# RevenueCat Shipaton 2026 — Next Gen Award submissions

Source: the [Devpost project gallery](https://revenuecat-shipaton-2026.devpost.com/project-gallery). I scanned all **164 pages** (3,922 projects) on 2026-10-07.

**Rule used:** the submission links to GitHub, either in the *Try it out* links or in the description. A Next Gen entry must provide a public open-source code repo, and no other category needs one. That gives **699 Next Gen submissions**:

- **676** list a GitHub link under *Try it out* (strong signal: this is where the required repo goes)
- **23** mention GitHub only in the description (weaker: some of these links point to third-party libraries)
- **5** link a GitHub profile instead of a repo
- Not counted: **54** projects whose only GitHub link is a `*.github.io` page (GitHub Pages, usually a privacy policy). That's a web page, not a code repo.

Each repo was also checked through the GitHub API (exists and public, license, commits, RevenueCat in the code, commits after the Sep 30 deadline), and each video through YouTube/Vimeo (availability and length). Flags are marked ⚠️. My winner prediction is in `winner_prediction.md`.

Interactive version: `site/index.html` (embedded videos, filters, search).

**Inspiration**

I'm a blind developer. I lost my vision to a stroke a few years ago, and had to adjust from being an avid competitive gamer, Redditor, marathon runner, computer user… to coming back online to an inaccessible internet. 
I struggled alone during the COVID shutdown, unable to find in-person rehabilitation, therapy, orientation classes, or anything. Looking online, I found next to nothing regarding stroke-related vision loss at the scale I experienced it. Accurately describing how I "see" the world was painfully difficult, and only added to the isolation. 

I created The Blind Spot website a couple of years ago, and am now a first-time mobile app creator because I want to create a mobile-first design tool so that people are better equipped with tools to more accurately articulate and represent their blindness and/or vision conditions. 

Image-heavy platforms became walls of nothing. Screen readers could only help when someone had bothered to add alt text, and almost no one had.

That experience led me to build AltText Guardian, a Reddit moderator tool that auto-generates alt text for image posts using computer vision. It won Best New Mod Tool at the Reddit Mod Tools Hackathon. But it solved only one side of the problem: making content accessible to people with vision impairments. The other side, the one nobody was building for, was making sighted people actually understand what vision impairment feels like.

According to the WHO, 2.2 billion people worldwide have a vision impairment, and at least 1 billion of those cases were preventable. It is a global health crisis, one that persists in part because the sighted majority has no frame of reference for what these conditions look and feel like.

The Blind Spot exists to close that empathy gap. If you can see through someone else's eyes for even a few seconds, you start to understand. And with understanding comes better design decisions, better policy, better care.

The RevenueCat Shipaton Peace Prize category, "greatest social good," gave me the perfect reason to bring the web-based simulator to mobile, where the phone's camera turns the simulation from a static demo into a lived experience.

**What it does**

The Blind Spot is a real-time vision-impairment simulator. It renders 59 medically-sourced vision conditions through your phone's camera at 30fps, letting you see your actual surroundings as someone with glaucoma, macular degeneration, cataracts, color blindness, or dozens of other conditions would see them.

It's web-native version lives at The Blind Spot

The core features:

- Live camera simulation of 59 conditions across 5 families: color vision, acuity and clarity, field loss, distortion, and other visual phenomena

- Severity slider that lets you experience conditions on a spectrum from mild to severe, because no two patients are alike

- Overlay builder for composing multiple conditions together (e.g., cataracts + glaucoma, which frequently co-occur in elderly patients)

- Voice-guided exploration via an ElevenLabs conversational AI agent that can switch conditions, adjust severity, and explain what you are seeing, all by voice

- Educational profiles of 210+ famous people with vision conditions, searchable and filterable

- Condition glossary with prevalence data, advocacy links, and medical sources

- "See What I See" sharing that generates a link others can open to experience the same condition

- 26-language support with WCAG-compliant accessibility throughout

The web version at theblind.spot supports image and YouTube video input. The mobile app takes it further: the camera makes the simulation visceral and immediate.

**How I built it**

**The ConditionSpec contract**

Everything in The Blind Spot flows from one abstraction: the ConditionSpec. Each of the 59 conditions is a JSON file describing an ordered pipeline of image transforms. The schema (v0.1) defines 11 operation types: colorMatrix, blur, fieldLoss (12 shapes), warp (3 kinds), contrast, directionalBlur, ghost, noise, floaters, shimmer, and starburst.

A single spec is the source of truth consumed by three independent interpreters:

- Mobile (Skia): TypeScript compiler generates a RenderPlan with SkSL shaders, applied via VisionCamera frame processor worklets

- Server (Elixir/libvips): Same semantics, different backend, used for sharing and the MCP surface

- Web (GLSL/CSS): Three.js shaders and SVG filters on theblind.spot (source on GitHub)

Golden tests assert perceptual similarity across interpreters. If any interpreter drifts from the schema's semantics, it is the one with the bug.

**The rendering math**

Operations compose with well-defined algebra. Gaussian blur sigmas combine in quadrature:

$$\sigma_{\text{combined}} = \sqrt{\sum_{i} \sigma_i^2}$$

Standard 4x5 color matrices compose via multiplication ($R = B \circ A$). Machado 2009 color vision deficiency matrices use linearized 3x3 transforms that operate in linear RGB space, requiring sRGB decode/encode in the shader:

$$c_{\text{linear}} = \begin{cases} \frac{c_{\text{sRGB}}}{12.92} & \text{if } c_{\text{sRGB}} \leq 0.04045 \ \left(\frac{c_{\text{sRGB}} + 0.055}{1.055}\right)^{2.4} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Contrast amounts multiply and lifts add. The strongest warp wins (stacking reads as noise). Every parameter can be a severity curve, interpolated between 0 and 1.

**The mobile stack**

Layer
Technology

Framework
Expo 52, expo-router

Camera
react-native-vision-camera 4.6.3

Graphics
@shopify/react-native-skia 1.6.0

Worklets
react-native-worklets-core 1.5.0

Animation
react-native-reanimated 3.16.3

State
Zustand 5

Payments
react-native-purchases (RevenueCat)

Voice AI
@elevenlabs/react-native

Monitoring
@sentry/react-native

Notifications
OneSignal

The camera pipeline runs entirely on the GPU. The compile.ts interpreter takes condition specs and severity, generates SkSL shader source and a flat uniform array, and the frame processor worklet applies it every frame. No JavaScript bridge crossing in the hot path.

**Raxol-powered MCP agent**

The Elixir backend uses Raxol to expose the condition library as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool surface. The Blindspot.MCP.Tools module defines four tools, annotated with @mcp_tool for auto-derived definitions via raxol_mcp:

- list_conditions - browse all 59 conditions

- get_condition - retrieve a full spec by ID

- list_families - conditions grouped by mechanism family

- compile_overlay - describe what a multi-condition overlay would look like

This means any MCP-compatible AI agent (Claude, GPT, or custom) can query the condition library, compose overlays, and reason about vision impairments programmatically. The Raxol integration made this nearly declarative: define the tool, annotate it, and the MCP surface is automatically derived.

**ElevenLabs voice guide**

The mobile app includes a conversational AI voice guide powered by ElevenLabs. The @elevenlabs/react-native SDK establishes a WebRTC session directly between the device and ElevenLabs with no backend in the audio path. The agent registers four client tools (show_condition, adjust_severity, save_overlay, list_conditions) that dispatch directly to the Zustand store, which triggers the Skia pipeline to update in real time.

You can say "show me what glaucoma looks like" and the camera view updates instantly while the agent explains the condition. This is especially valuable for educators and medical students who want a hands-free guided tour.

**Monetization**

RevenueCat manages a single non-consumable purchase (bs_overlay_builder) that unlocks the full 59-condition library and the overlay builder. Six of the most prevalent conditions (myopia, cataracts, deuteranomaly, hyperopia, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy) are always free, ensuring the educational core is accessible to everyone.

Web donations go through Stripe Checkout on the share pages, entirely separate from the mobile IAP flow. The "Support the Cause" button on the "See What I See" LiveView page lets web visitors contribute without installing anything.

**Challenges I ran into**

The biggest problem was ironically the administrative blockers of getting the app live. I'm submitting it via the NextGen track, but still want to enable The Blind Spot in every app store I can, but the administrative processes are really inaccessible. I'm working to add it to platforms such as Uptodown.dev, and soon Apple.

Mobile Testing. This was far and away the most difficult part of the build for me. I've been building out The Blind Spot for a couple years, but have never built a mobile app before. It was always in the plan to have an app, since most the world is mobile-first, so this hackathon pushed me to do so. But frankly, being a blind developer, and testing myself has been a hiccup. 

Color accuracy for color vision deficiency. Early versions used simple heuristic color matrices. The results looked wrong to ophthalmologists I consulted. I switched to Machado 2009 simulation matrices, which require operating in linearized RGB space (sRGB gamma decode, matrix multiply, gamma encode). This added complexity to the shader but made the simulations scientifically defensible.

Three interpreters, zero drift. The web simulator, the mobile app, and the Elixir server all interpret the same spec files. Any semantic difference between interpreters is a bug that would silently produce wrong simulations. We solved this with golden tests: run a reference image through all three pipelines and assert perceptual similarity. This caught several subtle issues, like the server applying blur before color matrix while mobile did the reverse.

Worklet closure semantics. VisionCamera frame processor worklets capture variables by copy, not by reference. Passing the compiled render plan into the worklet required shared values from Reanimated, and rebuilding Paint objects inside the worklet on every plan change. This was not documented anywhere and cost a full day of debugging.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- 59 medically-sourced conditions running at 30fps through a phone camera, each backed by cited research

- The ConditionSpec abstraction is genuinely portable: one JSON file drives rendering on three completely different graphics backends (Skia, GLSL/CSS, libvips) with verified consistency

- The web platform at theblind.spot already supports 265+ conditions, profiles 210+ famous people with vision conditions, and is available in 26 languages, all MIT-licensed and open source on GitHub

- The MCP integration via Raxol means any AI agent can programmatically explore and reason about vision conditions, opening doors for research and educational tooling we have not imagined yet

- The voice guide makes the simulator accessible to people who cannot easily use a touchscreen, which matters deeply for a tool about vision impairment

- WCAG AA compliance throughout the app, because a tool that teaches accessibility should itself be accessible

- AltText Guardian (Previous project) won Best New Mod Tool at the Reddit Hackathon. The Blind Spot continues that mission: not just making the internet accessible, but building empathy for why it needs to be

Privacy can be a feature. The Blind Spot has no accounts, no first-party analytics, no personal data collection, and overlays are stored as local JSON. A vision simulator that records what you look at would feel invasive, so the absence of tracking is part of the trust.

**What I learned**

Other than the unexpected pain of mobile testing, there were a couple: 

Technology outpaces accessibility. This was the lesson from AltText Guardian, and it is even more true for vision simulation. The tools to build empathy have existed for years (color matrices, field masks, blur), but nobody packaged them into something a designer or medical student could pick up and use in 30 seconds. The gap is not technical. It is prioritization.

**What's next for The Blind Spot**

- Expand the mobile library from 59 to 265+ conditions, matching the web platform's full catalog

- Narration system with ElevenLabs TTS: condition-specific empathy scripts that play while you experience each simulation, turning it into a guided educational moment

- Photo mode for capturing and sharing "before/after" comparison images

- Classroom mode for educators to present simulations to a group, with a teacher dashboard that controls what the audience sees

- AR overlay using ARKit/ARCore to label real-world objects that would be difficult or impossible to see under each condition

- Research API extending the Raxol MCP surface to let vision researchers run batch simulations programmatically

- Partnership outreach with ophthalmology programs, design schools, and accessibility advocacy organizations who could integrate The Blind Spot into their curricula

- Open-sourcing the mobile app to match the web platform's MIT license, so anyone can contribute conditions, translations, or interpreter implementations

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/046/283/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/046/283/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

SOLO: UNICORN RUN came from my own experience trying to build as a solo founder.

I have the same dream a lot of founders have: build something meaningful, grow it into a real company, and maybe one day create a unicorn.

But the reality of that journey is very different from the polished version people usually see online.

There are moments when everything feels like it is working.

Then there are days when something breaks, an idea does not work, progress slows down, money matters more than expected, a decision turns out to be wrong, or you realize that something you were confident about was never really validated.

There are wins.

There are failures.

There are moments where you feel like you are building the future, and others where you wonder whether you are building anything at all.

I realized that I was learning lessons through actually living this journey that would be difficult to explain through another article, course, or startup checklist.

So I started asking:

What if I could put the experience itself into a game?

That became SOLO: UNICORN RUN.

The idea is to take what I am learning, experiencing, getting right, and getting wrong as a real solo founder and turn those lessons into systems, decisions, consequences, and stories that other people can experience for themselves.

The simplest way I describe it is:

The Sims for AI solo founders.

**What SOLO is**

SOLO is a startup simulation game about trying to build a company from almost nothing.

You begin in a Founder Garage.

You have limited money, limited time, limited attention, limited energy, and a very large ambition.

You are also working with AI agents:

- Aurora — Research & Evidence

- Stacks — Engineering & Execution

- Brio — Growth & Campaigns

But the game is not about pressing a button and letting AI build your startup for you.

That would not reflect what I am experiencing in real life.

The real challenge is learning:

- What should I work on?

- What should I ignore?

- When should I trust AI?

- When should I verify something myself?

- Is this actually progress, or does it just feel like progress?

- Should I spend money now or protect runway?

- Should I keep building or talk to customers?

- Should I change direction?

- Am I moving too slowly?

- Am I moving too quickly without enough evidence?

- Should I intervene, or am I micromanaging?

- What happens when something I believed turns out to be wrong?

Those are the kinds of questions I want SOLO to turn into gameplay.

**Turning real founder experiences into game systems**

Many of SOLO's systems come directly from problems and lessons I encounter while building in real life.

The player has to manage things like:

- Runway

- Revenue

- Expenses

- Capital

- Trust

- Momentum

- Founder Energy

- Founder Attention

- Company Track Record

- Evidence

- AI agent reliability

- Agent workload

- Agent confidence

- Agent drift

These are not meant to be isolated statistics.

They interact.

A decision can improve momentum but hurt runway.

Moving quickly can create progress while increasing the chance that something was not properly validated.

Reviewing every AI decision may protect quality, but it can consume the founder's limited attention.

Giving an AI agent more autonomy may increase leverage, but now the founder has to decide how much that agent should actually be trusted.

That tension is a big part of what I am experiencing while building with AI today.

**Success and failure both matter**

One thing I do not want SOLO to become is a game where the player simply follows the "correct" startup formula and wins.

That is not how entrepreneurship works.

Sometimes a reasonable decision fails.

Sometimes a bad idea teaches you something important.

Sometimes something that looks like a failure becomes useful later.

Sometimes you get lucky.

And sometimes you make the right decision but do not understand why it worked until much later.

I want the player to experience those moments.

SOLO includes systems around evidence, hindsight, trust, momentum, and track record because I want decisions to have history.

The game should eventually be able to remind you:

You have been in a situation like this before. What did you learn?

That is something I am constantly doing as a founder myself.

**The AI founder problem**

Another major inspiration for SOLO is the rise of AI agents.

AI gives solo founders capabilities that would previously have required entire teams.

That is incredibly powerful.

But it creates a new problem:

Being able to generate more work does not mean you automatically know which work is good.

An AI agent can be confident and still be wrong.

It can complete exactly what you asked for even when what you asked for was the wrong thing.

It can produce something impressive that has very little evidence behind it.

And sometimes the founder becomes the bottleneck because everything still requires review.

I wanted that tension inside the game.

SOLO's agents are not meant to be perfect assistants.

They can have different levels of reliability, confidence, workload, calibration, and drift.

The founder has to learn how to manage them.

That creates situations where doing more is not always the best move.

Sometimes the right decision is to intervene.

Sometimes the right decision is to let the agent decide.

And sometimes the most important founder skill is recognizing the difference.

**Building the world**

I wanted the game world itself to reflect the founder journey.

SOLO begins in a small Founder Garage.

It is intentionally modest.

The player is sitting at a desk trying to build something much larger than the environment around them.

As the company grows, the physical world is designed to grow too.

The long-term progression moves from:

Founder Garage → Loft → Small Office → Office → Small Building → Big Building

The larger world is called Atlantis, a fictional technology hub populated by startups, investors, media organizations, and rival companies.

The goal is for company growth to become visible.

Instead of only seeing a revenue number increase, I want the player to eventually look around and realize:

I built this.

**How I built it**

SOLO is being built as a native Apple-platform experience using technologies including:

- Swift

- SwiftUI

- RealityKit

- Xcode

- Blender

- USD / USDZ

- Git

- GitHub

- AI-assisted development tools

One of the biggest technical principles behind the project is separating the startup simulation from the visual world.

The simulation controls the truth of the company:

finances, decisions, agents, evidence, progression, consequences, and saved state.

RealityKit and SwiftUI present that world to the player.

That separation lets me continue improving the graphics, animations, cameras, environments, and characters without changing the underlying business simulation every time.

**What I learned**

The biggest thing I have learned while building SOLO is that the game and my real founder journey are starting to teach each other.

Something happens while I am building my company, and I think:

That should be a mechanic.

Then I try to turn it into a mechanic and realize I do not fully understand the problem yet.

Designing the game forces me to think more clearly about the real decision.

Why was that difficult?

What information did I actually have?

What did I think I knew?

What turned out to be wrong?

What resource did the decision consume?

What would have happened if I had chosen differently?

That process has made SOLO more than a game project for me.

It has become a way of documenting and understanding the founder journey while I am still living it.

**Who I am building it for**

I am building SOLO for people who are curious about what it actually feels like to build a technology company.

That includes:

- Solo founders

- Aspiring founders

- Startup founders

- Builders

- Developers

- AI enthusiasts

- Tech enthusiasts

- People who enjoy simulation and management games

You should not need an MBA or years of startup experience to play it.

And you should not need to already want to become a founder.

My hope is that someone can play SOLO, make decisions, fail, recover, experiment, and come away understanding something about entrepreneurship that would have been much harder to learn from reading a definition.

**What makes SOLO personal**

I am not trying to build a game that pretends I already know everything about building a unicorn.

I do not.

That is actually part of the point.

I am building the game while I am living the journey.

As I encounter new problems, make mistakes, learn better approaches, discover tools, understand AI differently, and experience the emotional and strategic ups and downs of being a solo founder, those lessons can become part of SOLO.

The game can grow alongside the founder building it.

That makes SOLO, in a way, a living record of the journey.

**What's next**

My goal is to continue turning real founder experiences into playable systems.

That means expanding:

- AI agent behavior

- Founder decision-making

- Funding

- Customers and revenue

- Rivals

- Media attention

- Company growth

- Failure and recovery

- Founder energy and attention

- Team and AI autonomy

- Atlantis

- Character animation

- Environmental interaction

- Long-term company progression

Ultimately, I want SOLO to let someone experience the pursuit of building a startup from the Founder Garage all the way toward becoming a unicorn.

Not just the success story.

The whole journey.

The uncertainty.

The mistakes.

The late nights.

The breakthroughs.

The setbacks.

The decisions nobody sees.

And the feeling that despite everything that went wrong today, tomorrow you might still build something extraordinary.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We are a team of three developers from Tashkent who love Kotlin Multiplatform, development and games.

Wordle quietly assumes that one letter = one key = one tile. That's true for English, and it breaks for Uzbek. In Uzbek Latin, sh, ch, ng, oʻ and gʻ are single letters of the alphabet, each written with two characters. An Uzbek speaker counts shahar (city) as a five-letter word. Most clones count six and put s and h on separate tiles, which feels wrong to every native player.

Uzbek is also written in two scripts, Latin and Cyrillic, and both are in everyday use. Kazakh has 42 Cyrillic letters, which don't fit a Russian keyboard. We wanted a daily word game that treats these languages as first-class instead of patching them onto an English design. That became Harf ("letter" in Uzbek), with Uzbek (Latin + Cyrillic), Kazakh, Russian and English at launch.

**How we built it**

Harf is one Kotlin Multiplatform + Compose Multiplatform codebase that ships to Android, iOS, desktop and the browser (JS + Wasm), backed by a Ktor + PostgreSQL server.

The tile is a grapheme, not a character. A longest-match tokenizer splits each word into the letters a speaker actually counts, so digraphs win over their prefixes (sh before s, oʻ before o):

$$
\textit{shahar} \rightarrow \texttt{sh}\cdot\texttt{a}\cdot\texttt{h}\cdot\texttt{a}\cdot\texttt{r} \quad (5 \text{ tiles})
$$

Scoring follows the classic two-pass rule, applied to graphemes. Each tile is marked on the spot, in the word or absent. For a grapheme \( g \), the number of in the word marks is

$$
\text{present}(g) = \min\big(c_{\text{answer}}(g) - \text{correct}(g),\; c_{\text{guess}}(g) - \text{correct}(g)\big)
$$

so sh only ever matches sh, never s + h. Marks aren't Wordle's green and yellow: each board theme has its own palette and mark style (underline, half-fill), and the emoji share grid follows the active theme.

Each language gets its own on-screen keyboard where digraphs are real keys, so the player never has to guess how to type a letter.

Same puzzle, no network needed. The daily word is a pure function of the local day:

$$
w_d = \text{schedule}\left[\, d - d_0 \,\right]
$$

The schedule comes from the cached server pack, then a bundled snapshot, then a generated baseline. Every device shows the same word offline, and the rollover happens at midnight in each language's own time zone.

Content is the real moat. Vocabulary lives in a server-side word catalog with a staff web panel (Kotlin/JS, Kobweb). Curators pick daily words 60 days ahead under a no-repeat rule, and players can suggest missing words. Every catalog change republishes a versioned word pack, and the server refuses a pack that fails the same integrity check the app runs before adopting it. The grapheme engine and word rules live in one shared module, so the app, the server and the panel validate words identically.

Monetization via RevenueCat, never pay-to-win. Before selling anything we asked one question: does this purchase change the shared daily result? If it does, we don't sell it. The daily round is free forever and ad-free. You can pay for:

- Founder edition (one-time): the full archive of past days, a hard mode, and a Founder badge.

- Cosmetic board themes.

purchases-kmp powers Android and iOS. Desktop and web use a no-op implementation that reports unavailable instead of crashing. The RevenueCat app-user ID is bound to the Harf account (Google / Apple sign-in), so purchases follow the player across devices.

**Challenges**

- Ambiguous digraphs. n + g across a morpheme boundary isn't the letter ng. Trusting the tokenizer blindly would corrupt words, so the content pipeline has a human-reviewed exception list.

- Many apostrophes. In real text oʻ appears as o', oʼ, o‘ and even a backtick. Everything is normalized to the official U+02BB before tokenizing. Words containing the tutuq belgisi (sanʼat) are excluded at launch rather than turned into a confusing "non-letter" tile.

- Two scripts, one word. Uzbek Latin and Cyrillic are paired as one lexeme, so both scripts share the same daily answer. Switching script starts a new round so results can't leak between them.

- Store-review crunch. Sign in with Apple, custom Manage purchases and Paywall screens, and identity binding all landed in the final days of review.

**What we learned**

- Grapheme-first design pays off. Once "letter" meant grapheme everywhere (keyboard, scoring, share grid, word lists), most special cases disappeared, and four of our five script/language pairs became the trivial case.

- Offline-deterministic beats server-driven for a daily game: no loading spinner, no outage, the same puzzle for everyone.

- Pay-to-win is a design constraint, not a slogan. Deciding up front what we would never sell made the RevenueCat integration simpler and the game fairer.

- Kotlin Multiplatform scales. One codebase covered four platforms, a server and an admin panel for a three-person team in six weeks.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I watched a kid learn to read by following a parent's finger under each word. That's the entire trick: the word you hear and the word you see have to light up at the same time. Most "read-along" apps fake this, they scroll, or they highlight a whole line, or the timing drifts. I wanted the real thing: word-perfect highlighting, on a story that is about the child's own character, so they actually care what happens next.

It was also a deliberate engineering bet. The Shipaton has a "Ship Kotlin Everywhere" award, and I wanted to make the strongest honest version of that argument: one piece of read-along logic that behaves identically on Android, iPhone, desktop, and the web, not four apps that look similar.

**What it does**

Storymoji is a bedtime-story app for little kids. A child picks an emoji as a base: a cat, a robot, a ghost, decorates it with more emoji stickers, gives it a name, and says what kind of adventure they want. A few seconds later they have their own illustrated storybook, and the app reads it to them out loud, highlighting each word exactly as it's spoken so they can follow along. Stories are saved to the child's own shelf to re-read, and a family can choose to publish one to Storyland, a feed of stories other families have shared.

The reader is the whole point. Everything else exists to get a kid to that screen.

**How we built it**

The app is one shared Kotlin codebase that runs on four platforms. Every screen, the character editor, the story reader, the paywall, is written once in Compose Multiplatform. Each platform (Android, iOS, Desktop, Web) is a tiny shell whose only job is to call App().

Concretely, of the app's production code:

$$
\text{shared} = \frac{8{,}844 \text{ lines in commonMain}}{9{,}993 \text{ total lines}} \approx 88\%
$$

The remaining ~12% is the stuff a platform genuinely has to answer for itself, playing audio, making network calls, finding a folder to cache files in, talking to the app store, plus four almost-empty entry points (the whole iOS host is 26 lines of Swift; the web host is 10 lines of Kotlin; desktop is 27, most of which is loading the window icon).

The pieces:

- The character is a vector, never a picture. A character is stored as CharacterDoc(baseId, name, stickers = [...]), and every coordinate is a number from $0$ to $1$ measured against the character's own box. That's what lets the same character render pixel-identical as a tiny thumbnail in the picker, at full size on a storybook page, and in the web viewer and stay identical on page 1 and page 8 while the AI background art changes around it.

- The words come from Claude. The backend asks Claude Sonnet 5 to write a short story starring the child's exact character, then runs it past a word blocklist and Claude Haiku 4.5 as a safety check before a kid ever sees it. Moderation fails closed: if the checker times out or errors, the child gets a safe canned story, never unchecked model output. (Gemini is wired in as a drop-in alternative behind the same interface.)

- The voice comes with timings. Free stories are read by Amazon Polly Neural, paid stories by ElevenLabs. Both return not just the audio but when each word is spoken, in one shared format, so the app never knows which one ran. It plays the audio and, on every frame, asks "what millisecond are we at?" and lights up the matching word. Because that logic lives in shared code above the audio player, all four platforms highlight identically.

- The art arrives in beats. A story gets 3–6 background pictures, not one per page. Free stories use a hand-reviewed pack of scenes that appears instantly. Paid stories get backgrounds generated by Gemini. Until a picture is ready, or if one fails, the page shows the scene the child picked (bundled in the app), so a story is never blocked on a picture.

- Soft background music plays under the story and dips automatically while the narrator speaks.

- The paywall is RevenueCat. One hand-written Compose paywall, shared across platforms, backed by RevenueCat's Kotlin Multiplatform SDK on mobile.

The client and the backend even share the same Kotlin file for the network contract, the DTOs (data shapes) are defined once in the backend repo and pulled into the app as a Gradle composite build. So "Kotlin on the client and the server sharing definitions" isn't a slogan; it's literally the same source file compiled into both.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest bugs were the quiet ones:

- Page one narrated in silence. The reader opens before the audio finishes loading, so page one grabbed a silent placeholder player and never let go of it. The fix was keying the audio effect on the narration itself, not just the page number.

- A caching bug that gave away free stories. Each device gets a monthly story allowance tied to a token. Registering a second time mints a new token, a fresh free allowance. I had to make registration read from disk first and only ever happen when there's genuinely no token, and be very careful never to re-register just because the network hiccuped.

- Auto-advanced pages read on with nothing lit. Right after play(), every platform's player says "not playing yet" while it warms up. The reader copied that answer, so the next page read aloud with the button still saying "Read it" and no word highlighted. Now the reader tracks what it meant to do and checks that against the platform each frame.

- RevenueCat's iOS library only links on one specific machine, unless you fix it. Its prebuilt library hardcodes a path to someone else's Xcode. On any other Mac the build fails with an error that mentions neither Xcode nor RevenueCat. The build script now discovers this machine's own toolchain path and patches it in.

None of these show up in a demo. All of them would have shown up to a parent.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- It's actually out. Not a prototype, not a video of a prototype. You can download Storymoji from the App Store and Google Play, install it on Windows, macOS or Linux, or open it in a browser at storymojiapp.com/app/. Four platforms, all live, built by one person.

- One app, not four copies of one. About 88% of the code is written once and runs everywhere. When I fix a bug in the reader, it's fixed on your phone, your laptop and the web at the same time. Nobody has to remember to fix it three more times.

- The highlighting really is word-perfect. Every word lights up the moment the narrator says it, and it does that the same way on every device. It's the hardest thing in the app, and it's the thing I wanted most to get right.

- Free stories cost about one cent to make. Early on, every free story cost real money, so the more kids used it, the more it cost. Switching the free voice to Amazon Polly and the free pictures to a hand-checked set brought that down to about $0.011 a story. That means the free version can stay genuinely good instead of being a cut-down teaser.

- The paywall can't lie. It only lists things a purchase actually gives you today. That's not just a promise: there's a test that fails the build if the screen ever advertises something that isn't switched on yet.

- Safety fails closed. If the AI checker is slow or broken, the app shows a safe story, never an unchecked one. For a kids' app, "when in doubt, don't" is the only acceptable default.

- All the app's artwork fits in 84 KB. The web version had no emoji at all, so every character was an empty box. Instead of shipping a 24 MB font, I cut it down to just the ~60 emoji the app uses.

**What we learned**

A lot of this project was learning where "write once, run anywhere" quietly stops being true, and fixing each spot on purpose instead of by accident:

- Compose on the web ships no emoji font. Every emoji, and since the artwork is emoji, that's the entire app, rendered as an empty box in the browser. Fix: I subsetted Noto Color Emoji down to just the ~60 glyphs the app uses and bundled it. Whole font: 24 MB. The subset: 84 KB.

- The desktop JVM can't decode MP3 out of the box. The Java sound system ships every format except the one everybody uses. It needs a plug-in registered at runtime that no line of code imports, delete it as an "unused dependency" and narration breaks with a runtime error, not a compile error.

- Position reporting has to be precise or the highlighting looks broken. Android's default media player reports playback position in ~100 ms jumps. Invisible behind a progress bar; very visible when that number is choosing which word lights up. Switched to ExoPlayer for finer timing.

- A "debug build" is a fact each platform has to tell you itself, and I spent real time making sure a release build can never accidentally think it's a debug build and leak story text to a child's device.

The theme: shipping to four platforms honestly means meeting four sets of surprises, and writing them down so the next person (me, in a week) doesn't rediscover them.

**What's next for Storymoji: Bedtime stories**

Things I'd rather finish properly than rush for a deadline:

- More stories for subscribers. Right now everyone gets the same number of stories a month, and paying only changes the voice. Paying families should get more stories too. That needs the server to track each family's plan first, which is why the paywall doesn't promise it yet.

- Your character inside the picture. Today your character stands in front of the background. The next step is drawing them into the scene, climbing the tree or riding the rocket the page is talking about. It's already built and switched off while I make sure it looks right every time.

- Spanish. Stories, narration and the app itself in Spanish, so more families can read along in the language they speak at home.

- Drawing your own character. Right now you decorate an emoji with stickers. Next you'll be able to paint on it with your finger. The character format was designed with room for drawings from day one, so this adds to the app without breaking any character a kid has already made.

- More places to visit. A bigger set of hand-checked scenes that change with the mood of the story, so a spooky space adventure and a silly one don't look the same.

- Different voices for different stories. A calm voice for a sleepy story, a lively one for an adventure.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

You've been studying Japanese for six months. You land in Tokyo, walk into a ramen shop, and freeze.

LangCity is my answer to that. It's a pixel-art RPG where you walk around a Japanese city, and the only way to finish a quest is to actually say the thing — order the food, ask for directions, talk your way out of it. Speak Japanese, level up, unlock the city.

Tokyo is just the first stop. LangCity is built to become a world of cities: Paris for French, Seoul for Korean, and more after that.

**Inspiration**

I kept noticing the same gap. People grind vocabulary apps for months, hold a 300-day streak, and still go silent the moment a real person asks them something.

The problem isn't effort. It's that most apps teach words in a vacuum, far away from the moment you'd actually need them. You learn "excuse me" as a flashcard, not as the thing you say when you're lost at Shinjuku Station and your train leaves in four minutes.

So I built the moment instead of the flashcard. In LangCity, Japanese isn't a lesson sitting on top of a game. It is the game. It's how you finish quests, make friends in the city, earn progress, and open up the map.

**What it does**

LangCity is a top-down, pixel-art Japanese-learning RPG. You pick a character and wander a Tokyo-inspired town — the convenience store, the train station, the ramen shop, a café, a classroom, a gym, an office — meeting characters who each have their own personality, job, and way of talking to you.

The loop is simple:

- Explore the city and meet someone.

- Take a mission from real life — order lunch, ask for directions, buy something you need.

- Go find the right person or place.

- Say it in Japanese.

- Get feedback, earn XP, unlock more of the city.

There's a mission tracker and markers on screen, so you're never wandering around wondering what you're supposed to do. And the characters respond with AI, which matters more than it sounds: you finish a mission by getting your meaning across, not by typing one exact memorized sentence. Say it a different way and it still works. Say it badly and someone will help you fix it.

You're not thrown in cold, either. The game starts by teaching you hiragana and katakana in your first session. There's a study buddy who appears when you're stuck, on-screen suggestions when you have no idea what to say, and an alphabet reference you can pull up mid-conversation. Daily quests and streaks give you a reason to come back. Short mini-games keep vocabulary practice from feeling like homework. And if you want to hear real Japanese and say it out loud, you can turn on voice mode and actually speak.

Everything else is there to keep you moving: furigana and rōmaji reading aids, instant translation, saved progress, Google and Apple sign-in, cloud backup, and an optional LangCity Guild subscription for players who want more AI conversation. No account needed to start — open it, pick a character, and go.

**How I built it**

I built LangCity solo, in Flutter, so one codebase runs on Android, iOS, web, macOS, and Windows. The game itself runs on Flame and Bonfire — open-source engines that handle movement, collisions, and camera work, the same kind of toolkit behind a classic 2D RPG. Every street and interior is a hand-authored tile map, with custom loading code I wrote for backgrounds, doors, and where each character stands.

Architecturally I kept things boring on purpose. Small, focused pieces of code that each do one job — sign-in, AI conversation, missions and XP, sound, saving — instead of one giant system where everything touches everything. Boring paid off: I could add features fast without breaking what already worked, and a brand-new player can be walking around the city seconds after opening the app.

For the hard parts, I used specialists instead of reinventing them. Supabase handles sign-in and cloud saves. RevenueCat handles subscriptions and purchases. ElevenLabs gives the characters actual voices. AI conversations run on OpenAI, Gemini, or DeepSeek — I deliberately built it so LangCity isn't married to one AI company. Underneath all of it, a small memory model quietly tracks what you've learned and what you're starting to forget, so the game knows what to put in front of you next.

The full Japanese content pack — maps, audio, characters, a complete JLPT-level curriculum — is big. Too big to force on everyone at install. So the app ships a small starter version that's playable immediately and pulls in the rest only when you want it. Ads are rewarded and optional, never shoved in front of a conversation. Firebase Crashlytics tells me when something breaks in the wild, OneSignal handles notifications, and every code change gets tested and built automatically before it ships.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Making learning feel like a game instead of homework wearing a costume. Just letting people chat with an AI wasn't it. I had to build real missions — a place to go, a person to find, a goal, and a clear moment where you win — so every conversation was actually part of the game.

- Letting the AI be flexible without letting players get stuck. There are a dozen right ways to say almost anything in Japanese. The AI had to judge whether you got your meaning across, not whether you matched a script — while never leaving a player permanently blocked on a mission they technically completed.

- Building something you can start playing in seconds. No forced signup, no setup wall, no fifteen-screen onboarding. That meant sign-in, cloud saves, and subscriptions all had to be genuinely optional, and the free experience had to be a real game, not a locked demo.

- Getting a huge city and a tiny ramen shop to feel equally good to walk around in. The camera logic that works for a sprawling outdoor town falls apart in a single small room. It took a rewrite to make both feel natural instead of jittery or stuck.

- Making Japanese readable in a retro pixel-art style. Kana, kanji, pronunciation hints above characters, and English all want completely different spacing. I ended up writing custom text rendering so it all stays legible without ruining the pixel look.

- Shipping a big world without a punishing download. I built a system that only fetches the full content pack when a player wants it, verifies it arrived intact, and lets everyone else start playing immediately on a lighter starter version.

- Drawing an entire city by myself. A believable Tokyo needs dozens of characters, each with walk animations in four directions, plus streets, interiors, signage, and props. Hand-drawing all of that solo would have eaten the whole project. So instead of doing the art, I built the artist: a set of specialized AI agent skills, each one an expert at a single job — turning generated images into game-ready spritesheets, extracting tilesets, building interior maps, generating UI kits. I stopped producing assets one at a time and started producing the pipeline that produces them.

- Releasing to five platforms without a release team. LangCity ships on iOS, Android, web, macOS, and Windows. When something breaks in production, "I'll cut a build tomorrow" isn't good enough. I built a full CI/CD pipeline on Fastlane and GitHub Actions that takes a fix from commit to signed, uploaded builds on every store — so a critical fix can go out the same hour I write it, not the same week.

- Testing a game this big as one person. Missions branch, conversations are open-ended, and the UI is dense — there's no way to manually click through all of it before every release. So I leaned hard on automation: over 1,400 automated tests across 231 test files, including golden-image tests that catch a single pixel shifting in the UI, plus AI agents that review the suite itself and flag gaps in coverage. Every release runs the whole thing before it ships.

- Staying stable while shipping constantly. I release often, and some bugs only exist in the real store build — an Android crash that never once appeared during development showed up the moment I added proper crash reporting. Watching, catching, and fixing those is just part of running a live game.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- I built a real, explorable RPG where speaking Japanese is the gameplay — not a flashcard app in a pixel-art costume.

- The whole mission experience is complete end to end: a character offers you a quest, you accept it, the game guides you there, you have a real conversation, and you get rewarded for it.

- You can open LangCity and be playing in seconds, with no account and nothing to buy — then it gets richer as you sign in, talk to characters, and subscribe.

- Everything looks like it belongs to one world. The city, the characters, the dialogue boxes, the menus, even the subscription screen — all the same hand-crafted pixel art.

- LangCity isn't locked to one AI provider. It can run on several, which protects the game from any single company's pricing or outages.

- The business model matches the actual cost: exploring and playing are free, and you only pay for the AI-heavy features that genuinely cost money to run.

- Adding new missions and lessons doesn't mean rebuilding the game. The content is data, so the world can keep growing.

- The "keep coming back" loop is built into the RPG rather than bolted next to it — spaced review of what you've learned, daily quests, streaks, and a study buddy who lives in the world with you.

- Characters can speak Japanese out loud and listen to you speak back, so this isn't only a reading-and-typing game.

- The mini-games are their own reusable toolkit, so I can keep adding new ones quickly without putting the rest of the game at risk.

**What I learned**

- Context is what makes language stick. People remember a phrase far better when a character is standing there waiting to hear it and using it changes what happens next.

- AI is better with guardrails than without. Give it a clear character, a clear goal, and a fallback, and it becomes genuinely useful. Leave it open-ended and it becomes a chatbot people stop trusting.

- Removing the signup wall changed everything. Letting anyone start playing instantly made demos better, development faster, onboarding painless, and the free tier something I'm not embarrassed by.

- Feedback has to be instant without breaking the spell. Hints, translations, and corrections work best when they feel like part of the world instead of a popup interrupting it.

- Monetization should support the learning, not fight it. I can give away a genuinely generous game and still charge fairly for the parts that cost me real money.

**What's next for LangCity**

- More cities, more languages. Paris for French, Seoul for Korean, and onward. The city-and-language format was designed from day one to repeat, so LangCity becomes a world you learn in, not a single-language app.

- Launch early, watch how real players actually behave, and obsess over the path to a player's very first successful Japanese conversation.

- Make speaking practice faster and more responsive, and bring voice into more of the game than just dialogue.

- Let the game remember what you've learned across the entire world — not just the alphabet — and use that to decide what you see next.

- Add more neighborhoods, longer stories, real relationships with characters, and focused packs like Travel Japanese, Workplace Japanese, and Anime Japanese.

- Let characters teach on the fly — generating explanations, listening exercises, and corrections that fit the conversation you're actually having.

- Make notifications genuinely useful: nudge you about the specific words you're about to forget, instead of guilt-tripping you about a streak.

- Build a way to discover and try LangCity on the web and carry that progress straight into the app.

- Keep experimenting with pricing to find the line between a generous free game and a sustainable one.

- Add privacy-respecting analytics so I can measure real learning, not just downloads.

**Built with**

Dart · Flutter · Flame · Bonfire · Material 3 · Tiled · Flame Audio · Supabase · PostgreSQL · Google Sign-In · Sign in with Apple · RevenueCat · OpenAI / Gemini / DeepSeek · Genkit · GenUI · ElevenLabs · Firebase Crashlytics · OneSignal · Google AdMob · GitHub Actions · Android · iOS · Web · macOS · Windows

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

How much time do I waste every day?

That was the whole question. September 2024. I was living abroad, far from home, with a tiredness that had been piling up for a few years, and one day I caught myself swiping through my own days the way you swipe a feed. Morning turned into work, work into tiredness, and the evening dissolved into zoning out. That same month people at my work were let go in a single day, with no warning. It passed me by. In the moment it was just a very bad day, and only later did it become visible that Wastime counts from exactly there.

I started with a paper planner and wrote down where the time actually leaks away. Lost an hour here. A couple more here. And here it's anyone's guess where the whole day went. After about ten days I could see individual days, but the whole picture wasn't coming together. What do these small gaps turn into in a few years? No ready answer was at hand, so I sat down to make a prototype for myself. One button, three inputs, one list. One page.

I can still see the first screen. Only numbers on it and a short line underneath. If I keep pouring 10-15 hours a week into the usual “small stuff”, then over ten years that adds up to more than half a year of life. My first reaction, word for word, was “No f***ing way”. That's when something clicked. The number turned out to be stronger than any inner monologue. Time suddenly had weight.

The app was called Waste back then. Two years later it's Wastime, and the question got wider. Where does time go at all? What in it was alive? How much time do we have? And how much has already passed? 

**What it does**

Wastime is a mirror for your time and your life, built from your own data. No streaks, no motivational quotes, no feed. You put in what you actually do, and the app shows what it adds up to over years.

Inside there are a few tools, and all of them look at the same thing, only the scale changes.

- Calendars lay your whole life out as a grid, one square for one week. You see what's lived, where you are right now and how much may still be ahead. Three views, Life, Years and Ages. Milestones mark the events that shaped you, and Age Stories hold what each year was about.

- Time Diary is the everyday level, a diary of your hours. You log where they go and sort them into Wasted or Meaningful yourself. What counts as wasted, only you decide.

- Calculators. Wasted Calculator takes a small habit all the way to the end and shows the months it turns into. Planning Calculator counts backwards from a goal. 24H Calculator shows how many hours of the day actually stay yours. And Leftover Calculator, the hardest one, counts the time you may still have with the people you love.

- Converter turns the price of a purchase back into the working hours behind it.

- Life Expectancy sets the horizon for everything else. By country, by hand, or with a small calculator.

- Questions. More than 600 of them, and they show up right next to the number you're looking at. A question, I think, is often more useful than an answer.

- Wastime Journey. A story inside the app, written by me, about how each tool appeared and why. You can read it straight through or skip to what pulls you.

The one paid feature is publishing. Your Life calendar becomes a web page with its own address. You pick every Milestone that goes out, one by one, choose whether the page is Link, Public or Private, decide whether your name is on it, and give explicit consent before anything leaves the phone. The paywall for it runs on RevenueCat. Everything else in the app is free, and there are no ads.

**How I built it**

Alone, in the evenings and on weekends, next to a full-time job. Two years in, it's 2,024 hours and 50 minutes. I know the number to the minute because I log my time in my own app.

Why Ionic and Angular? Fair question. Because that's what I knew. Native, Flutter or React Native would have cost me months of learning before the first screen, and somewhere in the middle I'd most likely have dropped the whole idea. So the first version took one weekend, and on Sunday night it was on my phone. It turned out so simple and so absorbing that some hidden energy woke up in me.

From there the app grew one question at a time. A week in, I wanted to count useful time too, and that's how Wasted and Meaningful appeared. Two weeks in, my wife Krystsina mentioned in passing that there's this thing, a life calendar, one square for one week. I'd heard of such calendars myself, but the one who pushed me was her. I thought, why not, and threw the first grid together in one Sunday evening. From the outside the remark meant nothing. In reality this feature became key in the whole app. Later, digging around the topic, I found that Tim Urban wrote about exactly this calendar back in 2014, in “Your Life in Weeks” on Wait But Why.

Then the calculators, each out of a question I couldn't answer with what I had. Then Questions, because at some point they piled up and needed a place to live. Then the Journey, because the modules kept multiplying and I wanted a way in that explains why, and only then how.

Privacy was a design decision from the very start. Everything works offline. Entries, calculations and notes sit on your device and don't go anywhere on their own. The network is needed only for actions you start yourself, like publishing a calendar. The app asks you to sign in for the first time only at the publish screen, because a page that goes out into the world needs an owner who can take it down. Data Backup exports everything into one file you keep. Delete account takes the account and its cloud data down for good.

RevenueCat handles the purchase behind that one publishing flow.

**Challenges I ran into**

The hardest part was never the code.

Leftover Calculator counts how much time you may still have face to face with a particular person. My mom lives far away. When I first tried to explain the idea behind this calculator to my wife, I choked up and couldn't finish. While such a thought stays a calculation, it lives somewhere apart from you, almost like a task. Say it out loud, and it's about a concrete person. The calculator got built. I still wouldn't recommend it to everyone.

The second challenge was tone. An app called Wastime can very easily sound like a verdict. So the app never decides for you what was wasted. You sort your own hours, and an evening show can be Meaningful if that's what it was for you. I don't believe in the approach where “if you're not productive, then you're doing something wrong”. A completely lazy weekend is a normal part of a life that's alive. The app just shows how many such hours piled up over the week. What you're willing to live with is your choice alone.

The third was writing. Wastime Journey is a long text inside the app, in Russian and in English, one thought per page, every page held to about 900 characters. It took longer than some of the modules, and it's still being finished page by page. I’ve never had the knack for writing books, blogging, or working with text, so this is probably my biggest challenge.

And the boring one. Two years of evenings, more then 2000 hours, and then the release itself. Android is live in Google Play. iOS is in App Store review as I write this.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- The app helped me first. It pulled at least one person out of the swamp, so it's already not for nothing.

- Underneath, Wastime is a philosophical tool, and an incredibly complicated one. It has to be opened gradually, layer by layer. I still get surprised at how I manage to tie together things this different, when under every one of them lies one and the same thing, your time and mine. It's one of those cases when you look at all of it and think, “wow, did I really make all this?”

- The honesty and openness of the whole app. I was making it to help myself. And probably that's exactly why it came out as something other people can lean on too.

- Wastime has no dark patterns. No ads, no streaks, no endless feed, no notifications that beg you back. To be honest, it's an app that wants you to close it. In a good scenario you come in, see the reflection of your time you needed, understand something about yourself and go back to life beyond the screen.

**What I learned**

- Start with the tools you have. Angular was enough for the first weekend, and the first weekend was what mattered.

- A number is stronger than an inner monologue. You can tell yourself for years that the hours go somewhere wrong and do nothing. A concrete shape in front of you is harder to wave off.

- What's lost, only you decide. And not everything you once counted as lost or plain bad stays that way. Sometimes it turns out to be the best thing that could have happened to you.

- You can't add days. But depth to the day you have, you can sometimes give back.

**Why I think this counts as social good**

Let me name the problem first, the one a person runs into today.

The old ways of coping stop working in the world we now live in. Work gets automated, and people get let go in a single day, I've seen it from the inside. Loneliness. Loss of meaning, when life is full to the brim and there's less and less of the feeling of life left in it. And depression, which by now looks like the disease of the age, and it's only getting worse.

Wastime is my small answer to that. It doesn't fix any of it. It gives a person an honest picture of their own life, without anyone deciding for them what mattered. It can take back control of our lives and allow us to face reality. It brings the people they love back into the count, and after Leftover Calculator “not now” sounds different. It keeps their life data on their own phone. And everything except publishing is free and works without an account or the internet, so it costs nothing to try and nothing to walk away from.

I think people are going to need support and help. The problems are already huge, and I'm among the people who ran into them. So I'll dare to assume that in the coming years help will be needed like never before. I won't claim my app helps everyone, or even most. But some people, sometimes and in some places. Of that I'm sure.

And if each of us takes one small step against what today's world does to us, and each of us helps the person next to them, then together we might make this world a little happier and a little better.

**What's next for Wastime**

- iOS, as soon as review lets it through.

- Wastime Journey, part by part.

- The Calendar. It became the key feature by accident, and the list of ideas behind it is longer than the list of features I've shipped.

As a kid, somewhere between four and eight, I was building a time machine out of old TV remotes, old circuit boards and whatever wires I could find. My mom came over once and said that when I launch it, I should come get her, and we'd do it together. I never launched it. But a small app about time, I did build.

Keep feeling.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We wanted a fast, no fuss way to save and retrieve reusable snippets, 
text, links, and code, without digging through Notes apps or old chat 
threads. Existing clipboard managers felt cluttered, so we built 
something focused on speed: search, tap, copy, done.

**What it does**

SnapStash lets you save any text, link, or code snippet, auto detects 
its type, and organizes it into folders and tags. The search bar 
filters results instantly as you type, and tapping any saved item 
copies it to your clipboard immediately, no extra taps.

Free users get 20 snippets and 1 folder. Premium unlocks unlimited 
snippets, unlimited folders, and cloud sync, powered by RevenueCat, 
with Monthly, Yearly, and Lifetime purchase options.

**How we built it**

We used Replit's AI app builder to scaffold the app in React 
Native/Expo, then integrated the RevenueCat SDK for subscription 
management, wiring up entitlements, a custom offering with three 
pricing tiers, and a native paywall built with RevenueCat's visual 
paywall editor.

**Challenges we ran into**

Getting the RevenueCat SDK properly linked to Metro's bundler took 
some debugging, and the app's icon library wasn't loading correctly 
at first, causing broken glyphs across the UI. Both were fixed along 
the way. We also iterated on the app's visual design to move away 
from generic AI generated defaults toward something with a more 
distinct identity.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Going from an idea to a working app with a fully wired subscription 
flow, entitlements, and a published paywall, all within the Shipaton 
window. We're especially proud of the design pass that gave SnapStash 
a distinct visual identity instead of a generic template look.

**What we learned**

This was our first time wiring a real subscription/paywall flow end 
to end, from RevenueCat's dashboard configuration to entitlement 
checks in the app itself.

**What's next for SnapStash**

Cloud sync (iCloud/Google Drive), smarter auto tagging, and expanding 
to more platforms.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/424/863/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/424/863/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/424/864/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/424/864/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I have solar panels on my rooftop, but do they fulfill the expectations I had when I first installed them? No. Why? Because I never knew exactly what appliances I could run, or for how long. I didn't know why my bill kept rising even when I used solar, and I had no way of knowing whether running one heavy appliance meant I'd have to switch something else off.

I used to go upstairs every single day, every time, because a heavy appliance tripped the solar system off and that frustrated me endlessly. Whenever the bill arrived, we all used to blame each other, simply because we lacked management over our own appliances. We lacked control.

Before the bill even arrived, we'd literally become our own Einsteins, calculating the bill in our heads based on how much AC we'd run, scaring each other with jokes about how the house was about to "turn into hell" once the real number showed up. My mother would look at the bill and say, "There's definitely an error, the bill can't be this high, we don't use that much electricity" ,convinced something was broken, when really, nobody understood the system at all.

This isn't just my problem. Around 25 million households worldwide already rely on rooftop solar, a number projected to surge past 100 million by 2030. Off-grid solar is expected to bring first-time electricity access to almost 400 million people globally by the same year. Solar is becoming the world's answer to energy access but adoption means nothing without management. A solar system nobody understands how to use is just as frustrating as having no power at all.

That frustration is exactly why I built WattGuard.

**What it does**

WattGuard tracks your solar system in real time. Using live weather data, it calculates exactly how much energy your panels are producing right now, then tells you in plain language what you can safely run and for how long.

Setup is simple: register, enter basic details about your solar panels and battery, then add your appliances. From there, your dashboard shows everything you can run together right now, along with a time limit, and below that, what you could still run if you switched off one or two appliances from the list above.

If there's ever confusion, the WattGuard Assistant answers any question you have, based on your actual live data , not a generic guess.

On the bill side:

Bill Estimation tells you your expected monthly bill before it even arrives, based on your usage and your country's per-unit pricing so the number stops being a surprise.
Photo Bill Scanning (Pro) lets you snap a photo of your actual bill, and WattGuard explains exactly why it went up or down, using your solar/grid/battery history.
Budget Optimizer (Pro) builds you a full daily appliance schedule based on a target monthly bill you set turning a vague hope of "saving money" into an actual routine.
How we built it
Mobile app: Expo / React Native, with four core screens Auth, Setup, Dashboard, and Accurate Bill (Pro tools + paywall).
Backend: Python (Flask), handling weather lookups, power routing logic (solar/grid/battery decisions), appliance safe-to-run calculations, and bill estimation.
Weather data: Open-Meteo API free, no key required, pulling live sky conditions, cloud cover, and day/night state to drive the power-routing decisions.
AI Assistant: A chatbot wired directly into the user's live data, so every answer reflects their actual current appliance and power status, not a static script.
Monetization: RevenueCat handles the entire Free vs. Pro experience. A single entitlement (watt guard Pro) gates the two premium features. Users are identified to RevenueCat by their WattGuard account ID at login, so Pro status follows the account, not the device. A custom useIsPro() hook listens for real-time entitlement changes, so the UI updates instantly the moment a purchase completes no reload needed. RevenueCat's built-in paywall UI handles the entire purchase flow, and a Restore Purchases option is included per App Store requirements.

Along the way, mentors guided us closely at several key steps, which shaped a lot of the decisions above.

**Challenges we ran into**

Getting the mobile build pipeline stable was the hardest part. We hit native module errors after adding new packages (react-native-purchases-ui, expo-image-picker) that required full dev-client rebuilds rather than just a Metro refresh something that cost real time to properly diagnose. We also ran into an entitlement-identity issue: RevenueCat was initially tracking Pro status per-device instead of per-account, which meant a brand-new test account could incorrectly appear as "Pro" on a device that had already purchased it. Fixing this required properly wiring Purchases.logIn() and Purchases.logOut() into the authentication flow so entitlements correctly follow the actual user.

We also went through a full paywall screen removal an early custom paywall implementation had a broken import and needed to be scrapped entirely in favor of RevenueCat's own built-in paywall UI, which turned out to be both simpler and more reliable.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We're especially proud of Photo Bill Scanning and Budget Optimizer both solve real problems that almost every household faces. We're proud of successfully integrating RevenueCat as our monetization layer live entitlement checks, RevenueCat's built-in paywall, and restore purchases, all working end to end, not just installed but actually functional. We deliberately kept the core problem-solving experience free, and reserved Pro for the deeper, more resource-intensive tools, so the app is genuinely useful even without paying. We're also proud that WattGuard doesn't feel like a hackathon prototype ,it's built like a real, commercial-ready product from day one.

**What we learned**

What I learned is to solve a specific problem that irritates you first. If you actually solve a problem that irritates you, it will surely help others too. I never started WattGuard as some great, ambitious project, I had one vision, which was to solve the problem I faced almost every day.

For the first time, I learned how to integrate a Pro/Free tier system using RevenueCat and actually implement it end to end. I'm also grateful for the lessons from mentors along the way, they genuinely guided us very well at every step.

**What's next for WattGuard**

As we mentioned, we think of WattGuard as a commercial product, and we've already designed a path forward involving two directions.

While working on WattGuard, one problem kept spinning in my head: what if we could connect all appliances to a central point and let AI automatically power appliances on and off instead of just telling the user what's safe to run, actually managing it for them. Right now, if it rains or the battery dies, the app sends a notification, but I want to take that further using a small buzzer or physical alert, so everyone in the house can be aware immediately, not just whoever happens to be looking at their phone.

We've already sketched and designed this next step. There's a lot more coming to WattGuard soon.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Award category**

I'm entering the Next Gen Award. I'm a student, Larder is open source, and the Larder Plus subscription runs using RevenueCat .

**Inspiration**

Most nights I open the fridge, stare at it, close it, then open it again like something new is going to show up. There's usually food in there, just random stuff. Half an onion, a few eggs, some pasta. Ordering in costs way too much, and every recipe app I tried expected me to have a full kitchen and a grocery budget. I wanted an app that starts with what I actually have, as a student.

**What it does**

You take a photo of your fridge or cupboard and Larder figures out what's in it. You get to check the list first, so nothing gets saved until you've seen it. Then it shows you recipes you can make right now, with a rough cost and the calories, protein, carbs and fat for each serving.

There's a lot more in there too:

- Cook Mode takes you through each step while Nutmeg (the little mascot) cooks along with you. The timers are real alarms, so they keep counting down on your lock screen and ring even if the app is closed.

- Nutmeg chat knows what's in your pantry and what your goals are. You can ask him what to make, or tell him you bought something and he'll add them for you.

- Online recipes are optional. Turn them on and Larder pulls in thousands of recipes from Spoonacular that match your pantry. The 61 built-in ones will always work, even offline.

- The shopping list fills itself when you run out of something while cooking.

- Barcode scanning for packaged food. Point the camera at the barcode and its added straight to your pantry.

- Goals and Apple Health. Pick a goal and Larder tracks calories, protein, carbs and fat for every meal and saves them to Apple Health.

No accounts, and your photos never leave your phone. Everything is local.

**How RevenueCat powers Larder Plus**

I didn't want the useful stuff to cost money, so scanning, recipes, Cook Mode, nutrition, goals and the shopping list are all free. Larder Plus adds Nutmeg chat, weekly nutrition and budget insights, and seasonal looks for Nutmeg with matching app icons.

Larder Plus is one RevenueCat offering with two plans: Monthly for $2.99, and Semester for $10.99 (six months, so about $1.83 a month and 39% cheaper). I went with a semester plan instead of a yearly one because students think about money one term at a time, not by the year.

Both plans unlock one entitlement, larder_plus, and every Plus feature checks it. That means I can change plans in the dashboard without touching the app. I built the paywall myself in SwiftUI from the offering RevenueCat sends back, so the prices come straight from the packages and the "Save 39%" badge is worked out from the real prices. It only shows up once at the end of onboarding, after you've already scanned your fridge and seen a real recipe. The app listens to customerInfoStream, so Plus turns on the second a purchase or restore goes through, and then a welcome screen shows you what you got. Since Larder has no accounts, RevenueCat's anonymous IDs are all it needs. Everything runs on RevenueCat's Test Store, so you can try the whole purchase flow without paying.

I read a lot about how paywalls trick people with tiny "no thanks" links and fake countdowns, and I did the opposite. Two clear plans, prices up front, and "Not now" is one tap that feels exactly the same as buying.

**How I built it**

Larder is a native iPhone app written in Swift and SwiftUI, with SwiftData to save everything and no backend at all.

- The scanner uses Apple's on-device Foundation Models to guess what's in a photo, then Apple's Vision framework double-checks those guesses.

- Nutmeg's chat runs on Foundation Models too, right on the phone.

- Timers use AlarmKit, with a Live Activity on the lock screen.

- Nutrition comes from a table I built from the USDA's FoodData Central data.

- Online recipes come from the Spoonacular API. It only sends ingredient names plus your goal and diet, never photos, and if you're offline or out of daily requests it just falls back to the built-in recipes.

- Barcodes get looked up on Open Food Facts, and only the barcode number leaves the phone.

- Purchases go through RevenueCat.

All in all, it's just over 20,000 lines of Swift, 579 unit tests and 61 local recipes, as well as thousands more online recipes through Spoonacular.

**Challenges**

The scanner was the hardest part. I really wanted it to work completely on the phone, and more than once I almost gave up and just sent the photos to an online AI. On-device AI can be confidently wrong too. It once "saw" a pizza that definitely wasn't there. So Larder double-checks with Vision and always lets you fix the list.

The timers were another headache. At first they stopped as soon as the phone locked, which is pretty useless in a kitchen, so I rebuilt them on AlarmKit. And designing Nutmeg took way longer than I thought it would. I figured it'd be easy as pie. It wasn't, but it was worth it.

**What I learned**

Before Larder I'd never written any Swift or built a phone app. Almost everything I'd made before was in Python. Testing on my own phone every day caught bugs the simulator never would, and the more I used it, the more I realized this wasn't just my problem. Plenty of students open the same half-empty fridge every night.

**What's next**

- Getting it on the App Store once I have a paid developer account, then using RevenueCat's charts and Experiments to see how the paywall and the semester plan actually do.

- Moving online recipes to a paid Spoonacular plan, running through a small server so no API key ships inside the app.

- A social side, kind of like TikTok for recipes, where students can share what they cooked and what worked on a tight budget.

</details>
