**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/237/382/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/237/382/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/237/383/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/237/383/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/237/385/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/237/385/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/237/386/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/237/386/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/378/670/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/378/670/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/313/615/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/313/615/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/378/575/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/378/575/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/233/717/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/233/717/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

The video above covers what Veta is. This is what it doesn't have room for: the
rules underneath, and the things that went wrong on the way there.

**The design problem**

Streak counters are a threat that eventually gets carried out. They work by
holding something over you, and the day you slip they take it — which means the
mechanic that motivated you for two months is the same one that makes you delete
the app. The punishment is load-bearing.

I wanted to know whether a habit tracker could work with the threat removed
entirely: nothing to lose, nothing reset, no penalty of any kind. Kintsugi gave
me the shape of the answer, but the interesting part was never the metaphor. It
was whether an app can still feel like it matters when it has no leverage over
you.

**The rules that make it work**

Three, and they're the whole product:

A crack is a consequence, not a decoration. It isn't a "you failed" badge
drawn on top of the piece. Fracture.generate takes the vessel's form, a seed,
and a ceiling — how tall the piece was on the day it broke. A crack
physically cannot wander into ceramic that didn't exist yet, it dies against the
foot instead of bouncing off it, and its width is the number of days you were
gone. Two people who miss the same week get different vessels, forever, and
neither of them can be redrawn.

Repair is free, permanently. Charging to recover from a bad week would
monetise the exact moment the product exists to protect. Everything sold is
expansion — more concurrent pieces, the premium glazes, the museum — and never
restoration.

A window can only fail once it has closed. Not everything is daily; you can
ask a piece for three days a week. While that window is still open, nothing can
happen to the vessel no matter how many days are blank. The person who runs on
Saturdays must not find their piece broken on a Wednesday.

**How it's built**

Flutter, and not one bitmap of ceramic anywhere in the app. Every vessel is
a surface of revolution drawn at runtime with a CustomPainter: banded shading,
elliptical rim and base arcs, per-clay gloss and speckle across nine glazes.
The gold palette was sampled from photographs of real kintsugi rather than
picked from a colour wheel — its brightest tone is cream, never white, which is
why it reads as metal instead of a glowing UI accent.

Because the geometry is generated from a seed, a piece is reproducible from a
few integers: no images are stored, and the same scar redraws identically on any
device, forever.

**How RevenueCat is used**

One entitlement, plus, delivered by a default offering, and the paywall is
assembled entirely from what getOfferings() returns — package order, prices,
plan names and trial state are never hard-coded, so packaging changes from the
dashboard without shipping a build. The API key enters through --dart-define
at build time and is not in the repository.

Entitlement state is pushed, not polled. addCustomerInfoUpdateListener is
attached at startup, so a restore, a purchase made on another device or a grant
from the dashboard unlocks the app without it having to ask. restorePurchases
feeds the same listener, which means there is exactly one code path that can
flip the flag.

Billing never throws. A missing key, a dead network and a store that was
never configured all end the same way: the entitlement simply doesn't activate
and everything else keeps working. Nothing about purchases can stop someone
recording their day. It also means the app runs on an emulator or on web with
no store attached at all, which is how most of the 115-test suite runs.

The rest of the app has never heard of RevenueCat. Screens read one boolean,
VesselStore.isPlus; Billing exposes three members — isPlus, packages,
purchase — and lives behind them. It is 128 lines, in lib/data/billing.dart.

What is sold is expansion: more than one piece at a time, the five premium
glazes of the nine, the museum, and high-resolution export. What is not sold,
and never will be, is repair. Charging to recover from a bad week would
monetise the exact moment the product exists to protect, so the paywall was
designed around that constraint rather than having it bolted on afterwards.

**Challenges I ran into**

The hard ones were all in the boring layer, and all of them could have silently
robbed a user.

Daylight saving. The day index came from
DateTime(y,m,d).difference(epoch).inDays, which truncates the 23- and 25-hour
days a DST shift produces. Twice a year that would have deleted a day of
progress. It now uses civil-date arithmetic.

A save that could destroy the collection. load() cleared what was in
memory and then persisted it, so any read failure became permanent loss. Writing
is now a permission that has to be earned: nothing is saved until the app
knows what was on disk, and anything unreadable is quarantined verbatim —
"this build can't parse it" and "it's worthless" are different claims.

A two-phase write that rescued nothing. Saving writes a copy, promotes it,
then deletes the copy, so a kill mid-write leaves a whole version behind.
Except recovery preferred the main record — which always decodes in exactly
that scenario, because it holds the older, complete version. The newer copy was
found, ignored, and then overwritten by the very save that was meant to protect
it. Only a test that seeds the disk in that precise state exposes it.

The same lesson, three times. Ugly cracks were never a seed problem. A
fracture is generated against the height the piece had when it broke, so a
break on day 12 of 60 lives inside a disc of clay and comes out as a stub
against the foot. No width and no random number rescues that. What actually
needed choosing was when the piece broke.

**What I learned**

Measurements filter; they don't decide. I built instrument after instrument
to judge visual and audio work, and they misled me in the same direction every
single time. A gold-detection mask counted warm terracotta as gold. An
"attack time" metric measured the waveform's frequency instead of its envelope,
reporting 0.1 ms for everything. A one-second RMS window declared four sound
effects inaudible while they were playing perfectly — a 4 ms transient averaged
across 1000 ms moves the number by a tenth of a decibel. Every one of those
detected whether something changed, never whether the change was perceptible.

So the rule became: measure only to discard, and only where the descriptor
is a physical claim. A crack is a fast attack — if it takes time to peak it's
a thud, and that's not an opinion. A kiln is low-frequency. But whether gold
looks beautiful is not something a number can answer, and there the instrument
has to stay quiet.

Everything else went to blind comparison: candidates rendered, anonymised, and
judged with no context about the outcome I was hoping for. When I told the judge
what to look for it voted 6–0 in that direction — and 6–0 the opposite way
when asked neutrally. That is the most useful thing I learned building this, and
it had nothing to do with pottery.

**What's next**

Accounts and cloud storage. A collection currently lives entirely on the
device that made it, which means replacing a phone costs sixty days of work.
The next milestone is an account layer with server-side persistence, so that a
piece outlives the hardware that grew it and the same museum can be opened from
any device. It closes the last reachable state in which the app could still take
progress away unfairly — the one thing it promises never to do.

iOS. Veta is written in Flutter and its rendering engine is entirely
platform-independent, so reaching iPhone is a matter of adding a build target
rather than rewriting the app. The constraint is not engineering but access:
publishing to the App Store requires a Mac and an Apple Developer membership,
and neither is within reach on a student budget in Argentina. Any prize this
project earns is already committed to precisely that — the machine and the
membership, in that order — which makes an iOS release the first concrete use
of an award rather than an open-ended intention.

</details>

**Inspiration**

I've been getting into philosophy recently, and it's teaching me something: many things I don't agree with have valid arguments behind them.

John Stuart Mill put it plainly in On Liberty (1859): “He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.”

Understanding the other side can make your own convictions stronger. It can also make you realise you need to change them.

That is what I wanted to bring into 2 Minds: the knowledge of philosophy and manner of debating, which I've been learning. I wanted to put them into something people could pick up, understand, and argue with for themselves.

**What it does**

2 Minds is a library of puzzle challenges built around philosophical questions that philosophers have argued about for decades and centuries. Each puzzle introduces its question through a scenario that is easy to follow, then walks you through a connected series of choices which you, as the user, have to make.

Your answer determines which situation and question you meet next. For every opinion you choose, there is a counter argument to face. You can hold your position or take it back, but the app keeps asking you to think about what your answer commits you to.

By the end, you've learned a new concept and formed an opinion you've actually had to defend. The ending (close) tells you what philosophers have argued about the question, and the Sources screen gives you the citations, with notes and links, to go further. Afterwards, you can revisit any examined puzzle challenge and view the route you took through it. You can also open answers on the other branches and discover the arguments you didn't meet.

Your answers also shape which of six philosophical temperaments you lean toward, and the app shows it through its theme and gems, never a score. During the first-time onboarding, you will see these temperament definitions alongside their gems & reveal animations in the carousels, so you can get an early feel of what the theme changes look like.

**How I built it**

I built 2 Minds as a solo developer, using Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform. The first commit landed on August 1, and the app was live on the App Store on September 17. About 97% of the app's Kotlin and Swift source lines are shared, not counting tests or generated code. That includes the screens I designed, custom motion, puzzle logic, database and sync. The Swift side is seven small files.

One codebase ships to three stores. Room with the bundled SQLite driver gives iOS and Android the same database engine. Firebase, through GitLive's KMP SDK, handles sign-in and syncs content and records. RevenueCat's KMP SDK sells one subscription on the App Store, Google Play and the Galaxy Store, and Android ships two flavours from the same code, one for each billing system. The native side stays thin. Each app shell hands its sign-in, network and billing pieces to shared code once, at startup, and the entire expect/actual surface is six declarations.

It works offline first. Ten puzzles ship inside the app, and your record lives on your device. Signing in is optional and exists only to carry that record to your next device. When the library refreshes, it makes a single request that asks only for what changed since the last one.

The core screens and answer choreography started in Figma. In Compose, I built a small timeline system for the entrances, stamps, strikes and rewinds, then connected those moments to scrolling and visibility.

ThemeReveal is a separate library I created for this project. During a transition, it renders the content twice with different theme values and reveals the incoming version behind an animated entrance. To run it over a live, scrolling puzzle, I hoisted everything both copies have to agree on above the reveal: what you've read, every animation clock and every scroll position. That way the two worlds move as one. I extracted it, open-sourced it and published it to Maven Central. It now runs on Android, iOS, desktop and the web, with twelve reveal styles you can try in the live web demo.

Puzzles are data, checked twice. Each one is a JSON document: an opening, seven questions, fourteen answers and eight routes, with each answer's lean toward the six temperaments. A checker script holds every draft to the rulebook and a Node script publishes it to Firestore. Your temperament is plain arithmetic on your device, weighted toward your recent answers. There's no AI anywhere in the scoring, so the same answers always give the same result.

Tested on both platforms. I checked the app on devices, simulators and a foldable emulator in each posture, both half-open like a book and flat.

Along the way I gave a little back. I released anew version of compose-alert-banner 1.0.0-rc03, my own alert library, which 2 Minds uses for its notices. I also wrote up the whole build, including what iOS and Android each taught me, in a blog: Composing the app twice.

**Challenges I ran into**

The first challenge was engagement. Philosophy needs paragraphs of text, and reading texts cannot compete with other high-dopamine attention apps on your phone, so I designed the galley: a vertical feed of full-screen beats (like TikTok or Reels) where text appears as you reach it, and every choice, hold and take-back is something you see and feel.

The second was making that design work. Scrolling through paragraphs and turning to the next beat use the same finger movement, so I built a gesture layer that scrolls the text first and turns the page when you keep dragging past the end. The theme reveal needed the same care: two live copies of the puzzle had to stay perfectly in step while the new theme spread across them.

The third challenge was giving the puzzles a consistent formula and standard of reasoning. Each has an opening and three branching levels: seven questions, fourteen answers and eight possible routes. You follow one route through three questions, but every branch needs the same manual, dexterous care, requiring human eyes to validate, alongside using multiple LLMs to critique.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

Actually building the app.

I gave up in my head so many times. There were plenty of moments when I wanted to stop working on the puzzle sequence and call it good enough. But that sequence is the app. If reading, choosing, holding and reconsidering didn't feel right, the rest wouldn't make up for it.

I kept pushing and refining it. Seeing a puzzle run from its opening through to the closing gem makes me proud that I stayed with it. I'm glad that I've built something positive, that could potentially empower people with knowledge.

Additionally, I’ve spent the past 11 years building mobile apps and publishing them on Google Play and the App Store, but this was my first time launching on the Samsung Galaxy Store. It was refreshing to experience a different store’s submission process. This also marks the third personal project I’ve launched independently, without any company affiliation.

Building 2 Minds to this point, with this much detail and polish, is why I'm proud to enter it for four awards:

- RevenueCat Design Award

- RevenueCat Peace Prize

- Ship Kotlin Everywhere, by JetBrains

- Best App for Galaxy, by Samsung

**What I learned**

Design is hard. Making something attractive was only part of it. The harder question was whether a person could understand what was happening while giving the app ordinary, imperfect attention. As a developer, this was perhaps my greatest struggle.

Foldable Support. Agentic coding has made it much easier to support multiple layouts and form factors, and since 2 Minds is an app you read, I took the chance to build for foldable postures instead of stretching a phone layout across a bigger screen. On an Android foldable like the Galaxy Z Fold, the app reads the hinge: hold it half-open and a puzzle becomes a book, with the story on the left page, your choice on the right and a shadow down the crease. Apple announced the iPhone Duo while I was still building, which was good timing: I got to test a few of my screens on it.

I documented most of my learnings and journey in this article on Medium.

**What's next for 2 Minds**

I want to grow the puzzle library, then build support for puzzles that go beyond three symmetric levels of arguments. Currently, I have about 40 puzzles lined up for the app, and each puzzle is quite tricky to make due to the amount of research required and ensuring that it is readable and easily digestible by the readers.

The current structure gives every challenge a clear shape. Next, I want room for questions that need a different one: an argument that deserves another step, or a branch that needs more space than its neighbour. I want the structure to follow the question further.

</details>

**Inspiration**

**What it does**

**How we built it**

**Challenges we ran into**

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

**What we learned**

**What's next for Elderhub: Family Care Log**

**Inspiration**

Most medication apps assume the person holding the phone is tracking their own pills. Elderhub started with a different question: what does a family member need when they are helping a parent or spouse? The answer was not another alarm. It was one current care record that could be read and acted on by the people sharing the work.

**What it does**

Elderhub: Family Care Log gives each person their own medications, schedules, dose history, visits, vitals, tasks, bills, notes, contacts, check-in status, and emergency card. The Today screen brings the next actions together. Helpers can mark doses and tasks on someone else’s behalf, and the emergency card can be read or shared as plain text. The first person gets every feature free, invited family members are free, and the record stays usable offline.

**How we built it**

The app is a native iOS app built with Swift 6, SwiftUI, and SwiftData. SwiftData is the local mirror so every screen renders without waiting for a network. Supabase provides family circles and row-level access control. The sync engine is offline-first, with an outbox and per-entity conflict rules. RevenueCat powers Elderhub Plus, which unlocks additional care recipients while keeping invited helpers free. Scheduling, recurrence, Today summaries, reminders, and exports are pure or shared services so the rules stay testable outside the views.

**Challenges**

The hard part was not entering a medication. It was keeping the record trustworthy across family members and unreliable connectivity. We designed reminders around one request per person per dose time to fit the device budget, made dose log IDs deterministic so correcting a dose does not create duplicate history, and kept account and handset roles separate. Sharing is scoped per recipient, and losing access removes only that person’s local copy without deleting the family record.

**What I learned**

A family care product has to make the next action obvious while staying honest about what it does. Empty states, offline behavior, permission boundaries, and emergency presentation are part of the product, not edge cases. The result is a care log that can start locally and become a shared circle when the family is ready.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I'm a Christian and know that I should be praying more than I do. But with a demanding job and 2 young kids at home, it's easy to get so absorbed in the tasks of daily life that I'll go days without taking time throughout the day to stop and pray. There are a lot of prayer apps out there that have guided prayer audio, but I don't usually have 10+ minutes and a quiet space to take such a long and intentional break. But I do have 30 seconds. 

I got the idea for Vesper with my church's small group community. When people would post on GroupMe asking for prayer, the easy thing to do is say "I'll pray for you", but oftentimes I'll say that and never actually stop to do it. We've been intentionally trying to say instead, "I'm praying right now!", and this is the whole idea behind Vesper. Rather than asking you to fit a new habit into your life, I am trying to make it easy to take a short interruption in your day to pray for those who need it. 

**What it does**

Vesper works by making it easy for users to submit a prayer, which then gets matched to another user who will stop and pray for it right then. Users who get matched to a submitted prayer will receive a push notification telling them it's "Time to pray!", and they are encouraged to click it quickly and take just 30 seconds to pray for that request. After they have finished prayer, the submitter will then receive a push notification letting them know that someone just prayed for them, giving validation that a real human stranger just took time out of their day to support them in prayer.

The tendency for prayer apps like this is to either turn everything into a newsfeed of people in your church or in other faith-based organizations, which felt too much like a standard social media app. Vesper intentionally pushes back against becoming just a social media app so users can truly focus on what matters: recognizing our need to depend on the Lord every day, for all things big and small.

**How we built it**

As an Android developer and longstanding member of the Kotlin community, I decided to take this opportunity to see how far I could push Kotlin and see how well it can stand up to the complex demands of this application. Kotlin is the only programming language used, powering both the frontend Android and iOS apps with Kotlin Multiplatform, and the API server with Ktor, with data models, API endpoint definitions, and other contracts shared among them all.

Additionally, as the maintainer of a small state management library, Ballast, I wanted to see how far I could push its programming model and prove out an effective way to use its principles of Unidirectional Data Flow (UDF) for more than just UI. Ballast powers the state management for each screen in the app, as well as the data layer of the Android and iOS apps, and acts as an interface to Postgres-backed Job Queues and Schedules on the server.

The complete application stack includes:

- Kotlin Multiplatform (Android and iOS)

- Kotlin Ktor (API server)

- Postgresql

- Coolify as the reverse-proxy application server

- AWS EC2

- AWS SES

- Cloudflare DNS

**Challenges we ran into**

Kotlin works very well on the UI, and for server-side technologies there is a lot that can be done with Java interop, especially if the server is Spring Boot. But I wanted to stick to pure-Kotlin tech as much as possible, and the landscape for peripheral server-side technologies proved to be lacking. There was no standard library for handling things like sending emails, processing job queues, or running tasks on a schedule. But being able to use these specific technologies and having them implemented well in your backend is absolutely crucial for having an app that is reliable, where I don't have to worry that data could get lost because a 3rd-party system went down. 

Much of the development effort of Ballast was spent designing the backend system and building these features into Kotlin and Postgres. But while this did take a lot of time to get right, I now have the benefit of an app that processes expensive work in the background and can be proactive in engaging customers with push notifications and emails, without having to spend more money on these kinds of services as the userbase grows. 

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I'm very proud of the technical foundation I have laid with Vesper, as it not only makes for a reliable experience for my end-users, but is a platform upon which I will be able to reuse with future projects. I already have 2 or 3 other apps I plan on building over the next couple of years as I work toward a future where I can build a company and become self-employed selling services like this.

But the thing I'm most proud of is how much I have grown beyond just a software developer. By giving myself a clear vision for the functionality and thinking of it in terms of building a proper product, I have gained such an appreciation for the incredible amount of work it takes to start and run a business.

**What we learned**

While I'm certainly no expert yet, it has helped me understand the importance of thinking through the application from many angles, including the roles of:

- Product Owner: not just building a bunch of features, but constraining the features to build an experience

- Marketing: how to tell the story of the app rather than just describe its features

- Customer support: how to identify and correct issues reported by users

- Business analyst: what data to collect to help me understand the behavior of users

- CEO: how can I convert users into paying customers that may one day allow me to be self-employed

**What's next for Vesper**

As the father of small children, I don't have a ton of time to focus on Vesper, and could not build everything into it during the Shipaton that I would have liked. But I have gotten some valuable feedback from my beta testers, and have some clear goals I will be building in the product over the next few months, as well as starting a proper marketing campaign for it. 

Features

- Additional push notifications and email campaigns to increase engagement of sign-up users. These include things like:

- daily prayer reminders

- a weekly recap with prayer stats

- "Happy Birthday" emails

- long-term guided onboarding. Sending a series of emails and push notifications over the couse of several weeks or months to gently teach users understand how to use the app and remind them to engage with it regularly

- The core functionality is all global and anonymous right now, and I want to add a concept of Prayer Groups so users who already meet in person can have a safe space to submit prayer requests to be seen by others in the group

- Vesper as a SaaS product for churches to handle prayer submissions and pastoral follow-up

Marketing

I have several podcasts and newsletters I plan on connecting with to start prompting Vesper in full. Up until now, I have only tested it with friends and family, and have not done any external marketing. But now that I've validated that the core technology works, and have identified the gaps that still need to be filled, I am getting close to a point where I could do a full, paid marketing campaign.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**PoquitoTalk: speak to people in their language, and doors open**

In Bocas del Toro, Panama, you get between the islands by boat, and daily life runs on WhatsApp voice notes. PoquitoTalk lets English speakers type or say what they need and send it as a polite, natural voice note in Panamanian island Spanish. When the captain, plumber or clinic replies by voice, you hear it in English. They don't need an app, an account or a download: just a link.

Watch the demo (1:59): https://youtu.be/fTFZ1pqm_HQ. Every timestamp below opens the video at that moment.

**The problem, in 14 seconds (0:00)**

When your water pump dies or your boat engine won't start, you message a local worker in textbook Spanish from a translation app, and you get left on read (0:03). Formal text is the wrong tool in a place where people answer by voice, often from a boat. Newcomers hire middlemen or give up, and the local worker loses the job. I've lived here for 14 years and watched this happen every week in our community forums: "Who can recommend a plumber?", "Which captain can take us?"

**What PoquitoTalk does**

- English in, island Spanish out (0:30): you type or speak in English and get a warm, polite Spanish voice note that opens with "¡Buenas!" and uses the words people actually say here ("plomero", "dolor de barriga", "plata"). You pick your own voice, Diego or Sofia.

- One tap to WhatsApp (0:06): the voice note goes straight into the chat as audio.

- They answer by voice, with no app (0:10, 0:43): a 2-way voice link opens in any phone browser. The worker taps it in WhatsApp, answers in Spanish, and you hear the reply in English.

- The right words before you need them (0:36): 76 ready-made phrases for boats, doctors, water, power and more, voiced in both voices and built into the app, so they play without signal.

- A free local directory (0:24): 287 listings so far, from 77 boat captains and water taxis to hotels, restaurants, hardware stores, contractors and clinics. Listing is free, with no commission, and contact goes straight to the provider's WhatsApp.

- A website that does real work (poquitotalk.hero-apps.com): an online version of the directory that people can find on Google, free sign-up forms for captains, restaurants, lodging, tours and trades, the RevenueCat web funnel, and the 2-way voice page the worker opens. While the app was in review, it also held our waitlist.

**How we use RevenueCat (0:50–1:11)**

PoquitoTalk has two kinds of customers, and RevenueCat lets us serve both without building a billing backend.

1. Residents subscribe in the app, on Google Play (0:53).
Expats and off-grid homeowners use PoquitoTalk every week, so they get a subscription. The app uses the RevenueCat SDK (react-native-purchases) with Google Play Billing. One offering holds three packages: the Annual Explorer Pass ($39.99/year, 7-day free trial), the Monthly Resident Pass ($9.99) and the 7-Day Travel Pass ($4.99, non-renewing). Pro access comes from the entitlement in customerInfo, with restore purchases built in. The paywall itself was shaped in public: another builder on X pointed out that our purchase button used the same color as the rest of the app, so it now has a color used nowhere else, and a Google Play rejection taught us to show the yearly price first, not the per-month breakdown.

2. Tourists buy credits on the web, with no subscription (0:54).
Someone visiting Bocas for five days will never commit to a yearly subscription. So on the web we sell a one-time 50 Poquito Credits pack (never expires) through a RevenueCat Web Funnel with Stripe billing: three short slides, then checkout with Google Pay (0:59). With no store fee, we can offer a $3.74 launch price until October 15, against $4.99 in the app. You can see the Stripe transaction land in RevenueCat at 0:54.

3. Web purchases arrive in the app (1:05).
The funnel's thank-you page links into the app. PoquitoTalk handles that link with RevenueCat Web Purchase Redemption (parseAsWebPurchaseRedemption and redeemWebPurchase), finds the credits purchase in the customer's non-subscription transactions by its Stripe product, and adds the 50 credits once per transaction, so a link opened twice doesn't pay out twice. A guard makes sure a credits purchase never unlocks Pro: Pro comes only from a subscription or a pass.

4. Why the funnel matters. A payment on its own isn't enough: if nothing links the web purchase to the app, the buyer pays and then has nothing to open. In a RevenueCat funnel, the purchase becomes something the app can redeem, so a tourist who pays on the web lands in the app with their credits ready. That's why every web purchase goes through the funnel. We also connected RevenueCat to the Layers SDK, so revenue can be tied back to the posts that brought people in. All of this is live in v1.5.10, approved on Google Play on September 29, with working in-app purchases and web redemption.

**Built with the island (0:16)**

Before building anything, I asked the island's community forum what is hardest to explain in Spanish (0:18). The answers shaped the app: "Most of my calls are not repairs, but medical" became the medical and pharmacy phrases. Providers join the directory in two ways (0:24): a free sign-up portal, or we simply message them on WhatsApp and they reply, often by voice. We messaged six of the islands' Hope Spot certified boat captains this way, and five replied. For people who can't sign up online, I go and talk to them in person. The directory now lists 287 local businesses and providers, and nine signed up themselves through our website, from a water taxi and tour operator to a welder, an electrician and an A/C repairer.

**Growing it with Layers (1:11)**

Layers runs our growth loop: it makes a clip every day from our brand and app screens, posts it, and measures each post against our own median (1:27). Its honest verdict on our 805-view breakout was inconclusive (1:30), and it was right. Our small, promising signal came from useful posts: a cash-tips video and a bar skit that ends with a cheat sheet people save (1:31). The full loop, the SDK and our data, with screenshots: poquitotalk.hero-apps.com/growth-loop.html.

**Built in public (1:38)**

60 days, 60+ posts on X, two HackerNoon articles, and one page that collects it all: poquitotalk.hero-apps.com/build-in-public.html (1:53). Replies changed the app, from the paywall button color to the 2-way voice link.

**How it's built**

- App: React Native with Expo and TypeScript, live on Google Play (com.heroapps.poquitotalk).

- Speech to text: ElevenLabs Scribe, with Groq Whisper and OpenAI Whisper as fallbacks, and a cleaner for stutters and repeated words.

- Translation: a hand-written map of about 85 common island phrases first, then MyMemory, our own server and Google Translate, followed by a Panama polishing layer that swaps textbook words for island ones and fixes the Spanish ¿ and ¡ marks.

- Voices: ElevenLabs (eleven_multilingual_v2), Diego and Sofia; 152 phrase clips bundled for offline use.

- 2-way voice link: a small web page and PHP endpoint on our own server; the app checks for replies every 2.5 seconds.

- Directory: MongoDB Atlas, with a bundled copy that works offline.

- Payments and growth: RevenueCat (Google Play subscriptions, Web Funnel with Stripe, Web Purchase Redemption) and the Layers SDK.

**What we learned**

- Voice comes first here. A communication tool for this community needs audio at its center, in both directions.

- Design for the person who didn't choose the app. The worker on the other end installs nothing and pays nothing. That decision shaped everything else.

- Listen to your own output. When the app said "fontanero" or "dolor estomacal", which nobody says in Bocas, we changed the phrases and re-recorded both voices.

**What's next**

- Reach the 60+ remaining Hope Spot certified boat captains and build the region's first searchable captain directory.

- Replies spoken in a voice that matches the person who sent them (built, shipping in v1.5.11).

- QR codes where tourists already are: cards at hotel receptions and stickers on water taxis that open the web funnel, each with its own campaign tag, so we can see which hotel or boat brings buyers.

- iPhone: the waitlist is open on our website.

**More detail, one page per award**

- Funnel Vision: poquitotalk.hero-apps.com/funnel.html

- Peace Prize: poquitotalk.hero-apps.com/peace.html

- Growth Loop (Layers): poquitotalk.hero-apps.com/growth-loop.html

- #BuildInPublic: poquitotalk.hero-apps.com/build-in-public.html

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Over 430 million individuals globally experience disabling hearing loss, facing severe safety vulnerabilities when critical environmental cues occur. Conventional auditory alerts—such as commercial fire alarms, ambulance sirens, breaking glass, and cries of distress—fail to protect deaf and hard-of-hearing populations. Existing hardware alternatives, such as specialized strobe systems, remain cost-prohibitive, stationary, and confined to specific rooms.

EchoSense was engineered to eliminate this barrier by delivering continuous, on-device acoustic awareness. Operating entirely at the edge, it transforms critical environmental sounds into actionable visual, tactile, and systemic indicators in real time.

**What It Does**

EchoSense functions as a persistent, low-latency background service designed for comprehensive acoustic threat detection and accessible multi-modal feedback:

- Zero-Storage Privacy Framework: Ingests 16 kHz audio streams into a volatile 3-second circular RAM buffer, guaranteeing that raw audio files (.pcm, .wav) are never written to physical disk or uploaded to remote endpoints.

- Multi-Modal Threat Dispatch: Translates recognized acoustic hazards into instantaneous full-screen alert overlays, persistent custom haptic patterns, and prioritized system heads-up notifications.

- WCAG-Compliant Visual Hierarchy: Employs unambiguous geometric iconography (🛑 CRITICAL, ▲ HIGH, ◆ MEDIUM, ● LOW) alongside adaptive color tokens to ensure full legibility for color-blind users.

- Deterministic Simulation Engine: Features an integrated offline testing module that reliably simulates critical sound signatures (fire alarms, emergency sirens, infant cries, breaking glass) without network reliance.

- Encrypted Local Audit Logging: Indexes detected incident logs locally via an indexed Room SQLite database, complete with fast-filter chips for triage and review.

- Ethical Freemium Structure: Maintains all foundational emergency detection capabilities as permanently uninhibited public-interest utilities, while delegating advanced acoustic profiling and data analytics to premium tiers.

**Architecture & Engineering**

EchoSense leverages modern Android engineering standards to maintain high stability, low power draw, and determinism across the stack:

- Presentation & Pattern: Implemented Clean Architecture with Model-View-Intent (MVI) unidirectional data flow, orchestrated via Kotlin Coroutines and asynchronous StateFlow streams.

- Declarative UI Design: Crafted with Jetpack Compose and Material 3, incorporating an accessible high-contrast layout, fluid animations, and granular toggles for motion suppression and haptic calibration.

- Low-Level Audio Ingestion: Configured Android AudioRecord APIs to stream high-frequency acoustic data into non-allocating memory ring buffers with active hardware acoustic echo cancellation and noise suppression.

- Local Persistence: Structured an offline-first Room ORM abstraction layer over SQLite for low-overhead incident tracking.

- Entitlement Management: Integrated the RevenueCat Android SDK to arbitrate dynamic subscription tiers and telemetry without introducing barriers to emergency core functionalities.

**Technical Challenges & Mitigations**

- Aggressive OS Background Throttling: Non-standard OEM process management frameworks (such as HyperOS and OneUI) aggressively terminate long-running background tasks. This was resolved by binding the processing pipeline to an Android Foreground Service tied to persistent notification channels, paired with deep-linked system intents guiding users through battery-optimization exemptions.

- Asynchronous Test Concurrency: Coordinating multi-threaded audio buffer ingestion, mock classification streams, and reactive UI state dispatching introduced race conditions in testing environments. This was addressed by standardizing test suites on virtual coroutine test dispatchers and deterministic time manipulation.

**Key Achievements**

- Robust Test Coverage: Attained a comprehensive 100% pass rate across all 64 unit and integration tests, validating buffer integrity, concurrent state handling, and ViewModel stability.

- Privacy-Preserving Computation: Established a strictly ephemeral audio execution loop, validating that real-time machine listening can be deployed without persistent storage overhead or data harvesting risks.

- Universal Usability Compliance: Built an alerting interface adhering to rigorous WCAG 2.1 non-color-only sensory standards to guarantee rapid comprehension during emergencies.

**Key Insights**

- Low-Allocation Audio Handling: Gained deeper expertise in optimizing audio processing pipelines in Kotlin to bypass repetitive garbage collection cycles on the main render thread.

- Ethical Monetization Strategy: Successfully decoupled mission-critical life-safety features from revenue infrastructure, utilizing RevenueCat to drive sustainability through enterprise-tier telemetry and personalization rather than restricting foundational safety access.

**Roadmap**

- Edge Model Optimization: Deploying quantized, custom-trained on-device acoustic classification models to expand threat detection accuracy with minimal inference cost.

- Wear OS Extension: Building a companion wearable client to route targeted haptic pulses directly to the user's wrist during critical events.

- Spatial Acoustic Localization: Implementing multi-channel microphone phase comparison to provide directional visual vectors pointing toward sound origins.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I used to play the same ambient recordings to relax. After listening to them enough times, I began to remember which sound came next. That anticipation made it harder to rest. I wanted to make a soundscape I could return to without memorizing it, and a screen that felt calming even before playback began.

**What it does**

Ambient generates sounds such as rain, waves, and wind in real time. Their patterns and small details keep changing as you listen. Flowing ink responds to the sound. When you first open the app, you see a single play arrow. Tap it, and the arrow dissolves into the ink.

Try Ambient in your browser.

Because Ambient is designed for background listening, I wanted people to enjoy it on the devices they already use for work and relaxation. I also released it on TVs, smartwatches, and desktop computers.

I also wanted people to be able to listen to Ambient in the background while working in VR. Since there’s still little competition in the VR space, I think this would be an effective marketing strategy. For that reason, the app is now compatible with Vision Pro, which has been confirmed to support background playback. As of September 30, 2026, Ambient appeared first in search results for "ambient" in the Vision Pro App Store in both the US and Japan.

On Vision Pro, I use particle visuals instead of ink to make use of the surrounding space. On Apple Watch, I use a lighter particle renderer to help conserve battery power.

The app has no ads. Free listening lasts up to 60 minutes per session. Premium adds unlimited listening and background playback.

**How we built it**

**Cross-platform architecture**

KMP let me develop sound generation, scene transitions, playback state, and listening limits in one shared core. With separate implementations for all eight platform families, each core change would need equivalent regression checks in eight codebases. Instead, I maintain one implementation and one shared test suite, then validate each platform's audio, UI, and lifecycle integration.

Android calls Kotlin directly, Swift imports a generated Kotlin/Native framework, desktop apps use a C interface, and the web runs Kotlin/JS inside an AudioWorklet. These adapters connect each app's controls to the same engine and return shared state, so I can keep each platform's own interface without reimplementing the playback rules.

Platform
Shared engine bridge
Interface, audio, visuals

iOS / iPadOS
Kotlin/Native framework
SwiftUI, AVAudioEngine, Metal

Android / Android TV
Kotlin/JVM module
Android Views, AudioTrack, Vulkan or OpenGL ES

watchOS
Kotlin/Native framework
SwiftUI, AVAudioEngine, Canvas particles

visionOS
Custom Kotlin/Native target
SwiftUI, AVAudioEngine, RealityKit and Metal particles

macOS
Kotlin/Native C bridge
SwiftUI, AVAudioEngine, Metal

Windows
Kotlin/Native C bridge
Win32, WASAPI, Vulkan

Linux
Kotlin/Native C bridge
GTK4, ALSA, Vulkan

Web
Kotlin/JS in AudioWorklet
HTML controls, Web Audio, WebGPU

iPadOS uses the iOS app, and Android TV uses the Android APK with support for TV remote input. Web playback controls remain available without WebGPU.

The ink simulation builds on Stable Fluids with custom color mixing.

I extracted Ambient's reusable audio playback layer into KMP Procedural Audio, a lightweight Kotlin Multiplatform library released under the MIT license. It offers shared playback controls and source switching across Android, iOS, macOS, watchOS, Windows, Linux, and the web.

**Premium across devices**

Premium purchased in the iOS or Google Play Android app also works on Windows, Linux, and the web. The receiving device displays a QR code. The user scans it in the mobile app, checks the device name, and approves the link, without creating a separate account.

Kotlin Multiplatform shares the logic behind this flow. The same core manages pairing, waiting for approval, saved access, expiry, and removing linked devices. Each app connects it to its own interface, networking, credential storage, and store purchase SDK. This keeps the linking rules consistent while allowing each platform to use its native capabilities.

A Cloudflare Workers service verifies the StoreKit transaction or Google Play purchase token and checks that it matches an active Premium purchase in RevenueCat. D1 stores the registrations and allows up to three linked devices or browser profiles per eligible purchase. The QR code is valid for five minutes and contains an approval code, with a separate token used by the receiving device to check its access.

Previously verified Premium remains available offline only until the server's access deadline. Expired access or a check that reports Premium is no longer active returns playback to the free tier’s 60-minute session limit. Users can remove links from the mobile app. Network and store checks run separately from sound generation.

Read more about the shared engine, fluid visuals, and visionOS support in my dev.to article.

**Challenges we ran into**

Kotlin Multiplatform does not officially support visionOS. I forked Kotlin and added the target needed to build Ambient for Vision Pro. While researching how to contribute that work, I found KT-59571, the existing visionOS support request. Its earlier LLVM limitation had been resolved in the current Kotlin/Native version.

I refined my implementation and submitted draft PR #7797. JetBrains explained that adding an official target would increase CI and maintenance costs, so the PR was closed without being merged. I appreciated the care they took in explaining the decision.

The biggest implementation challenge was optimizing performance. Both audio and graphics required real-time processing, so I had to decide which tasks should run on the CPU and which on the GPU. Audio was especially sensitive to timing: missing an audio-buffer deadline could cause clicks or dropouts.

Physically faithful color mixing quickly made the ink look muddy. I chose a stylized color model that keeps the blends soft and visually distinct rather than strictly realistic.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

One shared core now supports builds across eight platform families, from phones and TVs to desktops, the web, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. I am especially proud that the Vision Pro app uses the shared Kotlin core and lets people purchase Premium in the app, with purchases powered by RevenueCat.

While the “Ship Kotlin Everywhere” category does not prioritize the number of supported platforms, reaching users through multiple app stores is an important part of Ambient’s strategy. Kotlin Multiplatform makes this possible while helping me deliver a consistent experience across devices.

**What we learned**

I chose an affordable monthly subscription without a free trial and offered a lifetime purchase alongside it. My hope was that the monthly price would make Premium approachable while giving people a clear alternative if they preferred to pay once. The first two paying customers bought lifetime access without first subscribing to the monthly plan.

The visionOS work also taught me that getting a target to build is only one part of official support. CI, libraries, distribution, and long-term maintenance matter too.

**What's next for ambient**

I plan to improve the quality of Ambient’s 50 sounds and add more variety. I also want to make the ink more relaxing to watch by refining how long it stays on screen and how its colors blend. There is still room to make both the audio and the visuals feel more natural and inviting.

I also plan to bring Ambient to Apple TV, Wear OS and Meta Quest. I couldn’t add support for these platforms during Shipaton. What matters to me is how they fit into people’s lives. Someone who enjoys Ambient on their phone should also be able to play it on their TV while relaxing at home. I want to help people discover these options and give them a consistent experience across the devices they use.

The market for ambient sounds and sleep music is crowded. I want to establish strong user retention before investing in paid advertising, so I plan to focus on ASO first. Ambient’s broad platform support is a key part of that strategy. Each store gives people another way to discover the app. I’ll tailor each listing to its platform and highlight how people can use Ambient on their other devices. The goal is not just to increase downloads but to help people make Ambient part of their routine. I’ll track retention and Premium purchases across stores to guide further development and decide when to start testing paid advertising.

ASO takes time to produce results. One reason I offered a lifetime plan alongside the monthly subscription was to generate revenue during Shipaton. The lifetime plan has brought in revenue and met that short-term goal.

With that short-term goal met, my next focus is long-term revenue. If retention data indicates that focusing on subscriptions would increase LTV, I’ll stop offering the lifetime plan to new users. As part of that shift, I’ll adjust the monthly subscription price and introduce an annual plan. Once I have enough evidence that the expected revenue per customer justifies the acquisition cost, I’ll start testing paid advertising to complement organic growth.

JetBrains also pointed me to KT-43974, a request to allow Kotlin targets to be maintained outside the main repository. I hope to contribute the visionOS support I developed for Ambient if that becomes possible.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Digging through a camera roll one photo at a time to free up space is just clunky and boring. TikTok already trained everyone's thumb to swipe through content nonstop without even thinking about it, so I figured that same gesture could make cleaning your gallery feel just as addictive instead of feeling like a chore.

**What it does**

SwipeGallery turns cleaning up your photos and videos into a quick swiping game. Swipe up or down to delete, swipe the other way to keep, and just fly through your camera roll instead of tapping into each photo and hitting delete one by one.

**How we built it**

Built the whole thing with Compose Multiplatform so the UI and logic are shared between Android and iOS from one codebase. CMP handles the shared business logic, and I plugged in native platform APIs where I needed real access to the photo library on each OS.

**Challenges we ran into**

Biggest challenge was making photo loading feel instant. Nobody wants to sit there staring at a spinner while their whole camera roll loads in. I ended up building a caching and batching system so photos load in small batches as you scroll, instead of trying to load everything up front. That way the first batch shows up fast and the rest keeps loading in the background while you're already swiping.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Got SwipeGallery to almost 200 downloads, which felt awesome for something I built solo. Also made my first real money from it, $40 from someone picking up a yearly subscription. Small numbers but it's proof people actually want this.

**What we learned**

Got a lot better at Compose Multiplatform and figured out how to actually ship a KMP app end to end. Also ended up spinning off the photo and video loading gallery piece into its own library called Pikto, which is my first published library ever.

**What's next for SwipeGallery**

Next up is running some A/B tests on different pricing models to see what actually converts. Also want to keep growing the user base and hit my first $100 in revenue before the Shipaton wraps up.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

The Littles: Edmonton School Run began with a real person named Danny. During a difficult time when I had nowhere to stay, Danny treated me with kindness and gave me somewhere safe to be. I have never forgotten that.

I lived in Edmonton for many years. I found love, lost love, built lasting friendships, and experienced both the best and worst of times. It eventually became too cold for me to stay, but part of my heart will always be there.

This game is my thank-you to Danny and to the people of Edmonton and Alberta. You deserve more recognition for the kindness, friendship, and hope you give others.

**What it does**

A fierce Edmonton snowstorm has scattered children throughout the neighbourhood. Danny chooses to search for them and bring them safely to school.

Across three levels, players explore streets, parks, houses, and the river valley. They find missing children, keep the growing group together, and guide everyone through the storm.

Later levels introduce darkness, a flashlight, wildlife, longer searches, dangerous weather, and larger groups of children. Danny’s mother also keeps checking on him while he tries to help the neighbourhood.

I wanted to create a nonviolent game. There are already many games about shooting and fighting. This game is about responsibility, community, persistence, and helping people.

**How we built it**

The game was built in Unity using C#. I normally develop with Unreal Engine, so changing engines was a major learning experience.

We created systems for exploration, dialogue, objectives, following children, group movement, snowstorms, flashlight use, level progression, mobile controls, and the final return to school.

The project had almost no budget, so it combines original work, custom code, in-house construction, and properly licensed assets.

ChatGPT and Codex were major development partners. They helped turn rough ideas into working systems, diagnose problems, test builds, and improve the experience. OpenAI also provided a month of access that helped make this development possible.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the greatest challenges was developing the game while I could effectively use only one arm. Ordinary development tasks took much longer, but I kept working.

Other challenges included learning Unity, building without a meaningful art budget, making groups of children follow Danny without colliding or getting stuck, adapting keyboard interactions for Android touch controls, and keeping the game understandable during a heavy snowstorm.

The project also taught us when to stop adding features and concentrate on finishing.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud that the game became a complete three-level experience rather than remaining an unfinished prototype.

Danny can explore the neighbourhood, find missing children, form a growing group, survive the whiteout, use a flashlight, encounter wildlife, and return everyone safely to school.

We are especially proud that the game tells a nonviolent story about ordinary kindness. Danny does not save the world by fighting. He helps children through dangerous weather and does his best for his community.

**What we learned**

We learned a great deal about Unity, Android development, player guidance, camera design, group-following behaviour, mobile controls, performance, accessibility, and testing a complete experience.

We also learned that limitations can encourage creativity. A small game made with limited resources can still carry a meaningful story.

Hackathon deadlines provide useful discipline. We do not enter expecting to win. We participate because the structure encourages us to learn, finish our work, and build within clear guidelines.

**What's next for The Littles: Edmonton School Run**

The Android release is waiting for Google Play developer verification and may not complete before the hackathon deadline. The game will remain free either way.

A directly installable Android build and the publishable project source will be available so the game can still be played and evaluated.

After release, we hope to improve the children’s movement, animations, mobile interface, accessibility, environmental detail, and overall polish.

Thank you to Danny, our friends, the people of Edmonton, OpenAI, and the Devpost community.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Family caregiving often depends on scattered messages, phone calls, and memory. When several relatives share responsibility, it is easy to miss a task, repeat an update, or lose important context during a handover.

I built CareRelay – Nối Chăm to give families one calm, private place to coordinate everyday care. The goal is not to diagnose medical conditions, but to help family members stay aligned around tasks, responsibilities, and handovers.

**What it does**

CareRelay helps a family create a shared care circle for one care recipient.

Members can:

- Organize daily care tasks with times, assignees, and completion status

- See shared progress for the day

- Create structured text handovers

- Record and play private voice handovers

- Follow recent updates in a shared care log

- Receive real-time updates across multiple devices

- Invite family members with clear Owner, Caregiver, and Viewer roles

- Keep data separated between different care circles

Role permissions are enforced in both the interface and backend. Owners manage the care circle, caregivers update care activities, and viewers can follow progress without modifying records.

**RevenueCat integration**

CareRelay uses RevenueCat to provide a simple optional subscription called CareRelay Plus.

The free plan supports voice handovers of up to 30 seconds. CareRelay Plus increases the limit to 120 seconds.

The app uses:

- RevenueCat Offerings and Packages

- A monthly subscription product

- The care_relay_plus entitlement

- RevenueCat CustomerInfo as the subscription source of truth

- Supabase Auth user IDs as RevenueCat App User IDs

- Restore purchases

- Account-level entitlement isolation

- Safe handling for purchase cancellation, failure, restart, and temporary network errors

The subscription only changes the recording duration. It never overrides care-circle roles or backend authorization.

**How I built it**

CareRelay is a mobile application built with:

- React Native

- Expo and Expo Router

- TypeScript

- Supabase Authentication

- PostgreSQL

- Supabase Realtime

- Supabase Storage

- Row Level Security

- RevenueCat

- Android development builds

Supabase stores users, care circles, memberships, invitations, tasks, handovers, and activity history. Realtime events notify the application when data changes, while the app reloads canonical data from the backend to avoid stale or duplicated state.

Voice recordings are stored in a private Supabase Storage bucket. Access is limited to authorized members of the correct care circle.

**Challenges**

One of the biggest challenges was keeping data and subscriptions isolated when users signed out, changed accounts, or switched care circles. Realtime listeners, cached state, and RevenueCat CustomerInfo all needed to be cleaned up and reconnected in the correct order.

Another challenge was protecting private voice recordings. A Storage URL alone must not give someone access, so the application uses private storage, short-lived authorized access, and backend policies tied to care-circle membership.

I also had to make purchase states reliable across cancellation, failed purchases, application restarts, account switching, and temporary connection failures.

**Accomplishments that I am proud of**

- Built a complete multi-user care coordination workflow

- Implemented Owner, Caregiver, and Viewer authorization

- Added real-time synchronization between independent clients

- Protected private voice recordings with backend access policies

- Prevented duplicate tasks, handovers, and activity events

- Integrated a working RevenueCat subscription flow

- Preserved subscription isolation when switching accounts

- Tested the main Android flow end to end on a Pixel 8 emulator

- Created a calm and accessible interface in Vietnamese and English

**What I learned**

This project taught me that a reliable mobile product is more than a collection of screens. Authentication, authorization, subscriptions, storage, real-time updates, offline behavior, and account cleanup must all work together.

I also learned to treat backend policies as the real security boundary instead of relying only on hidden buttons in the user interface.

RevenueCat helped me understand how to design subscription access around entitlements and verified CustomerInfo rather than local purchase assumptions.

**What is next for CareRelay**

The current version focuses on the core family coordination experience.

Future improvements may include:

- More flexible recurring care schedules

- Improved accessibility and localization

- Notification preferences

- Additional care-log filters

- Better support for larger care circles

- Native iOS purchase validation

- Production store deployment

CareRelay’s long-term goal is simple: help families share care responsibilities with less confusion and better continuity.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

While waiting in my car for my daughter outside the chess coaching center, I was trying to practice the accelerated London opening using a paid chess app. I was getting stuck at the same spot after the first ~ 10 moves. Everytime losing either my minor pieces or sacrificing my Queen. 

My daughter recently started learning chess and she had a lot of questions. So I decided to learn along with her. I tried three to four apps and realized that all were using the same chess engine with minor UI changes. However, the user experience was exactly the same: same massive jumps in level, same hints and lack of guidance if you feel stuck. So I decided to build an open-source game with the hope that other developers will contribute to make it better for everyone. 

**What it does**

It is a chess coaching app that feels like a coach watching every move and helping you think through it. Every move is graded based on how it changes your chances of winning. You can ask for a hint, best move or questions about the current position. 

Other apps have rigid jumps from beginner to intermediate level. In my other app, I win every game at beginner level and lose every game at intermediate level. In either situation, I lose my desire to play more. So I introduced 20 levels with human-like variation in game play. So the app simply doesn't pick the same moves everytime.

In addition, you can learn openings, solve puzzles and import games from other sources. 

**How we built it**

The app is built with Claude Code. I started with a concept and brainstormed through it. My goal for the app was to feel like I was playing along a coach who would help me when I needed help. Also, I wanted to minimize dopamine hits by reducing unnecessary graphics and allow people to personalize the app. 

All the core features will be free on the app store and available on GitHub for anyone. If you want access to online AI-based coaching, you have to pay a small fee to cover token usage. For 99 % players, the free version is more than enough. 

**Challenges we ran into**

The AI based coaching can be tricky since most LLMs are not as good as the chess engine. So we connected the chess engine to the LLMs, so both with together.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

This is my first open-source project and I enjoy using this app over the other apps that I paid for. All the code was written by Claude Code. 

**What we learned**

You can use AI to learn almost anything, including things that AI is not good at. Building, customizing and shipping apps is easier than ever. 

**What's next for Chess Coach**

Hoping to see people contribute to the open-source project so we can continue to make this better for everyone. I am considering adding a BYOK option for people who want to connect their own LLMs to the app.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

No single student captures everything said during a lecture.

One student writes down the definition. Another catches the lecturer’s example. Someone else records an important explanation or remembers what might appear in the exam. After class, that knowledge remains scattered across separate notebooks.

We asked:

What if every student could keep a personal notebook, while the class learned from everything its members captured?

That idea became HiveNotes: your own book, connected to the class hive.

**What HiveNotes does**

HiveNotes is a collaborative classroom notebook where every student receives a separate, password-protected journal.

Students can:

- Type notes on ruled digital pages

- Write naturally using a pen or stylus

- Convert handwriting into journal text

- Create diagrams with Excalidraw

- Upload photographs and classroom materials

- Record lectures and generate transcripts

- Read their classmates’ books without editing them

- Ask AI questions grounded in the class’s material

The teacher can compile the class’s contributions into a shared revision studio containing:

- A structured study guide

- Source citations

- A glossary

- Frequently asked questions

- Practice quizzes

- Knowledge-gap analysis

- An audio revision briefing

- Source-grounded AI assistance

Instead of expecting one student to capture an entire lecture perfectly, HiveNotes lets the whole class build a more complete understanding together.

You do not have to catch everything. You only have to catch something.

**How we built it**

HiveNotes is a full-stack TypeScript application.

The frontend uses Next.js 16, React 19 and Tailwind CSS. The backend is powered by Node.js and Express 5, with classroom information stored in PostgreSQL 16 and managed through Prisma 7.

Each classroom receives a unique room code. The person who creates the room becomes the teacher and owner of the hive. Students join using the room code and create password-protected personal journals.

A student can edit their own pages, while classmates’ books remain readable but locked. WebSockets support live classroom activity, while operational-transformation logic helps manage collaborative updates safely.

**Multimodal learning**

HiveNotes combines:

- Canvas-based handwriting

- Handwriting recognition

- Excalidraw diagrams

- Image understanding

- Browser-based audio recording

- Lecture transcription

- AI-generated revision tools

- Text-to-speech revision briefings

**Artificial intelligence**

The AI system is powered through Groq.

HiveNotes uses:

- Whisper Large V3 Turbo for lecture transcription

- GPT-OSS 120B for revision generation and questions

- Qwen for image, handwriting and diagram understanding

- Orpheus for audio revision briefings

The system constructs its revision context from the room’s actual pages, notes, diagrams, images and recordings. Generated revision content includes references such as [S1], connecting explanations to the original classroom sources.

**Deployment**

The application is deployed on Render as separate web and API services with a managed PostgreSQL database.

We also created a Capacitor mobile shell for demonstrating HiveNotes on an iPad with Apple Pencil.

**RevenueCat integration**

HiveNotes uses RevenueCat Web Billing to power Hive Pro.

Students can join a classroom and use the core learning tools for free. We deliberately do not paywall:

- Writing and note-taking

- Handwriting conversion

- Diagrams

- Photographs

- Lecture recording

- Voice notes

- Classroom participation

Every teacher receives the first class compilation for free.

Hive Pro costs $4.99 per class per month and unlocks additional class compilations.

RevenueCat manages the hive_pro entitlement, offerings, purchases and subscription status. The HiveNotes backend independently verifies the entitlement and synchronizes subscription changes through a RevenueCat webhook.

We chose this model because the teacher controls the shared revision experience, while students should never be prevented from contributing because they cannot pay.

**Challenges we faced**

**Protecting individual ownership**

A single shared document would have been easier to build, but it would not feel like a personal notebook.

We created separate student journals with ownership controls and password protection. Students can learn from their classmates’ books, but only the owner can edit a journal.

**Making handwriting useful to AI**

Ink strokes are meaningful to a student, but they cannot be passed directly to a language model.

We developed a process for rendering notebook ink, recognizing the handwriting and converting it into text that can contribute to the class revision.

**Grounding generated content**

A general AI summary can introduce information that was never taught.

HiveNotes constructs its revision context from the room’s actual pages, notes, diagrams, images and lecture transcripts. The generated revision then cites those classroom sources.

**Processing real classroom recordings**

Real lectures contain background noise, interruptions, different accents and incomplete sentences.

We had to transform imperfect transcripts into useful revision material without pretending that every transcribed sentence was completely reliable.

**Maintaining mobile notebooks**

Mobile browsers can suspend processes and interrupt saving.

We improved mobile persistence so students are less likely to lose their work when using phones and tablets.

**Designing fair monetization**

We wanted RevenueCat to support a sustainable product without restricting students’ ability to learn.

This led us to place the paid entitlement around repeated teacher-controlled compilations rather than basic student participation.

**What we learned**

We learned that collaborative learning does not require removing individual ownership. Students can contribute more confidently when they still have a space that feels like their own.

We also learned that educational AI works best when it is grounded in the learners’ real context.

HiveNotes is not intended to replace listening, studying or note-taking. It helps students recover what they missed, compare perspectives and transform fragmented classroom information into something the whole class can revise from.

RevenueCat encouraged us to treat monetization as part of the product architecture instead of adding it at the end. Its entitlement system gave us a clear distinction between free student participation and premium teacher tools.

**Accomplishments we are proud of**

We built the complete classroom learning loop:

- A teacher creates a classroom hive.

- Every student receives a separate personal book.

- Students contribute handwriting, typed notes, diagrams, images or recordings.

- Classmates can read one another’s books without overwriting them.

- The teacher compiles the room’s collective knowledge.

- HiveNotes creates a cited guide, glossary, FAQ, quiz, gap analysis and audio briefing.

- RevenueCat manages continued access through Hive Pro.

We are especially proud that HiveNotes does not feel like a generic AI chatbot with a note-taking feature added to it.

It feels like opening a real notebook first—and discovering the intelligence of the class when it is time to revise.

**What’s next**

Our next steps include:

- Native iPad and mobile releases

- Improved offline writing and synchronization

- Better speaker separation for lecture recordings

- Teacher dashboards and classroom management

- Downloadable revision packs

- More personalized quizzes and study plans

- Institutional plans for schools and universities

- Additional accessibility features for different learning needs

Our long-term vision is for every classroom to have a living knowledge base created by the students who were actually there.

**Try HiveNotes**

- Open the live HiveNotes application

- View the current source code

- Watch the video demonstration

Take your notes. Build the hive.

</details>

**💡 Inspiration**

Most people store sensitive documents (passports, driver's licenses, tax IDs, insurance cards) scattered across photos, emails, or unencrypted notes. I wanted to build a 100% private, on-device iOS document vault where families can scan, organize, and lock their critical documents without sending a single byte of personal data to a cloud server.

Built as part of RevenueCat's Ship-a-thon in a focused 7-day build sprint!

**🔒 What It Does**

Document Vault is a native iOS 17+ SwiftUI app designed for maximum privacy and zero friction:

- VisionKit Multi-Page Camera Scanning: High-res document scanning with automatic edge detection and perspective correction.

- Photo & PDF Import: Multi-page PDF conversion and photo import directly from Files or Photos.

- SwiftData Categorization & Tagging: Built-in category tags (Passports, Driver's Licenses, Insurance, Tax IDs) + custom tags with instant on-device search.

- Face ID & Touch ID Security: Biometric app lock on launch and backgrounding via LocalAuthentication.

- On-Device PDF Exporter: Generate password-protected PDF summaries for sharing via AirDrop, email, or messaging.

- Feedjar In-App Feedback: Integrated 1-tap feedback widget for real-time user feature requests and bug reporting.

**⚙️ How I Built It**

Built in 7 days using modern iOS frameworks and AI-assisted workflow:

- UI & Architecture: SwiftUI & SwiftData (iOS 17+)

- Document Scanning: Apple VisionKit (VNDocumentCameraViewController)

- Security & Biometrics: LocalAuthentication (LAContext)

- Monetization: RevenueCat SDK (Subscriptions)

- User Feedback: Feedjar SDK

- Development Workflow: Vibe-coded with Cursor AI

**💳 RevenueCat Monetization Integration**

Integrated using the RevenueCat iOS SDK to manage subscription entitlements:

- Free Tier: 1 profile, up to 3 document scans, basic search, and local export.

- Vault Pro Subscription ($4.99/mo or $29.99/yr): Unlocks unlimited document storage, multi-family member profiles, and priority PDF summary reports.

**🚧 Challenges I Ran Into**

- VisionKit SwiftUI Bridging: Wrapping UIKit's VNDocumentCameraViewController smoothly inside a SwiftUI sheet state while preserving multi-page scan data.

- On-Device SwiftData Relationships: Structuring SwiftData @Model relationships for multi-page document attachments and tags without cloud sync latency.

- 7-Day Build Constraint: Shipping a fully functional, monetized iOS app with TestFlight builds and App Store Connect setup within a strict 7-day window.

**🎉 Accomplishments That I am Proud Of**

- Shipped a working, native iOS app from scratch to TestFlight in 7 days.

- 100% on-device data architecture — zero backend server costs, zero user tracking.

- Fully integrated RevenueCat subscription paywall and entitlement system.

**🔮 What's Next for Document Vault**

- iCloud Encrypted Backup: Optional end-to-end encrypted backup.

- Home Screen Widgets: WidgetKit shortcuts for emergency document access.

- watchOS Companion App: Quick-glance ID verification on Apple Watch.
