**Inspiration**

Working out alone often means guessing if your form is correct, and hiring a personal trainer isn't accessible for everyone. My co-founder and I wanted to bridge this gap. We realized that modern smartphones have enough processing power to run complex computer vision models locally, so we decided to build a pocket personal trainer that actually watches you and gives real-time feedback.

**What it does**

Replix is a mobile fitness app that uses your phone's camera to analyze your workout form. It maps 33 3D skeletal landmarks on your body in real-time to automatically count your reps, correct your posture, and log your progress. Everything happens on-device, meaning zero lag and complete user privacy since no video feed is ever sent to a server.

**How we built it**

We built the cross-platform application using React Native and Expo, with Supabase handling our backend database and user authentication. The heavy lifting is done through custom Expo native modules we engineered to integrate Google MediaPipe Tasks Vision and CameraX. This architecture allows us to run complex pose estimation models directly on the mobile hardware.

**Challenges we ran into**

Our biggest hurdle was getting real-time computer vision to run smoothly on a mobile device without dropping frames or instantly draining the battery. Bridging native MediaPipe tracking libraries into a React Native environment required writing custom native code, which was a steep learning curve. We also spent a lot of time fine-tuning the rep-counting logic and handling dynamic screen orientation controls without interrupting the active tracking session.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are incredibly proud of achieving low-latency, on-device ML tracking within a React Native ecosystem. Getting the 3D skeletal mesh to overlay perfectly onto the live camera feed was a massive technical win. We're also proud of taking the project from a rough prototype to a polished application under our Skortan organization.

**What we learned**

We learned how to break out of the standard Expo managed workflow to write native code when performance is critical. We also gained deep insights into on-device machine learning constraints, managing memory during live camera feeds, and optimizing real-time state updates.

**What's next for Replix**

Since we are focusing on the Next Gen Award to showcase our open-source repo and core tech, our immediate next step is expanding our supported workout library. With our subscription testing already completed, our final steps are wrapping up internal testing and completing the official submission processes for the App Store and Google Play Store.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

As a mahjong player, I kept wishing for quick, bite-sized drills to sharpen tile efficiency and fu-scoring — skills that usually take years of table time to build. So I built Mahjong Tsujigiri! (麻雀 辻斬る！), a training app that turns those drills into 60-second rounds.

**What it does**

Mahjong Tsujigiri! offers three practice modes:

- Full Flush — advanced discard puzzles using a single suit

- What to Discard — build efficient hands under a 60-second clock

- Fu Practice — read a completed hand and calculate its fu, with a full breakdown afterward

Every mode also has an Oni Challenge: a 5-second-per-question sprint where consecutive correct answers double your score, up to 8x. Players track history, climb samurai-inspired ranks, and compare scores on global and weekly leaderboards. The app works in both Japanese and English.

**How I built it**

- Next.js 16 + TypeScript + React 19, compiled to a static export and wrapped with Capacitor 8 for iOS and Android

- Supabase for the problem bank and leaderboard

- RevenueCat + the Capacitor Purchases SDK power the freemium model: free players get 5 rounds a day (or a rewarded-ad refill), and Premium subscribers (monthly/annual) or a one-time Remove Ads purchase unlock more

- AdMob for banner/interstitial ads, gated by Google's UMP consent flow for EEA users

- The same Next.js codebase also ships as a web app and a LINE mini-app, so non-native players can practice too

**Challenges I ran into**

- A Capacitor "thenable" trap: Capacitor plugins are Proxies that return a function for every property access, so they look like they carry a .then method. An async function that returned the Purchases plugin made JavaScript treat it as a Promise and await a native .then call that never resolves — the purchase screen hung forever. The fix was to reference the plugin synchronously instead of returning it from an async function.

- iOS 27's UIScene enforcement: a build that had shipped fine for months started crashing on launch on iOS 27 devices, because the app had never adopted the UIScene lifecycle. Capacitor's own scene-delegate proxy doesn't implement UIWindowSceneDelegate, so I had to write a real SceneDelegate that builds the window itself and forwards Capacitor's own URL and continuity handling.

- Static export routing on native: Capacitor's local web server maps any extension-less path to the root index.html, which breaks a statically exported, localized Next.js site (e.g. /en/). Fixed with a custom iOS router plus a reload-safe path rewriter that works on both platforms.

**What's next**

- Monthly problem-set refreshes (the subscription's core promise)

- A daily-challenge mode and a "missed problems" review mode

- A wider Android rollout via Google Play

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Mental health and emotional wellbeing are more important than ever, yet many people struggle to find simple, accessible ways to manage their stress and emotions. I noticed that while there are many meditation apps, few actually adapt to how the user is feeling in the moment. I wanted to build something that meets people where they are emotionally and provides immediate, personalized comfort through the power of sound therapy. Soundscape Therapy was born from the idea that the right sounds at the right time can transform your mood and bring peace to your day.

**What it does**

Soundscape Therapy is an AI-powered mood-based sound therapy app that creates personalized soundscapes based on your current emotional state. Simply select how you're feeling from six moods: Happy, Focused, Stressed, Anxious, Sad, or Tired. The app then plays a unique therapeutic sound tailored to your mood, accompanied by an AI-generated message and visual feedback.

Key Features:

- 🎵 6 Mood-Based Soundscapes - Each mood triggers a unique therapeutic sound (alarm clock for Happy, beep for Focused, water droplet for Calm, bird chirp for Relaxing, soft alarm for Sleepy)

- 🧘 AI-Powered Recommendations - Each mood comes with a personalized AI message and sound recommendation

- 🔓 Premium Subscription - Unlock all moods with RevenueCat-powered premium subscription

- 📊 Session Tracking - Track your therapy sessions with AsyncStorage

- 🌙 Beautiful Dark Theme - Calming visual experience with animated backgrounds and sound wave visualization

- 🔊 Real Sound Effects - Plays actual audio using Expo AV from Google's sound library

**How we built it**

Built entirely on an Android phone using Termux!

**Technology Stack:**

- Framework: React Native with Expo (SDK 54)

- IDE: Termux, Nano (command-line editing)

- Testing: Expo Go app on Android

- State Management: React Hooks (useState, useEffect)

- Storage: AsyncStorage for session tracking

- Audio: Expo AV for sound playback

- Monetization: RevenueCat SDK for premium subscriptions

- UI: Animated API for smooth visual effects

**Development Process:**

- Project Setup: Used Expo CLI to initialize the project with SDK 54 (compatible with Expo Go version 54.0.8)

- UI Development: Built the interface with React Native components including SafeAreaView, ScrollView, TouchableOpacity, and Animated API

- Sound Integration: Integrated Expo AV to play sound effects from Google's sound library URLs

- RevenueCat Integration: Added react-native-purchases SDK with test API key for premium subscriptions

- State Management: Used React hooks for managing mood selection, session tracking, and premium status

- Storage: Implemented AsyncStorage to persist session count between app restarts

- Animations: Created pulsing animations, bounce effects, and color transitions for engaging user experience

- Testing: Tested everything on physical device via Expo Go

**Key Technical Implementation:**

- RevenueCat Setup: Configured with entitlement "Soundscape Therapy Pro" and three products (Monthly $4.99, Yearly $39.99, Lifetime $99.99)

- Sound System: Each mood triggers a specific sound URL using Google Actions sound library

- Visual Feedback: Wave animations, pulsing player circle, and color transitions provide engaging feedback even without sound

**Challenges we ran into**

1. SDK Version Compatibility

- Problem: Expo SDK 57 was incompatible with my Expo Go version (54.0.8)

- Solution: Created project with SDK 54 and used --legacy-peer-deps flag for dependency installation

2. Sound File Not Playing

- Problem: Initially tried using local MP3 files, but they were corrupted or blocked

- Solution: Switched to online sound URLs from Google Actions sound library which are reliable and always accessible

3. RevenueCat Test Purchase

- Problem: Test purchases weren't working initially

- Solution: Ensured proper API key configuration and used test mode in RevenueCat dashboard

4. TypeScript Issues

- Problem: TypeScript caused dependency conflicts with React Native

- Solution: Used JavaScript instead of TypeScript for simpler dependency management

5. Permission Errors

- Problem: npm install failed with permission errors on /sdcard

- Solution: Worked in Termux's home directory (~) instead of /sdcard

6. AsyncStorage Error

- Problem: "Native module is null" error

- Solution: Properly installed @react-native-async-storage/async-storage and used it correctly

7. Expo AV Deprecation Warning

- Problem: Expo AV is deprecated in SDK 54

- Solution: Continued using it as it still works, but documented the need to migrate to expo-audio in future versions

8. Building Entirely on Phone

- Problem: Limited development environment on Android

- Solution: Used Termux for npm commands, Nano for editing, and Expo Go for testing - proved you can build fully-functional apps on mobile!

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

🌟 Built on a Phone: Developed the entire app using only an Android phone - no computer needed! This proves anyone can start building mobile apps with minimal resources.

🎵 Working Sound Effects: Successfully integrated real sound effects that play with each mood selection, creating an immersive experience.

💰 RevenueCat Integration: Successfully implemented premium subscriptions with RevenueCat SDK, including test purchases working properly.

🎨 Beautiful UI Design: Created a polished, dark-themed interface with smooth animations, color transitions, and visual feedback.

📱 Fully Functional App: Complete working app with mood selection, sound playback, session tracking, and premium features.

🧘 Mental Health Focus: Built something that genuinely helps people manage their emotions and find peace.

⚡ Quick Development: Built from scratch in a short time using limited tools, demonstrating efficient development skills.

🤝 Open Source Ready: Clean, well-structured code ready for GitHub sharing.

**What we learned**

Technical Skills:

- 📱 React Native and Expo development fundamentals

- 🎵 Audio integration using Expo AV in React Native

- 💰 RevenueCat SDK integration for in-app purchases

- 📊 AsyncStorage for local data persistence

- 🎨 React Native animations and visual effects

- 🔧 Working with dependencies and version compatibility

- 🐛 Debugging without traditional IDE tools

Development Philosophy:

- 💪 You don't need expensive equipment to build apps - a phone and determination are enough

- 🔄 Adaptability is key - when one approach fails (local MP3 files), find another (online URLs)

- 📝 Documentation and persistence matter when building complex applications

- 🧪 Testing on real devices is crucial for catching issues early

Business & Monetization:

- 💰 Understanding subscription models and revenue strategies

- 🔑 Importance of proper payment processing integration

- 📈 How to structure premium features to provide real value

Personal Growth:

- 🚀 Overcame numerous technical challenges and setbacks

- 💡 Developed problem-solving skills under constraints

- 🌱 Built confidence in mobile app development

- 🔗 Learned the value of community resources and documentation

**What's next for Soundscape Therapy**

Immediate Future:

- 📱 Publish to Google Play Store (after connecting real Play Store account)

- 🎵 Add more sound effects for each mood (10+ sounds per mood)

- 🌐 Support multiple languages (English, Spanish, French, etc.)

- 📊 Add analytics to track user engagement and mood patterns

- 💬 User profiles with personalized mood history

Feature Roadmap:

- 🤖 Real AI Integration: Replace static responses with actual AI-generated sound recommendations using OpenAI or similar API

- 🎧 Custom Sound Mixing: Allow users to mix multiple sounds together

- 📈 Mood Insights: Visual dashboard showing mood patterns over time

- 👥 Social Features: Share soundscapes with friends and family

- 🏆 Gamification: Add daily challenges, achievements, and streaks

- 🔔 Reminders: Daily check-in notifications using OneSignal

- 🌙 Sleep Mode: Special night mode with sleep timers

- 📱 Watch App: Apple Watch and Wear OS companion app

Hackathon Plans:

- 🏆 Submit to Next Gen Award (student category)

- 🏆 Submit to RevenueCat Peace Prize (mental health/social good)

- 🏆 Submit to RevenueCat Design Award (beautiful UI)

- 🏆 Submit to HAMM Award (monetization strategy)

- 🏆 Submit to #BuildInPublic Award (sharing the journey)

Long-term Vision:
Transform Soundscape Therapy into a complete mental wellness platform that combines sound therapy with guided meditation, breathing exercises, and daily mental health check-ins - all powered by AI personalization.
Thank you to RevenueCat for this incredible hackathon opportunity and for providing the tools to help developers monetize their apps! 🙏

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Inspiration

Cyber scams are becoming increasingly common, especially through SMS, WhatsApp messages, emails, suspicious links, QR codes, and fake payment requests. Many people receive these messages but are unsure whether they are safe or fraudulent.

We wanted to build a simple mobile application that could help everyday users identify suspicious digital content, understand why it is risky, and learn how to stay safe.

This idea led us to create CyberShield AI, a personal cybersecurity companion that combines scam detection, security awareness, and interactive learning in one Android application.

What it does

CyberShield AI helps users detect and understand common cybersecurity threats through multiple tools:

🔗 URL Security Scanner – analyzes suspicious links and provides a risk score.
📱 Scam SMS Detector – identifies common SMS scam patterns such as OTP requests, fake bank alerts, UPI scams, and fraudulent offers.
💬 WhatsApp Scam Detector – analyzes suspicious WhatsApp messages.
📧 Email Phishing Detector – detects phishing indicators, suspicious links, urgent requests, and information-stealing attempts.
📷 QR Code Scanner – helps users identify potential risks associated with unknown QR codes.
🤖 CyberShield AI Assistant – provides cybersecurity guidance and analyzes suspicious content using local security logic.
🧠 Cyber Quiz + XP – helps users improve their cybersecurity knowledge through interactive questions.
📊 Security Score – provides a personalized security-awareness score based on user activity.
💡 Daily Cyber Tips – provides practical cybersecurity advice every day.
📚 Cyber Safety Awareness – teaches users about phishing, OTP safety, UPI scams, fake jobs, passwords, malware, and other threats.
🗂️ Scan History – stores previous security scan results locally for easy reference.

Our goal is not only to detect threats, but also to educate users about the warning signs behind them.

How we built it

CyberShield AI was developed as an Android application using Kotlin and Jetpack Compose.

We used:

Kotlin for application development
Jetpack Compose for the modern Android UI
Firebase Authentication for login and signup
Room Database for local scan history and quiz data
DataStore for persistent user preferences and XP
Android Camera/QR technologies for QR scanning
A rule-based security analysis engine for identifying common scam and phishing patterns

The application follows a modular structure so that scanners, navigation, database operations, and UI components can work together without affecting the existing functionality.

We also focused on creating a consistent dark navy and neon-blue cybersecurity interface that is easy to navigate and suitable for everyday users.

Challenges we ran into

One of the biggest challenges was combining multiple cybersecurity features into a single mobile application while keeping the interface simple.

We faced challenges with:

Integrating multiple scanner features
Managing navigation between many Jetpack Compose screens
Connecting Firebase Authentication
Maintaining scan history using Room Database
Making analysis results appear immediately after pressing the Analyze button
Persisting quiz XP between app sessions
Handling camera permissions for QR scanning
Creating an AI-style assistant without depending on a paid external AI API
Keeping the UI responsive across different screen sizes

We solved these challenges by breaking the application into reusable components and using a local rule-based security analysis system for the core detection features.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are proud to have developed a complete Android cybersecurity application that brings multiple security tools together in one platform.

Our major accomplishments include:

Building multiple functional scam detection tools
Creating a persistent scan history system
Implementing Firebase-based authentication
Developing a cybersecurity quiz with XP progression
Creating a personalized security score
Adding daily cybersecurity awareness tips
Building a local CyberShield AI security assistant
Creating a dedicated cybersecurity awareness section
Designing a consistent dark cybersecurity-themed interface
Successfully building and testing the application as an Android APK

Most importantly, we are proud that CyberShield AI focuses on both detection and education, helping users understand cyber threats instead of simply labeling content as dangerous.

What we learned

During development, we learned how to build a complete Android application using Kotlin and Jetpack Compose while integrating Firebase, Room Database, DataStore, camera functionality, navigation, and reusable UI components.

We also learned that cybersecurity applications need to communicate risks clearly. A detection result is much more useful when the user understands what the warning signs are and what action they should take next.

The project also helped us understand the importance of designing security tools for normal users rather than only for technical professionals.

What's next for CyberShield AI

We plan to continue improving CyberShield AI with more advanced cybersecurity capabilities.

Future improvements include:

AI-powered threat detection
Real-time phishing URL intelligence
Voice and call scam detection
Advanced QR and payment fraud detection
Deepfake and voice-clone detection
Multilingual support, including Tamil
Real-time threat intelligence
Automated scam reporting
More personalized cybersecurity recommendations
Cloud-based security analysis
Enterprise and financial-sector integrations

Our long-term vision is to make CyberShield AI a personal cybersecurity companion that helps people detect, understand, and avoid digital threats before they become victims.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**English Version**

**Inspiration**

It stems from the need to track issues reported to local authorities. Often, problems like potholes or broken streetlights are reported, but there is no prompt response or confirmation of the repairs to ensure transparency. Furthermore, there are cases where a pothole is fixed only to reappear shortly after because poor-quality materials were used.

**What it does**

It logs civic reports, which are initially verified in the backend to filter out unsafe images and comply with Apple's strict App Review Guidelines.

**How we built it**

We used various technologies to build the app. We utilized SwiftUI for the native interface and SQLite for the local database, which contains all the cities in El Salvador and their administrative divisions to accurately route each report to the correct authority. On the backend, we implemented Lambda functions written in Go to process requests; one of these Lambdas is dedicated exclusively to validating report content to block harmful material (NSFW).

**Challenges we ran into**

We faced challenges where entered city names didn't match the official registry names. We had to implement workarounds in our grouping logic to overcome these discrepancies and ensure accurate assignment.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Getting approved by the App Store. Since the app features social networking elements, it required strict content and message moderation. We managed to strike a balance that allows freedom of expression without offending others, providing a safe space for citizens to comment on reports and express their frustration about community issues.

**What we learned**

We learned how to integrate subscriptions and native payment methods using RevenueCat, as well as how to configure Google AdMob for ad-based monetization.

**What's next for Repórtamelo**

Expanding our services to other countries, which will require indexing new cities and their administrative details so that reports can be properly processed and routed internationally.

Versión en Español

**Inspiration**

Surge de la necesidad de darle seguimiento a los problemas reportados a las autoridades. En múltiples ocasiones, se reportan baches o lámparas quemadas y no hay una pronta respuesta, ni confirmación de los cambios para ofrecer transparencia. Además, se han presentado casos en los que reparan un bache y este vuelve a aparecer al poco tiempo porque usaron materiales de mala calidad.

What it does

**Registra reportes ciudadanos, los cuales son verificados inicialmente en el backend para filtrar imágenes con contenido no seguro y cumplir con las estrictas normas de Apple.**

**How we built it**

Utilizamos diferentes tecnologías para construir la app. Para la interfaz nativa empleamos SwiftUI, y como base de datos local usamos SQLite, la cual contiene todas las ciudades de El Salvador y sus divisiones administrativas para clasificar correctamente a qué entidad le corresponde cada reporte. En el backend, implementamos funciones Lambda escritas en Go para procesar las peticiones; una de estas Lambdas está dedicada exclusivamente a la validación del contenido del reporte para bloquear material dañino (NSFW).

**Challenges we ran into**

Nos enfrentamos a problemas porque algunos nombres de ciudades ingresados no coincidían con los nombres oficiales de los registros. Tuvimos que implementar soluciones alternativas (workarounds) en la lógica de agrupación para superar estas discrepancias y asegurar una asignación precisa.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Lograr la aprobación de la App Store, dado que la aplicación incluye funciones sociales que requieren moderación de contenido y mensajes. Conseguimos establecer un balance que permite la libertad de expresión sin ofender a los demás, brindando un espacio seguro para que los ciudadanos comenten y expresen su frustración sobre los problemas de su comunidad.

**What we learned**

Aprendimos a integrar suscripciones y métodos de pago nativos utilizando RevenueCat, así como a configurar Google AdMob para la monetización mediante anuncios.

**What's next for Repórtamelo**

Expandir el servicio a otros países, lo cual requerirá el indexado de nuevas ciudades y sus detalles administrativos para que los reportes se puedan procesar y asignar correctamente a nivel internacional.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

In 2041, greenhouse gas concentrations pushed planet Earth past an irreversible tipping point. The oceans warmed, forests turned into net carbon emitters, and a toxic yellowish-green haze settled over the atmosphere. By 2047, an unprecedented event known as the "Chlorophyll Awakening" occurred: pushed by severe evolutionary pressure, plant life mutated into predatory organisms capable of motor response and active hunting, driving over 90% of humanity into ruin.

Most survival games frame nature purely as a menace to be incinerated. Flora: The Earth Wants It Back turns that trope on its head. Playing as Sylva, a resilient botanist, the goal isn't just mindless slaughter; it's healing. Using Pure Seeds harvested from pre-crisis seed banks, Sylva neutralizes mutated flora, reverses chlorophyll aggression, and physically restores the earth zone by zone. We combined the addictive adrenaline of isometric roguelite Bullet Havens (Vampire Survivors) with environmental storytelling, vibrant low-poly aesthetics, and real-world ecological purpose.

**What it does**

Flora is a fast-paced 3D isometric Roguelite Bullet Haven + Reclamation game built for mobile (Android & iOS).

- 🌿 20-Wave Survival Gauntlet: Face off against swarms of mutant species (Moss, SporeHead, Ivy, Wolfey) culminating in a colossal boss battle against Chinar (The Ent).

- ⚔️ Dynamic Auto-Arsenal: Equip up to 4 specialized botanical weapons:

- Pollen Injector: Rapid-fire single-target seed darts.

- Flamethrower: High-temperature conical crowd control.

- Flying Orbiting Axe: Lethal spinning perimeter defense.

- UV Lamp: Continuous holy-purple aura dealing damage over time to swarming pests.

- 🃏 RNG Upgrade Deck: Harvest dropped seeds to level up and dynamically choose from 3 randomized skill cards backed by custom 3D-rendered icons (UpgradeManager.cs).

- 🌅 Visual Terraforming: When an infested sector is reclaimed, the toxic gloom and yellow smog immediately dissipate, unveiling a vibrant blue sky and blooming nature.

**💰 RevenueCat Integration & Purpose-Driven Economy**

- 🕊️ Peace Prize Category: Features an in-game "Plant a Tree" IAP package powered by RevenueCat (RevenueCatManager.cs). In-game purchases contribute directly to real-world reforestation efforts.

- 🐱 Catvertising Category: Zero intrusive interstitial pop-up ads! Players only encounter an opt-in "Double Your Harvest" rewarded video upon victory/defeat, with ad revenue telemetry tracked directly in real-time via RevenueCat's AdTracker.TrackAdRevenue API (AdManager.cs).

- 🛡️ Judge-Friendly Simulation Mode: Includes an automated fallback architecture so hackathon judges can test the full store and rewarded loop seamlessly without requiring real credit cards or getting stuck offline.

**How we built it**

- Game Engine: Built in Unity 6 (C#) targeting Android devices.

- 3D Art & Visuals: Handcrafted 3D low-poly models created in Blender, optimized materials, and clean 2D UI layouts.

- Mobile-First Performance: Bypassed heavy physics calculations by implementing squared-distance mathematical radius checks (sqrMagnitude), NavMesh pathfinding, and memory-safe Object Pooling to render hundreds of active enemies at a solid 60 FPS.

- RevenueCat & Monetization Stack:

- Configured com.revenuecat.purchases-unity for cross-platform IAP entitlement management.

- Integrated com.unity.ads linked with RevenueCat's AdRevenueData (TrackAdRevenue) for real-time rewarded ad impression tracking.

- Cross-Scene Architecture: Ensured persistent lifecycle management (DontDestroyOnLoad) between the base hub (BaseScene) and the combat arena (CombatScene).

- Deployment & Release Pipeline: Built and signed production .aab packages with LZ4HC compression and deployed directly to Google Play Store Production Track (com.budabigame.flora).

**Challenges we ran into**

- The 200 MB Google Play Size Limit: Our initial .aab build hit 211 MB due to uncompressed 4K baked normal maps. We migrated quality profiles to Mobile Mipmaps (MipmapLimit: 1), clamped oversized textures to 1024, and switched to high-ratio LZ4HC compression, shrinking the final package down to 188 MB.

- Unity 6 Gradle & EDM4U Compatibility: Unity 6's Gradle 8.10 and Java 17 toolchain conflicted with external dependency resolution. We manually configured mainTemplate.gradle and standard gradleTemplate.properties with AndroidX and Jetifier flags to ensure RevenueCat native Android libraries compiled flawlessly.

- Automated UI Cropping Operation: Original 2D UI designs were centered on 2000x2000 transparent canvases, causing UI distortion inside Unity. We wrote automated Python batch-cropping scripts to strip transparent padding, restoring true aspect ratios (such as 9:1 for health/XP bars) for pixel-perfect HUD alignment.

- Keystore & Security Hardening: Restructured our entire .gitignore to sanitize all keystores (*.keystore, *.jks) and RevenueCat private configurations, maintaining an audit-clean 43+ commit Git history.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- From Scratch to Google Play in 22 Days: Managed an intense 22-day daily sprint, taking Flora from an empty Unity scene to an approved production build on Google Play Console.

- Harmonious Art & Gameplay: Fused dark apocalyptic undertones with vibrant, low-poly aesthetics and satisfying visual payoff upon clearing waves.

- Ethical Monetization: Delivered a monetization model that never annoys the player, rewards engagement via RevenueCat's Catvertising standard, and creates real ecological impact (Peace Prize).

- Rock-Solid Stability: Zero game-breaking crashes across Android devices thanks to optimized pooling and bullet-proof fallback logic.

**What we learned**

- Performance is King on Mobile: Shifting damage calculations from physics colliders to vector math and managing mipmaps makes the difference between battery drain and buttery-smooth gameplay.

- Unified Revenue Analytics: Experiencing how easily RevenueCat bridges in-app purchases and ad impression revenue under a single telemetry roof changed how we view mobile monetization.

- The Power of Daily Milestones: Documenting daily progress, embracing peer review, and maintaining disciplined sprints kept our 3-person team aligned and moving forward every single day.

**What's next for Flora**

- 🏰 Full Base-Building & Survivor Management: Expand the Radio Tower base camp, build botanical laboratories, and manage rescued refugees as seen in our game design document (GDD).

- 🗺️ 5 Vast New Biomes: Introduce the Rotten City, Crimson Desert, Frozen North, and the Origin Laboratory.

- 🍎 iOS & App Store Launch: Bring Flora to iPhone and iPad utilizing RevenueCat’s cross-platform store abstraction.

- 🌳 Certified NGO Reforestation Partnerships: Partner with verified reforestation nonprofits (e.g., Eden Reforestation Projects or One Tree Planted) to turn every in-game "Plant a Tree" IAP into real saplings planted worldwide.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

The initial idea for this project came from one of my university lecturers who taught Decision Support Systems (DSS)—a core branch of practical AI. Around the same time, I was diving into basic accounting fundamentals, learning how balance sheets work and what truly constitutes a healthy business cash flow.

Seeing these two worlds, I asked myself: How can I blend predictive analytics with practical accounting principles into an intuitive tool for everyday business owners? That spark became the foundation for W-Spread.

**What it does**

W-Spread is an intelligent cash flow management and Decision Support System (DSS) tailored for small-to-medium businesses (MSMEs). Instead of overwhelming users with raw spreadsheets, W-Spread simplifies financial reporting and cash flow forecasting into clear, actionable insights.

Key features include:

- Automated E-Statement OCR Parsing: Users can upload bank PDF e-statements (such as BCA, Mandiri, or BRI). The backend automatically extracts, categorizes, and logs historical revenue and operating expenses line-by-line.

- Predictive Financial Analytics: Using historical monthly averages for revenue and expenses, the app projects future account balances while accounting for operational risk factors:

- Actionable DSS Insights: Translates complex accounting projections into intuitive visual risk indicators, helping entrepreneurs make fast, confident capital decisions before cash flow bottlenecks occur.

**How we built it**

Having joined the hackathon with less than two-thirds of the remaining time, I decided to challenge myself by going solo. I acted as the hustler and tech lead, while leveraging my Agentic AI (powered by Claude 3.5 Sonnet in Kiro IDE) as my dedicated hacker.

- Ideation & Architecture: I drafted initial blueprints, narrowed down candidate concepts, and picked W-Spread. I selected JavaScript as the primary ecosystem for rapid development—building a lightweight Express.js REST backend hosted on Vercel, paired with Supabase for database management and auth.

- Prototyping & Slicing: I designed a low-fidelity UI/UX tailored for fast mobile navigation, then worked alongside my AI agent to slice the components into a clean, functional Expo (React Native) mobile prototype.

- Core Engine & Refinement: Together with my AI agent, we structured the database migrations, implemented the backend pdf-parse / multer OCR pipeline, and established the REST API synchronization paths.

Remarkably, the entire implementation phase was completed in essentially a single high-efficiency AI agent session with about five major handover points.

**Challenges we ran into**

Building this under tight constraints came with its fair share of hurdles:

- Scope & Context Friction: In the planning phase, IDE biases and overly broad initial prompts caused delays. I had to quickly pivot to granular context tagging (@File) to keep execution sharp.

- Branding & Visual Identity: Finding a distinct visual color palette was tricky—several great color combinations I tested felt too close to existing fintech apps.

- Debugging Under Pressure: Truthfully, during implementation, I spent more time wrestling with runtime errors and identity sync bugs than writing fresh feature code! But staying optimistic through every broken build kept the project moving forward.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I am incredibly proud to see W-Spread fully functional and meeting every single design goal I laid out.

Building a complete full-stack app—from database schema and OCR parsing to custom state management and predictive analytics—in less than a month as a solo developer was something I wasn't sure was achievable within the timeframe. Hitting this milestone early proved to me what's possible with disciplined execution and modern AI pairing.

**What we learned**

The biggest takeaway from W-Spread was mastering patience under intense pressure. Hackathons operate on aggressive timelines, forcing you to cut vanity features, identify high-impact deliverables, and maintain a sharp product focus.

I learned to put my ego aside, push beyond my comfort zone, and explore the outer limits of my potential in the digital space. It was a reminder that staying in your comfort zone is the enemy of growth.

**What's next for W-Spread**

If luck is on our side in this competition, my ultimate goal is for W-Spread to contribute to the digital transformation of accounting for Indonesian micro-enterprises. I want small business owners to manage their financial health effortlessly from the palm of their hand.

In 2 to 3 years, I hope to see thriving businesses that scaled successfully because W-Spread helped them stay solvent. I firmly believe that sustainable businesses aren't built on shiny branding alone—they survive on the entrepreneur’s discipline in managing their cash flow.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Indonesia ranks second in the world for TB burden, with an estimated 1.08 million cases and around 125,000 deaths every year, meaning 14 people die from TB every hour in this country alone. Behind these numbers lies a quieter, more persistent problem: medication adherence.

According to Indonesia's 2023 Health Survey (SKI), national TB medication adherence sits at only 62.5%, far below the treatment standard. Patients are required to take medication daily for at least six months, and missing doses doesn't just delay recovery, it can lead to drug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), a far more dangerous and expensive condition to treat.

We didn't want to design this app based on assumptions, so we conducted research before building anything. We interviewed both TB patients undergoing treatment and doctors who manage TB cases directly. Patients told us they often lost track of their schedule, especially once symptoms started improving around the second month, a critical point where many patients mistakenly feel "cured" and quietly stop treatment. Doctors, on the other hand, told us they frequently have no way of knowing whether a patient actually took their medication between visits, they can only rely on the patient's word.

That gap between what doctors need to know and what patients actually do, is what inspired Remindy.

**What it does**

Remindy helps patients stay consistent with their treatment through:

Quick medicine input, adding a new medication only takes a few steps, with fields for dosage, schedule, and instructions (before/after meals).

Photo proof confirmation, patients snap a photo as proof after taking their medicine, building a trustworthy, verifiable record.

Adherence tracking, a home screen summary showing adherence rate and treatment progress (e.g. Day 45/180), so patients can see how far they've come.

Medicine history, a searchable record of every dose, taken or missed, organized by date, something doctors told us would help them follow up more effectively.

Family monitoring access, so loved ones can stay updated without needing to ask, since our interviews showed family support is one of the strongest factors in patient adherence.

**How we built it**

We started with research, not wireframes. Before designing a single screen, we gathered data on Indonesia's TB situation and conducted interviews with patients and doctors to understand the real, everyday friction in TB treatment, not just the clinical side of it.

From there, we built low-fidelity, greyscale wireframes to lock down the core flow: Home, Medicine Details, Add New Medicine, and Report/Upload, before touching any color. This let us focus entirely on hierarchy, spacing, and usability first.

Once the structure felt solid, we moved into visual design. We iterated through several color directions, from a high-saturation blue and green concept, to an orange and navy palette, before settling on a calmer, muted teal system with dusty rose accents. Each color was assigned a single clear meaning (teal for primary actions, green for "taken," soft rose for warnings) so patients could understand status at a glance, without needing to read every label.

We also designed the onboarding flow, a subscription/paywall screen, and supporting copy (taglines, microcopy, and a short pitch script) to present Remindy as a complete product experience.

**Challenges we ran into**

Designing around real stigma, not assumptions. TB still carries heavy social stigma in Indonesia. Patients we interviewed were hesitant to talk about their condition openly, which confirmed our decision to move away from alarming, high-saturation colors (like solid red) that could make an already anxious patient feel worse every time they opened the app.

Translating doctor needs into patient-facing design. Doctors wanted detailed, verifiable records. Patients wanted something simple they wouldn't dread opening every day. Balancing both without overwhelming the patient-facing side took several rounds of revision.

Status clarity. Early versions made it hard to tell which medicine had been taken versus which was still pending. We solved this by giving every status its own dedicated color and icon, instead of relying on text alone.

Keeping data consistent across screens. Details like dosage instructions (before/after meals) needed to match exactly between the home screen and the detail page, small inconsistencies could easily confuse patients taking real medication.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Grounding the entire product in real research, national TB data and direct interviews with both patients and doctors, instead of designing in a vacuum.

Designing a complete end-to-end flow, from onboarding to daily use to subscription, with a consistent design system.

Building a color system grounded in both usability and the emotional needs of chronic illness patients, not just aesthetics.

Including a family monitoring feature, recognizing that treatment adherence isn't just an individual effort, something both our patient and doctor interviews pointed to repeatedly.

Iterating through dozens of design revisions to arrive at a UI that's simple enough for first-time or elderly users.

**What we learned**

We learned that Indonesia's TB adherence problem isn't about awareness, most patients we spoke to understood why the medication mattered. It's about consistency over a long, invisible stretch of time, especially once symptoms fade. That reframed how we designed Remindy: less about reminding, and more about giving patients a reason to stay engaged day after day.

We also learned that in healthcare-related products, color and tone carry as much weight as functionality. A well-structured feature can still fail if its visual presentation creates stress instead of reassurance.

**What's next for Remindy**

Partnering with local clinics (Puskesmas) and TB programs for real-world pilot testing, following up directly with the patients and doctors we interviewed during research.

Adding multi-language and regional dialect support to reach more patients across Indonesia.
Expanding medicine input to support barcode or package scanning for faster logging.

Building a companion dashboard for doctors and health workers to monitor multiple patients at once, directly addressing the visibility gap doctors told us about.

Exploring integration with Indonesia's supervised treatment (DOTS/PMO) programs at the Puskesmas level.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Snap Closet: Outfit & Wardrobe**

**Inspiration**

I started Snap Closet two years ago because I had plenty of clothes but kept wearing the same few pieces, then buying more of the same. I wanted my closet on my phone: easy to add to, quick to filter, and clear at a glance. Seeing what I already owned felt like the first step toward wearing more of it.

The first attempt stalled. After six months of working on it after hours, I hadn't reached 40%, and I wasn't happy with how it looked. I put it aside for a year. Better AI tools gave me a reason to try again, and this time I rebuilt and shipped it in under three months.

“Snap” comes from “snapshot.” That's how I want the app to feel: take a photo, make a few choices, and let it handle the tedious parts. Clothing is personal and creative, so I also wanted browsing my wardrobe to feel inviting and playful. Making the app enjoyable to return to became part of the work from the beginning.

**What it does**

Build your wardrobe with less effort. Add photos of individual clothes, shoes, bags, and accessories, or select a person in an everyday photo and import multiple garments they are wearing. AI extracts and tags the items, with processing running in the background so you can keep adding clothes.

See what you own and find what you need. Browse a visual wardrobe and filter your clothes to narrow down your choices. A closet checkup helps surface overlooked pieces, new combinations, possible gaps, and suggestions for what you might let go of. Similar-item search can help you notice when you already own something like a piece you are considering.

Find more ways to wear it. Describe an occasion, choose a piece to build around, or upload a reference photo in Ask your closet. It suggests looks using clothes you already own. Bring one into the Fitting Room, adjust it, and save it to your calendar. In the Model Atelier, you can create a personal avatar and preview your clothes on it. Each avatar has a little blind-box surprise. You can also record an outfit with a photo of yourself wearing it.

**How we built it**

I built Snap Closet in Flutter for iOS and Android. At first, I copied the workflow from my day job. Even after work, I was creating tickets to guilt myself into doing more work.

This time, I kept the process lighter. I used coding agents throughout development, turned repeated tasks into reusable tools, and kept project decisions in a few Markdown files. My design-system Skill helped me redo the app's design and update the existing screens in a day. The structure I'd worked out by hand still helped; I just didn't need to maintain all the same intermediate work.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Making setup worth the effort. Photographing an entire closet is already a chore. Everyday-photo import helps people start with photos they already have, and background processing lets them keep going. The broader challenge is making the whole path from adding clothes to finding something useful feel manageable.

- Getting useful AI results. Early tagging applied too many custom labels. Evaluating them separately helped. For try-on, I tried several approaches before finding results I was happy with at a workable cost.

- Knowing when to change course. Building avatars from layers of artwork took more and more effort without looking much better. Switching to generation gave me better results, and the surprise became part of the fun.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- The app is live on both iOS and Android, in four languages. I use it myself.

- In under three months, I rebuilt the app, redesigned it, and launched it with a website. Virtual try-on followed in a week.

- The design-system Skill became something I could reuse beyond this app.

**What we learned**

Seeing something work quickly kept me going. For a solo project, that mattered more than having a polished development process. I needed to spend less time getting ready and more time finishing things.

The same concern for effort applies to the app. I don't want people to learn how to prompt a model just to get dressed. A photo or a simple choice often does the job. AI should fit into the things people already do and make them easier.

I expect better models to keep improving recognition and styling assistance. The product still has to make those capabilities useful: how quickly can someone add clothes, find a particular item, or understand what is in their wardrobe? Those are the interactions I want to get right. Visual clarity and small moments of delight help make the experience feel approachable, although it is still early and I need to learn which details bring people back.

I wrote more about this on my blog: Snap Closet Is Live on iOS and Android! Reflections on Indie Development.

**What's next for Snap Closet**

My next priority is to make the everyday workflows smoother: adding clothes, filtering them, and seeing the whole wardrobe clearly. I want to learn where new users hesitate, which steps feel tedious, and what helps them find something they actually want to wear.

As an indie developer, I can give a small interaction close attention and keep refining it. I want to earn a place in someone's routine by making those interactions especially useful and enjoyable.

Snap Closet's direction is to help people make more use of what they already own. Shopping integrations are outside my current focus. I want someone to open the app, rediscover a forgotten piece, and leave with an outfit they are excited to wear.

</details>

**Video (1:45):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7VvAWCkqP7g

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/7VvAWCkqP7g/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7VvAWCkqP7g)

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I wonder "What would travelling feel like if I didn't plan everything?" Usually, when I travel, I already know where I'm going, what places I'm visiting, where I'm eating, and what I'm doing next. But what if I just let the journey decide for me? Would it be chaotic, or would it be filled with unexpected discoveries and surprises? That thought inspired me to create Wondertrail—an app where I choose an area, set a few preferences, and simply roll to see where the adventure takes me. Instead of spending time planning every stop, I wanted travelling to feel a little more spontaneous, surprising, and exciting.

**What it does**

Wondertrail transforms map locations into spontaneous adventures. Users simply select an area to explore, set their preferences, and click "roll." The app instantly curates a complete, sequenced trail using available destinations in that region. Instead of planning stop-by-stop, travelers get a seamless journey out of the box. Each generated stop includes practical details like photos, descriptions, categories, time estimates, costs, and tips from other travelers.

**How I built it**

I built Wondertrail's frontend with Flutter and its backend with Appwrite. I integrated OpenStreetMap and flutter_map to handle geographical visualizations, while Appwrite manages destination data and photo storage. Rather than relying on static, pre-packaged routes, the app uses a dynamic, map-based point-of-interest system. Destinations are stored individually, enabling my algorithm to dynamically stitch nearby locations together into a logical trail the moment a user rolls. This generated route is then rendered as a connected, interactive journey on the map.

**Challenges I ran into**

My primary technical challenge was developing an algorithm that generates full trails that are both spontaneous and highly practical. Because the system dynamically selects multiple stops—rather than picking a single random point—it has to account for complex variables like distance, geographic clustering, and the logical flow between locations. Additionally, balancing the user experience was tricky: I needed the "roll" mechanic to feel fun and unpredictable, but the resulting itinerary still had to be realistic and easy to navigate.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

I successfully engineered a completely new paradigm for travel discovery. Instead of forcing users to sift through hundreds of reviews or settle for generic, pre-made guides, Wondertrail builds unique adventures on the fly using existing map data. My core philosophy—"roll once, get an entire adventure"—simplifies trip planning without sacrificing the thrill of discovering the unknown.

**What I learned**

I learned that pure randomness requires underlying structure to deliver a strong user experience. Picking destinations at random often yields disjointed, frustrating travel routes. Building Wondertrail pushed me to deeply analyze spatial relationships—figuring out how places connect geographically so my trails feel spontaneous but remain highly logical. Furthermore, I gained significant hands-on experience with the unique architectural demands of map-based applications, spanning location data storage, dynamic route generation, and journey visualization.

**What's next for Wondertrail**

Moving forward, I plan to upgrade my trail-generation algorithm to better factor in complex variables like real-time travel distance, operating hours, destination categories, and deeper user preferences. I am also focused on expanding my destination database, refining the map interface, and allowing users to lightly customize their itineraries without losing the magic of the spontaneous roll. Due to budget limitations during development, I currently use OpenStreetMap. If resources allow in the future, I plan to integrate Google Maps to provide more complete destination information and access to a wider range of reviews. Ultimately, my vision is to establish Wondertrail as the ultimate travel companion: just pick a region, roll the dice, and let the adventure unfold.

</details>

**Inspiration**

Everyday digital tasks often require switching between multiple apps and websites — one for OCR, another for speech-to-text, another for PDFs, another for translation, and another for QR scanning.

I wanted to solve this problem with one simple idea: why should users need a separate app for every small productivity task?

That idea became ToolCab, an all-in-one productivity toolkit designed to bring useful everyday tools together in a single, clean and easy-to-use application.

**What it does**

ToolCab combines multiple productivity and document utilities into one application.

Its core features include:

- 📝 Text → Audio — Convert written text into speech.

- 🎙️ Audio → Text — Convert speech into text.

- 🌐 Language Translator — Translate text between supported languages.

- 📷 Image → Text (OCR) — Extract text from images.

- 📅 Calendar & Events — Organize important events and dates.

- 🔳 QR Code Scanner — Scan QR codes quickly.

- 📄 Text → PDF — Generate PDF documents from text.

- 📖 PDF → Text — Extract text from PDF documents.

- 🔗 Merge PDFs — Combine multiple PDF files into one.

- ✂️ Split PDFs — Extract selected pages from PDFs.

- ⚡ Compress PDFs — Reduce PDF file size for easier sharing and storage.

The goal is to make these tools accessible from one consistent interface instead of forcing users to install and switch between many different applications.

**How I built it**

ToolCab was built as a cross-platform mobile application using Flutter and Dart.

The application uses a modular approach so individual tools can operate independently while sharing a consistent design system and navigation structure.

Key technologies and libraries include:

- Flutter & Dart

- Material 3

- Google ML Kit

- Speech recognition and text-to-speech technologies

- PDF processing libraries

- Local storage

- Mobile scanner capabilities

- Responsive UI components

- Google Fonts

- Platform APIs and permissions

I focused heavily on usability, responsive layouts, smooth interactions, dark/light themes, error handling, loading states, and a consistent visual experience across the application.

**Challenges I ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was bringing many completely different utilities into one application without making the experience feel complicated.

PDF processing required careful handling of files, pages, temporary storage, and different document operations.

Speech and OCR features also required proper permission handling and lifecycle management.

Another challenge was maintaining a polished and responsive interface while supporting multiple tools with different workflows.

I also spent significant time testing navigation, edge cases, responsive layouts, loading states, and resource handling to make the final application reliable enough for a hackathon submission.

**Accomplishments I'm proud of**

I'm proud that ToolCab evolved from an idea into a complete, functional productivity toolkit containing multiple independent utilities inside one application.

I'm especially proud of:

- Building a unified experience for many different productivity tasks.

- Implementing real document-processing workflows instead of relying on static demonstrations.

- Creating a professional Material 3 interface.

- Supporting dark and light themes.

- Making the application responsive across different screen sizes.

- Adding proper loading, error, and empty states.

- Testing the application and resolving issues before release.

- Preparing the project as a complete open-source hackathon submission with source code and release documentation.

Most importantly, ToolCab demonstrates that a collection of useful everyday utilities can be brought together into one focused application rather than scattered across many separate tools.

**What I learned**

Building ToolCab taught me that creating a multi-feature application is not only about implementing individual features.

I learned a lot about:

- Structuring a larger Flutter application.

- Managing application state and navigation.

- Working with device permissions.

- Handling files and temporary storage.

- Processing PDFs programmatically.

- Integrating OCR and speech technologies.

- Designing responsive interfaces.

- Managing different platform capabilities.

- Testing edge cases and handling failures gracefully.

- Using Git and GitHub to organize and publish a complete software project.

The biggest lesson was that polish, reliability, and user experience are just as important as the feature list.

**What's next for ToolCab**

ToolCab is designed to continue growing as a unified productivity platform.

Future improvements could include:

- More advanced AI-powered document tools.

- Smarter document summarization.

- More powerful translation capabilities.

- Batch PDF processing.

- Cloud synchronization and optional backup.

- More advanced file conversion tools.

- Additional accessibility features.

- More platform-specific optimizations.

- Expanded productivity and utility modules.

The long-term vision is to make ToolCab a reliable digital toolbox for everyday tasks, where users can find the tools they need without constantly switching between different applications.

</details>

## 34. Open Innings — Cricket Scoring

> Millions play cricket every weekend. Almost none of it is recorded. Open Innings scores every ball — offline-first, open source, and free to the person scoring, with no ads while they score.

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/open-innings-cricket-scoring (gallery page 11) · ❤️ 0 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [Biprayan Choudhuri](https://devpost.com/Code_Neuron58)
- **GitHub (Try it out):** https://github.com/CodeNeuron58/open-innings
- **Repo check:** public repo · license: AGPL-3.0 · 248 commits · TypeScript · RevenueCat found in code ✅
- **Other links:** https://openinnings.com
- **Built with:** admob, drizzle, expo.io, heroku, nextjs, pnpm, postgresql, react, react-native, revenuecat, sqlite, tailwind, typescript, zod

**Video (1:21):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8lQ1PKYm43A

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/8lQ1PKYm43A/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8lQ1PKYm43A)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/454/516/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/454/516/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/454/514/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/454/514/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/454/515/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/454/515/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/454/513/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/454/513/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Millions of people play cricket every weekend, and almost none of it is written down. Runs vanish into paper scorebooks that get lost, and a player can play for twenty years with no record of any of it.

The apps that would keep them exist, but they charge the one person doing three hours of unpaid work with a phone in one hand and eleven people waiting on them.

That inversion is the whole project. The scorer is the labour. The people reading the scorecard are the audience. So the scorer never pays and never sees an ad, and the app earns from the readers instead.

**What it does**

Ball-by-ball scoring for club, box and gully cricket — the games nobody else records.

- One thumb, one tap per ball. Extras are armed modifiers: arm a wide, tap the runs, and the key tells you what it will score before you commit.

- Works with no signal. Every tap writes to SQLite and to the screen and returns. A drain loop handles the network. Grounds have patchy signal or none, which is exactly when scoring cannot stop.

- Any delivery can be corrected, not just the last one. The innings replays around the change, so the strike, the over and every figure after it follow.

- A live link anyone can open — no app, no account, no signup to watch.

- Careers that outlive the club. Public player pages, club pages, and the whole ball log exportable as CSV or JSON.

Every feature is free. Not a trial, not a tier. A supporter subscription removes ads on the viewer surfaces and unlocks nothing, because nothing is held back.

**How we built it**

ball_events is the only source of truth. Every other number is derived.

The scoring engine is a pure function — applyBall(state, event) → newState — in its own package with no I/O, no framework and no dependencies. The scorecard, career averages, the club page and the share cards are all folds over the ball log through that one function.

That buys three things. Undo is not a reverse operation, it drops a row and replays. A correction cascades correctly for free. And because the engine has no runtime assumptions, the same code runs on the server and on the phone — which is what makes offline scoring honest rather than an optimistic guess. The console folds pending deliveries through the same applyBall the API runs, against the API's own last answer.

The Laws live as exported sets rather than if statements, because the same question gets asked in more than one place. "Which dismissals credit the bowler" is Law 25, and the SQL that computes career figures imports BOWLER_CREDITED_WICKETS instead of retyping it. Three copies would drift; one export cannot.

Validate on write, tolerate on read. Replay runs on every read, so a rule tightened today would otherwise be applied retroactively to deliveries recorded before it existed — and a shared scorecard would break because the laws improved. Recording is strict; reading back is lenient and records the objection instead.

Expo / React Native, Next.js, PostgreSQL, Drizzle, in a pnpm monorepo so the engine and the API contract are shared rather than reimplemented.

**How it earns — and why RevenueCat**

The scorer is never charged, so the money has to come from the people watching. Ads run on the viewing surfaces — the public scorecard and the match list — and never on the scoring console. A Supporter subscription removes them everywhere.

RevenueCat carries that, and the design rule was that the app should never know what somebody bought — only what they are entitled to.

- One entitlement, checked in one place. The app asks a single question — does this person have supporter? — and never names a product. Adding a plan, changing a price or running a promotion is a dashboard change, not a release.

- Packages by type, not by name. One default offering with $rc_monthly (₹49) and $rc_annual (₹199). The paywall reads offering.monthly and offering.annual, so it renders whatever the offering currently holds.

- Test Store and Play in the same offering. Each package holds a simulated product and a real Play product side by side, so development and production run from one configuration.

- Tied to the account, not the phone. The app calls Purchases.logIn with the user's id at sign-in, so supporter status follows them to a new device, and Restore sits on the Supporter screen.

- Honest when it cannot sell. A build without a store key shows "Purchases are not configured in this build yet" — a visibly unavailable button, never one that takes money and grants nothing.

- The whole paywall is one line. AdBar returns nothing for a supporter. No feature sits behind it, because nothing is held back.

**Challenges we ran into**

Three bugs, and what they had in common is the interesting part: none of them crashed, none failed a test, and all three produced perfectly plausible output.

A pure function that wasn't runtime-pure. The engine minted ball ids with globalThis.crypto.randomUUID(). Correct on a server, correct in a browser, and absent in React Native's Hermes. Harmless for as long as the engine only ran server-side — then offline scoring moved it onto the phone and the first ball anyone scored threw Cannot read property 'randomUUID' of undefined. Scoring didn't work at all. No test caught it because every test runs under Node, where the global exists.

Two write paths that disagreed. POST /ball built the engine's input as an object literal and left out four fields, so overthrows and the batters-crossed override were silently stored as null. PATCH went through different code and carried all four — so correcting a delivery put back what recording it had lost. The correction suite proved overthrows worked while recording one never did.

A validation rule that was unreachable. A cross-field check sat below an early return taken by every event type that names its own runs — precisely the deliveries the rule was for. It was live for extras, which never carry shot placement, and dead for every scoring shot, which does.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

489 unit tests, plus smoke suites that play whole matches against a real database and a production build, then replay the stored log to prove it still parses. The engine is covered two ways: example tests for the cases somebody thought of, and property tests over any sequence of deliveries for the ones nobody did.

The property tests assert the Laws as invariants over randomly generated innings — the total is always the sum of every delivery, a wide is never a ball faced, a dismissed batter never faces another ball — so they hold for inputs no one wrote down.

And the cricket is right. A wide is not a ball faced. A leg-bye doesn't break a maiden and is never charged to the bowler. A free hit carries a no-ball's dismissals and survives an intervening wide. A single off the last ball keeps the strike. A retirement isn't a delivery, so it doesn't use one up. If the app refuses a ball, it tells you which Law says so.

**What we learned**

A pure function is only pure if it makes no assumptions about its runtime. "No I/O, no framework" was in the file header the whole time, and one call to a Web API broke it the moment the code moved to a phone.

Two code paths for the same write will disagree, and only one of them will be tested. The fix wasn't the missing fields — it was noticing that recording and correcting a delivery had become different programs.

Order matters in validation, and getting it wrong is silent. A rule after an early return isn't a weaker rule; it's no rule at all, for exactly the inputs it was written for.

**What's next for Open Innings — Cricket Scoring**

Tournaments. Clubs don't adopt a scoring app, they adopt a tournament system — fixtures, points table, a league page. It's the single biggest adoption gate, and it's already built on a branch with its own tests. It ships as the first update after launch.

Deep analytics, free. Every delivery is stored forever, so batting zones, matchups and over-by-over comparisons are pure compute over data we already hold. The incumbent charges a subscription for this; giving it away is the clearest way to be better rather than cheaper.

Offline everything. Scoring and undo work with no signal today; creating a match, starting an innings and correcting a delivery the server already holds still need the network. Closing that makes this the app that works at a ground with no bars — the exact moment the alternatives fail.

The share loop, and languages. A share button on the public scorecard, club pages that search engines can find — then Hindi and two or three southern languages, which is the real audience definer.

And the thing that stays fixed: no feature will ever be paywalled, and the person doing the scoring will never pay.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

The Shipaton gaming brief helped crystallize an idea I already wanted to pursue: a game tracker that feels effortless to use.

I had previously built trackers for anime, Pokémon, One Piece, and other media, so I saw clear potential in bringing that experience to games. I am also an avid gamer who regularly discovers interesting titles through YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram. Those posts often provide little context, and once I scroll away, the game is usually lost.

That personal frustration became the central idea behind Joylogue: let people save a game at the exact moment they discover it, even when all they have is a social media link.

**What it does**

Joylogue is a game tracker built around the full journey from discovery to completion.

Users can share a YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram link with Joylogue, which analyzes the content, identifies the game, and creates a detailed entry in their library. Joylogue also remembers the original post so users can return to the reason they saved the game.

Games can be organized as Want to Play, Playing, Completed, Shelved, or Abandoned. Players can track their progress, record start and completion dates, rate completed games, receive upcoming-release alerts, and get help deciding what to play next.

Joylogue also includes social features that support the core tracking experience. Friends can compare libraries, see games they have in common, view each other’s progress and ratings, and send direct game recommendations.

**How we built it**

I designed and built Joylogue by myself in approximately three weeks.

The app was created with React Native, Expo Router, and TypeScript. Its local-first library uses SQLite and Drizzle ORM, keeping the core tracking experience fast and available without depending on a constant internet connection.

The social system uses Supabase for profiles, friendships, shared libraries, and recommendations. Game information comes from IGDB through a server-side API, keeping private credentials outside the mobile app.

The social-link feature uses a server-side pipeline that can download and process public video content from platforms such as YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram. It analyzes the available text, metadata, and media to identify recognizable games before matching them with structured game data.

RevenueCat powers Joylogue Pro, including native paywalls, purchases, entitlement checks, restores, and subscription management. OneSignal supports notification infrastructure, while PostHog helps measure the discovery, library, social, and purchase funnels.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge was making social-link identification feel dependable.

Social posts rarely provide clean, structured game information. A title might only appear briefly in the video, be mentioned in the audio, or be missing from the caption entirely. The server therefore needs to download and process the content, identify possible games, match the result against reliable game data, and return it quickly enough that saving never feels frustrating.

Building the backend was only part of that challenge. I also spent considerable time refining the loading states, animations, error handling, and confirmation screens. The experience needed to communicate what was happening without making the user think about the complexity behind it.

Another challenge was adding social features without allowing them to take over the product. Joylogue is first and foremost an intuitive personal game tracker. Friend comparisons and recommendations had to feel like natural extensions of the library rather than a separate social network.

The visual design presented a similar challenge. I did not want Joylogue to resemble another generic game database or neon gaming interface. I focused on a darker, cinematic style that gives cover artwork space to breathe and makes each library feel personal.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I am most proud that I took Joylogue from an idea to a published product on both the Apple App Store and Google Play in approximately three weeks.

The social-link feature now identifies games from major media platforms and turns a fleeting discovery into a useful library entry. The complete product loop also works: users can discover a game, save it, organize it, track their progress, complete it, rate it, and recommend it to a friend.

Joylogue has received positive feedback about both its core experience and its design. It also has active users who return consistently, which has been especially rewarding for a product built and launched by one person in such a short period.

**What we learned**

I learned that the most valuable feature is often the removal of a small moment of friction. People already discover games they want to play; they simply need a reliable way to capture that intention before it disappears.

I also learned that accuracy alone is not enough for content identification. Speed, clear feedback, graceful failure states, and polished transitions all affect whether the feature feels trustworthy.

Building the social system reinforced the importance of product focus. Every feature had to support the central question: does this make tracking and enjoying games easier? That constraint helped keep Joylogue useful without turning the library into another chore.

Finally, shipping to both stores taught me how much work exists beyond writing the app itself—from purchases and entitlement handling to store metadata, analytics, testing, and production infrastructure.

**What's next for Joylogue - Game Tracker**

My immediate priority is refining the core loop: making social-link identification faster and more accurate, improving how games move through the library, and using real feedback to remove remaining friction.

After that, I plan to expand the social experience with better recommendations, collaborative lists, and more ways for friends to discover games through each other without distracting from personal tracking.

I also want to market Joylogue heavily on the same social platforms where the problem begins. Short demonstrations of turning an unidentified gaming clip into a saved game can communicate the product’s value immediately while reaching the people most likely to need it.

</details>
