<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I wanted to build a small multiplayer game that felt like an actual game rather than another simple Unity prototype. I liked the idea of taking a very simple concept — two robots fighting to destroy each other's base — and adding enough strategy and progression to make each match feel different.

That turned into Robo Mania, a 1v1 robot arena game where players have to balance attacking, defending and managing their resources.

**What it does**

Robo Mania is a fast-paced 1v1 robot arena game.

Each player has a base to defend and a short build phase at the beginning of the match. Players can bring a loadout of build cards and place defensive/support structures before the fight starts.

Once combat begins, players move around the arena, aim and fire missiles, collect E-Cells and build enough energy to deploy a swarm of small six-legged robots called Spidys.

The game includes online multiplayer, private rooms, matchmaking, bot fallback, different robot skins, missions, XP, coins, progression, mobile controls and a build/loadout system.

For the Shipaton version, I also integrated the RevenueCat SDK so the Android build can use ad monetization and RevenueCat's ad tracking capabilities.

**How we built it**

The game was built in Unity with C#, with Photon Fusion handling multiplayer.

I also used AI heavily during development to speed up implementation, debugging and problem solving. I used it more like a programming partner than a tool that simply generated the whole game.

My workflow was usually:

build a system → test it → find what breaks → inspect the logs/code → use AI to help trace the problem → make a small fix → test again.

I used Blender to create and refine the game's 3D assets and gameplay structures, while keeping the models lightweight enough for mobile and web.

A lot of the work ended up being about connecting many small systems together: networking, movement, aiming, projectiles, structures, AI, UI, progression, saving, audio and platform-specific integrations.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest part was multiplayer.

Things that worked perfectly with one player sometimes broke as soon as a second client joined. We had issues with movement, spawning, player visibility, camera direction, state synchronization and race conditions between matchmaking and gameplay.

Another challenge was making the game work well on both desktop and mobile. Desktop needed proper movement and aiming controls, while mobile needed touch controls without changing the underlying gameplay.

Performance was another major challenge, especially with multiple structures, missiles, VFX and Spidy bots active at the same time.

There were also a lot of smaller problems that were surprisingly difficult to solve, such as UI state leaking between screens, audio triggering more than once, respawn timers appearing after a match had already ended, and keeping the game visually consistent across different assets.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The biggest accomplishment is simply taking the project from a small prototype to a complete playable multiplayer game that I could actually ship.

Robo Mania now has a working online multiplayer system, private rooms, matchmaking with bot fallback, a build/loadout system, multiple robot skins, progression, missions, mobile controls and platform integrations.

I'm also proud of the fact that the game was actually released on CrazyGames rather than staying as a project that only existed locally.

The project also pushed me to learn much more about multiplayer architecture, game optimization, 3D asset creation and building for different platforms.

**What we learned**

The biggest lesson was that getting something to compile is very different from getting it to actually work.

AI can make implementation much faster, but it still takes a lot of testing and understanding to build a real game. The best results came when I gave AI very specific problems and then verified the changes myself instead of blindly accepting large generated changes.

I also learned how important performance and UX are. A game can have a lot of features, but if the first match takes too long to start, the controls feel bad or the game stutters, players will leave before seeing most of those features.

Finally, I learned that visual consistency matters more than simply having more assets. Every model, card, UI screen and environment element needs to feel like it belongs to the same game.

**What's next for Robo Mania**

I want to keep improving Robo Mania based on real player behaviour rather than endlessly adding features.

The next focus is making matches more replayable, improving retention, balancing the build system, improving Android performance and continuing to polish the game's visuals and controls.

I also want to experiment with more build cards, more robot customization and additional gameplay strategies while keeping the core 1v1 experience simple and fast.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Most task managers answer "what should I do?" I kept needing an answer to a different question: "when will this actually be over?"

A to-do list of ten items tells you nothing about your day. It just sits there, growing. For people who struggle to start — including people with ADHD — that open-ended list is exactly the thing that makes starting impossible. You can't begin something with no visible end.

I also noticed that most productivity apps are built to push you: streaks, red overdue badges, "you failed today" summaries. The people who need the most help are the people who already feel bad about themselves. An app that scolds you gets deleted on the day you need it most.

So I built the opposite.

**What it does**

Fin asks one extra thing when you add a task: how many minutes will it take?

From that, it shows you a single number — the time your whole day will be done. Add a task, the number moves later. Finish one early, it moves earlier. That one number turns an infinite list into a day with an end.

When you start working, Fin shows only the current task, full screen, counting down. Nothing else is visible. It does not auto-advance to the next task — you decide when you're ready.

What Fin deliberately does not have:

- No streaks, no combos, no "you broke your chain"

- No red overdue warnings, no guilt screens

- No feeds, no social, no gamification

The whole design brief was one word: don't blame the user.

**How I built it**

- Next.js 15 + React 19 for the app itself, deployed on Vercel — which means it also runs as a full web app with no install required. You can try the entire thing in a browser before ever downloading anything.

- Capacitor 7 wraps the same codebase as a native iOS app.

- RevenueCat (@revenuecat/purchases-capacitor) handles Pro — monthly, yearly (with a 7-day trial) and a one-time lifetime purchase.

- Codemagic builds and ships to App Store Connect, so the whole iOS pipeline runs without owning a Mac.

- Tasks are stored locally on the device. No account, no sign-up, no server holding your tasks.

**Challenges I ran into**

Designing restraint is harder than designing features. Every instinct as a developer says "add a stat, add a chart, add a streak." Each one I added made the app feel more like every other productivity app, and more like something that would eventually make the user feel bad. Cutting them back out took longer than building them.

The screenshot problem. A "calm, spacious, low-contrast" app is exactly the app that disappears in an App Store search grid. I had to design the store screenshots almost inversely to the app: one huge number per frame, hard contrast, no explanatory text.

Shipping iOS without a Mac. Capacitor plus Codemagic made it possible, but the feedback loop on native config issues is long, and each mistake costs a full build cycle.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

The app does one thing, and the one thing works. There was a real temptation to launch with more, and not doing that was the hardest and best decision in the project.

It also runs fully in the browser, so the distance between "saw a link" and "used the app" is a single tap. No install, no account.

**What I learned**

Constraints are a feature. Deciding who this is not for made every other decision faster.

Also: the users who most need a tool like this are the ones most likely to have been let down by tools like this. Tone is not decoration — it is the product.

**What's next for Fin**

- Shipped: on the App Store since 2026-08-13; version 1.3 is live now

- Getting it into the hands of people who actually struggle to start, and rebuilding around what they say

- Android via the same Capacitor codebase

</details>

See it running: app walkthrough · engine explorer · source and technical report

**Inspiration**

I am a research master's student in Human Movement Sciences at VU Amsterdam. My specialization is the psychology of sport and performance. I am also a certified trainer, and I teach in a gym. I have built software for over a decade, some of it past 10 million downloads.

My research question, basically, is how much of effort is set by the body, and how much by what you tell yourself.

That question is why this app exists. More women are training in the gym than ever, and the apps they hand me were built around someone else. Hevy and Strong are excellent logs for people who already know what to do. Women's apps sell one trainer's program and skip the logging. Neither asks about the thing the women I train connect to most. Her month.

Women and the coaches who train them told me the same thing, again and again. Strength, energy, and mood move with her month. In a study of 6,812 exercising women, 86% reported tiredness around their period. A coach who trains women full time put it best. Gym fear fades as more women lift. The menstrual cycle does not.

The gym is also a place where you can be wrong in public. Wrong weight, wrong machine, wrong form. So the app removes the unknowns, one at a time.

I interview the coaches who train these women. And I am running a survey of women who lift, in their own words.

So I built Bloom to sell certainty. She should never wonder whether she is doing the right thing right now.

**What it does**

Bloom makes her gym plan, then walks her through it. Other apps ask her to adapt to them. Bloom adapts to her.

- A short quiz builds a six-week plan. It works around her days, goals, and experience. Pick glutes, and the plan leans into them while still training everything. The six weeks build on each other, with an easier week built in.

- It takes her month into account. Onboarding asks two questions. When her last period started, and her usual gap. That is the whole ask. It is not a period tracker, on purpose. Today shows a "Your month" card with what the research actually says.

- Starting weight calibration. "What do I even start with?" is a top beginner fear. Bloom picks a safe first weight, then adjusts it with her over the first sessions.

- Guided sessions, one exercise at a time. Weights, reps, and rest are pre-filled. Every move is shown from start to finish by a female demonstrator, with setup and form cues in plain language.

- One tap on how it felt. Very easy, Easy, Just right, Hard, Too hard. No RPE/RIR like in traditional gym trackers for men. Those scales take learning, and they are not intuitive. She knows her body best, and every answer shapes her next set and her next session.

- Life happens buttons. Machine taken? One tap swaps in a match for the same muscles. Only got 20 minutes? The session trims to what matters most. Low energy? Same session, lighter from here.

- It welcomes her back. Come back after two weeks off, and Bloom quietly eases the weights back in. No broken streak, no guilt.

- A recap to share with her coach or her friends after every workout.

**How I built it**

- The research behind it. The engine's method, model and evaluation are written up as a technical report in the open repository.

- Flutter, shipping on iOS and Android.

- A deterministic training engine in pure Dart. It builds the plan, progresses it, and adapts each session from rules I wrote as a certified trainer, and it is covered by tests.

- I build AI products for a living. I kept AI out of the coaching on purpose. Quiz answers select and shape structures I wrote. That makes the advice testable, explainable, and safe. It also works offline.

- I collect her period data, and I deliberately sit on it. Two answers, stored privately. The plan does not change by phase yet, on purpose. The evidence for phase-based training is thinner than the marketing around it. This is my field of study, so I am doing the literature review first. The app says only what the research supports, and says so when it is thin. Humble beats confident and wrong.

- Subscriptions with RevenueCat. She sees her full six-week plan first, then the paywall. $59.99 a year with a 7-day free trial, or $12.99 a month. Built with purchases_flutter, my own paywall screen, one premium entitlement, restore, and offer codes for testers and partner coaches. Purchases are tied to her private account.

- Offline first. Gyms often have no connection. So everything lives on her phone and syncs to Supabase in the background.

- Our own exercise visuals. A consistent female demonstrator, two positions per movement, across 40 exercises. I reviewed every image as a trainer, for neck position, camera angle, and range of motion, and regenerated the ones that were wrong.

- The training rules are the real work. Progression, safe defaults, and comeback rules. I wrote them, then I pressure-tested them against the coaches I interviewed.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Turning coaching intuition into rules. "Add a little next time" hides a dozen decisions. Reps or weight first. How much. What counts as evidence. What to do when she says nothing. My default everywhere. When unsure, hold.

- Honoring the menstrual cycle without turning into a period tracker or a doctor. The easy build tracks everything and promises phase-perfect workouts. I wanted the opposite. Ask the least. Claim nothing medical. Because the research is still thin, finding the middle ground between too much and too little advice about her period was hard.

- Compressing effort into one tap without losing what progression needs to know.

- Weights that exist. Every suggestion has to match the real dumbbells and plates in her gym.

- Tone is a feature. Praising her for showing up implies I expected her to fail. So the app handles the moment first, and teaches later.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- A plan generator built with working coaches, from real practice.

- A direction I validated in real life, with real women trainees and coachees.

- A clear, coherent product philosophy I developed for this project. Every feature removes an unknown or adapts to her. Nothing ships that adds doubt, judgment, or guilt. It has already killed features that initially looked good.

- The failure states are the best screens in the app. The taken machine. The short lunch break. The two-week comeback. Each one has a warm, designed path.

**What I learned**

I learned a lot by interviewing women's coaches, and even more by simply asking women who train. Friends, colleagues, other students. Here is what I learned:

- The subject women usually connect to most is not the workout. It is their body's month. So I lead with it, and build everything else around it.

- Learn her, do not lecture her. One coach put it best. Every woman is different, but not every period of the same woman is different. Her pattern is often stable and personal. A textbook four-phase curve is a starting guess, never the answer.

- Contain first, teach later. When something goes wrong mid session, the fix comes first. The lesson waits for a calm moment. Advice right after a mistake is often not truly accepted.

- In this case, deterministic beats generative. She wants the right number already filled in, not a chatty AI mid set.

**What's next for Bloom**

- Improved menstrual-aware coaching. Most women are meaningfully affected every month. The no-show days cluster on day one and day two of the period, so those absences will never break a streak or ask for a reason. A four-phase estimate is only the cold start. The real system should learn her own pattern, and let today's energy overrule the calendar. This part of the app still needs a lot more thought, research, and development, which I'm excited to do soon.

- Progress that means something. Photos, measurements, and an adherence-first progress tab.

- Co-branded coach presets. "Emma's plan, adapted to you," built with partner instructors.

- Shareable recap cards for her coach or her stories, in story format and with a coach view.

- Plans that work around her running, yoga, or classes. The quiz already asks. The engine will use it once it knows which days they fall on.

- Android, from the same codebase.

- A web quiz funnel, and marketing content that reaches the women this was built for.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Inspiration:
The starting frustration was real: people want short-form social content while their eyes or hands are busy (driving, working, commuting, gym), but Instagram/TikTok require visual attention and do not support true background scroll. Existing audio (music, podcasts, serial fiction) already occupies those windows but lacks the low-commitment, variable-reward feed mechanic that makes short-form video addictive.

The deeper inspiration, however, is incomplete. Multiple prior attempts (Pundit, Riffr, SOLVV, Shuffle, SoundByte-style products, and adjacent social-audio experiments) already chased the same “audio TikTok / micro-podcasting / voice-first social feed” framing between 2016–2025. None reached meaningful scale. The only large audio successes (Pocket FM, Kuku FM) used the opposite loop: long-form serialized narrative + cliffhangers + micro-payments. Both later added short-form video. The inspiration is therefore less “untapped need” and more “repeatedly tested form with structural headwinds that has not yet been killed or proven by this team.”

What it does:
Echoflow is conceived as a short-form audio social feed (Twitter/TikTok-style scroll) for eyes-busy moments. Core proposed loop: creators post short audio clips; users consume via smart auto-scroll (hands-free) with optional visual thumbnails or small looped videos for preference learning and discovery; pure audio mode for true background use; audio hooks at the start of clips to reduce sampling cost; and a community layer that claims stronger human connection via voice intimacy.

In practice, the product still rests on an unvalidated assumption: that the scroll-and-skip dopamine mechanic transfers to pure (or mostly) audio at low cognitive cost. Optional visuals are a partial admission that pure audio discovery is hard. The “more human connection” claim has been the explicit thesis of several prior failed or stalled audio-social apps and has not yet been shown to produce retention or network effects at scale.

How we built it:
We built Echoflow as an early prototype around the core short-form audio feed concept. The product was developed iteratively, exploring the main interaction ideas we identified during research: short audio clips, smart auto-scroll, optional visual elements, audio hooks, and a community layer.

We used the prototype and its development process to test and refine these ideas while continuously comparing them against what we learned from existing audio-social products and the broader market.

The current build should be treated as a prototype for validating the underlying product concept, rather than as a finished or fully validated product.

As the project stands, we have a deployed website with scrapped content for demo (https://app.echoflow.in). and an internal near finished android app prototype. You can see the code for the app in our repo (https://github.com/devansh1012007/EchoFlow), but it is still not available to real users.

Challenges we ran into:
The primary challenge is not technical; it is epistemic. 

- Structural discovery cost: audio lacks a cheap visual thumbnail equivalent. Users must listen before judging, raising decision cost versus video.

- Creator supply and vulnerability: raw voice is higher-stakes than filtered video; prior attempts never solved volume or quality.

- Growth and retention loops: network effects never formed in pure-audio short-form social; content libraries are copyable.

- Hybrid tension: adding optional thumbnails/loops/auto-scroll improves discovery for people who can look, but weakens the pure hands-free claim and creates a product that competes more directly with existing visual short-form.

- Moat illusion: “voice intimacy + better community” is not proprietary and is easily approachable by platforms that already own distribution and creator relationships.

- Safety/attention conflict if driving remains a flagship use case. Cognitive distraction research does not treat hands-free audio as risk-free.

These are not “execution challenges to overcome with better features.” They are pattern-level signals from the category’s history.

Accomplishments that we're proud of:
Honest inventory: secondary market research and competitive mapping of the prior attempts; recognition that the idea sits in a latent/aspirational rather than hair-on-fire category; early articulation of 4Ms/SLIP/MVS language; and willingness to iterate on x-factors (auto-scroll, optional visuals, audio hooks, community). 

What is missing, and therefore not yet an accomplishment: a cheap, dated, falsifiable test of the core mechanic; direct conversations with target users about existing eyes-busy behavior (not the pitch); a single clear flagship use case with its specific constraints; and a written kill criterion.

What we learned:

- Medium ≠ mechanic. Audio works for eyes-busy time. The short-form infinite-scroll dopamine loop has not been shown to transfer cleanly and has structural disadvantages relative to video.

- “Harder and more ambitious” is not the same as higher expected value. Choosing the form that multiple independent teams already stress-tested and failed to scale is often low-EV stubbornness, not courage.

- Starting with long-form for traction then switching to short-form is fragile: different user expectations, creator incentives, retention curves, and product identity.

- Feature creativity (smart auto-scroll, optional visuals, audio hooks, intimacy claims) is downstream of validating whether people can form fast, low-effort judgments on short audio at all. Optimizing a potentially broken base wastes time.

- Planning and feature lists feel like progress; they are not. The highest-leverage unknown remains untested.

What's next for Echoflow:
Highest-leverage next action (do this before any further feature design or “cooking in the background”):

- Run the cheapest possible mechanic test. Shared folder of 20–30 short audio clips. Half with a simple spoken audio hook + pure audio; half with optional thumbnail or 2–3s looped visual. 10–15 people from the actual target demographic. Measure decision time, subjective effort, and whether pure-audio skip/continue ever feels automatic and compulsive. Stopwatch + structured observation is enough. No app required.

- Decide in advance: if pure (or mostly) audio judgment remains high-cost or non-compulsive, either kill the scroll hypothesis or radically reframe to a different mechanic (e.g., commit/binge narrative or a narrow high-ROI vertical). Write the date and the kill criterion down.

- Parallel: 15–20 short interviews focused only on current eyes-busy behavior and workarounds—no pitching. Look for whether any sharp, unmet friction exists that music/podcasts/serial audio do not already cover.

- Explicitly choose one flagship use case and its constraints (not “all eyes-busy moments”). Design only for that context’s safety, session length, and interaction limits.

Everything else—smart auto-scroll sophistication, community features, audio-hook tooling, visual preference learning—is premature until the base sampling cost is proven low enough to support an addictive loop. Continuing to stack features on an unfalsified assumption is the path prior attempts already walked. The disciplined path is to attack the assumption first.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We cared for my grandmother, and the hardest part wasn't the caregiving itself — it was keeping track of it. Information about her lived scattered across private chats and family WhatsApp groups: did she take her medicine today? How did she feel this morning? Did she go for her walk? Every caregiver in the family had a different, incomplete picture, and things fell through the cracks constantly — not because anyone didn't care, but because there was no single place to see the full story.

We built CareRelay so no family has to reconstruct "what happened today" by scrolling up through a dozen chat threads ever again.

**What it does**

CareRelay replaces the family WhatsApp thread with a shared care app for iOS and Android:

- Today: the next task, who's on duty right now, and the most recent updates — the one screen everyone checks first.

- Timeline: every event — medication, meals, symptoms, mood, physical activity, appointments — in one shared, filterable feed.

- Plan: a shared task list (meds, calls, errands) grouped by day, so nothing is "someone else's job" by accident.

- Log: log an update by typing or recording a voice note — AI turns it into a structured event, but the family always reviews and confirms before it's published. CareRelay never diagnoses or gives clinical advice.

- Handoff: a clear summary of what happened and what's pending when care responsibility passes from one family member to another.

- Family: invite family members and caregivers with a code, assign roles, and know who's in charge at any moment.

- Profile: emergency contacts, medications, allergies, and preferences for the person being cared for, ready to hand to a new caregiver or bring to a doctor's visit.

- Family subscription: one subscription, powered by RevenueCat, covers the whole family circle.

**How we built it**

Family Care Relay is a single Compose Multiplatform codebase shared between Android and iOS:

- UI: Jetpack Compose + Material 3, one composeApp module for both platforms, with a calm, generous-typography design system — red is reserved strictly for true errors, never used to alarm caregivers over routine updates.

- Architecture: MVVM with one ViewModel per screen and Kotlin StateFlow, dependency injection via Koin (AppModule, NetworkModule, and an expect/actual PlatformModule for platform-specific bindings).

- Backend: a separate Ktor service (CareRelayBackend) backed by MongoDB, which calls OpenAI to turn a voice or text note into a structured timeline event proposal — the client never talks to OpenAI directly, keeping API keys off-device.

- Auth: Firebase Auth with Google Sign-In via KMPAuth.

- Voice-to-text: native on-device speech recognition on each platform (SpeechRecognizer on Android, SFSpeechRecognizer on iOS) behind a single expect/actual VoiceTranscriber interface, so the shared code never has to know which platform it's running on.

- Monetization: RevenueCat KMP (purchases-core + purchases-ui) powers the family subscription paywall on both platforms from one shared Kotlin implementation.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Keeping AI assistive, never authoritative. The whole point of CareRelay is trust between family members — so every AI-extracted event (medication, symptom, mood) is a proposal the family must confirm before it's published to the shared timeline. Getting that confirmation step to feel fast instead of like extra busywork took several iterations.

- One codebase, two native platforms. Voice transcription has completely different native APIs on Android and iOS. Wrapping that behind a single expect/actual interface so the shared ViewModel layer stays platform-agnostic took real Kotlin Multiplatform design work.

- Designing for a hard moment without looking clinical. Caregiving apps easily end up looking like hospital software. We deliberately built a calm color palette and warm typography so families don't feel like they're operating a medical device — because they're not diagnosing anything, just talking to each other.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A real, working cross-platform app — not a prototype — built from one shared Kotlin codebase for iOS and Android.

- An AI logging flow that's genuinely useful (a 10-second voice note becomes a structured update) while keeping a human-in-the-loop confirmation step, so the app never publishes something nobody actually said.

- A calm, non-clinical design system that makes a hard topic — caring for someone you love — feel a little less overwhelming to use every day.

**What we learned**

- How much of caregiver stress is really just information loss — not knowing what already happened, or who was supposed to do what — and how much a shared timeline alone reduces that anxiety, even before adding AI.

- Practical Kotlin Multiplatform patterns for isolating platform-specific APIs (like native speech-to-text) behind clean expect/actual interfaces without leaking platform details into the shared ViewModel/UI layer.

- That a paywall people are willing to pay for, for a family, needs to be framed around "protecting your family's peace of mind" — not "unlocking features."

**What's next**

We deliberately kept Family Care Relay's MVP focused: one person cared for at a time, no clinical claims, no doctor integrations. Next on the roadmap:

- Multiple people under care in the same account, for families juggling care for more than one relative at once.

- Doctor and caregiver collaboration features — starting with easier ways to share the Person Profile and the Relevo handoff summary with a professional caregiver or during a doctor's visit, without turning CareRelay into a clinical record.

- Publishing to Google Play alongside the App Store, since the app is already fully cross-platform.

- Growing with real families past the hackathon, and using what we learn from them to prioritize what comes next.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Live on the App Store — In Two Lights, approved 2026-08-19. 247 rooms, free, with a one-time Pro unlock through RevenueCat.

**Inspiration**

I wanted to know whether you could make a puzzle out of disagreement.

Shadow puzzles usually ask one question: turn the object until its outline matches the picture. One shadow, one answer, and the main skill is patience. Shadowmatic has done that beautifully for ten years.

So I added a second light — and with it a second shadow, which has to be true at the same time. Now the object can't just be turned until something looks right. Every rotation that fixes the left wall breaks the back wall. You have to reason your way to a pose that satisfies both, then go there.

That tension is the whole game, and the entire build was a bet on one question: is it actually interesting, or just annoying?

**What it does**

A sculpture of hinged low-poly arms hangs in the corner where two perpendicular walls meet, lit from two directions. Each wall shows a target silhouette. You drag to rotate the form and bend it at its joints. The room is solved when both cast shadows match their targets at once.

No words. No timer. No hints for the first minute.

- 247 rooms across thirteen chapters — Rotation, The Joint, Two Joints, Forms, Silhouettes, The Rod, The Wedge, The Bulb, The Angle, The Arrow, Assembly, Tangle, The Works. The opening four are hand-authored so a new player's first minutes are designed rather than sampled.

- Endless mode — rooms generated on the device, numbered from 1, running as deep as you want to go. Room 340 is the same room for everyone, so a depth is a claim you can check.

- A daily room — one puzzle a day, the same one for every player.

- Stars on precision, not speed. A timer would turn a contemplative puzzle into a twitch one.

**How I built it**

Flutter 3.44.8 / Dart 3.12.2, no game engine. The geometry is hand-rolled:

- Meshes — every piece is a triangle mesh. Lathed forms, extruded prisms and unions, built by ear clipping. (This replaced an earlier convex-hull approach, which could not represent anything concave — no ducks, no moths.)

- Projection — vertices rotate into world space and project onto two perpendicular planes. Two axis-aligned lights make wall A's shadow (z,y) and wall B's (x,y), which is what keeps the two constraints genuinely independent.

- Scoring — intersection-over-union against the target on a 64×64 occupancy raster, thresholded at 0.92.

- Latching — a solve is entered at 0.92 but only given up below 0.89. Without that gap a finger resting on the glass wanders across the threshold, the chord re-fires and the glow reverses, and the player stops trusting the silhouette they just reasoned out and starts stabilising a number.

- Determinism — endless uses a hand-written splitmix64 PRNG, not dart:math. Random's algorithm is not contractual, and rooms are generated at runtime on the player's device; an SDK upgrade could otherwise silently change everyone's room 340.

- Generation off the UI thread — a hinged room costs about a second to generate on a desktop and several times that on a phone, so endless generates in an isolate and prefetches room N+1 while you play room N.

The decision that made everything else cheap: rooms are authored as a solved pose, and the target silhouettes are derived from it. Every room is therefore solvable by construction. 94 tests, including ones that assert every sampled endless room scores 1.0 at its solution and none opens pre-solved.

RevenueCat gates a one-time unlock past the free first chapter. The entitlement check fails open — if the store can't be reached, the player keeps what they paid for. An outage should never paywall someone who already bought it.

**Challenges I ran into**

I built two difficulty metrics and both of them were wrong.

I'd convinced myself one of my hand-authored levels was under-constrained — that its two shadows agreed across too many poses, so the second light was doing no work. I had inferred that from screenshots, not from playing it.

So I built metrics to catch it: constraint correlation, and a hill-climb findability probe.

Metric
The level I called bad
The level I knew was good

Constraint correlation
0.40
0.67

Hill-climb findability
40%
35%

Both ranked it backwards. The correlation metric would have thrown out the single best level in the game.

So I shipped no difficulty filter at all. The code is still there, deliberately unused, with a comment explaining why. An unvalidated metric that discards your best work is worse than no metric, and I'd rather carry a known gap than a confident wrong number.

That gap got more expensive when I shipped endless mode, which generates from the same unvalidated bands. It is now the thing a real playtest has to settle, and I can't settle it myself: I know the generator, the solution families and the transformations, so my own solve time measures my familiarity rather than the room's difficulty.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

I wrote a kill gate before I wrote the game: three questions, a date, and a rule that "maybe" counts as no.

- Does fixing one shadow actually break the other?

- Is solving it deduction, or fiddling?

- Can you read the targets well enough to plan a move?

I passed it seven days early, on the hinge level. The answer to the second question was "deduction — I reasoned about it," which is the answer that justified continuing. "I wiggled it until it went amber" would have ended the project there.

**What I learned**

That a negative result is worth shipping. Two failed metrics told me more about my own game than a working one would have — mainly that I don't yet know what makes one of these rooms hard, and that no amount of arithmetic substitutes for handing it to a person.

I also learned to distrust a correction that comes from reasoning when the original reading came from evidence. I talked myself out of a build failure's actual cause once, and the next build proved the evidence right.

**What's next for In Two Lights**

- Five naive playtesters, screen-recorded, with the timestamp marked where they first say "oh — fixing that one breaks the other." If that moment lands later than ninety seconds, the opening is wrong and no amount of content further in compensates.

- Difficulty ordering rebuilt from what they do, not from an unvalidated number.

- Google Play. The Android track is open and the release build is signed; that store is next.

</details>

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/IxeHSYabO7Y/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IxeHSYabO7Y)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/993/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/993/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/484/032/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/484/032/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Kokage: a better 3D AI character chat app**

Kokage is an app where you talk with AI characters you can see and hear. It's available now on the App Store. What makes it better is that it has two sides. The local side runs the whole character on your own device, for free. The cloud side is optional and makes the character's performance more vivid. Together, local inference and a highly efficient cloud keep it affordable however long you use it. Every character is yours to customize and share, and it remembers you. The core libraries behind it are open source.

**Inspiration**

The project started as a game idea. We wanted to make a game whose characters were driven by AI models running on the player's own device, so they could talk and react freely instead of following a script.

While working on it, we realized that the character's performance had to come first. A character is only convincing if it can speak, move and react like someone who is really there. So we set the game aside and focused on making one AI character perform well. From there, the project naturally became a chat app: the simplest place to meet a character and talk to it.

The best AI models available today can make a character feel vivid, with its own voice, look and movement. But that only matters if people can afford to keep talking. So we combined on-device inference with an efficient cloud to keep Kokage affordable for long-term, everyday use, and added memory so the experience gets better the longer you stay with a character.

The name Kokage (木陰) is Japanese for "the shade of a tree": a quiet place you keep coming back to.

**What it does**

**Local: the whole character runs on your device**

Kokage puts a whole character on your phone: its mind, its ears, its voice and its body. After a one-time model download, you can talk to it by voice or text, and on devices with enough memory you can show it things through the camera.

Even without the cloud, the character performs. It's a 3D avatar that listens, thinks with a hand on its chin, and speaks with lip-sync and gestures.

The local side is free. It works offline and without an account, and nothing you say has to leave the device.

**Cloud: models that make the performance more vivid**

Kokage Cloud is separate and optional. It runs models that are too large for a phone: three tiers of stronger conversation models, plus ARDY motion, voice design and character model generation.

ARDY motion uses a motion-generation model called ARDY to create the character's body movement live, as it talks, so its gestures fit what it's saying.

Voice design lets you describe the voice you want, listen to a few candidates, and keep the one that fits your character. The voice can then deliver a line in different moods, from happy to whispering.

Character model generation turns a description, a picture or both into a complete 3D character model, rigged and ready to move and speak in the app.

**Every character is yours to customize and share**

You can write your own character, with its own personality and look. You can import characters in the card formats the character community already uses, and export yours in the same formats. You can also start more than one relationship with the same character, and each keeps its own history, memory and look.

**Local and cloud together keep it affordable**

Local inference carries the everyday conversation, and replies generated on your device cost nothing.

The cloud is used only where it adds something a phone can't do, and it's built to do that at low cost. We chose the models that give the best performance for their cost, and kept the cloud architecture lean and efficient. It's pay-as-you-go, with no subscription: you buy Leaves, the currency for cloud features, when you need them, and they don't expire.

**It remembers you**

For each character you talk to, Kokage keeps a long-term memory that you can read, edit and delete, and a running summary of your earlier conversations. This history is stored on your device, so the character you've come to know is still there next month.

**How we built it**

Kokage is a Flutter app for iOS and Android, and it also runs on macOS. To run a whole AI character on a phone, we wrote the core libraries ourselves and open-sourced them at github.com/projectkokage:

- fllamer runs language models on the device, using llama.cpp.

- flvtterm loads and animates VRM 3D avatars.

- fonix runs speech models through ONNX Runtime.

- misakid is a Dart port of the Misaki pronunciation engine, which the voice needs to speak English.

Kokage depends on these four libraries in the shipped app, so they're proven in real use. Any Flutter developer can use them to build on-device AI characters of their own.

Everything is sized to the device, so a phone with less memory gets a smaller model.

The cloud is a single, deliberately simple server. It sends chat to the models we chose and hands voice design, character model generation and ARDY motion to GPU workers.

Purchases go through RevenueCat. We sell Leaves as consumable packs instead of a subscription, because people who mostly chat locally shouldn't pay a monthly fee for a cloud they rarely use. The Android version is still in store review.

**Challenges**

The hardest part was fitting a whole character into a phone. A language model, speech recognition, a voice and a 3D body all compete for the same limited memory, and each had to give up a little so they could run together.

Small on-device models drift out of character and sometimes remember the wrong things. We learned to treat everything a model says as a suggestion, so the app checks it before letting it change anything.

Our first animations were hand-coded, and they looked stiff. We threw them all out and replaced them with motion clips made ahead of time by ARDY, the same model the cloud uses live.

**What we learned**

Running locally is not a compromise. Once replies don't depend on a server, privacy, offline use and free everyday conversation all follow.

Small models need good structure around them more than they need to be smarter.

The same words land very differently when they are spoken, timed to the lips and matched with a gesture than when they sit in a text bubble.

**What's next**

The character's performance comes first: more natural motion, more expressive voices, and better generated character models. We're also making the cloud features more responsive, so motion, voices and generated models arrive with less waiting. Alongside that, we're working on stability, so the app runs smoothly on more devices and through long conversations.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

FitCrate was born from a simple problem: fitness information is everywhere, but reliable, personalized guidance is difficult to find. People often have to jump between calorie trackers, workout apps, nutrition websites, and AI assistants to understand what they should actually do.

We wanted to build a single AI-powered fitness companion that could understand a user's goals, provide personalized guidance, and back health-related information with trustworthy sources. FitCrate aims to make fitness and nutrition guidance easier to understand, more accessible, and more actionable.

**What it does**

FitCrate is an AI-powered fitness and nutrition companion that helps users make better decisions about their health and daily routine.

Key features include:

- AI fitness assistant for personalized fitness and nutrition questions

- Nutrition and calorie guidance to help users understand foods, meals, and nutrition

- Workout guidance based on fitness goals and user requirements

- Evidence-based answers with web search and citations for health-related information

- Source-backed recommendations, allowing users to verify the information provided by the AI

- Conversational experience so users can ask questions naturally instead of navigating complicated menus

- Personalized guidance around goals such as weight management, fitness, nutrition, and healthier habits

**How we built it**

FitCrate was built around an AI-first architecture. We combined an AI SDK with web search and a curated set of reliable information sources to make responses more useful and verifiable.

The application uses a modern mobile-first architecture, with an AI layer responsible for understanding user questions, retrieving relevant information, and generating responses.

For health-related queries, the system can search relevant sources and provide citations alongside answers, rather than relying entirely on the model's internal knowledge.

We also designed the system so that fitness information can be presented in a simple conversational format, making complex nutritional and fitness concepts easier for everyday users to understand.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was AI reliability.

A fitness assistant cannot simply generate confident-sounding answers. Health and nutrition information needs to be accurate, contextual, and supported by reliable sources. We therefore had to work on improving how the AI retrieves information and how relevant sources are selected.

Another challenge was balancing personalization with safety. Fitness and nutrition recommendations can vary significantly depending on an individual's goals, lifestyle, and circumstances, so the AI needs to avoid treating every user the same.

We also had to solve challenges around:

- Finding relevant sources for specific questions

- Providing useful citations without overwhelming the user

- Reducing hallucinations and inconsistent AI responses

- Designing a simple conversational UX

- Making AI responses fast enough for a mobile application

- Structuring health information in a way that users can actually understand and use

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We're proud of turning FitCrate from a simple fitness concept into an AI-powered fitness companion that combines conversational AI with web-based research.

One of our biggest accomplishments is the addition of source-backed AI responses. Instead of asking users to blindly trust an AI-generated answer, FitCrate can provide references so they can explore where the information came from.

We're also proud of building an experience where users can simply ask questions in natural language rather than having to understand complicated fitness terminology or navigate multiple tools.

Most importantly, FitCrate represents our attempt to make AI genuinely useful for everyday fitness and nutrition decisions, rather than just another chatbot.

**What we learned**

Building FitCrate taught us that building an AI application is much more than connecting an LLM to an interface.

We learned that retrieval quality, source selection, prompting, context, and response validation can have a huge impact on the quality of an AI application.

We also learned that health-related AI requires a much higher standard of reliability than general-purpose chat. A response can sound convincing while still being incomplete or misleading, which makes citations and trustworthy sources extremely important.

Most importantly, we learned to treat AI as a system that needs continuous evaluation and improvement, rather than something that is automatically reliable once an LLM is integrated.

**What's next for FitCrate**

Our next goal is to make FitCrate significantly more personalized and useful as a long-term fitness companion.

We're looking at:

- Personalized fitness and nutrition plans

- Workout and activity tracking

- More advanced food and calorie analysis

- Better AI reasoning and source retrieval

- A larger curated knowledge base for fitness and nutrition

- Progress tracking and personalized insights

- Better integration with health and fitness data

- Stronger safety and validation for health-related responses

- More proactive AI coaching based on a user's progress

Ultimately, we want FitCrate to become a personal fitness companion that combines AI, reliable information, and real user progress into one experience.

</details>

## 45. FISHDEX: Fish ID by Photo

> FISHDEX uses AI-powered computer vision to identify fish species non-invasively from a simple photo, helping anglers, researchers, and conservationists track biodiversity without harming the fish.

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/fishdex-fish-id-by-photo (gallery page 15) · ❤️ 0 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [Daniel Junco](https://devpost.com/DanielAguilarJ)
- **GitHub (Try it out):** https://github.com/DanielAguilarJ/FISHDEX
- **Repo check:** public repo · ⚠️ no license detected · 107 commits · JavaScript · RevenueCat not found in manifests
- **Built with:** computer-vision, firebase, python, react-native, revenuecat, tensorflow, typescript

**Video (0:57):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ybUPmW8-Xh4

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/ybUPmW8-Xh4/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ybUPmW8-Xh4)

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Fish tagging and invasive marking methods cause stress and physical harm to fish, and they are costly and time-consuming for researchers, hatcheries, and anglers. Recent advances in non-invasive photo-identification research (using natural skin patterns, scale structures, and lateral line shapes) showed that fish individuals and species can be reliably recognized from a simple photograph. We wanted to bring that same non-invasive identification power into an accessible mobile app that anyone could use in the field.

**What it does**

FISHDEX lets users snap or upload a photo of a fish and instantly get a species identification based on its visual features, no tagging, handling, or specialized equipment required. It's designed for anglers who want to log their catches, researchers doing biodiversity surveys, and conservationists monitoring native and invasive species populations, all through a fast, non-invasive visual workflow.

**How we built it**

We combined a mobile-first app experience with an AI-powered image classification pipeline. Photos submitted by users are processed through a computer vision model trained to recognize distinguishing visual features of fish species (body shape, coloration, fin structure, and patterning). We integrated RevenueCat for subscription and monetization management, allowing us to offer premium identification and logging features while keeping the core experience accessible.

**Challenges we ran into**

Building a robust visual identification system that works across varying lighting conditions, angles, and partial occlusions in real-world field photos was the biggest technical hurdle. We also had to balance model accuracy with performance on mobile devices, and carefully design the monetization flow so it didn't get in the way of the core non-invasive identification experience.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We built a working end-to-end pipeline that takes a photo from a user's phone all the way to a species identification result, integrated with a smooth subscription experience via RevenueCat.

**What we learned**

We learned a great deal about applying computer vision techniques to biological identification problems, and about integrating in-app purchase and subscription infrastructure using RevenueCat within a mobile hackathon timeframe.

**What's next for FISHDEX**

We plan to expand our species database, improve model accuracy across more diverse aquatic environments, and add community features so users can contribute verified sightings to help track biodiversity and invasive species over time.

</details>

**Inspiration**

My own pain!!! I am a husband and father to three wonderful children, and I can't recall now the number of times I've asked or my wife have asked me "babe, when did the baby eat last time" and "how much did you give her/him?"

**What it does**

Livy - Fed on Time is a simple app that helps you log how often and how much you are feeding your formula-fed baby, reminding you 5 mins before it's time for the next bottle, it provides some helpful guidance, but the main value proposition is the simplicity and the gamification of the app, allowing people to choose a calm character to help them along the way.

**How we built it**

I built it using Flutter as my framework, and for now it's only available for iOS but for future releases can be also available on Android too, for the database, auth and cloud functions like push notifications, I am using firebase as my preferred choice, super simple to integrate with flutter and very cost effective, of course I leveraged a LOT of help from AI, in conjunction with Higgsfield for Voxel generated graphics.

**Challenges we ran into**

The main challenge for this app was when to choose a model in hope of making the build journey as cost effective as possible, with the launch of Fable it was the number 1 candidate to do the first and most labor intensive work, including the prompts to higgsfield to come up with nice graphics, but then just building the tool and the small fixes after the first version of the MVP, becomes extremely expensive to do it with the same model, so switching to something like Opus helps maintaining the quality of product while also staying within the quota of tokens.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The UI and simplicity of the app, I myself started using it of course, and both my wife and I loved it, I am specially proud of the onboarding experience, it makes it really feel personalized for something as important as feeding our children when they are in such a beautiful and busy stage.

**What we learned**

Simpler is better, this is not the only app in the space, but our differentiators are:
1- This is for formula-fed babies.
2- The app and its UI is very simplistic yet very beautiful

**What's next for Livy - Fed On Time**

On this V1 I build the core features that I was in need of, as user feedback continues to come in, I have in the pipeline to release it to android, translating it to spanish and portuguese.

**Inspiration**

Mechanical engineering is often taught through dense textbooks and static diagrams. These materials explain terminology and formulas, but they rarely show how parts interact inside a real mechanism. Bearings, gears, synchronizers, planetary transmissions, automatic gearboxes, and CVTs become much easier to understand when learners can see them move and inspect every component from any angle.

We created Machine Elements to turn this traditionally abstract subject into a visual and interactive learning experience. Our goal was to combine the clarity of an engineering textbook with the engagement of a learning game and the freedom of an interactive 3D workspace.

**What it does**

Machine Elements is an interactive mechanical-engineering course for Android and iOS.

Learners follow a structured, game-like path covering forces and moments, shafts, bearings, mechanical joints, belt and chain drives, gears, planetary systems, manual transmissions, automatic transmissions, and continuously variable transmissions.

Each lesson combines several learning formats:

- Animated engineering diagrams demonstrate motion, forces, torque, and mechanical relationships.

- Clear explanations introduce terminology, construction, operating principles, advantages, limitations, and applications.

- Interactive 3D assemblies can be rotated and zoomed using continuous touch gestures.

- Components can be selected, hidden, revealed, or separated using exploded views.

- Contextual descriptions explain the purpose of each selected component.

- Short quizzes verify understanding and preserve progress between sessions.

Advanced topics are available through Premium access powered by RevenueCat. The application supports English, Russian, Spanish, and Greek, with the system language used by default.

**How we built it**

Machine Elements is built with Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform. The shared Kotlin module contains the course structure, lesson content, navigation, progress tracking, localization, quizzes, animated diagrams, 3D scene descriptions, interaction logic, and most of the interface. Android and iOS use thin platform-specific hosts for application setup and store integration.

A major part of the project is ComposeScene3D, a 3D library that we designed and developed ourselves specifically for Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform.

Open-source library:

https://github.com/AleksandrKdev/compose-scene-3d

Instead of maintaining separate 3D implementations for Android and iOS, we built a reusable shared foundation for scene graphs, procedural geometry, cameras, materials, lighting, shadows, object selection, clipping, annotations, gestures, and Compose integration. We later published ComposeScene3D as a standalone open-source project so other Kotlin developers can build interactive 3D experiences without recreating the same cross-platform infrastructure.

The educational models are constructed using reusable procedural geometry rather than prerecorded animations. This allows learners to inspect mechanisms freely while shafts, gears, pulleys, chains, synchronizers, clutches, brakes, and CVT sheaves continue moving according to their mechanical relationships.

RevenueCat manages Premium entitlements, subscription state, and purchase restoration across both platforms. Store-specific purchase integration remains native while access state and the Premium interface are shared through Kotlin Multiplatform.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest challenge was making complex

**Challenges we ran into**

We had to keep the public demo easy to try while separating it from private production infrastructure. We also designed a clear handoff between the web marketplace experience and the mobile monetization layer without exposing credentials or unrelated project history.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We shipped a focused marketplace experience with category browsing, featured listings, search, verified seller details, exchange preparation, image-ready listing creation, and a public repository that documents the mobile RevenueCat integration.

**What we learned**

A trusted campus marketplace needs more than listings: it needs clear context, verified community signals, safe exchange preparation, and a low-friction demo path. We also learned how to isolate a public hackathon submission from a larger production codebase.

**What's next for LazosTech UniMarket**

We will continue validating the experience with Universidad del Valle students, strengthen the exchange workflow, and iterate on the mobile shell and monetization model based on real feedback.

UniMarket was built by students from Universidad del Valle as part of LazosTech.

- **Repo check:** public repo · license: MIT · 45 commits · Dart · RevenueCat found in code ✅
- **Built with:** dart, flutter, java, springboot

**Video (1:31):** https://vimeo.com/1230718898

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/413/513/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/413/513/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/413/514/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/413/514/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/413/515/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/413/515/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/413/516/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/413/516/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/413/517/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/413/517/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/413/518/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/413/518/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Students usually know what they need to study, but deciding when to study everything is much harder. Assignments, exams, multiple courses, limited free time, and missed study sessions can quickly make a manually created plan outdated.

StudyFlow was inspired by the idea of building something beyond a normal to-do list. Instead of only showing deadlines, the goal was to create a system that can understand a student's workload, availability, and preferences and turn them into realistic study sessions.

We also wanted the schedule to adapt when things do not go according to plan. Missing one session should not make the entire study plan useless.

**What it does**

StudyFlow is a mobile study-planning application that helps students organize their academic workload and automatically create practical study schedules.

Students can:

- Manage courses and academic tasks

- Set deadlines, priorities, task types, and estimated study time

- Define their weekly study availability

- Configure preferred study hours, session duration, breaks, and weekend studying

- Automatically generate conflict-aware study sessions

- Track progress using a persistent study-session timer

- Monitor completed and remaining study minutes

- Recover missed study work by finding future available time

- Upload course materials such as PDF, DOCX, PPTX, and TXT files

- Use Google Gemini to analyze course material and turn important topics into actionable study tasks

- Access premium functionality through RevenueCat

One of the main ideas behind StudyFlow is separating AI understanding from schedule generation.

Gemini helps determine what may need to be studied, while StudyFlow's deterministic scheduling engine determines when that work can realistically fit.

**How we built it**

The mobile application was built using Flutter and Dart, while the backend was developed with Java and Spring Boot.

PostgreSQL is used to store users, courses, tasks, study sessions, availability, preferences, course materials, subscriptions, and other application data.

The backend uses technologies including:

- Spring Security

- JWT authentication

- JPA / Hibernate

- REST APIs

- PostgreSQL

- PDFBox

- Apache POI

The scheduling engine was divided into separate components responsible for task prioritization, time allocation, session generation, and conflict detection.

When a student generates a schedule, StudyFlow considers factors such as:

- Task priority

- Deadline urgency

- Remaining workload

- Weekly availability

- Preferred study hours

- Maximum session duration

- Break duration

- Weekend preferences

- Existing study sessions

For AI-assisted planning, StudyFlow extracts text from uploaded course materials and sends the relevant content to Google Gemini. Gemini identifies useful study topics, and those results are converted into real StudyFlow tasks that can then participate in the normal scheduling process.

We also integrated RevenueCat to manage StudyFlow Pro and premium feature access, along with Google AdMob for advertising support for eligible free users.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was building a scheduler that does more than place tasks into random empty time slots.

The scheduler needs to respect multiple constraints at the same time. A session must fit within the student's availability, avoid conflicts with existing sessions, respect breaks and preferred hours, and still allocate useful study time before a task's deadline.

Another major challenge was handling missed study sessions. A useful study planner should be able to recover when the student falls behind. StudyFlow therefore attempts to redistribute missed work into future valid time instead of simply marking the session as failed.

Timer persistence was another challenge. A study timer should not reset just because the user leaves the screen, so session timing and progress needed to be stored through the backend instead of relying only on a local Flutter countdown.

AI integration also presented an interesting problem. We did not want Gemini to simply return text that disappears after the request. Its output needed to become meaningful application data, so StudyFlow converts AI-generated recommendations into actual course tasks.

Finally, integrating Flutter, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, authentication, AI, document processing, notifications, advertising, and RevenueCat into one connected workflow required careful handling of state and data consistency.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are especially proud that StudyFlow became more than a basic task-management application.

The core workflow connects:

Course → Task → Availability → Scheduling Engine → Study Session → Progress

StudyFlow also supports an AI-assisted workflow:

Course Material → Text Extraction → Gemini Analysis → Study Tasks → Scheduling Engine

The scheduling engine can create and persist study sessions while considering real constraints such as deadlines, workload, availability, breaks, and conflicts.

We are also proud of the persistent study timer and missed-session recovery system, because they make StudyFlow react to what actually happens during a student's day rather than assuming every original plan will be followed perfectly.

Another accomplishment was keeping AI and deterministic scheduling as separate systems. AI is used where understanding unstructured academic material is useful, while deterministic algorithms handle time constraints and scheduling rules.

**What we learned**

Building StudyFlow showed us that creating a useful scheduling application is much more complicated than displaying tasks on a calendar.

We learned how important it is to separate responsibilities across the system. AI is useful for understanding unstructured information, while deterministic algorithms are better for enforcing strict rules such as deadlines, availability, conflicts, and breaks.

We also gained practical experience with:

- Flutter and responsive mobile development

- Java and Spring Boot

- PostgreSQL and relational data modeling

- REST API design

- Authentication and authorization

- Scheduling algorithms

- Persistent timers and state

- Document processing

- Google Gemini integration

- RevenueCat subscriptions

- Google AdMob

- Notifications

- Frontend and backend testing

One of the most important lessons was that a feature is not complete simply because the code compiles. It needs to work as part of the complete user journey.

**What's next for Study Flow**

The next step is to continue improving StudyFlow into a more complete student companion.

Future improvements include:

- Longer and more flexible scheduling horizons

- More advanced study analytics

- Richer AI-assisted study features

- Improved reminders and notifications

- More flexible semester and course management

- Better Arabic and RTL support

- More complete dark-mode support

- Accessibility improvements

- Production deployment

- Testing with more students and collecting real feedback

Ultimately, the goal of StudyFlow is to help students continuously answer three important questions:

What should I study?

When should I study it?

What happens when my plan changes?

</details>

## 50. SEVER.

> One thumb.  One swipe.  No take-backs.  A committed-melee roguelite you play with a single gesture.

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/sever (gallery page 17) · ❤️ 0 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [Hristijan Petrovski](https://devpost.com/funkymuse620)
- **GitHub (description only):** https://github.com/FunkyMuse/godot-revenuecat
- **Repo check:** public repo · license: MIT · 40 commits · Makefile · RevenueCat found in code ✅
- **Other links:** https://apps.apple.com/us/app/sever-one-swipe-roguelite/id6791682247 · https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.pixezia.sever
- **Built with:** gdscript, godot, kotlin, revenuecat, swift

**Video (0:57):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fCaNBJcJMgA

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/fCaNBJcJMgA/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fCaNBJcJMgA)

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**SEVER — one swipe, no take-backs**

A one-finger committed-melee roguelite for Android and iOS. Built in Godot 4.7 / GDScript.

**What inspired it**

Mobile action games almost always resolve their control problem the same two ways: bolt a
twin-stick layout onto a touchscreen, or take the attack away from the player entirely and
auto-swing whenever something walks into range. The first is uncomfortable. The second is
a bit inflexiblel; it quietly removes the decision that makes an action game an action game.

I wanted the opposite trade: the smallest possible input carrying the largest possible
commitment.

That became the game's whole atom. In SEVER a swipe is your movement, your attack, your dodge
and your gamble: all at once, all in one gesture. You dash along the vector you drew, your
blade cuts everything on that path, and you are invulnerable only while you're travelling.
Before the dash you're winding up and exposed. After it you're rooted in recovery and can't
act. So a whiffed swing isn't a wasted button press — it's a debt you pay in the next half
second.

The visual identity fell out of the same idea: the app icon is a severed ensō, an ink brush
circle cut in two by a single tapered red slash. One draw, one cut, no second attempt. The
whole game in one mark.

Six non-negotiable pillars keep it honest. The bluntest is: no auto-attack, ever. Proximity
does not deal damage. Every fight in the game exists because a player chose to swing.

**How I built it**

7 months learning Godot, the idea for the game was from 10 years ago while I was still in high school, recently when moving places fell out of my notes and I took it as a sign.

Writing the code took roughly six-seven weeks, 185 commits, ~17,400 lines of GDScript across 114 files, currently at
v1.2.1.

The architecture follows GDQuest's modular game architecture, with dependencies pointing
strictly one way:

Layer
Holds

Add-ons
third-party plugins + my own engine-only helpers

Systems
the run loop, shared bases, 13 autoload services, and pure RefCounted rule catalogs

UI
every panel, built through a single skin-aware UiKit

Content
the concrete cast — enemies, bosses, elite modifiers

Composition root
the only file allowed to know every layer

Nothing depends on content/. The run loop spawns enemies by id through an injected
registry, so adding an enemy is a row in one binding table — the run loop never changes.
Nothing depends on ui/ at all.

I don't trust myself to hold that in my head, so I wrote tools/arch_check.py: it parses every
script for both class_name references and res:// preloads, ignores strings and comments,
prints the dependency matrix, and exits non-zero naming file:line on any violation.

Two conventions did more for stability than anything else:

- No wild string keys. Every id — loc keys, save keys, enemy archetypes, sprite keys,
sound ids, entitlement ids, product ids — comes from a const in a designated class. A
typo'd const is a compile error. A bare "chasr" is a group with no nodes that fails
silently three weeks later.

- Domain logic is node-free. Gesture timing, health, the upgrade catalogs — all pure
RefCounted. There's no formal test framework; instead I write a throwaway harness scene,
run it headless, grep for RESULT / EXPECT-FAIL, and delete it but this will change soon enough.

I am a mobile engineer and borrowed some code concepts for keeping the code tidy and clean.

Everything ships in two complete skins — a 2D "ink" look by default and an 8-bit "retro"
unlockable — which means every piece of visual content needs both an SVG and a pixel sprite,
and every telegraph must read as shape plus motion, never colour alone. That constraint is
annoying and it's also the single best accessibility decision in the project.

**The money layer, and why I forked the SDK**

Monetization is deliberately orthogonal to power. Cosmetics — skins, shield wards, robes,
per-blade camos — plus exactly one consumable: a deep-floor death revive, which has a free
rewarded-ad path alongside the paid one. The revive buys back time, never strength. Depth is
the only thing that gates progression, and depth can't be bought.

Game code never touches a storefront SDK. It calls Store.buy(id) and reads ownership.

Upstream's Godot RevenueCat plugin could not support this catalogue, so I forked it
https://github.com/FunkyMuse/godot-revenuecat and added three things:

- get_active_entitlements() → the entitlement ids. Upstream exposed only a .size count,
which tells you how many you own but not which — making ownership fundamentally
unreconcilable.

- get_purchased_products() → every purchased product id, including non-consumables carrying
no entitlement. This is the one that mattered: it let à-la-carte items resolve by
product-id instead of minting an entitlement per item, collapsing 26 entitlements down to
4.

- It now actually emits customer_info_changed. Upstream declared the signal but never
registered RevenueCat's listener — so a refund or chargeback could never reach the game. That
signal is the live revoke path.

So that a player on a plane does not get their cosmetics confiscated.

**Challenges**

The floor-20 plateau. My own playtest died at floor 27 / wave 108 and I realised the last
new enemy appeared around floor 5. Everything after that was the same roster with fatter HP
bars — which violates a pillar outright ("pressure comes from more telegraphs and tighter
timing, never bigger sponges"). The fix was to go generative: elite modifiers that recombine
enemy behaviour, and scaling pacts that trade real power for real cost.

The "Â" bug. StoreKit returns localized prices with a non-breaking space between currency
and amount. My pixel fonts have no glyph for U+00A0, and some SDK paths hand it over
double-encoded — UTF-8 bytes read as Latin-1 — so the shop cheerfully displayed USD Â 0.99.
The fix repairs the double-encoded forms first, then folds every non-breaking and thin space to
plain ASCII. A day of my life for one whitespace character.

**What I learned**

That the interesting constraint is the product. "One finger" sounded like a limitation and
turned out to be the entire design — it forced the commitment mechanic, which forced the
i-frame window, which forced telegraphs to be readable, which made the game good.

That an abstraction boundary is worth building before you need it. Putting a StoreProvider
interface between the game and RevenueCat felt like much needed on day one. It's why my headless
tests, my CI, and my desktop editor all run with zero storefront — and why forking the SDK
changed exactly one file.

And that the failure modes worth engineering for are the boring ones: the refund, the
offline launch, the cancelled purchase, the double-encoded space. Nobody demos those. They're
most of what separates a jam build from something you can put in front of a stranger.

</details>

**Inspiration**

I wanted to build a system who would help me to track my working hours, as I'm a new comer to Canada. As I've never done this before, the best idea I could come up with was to have something on my phone, so I could track my time and export it, whenever needed.

**What it does**

Basically, the app tracks hours. Pro users can run multiple parallel timers across different projects simultaneously. Each timer card on the Clock screen shows:

Project name and color
Live elapsed time (updating every second)
Break button (start/end break per timer)
Clock-out button (stops that specific timer)
"Forgot to clock out?" link — opens a time picker to set a past end time
Free users are limited to 1 active timer. Attempting to start a second timer shows an upgrade prompt.

Target alarms calculate based on total tracked hours (sum of all active + completed timers today), matching industry standards.

**How we built it**

Using windsurf IDE in React Native (Expo) with a Flask backend.

**Challenges we ran into**

Find something relevant, since my inspiration was creating something only to myself.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Creating something competitive that follows industry standards and helps people to manage their schedules.

**What we learned**

This is my first Apple app, so the whole process was learned there.

**What's next for TrackTwice**

Help people and make money using RevenueCat. :-)
