**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/060/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/060/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/350/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/350/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/355/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/355/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Casparel was inspired by a simple problem: students have access to more educational content than ever, but finding trustworthy material and knowing what to study next is still difficult. Teachers also need better ways to understand student progress without relying only on grades.

**What it does**

Casparel is an adaptive learning and education community platform. Students can create learning goals, build study paths, track progress, find and save resources, participate in classes, and continue studying with selected library materials. Teachers can monitor learning evidence, support students, approve resources, and manage classes. Casparel also includes an educational forum for sharing materials, posts, surveys, comments, and recommendations.

**How I built it**

I built Casparel as a full-stack TypeScript monorepo. The frontend uses React and a reusable component system, while the backend uses Express with PostgreSQL for persistent data. Supabase provides the hosted database, OpenAI supports resource research and content moderation, and Hostinger runs the production application. I designed role-based experiences for students, teachers, parents, and administrators.

**Challenges I ran into**

My biggest challenges involved deploying a large workspace-based application, handling native package permissions, connecting the production database, and debugging authentication errors. I also had to balance useful AI features with strict cost limits. Creating consistent permissions, translations, theme contrast, search quotas, and moderation behavior across every role required careful iteration.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

I am proud that Casparel grew beyond a basic resource finder into a working learning ecosystem. It combines adaptive goals, progress evidence, class insights, resource discovery, library-based study continuation, community uploads, moderation, and administrative controls. I also successfully deployed the complete application and made its AI features affordable enough for an MVP.

**What I learned**

I learned that education technology must be explainable, accessible, and flexible. Recommendations are more useful when learners control the resources attached to their goals. I also learned that AI should support core workflows rather than replace them, especially when reliability, privacy, and cost matter.

**What's next for Casparel**

Next, I plan to strengthen moderation, improve multilingual coverage, expand class analytics, and add richer collaboration around resources and goals. I also want to introduce verified teacher approvals, better notifications, deeper progress insights, mobile optimization, and pilot programs with real students and educators.

</details>

src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/482/319/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We don't just work together. We go out together, and somewhere along the way we always end up playing something. A card game, a silly challenge, whatever is on the table. Those nights became some of our favorite moments, and we wanted to make them even more unique.

So we built the game we wanted to play with each other, with one goal: connect people more. We wanted something digital that never loses the essence of traditional games: sitting around a table, looking at each other, laughing, arguing, and trying to convince everyone that your card goes first.

That shaped every decision. SHIFT is an app, but the screen is never the point. The talking is the game, and the phone is just the deck. Every design call came down to one question: does this help the table talk, or does it compete with it? No chat, no voice, no countdown timers, no remote play. Just people, in a room, together.

**What it does**

SHIFT ("Line it Up") is a cooperative party game for 3 to 8 people in the same room. It is live on the App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/shift-line-it-up/id6810001678

At the center of SHIFT are the Shifters: a cast of little creatures that represent each player around the table. Instead of flipping cards like in a physical game, your Shifter carries your secret and brings it to life throughout the round. Each one gives players their own presence at the table and helps give SHIFT its playful personality.

Here’s how a Classic round works:

A theme sets a scale between two extremes, like “spiciness of food: from plain white rice to pure Carolina Reaper.”

Each player’s Shifter receives a secret number from 1 to 100. Only you can peek at it by pressing and holding your Shifter.

You write an example that you think belongs at that point on the scale. Then the secrets disappear and the conversation begins.

Together, the group tries to line up everyone’s Shifters in the right order. Only the Host can move them, but everyone has to agree before the lineup is locked in.

Then comes the reveal: the Shifters show their numbers one by one, turning the lineup into either a tiny moment of collective genius… or complete chaos.

SHIFT has three game modes built around that same idea of reading the room. Classic challenges the group to build the right lineup, with an optional bonus for guessing another player’s exact number. Impostor secretly gives one player a different theme, and the group has to figure out who doesn't belong. In Zone Out, exact numbers disappear and players receive secret zones instead. Zones can repeat, making the conversation much less predictable.

The whole game is available in English and Portuguese.

**How we built it**

We are four friends. Rafaela designed the game, and Bernardo, Fernanda and Vicenzo built it as a native iPhone app.

The first big decision was to have no server at all. The phones in the room talk directly to each other, and the Host's phone acts as the referee: it deals the secrets, runs the reveal and keeps the result, and each player only ever receives their own secret. That is the right trade for a game played among friends. RevenueCat handles all purchases, and it is the only outside service we use.

**Monetization: who invites, pays**

Premium access belongs to the Host and applies to the whole table. If the Host owns a mode, everyone in the room plays it, so a guest never sees a paywall during a match. A free room holds 6 players, and a one-time upgrade reaches 8, offered only at the moment someone gets left out. Locked content is shown with a lock instead of hidden, and skins are cosmetic only. Each card on the table wears its owner's skin, so a purchase is something the whole table sees.

**Playtesting**

While we were building, we played with about 10 friends. Watching real people play changed how a match works: what information each person sees and when, and the rules behind the table.

**Challenges we ran into**

- A dropped connection is not someone leaving. A phone locking, going into a pocket or stepping out of range looks like "player left" to the system, and we were ending matches after two-second blips. Now the game waits 20 seconds and tells the table whose seat it is holding.

- Dragging a card fought with scrolling. The tower of cards is a scrolling screen, and a normal drag always lost to the scroll. We borrowed the iPhone Home Screen trick: press and hold briefly, and the card lifts and wobbles into your finger.

- A rule applied one step too wide. We decided that music plays only on the Host's phone, so eight phones never play the same song out of sync. It also silenced the menu completely, where nobody is the Host. The rule only belongs to the table.

- A wrong diagnosis. We thought all eight mascots had mismatched colors and were about to redraw every face. Measuring them properly showed seven of eight were fine. The real bug was a mislabeled file.

- 12 players became 8. The wireless technology we use caps a room at 8 devices. We cut the number instead of faking it.

**What we learned**

- A constraint is a design tool. "In person" removed chat, voice, timers and servers, and gave us the product.

- Measure before you fix. Our worst bug was a wrong diagnosis, not wrong code.

- Playing with real people finds what plans can't: eight phones playing music, a screen that locks mid-match.

**What's next**

Larger rooms and remote play, and more playtests to keep tuning Impostor mode.

</details>

src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/469/595/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

- Kana is the first step a Japanese learner needs: the reading and writing system. Unlike the English alphabet, there are 208 characters to memorise before you can start reading. Daunting as that sounds, a casual learner should be able to finish it in about two weeks, and that unlocks a lot of the menus and everyday signs a traveller runs into in Japan.

- That beginner is the largest group of people who want to start learning Japanese, so we wanted every feature in the app to be free, with ads as our main source of revenue.

**What we built**

- A sequential learning experience. The loop is simple: show new characters and their sounds, then quiz the learner in several different patterns so the memory sticks.

- We scale the frequency and difficulty of those quizzes to how the learner is performing, for example by growing or shrinking the answer grid.

- Free with ads; one purchase (RevenueCat) turns them off. Yearly $15.99, lifetime $24.99, no monthly — on an app you finish, lifetime is the honest offer.

- We wanted a learning companion in the app, so we built a React Native tool for creating these characters and their in-app reactions. Once it is polished we plan to open source it.

**The feel we wanted**

We wanted a hand-drawn, illustrated feel, with a friendly interactive avatar. The home screen carries an illustrated animation in the spirit of the YouTube study-video trend. The app should feel cosy, and put the learner in the mood to study.

**The companion**

- Built with @sovl/procedural-avatar, written for this and to be released MIT: https://github.com/jamesrjohnston/procedural-avatar (pending polish before we release)

- Procedural, reactive characters for React Native. A character is data, its state is data — ten lines of JSON, eight primitive shapes, a roundness dial. No native code, one peer dep (react-native-svg), Expo Go compatible.

- JSON-first means LLM-drivable: a model can author a character or drive its mood. spec/CHARACTER-DESIGN.md records building nine and scoring them.

- Five moods, no more. Five companions: one from the start, one at a milestone, three bought with points earned by studying. Each is an identity plus a colour pair, so swapping the placeholder for the real thing changed no screen.

**Audio**

- 208 sounds × two voices, generated with ElevenLabs eleven_multilingual_v2, then reviewed.

- One clip per sound, not per glyph — あ and ア are the same syllable, and two recordings would teach that the scripts sound different. 416 clips → 208, 1.7 MB.

- A small harness flags clips by duration and by ear; flagged ones are re-recorded by hand. Lesson: type the glyph, never the romaji — the model reads Latin letters as letter names.

- A missing clip silently turns a listening question into a recognition one. The lesson never breaks.

**How we built it**

- Expo 57, RevenueCat and AdMob. iOS and Android from one codebase, although a DUNS problem meant the Android and Galaxy versions did not make it out in time.

- New tools in the AI space, ElevenLabs and Claude Code in particular, are what made this possible in the time we had.

**Challenges**

- DUNS. Getting the business registered with the right details turned into a back and forth, and the Android version missed the deadline because of it.

- Scope. We wanted more: a path map, matching questions, more companions. We cut screens, not progression, to ship. We also wanted an audio back and forth that drills the learner by anticipation, which is the ideal exercise for an app like this. We could not get it to that level in time, but the groundwork for it is in place.

**What's next**

- Path map, more companions buyable with points, matching questions.

- Open @sovl/procedural-avatar properly — docs, examples, the LLM authoring flow.

- Not kanji. Reading real words with the kana you have.

</details>

**Inspiration**

Students today have access to countless learning materials but these resources are often scattered across PDF, lecture recordings, screenshots and personal notes. This creates a fragmented learning experience where students spend more time organising information than actually understanding it.

We created StudyNova to transform traditional studying into an intelligent and personalised learning experience by combining AI assistance with thoughtful mobile design. 

Our goal was to build a learning companion that does not replace students' learning process but enhances it by helping them understand, revise and interact with their study materials more effectively.

**What it does**

StudyNova is an AI-powered learning companion designed to help students learn smarter and more efficiently.

Students can:

- Upload PDF and learning materials

- Generate AI-powered summaries

- Automatically create flashcards for revision

- Ask questions through AI TalkBack, an interactive AI learning assistant

- Record lectures and transform them into useful study resources

- Track learning progress through Study Canvas

StudyNova focuses on creating a personalised learning experience through:

- English and Bahasa Melayu language support

- Light and dark theme customisation

- A clean and student-friendly interface

Instead of using separate tools for notes, summaries, revision and learning assistance, StudyNova brings these experiences together into one integrated learning platform.

**How we built it**

We focused on combining AI functionality with user-centred design principles. The app experience follows a simple learning journey:

Learn &gt; Understand &gt; Practice &gt; Review

We designed each feature around how students naturally study:

- Learn: Upload learning materials and record lectures

- Understand: Use AI summaries and AI TalkBack to clarify concepts

- Practice: Generate flashcards for active revision

- Review: Monitor progress through Study Canvas

The application was built with:

- AI-powered document understanding

- AI conversational learning assistance

- Lecture recording workflow

- Automatic flashcard generation

- Learning progress tracking

- Customisable themes and language settings

Beyond technical implementation, we focused on creating a polished mobile experience through intuitive navigation, clear information hierarchy and personalised interactions. Our design goal was to make AI feel approachable, simple and useful for everyday students rather than overwhelming.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was balancing powerful AI features with a simple and intuitive interface. Many AI applications can feel complicated or overwhelming, especially for students who only need quick assistance during studying. We focused on reducing unnecessary complexity and creating a natural interaction flow.

Another challenge was designing an environment suitable for long study sessions. Since students spend many hours using learning applications, we considered visual comfort and personal preferences by introducing theme customisation, language options and a clean navigation structure.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud of creating more than just another AI chatbot.

StudyNova combines multiple learning experiences into one complete ecosystem:

- Intelligent study material processing

- Interactive AI tutoring

- Automated revision material generation

- Personalised study management

- Thoughtful interface design with personalised themes, language options, and intuitive user interactions

We are especially proud of creating a learning experience that adapts to different students through flexible study tools and accessibility features. The project represents our vision of how AI can become a supportive learning partner rather than just another technology feature.

**What we learned**

Building StudyNova taught us that creating a successful AI product requires more than advanced technology.

A meaningful AI experience depends on:

- Understanding real user problems

- Designing simple and intuitive interactions

- Prioritising accessibility

- Creating meaningful experiences through thoughtful design

We learned that great products are created when technology and user experience work together.

**What's next for test**

Future improvements include:

- AI-generated quizzes

- Personalised learning recommendations

- Advanced learning analytics

- More AI tutor personalities

- Cloud synchronisation across devices

- Adaptive learning paths based on student progress

Our vision is to continue evolving StudyNova into a complete AI-powered learning ecosystem that helps students study more effectively, wherever they are.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Traditional Gregorian calendars are mathematically chaotic: months fluctuate between 28 and 31 days, and weekdays shift randomly every month. This creates friction for consistent habit formation, quarterly retrospectives, and predictable time-blocking. 

We engineered Calender28 (Matrix 28) around a fixed 28-day cyclical system (13 equal months of exactly 4 clean weeks). We paired this predictable time architecture with an automated Eisenhower prioritization engine, connected Markdown knowledge graphs, and local-first data persistence.

**What It Does**

- 28-Day Cyclical Calendar: Standardizes time into 13 equal months of 28 days, ensuring every month starts on Sunday and ends on Saturday.

- Automated Eisenhower Conflict Resolver: Organizes scheduled items into four urgency/importance quadrants. The scheduling engine detects overlapping blocks in real time and automatically calculates free buffer slots.

- Bi-directional Knowledge Graph: Personal notes written in standard Markdown with [[wiki-links]] rendered dynamically on an interactive force-directed canvas.

- 28-Day Habit Cycles & Sparky Companion: A digital companion that tracks habit completion, evaluates daily focus sessions, and evolves through 28-day cycles.

- Dual Monetization (RevenueCat & AdMob): Seamless monthly and annual Pro subscription tiers powered by the RevenueCat SDK, alongside an in-app CalCoin economy earned through two-step rewarded ad combos.

- Android Glance Widgets: Interactive home screen surfaces providing live cycle countdowns and real-time task agendas.

**How We Built It**

Calender28 is built 100% natively for Android:

- UI & Architecture: Jetpack Compose, Material 3, Clean Architecture (MVVM/MVI), Kotlin Coroutines, and reactive StateFlow.

- Database & Persistence: Room SQLite for local-first, zero-latency offline storage.

- Subscription Infrastructure: Integrated the RevenueCat Android SDK (Purchases) and RevenueCat Customer Center to handle Monthly and Yearly Pro subscription tiers, client-side entitlement state, and offline receipt validation.

- Ad Monetization: Google Mobile Ads SDK for rewarded video combos and interstitial placements.

- Widgets: Jetpack Glance for reactive home-screen surfaces.

**How RevenueCat Is Integrated**

Calender28 uses the RevenueCat Android SDK to gate advanced power-user workflows:

- Entitlement Management: Gating features such as raw Markdown (.md) note export and full ICS calendar sync behind active Pro subscriptions.

- Customer Center: Instant subscription restoration, plan management, and live entitlement state reflection directly inside the app settings.

- Zero Backend Overhead: Handled entirely client-side with RevenueCat's cached entitlement verification, keeping the app fast and local-first.

**Challenges We Ran Into**

- Building a deterministic conversion engine between standard Gregorian dates and the fixed 13-month, 28-day cyclical system without breaking standard .ics calendar imports.

- Implementing a physics-based, interactive force-directed graph canvas in pure Jetpack Compose that maintains 60 FPS while handling node collisions and drag gestures.

- Coordinating client-side entitlement state between RevenueCat subscription purchases and local in-app CalCoin economy rewards.

**Accomplishments That We're Proud Of**

- Shipping a fully functional, offline-first productivity suite with zero external backend dependencies.

- Creating a dynamic bi-directional graph visualization entirely within Jetpack Compose.

- Implementing full RevenueCat purchase, restore, and entitlement verification flows on Android.

**What's Next for Calender28**

- Bi-directional CalDAV synchronization to connect with self-hosted cloud calendars.

- Encrypted peer-to-peer note synchronization across devices.

- Advanced habit analytics and custom graph filtering queries.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Life Replay**

Life Replay is an AI-first collaborative video editor that turns everyone's photos and videos from an event into one finished story.

Instead of memories being scattered across everyone's camera rolls, Life Replay brings them together, uses AI to find and shape the best moments, and lets people relive the event through a finished, editable film.

**Inspiration**

Not every event can afford a videographer.

Whether it's a birthday, graduation, family trip, wedding, or even a small get-together, people are already capturing the moment on their phones. The footage exists, but it is scattered across everyone's camera rolls.

After the event, nobody wants to spend hours asking everyone to send their photos and videos, downloading hundreds of files, finding the best moments, removing duplicates, and then sitting down to edit everything.

The frustrating part is that some of the best memories of your own event are often sitting on someone else's phone.

We wanted to make that entire process happen automatically.

Life Replay was built around a simple idea: everyone captures the memory, and Life Replay brings those memories together into a story.

**What it does**

You create an event on the app and get a simple invite code that you can share with everyone who was there.

Guests can join the event and upload the photos and videos they captured. There is no complicated setup and no need to chase people for their footage afterward.

Life Replay then brings everything together and uses AI to understand the content, identify the important moments, find the best shots, and avoid unnecessary duplicates.

You can choose the kind of story you want, whether that's Highlights, Celebration, Cinematic, or Family Story, and Life Replay creates a finished film around those moments.

The soundtrack is also created specifically for the event, so the film feels personal rather than like a generic slideshow.

You can also select a smaller group of memories, such as just the ceremony or just the party, and create a separate film from them.

And if the AI doesn't make it exactly the way you imagined, you can open the film in the editor and change it yourself.

The goal is not to replace your memories with AI. It's to make sure the memories you already captured actually become something you can relive.

**How we built it**

We built Life Replay as a mobile experience focused on making the process as simple as possible for the people attending an event.

The app handles collecting memories from multiple people, while AI helps understand and organize all the different photos and videos into a coherent story.

We designed the experience so that the complicated work happens behind the scenes. People shouldn't have to understand how their memories are processed. They should simply be able to contribute, wait for their film, and enjoy the result.

Privacy was also a core part of how we designed Life Replay. We don't want to become another permanent storage service for people's personal memories. Media is handled securely for the purpose of creating the replay, with access restricted to the people who are part of that event. We also designed the experience so that users don't have to hand over their entire personal camera roll just to use the product.

We also wanted to keep the creative side in the user's hands. The AI creates the initial edit, but the result can still be opened and changed manually.

That was an important part of the product for us: AI should help tell the story, not decide what the story means to you.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was handling the sheer amount of content that can come from a single event.

A normal event can easily generate hundreds or even thousands of photos and videos, often from different phones, different angles, and different moments. We had to figure out how to turn all of that into something meaningful without making the user do the work themselves.

We also ran into a lot of challenges around making the experience reliable outside of a local development environment. Large uploads, processing videos, creating films in the background, and making sure people could access events they were invited to all introduced problems we didn't initially expect.

The editing experience was another challenge. We didn't want the product to simply generate a video and say "here you go." We wanted people to be able to actually interact with the edit and make it feel like their own.

A lot of the hackathon was spent solving these small but important problems that are easy to overlook when you're only thinking about the main idea.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We're proud that Life Replay is more than just an AI video editor.

The most important part for us is that it starts with a real problem: the best footage from an event is often spread across many people's phones, and nobody has the time to turn it into a finished memory.

We built a complete experience around solving that problem.

We're especially proud of the fact that the AI-edited film is editable. Instead of treating AI's output as final, we let people open the edit, change it, and make their own decisions.

We're also proud that the experience works across a group. One person doesn't have to be responsible for capturing everything. Everyone can contribute what they saw, and Life Replay brings those different perspectives together.

Most importantly, we went from an idea to a working, deployed product during the hackathon.

**What we learned**

We learned that the hardest part of building an AI product isn't necessarily getting the AI to work. It's figuring out how to use it in a way that genuinely removes work for the user.

We also learned that people still want control even when AI is doing most of the work. A fully automated result can be impressive, but giving someone the ability to change that result makes it feel personal.

Another big lesson was how different a real product is from a prototype. Uploads fail, processing takes time, permissions behave differently, and small issues in the user experience can completely change how a product feels.

Most importantly, we learned that the value of Life Replay isn't really the video.

It's the fact that a moment that would have otherwise stayed scattered across everyone's phones can become something the people who were actually there can sit down and relive together.

**What's next for Life Replay**

We want to make Life Replay faster, more reliable, and capable of handling much larger events.

We also want to improve the creative side of the product, giving people more ways to guide the story while still keeping the process almost effortless.

Beyond individual events, we see a much bigger possibility for Life Replay.

Today, it's about turning the photos and videos from one event into a film. Eventually, we want Life Replay to help people turn years of scattered memories into stories they can actually revisit.

Because taking the photos is already easy.

We want remembering them to be just as easy.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/382/504/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/382/504/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/382/506/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/382/506/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**What it does**

The Forgetting Stage is an AI improv game where three actors share a memory capped at 1,000 model tokens. You choose the premise, direct the performance and save one actor line. As new dialogue arrives, older unpinned facts disappear.

When a seeded fact is erased, the next two actors answer the same question. Each has to invent a confident replacement. At curtain, the report puts the lost fact beside both answers and the one line you protected.

**Why I built it**

I wanted forgetting to be something the player could see and influence. The project grew from my Thousand-Token Theater experiment into a small theatre with a cast, a daily ticket and a visible record of what went wrong.

The hardest part was making the forgetting real. An early version relied on approximate word counts and client-supplied context. I moved the live performance state to the server, used the serving model's tokenizer and added tests for eviction, pinned lines and contradictory answers.

**How it works**

The Expo and React Native app sends actions such as start, advance, pin, direct and finish. The server owns the live transcript and builds each prompt after evicting old memory. One pinned actor line sits outside the 1,000-token allowance.

The live generation path uses Hugging Face. If generation is unavailable, the app labels its deterministic fallback as offline and labels its memory count as estimated. An offline rehearsal also lets players learn the mechanics without spending their daily AI ticket.

The current source includes editable character names, backstories and speaking styles, animated paper-puppet actors, director cues and a curtain report. Cast edits are saved locally and apply to later performances.

**RevenueCat**

RevenueCat powers the native box office: a consumable encore ticket and a Director's Pass entitlement for unlimited performances. One AI performance is free each local day, and purchase offers stay outside an active scene.

On September 25, a real cloud Pixel 7 Pro running Android 13 displayed RevenueCat's Test Store purchase dialog. A simulated monthly purchase activated Director's Pass and unlocked unlimited performances. Earlier Android testing also observed a simulated encore purchase. These are sandbox transactions, not revenue. Restore handling exists and has automated tests, but a successful physical-device reinstall-and-restore flow is not claimed.

**What is verified**

On September 25, the submission source passed 133 automated tests, TypeScript checking and an Expo web export after a clean dependency install. A secret scan found no leaks in the Git history or updated source.

That day's native cloud tests opened the cast editor, pinned Meera's line and completed an offline rehearsal on Pixel devices. The curtain report showed 18 forgotten beats and one protected line. The demo combines edited native recordings with labeled still captures. Its gameplay uses a prepared offline script; live Hugging Face generation is not running in that recording.

Earlier Android emulator testing observed live Hugging Face narrator and actor responses, a pinned line and the authoritative model-token meter. The attached August 21 native screenshot records that earlier build; it is not a new physical-phone capture.

OneSignal and Layers adapters are present in the code. A delivered OneSignal campaign and an observed Layers dashboard experiment are not verified, so I am not claiming those sponsor categories.

**How I built it**

I am the sole participant. Codex helped with implementation, debugging and verification. Junie CLI contributed to earlier cast, access-guard and Android-scaffolding work.

**Source and testing**

This is a Next Gen entry with public MIT-licensed source instead of an app-store listing.

Submission branch: https://github.com/himanshu748/forgetting-stage/tree/codex/nextgen-submission-20260925

Run npm ci, npm test and npm run typecheck from that branch. npm run web provides a browser preview. The Android app needs a custom native build for RevenueCat; live AI also needs a configured generation gateway and server-side model credentials. Without them, use the explicitly labeled offline rehearsal.

The server currently keeps performance sessions in process memory. A scaled deployment needs durable shared state and quotas. No production store release, paid-user traction or successful physical-device restore is claimed.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Memory loses its sound first. Afterfade turns it into music.

**Inspiration**

I can tell you what last Tuesday looked like — there is a photo. I cannot tell you what it sounded like. Photos survive. Sound doesn't.

I wanted a journal that asked for five seconds and nothing else, and gave back something I would want to keep. Not a list of entries. A music video of the week.

**What it does**

Point your camera for five seconds. Do it seven times. The app collects colors and ambient sound from each clip, composes a lo-fi track on the device, and cuts your footage to the beat. An ordinary week becomes a music video. You can add a filter and a one-line caption before you export.

No account. Nothing you record leaves your phone.

**The design decisions**

- You don't have to write. The only input is pointing the camera. A one-line caption is there if you want it, but the app works without it.

- Throw most of it away. The app keeps about one second out of five, chosen at random. The song arrives after you have forgotten.

- No streak. No daily quota, no reminder. Fill a cassette in an afternoon or over a month.

- The AI does not compose. No generative images, no AI music. Every sound in the track was recorded by you.

**How I built it**

Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform, one codebase for iOS and Android. This was my first app on either platform. Android took six days of evenings and weekends, iOS took two.

**Challenges I ran into**

Music generation started as Python on AWS. It cost money per track, did nothing offline, and sent people's recordings to my server. None of that fit an app whose promise is that your day stays with you. So I rewrote the engine in Kotlin on the device, shared by both platforms. A track went from a minute to ten seconds, the bill went to zero, and I deleted the server on day six.

No ad budget, so every download came from SNS alone. I posted the actual music videos the app produces and a hand-drawn comic series on TikTok. Together they brought over 2,000 downloads.

**Accomplishments I'm proud of**

- One person, concept to code to two app stores to marketing, in two months alongside a full-time job. Concept, illustration, UI, audio engine, and the TikTok comics are all mine.

- The first comic episode on TikTok brought 66K views. Over 2,000 downloads with zero ad spend.

- People say some version of "a day with nothing in it turned emotional." One user wrote that a lonely, slightly scary night became "a stylish memory, as music."

- The audio engine is now an open-source library other KMP developers can use.

**What I learned**

The phone is the server. When the input is already on the device and the work is pure computation, there is no reason to send it anywhere. Faster, free, and private.

Building is the easy half. Getting people to install the app, and to come back, turned out to be harder than making it.

A worked-out concept made the decisions for me. You don't have to write, throw most of it away, no streak, the AI does not compose. Every later question — where the ad goes, whether videos get a watermark — had an answer waiting.

**What's next**

- More cassettes. Lo-fi and Dreamcore are out, and each new tape unlocks as you finish the ones before it. More genres are next.

- Growing the DSP library. The engine is open-sourced and I want to add more building blocks other KMP developers can use.

Engineering devlog: What It Took to Ship One Kotlin App to Both Stores

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Regaly started from a simple problem. Remembering birthdays is easy enough, but finding a gift that actually feels personal is much harder. Too often, gift shopping becomes a last minute search through generic lists that have little to do with the person you are buying for.

I wanted to build something that makes gift giving feel more thoughtful and less stressful. Regaly helps people remember the important moments in the lives of the people they care about and gives them personalized gift ideas based on who that person actually is.

**What I built**

Regaly is a personal gift giving assistant for iPhone and iPad.

Users add the people they care about, their important occasions, interests, preferences, and other useful context. When they need a gift, Regaly uses that information to generate personalized suggestions together with a short explanation of why each idea could be a good fit.

The goal is not just to suggest products. It is to help users feel like they really know what to give.

**How I built it**

Regaly is built natively for iOS using SwiftUI and SwiftData.

User data is stored locally and synchronized across a user's Apple devices through iCloud. The AI gift recommendation flow is powered by a custom backend hosted on Vercel, which receives the relevant context about a person and generates tailored gift suggestions.

Subscriptions are managed through RevenueCat, including purchases, entitlements, and receipt validation.

I designed and built the entire product end to end, including the user experience, visual identity, application architecture, backend integration, subscription system, and App Store submission process.

**What I learned**

Building Regaly taught me how different it is to create a complete consumer product rather than just a technical prototype.

A feature can work perfectly from an engineering perspective and still need significant refinement before it feels simple and intuitive to a user. I learned a lot about reducing friction in onboarding, deciding how much information to ask for, designing AI interactions that feel useful instead of generic, and keeping the overall experience focused.

I also learned much more about the operational side of shipping an iOS application, including App Store Connect, subscription configuration, RevenueCat, App Review requirements, iCloud synchronization, and the many small details required to turn an idea into something people can actually download and use.

**Challenges**

One of the biggest challenges was finding the right balance between personalization and simplicity.

The more Regaly knows about someone, the better its recommendations can become, but asking users for too much information creates friction. Designing a flow that captures meaningful context without feeling like a questionnaire required a lot of iteration.

Another challenge was making AI generated recommendations feel genuinely personal. I did not want Regaly to produce another generic collection of gift ideas. The recommendations needed to clearly connect back to the person, which is why every suggestion includes the reasoning behind it.

Shipping the product also came with practical challenges around subscriptions and App Store review. Integrating purchases through RevenueCat, configuring the subscription products correctly, and navigating Apple's submission requirements were all important parts of getting Regaly ready for release.

Ultimately, the project became much more than an AI gift generator. It became an exercise in designing a complete product around a very human problem: remembering what matters and making the people you care about feel genuinely known.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/362/096/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/362/096/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/361/933/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/361/933/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/361/938/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/361/938/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/361/941/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/361/941/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/361/943/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/361/943/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

If you play games, you own games you haven't played. A Steam library full of sale
purchases, a subscription catalogue you opened twice, two things a friend
insisted on, and a low-grade guilt attached to the whole pile. You know roughly
how big it is. You couldn't name what's in it.

The moment I actually built for is narrower than that. A game goes past in a
video at eleven at night, you think "that one", and by morning it's gone.

The Shipaton supplied the part I can't write for myself. I entered the Influencer
Award for Gaming, and the category description turned out to be a better
requirements document than any I've written for my own side projects: save games
at the moment of discovery, judged on how well people can organize, complete,
rate and share them, and on whether managing a backlog feels enjoyable rather
than like another chore.

Not because those two sentences are insightful. Because they're fixed. Side
projects don't die of bad code, they die of being redefined every week, and a
brief you didn't write and can't edit removes that failure mode. When I couldn't
pick between two data models I stopped deliberating about taste and re-read two
sentences.

**What it does**

Barklog tracks your gaming backlog on iOS, with a dog keeping score.

Four statuses: waiting, playing, completed, abandoned. Most trackers assume
you'll finish everything. Barklog doesn't, so abandoned is one tap away and it
counts as an answer rather than a failure.

Share a clip into it and you get the game. A YouTube link, a TikTok, a Vimeo
upload, an IGN review: Barklog reads the page's title and author, works out which
game the video is about, and hands you the candidates to pick from. That's the
eleven-at-night case, and it's the feature I'd demo first.

The rest is what you'd expect. IGDB's whole catalogue to explore and search,
covers and platforms and summaries and similar games, a rating on the ones you
finish. It's free for ten unfinished games, and finishing one gives the spot
back. Premium takes the cap off, which is the whole difference.

**How we built it**

A Turborepo monorepo, TypeScript throughout: an Expo SDK 57 app, a Hono API,
Postgres, a worker that wakes up once a night, and Valkey next to the API. Four
things it doesn't own: IGDB for game data, Clerk for identity, RevenueCat for
purchases, OpenAI for turning a shared link into a guess.

Almost every interesting decision was about which of those four a user waits for.
The answer is none of them, except the one that can't be mirrored.

A nightly worker copies IGDB's entire games table into Postgres. 374,000 rows,
about 748 requests, a few minutes once a night, and the API only ever reads from
that copy. Their rate limit isn't mine and their 2 a.m. outage isn't mine either.
The part I'd steal for other projects is how the boundary is enforced: @repo/igdb
is in the worker's dependencies and not the API's, so the design can't quietly
regress into a live proxy under deadline pressure. Conventions rot. Manifests
don't.

The sync worker has no error recovery path, which is the design rather than an
omission. A failed run writes no watermark, so the next run re-fetches the same
range, and every write is an upsert or a scoped replace, which makes replaying a
page free. There's no repair path to write because there's no partial state to
repair.

Search runs on Postgres trigram matching, on word_similarity rather than
similarity. Plain similarity compares whole strings, so zeld scores near zero
against The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for reasons that have nothing to do
with relevance. Ranking is 60% relevance and 40% clamped popularity, and that
second term is what stops mario returning an obscure ROM hack above Super Mario
Odyssey.

The share pipeline is where all the work is recovery. The URL gets canonicalised
first, with YouTube and TikTok rebuilt from their native ids, and its SHA-1 is the
cache key for everything downstream. Then a ladder: an igdb.com link resolves
straight to a row in the mirror, 332 vendored oEmbed endpoints answer for the
sites that have them, and anything else gets fetched and parsed for og:title. The
rungs fail differently on purpose. A 401, 403 or 404 from oEmbed is terminal,
because falling through to scrape a removed video reports "Video unavailable" as
a title and then goes hunting for a game by that name.

Then two passes against OpenAI's Responses API on gpt-5.4-mini. Pass one sees the
title, author and site at reasoning effort none. Only if it gives up does pass two
run with web search, at roughly eighty times the price. Each pass reports which
tier of evidence it used, and the two don't share an enum, so pass one can't claim
a web-search basis. The provenance is enforced by the decoder rather than by the
wording of a prompt, and that's the only reason I trust the label enough to print
it. The screen says "Matches for the title" or "Games this channel usually
covers", whichever the model earned.

The free tier is one function. slotDelta asks whether a status change consumes a
slot, gives one back, or does neither, and it lives in a package the API and the
app both already depend on so the client's optimistic check can't drift from the
server's enforcement. Enforcement is a single transaction that opens with a
SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the user's own row, counts only when the delta is
positive, and answers 402 carrying the count and the limit.

RevenueCat is the one third party that can't be mirrored, because a purchase is a
fact about money that just changed. It arrives twice, as a signed webhook and as a
REST refresh the app can ask for, and both end at the same upsert. Every write
carries its own timestamp and the upsert refuses to apply behind a value already
in the row, so the race between them is settled by Postgres instead of by a branch
somebody has to remember to write.

One more thing shaped all of it. An agent wrote most of the code, so over about
two weeks I wrote more English about Barklog than there is TypeScript in it. The
first thing in the repository that isn't scaffolding is a design document.

**Challenges we ran into**

Accepting links from strangers is the genuinely dangerous part. A server that
fetches whatever people send it can reach cloud metadata at 169.254.169.254, a
Postgres on 10.x, an admin panel on loopback. The version everyone writes, check
the address and then fetch the hostname, doesn't work, because the connector
re-resolves at connect time and an attacker's DNS answers public for the check and
private for the connection. The fix is pinning the address you verified into the
request's own dispatcher, and every redirect hop re-enters the whole check. The
oEmbed matcher had a smaller version of the same problem: a glob compiled with
.* lets https://evil.com/x.youtube.com/watch satisfy YouTube's scheme, and
excluding / isn't enough, because WHATWG URL treats a backslash as a path
separator too.

The cap I designed first was wrong. Ten backlog entries total is a rule everybody
understands, and it's consumed in the first session and never recovers, because a
finished game keeps its slot forever. The paywall would have arrived on exactly
the behaviour the app exists to encourage. Catching that in a document cost an
afternoon of rewriting. A week later it would have cost a migration.

Then a pile of small things that ate real days. Pass two truncating under a
256-token budget, which isn't an error, just a response that won't parse, because
reasoning items and tool calls land in the same output array. The SDK's default
retries buying a second web search for an answer I'd already paid for. An
Instagram reel at 745KB turning a perfectly readable page into a 502 until HTML
started truncating instead of refusing. Sign-out calling Purchases.logOut() on a
cold launch, when Clerk has resolved to signed-out and the SDK's user is still
anonymous. And a concurrency test that failed once in forty-four runs and never
reproduced across forty-three more, which I've written down rather than quietly
dropped.

Then App Review. The code was ready on 1 September and the app went live on the
14th, and almost nothing in those two weeks was code. Four submissions, three
rejections: more information about what the app does, fixed with a walkthrough
video; a missing EULA and empty fields in App Store Connect; and a reviewer who
couldn't find account deletion, fixed with a second video. A first in-app purchase
is reviewed alongside an app version and never on its own, so the entire free tier
had to exist before 1.0. A production Clerk instance inherits nothing from your
development one, which is why Apple and Google sign-in simply weren't listed, and
diffing /v1/environment between the two is what made that visible. The fourth
review took four days with nothing left to fix, and I was at the edge of my seat
for all of them.

The quiet one: review became the job. An agent that writes ten times faster
doesn't leave you with a tenth of the work. You get ten times the diff at the same
reading speed you had before, and my reading speed was the ceiling on the whole
project.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

It shipped, it's on the App Store, and the whole thing is open source at
github.com/chornonoh-vova/barklog with the design documents and their rejected
alternatives included.

The parts I'd defend hardest are the boring ones. Failure is a no-op wherever it
can be: a failed sync run, a redelivered webhook, a delete for a user who's
already gone. The cache is fail-open, so losing Valkey makes the app slower rather
than broken. The share screen tells you what kind of evidence produced its answer
instead of asserting a confidence nothing in the system holds. The cap counts
hoarding rather than saving, so finishing a game can never be the action that gets
refused, and a lapsed subscriber sitting at twenty games keeps all twenty and wins
a slot back with each one they finish.

I'm also glad the SSRF work is there. It's the part most hackathon apps skip, and
there's a test for the backslash case.

**What we learned**

A wrong document costs more than wrong code. Wrong code fails a test or fails
review. A wrong design document gets implemented faithfully, everywhere it
applies, and looks finished when it's done.

A prompt is advice and a schema isn't. If a label has to be trustworthy enough to
put in front of a user, enforce it where the response is decoded.

A cache key for a model call has to name everything that changes the answer:
prompt version, model, tool configuration. Anything you leave out is a cache
serving answers from code you already deleted. And caching that call is product
work before it's cost work, because without it the same link shared twice comes
back as two different games, and that doesn't read as probability to the person
holding the phone. It reads as a bug.

Owning a mirror makes you the publisher of somebody else's moderation lag. The
age-rating questionnaire asks what your app contains, and the honest answer about
374,000 rows arriving nightly turned into a filter on the way in plus a nightly
sweep for anything IGDB re-tagged later.

And shipping is mostly not code. The place the agent helped most was App Store
Connect, which is the furthest thing from a codebase, for someone who'd never done
it before.

**What's next for Barklog**

Localization. The app is English-only today and a backlog tracker has no reason to
be.

Home screen widgets. The one place the "what am I playing" question gets asked is
the home screen, before you've opened anything.

One question I'd rather have answered by people than by me: ten unfinished games,
finishing one gives the spot back. I'm honestly not sure ten is right rather than
merely defensible. If it's too tight, I'll ship the change.

And one open problem I'd rather write down than pretend I solved. A reviewer
couldn't find account deletion, and what I shipped was a video showing where it
lives. A real user hunting for the same thing doesn't get a video, and the path is
still behind the avatar under Security.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I used to play chess with my grandpa every summer day when I was a kid, and those games were about more than just moving pieces—they were about learning, discussing the game, and connecting. This project aims to recreate some of that magic by blending a nostalgic, tactile chess experience with an always-available, patient AI coach that can explain moves and strategies just like a mentor would.

**What it does**

AI Chess Coach 3D is a fully cross-platform chess application built with Compose Multiplatform. It features a highly realistic, high-fidelity 3D UI (including small details like wear and cracks on the board and pieces) and five distinct AI coaching surfaces:

- An on-device Move Coach and Game Summary that analyze your play in real-time.

- A Rules Q&A to help beginners.

- A cloud-backed Opening Explainer and Position Chat for deep-diving into specific board states. It includes full support for standard chess rules, Stockfish engine integration with adjustable difficulty, auto-saving, PGN export/import, and a seamless monetization flow using RevenueCat.

**Building process, challenges, accomplishments**

I am documenting the full engineering journey at https://medium.com/@gabor.berenyi.california and in the project's README.

- Architecture: We built it using Compose Multiplatform targeting Android, Desktop (JVM), Web (Wasm), and iOS. We strictly separated the platform-agnostic chess engine (:chess-core) from the UI and AI layers so there is no duplicated logic.

- 3D Rendering: The biggest challenge was the 3D pipeline. We built a renderer-agnostic state (Board3DScene) that translates FEN strings into 3D scenes, which is then implemented across platforms using Google's Filament engine (SceneView on Android, native C++ on Desktop, and WebGL on Web). The UI is a rewrite of the old and incomplete vkChess project, see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md in the repository.

- AI & Verification: We orchestrated both on-device inference (LiteRT-LM) and a Ktor/pgvector backend for cloud retrieval. To ensure the AI doesn't hallucinate, the model only narrates assessments generated by deterministic code. We also built a rigid verification rig to mathematically prove our move generator's correctness against ground-truth Stockfish counts.

**What we learned**

We also learned that shipping "AI" features in a game requires rigorous guardrails; we had to build a dedicated rule-based evaluation suite (:evals) to mathematically enforce the AI's grounding, tone, and reading level so it acts like a helpful coach rather than a generic chatbot.

**What's next for AI Chess Coach 3D**

Our immediate focus is a successful launch on the Google Play Store! After that, we plan to refine the RevenueCat monetization tiers, expand the AI coach's pedagogical ability by analyzing long-term player habits across multiple sessions, and continue optimizing our on-device LLM inference for even faster real-time coaching.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/481/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/481/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/482/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/482/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/483/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/483/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/484/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/484/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We often know what matters but still cannot get ourselves to begin.

For a student facing an exam, overwhelm and distracting apps can turn a simple first study block into an entire evening of avoidance. Generic AI chat can give advice. A timer can count down. An app blocker can interrupt a distraction.

I wanted Mazō to connect all of those missing pieces: help someone find clarity, turn that clarity into one real action, protect the time needed to start, and make it easier to return after a setback.

Mazō is built around a simple question:

Can AI help someone move from knowing what to do to actually doing it?

**What it does**

Mazō is a personalized AI coaching and follow-through app for moments when someone feels overwhelmed, indecisive, or distracted.

The core loop is:

Understand → Decide → Commit → Focus → Recover

Mazō turns a coaching conversation into one practical next step.

Users can choose between coaching modes such as Decision, Clarity, Planning, and Reflection, select the coach that fits the kind of support they want, create a custom coach, and personalize the Mazō experience.

But the goal is not to keep the conversation going forever.

The goal is to reach something the user can actually do.

For example, a student might say:

“I have a math exam coming up, but I keep opening Instagram instead of studying. I also want a reminder tomorrow morning.”

Instead of returning another long list of productivity tips, Mazō can help narrow that situation into a manageable commitment, such as:

Study for 25 focused minutes now.

Mazō can then propose relevant actions such as:

- saving a note

- creating an in-app alarm or reminder

- adding a calendar event

- beginning a focus session

- saving the next step to Journey

Nothing is executed automatically.

The user sees the proposed actions first and must approve them before Mazō changes anything.

Each action returns a receipt so the user can see what really happened.

The next step is also not trapped inside the conversation. Journey keeps the actionable commitment, while Mind stores useful notes and insights from the user's experience.

**Focus and recovery**

A real focus timer helps the user begin.

But Mazō is not designed around perfect streaks.

If someone ends a focus session early, the app can check in, understand what interrupted them, and help them choose a smaller restart rather than treating the unfinished timer as failure.

For example, a 25-minute session that did not work might become:

“Let's restart with five minutes.”

That recovery loop is an important part of Mazō.

The product is not only trying to help the user start.

It is trying to help them come back.

**Focus Guardian on Android**

On Android, Mazō goes beyond the normal AI-chat experience.

Focus Guardian is a native Android feature.

With explicit Usage Access and Display over other apps permission from the user, Mazō can detect selected distracting apps in the foreground and cover them with a focus wall during the approved focus session.

It can also show a configurable nudge encouraging the user to return to Mazō after prolonged use of a selected distracting app.

This is real native Android behavior, not a simulated screen inside the app.

**Focus experience on iPhone**

iOS exposes different system-level capabilities, so Mazō does not pretend both platforms behave identically.

The iPhone experience includes the real Mazō focus timer and a Focus Shield preview, but it does not claim to block third-party apps across iOS.

We chose to make that limitation explicit rather than overstate what the platform allows.

**RevenueCat-powered Pro experience**

Mazō integrates the RevenueCat React Native SDK for native subscription functionality.

The integration handles:

- offerings

- purchases

- restores

- Pro entitlement updates

This gives Mazō a centralized entitlement layer for premium functionality rather than scattering paywall logic throughout the product.

**How we built it**

Mazō is built with:

- Expo

- React Native

- TypeScript

- Expo Router

- Supabase

- OpenAI

- Kotlin

- RevenueCat

The architecture is intentionally split between AI reasoning and deterministic product actions.

AI helps understand the user's situation and determine what kind of next step may be useful.

But the model does not get unrestricted authority over the device.

The flow is closer to:

User context

↓

AI coaching and interpretation

↓

Structured action proposals

↓

User approval

↓

Deterministic action dispatcher

↓

Success / failure receipts

That separation became especially important once Mazō started interacting with device-level functionality.

A model can suggest an action.

The application decides whether and how that action is actually executed.

**AI and backend**

When provider-backed coaching is configured, a Supabase Edge Function keeps the AI provider key server-side rather than exposing it inside the client.

Structured coaching modes and coach-specific guidance shape the conversation.

Separate structured planning interprets requested actions into typed proposals that the rest of the app can inspect and validate.

**Android native implementation**

Focus Guardian is implemented as a local Expo module written in Kotlin.

The Android implementation uses:

- UsageStatsManager

- a foreground service

- TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY

The foreground service can monitor which app is currently in front and display the focus wall when a selected distracting package is detected.

This was one of the most technically challenging parts of the project because it required working beyond the normal React Native layer and dealing directly with Android permissions, services, app usage events, overlays, and lifecycle behavior.

**RevenueCat**

Mazō uses react-native-purchases for native RevenueCat integration.

The native purchase layer supports offerings, purchase flows, restore flows, and Pro entitlement updates.

The web purchase interface is a simulator and is not presented as a real store transaction.

**Challenges we ran into**

**Making AI stop talking**

The first product challenge was avoiding another open-ended AI chatbot.

Language models are extremely good at continuing a conversation.

But sometimes that is exactly the wrong behavior.

Mazō needed a deliberate exit:

Clarify → Approve → Begin → Check in → Save the next step → Leave

The purpose of the conversation is not to generate as much text as possible.

It is to help the user reach something they can act on.

**Turning natural language into reliable actions**

Humans speak casually.

Someone might say:

“I'll probably study later.”

That can make sense conversationally, but it is not reliable application state.

We had to separate general discussion from an actual action proposal and make sure the user approves the action before anything changes on the device.

This is why Mazō uses typed action proposals, an approval step, and execution receipts.

**Building real Android focus control**

The Android Focus Guardian required native work around:

- Usage Access

- foreground-app detection

- overlay permissions

- foreground services

- session timing

- application lifecycle

It also forced us to think carefully about platform differences.

Android can support this permissioned overlay architecture.

iOS cannot use the same implementation.

Instead of hiding that difference, Mazō communicates it clearly.

**Designing recovery instead of failure**

Most productivity apps are very good at showing users when they failed to complete something.

We wanted Mazō to react differently.

If a focus session ends early, the useful question is not:

“Why did you fail?”

It is:

“What is the smallest useful step you can restart with?”

**That led to the recovery check-in and smaller-restart flow.**

**What we learned**

**More conversation does not always mean more value**

One of the biggest lessons from building Mazō was that an AI product does not need to maximize conversation.

Sometimes the most useful thing an AI can do is help someone make a decision and then disappear.

**AI becomes more powerful when its output becomes structured**

A useful sentence inside a chat can disappear minutes later.

When that useful part becomes structured application state, the rest of the product can respond to it.

That is what lets Mazō connect:

Coaching → Action → Focus → Recovery

**Device capabilities can change what an AI product actually is**

Without native device behavior, Mazō could still be an AI coach.

Android Focus Guardian makes the product different because the system can support the user's decision after the conversation has ended.

**Platform honesty matters**

Cross-platform should not mean pretending every operating system exposes identical capabilities.

Being explicit about the difference between Android and iOS makes the product more credible and leads to better design decisions.

**What's next**

The long-term goal for Mazō is to learn what actually helps each person follow through.

Future versions could adapt based on patterns such as:

- which coaching styles lead to action

- which focus-session lengths work best

- which distractions repeatedly interrupt execution

- when the user tends to abandon commitments

- what kind of recovery helps them restart

We also want to improve cross-device continuity, deepen personalization, make recovery check-ins more adaptive, expand focus protection where platform APIs allow it, and continue refining the RevenueCat-backed Pro experience.

Over time, Mazō could become less about generic productivity advice and more about understanding the specific interventions that help an individual move forward.

The bigger idea behind Mazō is simple:

AI should not only help people think better.

It should help them move.

</details>

src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/578/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every one of us has needed help that wasn't available in a shop. The sink is broken at 11pm, your laptop won't boot the morning of a deadline, your kid needs tutoring in a language nobody at school speaks. Facebook groups solve this, but they solve it badly: everything is public, posts scroll away in hours, there's no way to tell whether a stranger offering help is reliable, and the moment you need a phone number you're pushed into handing over your contact details to anyone.
We kept noticing the same pattern. The help was always there, sitting a few streets away. What was missing was the layer of trust that would let two strangers actually go through with it. That's what Handover is: the neighborhood skill exchange that behaves like a marketplace instead of a public feed.

**What it does**

Handover lets people list the skills they have - plumbing, bike repair, Spanish tutoring, help with a computer - and find that skill offered nearby by someone else.
The core loop is deliberately small: add skills to your profile, search by keyword and radius, send a request, chat privately, then close the loop with a rating and an optional tip. Tipping routes 80% to the neighbor through Google Play Billing, and the price is always shown before purchase.
The part we're proudest of is what the app refuses to do. It never shows anyone's exact location. Search results return a rough area and a distance, and your phone number is encrypted at rest and only revealed to a neighbor who accepted your request and explicitly agreed to share theirs, for that one request. Chat rooms use 15-minute access tokens rather than open-ended sessions. Every post and photo passes automated safety screening, every report reaches a real moderator queue, and users can block each other permanently.
It's a neighborly app that takes privacy and safety as the default rather than as a settings screen.

**How we built it**

A Flutter client (Android, iOS, web, desktop) talking to a FastAPI + SQLAlchemy backend, served through nginx with TLS and WebSocket support, packaged with Docker Compose.

A few decisions worth calling out:

- Location privacy is architectural, not a setting. We implemented geohashing from scratch. Search results carry a grid cell that gets decoded into a bounding box for the map, so the app can draw an area without ever receiving a coordinate. The implementation lives in frontend/lib/services/geohash.dart and is covered by tests.

- No third-party auth dependency. Tokens are HS256 JWTs we sign ourselves, with jti claims checkable against a BlockedToken table so sessions can be revoked. Passwords use Argon2, and legacy PBKDF2 hashes are accepted and transparently migrated. Two-factor auth is built in with TOTP and recovery codes.

- Contacts encrypted with Fernet under a key derived from a separate config value, never stored in plaintext.

- Safety is layered. Detoxify handles text toxicity at a 0.75 threshold; images go through magic-byte validation, Pillow integrity checks, dimension limits to stop decompression abuse, and an optional NSFW classifier (Hive or Google Vision) at 0.85. Critically, when a model fails to load we route to human review rather than silently marking content as safe. A failure in the safety system must not fail open.

- Payments go through Google Play via RevenueCat, so we never touch card data.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest problem was making privacy feel invisible. We kept building screens where the "safe" version was strictly worse for the user, a map with a vague blob, a chat where you can't get a phone number - and the honest fix was to accept that friction as the product. Once we stopped treating it as a defect, the design got much easier.
Signing the release build was its own adventure. We lost the original upload keystore, so we generated a new one, submitted a reset request to Google Play with its certificate, and waited for approval before we could ship. A build that worked perfectly on our machines was rejected by Play purely because of a signing key mismatch. The new key is backed up in two places now.
We also spent real time on child-safety compliance before the app was ever public: a designated child safety contact, a public account-deletion page, a legal page served by the API itself, and reporting flows that route to humans. None of it is visible in a screenshot, and all of it was mandatory.
And we had to be honest with ourselves about scope. Tipping, two-factor, image cropping, an admin moderation console - each of these was a day we'd budgeted as an afternoon.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The moderation pipeline. Reports from the app land in a real console where a human can see the post, its owner, and the reporter's reason side by side, then either remove the post or dismiss the report. That loop closes in seconds rather than days, and it's the difference between "we have moderation" and moderation that actually functions.
We're also proud that the safety checks degrade into human review instead of into nothing. That's a small piece of engineering that took real thought, and it's the kind of thing that only matters until the day it matters.

Finally: the app is signed, built, and going to Play. Flutter, FastAPI, our own auth, our own geohash, a working moderation console, and a real payment split - two friends had put that together end to end.

**What we learned**

The most surprising lesson was that privacy features are trust features. Every rough area instead of a pin, every consent step, every short-lived token is a moment where the user decides whether we can be trusted. The work that felt like friction while we built it turned out to be the thing that makes the product credible.
We also learned that safety systems have to be designed for failure, not just for success. The first version of our moderation code would have marked content as safe whenever a model failed to load. Fail-closed, even if it means a queue full of manual reviews, is the only defensible default.
On the technical side: we underestimated how much of "just ship it" is packaging. Version codes, signing keys, Play target-API policy, and the reset procedure consumed more time than any single feature. None of it is interesting and all of it is the product reaching people.

**What's next for Handover**

The neighborhood layer. Right now an area is just a radius around you. The real goal is a local network: verified address or building-level presence, so a search means "in my building" or "on my street," not "within 5 km of a coordinate." That unlocks the genuinely valuable version of the product, the person who watches the building, the student who tutors in the same block, the elder who needs a hand with groceries three doors down.
Verified reputation. Ratings exist, but they aren't carried yet. We want review history, repeat handshakes, and a visible track record that means something, so a neighbor can tell a first-time helper from someone the block trusts.
Recurring help. Most real favors aren't one-time. A weekly walk for an older neighbor, a standing tutoring slot, a monthly filter change.
Onboarding that starts useful. Rather than an empty search page, a new user should be able to get their first request or offer going in under a minute, using a suggested skill and a suggested radius.
And a real moderation team. The tools work, but at our scale the moderators are volunteers. The goal is a small local team with clear escalation, which is what the community is actually ready to support.

</details>
