<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Last year I started traveling, which meant I also left my previous Shipaton project unfinished.

I wanted to backpack, explore places beyond the usual tourist attractions, and experience cities the way locals do. Like most travelers, I relied on Google Maps, Reddit, blogs, Instagram, and ChatGPT to plan my trips.

The problem was that Google Maps mostly showed highly-rated tourist spots, while Reddit recommendations were often outdated, scattered across different posts, or simply unavailable for smaller cities. I spent more time searching than actually exploring.

That's when the idea for AasPaas came to me.

I realized I wasn't just looking for places, I was looking for stories and experiences.

I wanted to know where someone goes after a difficult day to watch the sunset. Which small tea stall locals have been visiting for years. Which quiet street feels magical after it rains. Which noodle vendor on the corner everyone recommends but never appears in travel guides.

I wanted travelers to experience the memories, emotions, and little moments that make a city feel alive, not just visit the places with the highest ratings.

So this year, I came back to Shipaton to build AasPaas.

**What it does**

AasPaas is a community-driven travel app that helps you experience a city through locals — not through star ratings.

Instead of bouncing between Google Maps, Reddit, blogs, and ChatGPT, you get the vibe, the tips, and a day plan in one place.

With AasPaas, you can:

- Feel a city's pulse before you land — what's on tonight, what's packed, what's actually worth it

- Read notes from people who live there (sunsets after hard days, chaat stalls with a blue canopy, quiet streets after rain)

- Ask AasPaas tiny, location-specific questions and get answers grounded in community notes — not a guidebook dump

- Hit Make a Plan and turn the vibe into a real itinerary that matches your time and mood

- Unlock more planning with AasPaas Pro — Trip Pass, Travel Year, or Lifetime — because travel isn't monthly SaaS; people plan in windows

AasPaas isn't just about finding places. It's about the stories, people, and little moments that make a city feel alive.

**How we built it**

Mobile-first on Expo / React Native, with a Node + Prisma backend and embeddings-powered RAG so Ask AasPaas answers from real community notes instead of inventing tourist fluff.

The fun product bet: AI only when it helps. Browse and ask from locals first; generate a plan when you want a full day. Itineraries are grounded in what people shared — not generic “top 10” lists.

For Shipaton, monetization runs through RevenueCat + Google Play: one entitlement (aaspaas_pro), three ways in (14-Day Trip Pass, Travel Year, Lifetime Local). Free travelers get one AI plan; then the paywall — fair, not spammy.

We also shipped store listing assets, a timed demo video, and production Play wiring so the purchase path is real, not a mock.

**Challenges we ran into**

Cold-start community. The hardest part wasn't the UI — it was getting original posts from real people. Without locals sharing, Ask and Plan have nothing honest to stand on. Bootstrapping trust and contribution in a new city is still the long game.

Seeding city data without faking the soul. Empty cities feel dead; fake-sounding seed content kills trust. We had to seed enough pulse (updates, people notes, Ask answers) for Jaipur and friends so the demo feels alive — while keeping a path for real user posts to take over.

Travel billing isn't Netflix. Monthly subscriptions fight how people actually travel. Designing seasonal plans (Trip Pass / Travel Year / Lifetime) and wiring them cleanly through RevenueCat + Play took more product thinking than “add a subscribe button.”

Search vs. stories. Ranking by reviews is easy. Surfacing “the tea stall locals never leave” is harder — and that's the whole point of AasPaas.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Shipped a full loop: city vibe → local notes → Ask → Make a Plan → Pro unlock

- Ask that answers from community notes (RAG), not pasted guidebook sludge

- Travel-native Pro plans via RevenueCat — one entitlement, three packages, live on Play

- A Shipaton demo that shows the entitlement path for real: free → paywall → Pro

- Coming back after leaving last year's project unfinished — and actually finishing this one

**What we learned**

Community products don't start with scale; they start with one honest city and a few notes worth keeping.

AI is strongest when it's grounded — embeddings + local notes beat “ChatGPT, plan my Jaipur trip” every time.

Travel monetization should match travel behavior. People buy a planning window, not a forever subscription by default.

And finishing beats perfection: Shipaton was the deadline that turned a travel frustration into a shippable app.

**What's next for AasPaas**

Go global — city by city. Expand beyond the first India-focused set: more cities, more languages, more local voices.

Grow the community graph. Better prompts to share a vibe, city ambassadors, and lighter ways for travelers to leave one true tip before they leave town.

Smarter Ask & Plan. Richer retrieval, multi-day journeys, and plans that react to live pulse (“skip parking after 4,” “folk set starts in 40”).

Deeper Pro. Trip Pass experiments, group/friend plans, and offline-friendly day threads for when you're actually out walking.

The north star stays the same: help someone find the place a local whispered about — not the one with a thousand reviews.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Inspiration

Math is one of the subjects students struggle with the most. Many existing platforms rely on fixed question banks, meaning students eventually memorize answers instead of truly understanding concepts. As a student myself, I've experienced how frustrating it can be to run out of meaningful practice or receive explanations that don't match the way I learn.

I wanted to build a platform where every student could receive unlimited, personalized math practice with clear explanations generated in real time. My goal was simple: make learning math engaging, adaptive, and accessible so students build confidence through understanding rather than memorization.

What it does

GeniusMath AI is an AI-powered personalized math learning platform that generates fresh practice questions on demand.

Students can:

- Choose a math subject, including Algebra, Geometry, Trigonometry, Precalculus, and more.

- Select a difficulty level.

- Choose how many questions to generate.

- Practice in School or Competition mode.

- Receive detailed explanations for every correct and incorrect answer.

- View their score and review mistakes to strengthen weak areas.

Unlike traditional worksheets, every practice session is unique, giving students virtually unlimited opportunities to learn.

How we built it

GeniusMath AI was built as a native iOS application using SwiftUI and Xcode.

The app uses AI to dynamically generate original math questions and explanations in real time based on each student's selected settings. We focused heavily on creating a modern, intuitive user experience with smooth animations, responsive navigation, and a clean interface that keeps students focused on learning.

The project combines:

- SwiftUI

- AI-powered question generation

- Custom quiz engine

- Adaptive practice modes

- Native iOS design principles

- Challenges we ran into

One of the biggest challenges was ensuring the AI consistently generated mathematically accurate and appropriately difficult questions across multiple subjects.

Another challenge was balancing response speed with quality. We optimized prompts and application flow to minimize waiting while still providing detailed explanations.

Designing an interface that remained simple for beginners while still offering enough customization for advanced learners also required several iterations.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're proud of creating a platform that feels like a personal AI math tutor instead of another worksheet generator.

Some highlights include:

- Unlimited AI-generated practice questions

- Personalized learning experience

- Instant answer explanations

- School and Competition practice modes

- Clean, modern native iOS interface

- Fast and intuitive user experience

Most importantly, we built a tool that encourages students to understand mathematics instead of memorizing answers.

What we learned

Throughout this project, we learned that building an educational AI product requires much more than simply connecting to a language model.

We discovered the importance of prompt engineering, user experience design, handling AI edge cases, validating mathematical correctness, and designing interfaces that make learning feel enjoyable rather than overwhelming.

We also gained valuable experience integrating AI into a real-world mobile application.

What's next for GeniusMath AI

Our vision is to turn GeniusMath AI into a complete AI learning companion.

Future plans include:

- Adaptive learning paths that automatically adjust difficulty.

- Personalized study plans based on student performance.

- Progress tracking and analytics.

- Teacher and classroom dashboards.

- Support for SAT, ACT, AMC, Math Olympiad, AP Calculus, and other standardized exams.

- Image-based problem solving using the camera.

- Voice tutoring for interactive learning.

- Cross-platform support for iPad, Android, and the web.

- Multi-language support to make personalized math education accessible worldwide.

Our mission is to make high-quality, personalized math education available to every student, regardless of where they learn.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

A student can choose the right answer and still struggle to explain why it is right.

“Heavier things fall faster” sounds convincing. Then a feather and a hammer fall together on the Moon. What changed? Remembering the answer is one task; explaining the conditions is another.

I built Dekisugi-kun around that moment. Instead of asking a companion to explain science, the learner has to teach it.

**What it does**

Dekisugi-kun is a native science app for middle and high-school learners. Its central interaction is simple: predict, read, hide the material, explain, and apply.

The learner makes a prediction, explores a focused lesson, and then explains the idea in their own words with the source hidden. They reread their text or replay their voice before the companion asks a fixed follow-up question from the lesson catalog. If they miss a condition, the app offers a hint and asks them to try again. Uncertain ideas remain available for a matching repair activity.

The 67-second demo follows this loop through falling objects, then shows a free understanding check that asks the learner to explain a principle and apply it in a different situation. The reasoning becomes something the learner can inspect and revise, rather than an answer they can copy.

The current build includes 12 science units and 35 concepts, with Japanese and English curriculum, story cases, diagram activities, and review. Core lessons work offline without an account. Text is a complete learning route alongside voice. In the demonstrated route, explanations and voice recordings stay on-device and are not retained as durable records.

**Why someone would buy Plus**

A family reviewing science together has two practical questions: “What should we review next?” and “What should I ask?”

Plus turns the companion’s record into a local family review plan. It chooses a topic, explains the choice, gives a parent a useful question, and changes one condition to check whether the learner can apply the idea. A shareable report carries the review plan without answer text, audio, or personal scores. The Aurora Cape adds a visible supporter benefit.

Core lessons, text input, review, and understanding checks stay free. The paid value is a more convenient family review routine. The demo shows a RevenueCat Test Store purchase unlocking Plus and the family report, with no real charge.

**How I built it**

Flutter powers the native app, a bundled bilingual curriculum, and SQLite-backed progress. TypeScript on Vercel serves the catalog. Fixed checkpoints and canonical need codes connect an observed gap to its repair activity. Key-term coverage prompts reflection; it is not presented as a grade for understanding. External live AI is disabled in the current production build.

RevenueCat’s purchases_flutter SDK handles packages, purchase, restore, and the plus entitlement. Family review is a local plan and a report the user can copy; it does not require cloud-linked parent and child accounts.

**Challenges and what I learned**

The hardest design problem was keeping the companion helpful while leaving the thinking with the learner. Hiding the source, requiring rereading or playback, and offering a condition hint after a miss made that principle visible in the interface.

I learned to judge a feature by what it asks the learner to do. That changed both the learning loop and monetization: explaining and applying remain free, while Plus helps a family decide what to revisit.

**Accomplishments and what’s next**

I built a working native flow from prediction through explanation, follow-up, repair, and review. The app passed 1,340 client tests, with 399 server tests in the unchanged baseline. The English demo uses actual native Android emulator interactions, edited for pace, with separate editorial narration and captions.

Next I will extend the curriculum, refine delayed review, run classroom pilots comparing explanations and transfer to new situations, and complete physical-device recording and permission checks.

**For reviewers**

Watch the 67-second English demo, explore the MIT source, or follow the native run and Test Store guide.

Android application ID: jp.dekisugi.dekisugi.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Studying for exams has always been a battleground for me. Whenever test season approached and I tried to sit down with dense physiology PDFs, my mind wouldn’t just drift—it would spiral. The overwhelming pressure triggered intense anxiety, bringing up past traumatic experiences, sudden panic, and severe distress. Standard study tools and flashcards only made it worse by piling on the pressure, treating me like a machine that just needed more repetitive drilling.

I needed an environment that felt safe. I spent hours unwinding in games like Stardew Valley, where you can exist in a calm, welcoming world without the constant threat of failure. We asked ourselves: What if studying felt like stepping into a gentle, grounding sanctuary instead of a high-stress trial?
That became the soul of Focus Physiology. We built this app specifically for people who struggle with study-induced panic and trauma triggers:
A Cozy Safe Haven: Instead of staring at an intimidating textbook, you walk a peaceful pixel farm, harvest crops, and engage with your notes through low-stakes exploration.
An App That Responds to Panic: Instead of punishing you when your heart races, the app notices your stress via an opt-in webcam pulse sensor. When panic spikes, it doesn't throw more questions at you—it automatically fades in soft lullaby music and gives you space to breathe until you feel grounded again.
Story Before Mechanics: Instead of jumping straight into a nerve-wracking quiz, your lecture notes are first transformed into a peaceful four-chapter valley story. You read at your own pace before ever stepping onto the farm.
Studying shouldn't trigger a fight-or-flight response. Focus Physiology turns overwhelming medical notes into a calm valley where you can learn safely, step by step.

**What it does**

Focus Physiology turns intimidating lecture notes into a cozy, grounding farm adventure.
Storyteller Quest: Paste notes, upload a PDF, or snap a page with your camera. The app writes a peaceful four-chapter valley story from that material and extracts quiz questions. It keeps you on the narrative page first so you can read calmly—it never dumps you directly into high-pressure gameplay.
Valley Farm (RPG World): A top-down pixel farm. Walk around with WASD or a phone D-pad, tend crops, talk to the farmer, and encounter gentle red slimes. Combat consists of short 3-question checks drawn from your notes. HP, XP, and levels carry over.
Webcam Stress & Grounding Sensor: An opt-in camera feature reads your pulse from your face using green-channel rPPG. A clear top bar tracks your state from calm to elevated. It runs entirely on video analysis, so typing or note-taking never triggers fake stress alarms.
Valley Lullaby: When your stress meter rises, soft ambient pad music automatically fades in to help pull you out of a panic cycle. You can mute it anytime or preview it on the dashboard.
Focus Timer & Lesson Board: A customizable Pomodoro timer paired with a simple To-Do / In-Progress / Mastered task board.
Study Stake Arena: Four subject tables where you and a study partner put a simulated stake in a pot; whoever logs the highest focus time (tied to the timer) wins the pot.
Everything is instantly playable directly in the browser on desktop or mobile.

**How we built it**

App Shell & UI: Built with TanStack Start + React 19 + Tailwind v4 to deliver a responsive shell (Dashboard, Storyteller, RPG, Stake Arena, and Tasks).
Game Engine: A custom Canvas 2D pixel farm running at 320×180 integer-scaled resolution using requestAnimationFrame + delta time. Key presses live in a JavaScript Set(event.code) rather than React state, ensuring smooth movement that never stutters or freezes.
AI & OCR Storyteller: Powered by xAI Grok (grok-4.5) on the server to convert raw lecture notes into JSON-structured stories and quizzes, with vision OCR for image uploads. If the API is offline, a local fallback storyteller generates chapters on the fly so the user is never left with an empty screen.
PDF Processing: pdf.js parses and extracts selectable text directly inside the browser.
rPPG Stress Engine: A custom pulse detector that samples a forehead Region of Interest (ROI), estimates BPM from light fluctuations in the green channel, filters out micro-movements, and updates the header stress meter in real time.
Generative Audio: Built with the Web Audio API (layered ambient pads, slow chord morphs, and quiet bells). Audio nodes are unlocked on the same tap as "Start sensor" to ensure seamless playback across all mobile browsers.
State & Persistence: State managed via Zustand + localStorage. No user accounts or login screens are required to demo or use the app.

**Challenges we ran into**

The Two-Step Movement Freeze: Early movement prototypes used React key state and setInterval. Holding down WASD keys caused React state to update twice, locking the character in place. Fix: We moved key handling into a native Set and restricted movement updates strictly to the requestAnimationFrame loop scaled by delta time (dt).
Storyteller Jumping to the RPG: Uploading notes originally redirected the user immediately to the game, which felt abrupt and overwhelming. To preserve a calm flow, the transform step now displays the four-chapter story on the current page first, leaving entry to the farm as a deliberate, low-pressure button choice.
Separating Typing, Movement, and Stress: A stress guard that listened to keyboard inputs accidentally spiked the stress meter while typing notes and hijacked WASD game keys. We made the sensor strictly camera-only and configured game key events to ignore active INPUT and TEXTAREA elements.
Cozy Aesthetic vs. Scope Creep: Developing full sprite sheets and complex game worlds was out of scope for a quick demo. A tight pixel framebuffer with integer scaling, y-sorted entity rendering, and a simple harvest/slime loop captured the nostalgic, comforting feel of Stardew Valley without scope bloat.
iOS Audio Restrictions: Mobile browsers block web audio until an explicit user gesture occurs. We synchronized the audio context unlock to the "Start sensor" and "Play music" buttons, adding an auto-resume handler on tab focus.
Stake Arena Safety: We intentionally avoided real-money integration or banking APIs to keep the app safe, accessible, and free of financial anxiety or gambling mechanics. The Arena uses purely simulated study points.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

A Full Grounding Loop: Transformed intimidating PDFs into a gentle story, a soothing farm walk, and brief, manageable review checks.
Silky-Smooth Controls: Fluid pixel-farm movement using direct event tracking without key-sticking or state freezes.
A Supportive Stress System: An opt-in, non-punitive pulse tracker that actively helps soothe anxiety (music + breathing prompts) rather than penalizing high stress.
Consistent Aesthetic: Preserved a cozy pastel design language with custom fox icons, warm coral accents, and comforting UI framing throughout.
Cross-Platform Accessibility: Fully functional on both desktop browsers and mobile devices (complete with a responsive D-pad, mobile camera capture, and bottom navigation).

**What we learned**

Game Feel Requires Native Input Handling: Smooth movement depends on low-level input tracking (event.code, held-state sets, delta time) rather than framework state management (setState).
Trauma-Informed UX Design: Product structure dictates emotional safety. When the app prioritizes narrative immersion before introducing review mechanics, learning feels safe and earned rather than forced.
Biometric Calibration: Camera-based rPPG requires warm-up cycles, environmental light verification, and value smoothing (hysteresis) to prevent ambient lighting changes from falsely triggering stress alerts.
Generative Web Audio: Rich, soothing ambient audio can be generated directly in code using gain fading instead of starting heavy audio files cold.
Scope Discipline: A single, polished, calming location is far more effective for anxiety relief than an unfinished open world.

**What's next for Focus Physiology**

Shared Cooperative Pots: Invite classmates into shared study pots with live study-time leaderboards and school-safe goals.
Expanding the Farm: Introducing seasonal changes, new crops, helpful villager NPCs who quiz you by chapter, and unlockable fields as you master topics and better graphics.
Enhanced Biometrics: Implementing FaceDetector ROI tracking and an optional "Calm-Only Study Mode" that pauses game prompts until your pulse stabilizes.
Spaced Repetition Harvesting: Farm crops that regrow along a personalized forgetting curve to gently prompt review on older facts.
Classroom & Group Mode: Allowing teachers or study group leaders to upload a shared lecture PDF so an entire class can explore the same valley together.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I am obsessed with programming, and I wanted to work on my projects wherever I was. I tried several mobile coding tools, but none gave me the experience I wanted: a capable editor, a real terminal, and a comfortable way to code without a full keyboard. Eventually, I decided to build that workspace myself.

**What it does**

Codaloud brings a code editor, Git, an interactive cloud terminal, and an AI assistant together on your phone. You can import a GitHub repository, edit its files, run commands, review the diff, and commit your work in one workspace.

Inside a project, you can ask the assistant to open files and panels, explain code, make changes, or run commands. You can speak your instructions or type them into the same floating command bubble.

- Edit code on the go. Use syntax highlighting, autocomplete, search, formatting, diagnostics for supported languages, and customizable editor settings.

- Code with your voice or text. Describe a change aloud or switch the command bubble to text mode. Typed requests use AI credits without starting an audio session.

- Type comfortably. A dedicated symbols row puts brackets, punctuation, indentation, and other coding characters within reach.

- Use Git and GitHub. Import repositories, review diffs, stage changes, create commits, manage branches, and fetch, pull, or push connected repositories.

- Run real commands. An interactive Daytona terminal lets you install dependencies, run tests, and build projects. Incremental synchronization transfers changed files between the device and sandbox.

- Delegate longer tasks. Review an implementation plan, approve the work, and follow the agent’s progress and logs while continuing to use the editor.

- Capture ideas in drafts. Write standalone code or notes, get assistance with the open draft, and copy your work into a project later.

Projects and drafts remain on the device. AI assistance, cloud terminals, authentication, purchases, and remote Git operations require their respective online services.

**How we built it**

Codaloud targets iOS and Android using React Native and Expo. The submitted demo shows the iOS experience.

- CodeMirror provides the editor inside a mobile WebView.

- A native C++ workspace engine and libgit2 support local file and Git operations.

- Expo SQLite stores projects, drafts, and other on-device information.

- Drizzle and Neon Postgres support cloud accounts, usage records, and the credit ledger.

- Better Auth handles authentication.

- OpenRouter provides models for AI assistance and code generation.

- LiveKit supports live voice sessions, Deepgram transcribes speech, and ElevenLabs generates spoken responses.

- Daytona provides project sandboxes and interactive cloud terminals.

- Trigger.dev handles background jobs and longer-running agent tasks.

- Firecrawl supports the agent’s web search and scraping tools.

- RevenueCat powers subscription and credit-pack purchase flows, paywalls, and purchase restoration.

**RevenueCat and monetization**

Codaloud offers Pro and Premium subscriptions alongside credit-pack purchases. Credits account for usage across AI requests, voice sessions, background agents, and cloud terminals, helping connect the pricing model to the cost of providing those services.

Users can view plans and balances, restore purchases, and access subscription management from Billing. Eligible subscribers and users with an active paid-tier trial can purchase additional credits.

The development build uses RevenueCat Test Store for purchase testing. Production App Store and Google Play purchasing remains a release preparation step; the submission does not claim completed production-store purchase verification.

**Working with Codex**

The app was built with Codex. I came up with the idea, planned the experience, researched the technologies, chose the stack, and guided the implementation. Codex wrote and executed code alongside me as I tested the app and refined the product.

I also used MCP integrations, including the RevenueCat MCP server, to help configure the project, create paywall drafts, and manage the product catalog.

Throughout this description, “we” means me and Codex.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Connecting local projects to cloud execution. Files live on the device, while terminal commands run in a sandbox. We worked on incremental synchronization, batching, and conflict detection to make those environments feel like one workspace.

- Designing for a small screen. Editor controls, navigation, terminal output, and AI responses all compete for limited space. The interface went through several iterations to keep those tools accessible without covering the code unnecessarily.

- Making voice assistance actionable. Useful voice conversations require more than transcription. We had to coordinate audio, context, tool calls, file changes, and responses while handling interruptions and reconnects.

- Choosing credits and pricing. AI requests, spoken responses, background work, and sandbox execution have different costs. We researched those costs and designed a credit model to account for them.

- Supporting offline diagnostics. We bundled language analysis into the app so supported diagnostics could work locally. Balancing analysis speed and bundle size meant limiting the languages supported by the MVP.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- We built a working mobile coding workspace in less than a month.

- Users can move from GitHub import to editing, terminal execution, diff review, and commits within the app.

- The assistant can act on project files through voice or typed instructions.

- Longer implementation tasks have a plan-review flow and visible progress.

- The editor provides local diagnostic feedback for supported languages.

- RevenueCat purchase flows are integrated with the app’s subscription and credit system.

**What we learned**

Building Codaloud introduced me to tools across mobile development, AI, voice, cloud infrastructure, and payments. It also taught me a better way to work with AI: research the problem, make product decisions clearly, break the implementation into manageable pieces, and test the results as the app takes shape.

I learned that putting desktop capabilities on a phone is as much an interaction-design problem as an engineering problem. The tools need to work together, and their controls need to remain comfortable on a small screen.

**What's next for Codaloud**

- Expand support for programming languages and diagnostics.

- Improve interface consistency and responsiveness.

- Complete production-store purchase configuration and verification.

- Test and refine the Android experience.

- Explore Apple’s on-device models.

- Add terminal execution that can run locally.

- Improve the experience for iPad.

- Publish Codaloud on the App Store.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I am inspired by the open source community that builds tools that rival and sometimes surpass proprietary AI products. Open source tools offer self-hosting and control over one's own data, and they apply pressure to proprietary tech to improve their products.

PocketCoder is heavily inspired by OpenClaw and Claude Remote Control. I started building the first version in February and submitted a prototype PocketCoder to a previous hackathon (https://devpost.com/software/pocketcoder-r4oita). I learned a lot but thought that was it for PocketCoder. RevenueCat Shipaton encouraged me to productionize PocketCoder and actually ship it because they allowed previous work as long as it has never been shipped to an app store before.

**What it does**

1-tap setup from mobile:

- Provisions a VPS from Linode

- Installs NixOS

- Deploys dockerized PocketCoder backend

- Configures TLS certificates with Caddy

- Authenticates mobile app to the backend

PocketCoder enables:

- Users swap between coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Goose) while using their own subscriptions or API keys via Agent Client Protocol (ACP).

- Agents that ask for permissions and show tool calls, not just a chat

- Agentic memory that remembers why, not just what

- Variety of MCPs through the Docker MCP gateway

- File inspector

- SSH key setup for git repositories

**How we built it**

Stack:

- Flutter/cubit client

- PocketBase + AG-UI protocol as a contract

- SQLPage for observability

- Docker MCP Gateway for many MCPs

- Docker Compose

- Caddy

- NixOS

- RevenueCat handles billing and entitlements

- Firebase Cloud Messaging for push notifications

- Cloudflare Workers for OAuth, push notifications, and NixOS/Docker images

- GitHub attestations

I used agentic tools such as Claude Code and Codex to speed up the implementation, debugging, and iteration.

**Challenges we ran into**

The scope and time of the project exceeded my expectations. In order to turn a VPS into an "appliance" — restart, update, backup, and restore, all from the app — a lot of engineering and version compatibility needed to be thought through.

One bug nearly convinced me the project was dead. Provisioning the VPS would hang with no error, even though the exact same flow had worked before. Something had broken, and I couldn't tell what. For about a day or two I thought this was going to block the whole project from shipping. The VPS looked healthy over SSH, and the installer's own log said it had finished, but the client just sat there waiting forever. The answer was on neither side: to signal that an install is done, the VPS powers itself off, and the client watches for three consecutive offline reads. Linode has an account-level watchdog that reboots any instance powered off without its knowledge, and it was winning the race — rebooting the box faster than my poll could catch the shutdown. A fully successful install was disguising itself as a permanently stuck one. I only found this by opening Linode's web portal and reading the raw event log by hand; nothing in my own server or client logs could see it. The fix: disable the watchdog for the duration of a provision, and re-enable it once done.

Additionally, PocketCoder is still not on the Apple App Store at the time of writing despite being on the Google Play Store for 2 weeks already, and submitting PocketCoder to both stores at the same time with the same information and instructions.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Getting not only a mobile AI Agent but also a mobile server controller that enables provisioning, deploying, and controlling a real server entirely from a phone, with no desktop step required at any point.

**What we learned**

- Distributing software onto machines you don't control is a different discipline than shipping an app — image caches, attestation, revocation, signed manifests were new to me.

**What's next for Poco the PocketCoder**

- Get through iOS review

- Use PocketCoder on my own VPS for real work and to self improve itself.

</details>

src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/282/475/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Everyone has a home screen. Most people waste it.

The default widgets Apple and Google ship are either too simple or locked to
their own apps. We wanted a home screen that actually reflects you — your
data feeds, your habit trackers, your live API endpoints, your aesthetic.
We built Pandra because the tools to make that exist, but the friction to
wire them together never went away.

**What It Does**

Pandra is an AI-powered widget studio for iOS and Android. You describe
what you want in plain language — "Bitcoin and Ethereum live price tracker",
"daily water intake counter", "production server health checker" — and Pandra
builds it as a real home-screen widget, backed by live data.

Widgets are organized into workspaces, a deck you can switch between for
different contexts: work, personal, travel. Every widget syncs to your home
screen in real time through a native bridge layer, so your lock screen and
home screen stay current without you lifting a finger.

The engine supports eight widget types out of the box: live weather, REST API
fetchers, counters, notes, news feeds, battery monitors, photo widgets, and
static metrics — each configurable down to card style, color, sparkline
pattern, and size.

**How We Built It**

The app is built in React Native with Expo Router for navigation and
Tamagui for the design system. On iOS, home-screen widgets are powered by
expo-widgets via an App Extension; on Android, react-native-android-widget
handles rendering into the native widget host, with small and wide slot variants.

A native bridge layer (native-widget-bridge) serializes the active deck to
AsyncStorage and shared App Group storage, so the widget extension and the app
stay in sync across process boundaries.

The backend runs on Convex — storing user decks, workspace layouts, and
telemetry logs — with Clerk handling authentication (Google Sign-In on
Android, with Apple Sign-In on iOS). Monetization is RevenueCat, with a
Pandra Pro entitlement gating AI generation and advanced widget types.

The AI widget synthesizer parses a natural-language prompt, classifies it into
a widget type, resolves live data (geocoding for weather, JSON path evaluation
for REST APIs, Hacker News for news feeds), and emits a fully-formed widget
record ready to drop into the deck.

**What We Learned**

Cross-process widget state is the hardest part of home-screen development.
iOS widget extensions and Android widget hosts run in separate processes with
no shared memory. Getting the app and the widget to agree on the current state
— without race conditions or stale reads — required a careful serialization
contract through shared AsyncStorage and App Group containers.

We also learned that natural-language widget generation only works if the
classifier is precise about which live data source backs the widget. A prompt
like "water tracker" should never hit a weather API — building a tight intent
classifier before any data fetch was the move that made the AI feel reliable
rather than random.

**Challenges We Ran Into**

The iOS widget extension boundary. Widgets are a separate build target with
their own entitlements and App Group identifiers. Wiring Expo's managed workflow
to produce a correctly-signed extension — and keeping the shared storage keys
consistent between the app and the extension across EAS builds — required a
custom Expo config plugin and careful entitlement management.

Keeping Android wide and small widgets visually consistent. The
react-native-android-widget renderer supports a subset of React Native
primitives. Matching the design language of the iOS SwiftUI widgets — same dark
surface palette, same live-indicator dot, same sparkline bars — using only
FlexWidget and TextWidget primitives took considerably more iteration than
building the same UI in-app.

RevenueCat entitlements across platforms. Pro access has to be enforced in
both the client UI and the widget sync path. Threading the entitlement check
through the native bridge — so a widget slot cannot be written with Pro content
if the subscription has lapsed — required the bridge layer to be entitlement-aware.

**What's Next**

- iCloud-backed deck sync so workspaces roam across devices

- A community template gallery where users can publish and clone widget presets

- Deeper AI: multi-widget deck generation from a single prompt describing an
entire home-screen layout

- Shortcut and Focus Filter integrations so workspaces switch automatically
with iPhone Focus modes

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Studying has become incredibly fragmented.

Students jump between textbooks, past papers, YouTube videos, notes, AI chatbots, and revision websites, but most of these tools only solve one part of the learning process. They can give you an answer, but they don't necessarily understand why you got it wrong, remember your weaknesses, or adapt the next lesson to you.

That is where Chapter started.

**What Inspired Chapter**

The idea came from a simple question:

What if an AI tutor didn't just answer your questions, but actually understood how you learn?

Instead of treating every student like a blank slate, Chapter is designed around the idea of building a persistent learning profile.

A student can bring in a past-paper question, ask for an explanation, get a hint instead of the answer, translate difficult material, and receive targeted help. Over time, Chapter tracks patterns in the student's learning and uses them to make future studying more useful.

The goal isn't to replace teachers or textbooks. It's to make the gap between I don't understand this and I can solve this myself much smaller.

**What We Buil**

Chapter is an AI-powered study platform covering subjects such as Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Mathematics, Computer Science, Economics, English, and Business, alongside SAT preparation.

Students can:

- 📸 Scan questions from past papers and study material

- 🧠 Ask AI to explain concepts step-by-step

- 💡 Request hints instead of complete answers

- 🌍 Translate difficult questions and explanations

- 📚 Study across multiple subjects and exam formats

- 📈 Track progress and identify areas that need more work

- 🔥 Build streaks, goals, and study habits

- 🏆 Participate in leagues and XP-based progression

- 🤖 Get personalized help based on their previous learning

We also designed Chapter with a parent side in mind, allowing parents to understand progress without turning the product into a surveillance dashboard.

**How We Built It**

Chapter was built as a full-stack application rather than a simple AI chat interface.

The frontend was designed around a dark, glass-style interface with a focus on making the product feel like a polished study platform rather than an AI wrapper.

Behind the interface, we built systems for:

- Authentication and user accounts

- Persistent student progress

- AI-powered tutoring

- Usage limits and quotas

- XP, streaks, goals, and progression

- Leaderboards

- Subject and question tracking

- Role-based access

- Database security policies

- Subscription and payment infrastructure

A major part of the engineering process was making sure that important logic could not simply be trusted to the client.

For example, things such as XP, quotas, progress, and access permissions need to be validated server-side. Otherwise, a student could theoretically modify a request and give themselves unlimited XP or bypass usage restrictions.

That meant Chapter had to be treated as a real production application, not just a prototype that looks good in a demo.

**The Hard Parts**

The hardest part wasn't getting an AI model to answer a question.

That part is relatively easy.

The difficult part was building everything around the AI.

We had to think about questions like:

- How do we prevent students from abusing AI usage limits?

- How do we securely store and retrieve learning progress?

- How should the system distinguish between a student asking for a hint and asking for the answer?

- How do we prevent users from modifying their own XP or progress?

- How should parents see useful information without exposing unnecessary student data?

- How do we make AI responses educational rather than simply giving away answers?

- How do we make the entire experience fast enough that students actually want to use it?

Security became especially important as the project grew. During testing, we discovered several places where server-side authorization needed to be strengthened, including functions that could accept arbitrary user IDs and data that could potentially be exposed to unauthenticated users.

Those issues became part of the development process rather than something we ignored for the sake of a demo.

**What We Learned**

Building Chapter taught us that an AI product is much more than the AI model.

The model might be the most visible part, but the quality of the actual product depends on everything surrounding it: authentication, databases, security, UX, state management, usage limits, personalization, and reliability.

We also learned that automated tests are not enough by themselves.

Chapter ended up with tests covering application logic, database security, and browser behavior across desktop and mobile layouts. We used those tests to catch problems that would have been easy to miss by simply clicking around the application.

Most importantly, we learned to think about AI as a system, rather than a feature.

**What's Next**

Chapter is still evolving.

The long-term vision is to make it feel less like a collection of study tools and more like a personal learning system that continuously understands what a student knows, what they struggle with, and what they should work on next.

The ultimate goal is simple:

Don't just help students get the answer. Help them become the kind of student who can get it themselves.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**What Inspired It**

Most mystery games script the moment you solve them. You pick the right dialogue option and a cutscene tells you that you were clever. We wanted a mystery where that moment is computed, where the game can check whether you actually proved something.

A phone was the obvious place to set it. People leave alibis in their texts without meaning to: "still at the studio", "left at ten", "on the ferry". In Read Receipts you get the victim's phone and nothing else.

It started as one of three ideas we stress-tested before writing any code. This one came back with a condition attached: build a real deduction engine, or don't build it.

**How it plays**

Every message that matters carries a typed claim saying who was where, and when: Nadia was at the studio from 21:40 to 22:20. You long-press a message to put its claim on the record, pin two claims on the evidence board, and run the check.

If both claims can't be true, the contradiction is confirmed and a locked thread opens. If they can, the game tells you why: different people, different times, or one place under two names. That explanation is worked out from the claims themselves, so a wrong guess still teaches you something. You can only accuse someone once every contradiction the case needs is proven, which stops anyone solving it by tapping every suspect in turn.

**How we built it**

It's an Expo SDK 57 app in React Native 0.86 and strict TypeScript, with expo-router for navigation and Zustand for state.

The rules live in src/engine/, which is plain TypeScript with no React Native imports. A test reads every file in the engine and the case content and fails the build if any of them imports a native module. That boundary is what lets the whole rule layer run under Node in milliseconds.

Cases are data, never logic. Each of the 16 scripts is validated with Zod when it loads, and a shared contract compares every pair of claims in a case. A case with $n$ claims needs

$$\binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$$

comparisons, and if any pair contradicts without the author declaring it, the build fails.

The rest of the stack:

- RevenueCat, through its Test Store, for the in-app purchase. It runs the real purchase flow without a paid developer account.

- Supabase for optional accounts and syncing progress between devices, locked down with row-level security. The whole game plays as a guest.

- A Node script that synthesises all 26 sounds (9 cues and 17 music loops), so nothing in the app needs an audio licence.

- Vitest: 5,010 tests in 142 files, and 94.8% statement coverage on the engine and state layers.

The interface and all 16 cases are also translated into Spanish, French, German and Brazilian Portuguese.

**Challenges**

No Mac and no Android SDK. We built everything on a Windows laptop. Every iOS and Android binary was compiled on EAS Build, and we tested iOS on cloud simulators through Limrun.

Test Store keys only run in debug builds. A release build carrying one shows a "Wrong API Key" alert and quits. We wrote a small key policy module that keeps the key out of release builds, and split the builds into two profiles: one for playing, one for demonstrating a purchase.

Audio that passed review and failed on a phone. Our first music sat below 300 Hz, where a phone speaker produces almost nothing, so nobody heard it. Later, message tones played once per launch and then went silent, because expo-audio reports a finished sound as not loaded and our rewind never ran. Then stopping the music didn't stop it: remove() only unregisters a player, so every stopped loop kept playing under the next one. We found the last two by reading expo-audio's Kotlin and Swift source, and each now has a test that fails if it comes back.

Writing a machine can check. 795 messages, about 20,400 words, have to read like real people texting and still hold up under a rules engine. The player also has no name, gender or face anywhere in the text, and a test enforces that too.

**What we learned**

A passing test suite is not a playthrough. Every writing mistake we found came from someone reading a case for sense, and every audio bug came from someone listening on a real phone. What tests are good for is keeping a bug fixed once a person has found it. So we stopped writing rules in comments and started writing them as tests. The comments went stale. The tests didn't.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**SongFlip – Zero-Click Music Link Redirector & Universal Playlist Engine**

**Inspiration**

Music is one of the most personal things we share with friends, family, and communities. Yet, music sharing across different platforms has been frustratingly broken for over a decade.

We’ve all experienced it: a friend sends a Spotify playlist in WhatsApp, but you subscribe to YouTube Music. Your partner sends an Apple Music album, but you’re on Tidal for Hi-Fi audio. Tapping that link breaks your listening experience completely—you’re thrust into a web browser preview, prompted to create an unwanted free account, or forced to manually search for each song.

We asked a simple question: Why can't our phones simply play songs and playlists in the music app we already pay for and love—with zero extra clicks?

That frustration sparked the creation of SongFlip.

**What it does**

SongFlip is an open-source, zero-click music link redirector, playlist converter, and universal sharing suite for Android and iOS:

- Zero-Click Interception: When you tap a supported link (Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, Deezer, Tidal, Amazon Music) in any messaging app, SongFlip intercepts it under the hood and opens it in your chosen player in under 30 milliseconds.

- Full Playlist & Album Conversion: Converts entire multi-track playlists across platforms in seconds, directly opening or queueing them in your destination streaming service.

- True Offline-First Resolver: Songs and resolved links are cached locally on your device in a persistent L1 storage layer. Even without an active internet connection, previously resolved tracks play instantly.

- Universal Smart Share Pages (songflip.link/s/): Generates a single universal link with rich social previews (OpenGraph) that lets each recipient choose their preferred music service.

- Predictive Clipboard Smart-Banner: Automatically detects copied music links in the background and presents a floating 1-tap launcher.

- SongFlip PRO (Powered by RevenueCat): Unlocks full playlist conversions, global cloud caching (&lt;10ms resolution), unlimited history, and customized per-service routing rules.

**How we built it & RevenueCat Integration**

We architected SongFlip as a high-performance cross-platform system with a modern monetization backend:

- Monetization Engine (RevenueCat):

- Integrated the RevenueCat Purchases SDK on Android & iOS to power dynamic paywalls, monthly passes, and lifetime PRO access.

- Leveraged RevenueCat's dynamic Offerings to test pricing models on the fly without app updates.

- Built an atomic voucher & promo engine using Firebase Cloud Functions connected to the RevenueCat REST API, enabling secure device-bound promotions and instant entitlement granting.

- Shared Core Engine:

- Built with Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) and Ktor, sharing 100% of URL parsing, playlist batching, regex heuristics, and telemetry between Android and iOS.

- Modern Mobile UIs:

- Android: 100% native Jetpack Compose, Material You dynamic theming, and Android 13+ Per-App Language support.

- iOS: Native SwiftUI, iOS Share Sheet Extension, Action Button / Shortcuts App Intents, and App Group storage.

- Multi-Tier Caching & Offline Pipeline:

- L1 Cache (Offline): Ultra-fast local SQLite/in-memory LRU cache (&lt;5ms) for true offline capability.

- L2 Cache (Cloud): Server-side Cloud Firestore cache (l2_song_cache) deployed in Frankfurt (europe-west3) with automated TTL pruning.

- Multi-Source Resolver: Direct Odesli/Songlink extraction combined with iTunes Search, Deezer API, and YouTube scrapers with dead-link oEmbed guards.

- Privacy-First Analytics: Completely anonymous, 100% GDPR-compliant telemetry using self-hosted Aptabase and Umami.

**Challenges we ran into**

- High-Speed Playlist Batching & Rate Limits: Parsing and resolving 50+ tracks simultaneously without hitting downstream API rate limits or degrading UI responsiveness. We solved this with a reactive concurrency pipeline in Kotlin Coroutines that chunks requests and leverages L1/L2 caches before querying upstream resolvers.

- OS-Level Link Ownership (Android 12+ & iOS Universal Links): Modern operating systems enforce strict domain verification (Digital Asset Links and AASA). We engineered frictionless entry points: instant Share Sheet (ACTION_SEND) deep linking, quick tile shortcuts, and clipboard prefetching.

- Dead-Link Traps & Regional Metadata: Matching rare tracks or regional releases often returned fan covers or YouTube Shorts. We created automated oEmbed validation guards and regex cleaners that discard invalid media before caching.

**Accomplishments that we are proud of**

- First Paying Customers from Day 1: Thanks to RevenueCat's frictionless checkout and paywall architecture, we converted our first beta users into paying PRO subscribers within hours of launch.

- Full Playlist Conversion: Scaled from single-track redirection to multi-platform playlist transfers with zero audio interruptions.

- Instant Offline Execution (&lt;5ms): Offline-first architecture ensures cached tracks launch instantly even in airplane mode.

- Full 24-Language Parity: Translated every string across Android & iOS into 24 native languages (including RTL Arabic and East Asian locales).

- Rock-Solid Reliability: Over 60 automated unit tests verifying multi-platform links, playlist edge cases, and regional domain variants.

**What we learned**

- RevenueCat eliminates monetization friction: Integrating in-app purchases natively across two platforms is notoriously painful. RevenueCat allowed us to focus 100% on core product UX while giving us enterprise-grade receipt validation, cross-platform entitlement sync, and real-time subscription analytics out of the box.

- Zero-click UX requires defensive parsing: Streaming services have dozens of domain variations (music.amazon.de, geo.music.apple.com, open.spotify.com/intl-de/). Multi-tier heuristic fallbacks are crucial for 99.9% resolution success.

- Offline-first builds user trust: Users don't care about API latency; they expect their music to open instantly. Caching aggressive resolution hashes locally made the app feel like a native OS feature.

**What is next for SongFlip**

- Fuzzy Smart Playlist Matching: Smarter acoustic fingerprinting for live versions, acoustic covers, and unreleased bonus tracks.

- much more

</details>

Managing money digitally should be simple, fast, and accessible. We were inspired by the growing need for convenient financial tools that allow people to manage their money, make transactions, and keep track of their finances from one place.

We wanted to create an eWallet that reduces the complexity of everyday financial activities while providing users with a clean and intuitive experience.

**What it does**

eWallet is a digital wallet designed to make everyday financial management easier.

Users can securely manage their wallet balance, make and receive payments, view transaction history, and keep track of their financial activity from a single platform.

The goal is to provide a simple digital financial experience that is convenient for users while creating a foundation for additional financial services in the future.

**How we built it**

We focused on creating a user-friendly interface and structuring the application around the core functions of a digital wallet.

The system is designed around key components including:

- User authentication and account management

- Digital wallet and balance management

- Sending and receiving funds

- Transaction records and history

- Payment processing

- Responsive user interface

- Secure handling of financial data

We developed the project iteratively, starting with the core wallet functionality and then improving the user experience and overall flow.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was designing a financial application that was both simple for users and structured enough to handle sensitive financial operations.

We also had to think carefully about transaction flows, data validation, user authentication, and preventing incorrect or incomplete transactions.

Another challenge was deciding which features to prioritize within the available development time. We focused on building the essential wallet experience first before considering additional functionality.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud of turning the concept of a digital wallet into a working prototype.

Our key accomplishments include:

- Creating a simple and intuitive wallet interface

- Implementing the core wallet experience

- Organizing transaction activity in one place

- Designing the project with future scalability in mind

- Creating a foundation for additional financial features

Most importantly, we created a product concept that addresses a real-world need: making everyday digital financial management simpler and more accessible.

**What we learned**

Building eWallet taught us that financial applications require more than just a good interface.

We learned the importance of thinking carefully about security, data validation, transaction consistency, and user trust.

We also learned how important it is to prioritize the core user journey when developing under time constraints.

The project helped us better understand how technology can simplify financial experiences while still requiring careful consideration of reliability and security.

**What's next for eWallet**

There is significant potential to expand eWallet beyond the current prototype.

Future improvements could include:

- QR-code payments

- Mobile money integration

- Bank account integration

- Scheduled payments

- Budgeting and expense tracking

- Savings goals

- Bill payments

- Notifications and transaction alerts

- Multi-currency support

- Improved fraud detection

- Stronger authentication and security features

- Merchant payment tools

- Financial insights and personalized recommendations

Our long-term vision is to build an accessible digital financial platform that makes payments and money management simpler, safer, and more convenient.

eWallet — Your money, simplified.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Schedio started from a problem I lived myself: as a student, I never struggled with understanding content — I struggled with knowing what to study first when three exams landed the same week. Every planning app I tried was either a generic to-do list that didn't understand academic priority, or a heavy AI tutor that solved my homework instead of teaching me how to organize my own time.

I built the first version of Schedio during my last trimester of high school (2º Bachillerato), used it myself to prepare for real exams, and it worked — it genuinely changed how I approached studying. That's when I decided to turn it into a real product for other students facing the same problem, across Spain first and beyond later.

**What it does**

Schedio turns a student's subjects, exams, and difficulty levels into a smart, distraction-free study plan. At its core is a rules-based prioritization engine — no AI black box — that weighs how urgent an exam is, how hard the student says the subject is, and their current grade in it, to tell them exactly what to focus on today.

Beyond that: a weekly/monthly academic calendar, a "Mochila" to centralize notes and study materials, focused study sessions with streaks and progress tracking, and Schedio Prime, a subscription (via RevenueCat) that unlocks expanded storage, unlimited subjects, and full planning views — while the core prioritization engine stays free for everyone, always.

**How we built it**

Schedio is built with Expo / React Native for cross-platform mobile, backed by Firebase (Auth, Firestore, Cloud Storage, Cloud Messaging) for data and push notifications, and RevenueCat for subscription management. The design system is intentionally minimal — a black/white/blue palette, Inter typography, and a Notion-inspired visual language, built to reduce cognitive load rather than compete for attention.

As a solo founder, I leaned heavily on AI-assisted development (Claude Code, Antigravity) to move fast without sacrificing product discipline — every feature gets classified as launch-blocking or post-launch before a single line of code is written, to protect the deadline.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Scope discipline as a solo founder. The hardest part wasn't technical — it was constantly resisting the urge to add "one more feature" (AI coach, social features, community) before the core product was solid. I kept a strict rule: if it doesn't block the core hook — showing a student their whole academic course in one screen — it waits for v1.1.

- Play Store compliance. Data safety forms, account deletion flows, closed testing requirements — none of it is hard individually, but doing it right from day one (instead of scrambling at the end, a mistake I made on an earlier project) took real planning.

- Positioning against well-funded competitors. Apps like Astra AI or Knowunity have huge user bases, but they solve a different problem — content and community, not organization. Staying disciplined about not copying their noise (social feeds, content marketplaces) while they had more resources was a constant judgment call.

**What I learned**

That the hardest technical problem is rarely the algorithm — it's saying no. The prioritization engine that powers Schedio took one afternoon to specify properly once I stopped treating it as vague and forced myself to write the exact formula. Everything else took discipline, not cleverness.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Shipping something a real user already depended on. Before this was a hackathon project, it was the app I used myself to get through my last trimester of Bachillerato — and it worked. That's a bar most side projects never clear.

I'm proud of the discipline behind the product, not just the code. Every feature in Schedio got tested against one question: does this block the core hook, or can it wait? That discipline meant saying no to an AI coach, social features, and "smarter" premium algorithms — even when they were tempting and even when competitors already had them — to protect a clean, focused v1.

I'm also proud that the business model doesn't compromise the product. The prioritization engine — the single most valuable thing Schedio does — is free for every user, forever. Monetization (Schedio Prime) only touches storage limits, planning horizon, and convenience features. Nothing that makes Schedio useful sits behind a paywall.

And practically: going from a stalled, paused first attempt at this idea to a working cross-platform app (Android native + iOS PWA), with real Firebase infrastructure, RevenueCat billing, and Play Store compliance handled properly from week one — as a solo founder, alongside another active project — in a two-month window.

**What we learned**

That scope is the real enemy, not complexity. The prioritization algorithm — the technical heart of the app — took one focused afternoon to fully specify once I forced myself to write the exact formula instead of leaving it as a vague idea. Almost every delay I hit came from unspecified features, not hard ones. "We need better limitations for storage" or "the app should feel more premium" cost far more time than any algorithm, because vague ideas can't be estimated — they have to be defined first.

I learned to treat AI-assisted development tools (Claude Code, Antigravity) as capable of large, autonomous changes, but only when given real context — a codebase alone doesn't tell an AI why a decision was made. Writing that context down explicitly turned out to matter as much as writing the code itself.

And I learned, again, that "we'll make it viral" is not a strategy — it's a hope with a deadline attached. The lesson from an earlier project came back deliberately this time: build a distribution plan that doesn't depend on an algorithm's mood, starting with a waiting list and real beta testers before a single piece of content goes out.

**What's next for Schedio**

Post-launch, the plan is a genuine AI Study Coach — personalized long-term study plans and study-technique recommendations — built on the behavioral data Schedio is already collecting from day one (session feedback, grades, study patterns), so it launches with real signal instead of guesswork. In a few months we want to be in the App Store but now I need more money.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I had what looked like the finished version of a career at the age of 31. 

I was an executive at Ford Motor Company in Istanbul. An office with a sofa big enough that you could sleep on it, the kind of detail that quietly says you have done it. Good pay. Personal asistant. Premium health insurance. Car with a driver, which I miss that the most to be honest. From the outside, I had everything I needed.

From the inside, I did not enjoy a single second of the job.

So I quit. Not because I hated comfort, but because comfort without joy started to feel like a well-decorated cage. In December 2025 I began learning how apps are made. Slowly, clumsily, with AI as a co-pilot and something unexpected happened. Even while I was burning money, even while nothing was guaranteed, I was enjoying myself for the first time in four years.

I now have one app that generates real revenue. It sustains itself. I earn a little more than I spend on ads. It keeps the business breathing. But it does not answer the deeper question I could not stop asking: is this adding anything true to someone’s life? In my own perspective it wasnt. 

So right at this moment, Missuo came from my fiancée.

All day we sent each other funny photos like the soft warfare of love. Pictures taken while the other was sleeping. Mid-yawn. Looking away. Completely unposed. Tiny private museums of each other. Then she said it out loud: what if we had an app like that?

I searched. Similar apps existed. None of them felt like our way of loving.

So I built Missuo the way we already share affection: private photos on each other’s screens, secret notes, miss-yous and hugs that arrive as a ping, games and questions you can play across distance. Not content for an audience. A channel for two.

That is what inspired Missuo, leaving a sofa in a corporate office for a home-screen heart that actually means something.

**What it does**

Missuo is an iOS relationship app for couples who want presence without performance.

Two partners connect with an invite code and share one private space:

Main leverage is that there are many widgets that you can use on your home screen without even opening the app and of course you need premium account to unlock all the widgets
Send any photo to your partner’s widget which is sealed, personal, only for the two of you
Leave secret messages on their home screen
Tap Love / Hug / Miss you and send it as a push, even when the app is closed
Answer daily questions and play 2-choice games from distance; answers unlock when both have replied
Keep memories, plans, moods, and a couple-aware coach
Unlock Missuo Premium through RevenueCat. Interesting part is that you only need one subscription for the whole relationship. If one of the partner is premium then the other is automatically premium as well. 
Missuo is not trying to replace conversation. It is trying to keep the thread warm between conversations.

**How we built it**

We built Missuo as a shared system for two phones, not a single-player product with a “partner” label glued on.

SwiftUI for the main experience
WidgetKit so love can live on the home screen, not only inside the app
Firebase for pairing, shared data, and partner notifications
RevenueCat for paywalls, offerings, trials, and entitlements, including a secondary decline offer
A relationship-level Premium mirror, so when one partner subscribes, both unlock; when the relationship ends, inherited access ends cleanly
Localization across multiple languages, because couples are global and intimacy should feel native
Privacy treated as a feature: partner photos, notes, and distance access should not haunt an ex’s widgets after unpair
Under the hood, the product kept teaching us the same design principle as a healthy relationship: share what should be shared, seal what should stay sealed, and never confuse noise with closeness.

**Challenges we ran into**

Building for two people is philosophically and technically harder than building for one.

RevenueCat entitlements belong to a purchaser; a couple needs a shared key to the house. We had to design Premium as something the relationship can inherit and then revoke with dignity when that relationship ends.

Widgets forced honesty. If a photo, miss-you, or secret note only works while the app is open, it is not really a daily ritual. Making presence work when the app is killed meant caring about App Groups, pushes, intents, and edge cases more than pretty screenshots.

Privacy was another kind of challenge. Couples want closeness. They also deserve boundaries. Ending a relationship had to clear partner photos, secret notes, and distance tracking. Significant other should be able to leave without leaving surveillance behind.

There was also the human challenge: learning in public, spending money while learning, resisting the temptation to only ship what monetizes fastest. Missuo took some time. It asked me to choose meaning over the easier dopamine of “another app that prints ad money.”

And yes, the unglamorous shipping challenges too: store product approvals, Test Store versus Apple keys, privacy manifests, SDK conflicts.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud that Missuo feels invented by a couple, because it was. Also if this works, then I will have right to say to my fiancee that I made an app for us and it hit it off. I can always have the upper hand in the relationship in terms of presents :)

Proud that Premium can cover both partners through RevenueCat instead of punishing love with two separate checkouts. I have never seen an app like this so making it made me feel that I have accomplished something different (Duolingo family is kinda the same but different). I especially enjoyed of making widgets, where you can send a photo to other person's widget, it was also something that I haven't seen before while making market research. Proud of all my widgets to be honest. Every each one of them have a purpose, and for the first time in making apps I have really took time to think deep for every feature. Proud of games you can play from different cities and still feel like you are playing together. Proud that the app can be playful without becoming loud.

Most of all, proud that this project exists because someone I love said “what if…”, and I finally had the courage and craft to answer with something real.

**What we learned**

I learned that a beautiful office can still be an empty room.

I learned that revenue without meaning eventually feels like another job you do not enjoy, its something just with different dashboards.

I learned that AI can accelerate building, but it cannot invent the reason to build. That reason came from quitting, from enjoying learning again, and from the funny photos my fiance and I already sent each other before Missuo had a name.

I learned that for a couples product, monetization should feel like protecting a shared home, not selling a luxury skin. RevenueCat helped turn that idea into something shippable: offerings, entitlements, and a subscription model that can belong to us.

And I learned this, maybe most clearly: the best apps are not always born from market maps. Sometimes they are born from a person you love, a camera roll full of ridiculous private photos, and the decision to finally build the life you actually want to wake up inside.

**What's next for Missuo**

After shipping Missuo to the App Store with production RevenueCat billing fully live. Keep refining relationship-level Premium. Expand the private rituals, more questions, more games, more gentle ways for a home screen to say I’m thinking of you.

Keep building with my fiance’s original spark at the center.

Also most importantly, analyzing our couples to see what they are using the most, whats their take on the app and what they want. 

It was the beginning of work that finally feels like living.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/145/574/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/145/574/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/075/009/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/075/009/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/075/010/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/075/010/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/075/011/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/075/011/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Tender relevance is not a single company-wide yes or no. The same public notice can fit one legal entity, geography, service line, or deadline policy and fail another. Small supplier teams often repeat that screening manually, lose the reasoning, and notice missing metadata too late.

TenderVerdict began with a narrow promise: turn public-procurement metadata into an explainable review queue, never a black-box bid decision. Next Gen extends that promise from one supplier profile to a bounded portfolio without taking the useful single-profile workflow away from free users.

**What it does**

TenderVerdict loads one normalized CSV or JSON notice feed and one to five supplier profiles. The deterministic core evaluates CPV fit, geography, lead time, notice type, and missing fields. Every notice becomes open_documents, watch, or reject with reasons, unknowns, provenance, and a concrete human next step.

The native macOS app adds:

- a Profile Builder for creating, reordering, validating, and saving one to five profiles;

- an import preview with record counts, normalized examples, warnings, and full-file metadata gaps;

- a complete first-profile Free queue with search, buyer/deadline/verdict filters, reasoning, safe source links, and deterministic JSON export;

- a RevenueCat-gated Portfolio Workspace that compares the same ordered notices across profiles and opens the exact evidence behind every differing result;

- explicit opt-in file continuity that stores only security-scoped bookmarks and never persists tender content, reports, review dates, or billing configuration.

TenderVerdict never produces a cross-profile score, ranking, legal conclusion, or automatic bid.

**How I built it**

The canonical qualification engine is Python 3.11+ with strict bounded schemas, deterministic JSON, atomic export, a shared review date, and SHA-256 provenance. A private embedded-core adapter normalizes workspaces, previews notice files, and executes portfolio runs inside a self-contained macOS package.

The interface is SwiftUI. It decodes the canonical reports and rejects inconsistent counts, provenance, shared notices, identities, or ordering before presentation. Stable result identities keep filtered queues and comparison drill-down aligned.

The app uses the official RevenueCat Apple SDK 5.83.0. RevenueCat controls only the native visibility entitlement; it never changes qualification results. The Test Store path covers offering load, cancellation, simulated failure, purchase, CustomerInfo refresh, relaunch recovery, and restore. Judge Access uses a RevenueCat Granted Entitlement and explicitly states that no purchase was made. No usable SDK key is committed, bundled, logged, or stored.

The reproducible builder embeds the offline Python runtime, licenses, fixtures, and Swift resources; applies and verifies an ad-hoc signature; runs worktree-independent smoke checks; and produces a checksum-paired archive. This is a competition evaluation build, not a notarized consumer release or production-billing claim.

**Challenges I ran into**

The first challenge was monetization without weakening trust. Free had to remain a complete workflow, while Premium needed to solve a coherent repeated-use problem rather than hide basic reasoning.

The second was safe continuity. Convenience often invites accidental persistence, so the feature remembers only opt-in file bookmarks and never auto-runs analysis.

The third was preserving exact profile/notice identity through search and filtering. Comparison cells resolve by stable IDs instead of filtered array offsets.

The final challenge was keeping evidence honest across source, packages, RevenueCat state, screenshots, CI, and the submission form. Test Store activity is not a real payment, and a Next Gen repository/video entry is not a public store release.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- One notice feed is normalized once and evaluated consistently for up to five ordered profiles.

- Free remains useful: one complete analysis, all notice-level reasoning, filters, source access, and deterministic export.

- Premium reveals cross-profile comparison and exact drill-down without changing a single verdict.

- Invalid input preserves the last valid report and cannot silently replace exportable evidence.

- Missing or invalid RevenueCat configuration fails closed; there is no local Premium toggle.

- The official SDK, self-contained package, source security boundaries, deterministic core, native contracts, and remote CI are all covered by reproducible checks.

- Shipaton managers confirmed that macOS is eligible without a platform-only disadvantage and that Test Store is enough for the Next Gen category.

**What I learned**

Entitlement-backed UI is strongest when billing state and domain logic remain separate. A useful free workflow makes the paid value proposition clearer, not weaker. Evidence is also part of the product: every public claim should resolve to a reproducible source, artifact, or organizer answer.

**What's next for TenderVerdict Next Gen**

Next, I want to validate the workflow with small supplier teams and add a signed, notarized distribution path. I will move from Test Store evidence to production billing only after real demand is proven. The current app remains an ad-hoc-signed competition evaluation build; it is not a consumer release, and no real payment was made.

</details>
