<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Splitting bills with roommates always ends the same way: a messy spreadsheet, a group chat full of "you owe me $12.50," and that one person who never pays up. I wanted an app that makes shared expenses boring. Log it, split it, settle it, done. No awkward conversations.

**What it does**

BrokeTogether is a mobile app that takes the awkwardness out of shared living expenses:

Households in seconds. Create a home, share an invite code, and your roommates are in. No spreadsheets, no group-chat accounting.
Flexible splitting. Every bill can be split equally, selectively among specific people, or with fully custom amounts. Groceries for everyone, dinner for two. One flow handles both.
Real-time balances. A live dashboard shows exactly who owes whom, plus smart settlement suggestions that minimize the number of payments needed to square everyone up.
Recurring expenses. Rent, wifi, utilities. Set them once and they post themselves every cycle, so the boring bills never slip through the cracks.
Shared shopping list (Pro). The whole household adds items with price tracking, marks them off as they're bought, and converts the finished list into a split expense in one tap. The grocery run becomes the expense automatically.
Analytics and insights (Pro). See where the household money actually goes with spending breakdowns by category and member, then export everything to PDF or CSV when you need receipts.
BrokeTogether Pro. Premium subscription powered by RevenueCat, unlocking the shopping list, analytics, unlimited household members, and smart payment reminders.

**How I built it**

Client: React Native with Expo, NativeWind styling, React Navigation, Axios, and Expo SecureStore for tokens.
Backend: Spring Boot 3 on Java 17, Spring Security with JWT, Spring Data JPA, PostgreSQL. Containerized with Docker and deployed on Railway.
Auth: email and password plus Google and Apple mobile sign-in, with token-based password recovery.
Monetization: RevenueCat SDK (entitlement: Broketogether Pro) handling the paywall, subscriptions, and entitlement checks, with a RevenueCat webhook keeping the backend's premium status in sync.

**Challenges we ran into**

The trickiest part was money math you can trust. Every cent has to be accounted for across splits, settlements, and recurring charges, so the balance engine got the most testing of anything in the project. Second was subscription state: keeping the RevenueCat entitlement on the device and the backend's view of "is this user premium?" consistent through webhooks took real care, since each side reports truth on its own schedule. Apple sign-in token verification on the backend was its own adventure. And through all of it, the mobile client and API had to stay in lockstep while both were still evolving.

**Accomplishments that I am proud of**

Shipped a real monetization loop. The app doesn't just demo a paywall, it runs one: RevenueCat entitlements, a working premium tier, and webhook sync so premium status survives reinstalls and device switches.
Money math that holds up. 46 backend endpoints, and the balance engine underneath them accounts for every cent across equal, selective, and custom splits, settlements, and recurring charges. That's the part I tested hardest, because it's the part users have to trust.
Two sign-in worlds, one account. Email/password, Google, and Apple sign-in all resolve to a single user identity, with secure token storage and auto-logout on the device.
A shopping list that pays for itself. My favorite feature: the household builds a shared list, checks items off, and converts it into a split expense in one tap. It's the kind of small loop that makes the app sticky.
Production-grade habits. Dockerized backend on Railway, clean controller/service/repository separation, global exception handling, and docs I can actually hand to another developer.

**What I learned**

I came in knowing Spring Boot and came out understanding mobile monetization end to end: paywalls, entitlements, webhooks, and the edge cases of app-store billing. I also learned that financial logic deserves tests before features, not after. Most of all, I learned how much polish matters in something people trust with their money. A confusing balance screen kills confidence faster than any missing feature.

**What's next for BrokeTogether**

The Shipaton build is the foundation. From here:

App store launches. Finish the Google Play closed-testing track and ship to production, then bring the iOS build to the App Store.
Smarter money features. Budgets per category with overspend alerts, receipt scanning to create expenses from a photo, and multi-currency support for households splitting costs across borders.
Beyond the household. Trip and event groups with their own balances, so the same splitting engine works for vacations and one-off gatherings.
Web dashboard. A companion web app for the full analytics and export experience on desktop.
Deeper Pro value. More premium insights like spending trends and forecasts, plus richer payment reminders.
The goal stays the same: make shared money so boring you never have to think about it.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/301/298/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/301/298/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/301/299/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/301/299/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/301/300/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/301/300/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/301/301/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/301/301/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/301/387/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/301/387/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every mainstream messenger tells you your messages are private while keeping something readable
on its own servers. Maybe not the text, but at least who you talked to and when. I wanted to see
how far the opposite bet goes: not "we promise not to look" but "we deleted the column we would
have looked at."

There's a second thread tied to the hackathon. Shipaton rewards a real monetization story, and a
privacy app that puts safety behind a paywall isn't a privacy app. So the revenue line had to be
cosmetics and nothing else. That constraint ended up shaping the product instead of being bolted
on at the end to satisfy a prize category.

**What it does**

Nearside is an end-to-end encrypted messenger. Android is the shipping build; there's a Linux desktop shell for convenience, and an iOS project that has been configured for months and has never met a Mac. One-to-one chats, group rooms, photos, video, voice notes, voice and video calls, stickers, disappearing messages. English, Spanish, German, Russian, Chinese and more are supported translations. The keys stay on the phone and the server holds nothing readable.

Twelve recovery words generate a seed that lives in the Android Keystore and never leaves the
device. Three keys come off that one seed: one for one-to-one messages, one for signing, one for
a private self-chat vault. There is no reset path, which is the honest consequence of a server
that holds nothing.

There is also no user directory. You add someone by scanning their QR code or reading eight characters out loud. The QR carries their public key along with the code, so adding them and verifying them are the same step. No separate "compare your safety numbers" screen that every app offers and nobody opens. If a contact's key changes later, the composer locks until you look at why.

Group rooms use one symmetric key sealed separately to each member, with an Ed25519 signature
checked before anything is decrypted. Every member holds the room key, so the signature is the
only thing that establishes who actually wrote a message.

The server holds ciphertext. Migration 0023 dropped the message-content column and the
server-side search function that read it, so search and conversation previews run against a local
SQLite mirror of what your own device has decrypted. Push notifications carry a sender and never
a message. That isn't a policy decision; after 0023 there is no body left to leak.

Pictures get the same treatment as text. Attachments are sealed with a random per-file key, and photos are stripped of their location data before they go out, because encryption doesn't hide GPS coordinates from the person on the other end. Chat backgrounds used to be the one image that went up in the clear; migration 0039 sealed those too, under the owner's vault key, since a wallpaper is chosen by one person and shown to nobody. The app is also excluded from Android's system backup, because the pinned attachments and the decrypted local mirror were being copied to Google Drive in plaintext by an app whose whole claim is that the server holds nothing.

Two features are built on that premise rather than around it. Sealed exchange lets two people
answer the same question without either one reading the other's answer first: you commit your own
answer when you ask, and both open at once when both exist. The withholding is a row-level policy
in Postgres, not a check in the app, because this repository is public and a check in the app is
one anyone can delete. "In this conversation" lists the dates somebody named and the links
somebody sent, read from the decrypted copy sitting on the phone, and every row jumps back to the
message it came from so you can check it yourself.

Calls are peer-to-peer. The signalling is sealed too, SDP and ICE candidates alike, because a
candidate line carries your LAN address and your public IP. It travels over a broadcast channel
that persists nothing, so there is no calls table and no record that a call happened. A ring can
be answered from the lock screen of a phone whose app the system has already killed.

The revenue line is six cosmetic theme packs sold once through RevenueCat, three themes free
forever, and donation tiers that buy nothing at all. Nothing functional sits behind a payment,
and no advertising SDK is in the build, enforced by a test that fails the suite if one ever
appears.

**How we built it**

React, TypeScript and Vite, wrapped in Capacitor for the Android shell. Supabase for auth,
Postgres, realtime and storage. libsodium does the cryptography, WebRTC handles calls, RevenueCat
handles purchases, OneSignal delivers push.

One file is the most important place in the codebase: the seal boundary, the only module allowed
to open or close a message body. Every query returns rows still sealed, and opening happens at
the one layer holding both an identity and a peer key. Everything else only ever touches
ciphertext.

Two tests exist to keep the product's claims mechanically true instead of aspirational. One fails
if a plaintext body ever reaches a database insert; the other fails if an advertising SDK shows
up in package.json or the Gradle build. The suite is 900+ tests across ~80 files, all pure logic
pushed out of components and into lib/, and CI runs it with lint and typecheck on every push.
A separate script replays every migration into a throwaway Postgres container and diffs the
result against the single-file schema, so changing one without the other fails on my machine
rather than on a live database with no undo.

Every native plugin degrades to a no-op in a browser: secure storage, the SQLite mirror, media
pinning, push, purchases. Building the Electron desktop shell taught me to stop asking Capacitor
whether it is running natively, because it answers yes on Electron, where none of those plugins
exist. The app asks its own isMobileNative() instead. Left alone, the seed would have been
written into localStorage while the UI reported hardware-backed storage, which is worse than a
crash.

**Challenges we ran into**

Publishing, first. Apple and Galaxy store wants a D-U-N-S number. Google Play wants that as well or twelve testers on a closed track for fourteen days.

The bug I learned the most from: identity was keyed to the device rather than to the account. Add
a second account on the same phone and it inherited the first one's private key. It got worse
during a switch, because the session and the key derivation were separate state, so there was a
render where the session had already become the new account while the keypair was still the old
one, and the publisher wrote the wrong public key into the new profile row. Two phones then
hashed different key material and every safety number, word list and art grid disagreed. It is
all per-account now, and the pair is resolved during render so no caller can observe a mismatched
one.

Answering a call on a locked phone whose app the system has killed was the other hard one. The
caller's topic is joined from the notification rather than from the friend list, because the
friend list arrives during the answer. The answering side announces itself the moment its topic
goes live so the caller can re-offer at once, since broadcast has no replay. TURN credentials
warm up while that happens. Capture only ever starts after the user has actually accepted: a
microphone opened on a ring nobody answered is an app listening to a room that never agreed to
it.

Dropping the content column also meant rebuilding things nobody thinks of as features. Search,
conversation previews, and date and link extraction all had to be rewritten against the local
mirror, which is the only plaintext copy that exists.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The privacy claims are enforced, not just written down. The in-app transparency screen that lists
what the server knows is built from live queries against the real schema, so a future migration
that adds a readable column changes what the screen says instead of leaving it quietly wrong.
A second screen says where the protection stops: metadata is not hidden, a rooted phone is a
compromised phone, and anyone genuinely at risk should use Signal. Most of the industry oversells
this part.

The monetization held up under its own rule. Light mode and the OLED-black theme are free,
because charging for a screen someone needs to read outdoors would be a functional paywall
wearing a cosmetic label. The largest donation tier hands over cosmetics that were already for
sale, which is the only direction a payment is allowed to move in this app.

**What we learned**

A security claim means nothing unless something breaks when it stops being true. Once the build
started failing on a plaintext body reaching an insert, every later feature got designed around
"what would make that test fail" instead of "does this look private."

The second lesson is where a rule belongs. In a public repository, a check in the client is a
suggestion: anyone can delete a line of TypeScript and rebuild the APK. So the sealed-exchange
withholding is a row-level policy with no UPDATE grant behind it, and the write paths that a row
policy cannot see got closed in migration 0034 instead of in the app.

**What's next for Nearside**

Rounding up twelve testers and getting through Play's closed track, then testing the iOS
version, which has been configured for months and has never met a Mac. After that, metadata: the
server still knows who talks to whom and when, even though it cannot read a word of what they
say.

</details>

src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/083/011/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Trading strategies are easy to imagine. The difficult part is finding out whether an idea survives realistic contact with data.

I became interested in quantitative finance because of that gap. Financial mathematics can look intimidating when it is presented only through equations, while trading platforms often hide the mathematics behind simplified interfaces. I wanted to build something in between: a laboratory where someone could take a hypothesis about markets, experiment with it, and see how it behaves without putting real money at risk.

That became Quvanti Labs.

I didn't want to build another brokerage or a system that tells people what they should buy. I wanted to build an educational quantitative research sandbox—a place where students, aspiring quants, and curious traders can explore the relationship between mathematical assumptions and market behavior.

The central idea became simple:

Don't just believe a strategy. Experiment with it.

That idea shaped both the technical system and the interface.

**What Quvanti Labs Does**

Quvanti Labs is an AI-assisted quantitative research and educational terminal.

A user can formulate a trading hypothesis, investigate it using quantitative tools, and examine how the resulting strategy behaves under historical or simulated conditions. The goal isn't to produce a magic prediction of the market. It is to make the process of questioning, testing, and stress-testing an idea accessible.

The platform is deliberately a sandbox. It does not execute real trades or provide financial advice.

Depending on the workflow, Quvanti brings together things such as:

- AI-assisted strategy/logic generation

- Historical strategy testing

- Simulated market scenarios

- Stochastic analysis

- Statistical indicators

- Hurst exponent analysis

- Strategy and performance visualization

- Quantitative experimentation and parameter exploration

- Risk-free paper-trading/research workflows

The emphasis is on experimentation rather than simply producing a green or red "buy/sell" answer.

**How I Built It**

Quvanti evolved over several months through repeated development, experimentation, debugging, self education and redesign rather than being built as one finished application in a single pass.

I started with the basic idea of an accessible quantitative research environment and gradually developed it into a much larger application.

The project combines a web application interface with computational and analytical workflows. I designed the product around the mental model of a quantitative researcher rather than a conventional consumer finance app.

That influenced almost everything in the interface.

Instead of hiding information behind many separate pages, I wanted the user to be able to see relationships between inputs, calculations, simulations, and outputs. The result is a dense, dark research-oriented interface with dashboards, charts, controls, parameter inputs, and analytical panels.

I also spent significant time on details that are easy to overlook: spacing, typography, hierarchy, component behavior, interactions, information density, and how mathematical outputs are presented.

**AI-assisted development**

I also used AI-assisted development tools during the project, particularly for initial code generation and accelerating parts of implementation.

However, Quvanti was not simply a prompt that produced a finished application.

I directed the product, researched the concepts I wanted to incorporate, designed the workflows and interface, tested features, investigated failures, debugged behavior, iterated on the architecture, and repeatedly refined the product. I also made detailed decisions about the UX and visual design.

I am intentionally being explicit about this because I don't want to present AI-assisted development as entirely manual coding, nor do I want to misrepresent the role I played in building the product.

**The Quantitative Side**

One of the most interesting parts of building Quvanti was learning how much more complicated financial experimentation becomes once you move beyond a simple historical chart.

For example, the Hurst exponent provides one way of investigating long-term dependence in a time series. In simplified terms, values around (H=0.5) are associated with behavior resembling a random walk, while values below or above that level can indicate different forms of dependence.

That led me to think differently about what a research terminal should show.

Instead of only asking:

"Did this strategy make money historically?"

I wanted Quvanti to encourage questions such as:

- What kind of market behavior did the strategy encounter?

- How sensitive is the result to different assumptions?

- Does the behavior persist under different conditions?

- What happens when the environment becomes unusually volatile?

- Is an apparent result robust, or could it simply be historical noise?

That philosophy is why Quvanti includes analytical and simulation-oriented features rather than treating backtesting as a single final score.

**What I Learned**

The biggest thing I learned was that building a quantitative application from a user perspective is much harder than implementing individual mathematical formulas.

A formula can be correct while the system around it is misleading.

For example, a backtest can produce an attractive result while still giving a false sense of confidence if the experimental setup is flawed. That made me much more interested in reproducibility, assumptions, data handling, validation, and communicating uncertainty.

I also learned that mathematical sophistication doesn't automatically create a better user experience.

A researcher might understand a complicated statistical concept, but if the interface presents its output poorly, the information becomes difficult to use. I therefore spent a large amount of time translating dense quantitative information into visual structures that could be explored rather than merely read.

Another lesson was that AI-generated code is not the same thing as understanding the software it creates.

AI can produce code that looks convincing even when the underlying behavior is wrong or the implementation doesn't match what I intended. Debugging Quvanti repeatedly forced me to become more skeptical of apparently correct output and to verify what the system was actually doing.

That changed how I approach AI-assisted programming: I now treat generated code as something to investigate and test, not something to automatically trust.

**Challenges**

**1. Turning an idea into an actual system**

The initial concept of "an AI quantitative research laboratory" sounds straightforward. Building the individual workflows and making them work together was not.

The application contains many interacting pieces, and changing one part could affect another. I had to repeatedly trace behavior across the interface, application logic, calculations, and external services.

**2. Debugging AI-assisted code**

One of the most frustrating challenges was debugging code that looked correct.

An AI-generated implementation can be syntactically valid and still produce behavior that isn't mathematically or logically appropriate. I had to learn to reproduce problems, isolate their causes, inspect assumptions, and test changes instead of simply accepting the generated solution.

**3. Making advanced mathematics understandable**

Quantitative finance has no shortage of intimidating terminology.

Hurst exponents, stochastic processes, Bayesian inference, simulations, and statistical validation can quickly become inaccessible to someone encountering them for the first time.

A major design challenge was therefore deciding how much mathematical information to expose without turning the interface into an unreadable wall of numbers.

**4. Avoiding false confidence**

This was perhaps the most important conceptual challenge.

A backtest can look impressive and still tell you very little about whether an idea will work outside the data used to test it.

That realization influenced the educational philosophy of Quvanti. The platform is designed as a research sandbox, not a machine for promising financial outcomes.

**5. Designing for exploration**

I wanted the interface to encourage experimentation rather than passive consumption.

That meant creating controls and visualizations that let users change assumptions, inspect outputs, compare scenarios, and understand how the results change.

It required considerably more iteration than simply making a collection of static charts, this led me to avoid all templates and experiment with custom UI and UX and implement one coherent theme for accessibility and ease of navigation without compromising on depth of different features.

I also tried to make the platform as comfortable and easy to navigate as possible with tiny coherent details spread on different pages, as by its core genre the platform is itself very dense so I tried my best to prevent users from being overwhelmed from not knowing where to start from or where to go after what.

I'm most proud that Quvanti became more than the original idea I started with.

It evolved into a system where software engineering, mathematical modeling, AI-assisted development, interface design, and quantitative research meet in one place.

But I am especially proud of the educational philosophy behind it.

I don't want Quvanti to tell someone:

"This strategy works."

I want it to encourage them to ask:

"Why does it appear to work, under what assumptions, and does it survive when I try to break it?"

That difference is important to me.

**What's Next**

Quvanti is still evolving.

Future work includes improving the reliability and depth of its quantitative workflows, expanding experimentation and validation capabilities, improving reproducibility, and making advanced mathematical concepts easier for students to explore.

I also want to continue reducing the distance between understanding a mathematical idea and actually experimenting with it.

Ultimately, Quvanti Labs is my attempt to turn quantitative finance from something people primarily read about into something they can experiment with.

And the experiment is still ongoing.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

This one started at an actual sabji mandi, not a whiteboard.

I was picking out tomatoes and asked the seller a simple question — "are these natural, no chemicals?" She just shrugged and said "you can tell by the colour." That's it. That's the entire food-safety system most of us grow up trusting in India — vibe checks and folk wisdom, passed down because nobody ever gave us anything better.

And it's not just chemicals. Most people I know — myself included, until I started building this — can name maybe ten fruits and vegetables by heart. Apple, banana, tomato, potato, and then it gets fuzzy. Meanwhile there's a whole stall of stuff two feet away that nobody buys because nobody knows what it even is.

I didn't want to build another generic nutrition app. I wanted to build the thing that could've actually answered that seller's question honestly — and I wanted AI to be the reason it could, not just a buzzword bolted on top.

**What it does**

Sprout Atlas is a produce field guide that tries to give you the real answer instead of a guess.

- A growing library of specimen guides covering nutrition, storage, terroir, and season — not just "here's an apple," but water content, glycemic index, peak harvest window, where it's from

- An Identify & Wash tab and a Chemicals & Post-Harvest Treatments tab on every guide — this is the part I actually built the app around. It's the honest answer to "is this natural"

- A camera-based Scanner Vision tool that identifies produce from a photo and gives you a condition read — and if it gets it wrong, you can just tell it what it actually is and it'll look again instead of leaving you stuck with a bad guess

- A Nutrition Tutor you can ask real questions, a Meal Planner, and a Rainbow Challenge to make learning feel like a game instead of homework

- A personal Atlas — saved specimens, scan history, progress — so it's not a one-time lookup, it's something that grows with you

**How we built it**

Solo, with AI woven into the actual product, not just used to help me build it faster.

The app itself is a lightweight PWA — no heavy framework bloat, just fast HTML/JS with a service worker so it actually installs and works offline. The scanner runs on a vision-capable AI model for identification, with a manual correction loop built in because I knew early on the first guess wouldn't always be right, and pretending otherwise felt dishonest given the whole point of the app. The Nutrition Tutor is a real conversational AI feature, not a canned FAQ — you can ask it something specific and it'll actually try to answer the thing you asked, not just recite a nutrition label at you.

The brand identity went through a few complete rewrites before it stuck — I killed a chalkboard aesthetic, killed a sterile Apple/Linear-style minimal look, and landed on this kraft-paper, botanical specimen-plate feel because it actually matches what the app is: a field guide, not a dashboard.

**Challenges we ran into**

Getting the Chemicals tab right was harder than I expected — it's the single most important part of the app, and it's also the part where being vague or wrong actually matters. I had to be genuinely careful not to let placeholder-sounding copy slip through into something that's meant to be the app's core promise.

The AI tutor and scanner needed real testing, not just happy-path demos — I caught it giving a technically-true-but-not-actually-helpful answer to a real question during testing, which was a good reminder that "the AI responded" and "the AI answered the question" aren't the same thing. Getting the scanner's correction loop to actually feel useful (not just a retry button) took a few passes too.

And honestly, scope. It's tempting to keep adding AI features when you're building solo and nobody's telling you to stop. I had to keep cutting things back to what actually serves the core idea — you're holding a fruit, you have a question, get you a real answer — instead of turning this into ten AI gimmicks stitched together.

**What we learned**

That the best use of AI here isn't "add a chatbot," it's picking the one or two moments where a real answer actually changes what someone does — whether to buy something, how to wash it, what it actually is. Building around that instead of around "cool AI feature" made every other decision easier, including which AI features to leave out.

**What's next**

More AI, and a lot more guides. Specifically:

- Growing the specimen library well past 500 guides, with richer detail on each one

- Expanding the AI side — smarter scanning, a more capable tutor, and AI-assisted meal and diet planning that's actually personalized, not templated

- Tightening accuracy across the board so the AI features are something people can genuinely rely on, not just something impressive in a demo

Long-term, I want this to be something families and schools in India actually trust — not just another app in the pile, and not just another app that says "AI-powered" without doing much with it.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Most relationship apps are built for dating. Once you're married or committed, the tools dry up — yet that's exactly when small, daily connection matters most. We built EmoBond to be a couple's everyday companion: a private, judgment-free AI coach plus lightweight emotional check-ins that keep two people close.

**What it does**

- AI relationship coach — talk (by text or voice) to a coach that helps you navigate the day-to-day of a committed relationship.

- Emotional check-ins — quick daily reflections that build self-awareness and shared understanding.

- Private by design — your personal reflections stay yours; couple data is protected with row-level security.

- EmoBond Premium — unlimited AI coaching conversations, unlimited check-ins, and priority AI analysis, sold as an auto-renewable subscription.

**How we built it**

- React Native + Expo (TypeScript) — one cross-platform iOS/Android codebase, shipped with EAS.

- RevenueCat (react-native-purchases) — the full subscription layer: one premium entitlement, offerings/packages, purchase + restore, and a webhook that syncs entitlements into our database. Verified live against the SDK offerings endpoint.

- Supabase — auth (Sign in with Apple), Postgres with row-level security, storage, and edge functions (including the RevenueCat webhook).

- AI — an LLM-powered coach with in-app data disclosure and consent.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Shipping a first auto-renewable subscription cleanly across a separate RevenueCat project and App Store Connect (subscription + group + build submitted together).

- Keeping intimate relationship data genuinely private (per-user RLS, not just app-layer checks).

- Paid traffic that couldn't reach the App Store. During Shipaton week, a $100 TikTok test drove 1,100+ landing-page views on our share page, but on the first day App Store Connect recorded just 7 visits to our App Store page from all sources. The cause: TikTok opens links in its own built-in browser, which can't follow Apple's redirect from an apps.apple.com link into the App Store app, so tapping Download ended on a blank page. We fixed it on Sep 30: inside TikTok, Instagram or Facebook, the button now opens the App Store app directly, with an "Open in browser" fallback if it can't, and we confirmed the fix on a real iPhone inside TikTok.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A live app on the App Store with RevenueCat wired end-to-end and verified.

- Privacy-first architecture for sensitive couple data.

- Shipped past the original submission: EmoBond IQ, real-time voice coaching, reminders, and an Android build now in closed testing.

**What we learned**

- RevenueCat's entitlement model made "is this user premium?" a one-line, cross-platform check and let us manage the paywall without app updates.

**Progress since submission**

EmoBond has kept shipping past the 5-week build described above:

- EmoBond IQ — the AI Coach tab now runs goal-aware sessions (mood, live voice or text, an outcome card with what I heard / what I noticed / one move / a script) and remembers each couple's patterns across sessions.

- Real-time voice coaching — voice sessions over WebRTC, budgeted per Premium user so cost stays predictable.

- Reminders & partner activity — daily check-in nudges, a heads-up when your partner links or reflects, and shared "Our moments" (birthdays, anniversaries, date nights).

- Safety guardrails — rate limiting, crisis-resource surfacing, and prompt-injection filtering on every AI turn.

- Now on v2.1.3 on the App Store, up from the 2.0.1 build this was originally submitted with.

- Android closed testing is open — try it today: join the tester group at https://groups.google.com/g/emobond-testers, then opt in at https://play.google.com/apps/testing/com.emobond.app and install from the Play Store (same Google account for both steps).

**What's next for EmoBond**

- Love Language Discovery — a couple assessment with a mutual-reveal mechanic and a daily action engine, the first of several relationship modules on the same chassis.

- A couple-shared subscription (one purchase covers both partners) and a tester-feedback loop to shape the roadmap.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/971/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/971/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/972/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/972/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/929/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/929/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/951/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/951/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/955/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/955/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/956/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/956/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/958/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/958/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/959/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/959/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Advice about eating better arrives in two shapes: track everything, or cook something else. Neither
helps at nine in the evening when you are already holding a packet of instant noodles. The question
people actually have in that moment is smaller and more answerable — what one thing would make this
hold me until morning?

So the app answers only that. It never asks you to remove, swap or reduce anything. There is no
domain model for subtraction, and there never will be.

**What it does**

Type what you are about to eat. You get a plain-English read on what the meal is missing and up to
three things to add, sorted by effort, chosen for where you are and what you keep in your kitchen.

- Instant noodles → crack an egg in, throw in frozen peas.

- Toast → peanut butter, a boiled egg on the side.

- The same meal in an airport gives different answers, because nothing there asks you to cook.

Two of three components is the target, and a meal that already reaches two is told so rather than
pushed toward a third. Tap "not for me" and that ingredient never appears again. Tap Add and the
combination is saved, ready to repeat.

There are no calories, no macros, no weights, no daily totals, no streak to break, and nothing to
review later. Say a meal already covers you and the app agrees and stops talking.

**How we built it**

One Compose Multiplatform codebase for iOS and Android. 91% of application code is shared by
line — 9,354 lines in commonMain against 440 Android, 298 iOS Kotlin and 227 Swift — and all 36
UI and ViewModel files are shared. Platform code is limited to app entry, haptics, notification
permission, URL opening, the push bridge, the HTTP engine and the launch screen.

Two architectural rules did most of the work:

- Dependency injection instead of expect/actual. Every platform capability is an interface
injected with Koin, so each one can be faked in commonTest with no mocking framework.

- Nothing throws across the Kotlin/Swift boundary. An uncaught exception reaching Swift kills an
iOS app instantly, with no usable trace, so every fallible operation returns a sealed result that
maps to designed copy.

The suggestions come from an authored catalogue bundled in the app: 664 meals, 123 additions, 84
ingredients. Allergen data is written by hand, never generated, and excluded from the candidate set
before anything ranks it, so a flagged allergen is structurally unreachable rather than filtered
afterwards. Missing data counts as unknown and fails closed. An LLM tier and a Cloudflare Worker exist
in the repository but are switched off in the shipped builds: everything you see answers on-device, in
under a frame, with no network at all.

Purchases run through RevenueCat's Kotlin Multiplatform SDK on both stores. Push runs through a
wrapper we wrote and published as its own Apache-2.0 library.

241 unit tests, plus 28 design guards that fail the build — not lint rules, but the product's own
constraints written down as code: no digits in a suggestion, no banned vocabulary, no shadows, no
advertising ID, no ViewModel coroutine without an exception handler.

**Challenges we ran into**

The paywall opened underneath the iOS system alert. We asked for notification permission and
raised the upgrade sheet in the same breath. On iOS the permission prompt is asynchronous, so the
sheet arrived first and sat behind it. Found while recording the demo video, fixed by making the
permission call report its answer so the sheet waits.

A push told people to try something they had just done. Tags were written once per launch, so the
"has completed a check" flag stayed false until the app was next opened — and the permission prompt
appears seconds after that first check. Our activation journey, which enters two hours after a first
session, therefore nudged people who had already used the app. The dashboard said it plainly: 36
delivered, zero clicks, five unsubscribes. We stopped the journey, wrote the tag at the moment the
check completes, and added a guard so it cannot regress.

Google Play promo codes do not grant a subscription. They attach the offer to the account and
apply it when the person subscribes, which is the opposite of Apple's offer codes. We only learned
this by redeeming our own codes and hitting the paywall. Our instructions for reviewers said the
wrong thing and would have made working codes look broken.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Live on both stores, through three review cycles, with two real defects caught and shipped rather
than discovered by users. 91% shared code including every screen. A push wrapper extracted and
published for anyone else building on Kotlin Multiplatform. And a set of guards that make the
product's promises — it only ever adds, it never shows a number that reads as a budget — into things
the build enforces rather than things we remember.

**What we learned**

Rules survive only if a script enforces them. Every guard in this repository exists because a written
rule was broken anyway.

Store mechanics differ in ways no test suite can catch. The only way to find out what a reviewer will
experience is to redeem your own codes on your own phone.

Dashboard numbers are a bug report. A zero click-through with unsubscribes is not weak copy, it is
the wrong message reaching the wrong people.

**What's next**

Direct interop for the push library on iOS so it needs no Swift shim. More authored additions, which
is the only thing that widens what the app can answer. And an honest decision about the subscription
before the season ends: the tiering means the app keeps working with the backend switched off
entirely, and we intend to preserve that.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Skipping one walk feels harmless.

Then it happens again. The streak disappears, the fitness app becomes another silent icon, and nobody notices.

That was the problem behind Pamoja. Most people already know walking is good for them. What they often lack is a reason to take the next walk today. We wanted to create that reason through the people they already care about.

Pamoja turns individual steps into a shared commitment. Families, friends and small teams work toward one weekly goal. Every walk moves the whole group forward, and every missed day becomes visible in a supportive, private circle.

The name Pamoja means “together” in Swahili. That became our guiding idea: movement feels more meaningful when it belongs to something larger than one person.

**What it does**

A user creates a private group, invites people they trust and chooses a shared weekly step goal. Pamoja reads eligible step data through Health Connect and keeps the group’s progress and leaderboard synchronized across members.

The free experience includes step tracking, groups, invitations, shared progress and leaderboards.

Premium adds the features that help a group stay together over time:

- Weekly Review preserves completed weeks and shows how the group performed.

- Plan Next Week lets the group prepare its next target and allows every member to respond with “I’m in,” “Prefer gentler,” or “Resting this week.”

- Together Trail transforms ordinary walks into a shared adventure. The group unlocks illustrated chapters through its combined movement, while each member controls their own participation.

- Multi-group Premium allows one subscriber to support more than one circle.

One person can sponsor Premium for the group, and every member receives the benefits. This makes a purchase immediately useful to several people and gives each group a natural reason to invite others.

**How we built it**

Pamoja is a native Android application built with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose.

Health Connect provides permission-controlled step access. WorkManager supports background synchronization, while the app remains usable when background access is unavailable.

Authentication, group membership and synchronized activity use Firebase Authentication and Cloud Firestore. Sensitive operations—such as Premium assignment, weekly planning and Together Trail progress—are validated through server-controlled Cloud Functions.

Subscriptions use Google Play Billing through RevenueCat. RevenueCat verifies the customer’s entitlement, while Pamoja’s backend securely assigns that entitlement to the selected group. This separation allows purchases to be restored and moved without letting the Android client grant Premium access by itself.

The interface supports light and dark themes and is localized for US English, UK English, Spanish and Hindi.

**Challenges we faced**

The difficult part was making every shared number trustworthy.

People can live in different time zones, open the app on different days and synchronize from different devices. We had to give each group one consistent weekly boundary and ensure that completed weeks remain stable after they close.

Background step synchronization brought another challenge. Android manufacturers handle background work differently, and health permissions always belong to the individual. Pamoja therefore treats background access as optional, keeps synchronization explicit and avoids exposing one member’s private health records to another.

Group Premium required careful design as well. A RevenueCat entitlement belongs to a customer, while the benefit belongs to a group. We built a server-owned sponsorship layer that verifies membership, subscription status, expiration and group capacity before granting access. One subscriber can cover the group without every member purchasing separately.

We also learned that empty states matter. A new group cannot wait seven days before the product becomes understandable. Pamoja now explains what will happen, allows planning from the beginning and presents Together Trail clearly before the first adventure starts.

**What we learned**

Accountability works best when it feels supportive rather than punishing.

A shared goal creates a simple promise: my walk helps us. Weekly history gives that promise memory. Planning gives the group a recurring ritual. Together Trail gives progress a destination.

We also learned that Premium must improve the group’s outcome. People are more willing to pay when the purchase creates lasting value for everyone they invited—better planning, preserved history and an experience they can complete together.

The strongest product loop emerged naturally:

Create a group → invite people → walk together → review the week → plan the next one → continue the adventure.

Each cycle creates another reason to return.

**What’s next**

Our next focus is deeper long-term motivation: additional Together Trails, richer group milestones, smarter summaries and more ways to celebrate progress without turning Pamoja into a noisy social network.

The vision remains simple.

A walk that would have been skipped becomes a contribution someone else can see. One contribution becomes a shared week. Shared weeks become a habit.

And the habit lasts because nobody is walking alone.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Ideas are easy.

Shipping is hard.

A student can have an idea for an app in seconds. But then the questions start.

Who actually needs this? What should I build first? Is my idea solving the right problem? How do I test it? And when is it ready to ship?

There are thousands of resources that teach programming, design, and entrepreneurship. But knowing those skills individually is different from knowing how to turn an idea into a real product.

That is the problem we wanted to solve.

ShipingIT is an interactive learning app that teaches students how to go from an idea to something real — by actually building it.

Instead of watching another course about innovation, learners enter a playful world where every lesson moves their own project forward.

Learn it. Build it. Test it. Ship it.

**What it does**

ShipingIT turns the product-building process into a journey.

Students begin by discovering a problem instead of immediately jumping to a solution. They interview characters, collect clues, identify pain points, separate assumptions from evidence, and decide what is actually worth solving.

Then they move forward.

Insight → Idea → Scope → Design → Prototype → Test → Improve → Ship.

The app includes 8 learning units, 32 core lessons, 97 authored exercises, 24 builder challenges, and six interactive games, designed around one principle:

Every lesson should leave you closer to a real product than when you started.

Ami, ShipingIT's guide, helps learners through the journey. Story chapters introduce concepts in context, while interactive exercises turn them into decisions the learner has to make.

But ShipingIT isn't only a course.

Learners also get a workspace where they can build and experiment with projects such as Lunch Lens, CampusCompass, and StudyBuddy. Each project keeps its own draft, prototype, tests, and notes so learners can iterate without losing earlier work.

Progress earns Sparks, which can unlock customization and additional experiences. Learning becomes progression — but completing a lesson is never the final goal.

Building something is.

**Designing learning around doing**

One of the most important decisions we made was to avoid turning ShipingIT into a collection of quizzes.

If we wanted to teach product thinking, the product itself needed to encourage product thinking.

So lessons are built around decisions.

Instead of simply explaining user research, ShipingIT asks you to examine evidence.

Instead of defining an MVP, it asks you to decide what belongs in one.

Instead of describing prototypes, it gives you something to build and test.

And instead of telling students that iteration matters, their projects actually change as they learn.

The result sits somewhere between a learning app, a game, and a lightweight product-building environment.

That combination became the core experience of ShipingIT.

**Validation**

26 students, from high school to university, tried ShipingIT.

- 17 completed all missions.

- 11 reported a better understanding of product validation afterward.

I used their feedback to refine the app, then tested the revised version again before finalizing it for my Shipaton 2026 submission.

**How we built it**

ShipingIT is built as a mobile app using React Native, Expo, and TypeScript.

We used Expo Router for navigation and Zustand with local persistence for progress and project state. Learning logic is separated from the interface so lesson prerequisites, rewards, recovery, and progression can be tested independently from individual screens.

That became especially important because progression is not simply a list of completed lessons.

If a learner changes an important decision earlier in a project, later work may depend on it. ShipingIT has to understand that dependency rather than pretending nothing changed.

We also wanted the app to feel alive.

Original characters, illustrations, motion, haptic feedback, interactions, and small moments of personality are used throughout the experience. Reduced-motion options and alternative interactions were added so those details do not become requirements for using the product.

For accounts and backend services, we use Supabase.

Optional AI assistance is routed through a server-side backend using OpenRouter, keeping model credentials away from the client. AI-generated responses and authored learning content are deliberately distinguished, and AI does not determine lesson completion or rewards.

That was intentional.

AI should help a student think — not do the thinking for them.

**Building monetization into the product**

We didn't want monetization to appear as an unrelated paywall added at the end of the project.

So we asked a different question:

What should always be free, and what creates enough additional value that someone might choose to pay for it?

The core learning journey remains available after sign-in.

ShipingIT Pro extends the experience with additional helpers, bonus labs, expanded customization, and Project Pack capabilities.

We integrated RevenueCat to manage offerings, localized pricing, entitlements, purchase state, and restore flows. During development, we use RevenueCat's sandbox/Test Store environment so the complete purchase experience can be tested without pretending that development transactions are production revenue.

RevenueCat therefore isn't just an SDK connected to the project.

It defines a real boundary in the product:

Learning how to build should remain accessible. Power tools can support the business around it.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest problems were not the screens.

They were the invisible systems behind them.

**Making progress trustworthy**

A reward should only be earned once.

A failed save should recover safely.

One project should never overwrite another.

And if an earlier decision changes, dependent work needs to respond correctly.

Those rules sound small individually, but together they determine whether learners can trust the app.

**Making learning feel like building**

There is a difficult balance between giving students guidance and simply giving them answers.

Too much explanation turns the experience into a textbook.

Too little structure makes a beginner feel lost.

We iterated around short explanations followed quickly by interaction, decision-making, and building.

**Connecting real native services**

RevenueCat, authentication, local persistence, AI services, haptics, and mobile behavior all work differently from a static prototype.

We learned that successfully compiling an SDK is not the same as proving that the experience works.

So we separated states such as loading, unavailable, sandbox, restored, and successful instead of hiding them behind a perfect demo.

That made ShipingIT less magical internally — and much more reliable.

**What we learned**

The biggest lesson from building ShipingIT is also the lesson ShipingIT tries to teach:

Shipping changes how you think.

An idea can sound perfect when it exists only in your head.

Once you turn it into screens, interactions, state, edge cases, pricing, and an actual build, the unanswered questions become visible.

We learned to reduce scope.

We learned to design systems instead of isolated screens.

We learned that playful design only matters when the underlying experience is dependable.

We learned that monetization is a product decision, not just a payment screen.

And we learned that sometimes the most important feature is simply making the next step obvious.

ShipingIT became better when we stopped asking:

"How much can we add?"

and started asking:

"What does the learner need to do next?"

**What's next**

ShipingIT is already a working Android development preview, but this is only the first version of the idea.

Next, we want to put the complete journey in front of more students and observe where they hesitate, what they skip, what they enjoy, and — most importantly — whether they can take what they learn outside ShipingIT and use it to build something of their own.

We want to improve the curriculum from real learner feedback, expand project-building tools, strengthen export capabilities, validate the full native experience across platforms, and eventually let learners take a project from their first insight all the way to something they can actually share with the world.

Because ShipingIT isn't really about teaching students how apps are made.

It's about helping them experience the moment when an idea stops being an idea.

And becomes something real.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Inspiration
Perimenopause and menopause are too often treated as taboo or purely clinical. Women experience sweeping changes in energy, mood, and sleep, but most health trackers treat every day in isolation—forcing users into endless manual data entry. We wanted to build a "gentle companion"—an app that understands the seasons of a woman's body and proactively reaches out, rather than just being a sterile medical log. 

What it does
Inner Seasons is an AI-powered wellness companion designed specifically for perimenopause and menopause. 
• Frictionless Tracking: It securely syncs daily biometrics (HRV, skin temperature, sleep) via Health Connect, so the app knows how you're doing without you having to type a word. 
• Proactive AI: You can chat with "Sage," your AI companion, about your symptoms. Thanks to our OneSignal integration, Sage doesn't just wait for you to open the app—she proactively reaches out with personalized push notifications to check in on you.
• Wellness Space: Users can explore a library of restorative frequencies (optimized for relaxation and clarity) and interactive podcasts covering hormone tracking and menopause management.
• Premium Insights: Powered seamlessly by RevenueCat, our premium tier unlocks advanced hormonal forecasting and deep pattern detection (e.g., flagging nighttime temperature spikes as possible night sweats).

How we built it
• Frontend: React Native and Expo (EAS).
• Subscriptions & Entitlements: RevenueCat handles our entire paywall logic, entitlement verification, and subscription state, allowing us to gate premium AI insights effortlessly.
• Push Notifications: OneSignal drives the proactive AI check-ins, allowing the system to securely route users straight into personalized check-in flows.
• Biometrics: Health Connect API for seamless integration with wearables (Samsung Health, Galaxy Watch, Oura).
• Intelligence: Advanced LLM integrations power the conversational AI, strictly bounded by medical disclaimers to ensure safe, non-diagnostic empathy.

Challenges we ran into
Handling Android 15 edge-to-edge UI updates, securely managing local biometric data without compromising user privacy, and ensuring the AI stayed within strict, non-diagnostic medical boundaries. Calibrating the OneSignal push notifications to trigger based on AI-detected patterns (rather than annoying, generic daily reminders) required deep architectural planning.

Accomplishments that we're proud of
We are incredibly proud of the frictionless nature of the app. By tying Health Connect directly to the AI's context window, the user doesn't have to manually type "I slept poorly." The app already knows your HRV dropped, and Sage proactively reaches out via a OneSignal push notification to offer grounding exercises from the Wellness Space. We've built an app that actually feels alive.

What we learned
Integrating RevenueCat saved us days of backend billing logic and receipt validation, allowing us to focus entirely on the AI and the user experience. We also learned how to fine-tune AI system prompts to be empathetic and supportive rather than purely clinical. 

What's next for Inner Seasons
We have a massive roadmap ahead! First, we are expanding our OneSignal integration to create fully offline, agentic background loops—allowing the AI to orchestrate multi-day care plans. Secondly, we plan to introduce 3D, dynamically animated AI avatars that can change their facial expressions in real-time based on the sentiment of your conversation.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**🚀 Herbei — Project Submission**

**💡 Inspiration**

We live in an age of information overload. We take dozens of photos, write quick notes, and capture moments every day—yet finding a specific detail later feels like finding a needle in a haystack. Traditional keyword search fails when you can't remember the exact words you used, and cloud-based AI solutions raise major privacy concerns when analyzing personal photos and daily thoughts.

We built Herbei to solve this. Inspired by the concept of a "Second Brain," Herbei is a privacy-first, 100% on-device AI assistant that automatically understands images, creates semantic memories ("Neurons"), and lets you search your life using natural language—without a single byte leaving your phone.

**📱 What It Does**

Herbei is an intelligent, privacy-first Semantic Memory Assistant that acts as your personal "Second Brain." Here is how it works:

- Visual Understanding: Capture a photo or pick an image from your gallery, and Herbei's local Vision AI (SmolVLM2) automatically analyzes the image and generates a detailed description.

- Semantic Embedding ("Neurons"): Converts images, text notes, and tags into 384-dimensional vector embeddings, storing them as interconnected memory nodes ("Neurons").

- Natural Language Search: Find anything using conceptual queries instead of rigid keywords. Searching for "where did I leave my prescription" or "items from my trip to the park" instantly finds the right memory even if those exact words weren't typed.

- Memory & Node Exploration: Provides an interactive dashboard to explore past memories, search history, and tag networks with instant swipe-to-manage controls.

- 100% Offline & Private: All AI inference, image processing, and database storage happen strictly on your device. Your personal moments never touch a cloud server.

**🛠️ How We Built It**

Herbei is engineered as a modern, local-first Android application built with a Feature-based Clean Architecture:

- On-Device Vision AI: Integrated SmolVLM2-500M using Google’s LiteRT (TensorFlow Lite) Engine to analyze and describe photos locally.

- Semantic Search Engine: Utilized ONNX Runtime with the Sentence Transformer (MiniLM-L6-v2) model to convert descriptions and tags into normalized 384-dimensional vector embeddings.

- Vector Matching: Implemented a custom, high-performance Cosine Similarity algorithm in Kotlin to rank and retrieve memories semantically in real time.

- Local Data Persistence: Built with Room Database, using custom Little-Endian ByteBuffer converters to store high-dimensional float vectors compactly and efficiently.

- Modern Android Stack: Built entirely in Jetpack Compose (Material 3), Jetpack Navigation 3, Koin for Dependency Injection, and Ktor for chunked binary model downloads with real-time progress reporting.

**🚧 Challenges We Ran Into**

- Edge AI Memory & Hardware Limits: Running both a Vision-Language Model (VLM) and a Sentence Transformer on a mobile device required strict memory lifecycle management to avoid OutOfMemoryError during inference.

- Efficient Vector Storage: Standard JSON/string serialization for 384-element float vectors was slow and bloated Room database reads. We solved this by implementing direct binary ByteBuffer conversion, cutting storage overhead by 75% and speeding up vector loads.

- Large Model Onboarding: Distributing ~500MB of AI model weights required building a robust streaming downloader using Ktor channel buffers to prevent memory spikes and handle connection interrupts gracefully.

**🏆 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of**

- Running Multimodal AI 100% On-Device: Successfully executing both a Vision-Language Model (SmolVLM2) and a Sentence Transformer model locally on an Android device with minimal battery overhead and fast inference times.

- Sub-Millisecond Semantic Vector Search: Implementing custom Kotlin-native Cosine Similarity vector matching that searches through hundreds of high-dimensional embeddings instantly without UI jank.

- Ultra-Efficient Binary Vector Storage: Bypassing slow JSON parsing by engineering a custom ByteBuffer binary converter in Room, cutting vector storage size by 75% and making database reads lightning-fast.

- Polished Onboarding & Architecture: Crafting a smooth initial download flow for 500MB+ model weights using Ktor streaming channels, backed by a clean Jetpack Compose & Navigation 3 architecture.

**🎓 What We Learned**

- The Power of On-Device AI: Modern Edge AI frameworks (LiteRT & ONNX Runtime) are now mature enough to build rich, private, cloud-independent applications directly on phones.

- Vector Mathematics in Kotlin: Deepened our understanding of high-dimensional vector spaces, embedding normalization, and optimizing matrix similarity math for mobile CPUs.

- Cutting-Edge Jetpack Libraries: Mastered the new Jetpack Navigation 3 API and state synchronization patterns for Jetpack Compose.

**🔮 What's Next for Herbei**

- Encrypted Cloud Backup & Multi-Device Sync: Implement End-to-End Encrypted (E2EE) cloud backup, allowing users to securely back up their memory database to a server and sync across devices without compromising zero-knowledge privacy.

- Encrypted Secure Vault for Sensitive Info: Integrate biometric authentication (Fingerprint / Face Unlock) and AES-256 hardware encryption to let users safely store sensitive documents, personal credentials, and private notes.

- Interactive 3D Knowledge Graph: Build a visual 2D/3D graph view of "Neurons" so users can visually explore clusters of connected memories, tags, and ideas.

- System Widgets & AI Agent Shortcuts: Add homescreen widgets and Android AppFunctions integration to allow instant one-tap visual capture and voice-activated memory search without opening the app.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We are a group of Singaporean friends living in Toronto and Waterloo. Since we came to Canada in January, we've been sending each other reels on the many events and activities that Canada has to offer, yet we kept losing track of all of them... 

What we had was a mess of posts and reels in an Instagram group chat, and a burning desire to bring our plans out of it. We wanted to make something out of that mess, that 'ruckus' of half-baked plans, which is what birthed Ruckus. 

**What it does**

Smart Event Capture

Users can send an event or place they discover online directly into Ruckus. The app analyses the content and extracts useful information such as the event name, location, date, time, and category. 

Dens: Sharing with friends

Every friend group has its own Den: A shared space containing the places and events that group wants to explore together. Rather than losing ideas across multiple group chats, everyone in the Den can contribute to the same shared collection.

Expressing Interest

Saving something does not necessarily mean committing to it. Friends can indicate that they are interested in an event first, allowing the group to see where interest naturally overlaps before anyone has to finalise a plan.

Map View

Saved events and places can be explored geographically, helping users understand what is happening nearby and identify things their group wants to do in the same area.

Grouped by Time

Ruckus also organises plans by time, giving groups visibility into what is happening today, this week, or later. This turns saved inspiration into something that can actually fit into a group's schedule

Notifications

Remember that event you saved? Well, it happened last week. The good news is that Ruckus won't forget your next events like you did. Users can choose to be reminded of when an event is upcoming and which friends have already expressed interest. 

**How we built it**

We built it as an npm-workspaces monorepo: an iOS app using React Native, Expo, and TypeScript; shared JavaScript packages for the API and data processing; a Node.js/Express proxy deployed on Railway; and a Supabase backend with Postgres and SQL migrations. The proxy connects to Claude Haiku 4.5 via OpenRouter for place extracting and Google Places for geocoding, keeping their API keys off the mobile app. We tested the code with Node’s test runner, database tests, an extraction harness, and TypeScript checks. And finally, we used RevenueCat for handling our freemium model. 

**Challenges we ran into**

Legality of what we were doing :0

We initially almost scrapped the idea when we ran into Instagram's Terms of Use, and how us scraping Instagram posts for information could potentially be legally touchy. The good thing was that some more research landed us with a user-flow that would circumvent this. When a user shares a reel, the app fetches that one public page while logged out. It reads the three link-preview tags (og:title, og:description, og:image), plus one extra fetch per tagged @handle to get the business name (the same request other apps like imessage or slack makes to show a link preview). We have no account, session cookie, token, logged-in WebView, proxy rotation or rate-limit evasion, and we don't crawl. Each fetch happens because a person chose to share that link.

Actually Shipping the App

While we were mainly gunning for the Next Gen Award, we started thinking to ourselves: What if this was a real app?

And hence we began tackling the admin of actually bringing this to life. Navigating the legal stuff, drafting our own TOS and privacy policy, ensuring compliance, making sure the subscription stuff was properly implemented, maintaining accuracy of info, getting it available on TestFlight for people to be able to test it properly, were all a huge challenge. 

Unfortunately, we were unable to have the app published on the iOS App Store before the submission deadline :( but if you are a fan of this project, please stay tuned, this may very well be real soon!

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Data extraction
Our data extraction engine works really reliably and well! It's also way faster than we imagined it would be

Frontend and Music
We made an app that we ourselves find a joy to use, with cute music and visuals that keep us coming back. The user experience as well is smooth and enjoyable. 

Notification engine
We spent a while debugging the notification feature, so ultimately getting it to work reliable and non-intrusively was a huge accomplishment. It's also a feature that we ourselves find super useful. 

**What we learned**

Making the User Experience Intuitive
It was a journey, running through our frontend again and again as users, and learning how many features were designed with intention that we so easily overlook as consumers. Making the app intuitive depended so much on the features, the platform, the screen size, all these factors played a role. We never quite realised how nitpick-y we were with our apps until we had to make one ourselves. 

Whimsy on the Frontend
What would make users come back to our app? What could we do to drive home the message and value of our creation? Fleshing out the storyline of our animal pals and our main guy, Rascal the Raccoon, was crucial to the design language of our app. Rascal, together with his currently unnamed Squirrel, Chipmunk and Possum friends, would dig through their trashcan, their Ruckus, and find treasure. Through this story, we wanted users to form a personal connection with our app and whimsy, and keep coming back. 

**What's next for Ruckus**

Due to the lack of time, we scrapped a client-facing part of the app that we initially planned for. We wanted the platform to also support event organisers, allowing them to post their own events and pay a premium to have them be advertised or recommended to users of Ruckus. This would also have been another stream of revenue for the app. Past this submission, this would be our next goal. 

We would also like to come up with some names and backstories for our critters, and flesh out the visuals and animations and have a more cohesive design language throughout the app. 

Overall, we are excited to have our app out on the iOS App Store, and we can't wait to see what others think of our creation.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Students have access to more learning materials than ever, but having information is not the same as learning effectively. Many students spend hours rereading lecture notes, PDFs, and textbooks, yet still struggle to remember key concepts, test their understanding, and organize their revision.

This inspired me to build BrainySpark, an AI-powered, offline-first study companion designed around one simple goal:

Learn more in less time and smarter.

I wanted to create a tool that helps students move from simply consuming information to actively understanding, practicing, and reviewing what they learn.

**What it does**

BrainySpark transforms study materials into personalized learning resources.

Students can use BrainySpark to:

- Turn study material into AI-generated flashcards

- Review cards using active recall and spaced repetition

- Generate summaries, key concepts, definitions, and quizzes

- Capture learning material through supported text and document workflows

- Use a free-first experience, with additional capabilities available through Pro

- Manage Pro subscriptions and purchases through RevenueCat

- Keep their learning experience centered around an offline-first local learning space

The core workflow is simple:

Capture → Generate → Understand → Practice → Review

**How we built it**

BrainySpark was built as a Flutter/Dart Android application, with a service-based architecture designed to keep the major components separate and replaceable.

The learning system uses an AI service layer for generating structured learning content such as flashcards and study resources. The application is designed so the AI provider can be changed without rewriting the core learning experience.

For local-first learning, BrainySpark uses Isar for structured local data and persistence.

For monetization, we integrated RevenueCat with its Test Store for development and testing. The Pro experience is based on RevenueCat entitlements rather than a fake payment system.

The broader architecture also includes:

- Supabase for cloud-related functionality

- OpenRouter for configurable AI access

- Fish Audio for text-to-speech/podcast functionality

- Flutter's Android ecosystem for device capabilities and file workflows

The application was developed incrementally, with each major capability tested on a physical Android device.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was building a feature-rich AI application while working with limited development hardware and real-world mobile constraints.

We encountered Android build and dependency problems, including Java, Gradle, NDK, and AAPT2 issues. Some builds took a significant amount of time, which made repeated debugging difficult.

We also had to troubleshoot configuration issues involving AI providers and RevenueCat. In particular, the application initially built successfully but did not receive the development configuration required for AI and RevenueCat at runtime.

Another challenge was designing the Pro experience so that a user could move naturally from a locked feature to the RevenueCat paywall and then to entitlement-based access.

Finally, integrating AI introduces challenges such as provider rate limits, malformed responses, network delays, and the need for reliable error handling.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are humble that BrainySpark became a real installable Android application, rather than remaining only a prototype or concept.

We successfully implemented and demonstrated the core learning loop:

Study material → AI-generated flashcards → preview → review → active recall

The review system supports Again, Hard, Good, and Easy, creating the foundation for spaced repetition.

We also integrated RevenueCat into the Pro experience and successfully connected the upgrade flow to the Test Store for development testing.

Another accomplishment is the offline-first direction of the product. BrainySpark is designed so the student's local learning space remains useful even when internet connectivity is unavailable.

Most importantly, BrainySpark brings multiple study activities into one experience instead of treating flashcards, quizzes, summaries, and review as completely separate tools.

**What we learned**

We learned that building an AI application is not only about selecting a powerful model. The surrounding architecture matters just as much.

Reliable configuration, API error handling, structured responses, loading states, caching, local persistence, subscription entitlements, and mobile performance can determine whether an AI feature actually works for users.

We also learned the importance of testing on a real physical device. A feature that works during development can behave very differently when network conditions, device resources, permissions, and mobile storage are involved.

Most importantly, we learned to design BrainySpark around the student's learning workflow, rather than simply adding AI features because they are technically possible.

**What's next for BrainySpark**

The next phase is to move BrainySpark from a hackathon-ready product toward a production-ready learning platform.

We plan to improve and expand:

- Text-to-podcast, including more reliable TTS processing, audio caching, and offline playback

- PDF, image, OCR, and voice capture

- More advanced AI study assistance

- Stronger spaced repetition and progress tracking

- Cloud synchronization and multi-device learning

- Better personalization and study recommendations

- More robust performance, error handling, and security

- Production RevenueCat and Google Play integration

- Broader testing with real students and feedback from users

Our long-term vision is to make BrainySpark a practical learning companion that helps students turn almost any study material into a structured, personalized learning experience.

BrainySpark — Learn more in less time.

</details>
