<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

ANIMA is the Italian word for soul. We built this project because we believe culture is what gives a city its pulse. Without local music, art, street markets, and regional food, a city is just concrete, traffic, and a repetitive daily grind. 

Right now, local culture has a serious visibility problem. You could be sitting at home or working at your desk while an amazing exhibition or show is happening two blocks away, and you’d never know. To find out what's happening around you, you currently have to follow dozens of random Instagram accounts, hope you catch an ad on local radio, or just get lucky enough for someone to invite you (not in the sad way, we promise!).

We made ANIMA to fix this. It’s a space built to make local culture accessible to everyone, giving artists a place to be seen and helping people actually live in their city instead of just passing through it.

**What it does**

ANIMA connects local creators with people looking for something real to do in their city through two straightforward roles:

**Visitor Flow**

- Feed & Discovery: Browse local events categorized by "Happening Now", "Events I'm Attending", and "Following". Users can filter events by location, date, or category.

- Event Details: Check out dates, exact locations, rules, and schedules (whether it's a one-time thing or a recurring event). You can see real-time updates on event status (ongoing, upcoming, postponed, or canceled).

- RSVP: Tap once to mark "I'm going". This automatically saves the event to your personal "Events I'm Attending" tab so you don't miss it.

**Expositor (Organizer) Flow**

- Create Events: Post cultural events with details, rules, schedules, categories, and location tags.

- Dashboard: Manage active events and update their status in real time (e.g., changing an event from upcoming to ongoing, postponed, or canceled).

- Expositor Profile: Account verification for organizers to build trust with the community, alongside a dedicated host feed view.

**How we built it**

We built ANIMA with a decoupled, feature-first architecture to keep the codebase clean and maintainable as the app grows:

- Backend: Kotlin with Spring Boot, handling our REST API and business logic. All database operations are locked behind the backend, running on PostgreSQL.

- Mobile App: Built using Compose Multiplatform with an MVVM pattern and StateFlow for state management. Client-side dependency injection is handled by Koin.

- Custom Design System: We chose not to use default MaterialTheme UI components. Instead, we built our own design system from scratch using local tokens (core.theme) for colors, typography, spacing, and border radius. Our global icon component renders SVGs directly from Lucide Icons.

- Localization: Set up using composeResources with built-in support for English (default), Portuguese, and Spanish based on system language.

- Infrastructure: Hosted on Google Cloud Run and Firebase (analytics and web hosting). We enforced standard Git practices using type/module/label branching and Conventional Commits.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Backend Migration: Switching our backend strategy to Spring Boot mid-way meant refactoring our architecture and API integration while keeping Kotlin models aligned.

- Building UI from Scratch: Ditching default Material components gave us complete visual freedom, but it meant building every button, card, and layout component ourselves in Compose.

- Feature-First Discipline: Keeping the code separated into clear layers (data, domain, and presentation) took constant discipline to ensure feature modules remained truly independent.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Our Own Design System: Achieving a unique, cohesive visual identity that feels custom-built for ANIMA rather than a generic template.

- Clean Kotlin Integration: Connecting a Spring Boot backend smoothly with a Compose Multiplatform app without sacrificing clean code standards.

- Solving a Real Problem: Building a working tool aimed at solving an issue we personally experience in our hometown every day.

**What we learned**

- Modular Architecture: How to properly structure a feature-first Kotlin project to separate domain logic from UI and data layers.

- Design Token System: How building custom color, spacing, and typography tokens early on saves time when constructing UI screens.

- Spring Boot + Kotlin: Best practices for writing clean REST endpoints using Spring Boot in a Kotlin environment.

**What's next for ANIMA**

- Interactive Map: Adding a visual map to find street fairs and outdoor events near you.

- Direct Organizer Contacts: Allowing organizers to link their direct social media/contact channels on event pages.

- Push Notifications: Alerting users via Firebase when an event they saved is about to start.

- Community Feedback: Adding reviews, ratings, and reporting tools to build trust across the community.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/431/452/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/431/452/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/431/577/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/431/577/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

As someone balancing several areas of life at once, I found it hard to plan my days, and even 24 hours never felt like enough. I wanted a simple way to manage my time and stay consistent, so I built Ascend: one place to plan your daily tasks and build the habits you want to keep. Most apps focus on either tasks or habits, and Ascend brings both together in a single app.

**What it does**

Ascend is a cross-platform mobile app for tracking tasks and building habits. You can add daily to-dos and mark them complete, and log habits with streak tracking that calculates your current and longest streaks. A home dashboard shows your open tasks and active habits at a glance. Login and signup use JWT authentication, so your data stays synced and secure across sessions. It runs on both iOS and Android with a dark-mode interface.

**How we built it**

The frontend is React Native with Expo, using Expo Router for file-based navigation across the home, tasks and habits tabs. Styling is custom StyleSheet code with a shared colour palette. State is handled with React Hooks, and AsyncStorage keeps the user's session on the device. The app talks to a backend API using the Fetch API, and JWT tokens handle authentication. The backend is built with Python's FastAPI framework and uses PostgreSQL to store all the app's data.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest part of Ascend was getting habit streaks to work reliably. A streak looks simple on screen, but it depends on every habit session being stored correctly, so I had to design how each completion is logged in the database and how the current and longest streaks are calculated from those logs.

A key problem was stopping duplicate entries. Without a check, a user could log the same habit several times in one day and inflate their streak, which would defeat the purpose of the app. I fixed this by making sure a habit can only be logged once per calendar day, so a second attempt on the same day is rejected. I enforced this on the backend so it holds even if the app sends a repeat request.

Streaks also needed careful handling of dates: deciding when a streak continues, when it resets after a missed day, and when it becomes the new longest streak. Small mistakes here made the numbers wrong, so I tested it against different scenarios such as consecutive days, a skipped day and a repeat log on the same day.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I'm proud of building a complete working app for the first time, from the mobile frontend to a FastAPI and PostgreSQL backend. It covers the full flow from signup to daily use: authentication, task management, habit tracking with real streak logic, and a dashboard that ties them together. I'm also proud of the polish, with a consistent dark-mode design and custom components rather than default styling.

**What we learned**

Ascend was my first time building a mobile app, so a lot of what I learned was about how app development differs from the web projects I'd done before. I learned how a React Native app is structured with Expo, including file-based navigation with Expo Router, splitting an app into screens and tabs, and building reusable components with a consistent style. I also found that mobile brings its own concerns, like designing for a small screen, testing on both an emulator and a physical device, and keeping the experience consistent across iOS and Android.

I also learned how a mobile app and a backend work together. Building login and signup with JWT authentication showed me how much sits behind a simple screen: the app has to send credentials, store the token, attach it to later requests and handle failures. Working with FastAPI and PostgreSQL taught me that the rules of the app, like one log per habit per day, belong on the backend where the data is stored, and not only in the interface.

**What's next for Ascend**

Next, I plan to add notification reminders for each task and habit, and let users schedule their tasks for particular times of the day. I'd also like to add gamification features to help users stick to their daily commitments and remember to check in every day, which goes back to the problem that made me build Ascend in the first place.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I built Perchie because I lived it. Chasing this dream, I'd get so locked into building that I forgot to take care of myself. Skipped meals, ignored water, sat in the same terrible posture for hours.

I didn't want any other builder to end up like me.

Everything out there measures output or demands attention. Productivity trackers make you anxious about numbers. Task managers make you stop and context-switch. I needed something that cared about me, not my metrics, without ever breaking my flow.

**What it does**

Perchie is a tiny wellbeing companion that lives right in your MacBook's notch. It quietly watches safe, private signals in the background: how long you've been focused, your idle time, your calendar, and checks in at the exact right moment. Not on a rigid timer. It waits for a natural pause in your work, then drops down from the notch to ask if you need water, a stretch, a meal, or a break.

Every check-in is a single tap. No typing, no chatbot, no leaving your flow. Pick one of six personalities, Mom, Homie, Assistant, Mentor, Coach, or Spark, and Perchie talks to you the way you'd actually want to be talked to.

It's not a productivity tracker. It's a companion looking out for you while you're locked in.

**How I built it**

Built entirely native for macOS with Swift, SwiftUI, and AppKit, targeting the newest OS.

- Design: A custom Liquid Glass system for the notch drop-down and dashboard, glassEffect throughout, built to feel like a real part of macOS rather than an overlay bolted on top.

- Personality voice: Every check-in line is hand-written, two natural variants per personality per situation, chosen by an anti-repeat picker so Perchie never says the same thing twice in a row. It's the writing, not live generation, that makes Mom sound like Mom and Coach sound like Coach.

- PerchBrain: A local memory store that learns your habit timing (when you actually eat, drink, shower, focus) via rolling histograms and feeds that back into every check-in so the companion sounds like it knows you.

- Monetization: RevenueCat with StoreKit 2, a 3-day full-access trial with zero features held back, then a straightforward paywall.

- Shipping-prep: Audited the app against Apple's App Review guidelines before ever submitting, fixing what I could find on my own first.

**Challenges I ran into**

Keeping an always-on menu bar app from eating CPU meant leaning entirely on event timing and idle detection instead of polling. Getting the notch panel to drop down without stealing window focus took real NSPanel/AppKit work most SwiftUI apps never touch.

Auditing against App Review guidelines ahead of submission surfaced real bugs I'd have otherwise shipped: a permission button phrased "Allow" that would have visually doubled up with the system's own calendar-access dialog (Apple's guidance is to use neutral wording like "Continue" instead), and black text on a dark background that only shows up under macOS Light Mode, something I never caught locally because the app forces dark mode everywhere. That one taught me .preferredColorScheme(.dark) in SwiftUI doesn't fully reach AppKit-backed controls like DatePicker inside a Form. Every raw window in the app now sets its real NSAppearance explicitly.

Late in the process I also cut WeatherKit and location-based sky entirely, in favor of a simple day/night-only sky. One less permission to ask for, one less thing that could break.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- The design. The notch integration and glass animations feel premium enough that people assume it's an Apple feature, not a hackathon build.

- The non-toxic voice. Perchie never lectures, never mentions productivity metrics, never guilt-trips. It's strictly on your side.

- Catching my own mistakes first. Auditing against Apple's actual guidelines before submitting instead of finding out the hard way after a rejection.

**What I learned**

I started by generating every check-in line live with on-device Apple Intelligence. It taught me fast that small on-device models can't be trusted with logic, only with words. I once asked the model to judge "is it late right now" from a timestamp in the prompt. It couldn't, and told users to go to sleep at 2 PM. Worse, the phrasing drifted: sometimes warm, sometimes oddly stiff, never quite as consistent as a real personality should feel. I eventually replaced live generation with a hand-written message library instead, and the check-ins got more consistent, not less personal. Decide in code, write the words yourself, and a reminder app becomes something you can actually trust to sound right every time.

Choices beat conversation for a reminder app. I built a full chatbot with dictation, then watched it pull people away from the one thing Perchie is for. Nobody deep in focus wants to compose a message. They want to tap "drank water" and get back to work. I deleted the entire chat path rather than leave it dormant behind the UI.

Apple's guidelines are specific, not vague opinions. Reading them literally before submitting caught real bugs, wording that reads as a false permission prompt, black text nobody would see in dark mode alone, that I'd have otherwise found out about the hard way.

Dark mode in SwiftUI is a promise the framework makes, not a guarantee AppKit keeps. A .preferredColorScheme(.dark) on a view doesn't automatically reach a raw NSWindow hosting it. Set the real appearance yourself, every time.

**What's next for Perchie**

Submitting to the Mac App Store for the first time. After that, exploring iCloud sync for PerchBrain, still no server, still nothing but Apple's own infrastructure and your device.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every to-do app I looked at does the same thing: it shows you a list of deadlines and leaves you to figure out whether you can actually finish everything in time. I built Deadline Rescue because I wanted an app that tells the truth — that actually calculates whether my workload fits my available time, and says so honestly instead of letting me find out by missing something.

**What it does**

Deadline Rescue is a student task tracker built around one core feature: Rescue. You add your deadlines with an estimated time and priority, tell it how many hours you have available per day, and it builds a day-by-day recovery schedule using an urgency-scoring algorithm.

If your workload doesn't fit, it doesn't hide that. It tells you exactly how many hours won't fit, explains its reasoning in plain language ("Why this plan?"), and gives you three real choices: allow the leftover work to spill past its deadline, ignore the warning, or increase your available hours and try again.

The free tier tracks up to 5 tasks. Premium Planning ($9.99/mo, via RevenueCat) unlocks the full Rescue engine, unlimited tasks, and adjustable planning windows.

**How we built it**

- Frontend: React Native (Expo, Expo Router), tested on a physical Android device via a custom EAS development build.

- Backend: Python + FastAPI, deployed live on Render, with SQLite persistence via SQLAlchemy.

- Monetization: RevenueCat SDK gates the Rescue engine behind a subscription entitlement, with a working sandbox purchase and restore flow.

- The algorithm: urgency for each task is calculated as (hours_remaining × priority_weight) / days_until_deadline. Tasks are sorted by urgency and greedily allocated to the earliest available days before their own deadline; anything that doesn't fit is recorded honestly as unscheduled rather than silently dropped. This logic lives in its own module, separate from the API layer, and is covered by an automated pytest suite.

**Challenges we ran into**

The scheduling algorithm looked simple on paper but had real edge cases I didn't anticipate — overdue tasks were initially crashing the endpoint entirely, and an off-by-one bug meant tasks due today never got scheduled at all. Writing tests around these cases (rather than just eyeballing the output) is what actually surfaced them, and fixing them taught me a lot about how easy it is for "obviously correct" logic to quietly break at the edges.

I also learned React Native, TypeScript, and RevenueCat integration from scratch for this project, coming from a Python background — the campus network I was building on blocked local device connections, which meant learning USB debugging and EAS development builds just to get a working dev loop going.

**What we learned**

That honest, explainable output is a genuinely different product decision than "just build a scheduler" — deciding to report an infeasible plan instead of silently compressing it into something that looks fine was the single choice that shaped the most interesting engineering work in this project.

**What's next for Deadline Rescue**

Persistent accounts and a hosted production database (currently SQLite, which resets on backend redeploy — a known, documented limitation), an in-app editable progress tracker for partial task completion, and expanding the "Why this plan?" explanation into an interactive what-if planner.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/431/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/431/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/903/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/903/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/904/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/904/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/905/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/905/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/906/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/906/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/907/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/907/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Fixed-time reminders fail exactly the people who need them most. If you struggle with
prospective memory (remembering to do something later), a notification that fires at 6:00 PM
every day turns into noise you swipe away without reading.

EVE is built for micro-reminders: your keys as you walk out the door, your earphones
before the gym, your charger before a long day, your medication after breakfast. Each one is
tiny, easy to forget, and only useful at the right moment. Remind someone about their keys
an hour too early and they'll still leave without them.

**Who it's for**

People with ADHD and executive dysfunction first, and anyone who forgets small, time-sensitive
tasks. That audience shaped every design choice: one clear action per screen, tap-based
feedback instead of typing, and a calm interface with little visual load.

**What it does**

EVE runs one loop: learn the routine → detect the right moment → nudge → learn from the
response.

- Learns from your calendar. During onboarding, EVE reads your calendar and uses Apple's
on-device Foundation Models to learn patterns in your week. It then asks a few yes/no
questions about your own events to fill in what the calendar can't say.

- Prepares you for what's coming. For each calendar event, EVE writes a few concrete prep
items (things to bring, prepare, or check) and schedules them an hour before the event.
Today's reminders appear on the Home screen, grouped by part of the day.

- Tells you what matters now. A suggestion bubble on Home shows the single most useful
thing to do next, and refreshes when your location, your reminders, or the time changes.

- Knows where you are. Pin reminders to saved places and choose whether they fire when you
arrive or when you leave.

- Learns from your response. Notifications offer one-tap feedback (Done, Too Early,
Too Late) that tunes when future reminders fire.

- Shows its work. The Insights screen lists what EVE believes about your routine, in plain
sentences you can edit or delete.

**How it makes money: EVE Plus, through RevenueCat**

The free tier keeps the core benefit (adaptive reminders, on-device privacy, feedback), because
the people EVE is for shouldn't hit a wall before it helps them. EVE Plus is for people who
want EVE more deeply in their life:

- Unlimited saved places (free accounts keep one). Tapping + at the limit opens the
paywall, and the add flow picks up where it left off after the purchase.

- Personalized prep. Each event's prep list draws on what EVE has learned about you: your
confirmed answers, your insights, and what you actually did before similar events.

- Contextual learning questions. Before an upcoming event, EVE deduces what you might need
("Gym coming up. Should I remind you to bring your gloves?") and asks. Your answers make the
next reminder better.

Pricing is set in the RevenueCat dashboard: Annual $9.99/year or Quarterly
$3.49/quarter. EVE gates every feature on the eve_pro entitlement, never on a product ID,
so pricing can change without an app release. The paywall is RevenueCat-hosted and laid out
from the dashboard. Settings shows membership status, Restore Purchases, and RevenueCat's
Customer Center for subscribers. Entitlement changes arrive through RevenueCat's customer-info
stream, so a purchase unlocks Plus immediately, with no relaunch.

**What makes it different**

- Private by design. All AI reasoning runs on-device with Apple's Foundation Models.
Calendar events, locations, learned routines, and history never leave the phone. The only
network traffic is RevenueCat's, keyed to an anonymous user ID.

- Grounded, not guessed. A small on-device model will invent things if you let it. Every
prep item and suggestion is checked against the context it was built from, and anything that
names something absent from your calendar or notes is dropped before you see it.

- Safe with other people's text. Anyone who sends you a calendar invite controls that
text. EVE marks it as data, not instructions, before it reaches the model, and strips those
markers from everything the model returns.

- Timing that adapts. EVE doesn't ship a fixed schedule. It moves reminders based on your
calendar, where you are, and how you respond.

**Award category**

Next Gen Award (students). We're a team of five at the Apple Developer Academy.

**How we built it**

SwiftUI and SwiftData on iOS 26.2+, with Apple's Foundation Models as the reasoning core.
We chose not to add any third-party model or cloud AI, so everything we learned would be about
Apple's frameworks. EventKit supplies the calendar, CoreLocation the arrivals and
departures, UserNotifications the nudges and one-tap feedback, and Natural Language
keeps non-English text out of prompts the model can't handle reliably. RevenueCat
(purchases-ios-spm) powers EVE Plus: offerings, the hosted paywall, purchase, restore, the
entitlement, and Customer Center. All of it lives behind one SubscriptionService, the only
file that talks to Purchases.

The model is stateless, so SwiftData is EVE's long-term memory. Every prompt is assembled from
it: upcoming events, confirmed answers, learned insights, and past behavior.

**Challenges we ran into**

- A 4096-token window. The on-device model's context is small. We had to budget every
prompt: cap event notes, rank what to include, and keep each call to one job. Asking one call
to write a notification and extract beliefs made it store the notification as a "fact"
about the user.

- Hallucination. Early prep lists invented rooms, items, and locations. We moved from
"please don't invent things" in the prompt to a deterministic grounding gate in code.

- Prompt injection through the calendar. Calendar text isn't ours, so we added delimiting
on the way in and cleanup on the way out, and gave the model no tools. An injection can
poison data but can't do anything.

- Monetizing an accessibility app ethically. We decided what Plus sells so the free app is
still genuinely useful to the person who needs it most.

**Accomplishments we're proud of**

A working end-to-end loop on a real iPhone: the calendar is learned, reminders are prepared,
nudges fire, feedback is recorded, and a RevenueCat purchase unlocks Plus instantly. It all
runs on-device except the purchase.

**What we learned**

On-device AI is a design constraint, not only a technical one. The smaller the model, the more
the product has to do: structured output, deterministic checks, and prompts with one job each.
We also learned to gate on entitlements, not products, and to let the dashboard own pricing
and the paywall.

**What's next for EVE**

- A production App Store build (the current build uses RevenueCat's Test Store).

- More languages; EVE is English-only today.

- User testing with more people with ADHD, and tuning the timing model on real feedback.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

So me and my friend were trying to build a habit together, and I was trying to help keep him accountable. Then he started sending me spreadsheets. I love my friend, but I don't love going through a spreadsheet every single day to tick off that he did one thing.

I looked on the App Store and there were a couple of apps that kind of fit, but nothing that really ticked every box. I wanted something with the simplicity of BeReal. You take a photo and you're done. But I also wanted the fun gamification stuff Duolingo does really well, like streaks, a currency and streak freezes. That's what led me to build Menta.

**What it does**

You pick a promise, like reading for 10 minutes a day. You pick how you're going to prove it, a photo, a note or a video. Then you pick who keeps you accountable. That can be a friend, Menta Check (AI promise checker), or just yourself.

When you send your proof, your reviewer gets a notification. They either approve it or ask for a clearer photo, and if it's approved in time your day counts. It works one on one or in a group, and you don't all need to be doing the same promise.

Menta Check (AI promise checker) came from my testers. They kept asking how come the app can't tell when the proof is wrong. Honestly that was something I'd overlooked.

**How it makes money**

The whole app is centred around the in-app currency, Momenta. It comes from the word momentum. Pretty much every action that builds towards your promise costs Momenta, so creating a promise, creating a group or joining one. You earn it by keeping your streak, reviewing a friend's proof and inviting people. You can't buy it, so you can't just pay your way around a streak.

I wanted Menta to be free for as many people as possible. Every free user gets 4 promises a month and can have 3 going at the same time. But the app also has to make money. So when you're short on Momenta you can watch a reward ad or go Pro. Free users also get an ad break after every 2 proofs they send. I steered away from banner ads because they don't feel great in the app.

Pro is 99 cents for the first week, then $9.99 a week or $79.99 a year, all through RevenueCat. Pro used to just be a Momenta stipend. Now it comes with Menta Check (AI promise checker), no ad breaks and higher limits, and each check costs me less than a cent.

**How I built it**

I built it with Expo and React Native because that's what I had the most experience with. Supabase is the backend, RevenueCat handles Pro and the ads, and OneSignal handles notifications. The over the air updates have been huge. I can fix things the same day instead of waiting on Apple review. A lot of it was built with AI agents, and I designed every screen in Paper first.

**Challenges**

Retention is the hard part. You need someone who's already committed to building a habit, and then you have to keep them coming back. Getting my first users was honestly embarrassing. It was calling in favours and asking people to try it. And sometimes I'd use my own app and think, why don't I like using this? If I'm feeling friction, a user definitely is.

**What I learned**

The first step is to build something awesome. The second step is telling people about it. Marketing was all new to me, UGC, Facebook ads, Apple search ads. Our Noise videos have passed 24,000 views, and it took a while to find a format that worked.

**What's next**

Getting Menta in front of people beyond my own circle. I know there's a market for this because I've met the people who are it.

The code is open source at https://github.com/ImDanielGitHub/Menta

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**SAFEW — Your safety shouldn’t start with an emergency.**

**💡 Inspiration**

The inspiration behind SAFEW came from seeing the reality of crimes and safety concerns faced by women in India and asking myself a simple question:

Can I build something that is actually useful to women when they feel unsafe—not just another emergency button?

Many safety solutions focus primarily on what happens during an emergency. But unsafe situations can begin much earlier—with warning signs, uncertainty, unfamiliar surroundings, or simply not knowing what to do.

That motivated me to create SAFEW as a safety companion focused on preparation, awareness, guidance, and access to help.

The current legal and women's-rights information in SAFEW is specifically focused on India. In the future, I want to expand it with country-specific laws and rights information for users around the world.

**🛠️ How I Built It**

I built SAFEW as a mobile application using React Native with Expo.

The application brings several safety-focused features together:

- AI Safety Assistant — provides guidance when users are unsure what to do.

- Trusted Contacts — keeps important contacts accessible when help may be needed.

- Learn & Prepare — provides practical safety and awareness information, including Warning Signs to help users recognize potentially unsafe situations.

- Women's Rights — provides India-specific information about relevant rights and laws.

- Location & Emergency Support — connects safety features with the user's situation.

- Emergency Siren — plays a police-siren sound that can be activated in situations where someone feels in severe danger and has limited opportunity to escape. The intention is to create distraction and attract attention, potentially giving the user an opportunity to move toward safety.

**📚 What I Learned**

Building SAFEW taught me that developing a safety-focused application requires much more than writing code.

I learned about user-centred design, mobile permissions, location handling, AI integration, responsible communication, and designing clear user flows.

I also learned to think about the difference between a feature that technically works and a feature that is actually useful to someone in a stressful situation.

Most importantly, I learned that when building technology related to personal safety, accuracy, clarity, and responsible design matter just as much as functionality.

**🚧 Challenges I Faced**

One of my biggest challenges was balancing usefulness with responsibility. Safety guidance should be practical without creating unnecessary fear or giving users misleading information.

I also faced technical challenges with location permissions, mobile navigation, UI design, AI integration, and making features behave consistently across devices.

Another challenge was researching and presenting women's rights information responsibly. Since laws vary by jurisdiction, I had to make sure that the legal information in the current version was clearly presented as India-specific.

**🌱 What SAFEW Aims to Do**

SAFEW is designed to go beyond the traditional idea of an SOS button.

It aims to help users recognize warning signs, prepare themselves, understand their rights, seek guidance, and reach trusted help when necessary.

The current version focuses on India, with the long-term vision of expanding to country-specific safety, legal, and rights information worldwide.

Help people know what to do before they need an SOS button.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Why I made Daruma**

I’ve moved to Japan twice. I still kept finding out about rules after I needed to know them.

Japan’s rules for foreign residents have changed a lot. I was tired of searching through websites, piecing things together, and wondering what I’d missed.

I wanted a planner that knew my situation. Something that could tell me what to do, what to bring, and when it was due.

So I started building Daruma.

It helps people handle the paperwork of living in Japan. It tracks deadlines, scans Japanese letters, provides phrases for the counter, and has an AI coach for questions along the way.

**How I built it**

I started in January. Then I stopped.

This is my first app, and I’m building it alone. I got stuck on onboarding screens, character designs, and small details that ate whole weekends. There was always something else to fix before I felt ready.

Shipaton changed that. The competition gave me a deadline. The big launch party in Tokyo gave me another reason to get it done. I stopped polishing things nobody had seen and focused on getting the app into people’s hands.

Daruma went live on the App Store on 20 August. I didn’t find out until a few days later. So much for the big launch moment.

Without Shipaton, I might still be adjusting the onboarding.

**What was hard**

The paperwork itself is complicated. What you need depends on your visa, your city, and your circumstances. Rules change. Advice goes out of date.

The challenge was to make that easier to navigate without pretending there was one answer for everyone.

That also meant setting limits on AI and narrowing its scope to give better answers. Daruma helps people get organized. It does not replace an immigration office or a qualified adviser.

**What I learned**

I learned more from putting the app in front of people than from another round of polishing it alone.

After launch, I asked my friends to review it thoroughly. Their feedback led to several updates: more pricing tiers to make it accessible, AI usage limits, tighter scope for answers, themes, and smaller fixes.

I also learned that a release does not have to be the finished version of everything I imagined. It has to be useful enough to start helping someone.

**What’s next**

Daruma is live, and several updates have already shipped. I’ll keep improving it based on what people need and where they get stuck.

The reason for building it hasn’t changed. I want people to spend less time figuring out the paperwork and more time enjoying their life in Japan.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**💡 Inspiration**

Mental health fluctuations and sudden fatigue dips aren't personal failures—they are heavily dictated by subtle environmental stressors like barometric pressure drops and circadian vulnerability.

Inspired by 2026 research published in Drug Discoveries & Therapeutics (DOI: 10.5582/ddt.2026.01019), we built ChronoMind to empower individuals to stop blaming themselves for "bad days" and start scientifically predicting and managing their biological resilience.

**⚡ What it does**

ChronoMind acts as a proactive circadian health companion that bridges environmental data with personal well-being:

- Real-time Barometric Pressure Sync: Automatically fetches local pressure data via Open-Meteo API.

- 1-Second Micro Logging: Seamlessly tracks brain fatigue and physical fatigue with zero friction.

- 7-Day Forecast Alert: Predicts upcoming pressure drops and warns users before fatigue hits.

- Doctor-Ready PDF Correlation Report: Visualizes personal fatigue trends against pressure changes, complete with AI-generated notes for physicians.

- Deep Chrono-Therapy Prescription: Offers targeted interventions (light therapy, hydration, 4-7-8 breathing) grounded in 2026 chronobiology algorithms.

- Golden VIP Suite: Integrated RevenueCat Paywall with a seamless transition to a luxury gold-themed PRO suite for subscribers.

**🛠 How we built it**

- Frontend & Architecture: Native Android application built with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose.

- AI Pair Programming: Developed end-to-end utilizing JetBrains Junie (CLI & IDE Integration) as an autonomous AI pair programmer.

- Monetization & Paywall: Integrated RevenueCat SDK for managing subscription plans, dynamic paywalls, and free trials.

- Weather Infrastructure: Fetches real-time and 7-day forecast atmospheric pressure via Open-Meteo API.

**🥊 Challenges we ran into**

Designing a seamless transition between free and premium features without harming user experience was our biggest challenge. We spent significant effort tuning the Paywall logic and creating a distinct "Golden VIP Suite" UI that makes subscribers feel genuinely valued, while ensuring non-subscribers can preview premium capabilities with zero friction.

**🏆 Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Achieving a zero-friction "1-second log" experience that users can maintain long-term.

- Building a full-fledged, publication-backed health application with a cohesive, luxury dark-gold design.

- Successfully leveraging JetBrains Junie to accelerate development speed by over 3x.

**📚 What we learned**

We gained deep insights into translating complex chronobiology research into intuitive UX. We also mastered rapid Android development using JetBrains Junie and effective paywall architecture with RevenueCat.

**🚀 What's next for ChronoMind**

- Proactive Push Notifications: Integrating OneSignal to notify users hours before major pressure fronts arrive.

- Wearable Integration: WearOS and smartwatch support to collect continuous heart-rate variability (HRV) and sleep data.

**🏆 Target Awards**

- Next Gen Award (Student category)

- Keep Them Coming Back Award by OneSignal

</details>

**💡 Inspiration**

Over 285 million visually impaired individuals face daily challenges with spatial navigation, reading printed documents, and identifying currency. Existing tools are fragmented, slow, and lack conversational context. AuraVision AI was created to provide an all-in-one, eyes-free multimodal vision assistant that acts as a real-time visual companion.

**🚀 What it does**

AuraVision AI turns any smartphone into an intelligent visual and audio companion:

- Sub-Second Scene Perception: Instant spatial mapping and hazard narration powered by Google Gemini 1.5 Flash.

- Ultra-HD Document & Prescription OCR: Accurately reads printed books, letters, and prescription labels with crystal-clear voice narration.

- Instant Currency Detector: Identifies banknotes and denominations in real time.

- Conversational Vision Memory: Enables blind users to ask voice follow-up questions referencing previous visual context without re-scanning.

- Eyes-Free Blind UX: Full-screen double-tap scanning, voice commands, and tactile haptic feedback designed for non-visual usability.

- Samsung Galaxy Foldable Adaptive Layout: Multi-window and foldable-ready responsive architecture.

**🛠️ How we built it**

- Frontend: Flutter & Dart with zero-visual accessibility semantics and high-contrast styling.

- AI Core: Google Gemini 1.5 Flash API with optimized low-latency streaming and multimodal buffers.

- Monetization Engine: RevenueCat SDK powering flexible subscription tiers, paywalls, and judge evaluation code redemption.

**🎁 Judge Evaluation Code**

Hackathon judges can unlock full lifetime Pro features directly inside the app using the promo code:
SHIPATON2026

**🧗 Challenges we overcame**

- Zero-Visual Interaction: Designing a seamless UX where users never need to aim for tiny buttons—solved via tactile haptic cues and global double-tap triggers.

- Real-time Latency: Optimizing image compression before calling Gemini 1.5 Flash to ensure voice feedback within 1-2 seconds.

**🏅 Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Production-ready release APK/AAB builds deployed.

- Seamless multimodal vision + conversational memory integration.

- Robust RevenueCat monetization architecture with promo code support.

**🔮 What's next for AuraVision AI**

- Wearable integration for smart glasses and Galaxy Watch audio streams.

- Offline edge-AI obstacle detection for low-connectivity environments.

- Multi-language audio localization for global accessibility.

**Cálculo Trivial**

Master Calculus. Level up.

Development status: Cálculo Trivial is currently under active development for RevenueCat Shipaton 2026. The core learning experience is functional, but the app has not yet been officially released.

**Inspiration**

Cálculo Trivial was born from a problem I experienced personally as a university student.

Calculus can be frustrating. Sometimes I could follow a solved example but felt completely lost as soon as the problem changed. When this happens repeatedly, students may begin to believe that they are simply not capable of learning the subject.

Struggling with Calculus does not mean that a student lacks ability. Sometimes an explanation was too fast, a previous concept was not fully understood, or the student simply needs another example and an opportunity to try again without feeling judged.

I started building Cálculo Trivial because I wanted to create the kind of learning tool I would have liked to use during those moments.

**What it does**

Cálculo Trivial is a gamified Android learning app designed to help university students practise Calculus through a structured and progressive experience.

Instead of presenting a disconnected collection of formulas, the app organizes learning into lessons, exercises, feedback, review and visible progression.

The current version includes:

- 120 questions distributed across six Calculus topics;

- Randomized practice sessions containing 10 questions;

- A minimum score of 80% to pass;

- Different questions when starting a new attempt;

- A review stage for incorrectly answered questions;

- Explanations that help students understand their mistakes;

- XP, virtual gold and content unlocking only after passing;

- User authentication and password recovery;

- Local progress persistence and cloud synchronization;

- Separate progress for each user;

- Free and Premium content;

- Monthly, yearly and lifetime Premium options;

- Purchase restoration and Premium access protection.

The objective is not to provide answers without requiring students to think. Cálculo Trivial is designed to help students understand why a solution works, learn from mistakes and gradually become more confident when solving problems independently.

**How I built it**

I am developing Cálculo Trivial with Flutter and Dart, initially targeting Android.

Firebase Authentication manages user accounts, while Cloud Firestore stores and synchronizes student progress. Firebase App Check helps protect access to the backend.

RevenueCat manages the Premium entitlement, product offerings, paywall, purchase restoration and access control. Monthly, yearly and lifetime products are currently working through RevenueCat's Test Store. The production configuration will be connected to Google Play before the official release.

The project currently includes automated tests for critical learning rules. Thirty automated tests are passing, including tests that verify:

- Rewards are only granted after approval;

- Content is only unlocked after approval;

- Reviewing mistakes does not modify the final score;

- New attempts use different questions;

- User progress remains separated and synchronized.

Debug APK and release AAB builds have also been successfully compiled. The Android signing configuration is protected, and the project targets Android API 36.

**Challenges**

One of the greatest challenges has been balancing accessibility, academic value and gamification.

Rewards can motivate students, but they should not replace learning. For this reason, XP, virtual gold and new content are only granted when the student achieves the required score.

Another challenge was designing the error-review flow. Students need an opportunity to understand their mistakes, but reviewing an answer must not modify the score already earned during the session.

Integrating authentication, cloud synchronization and Premium access also required careful testing. The application must preserve each user's progress, behave correctly with unstable internet access and prevent Premium content from being unlocked incorrectly.

**What I learned**

Building Cálculo Trivial has taught me that creating an educational application involves much more than writing code.

I have learned about mobile development, software architecture, authentication, cloud databases, security, monetization, automated testing, interface design, accessibility and educational content organization.

Most importantly, I learned that a personal academic difficulty can become the starting point for something useful. Instead of viewing that experience only as a failure, I can use it to build a tool that may help other students persist.

Sharing the project publicly through #Shipaton and #BuildInPublic also gives me an opportunity to collect feedback, document lessons learned and improve the application before launch.

**What's next**

Cálculo Trivial is still in development. The next steps are:

- Complete functional testing on physical Android devices;

- Review all 120 questions and explanations;

- Improve the interface, splash screen and accessibility;

- Test offline and unstable-network behavior;

- Configure production products through Google Play and RevenueCat;

- Run the required Google Play testing process;

- Record the final demonstration video;

- Gather feedback from university students;

- Publish the first official Android version.

My goal is not to eliminate every difficulty associated with Calculus. It is to make the subject clearer, less intimidating and more possible to learn—one step at a time.

**Open source**

The source code is publicly available under the Apache License 2.0.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

AirDrop is fast once its panel is open, but reaching that panel interrupts the flow: select, Share, AirDrop, wait. AirFliq started with one question: what if sending a file felt like one continuous gesture?

**What it does**

AirFliq is a native macOS menu bar utility that opens Apple's AirDrop panel in one move, from wherever you already are:

- Finder's right-click menu: Send with AirFliq.

- A global shortcut (default ⌃⌥A, fully customizable) that opens the native file picker.

- The menu bar.

- A magnetic drag target that appears beside your cursor while you drag a file. Drop it and the card folds into a paper plane that flies off the screen while AirDrop opens.

Files go through Apple's own AirDrop. Nothing is uploaded to an AirFliq server, there is no account, and AirFliq only reads folders the user chooses. It never asks for Full Disk Access.

**Monetization with RevenueCat**

- Free forever (version 1.0.1): 5 sends a day on every route, no trial needed.

- 7-day trial of unlimited sending: a free App Store product the user starts explicitly; it never renews or charges.

- Lifetime Pro: one purchase, unlimited forever.

RevenueCat verifies the trial and the non-consumable Lifetime entitlement, powers restore, and syncs App Store offer-code redemptions. The trial's start date comes from the verified transaction, not the Mac's clock.

**How we built it**

Swift 6 with strict concurrency, SwiftUI and AppKit, a FinderSync extension, Carbon hot keys, security-scoped bookmarks, StoreKit offer-code redemption and the RevenueCat SDK. It is a universal binary for Apple Silicon and Intel, built and archived by Xcode Cloud.

**Challenges**

macOS permissions change outside the app. The Finder extension lives deep in System Settings, and on managed Macs it can be blocked by policy. Our first public release could leave people stuck on that step. Version 1.0.1:

- makes every optional step skippable, so setup always finishes;

- shows an animated miniature of the exact clicks before opening System Settings;

- docks a small guide beside System Settings that confirms the switch the moment macOS reports it.

The drag target needs AppKit to own the drop surface while SwiftUI renders hover, attraction and release. The release animation runs in a separate click-through overlay, so it never delays the AirDrop handoff.

**Accomplishments**

- Four routes around one native AirDrop flow.

- A free tier that is genuinely useful, and an honest trial.

- Setup that always finishes, with a guide that finds the Finder extension for you.

- A signature release moment: the card folds into a paper plane and flies off the screen, built with Core Animation at the display's refresh rate.

**What we learned**

Testing the live App Store build right after launch exposed a blocker: a setup that cannot finish loses the user. Optional now means skippable. Trust also comes from small things: a free send is used only when AirDrop really sends. On macOS 27 a cancelled AirDrop panel reports the same "shared" result as a real send, so AirFliq tells them apart by the AirDrop radio traffic before counting.

**What's next**

- Measure trial starts, conversions and restores in RevenueCat.

- Localize the app.

- Bring the paper-plane confirmation to every route.

**Try it**

- Website: https://airfliq.vercel.app

Version 1.0.0 is live on the Mac App Store. Version 1.0.1, with the free daily sends, skippable setup, Finder extension guide and the paper-plane release, has been submitted to App Review.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

As a student, I was juggling grades scattered across notebooks and school portals, exam dates I'd half-forget until the week of, and hours spent making flashcards from lecture notes by hand. I wanted one place that could do all three: track grades with real weighted averages, count down to exams so nothing sneaks up on me, and turn my own notes into a quiz automatically instead of me writing questions by hand. That became StudyPulse.

**What it does**

- Grade tracking — organize subjects, log weighted grades, and see a live average with color-coded performance.

- Exam countdown — add exams with a live day/hour/minute/second countdown and automatic reminder notifications.

- Grade prediction — calculates the grade needed on remaining exams to hit a target average or scholarship threshold.

- AI Tutor — paste course notes (or upload a PDF/TXT) and get a 5-question multiple-choice quiz with explanations, generated by Google's Gemini API.

- Study Timer — a distraction-free focus timer with an optional fullscreen mode.

- Cloud sync — sign in with email/password; subjects and exams follow you across devices via Firebase.

- Smart Alerts (PRO) — spaced-repetition study reminders (7/3/1 days before an exam) instead of a single night-before nudge.

- StudyPulse PRO — a RevenueCat-powered subscription that unlocks unlimited AI quizzes, grade predictions, and Smart Alerts, with a free tier (1 AI quiz/day) for everyone else.

**How I built it**

The app is built with Flutter and Dart, targeting Android (and web). State is managed with Provider, with a single AppProvider holding the signed-in user's subjects and exams and syncing them to Cloud Firestore. Firebase Authentication handles email/password sign-in, and Firestore security rules lock each account to its own document.

The AI Tutor calls the Gemini API directly with the pasted course text and a structured prompt asking for a JSON array of questions, options, the correct index, and an explanation — parsed straight into the quiz UI.

RevenueCat powers the whole premium layer: it gates the AI quiz daily limit, grade prediction, and Smart Alerts behind a premium entitlement, checked through Purchases.getCustomerInfo(), with a paywall dialog that lists live packages and prices from a configured offering.

Smart Alerts schedule local notifications via flutter_local_notifications, anchored to the device's real IANA timezone (via flutter_timezone) rather than assuming UTC, so a reminder set for "the day before" actually fires the day before in the student's own timezone.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Package/Firebase mismatch: partway through development I renamed the Android package, which silently broke google-services.json — Firebase kept looking for an app that no longer matched, and the Android build failed outright until I re-ran flutterfire configure against the existing project.

- Core library desugaring: flutter_local_notifications needs Java 8+ desugaring enabled on Android, which isn't on by default — a one-line Gradle fix, but a confusing first error.

- Timezone-correct reminders: package:timezone's tz.local silently defaults to UTC unless you explicitly set it from the device's real timezone — an easy bug to ship without ever noticing locally.

- No paid Apple/Google developer account as a student — RevenueCat's SDK, paywall, and entitlement logic are fully wired up and tested end-to-end (sandbox purchases, restores, Firestore sync), even though this submission ships as source + demo video rather than a live store listing.

**What I learned**

How much of "payments" is really state-sync and edge cases, not the purchase button — restoring purchases, keeping premium status in sync across sign-in/sign-out, and making sure a user's data (and their scheduled notifications) don't leak into the next person's session on a shared device. Also: test on a real timezone, not just the emulator's default.

**What's next for StudyPulse**

- A real subscription product configured in Google Play Console so the paywall shows live pricing end-to-end.

- PDF text extraction for the AI Tutor (currently PDF/TXT upload works, but PDF text still needs to be pasted in manually).

- iOS build and App Store listing.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

For years I've dealt with recurring TMJ issues and stress coming from running my own business and dealing with a large family with challenges. Part of managing it is slowing down: breathing exercises, a quiet mind, a few minutes at a time, a few times a day. And every timer I tried was built backwards for that. A timer's whole job is to interrupt you — you set five minutes, a buzzer goes off, you're done. But interruption is exactly wrong for breathing, planks, stretching, cold plunges, or focused work. The point of those is to keep going.

I didn't want a countdown. I wanted a floor: at least fifteen minutes, with permission to continue. So I built AtLeast — the timer I actually wanted, and as it turns out, one nobody else had built.

**What it does**

AtLeast inverts the timer. You set a minimum — at least X minutes — and it taps your wrist gently at an interval you choose. Each tap means keep going. When you pass your floor, the taps simply stop. Silence is the success state.

That's the entire interaction, and it's deliberately eyes-free: I close my eyes, put ear plugs in, set at least 15 minutes, and breathe. There is no countdown, no progress ring, no remaining-time display anywhere in the app — that's a hard design rule, not a missing feature. You feel the app; you never look at it. The Apple Watch Taptic Engine is the whole interface, with six selectable haptic strengths from gentle to max and a live preview so you can feel your choice before you begin. The timer runs on-device with no account and no network required.

The iPhone app can also run a session on its own. Each timer can also carry a Session Type that saves the finished session to Apple Health, as Mindful Minutes or as a workout (Yoga, Mind & Body, Flexibility, Cooldown, Core Training, or Traditional Strength). AtLeast only writes to Health; it never reads it.

**How I built it**

- watchOS-first, iPhone as companion. The watch runs the session; the iPhone configures presets and mirrors a live session ambiently (same rule there — no numbers, just an ambient pulse).

- WKExtendedRuntimeSession keeps the haptic rhythm alive with the screen off — deliberately not HKWorkoutSession, which would have been the easy-but-wrong shortcut.

- Absolute timestamps everywhere. The timer never counts elapsed seconds; it stores start and target Dates, so backgrounding, restarts, and clock drift can't corrupt a session.

- SwiftUI .sensoryFeedback() drives every tap declaratively.

- Watch↔phone sync: I built my own library, SundialKit, to use WatchConnectivity's application context as revisioned, latest-wins state snapshots with a heartbeat, so a dropped delivery self-heals — built for reliability first, features second.

- Accessibility and localization as launch features, not promises: VoiceOver labels and announcements, Voice Control input labels, Dynamic Type, Reduce Motion, and six languages (English, Spanish, German, French, Japanese, Arabic).

- Modular Swift packages with the core logic platform-portable and unit-tested (it even compiles for WASM in CI).

**How I used RevenueCat**

The core timer is free forever — including background reliability, which I refuse to monetize. AtLeast Pro is "memory": the free app deliberately stores nothing, and Pro is what remembers — saved custom presets and session history with streaks. RevenueCat powers the whole loop: subscriptions ($0.99/month, or $9.99/year with a 7-day free trial), a $49.99 Founder lifetime for a diverse revenue mix, a pro entitlement shared across iPhone and watch, and a RevenueCat-dashboard paywall I can iterate on without shipping app updates. And because AtLeast has no accounts, RevenueCat's anonymous app user IDs are what let monetization survive that promise: purchases and restores work with zero sign-in, and the privacy label stays "not linked to your identity."

**Challenges**

- Silence is a feature you have to engineer. Testers said the taps were too polite, but the obvious stronger feedback types can play sound — unacceptable for a silent timer. Getting "keep going" to read on a real wrist without ever breaking the silence promise took a haptic-strength ladder and on-wrist testing, not API defaults.

- A one-slot radio. WatchConnectivity's application context is a single latest-wins slot that silently drops identical payloads. Making sync rock-solid meant monotonic revisions, idempotent intents, and heartbeats — distributed-systems thinking for two devices in the same pocket.

- Pro on a watch that never buys. Purchases happen on the iPhone through RevenueCat, but the watch has to unlock too. Running RevenueCat on both devices meant two anonymous customers posting the same receipt, and the entitlement could bounce between them. So the watch dropped the RevenueCat SDK and reads StoreKit 2's Transaction.currentEntitlements itself, caching only answers StoreKit confirmed. The phone sends just a nudge (an entitlement revision riding the same revisioned sync snapshot), and the watch re-checks StoreKit. An unknown state looks exactly like free, with Restore always one tap away.

- CloudKit has to converge on its own. Timers and history sync through SwiftData's private CloudKit database, which forbids unique constraints, so the same record can arrive twice. Every device collapses duplicates with the same deterministic rule (highest version, then a fixed tie-break), so both land on the same copy instead of whichever arrived first. CloudKit merges per field, so I stopped storing values derived from each other: a session keeps its target instant, not a duration too, so two builds can't write contradictory halves of one row. "This device" vs. "the watch" means opposite things on each side of a shared database, so history stores an absolute device identity. And the device that hosts a session writes its record; nothing is relayed over WatchConnectivity for the other device to write.

- Eyes-free is a discipline. Every feature request gets tested against "does this make someone look at their wrist?" Saying no to a progress ring is harder than building one.

- Shipping the last 10% solo: six-language screenshot pipelines, accessibility audits, and App Review prep, as a solo developer and parent of six.

**What I learned**

The absence of feedback can be the product. Every platform pushes you toward more — more alerts, more numbers, more engagement. Building an app whose success state is silence meant fighting that current at every level, from API choices to App Store screenshots. I also learned that the "floor, not ceiling" shape fits far more of life than breathing exercises: minimum walks, minimum reading, minimum practice. Once you see floors, you can't unsee them.

**What's next**

Siri and Shortcuts (start and stop a session by voice), a Focus filter, session history insights, and growing Pro on the "memory" promise without ever compromising the free, silent core.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

The idea started with a simple question: when the same video appears on Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube, how can we figure out where it most likely came from?

At first, I thought video metadata would be enough. But while working on it, I realized how easily metadata can change or disappear when a video is downloaded, edited, compressed, or uploaded again.

That made me think that the answer shouldn't depend on just one thing. We needed to look at the video from different angles and combine the evidence.

That's how Video Origin Analyzer started.

**What it does**

Video Origin Analyzer investigates a video and tries to determine which platform it is most likely associated with: Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube.

It doesn't rely only on the video name or metadata. It analyzes multiple signals including:

- Video metadata and container information

- Video codecs and stream characteristics

- Audio characteristics

- File fingerprints

- Compression and re-encoding patterns

- Visual information

- OCR/text found in frames

- Online visual search results

- Public platform information

- Platform post dates and cross-platform timelines

One of the features I care about most is "Why did we reach this conclusion?"

Instead of just showing a platform and a confidence score, the app shows the evidence that contributed to the result. If the evidence conflicts or isn't strong enough, the app can also lower its confidence instead of pretending to know the answer.

**How we built it**

The application was built with Flutter so it can run on both Android and iOS.

The main video analysis is designed to be local-first. The video itself doesn't need to be uploaded to a server for the forensic analysis.

For online investigation, we use server-side APIs and Supabase Edge Functions. This also lets us keep API keys away from the mobile application.

We use visual search to find potentially related public pages, and when a relevant Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube URL is found, additional public platform information can be used as another piece of evidence.

The app also includes Firebase authentication, local analysis history, PDF reports, RevenueCat for the Pro version, and a formal/classic interface.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge was accuracy.

There isn't one piece of information that can always tell us where a video originally came from. A video can be downloaded from one platform, edited, compressed, and uploaded somewhere else. Sometimes different platforms can have very similar versions of the same video.

Another challenge was making sure that online evidence didn't become the only thing the application trusted. We wanted the result to come from multiple signals rather than simply saying "Google found this first, so this must be the original."

We also had to deal with API limits, security, different platforms, and plenty of bugs during development.

Since I am building this with limited resources, keeping everything within free or very low-cost services was another challenge.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I'm most proud that this went from an idea about reading video metadata into a complete working application with a much broader investigation system.

The "Why did we reach this conclusion?" feature is probably my favorite part because it makes the result understandable instead of giving the user a mysterious percentage.

I'm also proud of building the application as a cross-platform Flutter project, keeping the actual video analysis local-first, and integrating online investigation without exposing API keys inside the app.

Getting all of these different parts to work together was a much bigger challenge than I expected when I started.

**What we learned**

This project taught us that real-world detection is rarely about finding one perfect signal.

We learned how much information can be extracted from a video and how different signals can sometimes contradict each other.

We also learned a lot about Flutter, video analysis, OCR, visual search, Supabase Edge Functions, API security, Firebase authentication, RevenueCat, local storage, and building a larger application while continuously testing existing features.

Most importantly, we learned to treat uncertainty as part of the result. If the evidence isn't strong enough, it's better for the application to say that than to give a confident but unreliable answer.

**What's next for Video Origin Analyzer**

There are still many things we would like to improve.

The biggest one is accuracy. We want to improve how the application compares videos across platforms and how it handles cases where the same video has been heavily edited or re-encoded.

We also want to improve the visual and audio matching, make the timeline investigation more powerful, and eventually support more types of evidence.

For now, though, the main goal is to keep testing the application with difficult real-world videos and learn from the cases where it gets things wrong.

Video Origin Analyzer is still evolving, but this version is a strong starting point for something much bigger.

Built by Mahad and Mehdi Developers.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Weather apps tell us what the sky is about to do. I wanted to make one that also tells us who else has stood under a sky like this.

104 years ago — someone watched this rain.

The Enchanted April, 1922 · Elizabeth von Arnim

Almanac pairs live weather with public-domain literature. A rainy morning can lead to Walden; snow can lead to Dubliners. Every passage names its book, author, publication year, and the number of years between then and now.

**What it does**

Almanac reads local weather from MET Norway and classifies it into eight weather groups—clear, cloudy, fog, drizzle, rain, snow, thunder, and wind—and three times of day. That creates 24 reading contexts.

The app selects from 428 curated passages by 27 authors across 32 public-domain books published from 1847 to 1925. No passage is AI-generated. The free shelf contains 86 passages and covers every weather/time bucket. One non-consumable purchase unlocks the other 342; there is no subscription.

The experience is tactile. Only the words move: the page stays paper and ink, with no particles and no sound effects, so the weather lives in the typography itself. Rain drops words onto the page, snow lets them drift, fog brings them into focus, wind pushes them in from the left, and thunder flashes the page. Mobile haptics follow the same timing. Readers can swipe backward through previous passages, and iOS and Android widgets show the current passage without opening the app.

Almanac is for readers who want a quieter alternative to a conventional weather screen: a useful glance at the day that also leaves them with a sentence worth carrying around.

I am submitting Almanac for the RevenueCat Design Award and Ship Kotlin Everywhere (JetBrains) tracks: weather-responsive typography, motion, haptics, and widgets on top of one shared Kotlin selection and data engine.

**How I built it**

Almanac is a Kotlin Multiplatform project with five surfaces:

- Android app: Compose Multiplatform

- Android widget: Jetpack Glance

- iOS app: Compose Multiplatform inside a small SwiftUI shell

- iOS widget: WidgetKit backed by the shared Kotlin logic

- Desktop: Compose Multiplatform for macOS, Windows, and Linux

Shared Kotlin handles weather parsing, classification, passage selection, SQLDelight content and history databases, and startup. By repository line count, roughly 72% of the Kotlin and Swift application source is in commonMain. The whole Swift side, app shell and widget included, is 179 lines.

Selection is deterministic rather than random at display time. Inputs include local date, time of day, weather group, installation ID, and reading history. Recent passages are removed and the least-read candidates are preferred. Identical inputs return the same passage on every target. This keeps an installation's app and widget aligned while giving different readers their own sequences.

The hash behavior is pinned with golden test vectors, and the selection tests run on JVM, Android, and the iOS simulator. The animation scatter is deterministic too: a word's position supplies its motion seed, while a single page timeline coordinates the headline, words, byline, lightning, and mobile haptics.

RevenueCat manages the core-2026 entitlement for the full shelf. Its ID matches the content pack ID: an active entitlement means the pack is owned. RevenueCat is the source of truth; the local database caches offline access and refreshes after purchase, restore, or offer-code redemption.

**Challenges I faced**

**Making an Android widget look like the app**

RemoteViews cannot receive the app's custom Typeface. Text spans and appearances did not solve it; one attempt crashed the widget. I render the “N years ago” heading as a bitmap and keep the passage in a system serif. I also learned that widgets must be checked on a real home screen, not only in previews.

**Keeping RevenueCat compatible with the iOS build and tests**

With Xcode 26, the KMP RevenueCat interop required Swift compatibility libraries unavailable to Kotlin/Native test executables. The app linked, but the cross-platform tests did not. I moved billing into the app module; the WidgetKit extension sells nothing and links no purchases SDK. This preserved the shared tests without duplicating the product model.

**Recovering from an App Review rejection**

An early iOS build was rejected under guideline 2.1(a) because a clean launch could remain blank. Startup had waited for location, store state, and weather before drawing. I reversed it: render from a saved or default city, refine when location arrives, and sync the store independently. An unavailable service can no longer erase the interface.

**Keeping platforms in agreement**

The hard part was normalizing inputs: local ISO dates, lowercase installation IDs, rounded coordinate cache keys, and one shared weather mapping. A controlled demo supplies the same installation ID to Android, iPhone, and desktop to prove identical inputs produce identical results. Production installations keep separate IDs.

**What I learned**

- Determinism is a property of normalized inputs, not just the algorithm.

- Entitlements are a better source of truth than purchase events; purchase, restore, refunds, offline access, and offer codes can all follow one path.

- The first frame should never depend on a network service or permission prompt.

- Widgets need testing on the actual home screen.

- Kotlin Multiplatform is most valuable in the invisible parts: one weather model, one selection engine, and one test suite that cannot silently drift between platforms.

**What I am proud of**

Almanac is live on the App Store and Google Play from one Kotlin codebase. It has no account or ads and rounds coordinates to about 1.1 km before storage or transmission. Most importantly, typography and motion are not decoration: they turn weather into the reading interface.

**What's next**

Japanese passages from Aozora Bunko with a language setting, and a new collection each year as more books enter the public domain.

</details>
