<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Certain songs bring back more than a moment — they bring back a place. A track can remind you of the street you walked down, the café where you first heard it, or a city you were discovering for the first time.

I wanted a simple way to preserve that connection without turning it into another public profile or social feed. Dejamu began as the idea of a private map that slowly fills with music tied to real places.

**What it does**

Dejamu is a local-first iOS journal for musical memories.

You can search for a song, listen to its preview, add a short note and date, and optionally attach your current location. Dejamu then places the song on your map using its artwork as the pin.

From there, you can:

- revisit entries from the map, weekly strip, list, or calendar

- edit or delete past memories

- generate a shareable card for a single entry

- see today’s song or a resurfaced memory in a home screen widget

- optionally receive a recall notification when returning near a saved place

There are no accounts, friends, or feeds. Entries are stored locally on the device.

**How I built it**

Dejamu is built entirely with SwiftUI for iOS 17 and later.

SwiftData stores each entry locally, while MapKit and Core Location capture and display its location. Song search uses the iTunes Search API, and AVPlayer handles 30-second previews. The widget uses WidgetKit and reads from the same SwiftData store through a shared App Group.

RevenueCat manages the dejamu_pro entitlement and presents a remotely configured paywall through RevenueCatUI. Pro unlocks the complete map experience, calendar browsing, and optional recall notifications.

I deliberately kept the architecture small: there is no backend, login, or synchronization layer. This makes the app more private and keeps the code focused on its core interaction.

**Product and monetization thinking**

The product principle behind Dejamu is:

Writing is free. Looking back is paid.

Creating memories and browsing them as a list remain free and unlimited. New users can also experience their first pins landing on the map before encountering the paywall. Dejamu Pro charges for the richer ways of revisiting a growing collection rather than limiting the act of recording it.

This felt more respectful than placing a cap on the number of memories a person could save, while still giving the subscription a clear and relevant purpose.

**Challenges**

One challenge was combining an interactive MapKit screen with a persistent, draggable SwiftUI bottom sheet without creating conflicting presentation states.

Sharing data with the widget also required moving the SwiftData store into an App Group container so that both targets could read the same entries.

Location introduced another set of decisions. I wanted it to be useful without making it mandatory, so every entry can be saved without coordinates. Reverse geocoding, denied permissions, unavailable song previews, and empty search results all needed graceful fallback states.

I also had to design the paywall around the product’s value instead of simply locking entry creation. That led to the free-writing, paid-reflection model.

**What I learned**

Building Dejamu taught me to work in complete vertical slices: first making one entry appear on a map, then adding search, location, browsing, sharing, monetization, and finally the widget and recall experience.

I also learned how boundaries between an app and its extensions affect storage, how entitlement state should flow through a SwiftUI app, and how much product design is involved in deciding what should remain free.

**What’s next**

My next focus would be reliability testing on more devices, accessibility improvements, and refining the onboarding and paywall based on feedback from real users.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

As an avid art lover, I've always admired an artist’s ability to draw a recognizable portrait. I've tried countless times, but I just can’t do it. This made me realize, how many other people like me have stepped away from art due to the lack of structured guidance ?

What if an app could break down your friend's face into simple shapes and lines through a step-by-step walkthrough ? My goal is to make art feel approachable, so that confidence is never what keeps someone from drawing, and more people can enjoy the craft and the community around it.

Anyone, including you, can draw. And hopefully, so can I now. 

**What it does**

At its core, ArtHaven transforms a portrait photo into a step-by-step offline walkthrough using the classic Loomis Model, along with some other artsy methods. 

- Loomis Breakdown: Pick any face photo from your gallery as your reference. Front-facing ones work best. The app finds the face's landmarks and builds a Loomis construction guide.

- Step-by-Step Guide: The guide is revealed one stage at a time, so you can draw along on paper and understand why each line is there before moving to the next.

- Hand-Sketched Look: Guides are drawn with organic, curved construction lines like an artist's own sketchbook, not cold geometric shapes. The lines wobble differently every time you scroll. I'd love to say that was a deliberate anti-tracing feature, and honestly, it is now. 

- Loomi, Your Drawing Buddy: Tap the mascot for a random drawing tip whenever you need a nudge or get stuck.

- Gamified Loop: Earn coins as you complete sketches, bringing you closer to a free one. 

**How I built it**

I've experimented with vision technology, yet combining it with app development was extremely new territory. 

- Claude Code + Google Gemini: I was able to bring my ideas to life with tools like Claude and Gemini, who did much of the hard work.

- Figma: I used Figma to solidify my vision and design ideas. 

- Google Colab: I prototyped the initial geometry in Google Colab, adjusting proportions until the guides matched how artists actually construct a head, before it went into the app.

- RevenueCat: I used RevenueCat to power coin-based in-app purchases.

I really focused on creating a clean, intuitive Flutter experience designed to feel like a natural part of your creative workflow. 

**Challenges I ran into**

Doubting I could build it. The biggest hurdle was internal. I was a complete beginner to app development, and even with AI tools I wasn't sure I could develop a working app.

Avoiding AI servers. Many tools that analyze images rely on cloud AI, which means ongoing server costs. I didn't want to go down that road, so I built everything to run on-device with pre-trained models. That keeps the app affordable, works offline, and means photos never leave the phone.

Accurate, but not traced. I wanted the guides to be precise without turning into a tracing tool, because I want users to focus on the overall shape of the head, not copy lines. This is why I kept the construction lines simple and sketchy, using dashed lines for ideal proportions and solid lines for measurements from the face, so the guide shows where things go without handing over every outline. Finding that balance took many rounds of adjusting proportions.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

I built a working app with integrated purchases in just two months, as a 17-year-old who first downloaded Android Studio in July. Along the way I battled my inner critic, and I'd like to think I won. 

The best part about the journey, though, was the feedback I received from testers. People who had never touched a sketchbook before were able to create an admittedly rough, yet recognizable, sketch of a face. 

**What I learned**

Being a clueless beginner is not a limit, but a starting point. With time and effort, anything is possible. I look forward to sharing my experience with other students afraid of stepping into an unfamiliar field. 

My journey shines a spotlight on the remarkable ability of AI to lower the barrier of entry into app development, just as ArtHaven strives to lower the barrier to drawing. Yet, while AI gets you some of the way, building an app that truly resonates with your audience is still inherently a human task. I learned this fact the hard way, prompting me to stop and define my own approach, vision, and design before continuing development. 

As a bonus, I’m weirdly educated about portrait sketching now. I had to research various methods to develop an effective walkthrough. 

**What's next for ArtHaven**

Art is a never-ending lesson, and ArtHaven has only just begun. Because of the time limit, I focused on one thing, front-facing portraits, and tried to do it well. For my next steps, I plan to:

- Extend the engine to every head angle, using the face mesh's 3D geometry to build an accurate Loomis breakdown for each.

- Extend the walkthrough to include shading 

- Support photos with more than one face

- Add a home widget

Dreams

- Adding support for fictional human-like characters, such as fantasy and cartoon faces

- An engine for animal faces

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**What is Dayflow?**

Dayflow is a smart daily planning app designed around one simple idea:

Your schedule shouldn't fall apart just because one thing changes.

Traditional to do lists give you a static list of tasks. But real life isn't static. Meetings move, tasks take longer, plans change, and suddenly the rest of your day needs to be reorganized.

Dayflow creates a structured daily flow and helps adapt the remaining schedule when plans change.

**The Problem**

Most productivity apps help you create a schedule, but they don't help much when that schedule changes.

If a meeting moves from 4 PM to 5 PM, users often have to manually figure out what happens to everything afterward.

That creates friction and decision fatigue.

**Our Solution**

Dayflow introduces Adaptive Replanning.

Instead of treating your schedule as fixed, Dayflow treats it as a flow that can adapt.

For example:

4 PM meeting → moved to 5 PM

Dayflow can reorganize the remaining schedule, shift affected tasks, and provide a new flow for the rest of the day.

The goal is simple:

Your day changes. Dayflow adapts.

**Key Features**

- Adaptive daily planning

- Automatic schedule replanning

- Task management and completion tracking

- Calendar-based planning

- Productivity insights

- Smooth animations and microinteractions

- Premium monochrome Dark Mode

- Premium monochrome Light Mode

- Dayflow Pro experience

**How We Built It**

Dayflow was built with Flutter and Dart, using Flutter's built-in Material 3 components, animation APIs, responsive layouts, and a modular architecture.

The current MVP uses local simulated AI planning to demonstrate the adaptive scheduling experience without requiring external cloud AI services.

This allowed us to focus on the product experience and demonstrate how adaptive planning could work.

**What We Learned**

One of the biggest lessons from building Dayflow was that productivity isn't only about creating a plan.

A useful planner also needs to handle change.

We focused on designing the experience around what happens after a plan is created when real life inevitably changes it.

**Challenges**

The biggest challenge was creating an adaptive scheduling experience that feels simple to the user while still representing the complexity of reorganizing multiple tasks.

We also focused heavily on making the interface feel smooth and premium while keeping the application lightweight.

**What's Next**

Future versions of Dayflow could include:

- Real AI powered natural language planning

- Persistent task storage

- Notifications and daily briefings

- Calendar integrations

- More advanced scheduling intelligence

- Subscription/payment integration for Dayflow Pro

**Built For**

Dayflow was created as a hackathon MVP to explore how AI assisted development and adaptive scheduling can create a more flexible productivity experience.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I wanted to solve a simple problem: having too many movies and games I want to experience, but not having one place to organize everything. When a backlog gets too big, even choosing what to watch or play can become difficult.

That inspired me to build NextUp — a unified media backlog and decision hub for keeping track of entertainment and deciding what to experience next.

**What it does**

NextUp brings movies, TV series, anime, documentaries, and video games into one place.

Users can search and explore media, add titles to their backlog, track their progress, rate what they have experienced, and view their activity history.

The main feature is Pick My Next, which helps with decision paralysis. Users can filter their choices based on media type, mood, genre, and available time, or simply let NextUp randomly choose something from their backlog.

NextUp also supports guest mode with local storage and account-based cloud synchronization.

**How I built it**

I built NextUp using React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, with Motion for animations and Lucide React for icons.

I integrated external media databases to retrieve information such as titles, artwork, ratings, release dates, genres, platforms, and other metadata.

For persistence, NextUp uses Firebase Authentication and Firestore for account-based cloud storage, while local storage provides a fast offline experience for guests.

**Challenges I ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was bringing different types of entertainment into one consistent experience. Movies, TV series, and games have different metadata and progress systems, so I needed to create a structure that could handle them while keeping each media type useful and distinct.

Another challenge was making Pick My Next more useful than simply choosing a random title. I designed it around factors such as available time, mood, genre, and media type so that the result feels more relevant to the user.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

I'm proud of turning a simple idea into a complete working product with dedicated Movies, Games, Activity, and Profile experiences.

I'm especially happy with the Pick My Next feature because it addresses the actual problem behind the project: sometimes having too many choices makes it harder to choose anything at all.

I also wanted NextUp to be useful without forcing users to create an account immediately, which is why I included guest mode and local persistence alongside cloud synchronization.

**What I learned**

Building NextUp helped me improve my understanding of React, TypeScript, state management, API integration, Firebase, persistent data, reusable components, responsive design, and UI/UX.

I also learned that building a good product isn't just about adding features. Each feature should solve a real problem and work together as part of a simple user experience.

**What's next for NextUp**

I would like to continue improving NextUp with more personalized recommendations, richer statistics, additional media sources, improved streaming information, and more ways for users to organize and discover their entertainment.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Saving a link is easy. Remembering why it mattered—and finding the useful details again—is harder. A restaurant recommendation, a recipe, and an article can all end up in the same growing pile of links. Opening every page again turns a small decision into another research session.

WizMark starts with that everyday problem: a bookmark should preserve the context that made something worth saving. The goal is to make saved links useful when it is time to choose a place, revisit an idea, or plan something with another person.

**What it does**

WizMark is a native iPhone and iPad app for saving, organizing, and revisiting links. Send a URL through the iOS share sheet, and WizMark fetches page metadata for a recognizable bookmark. Add your own notes and tags, organize links into collections, and search across saved content.

WizMark Pro adds AI enrichment. Users choose the information they want, including summaries and place details. A page recommending several cafés can become a bookmark with separate place names, addresses, and opening hours. Places can open in a maps app. Collection settings can remember extraction preferences, and AI can suggest an existing collection for an unfiled bookmark.

Shared collections let people gather links together, with viewer and editor permissions. Basic personal bookmarking works without creating an account. Personal bookmarks are stored locally and can sync through iCloud; shared collections use a separate authenticated service.

**How we built it**

The app uses Swift 6 and SwiftUI, with SwiftData for local persistence and CloudKit for personal synchronization. A native Share Extension keeps saving close to the app where a link was discovered. MapKit connects saved place information with a visual map.

AI extraction runs through a Convex backend using Gemini 2.5 Flash with Google Search grounding. Clerk supports sign-in for shared features. The interface displays analysis status so a saved bookmark remains understandable while enrichment is pending or has failed.

RevenueCat handles subscription offerings, purchase and restore flows, and entitlement updates. The pro entitlement enables AI features, an ad-free experience, and data export. A separate ad_free entitlement supports a one-time purchase for people who only want to remove ads. Purchase status also reaches the Share Extension, keeping premium access consistent while saving.

**Challenges we ran into**

A bookmarked page does not always describe one thing. An article can recommend several places, and their names, addresses, and opening hours must stay together. WizMark represents those places as grouped records, preserving the information for each destination.

Another challenge is keeping saving dependable while network-dependent work happens separately. The bookmark and its enrichment have distinct states: a failed AI request should not erase the link the user wanted to keep. Coordinating local data, personal sync, collaboration, and purchase state also required clear boundaries between services.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

WizMark shipped on the App Store on August 2, 2026. It brings a native sharing workflow, local storage, AI enrichment, collaborative collections, and RevenueCat monetization into a single app available in English and Japanese. The result goes beyond storing URLs: a saved recommendation can become something a person can inspect, annotate, share, and act on.

**What we learned**

Useful AI needs a clear place in an ordinary workflow. Choosing what to extract, showing progress, preserving the original link, and making results easy to copy matter alongside the model itself. Separating Pro from ad removal also makes the product's paid choices easier to explain.

**What's next for WizMark**

The next priorities are to refine extraction quality across more kinds of pages, improve the path from saving to revisiting, and learn from real usage of collaborative collections. The guiding question remains simple: does this help someone do more with a link they already thought was worth keeping?

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every plan I make at UChicago starts the same way: a group chat, five "when are you free?" messages, and half the people never answering. Then I noticed the same problem in offices. Two coworkers ask each other about lunch every day, while a third friend nearby is free too but no one knows each other's schedule, so the poor guy ends up eating alone.
The problem isn't communication. It's that all scheduling infromation is not streamlined. SYNC makes that visible and turns it into a plan in one tap.

**What it does**

SYNC has two kinds of spaces in one app.

Community spaces (friends, campus, clubs, neighborhoods)

- Status per space, with an expiry. You can be "heads down" at work and "free after 6" at run club at the same time. Every status expires, so nothing goes stale.

- Pulses. A one-tap invite with a quorum: "Lunch at 12:30, need 3." When enough people tap In, it confirms. If not, it quietly expires, so nobody has to say no.

- Week view. Your schedule, with an overlay that lights up where friends are free.

Workplace spaces (teams and companies)

- Office days. See who's in on which day, with a suggested anchor day when most of the team overlaps.

- Focus hours. Protected team windows that set everyone to heads down.

- Mixer. Opt-in cross-team coffee pairings.

- Aggregate-only insights. Managers never see individual data. That rule is what makes people willing to install a workplace app.

The design idea is "lit windows": free time glows warm amber against a night-blue background, so a group reads like a building at night.

**How it makes money (RevenueCat)**

Free for communities, paid by workplaces.

- Community Pro (monthly or yearly) unlocks unlimited circle members, unlimited circles, weekly rituals and custom status words. The paywall appears only at the moment of need, such as adding a 13th member, never at launch.

- Workplace plans are annual seat tiers (Team 25, then Business 100/250/500). When a team hits its cap, the admin moves up a tier.

The Pro purchase runs through the RevenueCat Android SDK (Test Store, entitlement sync_unlimited), with prices loaded from the current offering and Pro gated on CustomerInfo. Restore purchases is wired up too. Workplace tiers buy through a RevenueCat "workplace" offering; in this build they're display-only until that offering is configured.

**How I built it**

SYNC is a native Android app in Kotlin with Jetpack Compose and Material 3, using Room for local storage and the RevenueCat SDK for purchases. I built it with Gemini in Google AI Studio and Claude, writing a detailed product spec first and then building and testing screen by screen on my own phone. This build runs on seeded local demo data; a real multi-user backend is the next step.

**Challenges**

- Scope. The idea started as a social app for students, then grew to cover workplaces. The hardest part was finding the shared core (status, availability, intent) so one app could serve both without becoming two apps.

- Changing platforms mid-build. I started in Expo, then switched to a native Kotlin version that was much further along.

- Honest payments. Reviewing the AI-generated code, I found the paywall unlocked Pro for free, checked the wrong entitlement, and used a placeholder key. I replaced it with real RevenueCat purchase calls right before the deadline.

- Privacy. Designing a workplace availability tool that can't be used for surveillance, which led to the aggregate-only rule.

**What I learned**

Reading AI-generated code critically matters as much as generating it. I also learned how entitlements and offerings work, and that the features that make people trust an app, like expiring statuses and no individual analytics, matter more than the flashy ones.

**What's next**

A real-time backend, a launch at UChicago with one UChicago dorm house, called Max P, and on RSO (Recognized Student Organization), — UChicago Quantum, and then workplace pilots in larger communities and companies.

</details>

href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/170/896/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/170/896/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Couples take thousands of photos together, but they end up scattered across camera rolls, group chats, and cloud backups with zero shared narrative. A shared album is a folder, not a story. We wanted something with the emotional weight of a physical scrapbook, kept together, that a couple actually opens and adds to — not another social feed optimized for other people's attention.

The idea crystallized around a single visual metaphor: a thread that runs through every milestone — first date, moving in together, trips, anniversaries — literally stitching the relationship's timeline together. Once we had that metaphor, the product language followed naturally: you don't "post" a memory, you "stitch a moment." An empty timeline isn't an empty state, it's "the thread awaits its first stitch." That consistency of voice is what pushed this from a CRUD photo app into something with a real point of view — which is also why we targeted the Design Award category alongside HAMM.

**Prize Categories**

Primary targets: HAMM (monetization) and the Design Award. We'd also be glad to be considered for the Grand Prize, but we built OurThread first and foremost to win on monetization strategy and visual craft.

**HAMM: monetization built around the couple, not the individual**

- One subscription per couple. A relationship app that charges each partner separately feels wrong, so one purchase unlocks premium for both. Entitlement is tied to the couple, not to a user. RevenueCat webhooks (INITIAL_PURCHASE, RENEWAL, EXPIRATION) go to a Supabase Edge Function, which updates the couple's subscription row. The backend decides access from that row, so the partner who didn't pay gets premium right away without any promotional-entitlement workarounds.

- The free tier is the trial. Free couples get one timeline, up to 5 moments and the default theme. We dropped a separate 7-day trial because it was redundant. Five stitched moments is enough to get a couple emotionally invested in their thread. When the paywall appears, it comes at the moment they want to keep going, not on an arbitrary timer.

- Premium grows with the relationship. Premium adds unlimited moments, 5 alternate color palettes with a matching adaptive app icon, seasonal and limited-edition themes, cloud backup, and an exportable Annual Recap. The Recap gives couples a reason to come back every year, and it's shareable, which helps new users find the app.

**Design Award: a point of view, executed with polish**

- The thread is how you navigate the app, not just decoration. A continuous terracotta thread connects every moment in chronological order. The timeline opens at the newest stitch, and you scroll up to relive the story from the beginning.

- Layouts are permanent. Card rotations, cover layouts (polaroid, duo-polaroid, circle, full-bleed and more) and thread connector shapes look varied but are derived from each moment's ID, never regenerated per session. Both partners see the exact same scrapbook on any device, every time, because the product's promise is a shared artifact that doesn't change.

- One design system across six themes. Every screen reads from shared tokens, so all six palettes work across the whole app without redesigning any screen.

- The copy uses the same metaphor throughout. You "stitch a moment," "unstitch" one, and an empty timeline "awaits its first stitch." Editorial serif titles, a warm cream background and no dating-app clichés (no saturated pinks, no generic hearts) make the app feel like a travel journal.

**What it does**

OurThread is a shared visual diary for couples, built for iOS. Two partners link their accounts through a single-use invite link, and from then on they both add to one collaborative timeline: photos plus a short note, pinned to a date and location. The timeline renders as a chronological, top-to-bottom thread — each moment gets one of several deterministically-varied layouts (polaroid, circle crop, full-bleed, duo-polaroid for two photos, wide) connected by hand-drawn-feeling thread connectors, so the same moment always looks the same on any device, in any session, for both partners.

The subscription is priced per couple, not per person — one partner pays, both get premium. Free gives you one timeline and up to five moments as a natural trial (we deliberately dropped a separate 7-day trial as redundant); premium unlocks unlimited moments, five additional color themes (including an adaptive iOS app icon per theme), cloud backup, and an exportable Annual Recap — a five-slide, story-style playback of the year's moments, styled like an end-of-year Spotify Wrapped but built entirely around the thread/stitch visual language, shareable straight to Instagram Stories.

**How we built it**

React Native + Expo for the client, Supabase for essentially everything on the backend — Postgres, Auth, Storage with Row Level Security scoped to couple_id, Edge Functions, and Realtime. Auth is Sign in with Apple and Google collapsed into a single tap on the welcome screen (Apple requires offering both once you offer any third-party social login). RevenueCat handles the paywall and entitlements; a Supabase Edge Function listens for RevenueCat's purchase/renewal/expiration webhooks and updates the couple's row in a subscriptions table keyed by couple_id rather than user_id — that one modeling decision let us support shared-per-couple premium without needing RevenueCat's one-to-many promotional-entitlement grant for the second partner; the backend just resolves access from the couple, which either partner's session can read.

Data fetching runs through TanStack Query, with a clean split we held to throughout: plain Supabase calls live in services/api.ts, and the hooks components actually use (useMoments, an infinite query paging the moments table, etc.) live in services/queries.ts. The design system is token-based rather than hardcoded per screen — colors, type, spacing, and radii all read from useTheme() — which is what let us ship six total palettes (default terracotta plus five premium ones) without re-implementing any screen per theme, including swapping the iOS app icon via setAlternateIconName. The whole visual language — including exact hex values and font stacks — was prototyped first as real interactive HTML/CSS files before any of it became React Native components, so we always had a literal source of truth to extract from instead of eyeballing a screenshot.

The trickiest interaction piece was the timeline itself: card rotation, layout choice per moment, and the connector shape between cards all needed to look organic and varied, but had to be fully deterministic — seeded from the moment's own id — so a shared timeline renders identically for both partners and doesn't visually drift between app sessions. We also built the thread connectors as a scroll-linked reveal, tracing in as you scroll rather than just appearing, and iterated through a few reveal techniques (SVG mask reveal, then a clipped-View approach) before landing on one that performed well on device. PostHog is wired in for product analytics on the moments/recap/paywall funnels, which is already shaping what we prioritize next.

This was also effectively a two-person team of one developer plus Claude: the entire visual system started as interactive HTML/CSS prototypes built in Claude Design, which is what let us lock in exact colors, typography, and spacing before a single React Native component existed, instead of translating screenshots by eye. Claude Code did the heavy lifting turning that design reference into the actual app — screens, the seeded timeline logic, the RevenueCat/Supabase webhook wiring — working directly from a project-level spec that encoded the data model, business rules, and design tokens so the output stayed consistent screen after screen. Building something with this much visual and logical polish (six themes, deterministic layout system, full onboarding/paywall/recap flow) solo, in the Shipaton's timeframe, wouldn't have been realistic without that workflow.

**Challenges we ran into**

Getting the timeline to feel alive without feeling random was the core design tension of the whole project — early passes used naive randomness for layout and connector selection, which looked fine in isolation but broke the moment you reopened the app and a moment's layout had changed, or a couple opened the same timeline on two different phones and saw two different things. Reworking that around a stable per-moment seed fixed it, but took a few iterations to get connector variety and layout selection (e.g., avoiding two "circle" layouts back to back) to still look intentional rather than mechanical.

The Annual Recap's share flow was its own multi-day fight — getting the exported share-preview image to actually match what's rendered on screen (rather than clipping content or losing styling) took several passes, including moving from a bottom sheet to a modal for the share preview to get reliable layout behavior.

Modeling the couple relationship correctly also took real thought: subscriptions, invite links, and even "has this person finished onboarding" all needed to be derived from relational state rather than flags, since a couple can legitimately exist with only one partner onboarded, invites must be provably single-use without silently overwriting an existing partner, and none of that can drift out of sync the way a boolean flag can.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The deterministic-but-organic timeline rendering is the piece we're proudest of — it's subtle, but it's the difference between an app that looks hand-crafted and one that looks templated. We're also proud of holding the sewing/thread metaphor all the way through the product, from microcopy to the Annual Recap's visual identity to the empty state, instead of it being a launch-screen gimmick that fades away three screens in. And the couple-level subscription model, worked out entirely through data modeling rather than a special-cased integration with RevenueCat's promotional entitlements, kept the payments code simple while still doing the right thing for both partners.

**What we learned**

Modeling shared, two-person state correctly from day one saves you from a lot of special-casing later — almost every "who sees what, who can do what" question in this app collapsed into "read it off the couple's row," once couples and subscriptions were modeled at the couple level instead of the user level. We also relearned that visual consistency is a much harder engineering problem than a design problem: getting variety and permanence to coexist in the same feature (the timeline layout) meant treating "randomness" as a first-class, testable, seeded system rather than a decoration layer.

**What's next for OurThread**

OurThread is already live on the App Store, with the full feature set — including settings/account and the theme switcher — shipped. From here, the focus shifts from building to growing: using Layers to run organic growth experiments (App Store listing, screenshots, positioning) and leaning on PostHog to actually understand user behavior across the moments/paywall/recap funnels — which themes get picked, where the paywall converts or drops off, whether the Annual Recap drives re-engagement — and letting that data, rather than guesses, decide what gets built next.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Full Calculus**

**Inspiration**

Calculus is one of those subjects where understanding the process matters just as much as getting the final answer. Many students, including me, struggle because they have to jump between lecture notes, textbooks, calculators, solution websites, and different learning platforms just to study one topic.

I wanted to build a single platform that could take a student from the fundamentals of Calculus I through the more advanced topics of Calculus II and III, while also allowing them to learn, practice, check their answers, and get help when they are stuck.

That idea became Full Calculus.

**What it does**

Full Calculus is an interactive calculus learning platform covering:

- Calculus I: functions, limits, continuity, derivatives, applications of derivatives, and introductory integration

- Calculus II: integration techniques, applications of integration, parametric equations, polar coordinates, sequences, series, convergence tests, and power series

- Calculus III: vectors, vector functions, multivariable calculus, multiple integrals, and vector calculus

The platform is designed to achieve active learning and practice, not simply providing formulas or answers.

**How I built it**

I built Full Calculus as a web-based application using JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with a modular JavaScript architecture for lessons, exercises, grading, and application functionality.

One of the more technically challenging parts was building the mathematical answer-validation system. Instead of relying on simple string comparisons, the system parses mathematical expressions and evaluates whether a student's answer is mathematically equivalent to the expected answer.

For example, expressions such as:

2x

and

2*x

can be interpreted consistently, while expressions involving fractions, powers, trigonometric functions, logarithms, and variables can also be validated.

The validation engine supports mathematical operators, parentheses, fractions, constants such as \(\pi\) and \(e\), and functions including \(sin\), \(cos\), \(tan\), \(sqrt{}\), \(log\), and \(ln\) It evaluates expressions across multiple sample points while safely handling singularities rather than relying on raw eval().

The project also includes an AI-powered solver to provide additional assistance when students get stuck, alongside account functionality and a mobile/PWA-oriented experience.

**Challenges**

The biggest challenge was making mathematical interaction reliable.

A traditional quiz system can simply compare a submitted answer with a stored string. Mathematics is different: two completely different-looking expressions can represent the same mathematical result.

I therefore had to think about:

- Parsing mathematical expressions safely

- Handling implicit multiplication

- Determining mathematical equivalence

- Supporting both numerical and algebraic answers

- Handling undefined values and singularities

- Providing useful feedback to students

- Designing lessons that work across hundreds of calculus concepts

Another challenge was organizing such a broad curriculum into a coherent learning experience. Full Calculus currently spans material from basic functions and limits all the way to topics such as Taylor series, multiple integrals, Green's Theorem, Stokes' Theorem, and the Divergence Theorem.

**What I learned**

Building Full Calculus taught me that educational software requires more than simply presenting information.

I learned how important it is to design around how users learn, rather than just what information an application contains. I also gained experience building mathematical parsing and validation logic, designing interactive exercises, integrating AI assistance, and structuring a large educational application into reusable components.

Most importantly, the project showed me how software engineering can be used to solve a problem I personally understand: making difficult technical subjects more accessible and interactive.

**What's next**

Full Calculus very young still evolving. Future improvements will include expanding interactive explanations, improving personalized learning paths, adding more sophisticated mathematical feedback, and continuing to improve the mobile experience.

The long-term goal is to make Full Calculus a practical companion for students studying calculus and making it a place where they can actually learn how to solve problems.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I'm a 15-year-old high school student in Turkey. Every time I sat down to study, I ended up on my phone five minutes later — and all my friends had the same problem. Existing apps were easy to cheat, so I wanted to build one that actually makes you keep your promise to yourself. That's where the name comes from: an oath you can't break, because it's locked.

**What it does**

Oathlock is an Android focus app:

- Real app blocking – pick distracting apps from the list of apps installed on your phone; during a focus session, opening them shows a block screen.

- Math alarm – built on Android's native alarm system; to turn it off you have to solve math problems, so you're actually awake.

- Tasks with deadlines and reminders – notifications arrive on time, even after a restart.

- AI coach – powered by Gemini; tell it "I can't start studying" and it gives you a short, practical plan.

- Screen time stats – see how much time you spend on your phone.

- 3 languages – English, Turkish and German.

- Oathlock Pro – $4.99/month or $40/year, powered by RevenueCat.

**How I built it**

- React 19 + TypeScript + Vite + Tailwind, wrapped with Capacitor 8 for Android.

- A custom native Java plugin for the parts the web can't do: Accessibility Service (app blocking), AlarmManager (alarms), UsageStats (screen time), foreground services and boot receivers.

- RevenueCat SDK for subscriptions: one "pro" entitlement with monthly and yearly products, shown through an offering in the paywall.

- Google Sign-In for accounts and the Gemini API for the AI coach.

- I used AI coding assistants to learn and move faster, while I designed the app, tested every feature on my own phone and made the decisions.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Making app blocking reliable on Android with the Accessibility Service.

- Making the alarm ring like a real alarm even when the phone is locked or the app is closed.

- Setting up RevenueCat products, entitlements and offerings correctly for the first time.

- Translating both the app interface and the native Android notifications into 3 languages.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

Building

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Chlora started with a simple question: What if taking a photo of a plant could give you more than just its name?

Plant identification is only the beginning. When a plant develops yellow leaves, spots, pests, or other symptoms, gardeners often have to search through articles, forums and conflicting advice to figure out what is actually wrong and what they should do next.

I wanted to build something that could shorten that journey.

The idea behind Chlora is to move from:

“What plant is this?”

to:

“What is wrong with it, why is it happening and what can I do to help it recover?”

I was also interested in building something where AI could solve a real-world problem rather than simply demonstrating an impressive model.

**What it does**

Chlora is a plant identification and diagnosis app utilizing machine learning and computer vision for plant disease detection.

Users can take a photo of a plant and use Chlora to:

- Identify the plant and provide its scientific name.

- Analyze visible symptoms and identify potential problems.

- Estimate the severity of a detected problem.

- Show likely causes behind the symptoms.

- Provide practical care and recovery guidance.

- Generate a 7-day recovery plan.

- Save plants and monitor them over time.

The goal is to make plant care more actionable. Instead of giving someone a disease name and leaving them to search for the next step, Chlora tries to connect identification, diagnosis, causes and recovery into one workflow.

**How we built it**

Chlora was built as a mobile-first application combining computer vision image analysis with structured plant knowledge.

The AI analyzes plant photographs and visible symptoms, while the knowledge layer provides the relationships between plants, diseases, environmental conditions, and treatments.

I designed the product around a simple workflow:

Photo → Identification → Diagnosis → Causes → Recovery

I also integrated analytics so I can understand how real users interact with the application, where they get stuck and which features they actually use.

Chlora is currently available on Google Play and I am using real-world feedback to continuously improve the product.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was realizing how messy real-world plant photographs are.

A photograph can contain shadows, different lighting conditions, soil, multiple leaves, insects, disease symptoms and environmental clues at the same time.

Small pests are particularly difficult because they can occupy only a tiny portion of an image. A full-image analysis may correctly recognize the plant while completely missing an insect sitting on one of its leaves.

Another challenge has been diagnosis severity. A visually severe symptom does not always mean the same thing for the plant's overall outcome. Feedback from gardeners has shown us that severity needs to reflect practical impact, not just how dramatic a symptom looks.

We have also had to think carefully about how much information to show. A gardener needs enough information to make a decision, but not so much that the diagnosis becomes overwhelming.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The biggest accomplishment is that Chlora has moved beyond an idea into a real product that people can download and use.

It is live on Google Play and is already being tested by real gardeners.

What makes us especially proud is the feedback coming from actual users. Experienced gardeners have been testing Chlora and giving detailed feedback about diagnosis accuracy, pest detection, severity levels, recovery guidance and features they would genuinely use.

That feedback is helping shape the product in ways that would be difficult to discover through development alone.

We are also proud of building the complete journey from plant identification to diagnosis and recovery rather than stopping at a simple plant-recognition model.

**What we learned**

The biggest lesson has been that building the AI is only part of building the product.

A technically impressive prediction is not enough if the recommendation doesn't make sense to the gardener.

Real users have already helped us discover problems we would not have found ourselves. For example, gardeners have pointed out situations where shadows can be mistaken for moisture problems, obvious yellow leaves can be missed and small insects can disappear inside a larger plant photograph.

We have also learned that product-market fit comes from listening closely to users rather than assuming we already know what they want.

The most valuable conversations have been with gardeners who actually use Chlora and tell us what they would change, what they don't trust and what would make them come back.

**What's next for Chlora**

The next goal is to make Chlora useful throughout the entire plant-growing journey, not just when something goes wrong.

We are working toward better plant diagnosis, improved insect identification, more personalized care recommendations, environmental context, seasonal reminders and better plant progress tracking.

We also want Chlora to eventually help gardeners understand their plants before problems become serious.

Ultimately, the vision is for Chlora to become a trusted plant-care companion something gardeners can turn to when they discover a new plant, notice something unusual, or simply want to help their plants thrive.

</details>

**Inspiration**

Most builders, developers, and founders start their weeks with ambitious backlogs, only to get derailed by context switching, decision fatigue, and friction in starting tasks. At the same time, turning high-engagement mobile apps into sustainable recurring revenue is often an afterthought—marred by static, one-size-fits-all paywalls and disconnected web funnels.

We were inspired to build ShipCat AI to solve both challenges in tandem:

- Personal Momentum & Execution: Provide an autonomous, dopamine-reinforcing execution companion that pairs real-time Gemini AI coaching with focused sprint intervals and real-time binaural sound synthesis.

- First-Class Mobile Monetization: Showcase how indie creators can leverage the full power of RevenueCat Paywalls V2, dynamic A/B experimentation, consumable token packs, OneSignal push journeys, and Stripe web-to-app funnels to build a sustainable business on Day 1.

**What it does**

ShipCat AI is a comprehensive mobile momentum, habit coaching, and career development engine:

- 🚀 Autonomous Momentum & Habit Engine: Track daily habit streaks, conquer procrastination with 25-minute deep focus sprints, and level up with gamified XP and celebratory haptic audio feedback.

- 🎧 Real-Time Binaural Soundscapes: Integrated Web Audio synthesizer generating real-time Alpha (108 Hz) and Gamma (216 Hz) focus soundscapes during active sprint sessions.

- 🤖 Shippy AI Coach (Gemini API): Autonomous, low-latency conversational coach that provides adaptive task breakdown, energy-level scheduling, and friction reduction.

- 💼 Leadership Heather Simulator (Career Coaching): Interactive roleplay environment where emerging managers can practice high-stakes workplace conversations (scope creep pushback, moving deadlines, performance reviews) with real-time scoring across Empathy, Clarity, and Boundary Setting.

- 💳 RevenueCat Paywalls V2 & HAMM Suite:

- Multi-tier dynamic subscriptions: Monthly ($9.99/mo with 7-day trial), Annual ($49.99/yr with 58% savings), and Lifetime Founder VIP Pass ($149.99).

- Consumable Spark AI Token Packs ($2.99 for 50, $8.99 for 250) for pay-per-use deep coaching.

- Live A/B Experimentation Engine across 4 high-converting templates (Value Hero, Feature Matrix Grid, Countdown Flash Urgency, and Creator Social Proof).

- Judge Promo Code redemption box (SHIPATON2026 / JUDGE_ACCESS) and sandbox receipt restoration.

- 🔄 Sponsor Growth Ecosystem:

- OneSignal Smart Re-Engagement Lab: Automated lifecycle push campaigns (Day 1 Welcome, Day 3 Streak Saver, Day 7 Trial Expiration, Day 14 Winback).

- Layers Growth Loop: Double-sided viral referral flywheel with measurable conversion telemetry.

- Stripe Web-to-App Funnel: Frictionless web landing page checkout (checkout.shipcat.app) syncing entitlements directly into the mobile app.

- 📱 Multi-Device & Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 6 Multi-Window: Responsive simulator switching between Pixel 9 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro, clean frameless store mode, and an unfolded dual-pane Samsung Galaxy Fold multi-window layout.

**How we built it**

- Frontend & Mobile UI: React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Lucide React icons, and motion/react for fluid spring physics and micro-interactions.

- AI & Intelligence Engine: Server-side Gemini 3.7 Flash with resilient automatic retry logic and fallback routing to Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, plus offline contextual heuristics.

- Audio Synthesis: Custom Web Audio API oscillator architecture for carrier-wave binaural beat generation and crisp UI acoustic feedback.

- Monetization & Analytics Layer: Native RevenueCat SDK V2 architecture mapping customer offerings, entitlement gates, and sandbox receipts.

- Backend Service: Node.js Express server handling API routing, secure Gemini key custody, and webhook entitlement synchronization.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Seamless Paywall Template Swapping: Constructing a unified state engine capable of swapping between radically different paywall layouts (Value Stack, Feature Comparison Matrix, Countdown Urgency, and Social Proof) while preserving subscription state and checkout flows.

- Resilient AI Pipeline During Demand Spikes: Upstream LLMs can encounter transient 503 or capacity spikes. We engineered an autonomous generateWithResilience backend middleware that performs exponential retries, model fallbacks, and smart heuristic continuations so users never hit dead ends.

- Adaptive Foldable Architecture: Designing the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 6 dual-pane interface so that the habit sprint tracker on the left pane seamlessly communicates with the AI workspace on the right without race conditions.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- 🏆 Comprehensive Multi-Category Alignment: Deeply engineered integrations across the Grand Prize ($100k), RevenueCat Design Award ($15k), HAMM Monetization Award ($15k), OneSignal Push Award ($25k), Layers Growth Loop ($15k), Stripe Funnel Vision ($15k), and Samsung Galaxy Fold.

- 🎨 Anti-Slop Craftsmanship: Designed a distinctive obsidian-and-aurora dark mode visual language without generic gradients or placeholder cards.

- ⚡ Zero-Lag Sound Engine: Integrated real-time binaural oscillators directly into browser memory without bulky audio files.

- 📦 1-Click Judge & App Store Readiness: Built-in 1024x1024 PNG App Icon exporter and frameless screenshot capture meeting Rule 4 requirements.

**What we learned**

- The power of RevenueCat Paywalls V2 in dramatically reducing time-to-market for mobile monetization and enabling rapid paywall iteration without app store re-submissions.

- How to structure multi-turn AI roleplay prompts to deliver quantitative soft-skill scoring (empathy, clarity, boundaries) that feels genuinely constructive.

- Designing for foldable and dual-screen form factors from day one unlocks immense productivity density for power users.

**What's next for ShipCat AI: Daily Momentum & Monetization Engine**

- Multiplayer Sprint Rooms: Shared focus co-working sprints with real-time presence for remote teams and hackathon cohorts.

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/969/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/969/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/970/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/970/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/972/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/972/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/990/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/990/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Most of us make decisions with a spreadsheet open and a body we've stopped listening to. Sensie started from a simple observation made from decades of coaching work: people already know how they feel about a decision. They just can't access it on demand, and no app asks.

In our founder's words: "I had to do 20 years of therapy to get the most simple thing. That simple thing is being able to trust self. Can I trust the anger, the fear, the sadness? When I don't trust them, I push them away. When I trust them, it opens up this whole kaleidoscope of possibilities." Notice sooner. Choose better. 

We wanted a check-in that takes less time than opening a journal. No camera, no wearable, no 40-question survey. Just hold your phone, think about the statement, flick your wrist, and get an honest read. We call that a vibecheck.

One early tester was heading into a high-stakes meeting convinced the other side was "a dragon on the hill." Big ego, hard to work with, a fight waiting to happen. Before walking in, he ran a three-second check-in. His body flagged it as a story, not a read on the person. He let it go, walked in open, and found a collaborator. It turned into one of his best deals.

We watched early testers catch stories like that again and again, just by pausing to check in with their body. Then AI agents started making decisions alongside us, and the idea got bigger. What if your agent could take that same pause? Before it acts on your behalf, it asks your body, and you answer with a three-second gesture instead of typing a word.

**What it does**

SomaCheck turns a 3-second phone gesture into a signal. You hold the phone, hold a first-person statement in mind ("I feel clear about what deserves my attention right now"), and flick your wrist. The app reads the motion, compares it against your own personal calibration, and returns Aligned or Unaligned with a confidence. It's not a diagnosis and it's not a decision. It's a signal worth noticing.

Vibe check anything, from anywhere:

- In the app. Calibrate once, then check any statement you type, any time: hold the phone, flick your wrist three times (a gong sounds on each flick), and the verdict lands. Tell it whether it got you right and it learns your signal over time. If the read is Unaligned, choose Apollo, a 2-3 minute voice-guided breathing reset, or go deeper with a 20-25 minute guided integration session that works on the trigger itself. Journey shows your timeline, streaks and patterns over time.

- From your AI agent (MCP). Connect Claude Code, Codex, or Claude.ai with one command. Your agent gets six tools, including request_vibecheck, which sends one consented statement to your phone and waits up to 45 seconds for the exact result. The agent is told to treat it as a signal, not a verdict, and to say what it changes.

- From any product (API). The Statement API lets anything - a Slack bot, a survey, a calendar reminder, a friend's text - say "offer this person this statement" and receive the embodied answer back with a signed share link and a webhook.

- World Vibe. Public topics anyone can vibecheck from a QR or link. Your own answer is private; the group split unlocks once five unique people have checked in. No tracking, no cookies, no identity shown.

**How we built it**

- iOS app: Swift + SwiftUI with CoreMotion, running Sensie's patented gesture and calibration algorithms, an ElevenLabs-powered voice agent for the Apollo reset, built with XcodeGen and fastlane, CI on GitHub Actions macOS runners.

- Backend: Supabase Postgres and Deno/TypeScript Edge Functions. One request-and-consent layer serves the app, the MCP and the API.

- MCP: @somacheck/vibecheck on npm (built on the official MCP TypeScript SDK) for local use with Claude Code and Codex, and a hosted Streamable-HTTP server at mcp.somacheck.com behind OAuth 2.1 for Claude.ai. Same six tools on both paths. Published from CI with GitHub OIDC trusted publishing, no long-lived tokens.

- Web: somacheck.com (marketing + docs) and go.somacheck.com (World Vibe portal, universal links, share fallbacks) on GitHub Pages - zero analytics, zero cookies by design.

- Process: a small human team plus a multi-model agent fleet (Claude, GPT, DeepSeek, MiniMax, GLM, Kimi) with adversarial cross-model reviews before anything merges. Those reviews caught a billing race and a data-integrity bug before any customer did.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Our signal can identify sources of stress before a person is aware of it, this led to potentially creating conflict for people, them wondering if there was algorithmic-fuckery going on or if the topic really was a source of stress. So we had to create a unique realtime continuous auditory feedback system that lets a person hear their emotional state in realtime.

- Presentation integrity. Our first live API round trip exposed a real edge case where a routine check-in could have been matched to the wrong statement. We now require the text shown on the phone to match the statement being answered, exactly, before a result is delivered. 

- Tests that lie. An earlier build passed 6/6 end-to-end tests while a key screen could never appear, because every test hit the backend over HTTP and none exercised the real client path. Rule now: cover the real client path or the test is theatre.

- Two deployment paths, one truth. Keeping the local npm MCP and the hosted OAuth MCP behaviourally identical (same tools, same fail-closed behaviour for unauthenticated calls) took more discipline than building either one.

- Outside testers found what we couldn't. Five independent testers ran a cold end-to-end before launch and found a silent failure our own tests never surfaced. That's why every release now has a written threat model with failure cases that must fail.

- CI economics. macOS runners without path filters burned the org's entire Actions budget in a day. We fixed the filters and added a push-cadence gate.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A 3-second, no-hardware check-in that runs against your own calibration, built on tens of thousands of recorded sessions and nine PhD-led research trials, on two granted US patents.

- Over a thousand automated tests green on the 1.0 release candidate, with a freeze list that requires the founder's personal sign-off on any change to the sensing code.

- A working, consent-first MCP integration: 13 npm releases since July 29, hosted OAuth server live, and real people using it - 34 linked agents across 12 users at the time of writing.

- The Statement API in production, with metering, signed share links and webhooks, so every growth surface (agents, share-by-text, surveys, Slack, Siri, World Vibe) is a client of one door.

- World Vibe live with QR-to-answer in under a minute and honest group results (suppressed until five people have answered).

- Researched with PhDs from Oxford, UC Berkeley, and Northwestern, with research trials pending at Mayo Clinic and UC Berkeley.

**What we learned**

- The gesture is the easy part. Consent, cadence and honesty about what a signal means are the product.

- People will let an agent ask them a question they'd never ask themselves, as long as the agent can't see the raw data and the person can revoke it in one tap.

- Binary is kinder than a scale. Aligned/Unaligned plus confidence made results readable in a second; anything more invited over-interpretation.

- "Free for individuals" is a feature, not a sacrifice. It lets clinics, teams and developers be the ones who pay.

**What's next**

- Now live on the App Store: SomaCheck: Vibecheck (https://apps.apple.com/us/app/somacheck-vibecheck/id6792978184), with the RevenueCat-powered SomaCheck Pro tier.

- Listing the vibecheck MCP on the official registry, Smithery and the Claude connector directory.

- Share-a-vibecheck by SMS/WhatsApp, an "embodied answer" question type for surveys, /vibecheck in Slack, and "Hey Siri, vibecheck."

- World Vibe topics for public moments, including a board where anyone can vibe check what the other Shipaton teams are building.

- Care-provider dashboards so clinicians can see the weeks between sessions.

- An agent that proposes the statement from context it already holds, so the check-in meets you at the moment it matters.

</details>

**Inspiration**

Fighting games are unique in that the magic happens at so called locals. Locals are tournaments where people attend physically. This means travel and travel means unreliable internet.

**What it does**

Fighting Nerd has two main functions:

- fully offline data - users can access information no matter their connectivity

- consistent search and filtering across various games

**How I built it**

The Fighting Nerd project started out as a Discord frame data bot, after the old one died. From the very beginning, I had two non-negotiables:

- it must support multiple games

- it must source data from community wikis

Because of those factors, the project was highly modular from the very beginning. This made adding mobile clients on top of the Discord client the natural next step. And Compose Multiplatform was the obvious tool for the job.

**Challenges we ran into**

The architecture was the biggest one. The project uses five wikis and supports 15 games. Modularity was critical.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

The bot was a success - it's currently in 550 Discord servers and has 300 uses every day. FightingNerd is the defacto frame data bot for Tekken, BlazBlue, Uni and Melty Blood. Breaking into other games is an on-going aspiration.

Another thing I'm proud of are the original functionalities for Tekken, which is the game I have most experience with.

**What I learned**

Even if you have a free and compelling product, communicating the selling points to strangers is very difficult.

**What's next for Fighting Nerd**

WASM.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**PlanDee**

**Inspiration**

In emerging markets like Nigeria, mobile data is expensive and telecom pricing is confusing. Carriers offer hundreds of overlapping bundles with tricky conditions—like night-only data, social-app quotas, and short validity periods. Most smartphone users end up overpaying, wasting unused bonus data, or losing money to pay-as-you-go airtime billing simply because tracking granular usage across multiple SIMs is manually impossible.

I built PlanDee to solve this: converting raw Android network statistics into clear, actionable telecom recommendations—helping everyday users pick the exact data plans that match their actual habits and save money.

**What It Does**

PlanDee tracks on-device data consumption and automatically matches users with the cheapest telecom plans:

- Automated Data Auditing: Monitors data usage per app, separating foreground activity, background drain, Wi-Fi usage, and off-peak (night) data windows.

- Smart Tariff Matching: Compares real user consumption against updated pricing catalogs across MTN, Airtel, Glo, and 9mobile to find the most cost-effective bundles.

- Runout & Expiry Alerts: Tracks daily burn rates to warn users before their data runs out or switches to expensive direct airtime billing.

- 1-Tap USSD & Purchase Actions: Generates pre-formatted dialer codes (USSD) and payment links to renew or switch plans in seconds.

**How I Built It**

I architected PlanDee as a native Android app backed by a lightweight Go microservice:

- Android App (Kotlin & Jetpack Compose): Native Android app using NetworkStatsManager to query byte-level network usage per UID, with WorkManager handling periodic background collection. UI state is driven by StateFlow streams following MVVM architecture.

- Backend Service (Go & PostgreSQL): Built in Go for fast response times. PostgreSQL stores carrier tariff catalogs, user usage summaries, and recommendation records.

- Optimization Engine: I framed plan selection as a multi-constraint Knapsack / Dynamic Programming problem in Go. Instead of guessing, my backend evaluates single plans and multi-bundle combinations against the user's budget, night usage ratio, and top app categories to find the global minimum cost.

$$\text{DP}(b, t) = \min_{p \in \mathcal{P}} \Big( \text{Price}(p) + \text{DP}\big(\max(0, b - \text{UsableBytes}(p)), \, \max(0, t - \text{Validity}(p))\big) \Big)$$

**Challenges I Ran Into**

- Sanitizing Android Network Telemetry: Android's raw NetworkStatsManager queries include kernel traffic, system daemons, and uninstalled app UIDs. I built a filtering pipeline to isolate real user apps.

- Jetpack Compose Performance: Parsing network logs and loading app icons initially caused UI stutter when executed on the main thread. I resolved this by moving telemetry aggregation to background coroutines (Dispatchers.IO).

- Multi-Constraint Optimization: Factoring in night-owl bonuses and app-specific allowances increased combination complexity. I optimized state transitions in Go to keep recommendation responses under a few milliseconds.

- In-App Purchase Testing: Testing subscription tiers locally without an active Google Play Console setup required building a mock repository layer and fallback entitlement handlers.

**Accomplishments I'm Proud Of**

- Sub-Millisecond Plan Matching: Built a Go recommendation engine that evaluates hundreds of tariff plan combinations under strict budget limits in less than 1 ms.

- Clean, Responsive Dashboard: Created a lightweight Jetpack Compose UI with intuitive charts that display usage breakdowns cleanly without lagging.

- Real-World Savings: Built an end-to-end working tool capable of saving smartphone users 15% to 30% on monthly mobile data expenses.

**What I Learned**

- Transitioning to Modern Android: Moving from core Java fundamentals to modern Kotlin, coroutines, StateFlow, and Jetpack Compose state management.

- Applied Algorithm Design: Implementing dynamic programming for a real production backend rather than just textbook exercises.

- Android OS Internals: Working directly with Linux UID network accounting, system usage buckets, and modern background execution constraints.

- System Design & Pragmatism: Designing clean API contracts between dynamic backend pricing catalogs and mobile client execution logic.

**What's Next for PlanDee**

- Direct In-App Bundle Purchases (VTU): Integrating direct payment gateways (Paystack/Flutterwave + VTU APIs) to let users buy data directly inside the app.

- Usage Forecasting: Adding time-series forecasting to predict heavy usage spikes before they happen.

- Dual-SIM Smart Routing: Automatically detecting dual-SIM slots to route recommendation advice per SIM card slot.
A rollout for most of the features listed on the Pro Plan

</details>

**Inspiration**

Embervale was inspired by classic dark-fantasy action RPGs and the challenge of creating a meaningful adventure that works well on mobile. We wanted to build a world that feels mysterious and rewarding to explore, while keeping combat readable and responsive on a small screen.

**What It Does**

Embervale is a stylized dark-fantasy action RPG built for Android and desktop. Players explore five distinct realms, fight enemies and bosses, gather materials, discover new locations, upgrade equipment, and forge weapons from blueprints.

The project includes:

- Five unique realms: Whispergrove, Bramblewood, Mistfen, Heartwood, and Moonfen

- Action combat with dodging, skills, enemy telegraphs, elites, and bosses

- Gathering, inventory, equipment, crafting, and blueprint-based forging

- A discovery codex and player-following minimap

- Portrait-oriented mobile controls and safe-area-aware UI

- Scalable visual quality settings for different devices

- A hosted RevenueCat and Stripe purchase flow designed to keep sensitive provider credentials server-side

**How We Built It**

The game was built with Godot 4.7 using typed GDScript. We created reusable systems for combat, world streaming, terrain materials, enemy behavior, bosses, inventory, forging, quests, UI, audio, and quality scaling.

The environment uses stylized physically based materials, procedural terrain details, realm-specific color palettes, landmarks, waterways, and exploration paths. Gameplay systems are data-driven so that weapons, enemies, rewards, and realm content can be expanded without rewriting the core systems.

Because Android is the primary target, the project uses capped visual effects, scalable particles, limited transient lights, optimized materials, portrait UI layouts, and touch-friendly interaction controls.

**Challenges**

One of the biggest challenges was balancing visual quality with mobile performance. Lower quality settings needed to reduce presentation cost without changing damage, collision, gameplay timing, or telegraph readability.

Another challenge was designing a complete RPG loop that feels understandable:

- Explore a realm

- Discover enemies and resources

- Gather materials

- Compare equipment

- Forge an upgrade

- Return to the world with new abilities and goals

We also had to make crafting transactional and save-safe, preventing duplicate rewards or repeated resource deductions when the player interacts multiple times, dies, reloads, or travels between realms.

**What We Learned**

We learned that mobile game design requires more than simply shrinking a desktop interface. Controls, menus, touch targets, safe areas, combat feedback, and text hierarchy all need to be designed around short play sessions and limited screen space.

We also learned the importance of separating gameplay contracts from visual effects. Combat must remain fair and readable even when particles, fog, lights, and other effects are reduced for performance.

**What's Next**

The next stage is to polish the complete 20–30 minute route from the Whispergrove introduction through the Bramblewood expedition, elite encounter, boss battle, equipment upgrade, and visible realm unlock.

Future work will focus on Android device profiling, audio polish, stronger realm identities, quest progression, accessibility settings, and additional weapons and boss encounters.

</details>

**3. Engineering Rigor & CI/CD Pipeline**

- Zero Evidence Modification Enforced via CI:
The spoliation-check.yml workflow mounts raw mock disk images (.raw, .E01), computes SHA256 hashes, runs the full autonomous agent suite against the mount point, unmounts, and re-computes SHA256. If a single byte differs, CI terminates with code 1.

- Deterministic Reproducibility:
All dependencies are locked with poetry.lock (Python) and package-lock.json (Node.js). Containerized setups provide identical kernel-level read-only guarantees across developer machines and judge workstations.

- Structured Logging:
All execution artifacts produce structured JSONL traces containing timestamps, token expenditure, tool invocation parameters, parser exit statuses, and analytical hypotheses.

**1. Video Overview & Specifications**

**2. Timed Execution Script & Storyboard**

protocol-sift triage --evidence /cases/evidence/evidence.E01 --memory /cases/evidence/memdump.raw \
--mode autonomous --mcp-server localhost:8920 --max-iterations 15

"Traditional DFIR scripts dump gigabytes of raw output, flooding junior analysts and overwhelming LLM context windows. Protocol SIFT changes this by embedding senior analyst cognitive workflows into a fully autonomous, architectural-isolated agent loop. Notice the evidence integrity check executing first: read-only loop devices mounted with kernel-level write-blocking, initial SHA-256 hashes registered."

[INIT] SHA256(evidence.E01) = 7f8a... VERIFIED READ-ONLY
[MCP] Connected to Forensic Tools Server (214 typed safe tools registered)

- Visual: Agent invokes extract_amcache() and volatility_pslist(). Split screen shows live tool execution and dynamic hypothesis tree updates.

- Narration:
"Rather than dumping raw text, the agent queries our custom MCP server. The server executes SIFT tools natively, parsing outputs into concise JSON summaries before returning them to the LLM. In memory, the agent identifies an anomalous process: svch0st.exe (spelled with a zero), PID 4112, with no parent process. Simultaneously, disk Amcache reveals an execution record at 14:22:10 UTC."

- Agent Output:
[FINDING] Suspicious process PID 4112 injected from C:\Windows\Temp\updater.bin
[CORRELATION] Disk timeline matches memory injection timestamp within 1.2 seconds.

**[02:00 - 03:30] Act III: The Live Self-Correction Sequence (Judges' Focal Point)**

- Visual: Agent encounters an apparent dead end.

- Incident Event:
The agent queries the Windows Task Scheduler (get_scheduled_tasks()) to identify persistence.
The initial scheduled task SystemUpdate points to a clean Microsoft binary.
Agent Initial Guess: "Attacker used scheduled task SystemUpdate for persistence."

- Self-Correction Trigger:
Agent inspects timestamp discrepancies between scheduled task creation (2021) and the malware binary modification (2026-03-12).

- Live Output on Terminal:

[SELF-CORRECTION EVALUATION]
Hypothesis H2 (Task Scheduler Persistence) contradicted by Evidence E-4:
- Task creation timestamp: 2021-08-14 09:12:00 (Pre-incident baseline)
- Malware first seen: 2026-03-12 14:22:10
Status: REJECTED HYPOTHESIS H2.
Course Correction: Pivoting to Registry Run keys and NTFS Alternate Data Streams (ADS).
Tool Selected: query_registry_key(path='HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run')
Tool Selected: scan_alternate_data_streams(volume='/mnt/ro_evidence')

- Narration:
"Here is genuine autonomous self-correction. The agent evaluates its own intermediate hypothesis against time-distance constraints. Recognizing that the scheduled task predated the compromise by five years, it rejects the false positive, refuses to hallucinate an explanation, and autonomously pivots to NTFS Alternate Data Streams, where it immediately identifies the hidden staging directory: C:\Users\Public\svchost.exe:hidden.ps1."

**[03:30 - 04:30] Act IV: Synthesis, MITRE Mapping & Executive Report**

- Visual: Terminal streams final synthesis into a structured JSON and Markdown report.

- Narration:
"In under five minutes, the agent has traversed memory dumps, Prefetch, Amcache, NTFS MFT, and Alternate Data Streams. It outputs a cryptographically signed incident dossier, fully mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques T1055 (Process Injection), T1564.004 (Alternate Data Streams), and T1071 (Application Layer Protocol)."

**PROJECT-4: Architecture Diagram & Security Boundary Specification**

**1. System Architecture Overview**

The system implements a Decoupled Autonomous Agent Architecture with Purpose-Built MCP Isolation. Raw evidence is strictly segregated from the reasoning engine by architectural boundaries enforced at the Linux kernel and container level, ensuring zero risk of evidence tampering regardless of model hallucinations.

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| SECURITY BOUNDARY 1 |
| UNTRUSTED / ADVERSARIAL EVIDENCE LAYER |
| |
