<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We live in a world where information is everywhere, yet the ability to focus, learn deeply, and understand ourselves is becoming increasingly difficult.

I was inspired by a simple question:

What if personal growth could be trained like a skill?

NeuroAscend was born from the intersection of two worlds—ancient practices around awareness and self-development and the modern understanding of cognition, learning, and attention.

Instead of creating another content-consumption app, I wanted to build a guided experience that encourages people to train, focus, reflect, and evolve.

**What it does**

NeuroAscend is a cognitive-wellness and personal development platform built around structured learning and daily practices.

The app guides users through a progressive journey designed to help them develop greater awareness, focus, discipline, and cognitive potential.

Rather than overwhelming users with endless content, NeuroAscend aims to turn personal development into a consistent, engaging experience—something users can return to every day.

The long-term vision is to make the experience increasingly personalized, adaptive, and measurable as the platform evolves.

**How we built it**

NeuroAscend was built as a native Android application using Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, and Material 3.

The initial product focused on creating a polished foundation: onboarding, authentication, navigation, the core learning experience, and a futuristic interface that reflects the idea of human potential meeting technology.

I designed the visual language around deep space-inspired backgrounds, blue/purple gradients, glassmorphism, and cognitive/neural imagery to make the experience feel distinctly different from conventional education or wellness applications.

For monetization, I integrated RevenueCat to handle the subscription and purchase infrastructure, allowing the product to move toward a scalable subscription-based model without having to build the entire billing infrastructure from scratch.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge wasn't simply writing the code.

It was translating an abstract idea like "human potential" into a product that feels tangible, understandable, and useful.

I had to make difficult decisions about what belongs in the first version, how to avoid overwhelming users, and how to turn a large long-term vision into a focused MVP.

Building the experience while simultaneously thinking about UX, monetization, technical architecture, branding, and scalability also meant constantly balancing what the product could become with what it needed to be today.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The biggest accomplishment is turning NeuroAscend from an idea into a functioning product foundation.

I'm particularly proud of:

- Building the Android application from the ground up.

- Creating a distinctive futuristic visual identity and user experience.

- Designing a guided onboarding and learning journey rather than a traditional content library.

- Establishing the foundation for authentication, navigation, and future personalization.

- Integrating RevenueCat to support the product's subscription model.

- Turning a broad vision around human development into a tangible technology product.

Most importantly, NeuroAscend is no longer just an idea—it's something people can experience.

**What we learned**

Building NeuroAscend taught me that creating a product around human behavior is fundamentally different from simply building software.

The technology is only one part of the equation.

People don't need more information. They need experiences that make them want to return, engage, practice, and change.

We also learned the importance of starting small. A large vision becomes achievable when it is broken into focused experiences that can be tested, improved, and expanded over time.

RevenueCat also reinforced an important product lesson: monetization should be considered as part of the product architecture from the beginning, rather than added as an afterthought.

**What's Next for Neuro Ascend**

This MVP is only the beginning.

The next evolution of NeuroAscend is to move from a guided course experience toward a personalized cognitive-growth platform.

Future iterations will explore:

- Adaptive learning journeys based on user progress.

- Personalized daily practices.

- Progress tracking and meaningful user insights.

- AI-assisted personalization.

- A broader library of cognitive and awareness exercises.

- More sophisticated subscription experiences.

- Cross-platform expansion.

- A growing ecosystem around lifelong cognitive development.

The ultimate vision is simple:

Build technology that doesn't just help people consume more but helps them become more capable.

NeuroAscend is our attempt to build toward that future.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/175/203/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/175/203/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/175/225/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/175/225/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/175/226/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/175/226/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Research code is often difficult to trust and reproduce. Important claims become separated from the exact files, revisions, and experiment conditions that support them. RepoLens helps researchers move from “this repository looks promising” to a source-grounded understanding of what the code does and what still needs to be verified.

**What it does**

RepoLens turns a public research repository into an evidence-grounded workspace. Each important claim can be traced to a fixed revision, source file, line range, excerpt, and stable evidence identifier. Researchers can:

- review an architecture brief and mechanism map

- inspect source-linked evidence cards

- follow staged research and reproduction tasks

- answer repository-specific verification questions

- export an evidence-preserving Markdown report

- record local experiment notes and deviations in the native macOS app

The core evidence workflow remains available without a paid entitlement. RepoLens Pro is designed for multi-repository collections, deeper analysis, synchronized history, and long-term repository tracking.

**How I built it**

The public web application uses Next.js, TypeScript, the GitHub API, and Cloudflare Workers. It resolves an immutable commit, selects research-relevant files, extracts bounded evidence windows, and validates every displayed citation and command. DeepSeek analysis and bounded Agent exploration are optional; the deterministic evidence engine provides the complete core workflow without a model key.

The native macOS application is built with SwiftUI and RevenueCat SDK 5.86.0. RevenueCat manages the repolens_pro entitlement through a default offering with monthly, yearly, and lifetime packages. The purchase interface reads the live offering, derives access from CustomerInfo, persists entitlement state across relaunches, and provides Restore Purchases.

**RevenueCat verification**

The full entitlement flow was verified with RevenueCat Test Store:

- fetch the current offering and packages

- simulate a package purchase

- confirm repolens_pro becomes active

- relaunch the app and confirm access persists

- restore purchases and verify entitlement recovery

The demonstration uses Test Store only, so it requires no real payment method or charge.

**Challenges**

The central challenge is preserving trust across product layers. A concise research explanation is useful only when its source remains inspectable. Likewise, premium access must come from a verified RevenueCat entitlement rather than a local client flag. RepoLens keeps both evidence provenance and entitlement state explicit throughout the interface.

The distributable macOS application also needs to work for judges without my development environment. The release is an ad-hoc-signed universal application for Apple Silicon and Intel Macs, with setup instructions, entitlement-policy checks, no embedded private keys, and a published SHA-256 checksum.

**Accomplishments**

- Built a public evidence-grounded research-code workspace

- Built a native macOS evidence and experiment workspace

- Integrated RevenueCat offerings, purchases, entitlements, and restoration

- Verified purchase-to-unlock behavior end to end with Test Store

- Kept core citation review outside the paid boundary

- Published source code and a downloadable universal macOS release

**What I learned**

RevenueCat’s separation of products, offerings, and entitlements makes monetization easier to evolve without hard-coding business rules into the interface. Responsible AI tooling also needs a transparent product boundary: users should know both where a claim comes from and which entitlement controls a feature.

**What's next**

Planned work includes iOS support, secure cross-device synchronization, repository-change alerts, shared lab workspaces, and richer experiment-version tracking.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We've all had conversations we wish we could redo. A difficult discussion with a manager, negotiating a salary, setting boundaries with someone, or delivering uncomfortable news. Sometimes, the right words only come to us afterward.

That frustration inspired Rehevia.

Most people prepare for important conversations by thinking about what they'll say. But real conversations rarely follow a script. The other person might disagree, interrupt, become defensive, or ask something unexpected.

I wanted to build a place where people could experience those moments before facing them in real life.

Rehevia's guiding idea is simple: Practice it before you say it.

**What it does**

Rehevia is a voice-first AI conversation simulator that lets people practice difficult conversations with a realistic AI counterpart.

Instead of reading advice or chatting with an assistant that always agrees, users enter a conversation room and actually speak.

The experience follows a practice loop:

1. Prepare

Choose from 12 curated conversation scenarios or create a custom situation. Define what you want to achieve and prepare for the discussion.

2. Practice

Enter a live voice conversation with an AI counterpart. The counterpart can challenge your position and introduce resistance, making the experience more realistic than a predefined script.

3. Reflect

After the conversation, receive a structured debrief to understand how the discussion unfolded and identify opportunities for improvement.

4. Rewind and try again

Revisit important moments and explore how different responses could change the conversation.

The goal is to create a repeatable learning experience where users can experiment, reflect, and gradually become more comfortable handling difficult conversations.

Rehevia also includes Pro access and a High-Stakes Pass model for its premium practice experiences.

**How I built it**

Rehevia is built as a mobile application using React Native, Expo, and TypeScript.

Supabase provides authentication, database services, and server-side functions. Apple Sign-In supports authentication on iOS.

The conversation experience combines OpenAI's Realtime capabilities with WebRTC to enable live voice interactions. A structured resistance engine helps control the counterpart's behavior, while the application manages conversation states, interruptions, and recovery.

The backend handles session authorization, credit consumption, entitlement reconciliation, scenario compilation, and debrief generation through dedicated Supabase Edge Functions.

RevenueCat manages subscriptions and purchases. Sentry supports error monitoring and operational diagnostics.

A significant part of the development effort went into connecting these systems reliably. A successful purchase needs to unlock the correct features, a reconnect must preserve the session, and a temporary interruption should not erase the user's progress.

The architecture separates the conversation lifecycle, access control, and purchase state so these components can be tested independently.

**Challenges I ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was making the complete experience reliable on a physical iPhone.

RevenueCat and subscription activation

The development app initially couldn't retrieve products from App Store Connect because its bundle identifier differed from the production app. I configured RevenueCat's Test Store for development while preserving Apple's store configuration for release builds.

I also encountered a purchase flow where the transaction succeeded but Pro activation remained stuck. The application was waiting indefinitely for backend reconciliation. The flow was repaired so valid entitlements unlock access immediately, while backend reconciliation runs with a bounded timeout.

Real-time conversation interruptions

The conversation room could connect successfully and then unexpectedly pause or disconnect. Reconnect and Resume sometimes competed with each other, leaving the user in confusing states.

The investigation identified an unsupported parameter in an initial Realtime tool request as a likely interruption cause. I removed it and reworked the room lifecycle around explicit state transitions, bounded recovery, and reliable cleanup. The original provider rejection could not be conclusively verified because its error code had been discarded.

Performance and diagnostics

WebRTC statistics were being polled approximately every 130–150 milliseconds, flooding the development console.

I reduced audio-meter polling to at most once per second and preserved useful warnings and errors.

I also removed raw diagnostic JSON from the normal room interface and moved sanitized diagnostics into a development-only view.

Session and credit integrity

Reconnecting should never create duplicate sessions or charge users again for the same eligible practice. This required careful handling of authorization, session identity, backend idempotency, and recovery paths.

The resulting system has automated coverage for these behaviors, with final physical-device verification still underway.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

I'm proud of turning a simple idea about practicing difficult conversations into an integrated mobile prototype.

The project now brings together live AI conversations, structured practice scenarios, debrief generation, subscription management, and session recovery.

I'm particularly proud of the reliability work. It required addressing problems across mobile state management, real-time connections, purchase synchronization, and backend authorization.

The latest reported validation included 696 passing mobile tests and 31 passing contract tests for the room repair work.

These automated results are an important milestone, although the repaired experience still needs its final round of physical-iPhone testing.

**What I learned**

Building Rehevia taught me that the conversation experience depends on much more than the intelligence of the AI model.

Latency, microphone handling, connection recovery, and consistent session state all shape whether a live interaction feels natural.

I also learned how important it is to separate a successful transaction from the backend processes that follow it. Users should not remain stuck after a purchase that has already granted the required entitlement.

The project reinforced the value of clear lifecycle ownership, meaningful diagnostics, and testing failure scenarios rather than focusing only on the happy path.

Most importantly, I learned that building a convincing AI experience requires paying as much attention to what happens when things go wrong as to what happens when everything works.

**What's next for Rehevia**

My immediate priority is completing physical-iPhone verification of the conversation room, reconnection behavior, and purchase experience.

After that, I want to refine the practice and debrief experience, expand the scenario library, and gather feedback from real users.

I also plan to improve how users can revisit important moments, compare attempts, and track their development over time.

The long-term vision is to make Rehevia a practical companion for preparing for conversations that matter.

Practice. Reflect. Progress.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

For the past five years, we’ve built apps designed to help people. Through our work on Sismos México, we learned how valuable clear earthquake information can be.

During earthquakes in Venezuela and elsewhere, we saw people outside Mexico finding the app too. That made something clear to us: information is only the first step. Knowing what happened does not answer the questions a family faces next. Is everyone okay? Who needs help? Do we know what each person should do?

We wanted to help families prepare before those questions become urgent. Agree on a meeting point. Share responsibilities. Practice together. And when a reported earthquake matters to them, give each person a simple way to tell their private circle how they are.

That is why we built Ready Together: to help families prepare, practice, and check in, whether they live under the same roof or far apart.

**What it does**

Ready Together helps families turn a plan into something they can practice together. Android and iPhone users join the same private drill, confirm they are ready, and receive different responsibilities. Their actions contribute to one shared report, so the family can review the practice together.

Each person practices their part. One shared report helps the circle see what they completed and what to work on next. In the session below, both people participated, and one action Alex left unconfirmed became the next thing to rehearse.

Before practicing, families can agree on a meeting point and share responsibilities. Their private circle connects people who share a home or live far apart, including in different countries. Earthquake context is tailored to their saved areas in Mexico and other supported countries.

When a reported earthquake is relevant to the circle, a check-in notification invites people to respond. Each person can say “I’m okay” or “I need help,” and their family can see the responses for that event. A missing response stays unknown. “I need help” informs the circle; it does not contact emergency services.

The SeedLink-to-check-in path is operating. Seismic observations are correlated with a reviewed earthquake event; Ready Together verifies the event and its relevance to the circle’s saved areas before opening a private check-in and sending a OneSignal invitation to eligible members. A station observation alone does not trigger a family notification. Ready Together does not predict earthquakes or provide official early-warning alerts.

Ready Together works in English and Spanish. Earthquake context, the private circle, check-ins, household agreements, day and night drills, and the essential report stay free. Family Supporter is an optional one-time purchase that adds two practice scenarios: pets and guests at home. RevenueCat manages the purchase and entitlement, helping us support the project without putting essential coordination behind a paywall.

**How we built it**

We built Ready Together with Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform. Android and iOS share Compose UI, MVI presentation state, domain rules, and networking. Pure business rules live separately from versioned client-server contracts and data access, so a change to a transport or native SDK does not redefine what a check-in or drill state means.

Native integrations stay explicit: Android uses Google Maps Compose, while iOS uses MapKit through UIKitView. Purchases and Family Supporter entitlements are managed through the RevenueCat SDK. Notifications, authentication, and lifecycle behavior use platform integrations. Shared Kotlin owns the decisions around them, including event relevance and how unknown or stale state is presented.

The backend runs on Kotlin with Ktor. It handles private-circle membership, invitations, event-scoped check-ins, and shared drill sessions. Firebase Authentication manages identity, while Firestore stores circles, memberships, check-ins, and reports.

For the earthquake feed, our Ktor backend consumes earthquake reports through a normalized data adapter. It filters events against each circle’s saved areas and provides the same event context to Android and iOS, including the source, event time, and preliminary or reviewed status.

Our independent detector receives station waveform data through SeedLink and produces preliminary observations. The operating backend path uses signed ingestion, correlation with an exact event from a reviewed source, and independent verification of that event’s current facts and relevance to the circle. For eligible events within enabled country and area configurations, it opens an event-scoped check-in and sends OneSignal notifications to eligible members. Duplicate observations reuse the same coordination event, and each response remains attached to its circle and event. Ambiguous, stale, or unverified observations do not activate a check-in. We explain the flow and its boundaries in From a seismic signal to a family response.

Operating SeedLink-to-check-in path: station observations → reviewed-event verification → circle relevance → private check-in. OneSignal invites eligible members to respond; the backend remains the source of truth.

A synchronized drill makes that architecture tangible. An Android participant and an iPhone participant join the same room, receive different responsibilities, and follow a start time assigned by the Ktor backend. Shared Kotlin interprets the same semantic action IDs and session states on both devices; the server validates transitions and brings their actions into one collective report. A notification can bring someone back to the app, but it is never the session clock.

Practice content is bundled locally so an ongoing drill can continue through a connection loss. When a device reconnects, it reconciles with the shared session. Delayed or duplicate commands must not repeat completed actions, and an unanswered check-in must remain unknown. These are shared product rules, alongside the shared interface. We explain the module boundaries and native adapters in our architecture article.

RevenueCat manages the optional lifetime Family Supporter entitlement on each platform. It unlocks the pets and guests scenarios, while the day and night drills and essential coordination remain free. Billing stays separate from check-in and drill state. Restore uses the current platform’s store account; purchases do not transfer automatically between Android and iOS.

We tested the shared experience across both platforms, including invitations, synchronized practice, check-in responses, and the final report.

We turned lessons from building Ready Together into two open-source agent skills: kmp-spec-driven-design, for planning features across shared and native code, and kmp-proof-of-parity, for verifying behavior across Android and iOS. We published the templates, worked examples, and validation tools in our KMP Spec-Driven Skills repository. Our engineering note explains how another team can use them to plan a shared feature and collect separate Android and iOS evidence.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was making the earthquake feed reliable and useful for families. Bringing in reports was only part of the work. We also had to handle updates, avoid duplicate events, and make the source and status of the information clear.

We shared the idea with a community of earthquake enthusiasts. Those conversations helped us validate that preparation matters alongside earthquake information. Preparedness is also part of civil protection programs in several countries, and we wanted to help families bring that practice into their everyday lives.

Another challenge was making a drill work as one shared experience across Android and iPhone. Each person has a different responsibility, but everyone needs to follow the same timeline and finish with a consistent report. We had to account for delayed messages, connection loss, and people returning to the app.

Push notifications were another challenge across Android and iOS. Permissions, registration, and notification opens behave differently across platforms and providers. We needed to distinguish receiving a notification from opening it, handle cold starts, and prevent duplicate opens from repeating an action. That experience led us to open-source KMP Push Client. It gives KMP apps shared permission, registration, and notification-event handling, with separate FCM and OneSignal adapters and explicit native integration points. We included test fakes and a sample covering foreground notifications, cold-start opens, and duplicate handling, so other developers can test those boundaries in their own apps.

Another challenge was making preparedness feel approachable. We did not want Ready Together to feel like a corporate app full of forms. We wanted something families would feel comfortable opening and using together.

That led us to create Rocky, a friendly rock character who welcomes people and accompanies them as they prepare. Rocky gives the app warmth and personality, while we keep instructions, earthquake information, and check-in responses clear. The challenge was finding that balance: making the experience friendly without making light of the situations families are preparing for.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We’re proud of bringing shared family preparedness to life on Android and iPhone.

During the September 19, 2026 earthquake drill, three beta families who use Sismos México completed a practice with Ready Together. The families had three to four members each, with 11 participants in total.

Seeing an Android phone and an iPhone join the same drill, receive different responsibilities, and finish with one shared report was an important milestone for us. It brought the idea of practicing together to life.

We launched Ready Together on both stores in English and Spanish, keeping essential earthquake information, check-ins, and the main drills free.

After sharing Ready Together with our existing earthquake community, people started using the app in production and leaving store reviews. Seeing it reach people beyond our own testing has been especially rewarding. One of our first reviews recommended it for people whose families live far away, which reflected exactly who we hoped to help.

Early use — September 30

As of September 30 at 16:19 UTC, our retained app records showed 91 circles, including 16 with two or more members. Across 37 circles, 48 app profiles had submitted 72 event-specific check-in responses. Nine circles had completed 15 shared practices with at least two participating profiles.

**What we learned**

Earthquakes cannot be predicted, but we can prepare for them. Building Ready Together reinforced how important it is to make preparedness part of everyday life: talk with our families, agree on responsibilities, and practice what to do before an earthquake happens.

Conversations with the earthquake community helped us understand that reliable information and practical preparation belong together. Early testing and feedback helped us improve member visibility, clarify responsibilities, and make the next action easier to understand. They also shaped how we present connectivity changes and recovery during practice. Our updated field note, What changed when people tried Ready Together, documents those earlier findings and the later September 19 milestone: three beta families, with 11 participants in total, completed a practice. The next question is whether families repeat the practice and use what they learn to improve their plans.

We also learned that building for Android and iPhone means testing how the devices work together. Shared code helped us keep the experience consistent, but we still needed to test timing, notifications, and reconnection across both platforms.

Finally, launching the app gave us a perspective we could not get from our own testing. The first users and reviews helped us see how people connected Ready Together to their own families, including relatives who live far away. That reminded us to keep the experience simple, personal, and useful.

We documented the journey in our public build journal: product decisions, tests that exposed problems, the fixes that followed, and milestones along the way. The linked field notes explain our architecture and what we learned from building and testing across Android and iPhone.

**What's next for Ready Together**

We want to keep learning from the families using Ready Together. Their feedback will help us improve the first-time experience, make shared drills easier to repeat, and understand what helps people build a habit of preparation.

We also want to keep improving the reliability of the earthquake feed and check-in notifications, while refining the experience across Android and iPhone.

As we grow, we want to work more closely with preparedness communities and civil protection professionals to review and improve the practice content for different countries.

Our goal is to help more families make a plan, practice it together, and know how to check in when it matters.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

After my team and I lost in a previous hackathon, we sat down together to ask ourselves a hard question: What can we build that truly stands out and solves a genuine, everyday pain point?

That was the moment the idea for Decox was born. 

We had experienced this frustration firsthand. Whenever we tried using generative AI tools to brainstorm room redesigns—whether for a home office, gym, bedroom, or kitchen—we consistently got back "AI slop": gorgeous fantasy renders filled with hallucinated furniture that does not exist in any store. You fall in love with a room concept, but there is no way to actually buy the sofa, the light fixture, or the rug. 

We asked ourselves: why shouldn't an AI room redesign be grounded entirely in products and craftsmanship you can actually buy in real life?

**What it does**

Decox is a mobile-first spatial redesign engine that bridges the gap between AI inspiration and real-world execution.

Instead of generating synthetic, unbuildable mockups from scratch, Decox grounds every design in reality:

- Snap & Specify: You take a photo of your existing room (living room, bedroom, office, or patio) and describe your style and preferences.

- Live Store Sourcing: Decox uses intelligent web retrieval agents to search real e-commerce stores (such as Jumia, Jiji, and Amazon), finding actual in-stock furniture and decor items with verifiable prices and direct purchase URLs.

- Hallucination-Free Spatial Staging: Rather than inventing fictional objects, Decox uses multimodal spatial image editing to realistically place the sourced items into your room photo, preserving your room's real-world geometry, walls, doors, windows, and natural lighting.

- Local Master Artisan Matching: For custom physical finishes that can't be bought off the shelf (such as POP ceilings, fluted wood paneling, screeding, or interlocking paving), Decox matches the design directly to vetted local human craftspeople with instant in-app contact.

The result is a photorealistic, achievable redesign where every single item can be bought or built with one tap.

**How we built it**

We built Decox with a production-grade, multimodal stack:

- Mobile Client (React Native & Expo): Developed with TypeScript, featuring native camera capture, responsive masonry inspiration feeds, interactive before/after redesign views, and in-app artisan messaging.

- Agentic AI Orchestration (Python & LangGraph): Structured as a stateful RoomDesignState graph running on FastAPI. It analyzes room architecture, routes tasks between retail commerce sourcing and artisan craftsmanship, and orchestrates the staging pipeline.

- Multimodal Spatial Reasoning (Google Gemini 3.8 Flash): Leveraged for room perception, structural boundary analysis, prompt synthesis, and spatial image composition.

- Live Commerce Extraction (Parallel.ai): Powers real-time search across e-commerce platforms to extract verifiable product titles, live pricing in Nigerian Naira (NGN), product photography, and direct checkout links.

- Semantic Artisan Matching (PostgreSQL & pgvector): Cloud SQL database utilizing pgvector embeddings to semantically index and match physical craftsmanship requirements with local artisan portfolios.

- Cloud Infrastructure (Google Cloud Platform): Containerized via Docker and deployed serverless on Google Cloud Run, with media stored securely in Google Cloud Storage (GCS).

**Challenges we ran into**

Originally, we set out to build an all-in-one residential estate platform where gated estates could manage daily tenant repairs through vetted artisans while offering AI redesign as a secondary feature. 

However, building an entire multi-tenant estate management system alongside an advanced multimodal AI staging engine quickly became overly complex, fragile, and prone to breaking. With the hackathon deadline looming, we were stuck and realized we were spreading ourselves too thin.

We made the tough but necessary decision to unstuck ourselves: we stripped away the bloated estate management features, trashed the secondary clutter, and laser-focused entirely on refining our core, high-impact solution—grounded AI room redesign with real products and real artisans.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Seeing the pipeline work end-to-end felt like magic—it is a dream come true for our team to build something that solves a real-world frustration so cleanly. 

You provide your prompt, pick your style, and the AI does the rest: sourcing real products from live stores, preserving your room's real layout, and staging real items with accurate pricing. No fake furniture, no hallucinated mockups—just a grounded, actionable room transformation ready for execution.

**What we learned**

We learned that a great product is not defined by how many features you cram into it, especially when those features are things users never asked for. 

The biggest lesson was the power of ruthless focus: sticking to one core idea and refining it until the user experience is smooth, reliable, and delightful.

**What's next for Decox**

Our immediate priority is hardening backend stability and polishing every flow:

- Enhancing room decluttering and spatial staging precision.

- Expanding live e-commerce coverage and localized retailer integrations.

- Growing the verified artisan portfolio network.

If we are fortunate enough to win, our goal is to fund our Google Play Console developer account, complete production RevenueCat in-app subscriptions, and officially launch Decox on the Google Play Store as our team's first-ever published mobile application!

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Lowalk was partly inspired by the power systems in Hunter x Hunter and Jujutsu Kaisen. What I liked about them was that abilities aren't just about having more power, the interesting part is the conditions and restrictions attached to them. A character might make an ability stronger by placing a specific limitation on themselves.I started wondering if that idea could work for something completely different: productivity.Instead of simply telling myself that I should stop using my phone and focus, what if I could set my own condition? If I want to study at the library for an hour, my distracting apps stay blocked until I actually go there and complete the session.That became Lowalk. The user makes the commitment, and Lowalk enforces the condition.

**What it does**

Lowalk starts with a place. You choose somewhere you want to be the gym, library, classroom, café, or anywhere else you normally want to focus and set it as an Anchor.You then choose the apps you don't want available during that session and decide when you want the block to start.The important part is that the apps don't wait until you arrive to get blocked. If I have a gym session at 7 PM, Lowalk blocks my selected apps before 7 PM. If I'm still at home, they're already blocked. The idea is that I now have a very simple choice: go to the gym, or sit there with the apps I wanted to avoid unavailable. When I arrive at the Anchor, Lowalk uses my location to recognise that I've actually made it there.After that, the focus session starts. If I've committed to an hour, I need to actually spend that hour there.

Unlike most screen-time apps, Lowalk doesn’t give you an easy way out of a session once you’ve committed to it. You can’t simply skip an active session, delete it, or edit the duration to get around the block. The only way to use an override is through Focus Coins, which you earn by consistently completing your goals. Otherwise, you have to check in at your Focus Zone and spend the time you committed to.

Most screen-time apps that use location treat it as an afterthought. They typically block an app only once you enter a certain geofence or arrive near a location. Lowalk works differently through pre-blocking. Your selected apps are blocked 15, 30, or 45 minutes before your session starts, meaning you have to actually make your way to the Focus Zone and complete the session you committed to.

And leaving early doesn’t simply end the block. If you leave your Focus Zone before completing your session, Lowalk can penalize you with additional block time. The goal is to make the commitment itself meaningful: you decide where you need to be, when you need to be there, and how long you need to stay — then Lowalk holds you to it.

**How we built it**

Lowalk is built with React Native and Expo, with location services handling the connection between the digital session and the physical world.

A lot of the work went into making the session behave like one continuous system rather than a collection of separate screens. A session can be scheduled, waiting to start, blocking apps while you're travelling, waiting for you to arrive, actively running, completed, or manually unlocked and the app needs to know exactly where you are in that process.

**Challenges we ran into**

Location sounds simple until you try to build a product around it.

A map can show a nice little circle around your gym, but GPS doesn't know that you've "arrived" in the human sense. Your position moves around, the signal isn't perfect, and briefly entering a geofence shouldn't suddenly turn a drive-by into a completed session.

We had to think carefully about what actually counts as arriving and what counts as staying.

The other challenge was making the blocking happen at the right time. Lowalk isn't just checking where you are and then blocking an app when you get there. The restriction begins before you arrive, because that's the entire point of the product.

Testing this on a real phone also changed things quickly. Location permissions, background behaviour and app-shielding behaviour don't feel nearly as predictable as they do when everything is happening inside a development environment.

And then there was the temptation to keep adding things.

A product like this can easily become another productivity dashboard: AI coaching, social feeds, achievements, complicated statistics, notifications everywhere.I kept asking myself whether each idea actually helped with the one thing Lowalk exists to do.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I'm most proud that the core idea actually works on a real phone.It is one thing to have a prototype where a circle appears on a map and a timer counts down. It's another thing to have your phone actually block the apps you selected, leave your house, arrive somewhere, and have the session recognise that you showed up.I'm also proud of how much the idea changed during development without losing its original purpose. Lowalk started as a much simpler idea around blocking distractions for things like going to the gym. As I built it, I realised the same mechanic could work for studying, classes, work, and basically anything where the problem isn't knowing what to do, but actually getting yourself there.

I also like that the app doesn't need to constantly compete for my attention. Most productivity apps want you to open them more. With Lowalk, the ideal outcome is almost the opposite: you set your session up, put your phone away, and go.

**What we learned**

The biggest thing I learned was that a good idea doesn't necessarily need a lot of features.

**What's next for Lowalk**

Launch on the play store, I'm also working toward better widgets, richer ways to see your consistency, more flexible scheduling and better support for different kinds of Anchors and routines.But I don't want Lowalk to become another app that demands more of your attention.The best version of Lowalk is probably the one you barely need to open.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Most habit apps sell a quiet contract with yourself. Open the app. Tap done. Close it. Nobody saw it, so nobody cares if you skip tomorrow. We kept watching people start January strong and go silent by February, and we kept watching the exceptions: gym partners who text “you coming?”, study groups that wait at the library, group chats that roast the person who skipped, and the friend who actually buys lunch when they lose the bet.

That is the insight we designed around. Accountability to yourself is easy to negotiate with. Accountability to people you like is harder to fake. Verdly exists to put that social heat inside the product, without turning into a shame machine.

We also refused to make this a lecture about the planet or a guilt dashboard. The grove language (planting, roots, showing up) is how the product feels, but the job is any habit that needs witnesses: early mornings, training, writing, quitting something, showing up for a duo. If a friend can see you planted today, the habit has a chance. If they can react, rank you, and hold a real world stake over you, it has a spine.

**What it does**

Verdly is two products that share one identity: a serious solo habit home, and a social challenge arena that is the feature we would put in front of judges first.

Your grove (solo). You plant habits, check them off, and build streaks that belong to a real local day, not a UTC timestamp. Completions are stored as “this habit, this local date,” frozen at the moment you actually did it, so flying across a timezone does not rewrite yesterday. When life punches a hole in the run, streak shields can bridge a missed day without pretending you completed it. That distinction mattered to us: a shield is mercy, not a fake check. Premium (RevenueCat) unlocks unlimited habits, focus sounds, deeper analytics, shields, and a monthly coin drip. At seven days, at a loss, and when a shield could still save you, the paywall talks about that exact moment instead of a generic “go pro.”

Friends Grove and last planted. Your crew is not a follower count. The grove shows who planted today, who is still waiting, last active (only if both of you allow it), and small social moves like “saw you” witnesses. The home feed is people doing the work, not a content network. You can nudge, gift grove cosmetics with coins, and feel the room wake up when the first person plants.

Duo streaks. Two people lock the same daily bar. The day is not closed until both of you are in. Milestones (3, 7, 14, 21, 30, and on to a year) pay XP and have names on purpose: Week Warriors, Iron Pair, Year of Two. If one of you is stuck, swap a day lets a partner gift a completion that counts without a photo. It is cooperative accountability, not a second leaderboard.

Goals that last longer than a streak. Build, quit, or maintain. Confirmations, silent gaps, urge check ins, and copy that talks to the person you are becoming, not a calorie number. This is the slow layer under the daily fire.

Home screen widgets and Wrapped. Glance widgets put today’s habits on the launcher so the app does not have to be open to be honest. Wrapped turns a week of showing up into a story you can actually feel proud of.

**The arena (the main event)**

Create. Friends create a challenge: habit name, a real world stake as text (“loser buys everyone’s lunch”), duration (7, 14, 21, or 30 days), a daily clock, and a scoring mode. Invites are a 6 letter code, a QR card, and a link, saintnico.site/c/XXXXXX, that auto joins after sign in. Rivals show up in the same room.

Post daily. Every day, each player posts one proof photo before the clock. The feed is attendance: who Planted, who is still Waiting, how many showed up out of the roster. After the deadline you can still post, but XP drops (8 instead of 10 plus streak bonuses). Between midnight and 3am we do not let you pretend it is still “today”; we give a late window for yesterday at 5 XP with the streak frozen. That is how we kept the clock strict without being cruel at 12:07.

React. Friends react with weighted stickers. Hype family is +3, love family is +2, wow family is +1. You cannot hype yourself. You get 10 reactions per day per challenge, so the board cannot be farmed. Switching a sticker only moves the point delta.

Score. The creator picks how winning works:

- Consistency Cup is longest streak.

- Crowd Favourite is reaction points.

- Hybrid is streak times 10 plus reaction points.

$$ \text{Hybrid} = 10 \times \text{streak} + \text{reaction points} $$

Standings have a podium, live scores, and “X score behind #1” so chase is visible. When ranks move, Cloud Functions push FCM: you took the lead, you climbed, someone overtook you. The arena is supposed to feel alive while you are not staring at it.

Trophies, badges, and titles. Showing up should leave something behind. Verdly has a tiered trophy cabinet of more than fifty trophies, and we deliberately never tell you the total. You find them by doing the work, not by chasing a checklist. Finishing an oath-backed challenge earns a stake trophy, so the coins you locked on yourself become something permanent instead of a number that vanishes.

Badges live where other people can see them. In an arena roster, the badge next to a name tells the room who has finished oaths before and who is still proving it. On the profile, the oath record is part of who you are, not a buried stat.

Titles are what you wear. Milestone names like Week Warriors, Iron Pair, and Year of Two, and the winner title an arena awards at the end, sit on your nameplate and profile card, so they show up everywhere you do. None of it can be bought. Trophies, badges, and titles are earned, and coins never buy them. That is why they mean something when a friend sees them.

Swear your consistency. Coins are recognition, never cash (there is no withdraw type in the economy on purpose). You can lock at least 10 coins and at most 50% of your wallet on yourself.

- Finish the challenge and the lock converts to trophy XP (1 per coin, 2 with Premium, 500 XP cap on free).

- Miss and you forfeit: half of the lock is redistributed to people still in as a consistency bonus.

New wallets get a 20 coin first oath so the 50% cap does not make the minimum stake impossible. That is skin in the game without gambling regulation theater.

Proof, report, leave. Photos upload compressed. You can report a proof. Leaving a tribe costs 50 XP. Ending the arena writes a result snapshot: winner title, final board, top posts. We wanted a closing ceremony, not a doc that just goes isActive: false.

**How we built it**

We built a native Android app in Kotlin 2.0 and Jetpack Compose (Material 3, Navigation Compose) because this product is motion, lists, photos, and rank changes, and we needed that to feel immediate.

Identity and data. Identity is Firebase Authentication (Google Sign In and email). Challenge documents, members, completions, reactions, and activity live in Cloud Firestore. User progress (XP, grove fields, inbox, presence) lives under users/{uid} with rules that let friends read a public slice and nobody else rewrite your wallet.

Proof images. Proof images go to Firebase Storage at proofs/{uid}/challenges/{challengeId}/.... Before upload we decode, cap the long edge at 1024px, and JPEG compress at 70%. Coil paints the feed. Invite cards and QR use ZXing. Share cards are bitmaps we export, not screenshots of Compose.

Invites. The 6 letter code is not the Firestore document id. We generate A–Z codes, write challenges/{autoId} and invites/{CODE} in one batch, and joiners get the invite mapping. App Links (https://saintnico.site/c/... with autoVerify) and verdly://challenge?code= land in the same parser. People without the app hit a static join page that shows the code, opens the app, or sends them to Play (com.saintnico.verdlyhabits).

Streaks. Streak math for personal habits is a local StreakEngine over Room, with WorkManager sync and a DayChangeCoordinator that re evaluates on calendar day, timezone, and boot. Shields are a ledger: they cover a gap, they do not increment the run. Challenge streaks recompute from the completions map (ISO local dates) with stored memberStreaks as a cache we distrust when it says 0 against real history.

Scoring. Scoring is one contract in Kotlin (STREAK, REACTIONS, HYBRID) and the same formula in Cloud Functions (Node 20, firebase-admin, firebase-functions v2) so FCM rank alerts match the board the user sees. Reactions and check ins run in Firestore transactions so two phones cannot double spend points. The client still applies an optimistic sticker so the UI does not wait on the round trip.

Coins and Premium. Coins, oaths, and gifts are Room first (challenge_stakes, wallet, transactions), then synced to users/{uid}/wallet. Forfeit and convert are idempotent against challenge missedDays and archive state. RevenueCat plus Play Billing own Premium entitlements. Glance widgets snapshot habits. Lottie and Konfetti are the ceremony layer (planted, converted, podium), not the product.

What we didn't build. We did not ship a Python CV microservice. Honesty on the photo is the crew, the report button, one proof per day, and a clock you cannot quietly skip. That was a product choice: social contract first, model later.

**Challenges we ran into**

Joining a private room without listing the whole collection. Firestore evaluates list queries against the query, not the document you hope exists. If only members can list challenges, a joiner’s whereEqualTo("inviteCode") is permission denied even when the challenge is sitting there. We learned that the hard way. The fix was a get-able index: invites/{CODE}. Join became: resolve code, get challenge by id (signed in users may get by id), then an update that is only allowed if you are adding yourself to members. Legacy challenges still try the old query and fail closed.

Links that survive WhatsApp, Play, and “I don’t have the app.” A code in a screenshot, a pasted URL, an App Link, and a custom scheme all had to become the same six letters. We wrote one normalizer (trim, letters only, take 6, path segment after /c/, query code=). The website is a handshake: show the code, try verdly://, fall through to Play. Auto join after login was the last mile. If that fails, the product feels broken even if Firestore is fine.

What “today” means. Ranking the world on UTC midnight punishes night people. Using “now” for both posting and history punishes travelers. Personal streaks freeze localDate at write in the zone the user was standing in. Challenge proofs key off ISO local dates and LocalTime.now() on the device for the daily window. The 3am grace exists because “I posted at 12:40 for yesterday” is a real human sentence. Late is not full XP and does not extend the streak. After deadline is reduced XP. We would still rather move the clock to the server next, because a client clock can be wrong on purpose.

Hype that cannot be farmed. If reactions are free, Crowd Favourite is a popularity contest with alts. Transactions: one sticker per reactor per proof, 10 proofs per day per challenge, no self react, point delta on swap, memberReactionPoints in the same write. Proof keys are {uid}_{date} so we know owner and day. Cloud Functions still label the original three keys (fire, heart, lightning) while the client has a larger sticker set. We papered that with meta.points on activity. It is a seam we know about.

Oaths without becoming a casino. People asked for money on the line. We put coins in and then wrote a hard constraint: no withdraw, no cash out. Finish becomes trophy XP. Fail feeds the group. First oath grant of 20 coins exists because floor(10 * 0.5) cannot stake 10. Premium doubles XP per coin on convert. The copy is “swear” and “plant,” not “wager.” That was product and legal taste in the same file.

Solo streaks that survive reinstall and silent nights. Room schema moved through migrations; we open the database at launch so a mismatch dies in a recoverable place, not in the first Flow collector. Pending ops queue work for when the network comes back. Widgets read a snapshot file so the home screen is not a live Firestore listener. None of that is glamorous. All of it is why the grove still feels true on Monday morning.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We shipped this to Google Play (package com.saintnico.verdlyhabits, version 1.0.8). Create an arena, share a code or QR or link, rival installs or already has the app, they land in the same challenge, they post a photo, the attendance row updates, stickers move Hybrid scores, the podium and “behind #1” update, and a push can tell you that you just got overtaken.

We are proud of the attendance feed more than any badge. “2/5 showed up” is a sentence that changes behavior. We are proud that Hybrid is a real formula (streak * 10 + reaction points) with deterministic tie breaks (points, then streak, then uid), duplicated in Cloud Functions so notifications cannot disagree with the UI.

We are proud of the oath loop that converts or forfeits without returning spendable coins, and of the invite architecture that respects Firestore rules instead of opening the whole challenges collection to the internet.

We are proud that the same app is a daily solo grove: StreakEngine, shields, duo lock, goals, Glance, Wrapped, trophies, grove gifts, referrals at saintnico.site/r/....

Habits are easier to keep when someone's watching. Verdly makes sure someone is.

**What we learned**

Nobody is in the room. People don't fail habits for lack of advice. They fail because nobody is watching. When even a small crew can see the proof, completion stops being a private mood. That's why the arena feed shows attendance (“2/5 showed up”) instead of a personal stats page.

A day is a cultural object. A streak belongs to your real local day, not a UTC timestamp. We store completions as “this habit, this local date,” frozen at the moment you act, so flying across a timezone can't rewrite yesterday. Once a streak feels unfair, trust is hard to win back.

Strict clocks need gentle edges. A daily deadline only works if it's real, so late posts drop from 10 XP to 8. But between midnight and 3am we open a late window for yesterday at 5 XP with the streak frozen, so 12:07 doesn't punish someone for being human. Strict about the rule, kind about the edge.

Make farming boring instead of impossible. Stickers are weighted (hype +3, love +2, wow +1). You can't hype yourself, and you get 10 reactions per day per challenge. Switching a sticker only moves the point delta. You can't stop every gamer, but you can make gaming the board not worth the effort.

Verification doesn't have to be a model. One photo, one day, a clock, a cap on hype, a report button, and friends who know your face are enough to keep the social contract. Better checks can come later. In v1, we chose not to fake them.

Security rules are product design. Private arenas and shareable invites pull in opposite directions. Instead of loosening privacy for everyone, we built invites as their own thing, so a link can get someone into one challenge without exposing anyone else's.

The same rule in two places will drift. Hybrid scoring ($$10 \times \text{streak} + \text{reaction points}$$) has deterministic tie-breaks: points, then streak, then uid. We duplicated that logic in Cloud Functions so a push saying “you were overtaken” can never disagree with the leaderboard on your screen.

Mercy has to be labeled honestly. A streak shield bridges a missed day without pretending you completed it. Swap a day lets a duo partner gift a completion that counts without a photo. Both are visible acts of mercy, not silent edits to the record, which is why they don't cheapen the streaks around them.

Coins work when they're identity, not an ATM. Skin in the game means XP, titles, and half of your forfeit going to the people still in. Nothing in the economy can be withdrawn, on purpose. New wallets get a 20-coin first oath so the 50%-of-wallet cap never makes the 10-coin minimum impossible.

Endings deserve a ceremony. When an arena closes, we write a result snapshot: winner title, final board, top posts. We wanted people to feel it finish, not watch a database flag flip to isActive: false.

**What's next for Verdly Habits**

- No cash out, ever. That is a promise in the coin model.

- Server-authoritative clock. We want the daily clock and proof window authoritative on the server, so a moved device clock cannot cheat the arena.

- Team versus team arenas. Campus, office, and friend groups as sides, building on the same proof and scoring engine.

- Optional proof assistance. On device or cloud checks that the photo is new, a person is in frame, or it is not a duplicate of yesterday, with humans still able to report. Captions can be suggested later. The feed should stay people, not generated sermons.

- Arena streak recovery. A freeze you earn by showing up for others, matching personal shields, not a mute button on failure.

- iOS. When the Android contract is boringly solid: invites, clocks, oaths, grove.

The north star stays the same. Make showing up visible. Make flaking expensive in pride, not in cash. Make the crew the product.

**Built With**

- Kotlin

- Jetpack Compose

- Material 3

- Navigation Compose

- Firebase Authentication

- Google Sign-In

- Cloud Firestore

- Firebase Storage

- Firebase Cloud Messaging

- Cloud Functions (Node 20, firebase-admin, firebase-functions v2)

- Room

- DataStore Preferences

- WorkManager

- Glance

- Coil

- Lottie

- Konfetti

- ZXing

- Gson

- RevenueCat

- Google Play Billing

- Play Services Location

- saintnico.site (App Links + invite landing)

</details>

**Inspiration**

I inspired form Meson, CMake and npm. 
I am a C++ begineer it annoys me find c++ libraries, configure those and sometimes we find the source repo instead of build repo. To make our project we need build managers too. (Or else type 100 line commands when your project becomes big)
As a Javascript developer npm is very comfortable. 
I thought what if CMake and npm come together in a single project manager. 

**What it does**

My project is C Operations a free and open source C++ Tool. 
It can install c++ packages.
It can publish packages.
It can build projects.

**How we built it**

You publish / host your package like libs/ and include/ files on the Git Providers like GitHub or GitLab and our registry hosts that single URL which contains the package.yaml and configurations using our coop-cli. (We implemented Authentication too)

Then you download packages from our coop by providing a name and our registry returns url to the GitHub or GitLab Repository. Git clones that and coop organized those files into the repos. 

Coop can also build projects. It handles a build-cache/ folder where it compiles every file into .o files. If .cpp file is NEWER then .o file that means source has been changed hence we compile that single file and link the rest, if the .o is NEWER then last .cpp write time that means source hasn't changed and we skip compiling it.

## 168. showmi

> showmi is about music discovery using the swipe gesture found in some apps: you swipe through songs, and when you find a sound you like, you ask for "more like this."

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/showmi (gallery page 58) · ❤️ 0 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [cpantaleon06-coder Pantaleon](https://devpost.com/cpantaleon06-coder)
- **GitHub (Try it out):** https://github.com/cpantaleon06-coder/showmi.git
- **Repo check:** public repo · license: MIT · 114 commits · TypeScript · RevenueCat found in code ✅
- **Built with:** claude, deno, expo.io, plpgsql, shell, typescript

**Video (0:57):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=llQAJqRGrGM

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/llQAJqRGrGM/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=llQAJqRGrGM)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/160/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/160/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Spotify's recommendation engine is very good at one thing: giving you more of what's already popular. It's much worse at the other thing, giving you more of what's genuinely alike. If your taste sits outside the mainstream, that gap turns into a wall. This project started as a "Tinder for movies" concept, but that format was already saturated. Music wasn't, and it connected to a real, personal frustration instead of a trend. The core bet: niche discovery shouldn't depend on how popular something already is.

**What it does**

Showmi is a swipe-based music discovery app. You swipe through 30-second clips: pass, like, or rate what you've already heard from 1 to 5 stars. The rating is what actually moves the recommendation engine, not the swipe itself. The differentiator is the anchor mechanic: lock the deck to one song or artist and ask for "more like this." That request builds a real similarity chain through Last.fm's community tagging data, not a popularity ranking wearing a disguise. A vibe selector lets you filter the session's mood without losing your genre thread. Everything you save lands in a personal library, and a companion pet grows in step with how deep you listen to each genre.

**How we built it**

Client: Expo (React Native) with TypeScript, Zustand for local state, TanStack Query for server state and caching.

Backend: Supabase, running 17+ Postgres tables with Row Level Security, six Edge Functions, and six scheduled cron jobs.

Recommendation engine: built and unit-tested as its own standalone package, then vendored into the app. Thompson Sampling (Beta-Bernoulli) across five dimensions (artist, decade, popularity, genre, vibe), with a hard filter that assembles the candidate pool before ranking, and relaxes automatically if that pool gets too thin.

Data, split by role instead of by convenience:

- iTunes Search API for the actual audio (30-second clips, no key required)

- Last.fm for similarity and genre tags, called through an Edge Function so the API key never reaches the client

- Spotify Web API via Client Credentials for the exact track link, with no user login and none of the developer-mode tester limits that a login flow would trigger

Cross-source matching runs on normalized artist + title, since iTunes never exposes an ISRC to match against.

Monetization: RevenueCat, with a showmi_more entitlement gating unlimited swipes, no ads, and exclusive cosmetics, behind a paywall built from scratch to match the app's own visual identity rather than a default template.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Building solo, as a law student. No engineering background going in, learning the stack while carrying a full course load in Mexican civil, criminal, constitutional, and labor law.

- A platform shift mid-project. Spotify deprecated both preview_url and its /recommendations endpoint in November 2024, I noticed right as this project needed them. The fix was rebuilding audio and discovery around iTunes and Last.fm instead of Spotify.

- A silent cold-start bug. Genre and vibe answered during onboarding were being ignored by the deck; the engine needed to be seeded before the first swipes, not after. Traced and fixed.

- A one-word bug that would have broken monetization invisibly. The code checked for an entitlement called premium; the real one configured in RevenueCat was showmi_more. Undetected, no purchase would ever have registered as valid, and there'd have been no error to point to why.

- A missing build configuration, caught the day before writing this. eas.json didn't declare environment variables in any profile. Since .env is gitignored, the next build would have shipped with empty RevenueCat and Supabase keys: the paywall would show no plans, and the deck would have nothing to load. Caught and fixed before it reached a device.

- No personal Android device. Testing the purchase flow end to end depends on borrowing one.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A recommendation engine that holds up under test: 37 of 37 passing.

- A real performance pass, measured before and after, not assumed: session request count per deck load down from 103 to 9, and total latency from 66 seconds to 7.2.

- A real security fix, not a hypothetical one: found and closed 12 unprotected database tables and one IDOR vulnerability the same session.

- A visual identity that says no more often than it says yes: one brand color, one atmospheric gradient reserved for exactly three screens, and a standing rule against decorative shadows and generic gradients everywhere else.

**What we learned**

That an unverified assumption, an entitlement name, an environment variable, can sit quietly wrong for weeks and only surface right before a build or a demo. That building alone means the second pair of eyes a team would normally provide has to be replaced by deliberately re-checking against the real, running project instead of trusting what worked yesterday. And that chasing "more like this" turned out to be a better problem than chasing "more accurate audio analysis": Last.fm's community tagging gets you further, faster, than trying to fingerprint sound itself.

**What's next for Showmi**

- Move the user's library and taste profile from local, on-device storage to full persistence on Supabase, so switching phones doesn't erase it.

- Real store credentials (Spotify Client ID/Secret, Apple Developer Program, production RevenueCat keys) to move from a Test Store to an actual public release.

- Expand genre-to-vibe tagging coverage beyond its current ~20%.

- Surface a visible signal when the deck's filter relaxes past an exact genre+vibe match, so the person swiping knows why they're seeing something slightly off their request.

</details>

- **Built with:** dart, firebase, flutter, tensorflow

**Video (1:17):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Si-jEThtZ4

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/3Si-jEThtZ4/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Si-jEThtZ4)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/578/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/578/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/579/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/579/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/580/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/580/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/582/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/582/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/581/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/581/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/583/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/583/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/584/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/584/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/585/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/234/585/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Water-related problems — pollution, oil spills, illegal dumping, leaking pipes — often go unreported simply because there's no easy way for ordinary citizens to flag them to the right people. As someone passionate about AI and full-stack development, I wanted to build something that turns everyday smartphone users into active environmental watchdogs, while giving officials and organizations the data they need to act quickly.

WaterGuard started as a prototype I had already built for reporting water issues with location and photo evidence. Shipaton gave me the perfect reason to take that prototype, add real monetization through RevenueCat, and ship it as a genuine product.

**What it does**

WaterGuard lets anyone report a water-related issue in seconds: pin the exact GPS location, attach a photo as evidence, and submit. An on-device AI model automatically classifies the type of problem — pollution, oil spill, garbage accumulation, or pipe leak — so reports are structured and actionable from the moment they're submitted.

- Free for everyone: submit reports with location and photo evidence, track status updates in real time.

- Premium Individual: priority report flagging, unlimited report history, a Verified Reporter badge, and detailed AI confidence scores.

- Organization Dashboard: a separate subscription tier for NGOs and community organizations, unlocking an analytics dashboard, category trend charts, and CSV data export.

- Behind the scenes, WaterGuard also supports internal Volunteer and Admin roles for monitoring incoming reports and managing verification — a small ecosystem built around one shared goal: cleaner water, faster action.

**How we built it**

WaterGuard is built with Flutter, using Firebase (Authentication and Firestore) for the backend and user data. Monetization runs entirely on RevenueCat, integrated with two subscription tiers, each tied to Firebase Auth identity through Purchases.logIn()/logOut().

The AI classification feature uses a lightweight TFLite image classifier — trained via Google's Teachable Machine on a custom dataset assembled from Kaggle and manually curated images — chosen specifically because it runs entirely on-device, keeping the app fast and usable even on lower-end Android phones, without needing a network call or a heavy multimodal model.

The Institution/Organization dashboard uses fl_chart for trend visualization and Firestore queries for filtering and CSV export, giving organizations a way to turn raw citizen reports into actionable insight.

**Challenges we ran into**

Almost every stage of shipping this app came with its own obstacle:

- Getting RevenueCat's Test Store dialogs to render at all required switching from a lightweight ATD emulator to a full Google Play system image — and even then, RAM limits on Google Play emulator images (locked at 2GB, non-editable) forced us to test purchases on a physical device instead.

- Integrating TFLite meant wrestling with native library loading errors (libtensorflowlite_jni.so not found) caused by ABI mismatches between emulator architecture and the model's supported architectures.

- Migrating from a placeholder applicationId (com.example.flutter_application_1) to our real package name broke Firebase configuration and required re-registering the app in Firebase Console.

- Generating a signed release build surfaced a Gradle daemon crash under the combined load of R8 minification and native TFLite libraries, solved by increasing Gradle's JVM memory allocation.

- We even had a real security scare: an API key and a keystore password were accidentally committed to a public GitHub repo. We rotated the exposed RevenueCat key immediately and cleaned up the repository history.

- Connecting RevenueCat to real Google Play billing meant creating a dedicated service account in Google Cloud, granting the exact right combination of Play Console permissions, and then waiting out Google's credential propagation delay (up to 36 hours) before purchases could validate against the live Play Store.

- Our Play Console submission was also initially rejected under the Government Apps policy simply for describing our institution tier as being for "government agencies" — resolved by rewording our listing to make clear WaterGuard is an independent, community-driven platform with no government affiliation.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A fully working end-to-end subscription flow: free trial, purchase, entitlement gating, and premium feature unlocking — verified on a real device against both RevenueCat's Test Store and, ultimately, live Google Play Billing.

- An on-device AI classifier that adds genuine, tangible value to every report submitted, without requiring an internet connection or a cloud API call.

- A clean separation between our free/premium individual tier and a completely independent B2G-style organization tier, each with its own RevenueCat entitlement and its own set of features designed around who's actually paying for them.

- Successfully navigating the full Google Play publishing pipeline — from signing keys, to privacy policy, to account deletion requirements, to passing Google Play policy review — as a solo developer.

**What we learned**

Shipping a monetized mobile app end-to-end is a very different skill from building a working prototype. Payment infrastructure, app store policy compliance, credential security, and platform-specific quirks (emulator limitations, ABI mismatches, Gradle memory limits) all demand just as much attention as the core product idea. I also learned firsthand how important it is to separate secrets from source code from day one, rather than retrofitting security after a mistake.

**What's next for WaterGuard**

- Expanding the AI classifier with a larger, more diverse training dataset to improve real-world accuracy.

- Adding a live heatmap visualization to the Organization Dashboard.

- Supporting multi-user access and volunteer/report assignment workflows for larger organizations.

- Exploring iOS support once cross-platform build infrastructure is available.

</details>
