<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I didn't get into the university I wanted. I spent those years on my phone instead of studying.

So I tried app blockers. All of them did the same thing: made unlocking harder. Twenty push-ups. A math problem. A hundred steps.

I did them all, and unlocked anyway. That's the whole problem. If you can get past a lock, sooner or later you get past it. Making it harder fixes nothing, because the thing that needs fixing isn't how hard your phone is to open. It's that you don't want to work.

The only thing that ever actually made me want to work was other people. A friend posting that they were studying. Someone who had already made it talking about how they got there. No amount of friction ever did that.

So I built the blocker around that instead.

**What it does**

Every other blocker is trying to make your phone harder to reach, whether by adding friction or by blocking hard.

1% Lock is trying to do something else: make you want to go back to work.

It blocks. Apple's Screen Time API handles that part: the apps you pick, for as long as you choose. Nothing new there.

Then it gives the urge somewhere to go. Blocking your apps doesn't remove the urge to scroll. It only removes the destination, and an urge with no destination is what makes you unlock in the first place. So 1% Lock gives it one. Inside the app there is a feed, and every post is screened by AI. Gambling, junk food, gaming, nights out. All filtered out. What is left is people working. Studying. Training.

When the urge hits, you scroll here instead, and somebody studying at 2 a.m. makes you want to get back to work.

Unlocking is designed the same way. Before the lock starts, you pick what it will take to end it:

- Declaration — write one line about what you'll do after the break. This is an implementation intention; the meta-analysis (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006, 94 independent tests) puts the effect at d = 0.65

- Feed — you have to look at five posts, three seconds each, before the unlock button appears. Scrolling past them doesn't count. Every post you see is about studying, training or working

- Your image — the same five and three seconds, but with pictures you picked yourself and keep on the device. A role model, a goal, whatever works on you

- Hard Lock — no way out until the timer ends (Pro)

None of these four is meant to be an obstacle. Push-ups make unlocking hard; these put something in front of you at the moment your willpower is weakest, to make you want to stay locked. And while you are looking, whether at the feed or at your own pictures, a button sits underneath the whole time, as prominent as the one that unlocks: "Actually, keep working."

Every blocker has a way out, and no developer can take it away. Delete the app and the blocks go with it, and no app on the App Store can stop you from deleting it. That is the limit of the whole approach: making the lock stronger can never be the fix. So instead of competing on how inventive the unlock could be, I put the work into making people want to keep going.

I don't try to close that exit, and I don't pretend that I have. What I can do is make leaving cost something, and make staying the easier choice.

**How I built it**

Alone, in SwiftUI, in about two months of real work.

- Blocking — FamilyControls / DeviceActivity / ManagedSettings, with a custom ShieldConfiguration so the block screen shows your own goal and a quote instead of a generic warning

- Feed & social — Supabase: Postgres with row-level security on every table, Edge Functions, Storage

- Moderation — Claude, running a discipline-ethos filter on every post

- Monetization — RevenueCat

Moderation had to be cheap enough to offer for free. Every post and comment is checked for two things at once: is it safe, and does it fit what the app is for. Unsafe posts are rejected. Safe posts that are off-topic, like a night out, stay out of the feed. Every check goes to Claude Haiku first, and only the ones Haiku is not sure about go to Sonnet. If someone appeals, Haiku and then Sonnet look at it again, and anything still unclear comes to me. A normal check costs under one US cent. Each account can post five times a day, so no single user can run up the AI bill.

RevenueCat is the source of truth for Pro. Scheduled locks, location locks and Hard Lock are Pro. The app logs in to RevenueCat with the same user ID as Supabase, so a purchase belongs to the account, not the phone. A webhook writes Pro status into the database, where users cannot change it themselves, and test purchases are ignored in production. Before a scheduled lock starts, the lock extension checks that status. The "3-day free trial" label only appears when RevenueCat says the user is eligible for it. I never wrote a single line of receipt validation.

Two problems came up before launch. In sandbox testing, buying Pro did not unlock anything: my code checked for an entitlement called "pro", the one in the dashboard was named "1% Pro", and the webhook was skipping every event without an error. And RevenueCat does not promise that webhooks arrive in order, so an old expiration could arrive after a new purchase and switch Pro off. The database now ignores any event older than the last one it applied.

I'm twenty, a university student in Japan, and I didn't come into this as a professional engineer. The subscription layer is the part most people my age assume is out of reach for one person working alone. It isn't out of reach, and RevenueCat is most of the reason why. I'd like more students in Japan to know that.

**How the monetization is designed**

Most Screen Time apps sit behind a hard paywall. I couldn't do that here. A social app behind a paywall ends up with nobody in it and nothing to look at.

So locking is free, permanently, and so is posting and scrolling. The profile is built out of cumulative lock time, streak, completion rate and rank. Somebody who has never been able to lock once has an empty profile and no reason to come back.

Pro sells automation rather than access. Scheduled locks and location locks are the only features that lock your phone without you choosing to at that moment. That is worth paying for; another unlock method isn't. Hard Lock is Pro because the competitors that have it put it there too.

That decision comes with a cost attached. Free users get the whole social side, and every post they make goes through an AI moderation call, on top of storage and feed queries. A new user adds that cost with certainty, and subscriptions do not necessarily grow in step with it. So I added ads, which are the part of the income that arrives with the user rather than with the subscription.

I was giving away far more for free than the blockers that sit behind a hard paywall, so I expected a low conversion rate and set the price low to match. It came in at around 17%, much higher than I had planned for. So I tested it and more than doubled the price. Conversion fell, and I am still testing to find the right price.

**Challenges I ran into**

A social network is a lot to build. Feed ranking, follows, comments, notifications, reporting, AI moderation, rate limits, access rules on every table. The blocking engine is the part Apple helps with; everything else I had to build and secure on my own.

The harder problem was a different one. Blocking apps does not make anyone want to work, and neither does making the lock stricter. Building something that does is where the real work went, and most of this app is an attempt at that.

I started where everyone starts. The first thing I built was camera-verified push-ups, because that is what every other blocker does. Then I realized I had just made the same mistake the app exists to fix: it makes unlocking harder, and it does nothing to make you want to work. I took it out. Getting from there to what is in the app now took far longer than writing any of the code did.

Most of the time went into one moment: the second before someone unlocks. Working out what to put in front of a person at the point where they most want to quit, and then getting it to actually hold them, was the hardest thing in this project. The declaration came out of research. I looked for something that had already been shown to work and that I could put into an app, which is how it ended up being an implementation intention. The others, the feed of other people's progress and the image you set for yourself, came out of my own experience and a long time spent reading around it. None of it was obvious, and none of it came quickly.

Those unlock screens are the last line of defense. Wanting to unlock at all is already a partial failure, and the rest of the app has to make that moment arrive less often. That is a separate design problem and it was not an easier one. Cumulative lock time sits on your profile the same way followers and likes do, as something you build up over time. That number, the ranking and the completion rate are all public, and the completion rate drops visibly when you end a session early. All of it is there so that you don't want to unlock in the first place, and it had to do that without becoming a punishment for the people who do.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

As of today, 808 people have signed up. They have locked away 4,667 hours across 2,471 lock sessions and posted 301 times, and every post was screened by AI. 41 of them have paid for it.

About 7 in 10 timer locks run to the end. And people come back: 131 have locked five times or more, and 34 have locked twenty times or more.

The people using it are young. The median age is 19 and 87% are under 25. More than half said during onboarding that they spend six or more hours a day on their phone, and 231 of them said eight or more. Six hours a day is more than 90 full days a year.

This is the age that decides most of what comes after it, and these are the people locking their phones and taking some of that time back.

It is also a real product rather than a demo: on the App Store, with paying subscribers, changed repeatedly on user feedback, and built by one student. On the Japanese App Store it has an average rating of 4.8 from 26 ratings. I am entering it for the Next Gen Award and the RevenueCat Peace Prize.

**What I learned**

After launch I was improving the app on guesswork. I could see what people did: how many of the people who installed it ever started a lock, how many of the people who locked went on to subscribe, how many came back the following week. What I could not see was why, or what they wanted next. So I kept changing whatever I thought was wrong.

Then I made a developer account inside the app's own feed and started talking to users as myself. Requests came back that I would never have arrived at on my own, and acting on them has done more for the app than anything I picked out of the numbers myself.

What I learned is that data and users answer different questions. The numbers told me what was happening, but never what people actually wanted, and the only way to find that out was to ask them.

**What's next for 1% Lock**

Turning what users say into what actually ships. A mandala chart for breaking a goal down, a streak for posting and not only for locking. Those are the requests sitting in front of me now, and keeping that process running is the first thing.

But asking only reaches the people who are still here. The ones it stopped working for have already left, and they only show up in the data: sessions that get ended early, people who stop starting locks, people who stop opening the app at all. There is enough of that now to find the patterns, and once I know where it breaks I can build alternatives and test them against each other instead of choosing by taste. Price belongs in that too. I tested it once by more than doubling it, and I want to keep testing until I know what the right number actually is.

Further out: an alarm feature, task management, and an Android build so this isn't limited to people on iPhones. Working toward something is a lonely thing to do, and locking your phone only makes it lonelier. Adding those pieces is how this turns into what I actually want: one app that holds the whole day of anybody, anywhere, who is trying to get something done, with other people doing the same thing alongside them.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Learning platforms often teach the same fixed path to everyone, even though people start with different skills, goals, confidence, and pace. We were inspired by how expensive and inefficient it can feel to keep changing courses or platforms just to learn what actually matters for the next step.

AdaptiveSkills is built around a different idea: the learning journey itself should adapt. What comes next should depend on the learner’s goal, current understanding, chosen depth, completed work, and evidence from labs — not on a static syllabus.

As skills grow and goals change, the path should grow with the learner.

**What it does**

AdaptiveSkills helps people upgrade any skill through a learning path that changes with them.

It:

- maps the learner’s goal, existing knowledge, experience, and desired depth

- builds only the skills and concepts actually needed

- teaches concepts progressively instead of forcing a fixed course

- uses labs and practical work to measure what the learner can really do

- captures notes, doubts, weak areas, and proven knowledge throughout the journey

- adapts upcoming units based on learning evidence, not just course completion

- lets learners go deeper where needed and move faster through what they already know

- continuously creates the next learning runway as the learner improves

V1 focuses on technical and software-engineering skill development, including frontend, backend, APIs, databases, cloud, DevOps, system design, AI/application engineering, and related programming skills.

The learning engine is designed so the same adaptive model can later support additional skill domains beyond software engineering.

The goal is not simply to finish a course. It is to continuously strengthen the skills needed for the learner’s real goal.

**How we built it**

We built AdaptiveSkills around the idea that skill development should begin with understanding the learner’s target deeply, rather than immediately placing them inside a fixed course.

1. Learner context

The first step is building the learner profile. AdaptiveSkills collects the learner’s current role, experience, existing skills, resume or background, learning goal, preferred depth, and the type of role, product, or capability they are trying to reach.

This becomes the context used throughout the learning journey instead of asking the learner to start from the same generic syllabus as everyone else.

2. Target and skill-gap analysis

If the learner provides a job description, role, project goal, or specific learning objective, AI analyzes that target and breaks it into the capabilities, sub-skills, concepts, dependencies, and practical abilities required to reach it.

AdaptiveSkills then compares that target with what the learner already knows and builds a structured skill map around the remaining gap.

3. Learner-controlled scope and depth

The generated skill map is not treated as final automatically.

The learner can review the proposed scope, keep recommended concepts, remove areas they do not need, add missing topics, and choose how deeply they want to study each area.

That selected depth influences how much theory, implementation detail, practice, and reasoning the system should provide.

4. Small adaptive learning runways

AdaptiveSkills does not generate an entire course upfront.

Instead, it creates a small learning runway first. In the current V1 trial, the learner receives two coherent learning units with practical labs.

This gives the system enough structure to begin teaching while also allowing future units to depend on real evidence collected from the learner rather than assumptions made at the beginning.

5. Goal-aware teaching

Each learning unit is generated around the learner’s target, selected concepts, current level, and chosen depth.

During learning, the learner can:

- create notes

- mark important material

- raise doubts

- request deeper explanations

- indicate that a concept is already known

- identify areas they do not understand

These interactions become part of the learner’s evolving learning context.

6. Practical labs as evidence

After the teaching portion, the learner enters a practical lab based directly on the concepts from that unit.

The learner works inside an editable workspace, can run their work, use a limited hint system, and submit the final result.

The lab is not just an exercise at the end of a lesson. It is one of the main sources of evidence AdaptiveSkills uses to understand the learner’s actual capability.

7. Learning evidence

AdaptiveSkills records more than whether a unit was completed.

It can capture evidence such as:

- what was completed independently

- where hints were required

- where additional explanation was requested

- which concepts were demonstrated successfully

- what the learner already knew

- what still appears weak

- what needs reinforcement

This allows progression to depend on demonstrated understanding rather than only completion percentage.

8. Continuation and adaptation

After the initial two-unit trial, AdaptiveSkills performs a continuation analysis.

It considers the original target together with:

- the remaining skill scope

- completed concepts

- practical lab evidence

- assistance and hints used

- concepts marked as already known

- unresolved doubts and weaknesses

- the learner’s selected depth

AI then proposes the next learning runway from the remaining gap, rather than returning the learner to a predefined course sequence.

As the learner improves, the same cycle continues and the path evolves with them.

9. Access and entitlement layer

RevenueCat is used for the access layer.

The initial trial and continued learning can be represented through entitlements, while AdaptiveSkills itself remains responsible for the learner profile, skill map, learning evidence, progress, adaptation state, and runway generation.

This keeps payment and access control separate from the actual learning intelligence.

10. AI and backend responsibilities

We deliberately separated adaptive intelligence from authoritative product state.

AI is responsible for tasks such as:

- understanding the learner’s target

- decomposing skills

- generating learning material

- explaining concepts

- interpreting learning evidence

- proposing the next learning runway

The backend remains responsible for:

- persistent learner state

- selected skill scope

- progress

- notes and learning evidence

- lab state

- entitlements

- workflow state

- deterministic product rules

The overall system therefore operates as a continuous loop:

target analysis → skill map → selected scope → focused teaching → practical lab → learning evidence → adaptation → next runway

Instead of creating a course once and asking the learner to follow it, AdaptiveSkills continuously rebuilds what should come next from the learner’s actual progress.

**Challenges we ran into**

Keeping adaptation simple for the learner

AdaptiveSkills has many moving parts — goal analysis, skill mapping, depth selection, teaching, labs, evidence, continuation, and payments. One of the hardest product challenges was making all of that feel like one clear learning journey rather than a complicated system.

Designing our first mobile learning app

This was our first mobile app, so we had to rethink interactions that are much easier on desktop. Code examples, editable lab files, notes, text selection, navigation, and contextual actions all had to stay usable on a small screen without reducing the depth of the experience.

Building practical labs on mobile

The lab experience was especially challenging. We had to handle editable and read-only files, autosave, run results, hints, submissions, file navigation, and touch interactions while still making the workspace feel practical for real learning.

Separating AI from product truth

AI generates explanations, skill scopes, labs, hints, and continuation plans, but learner progress, completed work, evidence, purchases, and resume state must remain reliable. We therefore separated AI reasoning from the deterministic backend rules that control the actual learner journey.

Generating only what the learner needs next

Generating a full course upfront would be expensive and could quickly become irrelevant. We moved to small learning runways generated progressively, using new learning evidence before deciding what should come next.

Keeping learner state persistent

Learners may leave halfway through a concept or lab and return later. Notes, markers, doubts, code, hint usage, progress, and exact resume position all needed to stay synchronized across the journey.

Reconciling RevenueCat with learning access

RevenueCat introduced another important state boundary. A purchase event alone could not define learning state, so entitlements had to stay consistent with our backend progression and continuation logic.

These challenges led us to a clear architecture: AI for understanding and adaptation, persistent backend state for truth, and a mobile interface that reveals complexity only when the learner needs it.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Building our first complete mobile learning app

AdaptiveSkills became more than an AI demo. We connected onboarding, skill analysis, learning, labs, evidence, payments, continuation, and resume state into one working mobile journey.

Closing the adaptive learning loop

The product can analyze a learner’s target, create a skill scope, teach selected concepts, test them through practical labs, capture evidence, and use that evidence to shape what comes next.

The full loop is:

goal → skill analysis → learning → lab → evidence → continuation → next adaptive runway

Making practical labs work on mobile

We are especially proud of the mobile lab experience, which brings editable files, code, hints, run results, submissions, notes, doubts, and learner state together on a small screen.

Integrating RevenueCat into the learning journey

RevenueCat is not just a checkout button. Entitlements are tied to learning access, so a learner can complete the initial runway, unlock continuation, and move into the next adaptive path while the backend remains responsible for progression and state.

**What we learned**

Adaptation is more than content generation

We learned that an adaptive learning product needs a clear separation between AI and product state. AI is useful for analysis, explanations, labs, hints, and continuation planning, while the backend should own progress, evidence, access, and deterministic rules.

Mobile changes the learning experience

Building our first mobile app showed us that code editing, text selection, navigation, notes, lab execution, and resume state require much more careful design on a phone than on the web.

Entitlements are product state

RevenueCat changed how we thought about payments. A purchase is not just a transaction; it unlocks a specific stage of the learner journey, while the application still decides what that learner should receive next.

Generate less, adapt more

We learned not to create an entire course upfront. Smaller learning runways are more useful because each new section can be shaped by fresh evidence from the learner.

Most importantly, we learned that real personalization comes from continuously combining goal, prior knowledge, chosen depth, learning behavior, practical evidence, assistance used, and remaining gaps to decide what should happen next.

**What's next for AdaptiveSkills**

Building a deeper learner model

The next step is to make AdaptiveSkills understand learners across longer periods, not just unit by unit. The system should learn how quickly someone progresses, where they repeatedly struggle, what they can do independently, which types of practice help most, and how their goals change as their skills improve.

Expanding into deep labs

We want to move beyond short exercises into realistic, multi-stage labs where learners build complete features, debug failures, make architecture decisions, work under constraints, and prove skills through sustained practical work.

These labs should adapt from the learner’s evidence instead of giving everyone the same project.

Adding human guidance where it matters

AdaptiveSkills should become more human-centered over time.

AI can prepare context, summarize the learner’s history, identify the exact gap, and suggest where help is needed. Mentors, reviewers, peers, and domain experts can then step in when human judgment adds more value than another automated response.

Supporting collaborative learning

Real professional capability is often demonstrated through teamwork.

Future versions can include shared labs where learners take different roles, contribute to the same project, review one another’s work, resolve dependencies, and build evidence around communication, ownership, collaboration, and technical skill.

Adapting experiences, not just lessons

The long-term adaptive model should combine concept mastery, lab performance, assistance usage, repeated mistakes, project outcomes, collaboration evidence, and long-term progress.

The goal is to move from:

“What lesson should come next?”

to:

“What experience will most effectively improve this learner’s capability next?”

Evolving monetization with the learning model

We want paid access to reflect the value being created rather than wrapping a generic subscription around a fixed content library.

Future paid experiences could include deeper learning runways, advanced labs, long-term adaptive progression, expert review, team environments, and specialized skill tracks.

RevenueCat can continue to manage access and entitlements while AdaptiveSkills determines what each learner actually receives.

Long-term vision

The goal is for AdaptiveSkills to become a platform where AI adaptation, practical evidence, human guidance, deep labs, and collaborative learning work together to help people continuously build real capability rather than simply complete courses.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Dietitian Abbey Sharp teaches a simple idea: a meal holds you when it contains two or more of protein, fibre and healthy fat. No counting, no tracking, no restricting.

Almost every nutrition app does the opposite. It asks what you ate after you ate it, converts it into a number, and compares that number to a target. That is a tool that can only ever tell you what you did wrong — and the Shipaton's Nutrition brief asks, in as many words, for an experience that works "without calorie counting, macro tracking, or restrictive meal plans".

The name came before the code. κρᾶσις is Greek for the blending of elements in due proportion; in Hippocratic medicine, health was a good krasis. It is the same idea applied to a plate, and it turned out to be the product thesis as well as the wordmark — which is why the app opens by explaining its own name rather than by asking for anything.

**What it does**

You type what you're about to eat. Krasis reads it for the three compounds, fills three vessels, and tells you whether it will hold you. If it won't, it names one thing to add — chosen only from staples you told it you actually own, so it never suggests quinoa to someone who has never owned quinoa.

Then, about two hours later, it asks one question: still full? One tap — starving, fine, stuffed. After a few answers it stops guessing and starts telling you what actually holds you, which is different for everyone and is the one thing no calorie count can tell you.

There are no calories in it. No macros, no logging, no streaks, no goals, no score.

**How we built it**

SwiftUI and SwiftData on iOS 18, Swift 6 with strict concurrency on, plus a WidgetKit extension and a watchOS app. The project is generated by XcodeGen (project.yml is the source of truth, the .xcodeproj is git-ignored), and GitLab CI turns a pushed tag into a TestFlight build in about seven minutes with nothing pressed.

**The food table is the actual work**

The app does not call a nutrition API. It ships 274 foods, each reduced to three booleans, built by merging four openly licensed national databases:

Source
Country
Licence

BLS 4.0
Germany
CC BY 4.0

Ciqual 2025
France
Etalab 2.0

CoFID 2021
UK
OGL v3.0

USDA SR Legacy
USA
Public domain

That is 21,304 rows of evidence collapsed into 173 derived foods, plus 101 hand-curated dishes the databases have no row for. Two findings were worth the trouble:

- Composition barely differs between countries. Chicken breast is 22.5 / 23.4 / 23.25 / 23.3 g of protein across the four. For a boolean, the source is almost irrelevant.

- Coverage differs enormously. USDA contains exactly one Greek cheese. That is why four sources, and why the hand-curated set exists at all.

**The threshold that made it honest**

The interesting part is deciding what "contains protein" means. A gram threshold alone does not work. Let $p$ be grams of protein per 100 g, $s$ the typical serving in grams, and $E$ the energy in kcal per 100 g:

$$
\text{protein} =
\begin{cases}
\text{true}, & p \ge 10 \[4pt]
\text{true}, & \dfrac{p\,s}{100} \ge 6 \;\wedge\; p \ge 3 \;\wedge\; \dfrac{4p}{E} \ge 0.20 \[4pt]
\text{false}, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

The second branch is the one that took a bug report to find. Pasta was reading as a protein source. At $p = 5.4$ on a 200 g plate it clears the per-serving bar easily:

$$\frac{5.4 \times 200}{100} = 10.8 \ge 6$$

Meanwhile bread — the same flour, with more protein per 100 g at $p = 8.7$ — fails, because a slice is 60 g:

$$\frac{8.7 \times 60}{100} = 5.2 &lt; 6$$

So the food with more protein was the one being rejected. And no gram threshold fixes it. Lowering the serving bar to admit bread admits pasta too. Raising the density floor above pasta's 5.4 throws out whole milk, which is only 3.4 g per 100 g and is unarguably a protein source in a 250 ml glass:

$$\frac{3.4 \times 250}{100} = 8.4 \ge 6, \qquad \frac{4 \times 3.4}{63} \approx 0.215 \; \ge \; 0.20$$

Milk and pasta sit on opposite sides of a line that no gram threshold can draw between them, because the thing that separates them is not how much protein is there — it is what fraction of the food is protein.

The energy share separates them. Protein supplies 4 kcal/g, and pasta is 147 kcal per 100 g:

$$\frac{4 \times 5.4}{147} \approx 0.147 \; &lt; \; 0.20$$

0.20 is EU Regulation 1924/2006's line for "high protein". Applying it demotes pasta, wholemeal pasta, couscous, bulgur, quinoa and buckwheat — and nothing else.

It gates the per-serving path only — the first branch of that formula takes no further test, and that is not a shortcut. Applied everywhere, the share demoted every nut and seed: almonds are 21 g of protein per 100 g but 598 kcal of mostly fat, so $4 \times 21 / 598 \approx 0.14$, comfortably under the line. Almonds are a protein source. The rule has to know that a food can be dense in protein and dense in fat.

Healthy fat has a pleasingly small rule — unsaturated must beat saturated:

$$\text{fat} = \Big(u \ge 5 \;\;\vee\;\; \big(\tfrac{u\,s}{100} \ge 5 \;\wedge\; u \ge 2\big)\Big) \;\wedge\; u \ge \sigma$$

where $u$ is unsaturated fat per 100 g and $\sigma$ is saturated.

That single comparison excludes butter, ghee and hard cheese while including olive oil, nuts and avocado.

**Monetization**

RevenueCat, with a live A/B experiment scored on revenue per customer rather than conversion rate — the two arms sell a €49.99 one-off against a €24.99/yr subscription behind a trial, so the arm that converts fewer people can still earn more. The app never picks an arm: it asks for the current offering and
draws what comes back, so shipping the winner is a dashboard change rather than a build.

**Challenges we ran into**

Four builds went out for one crash before anyone symbolicated the log. The frame offsets were byte-identical across two very different builds — the tell that the culprit had not moved while three fixes went past it — and that was sitting in the crash report a day before anyone noticed. The cause, once atos had resolved it in one line: an Objective-C delegate method written in Swift's async form. The compiler's @objc thunk calls the completion handler on whatever thread the continuation resumes on — the cooperative pool — and UIKit asserts main thread inside it. Reading the log was right; stopping at the log was not.

The same trap has a second, different shape. When the Watch app landed, its WCSessionDelegate crashed on launch with "Block was expected to execute on queue [com.apple.main-thread]". UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate callbacks arrive on the main queue, so the @MainActor + @preconcurrency pattern that is correct there is wrong for WatchConnectivity, whose callbacks arrive on its own background queue. @preconcurrency silences the compiler; it does not move the thread.

A settings switch nobody could switch. Every row carried .contentShape(Rectangle()) so the navigating rows would be tappable full-width — which took the hit area of the toggle rows too. The switches drew, read their stored value, animated nothing and could not be changed. It compiles, it screenshots perfectly, and no unit test reaches it. Found by tapping the thing.

The app answered for a dish it had never heard of. παστίτσιο matched nothing, so the reading was empty, so the verdict was "This won't hold you long." — evidence of absence from absence of evidence, on the one screen whose entire job is being trustworthy. Now an unread meal gets no vessels, no verdict and no rescue; it gets a question instead, and the answer is remembered.

"None of these" had to become sayable. The unknown-food card's confirm button was disabled until a compound was picked — so a food that genuinely has none of them (ketchup, a coffee, a spoon of jam) could never be taught. The only exit stored nothing, so the app asked again on the next plate and forever. That was most of what "the food database is poor" felt like.

A user report that the table was poor turned out to be four foods that were all present and all correctly empty. A cucumber will not hold you. But four blanks in a row reads as ignorance whether or not each blank is right, so the fix belonged on the read screen rather than in the data.

Accessibility was worse than it looked. VoiceOver labelling was good, but Font.system(size:) does not scale — and every size in the app is a literal point size from the design spec, so the whole thing was frozen at the default text size, including at all five accessibility sizes. Fixed by mapping each design size to the text style it most resembles: at AX5 body text grows about 3.1× while large titles grow about 1.9×, so scaling a 31pt wordmark off body would put it past 95pt and off the screen.

**What we learned**

Deriving a boolean is a completely different problem from deriving a number, and much more tractable. "Does this contain protein?" survives disagreement between four national databases; "how much protein is in this?" does not.

A food with none of the three is an answer, not a gap. Half the reported "missing food" bugs were foods that were present and correctly empty.

Thresholds need a worked example that is wrong, or you cannot tell whether they are right. The pasta-versus-bread pair did more to shape the data pipeline than any amount of reading the regulations.

The design decisions that survived are the ones with a reason attached. "No second colour, ever" sounds arbitrary until you notice that a green vessel would import exactly the pass/fail grammar the product argues against. Writing the reason down is what stopped it being relitigated at 1am.

**What's next for Krasis**

Voice entry — the entry screen was designed around it from the start. And closing the loop between the check-back answers and the rescue ranking, so the app suggests what has actually held this person rather than what the table says should.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

SkillQuest is a free Android learning app that helps you explore languages and programming through short lessons and interactive practice.

Choose a skill, open a level, and learn with clear explanations and examples. Then practise with different types of questions, including multiple choice, fill in the blank, true or false, matching, and sentence building. Follow your progress as you complete levels and earn XP.

SkillQuest also includes speaking practice using your device’s speech features, as well as background music and sound controls that you can adjust in Settings.

AI tools are optional. You can add your own Gemini API key in Settings to access AI tutoring, additional practice questions, and pronunciation help. AI requests are sent to Google Gemini, so an internet connection is required.

Optional SkillQuest Subscription

SkillQuest is free to use, with an optional subscription for users who want additional features.

• Monthly: $4/month
• Yearly: $42/year

The yearly plan is offered as an alternative to monthly billing. The subscription is completely optional, and the core learning experience remains available without a subscription.

Because SkillQuest is distributed through itch.io rather than Google Play, subscription availability and payment options may depend on the platform and the payment provider. Users under the applicable age should only make purchases with the permission and involvement of a parent or legal guardian.

Get SkillQuest

Download and try SkillQuest on itch.io:

https://rayane-6.itch.io/squillquest

The goal of SkillQuest is to make learning easier to fit into your day: choose a skill, practise at your own pace, and keep moving forward one lesson at a time.

About the Developer
SkillQuest was created by a 14-year-old developer from Morocco.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

**What it does**

**How we built it**

**Challenges we ran into**

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

**What we learned**

**What's next for ClipStack**

InspirationAs developers and power users, we constantly copy and paste the same snippets—API endpoints, configuration blocks, regex patterns, and shell commands—throughout the day. Traditional clipboard managers often clutter the desktop, require bloated cloud accounts, or compromise privacy by sending sensitive text to remote servers. We were inspired to build ClipStack: a lightweight, privacy-first, local-first mobile utility where your code and text snippets remain entirely on your device, accessible with a single tap.How We Built ItClipStack is crafted using modern cross-platform mobile architecture centered on performance and developer experience:Core Framework: Built with React Native 0.81 and Expo SDK 54, leveraging Expo Router 6 for file-based navigation.Styling & UI: Styled using NativeWind 4 for seamless Tailwind utility classes on mobile, combined with Expo Haptics for tactile touch feedback.Local Persistence: Powered by AsyncStorage, saving data directly to the host device with versioned storage keys (clipstack.snippets.v1).Search Mechanics: Implemented an in-memory linear-time filtering algorithm over local state. Given $N$ snippets, filtering against search query terms across title, body content, and tag arrays operates with a worst-case time complexity of:$$\mathcal{O}(N \times (M_t + M_c + T \cdot M_g))$$where $M_t$, $M_c$, and $M_g$ represent string matching evaluations across Title, Content, and Tags ($T$).What We LearnedLocal-First Architecture: Storing state locally eliminates network latency completely, bringing read operations down to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ runtime access post-hydration.Cross-Platform Haptics & Clipboard: Managing platform-specific APIs requires strict runtime guards. Ensuring native haptics trigger smoothly on iOS/Android while failing gracefully on Web builds was a critical design pattern.Deterministic Testing with Vitest: Decoupling storage logic from UI components enabled sub-second unit test execution for our filtering and serialization pipelines.Challenges We FacedWeb vs. Native Parity: Web browsers handle clipboard permissions asynchronously via the browser Permissions API, whereas React Native handles them directly. Harmonizing these differences required unified wrapper abstractions in lib/haptics.ts and lib/clipstack-storage.ts.Safe Layout Insets: Designing a multi-type capture drawer that respects notch boundaries across various Android and iOS screen geometries without layout jitter.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Living inside a language you don't speak yet is tiring in a specific way.

After moving from India to Munich, vocabulary became one of the biggest barriers to learning German. Without enough words, I could not follow what was being said around me, no matter how much grammar I studied.

Most vocabulary apps had the same problems for me:

- They mostly relied on boring flashcards.

- They rarely had images, so there was nothing to visualise a word with or relate it to.

- Example sentences were plain text: no text highlights following the audio, and no way to tap a word in the sentence to see what it means.

- The vocabulary was often generic, with very little personalization.

- Learning felt like another study session instead of something connected to daily life.

- Streaks were supposed to motivate me, but losing one often did the opposite.

- Once I broke a streak by missing a few days, it became much easier to stop using the app completely.

So we built Vocabloot around one idea:

Learn the words that are already part of your life.

**What it does**

Vocabloot turns the world around you into your personal vocabulary book, on your phone, your tablet and your watch.

**Snap a word**

Take a photo of an object and Vocabloot gives you:

- The word in the language you are learning.

- The meaning.

- Pronunciation.

- Part of speech.

- Example sentences, read aloud with each word highlighted as it is spoken.

- Tap any word in the sentence and its meaning opens, with the article, the plural and the part of speech.

Vocabloot teaches 10 languages, and the app itself is localized in 24, so you can learn German from a Tamil or Arabic screen, not only through English.

Every snapped object also becomes a die-cut sticker, and there is a WhatsApp sticker pack.

Share an image from another app or pick one from your gallery and it becomes a new word too.

Widgets on the iPhone lock screen and on iPhone and Android home screens show your own words, photos and translations during the day.

Notifications teach from your own wordbook, in the time window and number of words a day you choose:

- Learn notifications: one of your words with its meaning, or one of its example sentences with the word blanked out.

- Recall notifications: just the word, to check you still remember it.

- Practice notifications: an invitation to play a game with your words, at most once a day.

- Capture notifications: a nudge to snap something new, only when your wordbook has gone quiet.

- Comeback notifications: if you stop opening the app, it sends fewer and then goes silent after a week.

- Promo notifications: a new deck, feature or offer, at most once a week and never in your first week.

**8 arcade games that make your own words stick**

The thing you snapped this morning is the thing you practise tonight. Each game trains a different part of knowing a word:

- Sky Rescue, Pop Quiz and Warp Run: recognising the meaning fast.

- Kraken Escape: checking a translation under pressure.

- Flooded Hold: matching words to their translations.

- Grid Hack and The Vault: spelling the word letter by letter.

- Intercept: understanding words in context, by reading a short message and answering questions about it.

All eight are free and unlimited, drawn in Compose Multiplatform with one implementation on both phones. They also run in the browser at vocabloot.com/games.

**Share your wordbook**

Your whole wordbook, photos, stickers and sentences included, exports from Settings as one .vlbackup file. Send it to a friend, a classmate or your other phone, and Import a shared wordbook adds their words to yours. Words you already have are kept and nothing is deleted. Opening a .vlbackup from a chat or an email offers the same import.

Turn on backup and the same wordbook mirrors into your own iCloud Drive or Google Drive, with no account and nothing on our servers. Restore brings it back on a new phone.

Because a wordbook is one file, decks and Creator Studio are built on it.

**Decks: on the web, and made in ChatGPT**

Greetings and set phrases ("Freut mich", "Wie geht es dir?") are the words you need first, and you can't photograph them. A deck is a .vlbackup file the app opens as its own, and every word in it gets what a camera word gets: a sticker, example sentences, tap-a-word meanings, the sound.

- The deck pages run the app's own Kotlin. vocabloot.com/decks lets you search, filter and hear every card. Its reading rules and the deck format are the phones' shared Kotlin compiled to JavaScript with Kotlin/JS, so a card on the web behaves the same way as the card in the app.

- Anyone can make a deck with ChatGPT. The open source Vocabloot Deck Kit is six skills that run in ChatGPT, Codex or Claude Code. Say what you speak, what you learn and the topic; the assistant writes every card, and the kit checks and packs them with the same Kotlin. It is listed in the ChatGPT plugin directory. The first community deck, German Greetings, was made this way.

**Creator program and Creator Studio**

We started the creator program to get learners posting about Vocabloot. Post three times about how you use it on TikTok, Reels, Shorts or X. Small accounts are welcome, because we look at how the posts did, not at your follower count. Posts with 30+ likes earn one month of Premium, and posts with 100+ likes earn a full year of Premium.

Then we saw that making the content is the hard part, so we built Creator Studio. Share your wordbook as a .vlbackup file, import it into Studio, and six of your own stickers become a YouTube Short, an Instagram or TikTok Reel, or an interactive Instagram Reel your viewers play along with through Instagram's emoji slider.

**Your words on your wrist**

The wordbook follows you off the phone. The Apple Watch app shows your word cards with their stickers, swipe to see the sticker full-size, and a Smart Stack widget surfaces the word of the hour. The Wear OS app matches it screen for screen, with a Tile for the same word on your watch face.

**Privacy first**

There is no account to create. Your wordbook lives on your phone, and backup goes only to your own iCloud Drive or Google Drive.

**Pricing**

Vocabloot is freemium, and only snaps sit behind the paywall. Every game, the whole wordbook, stickers, widgets, decks and backup are free. Snaps work like energy in a game. An energy chip on the camera screen shows how many you have left: a green battery with a number, which turns coral at zero and refills the next day. Free users get 6 snaps on the first day and 2 a day after that. Premium turns the chip into ∞, unlimited snaps for $7.99/month or $19.99/year, sold through RevenueCat's Kotlin Multiplatform SDK.

**How we built it**

Vocabloot is one Kotlin Multiplatform codebase, and the UI is Compose Multiplatform on both phones. There are no native front ends sitting on top of shared logic. The screens, the navigation, the dependency graph and the games are written once, and Compose draws them on Android and on iOS.

The split below is production code, tests counted separately, as published on vocabloot.com/shipaton. All eight games live in the shared code too: 15,511 lines, with zero game files in androidMain or iosMain.

Production code only, tests counted separately. The watches and the web run the same 1,534 of the 81,468 shared lines, so they get their own rows instead of one blended percentage; counting both watch apps into the total anyway gives 81,468 of 99,496 lines, 81%. RevenueCat purchases are one flow in the shared code, on the Kotlin Multiplatform SDK.

The same Kotlin also runs on the web. The deck pages on vocabloot.com and the Deck Kit's packer have to make decisions the app already makes: which word a tap lands on, which word lights up while a sentence is spoken, whether a card is valid at all. We did not want a second copy of those rules in JavaScript, so shared/format (the deck file format) and shared/reading (tap-to-word and the spoken highlight) compile to Kotlin/JS and run in the browser and in Node. A deck made with the Deck Kit is the same file the app itself would write. I wrote up how this works on dev.to, with the same card on Android, iPhone and the browser: Kotlin on Android, iPhone and the web. Android Weekly #746 featured it in its Articles & Tutorials section on 27 September.

The same Kotlin reaches the wrist the same way it reaches the web: the UI is native, the rules are shared. SwiftUI draws the Apple Watch screens and Compose for Wear OS draws the Wear OS screens, neither one reusing the phones' Compose Multiplatform UI. Both lay out every word card with the same wordCardRows() from shared/reading and label the part of speech with the same PartOfSpeech from shared/format that the phones and vocabloot.com use: 1,534 lines of shared Kotlin under both watches.

- Apple Watch: shared/reading and shared/format cross-compile to watchosArm64, watchosDeviceArm64 and watchosSimulatorArm64 as VocablootReading, a small static framework exported alone rather than the whole shared framework, so the watch stays well clear of the memory ceiling that had already killed our first iOS widget. 779 lines of SwiftUI call into it, so 66% of the watch app is shared Kotlin.

- Wear OS: no cross-compile at all. Wear OS is Android, so the watch app depends on the same shared/reading and shared/format Gradle modules as the phone app, and the phone and the watch exchange words over the Data Layer as one Kotlin type, WatchWordPayload. 657 lines of its own Kotlin, so 70% of the watch app is shared.

- The words themselves come from the phones' shared widget feed, published through our WidgetBridge library; 121 lines of Kotlin on Android and 231 lines of Swift on the iPhone forward it to the watch.

One Kotlin module, five real compile targets: Android, iOS, watchOS, the JVM and JavaScript.

Our stack:

- Kotlin Multiplatform, Compose Multiplatform, Kotlin/JS

- Koin, Voyager, Ktor

- Firebase (Cloud Functions, Auth, App Check, Remote Config, Crashlytics)

- OpenAI models, behind our Cloud Functions

- RevenueCat

AI requests go through Firebase Cloud Functions with App Check enforced, so no provider keys live inside the app.

The wordbook is stored as files instead of a database: a JSON manifest plus the image files, with atomic commits and a last-good copy. This keeps the app local-first and makes full backup, restore and decks the same operation.

**Building in public**

Everything we built during Shipaton is on one dated page, vocabloot.com/shipaton: the code split, every Wordathon post, every TikTok and Instagram post, both libraries, the deck program and a day-by-day timeline. The page keeps updating after 30 September. When one of our write-ups or libraries gets picked up by Android Weekly, Kotlin Weekly or anyone else, it goes there first.

**On X: the #Wordathon, 101 words from the street**

I set myself a public challenge: 100 German words, one per post, each looted with Vocabloot in a tram, a park or a shop, with the snap video and the example sentences. In between, rounds of The Vault and Sky Rescue on the words so far. It ended at 101.

- First post, 1/100 der Bus: x.com/NirmalJeffrey/status/2095430186346914127

- Challenge complete, 101 words: x.com/NirmalJeffrey/status/2102492878958162276

- Every post: x.com/NirmalJeffrey

**On TikTok and Instagram**

- TikTok, @learnfrombarbarah: learning Spanish with Vocabloot.

- Instagram, @vocabloot: our reels and posts.

**Giving back to the Kotlin community**

Two libraries extracted from Vocabloot during Shipaton, on Maven Central under Apache 2.0, each with a docs site, samples and test fakes. Both were picked for the Libraries section of Android Weekly #744 (13 September), and BackupKit again in Kotlin Weekly #529 (20 September). Vocabloot itself uses both from Maven Central, like any other app.

- BackupKit: backup into the user's own iCloud Drive or Google Drive app-data folder, no server, no account, with differential updates and resumable transfers.

- WidgetBridge: typed handoff of data and images to Glance and WidgetKit widgets; the iOS extension never links Kotlin.

And a write-up other KMP teams can follow: Kotlin on Android, iPhone and the web on dev.to, on how the phones' shared Kotlin now powers our deck website through Kotlin/JS. Android Weekly #746 picked it up too, in its Articles & Tutorials section (27 September).

**What building in public changed**

- The decks idea came out of a Reddit thread. I posted Vocabloot on Reddit and the top reply asked, "How is abstract vocabulary done?" I did not have an answer. You cannot photograph "Freut mich". That reply is where decks started, then the open source Deck Kit, then the first community deck, German Greetings. The moderators removed the post later, so the screenshot below is what is left of it. The reply under it, about A2 and B1 exams, is why every deck carries a level.

- Posting a word a day meant I was in the app every day, and that is how I noticed that a freshly snapped photo stayed hidden until its translation came back. It is fixed.

- Our Android home-screen widget went blank, but only in the store build. The fix went into the app and into WidgetBridge, our open source widget library, the same day, so anyone using the library gets it without ever seeing the problem.

- Anita, a retired nurse who is learning Korean, told us our Korean example sentences read like a textbook and that nobody talks that way. We changed how sentences are written for Korean and Japanese.

- The deck pages on our website had their own copy of one rule from the app, and it got a simple word wrong. We deleted the copy and made the website run the app's own code.

- A month of daily posting showed us what one post costs in time. That is where the creator program came from, and then Creator Studio, which turns a learner's own words into a Reel or TikTok that is ready to post.

What it cost: the three of us have full-time jobs in three time zones. The day's Wordathon post was usually the last thing I did at night, and on some days it was the only thing that shipped. The count kept going anyway.

**Launch platforms**

- Product Hunt

- Fazier

- Uneed

- Maidensail

- Startup Fame

- Munich Startup

- TechBase Directory

- FoundrList

- AlternativeTo

- Aitoolnet

- TinyLaunch

**Challenges we ran into**

Shared code does not mean identical behaviour. Every trap we hit was a place where iOS and Android disagree underneath the shared Kotlin:

- Widgets. Our first iOS widget linked the shared framework and was killed at the 30 MB extension memory limit. The fix became WidgetBridge.

- Speech highlighting. Android and iOS report spoken words through callbacks that disagree (onRangeStart versus willSpeakRangeOfSpeechString); we reconciled them into one contract with a test both sides must pass.

- The camera. A live preview cannot be a Compose canvas, so it is the one native screen; its zoom, facing and flash state are shared anyway.

- Cloud backup. iCloud placeholders and Google Drive app-data behave nothing alike.

- Notifications. iOS keeps at most 64 pending notifications per app, so the schedule is capped at 19 and rebuilt every time the app opens. Android 14 wants a second permission for exact delivery; we chose a nudge that may arrive late over nagging for it. The library we started with said "scheduled" before the OS had answered, so both sides now call the system scheduler directly, behind one shared contract.

- Bugs JVM tests can't see. iOS sent Booleans as 0 and 1 to Cloud Functions and our strict schema rejected every snap; the Firebase wrapper maps every callable error to UNKNOWN on iOS. We now verify iOS-only paths on the simulator before every release.

Lag. Opening a word right after a snap stuttered. We traced it frame by frame and fixed it for 1.3: the word page now arrives over three frames, the reveal animation stopped recomposing on every frame, and the widget export and image uploads moved off the main thread.

AI output in 10 languages. Korean 물병 (water bottle) failed five retries in a row because the AI kept writing Hangul in the pronunciation field; we now blank a bad pronunciation instead of rejecting the whole word. Japanese の and Chinese 木 were rejected for a missing reading or measure word, until we checked those only on the headword.

The three of us work full-time jobs in three time zones, so this was built in early-morning calls, late-night reviews and weekends, with product, design and marketing coordinated across different schedules.

Shipping to both stores for a global audience meant that scripts and languages, AI accuracy, pricing, age ratings and privacy rules had to be right in every market, and then survive store policies, closed testing and review rounds on both sides.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Vocabloot is on both stores and people use it:

- 1.0 on Google Play on 24 August 2026 and on the App Store on 26 August, after Google Play's closed testing with our tester community; then four releases on both stores in a month.

- 1,500+ words looted by learners, and 14 store ratings, all 5 stars, with ten written reviews from Germany, India and the US.

- Two libraries on Maven Central, picked by Android Weekly and Kotlin Weekly within weeks of publishing.

- Our dev.to write-up, Kotlin on Android, iPhone and the web, featured in Android Weekly #746 on 27 September.

- The Deck Kit in the ChatGPT plugin directory, and the first community deck made with it on vocabloot.com/decks the next day.

- A 101-word #Wordathon finished in public.

- An Apple Watch app and a matching Wear OS app, the same wordbook now on your wrist.

What we are proudest of is that all of it works together, in one app, built by three people.

**What we learned**

One of our biggest lessons was that cross-platform does not mean both platforms behave the same. Sharing code saves a lot of time, but you still need to understand how iOS and Android work differently.

We also learned that pricing is very hard. Vocabloot is a global language-learning app, so we wanted it to be affordable for people in different countries. At the same time, we still need to cover AI costs, infrastructure, app store fees and development costs.

Finding a price that is fair for users and also sustainable for us was harder than we expected. We ended up with one flat price everywhere and a free tier generous enough to learn from.

And even after building and shipping the app, marketing and distribution are even harder. We are still trying different ways to reach the right people: content, SEO, communities, creators, social media and partnerships. This is still one of the biggest things we are trying to crack.

**What's next for Vocabloot**

Our roadmap is public: see what's planned, vote, or add an idea at vocabloot.featurebase.app/roadmap.

Everything we shipped during Shipaton, day by day: vocabloot.com/shipaton

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Since my first day at university, I saw studying as something tiring, boring and huge. Especially because I always loved learning and joining a lot of things, and studying kept ruining that for me.

So one day I sat down and started thinking about a way to solve this problem. I searched a lot, and I found that the methods most of us students use are the worst ways to study (re-reading and highlighting). Of course they are easy to do (just sit, read, repeat and highlight), but they are not effective at all and they take a very long time. If we had a pyramid that ranks study methods, these ones would live at the very bottom of it.

**What it does**

From here, me and my friend Abdelhafeez started moving to solve this problem, and to take the way students study, and their learning journey, from the worst methods to a journey that is fun, gamified and proven by science to be the best, all with the help of AI. Today, joining this competition in the Next Gen category is one of the steps we are taking to reach the goal of our journey: to turn studying from hard, tiring work into a daily journey where the student's mission is to take care of their trees by watering them every day.

**How we built it**

Our journey went through a lot of experiences and competitions before this one, and we learned a lot from them. We moved from pictures on Canva and Figma to a web page (of course everything was different in the past competitions, like the visual identity... in this competition we leveled up, thank God). The last idea we reached was that we want to turn studying into a game: every day the student comes, does a short session using the best learning methods, and then leaves. And from exactly this point, we started this Shipaton.

After I made a number of assets in Blender (the trees, the world, the character and some icons), I went to Flow and fed it a lot of my work, so it would understand my identity, my colors and my character, to help me and save me time (because rendering in programs like Blender takes a lot of time). Then I started making the screens. This time, and different from all the other times, we focused on the deepest details of the UI/UX, from small interactions with Coco to the idea that you can study together with your friends in a squad, and other things that we really got tired thinking about. But in the end, it gave our app a really beautiful vibe. After I finished all the screens with the help of Stitch, the app was ready in Figma. Then we started turning the app from pictures into a real app with the help of Claude Opus 5.5, and thank God, after long days of work and real effort, the app is fully ready.

So now, instead of chaos and random studying, the journey of a student using Drrys looks like this:

Every day, after they attend their lecture at university and go home, they open the app. The app already has all the files for the subject, the past exams and everything that helps the AI understand the full context and predict the exam patterns and questions. Then, for each subject, they do one of two things:

A full session: this is on the day they had the lecture, so the session is longer. It has active recall, the Feynman technique, and flashcards to review what was given in the lecture.
A flashcard session (faster): just a review of the flashcards, which follow a spaced repetition system and were made in the full sessions.

**Challenges we ran into**

The first and most important thing for us when we started was to change everything we had before in the visual identity and start a new, strong one. So I opened Blender and started working on our character Coco, the trees, the environment and the style in general. After a long effort and a lot of tries, it worked, and I made the app in the minimalist, clay style you're going to see.

also, one of the biggest challenge for us was turning the app from pictures into a real app with the help of Claude. Designing a screen in Figma is one thing, but making it actually work is something else. Every screen that looked finished in Figma needed a lot of real work behind it: saving the student's trees and cards, making Coco's animations play smoothly on the phone, and connecting everything together.

We also found a lot of bugs only when we tested the app on a real phone, like the app crashing , and other challenges . So we went through many rounds of testing, finding problems, fixing them and testing again. Another hard part was making Coco's AI stick only to the student's own lecture files and past exams, and not make things up. It took a lot of tries until the questions and flashcards felt right.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

One of the nice ideas we came up with, and learned about during this Shipaton, is discounts on Pro. They come in two ways:

The daily streak: study 30 days in a row and you get 25% off, 60 days and it's 30% off. We did this to encourage students to stay consistent.
The "squad": you and 3 friends join the app together with one code, and when the squad is full, each of you gets 25% off Pro while the squad stays together. This helps Drrys spread wider.

The two discounts stack, up to 50% off. On top of that, the free plan gives you one tree with one branch (one chapter), but if you bring a friend to the app and they finish their first session, you get two branches instead of one.

**What we learned**

We learned sooo many things from all of these problems. And the most important one, from our point of view, is that your app has to be the way the user wants it, not the way you want it.

**What's next for Drrys — Grow what you know**

I'm really happy with this competition because it was a very big step for the app, and what's coming next is going to be even bigger in every way, God willing. We want to add mnemonics, AI-made videos, live Ai chatting with coco, audio podcasts and a lot of other features we have in mind.

And I really want to thank the RevenueCat team for all the effort they put in before the submission, and the effort they will put in after it. I want to remind you that you helped me, and helped thousands of people, build apps, grow and learn. So thank you.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Award Category: Next Gen Award

**Inspiration**

I’ve been investing my own money (and whatever my parents would give me) since freshman year of high school, hoping to be the next TJR or big investing guru. I used platforms like Robinhood and Webull to trade everything from options to crypto, but I would spend hours each day looking for trades and studying charts. This eventually took time away from school, so my grades tanked freshman year, and the worst part was that I was still making bad trades. After losing almost all the money I had and all the money my parents lent me, I quit...

Luckily, during sophomore year of high school, I was able to build a YouTube channel that earned me back some money, so toward the end of sophomore year I decided to invest my money again, but this time I didn't want to waste my time looking for trades. So I decided to build Sight: something that could handle a lot of the hassle of trading for me and give me more time to focus on school and YouTube. 

**Who is it for?**

Sight is built for students, beginners, casual investors, and anyone in between who wants to understand the market without spending hours researching and looking for the right trades. Sight brings market data, AI analysis, charts, portfolio tracking, and investing tools together in one place to make investing simpler and less time-consuming for our audience.

**What does it let users do?**

Sight is basically an AI investing assistant built to take the hassle out of investing. From my own experience, I know that investing is super confusing, especially for a beginner, which is why Sight simplifies the whole process. Instead of using a bunch of different websites for charts, fundamentals, indicators, and market information, all you need is Sight, which brings everything together in one easy-to-use app that also integrates AI into your investing decisions. Users also have access to features like adding stocks to a watchlist and viewing advanced charts via TradingView.

Sight's AI also finds and analyzes the market for potential trades and gives you AI-generated analysis explaining its decision, which you can decide whether or not to act on. You can even snap a picture of any stock chart and have Sight analyze it. Users can also connect supported brokerage accounts to Sight, see their actual portfolio, and submit real trades all without leaving the app. Trades are then logged to a user's journal so they can see their trading progress directly in the app.

**How I built it?**

I built Sight with React Native and Expo, using Vibecoding AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, OnSpace, and Lovable. Supabase handles storage for certain aspects, while OnSpace handles things like user accounts, authentication, and email verification. I also connected multiple APIs to bring live stock prices, fundamentals, technical data, and other market information into the app. 

The AI works using OnSpace; it takes market data, technical information, GEX, price action, outside information, and order flow all into consideration when it makes its decisions. The AI moves system only surfaces 85% confidence-rate trades to minimize risk. Other features like the Camera let users upload a picture of any stock chart and get an AI breakdown. This system uses OnSpace's AI system as well. I also integrated TradingView through a webview for more advanced charting and SnapTrade to securely connect supported brokerage accounts, pull portfolio information, and support real trade submissions.

**How does it Make Money?**

Sight uses two subscription options through RevenueCat:

- Monthly: $17.99/month - includes a 3-day free trial

- Weekly: $2.99/week - no free trial

Sight offers two subscription options: a monthly plan with a 3-day free trial, and a lower-commitment weekly plan. RevenueCat powers the entire subscription system inside the app.

**What Makes it Interesting or Different?**

- Everything in one place - Market data, charts, technical indicators, AI analysis, portfolio tracking, and brokerage connectivity.

- AI-powered trade analysis - Sight analyzes potential trades and explains the reasoning behind them.

- Camera chart analysis - Users can take a picture of a stock chart and have Sight analyze it.

- Brokerage integration - Users can connect supported brokerage accounts, view their portfolio, and submit supported trades.

- Saves time - Sight reduces the need to jump between multiple investing apps and websites.

**Challenges I ran into**

The biggest challenge I've faced so far is definitely finding the time to build Sight. I’m currently taking 6 AP classes while balancing extracurriculars and a bunch of other academically demanding things. So far, there have been A LOT of school nights, listening to Drake while fixing one more bug or finishing one more feature.

Another challenge I faced that was SUPER annoying was that when I did have time over a weekend to work on Sight, the market would be closed, so features that relied on live market activity (which is basically everything) couldn't be fully tested. I also had to work through API limitations, inaccurate/missing data, brokerage integrations, and getting all the different parts of the app to work together.

Another big challenge has also been getting Sight to the App Store. Just when I thought that I fixed all of Apple's annoying issues, Apple informed me that I need to be a registered LLC/Company to have this type of financial app, and that I couldn't simply work with the Developer account under my mom's name (SUPER ANNOYING). Money has also been a major issue. I've probably spent $1,000+ of my own money building Sight, which has been a lot for me.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

My biggest accomplishment is definitely just seeing Sight exist where it is now. This app started as an idea I had to help me with investing that I thought was probably going nowhere, but somehow I actually turned this into a real prototype with AI analysis, live market data, technical indicators, chart analysis, trade tracking, and even the ability to connect real brokerage accounts through SnapTrade.

I'm also super proud that I was able to build most of this while being a busy full-time high school student. There were so many times that I thought a feature was impossible to build or a bug would never get fixed, and then a few hours (or days) later I would finally get it to work. Going through that trial-and-error process and then finally getting something to work is just super satisfying to see.

And lastly, I'm also super grateful that Shipaton gave me the motivation to keep working on this app that I probably would've left sitting unfinished. 

**What I learned**

The biggest thing I learned from building Sight is how much work it actually takes to make an app into a finished product. I thought that vibecoding would be easy and fast, but in reality it's still a super hard and long process to make a high-quality and actually useful app. 

I also learned a lot about managing my time. Building Sight as a high school student is super difficult and stressful. For example, I remember a couple of weeks ago coming home from school and instantly going to work on Sight until around 9:00 pm that night when I realised, "Oh shoot, I have a test in AP Chem tomorrow." (I ended up getting a 65% on that test.)

**What's next for Sight Ai - Investing Assistant**

My first goal is definitely to get Sight officially onto the App Store. Because of Apple's requirement for me to have an actual LLC/Company, I definitely want to get that set up with my parents and get anything else needed to actually launch Sight completed as soon as possible.

After that, I want to focus on getting actual users. I actually already have an influencer interested in promoting Sight, but I told him to wait until the app was completely ready before promoting it to his audience.

I am super passionate about Sight, and I will definitely keep working on this project beyond shipaton!!!

</details>
