<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Loneliness is the quiet epidemic of our generation. I see everywhere people having a bad day and having nobody to actually text about it.

AI chats have memory now, even the free ones. But they remember everything, and after a while it gets confused. More importantly, they don't remember like a friend does. A friend doesn't keep a log of you. A friend keeps the small things: the exam you were stressed about, the person you stopped talking to, the thing you were proud of and didn't tell anyone else. Those details are what make someone feel known.

That's the idea behind Lucy, and that's where most of the work went: a memory that remembers like a friend does.

**What it does**

Lucy is an AI friend. You text her like you'd text anyone.

- A short questionnaire at sign-up tells her who you are before the first message.

- She writes in short bubbles, lowercase, with actual opinions. No bullet points, no "would you like advice or would you rather vent?".

- In the background, a structured memory keeps what matters: who you are, your goals, your relationships, your traits, what you like, what's going on in your life. Small things expire on their own. Weeks later, she brings things up herself.

- You log your mood in one tap a day. Your mood today and your seven-day average reach her before every reply, so she goes gentle on a rough week without you having to say it. A mood tracker shows your streak, a wellbeing score and a chart.

- She knows what time it is for you, and how long it's been since you last talked.

- You can erase her memory in one tap, and delete your account just as easily. No ads.

**How I built it**

React Native with Expo, in TypeScript, with Expo Router and Reanimated. English and French.

Supabase for the database: Postgres with row-level security on every table, and triggers on the columns that decide access, so the app can't write them.

A Node/TypeScript server builds the prompt (memory, mood, questionnaire answers, local time), calls the model through the OpenAI Responses API, cleans the reply, and runs the memory worker. The worker reads the conversation in segments and extracts facts into typed tables. There's no vector database. Recency and strength scoring on plain Postgres tables is enough for one person's life.

Monetization runs on RevenueCat. After onboarding you really talk to Lucy and get five free exchanges, once and for all. The counter doesn't reset. The sixth send is refused by the server, which stamps the wall. The app never decides access itself: when the quota is spent, the server asks RevenueCat whether the entitlement is active, and answers 503 rather than let anyone through if RevenueCat is unreachable. Two subscriptions, monthly and yearly, both with a 7-day free trial, plus dedicated screens for lapsed subscriptions and billing issues.

**Challenges I ran into**

Making her sound like a person. Language models love bullet points, dashes and hedging. Replies are cleaned server-side, and each line becomes its own bubble, at the pace a friend would type.
I improved it by kepping the prompt short. Every time I added a rule, she got worse. The current version is a dry character sheet with one priority.

The paywall. The first version came before the chat, so people were asked to pay for something they had never tried. I moved it after five real exchanges, which meant the server had to become the only thing that decides who gets in. It's very new, so I haven't had the chance to get a lot of feedback yet, but since I noticed a huge drop in traffic right at the paywall, I think being able to see the product might be a factor in increasing the number of trials.

Finally, the App Store review process took quite a while for the app to be approved.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

Lucy is live on the App Store, and I built it alone. I had never written code or made an app before this.

What I'm most happy about is that I did it on the side of a full-time summer job, while also preparing for an exam. There wasn't a single week where Lucy was the only thing I had to do.

**What I learned**

I had never built anything before, and I loved it. Seeing an idea turn into something people can actually download was a revelation. I don't think I'll stop.

I learned to watch how people really use the app. I realized that tracking is absolutely necessary just to understand what users are doing and what might be causing them to abandon the app.

I also learned that a simple paywall wasn't what converted users. By observing how the best apps operated, I noticed that they provided users with a complete journey that gradually drew them deeper into the app until they finally reached the paywall. So that's what I've done, and that's what I'll continue to do.

And on a personal level, I've also learned to be much more organized, to stay disciplined, and that every hour I can devote to my project during the day is time well spent. I'm entering my final year of study this year, and this is clearly a skill that will allow me to take my project as far as possible while I'm still in college.

**What's next for Lucy**

Marketing first. I'm running an Apple Ads campaign to understand which keywords people search, how they behave, and to make the App Store listing more relevant, because conversion is what's holding me back right now. I've started a TikTok account for UGC-style content and I'll keep pushing it, along with more paid ads, to bring in enough users to see clearly what works and where the bottlenecks are. Right now I simply don't have enough data.

Product next. The next thing I want to build is Lucy writing a real message to you on her own, spontaneously. That's how I think Lucy stops being a chat you just open and becomes a presence in your week. It's also where I think she'll stand out: it won't be an another wellbeing app made of small tools nobody uses, but something personal, built around the relationship, that actually helps people feel better. And naturally, someone who texts you first is someone you come back to.

Then it's about pushing Lucy to make real revenue. This is my last year of studies, and I'd love for this to be the project I keep going with after.

</details>

**Inspiration**

Parents often struggle with baby‑care routines — feeding schedules, medical checkups, and growth tracking — while siblings feel left out. I wanted to create something that feels less like a tool and more like a friend + game + guide. That’s how NuzzleNest was born: a playful 3D world with a mascot that supports both parents and siblings.

**What it does**

NuzzleNest is a 3D companion app that makes baby‑care fun, educational, and magical.

👶 Parent Mode: Daily checklist, smart alarms, growth tracker, food guidance, product guide, and calendar with stickers.

🧒 Sibling Mode: Quizzes, mini‑games, finger‑tracking mascot, glowing background effects, and treasure box rewards.

🌍 Social Features: Custom avatars, streak competitions, leaderboards, and future community sharing.

🎨 3D Interactivity: Mascot animations, glowing backgrounds, and motion‑based effects that make learning playful.

**How we built it**

Design: Figma for UI/UX prototyping and mascot creation.

Prototype: Interactive flows designed to simulate finger tracking, glowing backgrounds, and treasure box rewards.

Conceptual Logic: Growth tracker built on simplified BMI formula:

𝐵
𝑀

**𝐼**

Weight (kg)
Height (m)
2
Converted into plain language outputs like “Healthy” or “Slightly underweight.”

**Challenges we ran into**

🎨 Designing a mascot that feels original yet universally appealing.

📊 Simplifying WHO/CDC growth charts into parent‑friendly language.

🗓️ Syncing calendar events with checklists and reminders.

🧩 Implementing smooth 3D interactivity (finger tracking, glowing effects).

🤝 Ensuring accessibility for parents with different education levels.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Created a unique mascot that reacts to finger movement and celebrates progress.

Simplified growth tracking into clear, friendly health messages.

Built a calendar with stickers that syncs into daily checklists.

Designed sibling engagement through quizzes, mini‑games, and treasure boxes.

Made the app inclusive by using simple language and visuals.

**What we learned**

How to gamify serious routines like feeding and medical checkups.

How to balance fun and education for siblings.

How immersive design (finger tracking, glowing backgrounds) transforms learning into play.

The importance of accessibility and inclusivity in health‑related apps.

**What's next for NuzzleNest**

🤖 AI‑powered food suggestions tailored to age and growth data.

📱 AR baby‑care mini‑games for siblings.

🌍 Community hub for parents and siblings to share tips and achievements.

🎨 More mascot variations (sleepy, excited, thoughtful).

🗓️ Smart calendar syncing with Google/Outlook.

🧩 Expanded quiz packs and treasure box themes.

📊 Analytics dashboard for growth and learning insights.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

When the network goes down, the rescue network comes alive.

RescueNet is an offline-first emergency communication and coordination platform built for disaster-prone regions — designed around Pakistan's flood and earthquake emergencies, and built to generalize anywhere normal infrastructure can fail exactly when people need it most.

The problem
During floods, earthquakes, and major infrastructure failures, the thing that fails first is the network — cellular towers go down, internet access disappears — right when people most need to report emergencies, find their families, and locate safe routes. Most emergency apps quietly assume the internet works. RescueNet doesn't.

The idea
Turn ordinary smartphones into nodes of a resilient emergency network:

When internet is available: reports flow straight to a backend and a live coordinator dashboard.
When it isn't: reports are encrypted, stored locally, and relayed phone-to-phone over Bluetooth until any device in the chain regains connectivity — at which point the report reaches the backend automatically, no matter whose phone actually delivered it.
An AI layer turns messy, code-switched speech (English/Urdu) into structured, prioritized incident data — always labeled with a confidence score, never presented as certain fact.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every group trip starts with excitement—and dies in the group chat. 

When friends try to travel together, planning breaks down under social friction:

- The Budget Dilemma: No one wants to be the first to admit their financial limit, leading people to either overspend uncomfortably or drop out silently with vague excuses.

- Date Deadlocks: Juggling blackout windows across school schedules and jobs leads to endless polling threads with zero resolution.

- The Organizer Burden: A single coordinator is left doing all the logistical heavy lifting and booking, only to be questioned when plans don't align.

This coordination failure is a classic Pareto inefficiency in microeconomics: an optimal overlap exists where everyone’s constraints are satisfied, but social discomfort prevents people from disclosing their true parameters. 

We built PACT to replace group chat paralysis with deterministic consensus: a platform where travelers enter private constraints securely, reach consensus mathematically, and transition into a shared living manifest and memory vault.

**What It Does**

PACT guides groups through the entire travel lifecycle across three structured phases:

**Phase 1: Pre-Trip Consensus Room**

- Zero-Knowledge Silent Ballot: Travelers submit private budgets, target dates, and vetoes. Private numbers are never shown to friends—only the computed group intersection is revealed.

- Deterministic Pareto Consensus Engine: Calculates group alignment across candidate itineraries using an objective scoring model:
$$\text{Score}(c) = w_b \cdot \Phi_b(c) + w_d \cdot \Phi_d(c) - \lambda \sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i(c)$$
where $\Phi_b$ represents budget feasibility, $\Phi_d$ represents date alignment, and $V_i(c) \in {0, 1}$ represents hard member vetoes.

- Tactile Wax Seal Climax: When votes exceed the supermajority threshold ($\tau \ge 0.70$), an emerald wax seal stamp locks the pact with spring recoil physics, unlocking an authenticated Trip Brief and exportable Pact Receipt.

**Phase 2: In-Trip Living Manifest**

- AI-Curated Highlights: Context-aware activity suggestions powered by Gemini that resolve dietary restrictions, cost caps, and operating hours.

- One-Tap Itinerary Pinning: Optimistic state updates that add verified spots directly to group schedules.

- Offline-Cached Local Support: Instant one-tap access to emergency hotlines (Dial 112) and verified local transport operators.

- Encrypted Circle Chat: Direct, focused in-trip messaging with persistent plan reminders.

**Phase 3: Post-Trip Vault & Shared Memories**

- Google Photos-Style Shared Canvas: High-resolution collaborative photo gallery preserving the adventure permanently.

- Audio Voice Capsules: An interactive recorder featuring real-time 8-bar equalizer waveforms and persistent audio memories.

- The Pact Story Receipt: An exportable, branded story card designed for social sharing that highlights unanimous consensus.

**How We Built It**

PACT is built as an offline-resilient, cross-platform mobile application utilizing:

- Framework & Core: React Native on Expo SDK 52 with TypeScript in strict mode.

- Animation Physics: React Native Reanimated 3 running at 60 FPS for spring-recoil wax seal stamps, pulsing audio equalizer bars, and optimistic layout transitions.

- State Management: Dual-layer Zustand architecture (useCircleStore and useGatherlyStore) separating authenticated Supabase cloud synchronization from an isolated 5-Minute Judge Sandbox to guarantee zero cold-start crashes.

- Data Layer & Security: Supabase PostgreSQL protected by Row-Level Security (RLS) policies. Private constraints, vetoes, and budgets are locked to user IDs and aggregated at the database edge.

- Monetization Engine (RevenueCat): Integrated with the RevenueCat React Native SDK to power our Pro Circle Inheritance model.

**The RevenueCat Pro Circle Inheritance Flywheel**

Traditional per-seat SaaS pricing fails in group travel because casual participants refuse to purchase monthly subscriptions. PACT solves this through circle inheritance:

- The Purchase: One organizer buys a flat $9.99 PACT Organizer Pass.

- The Entitlement Propagation: RevenueCat validates the organizer’s active entitlement. PACT automatically inherits and propagates pro tier status to all 24 member slots in that circle.

- The Viral Growth Loop: 1 paying customer introduces up to 23 active travelers into the ecosystem with zero onboarding friction.

**Challenges We Ran Into**

- Eliminating Floating-Point Leaks in Sealed Voting: To ensure private budgets could never be reverse-engineered from intermediate gauge states, we had to ensure the consensus engine computes score derivatives in isolated memoized selector graphs, publishing only normalized consensus percentages.

- Zero-Dummy Realtime Member Lifecycles: Designing an invite system that avoided placeholder dummy data while preventing race conditions when two travelers claim open circle slots simultaneously required atomic slot-reservation logic.

- Hermes Dynamic Currency Formatting: Formatting multi-currency amounts (USD, EUR, GBP, INR, JPY, AED) across web and Android without crashing the Hermes JavaScript engine required building an internal locale-safe formatting fallback dictionary.

- Android Hardware Safe-Area Collision: Addressing status bar clipping and keyboard overlay quirks across diverse Android aspect ratios without breaking iOS safe areas required strict layout auditing across all primary modal drawers.

**Accomplishments That We're Proud Of**

- 247 / 247 Automated Tests Passing: Achieved 100% test passage across 58 test suites with zero TypeScript compiler errors (tsc --noEmit), verifying privacy isolation, currency conversion, and member capacity limits.

- The 5-Minute Judge Sandbox: Built an instant, isolated sandbox mode pre-seeded with 5 unique traveler personas (Maya, Jake, Priya, Alex, Sam), enabling judges to test the full consensus loop without creating accounts.

- Hardware-Accelerated Interaction Design: Engineered custom Reanimated 3 wax seal physics with tactile haptic recoil and live-oscillating audio waveform equalizers.

**What We Learned**

- Multiplayer Monetization Dynamics: Designing paywalls for group utility requires shifting focus from individual subscriptions to collective group unlocking. Lowering friction for invited guests directly fuels organic viral distribution.

- Zero-Knowledge UX Design: Users care deeply about privacy in social coordination. Displaying explicit "Sealed Input" indicators creates the psychological safety necessary for honest inputs.

- Robust State Isolation: Isolating testable mock states from network-backed cloud persistence is essential for building production-grade demo experiences that never fail under unstable network conditions.

**What's Next for PACT**

- Agentic Auto-Booking via Amadeus APIs: Transitioning the Living Manifest from recommendation into autonomous group reservation and ticketing.

- Automated Expense Escrow: Integrating smart split-bill settlement directly into the post-trip vault to eliminate post-vacation debt chasing.

- Dynamic Travel eSIM Provisioning: Allowing organizers to provision group data packages for international trips in one tap through RevenueCat consumable passes.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Trackly — A Social Habit Tracker Built for Accountability**

**The Problem: Accountability Without the App**

My girlfriend and I weren't trying to change our lives. We just wanted to work out consistently instead of restarting every few weeks like usual.

The habit tracker ecosystem is full of apps that do the basics well: create a habit, check it off daily, watch your streak climb. But they're all built around a single assumption: you're doing this alone. I could see my own progress in vivid detail. I had no idea if she'd worked out yesterday. If she hit snooze and skipped a day, I'd only find out when she told me. We were trying to build a habit together, but the apps had no concept of "together."

That's a small gap, but it matters in a way I didn't fully appreciate until trying to close it: knowing someone else showed up that day is a huge part of why you show up the next day. Isolation kills consistency. Every tracker I tried solved it with a half-hearted friends list or a shared leaderboard that felt bolted on as an afterthought.

That frustration became the seed for Trackly.

**What It Actually Does**

Trackly is a social habit tracker where accountability is the core feature, not an add-on.

You create habits—"morning run," "read 30 min," "study JavaScript"—and mark them complete just like in any other tracker. You get streaks, progress views, calendar histories. But it's structured around a different question: How am I doing alongside the people building this with me?

Instead of tracking your habit in isolation and then bolting on a social layer, Trackly flips the model. When you log a habit completion:

- For individual habits: Only you see the completion. Your streak. Your progress.

- For shared tasks: You and the people you invited both see the same habit. Two separate streaks, one shared leaderboard so you can see how you're tracking against each other.

- For group challenges: Up to N people in a group, competing toward a shared weekly target. Quantified (run 5km, drink 8 glasses of water) or simple (practice piano 30 min). Real-time leaderboards.

The accountability isn't a separate feature you unlock—it's baked into how the app is structured from the data layer up. That distinction shaped almost every technical decision.

**How I Built It (and Why It Got Complicated)**

Stack:

- Frontend: Flutter (single codebase → iOS, Android, Web)

- Backend: Firebase (Firestore, Auth, Cloud Functions for push notifications)

- Real-time sync: Firestore listeners + Provider state management

- Monetization: RevenueCat integration for premium subscription flow

The simplest version would've been: store habits in Firestore, each user sees their own. Simple.

But the moment a second person joins a habit, everything gets harder.

**The Sync Problem**

When you mark a shared habit complete, that single action now touches multiple pieces of state across multiple devices:

- Your personal streak for that habit

- Your friend's leaderboard view (showing your completion)

- The shared progress graph for that habit

- Push notifications to your friend saying "they just completed it"

If you're not careful, one of these updates goes stale while another succeeds. Your friend sees you completed it, but the leaderboard doesn't update. You see a streak increase, but the shared view hasn't caught up.

The solution: Real-time Firestore listeners. Every Habit/Group is stored as a document with a completions map:

Map&lt;String, List&lt;DateTime&gt;&gt; completions; // { "uid1": [DateTime, DateTime...], "uid2": [...] }

This structure is the secret. Instead of separate records per user, completions live in one document. When you toggle a habit complete, you:

- Optimistically update your local UI immediately (feels instant)

- Fire a single write to that document with your updated completion list

- The Firestore listener on every participant's phone fires automatically, syncing everyone to ground truth

No coordination logic. No eventual consistency bugs. One source of truth, streamed to all participants in real-time.

**Calculating Streaks at Scale**

Once multiple people are involved, the streak logic can't just be "days in a row." It needs to answer:

- What's your streak on this shared habit?

- What's their streak on the same habit?

- How many consecutive days did you both complete it? (for accountability metrics)

For each participant, I calculate currentStreakFor(userId) by:

- Pulling their completion dates for that habit

- Sorting chronologically

- Checking each date: is it consecutive from today (or yesterday if today isn't done)?

- Stopping at the first gap

Sounds simple. It took iteration to get right because off-by-one errors in date comparison means your 12-day streak suddenly shows as 3. That kind of bug tanks the core motivation mechanic of the app.

**Multi-Participant State Management**

I use Provider (Flutter's go-to state management for real-time apps). Each Habit/Group streams from Firestore via HabitsProvider:

Stream&lt;List&lt;Habit&gt;&gt; streamHabits() {
 return _db
 .collection('habits')
 .where('participants', arrayContains: currentUserId)
 .snapshots()
 .map((snapshot) =&gt; snapshot.docs
 .map((doc) =&gt; Habit.fromMap(doc.data(), id: doc.id))
 .toList()
 );
}

The where('participants', arrayContains: currentUserId) query means Firestore only sends documents relevant to you. Combined with persistent caching enabled client-side (persistenceEnabled: true, cacheSizeBytes: UNLIMITED), the app works offline and syncs when you come back online.

When you toggle a habit completion, the optimistic update fires immediately (good UX), the server write happens in the background, and the Firestore listener reconciles everyone's state automatically. If there's a conflict (you toggled while offline, then came back online), Firestore's last-write-wins semantics resolve it. In practice, this is fine for habit completion—you're unlikely to have genuine conflicts on whether you worked out today.

**Groups and Quantified Challenges**

Beyond shared habits, groups are first-class citizens:

- Group tasks: Shared to-dos (e.g., "team book club, read chapter 5")

- Group challenges: Weekly quantified goals (e.g., "group of 5, 50km running total this week")

Each group has nested Firestore collections:

groups/{groupId}/tasks/{taskId}
groups/{groupId}/challenges/{challengeId}

Members can join via invite, see live leaderboards, log daily progress toward the challenge target. The challenge leaderboard updates in real time as members log progress.

**The Hard Part: Making "Social" Meaningful**

The technical challenges were solvable with time. The product challenge was harder.

It would've been easy to add a friends list and ship it. Easy to copy Strava's leaderboard UI. Easy to slap on a comment section.

But none of that would've helped with accountability. It would've just added clutter.

I kept asking: Does this feature actually make someone more likely to show up tomorrow?

- Friends list? Not by itself, no. But invite-to-habit? Yes—now you're explicitly saying "I want you to track this with me."

- Weekly leaderboard on a shared habit? Yes—you can see if they're keeping pace.

- Comments on completion? No—that's noise. Nobody reads them. Deleted it.

- Achievements? Helpful as confirmation. Kept them.

- Weekly report to your friend? Helpful as a prompt to check in. Added it.

This question—"does it actually help accountability?"—filtered way more ideas than the technical constraints did.

**The RevenueCat Integration (Test Setup)**

For monetization, Trackly includes a full subscription flow powered by RevenueCat (v10.4.1). Currently running on RevenueCat's test store for this contest build, but the production logic is identical:

- Premium unlocks: Groups, quantified challenges, analytics, mood tracking

- Non-blocking async init: RevenueCat is configured on app start without blocking the UI

- Entitlement checks: Each premium feature gates itself via subscriptionProvider.hasProAccess

- Purchase flow: Full RevenueCat paywall sheet for upgrade

The test paywall is functional. In production, it'd point to App Store / Play Store subscriptions.

**What I'm Proud Of**

I solved a real problem I had: I couldn't find a habit tracker that actually understood "we're doing this together." So I built it—from product thinking through design through implementation to a working app.

Technically:

- Real-time sync across multiple participants without eventual consistency bugs

- Streak calculation that's correct for shared vs. individual contexts

- Multi-participant state management that keeps UI snappy even with frequent updates

- Groups + quantified challenges on top of shared habits

- RevenueCat integration wired through the entire feature set

- Cross-platform Flutter codebase (iOS + Android + Web from one codebase)

- Firestore security rules covering every collection and action

- Push notification infrastructure (FCM) with invite/response tracking

Product-wise:

- Accountability built into the core, not bolted on

- Every feature exists because it helps people stay consistent, not because it's technically doable

- Invitation flow that makes it explicit: "I want to build this habit with you"

- Leaderboards and progress views designed around shared context, not isolation

**Technical Learnings**

Real-time sync is harder than it looks. Getting state aligned across devices requires discipline: single source of truth in the database, listeners on every client, optimistic updates with reconciliation. One bug in this layer breaks the core feature.

Streak calculation is more subtle than just counting days. Off-by-one errors in date comparison, timezone handling, "did today count?" logic—all of it matters because streaks are the core motivation mechanic.

Groups scale complexity exponentially. One person: simple. Two people on a habit: real-time sync required. Groups of 5+ on quantified challenges: now you need leaderboards, weekly rollup logic, member-defined vs. shared task modes. I ended up with separate GroupService, GroupTask, and GroupChallenge models to handle it.

Multi-platform Flutter is a superpower. Building native iOS + Android separately would've doubled the time. Flutter let me focus on the core product and ship everywhere.

**What's Next**

The immediate next step is getting Trackly on the App Store and Google Play with RevenueCat running as a live production paywall instead of the test store setup.

Beyond that, the focus stays on accountability:

- Better ways to feel connected to someone else's progress (not just a number next to their name)

- Weekly group summaries: "Here's how we did together"

- Optional public groups: build a habit with randos, see their streaks too

- Integration with health platforms (Apple Health, Google Fit) for auto-logging

- AI-powered peer verification: "Did you really run 5km? Validate with a photo"

The goal isn't more features for the sake of it. It's making Trackly the habit tracker people reach for because they're not trying to do this alone. That was the original gap. That's still the one that matters most.

**Why This Matters**

Habit trackers are common. Habit success is rare. The difference isn't the app—it's accountability. Most trackers ignore this entirely. Trackly doesn't. It's built around the specific context of "I'm building this with someone else," not bolted on after the fact.

That distinction is the entire product.

What started as frustration at not finding what I wanted became a working app that my girlfriend and I actually use, with a subscription model, a functioning premium layer, and the infrastructure to scale to groups of any size.

Trackly is proof that you don't need a network of millions to make social features meaningful. You just need to ask whether they actually help people stay consistent—and have the discipline to say no to everything else.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/185/236/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/185/236/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/185/237/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/185/237/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/185/238/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/185/238/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/185/252/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/185/252/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Hospitals have call bells. Homes don't.

Someone recovering in bed after a stroke can often press a button but cannot call out. So can many people living with ALS or severe motor impairment. Their caregiver is in the next room, or has stepped out for ten minutes. There is no way to reach them.

The existing options don't fit. A physical bell only works within earshot. A messaging app requires the ability to type. A cloud-based system fails exactly when home internet does, and home internet fails often.

What was missing was something that works in the room with no network, and that someone who cannot speak or swipe can still operate.

**What it does**

Two devices, one app, two roles.

Patient side sits on a tablet beside the bed. Full-screen buttons, one tap to send. It ships with two items, "Discomfort" and "Water". The caregiver can add, rename and reorder more: "Turn over", "Too hot", whatever this particular person actually needs.

Caregiver side goes in their pocket. When a call arrives, the phone raises an alarm and speaks the item name aloud, so the caregiver knows what is needed without looking at the screen. Urgent calls repeat until acknowledged or until three minutes pass.

After tapping, the patient sees whether the call was delivered and whether it was acknowledged. Each call carries its own state on both screens: delivered, waiting, or unanswered. For someone who cannot ask again, knowing they were heard is the whole point.

Accessibility was the starting point:

- Every control is a single tap. No swiping, no long press. That is what lets iOS Eye Tracking and Dwell Control operate it directly. The app implements no eye tracking of its own; it stays out of the way of the system's.

- VoiceOver fully supported, and verified on device. During testing I found that a long-press entry point was unusable with VoiceOver, so the design changed to a two-step tap.

- Large targets, high contrast, and connection state shown by icon, text and colour together, never by colour alone.

- The caregiver's alarm is not silenced by the ring switch.

Every feature is free. There are three optional tip options on the caregiver side. They unlock nothing. There is no entitlement check anywhere in the codebase, and the patient side has no purchase UI and no way to spend money at all.

**How I built it**

- Swift 6, SwiftUI + UIKit in an MVVMC architecture. Every screen is Models / View / ViewModel / HostController, with a single doAction entry point per ViewModel

- Core Bluetooth. The patient is the peripheral, the caregiver the central. A compact binary wire format avoids fragmentation, and state restoration lets calls arrive after iOS has reclaimed the app from memory

- SwiftData for on-device storage. Nothing leaves the devices

- RevenueCat for the tip options, deliberately confined to a single directory so the dependency's blast radius is visible

- Spec-driven development using Spectra. Behaviour was written into specs before the code. The repo carries 12 capability specs (4,647 lines) and 7 archived changes, each with its proposal, design note and task list

The whole thing is open source under MIT.

**Challenges I ran into**

Three defects, all found the day before submission, all of which had survived checklist entries marked ✅ passed.

1. The alarm never armed after iOS reclaimed the app. A caregiver whose phone had been idle would get one notification chime instead of a repeating alert. The cause: audio session activation was tied to the caregiver screen appearing. When the app is woken by a Bluetooth event in the background, that screen never appears.

Diagnosing it took two wrong turns. First, stopping the debugger in Xcode looked like a testing artifact. It isn't: iOS treats system reclaim and user force-quit completely differently, and the former still restores Bluetooth state. Second, a test 13 hours later worked perfectly, because I had opened the app in between and the "preparation succeeded" path writes no log at all.

That second one produced the most transferable lesson: when success leaves no trace, you cannot tell "it didn't happen" from "it happened but wasn't recorded."

2. Non-urgent calls lost their spoken announcement. Two causes, each hiding the other. The speech was being drowned by the first 1.5 seconds of the alarm tone, and a policy check was stopping playback immediately after it started. Fixing only the first produced no visible change. That is why looking for a single cause never found it.

3. A two-day-old conclusion turned out to be wrong. I had recorded that a custom notification sound was "unreliable" and switched to the system default. The file was fine, and all four specs checked out. The failure had come from defect #1, so the custom sound went back in.

And then: two weeks in the review queue. 2026 has been rough for App Store review times as AI-generated submissions flood the pipeline. Nothing to do but wait.

**What I'm proud of**

The app works, but the thing worth pointing at is the paper trail.

Every manual device test is written down with its actual result and OS version. That includes the ones that failed, and the entries that were marked passed and later turned out to be wrong. Every architectural decision that cost something to learn is in DECISIONS.md. The specs were written before the code and are still the source of truth.

That is what caught those three defects: a process that demands every claim be re-tested and every result recorded.

**What I learned**

A ✅ records what happened that one time. It is not a permanent fact. One check was marked passed on Aug 11 with "spoken announcement works" written beside it. It regressed by Aug 14, and a person noticed during ordinary use. No test caught it. That sentence now sits at the top of the release checklist.

Shortening the test loop matters more than fixing any single bug. One defect could originally only be reproduced by leaving devices idle overnight. Once I realised that stopping the Xcode debugger triggers the same code path as a system reclaim, it became a three-second cycle. Both earlier misdiagnoses had happened under the once-a-night rhythm.

Verification steps that need extra hardware get postponed indefinitely. My multi-caregiver test needs three devices while every other check needs two. It was always "next time." A real defect was hiding there, and it is documented in the repo rather than quietly omitted.

**Why this benefits people**

The people SideBell is for cannot advocate for themselves. That is the definition of the problem: someone who cannot speak or move easily also cannot tell you that the current arrangement isn't working.

Who it reaches. Not a large number, and it would be dishonest to imply otherwise. There is no path here to millions of users. There is a path to mattering a great deal in a few thousand households. A person with ALS in the middle stages. Someone recovering from a stroke. An elderly parent who has had a fall. And with each of them, the one family member trying to cook dinner while listening for a sound from the next room.

What changes for them. Before: shouting, banging on a wall, or waiting. After: a tap, and the caregiver's phone says "Water" out loud from their pocket. The patient's screen then shows whether the call was delivered and whether someone acknowledged it. For a person who cannot ask twice, not knowing whether you were heard is its own distress.

Why it can actually be adopted. Every barrier that usually stops assistive technology from reaching a home has been removed:

- No purchase. Every feature is free, permanently. The tip options unlock nothing.

- No account, no subscription, no server. Nothing to sign up for and nothing to cancel.

- No new hardware. Families in this situation almost always already have a spare tablet and a phone.

- No internet. Bluetooth only, so it works in an old apartment, in a rural house, during an outage, or in a hospital ward with no guest Wi-Fi.

- No new motor skill to learn. Single-tap targets only, which is what lets iOS Eye Tracking and Dwell Control drive the app directly. Someone who can only move their eyes can still call for help.

- Open source, MIT. If this project stops being maintained, the people relying on it are not stranded.

What it deliberately does not claim. It is not a medical alert service, it will not reach a caregiver who has left the house, and it cannot send a call if the app has been force-quit or the device has run out of battery. All three are stated in the app on first launch, in the App Store listing, and in the README. For a tool someone's safety may rest on, an honest boundary is worth more than an impressive claim.

**A note for judges on testing**

There is nothing to unlock. Every feature is free. The three tip options grant no entitlement, and no promo code is needed because there are no premium features behind one. You can verify this in the source: the codebase contains no entitlement check at all, and the patient side has no purchase UI and no path to spend money.

Bluetooth is unavailable in the Simulator, so seeing calls actually travel requires two real devices. The 43-second demo video shows the full loop on two physical devices in a single unbroken take. The patient taps, the caregiver's phone alarms and speaks, and the acknowledgement returns to the patient's screen.

**What's next for SideBell**

- Remote push as a complement to Bluetooth, not a replacement, for when the caregiver steps out of range. CloudKit on a single shared iCloud account first, because that answers the one question that matters: whether silent push is fast enough to be trusted

- Indonesian and Vietnamese. In home care in Taiwan, the person actually operating the caregiver's phone is often a migrant care worker: 212,000 of them work as home caregivers. Filipino workers are already served by the English build. Low cost, high value

- Fix the multi-caregiver acknowledgement relay. Right now, if two caregivers are connected and one acknowledges, the other's alarm keeps going until timeout

- Reach the people who need it: ALS associations, assistive technology centres, occupational therapists. They see the families that hospital systems don't reach

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Share Pray**

A quiet place for families and small churches to carry each other's prayers.

**What inspired it**

Distance is the ordinary condition now. Family in one country, friends in
another, a church you visit twice a year. Staying in each other's lives takes
more deliberate effort than it used to, and the thing that goes first is the
small stuff — not the news you announce, but the things you are quietly
carrying. Those get lost in a group chat, scrolled away under photos and links
by the evening.

I wanted somewhere those could sit still. You write what you would like prayer
for; the people who care about you see it and can say they are praying. That is
the whole app.

I first tried to build it in 2017 — Kotlin app, Kotlin backend — and never had
the evenings for it. It sat unfinished for years. What changed was not the idea.
It was that I finally had the time.

**How I built it**

Kotlin Multiplatform, with Compose Multiplatform for the interface and
my own Ktor backend. SQLDelight for storage on both ends, Koin for wiring.

The split is the point:

files

shared, platform-agnostic
109

Android-specific
18

iOS-specific
15 Kotlin + 3 Swift

Nearly everything — the feed rules, the session handling, the offline cache, the
validation — is written once. What stays platform-specific is what genuinely
differs: how a text field looks, how a link arrives from the system, how the
database driver opens, and how a native SDK like Google Sign-In is reached.

The backend is mine too, not a BaaS: accounts and email confirmation, prayers
and their visibility, communities with invite codes, a moderation panel with an
audit trail. Around 390 unit and integration tests, plus 81 instrumented
tests that drive the real app against a real server.

**Paying for it without charging for it**

Charging someone to ask for prayer was never going to happen. Nothing in the app
is behind a paywall and nothing ever will be.

So RevenueCat runs a tip jar instead of a gate. The Settings screen offers a
coffee, a coffee and a snack, lunch, dinner, or a standing subscription for
anyone who wants to keep it running. Everything about the offer — how many
tiers, what they cost, what the paywall says — comes from the offering
RevenueCat serves, not from constants in my source, because prices differ by
country and change without an app release.

Purchases are tied to the account rather than the device, so someone who
supports on their phone is still a supporter on their tablet. Restore is there
for the people who reinstall. And when no API key is built in — the ordinary
state of the test flavour — the app says support is unavailable and everything
else carries on. That had to be a state the app could be in, not a crash.

It is an unusual use of a purchases SDK: no entitlement gates anything. The
customer info exists only so the app can say thank you.

**What I learned**

The bugs that matter are the ones that fail silently. Not crashes — those
announce themselves. The ones that cost weeks are the ones where everything
looks fine.

A test asserted the very typo it existed to catch. The Digital Asset Links file
named kg.nongrate.share_pray where the app is kg.nongrate.sharepray, and
Android's response to a mismatch is not an error — it simply never offers to
open the app. The test had encoded the wrong spelling, so it went green every
time.

Google Sign-In failed for a week because I had registered the upload key's
fingerprint rather than the one Play re-signs with. The device log said
NoCredentialException, and my own error handler translated that to "no Google
account available" on a phone with two.

Ktor 3.2.0 compiled, passed all 390 tests, and then failed to build a release:
Space characters in SimpleName 'use streaming syntax' are not allowed prior to
DEX version 040. It needs minSdk 30; mine is 24. Only the release build
caught it.

And a feature can fail without anything being broken. I curated 98 prayer
tags and put a search box over them. Production ran for weeks with nine tags
ever used. Someone typed trevoga — Russian, transliterated — rather than
find anxiety, which was right there. You cannot search a set you have never
seen. A tag nobody can find is a tag that does not exist.

Cutting the list would have decided that most of what people pray about does not
deserve a word. Grouping was the third answer: six groups, ten tags in each, and
the picker shows six things at a time.

**Challenges**

The one I spent longest on was a faint ring around the launcher icon. Eight
diagnoses, each plausible, each wrong. It turned out to be an emulator rendering
artefact — invisible on a physical Pixel. I had been correcting artwork that was
already correct. Since then I check on real hardware before I believe anything.

Then there is measurement instead of taste. When a card needed lifting off dead
centre, the honest version is not a number I liked the look of but a bias over
the space actually left over, so a short prayer rises and a full one does not
move. Same for placing the logo: its weight sits above its bounding-box centre,
so the mark is positioned by a measured centroid,

$$\bar{y} = \frac{\sum_{y} y \cdot w_y}{\sum_{y} w_y}$$

where each row's weight $w_y$ is how far its pixels depart from the paper, in
the proportions the eye uses — a broad pale wash counting for less than a thin
dark stroke of the same area. That number is measured at build time, so it stays
true if the artwork is ever redrawn.

**Where it is**

Live on Google Play and Apple Store in English and Russian — the Russian
reviewed by a native speaker, because a devotional word and an everyday word are
not the same word.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Lunker is a fishing game where the notification is the game. The fish bite while the app is closed: the push is your rod twitching, and you have 60 seconds to tap in and win the reel before the catch escapes. Built on OneSignal and RevenueCat.

- Code: https://github.com/edycutjong/lunker

- Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=dev.edycu.lunker

- Landing page: https://lunker.edycu.dev/

- Live ledger: https://lunker.edycu.dev/verify/

- Demo video: https://youtu.be/RSfPnZU19P8

The Google Play listing is in review and may not load yet. The demo video was filmed on an Android 15 emulator; the reel is started from "Cast now", and that fish escaped.

**Inspiration**

Every game I have installed sends me the same notification: "Come back for your daily reward!" I mute it inside a week, and so does everyone else, because it carries no stakes. The thing it announces will still be there in six hours.

Real fishing is the opposite. The whole skill is being present at the moment the line moves. You cannot schedule a bite; you can only be there or not.

So I asked what would happen if the notification were not a reminder about the game but the game itself. The notification IS the game mechanic.

**What it does**

You install Lunker, pick a lake, and close the app.

Later, on a train or while making dinner, your phone buzzes: "Your rod is twitching at Willow Lake — 60s before it escapes." Tap it and you land directly in the reel, not on a home screen, with the clock already running. A needle moves across a tension bar; hold it inside the moving green zone for six seconds, with a haptic tick on every zone crossing, and the fish is yours. Miss, and it throws the hook and swims off.

Landed fish fill an album by rarity and pay out COIN. COIN unlocks Quarry Pool (1,200 COIN). The Angler's Pass subscription (7-day free trial) opens the Deep Sea, the only lake whose table holds Legendaries. Each lake has its own fish table and its own bite hours, so which notifications you get tomorrow depends on what you did today.

Delete OneSignal and there is no bite, so there is no game — not a degraded game, no game.

**How we built it**

The design question was: where does a bite come from, and who is allowed to decide what you caught?

Client: React Native 0.79 on Expo 53, TypeScript, Android only. Server: one Cloudflare Worker (7 routes plus a cron handler) over a Cloudflare D1 database with 5 tables. The lake table, fish table and reel-tension model live in one shared/ module imported by both the app and the Worker, so the two cannot disagree about what a Moonlight Koi weighs.

The bite is sent by a cron handler, and that was the key decision. Every fifteen minutes the Worker asks which players are due: at most one bite an hour, never before 08:00 or after 23:00 local time, capped per lake per day, weighted by whether the lake fishes by day or by night. For each due player it writes the roll seed to D1 first, then sends the push through the OneSignal REST API with a 60-second TTL and a deep link into the minigame. The ordering is the point: the seed has to exist before the notification leaves, because it is what makes the catch verifiable afterwards, and a OneSignal Journey cannot write a row to my database before it sends.

On the device, OneSignal owns identity and reach: OneSignal.initialize and OneSignal.login with the same user id RevenueCat uses, Notifications.addEventListener('click') for the deep link, User.addTags for current_lake, streak_days, unlocked_count and rare_count (the streak is computed server-side from your local calendar days), and an in-app permission prime triggered with InAppMessages.addTrigger after your first landed catch. The native prompt fires only from the prime's own accept button. The Worker also fires two OneSignal custom events, rare_landed and lake_unlocked.

The economy is server-settled. When you land a fish, the app posts to /catch-resolved and does not say what it caught. The Worker rolls the fish against the committed weight table using the seed it stored before the push, grants COIN through RevenueCat's Virtual Currency REST API (v2), and returns the result (no catch has settled on a device yet). A client-supplied fish, rarity or coins is ignored, and a test asserts it. The HUD balance is a read of RevenueCat's ledger via Purchases.invalidateVirtualCurrenciesCache() then Purchases.getVirtualCurrencies(), never a local counter. Spending is an atomic server-side debit; an insufficient balance returns a 422 the app shows as "1,200 COIN — you have 840".

Purchases run through Purchases.getOfferings() and Purchases.purchasePackage(): three consumable coin packs and the Angler's Pass subscription. The Deep Sea is gated by RevenueCatUI.presentPaywallIfNeeded against the anglers_pass entitlement, and the Worker re-checks the entitlement, so the paywall is not enforced only in the app. Purchases.restorePurchases() covers reinstalls. The paywall itself is designed in the RevenueCat dashboard; there is no paywall UI in the codebase. Purchase events come back to the Worker as a webhook, HMAC-verified over the raw body with event_id as the primary key, so retries are idempotent. That table is what /verify renders (0 purchases to date).

/verify is where I would point a judge first. It is a read-only, unauthenticated page that computes the answer-rate statistic from the live ledger with the same computeBench function the CLI runs, so the page and the command cannot disagree. As of 2026-09-30 it shows 145 bites sent to 7 testers and none answered within 60 seconds yet — the denominator is honest.

Built solo, with Claude Code doing most of the implementation. The judgement calls were mine: what a bite costs a player in attention, and who gets to decide what you caught.

**Challenges we ran into**

The 60-second window was not 60 seconds. The minigame clock advanced by the clamped frame delta, which is right for the physics and wrong for the countdown. On a phone dropping frames, the fish escaped after 80 real seconds at 15 fps and 120 at 10 fps, and a player could background mid-bite for ten minutes and come back to a full window. The existing "frame-rate independent" test could never have caught it, because 30 and 120 fps both sit under the clamp. There are now two clocks — one for physics, one for real time — and tests at 60/30/15/10/5 fps plus a ten-minute background.

The app typechecked green for weeks and could never have been built. The client imports shared game logic from the repo root. tsc resolved those imports fine; Metro, the React Native bundler, roots itself at app/ and refused. The first assembleRelease died in bundling. CI had been certifying "the types are consistent", not "the app builds". The fix was four lines of Metro config; CI now runs the bundler and greps the fish table out of the output.

A billing failure silently deleted the game. Boot configured RevenueCat, awaited its login, and only then initialised OneSignal, with no error handling. Any RevenueCat rejection meant that player never received another bite. Push was downstream of billing, which is backwards for a game whose premise is push. OneSignal now initialises first and every RevenueCat call is guarded on its own.

The economy I called unforgeable was forgeable. An adversarial audit wrote working exploits: the replay guard trusted a client-supplied key, and eight parallel claims produced eight RevenueCat grants. Both money routes now reserve the row before calling RevenueCat, so the reservation is the lock.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- The client cannot forge a catch or a coin. Fish are rolled server-side from a seed written before the push; the HUD only reads RevenueCat's balance. A replayed or parallel catch calls RevenueCat exactly once, and tests assert both.

- The answer-rate number is reproducible by a stranger. node scripts/lunker-verify.mjs bench --source remote --url https://lunker.edycu.workers.dev runs the same computeBench as /verify. The window is measured from send, and unanswered bites stay in the denominator, which makes the number worse on purpose.

- 274 tests across 13 files, run on Node 22 and 24, including route contracts against real SQLite running the real migration, and the bench arithmetic against a fixture whose answer was computed by hand before the code existed.

- The repo argues with itself and loses. README.md carries a dated "What we got wrong" section: a method that does not exist, a streak nothing incremented, a permission prime that did not prime.

**What we learned**

A green check mark is worth exactly what it checks. Typechecking is not building, and a "frame-rate independent" test that never drops a frame proves nothing. I also learned that in a push-first product the notification stack has to survive everything else failing — billing included — and that the server, not the phone, has to own anything worth money.

**What's next for Lunker**

Honestly listed, because the repo lists it too:

- Lifecycle Journeys: the tide reminder (only if no bite was answered that day), the milestone catch on rare_landed, and a lapsed-angler win-back. The events and tags they branch on already ship; the Journeys themselves are dashboard work I have not finished.

- The RevenueCat → OneSignal integration, so win-backs can branch on a lapsed Angler's Pass.

- More lakes and seasonal fish tables, and a bite cadence that adapts per player rather than per lake.

Thanks for reading. If you only have a minute, watch the demo video and open /verify.

— Edy

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Engineering tools record planned tickets and final commits, but much of the actual work remains invisible: debugging, investigation, code review, interruptions, experiments, and context switching. AI coding agents have accelerated implementation while increasing the review and debugging burden. After interviewing more than 50 engineers and engineering leaders, we built Meridian to capture this missing layer of development work automatically.

**What it does**

Meridian is a local-first, open-source AI work journal for developers and engineering teams. It runs quietly in the background on macOS and Windows, reconstructing work from activity across coding agents, IDEs, browsers, terminals, and related development tools.

It organizes activity into a meaningful timeline, connects work with relevant Jira and GitHub tickets, and generates:

- Daily work summaries

- Worklogs and stand-up notes

- Draft project updates

- A searchable record of completed and unplanned work

Users review and approve generated content before sharing it. Meridian requires no cloud account, keeps data on the device until the user chooses to share it, and is MIT-licensed for individual developers.

**How we built it**

We built Meridian with TypeScript, React, Rust, Swift, Python, Tauri, and SQLite. GitHub and Jira integrations use their APIs and OAuth to connect captured activity with project context. Local LLMs transform raw activity into structured summaries and updates.

We use PostHog and Sentry for product analytics and reliability monitoring, with GitHub Actions, Docker, and Kubernetes supporting development and delivery.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest challenge was converting fragmented activity into an accurate work timeline without overwhelming users with noise. We also had to make background capture reliable while preserving privacy and keeping processing local.

Other major challenges included AI provider connection failures, OAuth token-refresh race conditions, database corruption recovery, telemetry pruning stalls, daemon startup reliability, and maintaining stable integrations across macOS and Windows.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Built a working local-first product for macOS and Windows

- Released Meridian as an MIT-licensed open-source project

- Integrated GitHub and Jira into an automatic work-journaling workflow

- Tested the product with 20 beta users, including several who became regular users

- Reached #1 Product of the Day and #3 Product of the Week on Product Hunt

- Created a privacy-conscious system that keeps users in control of what gets shared

**What we learned**

Capturing activity is easier than understanding it. Useful work journals require context, careful filtering, and strong user control rather than simply collecting more data.

We also learned that AI coding tools do not eliminate engineering work. They shift more effort toward reviewing, debugging, validating, and coordinating changes. Those activities need better visibility if teams want an accurate understanding of how software gets built.

**What's next for Meridian**

Next, we will improve Meridian's memory, activity reconstruction, and local AI capabilities while expanding integrations with the tools engineering teams already use. We will also develop an enterprise offering in collaboration with engineering teams signed on as design partners, with stronger team insights, administration, and privacy controls.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

A birth chart is not a curse. It is a timestamp — an astronomical snapshot of the sky at the exact time and place someone was born. With the right coordinates, that moment can be reconstructed with real physics.

That part is astronomy. What that position means for a person's life is a completely different question — and that's exactly where most astrology apps stop being honest.

That is not what most people are told, though.

Since childhood, I have seen how deeply superstition still shapes real decisions — and how easily it turns into exploitation. Someone finds a "dosha" in their chart, and suddenly a stranger is selling them a ritual, a gemstone, or a puja to "fix" it. I have watched this move from street-corner astrologers to apps and websites doing the exact same thing, just with a chatbot instead of a person — a modern-day fraudster with a better UI.

I could not go from house to house explaining what astrology actually is. But I also did not want to just tell people to stop believing in it, because the people who dismiss it outright have usually never learned its actual history either. Before it became a fear-selling industry, astrology was tied to real mathematical and astronomical knowledge. That history deserves respect, even while the exploitation happening in its name needs to stop.

So I decided to make a small attempt: build one app, inside a market of thousands of astrology apps, that tries to clean up some of that noise instead of adding to it.

That attempt became Enuma Sky.

Hi, I'm Deepak — a second-year Data Science student at IIT Madras, and I built it solo.

**What it does**

Enuma Sky turns astrology from a fear-based industry into a science-grounded self-reflection tool.

Here's the problem it's solving: India's multi-billion dollar astrology industry runs on telling people their birth charts are "cursed." People pay for remedies — gemstones, rituals, pujas — to fix fabricated flaws like Manglik Dosh (Mars's placement blamed for marital conflict), Kaal Sarp Dosh (all planets trapped between two lunar nodes, blamed for prolonged misfortune), Pitra Dosh (ancestors blamed for your problems), or Vastu Dosh (your home's architecture blamed for your problems). Marriages get delayed, careers get abandoned, anxiety spirals — and this isn't hypothetical: in one documented case, a fake astrologer extorted ₹13 lakh from a techie by promising rituals to fix his marital and financial problems.

No birth chart is broken. Ever.

The app computes a complete birth chart — Lagna (Ascendant), 9 planetary bodies, 27 Nakshatras, Vimshottari Dashas, and daily Panchang — using real NASA JPL DE440s ephemeris data (the same data NASA uses to navigate spacecraft), accurate to within 1.7 arcseconds across 150 years.

The AI never predicts the future. It acts purely as an empathetic translator, treating the chart as a framework for introspection — closer to journaling than fortune-telling — explaining what it reflects about psychology, strengths, and growth areas. Every claim it makes is checked against the computed chart before it reaches the user.

The feature I'm proudest of isn't astrology at all — it's the Crisis Safety Net. If a user expresses self-harm, hopelessness, or despair, astrology stops immediately. No horoscope, no prediction — instead, the app surfaces real, verified helplines: Tele-MANAS (14416), AASRA, Women Helpline (181), Emergency (112). No chart reading is worth more than a human life.

Beyond readings, Enuma Sky teaches: a 38-chapter interactive course explains authentic astrological principles using the user's own chart as the textbook, not generic sun-sign articles. A deterministic 78-card Tarot system uses cryptographic seeds — fully reproducible, zero invented mysticism — reframed as Situation → Obstacle → Advice, where even reversed cards carry constructive meaning. Ashtakoot Kundli Matching computes the traditional 36-point compatibility score without ever labeling a match "bad" or "doomed."

Monetization is powered by RevenueCat and kept deliberately clean: all calculations, Panchang, the course, and tarot are free forever. Enuma Sky Pro (Weekly / Monthly / Yearly) unlocks unlimited AI conversations, validated server-side so entitlements can't be gamed.

In short: Enuma Sky treats astrology as a mirror, not a verdict — backed by NASA-grade math, ethically bounded AI, and a safety net that puts human life above horoscopes.

**How we built it**

The core architecture rests on one rule: math and language must never mix.

The backend is a Python FastAPI service on Render. Every astronomical calculation — planetary positions, Lagna, Nakshatras, Dashas, Panchang, sunrise/sunset — is computed deterministically from NASA JPL DE440s ephemeris kernels via the Skyfield library. No AI touches any calculation; the math is physics, not prediction.

I chose NASA JPL over the more common Swiss Ephemeris purely for licensing: Swiss Ephemeris is AGPL-3.0, which would have forced my entire backend open-source. NASA JPL kernels are public domain and Skyfield is MIT-licensed — no traps, and the accuracy trade-off is practically zero (within 1.7 arcseconds across 150 years of benchmarks).

The AI enters only after the math is done. It receives a pre-computed fact brief — exact degrees, houses, nakshatras, dashas — and its only job is to translate that into warm, non-fatalistic language. A custom Grounding Engine then inspects every response, matching planetary claims (in English, Hindi, and Sanskrit) against the computed chart; if even one claim is hallucinated, the response is flagged grounded: false.

Crisis intervention runs before any AI processing at all. If a message shows signals of self-harm or despair, the entire astrology pipeline halts, and the AI is instructed to respond only with empathy and verified helpline numbers.

The mobile app is React Native with Expo (SDK 57), using Expo Router with a glassmorphic dark-mode UI — deliberately calm, no ads, no pop-ups, no red-and-gold chaos. The birth chart renders as a pure SVG North Indian diamond Kundli, so there are no heavy image downloads. Supabase handles optional auth and Postgres with row-level security for chart sync — every core feature works without an account. RevenueCat powers the subscription layer end to end, with entitlements checked server-side against a 60-second cache and instant refresh after purchase.

I built the whole thing solo — every line of code, every design decision, every ethical guardrail — over about three weeks (August 18 – September 8).

**Challenges we ran into**

- Racing the clock — building solo while exams loomed. I built the entire architecture — frontend, FastAPI backend, Supabase integration, the AI Grounding Engine — completely solo in three weeks (August 18 – September 8), with IIT Madras exams starting September 13th. The hardest part wasn't a bug, it was endurance: coding late into the night, studying during the day, with no team to share the load.

- AI cannot do math — and most astrology apps pretend it can. Language models can't reliably do spherical trigonometry or calculate planetary degrees. Most AI astrology apps let the LLM do everything — generate charts, compute positions, interpret results — which produces confident-sounding but astronomically wrong readings. I had to fully separate the calculation layer (deterministic NASA JPL math) from the interpretation layer; the AI never sees a calculator, only pre-verified numbers.

- Stopping hallucinations across three languages. Even with pre-computed data, the AI sometimes invents planetary placements that aren't in the chart. Catching these hallucinations meant pattern-matching across English ("Jupiter in the 7th house"), Hindi ("सातवें भाव में गुरु"), and Sanskrit terminology simultaneously — one missed variant, and a user gets false information wearing a confidence badge.

- Making the crisis safety net impossible to bypass. When someone tells an astrology app "I don't want to live anymore," the worst possible response is a horoscope. No prompt injection, conversation history, or edge case could be allowed to trick the system into resuming astrology mid-crisis. The detector runs before any AI processing, and once triggered, the AI's entire system prompt is overridden to respond only with empathy and real helpline numbers — tested across English, Hindi, and Hinglish phrasing.

- Licensing traps in open-source astronomy. I initially used Swiss Ephemeris, the industry standard, only to discover its AGPL-3.0 license would have forced me to publish the server's full source code under the same license. Migrating to NASA JPL DE440s + Skyfield took weeks of rewriting and re-benchmarking every calculation—the result: identical accuracy, zero licensing risk.

- Building a subscription system that can't be cheated. An early client-side credit ledger was trivially exploitable via request replay. I scrapped it and rebuilt entitlements on RevenueCat's server-side verification — every AI request checks against RevenueCat's REST API before processing, with no local trust and no stored tokens.

- Beating the Google Play clock, solo. Because I'm publishing under a personal Google Play account, Google's 14-day closed-testing rule required 12+ opted-in testers before the app could go live. With the hackathon deadline approaching, I gathered 15 testers and got the app into Closed Testing by September 11th — timed so the mandatory 14 days would finish right before submission.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

240+ automated tests passing. The pytest suite covers ephemeris accuracy against known historical charts, grounding logic across three scripts, entitlement gate enforcement, crisis detection across English/Hindi/Hinglish, and reproducible tarot shuffles.

The Grounded badge is visible to users. Most AI apps hide their verification step. Enuma Sky shows a ✅ Grounded badge on every verified reading, and flags it when verification fails — users see the math behind the reading, not just a claim.

Crisis intervention actually works, and is tested. The crisis path has been tested against real-world phrasing in three languages so it never fails silently. When it triggers, astrology stops completely and verified helpline numbers appear immediately.

14 seconds → 75 milliseconds. A dual-layer cache (in-memory + disk) cut AI response latency from 14 seconds to 75ms for repeat queries — faster for users, and cheaper on API costs.

Zero ads. Zero dark patterns. Zero fear. No pop-ups, no fake urgency timers, no fear-driven upsells. The core astronomical features are genuinely free forever, not free-trial-then-locked. RevenueCat's native paywall keeps the upgrade experience calm and honest.

Live in production on Google Play — solo, as a second-year student. A Python backend, a NASA-grade astronomy engine, an AI grounding system, and full RevenueCat subscription infrastructure, built entirely alone.

**What we learned**

LLMs should interpret, never compute. The moment a language model does the math, accuracy drops and hallucinations rise. The cleanest architecture is: deterministic code computes, AI translates — not just good engineering, but the only way to build trust in a domain where wrong numbers can shape someone's real decisions.

Ethical software is a competitive advantage. Every astrology app in the market uses fear to drive engagement. Refusing to do that — no doshas, no doom, no fake remedies — doesn't just feel different, it is different, and users notice when an app respects them instead of manipulating them.

Monetization doesn't have to be manipulative. RevenueCat made it possible to keep the free tier genuinely generous (all math, all courses, all tarot) and the paid tier genuinely valuable (unlimited AI conversations) — no countdown timers, no "your trial expires in 2 hours" pressure.

You don't need years of experience to ship something real. I started this as a second-year Data Science student. Tools like Expo, Supabase, RevenueCat, the AI API, and Skyfield make it possible for a solo builder to ship something that would have needed a full team just a few years ago.

**What's next for Enuma sky**

iOS launch is the immediate next step. Enuma Sky is built with Expo + EAS, which fully supports both iOS and Android from the same codebase — no rewrite needed. The iOS build has been tested and the pipeline is ready. Once Apple Developer Program enrollment is complete, Enuma Sky ships to iOS.

Going global — worldwide city coverage. The app currently supports roughly 3,000 Indian cities for birth location (entered manually, since a chart depends on where someone was born, not where they are now). The next step is expanding that gazetteer worldwide.

Western Astrology (Tropical Zodiac): Adding support for Western charts to cater to a global audience. Since our underlying astronomy engine (Skyfield) already performs high-precision planetary calculations, integrating the Tropical Zodiac system will be a seamless update that significantly expands our user base in the West.
Deepening the 38-chapter course. The plan is to make it richer — more chapters, deeper explanations, and stronger personalized "In Your Chart" examples that make every lesson feel written for the reader.

Multi-language expansion. The app currently supports English, Hindi, and conversational Hinglish. Adding regional Indian languages — Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Marathi — would reach more of the people most vulnerable to fear-based exploitation in their own language.

Real-time voice conversation with AI. Integrating a multimodal live API for real-time voice would replace the exploitative pay-per-minute human astrologer call model with a calm, ethical, and infinitely scalable AI voice companion.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Turkmenistan has almost no legal digital reading market — most books get pirated on Telegram, and Kindle/Apple Books don't operate there. We built Aýkitap to fix that with local bank/wallet payments. Shipaton pushed us to open it to the rest of the world with RevenueCat.

**What it does**

A full reading platform — EPUB/PDF/CBZ books, subscriptions, single-book purchases, streaks — across a Flutter app, NestJS backend, React admin panel, and Next.js website. Turkmen users pay by bank/wallet; everyone else now pays through RevenueCat via the App Store/Play Store, both landing on the same backend entitlement.

**How we built it**

Flutter + purchases_flutter for the app, NestJS/Postgres backend with a webhook + reconciliation layer for RevenueCat, Firebase for international login alongside the existing phone-OTP system, and a React/Mantine admin panel for mapping store products to books.

**Challenges we ran into**

Running two payment systems on one entitlement without conflicts, verifying store purchases server-side instead of trusting the client, and merging phone and Firebase logins into one identity without accidentally merging two different people.

**What we learned**

Building local-first, then generalizing, forces better infrastructure than building global-first — canonical account IDs and a purchase_mode capability instead of hardcoded payment UI.

</details>
