<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

A modern phone is a firehose. On an average day ours take several hundred notifications, emails, and texts, and maybe five of them actually matter: a delivery window, a card debit, an appointment confirmation, a bill due Friday.

Every "smart inbox" we tried solved this the same way — an opaque model decides what you see, quietly deletes what it thinks is noise, and does it on a server holding a permanent plaintext copy of your mail. You get quiet, but you can never ask why it was quiet, and you can't tell "nothing happened" apart from "something important was silently swallowed."

Relay takes the opposite trade. It is built on one rule: convenience never outranks privacy, consent, provenance, or idempotency. Quiet by default — but every decision (category, extraction, filter, disclosure, action) keeps a record of how it was made.

**What it does**

Relay is an Android-first app plus an edge pipeline that turns three noisy sources into one calm, searchable archive and a short list of things you might want to do.

Capture, with consent as the gate. Gmail through its own connector OAuth (deliberately not your login session), Android notifications through NotificationListenerService, and SMS in sideload builds. Each source needs an explicit OS permission plus an in-app disclosure, supports per-app allowlists, and is revocable. Relay never requests QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES — the installed-app list is resolved through a narrow package-visibility query, stays on the device, and is never logged or uploaded.

Encrypt before anything leaves the device. The Android capture queue stores only AES-256-GCM ciphertext in SQLite under a non-exportable Android Keystore key, bounded to 500 items / 2 MiB per tenant, and deletes an item only when the server returns a validated durable acknowledgement for that exact envelope. Sign-out and device revocation destroy the Keystore key before the rows, so an interrupted wipe can't leave decryptable data behind. Server-side, every raw payload is envelope-encrypted with a per-record data key wrapped by a versioned, Cloudflare-held KEK. Tenant, record, and purpose are bound into the AES-GCM associated data, so a row cannot be replayed into another user's context. Raw payloads expire after seven days — and the expiry is authenticated inside the ciphertext, so a delayed or replayed queue message can't quietly extend retention.

Deduplicate like it matters. Cloudflare Queues are at-least-once, so every stage can repeat after a timeout or a deploy. Relay runs two independent layers: a per-tenant Durable Object that serializes decrypt → dedupe → persist and keeps bound markers across evictions, and Postgres unique constraints on (user_id, source, source_account_id, external_id) and (user_id, content_fingerprint) as final arbitration. The second layer is what makes a lost HTTP response safe — the coordinator genuinely cannot tell "committed, reply lost" from "never arrived", so it always retries, and the retry converges on duplicate rather than a second row. Content fingerprints are a versioned algorithm, not a formatting detail: changing the canonicalization is a version bump with a migration plan, never a silent behaviour change.

Normalize into typed facts, not a text blob. A version-pinned normalizer emits sender, date, amount, currency, merchant, location, and reference facts from allowlisted envelope fields — the source kind never selects the extraction logic. Amounts stay bounded decimal strings and never pass through a JavaScript number. Dates resolve to exactly 30 UTC characters with nine fractional digits, so equivalent offset forms agree before contradiction checks while genuinely distinct sub-millisecond instants stay distinct. Every fact carries a normalizer version, a deterministic ordinal, a certainty, and the field path it came from; provenance stores paths and offsets, never source snippets. A candidate that fails validation becomes uncertain/invalid, and two candidates that disagree become uncertain/contradictory, with the values omitted. Relay would rather say "I'm not sure" than guess.

Deterministic filters first; AI only where nothing else will do. You state intent in natural language and Relay compiles it into a versioned, inspectable FilterPlan of typed predicates. Evaluation is tri-state: match, no-match, undecided. Only an explicitly declared semantic clause may reach a model — using your OpenAI key (validated server-side, envelope-encrypted, never returned to the client), disclosing only the allowlisted fields that clause declares, after redaction. Model, disclosed fields, redactions, purpose, confidence, and rationale are all recorded. Low confidence stays undecided and can never trigger an effect. Filter versions are immutable once used, so an audit record from last month can still explain itself.

Propose actions; never take them. Filters produce typed action proposals for Google Tasks, Nextcloud Budget, and signed webhooks. Provider, operation, connection, and input template come from a user-owned rule — never from source content, never from model output. That single constraint closes the prompt-injection path from "an email said so" to "an external thing happened." Default state is awaiting-approval; automatic execution is per-rule opt-in. Every action carries a stable Relay UUID plus a provider-specific idempotency strategy (Nextcloud accepts it directly, webhook receivers dedupe on it, Google Tasks needs reconcile-before-retry because its insert offers no equivalent guarantee). Dismissing a notification is deliberately harder than any of that: explicit source and filter scope, a deterministic match, a completed dry-run period, and an audit record. An AI-only match can never dismiss anything.

**How we built it**

A pnpm + Turborepo TypeScript monorepo with boundaries that are enforced, not just documented:

- apps/mobile — Expo (SDK 57) / React Native 0.86 with Expo Router, plus a local Kotlin module for notification capture, the Keystore-backed queue, and SMS. Continuous Native Generation, two EAS profiles (development with SMS permissions stripped at prebuild, sideload with them present), and a checked-in build-config gate that runs before any build.

- apps/api — Next.js on Cloudflare (OpenNext). Auth boundary and connector callbacks only. It never classifies and never calls providers. It doesn't decode unverified tokens either — it asks Supabase Auth who the user is, validates the returned UUID, and forwards only that.

- apps/pipeline — Cloudflare Worker with Queues, a per-tenant Durable Object, Workflows, dead-letter recovery, and KEK rotation.

- packages/contracts — Zod schemas for every cross-runtime wire shape; untrusted input is validated at each boundary, including internal queue messages, because retries and rolling deploys mix versions.

- packages/domain — pure, runtime-neutral filter and dedupe logic. packages/crypto — WebCrypto envelope encryption.

- Supabase / Postgres — seven migrations, RLS tenant isolation, and the important invariants pushed down into SQL: fixed-result persistence RPCs that report stored / duplicate / fact-integrity-conflict / tenant-conflict without leaking database detail, plus checks that reject impossible calendar values and non-canonical persisted precision.

Verification is the part we are proudest of: 38 test suites across contracts, crypto, domain, pipeline, API routes and mobile; pnpm verify chaining format/lint/typecheck/test/build/config gates; and pnpm e2e:local — a real end-to-end harness that resets a local Supabase stack, boots API + Wrangler, pushes one deterministic synthetic fixture through the full encrypted path, and asserts encrypted persistence, typed facts with exact money provenance, both dedupe layers, acknowledge-after-durability, cold-database conflicts, dead-letter metadata, operator inspection, exact encrypted replay, and seven-day retention cleanup. It refuses any non-loopback Supabase URL and creates zero remote resources. Child-process logs are scanned as streams for fixture or credential leakage.

The whole thing is developed one GitHub issue at a time against a dependency map, with accepted ADRs as the record for every architectural decision, and documentation treated as a source of truth to be fixed in the same change rather than left to drift.

**Challenges we ran into**

"Committed, but the response was lost." The single hardest problem. Once you accept that at-least-once delivery and a dropped reply are indistinguishable from a failure, you stop trying to detect the difference and instead make retry converge — unique constraints as arbitration, digests as idempotency identity, and acknowledgement only after both durable stages agree.

Money and time are traps. Parsing an amount into a float is the kind of bug you don't notice until a budget line is wrong by a cent, so amounts stay strings end to end. Dates were worse: two representations of the same instant were being flagged as contradictory until normalization resolved everything to one canonical nine-digit UTC form, with the database checking that the stored precision is exactly that.

Rotating keys without decrypting anything. Getting KEK rotation to rewrap data keys — via compare-and-set batches, stable encryption scope, and historical canaries — without ever touching plaintext took several attempts, and the dead-letter path had to preserve original AAD casing because those IDs are authenticated data, not just identifiers.

Android lifecycle versus cryptographic state. Development-local mode, real sessions, sideload transitions that retain app data, and unexpected session loss all had to converge on one rule: clear the previous tenant's key, queue, and capture config before anything else, with generation ordering so a superseded auth transition can't mutate current capture state.

Platform policy is a design input. READ_SMS / RECEIVE_SMS are restricted Play permissions, and iOS exposes no equivalent notification or SMS API at all. That is why SMS lives in a sideload profile, why a Play-safe non-SMS build is an architectural requirement rather than a later chore, and why iOS scope is Gmail plus Relay's own inbox.

**Accomplishments that we are proud of**

An end-to-end encrypted ingestion path that is genuinely testable locally, with no cloud resources and no real user data. A fact normalizer whose output is reproducible enough to be used as an idempotency key. A privacy model where "AI cannot select an endpoint, credential, provider operation, or irreversible action" is a structural property of the code rather than a promise on a policy page. And a dead-letter recovery flow whose operator API exposes metadata only, with no decrypt route anywhere in it.

**What we learned**

Explainability is an architectural decision made early, not a UI feature added late — provenance has to be carried from the first parse or it simply doesn't exist later. Idempotency is a product feature: anything users trust with money and calendars needs a stable ID and a defined ambiguous-retry strategy per provider. And the most valuable thing we built was the local harness; being able to run the entire encrypted path against a synthetic fixture in one command changed how fast everything else could move.

**What's next for Relay**

The foundation — encrypted ingestion, durable deduplication, typed facts, connector OAuth for Gmail / Google Tasks / BYOK OpenAI, Android notification capture with consent, and dead-letter recovery — is in place. Next, in dependency order: the natural-language filter compiler and deterministic evaluator, redacted semantic evaluation with disclosure audit, the action approval ledger, and provider dispatch behind durable workflows; then the curated quiet inbox, the approval timeline, and the notification-dismissal dry run. After that: Gmail OAuth verification and Limited Use review, an SMS distribution policy with a Play-safe build, a pre-release privacy and security audit, and resilience/disaster-recovery validation before public release.

Everything is AGPL-3.0-or-later and developed in the open at github.com/redsteadz/relay.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Your teammate's slides are late. The presentation is Friday. You need to say something, but how do you start?

Second Take gives that moment a second attempt. Instead of starting a new roleplay with potentially different facts, you rewind to a preserved checkpoint and change your choice. The point is to inspect a concrete difference, not to predict how a real person will behave.

**What it does**

In the recorded Alex rehearsal, “I am worried about the project” gets “Can you be more specific?” After a rewind, “Can you finish today?” leads to “I can get the sources done by nine tonight.” The comparison puts those choices and immediate responses together.

The useful detail is the limit of that offer: sources by nine, not the whole project. Reading both responses side by side helps distinguish an unresolved concern from a specific next step. The app now provides deterministic reading notes grounded in the visible replies: clarification is still needed in version A; version B names a scope and deadline. It asks what remains open, without scoring a winning path. These notes are not free-form AI coaching or proof that one phrasing always works better.

Intent Lock lets the user confirm whether an ambiguous message asks about ability or requests action. The conversation, rewind and second attempt are free. RevenueCat gates Full A/B Comparison after both attempts, when the user has a reason to review what changed.

**How we built it**

Kotlin and Jetpack Compose provide the Android interface. A TypeScript/Fastify backend owns state and checkpoints. Gemini 3.7 Flash interprets text and selects only among policy-approved actions. Alex's final replies are authored, not freely generated.

A selector failure can use a deterministic safe candidate. A router failure returns a clear interruption rather than inventing the user's intention. Application deadlines bound the wait; they do not make an unavailable provider available.

RevenueCat Test Store provides the offering, purchase, CustomerInfo update, active pro entitlement, restore and relaunch recognition. No real charge is claimed, and there is no local premium bypass.

**What we learned**

A controlled second attempt requires more than a new chatbot answer: it needs preserved context, explicit user intent and consistent state transitions. We also learned to distinguish passing local tests from reliable cloud service. A late provider sample exposed latency failures, so we added application-level deadlines and tested late responses for unwanted state changes.

**Monetization and next steps**

The hypothesis is that an organized comparison is valuable after a free rehearsal. The current monthly Test Store price is experimental; one scenario does not establish recurring willingness to pay. We have not validated demand, retention or revenue.

The next product questions are whether people understand the difference between their attempts and whether they return for another rehearsal. More authored scenarios, production hosting, store billing and deeper accessibility validation remain future work.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Ecos Profundos was born from pure nostalgia and a passion for dark fantasy anime series and the classic video games of our childhood. Every pixel, every mechanic, and every corner of the lore aims to bring back that sense of wonder we felt when discovering fantastical worlds on retro screens, now reimagined with modern technology.

**What it does**

Ecos Profundos is a dark fantasy action RPG where every battle is about more than simply attacking.

Fight your way through increasingly dangerous waves of enemies, manage your stamina, choose when to attack or retreat, and use positioning and your enemies' weaknesses to turn the odds in your favor. No two hits are exactly the same: damage can change depending on the situation, rewarding players who observe, adapt, and learn how the world reacts to their actions.

Defeating enemies allows your character to grow stronger and face increasingly demanding stages. Progression is meant to be felt: challenges that once seemed dangerous should gradually become easier as your character evolves.

Each stage pushes the player further, introducing tougher enemies and more demanding encounters before opening the path to the next challenge.

In the future, Ecos Profundos will also explore a more narrative and introspective side. A mysterious voice will accompany the player through fragments of text, reflections, and questions about doubt, destiny, failure, hope, and the paths we choose.

Sometimes, progressing will mean defeating another wave of enemies.

Sometimes, it may simply mean understanding what the journey is trying to tell you.

**How we built it**

The project was developed entirely natively using Apple’s ecosystem. It is powered by Swift 6, using SpriteKit for high-performance rendering and GameplayKit to structure the game logic through state machines and entities.

Character behavior is organized around gameplay states, keeping movement and animation transitions separate from the rendering logic. A custom virtual joystick provides normalized movement vectors that are translated into character velocity, movement states, and sprite orientation.

Sprite animations are organized into texture atlases for the different movement states and directions, allowing the game to switch animations efficiently while avoiding unnecessary texture loading.

Due to the time constraints imposed by the deadline, the pixel art assets were purchased from the itch.io platform and created by artist jfranciPX, under a license that allows their use in commercial projects. They were integrated into the project together with the custom touch controls and gameplay architecture.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the main challenges was preventing animation re-entry. Since the game loop updates continuously, repeatedly requesting the same state caused animations to restart from the first frame. I had to ensure that state transitions only occurred when the character's actual movement state changed.

Another challenge was tuning the virtual joystick thresholds. The joystick produces continuous vector values, so I needed to define clear boundaries between Idle, Walk, and Run without causing unstable transitions when the input magnitude was close to a threshold.

Managing directional sprites was also an important challenge. The character uses different animations for Front, Back, and Side, while horizontal mirroring is applied dynamically for left-facing movement. Keeping this logic clean and synchronized with the current movement state required careful separation of responsibilities.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I'm especially proud of building the gameplay foundation entirely with native Apple technologies, without relying on an external game engine.

The combination of SpriteKit, GameplayKit, and Swift 6 has allowed me to create a clean architecture where character movement, animation, state transitions, combat, progression, and future gameplay systems can evolve independently without having to constantly redesign the core of the game.

I'm also proud of achieving smooth transitions between idle, walking, and running animations while keeping directional movement responsive to the virtual joystick. Although these may seem like small details from the player's perspective, getting them to feel natural required solving several problems related to animation states, movement vectors, and the real-time game loop.

Another accomplishment I'm particularly proud of is integrating RevenueCat and defining a monetization model that respects the player experience.

For the Shipathon version, the game includes three optional "Buy Me a Coffee" support options. I have also prepared the idea of unlocking the complete game through a single purchase, although that option remains disabled in the current version.

Rather than building the game around aggressive monetization or randomized purchases, I want players to understand exactly what they are paying for. In the future, I may introduce optional equipment, items, or progression-related purchases, but always with the goal of supporting the adventure rather than replacing progression, skill, or exploration.

**What we learned**

During development, I gained a deeper understanding of real-time state management and how seemingly small architectural decisions can directly affect how a game feels when played.

I learned how to coordinate continuous joystick input with discrete gameplay states, how to structure and reuse directional sprite animations efficiently, and how to prevent unnecessary state transitions from restarting animations inside a real-time game loop.

The project also helped me better understand how GameplayKit state machines can work alongside SpriteKit, and how both frameworks can be combined to keep gameplay logic modular and maintainable.

Beyond the technical side, I also learned that designing a game means making decisions about the player experience long before every mechanic exists. Progression, difficulty, rewards, monetization, and combat are interconnected systems, and changing one of them can affect how the rest of the game feels.

Working on the monetization model made this especially clear to me. I had to think not only about how purchases could be implemented, but also about where I personally want to draw the line between monetization and preserving a fair and enjoyable progression system.

**What's next for EcosProfundos**

After Shipathon 2026, I plan to gradually expand Ecos Profundos into a much deeper action RPG.

The current prototype already includes movement, basic attacks, damage, a first contextual advantage when attacking from behind, health and stamina recovery items, wave-based progression, and the initial monetization structure. The full-game purchase option is planned but remains disabled in the Shipathon version.

Future updates will introduce more weapons, equipment, consumable items, character progression systems, enemy types, combat mechanics, and contextual advantages based on positioning and enemy states.

I also want to keep expanding the number and variety of stages, with the long-term goal of reaching around 100 phases while progressively increasing difficulty and encounter complexity.

The monetization model will continue to focus on transparency. Players will be able to experience the first stages for free and later unlock the complete game through a single purchase. Optional equipment and progression-related purchases may also be introduced, but I want to avoid casino-like systems or randomized purchases designed to pressure players into spending.

Beyond combat and progression, the game will continue to grow through new mechanics, narrative elements, environmental storytelling, and the mysterious voice that accompanies the player throughout the journey.

My goal is not simply to add more content, but to keep expanding a world where becoming stronger also means learning how to fight smarter, understanding its rules, and discovering what lies deeper within Ecos Profundos.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Technical interviews are notoriously high-stress, and traditional preparation is fundamentally broken. Algorithmic platforms only test code in silence, completely ignoring spoken communication and technical articulation. Meanwhile, human mock interview coaches charge upwards of $150 per hour, putting realistic interview prep out of reach for most candidates. We built InterviewAce to democratize elite technical coaching. Inspired by the low-latency intelligence of Gemini 2.0 Flash and seamless subscription monetization through RevenueCat, we set out to create an on-demand, 24/7 mock interviewer that combines verbal dialogue, an integrated live-coding IDE, and instantaneous feedback at an accessible price point.

**What it does**

InterviewAce is an AI-driven technical interview simulator that combines real-time verbal dialogue and an integrated multi-language coding IDE to deliver realistic, high-pressure interview practice. Powered by Gemini 2.0 Flash, it adapts dynamically to a candidate's domain and seniority, runs and tests code in an in-browser sandbox terminal, and generates instant performance scores with calibrated benchmark solutions—all monetized seamlessly through RevenueCat’s freemium quota system and multi-tier subscription paywalls.

**How we built it**

We built InterviewAce using high-performance Vanilla HTML5, CSS3, and modern JavaScript, featuring a glassmorphism design system with seamless Dark and Light theme support. For the AI engine, we integrated the Google Gemini 2.0 Flash API for sub-second question generation and code evaluation, alongside the browser-native Web Speech and Web Audio APIs for voice recognition, text-to-speech, and synthetic UI sound effects. Monetization was engineered with the RevenueCat Web SDK to manage subscriber entitlements and flexible paywalls, while the entire development and end-to-end validation was accelerated using Google Antigravity IDE's autonomous browser agents.

**Challenges we ran into**

Our primary challenge was delivering a realistic, low-latency coding and verbal interview experience entirely within the browser without heavy backend infrastructure. We solved this by pairing browser-native Web Speech and Web Audio APIs with Gemini 2.0 Flash’s sub-second inference, preventing conversational lag during live candidate responses. Additionally, cleanly implementing RevenueCat’s entitlement lifecycle and weekly quota gating on a client-side web application required designing persistent local state caches that trigger soft paywalls without disrupting candidate momentum. Finally, maintaining flawless glassmorphism readability across both Dark and Light themes required meticulously re-architecting our CSS tokens for code editors, modals, and terminal windows.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are most proud of creating a friction-free, ultra-responsive technical interview platform that genuinely replicates the pressure and depth of a live human engineering interview. Building an in-browser multi-language IDE (JavaScript, Python, C++, Java) with sandbox terminal execution, real-time voice dialogue, and instant Gemini 2.0 Flash code critique—with zero backend server overhead—was a major technical triumph. Above all, seamlessly integrating RevenueCat’s multi-tier subscription engine alongside an adaptable Dark and Light design system turned our vision into a polished, commercially viable product ready for real candidates.

**What we learned**

Building InterviewAce gave us deep insights into modern subscription architecture with RevenueCat—specifically how value-first freemium quotas (offering 3 high-impact free sessions) and non-intrusive, context-aware paywalls cultivate candidate trust and maximize conversion. Technically, we mastered combining Gemini 2.0 Flash’s rapid inference with native Web Speech and Web Audio APIs to eliminate server overhead and deliver desktop-grade performance directly in the browser. Finally, we experienced the transformative power of agentic development in the Google Antigravity IDE, demonstrating how automated browser verification and iterative AI pair-programming can compress weeks of full-stack engineering into days.

**What's next for Interview_ace**

Looking ahead, we are expanding InterviewAce into native iOS and Android apps using React Native and RevenueCat’s native mobile SDKs to capture cross-platform App Store and Google Play subscriptions. On the AI front, we plan to implement Gemini 2.0’s real-time bidirectional multimodal audio and vision streaming to critique candidate whiteboard system architecture diagrams and conversational body language. Finally, we are introducing a B2B University & Bootcamp tier via RevenueCat Web Billing, enabling college career centers and engineering accelerators to offer cohort-wide mock interview prep at scale.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/327/763/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/327/763/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/327/764/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/327/764/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/327/765/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/327/765/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/327/766/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/327/766/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Ngao started from something I observed close to home.

A close relative was struggling with alcohol use and poor financial discipline. What stood out to me was that they often understood their financial priorities while sober. They knew what their money was supposed to cover, but during periods of stress, cravings, or drinking, those decisions became much harder to maintain.

I noticed a recurring pattern:

Stress → craving → alcohol becomes accessible → money becomes accessible → impulsive spending → essential funds are depleted → financial stress → regret → another recovery attempt.

That made me realize that this was not simply a budgeting problem. The person often already knew what they should do.

The real question became:

How do we help someone protect the financial decisions they made while clear headed when they enter a high risk state?

That question became Ngao.

**What it does**

Ngao is a mobile financial self protection and recovery support system built around one principle:

Don't ask future-you to make a decision that sober-you could make today.

While sober, users create a protection plan for the money that matters most to them. They can define priorities such as rent, family obligations, savings, emergency funds, and discretionary spending.

Ngao then helps users identify predictable high risk periods such as payday, weekends, evenings, stressful situations, and personal triggers.

When a high risk period arrives, Ngao changes the experience from simply tracking money to protecting decisions.

A user can activate an intervention that introduces friction before an impulsive decision is made. They can start a cooldown, listen to a personal message they recorded while sober, contact a trusted person, review what they previously decided to protect, and reflect on what happened afterward.

Ngao is not intended to shame users or claim to cure alcohol dependence. It is designed to help people prepare for moments when their decision making may be most vulnerable.

**How we built it**

We built Ngao as a mobile first product using Bilt.me, which allowed us to move quickly from the idea and user flows into a working application.

The core experience follows:

PLAN → PREDICT → INTERRUPT → PROTECT → LEARN

Users first create their financial protection plan and identify triggers or high risk periods. Ngao then prepares them for those periods and provides an intervention when an urge occurs.

The intervention combines practical tools such as cooldowns, sober messages, trusted person support, and reminders of previously defined financial priorities.

We also integrated RevenueCat for subscription management and premium entitlements. This allowed us to build the monetization layer into the product rather than treating it as something to add later.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was designing for a sensitive problem without making the product feel judgmental or reducing the user to their alcohol use.

We also had to decide what we could realistically prove with an MVP.

The initial version cannot actually control a user's bank account or physically lock away their money. Rather than pretending that it could, we focused on behavioral protection through planning, reminders, cooldowns, trusted support, and financial commitments.

Another challenge was turning a highly personal problem into a repeatable product experience that could eventually work for people with different triggers, financial situations, and patterns.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud that Ngao started from a real world observation and became a working product rather than remaining an idea.

We are particularly proud of the way the product connects financial protection, behavioral intervention, and social support instead of treating them as completely separate problems.

We are also proud of taking the project beyond functionality and thinking about it as a real business. Integrating RevenueCat gave us the opportunity to build a subscription model around recurring value and consider how Ngao could sustain itself after the hackathon.

Most importantly, we are proud of building a product around a simple but meaningful idea:

Sober-you already knows what matters. Ngao helps protect it.

**What we learned**

We learned that building a product is much more than building the technology.

We learned about launching a product and the importance of validating whether users actually understand the problem being solved and find the solution valuable.

We learned that marketing a product around a sensitive personal problem requires trust and careful language. People should feel supported rather than judged.

RevenueCat also gave us practical experience with subscription products. We learned that monetization is not simply adding a paywall. It requires deciding what creates recurring value, what should remain accessible, and how premium access is managed through entitlements.

We also learned to think about scaling from the beginning. A product inspired by one person's experience has to become flexible enough to serve many different users and contexts.

**What's next for Ngao**

The next step is to test Ngao with more users and learn which interventions are actually useful during high risk periods.

We want to improve personalization, strengthen the financial protection mechanisms, expand trusted person support, and eventually explore integrations with real financial services.

We also want to scale Ngao across different communities and regions, starting with Kenya and eventually reaching other markets where similar financial and behavioral patterns exist.

Long term, we see Ngao growing beyond its initial alcohol related use case into a broader personal resilience and financial self protection platform.

Protect what sober-you built.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

New managers are often promoted for doing strong individual work and then immediately asked to give difficult feedback, set boundaries, resolve conflict, and say no fairly. Reading advice is not the same as finding the words under pressure. ReplayLead creates a private rehearsal space where the real conversation does not have to be the first practice.

**What it does**

ReplayLead is an Android conversation-rehearsal coach for new managers. The user chooses a realistic management scenario, rates how prepared they feel, and practices against an AI counterpart that responds to what they actually say. At any manager message, Rewind removes the later conversation and starts a genuine alternate branch. After practice, ReplayLead scores clarity, empathy, assertiveness, and actionability, identifies one strong moment, gives one focused improvement, and suggests a stronger response.

The app is resilient by design: it labels whether coaching comes from the secure cloud AI service or the deterministic on-device fallback, so a temporary network failure never destroys a rehearsal.

**How we built it**

- Kotlin and Jetpack Compose with a small state-driven Android architecture.

- RevenueCat Android SDK 10.19.1 for live Offering lookup, localized pricing, purchase, entitlement verification, and user-triggered restore.

- Cloudflare Workers and Workers AI for in-character replies and structured coaching reports.

- Server-side scenario allowlisting, transcript limits, output validation, and a 20-requests-per-minute per-IP limit.

- Gradle, Android unit tests and lint, Vitest, TypeScript typechecking, and GitHub Actions.

**RevenueCat implementation**

The paywall fetches the current RevenueCat Offering only when opened, displays the StoreProduct's localized price, and unlocks only when the configured replaylead_pro entitlement is active. Restore is always an explicit user action. Release builds fail if the public SDK key is missing or uses the Test Store test_ prefix.

For Google Play, monthly, annual, and lifetime products are active and mapped to the RevenueCat default Offering through the monthly, annual, and lifetime packages. Google Play real-time developer notifications cover subscriptions, voided purchases, and all one-time products; an end-to-end test notification was received by RevenueCat. The demo transaction uses RevenueCat Test Store, so it is simulated and is not presented as revenue.

**Challenges we ran into**

The first challenge was preventing Rewind from becoming a scripted visual trick. It therefore changes the underlying conversation state and preserves a real alternate branch. The second was honest monetization: the purchase button only enables after RevenueCat returns a real package and localized price. The third was AI reliability, solved with strict response validation, score normalization, rate limiting, and a clearly labeled local fallback.

**Accomplishments that we are proud of**

- A complete scenario-to-coaching journey that runs on an Android device.

- A real alternate-branch interaction that is understandable in seconds.

- Specific coaching tied to the Career Coaching criteria: realistic practice, useful feedback, and confidence building.

- Production-shaped RevenueCat and Google Play configuration without pretending that a simulated test purchase is revenue.

- A public MIT-licensed repository with passing Android and backend CI.

**What we learned**

Practice feels useful when feedback is narrow enough to act on immediately. One concrete improvement and a sentence the manager can actually say are more valuable than a long generic analysis. We also learned that monetization trust starts before checkout: live pricing, explicit restore, clear fallback states, and accurate claims matter as much as the purchase button.

**What's next**

Closed testing and a public Google Play release, followed by branch comparison, spaced practice plans, private progress history, voice rehearsal, and more scenarios for first-time team leads.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Students have access to countless opportunities—competitions, programs, projects, scholarships, and ways to develop skills. The problem is that finding the right opportunity and figuring out what to do next can be difficult.

I wanted to build something that helps students move beyond simply discovering opportunities and actually take action on them.

That idea became Student OPS: a platform designed to help students turn their interests and goals into opportunities, projects, skills, and measurable achievements.

**What it does**

Student OPS utilizes AI to help students:

- Discover opportunities that match their interests, skills, and goals

- Find projects they can realistically build and use to develop their skills

- Create roadmaps that break larger goals into actionable milestones

- Track projects and achievements as they progress

- Build a portfolio using evidence from their real work

- Identify skill gaps and understand what they can work on next

The goal is to connect the entire journey:

Goals → Opportunities → Projects → Skills → Evidence → Achievements

**How i built it**

Student OPS was built as a native iOS application using SwiftUI and Swift in Xcode.

The app uses AI through Groq to generate recommendations and insights while keeping the experience structured around specific student workflows rather than functioning as a generic chatbot.

I also built systems for opportunity matching, skill-gap analysis, project recommendations, roadmap generation, evidence quality, portfolio building, and progress tracking.

The project i through multiple iterations, with testing and refinement across the major features to make sure the different parts of the app worked together as one system.

**Challenges i ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was deciding how AI should actually be used.

It would have been easy to make Student OPS a chatbot that simply gives students suggestions. Instead, I wanted AI to work behind structured features and produce actionable results.

Another challenge was connecting opportunities, skills, projects, roadmaps, and portfolios without making the experience feel overwhelming. Each feature had to contribute to the same overall student journey.

I also had to balance building new functionality with fixing bugs, testing existing features, and polishing the experience for a real demonstration.

**Accomplishments that I am proud of**

I'm proud that Student OPS became more than an opportunity-search tool. It connects discovery with action.

A student can start with a goal, discover relevant opportunities, receive project recommendations, build skills through those projects, and eventually turn the work into evidence for their portfolio.

I'm also proud of building the application as a functional native iOS experience and developing multiple systems that work together rather than relying on a single AI prompt.

**What I have learned**

This project taught me that building with AI is not just about generating responses. The most useful AI experiences combine AI with good product structure, reliable data, and clear actions.

I also learned a lot about SwiftUI, application architecture, API integration, product design, testing, and iterating based on feedback.

Most importantly, I learned how much work goes into turning an idea into a product that someone can actually use.

**What's next for StudentOPS**

The next step is making Student OPS even more personalized and useful for students.

I want to expand the opportunity database, improve AI matching, add more project recommendations, strengthen portfolio generation, and make the roadmaps even more adaptive to each student's progress.

The long-term goal is to make Student OPS a place where students can go from "I want to achieve something" to "I know exactly what I can do next."

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I fell into Fourth Cone's poster restoration videos and didn't come out for a
while. At some point I noticed I'd started daydreaming about doing it myself —
about the specific satisfaction of bringing a piece back — and that's when it
clicked that I should make a game out of it.

The story came from the same place. Most ASMR games feel empty to me. They have
the texture and the sound and nothing underneath, and that wasn't what I wanted
to make. So I asked what's actually alluring about restoration, and the answer
wasn't the tools. It's the magic of recovering a lost past, and the mysteries
sitting inside the object. A stain is a record of something. A bad repair means
somebody was here before you.

So the story had to be a mystery where the restoration is the investigation —
not a plot delivered between levels, but something you uncover with your hands,
one layer at a time. Underneath that, the game is about the tension between
preservation and restoration: whether you hold an object still or let it change.
That's a live argument in the conservation community, and it turned out to be a
good argument to build characters out of.

**What it is**

You run a paper conservation shop. Damaged posters arrive, and you repair them
through a process grounded in real practice — surface cleaning, washing,
deacidification, lining, mending, inpainting. Then you catalogue the piece, and
the town printed on the first one returns no records. No map, no headline,
nothing.

Restoring a piece pays out coins, which you spend in a shop on small objects for
your desk.

**How I built it**

Unity and C#, solo.

Every poster is a ScriptableObject: its damage profile, which restoration stages
apply, the art layers for each stage, the catalogue fields, and the narrative
beats attached to it. Adding a cycle means authoring a data asset, not writing
code. That was the architectural bet of the whole project — the game is planned
at around twenty cycles, and one person can only ship that many if content
authoring is separated from systems work.

Monetization runs through the RevenueCat SDK as consumable coin packs, developed
against the Test Store.

**What I learned**

I came from Godot and 2D, so this was my first real project in Unity. Most of what I learned was the unglamorous half of shipping mobile:
Android build configuration, dependency resolution, and the fact that the
RevenueCat SDK doesn't run in the Editor at all, so every purchase test costs a
device build. That changes how you schedule a week.

I also learned that a lot of the development work happens outside of the game, so just because the game is wonderful and finished doesn't mean it will be successful. There are plenty of battles you've yet to fight, getting your developer account, the 14 days testing period, keeping your players coming back to the game with notifications, monetization set up, and so much more.

The bigger lesson was about scope. I originally planned to have the full 4 chapters of the game released this month.

What's here is two complete posters instead, after all, two finished pieces say more about what the game is than twenty rough ones would.

**Challenges**

Time, mostly. I lost a stretch of the build window to health issues and came back
to a deadline rather than a schedule, which forced the scope decision above
earlier and harder than I'd have liked. The correspondence system and the shop
objects that carry their own memories are both designed and both cut from this
build.

The other challenge was making the mystery legible through gameplay alone. The
second poster has a tear somebody already mended badly with tape, and lifting
that tape reveals an older repair underneath, done properly, by someone who was
still learning. Nobody tells you that. You have to notice it — which meant the
restoration mechanic had to be precise enough that noticing is possible. (I was really happy when all my playtesters noticed the details and got curious to know more, just like I wanted!)

A big challenge, which I was not able to overcome in these two months, was to register on google play in time, I underestimated the time it would take for them to analyse my documents for me to start playtesting, so I couldn't participate in the game/design categories.

**What's next**

The remaining cycles, released in chapters. The letters that arrive with each
piece. 
And shop objects that remember where they came from, so decorating becomes
a second way of reading the story.

</details>

src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/478/485/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Hackathon teams don't fail because they write bad code. They fail because of the illusion of agreement.

Around hour 30 of a sprint, someone goes AFK to sleep or eat. One dev wires up Firebase. The other defines the schema in Postgres. Both said "sounds good" in chat. Neither finds out until 3 AM on Sunday, when integration hell arrives with no time left to survive it.

The tools we already have don't fix this. Slack and Discord bury decisions under memes and panic. Jira is too heavy, because nobody moves tickets in a 48-hour sprint. We wanted a truth beacon in your pocket that costs nothing to feed, ignores chat noise, and tells you the second your team's reality splits.

**What it does**

Isolyne is an automated architectural referee for teams that move too fast to argue.

- Log casually. Type what you're doing, like "Setting up Zustand for state." No tickets, no forms. Our rule is Zero Double-Logging.

- Detect deterministically. Every new statement is checked against the team's entire established decision tree.

- Feel the alert. On a contradiction, a full-screen red Radar Alert fires with distinct haptics for alignment versus divergence.

- Resolve from your phone. Agree, challenge, or claim ownership, and the diverging branches merge back into one shared reality.

**Five kinds of drift it catches**

- Consensus: two devs choose different tech for the same topic.

- Interpretation: teammates define a feature's scope differently.

- Ownership: two people claim the same component.

- Timeline: disagreement about when something gets built.

- Execution: one says "done," another says "still working."

**How we built it**

The most important thing about Isolyne is what it refuses to do: it never asks an LLM to judge whether your team is aligned.

**Layer 1: LLM extraction, strictly sandboxed**

Groq (Llama 3) turns casual text into strict structured data, such as topic: "database" and choice: "Postgres". If Groq fails, Gemini takes over. If that fails, a fully offline keyword parser keeps the app working with no network. The model parses and nothing else.

**Layer 2: a deterministic CQRS event-sourced kernel**

All judgment happens in pure TypeScript with no model in the loop. Every input flows through one pipeline:

Signal → AwarenessGap → DecisionProposal → Commitment → CollaborationMemory

This gives us reproducible verdicts, an immutable and auditable timeline, and zero hallucinated conflicts. A radar that cries wolf gets muted, so a false alarm would kill the product.

**The stack**

React Native with Expo SDK 57 (New Architecture), Expo Router, Reanimated physics animations, expo-blur glassmorphism, expo-haptics, AsyncStorage-backed offline-first persistence, a custom React Context wrapping the kernel, and RevenueCat for entitlements and paywalls. The design language is brutalist dark mode (#07080F) with Orbitron headers and monospace logs.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Keeping the LLM out of the verdict. It's tempting to ask a model "do these two statements disagree?" We drew a hard line instead: models parse, code decides.

- Gaps that resolve themselves. If Anu changes her mind and aligns with Abhi before anyone formally resolves the conflict, the alert should vanish. We built these "evaporating gaps" into the state machine and tested the edge cases explicitly.

- Hostile conditions. Hackathon Wi-Fi is unreliable, so parsing degrades across three tiers and logging is never blocked.

- Alerts that mean something. The haptics and visuals had to be loud enough to wake someone mid-nap without turning into noise.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A fully deterministic kernel with 72 passing Vitest tests, including the hard state-machine edge cases.

- An architecture where the AI can fail completely and the product still works.

- A paywall placed at a moment of real emotional value instead of buried in settings.

- A demo that hooks in seconds: the app boots straight into a live conflict.

**What we learned**

- Trust in a coordination tool comes from predictability, and determinism beats cleverness here.

- The best time to ask for money is right after the product has just earned it.

- Writing about each decision in public forced us to defend it.

**Monetization: the "Moment of Doubt" (HAMM Award)**

We didn't bolt a subscription onto a random feature. We designed the paywall around one specific emotion.

- Free forever: unlimited real-time drift detection and alerts. The core value is never walled off, so teams trust it and adopt it.

- The trigger: a team resolves a serious conflict, the kind that would have wrecked their sprint. That is the Moment of Doubt: relief, plus the realization that the app just saved them.

- The paywall: at exactly that moment, Isolyne Pro offers the full immutable decision timeline and its export. Free users see only the most recent events. Pro users get the complete record, formatted to attach to a Devpost post-mortem as proof of engineering rigor.

The paywall appears when perceived value peaks, and it sells something the user immediately wants: evidence to show judges. RevenueCat handles purchases and entitlements through the React Native Purchases SDK, keeping free and Pro states in sync with the kernel's timeline gating.

**Built by the next generation (Next Gen Award)**

Isolyne is built by students using the toolchain of a seasoned team: Expo SDK 57 on the New Architecture, strict TypeScript, Reanimated 4, an event-sourced CQRS core, a three-tier LLM fallback chain, and a 72-test suite. We treated a hackathon app like production software. The part we're proudest of is the architectural restraint of keeping AI out of the decision loop.

**Built in public**

We documented the build instead of waiting for launch. Our HackerNoon stories cover our architectural decisions, UI iterations, and hackathon progress as they happened, so the problem was validated with real developers before the app shipped.

- https://hackernoon.com/u/abhi15

**A note on the demo**

To make the alert instantly visible, the demo loads a scripted scenario: five aligned decisions, then Abhi logging "Firebase" while Anu logs "PostgreSQL." The detection and resolution that follow run on the real kernel.

**What's next**

- Team sync across devices, so one team shares one live radar.

- Capturing decisions from commits and PR descriptions.

- Expanding beyond hackathons to early-stage startups and any small team that outpaces its process.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Encouragement Although energy systems generate a lot of data, data on its own does not lead to better decisions. The possibility to combine AI, data engineering, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, and blockchain to develop a more effective energy management strategy inspired us. As a result, we developed GridAware AI, a platform that transforms energy data into intelligent, actionable insights that can assist in identifying inefficiencies, identifying unusual consumption patterns, and supporting improved energy decisions. **

**What it does**

Energy-related data is analyzed and transformed into useful intelligence by GridAware AI. Some important capabilities are: 🤖 AI-powered energy analysis

- 📊 Energy consumption monitoring and pattern analysis

- Detection of anomalies and unusual usage * 💡 Intelligent recommendations for improving efficiency

- Safe data verification and handling * 🔗 Blockchain and smart-contract integration for trusted records

- ☁️ Cloud-ready architecture for scalability
The goal is to move energy management from simply monitoring consumption to understanding and optimizing it.

**How we constructed it GridAware AI was built with a modular architecture that combined several technology layers. Energy Data → Data Pipeline → AI Analysis → Insights → Optimization**

The data pipeline processes energy data and prepares it for analysis. The AI layer identifies patterns and potential anomalies, while the application layer presents the results as actionable insights.
 We also designed security and cryptographic capabilities into the architecture and explored blockchain and smart contracts for data verification and transparency.
 The platform is designed to be cloud-ready and scalable, allowing additional data sources, AI models, and integrations to be added in the future.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was integrating multiple technologies into a single cohesive prototype while working within a limited development timeframe.
 We needed to think about: Preparation and quality of the data 

- AI analysis accuracy

- Integration between different system components

- Safe data management * Scalability and infrastructure design

- Finding a balance between practical user experience and technical complexity We were forced to quickly iterate, prioritize the most important features, and simplify our architecture as a result of these difficulties. 

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud of bringing together AI, data engineering, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, and blockchain concepts into one project.
 More importantly, we created a foundation that can evolve beyond a prototype. GridAware AI is designed with modularity and scalability in mind, allowing us to continue improving the intelligence, security, and usability of the platform.
 We're also proud of the collaboration within our team and how different technical skills came together to build the solution.
 # What we learned
 GridAware AI taught us that building an AI-powered solution is about much more than developing an AI model.
 We learned the importance of:

- Establishing trustworthy data pipelines

- Designing scalable infrastructure

- Integrating security from the beginning

- Connecting different technologies effectively

- Converting technical outputs into user-friendly insights 

- Rapid prototyping and continuous iteration

We also learned that AI and blockchain can serve different but complementary purposes — AI provides intelligence, while cryptographic technologies can help establish trust and verifiability.

**What's next for GridAware AI**

Our next step is to continue transforming the prototype into a more complete intelligent energy platform.
 We plan to:

- 🚀 Improve AI-powered predictions and recommendations

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/434/015/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/434/015/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/383/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/383/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/384/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/384/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/385/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/385/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/386/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/386/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Froglight**

**Inspiration**

I’m an aerospace engineering student, and Froglight started from a problem I kept running into while studying.

The way I take notes changes constantly. In one lecture I may type theory, in another I need to work through equations by hand, annotate a PDF, sketch a control system, or organize ideas spatially on a whiteboard.

Each tool can be good at one of those things, but my knowledge ends up fragmented between different apps and different representations.

I wanted one workspace where those different ways of thinking could stay connected, without forcing everything into the same kind of document.

That became Froglight.

**What it does**

Froglight is a local-first knowledge workspace where different document types can coexist inside the same vault.

It currently includes structured pages, Markdown, handwriting and ink, paged notebooks, whiteboards, PDFs, LaTeX, databases, links, embeds, graph-based relationships, and other workspace tools.

The goal is not to turn all of those into one universal editor. Each kind of work keeps an interaction model that fits it, while remaining connected to the rest of the user’s knowledge.

For the Shipaton demo I created Asteria, a fictional aerospace study project. The same project moves between theory, handwritten equations, engineering sketches and design decisions.

A particularly important part of Froglight is source ownership: for example, a sketch can be embedded elsewhere in the workspace while remaining one editable source. Change the original, save it, and the linked view reflects that same document instead of becoming another disconnected copy.

**Software should adapt to the user**

Keeping many document types in one app still wasn’t enough for me.

Every student works differently, and even my own workflow changes depending on the course or professor. I often find myself wishing an application had one more tool, behaved slightly differently, or supported another way of working.

I didn’t want Froglight to become one more large but rigid application.

So its architecture is built around replaceable capabilities and plugins. Editors and document features are composed through the runtime, and vault plugins can contribute additional functionality.

In the demo, a Calculator plugin can be enabled inside the Asteria vault and immediately adds a new tool to the workspace. It is intentionally a small example, but it demonstrates the larger product idea:

the user should not have to adapt their workflow to the software; the software should be able to evolve around the user.

Friends from university have already started using Froglight as well, and I’m collecting their feedback to decide what to improve next.

**Froglight Pro and RevenueCat**

Cross-device synchronization has ongoing infrastructure costs, so I chose it as the first Froglight Pro feature rather than arbitrarily locking core note-taking functionality behind a paywall.

Froglight Pro uses RevenueCat for subscriptions and entitlement state.

The purchase unlocks a real hosted capability with recurring infrastructure costs, while local notes remain independent.

**How I built it**

Froglight is a pre-release application built primarily with TypeScript/React and Tauri 2, with shared application code across native and web hosts.

The architecture separates canonical user data from editors and platform-specific implementations. Different document families keep their own models, while shared runtime capabilities connect them inside one workspace.

For iOS purchases, I built a Froglight-owned Tauri plugin around the native RevenueCat SDK.

Optional account and vault synchronization use Firebase-backed providers.

A major focus throughout development has been making the iPad experience feel appropriate for actual study: Apple Pencil input, handwriting, touch interaction, notebook navigation, whiteboards, selection and editing behavior have all required substantial iteration on real-device workflows.

**Challenges**

One of the hardest parts was keeping Froglight extensible without turning it into a collection of unrelated editors.

Features need clear ownership: documents must survive editor changes, linked content must preserve its source, plugins need reversible lifecycles, local work must not depend on cloud services, and native functionality must not leak into portable document formats.

Handwriting was another significant challenge. Fast Pencil input exposes performance and latency problems immediately, so the Surface and ink pipeline has gone through repeated work around input batching, stroke rendering, erasing, selection and persistence.

**What’s next**

My immediate priority is reliability and refinement of the workflows that already exist, especially handwriting, notebooks, touch interaction and cross-device use.

After that, I want to continue expanding the plugin platform so more of the workspace can be shaped by users and plugin authors.

**Shipaton**

I’m submitting Froglight for the Shipaton 2026 Next Gen Award.

As a student, this project represents both the problem I personally wanted to solve and the kind of software architecture I wanted to explore: a serious local-first workspace that can grow around the way different people actually work.

</details>

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/12dR9GeYn1E/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=12dR9GeYn1E)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/866/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/866/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/870/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/870/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/867/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/867/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/868/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/868/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/869/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/869/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/864/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/864/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/863/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/863/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/862/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/862/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

When I was trying to come up with an idea for the hackathon, I really just wanted to make something that would bring me joy. I asked Claude and ChatGPT for ideas. Two ideas caught my attention: an app where a user taps an egg and a creature hatches, and an app where the user photographs an everyday object and that object turns into a googly-eyed character.

I decided to combine the two ideas to create Aurie: Hatch & Collect. The user takes a picture of an everyday object, and Aurie uses characteristics such as its shape and color to inspire a new creature.

The name Aurie comes from the aura that surrounds each creature. Every Aurie has its own glow, influenced by the family it belongs to, which became an important part of both the character design and the name.

The central loop of the app is:

Find something → photograph it → create an egg → hatch an Aurie → collect and interact with it.

From there, the idea grew into more than just a creature generator. I wanted each Aurie to feel like a small companion with its own appearance, family, environment, expressions, charms, and personality.

My goal was to make opening the app feel like there is always a little possibility waiting in the world around you.

**What it does**

The player begins by taking a photo of an object. The image is analyzed locally on the device, and the app uses characteristics of the image to influence the Aurie's body shape, color family, and other generated characteristics.

The photographed object inspires an egg that the player hatches through an animated sequence. Each Aurie is assembled from a collection of interchangeable character components, including:

- Multiple body shapes

- Different arm and leg styles

- Hairstyles

- Facial expressions

- Family-specific visual traits

- Collectible charms

Auries belong to visual families with their own environments and personalities. The families include Moss, Tide, Ember, Glow, Dusk, Starlight, and Stone.

Players can spend time with their current Aurie, play with toys, collect charms to equip on their Auries, discover new Auries, and explore quieter interactions when they want something less stimulating.

The Home screen is designed as an interactive play space rather than a static collection screen. Auries can move around their environment, react to the player, play with objects from a Toy Box, respond to actions such as shaking the phone, and use contextual dialogue to suggest activities naturally.

I also built quieter features, including a breathing experience and a Worry Jar, where a player can write down something that is bothering them, let their Aurie hold onto it for a while, and then release it visually with particles and fireflies.

For monetization, Aurie uses RevenueCat and Apple's in-app purchase system for optional hatch packs. The app still provides free hatches, so purchasing is not required to continue discovering Auries.

**How we built it**

Aurie is a native iOS and iPadOS app built in Swift.

The image is analyzed locally on the device using Apple's image-processing and Vision technologies to extract useful visual information. The app then uses those signals to influence the Aurie's body shape, color family, and other generated characteristics.

I created a modular character system where bodies, limbs, hair, expressions, colors, and charms can be combined. As the number of possible combinations increased, I had to build compatibility rules so that the system would not generate combinations that looked visually wrong, such as very long arms on a very short Aurie body.

The photo pipeline also required several stages. Rather than uploading user photos to a server, Aurie's image analysis happens locally on the device. The app extracts image signals, performs object classification using Apple's Vision framework, and uses the results as inputs to the Aurie-generation system.

A major part of development was visual iteration. The family environments went through many revisions so that every environment had a consistent playable area while still feeling distinct. I created a shared layout system so Auries remain approximately the same visual size and occupy the same movement space regardless of which family environment is displayed.

I also spent a significant amount of time building and refining the hatch sequence, character movement, expressions, interactions, sound behavior, responsive iPhone and iPad layouts, and App Store purchase flow.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest part of Aurie was that almost every feature affected several other systems.

For example, adding a new body type was not simply a matter of creating another shape. It also affected:

- Arm placement

- Leg placement

- Hair placement

- Movement

- Animation

- Charm positioning

- Expression placement

- Collision boundaries

A character could look great while standing still but break when kicking a ball, moving, or performing another animation.

The environments created a similar problem. Early versions contained too much sky or visually placed the Aurie in areas that did not look walkable. I eventually standardized the environments around a consistent walkable horizon and shared play-space dimensions so that movement feels believable across every family.

Another major challenge was translating photographed objects into Auries in a way that feels intentional. A completely random creature would be easy to generate, but that would defeat the central idea of the app. I had to work on making shape and color influence the result while still preserving enough randomness for each hatch to feel surprising.

I also learned that designing a character app requires thinking about personality as much as graphics. Small details, like an Aurie saying that it is happy to see the player again, asking to play ball, daring the player to shake the phone, or a Stone-family Aurie insisting that it does not want to dance, can make the character feel dramatically more alive.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I am especially proud that Aurie grew from a simple idea about hatching a creature into a complete interactive app with procedural character generation, multiple environments, character personalities, animations, toys, charms, quieter experiences, and an App Store purchase system.

I am also proud of the amount of variation possible within the Aurie system. Bodies, limbs, hair, expressions, colors, families, and charms can be combined while compatibility rules help keep the generated characters visually coherent.

Another accomplishment was getting the same system to work across both iPhone and iPad while keeping the Auries, environments, movement areas, and interactions visually consistent.

Most importantly, the core idea works: a player can photograph something in the real world, hatch an egg inspired by it, and meet a new Aurie.

**What we learned**

This project taught me how interconnected product design, engineering, animation, and user experience really are.

I learned a great deal about:

- Swift and native iOS development

- Apple's Vision framework and on-device image analysis

- Procedural character generation

- Character rigging and animation

- Responsive layouts across iPhone and iPad

- Designing reusable visual systems

- In-app purchases with StoreKit and RevenueCat

- TestFlight and App Store distribution

- Designing interactions that teach users without relying on traditional tutorial screens

The biggest lesson, though, was the importance of iteration.

Many of the things that looked good in a simulator did not feel right once I installed the app on a physical phone. Character scale, environment composition, movement distances, text readability, animation timing, and even seemingly minor UI decisions became much more obvious when using the app as a real player.

Aurie changed substantially because of that testing.

**What's next for Auries**

There is still a lot I want to explore with Aurie.

I want to expand the variety of character parts and charms, make each family feel even more distinct, add more contextual interactions and animations, and continue making the characters feel more responsive to the player.

I am also still refining the image-analysis pipeline so that object identification, shape detection, and color extraction more strongly influence the Aurie that is generated. One of my next goals is to make the final creature feel more obviously connected to the object the player photographed while still preserving enough randomness for each hatch to feel surprising.

My twin daughters have also become an unexpected source of product ideas. They keep suggesting new ways to make the Auries feel more alive, including feeding them, giving them tools or abilities based on their family, and eventually letting players talk directly to their Auries. One of my daughters suggested that the Auries should dance, but that the Stone family, which is the grumpier family, should act like it does not want to dance. That idea has already become part of the personality system I am building, where different families can react differently to the same activity.

The long-term idea is for Aurie to become a world where the objects around you are not just objects, but opportunities to discover a new little character.

There is an Aurie hiding in everything.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/484/017/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/484/017/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/484/319/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/484/319/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I type the same things on my phone all day: email replies, links, code snippets, my IBAN. The usual routine is to leave the chat app, open Notes, search, copy and switch back. SnipFlow removes that detour by putting your snippets inside the keyboard, in every app.

**What it does**

SnipFlow is a native iOS power-snippet vault and custom system keyboard.

- System keyboard: tap a snippet card to paste it into WhatsApp, Slack, Mail, Safari or Messages.

- Slash commands: type /email, /iban or /meeting and the shortcut expands into the full text.

- Smart variables: {date}, {time}, {clipboard} and {cursor} are resolved when a snippet is inserted.

- Encrypted vault: sensitive snippets are locked with Face ID or a master PIN and encrypted with AES-256-GCM and PBKDF2 (100,000 iterations).

- Share extension: select text anywhere in iOS and tap "Save to SnipFlow".

- Themes: four brutalist themes (Neon Mint, Cyber Amber, Electric Cyan, Dark Violet) with matching alternate app icons.

**How I built it**

SnipFlow is a native iOS app written in Swift, with a keyboard extension and a share extension. All snippets are stored on the device. The keyboard extension makes no network connections and contains no third-party SDKs.

**How I use RevenueCat**

- The RevenueCat SDK runs only in the main app. A single entitlement, pro_access, unlocks SnipFlow Pro.

- Three products are mapped to that entitlement: a monthly subscription, an annual subscription with a 3-day free trial, and a one-time Founder Lifetime purchase.

- After a purchase, a restore or a customer info refresh, the main app writes the entitlement state to a shared App Group. The air-gapped keyboard reads that flag locally, so it can switch between the free tier and Pro without ever touching the network.

- Pro unlocks unlimited snippets and categories, the full smart variable engine, Face ID vault locking and all themes and icons.

**Challenges**

A keyboard with Full Access can see what people type, so I wanted the privacy promise to be enforceable in the architecture, not just in the marketing text. Keeping RevenueCat and all networking out of the keyboard extension and passing only the entitlement flag through the App Group was the key design decision.

</details>
