<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I lost two people close to me during pregnancy and childbirth. After that, I kept thinking about how much can go wrong for a woman when there's no one checking in, no record of what happened, and no easy way to get support. Selina came out of that. It's not one feature. It's a few small things a woman might need on a hard day, put in one place.

**What it does**

Selina has a home screen that shows what's happening across different areas of your life: safety, health, academics, work, career, business etc depending on who the user is, and a companion to talk to when you just need to talk.

The free tier already does real work:

- Safety check-in: set a timer before you go somewhere. If you don't check back in, your emergency contacts get notified on their own, you don't need to be holding your phone for that to happen.

- Health: tracks your cycle and sets medication reminders.

- Academic chat and deadlines: ask questions, get quizzed, work through a problem, and keep a running list of what's due and when.

- Companion: a space to talk when you just need to talk.

Selina Plus, the subscription tier built with RevenueCat, adds a deeper layer on top of what's already there. The plan is for every section, Safety, Health, Academic, Companion, Career and Financial, and so on, to have its own deeper Plus layer. What's live now is a working slice of that.

**How we built it**

The app is React Native with Expo. The backend is a Python Flask API that runs nine small agents behind one orchestrator, one for safety, one for health, one for academics, and so on. It started on a mock reasoning provider I built myself, so the whole thing could run and be tested with no external API key needed. It now runs on real reasoning through Groq, with the mock provider still there as a fallback if the real one is ever unreachable. The interface didn't need to change at all when I made that switch, which was the whole point of building it that way from the start.

RevenueCat handles the subscription logic. I used their Test Store to build and test the whole purchase flow without needing a paid Apple or Google developer account, which mattered a lot working with a limited budget as a student.

**Challenges we ran into**

Getting comfortable with mobile builds took a while, especially the difference between a debug build that needs a live server and a standalone release build judges can actually install and use on their own. I also had to be careful with scope. It would have been easy to keep adding agents and features, but with a deadline, the harder job was deciding what to finish properly instead of what to add next.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Getting a full purchase flow working end to end, from offering to entitlement to unlocking a feature in the app. Also proud of keeping the app usable and calm-looking for something built around a heavy subject.

**What we learned**

A good chunk of building something like this is just plumbing, getting the app, the backend, and RevenueCat to actually agree with each other. I spent longer than I expected debugging a purchase flow that looked broken but was actually just missing a properly configured offering.

**What's next for Selina**

The biggest next step is letting Selina use photos and video, not just text. I'm building a vision pipeline with OpenCV 5 that can take a photo or short video from a moment that felt unsafe and turn it into a structured record: what was in the scene, when it happened, and what matters. Faces and other private details are protected, so the evidence is useful without exposing anyone. What Selina finds then decides what the Safety agent does next, like nudging you to check in with a contact or adding it to your private case timeline.

After that, I want to build out more Selina Plus features across Safety, Health and Companion, and add Career (Work), Business & Finance and Opportunity.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Gift giving is my love language. I love finding something that makes someone feel truly seen. But I have far too many birthdays, anniversaries and dates to keep track of. My grandma was living on the other side of the world, and I forgot her birthday entirely. I didn't call and I didn't send a gift. Being far apart is exactly when a small gesture matters most, and I missed it.

That's when I realized that caring wasn't my problem. My problem was memory. The best gift ideas come up in passing, months earlier: something a friend says they've been wanting to try, or something they keep talking about. By the time the date arrives, those details are gone. I built Preci so I never miss someone I love again, and so that when their day comes, I already know what would make them feel remembered.

**What it does**

Preci is an AI gift agent that remembers what people mention and researches gifts that fit them.

☀ Remember the little things. Save what someone mentioned, likes, needs or wants to avoid. Each person has a relationship, a color, an optional photo and their important dates (birthday, anniversary or a custom date, with an optional year so Preci can show "turns 30" or "10 years").
✿ Never miss the date. Import birthdays from Contacts or your calendar, and add an iPhone Reminder 2 weeks, 1 week or 3 days ahead with one tap.
❤ Find gifts that they will actually remember and use. Pick a budget (a preset or a custom range) and Preci searches the live web for real gift ideas. Each idea comes with a reason that ties back to what that person actually said.
☂ Private by design. People, notes and photos stay on your phone. Gift search sends the relationship, interests, saved notes, occasion and budget. It never sends names or contact details. No ads, no tracking.
☻ Fair monetization. Everyone gets 3 free gift searches. The Occasion Pass is a one-time $4.99 purchase through RevenueCat that unlocks unlimited searches and can be restored on any device.

**How we built it**

★ App: Expo (SDK 57) and React Native with TypeScript, built and shipped to the App Store with EAS Build and EAS Submit.
★ Payments: RevenueCat with a non-consumable lifetime product, a default offering, and an entitlement that gates gift search. The paywall checks the entitlement live, supports Restore Purchases, and changes to a thank-you state once the pass is owned.
★ AI gift research: OpenRouter routing to Perplexity Sonar, a web-search model, so suggestions are real products available now, not made-up ones. The prompt is built from the person's saved context and budget, and the response is structured into ideas with reasons and links.
★ Native integrations: expo-contacts and expo-calendar for importing birthdays, expo-calendar's - Reminders API for yearly reminders, and expo-image-picker for person photos.
★ Accounts (optional): Supabase Auth with email OTP codes and Sign in with Apple, so a purchase can follow you to a new phone.
★ Storage: Everything else is local (AsyncStorage). Privacy policy and support pages are hosted on Vercel.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Environment variables vs. cloud builds. My API keys were in .env.local, which is gitignored, so EAS builds shipped without them and gift search quietly failed. I moved every key into EAS environment 

- Showing the real product image. I wanted each gift idea to show a photo of the actual product, but keeping the image matched to the product was harder than finding the idea. The web-search model returns good product names and links, but its image URLs were often broken, expired, or of a different item. Many retailers also block their images from being loaded inside other apps. Pulling the preview image from each product page on the phone made results slow and still failed on a lot of stores. A gift card showing the wrong product would hurt trust more than having no photo, so for launch I show the idea, the reason it fits, and a link to the real store page. I left photos out until I can reliably match them to the right product.

- The entitlement mismatch. The app checked one entitlement ID while RevenueCat had another, so purchases went through but nothing unlocked. Matching them fixed the Occasion Pass.

- Auth edge cases. Google OAuth showed an "unverified app" screen, and Supabase confirmation links redirected to localhost. I fixed the site URL, published the OAuth consent screen, and moved signup to one-time codes.

- **Solo time pressure. **Design, engineering, copy, legal pages and store submission, all by me, against the deadline.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

✪ Shipped a real, submitted App Store app with a working RevenueCat purchase, not a prototype.
✪ Gift ideas that cite why they fit ("she mentioned wanting to try wheel throwing") instead of generic top-10 lists.
✪ A privacy model I'd be comfortable explaining to the people in my own app: no names leave the phone.
✪ A monetization model that respects users: 3 free searches and one honest price, with no subscription.
♥ Small details that make it feel finished: custom relationships and colors, milestone ages, one-tap iPhone reminders, and a paywall that thanks you once you've bought.

**What we learned**

❁ The hard part of shipping isn't the feature. It's the last 10%: keys, entitlements, review screenshots, privacy disclosures and auth redirects.
❁ RevenueCat removes most of the StoreKit pain, but the entitlement is the source of truth, and the app must agree with it exactly.
❁ Grounding an LLM in a web-search model and in the user's own notes makes the output much more useful than "creative" generation.
❁ As a product designer, writing the App Store page and the paywall copy was as much a product decision as any screen.

**What's next for Preci**

Proactive agent: before each occasion, Preci researches on its own and sends a nudge with ideas already waiting.
Price and availability tracking for saved ideas.
Quick capture: a share sheet and widget to save "they mentioned…" moments from Messages or Notes in a second.
iCloud sync across devices, and Android through the same Expo codebase.
Gift history so you never give the same thing twice, and learning from which ideas you actually picked.
Verified product images: fetch and check each product's preview image on a server, cache it, and show it only when it matches the linked product.
Connect to Facebook: Sync all the birthdays and important occasions of friends and family members from Facebook.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Oops! Bomb · 雷包點點名**

Less “Oops.” More “Done.”

Oops! Bomb is a collaborative iOS app for teams working toward a shared deadline. It connects the work before, during, and after a project: choosing teammates, assigning responsibilities, preparing meetings, sharing proof of work, and learning from the collaboration.

Group projects often scatter important information across chats, files, and individual to-do lists. Oops! Bomb brings those pieces together so members can see what needs doing, what has been submitted, and what still needs the team's attention. Its yellow-and-black American retro design, bomb-themed countdown, and playful reminders give accountability a recognizable personality.

Built by Oops Lab.

**Features**

**1. Teamwork Profile**

Your teamwork leaves a track record.

A project ends, but the experience of working together can inform the next one. Teamwork Profile brings a member's published peer-review results and project history into a personal collaboration record.

- View a five-dimension profile covering task completion, discussion participation, proactive help, problem solving, and reliability.

- Review results from individual projects alongside an overview of past collaboration.

- Export a personal performance report as a PDF.

- When applying to join a group, let its leader review the published performance summary and project history before approving the request. This view does not expose raw reviews, private comments, or reviewer identities.

This connects project feedback → collaboration history → more informed team formation. The profile reflects received peer feedback; it is not a guarantee of future performance.

**2. My Tasks**

Every task. Every project. One clear view.

My Tasks collects the signed-in member's assignments across projects, making it easier to decide what to work on next without opening each group separately.

- Switch between pending and completed tasks, ordered by deadline.

- Open a task to review its requirements, update subtasks, and manage deliverables.

- Check or uncheck a subtask to update its completion state. Weighted subtasks drive the displayed task percentage and feed member and project progress.

- See each assignment's project context rather than losing track of which team needs the work.

Home Screen widgets extend that view beyond the app. The My Tasks widget displays a compact checklist of pending work grouped by task, with a link back into My Tasks. A separate project widget shows countdowns and progress. Both use snapshots shared by the app.

Your next task, right where you can see it.

**3. Smart Agenda**

Come prepared. Stay on point.

Smart Agenda, shown as 自動化議程 in the Traditional Chinese interface, combines meeting preparation with a time-limited discussion plan. It helps the team arrive with something to discuss and leave each phase with a concrete outcome.

Meeting setup: The leader can create, edit, and delete multiple meetings within the same project. Each meeting has its own topic, date, time, duration, preparation materials, links, and plan.

Preparation and planning:

- The leader sets the meeting topic, date, time, and duration.

- Each member adds preparation notes, an attachment, or both. Members can edit only their own preparation.

- The agenda counts prepared members, including the leader. Additional entries from the same person do not inflate the count.

- Once everyone is prepared, a supported device uses Apple Intelligence to generate 3–4 phases, each with a time range, discussion topic, and concrete goal. Phase durations add up to the meeting's total length.

- Firebase validates and stores the plan so other members can view it, including on devices that cannot generate AI content themselves.

For example, a 20-minute meeting could allocate 5 minutes to reviewing materials, 7 minutes to deciding feature order, and 8 minutes to approving the next steps. This is an illustrative plan; actual output is generated from the team's preparation.

Before the meeting: Members can access shared meeting links, and a scheduled summary appears in group chat within the 30 minutes before the start. It highlights the topic, timing, prepared members, missing preparation, and available discussion topics.

Generation uses the meeting topic, duration, preparation notes, and attachment filenames. It does not analyze attachment contents. Model inference runs on the device; preparation and the generated plan are shared through Firebase.

**4. AI Detective**

From messy chats to clear goals.

AI Detective brings a collaboration assistant into the group conversation. When ideas, questions, and competing suggestions pile up, members can ask for help interpreting the discussion and identifying a useful next step.

- Mention the assistant in chat or use its shortcuts to ask a question about the recent conversation.

- Ask it to summarize a disagreement, clarify the options, or suggest a shared objective. Suggestions appear in the conversation for the team to discuss.

- Request project analysis using the team's task records and recent chat. The result includes a summary, strengths, improvement suggestions, and five project-level scores.

- Share the generated response or analysis through the group chat so the team can work from the same information.

The assistant uses Apple Intelligence on a supported device. It is instructed to use the supplied evidence and identify missing information. Its suggestions support the team's decisions; they do not automatically assign tasks, resolve disagreements, or change deadlines.

**5. Nudge**

Can't reach through the screen? Send a Nudge.

Nudge gives members a playful way to get a teammate's attention without typing another reminder into the chat.

- Send a poke to another member of the same group from the member-progress interface.

- Choose a reminder style that fits the moment, including a lighthearted meme-style nudge.

- Deliver the nudge through Firebase, with an in-app reception effect and push notifications when configured and permitted.

- Control poke reception in notification preferences.

It carries Oops! Bomb's humor into everyday coordination while keeping the recipient in control of notifications.

**6. Verified Submission**

It's not done until the team says it's done.

Finishing a checklist and having teammates accept the result are two distinct steps. Verified Submission connects a deliverable to the people who need to review it.

- The task owner completes the subtasks and uploads proof of work, or attaches an external result link.

- Other group members can open or download the shared submission.

- Each eligible teammate confirms the result. The task owner does not review their own task.

- The backend records verification against the current submission and marks its review complete when the required confirmations are present.

Reviewer avatars make the confirmation state visible: pending reviewers are dimmed, and confirmed reviewers are highlighted. Changing the checklist or replacing the current submission requires renewed confirmation, so an earlier approval does not silently carry over to different work.

Checklist percentages and submission verification are tracked separately: the percentage shows work progress, while confirmations record the team's acceptance of the deliverable.

No proof. No pass.

**7. Anonymous AI Review**

Speak honestly. Improve together.

The end-of-project experience combines two perspectives: anonymous feedback from teammates and AI analysis of the project's recorded work and discussion.

Anonymous peer review

- Members evaluate their teammates across five collaboration dimensions and can leave written feedback.

- The app tracks completion of the review round and releases results after all participating members have finished.

- Members see the feedback they received without reviewer identities. Published personal results contribute to their Teamwork Profile and project history.

AI project analysis

- Apple Intelligence uses task facts and team conversation to produce project-level scores, a summary, strengths, and improvement suggestions.

- The prompt asks for evidence-based assessment and explicitly identifies situations where information is insufficient.

- AI analysis is separate from peer-review calculations: private anonymous feedback is not sent to the model to generate those project scores.

Together, these views help teams reflect on what happened and carry useful lessons into the next project. AI output remains a reference for discussion, not an authoritative judgment of an individual.

**8. AI Project Meme**

Turn project chaos into a meme.

Project endings have a visual punchline. Oops! Bomb presents a project-specific meme when a project succeeds or reaches its deadline with unfinished work, keeping the outcome connected to the app's bomb-themed personality.

- Show the project's name in the outcome artwork.

- Use different success and unfinished-project presentations.

- Reopen the outcome meme from the settlement screen and share the rendered image.

Current implementation: This demo feature uses bundled artwork and programmatically composed project captions. Despite the demo chapter name, the current build does not generate new meme images with an AI model.

**9. Project Essentials**

Everything your team needs, all in one place.

The everyday collaboration tools connect the feature highlights into a usable project workflow:

- Create and join: Set up a group and deadline, share its code or QR invitation, and manage join requests. The creator becomes the initial leader.

- Assign and organize: Publish tasks, select owners, add weighted subtasks, and edit task details. Pin a member's card in the progress list and keep the project countdown visible.

- Upload and share: Add multiple attachments, manage their titles and descriptions, replace or delete files, and share external links. Firebase Storage stores file contents, while Firestore stores their shared metadata.

- Keep membership current: Transfer leadership, vote for a replacement when needed, and decide whether departed members' archived work remains in project progress. Rejoining members start without taking back their old assignments.

- Stay connected: Use group chat, read receipts, pinned messages, deadline reminders, and a notification inbox.

- Make it personal: Set a nickname and photo, use English or Traditional Chinese, and choose notification preferences. The interface can follow the system language.

These features use the same project and member data, so task details, attachments, preparation, and review state can be shared across accounts and devices through Firebase.

**Supported attachments**

Location
Formats

Task deliverables
PNG, JPG/JPEG, PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, ZIP, and external links

Agenda preparation
PNG, JPG/JPEG, PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, ZIP, MOV, and MP4

Files must be non-empty and no larger than 20 MB. Task PNG and JPEG uploads preserve their original format and bytes. Profile photos are resized and stored separately as JPEG.

**Tech Stack**

Area
Technology

iOS app
Swift, SwiftUI, Swift Observation

On-device AI
Apple Intelligence through the Foundation Models framework

Authentication
Firebase Authentication: email/password and anonymous sessions

Shared data and files
Cloud Firestore, Firebase Storage, Security Rules

Backend
Cloud Functions for Firebase, Node.js 22, scheduled meeting reminders

Notifications
Firebase Cloud Messaging, APNs, UserNotifications

App verification
Firebase App Check: debug provider in Debug, App Attest in Release

Widgets
WidgetKit and a shared App Group

Dependencies
Swift Package Manager and npm

The current app does not integrate RevenueCat or a subscription paywall. No RevenueCat configuration or OpenAI API key is required to run this version.

**Setup Instructions**

**Requirements**

- A Mac with Xcode 26.5 or later and the iOS 26.5 SDK. The app and widget currently target iOS 26.5+.

- An iOS 26.5+ simulator or compatible iPhone. Use a physical device to verify Apple Intelligence generation and push notifications.

- For AI features: Apple Intelligence must be supported, enabled, and fully downloaded. Agenda generation checks support for both English and Traditional Chinese. See Apple's Foundation Models documentation.

- Your own Firebase project with Authentication, Firestore, and Storage enabled. Deploying the backend requires the Firebase Blaze plan; cloud usage is billed to that project.

- Node.js 22, npm, and the Firebase CLI for backend setup. Use JDK 21+ for local emulator testing.

- An Apple development team with the capabilities needed to sign the app and widget when running on a physical device.

**1. Clone the repository**

git clone --branch main https://github.com/sylvia0716/Slacker-ios-summer-camp.git OopsBomb
cd OopsBomb

**2. Configure Xcode signing and identifiers**

Open group.xcodeproj and select the group scheme. Allow Xcode to resolve the Swift Package Manager dependencies.

In Signing & Capabilities, select your development team for both group and GroupBombWidget. Use bundle identifiers registered to your team. The repository currently uses con.sylvia.group and con.sylvia.group.widget.

Register a shared App Group and use the same identifier in all four locations:

- group/group.entitlements

- GroupBombWidget/GroupBombWidget.entitlements

- group/Shared/Services/WidgetSnapshotStore.swift

- GroupBombWidget/WidgetSnapshotStore.swift

The current App Group identifier is group.con.sylvia.group. Both targets must have access to the same group for widgets to receive app snapshots.

**3. Configure your Firebase project**

- Register an iOS app in the Firebase Console using the app bundle identifier from the previous step.

- Download its GoogleService-Info.plist and replace group/GoogleService-Info.plist. Verify that the file belongs to the group app target.

- In Authentication, enable Email/Password and Anonymous sign-in. Anonymous sign-in supports entering without an email account.

- Create the default Firestore database and a default Storage bucket.

- Configure App Check for your iOS app. For simulator/Debug builds, register the debug token printed by Xcode in your own Firebase project. Release builds use App Attest. See Firebase's debug-provider setup.

The checked-in Firebase configuration and .firebaserc reference the team's project. Replace the client configuration and explicitly select your own project for deployment.

**4. Install and deploy the backend**

From the repository root:

npm install -g firebase-tools
npm ci --prefix functions
firebase login

FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID="your-firebase-project-id"
firebase deploy --project "$FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID" \
 --only firestore:rules,firestore:indexes,storage,functions

Use the existing firebase.json; there is no need to initialize a new backend in this repository. The app calls Functions in asia-east1, matching the backend source. Deploy all exported functions so membership, tasks, account notification cleanup, agendas, and reminders are available together.

This deployment includes scheduled meeting reminders. Firestore indexes may take time to become ready. File access and data mutations rely on the supplied Security Rules and authenticated backend checks.

**5. Configure push notifications and password reset**

- Push notifications: Enable Push Notifications for the app identifier and upload your APNs authentication key to Firebase Cloud Messaging. Build with your team's signing configuration and allow notifications on the device. See Firebase's Apple-platform messaging setup.

- Password reset: The app sends reset emails through Firebase Authentication. Firebase's default reset page can be used without deploying a separate website.

- Optional branded reset page: auth-web/ contains a bilingual reset page and email templates. Before hosting your own copy, replace the project API configuration in auth-web/public/config.js and the fallback Firebase action-page domain in auth-web/public/app.js. Follow the auth-web setup notes and configure your own Firebase email action URL.

**6. Build and try the app**

Select an iOS 26.5+ destination in Xcode and press Run using the group scheme.

For a collaboration walkthrough:

- Register two test accounts on your Firebase project.

- Create a group with the first account. Submit a join request from the second account using its invitation code, then approve it as the leader.

- Assign tasks and subtasks, upload a deliverable, and check that the other account can see it.

- Open the agenda-management icon beside Share, create a meeting, and submit preparation from both accounts.

- On an eligible device, generate the meeting plan and verify that the other account receives the saved result.

The simulator can exercise the interface and Firebase flows. If its system language model is unavailable, it cannot validate actual AI generation. Existing shared plans remain readable. Developer-only sample-data tools require an administrator-granted claim and are not part of normal registration; ordinary test accounts can create their own projects.

**Run tests**

From the repository root, after selecting the full Xcode toolchain:

export DEVELOPER_DIR=/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer

**Swift model, repository, localization, and state tests**
swift test

**Backend unit tests**
npm ci --prefix functions
node --test functions/*.test.js functions/*.test.cjs

**Firebase integration and Security Rules tests**
npm ci --prefix firebase-rules-tests
firebase emulators:exec --project demo-group-bomb \
 --only auth,functions,firestore,storage \
 'npm --prefix firebase-rules-tests run test:rules'

The integration suite targets the local demo-group-bomb emulator project. Its endpoints are configured by the tests; starting emulators does not automatically redirect the iOS app away from the project in its plist.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Studying today is chaotic. Students juggle between PDFs, notes, assignments, and random resources, often switching between multiple apps just to understand one concept. Most tools are either passive (just reading) or too rigid, with no real interaction.

We wanted to build something that feels natural—where learning isn’t just consuming content, but actively engaging with it. The idea was simple: what if your study material could talk back, guide you, and adapt to you?

That’s how Sidenote was born.

**What it does**

Sidenote transforms scattered study materials into an interactive learning experience.

Users can:

- Chat with their study content and get instant explanations

- Practice concepts through contextual questions

- Capture insights using in-chat sticky notes

- Organize learning without switching between apps

Instead of jumping across tools, everything happens in one seamless flow.

**How we built it**

We built Sidenote as a mobile-first application using:

- React Native (Expo) for cross-platform development

- Backend APIs + AI models to power chat, explanations, and practice

- Supabase for data handling

- RevenueCat for monetization (credits + paywall system)

The core idea was to keep everything modular:

- Chat system for learning flow

- Sticky notes as an interactive layer

- Action buttons for guided learning (practice, notes, etc.)

**Challenges we ran into**

- Backend integration issues: Handling real-time uploads and API communication across devices was tricky, especially with network constraints.

- State management in chat: Ensuring messages, notes, and actions stayed in sync without breaking flow required careful handling.

- Mobile performance: Features like draggable and resizable sticky notes needed optimization to work smoothly on mobile.

- Build and deployment issues: Setting up APK builds and resolving environment/config issues took significant effort.

**What we learned**

- Building for mobile requires constant trade-offs between performance and features

- A smooth demo experience is as important as the actual functionality

- Monetization should feel natural, not forced

- Small UX details (like sticky notes) can significantly improve user engagement

**What’s next**

We plan to:

- Improve backend reliability and real-time syncing

- Enhance personalization in learning

- Expand note and archive features

- Refine the monetization system for real-world use

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Spino Ghost Racing: race other players' ghosts, build your own tracks and run championships in a 2D top-down racing game. Entering the Best Game Award, the RevenueCat Design Award, the Keep Them Coming Back Award and the #BuildInPublic Award.

**Inspiration**

Spino Ghost Racing started as a 2D racer on Reddit. A community of racers grew around it, and they kept asking for more, including a real app. A game inside a web feed had its limits, so I rebuilt it from scratch as a native mobile game, first commit on August 18. 

**What it does**

The game allows players to race each other ghost replays, make tracks and run championships.

Features:

- Race other players' ghosts on any track

- Race in multi-track championships

- Build your own tracks

- Trace a doodle and turn it into a track

- Run your own championships (they go live after a review)

- Doomscroll the feed of tracks and championships

- Get notified when someone beats your time, with your new place

- Fair on every device: replays are deterministic, so a track drives the same anywhere

- Runs smoothly even on a 2015 phone

- Buy car colors and chassis

- Buy ads on the track: billboards beside the road and text on the track surface

- Play with touch, keyboard or a controller

- Lots of settings: personal best ghost toggle, how many ghosts, on-screen controls position, engine sound and more

- Android

- iOS (in App Store review-land at the time of writing)

**How we built it**

I gave an AI coding agent the previous project and went from there. At first it looked like a lot could be brought over, but in the end very little could move from the web version to Godot, so a complete rewrite was unavoidable. I chose Godot 4.7 because it's lightweight, powerful, free and flexible, and I've used it before.

A lot of time went into making the replays deterministic, so the server can replay every track and check it before a time goes on the board. The simulation is written in Rust: the same code runs in the game and, compiled to WebAssembly, on the server (Supabase Edge Functions), so nobody can fake a time. Rust also gave a nice performance boost: it runs beautifully on my 2015 phone.

Purchases go through RevenueCat on both stores: the server records each purchase and puts the player's billboard or road text up on the track. Push notifications go through OneSignal: when someone passes your time, the server tells you, with your new place. Along the way I wrote a OneSignal bridge for Godot (Android and iOS) and let others save some tokens: https://github.com/ksvslk/godot-onesignal 

**Challenges we ran into**

Responsive design in Godot took a lot of time. Adding new UI elements was a struggle. I've done it myself in the past too, and it's not as straightforward as on the web. AI agents probably don't have much training data on it either.

The feed was also a challenge. Every page in the feed is a live track with a car driving on it, not a picture. At first, swiping fast froze the game and scrolling stuttered. It took a lot of fixes to make it smooth: pages now get ready in the background, and the live track takes a break whenever a menu covers it. The feed also updates while you scroll, so the page you're on must never jump to another track. This still needs work.

If you think that you will make a racing game (even a 2D one) and it just runs 60 FPS on a 2015 phone, then think again. The physics and replays are written in Rust, which is much faster, and then everything that slowed the old phone down had to go: I measured every frame on the phone itself and cut the work in half, made the scenery lighter, and stopped redrawing things that didn't change.

And when I say "I", I mean "me and my AI agents".

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- I did not give up on getting the FPS up, and the performance is where I wanted it: smooth, even on my 2015 phone.

- Track editor with tracing: 32 tracks on the feed already, and it's really fun to see what players make.

- Doomscrolling (but not toxic 😍)… through race tracks?!

- Onboarding is just a few taps.

- No ad network, no pop-ups and no paywall: you can just play. 

- Every lap is checked by the server before it counts, so nobody can fake a time.

- From the first commit (August 18) to live on Google Play (September 24) in 37 days.

- I got a very warm welcome from the community: all 10 ratings on Google Play are five stars, and 6 of them came with a written review. So I must have done something right!

**What we learned**

Players appreciate when you listen to them.

**What's next for Spino Ghost Racing**

Steam! Better support for big screens.

</details>

**About the Project**

I built StudyOS because I kept running into the same problem while studying: making a study plan was easy, but actually following one was not.

A normal to-do list might say “Study Maths for 2 hours,” but it doesn't answer the questions that matter when you're sitting at your desk: What should I do right now? How long should I spend on it? What happens if I fall behind?

That became the idea behind StudyOS — a study system that adapts to the student instead of expecting the student to perfectly follow a plan.

StudyOS takes a student's syllabus, goals, and available study hours and turns them into a clock-time routine. It then guides the student through focused study sessions and tracks what actually happens. If a session takes longer than expected, a student finishes early, or their available time changes, StudyOS can adapt the remaining routine instead of leaving them with a broken plan.

**What I Learned**

One of the biggest things I learned was that adding more features doesn't necessarily make a product better. My first instinct was to keep adding AI features, dashboards, and tools. But as I tested the product, I realized that students don't need more things to look at — they need more clarity about what to do next.

That changed how I approached the entire product. I started designing around one question:

“What is my next step?”

I also learned a lot about building reliable stateful systems. StudyOS has to coordinate scheduling, task completion, focus sessions, availability, and real-time schedule adaptation without losing track of what the student has already done.

**How I Built It**

I built StudyOS with React Native, TypeScript, Expo, Zustand, Google Gemini, and RevenueCat.

The core scheduling system is deterministic, while Gemini is used where AI can genuinely improve the experience. I also built the project around a continuous loop:

GOAL → PLAN → DO → MEASURE → ADAPT

The app has four main areas:

- Today — shows the student what they should do right now.

- Subjects — organizes their curriculum from subject → syllabus → chapter → topic.

- Routine — manages when they are actually available to study.

- Sanctuary — helps them reset when they're overwhelmed or struggling to focus.

RevenueCat powers the subscription layer for premium capabilities, allowing StudyOS to experiment with a sustainable model rather than treating AI usage as an unlimited free resource.

**Challenges**

The hardest challenge wasn't getting an AI model to generate a study plan. It was making the entire system behave reliably when reality doesn't follow the plan.

I had to deal with things like changing availability, unfinished tasks, completed sessions, breaks, schedule recalculation, and maintaining state across different screens. I also encountered React hook-order issues while restructuring the app's navigation, which forced me to become much more careful about how stateful React components are designed.

Another challenge was realizing that my early interface had become too complicated. I eventually redesigned StudyOS around a much simpler information architecture so that opening the app immediately answers one question:

What should I do right now?

Building StudyOS taught me that good software isn't just about how much you can build. It's about knowing what to remove

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I lost part of my own hostel deposit in a dispute I couldn't win.

The warden said a cupboard door was damaged. I knew it had been like that when I moved in. But I had no photos, no dates, no signature — just my memory against his. Memory loses that argument every time.

This happens to students and young renters across India every move-out season. "It was already like that" is the most common defence a tenant has, and the weakest. The landlord holds the money. The tenant holds nothing.

I didn't want to build another photo app. Anyone can take photos — and anyone can claim photos were taken later, edited, or picked selectively. I wanted to build evidence: a verifiable record of a room that is harder to alter or dispute later, and acknowledged by the other side before any conflict starts.

That's Verity. Things happen. Keep the proof.

**What it does**

Verity follows a tenancy from move-in to move-out and turns a room into a sealed, verifiable record.

1. Guided move-in capture
Verity walks you through your room area by area — ceiling, walls, floor, furniture, bathroom, keys — so nothing gets missed. The camera is live-only: no gallery imports, no screenshots, no edited photos.

2. The seal
Every photo is SHA-256 hashed at the moment of capture and locked at save. The timestamp comes from Verity's server rather than relying only on the phone's clock, so the recorded time is independently anchored. If you're offline, the record waits as pending seal and is verified when you reconnect. A "How was this sealed?" screen explains the full chain in plain language.

3. "Whose is this?"
Every item gets an owner: Landlord's, Mine, Roommate's, or Shared. Ownership can become part of a deposit dispute — Verity records whose item it is on day one.

4. Owner signature
You send your landlord a link. They review the sealed move-in record on the web and sign it with their finger — no app, no account. The record now reads Owner signed · Verity sealed: the owner has acknowledged the room's condition before there's anything to argue about.

5. Issue timeline
Something breaks mid-tenancy? Log it in seconds from a home-screen widget or app shortcut — photo, one-line note, date — and optionally notify the owner. Every issue lives on a dated timeline, through to resolved.

6. Move-out comparison
At move-out, a ghost overlay of your move-in photo helps you recreate the same angle. Verity then shows each item side by side — move-in vs. move-out — with ownership and owner-signature status attached.

7. Filing Assist
If your deposit is withheld unfairly, Verity prepares a deposit summary, deduction breakdown, evidence index, and a formal notice to send your landlord. If that doesn't resolve it, Verity walks you through what the government's e-Jagriti consumer complaint portal asks for and hands you a ready evidence pack, so you can file yourself.

Verity is not a lawyer and never pretends to be. It keeps your records and prepares your documents — you decide whether to file and what to submit.

Pricing: built so nobody is locked out of proof

- Capturing and sealing are always free

- ₹99 — Protect this room (at move-in): Evidence Certificate, owner signing flow, and Filing Assist if you ever need it

- ₹149 — Filing Assist (at move-out): for anyone who didn't protect their room at move-in, unlocked only when something has gone wrong

- One purchase per room via RevenueCat. No subscription. Protecting early costs less.

**How I built it**

Verity is a solo build — design, frontend, backend, everything.

- React Native + Expo with TypeScript (strict)

- expo-camera in live-only mode for capture

- expo-crypto for SHA-256 hashing at the moment of capture

- expo-sqlite for an offline-first local record, so capture and hashing work without signal

- Supabase for server-side timestamps, seal verification, and the owner-signing web flow

- RevenueCat for per-room entitlements (₹99 / ₹149)

- OneSignal for owner and issue notifications

- Sentry for crash and error monitoring

- Claude Code as my pair programmer across the build

Design came first. Before writing backend code I designed all 51 screens around one idea: Verity should feel like a document, not a gallery app. Warm ivory paper, near-black ink, and a maroon stamped "V" that works as an authentication seal. The splash is a linocut-textured animation where hand-drawn lines converge into the seal. Every screen is meant to feel like something you could print and hand to someone — because eventually, you might.

**Challenges I ran into**

Making "proof" mean something. A photo with a date on it proves very little — phone clocks can be changed and galleries can be edited. The hard part was designing a chain that holds up: live-only capture, hash at capture, lock at save, server timestamp, and an owner signature on top. Each layer closes a gap the previous one left open.

Offline sealing. Students move into rooms with bad signal. Verity had to capture and hash offline, hold the record as pending seal, and verify it later without letting anything change in between.

Getting the other side to participate. A record only the tenant signs is still one-sided. The owner flow had to be frictionless — no install, no account, just a link, a review, and a signature.

Scoping honestly around the law. It would have been easy to promise "we'll get your deposit back." That isn't true and isn't responsible. Filing Assist prepares and guides, and makes clear at every step that the user decides.

Time. I built this solo and lost several days in the middle to university exams. I dropped tools that weren't working, refocused on the Next Gen category, and spent the final week making it genuinely good rather than just finished.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- A complete tenancy journey across 51 designed screens — move-in, seal, owner signature, issues, move-out, comparison, and filing

- An evidence chain where every layer has a reason to exist

- An owner-signature flow that turns the landlord from an opponent into a co-signer

- A visual identity that feels like a trusted document, not a utility app

- Pricing where the core protection — capture and seal — is free for everyone

**What I learned**

- Trust is a product feature. The live-only camera, server timestamps, and "How was this sealed?" screen all exist to make a stranger believe the record.

- The best time to prevent a dispute is before it exists. An owner signature at move-in is worth more than any evidence at move-out.

- Restraint matters. I dropped features I liked — group complaints, deduction groups, lending — so the core flow could be excellent.

- How to ship a full product alone under a hard deadline, and how to use an AI coding partner well, not just fast.

**What's next for Verity**

- Public launch on Google Play for students and renters across India

- Hindi and regional languages, so more of the people losing deposits can use it

- Hostel and PG partnerships, making Verity the standard move-in check

- Item lending records — the data model is already in place

- Beyond rooms — rented bikes, cameras, equipment: anything you hand back and might be blamed for

Deposits are lost to memory every year. Verity makes sure the next person has proof.

Things happen. Keep the proof.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/788/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/788/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/792/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/792/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/795/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/795/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/797/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/797/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/799/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/799/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/801/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/801/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/803/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/385/803/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I fly a lot, and the day of a flight is always the same juggling act: one app for the boarding pass, another to see whether the flight is on time, the airline's app for the gate, and a group chat where everyone asks "did you land?". When something goes wrong, a fourth thing appears days later: a web form from a claims company that keeps a third of whatever the airline owes you.

FlyRight started from a simpler idea. The app that is with you for the whole travel day is the one that should keep your people in the loop, and it is the one that already knows what happened when the flight goes wrong.

So FlyRight is a travel buddy first. It tracks the flight and walks you through the day step by step: at the airport, checked in, bags dropped, through security, passport control, on board, in the air, landed. That walk lives on your Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island as a Live Activity on iPhone, and as a live notification on Android, counting down on its own with the app closed. The people you choose follow the trip live — the plane riding the route, delays as they happen, the moment you land. Nobody has to ask.

And when the flight is three hours late, FlyRight already knows. It says in plain words what the airline owes you under EU261, drafts the claim letter and points you at the airline's own claim channel. It doesn't file for you and it doesn't take a cut.

**What it does**

FlyRight is live on the App Store and Google Play as FlyRight: Flight Tracker — Travel buddy & delay claims. Since the first Shipaton submission on 12 September it has shipped eighteen releases in nineteen days, 1.0.32 through 1.1.9, and the product changed shape twice in that window: the map became a globe, and the paywall moved.

Keeping flights and keeping up with people is free.

- Your flights, grouped into trips. The Flights tab no longer lists legs; it groups them into destination trips. The outbound and the return sit together under one heading with the destination city, the country's flag faded across it, the dates and the days spent there. Connections stay inside their trip. Past travel reads newest destination first. A friend's travel groups exactly the same way.

- Add a flight in seconds. Type the number, scan the boarding pass, or share the airline's confirmation PDF — or a screenshot of the email — and every leg imports on its own. Lufthansa, Emirates, Etihad, IndiGo, Goibibo and Amadeus-style receipts are read by barcode or on-device OCR. Adding the same flight twice, even from a codeshare pass, updates the trip instead of duplicating it. Five live lookups a day work before you make an account at all, and your guest flights follow you in when you sign up.

- The boarding pass itself. Scanned or imported once, then full-screen at the gate with the brightness up and no signal needed. Seat, sequence and booking reference fill themselves in.

- A journal worth keeping. Notes, a rating, seat and booking reference, private photos, travel stats down to the aircraft type and maker — all free, with no cap on how many flights you keep.

- Your world as a globe. The World tab is a real earth you turn with a finger and pinch down to coastlines, lit by the actual sun: the terminator falls where it falls right now, and a trip's own globe puts the sun where it was at take-off or landing. Routes, airports and a radar beacon on the trip of the day live on it. Share it as a poster, story or square, with a GPU-drawn glow over the corridors you fly most.

- The people, free on both sides. Follow family and friends, approve who follows you, choose an audience per trip. Read, heart and reply to their postcards — the photo or the line someone sent from inside a trip. Pin a friend's trip to your own Lock Screen as a Live Activity and the countdown runs there too. There is no longer any cap on how many people can follow you.

Pro is the day itself. Automatic monitoring of your own flights — gate, terminal, delay, baggage belt, inbound-aircraft warnings, the live position on the globe — your own Live Activity and travel-day alerts, publishing postcards to your people, and preparing a new claim. Your family never pays to watch: following, reading and replying stay free, and whether their Lock Screen lights up depends on the traveller's subscription, not theirs. You pay to broadcast, not to receive.

- Know what you're owed. A pure-TypeScript rules engine maps the disruption to EU261 and returns a plain payout figure with the reason behind it, not legalese. This release corrected two of its own answers: intra-EU flights over 1,500 km cap at €400, and the EU's outermost regions are covered. Saved claims that carried the old amount were repaired in place.

- Claim, don't decode. The wizard drafts the airline correspondence, routes it to where that airline actually takes claims (a table covering 41 airlines) and tracks the deadline. Letters you already have stay readable forever, subscription or not.

- Wide screens. On an iPad in portrait, an Android tablet or an unfolded Fold, flights, friends and claims open beside their details instead of pushing a new screen.

- Ask for it out loud. "Show my next flight", "Show my boarding pass", "Add a flight" through Siri and Shortcuts on iPhone; the Android twin is registered as AppFunctions for Gemini.

**How we built it**

Expo SDK 57 and React Native with Expo Router, both stores through EAS Build, EAS Hosting for the website and API routes. The journal is Drizzle over SQLite, so it opens instantly and works offline. Convex is the sync backend, Clerk is auth, and the Clerk user id is deliberately the same key RevenueCat uses for app_user_id and Layers uses for identity — one id across auth, sync, entitlements, attribution and push, so an install joins to the revenue it produced.

RevenueCat, and the week we moved the paywall. The catalogue is monthly, yearly and lifetime in one offering, with a 14-day trial on the store subscriptions and RevenueCat Web Billing running the same entitlement on the web in 18 currencies — a free EU261 checker at getflyright.com/check, then Pro bought on the web keyed to the Clerk id so it is already attached when the app is installed.

What changed on 23 September is not the catalogue but the line it sells across. FlyRight used to cap a free account at three followers. That cap taxed the exact loop that grows the app: every person who invited their family hit a wall, and the people on the other side of the wall were the ones who would have installed it. So the cap is gone, journals and following are free, and Pro became the travel day — monitoring, publishing and claim preparation.

The enforcement is server-side, not a client flag. isPro() in Convex guards the provider calls (freeFlightDetails() strips gate, terminal, position and inbound from a free response, and only returns a delay once the flight has actually landed — so a free traveller can still run a manual EU261 check on a past delay), the Live Activity meter, postcard publishing and claim generation. The RevenueCat webhook writes the mirror; a reconcileAccess job stops paid polling and pushes at expiry, and cancels any pending acquisition reminder the moment someone buys.

The offer itself is trip-shaped. There is no paywall on launch and none when you save a flight. One compact "Live updates off · See Pro" row sits on an upcoming trip, opening a short sheet — three things Pro adds, "Family follows free", plans, and a third option we think matters more than either: "Remind me 2 days before this trip." It is an in-app reminder, not a deferred purchase; it starts no billing, sends no push, and is cancelled by a deletion, a reschedule, departure or an actual subscription. The × on the home card writes a permanent, account-scoped, cross-device preference — a dismissal that a reinstall cannot undo, because a promotion that comes back is a promotion that gets the app deleted. Acquisition cards only ever appear on a future, owned flight: never on an empty journal, never on a past trip, never while reading someone else's travel. Signed-out guests can browse real RevenueCat prices, and the chosen plan and flight survive the sign-up.

The globe is ours. react-native-maps is gone. Both MapKit and Google Maps floor zoom-out at roughly a hemisphere — you cannot see a life of flying at once — and the issue asking to lift it is closed "not planned". So the World tab, the trip inset and a person's travel card are a globe drawn in react-native-skia from a runtime shader, with the projection maths in TypeScript and textures generated by a script. src/services/sun.ts computes the subsolar point and the shader mixes real sunlight with a studio light through a daylight uniform. The plane on an active route moves from the provider's last reported position carried forward along its track, and falls back to the timetable when the position is null — which, over an ocean, it usually is.

One WebGPU feature, on purpose. The share poster's route-density glow runs on react-native-webgpu with shaders written as 'use gpu' TypeScript and compiled to WGSL at build time by TypeGPU: two compute passes, an atomicMax peak feeding a CPU auto-exposure gain, a colour ramp packed to RGBA, then a Skia image drawn under the atlas. No adapter means the switch simply isn't there and the poster is the plain atlas. The globe stayed on Skia — this is the one place the GPU earned its 20 MB.

iOS 27, built on this desk. An app linked against the iOS 27 SDK without UIKit scene-lifecycle adoption is refused at launch by iOS 27; we measured it both ways on the same simulator. Expo backported scene support to SDK 57.0.23, so FlyRight adopted it without waiting for SDK 58 — but EAS Build has no Xcode 27 image, so every 1.1.x release since has been an eas build --local IPA off this Mac, submitted through EAS, with Android still building in the cloud.

Measured on real phones, not our desk. Expo Observe reports startup time from every install, and the first thing it taught us was to distrust it: most of our "slow startups" were Google Play's pre-launch test robots and our own emulator builds. FlyRight now stops reporting from Firebase Test Lab devices and emulators, and strips private trip details from screen reports. With clean data we profiled a release build on a Pixel and found the launch spent its time loading code for screens nobody had opened yet. Loading modules on first use, a lazy React Native UIManager and tabs built on first open cut JavaScript bundle load by about 70% for real Android users and 60% on iPhone. The Android p90 is still slower than we want.

OneSignal carries follower pushes, travel-day alerts and the notification that a new version has reached the store, addressed through secret aliases rather than user ids. Layers carries growth analytics and install attribution on the same id as the revenue. Detour makes an invite link survive the install, so someone who taps "follow Maja" in a message lands on that invitation after installing from the store. Flight status is AeroDataBox behind a shared cache and a per-user daily quota; Cloudflare Email Routing and a Worker run the two-way support relay.

**Challenges we ran into**

We put the paywall on the wrong side of the product. Three followers seemed generous when the feature was new. It took a month of data to see it was charging people for the thing that spreads the app. Undoing it was the largest single commit of the hackathon — 184 files — because "free" had to be true on the server too: every cap, every push string, every gate in a query. The hard part wasn't removing a constant, it was deciding what Pro is for and keeping the app honest about it, down to refusing to market "automatic seat changes" because the provider does not actually expose seat changes.

Live Activities have five sync points. The lock-screen card, the app's own state, the push payload, the widget extension and the backend's content builder must all agree on one shape; any drift and the Lock Screen quietly lies about your flight. Then iOS kills every activity after eight hours, so a long-haul day needs a liveness sweep and a countdown that ticks natively instead of from pushes.

Time zones bit a real user. Manually entered flights stored bare wall-clock times and drifted two and a half hours when the phone changed zone mid-trip. The rule now: print the digits as written, do every calculation on a pinned instant in the airport's own zone.

Our own compensation engine was wrong about two cases. A flight inside the EU over 1,500 km caps at €400, not €600, and the outermost regions — Réunion, the Canaries, the Azores — are EU departures. We found both, fixed the engine, and then went back and corrected the saved claims that had already been told the wrong number. The one part of the app that must never be wrong is the part that says what you're owed, and it was, twice.

The reorder we had to undo. 1.1.0 moved the app to open on a Home feed of other people's travel. TestFlight feedback was immediate and consistent: I open this to see my flight. 1.1.1 put Flights back first, kept the feed as an Updates tab, and never reached the App Store as 1.1.0 at all — we withdrew the review and renamed the version record. Shipping fast is only useful if you can also un-ship.

Grouping legs into trips is not a sort. A return that hasn't been booked yet, a connection that looks like a stay, a flight saved with no real arrival time, a second city in the same country — each one breaks a naive grouping in a different way, and the grouping has to recompute silently every time a flight is added.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Eighteen releases in nineteen days, one developer, on two stores that both had to accept them. 1.1.9 is live on Google Play and in App Review on iOS, where 1.1.8 is live. 586 people used FlyRight in the last 28 days, 574 of whom arrived inside that window — 795 new users since launch on 1 August.

The globe. Not because a globe is hard, but because the right answer to "the map SDK won't zoom out far enough" turned out to be writing the earth ourselves, with a shader, a sun and a projection — and it shipped in five days.

Moving the paywall mid-hackathon, with a week left, because the data said the free tier was the growth engine and we were charging rent on it.

And the product is honest about the boring half: most flights are fine, so most days FlyRight is just a good travel journal that keeps your people in the loop.

**What we learned**

Never put a price on the part of your product that spreads it. The follower cap looked like the obvious upgrade trigger and was actually a tax on word of mouth. What people will pay for is the day something is at stake — the gate changing, the delay, the claim — not the right to have their mother watch them land.

The server has to know about Pro. A client-side check is fine for a paywall. The moment an entitlement has a social side — whose family gets live updates — the backend has to be the one saying yes, and "free" has to be true in the query, not just in the UI.

The platform will set your deadlines for you. Adopting the iOS 27 scene lifecycle wasn't a feature; it was the difference between an app that launches and one that doesn't, and it arrived with no cloud builder that could compile it.

**What's next for FlyRight**

The Samsung Galaxy Store, where a billing-free build variant already runs. Real flown tracks on the trip globe — the FlightAware integration is written and sitting behind an unset key until the licence question is settled. UK261, Canada's APPR and Brazil. And closing the loop from claim drafted to money actually received, which is the only metric that counts.

Links: App Store · Google Play · getflyright.com · Source on GitHub

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**What it does**

- Screen-Free Voice Capture: Tap an NFC sticker on your pill bottle, tap the Action Button, or tell Siri "Record check-in." Speak for 30 seconds while walking down the hall, and walk away.

- 100% On-Device Signal Extraction: Transcribes locally and extracts mood, focus, energy, and medication side effects into a visual timeline.

- Zero Shame: No streaks, no red badges. If you miss two weeks, Squirl simply says: "Welcome back."

- Absolute Privacy: No accounts, no servers, and zero cloud leaks ($\text{Marginal Cloud Inference COGS} = \$0.00$). Your journal never leaves your iPhone.
**How we built it**

- WhisperKit (CoreML): Runs openai_whisper-small directly on the Apple Neural Engine.

- On-Device LLM (Apple MLX): Runs Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct-4bit locally in a two-pass pipeline (narrative summary + structured JSON extraction against a 718-entry ADHD clinical lexicon).

- RevenueCat: Powers our $29.99/year subscription and 7-day free trial.

- Fail-Open Architecture: If offline or if entitlement check fails, the app automatically unlocks. Your private journal is never held hostage.
**Challenges we ran into**

- Local RAM & Thermals: Running Whisper + a 1.5B LLM on-device risks memory pressure ($&gt;1\text{ GB}$). Solved with a 1.5s staggered preload, a $20\text{ MB}$ MLX cache limit, and 3-minute idle memory eviction.

- Interrupted Model Downloads: Large weight downloads often broke on mobile data. Built an out-of-process BackgroundLLMDownloadService with byte-range resume so interrupted downloads never start from zero.

- Ethical Paywall Design: Avoided dark patterns, fake countdowns, and streak threats. Existing 1.0 users are grandfathered, and journal export remains free forever.
**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Shipped Solo: Built, tuned, and published code-complete to the App Store with $\$0$ outside capital.

- $\mathbf{\$0.00}$ Server Bills: 100% on-device AI gives us $85\%$ net margin realization on every subscriber.

- Proven Accuracy: On-device benchmark gate scored $0.941$ precision/recall on ADHD medication extraction.
**What we learned**

- Lower activation energy &gt; more features: A 30-second voice note beats a 10-minute form every single time.

- Calm technology wins: ADHD users don't need gamified streaks; they need permission to pause and psychological safety when they return.

- Edge AI is production-ready: Local inference delivers instant privacy, zero latency, and zero server scaling headaches.
**What's next for Squirl - Voice Journal**

- Squirl Connect: Opt-in clinical summaries to export structured titration and symptom reports directly to your psychiatrist.

- Apple Watch & Lock Screen Widgets: One-tap complication logging.

- Encrypted CloudKit Sync: Optional private end-to-end sync across iPhone and Mac without compromising the on-device privacy guarantee.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**💡 What Inspired Me**

My family runs J&C Impresiones 3D, a workshop specializing in 3D printing and laser cutting. Everything was running smoothly until I moved from Arribeños to Junín to pursue my degree in Computer Engineering. Suddenly, managing the business remotely became a logistical nightmare. 

I was receiving the orders and preparing the designs, but I had to communicate all the technical instructions to my mom back at the workshop so she could execute them. She then had to report the progress back to me so I could update the clients. The workflow became chaotic. I needed a centralized system to bridge the physical distance, and that chaos inspired the creation of Gestión J&C.

**⚙️ How I Built It**

I wanted an application that was fast, reliable, and accessible from anywhere. I built the frontend using Flutter and Dart, ensuring a smooth, native-like experience on mobile devices. To keep the codebase maintainable and scalable as the business grew, I implemented Clean Architecture principles alongside robust State Management.

For the backend, I needed a database and authentication system capable of syncing in real-time, allowing my mom and me to see order updates instantaneously without refreshing. To achieve this, I used Supabase.

**⚠️ Challenges I Faced**

As the app became an integral part of our business—handling quotes, job tracking, and sales—I decided to tackle our biggest bottleneck: tax billing. Previously, issuing an invoice meant logging into the ARCA (Argentine tax authority) portal, manually entering client data, calculating amounts, generating the invoice, and downloading a PDF. It was incredibly tedious.

I integrated the ARCA API to reduce this process to a single click, but it became the most complex challenge of the project. I had to build a system to handle complex authentication mechanisms, specifically managing cryptographic certificates that expire every few hours, while also parsing and handling very specific and obscure API error codes to prevent billing failures. 

**🧠 What I Learned**

Beyond the technical leaps in API integration and security certificate management, the biggest lesson was understanding how to map real-world physical workflows into a digital interface that is actually easier to use than pen and paper. 

I learned that the best software doesn't just store data; it actively removes friction. The true measure of success for this project wasn't just the complex backend, but the user experience: the interface is so intuitive and accessible that my mom can seamlessly manage the workshop's daily production and customer updates without any technical headaches.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/434/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/434/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/431/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/431/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/433/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/433/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/435/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/435/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/432/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/432/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Learning to handle money is hard, mostly because the real world charges you for every mistake. New investors usually end up bouncing between a trading app, a budgeting app, and whatever lessons they can find online, and they tend to start doing this after they've already put money in. We wanted one safe place where anyone could practise investing and get a handle on their spending, so the good habits are already there before real money is involved. That's why we built Markva.

**What it does**

Markva puts a paper-trading simulator, a personal expense tracker, and an interactive finance tutor into one mobile app.

In Markva, you can:

- Build simulated stock portfolios and manage them with market orders, limit orders, and recurring investments

- Keep watchlists and look at price history, portfolio performance, dividends, diversification, and backtests

- Track your expenses, budgets, savings goals, and recurring bills, and set up round-up savings

- Learn through lessons, quizzes, flashcards, and daily challenges, and earn streaks and achievements along the way

- Use AI to explain concepts, analyse your portfolio or spending, help with receipts, and add an explanation and next step to your weekly recap

- Pick between Free, Pro, and Max plans, with subscriptions handled by RevenueCat

All the money in Markva is pretend. It never connects to a brokerage or a bank, and it never places a real trade.

**How we built it**

Markva is a React Native app built with Expo SDK 57 and TypeScript, and we built it for Android first. Expo Router handles the six-tab navigation. Zustand and AsyncStorage keep all core app state local: portfolios, expenses, learning progress, preferences, and recurring schedules stay on the device, so the app is quick and remembers where you left off. The only Markva backend is Supabase, used solely for the optional friends and duels feature. AI, market-data, RevenueCat, and Sentry integrations are direct client-side service calls rather than Markva-hosted storage.

RevenueCat controls who gets access to what across the Free, Pro, and Max tiers. Pro unlocks the deeper insights and premium tools, and Max adds features for power users, like multiple portfolios and backtesting. The judge build runs on RevenueCat Test Store, so judges can go through the whole purchase flow and watch features unlock without paying anything.

Market data comes from Twelve Data when it's configured. If it isn't, the app falls back to a deterministic local market engine, so the demo still works offline. All the AI features go through one shared dispatch layer that works with Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, and OpenRouter, which means we can swap providers without touching the features. We also added Reanimated animations, haptics, local notifications, biometric app lock, Sentry monitoring, CSV export, and portfolio snapshots you can share.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest part was getting a lot of connected financial systems to behave reliably while keeping nearly all app state on the device. Recurring expenses, dividends, limit orders, auto-invest plans, goal contributions, and reminders all have to catch up properly after the app has been closed for a while. We handled this with persisted cursors and processing loops that have a hard cap on how many times they can run.

Animated navigation was another headache. We wanted it to look polished, but the animations kept getting in the way of taps. Expo tabs keep screens mounted, so we wrote entrance animations that trigger when a tab comes into focus and replay each time without remounting any of the controls you interact with. We also made sure every outside integration fails gracefully. If a market-data or AI key is missing, Markva still works as a full demo.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We're proud that the three parts of Markva actually work together. Your trades show up in your portfolio analytics, your spending feeds into your budgets and goals, and the lessons explain the ideas you run into everywhere else in the app.

We also managed to fit a lot in without making the app hard to use: multiple portfolios, benchmark comparisons, automatic investing, dividends, AI insights, spaced repetition, gamification, accessibility settings, local-first privacy, and a working premium tier through RevenueCat.

**What we learned**

The biggest lesson was that financial education works better when you can act on it straight away. A lesson on diversification means a lot more when you can open your own simulated portfolio right after and check how spread out it is. Budgeting ideas stick better when you see them in your own expense categories and savings goals.

On the technical side, we learned how much fallbacks, stable state selectors, careful date maths, and idempotent background processing matter in a mobile app that holds this much state. We also learned that subscriptions should be planned as part of the product from early on. A paywall added at the last minute feels exactly like that.

**What's next for Markva: Predict the Market**

Next up are debt and loan payoff tracking, an activity heatmap for financial habits, custom expense categories, and savings-goal milestones on the net-worth chart. Further out, we want to add more learning paths and social challenges, and use privacy-conscious personalisation to help each user build a money routine they'll actually stick to.

</details>
