<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every alarm clock has the same flaw: a button that lets you lie.

We'd set a 6:00 alarm to run, tap Stop, and go back to sleep. We'd sit down to study, put the phone face down, and pick it up "for a second" forty minutes later. Habit apps didn't help. They ask you to tick a box, and a box can't tell whether you did the thing.

So we asked a different question: what if the alarm didn't stop until your phone could tell you'd actually shown up? No done button. No snooze-and-forget. Just proof.

Research backed the idea that friction works. A short pause before opening a distracting app cut app opens by 57% over six weeks (Grüning et al., PNAS 2023). ShowdUp turns that friction into proof.

**What it does**

ShowdUp is an Android alarm you have to show up for. You pick a time window and what showing up means. Then it rings, and keeps coming back, until your phone can tell you did it.

Setup starts with why you're here: Study or focus, Move or run, or Wake up. Each one shows only the proofs that fit it, and every proof says in one line how it's checked:

- Phone-down focus: the apps you pick (for most of our testers, Instagram) stay shut until the timer ends. Open one and you get caught: a full screen the first time, showing the reason you wrote ("Exam on Monday"). After that, a small card and Android goes home.

- Wake up with a tag: scan a code you placed away from your bed. In our demo it's the barcode on a face wash in the bathroom. Only that exact code stops the alarm.

- Run or walk: GPS distance or time. Fake locations and car speeds don't count. When you hit the goal the ringing stops, but the run keeps recording, then gives you pace, kilometre splits and your route drawn as art.

- Steps, counted by the phone's step sensor (shaking it doesn't count), and LeetCode, read from your public profile.

- Gym or a place (Pro): GPS sees you arrive and stay.

The logo is the interface. ShowdUp's mark is a dot above a cup: a person with their arms up. Turn it upside down and it's a bell. So the mark is the alarm's state:

- Ringing: the bell rocks while you're due.

- Showed up: proof lands and the bell turns over. The dot is you, standing up.

- Missed: an empty cup. No dot, and no shame.

- Couldn't tell: a dotted dot. A failed sensor never counts as a miss.

The same marks fill your History grid, with a key one tap away, next to your records: days showed up per activity, best streaks, badges and every run.

It's honest on bad days too. Hold End today and the reminders stop, recorded as an ended day, not a fake win. Missed today? Never miss twice.

Everything stays on your phone. No account, no ads, no data sold.

**How we built it**

- Flutter + Riverpod for the app: about 17,300 lines of Dart. It's local-first, with no sign-up, and the logic that decides whether you showed up lives in pure, unit-tested Dart classes.

- Native Kotlin (about 2,850 lines) for everything that must survive Android closing the app:

- EscalatingAlarmEngine: exact alarms that keep returning inside your window, even after a reboot.

- TrackingService + RoutePolicy: a foreground GPS service that filters fixes, proves the run, then keeps recording until you finish.

- AppBlocker + CatchPolicy + CaughtFlash: an Accessibility service that reads only which app is in front, then closes it.

- FocusTracker: the phone-down timer, which restarts if a held app stays open.

- OverlayService: an optional companion bubble that floats over other apps.

- Google's code scanner for tags, so ShowdUp never needs camera permission. It stores only a scrambled fingerprint of the code.

- RevenueCat + Google Play Billing for Pro, priced per country.

- Firebase (Auth, Firestore, Cloud Functions in TypeScript with zod) for optional friend Battles, which never see your proof.

- Website on Firebase Hosting, with the APK on GitHub Releases.

**The maths of an honest run**

Every GPS fix passes four gates before it counts: it can't be mocked, its accuracy must be within 50 m and it must be under two minutes old, and the speed between fixes must be between 0.5 and 8 m/s, because anything faster is a car. Standing still makes GPS wander, so a new fix only counts as movement once it leaves a jitter radius around the last point:

$$
r = \max\left(5\ \text{m},\ 0.5 \times \text{reported accuracy}\right)
$$

The distance between two fixes uses the haversine formula:

$$
d = 2R \arcsin\sqrt{\sin^2!\left(\frac{\Delta\varphi}{2}\right) + \cos\varphi_1 \cos\varphi_2 \, \sin^2!\left(\frac{\Delta\lambda}{2}\right)}, \qquad R = 6371\ \text{km}
$$

Splits are timed at the exact moment the route crosses each kilometre. When a boundary falls between two fixes, we interpolate the crossing time from the distance on either side of it:

$$
t_k = t_a + (t_b - t_a)\,\frac{D_k - s_a}{s_b - s_a}
$$

The route is drawn as a line on ink with no map tiles, so a shared run card never shows the streets where you live.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Proving without spying. Every proof had to be believable and private. Accessibility can read whole screens, but ours only ever reads the package name of the front app. The tag stores a fingerprint, not the code. Routes never leave the phone.

- Android fights background work. We had to handle exact-alarm permissions, foreground-service types, battery optimisation and reboots so that a 6:00 alarm really rings at 6:00, and keeps ringing.

- GPS lies. Mock locations, jitter while standing still, stale fixes and car speeds all had to be filtered before a single metre counted.

- A bug that only shows up abroad. Our early builds silently put every user on India time, so someone in London would have woken at the wrong hour. ShowdUp now follows the phone's timezone and its 12- or 24-hour clock, and shows kilometres or miles by region.

- Distribution is a policy problem. Google Play needs a declaration and demo video for Accessibility use. Play Protect blocks apps installed from outside the store that use Accessibility in some regions, including India. And Firebase's free plan refuses to host APK files, so our download moved to GitHub Releases.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A real, signed Android app you can install today, not a prototype. Alarms fire after the app is killed and after a reboot.

- A logo that works as a state machine. One shape tells you whether you're due, done, missed, or unsure, from the onboarding to the History grid to the website.

- Six ways to prove you showed up, none of them a button, each with a plain-language line explaining how it's checked.

- Strava-style run summaries with zero location exposure.

- 123 automated tests across Flutter, Kotlin and Cloud Functions, all passing, and zero analyzer issues.

- Ready for the world: device timezone, local clock, km or miles, and regional pricing.

**What we learned**

- Real users rewrite your roadmap. Our first tester ignored half the features. What stuck was locking Instagram while studying. What they asked for was Strava-like runs and badges. That one session made runs free, put an intent picker at the start of setup, and gave us records and badges.

- Trust has to be visible. The first question every tester asked was "how does it know I really did it?" Now every proof answers that in one line, right where you choose it.

- Accountability needs a dignified exit. An app that holds you to a promise must also let you off the hook honestly on a bad day. "Couldn't tell" and "Never miss twice" came from that.

- Design is behaviour. Making the mark carry meaning did more for understanding than any tutorial text.

**What's next for ShowdUp**

- Google Play. Closed testing first, then a public launch, so installs are one tap with no Play Protect warnings.

- Friends ranking by days showed up. The server side is already built behind a feature flag.

- More languages, and more proofs (Health Connect workouts are next).

- iOS, once the Android version has proved itself.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

[ REVENUECAT SHIPATON 2026: NEXT GEN SUBMISSION ]

Update: Konvo just crossed 2,000,000+ organic views in less than 24 hours. Watch here: https://www.instagram.com/p/Dd0TQrPo5mZ/

Now you may be thinking... what?? how??? well.. lets start with my story below. 

Have you ever opened Instagram to reply to one message, but end up scrolling 36 minutes later?

I'm 16, and for the past 2 years, I've been constantly trying to end my screen time addiction. I've tried dozens of screen time apps, but I kept running into the same problem:

Whether I unlocked Instagram for 5, 15, or 30 minutes to reply to someone, Reels was still right there. And Instagram is so freaking addictive.

So on July 1st, 2026, I promised myself I'd delete Instagram completely for 2 weeks.

2 weeks later, I redownloaded Instagram and realised I didn't have the urge to scroll anymore. But when I opened my messages, I saw 15+ unread messages from friends asking to hang out, call, or get advice.

I had just ghosted all of them and left them on delivered. Which didn't feel good, because you know I love all my friends.

At my school, we don't really ask for each other's phone numbers anymore. We ask, "yo whats your insta", and talk & message from there.

So I thought, what if I could keep my Instagram messages without the feed, Explore, and Reels pages?

Maybe like a WhatsApp for "Instagram messages"?

**What it does**

So that's why I built Konvo: DM's Only.

You sign in on Instagram's own login page inside the app, and it opens straight to your inbox. Your password and message contents aren't sent to Konvo's servers.

Your DMs, group chats, story replies, profiles, and notifications still work. The feed, Explore, and Reels pages are hidden. Individual posts or reels shared in a conversation can still open.

There's also the option to lock the real Instagram app with Screen Time, with 2 short passes a day to post a story or call someone.

**How we built it**

I initially tried the official Instagram API, but the restrictions didn't work for what I wanted to build, especially normal conversations and group chats. So I pivoted after 2 days.

Then I tried loading instagram.com in a web view and injecting a script before Instagram's own code runs. And it worked! I could hide the distracting pages and add my own buttons.

URL rules send the feed pages back to the inbox, and CSS hides the buttons that lead to them. When Instagram changes its layout, I can update those rules through a JSON file on my site without waiting for an app update.

I built Konvo on my MacBook first, saw it worked like really well, then moved it to iPhone. Tauri + Rust for the app, Swift for RevenueCat, Screen Time, and notifications.

Most of Konvo was built in the back row of 3-hour lectures at a 2-week high school business program in Hong Kong, and in my bedroom over the summer.

**How Konvo uses RevenueCat**

RevenueCat handles Konvo's monthly and annual subscriptions. The paywall loads the actual prices in your currency from its offering, checks whether you're eligible for the annual plan's 7-day trial, and uses the Pro entitlement to unlock access. It also restores purchases, so someone who's already paid doesn't have to pay again. The trial gives people time to see whether Konvo helps them stop scrolling while keeping their messages. I also send RevenueCat's subscription events to PostHog through webhooks. Seeing people cancel in the first few minutes helped me improve the trial explanation and what happens after purchase.

**Challenges we ran into**

App Store review took multiple attempts, including fixes to description details & getting Apple's testers access to the verification code for my test Instagram account.

Then the paywall broke when I launched it on LinkedIn.

My LinkedIn app launch post reached 210,000+ impressions, but people who downloaded Konvo were getting stuck on "Loading your plans". 10 people messaged me and one emailed.

The cause was: my paywall waited for 3 products from RevenueCat, and the 3rd, a lifetime purchase, was never approved in App Store Connect. So the real store never sent it. My phone had a local StoreKit file that still had it, which is why I never saw the problem.

I fixed it in build 82 by only waiting for the products I was actually selling, submitted it through Apple's expedited review & got accepted.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I got my first viral reel on september 8th 2026, it got over 2,000,000 views: https://www.instagram.com/p/Dd0TQrPo5mZ/ 

I've posted consistently 2 times a day for 2 weeks straight and saw no results.

I had doubts; I was sad, worried but the one thing I did not do was: give up. 

Konvo is published on the App Store. By September 28st, 2026:

- 10,000+ downloads

- 5 figs in revenue

- 2,500,000+ combined views and impressions across my social posts

- peaked ranked #61 in productivity (higher than wisperflow, notion, obsidian & goodnotes)

The demo shows an earlier build. On September 25th, I submitted v1.9.0, build 130, for App Store review. The matching source and version notes are linked at the top of my public repository.

This is my first time building an app, and my first time making money online. It has been an unbelievable experience, and I would like to thank my parents for supporting me :)

**Why this fits the Next Gen award**

I'm 16, and Konvo is my first app. I started with a problem I was having myself, and had to figure out everything from getting Instagram messages to work to setting up subscriptions with RevenueCat. I also got to learn what happens when your paywall breaks on launch day and real people start messaging you about it. Now Konvo is on the App Store, the source is public, and people are actually using and paying for it. This is my first time making money online, which still feels a little crazy because it started with me just trying to stop scrolling :)

**What we learned**

I thought modifying Instagram's UI was too ambitious. But I was like, freak it, why don't I give it a shot anyway, and that's how Konvo started.

Building something for myself also meant I knew exactly what was working and what wasn't. Deleting Instagram stopped me from scrolling, but I couldn't keep it deleted because of my messages & friends.

And the launch-day bug taught me that working on my phone doesn't mean it works for someone downloading it from the App Store. My test setup had hidden the exact problem real users ran into.

**What's next for Konvo: DM's Only**

Number 1 priority: BRING KONVO TO ANDROID, GOOGLE PLAY STORE.
I have a waitlist of over 1500 people who want konvo on android.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We were inspired by the difficulty many people face when trying to find the right mentor for their career goals. Searching through profiles is often time-consuming, and it can be difficult to know which person has the experience and skills that best match your needs.

We wanted to create a platform that makes mentorship more accessible by combining personalized matching, career guidance, scheduling, and communication into one place.

**What it does**

MentorHer is an AI-powered mentorship and career discovery platform that helps users find mentors based on their career goals, skills, interests, and aspirations.

Users can create profiles, discover recommended mentors, explore personalized career paths, schedule mentorship sessions, communicate with mentors, and participate in a community for knowledge sharing.

The platform is designed to support both mentors and mentees through personalized dashboards and tools for managing their mentorship experience.

**How we built it**

We built MentorHer as a full-stack web application using Next.js and React for the frontend and Node.js for backend functionality.

We used Firebase and MongoDB to handle application data and user-related functionality. AI-powered functionality is used to support mentor matching, career-path recommendations, and personalized guidance.

We also integrated scheduling and real-time communication capabilities so that users can move from discovering a mentor to actually arranging and conducting a mentorship session.

The interface was designed to be responsive and easy to navigate, with separate experiences for mentors and mentees.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was bringing several different systems together into a single platform. User authentication, profiles, AI recommendations, scheduling, dashboards, community features, and real-time communication all needed to work together reliably.

Another challenge was designing a useful matching experience. Simply matching users based on one characteristic would not provide meaningful recommendations, so we had to consider multiple aspects of a user's goals, skills, and aspirations.

Working within a limited development timeline also meant that we had to prioritize the most important features and continuously test the application as new functionality was added.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud of building a complete mentorship experience rather than limiting the project to a simple mentor directory.

MentorHer brings together mentor discovery, AI-assisted recommendations, career guidance, scheduling, communication, personalized dashboards, and community interaction in one platform.

We are especially proud of creating a foundation that can be expanded into a more personalized career-development ecosystem.

**What we learned**

We learned that building an AI-powered product requires careful consideration of both the technology and the user experience. An intelligent recommendation is only valuable when it helps users make better decisions.

We also gained experience with full-stack development, database integration, authentication, API integration, AI functionality, scheduling, real-time communication, responsive UI development, and debugging a multi-feature application.

Most importantly, we learned how to prioritize features and make architectural decisions while working under a hackathon deadline.

**What's next for MentorHer**

Our next step is to make the matching system more personalized and accurate. We want to incorporate additional information about users' experience, skills, interests, goals, and previous mentorship interactions.

We also want to improve the career-path generator, enhance scheduling and communication, expand the community features, and introduce additional AI-powered career tools.

Our long-term goal is for MentorHer to become a complete career and mentorship ecosystem that helps people discover the right mentors, guidance, resources, and opportunities at the right time.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Cognita Hub started with a simple question:

What if educational technology supported the people who know the child instead of trying to replace them?

Cognita was initially created to support mathematics learning for autistic children aged 5–9 and other children who may benefit from more accessible and configurable learning experiences.

As we developed the project, however, we realized that simply creating “accessible exercises” was not enough.

Conversations with educators and researchers at UFPA changed the way we thought about the product. We learned to look at a learning activity as more than content plus a correct answer.

Instructions, support, engagement, context, environment, and human observation can all shape the experience.

That became especially important when thinking about autism.

Children on the autism spectrum do not form a single learning profile. A visual stimulus, animation, instruction style, amount of movement, or support strategy that helps one child may create friction for another.

Because of that, Cognita does not try to translate a diagnosis into a prescribed interface.

Instead, it follows a principle that became central to the project:

Person before diagnosis.

The experience should be adaptable to the child, while important pedagogical decisions remain in human hands.

This pushed Cognita from being “a platform with math exercises” toward becoming a connected learning ecosystem built around preparation, experience, observation, feedback, and adaptation.

**What it does**

Cognita Hub is a connected educational ecosystem for children, tutors, families, and schools.

It was designed with an initial focus on autistic children, while avoiding the assumption that every autistic child should interact with technology in the same way.

Instead of treating each user as an isolated part of the product, Cognita connects what happens before, during, and after a learning activity.

**For children**

- Interactive mathematics learning journeys

- Visual and configurable activities

- A dedicated Android experience designed around exploration rather than adult-style dashboards

- Individual settings for text, motion, and interaction

- Learning experiences that can be adjusted without defining the child by a diagnosis

**For tutors**

- Activity preparation and customization

- Personalized learning journeys

- Session management

- Observation and engagement records

- Context about how the child interacted with each experience

- Reviewed feedback and next-step planning

- Human control over progression between learning modules

**For families**

- Clear summaries of learning sessions

- Progress through the child's learning journey

- Reviewed tutor feedback

- Suggested next steps

- Access to meaningful context without exposing private tutor notes

Instead of reducing learning to a score, Cognita preserves the context around each session:

What support was needed? How did the child participate? What did the tutor observe? What could be tried next?

This is especially important in our initial autism-focused use case, where the same activity may work very differently depending on the child, the environment, the instructions, and the support provided.

The product follows a continuous cycle:

Prepare → Experience → Observe → Reflect → Adapt

Cognita does not diagnose children, replace educators, or claim to prescribe the “correct” experience for autism.

Its role is to help the people around the child prepare, observe, record, and make better-informed decisions.

For Shipaton, we also developed Cognita for Schools, our institutional licensing concept powered by RevenueCat.

A school can activate institutional access through a RevenueCat purchase flow, unlocking the connected tutor, child, and family ecosystem while keeping the child-facing learning experience free from ads, purchases, and monetization prompts.

**How we built it**

Cognita combines a web platform for adults with a dedicated Android experience for children.

**Web**

- Vanilla JavaScript

- HTML5

- CSS

- Vite

- Supabase

**Android**

- Vanilla JavaScript

- Vite

- Capacitor 8

- Supabase

- RevenueCat Purchases SDK

Supabase powers our PostgreSQL database, authentication, Row Level Security, storage, pairing, and shared learning records.

The web platform provides the tutor and family experiences, while the Android app provides the child-facing experience and the institutional Cognita for Schools demo.

The different interfaces share the same learning context, but they deliberately expose different information.

For example, a tutor can record an internal observation about a session, while the family receives only reviewed feedback and a clear next step.

This separation is important because Cognita is not intended to automate pedagogical interpretation or expose raw observations without context.

For Shipaton, we integrated the RevenueCat Purchases SDK into our Capacitor Android application.

Our institutional prototype uses:

- Offering: cognita_school

- Monthly package: $rc_monthly

- Product: cognita_school_pilot_monthly

- Entitlement: school_access

We validated the RevenueCat Test Store flow on a physical Android device, including:

- Successful purchase

- Failed purchase

- Purchase cancellation

- school_access entitlement activation

Once the entitlement is active, the app unlocks the Cognita for Schools ecosystem, where the user can explore the tutor, child, and family experiences.

The current purchase flow uses RevenueCat's Test Store and represents a prototype rather than validated commercial pricing.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was designing for three very different perspectives at the same time:

- the child experiencing the activity,

- the adult guiding and observing the process,

- and the family trying to understand what happened.

Each one needs different information, language, and interaction patterns.

Another major challenge came directly from our initial focus on autism.

There is no universal “autism mode” or “accessible mode.”

Autism does not describe one interface preference, one learning strategy, or one support need.

An animation that helps one child stay engaged may distract another.

A highly visual activity may support one child and overwhelm another.

A short instruction may work better in one context, while another child may benefit from additional visual support.

Because of that, Cognita focuses on configurable experiences instead of prescribing one interface based on a diagnosis.

This also influenced how we think about data.

A result such as “8 out of 10 correct” does not explain:

- whether support was needed,

- whether the child stayed engaged,

- whether the instruction had to be changed,

- whether the environment affected the activity,

- or what the tutor observed during the session.

Another challenge was deciding what information should move between users.

Tutors can keep internal observations that should not automatically be exposed to families.

Families instead receive reviewed feedback and a clear next step.

On the technical side, moving from a web-first ecosystem to Android with Capacitor forced us to rethink:

- Navigation

- Native application lifecycle

- Mobile performance

- Initialization

- Touch interactions

- Animations

- Device-specific behavior

Testing on a physical Android device revealed issues that were invisible in the browser and forced us to optimize assets, transitions, layouts, and initialization.

RevenueCat also created an important product challenge:

How do we monetize Cognita without putting accessibility behind a child's paywall?

Our answer was to explore institutional licensing through Cognita for Schools.

Instead of monetizing the child-facing experience directly, the institution licenses the connected ecosystem around it.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We're proud that Cognita is no longer just an idea.

Today, the prototype includes:

- A working Android child application

- Web experiences for tutors and families

- Device pairing

- Interactive mathematics activities

- Configurable learning experiences

- Personalized learning journeys

- Tutor-created activities

- Journey and module management

- Session and observation records

- Reviewed family feedback

- Shared progress between the different experiences

- RevenueCat integration

- A working institutional licensing prototype

For Shipaton, we built a complete demonstration flow:

Institutional license → Tutor prepares → Child experiences → Tutor observes → Family receives context

The tutor can configure an activity, place it inside a learning journey, assign it to the child, review the resulting session, and transform observations into reviewed family feedback.

The child experience remains intentionally different from the adult interfaces.

Instead of dashboards and management tools, the Android experience uses visual journeys and focused interactions designed around exploration.

We are especially proud of successfully validating the RevenueCat purchase lifecycle on a real Android device.

Cognita Hub also advanced to the national stage of Desafio Liga Jovem, where we presented the working product and ecosystem to external judges.

But our biggest accomplishment was changing the way we thought about the product itself.

Cognita evolved from:

“a platform with math exercises”

into:

a connected learning cycle built around human mediation.

And our understanding of accessibility also evolved.

We stopped asking:

“What interface should an autistic child use?”

and started asking:

“What does this child need in this experience, and how can technology help the adults around them respond?”

**What we learned**

We learned that educational technology does not need to automate every pedagogical decision to be useful.

A correct answer alone does not describe a learning experience.

Context matters.

Participation, support, engagement, observation, and the way the child experienced an activity can all contribute meaningful information.

Our work around autism reinforced this lesson.

A diagnosis can provide important context, but it should not become a shortcut for assuming what a child can do, what they prefer, or what interface they need.

That is why Cognita is built around configurable experiences rather than diagnosis-based presets.

We also learned that technology becomes more useful when it helps adults make better-informed decisions instead of trying to replace those decisions.

That principle influenced several parts of Cognita:

- the child does not automatically advance to the next learning module;

- the tutor reviews a session before feedback reaches the family;

- internal tutor notes remain private;

- activities and journeys can be adjusted before they reach the child;

- accessibility settings are configurable instead of being automatically assigned based on diagnosis.

We also learned that monetization is not just a technical integration.

RevenueCat pushed us to think about who should actually pay for the product.

For a project centered on accessibility and inclusion, monetizing individual child-facing accommodations felt inconsistent with the direction of the product.

That led us toward an institutional model instead of monetizing the child's experience directly.

And technically, testing on a physical Android device reminded us very quickly that:

“It works in the browser” does not mean “the mobile app is finished.”

**What's next for Cognita Hub**

Our next step is to expand Cognita with more multimodal learning experiences, including richer visual and auditory interactions.

Today, the activity library is still intentionally small.

We want to explore more ways of presenting mathematics beyond counting and number identification, while preserving the same configurable and human-centered model.

We also want to continue improving:

- Accessibility configuration

- Visual, auditory, and multimodal activities

- Tutor observations

- Connections between one session and the next

- Personalized learning journeys

- Institutional tools for schools

- More mathematics activity formats

- Better support for different learning contexts

- Research-informed product validation

Our initial focus will continue to include autistic children, but we want future decisions to come from real observation and collaboration rather than assumptions about diagnosis.

We want to keep validating Cognita with educators, researchers, families, and children so that new features respond to real needs.

Cognita for Schools can also evolve from our current RevenueCat Test Store prototype into a real licensing model for schools and educational organizations.

Most importantly, we want to preserve the principle that shaped the project:

Person before diagnosis.

Our long-term goal remains simple:

Technology should support the people who know the child, not pretend to replace them.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**🌱 Inspiration**

Ever thought of a great business idea but didn’t know where to start? This is the problem many students face in the Philippines, where entrepreneurship opens the door to income, survival, and self-empowerment—yet remains locked behind limited market access, operational challenges, and gaps in business knowledge. 

As two students tasked to run a business from start to finish as part of our high school curriculum, we experienced all the challenges that come with starting a business venture. We built from scratch—running marketing campaigns on social media, creating order forms, curating aesthetic websites, coordinating payments and deliveries, and tracking sales in complex spreadsheets. 

It was during this lengthy process that we noticed a gap in existing infrastructure and educational support provided to students nurturing an entrepreneurial spark. We thought: if only there was a platform to guide us through this end-to-end process.

So we did what any frustrated entrepreneur would do—we built it.

**🌿 What It Does**

An all-in-one marketplace for students to plant, grow, and sustain their own businesses, SproutSquad supports aspiring entrepreneurs through the end-to-end process of starting one’s very own business venture. 

From tracking orders to managing finances, this educational e-commerce app streamlines messy, separate business functions into an interactive, beginner-friendly platform. It offers three core features:

**🌱 1. Marketplace**

SproutSquad is home to an online marketplace where buyers and sellers meet. Eliminating the need for a separate website or order form, it gives startups visibility through the app’s catalog of registered shops and product listings. Customers can view student sellers’ social media pages and ratings and place orders as they would in any other e-commerce platform. Shops that are rapidly growing or are nominated by the community will earn a special feature in the SproutUp! showcase.

**🪴 2. Shop**

SproutSquad’s Shop dashboard translates numbers into readable, actionable metrics and automates the manual processes every budding entrepreneur runs into. By tracking sales and inventory and evaluating a shop’s business health score from financial metrics, it saves student sellers time and energy to focus on growing their startup instead of handling administrative work. Here, shop owners can collaborate with business partners, track incoming orders and expenses, and customize their shop profile for customers to see in the marketplace.

**🌻 3. SproutAcademy**

Perhaps the app’s most distinguishing feature versus other e-commerce apps, SproutAcademy is an interactive, gamified platform that teaches students how to grow their own businesses from scratch. Backed by credible sources, including the Philippine Department of Education (DepEd) curriculum, key lessons are delivered across eight modules featuring daily quests, short lessons, and real-world business simulations. With these educational resources, young entrepreneurs can learn the basics of business, from ideation and marketing to finance and funding.

**🌳 How We Built It**

We wanted SproutSquad to feel like one connected platform, rather than another collection of separate tools, so we built it using React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, with Supabase handling our database, authentication, security, and real-time features. We then used Capacitor 8 to bring the web app to iOS, letting us use native Apple technologies such as StoreKit, while keeping most of our codebase shared. 

For the SproutSquad subscription system, we integrated RevenueCat through two SDKs: @revenuecat/purchases-capacitor for native iOS purchases and @revenuecat/purchases-js for Web Billing. Rather than hardcoding subscription plans into the app, we connected both our monthly Sprout+ and yearly Bloom+ plans to a single sproutsquad_membership entitlement. This lets the app check whether a user has an active membership, so all six premium tools—inventory tracking, pre-orders, coupons, bundles, order exports, and scheduled product drops—unlock the same way on either plan. Meanwhile, RevenueCat handles the actual purchase, renewal, and cancellation process.

We also wanted our subscription system to work reliably beyond the paywall itself. Thus, we connected RevenueCat to our Express/Netlify backend and Supabase through a secure webhook that processes subscription events and keeps our in-app subscription status and notifications updated. We use the user’s Supabase ID as their RevenueCat User ID so their subscription follows their account, while signing out resets the RevenueCat session to prevent another user from inheriting access. We also implemented live entitlement updates, Restore Purchases, subscription status tracking, and a server-side 30-day promotional entitlement for Shipaton judges, granted through RevenueCat's V2 API.

**🌱 Challenges We Ran Into**

**🌿 1. Condensing Multiple Features into One Cohesive App**

Since SproutSquad brings together a marketplace, seller management tools, an educational platform, and a discovery system, we had to be intentional about how we structured the experience. It had to feel like one cohesive app, not several unrelated features stitched together.

**🌻 2. Grounding Sprout Academy in Real Business Principles**

We had to ensure that the Sprout Academy curriculum had a real educational foundation backed by credible sources, balancing relevant learning with gamification. We curated lessons, simulations, and quizzes around practical business concepts while keeping the experience fun and engaging. 

**🪴 3. Making SproutSquad Work Across iOS, Web, and Supabase**

We also had to figure out how to make RevenueCat’s SDK fit naturally into our existing architecture, accounting for different purchasing systems across web and native iOS while keeping subscription access consistent. Testing the full purchase-to-entitlement flow helped us catch issues that weren’t visible during development, including a scramble to fix last-minute bugs that emerged during the last 12 hours before submission.

**🌱 4. Working Within Funding Constraints**

As the project grew, we struggled to manage the app’s scope given our limited access to resources as minors and students. We had ambitions we wanted to achieve, such as an AI business assistant, that we had to set aside for now, since they didn’t align with our current resources and funding. That constraint pushed us to focus on features within our reach that deliver real value to student entrepreneurs, such as SproutUp!, which features student businesses based on their performance and potential.

**🌼 What We Learned**

When it comes to educational content, we learned that building something fun and something educational are far from the same thing. Doing one doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve done the other. Early on, we relied on credible content based on the DepEd curriculum to design accurate, comprehensive, and understandable lessons, only to realize that accuracy doesn’t make learning worthwhile on its own. In building SproutAcademy, we had to treat gamification as not just a decoration but rather a core part of its design.

From a product design standpoint, the project taught us to make compromises between technical accuracy and usability. We started out wanting to faithfully represent each shop’s profit margins and expenses based on fundamental accounting principles, but eventually ran into the risk of overcomplicating the numbers and confusing student sellers—the exact opposite of what we set out to do. We learned that sometimes making a useful product means sacrificing 100% completeness for clarity.

Finally, integrating an online marketplace, a discovery system, seller tools, and a learning platform into one app taught us the skill of scope discipline. We pivoted from our idea of building an AI business assistant because it didn’t fit our current direction or resources. That decision freed us to focus on features like SproutUp! that deliver real value to entrepreneurs, and made the product better for it.

**🌱 What’s Next**

Our next step is to publish the app to the App Store so it can be used widely by aspiring student entrepreneurs beyond just the two of us. From there, we want to keep expanding SproutAcademy simulations and content (perhaps outside the Philippines), enhance the SproutUp! showcase as a real-time discovery engine for student startups, and explore partnerships with schools to help Filipino students going through the same Business Enterprise Simulation project we did. In the future, we may revisit our idea of an AI business assistant once SproutSquad gains the traction and resources to sustain it the way we want to.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/456/661/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/456/661/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/456/662/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/456/662/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/456/663/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/456/663/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/456/664/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/456/664/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Sarthi — Your destination. Your voice. Your way forward.**

**Inspiration**

For someone who cannot rely on vision, navigating the world is not simply a matter of knowing where to go. The difficult part is understanding what is happening around them right now.

A map can tell you that a pharmacy is 700 meters away. It cannot tell you that there are stairs directly ahead, that an obstacle is blocking the walking path, or that the real-world environment no longer matches what was expected.

That led us to a simple idea:

You choose the destination. Sarthi figures out the way.

We wanted to build something closer to a mobility companion than a camera that simply describes objects.

**What it does**

Sarthi is a voice-first AI mobility companion designed to help visually impaired users navigate dynamic environments.

The interaction starts naturally: the user simply tells Sarthi where they want to go.

For example:

“Take me to the nearest pharmacy.”

Sarthi can then:

- Understand the user's destination.

- Find relevant nearby places.

- Compare available walking routes.

- Start a navigation journey.

- Provide turn-by-turn guidance through voice.

- Continuously observe the surrounding environment through the camera.

- Identify mobility-relevant hazards such as stairs, curbs, potholes and obstacles.

- Maintain a persistent understanding of the surrounding world.

- Decide which information actually requires the user's attention.

- Communicate important information proactively instead of waiting for the user to ask.

- Handle uncertain, stale or unavailable perception explicitly.

- Reconcile the planned route with the physical environment.

This creates a continuous loop:

Intent → Search → Route → Perceive → Reason → Prioritize → Guide → Recheck → Adapt

The map answers:

“Where should I go?”

Sarthi also tries to answer the more immediate question:

“What do I need to know right now?”

Importantly, Sarthi is designed as an assistive system, not a replacement for a cane, guide dog, or the user's own judgment. When perception is uncertain, the system communicates that uncertainty rather than pretending it knows.

**Key Features**

**🎙️ Voice-First Interaction**

Voice is the primary interface of Sarthi.

Users can interact naturally without needing to navigate complex visual controls.

- Voice-based destination requests

- Speech recognition

- Spoken navigation instructions

- Proactive hazard warnings

- Text-to-speech guidance

- Multilingual interaction foundations for English, Hindi and Marathi

A user can simply say:

“Which is the nearest pharmacy to me?”

and Sarthi can interpret the request as a navigation task rather than a generic visual question.

**📍 Natural-Language Destination Discovery**

Users don't need to know the exact name of a location.

Sarthi understands destination-oriented requests such as:

- “Take me to the nearest pharmacy.”

- “Find me a hospital.”

- “Where is the nearest café?”

- “Can you find me a hotel?”

It extracts the destination intent, searches for relevant nearby places, and prepares them for route selection.

**🗺️ Route-Aware Walking Navigation**

Sarthi does not simply assume that the geographically closest place is the easiest to reach.

Candidate destinations are evaluated using their actual walking routes.

The navigation system includes:

- Place discovery

- Walking-route planning

- Route distance and duration

- Turn-by-turn guidance

- Navigation state

- Route progress

- Current-position tracking

- Route-aware destination selection

This allows Sarthi to distinguish between:

“closest as the crow flies”

and

“closest to reach by walking.”

**👁️ Continuous Environmental Perception**

The camera provides Sarthi with a live view of the user's surroundings.

Rather than treating every camera frame as an isolated image, Sarthi maintains a structured World State.

The perception layer can track information such as:

- Object/class

- Confidence

- Bounding box

- Relative position

- Approximate distance

- Perception freshness

- Camera movement context

This gives the rest of the system a continuously updated representation of the environment.

**⚠️ Mobility-Focused Hazard Detection**

Sarthi is not designed to describe everything that appears in front of the camera.

It focuses on information that can affect the user's movement.

The system can reason about situations such as:

- Stairs and steps

- Curbs and step-downs

- Obstacles in the walking path

- Potholes and holes

- Uneven walking surfaces

- Doorways and entrances

- Large blockers

For example:

“Stop. Stairs ahead.”

The objective is not maximum object recognition.

The objective is useful environmental awareness.

**🧠 Intelligent Attention Prioritization**

A major challenge in assistive AI is deciding when the system should speak.

A camera can detect many objects at once. Announcing all of them would increase cognitive load and potentially make navigation harder.

Sarthi therefore prioritizes information using:

CRITICAL → CAUTION → GUIDANCE → INFORMATION

Important events can interrupt normal navigation guidance, while irrelevant observations remain silent.

The system also incorporates:

- Relevance filtering

- Warning cooldowns

- Duplicate-warning prevention

- Hazard persistence checks

- Route-corridor filtering

- Perception freshness

This allows Sarthi to focus on what matters now rather than everything it can see.

**🧭 Route ↔ Environment Reconciliation**

One of Sarthi's central ideas is connecting two different sources of truth:

The map knows the planned journey.

The camera observes the physical world.

Sarthi brings these together through:

Planned Route ↔ GPS Position ↔ Observed World

This creates the foundation for identifying situations where the environment and the planned navigation context do not perfectly align.

Instead of treating navigation as:

GPS → instruction → GPS → instruction

Sarthi is designed around a continuous perception-navigation loop.

**🛡️ Uncertainty-Aware Safety**

Sarthi explicitly distinguishes between absence of evidence and evidence of absence.

For example:

No detection ≠ no obstacle.

A failed perception request does not mean that the path is clear.

The system tracks states such as:

- Detected

- Not detected

- Unknown

- Unavailable

- Stale

When perception becomes unavailable, Sarthi preserves uncertainty instead of generating a false “all clear” conclusion.

Similarly, safety-critical decisions are not delegated entirely to a generative language model.

Deterministic logic handles important safety and prioritization behavior.

**☁️ Cloudinary-Powered Visual Pipeline**

Cloudinary forms an important part of Sarthi's visual media pipeline.

Camera frames can be delivered through Cloudinary, while the architecture supports targeted AI Vision analysis for mobility-specific questions.

Instead of asking an AI system to describe every frame in detail, Sarthi can ask focused questions when the navigation system needs additional information, such as:

“Are there stairs or steps visible in this image?”

“Is there a curb or step-down at ground level?”

“Is there an obstacle directly in the walking path?”

“Is there a pothole or hole in the walking surface?”

This makes Cloudinary part of the mobility intelligence pipeline, rather than simply being used as image storage.

**📱 Mobile-First PWA**

Sarthi is designed as a mobile-first Progressive Web App.

The mobile experience integrates:

- Camera access

- GPS positioning

- Voice input

- Voice output

- Navigation map

- Live environmental perception

- Responsive controls

- PWA installation support

The visual interface provides navigation context, while voice remains central to the experience.

**🔄 Resilient Real-Time Perception**

Real-time AI systems introduce practical problems such as latency, overlapping requests, network failures and rate limits.

Sarthi is designed around these constraints.

The perception loop uses:

- One perception request in flight

- Controlled perception intervals

- No request backlog

- Rate-limit backoff

- Stale-state handling

- Provider failure handling

- Malformed-output handling

If the perception provider temporarily becomes unavailable, Sarthi does not convert that failure into a false statement about the environment.

Instead, it communicates the limitation and continues operating with the information that remains trustworthy.

**How we built it**

Sarthi is built as a React + Vite frontend with a Node.js + Express backend, with a modular navigation, perception and AI architecture.

**🧭 Navigation Architecture**

We separated navigation into dedicated services for:

- Destination intent extraction

- Place search

- Walking-route planning

- Navigation state

- Route progress

- Turn-by-turn guidance

This separation allows navigation decisions to remain structured and testable rather than putting the entire journey inside a single AI prompt.

**👁️ Perception Architecture**

The camera feeds into a perception pipeline that converts visual observations into structured world information.

Instead of asking:

“What does this image contain?”

the system is designed around the more useful question:

“What information from this image matters for the user's current journey?”

**🧠 Reasoning + Deterministic Safety**

One of our most important architectural decisions was separating AI reasoning from deterministic safety logic.

Generative AI can help interpret complex visual and natural-language information, while deterministic services handle things such as:

- Safety prioritization

- Freshness

- Relevance

- Cooldowns

- State transitions

- Validation

- Failure handling

This reduces the risk of allowing a language model to make unsupported safety conclusions.

**🗣️ Voice Architecture**

Voice is treated as a first-class interaction layer rather than an additional feature.

The user can provide intent through speech, receive navigation instructions through speech, and receive proactive warnings when the system determines that something important requires attention.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest problem wasn't getting an AI model to recognize an object.

It was deciding when that information actually matters.

A camera can detect dozens of things in a single frame. Telling the user about all of them would make navigation worse, not better.

We therefore had to solve several deeper problems.

**1. When should Sarthi speak?**

We introduced relevance, priority, deduplication and cooldown logic so that Sarthi doesn't continuously repeat itself.

The goal is not maximum narration.

The goal is minimum necessary interruption.

**2. How do we handle uncertainty?**

No detection does not mean no obstacle.

A stale frame, failed model request or unavailable provider cannot be treated as a clear environment.

Sarthi therefore tracks perception freshness and explicitly preserves uncertainty.

**3. AI hallucination vs. deterministic safety**

We didn't want a language model deciding something like:

“The road is safe to cross.”

Safety-critical behavior requires fresh information and deterministic rules.

AI can assist with perception and reasoning, but it should not manufacture certainty when the underlying evidence is missing.

**4. Maps vs. reality**

A route can be geographically correct while the immediate environment has changed.

That means navigation cannot simply be:

GPS → instruction → GPS → instruction

Sarthi instead works toward continuously comparing:

planned route ↔ observed world

and responding when those two sources disagree.

**5. Real-time constraints**

Continuous vision requests introduced latency, overlapping requests and API rate-limit problems.

We built around:

- One perception request in flight

- Controlled perception intervals

- No request backlog

- Rate-limit backoff

- Stale-state handling

This makes the architecture more suitable for real-time mobile use than simply sending every camera frame to an AI model.

**Accomplishments we're proud of**

We're proud that Sarthi evolved beyond a simple “AI camera for the visually impaired.”

We built the foundations of an actual mobility system:

- 🧭 Natural-language destination understanding

- 📍 Nearby place discovery

- 🗺️ Route-aware walking navigation

- 🎙️ Voice-first interaction

- 👁️ Continuous visual perception

- 🧠 Persistent world-state reasoning

- ⚠️ Deterministic safety prioritization

- 🔄 Route ↔ environment reconciliation

- 🔁 Adaptive navigation architecture

- 🌐 Multilingual interaction foundations

- 📱 Mobile-first PWA architecture

- ☁️ Cloudinary-powered visual media pipeline

- 🛡️ Explicit uncertainty and failure handling

We also built extensive automated validation around the navigation and perception layers, including negative cases where the system must refuse to make an unsafe assumption.

One principle became particularly important to us:

An AI mobility assistant should know when it doesn't know.

**What we learned**

We initially thought the biggest challenge would be computer vision.

It wasn't.

The deeper challenge was decision-making under uncertainty.

We learned that building an assistive AI system requires much more than connecting a vision model to text-to-speech.

The system has to understand:

What is happening?
Does it matter?
How urgent is it?
Is the information fresh?
What should the user do next?
And how certain are we?

We also learned that AI should not control every part of the system.

Generative AI is useful for perception and reasoning, but critical safety behavior benefits from deterministic state machines, validation and explicit failure handling.

Most importantly, we learned to design around the user's cognitive load.

The goal isn't to tell the user everything the AI can see.

The goal is to tell them:

the right thing at the right moment.

**What's next for Sarthi**

Our next step is to make the existing navigation architecture more complete and reliable for continuous real-world journeys.

We're working toward a journey where:

Take me to the nearest pharmacy.

becomes:

Find → Route → Navigate → Observe → Detect → Warn → Reconcile → Reroute → Arrive

Future work includes:

- More reliable real-world walking navigation

- More robust live rerouting

- Stronger route ↔ camera reconciliation

- More robust obstacle and hazard detection

- Interactive camera-guided environmental scanning

- Stronger multilingual voice interaction

- Better handling of GPS and perception uncertainty

- Extensive testing across real mobile devices and real-world routes

Ultimately, we don't want Sarthi to be an app that users constantly have to operate.

We want it to become a quiet companion that understands when to speak, knows when to stay silent, and helps the user move through a changing world with greater awareness.

You choose the destination. Sarthi figures out the way.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I wanted to build something more ambitious than a typical first project — a 2D stealth game with a real story, not just a tech demo. I'm a beginner solo developer, and Godot 4.7 felt like the right engine to learn game architecture from the ground up while shipping something complete for Shipaton 2026.

The story follows Hector Miller, a father who lost his daughter Laura to the mafia and becomes a vigilante seeking revenge. I wanted the mechanics (staying hidden, timing your strikes) to mirror the tension of someone who has to be careful and calculated, not reckless.

**What it does**

Hector Miller is a linear 2D stealth game built in Godot 4.7. The player sneaks past patrolling enemies using cover (columns), reads a document that reveals the protagonist's backstory, and eliminates two targets in sequence. Getting spotted sends you to a game over screen; defeating the final target triggers the ending.

**How I built it**

- Engine: Godot 4.7, GDScript only, no external plugins.

- Stealth detection: enemies check line-of-sight and distance to the player, and Area2D-based "columns" (grouped as "colonna") let the player hide from view without blocking movement physically.

- State persistence: since I couldn't get Godot's Autoload UI to register a script in my editor setup, I used a class_name GameManager extends Node with static variables instead, to persist things like which enemies are already dead, spawn points between scenes, and background music playback position across scene changes.

- Android export: I set up a lightweight Android export pipeline (OpenJDK 17 + Android SDK command-line tools only, no full Android Studio) to keep the build environment small, and tested the final APK on a real device.

**Challenges I faced**

- Getting stealth detection to work correctly with Area2D-based cover objects instead of physical colliders (RayCast2D doesn't detect Area2D by default).

- Synchronizing enemy attack animations with actual hit frames.

- A recurring input-bleed bug where interacting with an in-game document while paused would also trigger the player's attack animation once gameplay resumed — solved with a short input-lock window after unpausing.

- Setting up Android export without Android Studio, using only the command-line SDK tools to keep the toolchain lightweight.

**What I learned**

This was my first time building a complete game loop from scratch: stealth AI, state persistence across scenes, UI/pause interactions, and a full Android export pipeline. I learned a lot about Godot's node-based architecture and how much simpler state management becomes once you stop fighting the engine's paradigms.

**Next Gen Award**

I'm a student submitting under the Next Gen Award: the project is fully open-source (MIT License) on GitHub, and I'm not using the RevenueCat SDK, since Next Gen doesn't require a store listing or monetization. The repository contains the complete Godot project — anyone can open it and run it directly in the editor or export it themselves.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

When people feel depleted, reaching out can feel harder than it should. Many wellbeing products keep attention inside the app through content, tracking, or chat. We wanted to build something that helps a person leave the screen and take one small step toward someone who matters.

**What it does**

One Good Reach is a private daily mobile ritual:

- Check in with Soul, Mind, and Body.

- Choose a person who matters.

- Receive one safe action designed to take about five minutes.

- Prepare an editable message or conversation.

- Reconnect in real life.

- Mark the action complete and reflect privately.

Actions include gratitude, checking in, making an invitation, asking for support, and preparing a repair. The app does not try to become the user's companion. It helps the user move from technology back into a human relationship.

**How we built it**

One Good Reach is built with Expo React Native, strict TypeScript, and Expo Router. Screens call service interfaces for local data, recommendations, profile state, and purchases.

Personal check-ins, labels, messages, and reflections are stored on the device with AsyncStorage. A pure safety gate runs before action generation. The recommendation engine is bounded and local, combining Soul, Mind, and Body ratings with recent history to choose an appropriate action template. Private notes do not need to leave the device.

RevenueCat is integrated through react-native-purchases to manage offerings, the Premium entitlement, purchase state, and restoration. The production path uses an Expo development or store build with the Android public SDK key.

**Privacy and safety**

One Good Reach has no public profiles, community feed, address-book access, or automatic message sending. It is a wellbeing and relationship-support tool, not therapy, diagnosis, crisis care, or an AI companion. If crisis language is detected, the normal recommendation flow stops and the app redirects to a safety screen.

**RevenueCat and monetization**

The model is freemium. The core daily check-in, one safe reconnection action, safety routing, and useful personal history remain available without payment. Premium is designed for deeper pattern insights, additional guided reconnection journeys, and more choice in action formats.

A subscription fits the recurring value of an ongoing relationship practice, while a free trial lets users experience the complete loop before paying. We do not monetize private emotional data or place safety behind a paywall.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest product decision was restraint. It would have been easy to add open-ended AI chat, a social feed, gamified streaks, or automatic message sending. Each would make the app look busier while weakening the central idea. We instead kept the flow linear, private, and focused on one real-world action.

Technically, we also separated purchase logic from the UI so the app can run in a safe preview mode during development while using real RevenueCat offerings and entitlements in Android builds.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A complete check-in to action to reflection vertical slice

- Private, local-first storage for sensitive content

- RevenueCat purchase, restore, offering, and entitlement integration

- A safety gate that cannot be skipped by an asynchronous race

- A calm visual language without feeds, rankings, or streak pressure

- 19 passing Jest tests, strict TypeScript, ESLint, and 18 of 18 Expo Doctor checks

**What we learned**

Relationship technology can be valuable without pretending to be a relationship. The best role for the app is to reduce the activation energy of reaching out, then get out of the way.

We also learned that privacy can shape the product itself. Keeping notes local and using bounded recommendations makes the experience more trustworthy and keeps the engineering aligned with the product promise.

**What's next**

Next steps include deeper private pattern insights, more guided reconnection journeys, accessibility testing on a wider range of Android devices, and careful user research on which prompts most often lead to meaningful real-world contact.

**Award fit**

**RevenueCat Peace Prize**

One Good Reach was designed to create social good at the scale of one relationship at a time. It turns a private emotional check-in into a small, achievable act of gratitude, care, invitation, support, or repair with a real person. Its purpose is not to keep people talking to technology. It is to help them take a safer first step back toward one another.

**RevenueCat Design Award**

The design treats reconnection as a calm private ritual rather than a productivity contest. Warm ivory surfaces, coral and aubergine accents, rounded organic forms, generous spacing, and clear adult typography create a sense of safety without becoming clinical. The paired reaching forms in the app icon express the product idea in one symbol: two people moving toward a shared point of connection.

**HAMM Award**

RevenueCat powers the Premium entitlement, offerings, purchase flow, and restoration. The monetization model protects the useful daily core while reserving deeper ongoing value for subscribers.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Devpost project page — RevenueCat Shipaton 2026, Next Gen Award**

Paste-ready English copy. Devpost's default headings are used, so each block maps
onto a field on the submission form. Nothing here claims a capability the repo
does not contain — check every number against npm test and node eval/khoanbench.js
before you paste.

**Tagline (one line, shown under the title)**

Hold on. Verify. Then act. — a scam-awareness assistant for older people, where
the AI is never the thing that decides.

**Inspiration**

Impersonating the police was the most common online scam in Vietnam in 2025,
according to a survey of 60,300 people by the National Cyber Security
Association. Scammers build fake offices, wear uniforms, and make video calls.

Three numbers explain why a tool has to intervene before the money moves:

- Over 6,000 billion VND lost to online scams in the first 11 months of 2025
(Ministry of Public Security).

- Only 32.12% of victims reported it to the authorities; 12.03% accepted
the loss and did nothing (NCA, 60,300 respondents, Dec 2025).

- Victim rate in 2025 was 0.18%, one person in 555.

Two thirds of victims tell no one. Help that arrives after the money is gone
barely happens. That leaves one moment that matters: while the scammer is still
on the phone.

**What it does**

The first design constraint is not a feature: the person being scammed does
not have to open anything. Someone who is being told by a fake police officer
to stay on the line will not open an app, find a paste box, and wait for a
result. An assistant that only works when opened does not work.

So the phone runs a quiet local screen and the intervention appears where the
person is already looking:

- On-device pre-screening. A message arriving with two or more signals at
once — a code request plus pressure, an agency name plus a transfer demand —
raises a local prompt. No network call, no AI, and deliberately no verdict of
its own. It is a bell, not a scale.

- An overlay warning strip draws over whatever is on screen, including the
call screen, when the engine returns High risk. It never covers the full
screen and always has a dismiss button.

- A long-call reminder. Police-impersonation calls run for hours. After 25
minutes the app asks one question: is someone telling you to transfer money?
It counts time; it does not listen to, record, or identify the call.

- The adult child gets the alert, because the person who will reliably open
an app is not the person being scammed.

When someone does open it, they type, speak, or send a screenshot, and get one
of three levels, the reasons behind it, and — at the same text size as the
verdict — what it could not check.

**Two layers, and only one of them decides**

AI layer reads the text and raises FLAGS (present | unknown)
 it never returns a score or a level
 ↓
Rule engine the ONLY thing that decides the level
 deterministic, offline-capable, testable

The response schema forbids the model from returning riskScore,
riskLabel, critical, interventionLevel or safe. If a model returns one,
validation rejects the response.

Four rules that never bend:

- Three levels, fixed wording. High risk · Suspicious · No clear risk
signals found. There is deliberately no "Safe" label, in any language.
The system reports what it did not find in what it was given; it does not
promise safety.

- Codes, not sentences. The engine emits enum codes; display text is looked
up in a catalog, so switching language cannot change a verdict.

- "Could not check" ≠ "checked, found nothing."

- Anything clever may only raise caution, never lower it.

**How we built it**

React 19 + Vite PWA, TypeScript, Tailwind, packaged for Android with Capacitor;
Node/Express backend; Postgres for the family circle. The rule engine is plain
JavaScript with no model dependency, so it runs with the network off.

Tests enforce the product rules rather than just the code: a floor of 14px on
every font size, every t() key required to exist in the English block, and the
three risk labels locked so no one can quietly add a "Safe".

**Measurements — reported against two different sets**

Numbers are measured, not targets, and every one is reproducible from the repo.
They are given twice, because the difference between the two is the point.

Development set (test/du-lieu/, reproduce with npm test) — the rule
patterns were tuned against these, so read it as an upper bound:

Layer
Catches
False alarms
Set

Rule engine, Vietnamese
80%
0%
100 scenarios (49 scam / 51 benign)

Rule engine, English
70%
0%
200 scenarios (100 / 100)

Held-out set (eval/dataset/, 597 labelled samples never used for tuning,
reproduce with node eval/khoanbench.js) — this is the number that predicts
behaviour on a message nobody has seen:

Layer
Recall
False alarms

Rule engine, Vietnamese
14.4%
3.3%

Rule engine, English
6.1%
1.0%

Rule engine, mixed VI/EN
11.4%
0.0%

The two tables count different things. In the development table a scam counts as
caught at Suspicious or above; in the harness, recall requires High risk.
Under the looser definition the held-out set gives 34% Vietnamese and 33%
English. Six reproducible numbers, and none of them is a single headline figure.

We publish the low ones on purpose. A safety tool that only reports its best
number is training its users to trust it more than it has earned.

**Monetization — RevenueCat**

The rule we set before writing any of it: nothing that reduces someone's
protection is ever behind a paywall.

Everything on the at-risk person's phone is free forever and works offline —
checking a message, the overlay warning, the long-call reminder, the family
password, the lessons, the verified emergency numbers. That side of the product
never sees a price.

The subscription lives on the other side, in the guardian view used by the
adult child, sold through RevenueCat Web Billing so it works in the PWA:

Free
Khoan Đã Family (subscription)

One guardian per elder
Several guardians share one elder — siblings, in-laws

The alert itself
Alert history, and a weekly digest of what was checked

One connected elder
Several elders on one account

The person paying is the person with income and a reason to pay, and the person
at risk is never the one being sold to. Ads were ruled out at the start: an
advertisement inside a scam warning is a scam-shaped object.

**Challenges we ran into**

The false-alarm budget is the whole product. For an older user, a false
alarm costs more than a miss — cry wolf a few times and the app gets
uninstalled. That is why the benign half of every test set is as large as the
scam half, and why the model is not allowed to raise the verdict on its own.

Screenshots must not get a softer verdict. Text inside an image goes through
the identical rule engine as typed text. If the image cannot be read, the app
says that — it never reports an unread image as one it checked.

Every escape hatch has to stay. Even the most critical screen keeps an "I'm
fine, nothing dangerous" exit. A false alarm the user cannot escape is how an
app gets deleted.

**What we learned**

That the honest version of an accuracy table has more than one row in it, and
that writing the disappointing row down is what makes the good row worth
anything.

**What's next**

Bringing it to local elder associations in Hanoi, and a version that can warn
during the incoming call itself.

**AI tools disclosure**

Claude Code was used as a coding assistant throughout. The rule engine's
patterns, the risk-label contract, the test sets, and the research behind the
numbers above are the author's own work. Two hosted models (Anthropic Claude,
Google Gemini) are used at runtime as the flag-raising layer only; neither is
permitted to return a risk level.

</details>
