<details><summary>Description</summary>

A lease arrives with twenty minutes to sign it. The clauses that take your money are the quiet ones: a deposit of ten months' rent, a refund that waits ninety days, repairs deducted "in the landlord's sole discretion".

Redline reads the lease on your phone and marks each of those clauses in red, with what it costs you and, where a local law caps it, the statute that says so.

The lease text never leaves the phone. No account, no login, no upload.

Entering the Next Gen Award. Student entry: a working open-source Android app (MIT), a demo video and a public repository. There is no store listing, as the Next Gen rules allow.

**Try it in one minute**

- Install app-release.apk from the latest release, or scan the QR code in the README. Android asks twice because the app is not on Google Play: allow installs from the browser, then on the Play Protect warning tap More details, then Install anyway.

- Tap No lease to hand? Open a sample lease, or photograph your own lease.

- Turn on airplane mode first if you like. The scan runs entirely on the phone.

**What you see**

**The scan**

Photograph a paper lease inside the app. CameraX feeds ML Kit text recognition about five times a second, boxes appear over the text it has found, and the screen tells you when the page is steady enough to shoot. The shutter answers with a haptic tap, the torch is one button away, and a long lease goes in page by page in one scan.

**The lease card**

The start screen holds a lease drawn in 3D. Drag it and the page tilts under your finger; let go and it springs back.

**The report**

A 0 to 100 gauge drawn with a sweep gradient leads the report: Low risk under 30, Caution from 30 to 59, Toxic clauses from 60. Under it, a four-part bento grid splits the risk into Financial exposure, Privacy & entry, Termination traps and Maintenance shifting. A money card works out the sums the lease itself states, so the tenant reads a figure, not a warning. Where a clause has no effect under local law, a separate card names the law.

**The document**

The whole lease, set in Source Serif, with every flagged clause marked by an irregular highlighter stroke drawn under the text, the way a pen would. Tap a mark to open the finding. A rail down the right edge shows where every mark sits in the lease.

**The reply**

Finding the problem is half the job; the tenant still has to answer the landlord. Redline drafts the reply as a formal email or a short WhatsApp message, in a friendly or a firm tone.

**Two flats, side by side**

Scans are saved on the phone. Open two and a butterfly chart sets their risk against each other across all four categories.

**Why the result can be trusted**

On-device OCR. ML Kit text recognition 16.0.1 is bundled in the APK (about 11 MB per ABI), so a scan works in airplane mode. The recognised text stays on the phone. Google's ML Kit library does send its own usage diagnostics (device, app and performance data, not the text), as its data disclosure states.

38 deterministic rules, not a model. The same lease gives the same findings on every run, and every flag points at the exact sentence that triggered it. When no rule fires, the report says "Nothing matched" rather than calling the lease clean.

Six places, cited. You choose the place, and the rules shift their thresholds to it and cite the law behind each one. Cells marked * are cited in the report but not yet checked automatically.

Place
Deposit cap
Deposit back within
Late fees
Law cited

California
1 month (2 for small landlords)
21 days
Fair estimate of the landlord's cost
Civil Code 1950.5, 1671

New York
1 month
14 days
Only after 5 days late; lesser of $50 or 5% *
General Obligations Law 7-108, Real Property Law 238-a

Massachusetts
1 month
30 days
None until rent is 30 days overdue *
M.G.L. ch. 186 § 15B

Texas
No cap
30 days after a forwarding address
12% (four homes or fewer) or 10%, after 2 full days
Property Code 92.103, 92.019

England
5 weeks' rent (6 at £50,000 a year or more) *
10 days from agreement
No fee; interest at most 3% over base rate, once 14 days late
Tenant Fees Act 2019

India
None in most states; the Model Tenancy Act proposes 2 months, Tamil Nadu sets 3
No figure used
No figure used
Model Tenancy Act 2021

Why not paste the lease into a chatbot? A chatbot can read a lease well and name the law, but the lease then sits on an AI company's servers. A lease carries names, home addresses, signatures, phone numbers and often the bank account the rent is paid into, and anything stored on someone else's server can be kept, reviewed or exposed in a breach. The chatbot's answer can also change from one run to the next, and nobody publishes how often it is right. Redline keeps the lease on the phone, gives the same flags every time, and its measured accuracy is below. That also makes it usable by someone checking a lease for another person, such as a tenant-union volunteer, who often cannot upload it.

Why rules instead of sentence embeddings. Thirty real lease clauses (twenty costly, ten benign) were labelled first, with two pass marks set in advance: the right category for at least 14 of 20, and true-positive margins at least three times the benign margin.

Approach
Costly clauses caught
Margin ratio (pass needs 3x)

Embeddings (Universal Sentence Encoder, two runs)
8 / 20
1.14x and 0.89x

Deterministic rules
20 / 20, benign 10 / 10
not applicable

The embeddings did worse than miss: a clause saying the tenant pays their own electricity scored higher than sixteen of the twenty costly clauses. The rules were written with those thirty clauses open, so that result only proves they fire where intended. The fairer numbers come from clauses they had never seen: 4 of 5 costly and 5 of 5 benign on a held-out set written afterwards in different wording, 18 of 26 costly on United States leases and 13 of 19 on English ones. The misses and their reasons are written up in eval/README.md.

**How RevenueCat is used**

The paywall comes after the scan, never before it. Charging before the scan would mean charging for something the reader has had no reason to want yet.

- Free: the scan, the gauge and its band, the bento grid, the clause counts, the first flagged clause in full (with its citation once a place is set), the money card's figures, and the topic of every locked finding ("Your deposit", "Leaving early"). A lease with one flagged clause, or text that is not a lease, is shown in full for free, so the paywall never asks money for nothing.

- Paid: every other clause in full, the email and WhatsApp drafts, sharing and PDF export, and the side-by-side comparison.

- Renter Pro, from the RevenueCat offering. One plan, sold as lifetime or monthly, opens every lease plus the comparison. Prices come from the store through the offering, never from the code. The price line says "From" only when more than one plan is on offer, and "paid once" only when no plan recurs.

- Entitlement full_report, read from CustomerInfo. The report is drawn locked until that answer arrives, and the buy button stays disabled while ownership is being checked, so nothing flashes open and nobody pays twice.

- Restore without an account. The RevenueCat app user ID is a salted SHA-256 hash of ANDROID_ID, which Android fixes per signing key, user and device. On an Android 16 emulator (API 36), Renter Pro survived an uninstall and reinstall: the report opened in full on first launch, before Restore was tapped.

- Offline first. Without a network the scan still runs and the paywall waits. An UpdatedCustomerInfoListener applies entitlement changes the moment they arrive, with no restart.

- No keys in the repo. BuildConfig.REVENUECAT_API_KEY comes from local.properties. Built without one, the app compiles and scans, and the paywall stays locked.

**Accessibility**

- Motion follows Android's animator duration scale, so with animations off, transitions are skipped.

- Screens are render-tested at 200% font scale.

- Rows and buttons hold a 48dp minimum touch target.

**Built from a clean clone**

git clone https://github.com/Kesav2k04/redline
cd redline
./gradlew :app:assembleDebug
./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest

230 unit tests, 0 failures, and the repo builds from a clean clone with no keys.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Programme dashboard — guide for judges**

URL: https://prufture.voltarut.com/dashboard
TestFlight (iOS, no account needed): https://testflight.apple.com/join/rBhq72De

- Sign in

- Open the URL and sign in with your Gmail account

- If asked for an invitation code, enter LIMA-TEAM-2026 or BOGOTA-OPS-2026. Staff accounts need it once; the browser remembers it.

- What to look at (left sidebar)

• Overview: this week's reports, how many are ready to review, how many still need another community report, and the programmes covered. Shows a review pipeline and the latest reports received.

• Reports: every report received, filterable by status, programme, area or date, plus text search. The URL keeps your filters. Open a report to see:

• its evidence summary and review timeline (signed on the phone → delivered → second community report → anchored as a public record);

• Open public record, the same page anyone can verify without an account.

• Use j / k to move between reports.

• Alerts: reports that need a decision or a follow-up.

• Programmes: coverage by programme and activity type.

• Communities: coverage by approximate region. Exact locations of households, schools or people are never shown.

• Coverage: a map of zones by report count. Only approximate 5-character cells, never a pin.

• Exports: the coarse report list as CSV, for offline review.

• Settings: what the dashboard shows and what it never shows.

- What you will never see
No reporter name, phone, email or identity; no exact coordinates; no original photos. A photo exists only if the reporter chose to share it; it is encrypted to the programme key and never shown here.

- Please avoid

• Programmes → Enrolment acts on the live programme pass group: it adds members and starts new rounds. Viewing it is fine. Please do not enrol commitments or start a new round.

• "Mark reviewed" on a report page is disabled in this version. Accept/reject review lives in the app (Me → Coordinator review). With the offer code, that screen shows a sample inbox you can freely accept and reject.

**Inspiration**

Field teams document work that matters—solar installations, vaccine refrigeration, water access—but
connectivity is unreliable and the people collecting evidence should not have to trade away their
privacy. Prufture started from a simple question: can a report remain useful and independently
verifiable without publishing the reporter's identity or exact location?

**What it does**

Prufture is an offline-first iPhone app for humanitarian field reporting. A volunteer can photograph
completed work, answer a short activity-specific checklist, and save the report with no account and
no network. The phone hashes and signs the evidence locally, queues it, and sends it when connectivity
returns.

The public record contains only the activity, date, a deliberately approximate area, and a verification
reference. Original photos remain on the device unless the reporter explicitly agrees to share them
with the programme team. Optional Face check and Programme pass flows add assurance without blocking
basic reporting.

Reporting is free. Programme coordinators can subscribe to the Coordinator plan through RevenueCat to
review reports, accept or reject them, restore purchases, redeem Apple offer codes, and draft an email
summary. This keeps the field workflow accessible while charging the organizational role that receives
ongoing operational value.

**How we built it**

The mobile app uses Expo, React Native, TypeScript, Expo Router, SQLite, SecureStore, and RevenueCat.
Capture, local signing, the offline queue, sync, and public attestation are separate layers so a vendor
outage never destroys the core reporting flow. The backend uses Express and Render; the public
verification site and coordinator dashboard use Next.js and Vercel. Report fingerprints are anchored
on Base Sepolia. Optional liveness uses AWS Rekognition, while the staff dashboard uses Clerk.

Every external integration returns a typed availability result instead of throwing through the user
flow. Sync retries are idempotent by proof hash. The public payload is intentionally small: proof hash,
task ID, coarse geohash, and capture time—never a name, email address, exact GPS point, photo, or face
image.

RevenueCat is a product boundary, not a decorative paywall. The app identifies the anonymous App Store
customer, loads monthly and annual offerings, purchases through Apple, restores entitlements, supports
offer-code redemption, and re-checks the coordinator entitlement server-side before returning protected
programme data.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest part was combining offline reliability, verifiability, and privacy without making the
interface feel technical. We narrowed what leaves the phone, built explicit pending/synced/attested
states, and made every optional assurance step degradable.

Store review added another real-world constraint: reviewers must understand why location and camera
access are needed, how the app works without accounts, and where the paid coordinator experience
begins. We built a complete no-login path, clear permission copy, restore purchases, offer-code
redemption, privacy and support pages, and a physical-device walkthrough.

We also found and fixed production-only integration problems: platform-specific RevenueCat keys,
server-side project scoping, unknown-customer behavior, and entitlement failures that must be shown as
unavailable rather than falsely interpreted as unpaid.

**Accomplishments that we are proud of**

- A full report can be captured, signed, and queued without connectivity.

- The reporter does not need an account, and no PII is written to the public record.

- RevenueCat subscriptions unlock a real coordinator workflow rather than a cosmetic screen.

- Original evidence remains under the reporter's control.

- Public verification is useful without exposing exact field locations.

- The iOS build runs on a physical iPhone through TestFlight.

**What we learned**

Privacy is strongest when enforced by data shape, not only promised in copy. Offline-first design is
more than caching: every state transition needs a visible, recoverable meaning. Monetization works best
here when it follows the value chain—volunteers report for free, while coordinators pay for the
operational review layer.

**What's next**

Next we will complete App Store publication, expand programme onboarding, harden multi-programme
coordinator workflows, and test with more field teams. We also plan to improve accessibility and
localization while keeping the same privacy rule: useful public proof, minimal public data.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**LinguaLeap: Bridging Global Conversations with Social AI Voice Matches**

**Inspiration**

Traveling across non-English speaking countries opened my eyes to a profound reality: language is the ultimate bridge to human connection. Sitting in local cafes, navigating transit, or asking for help, I repeatedly experienced the frustration and isolation of not being able to communicate in the most fundamental form. It hurts when you cannot share a basic interaction or express gratitude in a local tongue.

Existing language apps felt like isolated flashcard drills that prepared you for tests, not for real conversations. I was inspired to create LinguaLeap—a social, AI-powered interactive language learning app designed to transform language acquisition into live, voice-driven multiplayer games and community practice.

**What LinguaLeap Does & How We Built It**

LinguaLeap turns language practice into an engaging, real-time multiplayer experience:

- Voice Match Gameplay: Players challenge global opponents or friends in 10-round speech matches. Players tap START TURN, hold the microphone to speak in the target language, preview their live transcribed speech, and submit it for real-time AI evaluation.

- AI-Powered Evaluation: Powered by Google Gemini AI and Cloud Functions, the backend evaluates phonetic accuracy and translation context, awarding \(+10\) points per accurate turn.

- Global Radar & Friendly Matchmaking: Features a real-time global matchmaking radar matching players based on language, skill level, and geographical proximity.

- In-App Monetization via RevenueCat: Integrated using purchases_flutter to manage Free vs. Premium tiers. Premium subscribers unlock advanced language strength levels (Intermediate & Pro), unlimited topics, and full immersion group challenges.

**Tech Stack & Architecture**

- Frontend: Flutter & Dart (Cross-platform iOS & Android)

- State Management & UI: Provider, Shadcn UI (shadcn_ui), and custom Material themes

- In-App Purchases & Subscriptions: RevenueCat (purchases_flutter)

- Backend & Real-Time Sync: Firebase Authentication, Cloud Firestore, Cloud Storage, and FCM

- Serverless AI Logic: Firebase Cloud Functions (TypeScript) & Google Gemini AI API

- Speech Engine: speech_to_text with dynamic locale resolution and permission handling

**Mathematical Models & What We Learned**

Building LinguaLeap taught us deep insights into real-time audio pipeline management, serverless architecture, and subscription monetization with RevenueCat. 

**1. Gamification & Progression Model**

Player progression follows a discrete level step function based on cumulative scores:

$$\text{Level}(S) = \left\lfloor \frac{S}{1000} \right\rfloor$$

$$\text{Progress}(S) = \frac{S \bmod 1000}{1000}$$

Where the updated score after turn \(t\) is calculated as:

$$\S_{t+1}=S_t+10\cdot\mathbb{I}\left(\operatorname{AI_Validation}\left(\text{transcribed},\text{target}\right)=\text{true}\right)$$

Where \(\mathbb{I}( \cdot)\) is an indicator function returning \(1\) for correct pronunciations and \(0\) otherwise.

**2. Global Matchmaking Compatibility Score**

To ensure fair play, matchmaking compatibility $$\mathcal{M}(u_1, u_2)$$ between user \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) is formulated as:

$$\mathcal{M}(u_1, u_2) = \mathbb{I}\left(L_{u_1} = L_{u_2}\right) \times \mathbb{I}\left(S_{u_1} = S_{u_2}\right) \times \exp\left(-\gamma \cdot d(p_1, p_2)\right)$$

Where \(L\) represents learning language, \(S\) represents skill strength, \(d(p_1, p_2)\) is the Haversine geographical distance between location coordinates, and \(\gamma\) is a distance decay parameter.

**Challenges We Faced**

- Microphone Hardware Contention:

- Challenge: On Android/iOS, running background audio recorders concurrently with speech recognition caused hardware input locks, leading to empty transcriptions.

- Solution: We re-engineered the audio pipeline to grant exclusive, unhindered mic access to the speech-to-text engine with an asynchronous \(250\text{ ms}\) result buffer, guaranteeing seamless speech capture.

- Real-Time Multiplayer Timer Synchronization:

- Challenge: Syncing 30-second turn countdowns and waiting periods across devices with varying network latencies.

- Solution: Leveraged Firestore server timestamps to derive elapsed time dynamically relative to device clocks between two or multi players.

- Seamless Paywall Integration with RevenueCat:

- Challenge: Dynamically restricting advanced language strength levels (Intermediate/Pro) and unlimited group topics without degrading user experience.

- Solution: RevenueCat's SDK allowed us to query entitlement states effortlessly and present paywall screens smoothly when free users attempt to access premium features.

**What's Next for LinguaLeap**

We plan to introduce live AI speech pitch analysis, multi-party voice rooms, and localized offline lesson caching to continue making global conversations accessible to everyone.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

The work is done, but the day’s story is scattered.

Work happens throughout the day, but important details quickly become scattered across meetings, messages, notes, and memory.

A meeting creates a decision. A message creates an action item. A task gets completed. A blocker appears. A quick note is saved somewhere.

By the end of the day, these details are spread across conversations, notes, and memory. The user then has to search through everything and rebuild the story of the day.

I noticed this problem during my internship. People around me often spent long days in meetings, discussions, and follow-up work. Afterward, they still had to remember what was discussed, what decisions were made, and what needed to happen next.

The problem was not a lack of effort. It was the amount of information people had to keep in their heads.

That observation led me to build DaySumm.

The product changes the process from:

Work, forget, search, reconstruct

to:

Work, capture, continue, review

**What it does**

DaySumm helps users capture small moments while they are still fresh.

Users can record a voice note or write a quick entry. DaySumm then organizes those entries and turns them into a structured daily digest.

The digest includes:

- Key highlights

- Action items

- Decisions

- Blockers

- A concise status update

Voice entries are transcribed and translated into English when needed. Entries are automatically classified so users do not need to organize everything manually.

The experience follows a simple flow:

Capture a moment → Save it instantly → Organize it automatically → Review a clear daily story

DaySumm is not designed to become another task users have to maintain.

Its purpose is to help people remember the work they already did.

**How I built it**

DaySumm is an Android-first mobile app built with React Native, Expo, and TypeScript.

**Local-first capture**

New entries are saved locally using SQLite with a stable local ID, timestamp, source, and sync status.

This allows users to capture thoughts quickly, even when the network is unavailable. Entries remain available locally and are synchronized with Firestore when the connection returns.

**Voice processing**

Voice entries are sent through authenticated Firebase Cloud Functions.

Groq Whisper handles transcription and English translation. If transcription fails, DaySumm keeps a local fallback entry so the user's thought is not lost.

**Automatic classification**

Entries are classified into five useful categories:

- highlight

- actionItem

- blocker

- decision

- note

Users can edit entries and correct classifications. Manual corrections are protected from being overwritten by later automatic processing.

**AI-generated daily digest**

At the end of the day, the backend collects the user's entries and prepares them for digest generation.

The AI creates a structured summary with a headline, highlights, action items, decisions, blockers, and a status update.

The result is validated before being stored. If the user's entries have not changed, DaySumm reuses the existing digest instead of making another AI request.

**Notifications and subscriptions**

Firebase Cloud Functions handle scheduled digest generation and timezone-aware notifications through Firebase Cloud Messaging.

RevenueCat manages the free and Pro experience:

- Free users: limited daily AI digest generation

- Pro users: unlimited digests, longer digest history, and faster processing priority

RevenueCat manages the mobile offerings and purchases. The backend also verifies the user's Pro entitlement independently before allowing premium access.

This gives DaySumm a clear business model while keeping the core capture experience accessible.

**Challenges I ran into**

The first challenge was making capture feel effortless.

If recording a thought requires too many steps, users may postpone it and forget the detail. I designed the app around quick voice capture and short written entries.

The second challenge was reliability.

Entries need to be saved immediately, synchronized safely, and recovered when the device goes offline. I built a local queue so entries remain on the device until they are successfully synchronized.

Voice transcription also needed a safe fallback. If transcription fails, DaySumm keeps a local entry so the user's thought is not lost.

Another challenge was making the AI output trustworthy. Users should be able to review the result, correct the system, and keep control of their original information.

To support this, DaySumm allows users to edit entries, correct categories, delete information, and preserve manual corrections.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

I built a complete flow from capturing a thought to creating a daily digest.

The strongest parts of the current version are:

- Fast voice and text capture

- Offline-first local storage and synchronization

- Automatic transcription and classification

- Structured AI-generated daily digests

- Timezone-aware scheduled notifications

- RevenueCat-powered free and Pro access

I also tested DaySumm with one person for seven days.

They found it easier to record thoughts through voice and review the day from one place. They felt that the summary reduced the need to keep every detail in their head.

Friends gave a different type of feedback. They did not experience the same daily work pressure, but they still found the app useful for important notes, special occasions, and moments they wanted to remember.

This showed me that DaySumm has its strongest daily value for people who handle a large amount of work information, while the same experience can also support personal memory and reflection.

**What I learned**

Building DaySumm taught me that a focused product can begin with one repeated moment of frustration.

People do not always need more productivity features. Sometimes they need a better way to remember meaningful work without carrying the entire day in their heads.

I also learned that automation needs trust. A useful AI feature should not take control away from the user. It should make the user's information easier to understand while still allowing them to review and correct the result.

The strongest product direction came from connecting three simple ideas:

- Capture moments while they are fresh.

- Organize them automatically.

- Turn them into a clear story at the end of the day.

**What's next for DaySumm**

The current version focuses on building the habit of capturing moments through voice and quick writing.

The next step is to make this process more passive by connecting DaySumm with tools people already use, such as:

- Calendar and meeting tools

- Notion

- Slack

- GitHub

- Jira

- Other workplace systems

Instead of asking users to record every important moment manually, DaySumm could collect relevant context from their existing workflow and create a more complete daily story.

The long-term vision is to make the end of the workday feel less like a memory test.

Capture work while it happens. End your day with the story already clear.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/261/357/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/261/357/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/261/358/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/261/358/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/261/359/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/261/359/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/261/360/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/261/360/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

.io games are the purest "one more round" loop — but most of them are grim tanks and snakes. We wanted that same instant, skill-based arena feel with characters you actually want to be: a squishy cat, a tanky pig, a glass-cannon rabbit. Cute on the outside, real dodge-and-aim on the inside.

**What it does**

- Instant real-time multiplayer arena. No sign-up, no tutorial — type a nickname, tap Fight!

- Eat snacks to level up, then pick Damage / Fire rate / Speed / Max HP. Take down rivals, climb the top-10 board, respawn 3 seconds after you fall.

- Rooms of 12 are always filled with bots so the arena is never empty; the server scales to 20 rooms.

- Works offline. If the server is unreachable you drop straight into smart bots and get a one-tap "Join online room" the moment it's back.

- Three free animals (🐱 cat, 🐶 dog, 🐷 pig) and a one-time Premium Animals unlock (🐰 rabbit, 🦆 duck, 🦊 fox).

- Korean/English UI, mobile touch controls (left stick + right aim/fire), and compatibility down to old Android WebViews.

**How we built it**

- A shared ES-module simulation (shared/) runs identically on the Node server and in the browser — same physics, same bots, same level curve. That is what makes the offline→online handoff seamless.

- Server: Node + ws, 30 Hz tick, 20 Hz snapshots, client-side interpolation for smooth 60 fps rendering. Pellets are sent at 5 Hz as deltas to cut bandwidth.

- Android app is a thin WebView (WebViewAssetLoader) around the same game with a small JS↔Java bridge.

- RevenueCat powers monetization: one product (premium_animals) maps to one entitlement (premium). Unlock state is derived only from customerInfo.entitlements["premium"].isActive — so restores, reinstalls and device changes just work, and the game never trusts local state.

- Free-tier infrastructure: Render for the server, GitHub Pages for the web build, and a 10-minute GitHub Actions ping to keep the free dyno warm.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Old Android WebViews (Chrome 53) choke on ?./?? and CSS inset/gap — we rewrote those paths so the game runs on cheap devices.

- ES modules can't load from file:// inside a WebView, so assets are served over https://appassets.androidplatform.net.

- A single malformed WebSocket message used to kill the whole server. Inputs are now sanitized and dispatch is fenced — with a regression test.

- Free-tier cold starts made first impressions "bot mode". Solved with a keep-alive plus a graceful offline→online handoff instead of an error screen.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Shipped to 177 countries with live multiplayer on a $0/month server.

- 19 automated tests covering combat, growth, bots, room isolation, bandwidth and input hardening.

- The offline mode isn't a fallback screen — it's the full game, so the app is never "broken".

**What we learned**

Deriving entitlement purely from RevenueCat instead of caching a local flag removed an entire class of "I paid but lost it" bugs. And on a free tier, perceived latency is a design problem, not just an infra one.

**What's next for PawPaw Arena**

Seasonal skins as further RevenueCat products, a weekly leaderboard, and private friend rooms.

**Note for judges**

The game is free with no ads and no sign-up — all core gameplay, online multiplayer and the three starter animals are fully playable without any purchase. The single in-app product unlocks three extra animals that are side-grades, not power-ups, so judging does not require a purchase. A promo code can be provided on request.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Most consumer travel applications are built on an unrealistic premise: permanent, high-bandwidth cellular connectivity. 

When travel disruptions strike—canceled underground subway connections, delayed airport tarmac transfers, or sudden rainstorms—they invariably happen where roaming and cellular signals fail completely. Traditional apps present an endless loading spinner because their rerouting engines are tethered to remote servers. 

I built WayPoint as a solo developer to flip this architecture: turning the device itself into the autonomous, single source of operational truth.

**What It Does**

WayPoint is an edge-first iOS travel co-pilot engineered to function continuously with zero bytes of cellular data:

- ~260ms On-Device Panic Pivot: When bad weather or transit cancelations occur, WayPoint calculates alternative topological routing directly on Apple Silicon in sub-second time.

- AES-256 Secure Enclave Ticket Vault: Offline boarding passes and transit barcodes are encrypted locally on hardware. Turnstiles and airport gates scan instantly in airplane mode without remote authentication handshakes.

- Live Journey Telemetry: Real-time platform track numbers and departure countdowns stream natively to the Dynamic Island and Apple Watch via ActivityKit.

- Next Gen Architecture: Designed for resilient transit without ongoing server reliance.

**How I Built It**

- Frontend & UX: Built natively in SwiftUI with fluid gesture interactions, tactile haptics, and Dynamic Island Live Activities.

- Local Data & Graph Solver: Implemented using SwiftData on-device models to traverse pre-compiled transit graphs and station topologies.

- Hardware Security: Leveraged Apple's LocalAuthentication and CryptoKit to interface with the Secure Enclave for biometric-locked AES-256 pass storage.

- Monetization Architecture: Architected with RevenueCat to manage multi-city offline vector graph downloads and premium vault features (waypoint_pro).

- Web Simulation Sandbox: Deployed a synchronized Next.js simulation engine to Vercel to allow judges and beta testers to test the disruption state machine directly in the browser.

**Challenges I Faced**

- Local Graph Traversal Overhead: Optimizing Dijkstra and topological routing algorithms to run within strict mobile memory footprints while executing in under 300 milliseconds.

- Offline Hardware Encryption: Guaranteeing that pass barcodes decrypt instantly via Secure Enclave without causing UI stutter at turnstile scanners.

- Graceful Degradation: Designing an architecture that seamlessly balances cached topological layers with live network states when connectivity occasionally returns.

**What I Learned**

Treating offline mode as an active edge-computing system rather than passive static caching transforms the entire user experience. Mobile apps do not need to rely on remote server round-trips for core decision-making when local silicon can handle complex graph evaluation natively.

**What's Next for WayPoint**

- Multi-modal offline routing including ferry networks and bike-share hubs.

- Rollout to my first 50 TestFlight beta testers.

- Production integration of RevenueCat in-app subscriptions across global city graph packs.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**💡 Inspiration**

I'm someone who always loves capturing every moment of life, every emotion, and everything I want to remember so that at the end of the day—or some day in the past, maybe a week, a month, or a year later - I can look back at those moments, the feelings back then, and what I needed to remember, as well as quickly share what I've been through with my friends. Sounds interesting, right?

Currently, we have camera apps, but our busy lives clutter the camera gallery with so many things (photos, screenshots... ahhh, way too many things). Note-taking apps require too much time to organize, format, and make them look good, and when we want to share, we have to filter them out and search for beautiful templates to post.

I realized that many people also want an app to aggregate and quickly note down their emotions at that moment, quickly capture or record everything, and when it's time to share, they can just pick a ready-made template they like. Plus, it helps look after mental health and build a habit through streaks (just like other social media platforms) to preserve beautiful memories in life, especially now when everyone has a tendency toward nostalgia.

=&gt; That is why Loggoo was born.

**✨ What it does**

Loggoo is a app that helps you to note down your life with captured images, notes and moods, share your life with your friends via beautiful frame, take care of your mental health and help you to keep your memories alive.

Features in Loggoo:

- Capture in seconds: Take a photo / Record video, choose one from your library, tap a mood, or write a short note.

- 24-hour visual timeline: Photos, moods, videos, and notes appear together in the order they happened.

- Frame Studio: Turn a day into a shareable story or post using built-in layouts available at launch. New seasonal and holiday-themed templates are added regularly.

- Mood calendar and trends: Review how you felt throughout the month and explore patterns and advices across weeks and months.

- Home Screen widgets: See your current day, mood, or streak and jump directly into logging.

- Cute mood face packs: Personalize every mood across the timeline, calendar, widgets, and exported frames.

**🛠️ How I built it**

Initially, I planned to use Flutter due to my extensive cross-platform experience. However, I decided to bet on Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform to test its ecosystem maturity, performance, and its integration with deep native features like camera hardware, video playback, and home widgets. They are things that Flutter does not yet handle well, requiring reliance on external libraries.

Tech Stack:

- Core & UI: Kotlin Multiplatform & Compose Multiplatform

- Camera & Capture: CameraX (Android) & AVFoundation (iOS) for native recording.

- Video Playback: Media3 (Android) & AVKit (iOS) for timeline playback.

- Home Widgets: Jetpack Glance (Android) & WidgetKit (iOS).

- Data Sync: CloudKit for iOS cloud backup and sync.

- Monetization: RevenueCat for robust in-app purchases, yeahh 100% percent of course

- OneSignal: for automated user journeys, personalized notifications and campaign notification.

- Analytics & Stability: Firebase Analytics & Crashlytics, configured using my own custom open-source CLI setup tool, auto register app to Firebase and download configuration files quickly

- I also built landing page and frame generator with Astro to transfer beautiful frames to Loggoo too.

- And Thank you Claude Design for helping me on giving idea about color palatte for my design system and helping me to create beautiful frames for Loggoo.

**🧗 Challenges I ran into**

**Camera speed and quality, OMGGG but it so fun and real technical challenging**

"Snap it, mood it, frame it" only works if the camera is fast on both Android and iOS, and the photo still looks good. The usual path is shoot, wait for the phone to process the picture, then show it. That wait killed the snap, especially on a slower Android phone.

So I skipped that processing. A tap keeps the frame already on screen, crops it square, saves it, and shows that same picture at once. It stays clear because the camera takes a middle size, not a giant file and not a soft one, and in the dark it shoots a little slower so the photo stays bright.

Here is a gif of Loggoo snapping:

Then the iPhone 17 front camera showed up already upright, while older iPhones lie on their side. The app still rotated every photo 90 degrees, so those selfies came out sideways. I left the new sensor alone and kept rotating the older ones. Photos, video, and the cover image stand upright now.

Of every challenge in Loggoo, the camera is the one I had the most fun with, really technical challenging but so fun. I shared the result on X

**Beautiful frames but different densities for different devices**

The same frame had to look the same on every phone. It did not. Android and iPhone measure the screen differently, a small phone is not a big one, and a bigger system text size shoved the layout around.

So a frame no longer follows the device. Every template sits on one fixed canvas, and system text size cannot blow it up. When you share, that same layout is drawn again as a full-size image, so the preview and the picture you send match. So nicee when I share frames to my friends, they look the same on their phones.

**A data bridge for widgets, written from scratch**

Home screen widgets were new territory for me, on both platforms. A widget does not live inside the app. It cannot just peek at the journal. Android and iOS each want their own little bridge, and nothing off the shelf did both. So I wrote it. The app saves a small snapshot of the day, the mood, and the streak, and each widget reads that same snapshot. Log a moment, and the tile on the home screen catches up. Same story on both phones, two completely different doors. Here is day 18 of me with my Loggoo widgets

**Keeping the timeline smooth with photos, video, and voice**

A day in Loggoo is a long scroll of heavy things: photos, video, and voice notes. Load every full file while you flick, and the list stutters. On a slower phone it stops feeling like a journal.

So the list only does the work for what is on screen. Small photos use a light preview, and the big tile is the one that reads the real picture. A video plays only while its card is showing, then lets go, so two clips never run at once. A voice note draws a saved waveform instead of opening the recording just to scroll past it. The day stays full. The scroll stays light. Compose Multiplatform helps me to achieve this for both Android and iOS

**Removed from the App Store, and the appeal**

This one is not a fun engineering puzzle. Apple says Loggoo is misleading because the features were switched after review. I do not agree. There is no feature flag in the app. What they reviewed is what shipped. I am appealing. The iOS app had already been live for more than a month when it was removed from the store. I am actively looking for help and pushing the appeal, because the Android build is still up and the iPhone one should be too. I'm not sure if it will be approved again, but I'm trying my best. Here is day 22 of me when Apple removed Loggoo from the App Store.

**🏆 Accomplishments that I're proud of**

**App Performance and beyond expectations**

What I am proud of is that Loggoo launching is fast and smooth. The native pieces run cleanly because of Kotlin Multiplatform. I bet on it, and it held up. Camera, video recording, and home widgets all work better than I expected, thank you JetBrains.

**Have great feedbacks from users**

The first time I tried it on Reddit, I got a lot of feedback. People said the idea had promise, the UI was striking, and the templates were beautiful. They also asked for a lot of features. I built many of the ones they asked for, and they were happy with them, here are their feedbacks:

Great rating number on App Store too (before Apple removed it :)) )

**I got my first paying users**

This one is honestly the happiest. I got my first paying users. They really like Loggoo, and it actually solves the problem they had. Here is my happy moment on X

**I built an open source CLI tool to share with the community**

While building Loggoo I realized that configuring Firebase for a KMP project is genuinely tiring. You register the app, download the configuration files, and set them up for each project. It felt like work that should not take that long, so I built a tool that does it automatically. It made Firebase setup for KMP fast and easy. Flutter already has something like this. This one is for KMP. 

And it is 🔥 kmpfire_cli, an open source CLI for quickly configuring Firebase on a KMP project. Here is the repository and my story on X.

**OneSignal helps me alot in user engagement and retention**

I never thought about user engagement retention via notification in before, but OneSignal helps me a lot. OneSignal provides me a lot of features to help me to engage with users and retain them through automated user journeys, personalized notifications and campaign notification. I can easily send notifications to:

- Gently remind users to log their record to keep streak.

- Notify users about new frames, collaborator updates, and new features.

- Engage users with targeted campaigns, journeys event like recap week.

- Notify them to look back at their previous week or month activity

This helps users have habit to log their record daily, and keep them engaged with the app. OneSignal is my hero, thank you for your help. Here is my story on X

**And I might be the first person in Shipaton to get removed by Apple LOL**

This one was not on the plan. The iOS app had already been live for more than a month when Apple said it was misleading, because the features had been switched after review. I do not agree. Loggoo has no feature flags at all. What they reviewed is what shipped. I am appealing, and the iOS build is off the store. Android is still up and doing fine. If Shipaton had a prize for "removed first," I might be leading it, and I am still trying to get the iOS app back. Let's look back my 22rd day.

**📚 What I learned**

- Cross platform but still native feeling, Kotlin Multiplatform / Compose Multiplatform is a great choice. From Android native developer and Flutter developer, now I have a new weapon to build cross platform apps with native feeling and performance. Write own native code for both platforms and share the codebase between them is interesting and challenging.

- Before adding a feature, ask whether users actually need it. Listen to their feedback and try it more than once before the final call. A personal experience is what sets the app apart, keeps people, and helps it grow.

- Building the app can be fast. Getting people to actually find it is the long part, and that means learning marketing and promotion. As a developer, this is the lesson I keep coming back to.

**🚀 What's next for Loggoo: Photo Journal & Mood**

I have a lot of plans for Loggoo, but here are the top 5:

- Improve the app performance and stability: The app is still new, and there are still a lot of things to improve. I need to improve the app performance and stability to make the app more reliable and user-friendly.

- Marketing and Promotion: Yeahhh to be honest, marketing is really hard, I need to learn a lot. Currently I'm learning some marketing strategies, find some "Study with me" or "Lifestyle" TikTokers / Hot Instagram to collaborate with me to create content for Loggoo.

- Timeline collaborator feature: I want to add a feature to allow users to collaborate with each other on the timeline. Users can add each other as collaborators and see each other's timeline and keep memories together. This is really interesting and challenging, I need to think about how to implement it.

- Collab with brands in Frames: For frames, I created a Studio that brings special frames to Loggoo to expand the frames libraries, I'm thinking about collab with brands to create frames in Loggoo, this will help brands to increase brand recognition and Loggoo to increase revenue.

- Maximize the power of OneSignal: OneSignal helps me a lot in understanding user journey and personalized notifications, help users to have habit to log their record daily, and keep them engaged with the app. They have alot features that I haven't even touched yet, I need to explore and use them to the fullest.

**💬 Final words**

Thank you for reading this far. I am grateful to be part of Shipaton, and glad I got to tell the Loggoo story here. I would love to hear what you think of the app, and I am excited to keep building what comes next.

Dung Nguyen Minh - @dzungngminh

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Independent financial advisors, family office managers, and private wealth consultants are responsible for managing multi-crore portfolios while adhering to stringent fiduciary and privacy standards. Yet, the software ecosystem available to them is frustratingly polarized: it is either legacy, clunky enterprise software built in the 2000s, or disconnected personal finance spreadsheets that fail to impress high-net-worth clients.

We asked ourselves: Why can't wealth advisors have a tool that combines the raw execution speed of an institutional Bloomberg terminal, the privacy of a hardware crypto wallet, and the elegance of an executive luxury dashboard?

That vision led to Asset Array: a private wealth operating system engineered with an obsidian and champagne gold aesthetic, end-to-end zero-knowledge encryption, and a built-in Gemini-powered portfolio intelligence co-pilot.

**What it does**

Asset Array is an executive-grade wealth management CRM, portfolio rebalancer, and client reporting suite:

*Executive Portfolio Command: Real-time visibility into Total Assets Under Advisory (AUA), asset allocation distributions (Equities, Fixed Income, Real Estate, Alternatives, Cash), client risk profiles, and urgent follow-up deadlines.
*AI Portfolio Co-Pilot (Google Gemini): Analyzes individual client holdings against macroeconomic market sentiment to generate institutional-grade rebalancing rationales, risk commentary, and tailored client updates ready for WhatsApp or Email dispatch.
*Executive PDF Report Studio: Creates high-resolution, branded portfolio appraisal summaries on-device using custom HTML-to-PDF compilation, complete with fiduciary disclaimers and allocation charts.
*Client Dossiers & Relationship Hub: Centralizes investor contact preferences, portfolio holdings, liquidity requirements, and private meeting notes.
*Universal Desktop & Mobile Workspace: Automatically adapts to the device form factor — providing a wide-screen command center with keyboard shortcuts (⌘K, ⌘B, ⌘L, Esc) on desktop (≥1024px), and a tactile bottom-sheet mobile app on smartphones.
*Zero-Knowledge Cloud Sync: Client financial data is encrypted on-device via AES-256 before leaving the browser, ensuring only the advisor holds the decryption keys.
*Pro Fiduciary Monetization (RevenueCat): Seamless in-app subscription paywall gating premium features like the Gemini AI Co-Pilot and Unlimited PDF Exports across Monthly and Annual plans.

**How we built it**

We implemented a modern, scalable, decoupled architecture spanning client, edge, and cloud:

*Frontend Framework: Built with React Native / Expo utilizing a custom Platform Adaptation Layer (PAL). This allows a single, unified TypeScript codebase to render natively on iOS, Android, and the Web without code duplication.

*Design & Aesthetics: Styled in custom Vanilla React Native Stylesheets using an Obsidian (#030712) & Champagne Gold (#E0A84C) palette, complete with glassmorphism cards and responsive modal windows.

*Monetization Engine: Integrated RevenueCat (react-native-purchases) to manage subscriptions, verify entitlements (pro_advisor), and orchestrate the Pro paywall UI.

*AI Engine: Powered by Google Gemini 2.5 Flash via @google/genai on the backend, processing portfolio summaries with structured JSON schemas and low-latency token generation.

*Backend API: Built with Node.js and Express, featuring custom rate limiting, HMAC-SHA256 JWT access and refresh token rotation, and audit logging.

Cloud Infrastructure & Zero-Cost Production Stack:
Frontend: Hosted on Firebase Hosting Global CDN (https://asset-array.web.app).
Backend API: Containerized and hosted as a live Web Service on Render (https://assetarray.onrender.com).
Database: Multi-region MongoDB Atlas (M0) replica set.

**Challenges we ran into**

*Responsive Dual-Ergonomics (Mobile vs. Desktop): Financial dashboards are information-dense. Mobile needs bottom-sheets and thumb-accessible navigation, while desktop needs persistent sidebars and centered dialog modals. We solved this by developing responsive layout hooks and centering abstractions that adapt layout and animations at runtime based on viewport width (≥1024px).

*True Zero-Knowledge Encryption: We needed multi-device synchronization without the cloud database ever knowing client net worth, holding names, or portfolio balances. We architected client-side AES-256 payload encryption with PBKDF2 key derivation; the database only stores encrypted ciphertext blobs with hash integrity checks.

*Web Vector Font Hydration: When compiling Expo to pure static web bundles, vector icon glyphs often render as missing character boxes. We solved this by creating a startup font-loader routine (Font.loadAsync) that dynamically injects font-faces into the browser DOM before rendering.

*Deploying a Free, Permanent Production Stack: Setting up scalable hosting without credit card billing was a major puzzle. By pairing Firebase Hosting for the frontend, Render for the containerized backend, and MongoDB Atlas for database storage, we built a 100% free, 24/7 accessible production environment.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

*Flawless Production Deployment: Deployed a complete three-tier production stack that is publicly live, responsive, and secure: asset-array.web.app.

*Enterprise Security First: Built a system where sensitive client financial data is cryptographically protected with AES-256 before transit.

*RevenueCat Monetization Integration: Engineered a high-converting, luxury subscription paywall with native tier toggling and instant entitlement unlocking.

*Luxury Executive Aesthetic: Created a UI that feels premium and authoritative — steering away from cookie-cutter AI apps to build something a real private banker would proudly open in front of an Ultra-High-Net-Worth client.

**What we learned**

Power of Cross-Platform React Native Web: React Native Web combined with the PAL pattern can deliver desktop experiences that rival native web frameworks when designed with keyboard accessibility and responsive layouts.

Subscription Mechanics with RevenueCat: Gaining hands-on mastery of entitlements, offerings, and sandbox testing flows taught us how to design monetization flows that feel natural rather than intrusive.
AI Prompt Engineering for Strict Financial Output: Instructing Gemini to output strict JSON schemas with fallback handling ensures the UI never crashes even when processing unpredictable portfolio data.

**What's next for Asset Array**

*Plaid / Account Aggregator API Integration: Automated real-time balance syncing from bank accounts, demat accounts, and mutual fund central depositories.

*Multi-Advisor Team Permissions: Role-based access control (RBAC) allowing senior partners to delegate client accounts to junior associates while retaining audit trails.

*Client Portal Companion App: A read-only, end-to-end encrypted mobile app for clients to view quarterly performance reports, approve rebalancing requests, and chat securely with their advisor.

*Native App Store & Play Store Release: Packaging the existing codebase into standalone iOS and Android binaries to publish on the Apple App Store and Google Play Store via RevenueCat production keys.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I have always had a deep passion for space exploration games, especially the thrill of touching down and surviving on alien worlds no one has ever charted or imagined before. But in the mobile gaming landscape, that wonder is almost always broken. Titles either demand flagship hardware that overheats budget phones, or lock the experience behind aggressive paywalls, energy meters, and predatory microtransactions.

CIVITUS was born from a personal ambition, to combine what I love most from games like SA2138 and Waste of Space into something I had never dared attempt before. I set out to build a full 3D procedural space survival game for Android with living biomes, procedural terrain, strange flora, reactive alien fauna, and distinct planetary ecosystems where every world and star system feels genuinely unique.

Crucially, it had to run on everyday low-end hardware without loading screens or fake backdrops. Integrating RevenueCat became the cornerstone of this vision: proving that an ambitious mobile 3D game can deliver real scientific grounding, procedural wonder, and an uncompromised survival loop through an ethical, transparent purchasing architecture that treats players with respect.

**What It Does**

The player controls an astronaut surviving on procedural spherical planets with a fixed diorama radius of (R = 160\text{m}).

Key gameplay systems:

- Radial Gravity: Omnidirectional physics anchored to planetary mass centers, eliminating gimbal lock during global traversal.

- Barometric Atmosphere: Density calculated via the physical scale-height formula (P(h) = P_0 \cdot e^{-h/H}), dynamically driving aerodynamic drag, engine ISP, wind, and sky Rayleigh extinction.

- Dynamic Ecosystems: 21 procedural creature archetypes (terrestrial, aquatic, aerial) with physical interactions (lifting, carrying, and aquatic rescue mechanics).

- Spacecraft & Life Support: Modular interior modules (pilot seat, hyperdrive core, oxygen generator, gravity gimbal, storage bin, crafting workbench) requiring salvaged components for orbital departure.

Monetization Architecture (RevenueCat):

- Entitlement no_ads ($0.99 USD): Permanently suppresses all interstitial transmissions.

- Entitlement planet_editor ($1.99 USD): Unlocks sandbox generation sliders (noise scale, sea level thresholds, atmospheric composition).

- Entitlement full_game ($2.99 USD): Founder license unlocking all sandbox tools and advanced planetary sectors.

- In-Game Economy: Luna Coins earned through mineral salvage or optional 3-second diegetic radio transmissions (rewarded callbacks).

**How We Built It**

- Engine: Godot 4.7.2 Stable using GDScript and custom GLSL PBR shaders.

- Procedural Planetary Mesh: Cubed-sphere topology generating 12,288 continuous triangles with multi-octave simplex elevation noise, coastal thresholds, and oceanic depressions ((-14\text{m}) to (+24\text{m})).

- Normal & Wave Calculation: Analytical wave derivatives and view-space normal perturbation to ensure camera-angle invariant sunlight reflection on fluid surfaces.

- RevenueCat SDK Wrapper: A custom RevenueCatManager singleton abstracting Google Play Billing and RevenueCat REST endpoints, paired with an offline state machine for deterministic local testing.

- Automated Testing: Developed strictly under Test-Driven Development (TDD). Over 640 headless assertions validate movement math, atmospheric decay, craft recipes, and entitlement unlock states without requiring graphical display servers.

**Technical Challenges**

- Cubed-Sphere Seams: Normalizing cube faces to a sphere created vertex stretching and tangent discontinuities at the corners. Resolved by applying elliptical projection and continuous 3D noise sampling.

- View-Space Normal Lighting: Initial ocean and terrain shaders had normal vectors sliding across camera angles. Fixed by transforming perturbed surface normals directly into view space before lighting passes.

- Offline Entitlement Resilience: Implementing reliable local caching so players venturing outside network coverage retain their unlocked entitlements without interruption.

**Metrics & Accomplishments**

- 60 FPS performance maintained on baseline hardware targets (ARMv7 32-bit architecture).

- Zero-freeze asynchronous chunk generation during suborbital entry.

- 640+ automated headless test assertions executing in under 1.2 seconds with 0 failures.

- Non-coercive freemium design: full base game completion without paywalls.

**What We Learned**

Architecting a clean bridge between an open-source game engine (Godot GDScript) and the RevenueCat ecosystem, decoupling game logic from store verification through event-driven entitlement listeners.

**What Is Next**

- Gas giants with physical ring navigation and atmospheric skimming.

- Surface base construction modules.

- Additional cosmetic spacesuit configurations integrated into RevenueCat offerings.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

My main inspiration was the people around me:

- the people who worked hard for their income

- the people who are the base of the economy

- the people who put their blood and sweat into their work

- the people who truly deserve something built for them
Many people like this fall into debt and face financial problems. Nidhi aims to make their lives better by helping them become financially disciplined, providing some form of prescriptive financial literacy, and providing them a potential safety net against the problems and hurdles that come in their life.

**What it does**

Nidhi is literally the simplest financial app for people who deserve it the most: the kirana shop owners, the farmers, the people who truly put in all their hard work just to make our lives better and are the base of our economy.

Nidhi has mainly these features :

- Monthly savings goals and locked savings to ensure that money is saved.

- Emergency fund deposits to ensure that, in case of any emergencies, money is always there and debt isn't required

- Tracking their loans and other debt to ensure that they know how much money they truly have that they can spend without thinking.

- A daily log for tracking how much they have spent that day which includes a voice feature for documentation 

- Describing, not prescribing, their spending habits and analyzing their spending trends 

Nidhi also includes notifications and multilingual support to ensure everyone is included. My only monetization is ads.I don't want our users to pay a single rupee. They already work hard for their money, and this app should empower them to manage and be mindful of it.

**How we built it**

I built it using GLM 5.2. I used Gemini and Claude to engineer the prompts, and I manually entered the commands and ensured that the environments and the assets were created. For the assets, I used AI tools such as Gemini for image generation. I ran the prototype on a development build, scanned the QR code, and actively tested and fixed the app. This experience taught me a lot about how code and APIs work and how mobile apps are made and tested. We used mainly two integrations: RevenueCat for ad monitoring and Sarvam for voice API. 

**Challenges we ran into**

I ran into multiple challenges. 

- The first challenge was that the dependencies weren't matching. For this, I had to research the compatibility of the dependencies.

- The second was the UI; I had to actively ask GLM to fix the UI to ensure that it was built for a phone, not for a website, and make it premium for our users

- The third was the Expo build. While I was loading my app, I had a Gradle error due to some dependency mismatches and also because of other requirements. I spent a lot of time on this, and it took a lot of time to debug. 

- The Sarvam gateway wasn't working. This was one of the most challenging errors to solve because even GLM couldn't figure it out. I had to research and fix the problem with Claude. Claude recognized the bug immediately and helped rectify it by changing the code. I ran the app's test servers once again and monitored the logs to make sure that all the languages were being parsed and transcribed properly.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I am happy to say that my app successfully runs without any major issues. Despite the challenges with the APIs and the problems I faced, I am happy that I overcame them and I was able to deliver a properly functioning app with integrations.

I hope that this app can make a real impact in the world by serving the people in need. I spent a whole 2 weeks brainstorming the perfect idea so that I could make an app that makes a real impact in the world, not just another generic app. I feel truly accomplished by shipping this project successfully despite multiple hurdles.

**What we learned**

I learned that app making requires a lot of patience and a lot of trial and error. You should be really careful and patient even when building with AI. I also learned that when making a product, the execution and the ideation matter equally. I just didn't want to make another generic app. I wanted to make an app that actually serves a purpose and an audience that is actually underserved. Hence, I have the dialogue: serve the underserved. This journey has taught me a lot about being patient and resilient in times of challenges, and it also taught me how to make a mobile app from scratch using AI. 

**What's next for Nidhi**

I hope to take this app beyond India, throughout the world, so everyone can benefit. I want to also add a banking integration where people are actually forced to save their money to ensure that everybody has financial security in their lives. The whole goal of making this app was to make an impact in the world for the people who do the most and work the most behind the scenes, and are basically the foundation of our economy and the modern world. They deserve financial security and a promising future.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

The idea came from a real experience: while boarding a matatu, M-Pesa stopped working, leaving me unable to pay my fare. This made us think of a more reliable, dedicated digital payment solution for public transport. That’s how Transit Pay was born.
Inspired by cashless transport systems in other countries, we developed Transit Pay — a platform where passengers can preload money into a digital wallet, scan a QR code when boarding, and have their fare calculated based on the distance travelled.

**What it does**

Transit Pay allows passengers to:
-Preload money into a digital wallet.
-Scan a QR code when boarding a matatu.
-Track their journey and calculate fares based on distance.
-View nearby matatu stages and get fare estimates.
-View their trip and transaction history.
-Pay without using cash.

**How we built it**

Transit Pay was built using Flutter and Dart for the mobile application, with Firebase providing the backend infrastructure.
Flutter & Dart — mobile app development
Firebase Authentication — user authentication
Cloud Firestore — storing users, vehicles, trips, wallets and transactions
Firebase Cloud Functions — secure backend operations and payment settlement
Firebase Storage — file storage
Geolocator — location and distance tracking
QR code technology — vehicle identification and trip initiation
Git & GitHub — version control and collaboration

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was designing a secure wallet and transaction system. We needed to make sure that passengers could not directly manipulate their wallet balances from the app.
We also faced challenges with:
-Configuring Firebase Cloud Functions.
-Setting up Firestore security rules and indexes.
-Handling authentication and connectivity issues during development.
-Connecting different parts of the application, including the wallet, trips, QR scanning and backend services.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud of turning the idea into a working mobile application rather than keeping it as just a concept. A structure that can be expanded for real-world payment integrations.
We successfully implemented:

-Passenger and driver experiences.
-Digital wallet functionality.
-QR-based vehicle identification.
-Trip tracking.
-Transaction records.
-Firebase backend integration.

**What we learned**

Building Transit Pay taught us that developing an application is much more than designing screens.

We learned how different technologies work together to create a complete system, particularly Flutter, Firebase, Firestore, Cloud Functions, authentication, QR codes and location services.

We also learned the importance of security when dealing with financial data. Operations such as changing wallet balances should not simply be trusted to the mobile application; they need to be handled securely on the backend.

Most importantly, we learned how to take an idea, break it into smaller technical problems, troubleshoot those problems, and gradually turn the idea into a working product.

**What's next for Transit Pay**

Offline functionality for areas with poor network connectivity.
M-Pesa integration for seamless top-ups.
Expand to more matatu routes and stages.
Improve fare accuracy and real-world testing.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I've collected trading cards for years, and I also run a small vintage card business on the side. Between the two, I'm constantly checking what I own, what I'm missing from a set and what something is worth. For a long time that meant a mix of spreadsheets (I know, right!) and apps that didn't do everything that I needed. Alongside that, they we're pleasant to use - they were either full of advertising, poorly designed UX or not performant due to hybrid frameworks.

I wanted an app that had a range of features in one place that worked fast, while also working offline at card shows where signal tends to not be great. From all of my wants and needs, this is where Sleevd was born.

**What it does**

Sleevd is a trading card collection tracker for Android and iOS. Across a range of popular trading card games, collectors can browse every single set and track the cards, graded slabs and sealed products that they own.

Features of the app include:

Card scanning - use your camera to scan cards and graded slabs, this saves you manually searching for cards one by one.

Market Pricing - view market prices for cards, graded slabs and sealed products across all conditions and grades.

Grading Populations - view population data for graded slabs, so you know exactly how many cards have been rated at each grade with your chosen vender.

Portfolio management - track the growth of your trading card and its value over time

Grading ROI - spot opportunities to grow your portfolio from grading valuable cards in your collection

Collection Analytics - see complete analytics for your collection spread across games and sets, while also being able to spot behaviours in your collection habits

Sales Management - keep track of any sales you make directly in the app! This allows you to see your profit from sales over time, which comes in handy to know if you're making more than your spending!

Trade Management - nothing hurts more than getting ripped off in a trade, so you can use the trade manager to calculate if a trade is fair based on the current market value of the cards on offer!

Budgeting - collecting is fun but its easy to get carried away in the moment. Use the budgeting feature to create budgets for your spending and get notified for when you hit/exceed this.

Pull Tracker - when opening packs, bundles and boxes, its helpful to know your hit rate and what products perform better. The Pull Tracker allows you to record the product you've opened, what you got from it and then view the returns of your pulls.

Achievements - to help users explore and learn about different parts of the app we built achievements. Get rewarded for completing different tasks, growing your collection and trying features of the app!

Release Calendar - so you can grow your collection, you need to know when the new sets are coming out. The release calendar is kept up-to-date with all the new releases and you can create reminders directly from here.

Offline-first - anything that you do in the app is cached locally and available offline

**How we built it**

Sleevd is built with Compose Multiplatform and Kotlin Multiplatform - all of the core implementation (data, business logic and networking) is written in Kotlin, and the user Interface is written using Compose Multiplatform, so everything is completely shared between Android and iOS. The API for the app is also built with Kotlin, so it's a 100% Kotlin project.

Card scanning uses each platform's native tools behind a shared contract. On Android, I used CameraX with ML Kit text recognition, and on iOS the Vision framework. For Paid plans, the card image is sent directly to my API for AI analysis, but for free users the recognised text is then passed through to a search query to find matching cards.

I'm using the Scrydex API for all trading card data and market pricing, on their scale plan. However, it would be easy for me to eat through my credits if I was calling this directly through the app. So instead, I built my own API using Kotlin - hosted on Railway and caching data using Neon. Whenever a request is made to my API, we first check Neon to see if there is cached data available and if not, we hit Scrydex and then cache the data before returning it to the client. This means that for most data clients are requesting from the API is coming from our cache, which saves a huge amount of credits. And because I am hosting my own API, I added device attestation using Play Integrity on Android and App Attest on iOS. This means that the app completes a challenge/nonce exchange to receive a signed session token, which is then checked on every API request through a Ktor plugin. This means that my API can only be called from either of my official apps, protecting me from any unauthorised use.

Alongside API caching, everything is also cached on the device using SQLDelight - this is what allows the app to work completely offline for data that has already been accessed. Whenever data is received from the API we cache it, and use the cache first whenever accessing any screen. This is what allows the app to feel so snappy!

When building Sleevd, I was really intentional about the feel of the app and ensuring that it felt delightful to use. I spent a lot of time working on animations and transitions to allow the app to feel more connected, and feel more like a journey through one screen, rather than it feel like you are constantly jumping between different screens. There's still some work to do here but I'm really happy with how things are feeling so far.

Sleevd supports two plans, Pro and Ultimate. To support these two plans I used RevenueCat using the KMP SDK, and I also utilised RevenueCat Paywalls for the first time to display the upgrade screens within the app. Alongside this, both platforms support free trials so that users can try out all of the paid features in the app before they commit to upgrading. One thing I also did through the app to guide users to start a trial was two things:

- Seed real 'sample' data into the apps: so for example, only Pro users can track graded slabs. For free users, the graded slabs screen will show all data for a hardcoded graded slab, allowing the user to see exactly how this feature feels. I do this in a few places and each screen features a paywall button to guide the user into upgrading.

- Pixelate the users data in views that requires a paid plan: for example, the portfolio screen will use the users real data to build the graph and pricing information, but this information is pixellated until they upgrade. This acts as a 'teaser' for the feature and gives another opportunity to guide them to upgrade.

**Challenges we ran into**

Protecting the backend proxy was also more involved than I expected. Play Integrity and App Attest each have their own flow and failure cases, and I needed a session approach that didn't add an attestation round trip to every request. It took a few iterations for me to get this right and find the balance between being secure and ensuring that the UX was not affected.

Card scanning was another big challenge as originally, I was trying to do everything on device. Starting with OCR it felt OK when my testing was isolated, but as soon as I expanded the cards and sets I was testing with I could see the gaps in accuracy. After a few iterations I managed to get to a solution with OCR that was good enough, but it didn't feel premium enough for paying users, which is why I switched to AI card analysis through my API. This is super accurate, meaning that paid users will get a premium experience through the app - this also allowed me to create another upgrade path by providing a few AI scans to free users.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Shipping Sleevd on both Google Play and the App Store from a single codebase

- Building my own API in a way that allows me to easily scale, while also ensuring it is well protected

- I spent a lot of effort adding animations so that the app was delightful to use and didn't just feel like stock UI elements

- Providing a generous free plan, while at the same time creating many opportunities to guide users to free trials and upgrades

- Building a website for the app at sleevd.cards with some free tools (downloadable binder inserts and checklists) to drive traffic to the website and app downloads

- Offline support, allowing the app to work from anywhere!

- Focus: I added the features which I felt were the most useful, without getting carried away with bloating the app too much

- Open-sourcing two components - Pixelate and MorphingFab

**What we learned**

I felt like I learn a huge amount from this project! It was my first time shipping my own iOS app, so going through the whole review process was an experience - it was definitely a lot stricter than Google!

When I started seeing my API credits for Scrydex spiking, I knew I needed to do something about it. I have not built such a system for my own projects before so adding the API and cache layer (and getting it right) had a lot of learnings.

Finally, the animations! I've built basic animations before, but have not usually invested too much time on this front. They took a lot of tweaking to get right but I'm super happy with the results - this process taught me how to think about animating components (without getting carried away), as well as how to create a cohesive experience while the user is navigating through the app.

**What's next for Sleevd - Trading Card Manager**

The next main thing I want to work on are accounts - currently, everything is local to the device. While you can export and import your data, being able to create and account will allow data to be saved on my API and also allow account sharing (my wife and I collect together, so we both need access to our collection!). 

Once I have accounts, this will unlock so much around social connections in the app and public sharing. Currently we have a collection image sharing feature (accessible from the share menu within a binder), but I would love for users to be able to connect in the app, create trades with people who live near by and even share a public facing portfolio. There's so much that can be done here, so it's something I am going to start working on right away!

</details>
