[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/fz2dSqMpcFg/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fz2dSqMpcFg)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/981/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/981/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/482/178/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/482/178/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Learning American Sign Language (ASL) usually means paying for an expensive tutor or watching static videos without knowing if you're making hand shapes correctly. We wanted a fast and private tool that watches your hands through your phone camera and gives feedback in real time.

**What it does**

Handspell is a native Android app that tracks your hand shapes in real time using your front camera. It guides you through ASL letters and word signs, showing landmark wireframe overlays alongside clear three-state indicators (no hand / adjust position / match). It includes all 26 alphabet letters, core word signs, daily challenges, and story-based lessons.

**How we built it**

We built Handspell natively using Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, CameraX, and Google MediaPipe. 

CameraX passes live video frames to MediaPipe to extract 21 3D hand landmarks. To keep recognition accurate regardless of hand distance or left/right orientation, we normalize raw coordinates around the wrist origin W₀ = (x₀, y₀, z₀) and scale them by palm length:

$$p_i' = \frac{p_i - W_0}{\Vert{}p_{\text{middle_mcp}} - W_0\Vert{}}$$

Left hands are mirrored across the x-axis (x' = -x).

For classification:

- Static Letters (A–Z): A small on-device MLP and k-NN classifier handles single-frame shapes, combined with a hold-to-confirm temporal filter so the screen doesn't flicker.

- Dynamic Signs (J, Z, and Word Signs): Fingertip motion paths across frames are passed to a lightweight 1D CNN.

RevenueCat Integration:
We integrated the RevenueCat Android SDK (Purchases) to power our Freemium model. Basic fingerspelling and core signs are free, while Handspell Pro ($2.00/month or $10.00/year) unlocks extra word signs, unlimited speed challenges, and story lessons. Both plans map to a single handspell_pro entitlement. RevenueCat handles purchases, renewals, and entitlement checks on-device. We also added a local 3-day demo mode so testers can preview Pro features without hitting live store APIs.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Look-alike hand shapes: Letters like A, E, M, N, S, and T all look like fists. We had to focus on small thumb-over-finger joint offsets to tell them apart.

- Face and body overlap: Signs near the face or chest (like "mom" or "sad") caused tracking issues when hand points overlapped with facial landmarks.

- Performance: Running vision models and normalization on every camera frame choked the main thread at first, so we moved landmark extraction to background coroutines.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Getting real-time gesture recognition running smoothly on-device at 60 FPS without battery drain or screen stutter.

- Keeping 100% of video processing private in temporary memory without sending a single frame to a server.

- Designing a clean UI with nested corner geometry where inner card radii scale naturally: r_inner = max(0, r_outer - inset).

**What we learned**

We learned that high model accuracy on paper doesn't guarantee a good app experience. Raw predictions were originally too twitchy, so adding a brief temporal buffer sacrificed a fraction of a second in raw speed but made feedback feel smooth and forgiving. We also learned how to handle continuous video streams in CameraX without overloading Android's main thread.

**What's next for Handspell**

We're working on publishing Handspell to the Google Play Store. After that, we plan to expand our sign vocabulary, improve face-overlap tracking, and partner with local educators to bring Handspell into introductory ASL classes.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Communities often experience important problems long before those problems become visible in formal datasets or decision-making systems. Local concerns may be scattered across individual reports, conversations, and observations, making it difficult to identify patterns and decide what to do next.

DscienTia was inspired by a simple question:

What if community voices could be transformed into useful, actionable intelligence?

We wanted to build a platform that helps people move from reporting a local challenge to understanding its potential impact and identifying practical actions that can strengthen community resilience.

The name DscienTia reflects our vision of combining data, science, technology, and human-centered innovation to create positive social impact.

**What it does**

DscienTia allows users to submit community reports describing local challenges or concerns. The platform transforms these reports into structured information and AI-assisted insights that can help users understand patterns, potential risks, and possible resilience actions.

Instead of treating AI as the final decision-maker, DscienTia uses AI as an assistant for understanding information and supporting better human decisions.

Our goal is to make community intelligence more accessible, understandable, and actionable.

**How we built it**

DscienTia is built as a full-stack application with a Flutter client and a Laravel-based backend API.

The architecture separates the user experience, application logic, data layer, and AI insight generation so that the system can evolve without tightly coupling the application to a single AI provider.

The backend provides APIs for community reports and AI-generated insights. We also designed an AI provider abstraction that allows DscienTia to work with different AI implementations while maintaining a consistent application interface.

For the Ship-a-ton edition, we are extending the existing DscienTia application into a mobile-first product and integrating RevenueCat to support a sustainable product model while keeping core community participation accessible.

**What we learned**

Building DscienTia taught us that creating an AI product is not only about choosing a model.

We learned the importance of:

- designing clear boundaries between AI assistance and human decision-making;

- creating reliable contracts between frontend and backend systems;

- handling AI failures and fallback scenarios gracefully;

- thinking about privacy, fairness, and responsible use of community-generated data;

- designing an interface that makes complex insights understandable;

- building a sustainable product model without losing sight of social impact.

We also learned that a good social-impact product needs both technical feasibility and a realistic path toward long-term sustainability.

**Challenges**

One of our biggest challenges was balancing ambitious AI capabilities with the reliability expected from a real product.

AI services can fail, produce unexpected responses, or change over time, so we designed the backend with provider abstraction, validation, error handling, retry behavior, and fallback mechanisms.

Another challenge was turning a broad idea—community resilience—into a focused user experience. We continuously refined the product so that users can move through a simple journey:

Report → Understand → Discover insights → Take action

We also had to work within limited resources while building the product across frontend, backend, AI integration, deployment, and product design.

**What's next**

DscienTia is still evolving.

Our next step is to make the mobile experience more polished and accessible, strengthen the AI-assisted insight workflow, and introduce sustainable monetization through RevenueCat without compromising the project's community-oriented mission.

Ultimately, we want DscienTia to demonstrate that technology can help communities not only identify problems, but also understand them, collaborate around them, and build practical pathways toward a safer and more resilient future.

</details>

src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/467/956/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I have about four hundred screenshots of lecture slides on my phone. I've opened maybe six of them.

That is the actual problem. Capturing something is easy and feels productive, and it does almost nothing for memory. The part that works, going back to the material right before you would have forgotten it, is the part nobody does, because deciding when to review is tedious and easy to skip.

So the app makes that decision for you. You capture something once, or describe a topic and let it build the set, and Interval brings it back on a widening schedule: 1 day, 3, 7, 30, 90. Recall it and the gap widens. Miss it and it comes straight back tomorrow.

The honest origin story: this started as a team of four. Nobody started. With three days left I decided that submitting something working alone beat submitting nothing together, and only then the team took action. We had never written a line of Kotlin before this week.

**What it does**

Three question types over one scheduler. Flashcards you grade yourself, plus multiple choice and true/false that grade themselves. They share one model, so the ladder, the statistics and the storage never branch on type.

AI in three places, each tied to a real moment:
1) Generate - name a topic or paste your notes and get a mixed study set back. Nothing is saved until you tick it, so a hallucinated fact costs one tap to reject rather than sitting in your rotation for a month.
2) Explain this - appears the instant you get a card wrong, which is the one moment you actually want an explanation.
3) Coach - a chat tab for everything else.

It works with Gemini, OpenAI or OpenRouter. You bring your own key; the app never ships one.

Notifications that are the product, not a retention tactic. A card coming due arms the alarm. Tapping the notification opens straight into that session.

A reward loop with a punchline. Correct answers pay XP, streaks pay more, and there is a milestone ladder. The top tier is at one million XP and reads: "the developer will genuinely buy you a five dollar lunch. Anywhere you like. Just email him. Nobody has ever emailed him." At ten to twenty XP a card that is north of fifty thousand correct answers, so it is a promise I can actually afford to keep.

**How we built it**

Native Android - Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, Material 3, minSdk 26.

The whole app has exactly one external dependency: the RevenueCat SDK. Everything else is framework:
| Need | What I Used | Instead Of |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Storage | org.json` + single file (atomic writes) | Room |
| Background Work | AlarmManager | WorkManager |
| Navigation | Sealed interface + when | navigation-compose |
| AI HTTP Calls | HttpURLConnection | Retrofit / OkHttp / Ktor |
| Visuals & Assets | Compose Canvas | Icon packs & charting libraries |

That was a deliberate constraint, not minimalism for its own sake. As someone who had never used Kotlin, we could not debug a Gradle version conflict quickly. Every dependency is a version to keep compatible and a failure mode to diagnose, and on a three-day clock the framework version wins every time. It also means anyone can clone the repo and it just builds.

Monetization. One entitlement, one flag. Billing.isPro is the only thing any gated feature reads, scattering purchase checks through the UI is how an app ends up with one screen that thinks you paid and another that doesn't. Pro is defined as any active entitlement rather than a hardcoded string, so renaming something in the RevenueCat dashboard cannot silently lock a paying customer out. The paywall renders whatever packages the default offering contains, so prices change server-side with no app update.

The detail we are most pleased with: the local profile's id is passed to Purchases.logIn(), so a purchase belongs to the person, not to the install. Delete the app, reinstall, and Pro comes back.

**Challenges we ran into**

Shipping was harder than building. Google Play requires new personal developer accounts to run a closed test with twelve testers opted in for fourteen continuous days before you can even apply for production. The Galaxy Store now requires corporate seller status for Android content. Apple needs a Mac I don't have. Working that out early is why we targeted Next Gen and used RevenueCat's Test Store, which gave me a fully working purchase flow with no store account at all.

Three AI providers, because the first two fought me. Gemini kept rejecting model ids that the documentation said were valid, and the failure looked identical to a bad key. Rather than keep guessing names, we added a Find models button that asks the provider which models that specific key can actually call and lists them. That turned an opaque dead end into a working picker, and it is better for anyone cloning the repo too.

A blurred orb, not a shader. The loading animation we wanted was a WebGL shader orb. There is no GLSL here, so it is six coloured lobes on three co-prime orbits drawn to a Canvas, run through a real Gaussian blur so their edges dissolve into each other, with a crisp unblurred pass on top carrying the rim and a specular highlight. That last part matters, without it a blurred blob just reads as an out-of-focus mistake.

Bugs that taught me something. A card promoted to the three-day rung rendered as "Due in 2 d", because integer division floored three-days-minus-two-seconds. The undo snackbar spawned exactly on top of the grade buttons and blocked the next card. Neither is clever; both are the kind of thing you only find by using your own app.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

It exists. Three days ago we had never written a line of Kotlin, and the team this was meant to be had not started. Choosing to build something small and finished alone, instead of something ambitious and broken together, is the decision the whole project rests on.

One external dependency. The RevenueCat SDK, and nothing else. Storage is org.json and a file written atomically, scheduling is AlarmManager, navigation is a sealed interface and a when, HTTP to three different AI providers is HttpURLConnection, and every icon, chart and animation is Compose Canvas. That started as a survival tactic, we couldn't debug a Gradle conflict quickly, but it ended up as the thing I'd defend hardest. Clone the repo and it builds, first try, with no setup.

Purchases belong to the person, not the install. The local profile's id is passed to Purchases.logIn(), so deleting the app and reinstalling brings Pro back without a restore tap. It's three lines and most hackathon integrations skip it.

Turning a dead end into a feature. Gemini kept rejecting model ids the docs said were valid, and the failure looked identical to a bad API key. Instead of guessing names for another hour, we added a Find models button that asks the provider which models your specific key can actually call. That fixed my problem and made the app better for everyone who clones it.

An orb with no shader. The loading animation we wanted was WebGL. There's no GLSL here, so it's six coloured lobes on three co-prime orbits drawn to a Canvas, run through a real Gaussian blur so their edges dissolve, with a crisp pass on top for the rim and specular. Working out why the first version looked wrong, a blurred blob with no edge reads as a mistake, not a material, taught me more than the code did.

Knowing what to cut. we scoped Kotlin Multiplatform, OneSignal push, and OCR card generation, and dropped all three. Each was chasing a prize category that required a store release we structurally could not get. Cutting them is the only reason the parts that shipped actually work.

**What we learned**

That most of the difference between an app that feels amateur and one that doesn't is motion. Halfway through we replaced every fixed-duration animation with a spring. A tween always arrives at the same moment no matter how far it travelled, which is exactly what makes an interface feel mechanical. we also redefined the app's tap modifier so every surface dips under your finger, one edit, and the whole app stopped feeling like rectangles with listeners attached.

And that scope is a skill. we planned Kotlin Multiplatform, OneSignal push, and OCR card generation. we cut all three, each was chasing a prize category that required a store release we could not get, and cutting them is the reason the parts that shipped actually work.

**What's next for Interval**

Sync, card editing from inside a review, and real PDF and image parsing, the app currently accepts those attachments and says plainly that it is only using the filename as a hint, rather than pretending it read the page.

</details>

## 273. Circa — your body clock, dialed in

- **Team:** [ANUKA R GOWDA](https://devpost.com/anukargowda)

- **Built with:** android, dart, flutter, go-router, google-play-billing, ios, noaa-solar-algorithm, purchases-flutter, revenuecat, riverpod, sqflite, sqlite, wcag-2.2

**Video (1:52):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a2lLMDaexKk

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/a2lLMDaexKk/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a2lLMDaexKk)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/293/568/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/293/568/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/293/570/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/293/570/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/293/571/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/293/571/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/293/572/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/293/572/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/293/573/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/293/573/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I didn't need another sleep tracker. I had several, and between them they told
me — in increasingly beautiful charts — that I slept badly. Not one of them ever
told me what to do about it on Tuesday.

The science isn't the bottleneck. Morning light advances your body clock and
evening light delays it. Caffeine at 4pm is still measurably in you at midnight.
Your alertness through the day is the sum of two well-characterised processes.
All of this is decades old, and almost none of it reaches the person holding the
phone. The gap isn't measurement. It's prescription.

So Circa skips tracking entirely — no wearable, no account, no network — and
spends its effort on the timing instead.

**What it does**

Circa computes where the sun actually is above you, estimates where your body
clock currently sits, and turns both into a short daily protocol you can follow:

- Today — your light window, caffeine cutoff, wind-down time and target
bedtime, over a sky that renders the real sun at your coordinates right now.

- Sleep — five-second logging and a seven-day sleep-debt ledger with an
honest confidence level, because three nights of data is not five.

- Plan — your melatonin onset, temperature minimum and chronotype, with a
protocol chosen to match them.

- Jet Lag Planner — a day-by-day pre-adaptation plan built before you fly,
from the light phase-response curve rather than a rule of thumb.

- Forecast — tomorrow's predicted alertness curve, dip and all.

**How I built it**

Flutter 3.44.7 · Dart 3.12.2 · Riverpod 3.3.2 · GoRouter 17.3.0 · sqflite 2.4.3 ·
purchases_flutter 9.16.1. Seven packages, every one load-bearing.

The centre of the app is lib/domain/chrono — nine pure Dart modules with zero
package dependencies:

- solar_engine — the NOAA solar position algorithm: sunrise, sunset, civil and
nautical twilight, solar noon, altitude at any instant.

- circadian_phase_model — phase estimated from sleep timing via the MCTQ
construct, yielding melatonin onset and temperature minimum.

- two_process_model — Borbély's homeostatic sleep pressure against the
circadian process, producing the alertness curve.

- light_prc — the light phase-response curve: how much a given light exposure
moves your clock, and in which direction.

- caffeine_model, sleep_debt_ledger, chronotype_estimator,
jet_lag_planner, protocol_engine.

Every one is unit-tested against published values rather than against itself.

Offline-first is the architecture, not a feature. Solar geometry is pure
maths from latitude, longitude and date, so there is nothing to fetch. Location
resolves from the device time zone through a bundled dataset — 4,461 cities, 361
IANA zones, 218 countries, 247 KB, with prefix search and haversine reverse
geocoding. geolocator was removed deliberately: it merges
ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION into the manifest for a capability the app doesn't use,
which is a Play data-safety problem before it's a code smell. There is no
account, no server and no analytics. Sleep data never leaves the device.

Monetisation is RevenueCat. One entitlement, pro — everything gates on
customerInfo.entitlements.active['pro'], because multi-tier entitlements are
where gating bugs are born. Three packages in the default offering: monthly as
a deliberate decoy anchor, annual with a 7-day trial as the target, and lifetime
for people who hate subscriptions. Annual is the hero because a circadian
intervention takes weeks to show results, and a monthly plan churns before the
user ever feels it work.

**Challenges I ran into**

A code generator that silently dropped my data. drift_dev 2.34.0 — the
newest release compatible with the analyzer flutter_test pins — omits every
IntegerColumn from its generated code. Not an error; just absent columns.
Nearly every column in this schema is an integer timestamp. I confirmed it with a
minimal probe table and moved the data layer to hand-written SQL on sqflite.

I published a contrast ratio that was wrong. My design doc claimed the
light-theme amber was 4.0:1. I wrote a test that recomputes all 17 palette tokens
from source and checks them against WCAG 2.2 AA — and it failed. The real ratio
was 2.55:1. Amber is now split into solar (fills and icons only, 3.28:1)
and solarInk (text-safe, 5.81:1), and the test asserts that solar stays
below 4.5:1, so nobody can quietly start using it for text later.

Two RevenueCat bugs that only a real store could surface. I drove the paywall
end to end against RevenueCat's Test Store before the Play account existed. It
found two things that would have shipped:

- startListening lost a race with configure. main() deliberately doesn't
await configuration — a slow store must never delay the first frame — but the
listener ran from a post-frame callback, found _configured == false, marked
the store unavailable and returned without attaching. Nothing retried. A
paying customer relaunching the app would have sat on the free tier for the
whole session.

- Bundled marketing copy survived into the live-price path. copyWith only
overrode displayPrice, so the annual tile printed the store's real price
beside the hardcoded subtitle "$3.33 / month · save 52%" — wrong arithmetic at
any price but the US one, and dollars shown to a shopper whose price directly
above reads ₹ or €. The CTA also promised "Start 7 days free" for a product
with no free phase, which is a review rejection rather than a cosmetic slip.
The subtitle is now rebuilt from pricePerMonthString against the live
monthly package, and trial length is read from the store's own free phase.

A model with no afternoon dip. The naive formulation of the two-process model
produced a monotonic curve — no post-lunch dip at all, which is the one feature
of the day everybody actually recognises. I fitted the parameters numerically
against published data until the curve matched lived experience.

Tests that passed on the day I wrote them. Three repository cases inserted
records at a hardcoded date, then read them back through rolling 14-day and
7-day windows measured from DateTime.now(). They went red on a morning nobody
had touched the code. The production behaviour was correct; the tests simply
weren't hermetic. The fix was to inject the clock as a dependency, not to widen
the window — widening it would have hidden the rot instead of removing it.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

The engine computes; it doesn't render fixtures. Computed sunrise and sunset
against published almanac times for the 2026 solstices, locked in as golden tests
at ±2 minutes:

City
Date
Computed
Published
Δ

London
21 Jun
04:43 / 21:21
04:43 / 21:21

07:16 / 16:32

07:00 / 16:54

Polar cases are first-class states rather than errors: Tromsø returns midnight
sun in June and polar night in December.

The same build in two places, which is the evidence I trust most — an iPhone
simulator on a London profile with five logged nights, against a Pixel emulator
in Mumbai at 22:11 on a fresh install. London: a daylight arc with the sun 29%
along, "Good morning", sunrise 05:09 against a published 05:12, sleep debt 4h 59m
at medium confidence. Mumbai: a star field with a crescent moon, "Good evening",
sunrise 06:11 against a published 06:10, and an active "NOW — dim the lights"
window. Nothing there is a fixture.

Accessibility is tested, not asserted. All 17 tokens machine-checked against
WCAG 2.2 AA on every run, plus minimum tap-target height at every button size,
1.6× text scaling without overflow, screen-reader semantics and reduced-motion
behaviour.

186 tests, all passing. flutter analyze: no issues.

**What I learned**

A store that returns real data is a test environment you cannot simulate. Both
paywall bugs above were invisible against mocks and would have reached paying
users.

If you publish a number, write the test that checks it. The contrast bug was in
my own design documentation, stated with confidence, and it took thirty lines of
test code to disprove.

And the schedule constraint that mattered had nothing to do with code: an
individual Play account needs 12 testers opted in for 14 consecutive days before
production. That is wall-clock time. It cannot be compressed by working weekends.

**What's next for Circa**

- The notification scheduler — protocol events already emit stable idempotent
keys; the reconciler into the OS queue is the remaining piece.

- Trends, with a consistency raster plot over months rather than a week.

- Health Connect import for people who do own a wearable and want it to feed the
model rather than replace it.

- An iOS release. The engine is platform-agnostic; only the store work differs.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Category: Shipaton 2026 Next Gen Award (Student Track)

Quick Demo for Judges: Sign in with demo@gmail.com / 1234 (seeds 30 days of medical history) or tap [Demo] Instant Unlock Pro on the paywall to test all Pro features without needing sandbox store accounts.

**Technical Deep-Dive & Journey**

We documented our architecture and design decisions on HackerNoon:

-&gt; CareBridge: Senior-Friendly Design Ahead of Cloud Complexity

**Inspiration: Building for My Grandma in Rural Vietnam**

I'm a final-year Computer Science student at UIT in Ho Chi Minh City.

Earlier this year, an astrology website I spent six months coding died overnight after a Google search update. Traffic plunged from 600,000 impressions to zero. Broke and burned out, I packed a single backpack and took the bus back to my hometown in Ea Kar, Dak Lak (a rural farming district in Vietnam) to stay with my grandmother during summer break.

Living with her, I saw a quiet, everyday struggle that never crossed my mind while chasing search rankings in the city. 

My grandma lives with diabetes and severe high blood pressure, taking 6 to 8 different pills every day. Her eyesight is failing, and her fingers tremble with arthritis. Every morning, I watched her hold generic blister packs up to the sunlight, squinting through thick glasses, terrified she might take the wrong dose or double-dose by mistake. Whenever a tiny pill slipped from her shaking fingers onto the floor, she would apologize to me—as if growing old were her fault.

I tried installing popular medication apps on her phone. None of them worked. They had tiny grey buttons her thumbs couldn't hit, loud banner ads covering the screen, and mandatory cloud logins that locked her out. She looked bewildered, handed the phone back to me, and whispered: "Con ơi, cái này khó quá, bà không biết bấm." ("My child, this is too hard. I don't know how to press this.")

That broke something inside me. I realized I had spent years in university learning algorithms to optimize ad clicks, while the woman who raised me couldn't safely take her heart medicine.

I dropped everything to build CareBridge for this Shipaton. I had one goal: make an app so gentle, big, and reliable that my grandma never has to feel scared or confused about her pills again.

I built test builds, walked down the red-dirt roads of my village in Ea Kar, and sat on porches with elderly neighbors in their 70s and 80s. I handed them my phone. If an auntie hesitated or had to squint, I went back inside and made the buttons twice as big and the voice twice as clear. CareBridge wasn't built in a startup incubator—it was shaped on the front porches of Ea Kar.

**What It Does**

CareBridge is built on dignity and simplicity:

- Bedside Nightstand Clock: Turns an old phone into a glowing bedside clock. When it's pill time, it speaks the exact medication name in a slow, soothing voice (expo-speech calibrated at 85% speed) and shows a massive confirmation button with heavy vibration feedback.

- Punch-Card Adherence Grid: A visual weekly matrix showing unbroken streaks of taken doses. It automatically tracks pill inventory and gently warns days in advance before a prescription runs out.

- 1-Tap Clinical Observations: Seniors or caregivers can tap a single colored tag to record how they felt (Taken with food, Dizzy, Nausea, Normal).

- Doctor Clinical PDF Export: 1-tap generates a clean, printable A4 medical report with 30-day adherence and blood pressure / blood sugar charts that my grandma can hand directly to her doctor during monthly checkups.

- Samsung Galaxy Flex Mode: Automatically splits into a bedside stand display when folded at 90° on Galaxy Z Fold devices.

**How We Built It**

- Frontend: React Native with Expo SDK 54 and strict TypeScript (0 errors on strict tsc).

- 100% Offline-First SQLite: Everything runs on local SQLite (expo-sqlite, WAL mode). Zero cloud latency, zero tracking, and no remote servers—my grandma's medical data never leaves her device.

- Guaranteed Offline Alarms: Scheduled via native expo-notifications (DAILY triggers) that ring reliably even in airplane mode.

- A4 Print Engine: On-device clinical PDF rendering using expo-print with strict CSS pagination guards (page-break-inside: avoid;) preventing broken tables at local clinic printers.

**RevenueCat & Monetization**

We built an honest freemium model using the RevenueCat SDK (react-native-purchases):

- Free Plan: Bedside clock, daily reminders, up to 2 active prescriptions, 7-day history. Basic daily care habits (drinking water, walking, blood pressure checks) are 100% free and unlimited so no elderly patient is ever locked out of basic health tracking.

- CareBridge Pro: Unlimited prescriptions, full 52-week punch cards, and Doctor PDF Export ($9.99/mo, $79.99/yr, $99.99 lifetime).

- Offline Caching: Subscription entitlements are cached in SQLite so patients never lose access to their tools during network outages.

- Judge Sandbox Bypass: Built-in [Demo] Instant Unlock Pro and [Judge Demo] Reset to Free Plan buttons inside PaywallModal.tsx so judges can test both Free and Pro tiers instantly without a sandbox account.

**Real Bugs & Technical Hurdles**

**1. RevenueCat Overwriting the Demo Override**

When we built the [Demo] Instant Unlock Pro button for judges, we set isPro = true. But milliseconds later, our listener queried Purchases.getCustomerInfo(). Because there was no active store receipt on emulators, the SDK flipped it right back to false.

Fix: We wrote a small circuit breaker (isDemoOverride) inside our service to prioritize the demo flag during test sessions while leaving real store logic intact.

**2. React Native Native Modal Collisions**

Closing the Paywall modal while immediately opening our custom "Pro Unlocked!" alert caused a native thread crash on Android—the OS destroyed the alert view along with the unmounting paywall.

Fix: Added a 350ms transition delay to let the native view tree finish closing the first modal before mounting the next one.

**3. Timezone Off-by-One Errors**

Mapping 52 weeks of intake logs into Monday–Sunday columns across different timezones kept causing off-by-one day bugs. We fixed this by pinning all date parsing strictly to local solar noon (12:00:00) to dodge daylight saving and midnight boundary glitches.

**4. Realistic Demo Data**

To give judges realistic 30-day vitals charts on login, we wrote a small generator using sine/cosine waves plus random noise to simulate natural human fluctuations in blood pressure and fasting glucose.

**What I Learned**

- Accessibility is an act of empathy: It's not just large text—it's 48px touch targets for arthritic fingers, slower speech cadence for tired ears, and zero cognitive friction.

- Local-first protects human dignity: Medical software shouldn't force an 80-year-old grandmother to reset a forgotten cloud password just to remember her blood pressure pill.

- The best code serves someone you love: Months of chasing SEO algorithms felt empty. Watching my grandmother confidently tap a big green button and smile because she remembered her morning pills—that gave me my purpose back.

**What's Next**

- Remote Family Bridge (RevenueCat Family Tier): Adding an encrypted, peer-to-peer sync engine (via PowerSync) so children working in distant cities can see that their elderly parents took their morning pills, receiving quiet alerts only if a vital dose is missed.

- Regional Pricing for Rural Families: Setting up localized RevenueCat pricing (~49,000–69,000 VND / $1.99–$2.99/mo in Vietnam) so rural families in communities like Ea Kar can easily afford it.

- Bluetooth Vitals Integration: Direct BLE pairing with Omron blood pressure monitors to eliminate manual typing for trembling hands entirely.

- Smart Pillbox & Galaxy Ecosystem: Bluetooth pairing with physical smart dispensers and S-Pen gesture shortcuts for Samsung tablets.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Fix the step, not just the final answer**

Counterstep Pocket is native Android algebra practice built around one idea: correcting an answer should not erase how you got there. Enter an expanded expression, see which term needs attention, request a hint, and repair the line while retaining the original attempt and hint history.

For example, entering 2x+3 for 2(x+3) produces feedback on the constant. Repairing it to 2x+6 records a successful repair without relabeling the first attempt as independently correct.

Download the verified 0.5 preview and matching source | Source and setup instructions

**What works**

Free practice, term-specific feedback, progressive hints, saving and sharing work without connecting a store. Unfinished expressions survive closing and reopening the app. Edited answers must be checked again; earlier attempts remain in the record. Sharing opens Android's chooser with a personal practice note, not an authenticated grade.

The optional mixed-sign pack adds practice with negative coefficients and constants. RevenueCat's SDK entitlement response controls access; a saved study file cannot grant it. Purchase callbacks do not replace newer practice work.

**RevenueCat integration**

The Android app uses RevenueCat SDK 9.9.0 to load its current offering, display the product and sandbox price in a native paywall, make a Test Store purchase, refresh access, and restore the same sandbox customer's current access. The mixed_signs package and entitlement are connected to a non-consumable practice-pack product. Core practice, hints and saving remain free; the USD 2.99 price shown is a sandbox display price, not a real charge.

The demo captures RevenueCat's actual Test Store dialog and separate cancellation, failure and success outcomes. It then shows process restart, retained draft, restored test access and a correctly answered premium exercise. An authenticated RevenueCat API read separately confirmed the 0.5 preview's sandbox purchase and active entitlement. The redacted verification summary is included in the release.

**How it was built and checked**

Kotlin, native Android views, a deliberately narrow integer-linear checker, Gradle and GitHub Actions. There is no OCR or conversational model running inside the application.

Verified application run 36161609006 passed 108 JVM tests, 26 Android emulator tests and eight end-to-end workflow assertions. These cover repair history, cancellation and failure without losing work, a successful SDK entitlement response, process restart, Test Store restore, pack unlock and premium-answer checking.

An actual checkout exposed a missing Android Main coroutine dispatcher after the provider accepted a purchase. Version 0.5 fixes that dependency and adds a native regression test. The later successful run, not the earlier failed run, supports the verification claim.

The APK and matching source archive come unchanged from application commit b903185484d71eda809718e9d7584670ccfe9c3b. Release packaging checks their hashes and all 15 public downloads without authentication. The captioned demo contains edited, original-speed Android emulator footage. Full-resolution screenshots, icon, checksums and reproduction instructions are included.

**Try it and understand the scope**

Install the debug preview on Android API 26 or later. Try the free exercise first. For the optional purchase flow, follow START-HERE.md and explicitly connect the provided public Test Store SDK key. Remembering that public key is opt-in. No administrative secret belongs in the app. Preserve practice notes before replacing an older APK signed by a different build runner.

This is a development preview, not an app-store release. All demonstrated purchases are sandbox events; no real revenue is claimed. Test Store restoration is not a Google Play or cross-account restore test. The device evidence is from an Android API 35 emulator, not a physical phone. Software-test results are not evidence of measured learning improvement.

**Provenance and next steps**

Original native implementation by Joseph Ayanda, adapted from his earlier Counterstep practice concept with substantial AI assistance for implementation, debugging, tests and submission preparation. Original code is MIT licensed; third-party licenses remain applicable. The separate Amazon Relay and Prom web entries are unchanged.

Next: learner usability feedback, physical-device checks and a separately configured production-store release.

</details>

**Why I built Voino**

In a lecture or meeting, I want to follow the discussion instead of typing the whole time. Afterward, useful points can get lost in a long transcript. Voino turns captured words into notes I can review and a visual board I can edit.

**What it does**

Voino is a Flutter Android prototype. Tap the mic to capture an editable live transcript, or type and paste text instead. The default note extractor uses rules, not AI. Review its key points against the transcript, then make a board with editable cards, arrows and shapes. Listening, notes, board editing and text export stay free.

**How I built it**

I used Flutter and Dart, speech_to_text for Android speech recognition, and a custom hand-drawn board. RevenueCat's purchases_flutter SDK connects the Android Test Store to the voino_pro entitlement. Test Pro gates board JSON save, copy, open and pasted import. It is sandbox billing only, with no real charge. The public repository is MIT licensed.

**Challenges and what I learned**

Speech recognizers revise interim results and can stop at device-imposed session limits. I worked on transcript stitching, visible microphone state and a type/paste fallback. Notes stay editable because recognition and rule-based extraction can miss things. Building the board also meant handling selection, shapes, pan and zoom on a small screen. Testing the real phone mattered more than a desktop preview.

**Demo and current limits**

The video is recorded on an Android phone and shows live transcript capture, rule-based notes, board editing and drawing, plus the RevenueCat Test Store unlock. It does not demonstrate JSON save or open, so those paths are not claimed as verified in the video. The app is not published on Google Play or another store. There is no account-based history or cloud sync. Android device speech may use its vendor's online service; this is not a claim of fully offline recording. The repo has optional AI work, but this submission's recorded flow uses rule-based notes.

**What comes next**

Verify board-file save/open and restore on the physical phone, improve capture reliability and mobile board controls, then review production signing and billing before a store release.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

SciNova AI — Project Story
Inspiration
Science and technology are changing quickly, but finding useful scientific information is not always easy. Information is often spread across different websites, apps, and platforms, and complex topics can be difficult to understand.
That is where the idea for SciNova AI came from.
We wanted to create one simple place where people could ask science questions, learn about different topics, follow international science news, and explore the world through interactive maps.
Our goal was to make science feel less complicated and more accessible—especially for students, learners, and anyone who is simply curious about how the world works.
What We Built
SciNova AI is a modern digital Science Hub that brings several science-focused tools together in one platform.
The main platform includes:
AI Science Chat — Ask questions about science, space, biology, physics, climate, technology, astronomy, and scientific discoveries.
International Science News — Discover important scientific news, research, and breakthroughs from around the world.
Interactive Map — Explore locations and geographic information through an interactive map experience.
About SciNova AI — Learn about the platform, its purpose, and the technology behind it.
Project Overview — See how the project was created, what we focused on, and where we want to take it next.
We designed SciNova AI with a futuristic science-inspired interface that works across both mobile and desktop screens.
How We Built It
We wanted the experience to feel simple from the moment a user opens the platform.
The dashboard brings the main features together so users can quickly move between the AI assistant, science news, interactive map, and project information.
The AI Science Chat is at the center of the experience. Instead of presenting it as just another general chatbot, we designed it around science learning and exploration.
We also focused heavily on the interface itself—using a dark futuristic design, clear sections, responsive layouts, simple navigation, and a visual style inspired by science, technology, and space.
The project brings together AI, web development, APIs, mapping technology, and responsive UI design into one lightweight Science Hub.
Challenges We Faced
One of the biggest challenges was bringing several different features together without making the platform feel complicated.
We had to think carefully about how the AI assistant, news section, and interactive map could work together while keeping navigation straightforward.
Another challenge was making the AI feel useful for learning rather than simply answering random questions. We wanted users to be able to use it as a starting point for understanding scientific topics and discovering new information.
Keeping the interface responsive and lightweight while combining different technologies was also an important part of the development process.
What We Learned
Building SciNova AI gave us practical experience with AI applications, responsive web development, UI/UX design, API integration, mapping technology, and educational technology.
More importantly, we learned that a good AI product is not only about generating answers.
The way information is presented matters just as much. A useful platform should help people ask better questions, understand difficult concepts, discover new information, and continue exploring.
That idea influenced many of the decisions we made while building SciNova AI.
What's Next
SciNova AI is only the beginning.
Our next goal is to expand the platform with more tools that allow users to do more than simply read or ask questions.
We plan to introduce:
Advanced AI science assistance
Interactive scientific simulations
Virtual experiments
Scientific visualizations
Better science and research news discovery
Expanded educational resources
More powerful interactive maps
Space and astronomy exploration tools
Biology and life-science resources
Physics and chemistry learning tools
Support for emerging technologies
We also want to make the AI better at explaining difficult scientific concepts in simple language, helping students work through problems step by step, and directing users toward reliable scientific information.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every focus app asks you to be disciplined at exactly the moment you have no discipline left. They give you a countdown and a guilt trip. Neither helps a hand that wants to reach for a phone.

**What it does**

Squishflow puts a soft body between you and the work.

You tell it what you want to finish. It hands back blocks short enough to believe — the first one deliberately shorter, because starting is the expensive part of focus, not continuing. Then, while you sit with the tension, you push your thumb into Squishy and it pushes back.

The squishy is a physics model, not an animation. The silhouette is a ring of 26 coupled radial samples with real stiffness, damping and neighbour coupling. A press opens a dent exactly under your finger, the wave travels around the surface, and volume conservation means denting one side bulges the other. It has haptics tied to pressure and a synthesised voice: no audio files ship, and every material's squelch is derived from the same three numbers that drive its shape — stiffness sets the pitch, damping the length, coupling the wetness — so a stress ball snaps high and dry and a bubble rings. Left alone, it wakes up, blinks on an irregular rhythm, looks around, and occasionally stretches. Squeeze it and it answers with a word for a beat (Oof. — mid-block only Mm., Back to it.); press hard and the mouth purses; finish a block and the eyes close for a moment while the smile widens. Each of the five materials wears its own face: smaller eyes on foam, heavy lids on mochi, a startled bubble.

It does the thing it asks of you. Over a focus block the body softens and stops wobbling. The same drag gives about a fifth further at minute twenty-four than at minute one. Then, in the last sixty seconds, it breaks the pattern: the breath quickens and the line changes to Almost banked. A session visibly has depth, not just a countdown.

It has a position on streaks. Come back after three days away and it says Been a while. Nothing to catch up on. That is the moment a streak app shows a broken chain; this one says the gap does not count — and that sentence, like every line the app says, is held to rules by unit tests: no exclamation marks, no failure language, nothing longer than one line. The journey screen shows the last seven days as minutes per day, scaled to your own best day, because minutes done cannot break and days missed are nobody's business. When a block ends with the phone face down, one notification says so — "Banked. 15 min of focus." — and that is the only notification the app will ever send.

**Monetisation: focus is the currency**

There are five bodies. Every one can be earned with focused minutes. Pro buys them now.

A focus app that locks its rewards behind a card is working against the thing it claims to want — it profits when you pay, not when you concentrate. Making focused minutes the free currency means the app only gets more rewarding the more it actually works. The subscription is a shortcut for people who would rather not wait, and the reason there are no ads and no analytics on anyone, paying or not. The one Pro benefit that is not cosmetic is utility: free protects three apps behind Squishy, Pro protects every one — and that limit lives in product logic with a test, not in paywall copy.

Two consequences, both unit-tested: a lapsed subscription keeps everything you earned, and a locked body shows how close you are rather than a padlock. And because only one body is free at the start, tapping a locked one hands it to you for six seconds before the paywall appears. A list of names cannot communicate what dense foam feels like.

The materials are not reskins. A test asserts that a stress ball settles in fewer frames than jelly and a water balloon in more, and another that it sounds higher and shorter. If two of them ever came to rest at the same rate, the entitlement would be selling paint. The shelf plays each body's voice when you tap it, locked or not: the difference is heard before it is paid for.

The plans screen is drawn in the app's own style over RevenueCat's SDK: three plain rows with the yearly price explained per month, a store trial said in plain words when one exists, Restore purchases, privacy and terms beside the button, and no countdown or "most popular" badge. A purchase unlocks on the spot. The release build is minified, signed from the environment and refuses the Test Store key, so the distance from here to charging real money is two store accounts and two keys.

**How we built it**

Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform. The UI, timer, planner, physics and audio synthesis are all in commonMain; the platform source sets hold only what genuinely differs — haptics, persistence, app selection. RevenueCat's KMP SDK handles offerings, purchase, restore and the Pro entitlement; the plans screen itself is drawn in the app's own style.

It runs on Android and iPhone from one codebase. The iOS build lives in GitHub Actions because the only Mac available runs Monterey: a hosted Mac compiles the shared Kotlin for Apple, builds the Xcode project, boots a simulator and photographs the app on every push. The shared Kotlin compiled for iOS on the first attempt.

A few design decisions worth knowing:

- Hue carries state. Coral is tension, sage is focus, lavender is interruption — across the whole product. Materials therefore never repaint the body; they differ by finish.

- Motion has a grammar. Going deeper rises, going back falls, overlays travel their own axis, and an interruption arrives with no motion at all, because being pulled out of a distraction should feel like a stop.

- The first screen is the product. One body and nothing to read before you touch it. The list of apps and the one permission come after you have squeezed it, not before.

- Reduced motion is honoured. The body still deforms under a finger — that is the interaction — but nothing moves that you did not move.

- The copy is tested. No exclamation marks, no failure or streak language, nothing longer than one line. The rules are assertions.

Honesty: the planner is deterministic and on-device. It does not learn and there is no model behind it. The interface says "adaptive focus," never "AI."

**Challenges we ran into**

The project is developed entirely on Windows. The only Mac available for iOS work runs Monterey and cannot target a current iPhone or run a current Xcode, so the whole iOS path — compiling the shared Kotlin for Apple, building the Xcode project, running it in a simulator, and archiving an unsigned IPA for sideloading — was built to run in GitHub Actions on a hosted Mac instead. Getting Kotlin/Native to link against RevenueCat's Swift UI framework outside of Xcode, and getting a synthesised audio engine to sound "squishy" rather than like filtered noise, were the two places that took the most iteration.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

That the physics model is real rather than decorative — a test asserts a stress ball settles in fewer frames than jelly and that a water balloon sounds lower and longer, so the materials could not fake being different. And that the monetisation model survived contact with its own tests: a lapsed subscription keeps everything earned, and the plans screen refuses to run on the Test Store key outside of debug builds, so what a judge tries is the same code path a real purchase would take.

**What we learned**

That copy can be held to the same discipline as code. Every line the app says is checked by a unit test — no exclamation marks, no streak or failure language, one line only — which turned "does this feel calm" from a vibe into something that fails a build.

**What's next**

The store release path (docs/MONETIZATION_LAUNCH.md) is ready — signed release build, real RevenueCat keys, App Store and Play Store products — pending the store accounts.

**For judges: testing Pro**

The build in the repository uses RevenueCat's public Test Store key, so the plans screen loads real offerings and every purchase is simulated and succeeds: tap any plan, confirm the Test Store dialog, and every body unlocks on the spot. "Restore purchases" works the same way. No promo code is needed. On a store build the key changes and nothing else does.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I love to travel, and I want more people to love it too.

For a lot of people, the destination isn't what keeps them at home. The problem is everything around the trip. Planning feels overwhelming if you've never done it. Ideas are scattered across saved posts and browser tabs. Once you've booked, your confirmations are spread over a dozen emails, three airline apps and a camera roll full of screenshots. The trip starts to feel like work before you've even left.

The best travel inspiration I know of is other travelers. You see where real people went and what they did each day, and you think, "I could do that." That idea is where Supernova started. It puts the inspiration, the planning and the logistics in one app, so a trip somewhere new feels possible instead of intimidating.

**What it does**

Supernova is a social travel app with four parts.

Discover. Browse a feed of photos and video clips from other travelers. A 3D globe shows the destinations people save most, and you can search for travelers and trips.

Plan. Build a trip yourself, copy another traveler's itinerary and make it your own, or have AI build one for you. Tell it where you're going (one city or several), when you're going, your travel style and anything you don't want to miss. You get a day-by-day itinerary that covers every city in order, with travel days between cities and costs in each city's local currency. Every stop is pinned on the trip map.

Carry. The travel wallet holds your boarding passes, hotels, car rentals, restaurant reservations, shows and loyalty programs. You don't have to type any of it in. Paste a confirmation email or add a screenshot, and AI fills in the form for you to review before it's saved. Supernova checks your upcoming flights automatically and sends you push notifications with updates.

Connect. Follow travelers, like and comment on their posts, invite friends to plan a trip with you, and message friends one-on-one or in groups.

Supernova Pro runs on RevenueCat and comes monthly, yearly or as a one-time lifetime unlock. The free tier is enough to plan real trips: one AI-generated trip every week, plus one AI wallet import to try the feature. Pro removes both limits, lets you post 30-second video clips and turns on flight alerts.

**Why I built it**

I want travel to be easier and more accessible.

Each part of the app removes a reason people put off a trip. If you don't know where to go, the feed and the globe show you where other travelers are going. If you've never planned a trip, you can copy one from someone who's been there, or let AI draft one for you. If keeping track of bookings stresses you out, the wallet keeps every flight, hotel and reservation in one place.

I also wanted the free version to be useful by itself, so you can plan a real trip without paying anything. Pro is for people who travel often.

**How I built it**

I'm a solo developer, and I built Supernova under my studio, Galaxie Labs. I design before I build. Every feature starts as a written spec that covers the decisions, the tradeoffs and the architecture rules. I turn each spec into a phased plan, build it with Claude Code one checkpoint at a time, and commit between milestones. A CLAUDE.md file in the repo holds the rules every change has to follow, from "never call a secret API from the client" to "no emoji in the UI."

App. React Native with Expo SDK 54 on the New Architecture, written in TypeScript. Expo Router handles file-based navigation, Zustand holds app state, and TanStack Query fetches and caches data. FlashList renders every feed and list, and Reanimated drives the spring animations. Phosphor duotone icons and haptics run throughout. EAS builds both the development client and the store builds.

Backend. Firebase: Authentication (email and Google sign-in), Cloud Firestore with detailed security rules, Cloud Storage for media, and Cloud Functions v2 on Node 20. Every call to a paid or secret API goes through a Cloud Function, never through the app.

AI. Gemini 2.5 Flash runs in two Cloud Functions. generateTrip turns a destination, dates, travel style and must-sees into a structured itinerary. parseTravelConfirmation reads pasted text or a screenshot, works out what kind of booking it is and extracts the details. Usage limits are enforced on the server, so the app can't get around them.

Maps and places. The globe is built with Mapbox (@rnmapbox/maps) and uses fly-in camera animations. The Mapbox Search Box API places AI-suggested stops on the map. Google Places API (New) provides place details, and it's only called when a user asks for something. Its data is never drawn on the map as pins.

Search, flights and notifications. Algolia powers traveler and trip search, and Firestore triggers keep it in sync. A scheduled Cloud Function checks upcoming flights with AviationStack every 30 minutes and sends updates as Expo push notifications.

Monetization with RevenueCat. react-native-purchases handles purchases. All three products (monthly, yearly and lifetime) grant a single supernova_pro entitlement. The app only asks whether Pro is unlocked, never which plan someone bought. Plans come from a default offering that's configured remotely, so I can change what's on sale from the RevenueCat dashboard without an app update.

There are two paywalls. My own paywall follows the app's design system and is shown to people who go looking for Pro. RevenueCat's hosted paywall appears when a user hits a feature limit, and I can restyle and A/B test it from the dashboard. RevenueCat's Customer Center handles cancellations, plan changes, refund requests and missing purchases.

A webhook Cloud Function, syncTier, copies each user's entitlement into Firestore so the server can enforce the AI limits. Each user's Firebase ID is also their RevenueCat app user ID, so no lookup table is needed to connect a purchase to an account.

**Challenges I ran into**

A Pro upgrade that didn't stick. My first purchase flow seemed to work: you paid, and the app switched to Pro. But the server sets the AI trip limit based on the user's tier in Firestore, and nothing ever wrote that tier there. The security rules correctly block the app from writing its own tier. So a paying user had Pro for one session, stayed rate-limited on the server, and went back to free on the next launch.

The fix was the syncTier webhook:

- It checks a shared secret on every call.

- It ignores events older than the last one it applied, and a repeated event changes nothing.

- It doesn't remove Pro on a CANCELLATION event, because that user has paid through a future date. It doesn't remove Pro on BILLING_ISSUE either, because that event starts a grace period.

- If an event arrives before the user's profile exists, it returns a 500 so RevenueCat tries again. A 200 would have silently lost the purchase.

I tested the webhook with curl before connecting it to RevenueCat. That way, if something failed later, I'd know the problem was configuration, not code.

Setup mistakes that show no error. Four different store setup mistakes look exactly the same inside the app, an empty paywall or a purchase that doesn't stick, with nothing in any log:

- The Paid Applications Agreement isn't active.

- A product is stuck in Missing Metadata.

- The entitlement ID has a typo.

- A RevenueCat test key is left in the environment, where it overrides the real key.

I wrote a phased setup checklist with a checkpoint for each one. I also added a guard that won't configure the SDK with a test key in a release build. Users see an unavailable paywall instead of a purchase flow that fails without saying why.

AI stops in the wrong country. A trip to La Paz, Baja California Sur came back with stops in La Paz, Bolivia. The place search was running against the whole planet, and it had put "Playa El Tecolote" in San Diego and a Mexican market in Brazil.

Before choosing a fix, I ran ten real stop names through four approaches. Mapbox with only a nearby-location hint was still wrong three times out of ten. Mapbox restricted to a bounding box around the destination was right nine times, wrong zero times, and returned no result once. That settled it: a restricted search either finds the right place or says it can't find one, and it never saves a wrong answer. Mapbox now places about 90% of stops for free. Google, biased toward the destination, handles the rest on a cheaper billing tier than before.

Adding multi-city trips without breaking single-city ones. Most AI trips are to a single city, and I didn't want the new multi-city prompt to change them at all. The prompt builder now branches on whether a trip has extra destinations. With none, it produces exactly the same prompt as before, character for character. The code enforces that, so I don't have to remember it.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- Building a social network, an AI trip planner, a travel wallet and a subscription business into one app as a solo developer.

- Keeping the server in control of monetization. Pro holds through relaunches, account switches, renewals and refunds, and the free tier can't be bypassed from the app.

- Pinning AI itinerary stops to the map automatically, with no wrong-country results in testing.

- A design that looks like a travel magazine, not a template.

**What I learned**

- Failures that report no error are the most expensive kind. Every step should either work or fail in a way you can see.

- Build around entitlements, not product IDs. Adding a plan shouldn't require an app update.

- Measure before you choose. Ten test searches settled a question I could have argued about for a week.

- Writing a spec before the code costs less than rewriting the code later.

**What's next for Supernova**

- Travel Tracker: record your route in the background, show the path you actually took on the map, and count the countries and regions you've visited, with England, Scotland and Wales counted separately.

- Android: release on Google Play.

- Smarter flight alerts: add gate and terminal changes.

- Better messaging: photo sharing, and adding or removing people in group chats.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

"That one was quicker than yours."
"No chance, mine was faster."

Go to any net session or street match and you'll hear this argument. Every bowler is sure he's the quickest in the group, and nobody can prove it. Radar guns cost hundreds of dollars and belong on TV, not at the local nets, so the argument never ends.

We wanted to settle it. Almost everyone already carries a phone that films at 60 fps, so we asked: can a phone video give a speed both bowlers have to accept? And if it can't be sure, can it at least say so honestly, instead of handing the loudest bowler a number to brag about?

That became Paceball: a speed gun that shows its working, so the answer is something you can check, not just believe.

**What it does**

- Record a delivery side-on, with both ends of a known distance in frame: the stumps, two markers, or even the ball itself as a ruler.

- Mark the reference, then step frame by frame and tap the ball at release and where it bounces.

- Read the average speed from release to bounce, with an honest ± range worked out for that exact reading.

Every result shows its working: the frames you marked, the fps read from the file, the flight time, the scale and the distance. The frame is labelled "Marked, not tracked", because the line joins the points you tapped and nothing more.

On top of that:

- A personal best on Home, with a speedometer that sweeps to your reading

- History, Stats (speed over time, deliveries per day, bounce confidence) and Compare

- Multiple players on one phone

- Share cards and video clips with the reading burned in

**How the measurement works**

Speed is distance over time:

$$
v = \frac{d}{t}
$$

The distance comes from the reference you marked, and the time comes from frames:

$$
d = \frac{\text{pixels from release to bounce}}{\text{pixels per metre}} \qquad t = \frac{\Delta f}{\text{fps}}
$$

A real delivery from our screenshots:

Input
Value

Marked frames
253 to 277

Frame delta \(\Delta f\)
24 frames

fps (read from the file)
60.03

Flight time \(t\)
0.3998 s

Distance \(d\)
8.92 m

Speed
80.3 km/h ± 8

$$
v = \frac{8.92 \text{ m}}{0.3998 \text{ s}} = 22.3 \text{ m/s} \approx 80.3 \text{ km/h}
$$

The ± range is the honest part. You can only mark to the nearest frame, and the scale comes from one reference distance, so every reading carries its own uncertainty, and Paceball shows it instead of hiding it.

**Honesty rules, enforced in code**

- No guessing: a guessed bounce gives no speed at all.

- No assumed fps: the frame rate is read from each video's own track, never assumed to be 60.

- No fake records: readings that can't be right (over 180 km/h, or a range wider than ±25 km/h) are tagged "Check this reading" and never count as a personal best, in Stats or in Compare.

**How we built it**

- Expo SDK 57, React Native 0.86 and TypeScript, with expo-router

- A native Kotlin module that reads the real frame rate from the video track and extracts exact frames for marking

- Media3 Transformer (Kotlin) to export shareable video clips with the reading and marks drawn in

- React Native Skia and Reanimated for the speedometer, share cards, charts and celebration, all animated on the UI thread

- VisionCamera for capture, with exposure, zoom, start delay, sound and record length

- MMKV for fast on-device storage. Deliveries never leave the phone

- Sentry, strictly opt-in

- 454 automated tests, run before every commit

**How we use RevenueCat**

- One entitlement, pro, read from RevenueCat's CustomerInfo. Pro is never assumed or cached as true.

- The default offering with a monthly and an annual plan. The annual plan has a 7-day free trial, and the paywall only mentions a trial when the store actually offers one to that user.

- Prices from the store, in the user's own currency. Nothing is hard-coded.

- Purchase, restore and a live listener, so Pro unlocks the moment a purchase lands, followed by a celebration screen.

- A weekly free allowance: 3 analyses per 7-day period, shared across players. Pro removes the limit and unlocks clean exports, Stats, Compare and higher recording quality.

- Runs without keys: a build with no RevenueCat key shows a clearly labelled sample paywall with purchasing off, so anyone can clone the repo and run it.

**Challenges we ran into**

- The frame rate lie. Early on, some readings were quietly wrong because the fps the app trusted wasn't the rate the video was actually recorded at. We moved fps reading into native code that measures the video track itself, and now every result shows the fps it used.

- Deciding what not to show. It's tempting to always print a number. We chose to show no speed from a guessed bounce and to flag readings that can't be real, even though a big number looks better in a demo.

- Running out of builds. We used up our free cloud builds days before the deadline, so we moved to building on a free CI machine with EAS local builds and the same signing credentials, and kept shipping to Google Play testing.

- Burning the reading into video. Exporting clips with the speed, marks and watermark drawn in meant writing a Media3 pipeline in Kotlin that we could only test on a real build.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A working app on Google Play testing that gives a believable speed from an ordinary phone video

- A measurement that explains itself: every reading shows its frames, fps, scale and range

- A calm, precise design, from the speedometer sweep to the share card

- A public, MIT-licensed repo with 454 tests and a README anyone can follow

**What we learned**

- Honesty is a feature. Players trust a range more than a suspiciously exact number, and it ends arguments faster.

- RevenueCat made subscriptions the easy part, which let us spend our time on the measurement.

- Test on real devices early. Assumptions about fps hide exactly the bugs that matter.

**What's next for Paceball**

**Settle more arguments, faster**

- Ball tracking across every frame. Detect the ball in all ~30 frames between release and bounce and fit a curve through them, instead of relying on two taps. The range tightens from about ±4 km/h to ±1-2 km/h on the same phone, and marking drops from four taps to two. It's classical computer vision, no machine learning needed.

- Any camera angle. Perspective correction (homography) using the pitch itself (20.12 m × 3.05 m) as the reference, so you can film from behind the bowler like a broadcast camera, not only side-on.

- Automatic stump and crease detection, so calibration happens by itself.

- Automatic release frame using on-device pose detection.

- A whole over in one clip. Record six deliveries once, calibrate once, get six speeds.

**Every automatic mark stays honest**

- Detection assists, never replaces: every automatic mark stays draggable.

- If it can't find the ball, it says so and falls back to manual marking. It never guesses.

- The ± range is always shown. Better precision means a smaller range, never no range.

- Measurement stays on-device and works offline.

**For players, coaches and academies**

- Proof, not just a number: optional cloud backup of your top 5 deliveries with the video ( will also be added on single players too) they came from, so a personal best can be verified.

- Coach and academy tools on the web: squads, sessions and progress over a season, with seat-based plans.

- Form insights from on-device pose detection.

- Batsman mode, and other sports. The engine only needs a known distance.

**Growth**

- A public release on Google Play, then iOS.

- A lifetime plan alongside monthly and annual, and regional pricing for Pakistan, India and neighbouring markets.

- Smart reminders: a nudge after a quiet week, a personal-best celebration, a heads-up before a trial ends.

**UI and Design**

- A full rework of the current design, as it was done in a very limited time and we didn't had the time test other shaders on mobile like Threejs etc.

- A proper premium app feel.

- More ways to make user experience smooth and automatic.

</details>
