<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/353/695/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/353/695/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/353/697/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/353/697/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/353/698/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/353/698/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/353/699/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/353/699/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/353/700/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/353/700/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/353/701/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/353/701/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

During catastrophic wildfires like the Marshall Fire in Colorado or the Caldor Fire in Lake Tahoe, thousands of families watched emergency maps showing fire perimeters miles away—only to have burning embers crash through their attic vents and ignite their roofs minutes later.
Post-wildfire forensic studies from NIST and CAL FIRE reveal a chilling reality: up to 90% of homes destroyed in wildland-urban interface (WUI) fires are never touched by the main flame front. They are ignited by windborne embers (firebrands) projected miles ahead of the blaze.
Standard fire alert apps only show where the fire has already burned. They treat wildfires like static perimeters, leaving millions of homeowners in forest-bordering communities blind to the single most critical predictor of immediate danger: wind direction relative to the fire and their property.
We built EmberWatch to make this invisible danger visible and actionable. By fusing real-time satellite hotspot feeds with live meteorological wind vectors, EmberWatch calculates a pinpoint, downwind Ember Threat Index (0–100) right on a resident's phone—giving families the life-saving minutes they need to harden their homes or evacuate safely.

**What it does**

EmberWatch is a native Android and iOS mobile application specifically engineered for citizens living in and around forest borders and WUI communities.

- Hyperlocal 6-Factor Ember Threat Index
Instead of generic "fire danger" ratings that cover entire counties, EmberWatch computes an exact hyperlocal threat score:
Ember Threat Index=Fprox+Fwind+Fdir+Fint+Fdry+FvegEmber Threat Index=Fprox​+Fwind​+Fdir​+Fint​+Fdry​+Fveg​

- Fire Proximity (Fprox∈[0,30]Fprox​∈[0,30] pts): Great-circle distance calculated via the Haversine formula within a 50 km threat radius: Fprox=max⁡(0,round(30×(1−dkm50)))Fprox​=max(0,round(30×(1−50dkm​​)))

- Wind Velocity (Fwind∈[0,25]Fwind​∈[0,25] pts): Dynamic wind force scaling danger propagation: Fwind=min⁡(25,max⁡(0,round(vmph×0.65)))Fwind​=min(25,max(0,round(vmph​×0.65)))

- Wind Direction Toward Property (Fdir∈[0,20]Fdir​∈[0,20] pts): Evaluates whether the user's property sits in the crosshairs of the fire's downwind ember plume: Fdir=max⁡(0,round(20×(1−Δθ90∘)))for Δθ≤90∘Fdir​=max(0,round(20×(1−90∘Δθ​)))for Δθ≤90∘

- Fire Intensity (Fint∈[0,10]Fint​∈[0,10] pts): Derived from VIIRS satellite thermal radiative power (FRP) and NIFC reported burn acreage.

- Atmospheric Dryness (Fdry∈[0,10]Fdry​∈[0,10] pts): Fuel moisture proxy based on real-time relative humidity (RH ≤12%≤12% triggers peak Red Flag scores).

- Vegetation & Fuelbed Risk (Fveg∈[0,10]Fveg​∈[0,10] pts): Proximity to USFS National Forest boundaries and wildland-urban interface borders.
**How we built it**
Frontend Framework: React Native with Expo SDK 57 (TypeScript).

- Mapping Engine: Leaflet integrated via react-native-webview rendering Carto Voyager raster tiles with authentic API key authentication, eliminating external Google Maps API key dependencies and blank-screen bugs.

- Weather & Wind Sensors: Parallel queries to NOAA National Weather Service (api.weather.gov) and high-resolution Open-Meteo satellite observational grids with decimal wind velocity (0.1 mph) and live timestamp cache-busting.

- Wildfire Hotspots: NASA FIRMS VIIRS satellite thermal detection (375m resolution) + National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC) ArcGIS Open Data REST API.

- Forest Boundaries: USFS National Forest boundary polygons bundled locally for instant offline spatial intersection.

- Native Android Toolchain: OpenJDK 17, Android SDK 35, and Gradle building release-signed standalone APKs.
**Challenges we ran into**

- Inverting Meteorological Wind Vectors: In meteorology, wind direction is reported as the direction the wind is coming from (e.g., a "North wind" at 0∘0∘ blows toward the South at 180∘180∘). Early prototypes inverted this, pointing the ember plume backward! We corrected the vector physics: θember_travel=(θwind_from+180∘)(mod360∘)θember_travel​=(θwind_from​+180∘)(mod360∘) This guaranteed that the ember cone always points directly downwind from the active fire.

- The "API Key Required" Tile Watermark: When testing Carto basemaps, tiles suddenly rendered with a diagonal "API KEY REQUIRED" watermark across the entire screen. Researching the API revealed that while Carto documentation mentions api_key=, their new raster endpoint strictly validates the query parameter ?key=YOUR_KEY. Passing the key correctly eliminated the watermark completely.

- Coordinate-Specific Wind Persistence: When users selected different cities from search chips, the wind speed occasionally appeared static because an earlier simulation preset kept state in storage. We restructured the context pipeline to force an immediate switch to live mode and added micro-timestamp query parameters, ensuring every coordinate change triggers a real-time wind query.

- Windows Device Guard Policy during APK Compilation: During the release APK build, Windows Application Control blocked the local Hermes compiler binary inside node_modules. Instead of disabling Hermes and sacrificing runtime performance, we routed Gradle's hermesCommand in app/build.gradle to the system's trusted, signed compiler binary, allowing the release build to succeed in Hermes bytecode format.

- Android 15 Edge-to-Edge Navigation Overlap: On Android 15 devices with gesture navigation, standard tab bars were clipped beneath the system bar. We resolved this by integrating useSafeAreaInsets to dynamically float the navigation and map overlays above the native system bar.
**Accomplishments that we're proud of**
Zero-Proprietary Lock-in: The app requires zero paid Google Maps or Mapbox API keys. It renders fully interactive, satellite-switchable terrain maps out of the box.

- 100% Test Coverage on Risk Calibration: Designed a 28-test automated suite verifying each factor of the Ember Threat Index against live NOAA and NIFC endpoints.

- Standalone Release APK: Compiled a complete 34.9 MB release-signed Android package (EmberWood-v4.apk) that installs seamlessly on Android 9 through Android 15 devices.

- Turning Fear into Action: Instead of panic-inducing red maps, EmberWatch gives clear, practical directives (e.g., "Move outdoor cushions downwind; shut crawlspace vents; escape heading: SE").
**What we learned**
Wildfire Dynamics: How wind velocity exponentially widens the ember cast corridor, and why small defensible-space actions in the first 5 feet (Zone 0) prevent the majority of home structure fires.

- Resilient API Architecture: How to build dual-layer fallback systems (NOAA NWS + Open-Meteo satellite observations) so life-safety tools never crash when a single government server is congested.

- Cross-Platform Map Optimization: How to embed lightweight, responsive Leaflet webviews in React Native that render satellite imagery, vector polygons, and custom pulse markers at 60 FPS.
**What's next for EmberWood**
Neighborhood Mesh Alerts: Peer-to-peer Bluetooth/Wi-Fi Direct alert propagation to notify neighbors even when cellular towers burn down.

- 3D Terrain Ember Trajectories: Integrating USGS digital elevation models (DEM) to simulate how canyon winds and mountain ridges channel ember storms.

- Smart Home Vent Triggers: Home Assistant and IoT integrations that automatically close motorized attic vents and activate exterior sprinkler defenses when high ember risks are detected.

</details>

**Inspiration**

Managing assemblies for clubs, associations, and residential complexes is often a logistical nightmare. Organizers struggle with verifying attendee identities, while participants often worry about the lack of privacy or integrity in traditional hand-raising or paper voting. I wanted to bring physical and hybrid assemblies into the 21st century by building a mobile-first solution that makes accreditation frictionless and guarantees truly anonymous, cryptographically safe voting.

**What it does**

Quorum is a modern mobile platform that simplifies assembly management. For organizers, it provides seamless check-ins using dynamic QR codes. For participants, it offers a secure voting interface where votes are cast entirely anonymously—the server never links a user ID to a vote. Instead, a unique receipt hash is generated and stored locally on the user's device, ensuring the vote is verifiable but private. Once a voting urn closes, results are calculated and published to everyone in real-time. 

**How I built it**

I built Quorum using a scalable, modern, and cross-platform tech stack:

- Frontend: React Native and Expo (SDK 57) to deliver a flawless native experience on Android.

- Styling: NativeWind (Tailwind CSS for React Native) for a clean and responsive UI.

- Backend: Supabase (PostgreSQL, Row Level Security, Edge Functions, and Realtime) to handle my database, secure the data, and publish live voting results.

- Security: Integrated device biometric security (Face ID/Touch ID) to confirm votes and prevent unauthorized actions.

- Monetization: RevenueCat seamlessly handles my in-app purchases and premium paywalls, unlocking advanced assembly management tools and expanded capacities for organizers.

**Challenges I ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was engineering a system that guarantees absolute voting anonymity while strictly preventing duplicate votes. I had to carefully design an architecture where a user is authorized to vote, but the backend stores the vote completely unlinked from their identity. Implementing the receipt hash system, which is generated and stored securely on the user's local device, required precise state management. Additionally, seamlessly integrating RevenueCat paywalls to feel like a natural part of the user journey required careful fine-tuning.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

I am incredibly proud of achieving cryptographic anonymity in the voting process without sacrificing user experience. Building a system where users can genuinely trust that their privacy is protected is highly rewarding. I am also proud of the QR accreditation flow—it's incredibly fast and drastically cuts down the time people spend in line before an assembly. Finally, getting the RevenueCat premium upgrade flow working so smoothly was a major win for me.

**What I learned**

I deepened my expertise in React Native and Expo, particularly working with the latest SDK 57 features. I learned how to effectively implement advanced Row Level Security (RLS) in Supabase to lock down database tables, ensuring the integrity of the voting data. Furthermore, integrating RevenueCat taught me a lot about structuring in-app purchases and managing entitlements for a SaaS mobile product.

**What's next for quorum**

My immediate next step is to officially release Quorum on the Google Play Store so that organizations can start using it in the real world. Ultimately, I aim to make Quorum the gold standard for modern, secure governance across all types of communities.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Football management games often lean toward opposite extremes: they are either dense, spreadsheet-heavy simulators that take hours to reach match day, or uninspired mobile clickers that lack genuine on-pitch identity. We wanted to build something nostalgic, responsive, and tactile. Our goal was to create an indie football experience that strips away bloated sub-menus, letting players rip open packs, set up their tactical formations, and instantly watch their squad battle it out on a dynamic, physics-driven pitch.

**What it does**

PackedFootball combines collectible card mechanics with an active, physics-based match simulation into a fast-paced managerial experience. Players tear into randomized player card packs, supported by in-game currency and optional microtransactions, to get better players and items to improve those players. Once a lineup is assembled and positioned in custom tactical formations like a 4-2-3-1 or 3-5-2, players dive into real-time 2D matches where outcomes are determined by emergent pitch geometry, collision, and player positioning. Outside of matches, managers climb competitive league tables for promotion, earn rewards, and customize their club's aesthetics, player appearances, and goal celebrations.

**How we built it**

We architected the game around a responsive client interface coupled with a custom 2D physics simulation loop where on-pitch action unfolds organically from spatial dynamics rather than arbitrary probabilistic die rolls. Instead of relying on abstract shooting formulas, a striker's chance to score is dictated by pure physical interactions: their instantaneous velocity, proximity vector to the ball, diving reach, and shot trajectory angles toward the net. The only direct attribute-comparison checks evaluate physical ground clashes, specifically pitting the defender’s tackling rating against the carrier’s ball control value, while the rest of the match emerges naturally from collision geometry, clearance vectors, and continuous spatial bounds.

**Challenges we ran into**

Engineering a physics-based football engine with 22 autonomous agents was our most demanding challenge, as early builds easily devolved into chaotic scrums around the ball or erratic pinball bounces off the touchlines. Tuning player dive triggers, clearance impulse vectors, and collision damping took countless iterations so that positioning felt deliberate, loose balls felt contestable, and scorelines stayed believable. 
On the production side, navigating the App Store submission process presented steep hurdles around properly integrating microtransaction architectures, configuring data privacy manifests, and ensuring full compliance with Apple’s guidelines regarding transparent pack drop-rate disclosures in the store UI.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We successfully built a responsive, physics-driven match engine where goals feel earned through spatial movement, timely tackles, and natural pitch physics rather than predetermined dice rolls. Seeing a lineup you assembled from raw card packs execute clean defensive clearances, win contested ground duels, and dive for loose balls in the box makes the entire managerial loop deeply satisfying. We are also immensely proud to have taken PackedFootball from an initial blank canvas all the way through full mobile deployment, delivering snappy UI, authentic retro pixel aesthetics, and a fun pack-opening experience to players' hands.

**What we learned**

Developing PackedFootball taught us that physical interactions in sports simulations often create far more exciting, emergent moments than purely statistical calculation tables, provided the collision and control checks are tightly bounded. We also discovered that shipping a live mobile game with in-app microtransactions requires an immense amount of operational discipline beyond writing simulation code. From balancing in-game store economies and satisfying strict store review mandates to handling responsive layout scaling across different mobile screen dimensions.

**What's next for PackedFootball**

The roadmap for PackedFootball centers heavily around social connectivity and community competition. We are actively developing a comprehensive Clan system where managers can band together, form clubs with their friends, and battle in high-stakes Clan Tournaments for collective glory and exclusive pack rewards. Alongside friend-list interactions and direct head-to-head challenges, we plan to continue rolling out fresh card drops, expanding cosmetic customization with community-voted celebration animations, and refining our physics engine to introduce new physical clash dynamics and set-piece opportunities.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

When I was preparing for my final examinations, I would frequently come across this small YouTube channel that hosted a bunch of great quotes. On some days, I would scroll through the channel endlessly. It served as a mental reset from all the studying. I figured this application could serve the same purpose for someone else.

**What it does**

myQuote is a simple quotes app. Its main features are speech synthesis and a minimal user interface guided by the 60-30-10 color rule: a dominant background color, a secondary text color, and an accent color for controls and highlights.

Users can read quotes, listen to them, save favorites, and share them. The app also offers a collection of premium themes and bundled fonts without changing the underlying UI structure. Pro users can set their own notification time.

**How we built it**

Initially, I wanted to program the app locally, solo and slowly, but my hardware was simply not good enough for the workflow I had in mind. So, I decided to build it using AI and cloud infrastructure. I used a promotional ChatGPT Plus trial that coincided with Shipaton’s competition period.

The app is written in Kotlin, with Jetpack Compose and Material 3 handling the interface. Jetpack DataStore stores local preferences, Android’s text-to-speech system reads the quotes, and RevenueCat manages purchases and premium access.

All the APKs were compiled through GitHub Actions. The entire process was iterative: I gave ChatGPT instructions, downloaded the resulting builds, and tested the app on physical devices to see whether it met my specifications. When something failed or looked wrong, that became the next round of work.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest initial challenge was not having enough computational power to build the application comfortably on my own machine. Moving the builds to GitHub Actions made the project practical. Without the promotional ChatGPT offer, I would probably have abandoned it.

Testing brought its own challenges. Speech synthesis depended on the voices installed on each device, and an interface that scrolled smoothly on one device could struggle on another. Premium access also needed attention: a successful purchase had to remain correctly recognized after reopening the app. The implementation uses RevenueCat’s customer information to determine whether the premium entitlement is active.

Getting an APK to compile was only part of the job. I still had to check what it actually did.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The first fully functioning prototype was built in six days. 

From there, I refined the interface, themes, speech controls, and purchase behavior through repeated testing.

The quote collection and fonts are bundled with the app. Quotes can be read locally, and speech works offline when a suitable offline voice is installed. Online voices and RevenueCat purchase checks use network access.

I also ended up with a repeatable cloud build process that let me keep developing despite my hardware limitations.

**What we learned**

You can build an entire application using cloud infrastructure, even when your own machine cannot comfortably handle the development environment.

AI made implementation faster, but I still had to define what I wanted, test the results, and identify where the behavior fell short. The more precise my instructions and feedback became, the more useful the process was.

The biggest lesson for me was that I could change how I approached the work. I did not need to wait for better hardware before starting.

**What's next for myQuote**

I plan to publish myQuote on the Google Play Store. For now, I am submitting it to Shipaton’s Next Gen category, with public source code and a judge build that uses RevenueCat’s Test Store for purchases.

</details>

**What it does**

NovaED combines social discovery with creator business tools in one mobile-first experience:

- Pulse feed for photo and video content

- New & Rising discovery to give emerging creators a fairer path to visibility

- Creator profiles with posts, followers, saves, and engagement

- Creator Studio for drafts, publishing, content management, and analytics

- Creator analytics for engagement and audience performance

- Nova Companion and creator-assistance tools for planning, brainstorming, hooks, and workflow support

- Marketplace and monetization surfaces for creator-focused premium features and supported offerings

- Safety and privacy controls including reporting, blocking, protected account data, and secure authentication patterns

**How RevenueCat fits in**

NovaED is integrating the RevenueCat SDK as the entitlement layer for premium mobile access. The goal is to keep the core social experience understandable while using RevenueCat for at least one paid premium purchase or subscription.

Premium access is designed around creator-focused upgrades such as Creator Boost and Pro features. RevenueCat handles purchase/entitlement state, while sensitive server-side secrets remain outside client code. The app uses the public RevenueCat SDK key on the client and reserves secret API credentials for backend-only use.

**Discovery model**

NovaED is designed around a balanced ranking concept rather than pure popularity. The working feed model combines engagement, watch/dwell time, monetization yield, and time decay, alongside a dedicated New & Rising experience so smaller creators have a realistic chance to surface.

**Design**

NovaED uses a light, futuristic creator-economy visual direction with high-resolution media, clean navigation, responsive phone/tablet layouts, and creator-focused dashboards. The goal is professional and modern rather than generic or playful.

**Safety and privacy**

The production path includes account-level authorization and data isolation, protected environment variables, server-side validation for sensitive monetization actions, file/input validation, fraud and duplicate-request protections, privacy policy, terms, community guidelines, creator monetization terms, and account-deletion instructions.

**Current Shipaton work**

The Shipaton build is focused on completing RevenueCat premium access, production QA, mobile testing, store-ready assets, and a concise device demo that shows the creator workflow and premium experience.

**Why it matters**

Creators often have to piece together publishing, analytics, monetization, workflow, and discovery across separate services. NovaED is designed to bring those pieces into one product while giving emerging creators more visibility and clearer monetization tools.

The long-term goal is to make creator growth more accessible, measurable, and sustainable without removing creator control from the process.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

It is easy to miss hazards around your home because you see the same rooms every day. A loose cable, blocked exit, unstable object, or exposed knife might not seem serious until someone gets hurt.

I wanted to build Safesight as a second set of eyes for your home. It helps people notice potential dangers and gives them practical ways to fix them.

**What it does**

Safesight uses AI to scan photos of rooms and find possible safety hazards. It highlights each hazard, explains why it could be dangerous, gives it a severity level, and suggests how to fix it.

Designed for parents child-proofing their homes, new homeowners, renters, homebuyers, real estate agents, and senior citizens, Safesight makes identifying everyday household risks more accessible.

After making a change, users can scan the room again to see if the hazard is gone. The app also includes a House Score, scan history, hazard tracking, and shareable reports.

Safesight is meant to be a helpful tool, not a replacement for a professional safety inspection.

**How we built it**

Safesight is an iOS app built with Swift and SwiftUI. It sends images to a backend server, which securely processes them with Google Gemini. The Gemini API key is stored on the server instead of inside the app.

The AI returns structured information about each hazard, including its name, location, severity, confidence, explanation, and suggested fix.

I also added scan history, image uploads, rate limiting, hazard tracking, and RevenueCat for the optional Premium features.

To test the app, I created a benchmark using 20 room photos with manually labeled hazards. Safesight found 96.4% of the hazards in the benchmark, with a precision of 94.6% and an F1 score of 95.5%.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the hardest parts was making the results useful. I did not want Safesight to simply list objects in a room. It needed to explain what might be dangerous and tell the user what they could do about it.

AI is also not always correct. I had to think about confidence levels, severity scores, false positives, and how to make it clear that Safesight cannot guarantee that a home is completely safe.

I also had to work through problems involving image uploads, API costs, server security, different lighting conditions, and keeping track of hazards between scans.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I am most proud of the complete process Safesight provides:

Find a problem, understand it, fix it, and scan again.

I am also proud that I was able to:

Build a working iOS app with SwiftUI.

- Added hazard explanations and recommended fixes.

- Included bounding boxes, severity levels, and confidence scores.

- Created a House Score that changes as hazards are fixed.

- Added scan history and hazard tracking.

- Built a backend with security features and request limits.

- Created a benchmark to test how well the system works.

- Built the project independently at 14 years old.

**How We Integrated RevenueCat**

We integrated RevenueCat to power Safesight's freemium model and manage Premium entitlements.

Users get 2 free scans and access to 6 Focus areas. Premium unlocks unlimited scans, 25+ Focus areas, AI summaries, product recommendations, unlimited exports, and higher-tier AI models.

RevenueCat handles the subscription state, purchase flow, and entitlement checks, so Safesight can instantly unlock or restrict Premium features based on a user's subscription.

$9.99/month or $79.99/year.

**What we learned**

I learned that building an AI app involves much more than connecting an app to an AI model. I had to think about the design, privacy, security, cost, testing, and how much users should trust the results.

I also learned that testing computer vision is difficult. An app might recognize the right hazard but still place the box incorrectly or give the wrong severity level. This showed me why real testing and honest limitations are important.

**What's next for Safesight**

I want to test Safesight with more rooms and a larger set of manually labeled images. I also want to improve the accuracy of the hazard boxes and reduce false positives.

Other improvements I am considering include better handling of unclear photos, more accessibility features, support for more types of homes, and possibly processing some images directly on the device for better privacy.

The final step would be to launch Safesight publicly on the App Store so people can use it in their own homes.

The long-term goal is to make Safesight a useful and trustworthy tool that helps people notice and fix hazards around them.

</details>

**Inspiration**

As a university student, my daily lives are scattered across half a dozen clunky apps: one for class timetables, another for tracking spending, a third for assignment deadlines, and isolated notes for health habits. Most campus tools are outdated, confusing, and stressful to navigate. 

I built Varsity to solve this exact problem: creating a unified, elegant "Campus Life OS" that simplifies academic scheduling, daily financial budgeting, and health tracking into a single cohesive web experience.

**What it does**

Varsity acts as an all-in-one personal operating system for students, organized into three core pillars:

- Academics: Interactive class timetable builder, exam countdown trackers, and prioritized assignment management.

- Finance: Campus expense logger and allowance calculator designed specifically for student living expenses.

- Health & Wellness: Daily wellness check-ins, hydration/sleep logs, and focus timers to combat study burnout.

- Campus Social & Study Hub: Real-time peer chat channels and study rooms where students can collaborate on assignments, form study groups, have a date and connect across campus.

**Monetization & RevenueCat Integration**

Varsity operates on a freemium model powered by RevenueCat Web Billing:

- Free Tier: Core timetable builder, basic expense logging, and daily wellness logs.

- Varsity Pro ($2.99/mo or $19.99/yr): Unlocks budget analytics, custom UI themes, automated schedule export, and advanced health habit insights via a seamless RevenueCat paywall.

**How I built it**

Varsity was built using a web-first architecture designed for rapid iteration and $0 upfront infrastructure cost:

- Frontend: Built with React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS.

- UI/UX Design: Lovable AI assistant was used as a rapid component builder to craft an intuitive Navy-on-Cream aesthetic.

- Database & Auth: Supabase handles real-time data persistence for class schedules, financial records, and user authentication.

- Monetization Engine: RevenueCat Web SDK (@revenuecat/purchases-js) manages subscription entitlements, paywall rendering, and Stripe payment processing.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Seamless Paywall Logic: Ensuring entitlement states (varsity_pro) instantly updated across all device sessions without forcing full page refreshes required careful state management around the RevenueCat Web SDK initialization.

- Multi-Pillar Data Sync: Designing a database schema in Supabase that gracefully handles real-time updates for academic tasks, budget transactions, and wellness logs under a single unified dashboard.

- Universal Aesthetic: Balancing UI warmth to create an approachable design for all students without leaning too heavily toward a single demographic.

**Accomplishments that I am proud of**

- End-to-End Monetization: Successfully implementing a working subscription paywall using RevenueCat Web Billing on a web app.

- Unified Student UX: Bringing academic, financial, and wellness tracking under one roof with zero clutter.

- Zero-Budget Execution: Delivering a fully functional, production-ready SaaS application with $0 spend.

**What I learned**

- Web Monetization Flexibility: Harnessing RevenueCat for web billing allows developers to implement cross-platform subscription logic effortlessly without being bound to app store review delays.

- AI-Assisted Workflows: Leveraging AI tools for component generation dramatically speeds up design-to-code pipelines for solo developers.

**What's next for Varsity: An All-in-One Campus OS**

- Native Mobile Apps: Packaging the web platform into native iOS and Android builds (including Samsung Galaxy Store) via Capacitor.

- Campus Community Hubs: Expanding into localized university news, peer study groups, and shared campus marketplace features.

- AI Study Assistant: Integrating smart exam preparation tools and automated timetable parsing from university PDFs.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/357/568/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/357/568/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/357/541/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/357/541/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/357/542/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/357/542/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/357/537/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/357/537/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**About the Project**

In an emergency, can someone stay calm enough to unlock their phone, find an SOS button, and press it at the right moment?

Often, they may not be able to. They may run for help, shout, or repeatedly cry “Help, help!” We built Abhaya around this possibility.

Most existing SOS applications depend on a single manual action. But in a real emergency, a person may not be able to unlock the phone, find the button, or press it in time.

Abhaya takes a different approach.

If a user starts running for help, the app can use the mobile phone’s built-in sensors to detect a configured rapid-movement pattern and trigger an automatic SOS. If the user shouts for help or says the keyword Abhaya, our Edge ML model can recognize the voice signal and start the SOS process.

The app also provides many other modern ways to trigger SOS, including manual tap, press and hold, triple tap, voice keyword detection, and sensor-based movement detection. After a trigger is detected, Abhaya starts a short countdown so the user can cancel the alert if it was activated accidentally.

Once the SOS is confirmed, Abhaya can share the user’s latest location, alert emergency contacts via SMS, create a live safety link, and let trusted people follow the situation. Features like route check-ins, crime-data maps, role-based contacts, haptic feedback, and Discreet Mode extend it beyond a traditional panic button.

Our goal is to build a modern, out-of-the-box safety solution that recognizes people may react differently in emergencies. Abhaya provides multiple ways to get help when using the phone normally may not be possible.

**What Inspired Us**

We realized that in a real emergency, people may not have the time—or even the ability—to calmly unlock their phone and press an SOS button. They could be running, unable to speak, carrying something, or trying not to attract attention.

That made us ask:

What if getting help didn’t depend on pressing a button?

How can a mobile phone recognize several meaningful safety signals and begin a controlled SOS flow without relying on only one visible button?

**How We Built It**

We wanted Abhaya to feel simple for the person using it, while doing a lot of the hard work quietly in the background. So we built it as a mobile-first safety system with a backend service and a public live-viewer flow.

The mobile application is built with React Native and Expo. It brings everything together in one place—from a clear permission explainer and home map to route check-ins, emergency contact management, sensor dashboard, subscription settings, and a low-attention Discreet Mode for premium users.

Behind the app, the backend is built with Node.js, Express, Prisma, and PostgreSQL. It manages user profiles, emergency contacts, route history, safety sessions, public viewer tokens, and SOS relay endpoints. For communication, SMS delivery is connected through Twilio, while OpenStreetMap-based services provide map data and nearby police-location information. A real-time WebSocket engine keeps live location updates flowing during an active safety session.

One of the most important parts of Abhaya is that not everything needs to depend on the internet. Our Edge ML and sensor layer is designed to keep critical detection close to the device. Voice and sensor signals can be evaluated locally before the application starts the SOS countdown. This reduces dependence on continuous network availability during the first detection step and helps keep the experience fast, responsive, and practical when every second matters.

In simple terms, we built Abhaya so that the phone can do more than wait for someone to press a button—it can actively help recognize when assistance may be needed.

**High-Level Structure**

**Key Features**

**Situation-Based SOS Triggers**

Abhaya supports multiple trigger paths so the user is not dependent on one interaction method:

- Manual safety action

- Press-and-hold gesture

- Triple-tap gesture

- Voice keyword through the optional Edge ML audio model

- Configured motion detection such as rapid shaking

- Missed route check-in escalation, where enabled by the journey flow

The countdown and cancellation step help reduce accidental emergency notifications.

**Live Location and Safety Sessions**

When a safety session begins, Abhaya creates a server-hosted link that trusted recipients can open. The session can provide the user identity, current status, last known location, start time, expiration, acknowledgement state, and resolution state. This gives recipients more useful information than a single static alert.

**Route Check-In**

Users can define a destination and expected arrival time. During the journey, the app maintains an active check-in state. The user can mark the route as completed, and the journey can be reviewed later through route history. A missed check-in can become an additional signal for escalation, depending on the configured flow.

**Role-Based Emergency Contacts**

Contacts can be assigned meaningful roles such as primary responder, family member, friend, nearby helper, or medical contact. This makes the response plan easier to understand and allows the incident interface to communicate statuses such as:

Primary responder — notified
Friend — viewer opened
Family member — not reached

**Crime Data and Map Context**

The home map can display safety-related crime-data zones and nearby context. These visual overlays are intended to support awareness and route planning; they are not presented as a guarantee that an area is safe or unsafe.

**Discreet Mode**

Discreet Mode provides:

A low-attention interface for situations where drawing attention may be unsafe.

It uses a neutral confirmation surface, configurable low-attention triggers, haptic countdown feedback, and a notification-shade update. It is a premium feature. It is not completely invisible and does not guarantee that Android restrictions can be bypassed.

**What We Learned**

Abhaya taught us that safety is not just about adding more detection features. It is about building a trustworthy chain from signal to decision to response.

We learned to balance on-device processing and backend services, while keeping the app useful even when the network is unreliable. We also learned that permissions like location, microphone, notifications, and background access need to be explained clearly so users know what they are allowing.

Most importantly, we learned to design for things going wrong. GPS can fail, requests can time out, permissions can be denied, and Android can suspend background tasks. So we built around cancellation, retries, offline persistence, clear status messages, and honest limitations.

And we realized one more thing: the alert is only as good as the help that follows it. A useful SOS should give the recipient the location, live link, contact role, acknowledgement, and clear context about what happened.

**Challenges We Faced**

**Balancing Automatic Detection and False Alarms**

Automatic SOS is powerful but sensitive. Motion, voice, or environmental signals can be ambiguous. We addressed this by using a configurable trigger model, confidence information for the Edge ML keyword flow, a countdown, and an explicit cancellation path.

**Background Execution and Android Restrictions**

A safety feature that only works while the app is open is incomplete, but mobile operating systems restrict background execution for privacy and battery reasons. We implemented background-aware notification and pending-state handling while keeping the product language honest: the app supports continued safety behavior where the platform and permissions allow it, but it does not promise unrestricted background execution.

**Reliable Emergency Delivery**

The notification pipeline crosses several boundaries: the mobile device, the REST API, the database, the SMS provider, and the recipient’s device. Each boundary can fail independently. We added API fallbacks, persisted pending SOS state, delivery results, and recipient response states to make failures visible instead of silently presenting a false success state.

**Avoiding Duplicate Notifications**

A live safety session and an SOS alert can both appear to be notification events. Treating them as unrelated flows can cause duplicate messages to recipients. The architecture therefore separates session creation, live tracking, and emergency delivery responsibilities so the system can evolve toward one consistent incident pipeline.

**Privacy and Trust**

The app handles phone numbers, location, microphone access, emergency contacts, and potentially sensitive incident information. We designed contextual permission screens, role-based contact presentation, neutral messaging for Discreet Mode, and clear limitations to make the system more understandable and trustworthy.

**Closing**

When an emergency happens, every second matters—and every person may react differently.

Abhaya brings together Edge ML, built-in mobile sensors, live maps, crime-data context, route monitoring, emergency contacts, SMS delivery, and real-time location sharing into one connected safety workflow.

But Abhaya is not about making unrealistic promises.
It is about making sure that when someone needs help, there is more than one way to ask for it.

It is about giving trusted people the right information at the right time, while keeping the entire experience calm, transparent, and practical.

Because sometimes, the person who needs help may not be able to reach a button.

Abhaya — situation-aware mobile safety that stays ready when the user may not be able to reach the SOS button.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Getting dressed every morning sounds simple, but it routinely devolves into decision fatigue. Most outfit recommendations online suggest clothes you don't own, ignore whether your favorite pants are sitting at the bottom of a laundry basket, or fail to account for local weather changes.

I wanted to build FitFlow as a privacy-focused, local-first "wardrobe OS" that solves this exact daily friction. Instead of relying purely on generic cloud styling services, FitFlow treats your physical closet as a deterministic state machine: tracking laundry availability, parsing personal aesthetic notes, and factoring in real-time climate data to algorithmically generate the right fit for the day.

**How I Built It**

FitFlow is designed as a hybrid architecture: combining local-first privacy with optional LLM styling capabilities.

- UI & Client Polish: Built with a dark tactical design system, an iOS-style translucent floating navigation bar, tactile haptic feedback, and custom UI audio triggers to make daily wardrobe management feel responsive and polished.

- Deterministic Laundry Engine: Keeps full state management of every clothing item ($i \in I$). An item's availability state $S(i)$ transitions through a defined state cycle:

$$S(i) \in {\text{Clean}, \text{In Wash}, \text{Drying}, \text{Dry Cleaning}}$$

If an item's state is not Clean, it is strictly excluded from the recommendation candidate pool $C$.

- Contextual Outfit Scoring Algorithm: The outfit generator scores valid combinations based on weather compatibility $W$, recent wear frequency penalization $R$, and style context flags $V$ (e.g., excluding "home-only" gear when toggled for "Heading Out"):

$$\text{Score}(\text{Outfit}) = \alpha \cdot W(i) + \beta \cdot V(i) - \gamma \cdot R(i)$$

- AI Stylist & Local Privacy: Sensitive wardrobe photos and closet metadata remain entirely on-device (stored securely using Android Keystore). Users can optionally provide a Gemini API key to trigger deep natural language style note parsing without sacrificing local data control.

- Monetization (RevenueCat): Integrated the RevenueCat SDK to handle freemium feature gating — free users get core wardrobe tracking, laundry state management, and basic outfit recommendations, while Daily Fit Pro unlocks the AI Stylist (Gemini-powered style parsing) and AI-driven Wardrobe Gap Recommendations (suggested items to fill gaps in your closet, linked out to Amazon/Myntra).

**Challenges I Faced**

- Managing Micro-Interactions & State: Balancing smooth UI transitions with instant state updates—such as long-press gestures to toggle laundry states—required tuning haptic feedback timing and audio cues so the app felt instantaneous without dropping frames.

- Edge-Case Filtering: Designing the algorithm to handle depleted wardrobes gracefully (e.g., when all tops in a specific weather bracket are currently in the wash) without breaking the recommendation pipeline.

**What I Learned**

Building FitFlow highlighted the power of combining deterministic rule engines with modern generative AI. Relying on strict state rules for constraints like laundry availability while delegating subjective tasks like style coordination to LLMs produces a much more reliable user experience than using AI alone.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Washington caps how much a 16- or 17-year-old can work in a school week. Most teens never see the statute. The person writing the schedule is usually the person breaking it. I wanted one place for "that shift felt wrong": the rule, a link to the published text, and the dollar amount.

**What it does**

Off the Clock is an Android app for teen workers in Washington.

- Log a shift by typing it in, or photograph the schedule your manager posted. OCR runs on the phone; the photo never leaves the device; nothing is saved until you confirm.

- Every shift runs through a rules engine built from chapter 296-125 WAC (as amended by WSR 26-11-048, effective July 1 2026), plus WAC 296-126-092 and RCW 49.46.130. Each problem quotes the statute and links the published text.

- Missed rest breaks, docked time, pay under the wage floor, and unpaid overtime are summed in integer cents and shown as one figure, with every problem listed underneath.

Finding violations is free. The paid unlock is a dated PDF evidence record: every shift, every rule broken, and the statute behind each one: the form you hand to someone else.

**How I built it**

- Expo SDK 57, React Native 0.86 (New Architecture), TypeScript, expo-router

- React Native Paper (Material 3), light and dark

- On-device schedule scan via ML Kit (expo-mlkit-ocr)

- Local-only storage (AsyncStorage). No account, no server, no upload.

- Evidence PDF via expo-print + expo-sharing

- 55 tests under plain node --test covering hours caps, breaks, wage floor, overtime, OCR regrouping, PDF escaping, WCAG AA contrast, and entitlement logic

**Monetization with RevenueCat (Next Gen judges: read this)**

Violation findings are free. The $4.99 Pro unlock is a dated PDF evidence export (entitlement: evidence_export). Parent pays via RevenueCat: in-app one-time purchase, or Web Purchase Link / Web Billing on Stripe with the same customer ID. The app refreshes entitlement when a parent already paid. Built against Test Store + Stripe test mode for Next Gen.

Key files: src/entitlement.ts, src/purchases.tsx, app/export.tsx. See also SANDBOX-PURCHASE-TERMS.md.

**Challenges I ran into**

Encoding chapter 296-125 into deterministic tests: daily/weekly caps, night cutoffs, and break math differ by age band. OCR from real posted schedules is messy; the parser has to refuse bad reads instead of inventing shifts. Connecting Web Billing to the same customer ID as the native SDK so a parent payment unlocks without a second account.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- Working rules engine with statute citations (each hit links published WAC/RCW text)

- Dual RevenueCat rails (SDK + Web Purchase Link) aimed at the actual payer (the parent)

- On-device OCR with an explicit privacy boundary

- 55 focused unit tests on the money and time math

- MIT open-source repo ready for Next Gen review

**What I learned**

Labor rules are precise; an app that misquotes them is worse than no app. Monetizing discovery of underpayment would tax the person with the least power, so the free/paid split follows who holds the card. RevenueCat Web Billing is what makes "parent pays, teen unlocks" work without building a custom checkout.

**What's next for Off the Clock**

Ship a production Play Store build with live RevenueCat keys once eligible; expand coverage if other states publish similarly clear hour/break rules; keep the local-first privacy model.

**Awards I am competing for**

Next Gen Award: solo student submission judged on video + open-source code. This entry is a minor entrant with guardian consent; Next Gen is the eligible lane.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/357/851/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/357/851/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/357/852/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/357/852/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/393/314/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/393/314/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Moving a link or a file from my phone to my laptop is still oddly painful. I end up emailing it to myself, messaging it on Slack, or hunting for a cable. AirDrop solves this beautifully, but only inside Apple's ecosystem. I wanted that same "it just appears" feeling across Android, iOS, and desktop, and I wanted to build it once, which made Kotlin Multiplatform the obvious choice for the RevenueCat Shipaton.

**What it does**

Beam is an AirDrop-style drop zone for your own devices. Open it on two devices on the same Wi-Fi and they find each other automatically. Pair once with a one-time PIN or a QR code, and from then on you can send text, links, and files with a tap.

The flow I care about most: on your phone, open a web page, hit Share → Beam, pick your laptop, and the page opens there immediately.

Everything stays on your local network. There are no accounts and no cloud.

Beam Pro (RevenueCat): text and links are free, and pairing is free for up to 2 devices. Sending files and pairing more devices are behind a Beam Pro paywall, built with RevenueCat's purchases-kmp and Paywalls.

**How we built it**

One codebase: discovery, pairing, transport, persistence, and the whole UI live in one Kotlin Multiplatform module, using Compose Multiplatform for Android, iOS, and desktop.
Discovery: mDNS/Bonjour, using each platform's native API (NsdManager, NSNetService, jmdns) behind a shared interface.
Transport: every device runs a small embedded Ktor server (/pair, /text, /file, /status) and talks to peers over the LAN. If the default port is taken, it falls back to the next free one and advertises whichever it actually bound.
Trust: a single-use, time-limited PIN (or QR) must be verified before any device counts as paired, and text and file requests from unpaired senders are rejected.
Persistence: SQLDelight for paired devices and history, plus each platform's native key-value store for the device identity and settings.
Always on: an Android foreground service and a macOS menu-bar tray keep Beam reachable when its window is closed.
RevenueCat: the paywall, purchases, and a Thingsenz Pro entitlement gate file transfers and the device limit.

**Challenges we ran into**

RevenueCat has no desktop SDK. So the desktop app can't sell Pro. I made it inherit Pro from a paired phone: it asks each paired, reachable phone whether it holds the entitlement, and unlocks while any says yes. That turned a limitation into a feature that fits Beam's "your devices work together" idea.
A thread-visibility bug. Correct PINs were being rejected as wrong. The PIN was written on the UI thread and read on the server's threads without @Volatile, so the server kept comparing against a stale value. It took ruling out expiry, duplicate processes, and the random generator before I found it.
"Ghost" devices. I generated a fresh random device ID on every launch, so each relaunch looked like a brand-new device. Persisting the ID fixed the ghost entries and pairing surviving restarts.
Kotlin/Native crashes. An uncaught error in a background coroutine kills an iOS app. That showed up when two Beam instances shared one machine, and led to the port fallback.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

A single shared codebase that actually discovers, pairs, and transfers between an Android phone, an iOS simulator, and a Mac.
The share-a-link-and-it-opens-on-my-laptop flow works reliably.
A working end-to-end paywall: free-plan lock, RevenueCat paywall, a test purchase, and the desktop unlocking itself.

**What we learned**

Multiplatform is strongest when you share the boring 90% and keep the platform edges thin. I also learned to distrust "it works on my machine" for threading, and that a small paywall design decision (desktop inherits Pro) can matter more than the paywall itself.

**What's next for Beam**

QR scanning and showing the device's own LAN address on iOS (both are Android-only today).
Verifying the Windows and Linux tray and launch-on-login code on real machines.
Real Play Store and App Store products in place of RevenueCat's Test Store, and a proper unpair option.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Kin — A Messenger That Remembers What Matters**

**Inspiration**

Messaging apps are excellent at helping us talk, but poor at helping us remember. The conversations that matter most — with a partner, best friend, parent, or sibling — eventually disappear inside thousands of messages. Photos, first dates, favourite places, plans, and small promises are still there, but retrieving and reliving them is work.

Every relationship also receives nearly the same generic chat interface. The history shared with a partner feels no more personal than a project group, even though those relationships carry very different meaning.

**What it does**

Kin is a private messenger built around the relationship rather than the inbox. Each one-to-one Kin Space combines a familiar conversation with a second layer for the relationship itself.

A person can long-press any meaningful message and choose Remember this, then preserve it as a Moment, important date, or plan. Saved items appear in the relationship view and chronological timeline, retain a link to the source conversation, and can resurface through On This Day. Each Space can also have its own nickname, accent, wallpaper, shared media, and relationship sticker.

Key features include:

- private, invitation-based one-to-one Kin Spaces;

- text and image messages, reactions, timestamps, relationship stickers, realtime updates, retry, and offline states;

- Remember this for turning a source message into a Moment, date, or plan without losing its conversational context;

- relationship views, shared media, future plans, and a chronological timeline;

- On This Day anniversary resurfacing;

- per-relationship nicknames, accents, themes, and wallpapers;

- archive, leave, block, report, account export, and account deletion;

- private-by-default notifications with retry and receipt reconciliation; and

- a deterministic fictional demo story that never silently replaces connected production services.

Kin is intentionally not a public social network, relationship score, surveillance tool, or automated relationship coach. Ordinary messaging remains free, existing saved history remains available after a subscription ends, private conversations contain no ads, and relationship data is not sold.

**How we built it**

Kin is a TypeScript application built with Expo SDK 57, React Native, and Expo Router for Android, iOS, and a browser-compatible demo.

The client depends on a KinRepository interface so the UI is not tied to one data provider. A local AsyncStorage adapter supplies the deterministic Maya-and-Jamie demo story. The connected implementation uses Supabase Auth, Postgres, Row Level Security, Realtime, private Storage, RPCs, Edge Functions, Cron, and Vault.

EAS owns the native build profiles. Isolated Supabase production and staging projects run in Singapore, and Vercel hosts the public demo. Production bundle validation rejects missing or wrong-platform public keys and checks that server secrets never enter client bundles.

**How RevenueCat powers Kin+**

Kin+ adds unlimited creation of new Moments and relationship themes while leaving ordinary messaging and previously saved history available to everyone.

The native RevenueCat adapter identifies customers with the signed-in Supabase UUID. A signed, idempotent Supabase webhook refreshes RevenueCat's current subscriber state instead of trusting individual lifecycle events, then stores a private entitlement projection used for server-authoritative limits.

For judge testing, the standalone Android build uses an isolated staging backend and RevenueCat Test Store. Purchases are simulated, never charge real money, and create no real revenue. The build is intentionally debuggable because RevenueCat Test Store rejects non-debuggable binaries; it is not a production-store binary.

**Privacy and AI choices**

Kin does not send private relationship content to a generative model and does not place an AI participant inside a relationship. Memory creation is explicit: a person chooses what to save, while deterministic date logic powers timeline ordering and On This Day resurfacing. This is a deliberate privacy and product decision.

AI was used during development to turn the product thesis into an implementation plan, evaluate edge cases, generate test scenarios, review interaction copy, and check whether monetization and recovery states stayed aligned with the emotional and privacy goals. The fictional demo story and original demo assets were also developed as a safe, non-personal narrative for repeatable testing and presentation.

**How we used Codex**

Codex helped translate the product requirements into the Expo, Supabase, and RevenueCat architecture; implement test-driven slices for authentication, account lifecycle, invitations, messaging, Moments, personalization, safety, notifications, billing, and deployment; review RLS and privacy boundaries; build the RevenueCat adapters and webhook; create and inspect the brand assets and screenshots; and run CI-equivalent tests, browser journeys, bundle scans, deployment checks, and provider-boundary audits.

Codex also helped challenge ideas that weakened the product thesis. Relationship scoring, silent AI inference, public feeds, ads inside conversations, and locking old memories behind a subscription were deliberately excluded.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest boundary was making premium access convenient without letting billing state become a client-side trust decision. RevenueCat remains the billing authority, while the server refreshes current subscriber state and applies limits from a private entitlement projection.

We also had to keep three environments honest: a deterministic public web demo, a connected staging Android build, and production services. Explicit environment labels, isolated projects, bundle validation, and separate adapters prevent demo behaviour from silently masking provider failures.

RevenueCat Test Store introduced one more constraint: it intentionally rejects nondebuggable apps. We therefore produced a standalone debuggable judge APK with an embedded JavaScript bundle, then verified that it cold-starts without Metro and completes purchase and restore in an Android 15 emulator.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- The central conversation-to-memory flow works end to end: message → Remember this → Moment → relationship view → timeline → On This Day.

- RevenueCat Test Store purchase and restore were verified in the native Android UI, and staging Supabase received the active kin_plus entitlement.

- The release gate passes 67 Jest suites / 340 app tests, 36 Edge Function and operator-tool tests, and 14 Playwright journeys, together with TypeScript, lint, web export, production bundle isolation, and dependency checks.

- The production backend includes eight migrations, 17 RLS-enabled public tables, private Storage, five active Edge Functions, and two scheduled workers.

- The public demo uses only fictional data and visibly labels simulated billing.

**What we learned**

Relationship software benefits from restraint. The most useful memory feature was not automatic extraction; it was a clear, intentional action that preserves context. Monetization also feels more respectful when it expands future creation and expression without taking away messages or memories people already made.

Technically, we learned to treat purchase events as prompts to refresh authoritative state, keep client and server responsibilities explicit, and test provider boundaries separately from local application behaviour.

**What's next**

The next production steps are real Google Play subscription products and receipt proof, physical-device push verification, and a custom SMTP sender before broad consumer signup. Longer-term ideas include group Kin Spaces, voice and video calls, and message import, but only where they preserve the relationship-first, privacy-conscious product direction.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

“Has anyone given Mochi her medicine today?”

In a household where several people care for a pet, answering that question often means searching group chats, calling someone, or relying on memory.

A study published in 2024 surveyed 151 dog owners at a veterinary teaching hospital in New Zealand: 38% shared medication administration with others, while approximately 30% of the 132 owners managing oral medication reported missed doses (Odom et al., 2024).

We built Pet Together to give caregivers a shared view of what needs doing, who is responsible, and what has been recorded—connecting everyday care with a clearer history for vet visits.

**What it does**

Pet Together helps households coordinate daily care, track medication, and prepare for vet visits.

- Shared care: Create recurring or one-time tasks, claim them, or offer them to another caregiver. Calendars, reminders, and per-pet views keep responsibilities and progress visible.

- Medication tracking: Set up medication courses and dose times, record administrations or skips, and review adherence. The history distinguishes given, skipped, and not recorded.

- Health records and vet preparation: Keep symptoms, weight, vaccinations, past visits, and supporting photos together. Generate a Vet Visit Pack for a selected period and export it as a shareable PDF.

- AI-assisted entry: Type or say an instruction such as “Feed Mochi every day at 8 a.m.” Gemini proposes a schedule that the caregiver reviews and confirms.

- Household access: Members join through invitations with owner approval. The app supports English, Japanese, Chinese, and Korean.

**How we built it**

We built the app with Flutter and Dart. Firebase Authentication handles sign-in, Cloud Firestore synchronizes household data, and Firebase Storage stores photos and attachments. Cloud Functions and Firebase Cloud Messaging support reminders and household updates.

Firebase AI Logic connects to Gemini to turn typed or transcribed instructions into structured task proposals. Charts visualize care activity, and PDFs are generated on the device.

RevenueCat handles purchases, restoration, and subscription entitlements, with eligible access shared across household members. A common service interface supports both the Firebase implementation and a local demo.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Shared responsibility: We needed clear rules for claiming tasks, requesting handoffs, and handling simultaneous updates. Explicit states and transactional updates help keep responsibility consistent.

- Recurring care: Recurring routines must remain separate from individual occurrences, so skipping today’s walk preserves tomorrow’s schedule.

- Reliable health records: A medication update awaiting server confirmation must not count as a confirmed administration. The vet summary also needs to identify missing information clearly.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Connecting daily coordination, medication tracking, and vet preparation.

- Making caregiver responsibilities and handoffs visible.

- Preserving the distinction between given, skipped, and unrecorded doses.

- Turning household records into a shareable Vet Visit Pack.

- Adding Voice to Action to simplify task entry.

- Providing a local demo alongside the cloud implementation.

**What we learned**

- Clarity is a safety feature: In shared care, ambiguous statuses lead to missed or duplicated doses. Clearly distinguishing between given, skipped, and unrecorded directly impacts how a caregiver decides what to do next.

- Keep AI bounded and transparent: Natural language processing works best when focused on drafting structured schedules, leaving final review and confirmation firmly in the hands of the caregiver.

**What's next for Pet Together**

On the product side, we plan to strengthen health-related features, including automated alerts for unusual changes in recorded weight and other health data.

To guide broader improvements, we have created a multilingual survey exploring care habits, coordination difficulties, feature priorities, and pricing preferences. We will use the responses to refine our workflows and offerings, inviting respondents to a beta to test updates with real households.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**LampLight: Learn Languages Through Living Books**

Read real stories in the language you're learning, with translation close enough to help but quiet enough to let you keep reading.

**Inspiration**

Learning a language through isolated exercises is useful, but reading a real story creates a different kind of connection.

Growing up in Bangladesh, we often found ourselves reading literature in another language with a book in one hand and a phone dictionary in the other. Looking up a word meant leaving the page, opening another app, finding the translation, and then trying to remember where we were in the story. The same problem becomes even harder with languages and writing systems that are poorly supported by existing bilingual reading tools.

We built LampLight around a simple idea: language learning should happen inside meaningful reading.

Instead of replacing books with exercises, LampLight puts real literature at the center and keeps language assistance available when the reader needs it.

**What It Does**

LampLight is a mobile reading app for people who want to improve a language by reading actual books.

**Two-Shelf Library**

The library is divided into two shelves: books in the reader's familiar language and books in the language they are learning.

LampLight currently supports collections across English, Bengali, Japanese, Korean, and Arabic, including public-domain literature from sources such as Project Gutenberg and Aozora Bunko.

**Parallel Bilingual Reading**

Readers can tap a sentence or word to see its translation without leaving the page or losing their reading position.

The goal is not to translate everything automatically. It is to make help available exactly when it is needed.

**Contextual Flashcards**

Any word can be saved while reading.

LampLight turns saved words into review cards and schedules them using the SM-2 spaced-repetition algorithm, allowing vocabulary review to come directly from the books the reader is actually reading.

**Bring Your Own Books**

Readers can import their own EPUB files and use the same reading, translation, and vocabulary features with them.

**Culturally Adapted Reading Environments**

Different literary collections have their own visual treatment inspired by their cultural and writing traditions, including Bengali paper textures, Japanese washi-inspired details, Korean hanji elements, and Arabic geometric patterns.

These are used to change the atmosphere of the reading experience without changing the underlying reading system.

**Quote Cards**

Readers can turn passages they like into formatted quote cards for saving or sharing.

**The Sacred Table**

LampLight also includes a separate reading space for the Quran, Bible, Torah, and Vedas, with references attached to the text so readers can explore primary sources directly rather than relying only on secondhand explanations.

**Offline Reading**

Books, saved words, flashcards, and core reading features continue to work without an internet connection.

LampLight also includes ambient rain and forest sounds, native pronunciation, warm reading themes, and an offline-first architecture designed for uninterrupted reading.

**Who It's For**

LampLight is designed for language learners who already enjoy reading and want to use books as part of their learning process.

It is especially useful for readers dealing with languages that use different scripts or writing conventions, where switching between books, dictionaries, and translation tools can interrupt the reading experience.

**Business Model**

The core reading experience is free and includes unlimited reading, EPUB import, and offline downloads.

The free plan includes:

- 50 translations per day

- 30 saved words per book

- 15 saved quotes

- 4 quote-card styles

- Starter soundscapes

LampLight Premium costs $5.99/month or $44.99/year.

Premium removes the usage limits and adds unlimited translations, custom vocabulary decks, all quote-card themes, and the complete soundscape collection.

Subscriptions, purchases, and restore flows are handled through RevenueCat.

**How We Built It**

Mobile: React Native with Expo SDK 57, Expo Router, and React Native Reanimated.

Local storage: expo-sqlite with an asynchronous serialized database queue. This prevents concurrent database operations from interfering with each other during rapid page turns, word saving, and background synchronization.

Pagination: We built a custom typography and pagination system that measures actual glyph widths instead of treating every character the same. This was important for Bengali ligatures, Japanese kanji, and other non-Latin writing systems.

Backend: Supabase for authentication, database services, and server-side functionality.

Subscriptions: react-native-purchases with RevenueCat for subscriptions and restore flows. A Supabase Edge Function verifies subscription events and synchronizes entitlements, while the app maintains a 72-hour offline grace period.

Literary assistance: Gemini Flash with Groq as a fallback for contextual literary lookups and translation-related features.

**Challenges We Overcame**

**Making Different Writing Systems Behave Like Real Books**

Traditional pagination assumptions break quickly with Bengali, Japanese, and other scripts.

We had to account for actual glyph widths, line height, margins, and script-specific behavior to prevent clipping, awkward breaks, and inconsistent pages.

**Reliable Offline Storage**

Reading and writing data at the same time caused SQLite locking problems on Android, particularly when users rapidly turned pages, saved words, and triggered background synchronization.

We solved this by serializing database operations and using Write-Ahead Logging.

**Keeping Assistance Out of the Way**

Translation is useful only when it does not destroy the reason someone is reading.

A major part of the design was making translation, vocabulary saving, audio, and other tools easy to reach without covering the page or forcing the reader into another screen.

**Accomplishments We're Proud Of**

We built a reading experience where an unfamiliar language does not immediately feel like a barrier.

We also built the app around offline use rather than treating offline support as an afterthought. Reading, saved vocabulary, and flashcard review can continue without a constant connection.

Most importantly, we brought literature from multiple writing systems and cultures into the same reading system without forcing them into the same visual treatment.

**What We Learned**

A language-learning app does not have to feel like a language class.

During development, we found that many of the hardest problems were not about adding more features. They were about typography, pagination, storage reliability, and deciding when the app should stay completely out of the reader's way.

The best interaction is often the one that helps without interrupting.

**What's Next**

We plan to expand the library with Spanish, French, German, and Urdu literature and continue improving support for different writing systems.

We also want to improve contextual translation so that sentence meaning can take surrounding narrative context into account, add synchronized read-along narration, and make it possible to download entire author collections for offline reading.

**Judge Access**

To test Premium features without restrictions:

Settings → Redeem promo code → SHIPATON2026

The code grants 30 days of full Premium access.

A free trial is also available directly from the paywall.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Most astrology apps use the tropical zodiac, locked in place over 2,000 years ago. The actual sky has shifted since then, planets aren't where tropical astrology says they are anymore. Sidereal Sky shows you where they really are.

**What it does**

Sidereal Sky calculates real-time sidereal planetary positions using JPL ephemeris data, shows daily moon phases and sign changes, and lets users unlock their full sidereal birth chart with Sun, Moon, and planetary placements, plus a personalized reading based on their Sun and Moon signs.

**How we built it**

Built using Flutter, pulling planetary position data from the JPL API. Monetization is handled through RevenueCat with a one-time non-consumable purchase to unlock the full birth chart feature.

**Challenges we ran into**

Getting accurate sidereal calculations right (correcting for the ayanamsa offset from tropical positions), and building a complete paywall-gated feature under hackathon time constraints.

**What we learned**

How much of astrology's modern framing comes from tropical convention rather than the actual sky! And also it was really cool that JPL has this API available. This was also my first time using Flutter which was great

**What's next**

Adding rising sign calculation, deeper AI-generated chart readings, and app store launch.

</details>
