<details><summary>Description</summary>

**💡 Inspiration**

Most health and fasting apps on the market today share the same three fatal flaws:

- Invasive Privacy Practices: They mandate cloud accounts, sell sensitive biometric habits, and force continuous tracking.

- Predatory Monetization & Dark Patterns: Confusing trial traps, bloated yearly plans, and artificial lock-outs.

- Generative "AI Slop": Unreliable, hallucinated health advice that overwhelms users with medical pseudo-science.

We built KYNIO around an uncompromising philosophy: Local-First, Zero AI Slop, and Circadian Harmony. Your body's metabolism evolved around the natural cycle of sunlight (melatonin surge, insulin sensitivity, and cellular autophagy). KYNIO translates that biological rhythm into a tactile, gamified mobile experience where 100% of your data stays on your device.

**⚡ What It Does**

KYNIO is a gamified circadian fasting and metabolic lifestyle tracker for Android and Web:

- Circadian Solar Dial: A signature dome arc and dot-matrix clock that tracks your fast against the 5 metabolic phases (Digestion, Fat Burning, Ketosis, Autophagy, and Deep Renewal), complete with local solar calculation (Sunrise, Solar Noon, and Sunset) without GPS tracking.

- 100% Local-First (SQLite + Drizzle ORM): Fasting intervals, water intake, body weight, and workout logs are stored exclusively in an on-device encrypted SQLite database. Zero account requirement.

- Deterministic RPG Gamification: Earn XP, level up, maintain streaks, and complete weekly challenges generated deterministically from the ISO calendar. No pay-to-win mechanics or dopamine exploitation.

- AI Meal Vision with Strict JSON: Snap a photo of your dish to estimate macros and calories via a secure Gemini Edge Function. Images are never stored, user identifiers are stripped, and output is strictly validated against TypeScript schemas before rendering.

- Android Ecosystem Integration: Native Persistent Foreground Service (chronometer in notification bar), Home Screen AppWidget (fasting progress + 1-tap hydration), and Google Health Connect sync.

**🛠️ How We Built It**

KYNIO is built with an ultra-modern, production-hardened tech stack:

- Frontend & Core: Expo SDK 57 (React Native 0.86, React 19, TypeScript strict mode) with expo-router typed routes.

- Styling & Aesthetics: NativeWind v4 (Tailwind CSS) implementing the bespoke "Circadiano" design system (warm paper #EDE6D3, charcoal ink #3A3A38, and solar amber #D9922E).

- Data Persistence: Expo SQLite coupled with Drizzle ORM for local transactional integrity, composite indexing, and soft-delete capabilities.

- Monetization & In-App Purchases: Native billing via react-native-iap with server-side validation via Supabase Edge Functions (verify-purchase) ensuring tamper-proof Pro unlocks.

- Optional Cloud Backup: Google OAuth with Supabase Row-Level Security (RLS) policies—activated only on voluntary opt-in.

- Automated Quality: Full test pyramid with Jest (55 suites, 295 passing unit tests), contract tests for AI and legal sites, and end-to-end Maestro flows.

**🧗 Challenges We Faced**

- Android 14+ Foreground Service Rigor: Google Play enforces strict foregroundServiceType="specialUse" policies. We engineered a native Kotlin module (FastingForegroundService) that updates the notification chronometer directly via Android SystemUI without draining battery or waking the JS thread.

- Pure Local-First Analytics: Generating factual correlation insights (e.g. Early Time-Restricted Feeding adherence and hydration-to-completion rates) entirely on SQLite without relying on external cloud analytics or LLM tokens.

- Rock-solid Version Synchronization: Coordinating synchronized version bumps across package.json, app.json, and native Gradle scripts to ensure reproducible AAB builds for the Google Play Store.

**🏆 Accomplishments We're Proud Of**

- 100% GDPR Compliant from Day One: Zero medical liability, one-click full data export (JSON), and instant cryptographic erasure.

- Google Play Production Release: Successfully verified and packaged for 18,800+ Android devices with high-level code obfuscation (R8/ProGuard) and optimal bundle size.

- 295 Automated Tests: 100% test coverage across stores, metabolic calculators, and local encryption services.

**🚀 What's Next for KYNIO**

- Expanding native Glance AppWidgets for more customization on the Android home screen.

- Deep Wear OS companion tile for quick glance while on workouts.

- Bringing the PWA web export to parity with native push notifications.

</details>

**Video (1:34):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ykJ4I0GMk9Y

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/ykJ4I0GMk9Y/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ykJ4I0GMk9Y)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/318/470/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/318/470/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/389/438/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/389/438/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/389/443/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/389/443/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

A progress photo can show what you made without showing where to begin again. For an embroidery piece, model or collage that takes several sittings, the missing detail may be a particular spot and one short instruction.

Benchkeep brings those two things together. It is a visual bookmark for unfinished craft work: a photo, a point on that photo and the maker's own next move. The goal is a clear return to the work, without having to reconnect a camera-roll image with a separate note. This is a product hypothesis, not a claim from a user study.

**What it does**

Choose a photo, place a point, name the piece and write the next move. Direction controls provide another way to position the point. Save the checkpoint, then reopen the piece with its photo, point and note together. “Look closer” focuses on the marked detail; “Whole piece” restores the context.

Each new checkpoint preserves the previous note in a trail. A finished piece remains readable and can return to the bench. Craft photos and notes are stored locally. The built-in Autumn leaves example is labeled as sample content.

Portable backups include photos and project data. Import validates the file before replacing the bench. Reading and exporting existing work remain available even when the free plan's capacity is exceeded. Native backup controls are implemented; their Android export/import flow was not part of the final emulator walkthrough.

**How it was built**

Benchkeep uses React Native, Expo and TypeScript. Photo points are stored relative to the image rather than screen pixels, so the location is preserved when the layout changes. Serialized writes prevent an earlier autosave from replacing a newer checkpoint. A recoverable local backup and validated portable backups address failed writes and malformed data.

The visual design gives the piece priority: quiet typography, a large image and a short next action. Focus motion respects reduced-motion preferences. The privacy notice and fonts are bundled in the app.

The final source passed 27 automated tests and TypeScript checking. The tests cover geometry, checkpoint history, capacity rules, persistence failures, purchase-state handling, backup validation and the Android embedded-development bootstrap.

**RevenueCat and the business model**

The free bench holds two active pieces. Full bench is a one-time unlock for more active pieces. This packaging fits a small personal tool used whenever a maker returns to a project; it does not require an ongoing subscription to keep reading their work.

RevenueCat supplies the offering, localized price and benchkeep_plus entitlement. Benchkeep does not unlock premium from a local flag. Cancellation, pending or failed responses and a response without the expected active entitlement cannot grant access. A data backup contains craft work, not a premium entitlement.

The Android demonstration uses RevenueCat Test Store and is explicitly labeled “Test purchase · no real charge.” On the final APK, the native SDK loaded the $4.99 sandbox product. Cancelling kept access locked; a valid sandbox purchase unlocked Full bench. The restore action and another app restart retained access in the same sandbox installation. These checks are not real-money sales, Google Play/Galaxy purchases or cross-device store restoration.

**Challenges and evidence**

Keeping a point attached to a photo involves more than drawing a marker. Letterboxing, layout changes and focus near an edge all affect where that point appears. Another boundary was separating craft data from paid capacity: importing a backup must preserve readable work without granting premium or silently discarding extra pieces.

Actual Android execution caught a bootstrap problem that passing unit tests and a compiled APK had missed: Expo's development message socket expected a Metro server. A narrowly scoped adapter now skips that tooling socket only for an embedded Test Store development bundle. The APK remains genuinely debuggable, as RevenueCat requires, while its native host loads the embedded JavaScript without Metro. Purchase guards remain intact.

The final APK was tested on an Android 16 emulator. The run covered photo-picker import, point placement, checkpoint saving, focus and resume. With networking disabled, force-stop and relaunch preserved the photo, point and next move even when RevenueCat could not connect. The sandbox purchase outcomes above were then checked with networking restored.

**Current scope and next steps**

This entry targets Next Gen, with public MIT-licensed source and a downloadable Android judging sandbox. Benchkeep has no public app-store release, verified paid customers or measured time-saving results. It does not provide cloud sync, collaboration or automatic interpretation of craft photos. The maker writes the next move.

The final native run did not cover camera capture, native backup export/import or the failed-purchase option. Failure/pending cases have automated coverage, with separately recorded Web SDK failure evidence. There was no physical-device test or production store restoration. Those checks, followed by a small user trial, are next steps before a production release.

The code and project materials were developed with AI assistance. The generated embroidery imagery is demonstration content, not a customer's work or evidence of adoption.

</details>

> A private practice space for the hardest conversations nurses have — with each other, not patients. Rehearse, get real feedback, build the confidence to have it for real.

**Video (1:24):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ti8VLprNZ4c

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/Ti8VLprNZ4c/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ti8VLprNZ4c)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/160/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/160/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/161/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/161/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/162/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/162/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/163/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/163/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/164/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/164/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/165/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/165/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/166/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/166/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Charge nurses and nurse managers are expected to have some of the hardest conversations in healthcare telling a colleague their documentation was wrong, saying no to unsafe overtime, de-escalating conflict mid-shift — and almost none of them get trained for it. Clinical skills are rehearsed constantly before they're used on a real patient. Interpersonal leadership skills usually aren't rehearsed at all; the first real attempt often happens under pressure, with real relationships and real consequences on the line.

Every existing tool we found in this space is enterprise software — sold to hospital systems, not to the individual nurse who needs it tonight before tomorrow's shift. We wanted to build something a nurse could actually download and use on their own.

**What it does**

PrepRounds is a private practice space for the conversations charge nurses and nurse managers dread most. You pick a real scenario, have a live conversation with an AI colleague persona that responds the way a real person would — with resistance, defensiveness, and pushback, not just agreement — and afterward get a structured debrief: what you said that actually worked, quoted directly from your own words, and one concrete thing to try differently next time.

The app is personalized to your role (Charge Nurse, Aspiring Charge Nurse, or New Nurse Manager), tracks your practice history and confidence trend over time, and is explicitly grounded in real nursing leadership and communication frameworks — AACN's communication competency standards, AONL's Nurse Leader Core Competencies, and AHRQ's TeamSTEPPS tools (DESC and CUS) — cited directly in the app so it doesn't just feel evidence-informed, it is.

**How we built it**

React Native (Expo) on the client, with Supabase (Postgres + Row-Level Security, anonymous auth) as the backend. The AI persona and feedback generation run server-side through a Supabase Edge Function calling Google's Gemini API — the API key never touches the client. RevenueCat handles the entire subscription lifecycle: a shared pro entitlement across a Test Store app (for development) and a real App Store app (for production), one offering, and a custom-built paywall with a real free/Pro comparison table. OneSignal handles optional daily practice reminders, and Google AdMob powers rewarded bonus sessions for free-tier users.

The build process itself was an architect/implementation-agent workflow: Claude as spec-owner making explicit product decisions and recording them in versioned spec docs, Claude Code as the hands-on implementation agent — investigating, verifying, and flagging ambiguity back rather than deciding unilaterally.

**Challenges we ran into**

The honest version: several real production bugs, each one only fully understood after real investigation, not assumption.

The roleplay engine was ending conversations after one exchange. The model was emitting a scene-complete signal almost immediately — confirmed across three different scenarios, all collapsing by turn 2-3 instead of the intended 4-8. The fix was a combination of prompt rewrite and a deterministic server-side minimum-turn floor, verified with real transcripts before and after: baseline turns of 2/3/3 became a consistent 4/4/4, with personas holding position and introducing fresh objections rather than folding.

A feedback-generation bug with a 62% failure rate, traced through Supabase's actual server logs to a single missing schema constraint — the AI's response schema allowed empty arrays, but the validator rejected them. A genuinely good model response (real quotes, coherent reasoning) was being thrown away because the schema never told the model an empty try_instead array wasn't allowed. Tightening the schema to match the validator's actual requirements took the failure rate to zero.

A RevenueCat key mixed up between Test Store and production, caught live on a real device via TestFlight rather than in review — better there than in front of App Review.

Apple's own review process flagged a stale, unused tracking permission string and a default-on iPad device family neither of which reflected the app's actual behavior — both traced to source, confirmed via the compiled binary (not just the config), and resolved cleanly.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Getting a real, working, multi-turn AI roleplay engine that holds a consistent persona under pushback — not a chatbot that agrees with everything the user says. Building a debrief that's evidence-grounded: every quote it shows the user was programmatically verified as a real substring of what they actually typed, not a plausible-sounding hallucination. And doing all of it with a debugging discipline that treated "it should work" as never good enough — every real fix was verified against real data, real logs, or a real device before being called done.

**What we learned**

That the gap between "looks right in a code read" and "actually works" is often exactly where the real bugs live — the feedback schema issue passed every obvious check and still failed 62% of the time in production. And that shipping something narrow and genuinely working beats shipping something broad and half-verified, especially against a deadline.

**What's next for PrepRounds**

A stateful persona engine with formal emotional variables (openness, defensiveness, trust) instead of prompt-only behavior; a five-dimension evaluation rubric (psychological safety, clarity, active listening, resistance handling, actionability) replacing today's prose-based scoring; a "Custom Round" generator letting Pro users describe their own real situation (with a privacy guardrail to keep patient-identifiable information out); and unit-specific scenario variation alongside the role-based personalization already shipped. All of it is scoped and written down — the next phase is building it.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

The inspiration for the project stems from a lifelong draw to cultures and languages. We repeatedly encountered individuals who could recognize their grandmother's greetings or name traditional family dishes, but who could not respond in their indigenous language. This language loss often occurs because these individuals grew up away from where the language is spoken daily, often in cities, foreign countries, or English-speaking school environments. Because major language apps are largely built for tourists looking to navigate hotels or cafes, the team built Root specifically for heritage learners who want to greet elders properly and understand cultural proverbs. The project is built around the single belief that distance from home should not equate to distance from one's language.

**What it does**

Root is a calm Android app designed for reconnecting with heritage languages, currently featuring Dholuo, Shona, Swahili, and Amharic. It features a "Practice" mode with recall cards where users rate their memory honestly (Missed, Close, or Got it), without streaks, leaderboards, or guilt. The "Learn" section offers a gentle path of guided conversations, pattern workshops, and stories where finished lessons stay finished. An "Explore" section covers everyday situations, culture notes, and a notebook for users to save and record their own family's specific phrases. The app uses only real voices, crediting the volunteer speaker by name, and explicitly states when a recording is unavailable rather than faking one with text-to-speech. It works entirely offline without requiring an account, and includes warm-paper light and warm-charcoal dark themes, a home-screen widget, and a shareable card.

**How we built it**

Root was built natively using Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, and Material 3. It utilizes a versioned Room database to store all progress, saved phrases, and recordings locally on the device, while WorkManager handles hash-verified, size-bounded content downloads and Glance powers the widget. Content is managed through a Python toolchain, and every starter phrase was verified against public references like Wikivoyage, Omniglot, Wiktionary, or the FSI Amharic course. For monetization, RevenueCat powers a non-subscription, one-time unlock for either a single language or all languages, which provides access to premium conversational sets like "Heart words" and "Keep talking". The app's quiet design pairs the Source Serif 4 font for words and Inter for the interface, featuring a hand-drawn root animation and an original startup sound.

**Challenges we ran into**

Earning money without betraying the mission: Finding a monetization model that kept all basic practice free while only charging for extra premium sets, ensuring nothing is sold before it exists in the app.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Delivering a fully working app across four African languages, featuring over 220 source-checked phrases, 24 lessons, 8 short stories, and 8 culture notes.

**What we learned**

The technological aspect of a language app is easy, but finding an app flow that works, building trust through accurate sources, authentic recordings, and proper credits is the hard part.

Heritage learners don't need pressure or gamification; they simply need a doorway to the language and a reason to return.

**What's next for Root**

Working directly with native speakers and elders to review phrases and record them with proper consent and credit.

Expanding to more languages based on what learners ask for. 

Including proverbs and longer spoken stories. 

Publishing the Root app on Google Play.

</details>

**MIMORY**

Your people. Your moments. Your world. ♡

What if we don't have a memory problem — we have a remembering problem?

MIMORY turns the moments you share with the people who matter into little worlds you can revisit.

**Inspiration**

We all have people who become part of our story.

Not just through the big moments, but through hundreds of tiny ones we barely notice while they're happening.

A photograph from a trip.

A ridiculous inside joke.

A birthday celebration.

A random evening that meant nothing at the time — until years later, when it means everything.

We keep these moments everywhere.

In camera rolls.

In old chats.

In screenshots.

In forgotten folders.

We are surrounded by memories, yet somehow, we can still lose touch with the feeling behind them.

The idea for MIMORY began with a story a friend once shared with me.

There was a couple who had spent around eight years together.

Eight years is a long time to build a story with someone.

There were trips they had taken, places they had been, celebrations they had shared, silly photographs, ordinary days, private jokes, and countless little moments that had quietly become theirs.

Then they entered a difficult chapter.

A disagreement became distance.

And, as sometimes happens in difficult moments, the present began to feel bigger than the past.

The years of memories were still there.

But emotionally, they felt far away.

Then, during one of their conversations, they started going through their old photographs.

They weren't looking for an answer.

They were just remembering.

One photograph became another.

A trip.

A celebration.

A silly picture.

An ordinary day.

A moment they had almost forgotten.

And something changed.

For a little while, the difficult moment wasn't the whole story anymore.

There was a much bigger story sitting behind it.

Eight years of laughter.

Eight years of places.

Eight years of ordinary and extraordinary moments.

Eight years of being there for each other.

The photographs hadn't changed what happened.

They simply made the rest of the story visible again.

That stayed with me.

Because it made me realize something:

Maybe we don't have a memory problem.

Maybe we have a remembering problem.

Technology has become incredibly good at storing our lives.

Our phones can hold thousands of photographs.

Our chats can preserve years of conversations.

Our storage can keep almost everything.

But storing a memory and returning to it are two very different things.

A camera roll gives you a grid.

A chat gives you a timeline.

A folder gives you files.

But none of them gives you the feeling of walking back into a moment that mattered.

So I started asking:

What if memories weren't just things we stored, but places we could return to?

What if a photograph could become a little landmark?

What if a collection of moments could become a world?

What if the people who matter to us could have a world that slowly grows with every memory we add?

And most importantly:

What if, instead of scrolling through our memories, we could walk through them?

That question became MIMORY.

MIMORY isn't meant to replace real relationships.

It isn't meant to judge them, score them, or tell us how we should feel.

It simply gives the memories that already matter somewhere to live.

A place to revisit.

A place to explore.

A place where one difficult moment doesn't have to become the entire story.

Because sometimes, we don't need another notification telling us what to do.

We just need a little reminder of what we've shared.

**What it does**

MIMORY transforms shared memories into a living, explorable storybook world.

You begin by creating a world around someone important to you:

- Best friends

- Partners

- Parents & family

- People who matter to you

Then you add the moments that make that relationship yours:

Photos · Stories · Places · Milestones · Inside jokes · Voice memories

Instead of becoming another item in a feed, those moments become part of the world itself.

A moment you save
What it becomes

📷 Photograph
A framed keepsake

🗺️ Trip
A landmark in the world

🎉 Milestone
A meaningful world element

💬 Story
A storybook memory

🎙️ Voice memory
A keepsake to revisit

❤️ Meaningful moment
A place worth discovering

As memories accumulate, the world grows with them.

**Memory Walk**

The heart of MIMORY is Memory Walk.

Instead of scrolling through a conventional timeline, you enter your world and physically explore it.

Walk along its paths.

Discover memory landmarks.

Find photographs embedded into the environment.

Explore tiny storybook details.

Follow signs.

Encounter animals and small discoveries.

And when you find a memory you want to revisit, you choose to visit it.

You don't just look at a memory.

You walk toward it.

That is the interaction at the heart of MIMORY.

**A world that feels personal**

MIMORY is designed to feel less like a dashboard and more like a little world that belongs to you.

Soft landscapes.

Personal characters.

Storybook environments.

Memory landmarks.

Scrapbook-style keepsakes.

Small discoveries.

Gentle movement.

The visual world isn't simply decoration.

The world is the interface.

**What MIMORY deliberately avoids**

MIMORY is not designed to turn relationships into a game.

- No relationship scores

- No streaks

- No guilt mechanics

- No relationship-health diagnosis

- No algorithm telling you how you should feel

MIMORY doesn't judge the relationship.

It simply gives your memories somewhere beautiful to live.

**The emotional loop**

The experience is built around a simple loop:

Remember
 ↓
Revisit
 ↓
Feel
 ↓
Remember what matters

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**The Problem I Saw Firsthand**

FlowDesk started with a problem I saw in my own family.

My aunt started a consulting company that helps social projects find funding. As I watched her work, I noticed how much of her time was spent on tasks that were necessary but repetitive: reviewing project information, working through documentation, preparing responses, and answering similar questions from different people.

The problem was not a lack of expertise. It was that her expertise was constantly being pulled into the same kinds of tasks.

That made me wonder: what if an AI system could take on some of these repetitive responsibilities while still working from the company's own knowledge?

I did not want to build another chatbot that simply answers questions. I wanted to build something closer to a digital employee: a specialized AI worker that understands a business, performs a specific role, and can be given real tasks.

**From Chatbot to AI Employee**

This became the idea behind FlowDesk — AI Employees for Small Businesses.

The core concept is simple:

Company knowledge → Specialized AI employee → Delegated task → Business output

Instead of asking one general-purpose chatbot to do everything, a business can create different AI employees for different responsibilities.

A sales employee can handle customer questions.
A marketing employee can create campaigns.
A support employee can work from company documentation.
A business can also create custom employees for its own workflows.

The important part is that these employees are connected to the company's own knowledge rather than relying only on generic AI knowledge.

**How I Built It**

I built FlowDesk as a full-stack web application.

The backend is built with Python and Flask, with SQLite for data storage and OpenRouter for connecting the application to large language models. The interface uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

I designed the application around a workspace model:

- A company creates its workspace.

- The company adds its internal knowledge and documents.

- It creates specialized AI employees.

- Each employee is given a specific role.

- The employee uses the company's knowledge to complete tasks or interact with customers.

I also built separate interfaces for managing employees, company knowledge, and AI interactions so that the system feels like a business tool rather than a simple AI demo.

**The Biggest Challenge**

The hardest part was not getting an AI model to generate text. That part is relatively easy.

The harder problem was making the AI useful and business-specific.

A generic chatbot can produce a convincing answer, but that does not necessarily make the answer correct for a particular company. FlowDesk therefore needed a way to connect an employee's work to the information that actually belongs to the business.

This changed how I thought about the project. I stopped asking, “How can I make the AI generate better answers?” and started asking, “How can I give the AI the right context to perform a specific job?”

That shift shaped the architecture of FlowDesk.

**What I Learned**

Building FlowDesk taught me that building an AI product is much more than connecting an application to an LLM.

I learned how to combine backend development, databases, frontend design, document-based knowledge, API integration, and AI prompting into one working system.

More importantly, I learned to start with the workflow rather than the technology.

The original inspiration came from watching someone spend valuable time answering repetitive questions. That made the goal of FlowDesk clear: use AI to remove repetitive work so people can spend more time on the work that actually requires their expertise.

FlowDesk is my attempt to turn that observation into a practical product.

</details>

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/c-QuzpH1JUU/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c-QuzpH1JUU)

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Inspiration

College students often practice many questions but still struggle to understand what they are actually weak at. Generic recommendations usually react to a single wrong answer instead of looking at persistent patterns.

We wanted to build a placement coach that identifies genuine skill gaps from repeated assessment behavior and then turns those gaps into a personalized learning path.

What we built

Place Path is an AI-powered placement assistant for college students.

Instead of treating one wrong answer as a skill gap, Place Path analyzes repeated performance patterns, question difficulty, consistency, and error behavior to identify persistent weaknesses.

The flow is:

Assessment → Multi-attempt Analysis → Skill Gap Detection → Confidence Check → Targeted Diagnostic → Personalized Learning Path → Reassessment

This creates a continuous assess → diagnose → learn → reassess loop.

How it works

A student's assessment attempts and performance data are analyzed to build a skill profile.

When the evidence is weak, the system can use a targeted diagnostic question before making a stronger skill-gap conclusion.

The recommendation layer then produces a personalized learning path focused on the student's weak areas.

Why it is different

A simple approach is:

Wrong answer → Recommend a similar question

Place Path aims for:

Multiple attempts → Error pattern analysis → Skill-gap detection → Confidence estimation → Targeted diagnostic → Personalized recommendation

Technical approach

The prototype uses a React/TypeScript frontend, a Node.js backend with REST APIs, PostgreSQL for data, and AI services for analysis and recommendations. The AI architecture is designed around structured outputs and validation before results are exposed to the frontend.

Challenges

The main challenges were sparse student history, avoiding false skill-gap diagnoses, maintaining consistent AI outputs, and keeping recommendations useful.

We addressed these with minimum evidence thresholds, confidence-aware analysis, rule-based validation, and controlled test cases.

What we learned

We learned that useful AI placement guidance needs more than a single assessment score. Looking at performance patterns over multiple attempts gives a better basis for deciding whether a weakness is persistent and what the student should learn next.

Future direction

The prototype is designed to grow into a broader placement-preparation platform with continuous skill tracking, targeted practice, personalized roadmaps, mock interviews, progress tracking, and premium capabilities.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**About the Project**

Starting a career in tech can feel overwhelming. Students often know the role they want, but not which skills to build, what projects to complete, or how to show their progress to employers. Maven was created to turn that uncertainty into a clear and practical next step.

Maven gives students a personalized roadmap toward a tech role, tracks their progress with a readiness score based on completed tasks, and helps turn real experience into strong CV bullet points.

Students can also upload an existing CV to quickly prefill their experience. Maven extracts relevant information, presents it back to the student for review, and lets them edit or confirm everything before it is used to personalize their roadmap.

**What We Learned**

Building Maven taught us that career guidance needs to be both personal and trustworthy.

AI is useful for tailoring roadmaps, understanding a student's background, and helping shape CV bullet points. However, we felt that progress scoring should remain transparent and that students should stay in control of every claim made about their experience.

One of our main challenges was balancing useful AI features with privacy and clear user control.

We designed CV intake as an optional shortcut. The uploaded file is used to extract an experience summary, which the student reviews and confirms. The rest of Maven's roadmap generation then works from that confirmed information.

We also kept the readiness score arithmetic-based rather than AI-generated. This means students can understand exactly how their score changes and which completed tasks contributed to it.

**Why Maven**

Maven helps students move from:

"I want to work in tech, but I don't know what to do next."

to:

"I know what skills I need, what I should build next, and what I can already show employers."

Instead of simply suggesting a career, Maven gives students a structured path toward it and helps them build evidence of what they have achieved along the way.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I've used a bunch of budgeting apps before and honestly got tired of the same thing every time you open it, see a pie chart, close it, forget about it a week later. Nothing actually told me what to change. I'm a student building my first real app with actual monetization behind it, so I wanted to try solving that instead of just making another tracker.

**What it does**

It's an income/expense tracker dashboard, monthly totals, recent transactions, the basics. But the part I actually care about is the AI Assistant I added on top. It's not hooked up to any external AI model; it just reads your own transaction data and works out things like:

If you're spending more than usual in a category this month
What a realistic savings target looks like based on what you're actually earning vs spending
Answering stuff you type in, like "how do I save more this month," using your real numbers instead of generic advice

For the money side, there are two tiers. A one-time $1.99 lifetime purchase unlocks the core app, and the AI Assistant is a separate monthly subscription through RevenueCat. If you already bought the lifetime version, you get the AI subscription at half price I didn't want people who already paid once to feel like I was charging them again for something that should've just been included.

**How we built it**

Everything was built solo on Replit using Replit Agent I'd describe what I wanted and iterate from there. It's React Native/Expo underneath. RevenueCat handles both purchase types: the lifetime entitlement and a separate "Ai assistant" monthly entitlement, with the discounted pricing kicking in automatically depending on whether the user already holds the lifetime one.

**Challenges we ran into**

The annoying bug: before I'd actually set up the AI offerings in RevenueCat's dashboard, tapping the AI icon would sometimes trigger the "lifetime" paywall instead wrong purchase flow entirely. Had to go back and add a proper check so it fails safely instead of routing people to the wrong product.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Getting the dual-entitlement RevenueCat setup actually working end to end lifetime purchase, separate AI subscription, and the discount logic all talking to each other correctly without conflicting. Also, proud that the AI Assistant runs entirely off the user's own data with zero external API calls, so there's no ongoing cost per user and nothing about their spending ever leaves the app.

**What we learned**

Mainly that pricing isn't just a business decision, it's a UX one too. Every single paywall trigger had to know exactly which entitlement it was checking, otherwise you end up accidentally breaking trust with someone who already paid you once.

**What's next for Budget Manager Pro**

Getting the RevenueCat products and offerings fully live so the AI subscription can actually be purchased end to end, then testing the whole flow with real transaction data before the app goes any further.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**After You**

Catch something your friend threw yesterday.

After You is an asynchronous cooperative Android puzzle game. Made for people who live apart but love close together in heart.

**Inspiration**

I have a lot of friends in different timezones and I wanted to be able to show that I care about them without being glued to my phone, so I made After You. It has a really unique mechanic equivalent to messaging but for video games. Both players don't have to be online to play the game, but the replays are together.

Playing the Conservatory level with a friend

**What it does**

It is an Android game that is played by two people at different times. You send your turn and then close the app. Your friend can send theirs hours, or days later. Then you can watch the replay with both runs coexisting together.

A replay is a mini recording of actions and checkpoints, not a video. The puzzle simulation is performed on the phone. The server will take care of the handoff between players, so they don't need to keep the game open together.

Home Screen With All 50 Collectibles

**How I built it**

- I used Godot and GDScript for the game, and Kotlin for the native Android integrations.

- RevenueCat manages the Full Journey purchase and restore via Google Play Billing.

- The backend is built with TypeScript, Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects.

- Optional turn notifications use Firebase Cloud Messaging.

The code is on GitHub.

Full Journey Purchase Screen | Fulfilled Using RevenueCat

**What I learned**

I learned what goes into making an engaging game. My later levels were so much better than my previous ones that I archived the older ones and put them under "Earlier Islands" I also underestimated the importance of navigation and small quality of life things. The Friends page, room sharing, loading the replay, progress bars and photo frames were all changed. These were minor things, but they added up to making the game easier to use and feel more polished.

**Challenges**

The biggest challenge I faced was obviously the emergency surgery. I couldn't predict that at all. Even without the surgery, I was already finding it really difficult to get an intuitive understanding for how to develop the levels to be engaging. I only figured it out through trial and error, but add that on top and it was something else.

The UI went through so many changes. I had to delete and remake these screenshots so many times. I really like the latest revamp of the friends and hosting menus, they seem very well polished to me now. The navigation was changed so much too. I tested the app with my friends and almost every time I found out that something could have been done or shown in a simpler way.

You don't really notice what's wrong or not obvious in your app when you've been looking at it for so long. That's why you test with friends! And if it's a game, it's fun too!

New Polished UI

**Next steps**

I want to add more complex levels, maybe even add more than just two players. I want to see what parts of the game people enjoy the most and what parts of the game people have problems with and target those accordingly.

My friends also suggested a more chaotic mode to rival the peaceful nature of After You. I've also been thinking about adding free and paid user skins as well as hints on levels.

A server browser (so you can meet new friends) and chat are on my mind too.

**Word of Advice**

I strongly recommend making your own unique ideas. It just feels more rewarding even if it's harder. As far as I know, no game has the mechanic that After You has and that makes it feel so much more personal to me.

It reminds me of this quote:

“To go wrong in one's own way is better than to go right in someone else's.”
― Fyodor Dostoevsky, Crime and Punishment

Thank you, and I hope After You brings you closer with your friends!

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**For judges**

- Install. iOS beta on TestFlight:
https://testflight.apple.com/join/EvbxqXGU. This is build 1.0 (2),
approved by Apple for external testers. TestFlight is a beta channel, not
a public App Store release.

- Sign in. The demo account's email and password are in the
README's For judges section.
It already has three generated briefs, two of them translated to Spanish.
Pro is deliberately inactive so that you meet the paywall.

- Reach the paywall. Tap Upgrade in the dashboard header, or tap any
locked Pro feature: Pro to translate on a brief, the upgrade ribbon
on a brief, or adding a family profile.

- Purchases on TestFlight are free. In-app purchases in a TestFlight
build run in Apple's sandbox and are never charged. You can buy Monthly or
Lifetime and watch Pro unlock without paying anything.

- The demo account is shared. The entitlement follows the account, so a
purchase on it unlocks Pro for every judge who signs in after you. To test
the purchase itself, create your own account from the sign-in screen.

- After the App Store release, Pro access for judges will be by App
Store offer code.

**Elevator pitch**

Anteroom converts a shoebox of referrals, lab printouts, and medication
boxes into one structured brief your doctor can read in 30 seconds — in
English or Spanish, with every claim traceable to the original photo.

**Inspiration**

In Spain, the appointment is short and the paperwork is long. An expat or a
retiree arrives at a consulta with a plastic folder: a referral from a GP in
another country, a lab printout in a third language, three medication boxes,
and a memory of what a specialist said eight months ago. The physician
spends the first half of a 10-minute slot doing document triage instead of
medicine.

The friction is specific, and it has two halves:

- The intake bottleneck. Nobody has structured the patient's history
before the consultation starts. The doctor does it live, under time
pressure, from paper.

- The language bottleneck. The patient's documents and the doctor's
working language often differ. Translation happens ad hoc, by a family
member, at the worst possible moment.

Anteroom moves both jobs out of the consultation room and into the waiting
room — the anteroom. That's the name.

The clinical framing comes from 12 years of emergency and general practice.
The failure mode we care most about isn't a missing document; it's a
confidently wrong one. A medication dose transcribed incorrectly is more
dangerous than a medication that was never transcribed at all.

**What it does**

Anteroom gives one family a shared, structured medical record they control.

- Capture. Photograph referrals, lab results, and medication lists with
the device camera, or import from the photo library.

- Classify. Each capture is typed as a referral, medication list, lab
result, or other, with a confidence level. You can override the
classification with one tap.

- Generate a brief. The captures collapse into a single BriefContent
record: patient identifiers, referral reason, medications with dose and
frequency, allergies with reactions, and a list of flagged items.

- Flag, don't guess. Anything ambiguous or contradictory lands in
flagged_items and renders as a red "Flagged for clinical review" banner
instead of being silently resolved. A dose that reads 20 mg on the
referral and 10 mg on the bottle becomes a flag, not an answer.

- Keep the source. Original photos stay attached to the brief, and a
photo verification view lets the doctor check any line against the paper
it came from.

- Translate. A brief generated in English can be rendered in Spanish,
and the reverse, with the source language recorded on the record.

- Manage a family. Profiles cover you, a partner, children, and parents,
each with their own briefs.

- Export. Produce a PDF for the clinic. The free tier watermarks it; Pro
doesn't.

**The zero-hallucination design constraint**

"Zero-hallucination" is a constraint on the data model, not a claim about a
model's accuracy. Three decisions enforce it:

- A closed schema. BriefContent has fixed fields. There is no
free-text summary field for a model to fill with plausible prose, so
there's nothing for a narrative hallucination to occupy.

- Uncertainty is a first-class value. flagged_items,
detected_confidence, and doc_type_manual_override exist so the app
can say "these two documents disagree" rather than picking a winner.

- Provenance survives. Extracted fields never replace the source. The
original photographs remain on the brief and are reachable from the
clinical view, so every line is falsifiable in one tap.

A clinician doesn't need the app to be right. A clinician needs to know,
fast, where the app is unsure.

This is tested, not asserted. tools/sample_page_illegible.jpg is a
prescription whose Warfarin dose has been blurred and blotted out. A model
that guesses a plausible dose passes any test that only checks the readable
rows, so the end-to-end suite asserts the opposite: that the dose is
absent from medications and present in flagged_items. Against
the live backend it comes back as

medications: ... Warfarin (no dose) as directed
flagged: Warfarin dose unreadable on page 2

and the brief screen renders Warfarin as the one medication in the list
with no dose line under it.

**How we built it**

The whole product is one Kotlin Multiplatform codebase.

Layer
Technology

UI
Compose Multiplatform 1.12, Material 3, shared across all targets

Shared logic
Kotlin Multiplatform 2.4.20

Targets
Android, iOS (arm64 and simulator), Desktop (JVM), Web (JS)

Auth and data
Firebase Auth, Firestore, and Storage through GitLive

Backend
Firebase Cloud Functions, Python 3.12, europe-west1

Extraction
Gemini 2.5 Pro and 2.5 Flash on Vertex AI, europe-west1

Billing
RevenueCat purchases-kmp 3.8.0

Networking
Ktor client

There is no per-platform UI code. App.kt is the single entry point that
MainActivity on Android, MainViewController on iOS, the Compose desktop
window, and the web viewport all render. Screens, the paywall, the family
profile strip, and the clinical brief view are written once.

**The RevenueCat integration**

The entitlement is anteroom_pro. The default offering carries two
packages: $rc_monthly and $rc_lifetime.

The interesting engineering problem is that purchases-kmp publishes
artifacts for Android and Apple targets only, while Anteroom also ships
Desktop and Web. Putting the SDK in commonMain breaks the JVM and JS
compilations.

The solution is a small expect/actual seam in the subscription package
under app/shared/src:

- RevenueCatService is the common interface: four StateFlows plus
initialize, fetchOfferings, purchasePackage, restorePurchases,
and refreshCustomerInfo.

- expect fun createRevenueCatService() picks the implementation per
target.

- The store-backed RevenueCatServiceImpl lives in src/mobileMain/kotlin,
which is compiled into both androidMain and iosMain. One
implementation, zero duplication: the same Kotlin runs against StoreKit on
iOS and Google Play Billing on Android, with no platform branches in the
calling code.

- What is live today: in-app purchases are active on iOS, through
StoreKit, on a public TestFlight build that anyone can install:
https://testflight.apple.com/join/EvbxqXGU. The monthly and lifetime
products exist in App Store Connect and the paywall resolves their prices
from the store at runtime.

- Android runs the identical code from the identical source set and
installs as an APK built from this repo with
./gradlew :app:androidApp:assembleDebug. Its Play Store products are not
registered yet, so purchases cannot complete there. A new Google Play
Console account has to run a 14-day closed test with 20 testers before it
can publish, which does not fit inside this hackathon — so Play
registration is scheduled for after the beta rather than rushed. The app
handles the unconfigured state rather than leaking it: the RevenueCat SDK
returns ConfigurationError, and the paywall shows one sentence, falls back
to the catalogue price, and logs the diagnostic.

- Desktop and Web get SimulatedRevenueCatService, which keeps the paywall
navigable on a laptop and reports isSimulated = true so the UI says out
loud that no charge occurred.

Entitlement state has exactly one source of truth. applyEntitlement()
reads customerInfo.entitlements["anteroom_pro"]?.isActive and pushes the
result into the app-wide SubscriptionService. Everything else in the app —
locked family profile avatars, the watermark notice on export, the
translation lock, the upgrade banner — observes that flow. Nothing in the UI
sets the entitlement directly.

Because the app registers a PurchasesDelegate, entitlement changes that
originate outside the paywall propagate on their own: a renewal, a lapse, a
restore performed on another device, or a promoted App Store purchase. If
the paywall happens to be open when anteroom_pro turns on, it closes
itself.

Failures are handled as distinct cases rather than one generic error:

- A user dismissing the store sheet is a cancellation, not an error, and
shows no red text.

- A purchase that succeeds without granting the entitlement says so and
points you at Restore purchases.

- A restore that finds nothing says it found nothing instead of silently
unlocking.

- An unreachable store falls back to dashboard pricing so the paywall still
renders, and surfaces the reason.

**The extraction pipeline**

Four callables and a webhook, deployed to europe-west1. The client never
writes a clinical field: firestore.rules rejects content, status,
generated_at and the share token from any client, and the Admin SDK inside
these functions is the only thing that may. "Nothing invented" is therefore
a property of the system rather than a promise about the UI.

Function
Model
Owns

classifyDocType
Gemini 2.5 Flash
detected_doc_type, detected_confidence

generateBrief
Gemini 2.5 Pro
content, status, generated_at

translateBrief
Gemini 2.5 Pro
content_translations

renderBriefPdf
none
nothing — returns bytes

revenuecatWebhook
none
users/{uid}/billing/entitlement

Everything stays in the EU. Firestore is eur3, functions and Vertex AI
are both pinned to europe-west1. That costs us model capability and we
took the trade knowingly: Gemini 3.x exists on Vertex, but only on the
global endpoint, which routes a photograph of someone's referral letter to
whichever region Google picks. These are medical documents, so the residency
is worth more than the newer model.

Translation cannot touch a dose. merge_translation takes prose from
the model and every clinical field from the already-extracted content, so a
translation pass is structurally unable to alter a drug name, a dose, a
frequency, a patient's name or an ID. The test feeds it a deliberately
hostile response that corrupts all of those and asserts none of it lands.
Dosing frequency is localised for Spanish clinicians — by a fixed lookup
table, not the model, and anything the table doesn't recognise is left in
the source language rather than guessed at.

The paywall moved server-side. renderBriefPdf takes no watermarked
argument. The server derives it from the entitlement, so the clean export —
one of the two things Pro sells — stopped being a boolean the client could
flip. translateBrief returns PERMISSION_DENIED to a free caller. The
RevenueCat webhook is the only writer of that entitlement document.

It spends real money, so it has a brake. A per-user daily cap charged
transactionally before the model call, and a kill switch at
config/runtime.ai_enabled read on every call — flip it and spend stops
within seconds, with no deploy. Pages are downscaled to a 1536px long edge on
both the client and the server, because the server must not depend on a
client having behaved. A two-page brief costs about $0.02 end to end.

**What runs today**

Being precise about this matters more than the pitch does.

Live and verified against the deployed project:

- The complete Compose Multiplatform UI across Android, iOS, Desktop, and
Web.

- RevenueCat billing through purchases-kmp: offerings fetch, package
purchase, restore, customer info refresh, and delegate-driven entitlement
updates, all verified against anteroom_pro. Purchases complete on iOS,
through StoreKit, on a TestFlight build Apple has approved for external
testers: https://testflight.apple.com/join/EvbxqXGU

- Firebase authentication, Firestore persistence, and Storage photo upload —
including on Desktop, which uploads over the Storage REST API because
GitLive ships no JVM implementation.

- Real extraction: a photographed referral and a photographed prescription
become a populated BriefContent in about 13 seconds, with the illegible
dose flagged rather than guessed.

- Translation into Spanish, and PDF export whose watermark is decided by the
server.

- Family profile management and the clinical brief view with flagged-item
banners and photo verification against the original page.

Honest limits:

- Android purchases do not complete yet. The Play products are not
registered, so the store returns no offering and the paywall falls back to
the catalogue price with a plain "Plans aren't available on this device
right now." A new Google Play Console account must run a 14-day closed test
with 20 testers before it can publish, which cannot finish before the
deadline — so Android ships as a direct APK this cycle and Play
registration follows. The billing code itself is the same source set that
is live on iOS; what is missing is a store listing, not an implementation.

- Two languages, English and Spanish.

- Six pages per brief. The cap is the spend ceiling as much as a product
limit, and it is enforced in the security rules, not just the client.

- The public share page was cut. An earlier build advertised a QR code
pointing at a guessable /s/{brief_id} URL; the page, the QR and the
claim were removed together.

- Desktop and Web run SimulatedRevenueCatService for billing and label
themselves as a simulation on screen. Everything else on those targets is
the real backend.

- The Ktor server module is a scaffold and is unused.

**How we know**

Four suites, all runnable against the live project rather than a mock:

Suite
Checks
Proves

tools/verify_rules.py
21
Cross-user denial, server-only clinical fields, storage limits

tools/verify_pipeline.py
43
The whole pipeline, both paywall gates, entitlement grant and revoke

tools/verify_account_deletion.py
17
That deleting an account really erases it, checked from outside

functions/tests/test_pipeline.py
56
Translation safety boundary, PDF, frequency lookup

The rules suite earned its keep immediately. It found that our brief-create
rule could never have passed: it required status == 'draft' while also
requiring the key status to be absent, and the Kotlin client serialises
defaults, so every nullable field arrives as an explicit null. A test
written from the rules would have agreed with the rules. Only a test built
from the real client payload caught it.

**Challenges we ran into**

- A multiplatform SDK that isn't available on every platform.
Reconciling purchases-kmp's Android-and-Apple artifact set with a
four-target app took the shared-source-directory approach described above.
The obvious fix — an intermediate source set wired with dependsOn() —
disables Kotlin's default hierarchy template and breaks iosMain.

- Two SDKs configuring one singleton. An earlier build configured the
native Android RevenueCat SDK in MainActivity while purchases-kmp
pulled in a different major version of the same library. Removing the
native call and letting shared code configure once fixed both the version
conflict and the double configuration.

- Designing for uncertainty. The hard product question wasn't extraction
accuracy. It was what the screen does when two documents disagree. Showing
both and flagging the conflict took more UI work than picking one would
have.

- A security rule that no client could satisfy. Described above. The
general lesson: a test written from your rules will agree with your rules.
Build the payload the way the client actually builds it.

- Deleting the fallbacks was the risky part. The repositories used to
swallow every failure and return mock data, so a permission error, an
offline device and an empty account were indistinguishable — from each
other and from success. Removing that turned silent wrong answers into
crashes until there was somewhere for failures to go, so the error banner
and try/finally on every long call had to land in the same change.

- Firebase on Desktop fails twice, late, and somewhere else.
Firebase.initialize(context = null) is correct on Web and leaves the
JVM app uninitialised — which surfaces at the first auth call as
"Default FirebaseApp is not initialized". Passing a Context gets
further: auth succeeds, and Firestore then dies on its own async queue
because it casts to android.app.Application. Writing the integration
test before the implementation is the only reason both were found.

**Accomplishments we're proud of**

- One RevenueCatService implementation drives billing on iOS and Android
with no platform branches in the calling code — live against StoreKit
today, and pointed at Google Play Billing by the same source set the moment
the Play products exist.

- A paywall that reacts to entitlement state rather than to button taps, so
it behaves correctly when a subscription changes somewhere else.

- A clinical data model that treats "we don't know" as information worth
rendering — and a test that proves the model honours it, by handing it a
dose it cannot read and checking that the field stays empty.

- Both Pro gates enforced on the server. The clean export is not a flag the
client can set.

- A pipeline that spends real money behind a daily per-user cap and a kill
switch that stops it in seconds without a deploy.

**What we learned**

purchases-kmp collapses two native billing integrations into one Kotlin
surface, and the remaining work is almost entirely about state, not stores.
The lesson that transferred best from clinical practice: the value of an
intake document is not how much it asserts, it's how clearly it marks what
it can't confirm.

**What's next**

- Validate the brief format with clinicians, as a student research
project. The question we want answered is not "is it accurate"
but "does the flagged-items section change what you ask the patient".

- Expand language coverage beyond English and Spanish. The frequency lookup
table is per-language and the extraction prompt is language-agnostic, so
the work is mostly clinical review of the wording.

- Google Play registration, then the 14-day closed test, then Play Billing
live against the same RevenueCatServiceImpl that already runs on
StoreKit.

- On-device classification, so the doc-type triage costs nothing and works
offline.

- A clinic handoff that is safe by construction — the previous design was a
guessable URL, and we would rather ship nothing than ship that again.

**Award tracks**

- Main prizes. These require the first public version to be released on
the App Store, Google Play or Galaxy Store during the submission period,
and TestFlight does not count. Anteroom 1.0 is being submitted to the App
Store this week. It is eligible if Apple approves the release before the
deadline, and not otherwise.

- Next Gen / Student Award. No store release is required. Anteroom is
submitted with a demo video and a public open-source repository,
github.com/sorarx27/anteroom-mobile
(branch kotlin), under the MIT license in LICENSE. It
is built by an actively enrolled Master's student.

- Ship Kotlin Everywhere. This award needs live App Store and Google Play
listings. The code qualifies: 100% Compose Multiplatform UI and one
purchases-kmp implementation for both stores. The listings do not yet.
The Play products do not exist, and a new personal Play Console account
must run a 14-day closed test with 20 testers before it can publish.
Anteroom is eligible only if the Play listing is live by the deadline, and
we are not counting on it.

- Most Likely to Make Money. The clinical intake and language bottleneck
for expats and retirees seeing doctors in Spain is a recurring,
paid-for problem with a clear willingness to pay at the household level.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We were inspired by a simple problem: finding reliable workers for everyday services can be difficult, while many skilled workers struggle to find consistent customers and new opportunities. We wanted to build a platform that could bring both sides together in a simple and organized way.

**What it does**

ShramikSetu connects customers with local service providers through one platform. Customers can discover services, receive recommendations, send requests, book workers, communicate with them, make payments, and track their bookings. Workers can showcase their skills, manage services and job requests, communicate with customers, and keep track of their work. The platform also includes AI-powered assistance to make finding and managing services easier.

**How we built it**

We built ShramikSetu as a full-stack web and mobile application with separate experiences for customers, workers, and administrators. We connected the frontend with a backend API and database to manage users, services, bookings, requests, notifications, and payments. We also integrated AI assistance, real-time communication, authentication, and a payment gateway to make the platform more complete and practical.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was getting all the different parts of the application to work together smoothly. We dealt with API integration, authentication, database connectivity, payment flows, notifications, real-time communication, deployment, and differences between local and production environments. Debugging these issues helped us understand how the different layers of a real-world application depend on each other.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud that we were able to turn our initial idea into a working platform with multiple user roles and real-world functionality. Integrating AI assistance, service discovery, booking management, communication, notifications, and payments into one platform was a major achievement for our team.

**What we learned**

This project taught us that building a complete product is much more than writing individual features. We learned how frontend, backend, databases, APIs, third-party services, and deployment work together. We also improved our debugging, teamwork, problem-solving, and ability to turn an idea into a usable product.

**What's next for ShramikSetu**

We want to continue improving ShramikSetu based on real user feedback. Our next steps include making the AI assistant more capable, improving service recommendations, strengthening security and payment reliability, adding better worker verification and reviews, and making the platform more scalable and accessible.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I was planning two years abroad on savings, and I worked it out in a spreadsheet. A spreadsheet does the job. It is just not my thing. I wanted the answer on my phone in two seconds, so I built that. I have not opened the spreadsheet since.

It came from Breath of the Wild. It is the best-designed survival game I know. Hearts and stamina are there so you can keep going, not to stop you. Keeping it going is the whole game.

The runway number looks like a countdown. It isn't. It is how long you can keep going.

**What it does**

Financial Runway shows how many months your money covers, counted from today, and the month it would run out. Knowing your runway is an opportunity to adjust.

Two kinds of cost, not twenty categories. Some costs are already decided: rent, loan payments, subscriptions. The living budget is what you plan to spend. Logging a coffee uses that budget up instead of adding to your costs, so the number only moves if you go over. What you do not spend comes back at the end of the month.

It asks instead of assuming. The app knows when a subscription should have billed and what a loan payment should be, but only you know what actually left the account. A subscription either billed or it did not. A loan leaves the amount to you, because you can pay more than the schedule.

Logging is three taps and a number. Tap the button, tap what it was for, type the amount. A line under the tiles takes you straight to logging income instead.

Set a goal in months, and see the cash it needs. The app turns that into a cash target, shows how much is still to go, and tells you the months of cover left to build.

Plan it before you do it. Change a cost or your income, run it, and see the months move.

The number tells you how it is doing before you read it. Above six months of cover it is mint, between three and six it turns amber, and under three it goes pink. A soft glow behind it keeps time with the same three states: slow and faint when you are stable, quicker and brighter as the cover shortens. Turn on Reduce Motion and it holds still instead of pulsing.

**How it's built**

Flutter, Drift, SQLCipher. A local database on the phone, locked with a key made on the device and kept in the Keychain.

The maths is ordinary bookkeeping. You set a budget for rent and one for living. If you spend more than a budget, the bigger number counts. Add subscriptions and loan payments, and that is your monthly cost. Runway is your cash, minus what is still due this month, divided by that, counted from today. Income works on the same scale, so the simulator can show a cost cut and a pay rise in the same unit: months.

No account and no server. Your data stays on your phone and I never see it, so you do not have to take my word for how careful I am. The app sends no analytics events of its own: not an amount, not a balance, not even which screen you opened. Firebase is initialised, so Google's SDK collects its standard app-level signals such as session starts, and that is the whole of what leaves. Pro is the exception, and it belongs to the Apple ID rather than the app, so Delete all data cannot take away what you paid for.

A lot of it was vibe coding, so most of the work was checking. Claude Code wrote most of the app and I used Codex for the visuals. I described what I wanted and kept what worked. That is the only reason this got built in the time I had. It is also where most of the bugs came from. So there are checks for the things I cannot see by looking:

- The database is asked which cipher it is running, and refuses to open if the answer comes back empty.

- Tests hold the signing setup and the languages the App Store will list.

- Tests hold the contrast of every colour pair, and cap how many raw colours one screen may use.

**Challenges**

Getting the tone right. It started as a game: hearts and EXP for keeping your runway going, and a rank worked out from your number. The ranking was the part that had to go.

A rank turns a fact about your month into a verdict about you.

So I cut anything that scored you, and changed the words too: burn and survive became monthly costs and months covered.

A loan had no obvious place to sit. It arrives as money you can spend, so it lifts the runway. It leaves every month, so it is also a cost. And it is still owed. My first version worked like a bank: principal, balance, interest rate, schedule. That was a mistake. What matters is how much leaves each month and when it stops. Modelling it that way turned up a bug: a loan dropped out of monthly costs as soon as the principal was repaid, with payments still to go. I thought about warning you not to spend it all, and left it out: what you owe sits beside what you have. A loan does not add runway. It borrows it.

It is a rough number, and it still has to be right. Your cash divided by your costs. Nobody spends in even months and nobody knows the next one, so it was never going to be exact. Close enough is fine. Wrong is not. A typo put the run out date in the year 275360. Someone whose cash really is zero should see zero months, not a negative number. And before any costs are entered the answer is not an error. It is unlimited.

**What went right**

Narrowing it down. I wanted it to handle every situation I could think of. Most of the work turned out to be deciding what not to build. Onboarding went from five pages to three, and then to one. A chart was cut. The runway number moved above everything else and became the only big number in the app.

I use it. Not to check how I am doing, which is what the spreadsheet was for. To decide: whether this month can take a flight, whether I can turn work down. That was the whole ambition, and it is done.

It left my laptop. One number, a few screens, six languages, and a real app submitted to the App Store instead of a prototype in a folder. Simple took longer than any of it.

**What's next for Financial Runway**

- Capture without connecting. The cost of no bank connection is typing, and that is the fair objection to everything above. The answer is not a bank login, it is making capture cost almost nothing. Subscriptions should record themselves: the app already holds the date and the amount of the next charge, which beats a bank feed, because a feed learns afterwards and a schedule knows in advance. Spending should be loggable by voice from the Lock Screen without opening anything. A receipt should scan, exactly in Taiwan where the fiscal QR carries the date and the total, and by text recognition elsewhere. A statement should import once at the start, so the first runway is true rather than provisional. All of it runs on the device, so none of it adds an account, a server or a credential.

- The income half. Costs have four screens. Income has an entry field. You can log what arrives and see each entry, but nothing shows whether it is growing, and that is the other half of the answer.

- Not credit cards. A card spend leaves your cash when the bill is paid, not when you tap, so there is a real bookkeeping case for deferring it. I worked it through and dropped it. The runway lands on the same number either way, and counting the spend on the day you make it is the point: cards erode awareness precisely because the money leaves without you feeling it. Better bookkeeping that reproduces the problem is not an improvement.

- Fewer numbers, better joined. A dozen figures, each added for a good reason, which is how a screen gets crowded. The app knows your cash lasts 12 months while the loan has 43 to go, and leaves you to notice. Saying it would be worth more than most of the figures it replaces.

Everything above this is a guess until there are users. I built this for my own problem and I think other people have it too. Asking does not settle it, because people say yes to things they never open. So the order is: publish, be loud enough to be found, then let real use decide what gets polished and what gets cut. Building it was the quiet half. The noisy half is next: going to the people who already count months rather than budgets, on work-exchange and volunteering placements, career breaks, long stretches between contracts, and asking the organisations they pass through for a line on a resources page rather than a discount nobody needed.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Most chore-tracking and shared calendar apps feel like enterprise ticketing systems—cold, rigid, and tedious. But shared living—whether with a partner, family, or roommates—is deeply personal. It should feel collaborative, encouraging, and delightful.

We built Stewardie to replace household friction and mental load with harmony, tactile charm, and clear communication.

**What It Does**

Stewardie is an everyday shared-life companion structured around three core pillars:

- Shared Spaces & Responsibilities: Create shared spaces (home, apartment, family) where chores and plans aren’t just assigned, but requested, claimed, and celebrated. Tasks support photo verification proof and handoffs.

- Little Moments & Mood Check-Ins: A private daily feed for shared victories, photo memories with bespoke clay television framing, and one-tap emotional check-ins to stay connected.

- Privacy-First Live Location: Voluntary, time-bounded (15, 30, or 60 minutes) temporary location sharing on interactive maps with automatic expiration.

- Stewardie Plus (Powered by RevenueCat): A fair, transparent subscription tier ($4.99/mo or $39.99/yr) that belongs to the individual subscriber across all their spaces. Plus unlocks up to 20 spaces, unlimited task history, and multi-photo attachments, while ensuring Basic members always retain access to complete tasks and participate freely.

**How We Built It**

- Frontend / Client: Built in Flutter with a completely bespoke Soft Pop pastel clay design system—featuring warm cream surfaces, custom clay cards, spring physics, and 10 custom synthesized acoustic sound effects.

- Monetization (RevenueCat): Integrated using purchases_flutter for seamless subscription lifecycle management, entitlement verification (stewardie_plus), and non-intrusive paywalls.

- Backend & Real-Time Sync: Firebase Authentication and Cloud Firestore for live state synchronization, with strict security rules governing quota enforcement and role boundaries.

- Media Pipeline: Supabase Storage & Edge Functions for photo verification attachments and Moments media handling.

**Challenges We Faced**

- Fair Monetization Architecture: We refused to use hostile paywalls that lock other household members out. Designing the entitlement model so a Plus subscription belongs to an individual across multiple spaces without breaking the experience for free invited members required deliberate architecture.

- High-Performance Tactile UI: Achieving a soft claymorphic depth without sacrificing 60 FPS mobile performance required custom painters and avoiding heavy nested shadows.

- Real-Time Quota Optimization: Balancing continuous collaborative streams with cloud database quotas led us to design custom avatar caching and efficient storage URL pipelines.

**Accomplishments We're Proud Of**

- Over 210+ comprehensive automated tests validating onboarding tours, offline fallbacks, RevenueCat purchase states, and accessibility layouts.

- Zero generic template aesthetics—every screen, chip, button, sound effect, and clay frame was custom-crafted.

- A functional, end-to-end RevenueCat subscription flow that feels native and rewarding.

**What We Learned**

Integrating RevenueCat taught us the importance of clean separation between client-side purchase states, store sandboxes, and server-side entitlement reconciliation. We also learned how positive micro-interactions and transparent pricing build immediate user trust.

**What's Next for Stewardie**

- Official launch on the Apple App Store and Google Play Store.

- Advanced recurring routines and calendar integrations (Google Calendar / Apple Calendar).

- Expanding RevenueCat Experiments to test localized introductory pricing for international households.

</details>
