[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/OjRnKjV0_O8/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OjRnKjV0_O8)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/330/218/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/330/218/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We take so many videos of the people we care about — days out with friends, family gatherings, weddings, trips, and everyday moments.

But when it comes to sharing them, I noticed there was a gap. Platforms like YouTube are built around public or broadly accessible sharing, while sending videos privately can mean sending huge files one person at a time.

This became especially relatable with family weddings. In Pakistan, wedding videos can easily turn into hours of footage. Family members living abroad may want to watch those memories, but uploading them publicly isn't appropriate because of privacy concerns, and sending such large files individually isn't practical.

I also have family members who have moved abroad, and I often record little moments that I would like to share with them. That made me think: what if I could upload a video once and simply choose exactly which people could watch it?

That idea became WithYou — a private video diary for the people you actually know.

**What It Does**

WithYou lets users upload videos and give each video its own privacy settings.

A video can be:

- Public — visible to all contacts

- Selected Contacts — visible only to chosen people

- Private — visible only to the owner

The key idea is that not every video is for everyone.

A video from a day out with friends can be shared with those friends, a family video can be shared with family members, and a personal video can remain completely private.

**How I Built It**

I built WithYou as an Android application using Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, following an MVVM architecture.

For authentication and application data, I used Firebase Authentication and Cloud Firestore. Videos are stored using Supabase Storage, while a separate backend supports secure video playback.

The application also uses Hilt for dependency injection and Media3/ExoPlayer for video playback.

One of the most important parts of the implementation was designing the video access model. Instead of treating privacy as a single account-level setting, every video stores its own visibility and, when necessary, a list of users who are allowed to access it.

The app then filters content based on those permissions so that users don't simply receive videos they aren't authorised to see.

**Challenges**

The biggest challenge was not uploading a video — it was making sure that the right person could access the right video.

Implementing the three privacy levels meant dealing with several cases:

- Making private videos visible only to their owner

- Allowing selected contacts to access specific videos

- Making public videos visible to all contacts

- Preventing unauthorised videos from appearing in feeds and profiles

- Keeping the video playback flow secure

I also had to work through the interaction between Firebase, Firestore, Supabase Storage, and the backend. Getting authentication, metadata, storage, access control, and playback to work together required a lot of debugging.

Another challenge was designing the video player experience. I wanted users to be able to watch videos naturally in both portrait and landscape orientations, including an expanded/fullscreen experience.

**What I Learned**

Building WithYou taught me that creating a real application is much more than implementing individual features.

I learned how different services have to work together as one system — authentication, database, storage, backend services, permissions, and the Android UI all have to agree about the same user and the same piece of content.

I also learned a lot about access control and privacy-aware application design. A privacy feature isn't complete just because the UI lets you select "private." The backend and data-access logic also have to enforce that decision.

Most importantly, I learned to think about software from the user's perspective first.

The question wasn't:

"How do I build another video-sharing app?"

It was:

"Why is sharing a personal video still so inconvenient when I only want certain people to see it?"

WithYou is my attempt to solve that problem.

🚀 What's Next for WithYou?
WithYou is still evolving. One of the features I want to add next is AI-powered subtitles and translation.

</details>

**Video (0:54):** https://vimeo.com/1231979543

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/606/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/606/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/607/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/607/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

OnMe started with something very familiar in our house: my wife loves clothes.

She'll go to the mall, find something she likes, try it on, look at herself from every angle, decide it isn't quite right, return it to the rack... and then move on to the next one. 😄

Online shopping makes the problem even harder. She can see a beautiful dress on a model, but the question is always the same:

"But how would this actually look on me?"

That got me thinking: why should she have to travel to a mall and physically try on ten different outfits just to answer that one question?

With today's generative AI, couldn't we make it as simple as taking a photo?

That became OnMe.

The idea is deliberately simple: upload a photo of yourself, upload a photo of something you'd like to wear, and see it on you.

Hopefully, that means a few fewer trips to the fitting room. 😄

**What it does**

OnMe is an AI-powered virtual try-on app with an intentionally simple interface.

You give it just two images:

- A full-body photo of yourself

- A photo of an outfit you want to try

The outfit could be something you saw in an online store, on social media, in a screenshot, or simply a photo of clothing you liked.

OnMe uses AI to generate a realistic visualization of you wearing that outfit.

The goal isn't to create a different or "improved" version of you. OnMe aims to preserve your identity, face, hair, skin tone, natural body proportions, and overall appearance while transferring the clothing from the reference image.

No prompts.

No body sliders.

No complicated configuration.

Just:

You + an outfit → See it on you.

**How we built it**

We designed OnMe around an image-to-image generative AI workflow rather than a traditional text-prompt experience.

The system receives two visual inputs:

- the person image

- the outfit reference

The AI pipeline then has to understand both independently and generate a new image that combines them.

For the person, we want to preserve:

- identity and facial appearance

- hair

- skin tone

- natural body proportions

- pose and overall appearance

For the outfit, we want to preserve:

- color

- silhouette

- neckline

- sleeves

- length

- patterns

- fabric appearance

- important design details

The difficult AI work happens behind the scenes.

For the user, we deliberately reduced the experience to:

Upload yourself → Upload the outfit → Try it on → See the result.

We believe the interface should almost disappear. The result is what matters.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge is that virtual try-on is much harder than simply generating an attractive AI image.

A generated picture can look impressive while still being completely wrong.

The AI might subtly change someone's face, make their body thinner or taller, alter the shape of the garment, change its color, lose a pattern, modify the neckline, or invent details that weren't present in the original outfit.

That means we're solving for two kinds of fidelity at the same time:

Person fidelity — does the result still genuinely look like the same person?

Garment fidelity — does it still genuinely look like the outfit they selected?

Getting one right while losing the other isn't enough.

Another challenge was actually simplicity.

It's tempting to keep adding AI controls: prompts, body settings, styles, poses, sliders, editing tools, and dozens of options.

We kept asking ourselves:

Does the user actually need this?

If not, we removed it.

OnMe should be understandable within seconds of opening it.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We're proud that OnMe turns a sophisticated generative-AI problem into an interaction almost anyone can understand.

You don't need to know how to write an AI prompt.

You don't need fashion terminology.

You don't need to enter dozens of measurements.

You don't need to configure a generation model.

You simply show OnMe yourself and what you want to wear.

We're also proud of one important principle behind the product:

The AI shouldn't change you just to make the result look good.

The goal isn't to make you thinner, taller, younger, or turn you into an AI fashion model.

The goal is much simpler:

"Show me how this would look on me."

**What we learned**

One of our biggest lessons was that the quality of virtual try-on isn't just about photorealism.

Preservation matters.

If the image looks incredibly realistic but changes the person's face, it has failed.

If it preserves the person perfectly but changes the outfit, it has also failed.

The best result is one where the technology almost disappears and your immediate reaction is:

"That's me wearing that."

We also learned something broader about building AI products.

Powerful AI doesn't necessarily need a powerful-looking interface.

Sometimes the best AI experience is the one where the user barely has to interact with the AI at all.

Give it what it needs and let it do the complicated work.

**What's next for OnMe**

A single AI-generated image is only the beginning.

Our next goal is to make OnMe feel less like looking at a photo and more like standing in front of a virtual fitting-room mirror.

We want to explore:

- 360° View — turn around and see how the outfit looks from the front, side, and back.

- Zoom & Detail — inspect fabric, patterns, stitching, neckline, sleeves, and other garment details up close.

- Multiple Poses — see the same outfit while standing, walking, sitting, or turning.

- More Clothing Categories — dresses, shirts, jackets, suits, sarees, trousers, skirts, traditional clothing, and more.

- Better Fit Fidelity — preserve your real body proportions while showing how different cuts and silhouettes may look.

- Outfit History — quickly compare things you've already tried.

- Try Another Color — when a garment comes in multiple colors, visualize different options without changing the design.

- Instant Try-On from Anywhere — see an outfit online, share or upload the image to OnMe, and immediately see it on yourself.

Longer term, we imagine opening OnMe and having your own AI fitting room.

Upload yourself once. Then whenever you find something you like:

Add outfit → Try it on → Rotate → Zoom → Compare → Decide.

No trip to the fitting room required just to find out whether you like the look.

Our vision is simple:

If you can see it, you should be able to see it on you.

**OnMe — See it on you.**

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Don't Go To Bed started with my boys, Leo and Ian, and the sort of game ideas that make perfect sense when you're a child: build things, fight monsters, turn the world sideways, and find Mammy.

Inspired by Minecraft, Super Mario Bros. and the boys’ own drawings and ideas, we wanted to make something together as a family. Leo, Ian and Papa became the playable characters.

The story is simple: Mammy has gone out, Daddy has forgotten where, and we need to find her before dark. We have some building blocks and a plan.

The plan is mostly building blocks.

**What it does**

Don't Go To Bed is a 2.5D adventure, now available on Google Play and the App Store for iPhone and iPad.

Players can explore, break and place blocks, collect materials, fight zombies and skeleton archers, use potions and search for Mammy before nightfall. Turning the world switches between two directions through the same world, revealing different routes and nearby terrain.

You can play solo or join another player over local Wi-Fi. Multiplayer shares the adventure: players see one another, change the same terrain and face the same enemies.

The game includes music that changes between the menu, the search and the night-time panic, alongside sound effects, separate volume controls and accessibility options for movement and reduced flashing.

All characters and gameplay are free. RevenueCat powers optional, repeatable one-time tips in a grown-up support section. Tips do not unlock content or give players an advantage, and there is no subscription.

**How we built it**

The project began as an Android game and grew into a Kotlin Multiplatform application.

Shared Kotlin code handles the game rules, world, inventory, combat and multiplayer messages. Compose Multiplatform provides the interface and rendering, with platform-specific integrations for networking, audio and device settings.

We built it without a dedicated game engine. That meant implementing systems such as movement, collisions, enemy behaviour, world projection and animation ourselves.

Multiplayer uses a host-controlled world with WebSocket connections. The host coordinates terrain changes and shared entities so that actions such as mining a block or firing an arrow can stay consistent between players.

Testing has included Android emulators and physical Apple and Android devices, including an older iPad. We have played together across physical Android and iOS devices; multiplayer still has bugs. Automated tests cover shared game logic. Release preparation included device checks and real gameplay footage.

**Challenges we faced**

One of the biggest challenges was making a world that turns without making the game lose track of where everything belongs. Terrain, enemies, arrows and other players all need to remain consistent when viewed from a different direction.

Multiplayer added another layer: two players can act at the same time, join at different moments or leave unexpectedly. We had to think carefully about which device owns the world state and how actions and updates travel between devices.

Performance also mattered. A game that feels fine on a development machine can behave very differently on an older tablet.

One particularly surprising crash came from a skeleton archer's flashing effect. A tiny positive opacity value rounded down to fully transparent in the graphics library, triggering a native rendering failure. It looked random while playing, but several device crash reports led us to the same cause. We added a guard and regression tests for that boundary.

And, of course, there was the ongoing challenge of turning an enthusiastic family wish list into something we could actually finish.

**What we learned**

Sharing code across platforms is valuable, but it doesn't remove the need to understand and test each platform.

We learned to separate game rules from rendering, make ownership explicit in multiplayer, and use real crash reports rather than guessing from what a player sees.

We also learned that “it builds,” “it opens,” and “it survives a proper play session” are three different milestones.

Most of all, we learned how much personality a project gains when the people helping to imagine it also become its characters.

**Accomplishments we're proud of**

- Releasing our family game on both Google Play and the Apple App Store.

- Receiving our first €9.99 Android support tip while keeping all gameplay free.

- Building shared gameplay and local multiplayer without a dedicated game engine.

- Making world turning part of exploration.

- Adding music, sound effects and accessibility settings.

- Creating a trailer with our own narration and real two-player footage.

- Preparing the code for public collaboration, while keeping private release material and credentials separate.

During the multiplatform migration, the build passed 92 Android unit tests and an unsigned iOS Release build. Since then, we have released on both stores and played together across physical Android and iOS devices. Multiplayer still has bugs to resolve.

**What's next**

The game is released on Android and iOS. Next comes improving the experience on real devices and choosing small additions with the boys.

In our September 28 family discussion, we worked through a crafting idea together: a workbench opens a recipe list, and we start with a simple version the boys can play and refine. Crafting is not in the released build. We also revisited character specials: a drum-kit ability and a giant dog, replacing an earlier giant-cat idea. Larger worlds, more building materials and Jenny's quests remain future candidates rather than promised release features.

The code is MIT licensed, with separate terms for family artwork and branding. We welcome people exploring the code and making their own versions with their own identities and assets.

For now, we just need to find Mammy.

Preferably before somebody puts another twelve blocks of dirt in the bag.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

DSA Mentor is a mobile study companion for anyone grinding through data structures and algorithms problems. Instead of dumping a full solution, it gives you layered hints — a subtle nudge first, then a bigger push, then the approach — so you actually learn to recognize patterns instead of memorizing answers.

How it works: paste any DSA problem statement, and Gemini identifies the underlying pattern (hash map, two pointers, sliding window, DP, etc.) and generates a hint calibrated to how much help you've already asked for. Mark problems as solved, and your session history tracks what you've worked through and which patterns you're still shaky on.

Built with: Expo (React Native), Google Gemini for pattern-aware hint generation, Supabase for auth and session storage, and RevenueCat for subscription management — free users get 3 hint sessions a day and their last 3 sessions in history; premium unlocks unlimited sessions and full history.

This was built solo end-to-end for the Next Gen category — from auth flow to AI integration to a working RevenueCat paywall — as a tool I'll actually keep using for my own DSA practice.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

PickMe came from a real commuting problem. My teammate Laiba and I realized that even when our routes didn't perfectly overlap, we could still carpool. However, we couldn't find a single platform to easily connect people with similar routes and schedules, which inspired us to build one.

**What it does**

PickMe connects people traveling along similar routes and schedules so they can find potential carpool partners, share rides, and reduce commuting costs.

**How we built it**

We developed PickMe as a rapid prototype during the RevenueCat hackathon, working remotely as a team. With only seven days, we focused on defining the core workflow and implementing the most important features needed for a functional app.

**Challenges we ran into**

Our biggest challenges were the seven-day deadline, remote coordination, and late finalization of the app workflow. The complete workflow was only finalized three days before submission, leaving limited time for development and polishing.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Despite the limited time, we managed to turn an idea into a working carpooling application within seven days. We are especially proud that we kept experimenting and adapting instead of getting stuck in the planning stage.

**What we learned**

We learned that experimentation goes a long way. It is easy to spend too much time researching and planning, but building and testing early can help overcome those limitations and reveal what actually works.

**What's next for PickMe**

We would like to further develop PickMe by improving its user experience, matching system, reliability, and overall feature set, turning the prototype into a more complete and polished carpooling platform.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Finding reliable pet care can be surprisingly fragmented. Pet owners often depend on social media posts, informal referrals, phone calls, and disconnected payment or messaging tools. At the same time, independent pet-care providers need a simple way to present their services, manage bookings, communicate with clients, and understand their earnings. I built Boo Pet Care to bring those experiences into one mobile marketplace. Owners can discover suitable providers, manage their pets, create bookings, chat with providers, receive notifications, and leave reviews. Providers can create service profiles, set availability, manage bookings, communicate with clients, and monitor their work from a dedicated dashboard.

**What it does**

Boo Pet Care supports two types of users:

**Pet owners**

- Create and manage pet profiles

- Discover nearby pet-care providers

- Review provider services and availability

- Create and manage bookings

- Chat with providers within an existing booking

- Receive booking and account notifications

- Leave reviews after completed services

**Pet-care providers**

- Build a provider profile

- Configure services, pricing, availability, and working hours

- Receive and manage booking requests

- Communicate with owners through booking chat

- Record completed service payments

- View ordinary dashboard statistics

Boo also includes two optional premium memberships powered by RevenueCat:

- Boo Plus allows owners to create additional pet profiles beyond the first free pet.

- Boo Pro provides advanced recorded-earnings insights for providers.

The free experience remains useful: owners retain discovery, booking, chat, notifications, reviews, and one pet profile, while providers retain profiles, services, bookings, availability, chat, and ordinary statistics.

**How I built it**

The mobile application was built with Flutter. The backend uses NestJS, TypeORM, and PostgreSQL, and is deployed on Render. On admin web view side , Cloudinary stores provider-verification documents, while the backend controls the associated verification workflow and access.

I used:

- RevenueCat for Test Store purchases, role-specific offerings, subscription restoration, and entitlement lifecycle management

- RevenueCat webhooks to project subscription state into PostgreSQL

- Stream Chat for booking conversations

- OneSignal for push-notification integration

- PostgreSQL as the authoritative source for application and entitlement data

RevenueCat uses the authenticated Boo user UUID as the App User ID. Owners and providers have separate offerings and entitlements, preventing Boo Plus from unlocking provider features or Boo Pro from unlocking owner features.
Premium enforcement is not based solely on the Flutter interface. RevenueCat sends authenticated webhook events to the backend, where entitlement state is processed idempotently and stored in PostgreSQL. When an owner attempts to create an additional pet, the backend checks for an active and unexpired boo_plus entitlement inside a database transaction.

**Challenges I faced**

The most difficult challenge was synchronizing identity and subscription state across Flutter, RevenueCat, the backend, and PostgreSQL.
RevenueCat initially created anonymous customers before authentication completed. Logout and login operations could also overlap, allowing an older logout operation to clear a newer user identity. I corrected this by serializing identity mutations, tracking the active SDK identity, rejecting stale results, and verifying the RevenueCat App User ID after login. Another challenge was keeping the app synchronized immediately after a Test Store purchase. A purchase could succeed while the interface continued showing the free membership state. I added reactive entitlement updates, CustomerInfo reconciliation, expiration timers, cache invalidation, and protection against stale entitlement snapshots.
The additional-pet flow exposed an important architectural lesson: client-side premium checks improve the user experience, but they must not be the security boundary. The backend now makes the final decision. It locks the owner record, counts existing pets, verifies the projected entitlement, and inserts the new pet transactionally.
I also had to handle subscription expiration, account switching, delayed webhooks, duplicate events, role mismatches, slow emulator initialization, and responsive premium screens without allowing stale access to leak between accounts.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I am particularly proud that Boo Pet Care is more than a paywall demonstration. It is a working two-sided marketplace with separate owner and provider experiences, booking management, chat, notifications, reviews, provider availability, and premium features connected to real application value.
The RevenueCat integration supports role-specific offerings, authenticated Boo UUID identities, purchases, restoration, expiration, logout, and account switching. RevenueCat webhooks project subscription events into PostgreSQL, while the backend independently enforces Boo Plus access for additional pet creation.
The focused premium-access suite contains 15 passing tests. I also successfully demonstrated Boo Plus unlocking additional pet creation and Boo Pro unlocking advanced provider earnings insights through RevenueCat’s Test Store.

**What I learned**

This project taught me that subscription integration is much more than displaying a paywall. A reliable implementation must account for identity transitions, webhook authentication, idempotency, stale asynchronous results, expiration, account switching, and server-side authorization.
I also learned how important it is to distinguish presentation state from authoritative access control. Flutter can show whether a feature appears available, but protected backend mutations must independently verify entitlement state.
The focused premium-access test suite now contains 15 passing tests covering free access, role separation, entitlement mismatch, expiration, account switching, immediate post-purchase activation, and premium upgrade routing.

**What’s next for Boo**

Future versions of Boo Pet Care could introduce pet health timelines, health-record exports, care reminders, CareLoop rebooking, advanced booking analytics, private client notes, automated rebooking suggestions, and featured provider listings.
These features are currently presented only as Coming soon and are not represented as completed functionality. The current premium implementation focuses on two working, demonstrable value slices: additional pet profiles through Boo Plus and advanced earnings insights through Boo Pro.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/476/383/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/476/383/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/844/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/844/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/845/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/845/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/846/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/846/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/847/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/847/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**2.1 Inspiration**

Growing up, one of my all-time favorite childhood games was Glu Mobile's (Glu Studio) legendary mobile title, Blood & Glory. The visceral gladiator duels, directional swiping, frame-tight parries, dodges, and exhilarating counter-attacks made it one of the most engaging combat experiences on mobile.

Tragically, Glu Mobile discontinued Blood & Glory years ago, taking it off app stores and leaving it completely unplayable on modern devices. For years, I missed that pulse-pounding rhythm—the rush of reading an incoming blade strike, executing a frame-perfect parry at the last fraction of a second, and shattering the enemy's guard with a cinematic counter-combo.

**ColoSynth was born out of a passionate mission to resurrect and recreate that cherished childhood combat experience. I set out to replicate the core directional swipe-and-parry gladiatorial combat loop of Blood & Glory, while reimagining it in an electrifying cyberpunk synthwave comic universe. Furthermore, whereas classic mobile titles often relied on frustrating pay-to-win walls and clunky billing, I wanted an ethical, transparent player progression model—making RevenueCat the ultimate engine to power a modern, rewarding in-game economy.**

**2.2 What It Does**

ColoSynth is a full-featured mobile action game with the following core systems:

- Directional Combat & Parry Mechanics: Real-time swordplay where players read enemy attack vectors, execute frame-precise parries, trigger cinematic counter-slashes, and stagger opponents.

- Comic Book Visual Presentation: Hand-crafted comic layouts, expressive halftone styling, onomatopoeic visual effects (SFX text pops), dynamic camera shakes, and diagonal slice screen transitions.

- 3D Character Model Inspector: An interactive 3D model viewer powered by Google's model-viewer web engine, allowing players to rotate and inspect their unlocked synthesized fighters.

- Dual Economy & Progression: In-game Ink (earned through skill and tournament victories) and Paint (premium chromatic currency) allow players to upgrade skill trees, unlock characters, and acquire battle buffs.

- Integrated In-App Purchases via RevenueCat:

- Consumable Currencies: Tiered Ink and Paint currency packs (ink_tier_1/2/3 and paint_tier_1/2/3).

- Non-Consumable Entitlements: An "Ad-Free" pass (com.drillacatz.colosynth.ad_free) with instantaneous entitlement unlocking (ad_free) that disables interstitials and rewards bonus multipliers.

- Purchase Ledger & Integrity: A tamper-evident local purchase ledger and cryptographic HMAC signature validation for secure guest and authenticated profiles.

- Zero-Friction Offline Fallback: Complete graceful degradation so judges and players without live sandbox accounts can still evaluate store offerings, item flows, and pricing effortlessly.

**2.3 How We Built It**

- Engine & Framework: Developed entirely in Flutter (Dart SDK 3.3+) using the Flame 2D game engine for physics, collision detection, and particle systems.

- Monetization & Subscriptions: Integrated the official RevenueCat SDK (purchases_flutter). We configured dynamic paywalls, purchase streams (customerInfoStream), and entitlement listeners that unlock game features in real time.

- State Architecture: Powered by Flutter Riverpod for declarative, predictable state propagation across battle mechanics, wallet states, and UI overlays.

- Persistence & Cloud Sync: Hybrid offline-first architecture utilizing SharedPreferences with local SHA-256 entropy keys, tamper-resistant HMAC data verification, and cloud synchronization with Firebase Firestore.

- Visual Design & Audio: Custom procedural 3D comic chest shaders, 2D particle systems, dynamic hit-stop effects, and a custom audio repository managing contextual BGM and slashing sound effects.

**2.4 How We Integrated RevenueCat**

RevenueCat serves as the central billing and entitlement engine for ColoSynth:

- Unified IAP Service (IapService):

- Initialized at startup with asynchronous configuration and entitlement observation.

- Listens to Purchases.customerInfoStream to update local reactive providers when the user's entitlements change.

- Entitlement-Based Feature Gating:

- The ad_free entitlement is checked dynamically before triggering interstitial ad sequences across battle stages.

- Restoring purchases (Purchases.restorePurchases()) queries active entitlements and updates UI state with immediate visual comic banners.

- Transaction Resilience & Purchase Ledger:

- Every purchase completion updates our PurchaseLedgerService, persisting transaction metadata, status, and product IDs with tamper-evident HMAC signing.

- Judge & Reviewer Accessibility:

- Built with an intelligent development mode fallback: if live RevenueCat credentials are not injected at compile time, the store gracefully displays localized fallback pricing tiers, preventing startup crashes and allowing seamless review of the full UI/UX flow.

**2.5 Challenges We Ran Into**

- Balancing Game Loop Tick Rates with UI Rendering: Flame's render loops needed tight synchronization with Flutter's widget tree, especially during dramatic battle cut-ins, slow-motion parry effects, and full-screen comic dialogs.

- Sandboxed In-App Purchase Testing: Ensuring deterministic, non-blocking store behavior across both online sandbox environments and local offline demo scenarios required building clean abstractions and defensive error boundaries around payment flows.

- Preventing Memory Overhead: High-resolution comic sprites and 3D GLB model assets required proactive cache management via an AppMemoryManager to maintain smooth 60 FPS performance on resource-constrained mobile devices.

**2.6 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of**

- Designing a complete, original combat and parrying feel that rewards player reflex and practice.

- Delivering a consistent, high-energy graphic novel comic aesthetic across every single screen, dialog, and battle HUD.

- Achieving an automated test suite containing 49+ unit and widget tests covering damage formulas, daily task milestones, economy bounds, and RevenueCat purchase mocks.

- Building a 100% open-source, launchable codebase with zero external credential requirements for judges.

**2.7 What We Learned**

- How to structure clean, maintainable monetization pipelines in mobile games using RevenueCat.

- The power of decoupled architecture: separating game simulation logic (Flame) from reactive UI states (Riverpod) and billing services (RevenueCat).

- The importance of offline-first resilience in mobile apps so users retain full access to their locally unlocked content regardless of network connectivity.

**2.8 What's Next for ColoSynth**

- Additional weapon classes with unique parry timings and combo trees.

- Live multiplayer asynchronous ghost duels.

- Expanded subscription tiers via RevenueCat (such as a seasonal "Syndicate Battle Pass").

- Full publishing to Google Play Store and Apple App Store.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Research experience is close to required for med school and PhD applications, and a big edge for internships. But the only way in is cold-emailing professors, and most emails go unanswered because they're generic. Families pay research-mentorship programs $2,900 to $8,900 just to get a foot in the door. We're students who went through this, and we wanted to build the tool we wished we'd had.

**What it does**

- Lab Radar: pick your university and interests. Labmate reads three years of papers from your school (OpenAlex) and ranks every active researcher by fit, weighted toward the people who run labs.

- Money just landed: Labmate cross-checks NIH RePORTER and NSF awards. A lab that got a new grant weeks ago probably needs hands now, and almost no student knows to look for this.

- Their email, one tap: Labmate finds the professor's address in the author details of their own published papers (Europe PMC) and shows which paper lists it. Real public data, never guessed.

- Paper brief: any recent paper explained in plain English, with key terms and smart questions to ask.

- Understanding gate: before Labmate writes anything, you pass a 3-question quiz on the paper and write your own takeaway. The email is built around your words, addressed to the professor, and it never invents experience you don't have.

- Your inbox, not ours: open the draft in your own Gmail, Outlook or Mail app. Labmate never sends anything for you.

- Outreach tracker: follow-up reminders at day 7 and a cap of 5 emails a week, so professors get fewer, better emails.

**How we built it**

- Expo (SDK 57) + Expo Router + TypeScript, for iOS, Android and the web.

- Designed to Apple's Human Interface Guidelines for iOS 26: Liquid Glass (expo-glass-effect) on the controls only, SF Symbols, SF Pro and SF Pro Rounded, system colors with dark mode, native large-title headers and haptics.

- Data: OpenAlex (researchers and papers), NIH RePORTER and NSF Awards (grants), Europe PMC (professor emails). The ranking is a pure, unit-tested function.

- AI: structured outputs (zod schemas → JSON Schema) for briefs, quizzes and drafts, served from Vercel functions. It runs on Qwen through OpenRouter for about $0.0006 per brief (Claude is supported as a drop-in). Slow or broken answers are retried on another provider, and a brief is prefetched when the lab page opens so it's usually ready by the tap. Keys stay server-side; OpenAlex and NIH are proxied with caching, a parameter allowlist and a per-IP rate limit.

- RevenueCat: entitlement pro, an offering with a 3-month Research Season Pass ($27.99) and a monthly plan ($9.99), a plan picker, restore purchases, and the customer-info listener so Pro unlocks instantly. Free tier: 3 briefs. The same RevenueCat setup runs in the web build.

- Tooling: ESLint, Vitest (app + server tests), GitHub Actions CI on every PR, EAS build profiles.

**How it uses RevenueCat**

- Seasonal pricing that matches how students actually search for labs: a Research Season Pass instead of a forever subscription.

- A natural upsell: the fresh-grant details and unlimited briefs are gated behind pro, and free users can see that a lab just got funded.

- Parent checkout: "Ask a Parent to Pay" shares a RevenueCat Web Purchase Link (RevenueCat Billing + Stripe) tied to the student's app user ID, so a parent can pay on the web and the student's Pro unlocks live.

**Challenges we ran into**

- OpenAlex started requiring API keys in 2026, so we moved every call behind a caching proxy.

- Matching the same person across OpenAlex, NIH, NSF and Europe PMC, which all format names and institutions differently.

- Making an AI email tool that professors won't hate. The quiz gate and the weekly cap are product decisions, not just features.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Works for any university on day one, with no partnerships and no scraping, using only open data.

- The "money just landed" signal: public grant data turned into an unfair advantage for students.

**What we learned**

Monetization design is product design: who pays (parents), when (application season) and what feels fair (a season pass).

**What's next for Labmate**

- Mock lab interviews generated from the lab's own papers.

- A high-school edition: summer research programs and mentor matching.

- Publishing to the App Store and Google Play before the spring research season.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

You open a drawer and find the project you loved three weeks ago. You have ten free minutes. But where did you stop? What comes next? Where did you put the materials?

Maker communities describe leaving notes with stored projects so they can reconstruct their plans later. That small act became Unpause: a note to your future self, designed around the moment you return.

**What it does**

Unpause saves a handoff for an unfinished physical hobby: a photo, where you stopped, one tiny next action, and where the materials live.

When time opens up, choose your available time and energy. Find a project with a step that fits, open its resume card, and make a little. Leave a fresh checkpoint when you stop. Your photos, notes, and past sessions build a history of small returns.

Three unfinished projects are free. Finishing one opens a slot for another idea. Studio is the planned lifetime upgrade for unlimited unfinished projects within device storage limits. Reminders, finished projects, and portable backups stay free.

**How we built it**

Shivam Gupta created Unpause with AI-assisted research, implementation, and testing. React Native, Expo, and TypeScript share the core experience across Android, iOS, and web.

The app works locally without signup. Firebase supplies optional account identity. Supabase hosts coordinated Firebase/RevenueCat account deletion. Signing in does not upload or synchronize project notes and photos.

RevenueCat handles lifetime Studio entitlements, restoration, and account identity across Galaxy, iOS, Google Play, and Test Store. Native storage uses bounded chunks and an atomic manifest. Validated backups preserve photos as well as text.

Warm paper colors, Fraunces headings, and original craft illustrations make the shelf inviting.

**Challenges we ran into**

A hobby journal can become a large archive. We reproduced an Android storage risk above two megabytes, then tested a 300-checkpoint archive through import and restart, including its latest note and photo.

We also protected unsaved drafts, prevented account changes from applying stale purchase results, and handled failed writes and cancelled imports. Accessibility testing exposed contrast, navigation-role, and narrow-screen layout issues that led to fixes and regression checks.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The complete pause, return, make, and checkpoint loop works in a live web app and an installable Android preview. 154 unit tests and 30 browser scenarios pass. Hosted Firebase account flows and coordinated deletion passed live tests. The native RevenueCat Test Store also passed cancellation, simulated failure, success, restore, and cold restart. These simulated transactions do not establish production billing or revenue.

The commercial model fits occasional hobby use: a useful free tier and one understandable lifetime upgrade. US $19.99 is the proposed price to validate with actual buyers.

**What we learned**

The next physical action can be more useful than a long plan. A materials note can matter as much as a photo. Preserving that context reliably is part of the product experience.

Notes, Krafio, Purlsy, and Tapcord are credible alternatives. Unpause's bet is a calmer, faster return ritual organized around the time and energy available. That differentiation still needs testing with people's own projects.

**What's next for Unpause**

Resolve Samsung corporate commercial seller approval, then complete physical-device store purchases, signing, and a qualifying public release. iOS source and build configuration are prepared; a compiled iOS binary remains to be produced.

Then invite makers to capture a handoff and return on another day. Observe whether they can start, whether they leave a second checkpoint, and whether Studio earns a purchase. Let that evidence guide better capture and craft-specific prompts.

The immediate aim is concrete: help someone reopen the drawer and keep making.

Try Unpause: Web app · Android preview and submission kit · Source code · Demo video · PDF brief · Pitch deck.

The Android download is a development preview. A public Galaxy Store listing is pending Samsung corporate commercial seller approval.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I built Improkinz because studying often means jumping between many different tools. One app is used for notes, another for flashcards, another for quizzes, another for productivity, and opportunities and student communities are somewhere else entirely.

I wanted to create one place where students could learn, stay organized, connect with other students, and discover opportunities.

That idea became Improkinz — an all-in-one student platform designed to make the learning experience more connected and useful.

**What It Does**

Improkinz combines AI-powered study tools with productivity, community, and opportunity features.

Students can use AI to create flashcards, summarize material, generate quizzes, organize notes, and interact with a study chatbot. They can also use tools such as a Pomodoro timer, calculator, to-do list, and study board.

Beyond studying, Improkinz includes a student community feed, profiles, study groups, educational videos, and an opportunities section where students can discover things such as competitions, programs, and other learning opportunities.

The goal is not just to help students study for one exam, but to create a platform that supports different parts of their student journey.

**How I Built It**

I built Improkinz using React Native and Expo, with TypeScript/JavaScript across the application. I used Firebase/Firestore for backend data and authentication-related services, Clerk for user authentication, and RevenueCat for the subscription/paywall system.

The AI features are connected through an API layer, allowing the app to provide tools such as summarization, quiz generation, and flashcard generation.

I also built the application as a multi-screen mobile experience with features including onboarding, profiles, community posts, opportunities, study tools, and a subscription experience.

**What I Learned**

Building Improkinz taught me that creating an app is much more than writing individual features.

I learned how different systems have to work together — authentication, databases, APIs, mobile UI, AI services, subscriptions, environment variables, and deployment all have to communicate correctly.

I also learned a lot about debugging. A feature can appear completely broken on the screen while the real problem is somewhere else in the backend, authentication flow, API configuration, or database.

Most importantly, I learned how to take an idea and keep improving it through real problems instead of stopping when something doesn't work.

**Challenges**

One of the biggest challenges was integrating multiple services while keeping the application reliable.

Authentication and Firebase integration required careful handling of user identities and profile data. I also had to debug issues where information appeared correctly in one environment but not another.

Another challenge was building the community and opportunity systems. Features such as profiles, posts, reactions, opportunities, and user-specific data require many pieces of backend logic to work together.

The AI features also presented a challenge because AI-generated results need to be useful to students rather than simply producing text.

Finally, building and testing the project as a young solo developer meant that I had to learn many technologies while simultaneously solving problems in the application.

**Why I Built It**

Improkinz started as an idea for making studying easier, but it grew into something bigger: a platform where students can study, organize, connect, and discover without constantly switching between different tools.

I built it to solve a problem I could actually see in the student experience, and building it has taught me how to turn that problem into a working product.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Break the Loop.**

**Inspiration**

The internet is full of self-improvement advice.

There are thousands of videos, articles, posts, and AI-generated suggestions telling us how to become more confident, disciplined, social, productive, or adventurous. But having more information doesn't necessarily lead to taking action.

We wanted to solve a simpler problem:

What if, instead of giving people more advice, we gave them one thing to actually do?

That idea became Go Beyond.

**What We Built**

Go Beyond is a personalized self-improvement app that helps people step outside their comfort zone through small, actionable challenges.

Instead of giving users a long list of recommendations, Go Beyond learns their starting point through a short baseline assessment and gives them one clear next move.

For example:

"Start a 2-minute conversation with someone you don't normally talk to."

After completing a challenge, the app tracks the action, rewards progress, and adapts future challenges based on the user's behavior.

The core loop is:

Baseline → Challenge → Action → Completion → Reward → Progress → Next Challenge

The goal isn't to tell someone how to change their life.

It's to help them make one meaningful change today.

**Personalization**

We built a RAG-powered personalization layer behind the challenge system.

Instead of using AI as a chatbot that generates endless suggestions, the system retrieves relevant challenges based on the user's behavioral profile, previous challenges, completion history, and current progression.

The system then selects a challenge appropriate for the user's current level while avoiding excessive repetition or jumps in difficulty.

This allows the experience to become more personalized as the user actually takes action.

**Privacy**

We also wanted personalization without unnecessarily exposing identity.

The personalization layer works primarily with a minimized behavioral representation rather than directly exposing information such as the user's email or identity.

Identity tells us who you are. Behavior tells us what you need next.

**Monetization**

Go Beyond uses RevenueCat to power its Pro subscription.

Users can experience their first five challenges for free before reaching the Pro experience.

Pro unlocks:

- Unlimited personalized challenges

- Adaptive difficulty

- Advanced personalization

- Push Me

- Advanced progress insights

- Long-term growth tracking

RevenueCat handles subscription and entitlement state so premium access isn't hardcoded into the application.

**How We Built It**

Go Beyond is built as a mobile-first application using:

- React Native

- TypeScript

- Expo

- Supabase

- RAG / AI personalization

- RevenueCat

We focused heavily on making progress visible through the UI. Completing a challenge should feel like an achievement rather than simply checking an item off a list.

**Challenges**

One of the hardest parts wasn't generating challenges — it was deciding which challenge should come next.

A challenge that is too easy becomes meaningless. A challenge that is too difficult can discourage the user.

We therefore had to think about progression, difficulty, repetition, previous behavior, and personalization together.

Another challenge was integrating monetization without making the product feel like it was blocking the user before they understood its value.

**What We Learned**

We learned that personalization doesn't necessarily require knowing everything about a user.

A small amount of meaningful behavioral information can be enough to make the next action feel relevant.

We also learned that progress itself can be part of the product. When users can see their actions accumulating into something larger, completing the next challenge becomes more meaningful.

**What's Next**

We want Go Beyond to become increasingly adaptive as users build a history of real-world actions.

The long-term vision is simple:

Less scrolling. Less overthinking. Less noise. More doing.

You don't need more advice.

You need your next move.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I love software, even though my field of study doesn't directly involve building it. That love grew at university, as I began to understand how software really works.

A friend introduced me to Devpost in 2025, and that's when I first saw the RevenueCat Shipaton. I had an idea I wanted to enter, so I registered. But I didn't yet have the skills to build an app, and the Shipaton clashed with my end-of-semester exams, so the idea never got built.

Later I realised that vibe coding had closed that skill gap, and that many winners were building this way. So I came back in 2026 with high spirits, determined to finally ship my idea.

**What it does**

Kandoo is a context-aware memory and action assistant that you talk to the way you'd talk to a friend. No forms, no picking dates from a calendar. You just say it:

"Just left lunch with Kofi. His daughter Adwoa starts at Achimota next week. He finally agreed to the 2.5 percent merchant fee, but only if we waive it for the first three months. Remind me to send him the contract before Friday, and to get Adwoa a small gift this weekend."

From that one breath, Kandoo pulls out everything inside it:

- The facts worth remembering, written as clean standalone statements, with "he" and "his" resolved to Kofi.

- The reminders, with "before Friday" and "this weekend" turned into real dates and times.

- The people involved, each with their own page.

- A tidy written note of the whole conversation.

You stay in control. Nothing is saved or scheduled until you've looked it over, so Kandoo never quietly commits a wrong guess to your day.

Reminders that get your attention. A reminder fires as a local notification on your phone, even with no internet. If the screen is off, Kandoo wakes the phone with a full-screen alert where you can snooze it, mark it done or dismiss it. Reminders can repeat on the days you choose.

Reminders that wait for a place. Draw any place on the map, such as home, campus or church, and say "Remind me to give Jane her notebook when I get to campus." The reminder fires the moment you arrive. Kandoo never tracks you. It only watches the few places you've drawn, and your location never leaves the phone.

Ask it anything later. For example: "What did we agree on pricing with Kofi?" Kandoo searches what you've told it by meaning, not just by exact words. You never said "pricing", but it still finds the fee deal and answers in plain language.

Show it the world. Photograph a flyer, a business card or a whiteboard, and Kandoo pulls out the event, the date and the people. Photograph a page of handwritten notes, and it becomes an organised note filed in your Library, which you can open in Microsoft Word.

Mr. Kandoo. A voice assistant you hold a real conversation with. He creates reminders and notes, researches topics with real references, reads pages through the camera, and runs your team. Every change he makes appears as a card, and nothing is saved until you say yes.

Teams. Create a team, invite people with a link, and share notes, research, PDFs and photos, with each file showing who sent it. A team leader can send tasks, and each member accepts them into their own reminders.

Insights. Charts of how you've used Kandoo this week or month: your busiest day, how you capture, your reminders done and overdue, and the people and places that came up most.

Four plans, handled through RevenueCat:

- Free: capture, reminders, your Library, and answers from the last ten days.

- Personal ($3.99/month): your whole history, Places, kept photos, Insights and Kandoo's own voice.

- Pro ($9.99/month): work tools, turning pages into notes, and being part of a team.

- Elite ($19.99/month): Mr. Kandoo, research with references, and leading a team.

The paywall appears at the moment a feature is worth something to you, such as when a question reaches an older memory, and it opens on the cheapest plan that unlocks it.

**How I built it**

The way I started building Kandoo was quite interesting. I had a history of trying to vibe code things that never became real. So I went to ChatGPT's Projects mode, which I had never used before. I explained the problems I'd had building apps this way and asked it to break app building down into steps I could understand. We went through lessons until I was ready. Then we started on the app itself and built much of the backend, until the project began to show real potential.

When I started hitting ChatGPT's usage limits, I switched to Claude Code to take what I had started and finish it.

The stack:

- App: React Native with Expo and TypeScript, Android first.

- Backend: Node and Express, hosted on Render.

- Database and sign-in: Supabase, a Postgres database with pgvector for searching by meaning.

- AI: Google Gemini, which interprets what you say, reads photos and documents, and powers search by meaning.

- Mr. Kandoo: an ElevenLabs voice agent whose tools run on the phone.

- Subscriptions: RevenueCat, with every plan checked on the server.

A few decisions I'm glad I made:

- The AI understands; it never acts. Gemini only turns speech into structured data. That data is checked against a strict schema, and ordinary code decides what gets saved. Kandoo is not "an AI with access to your database."

- One sentence, many actions. My first version could only pull one thing out of a sentence. I rebuilt it so a single capture can produce any number of memories and reminders, because real life comes in messy recaps, not neat commands.

- Your phone owns time and place. Reminders are scheduled on the device, not on a server, so they fire even when the internet is off. Location is never streamed anywhere.

- Search that understands meaning. Recall combines search by meaning (vector embeddings) with ordinary keyword search, so a question worded differently from the memory still finds it.

- Built to stay up. If the main AI model is overloaded, Kandoo automatically falls back to a backup model. Notes and memories save on the phone first and sync once the connection is back.

**Challenges I ran into**

As someone who hadn't vibe coded a fully working app before, I ran into the usual challenges:

- fixing broken code;

- finding my way around the different services I had to connect.

I also hit usage limits more than once: first on ChatGPT, before the project reached the stage I wanted, and then on my Claude Pro weekly limit when I was close to finishing. I had to pay for another account to keep going.

There were technical walls too:

- The full-screen alert. Getting a reminder to wake a locked phone meant going below what Expo supports out of the box and patching the notification library myself.

- Free-tier AI limits. At one point Gemini's servers were overloaded, and my own retries were using up the daily quota. I redesigned how Kandoo handles failures, so the app stays useful when the AI is busy instead of breaking.

- Teaching an AI to count days. Mr. Kandoo kept turning "Friday" into Saturday, even when he had the right date in front of him. I stopped trusting him with dates: the phone now checks that the date he picks really falls on the day you said.

Around the middle of the project I got really discouraged. I was facing serious hurdles adding new screens and features, and I thought I wouldn't finish in time. I decided to keep going anyway, even if I finished late. A few days later, I realised I was going to make it.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

I'm proud that Kandoo grew from my first MVP into a full product that works end to end:

- One spoken sentence becomes several memories and reminders, with real times.

- A reminder can wake a locked phone, or wait until you arrive somewhere.

- You can ask a question in your own words and get the right memory back.

- Mr. Kandoo holds a real conversation and acts across the whole app, and never acts without your yes.

- A team can share files and hand out tasks from their phones.

- The whole project is open source.

**What I learned**

The most important things I learned on this journey are resilience and consistency. I had to show up every single day. At the start, I couldn't picture what I was building and didn't really understand what I was doing. But as I worked through errors and kept building, it began to make sense, until I finally saw the app come to life.

On the technical side, I learned that trust is the real product. An AI assistant is only useful if it never acts behind your back, which is why everything in Kandoo waits for your review. I also learned that an error you hide becomes a bug you can never find.

**What's next for Kandoo**

- Google Play release, with local prices for Ghana and a smaller download.

- Kandoo Moments. When you arrive somewhere, Kandoo reminds you what happened there last time, and shows who is usually around you there.

- More languages, so people can talk to Kandoo the way they actually speak at home.

- iOS, once Android is solid.

See everything Kandoo can do: greatman-david.github.io/kandoo

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We’ve all experienced the same problem: a warranty document buried somewhere in our phone, a subscription renewal we forgot about, or a receipt we can’t find when we actually need it. Important purchase information is scattered across emails, PDFs, photos, and paper receipts. We wanted to turn that chaos into one simple, intelligent place.

**What it does**

Warranty Vault securely stores warranties, subscriptions, and purchase documents in one place. Users can manually enter details or capture documents, extract information using on-device OCR and AI, review the extracted data, and confirm before saving it. The app tracks expiration and renewal dates, sends timely reminders, and provides direct access to official claim or service pages.

**How we built it**

We built the mobile app with Flutter, backed by FastAPI and Supabase for authentication, database, and secure document storage. Google ML Kit performs on-device OCR, while Gemini helps interpret extracted information into structured warranty and subscription data. RevenueCat handles the Pro subscription layer, and local Android notifications handle reminders. Security is reinforced through Supabase Row Level Security, ensuring users can only access their own data.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest part was connecting everything into one reliable end-to-end workflow. OCR had to work on a real Android device, extracted information needed validation before reaching the database, and notifications had to work reliably even when the app was closed. We also had to handle authentication, storage permissions, user isolation, AI failures, and subscription states without compromising the core experience.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We’re proud that Warranty Vault became more than just a document-storage app. It can take an unstructured document, extract meaningful information, let the user verify it, securely store it, track important dates, and proactively remind the user when action is needed. We also validated the core workflows on a physical Android device, including OCR, secure storage, notifications, authentication, warranties, and subscriptions.

**What we learned**

We learned that building an AI application is not just about getting an LLM to produce an answer. Validation, user confirmation, security, error handling, and reliable system integration matter just as much. We also learned the importance of testing the complete journey—from the user's action through the frontend, backend, database, AI processing, and back to the user.

**What's next for Warranty Vault**

We want to make Warranty Vault evolve from a passive vault into a personal ownership assistant. Future versions could intelligently organize purchases, provide better warranty and subscription insights, improve document understanding, and help users navigate the appropriate support or claim process faster—while keeping the user in control of every important action.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

As a USC student and huge football fan, I wanted an easier way to learn more about the team I was watching every week. At games, I would often want to look up a player, an old season, or something about USC football history, but the internet at the Coliseum can be extremely spotty.

At the same time, I had been working through 100 Days of SwiftUI and wanted to challenge myself to turn what I learned into my first published iOS app. I decided to combine that with my interest in sports analytics and build USC Football Tracker.

**What it does**

USC Football Tracker puts more than 130 years of USC football information in one place. Users can explore historical seasons, game results, rosters, coaches, national championships, Heisman winners, and other program accolades.

The app also includes the current 2026 roster and schedule, with current-season game results automatically updating through an API. Much of the app's historical data is stored locally, so users can still explore USC football information when they have poor or no internet connection.

I also built a season predictor that gives win probabilities for USC's schedule and simulates the season using a machine learning model.

**How we built it**

I built the iOS app using Swift and SwiftUI.

For the data pipeline, I used Python to collect and process USC football data from CollegeFootballData.com. I transformed the historical information into JSON files, then used Swift's Codable and JSONDecoder to convert that data into models that could be displayed throughout the app.

For the season predictor, I used Python to create a CSV training dataset from historical USC games. The dataset included features such as home/away status, conference-game status, USC's AP ranking, and the opponent's AP ranking. I trained and evaluated the model using Create ML, then integrated the trained model into the app using Core ML.

For the current season, I also built a small backend using Vercel that communicates with the CollegeFootballData API. The Swift app uses URLSession to retrieve the latest 2026 game data while falling back to locally bundled data if the request fails.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of my biggest challenges was figuring out how to turn a large amount of football data into something that was actually useful inside an iOS app. I had to learn how to clean and restructure API data with Python, decode JSON in Swift, and design reusable SwiftUI components to display it.

I also ran into issues I didn't initially see while developing in Xcode. For example, some text became difficult to read when I tested the app on iPhones using Dark Mode. Testing on actual devices helped me identify and fix those problems by using preferred color scheme on light mode.

My other challenges were not regarding code but through the process of getting the app released to the app store. I kept getting errors within my reviews in the privacy policies or other small things. Eventually, my app was released and it was amazing!

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

My biggest accomplishment that I'm proud of was being able to ship a real app onto the app store and have others view and use my app. From the early stages of my developer career, not once did I think about how apps were made, until I really got into SwiftUI. Learning the language and framework itself was fun for me as it is very different from other coding languages. Being able to take what I learned into a real product and showcase my skills to others felt super rewarding.

**What we learned**

The main lesson I learned was the timeline of how a real app is made. Before this project, I had mostly worked on smaller projects where the goal was to learn one aspect of SwiftUI. USC Football Tracker showed me how to combine everything I was taught. I learned how an idea is able to shape into a real application. I also learned that an app is never really "finished." After using it myself and hearing from other USC students, I found new problems to solve and features to add, such as current 2026 team data. This project taught me how important iteration and user feedback are to the development process..

**What's next for USC Football Tracker**

I want USC Football Tracker to continue improving throughout the 2026 season. My next goal is to make the current-season experience even more useful on game day and continue improving how live information is presented. Whether this means better UI or more information, I want to continue working on this app. 

Longer term, I'd like to improve the season predictor with a larger training dataset and better metrics, leading to overall better predictions. My ultimate goal is for this app to be the best app for Trojans to learn more about the team and USC football history before, during, and after games.

</details>

src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/439/515/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

My teammate and I have been longtime users of Flighty whenever we travel. We love how it takes something that can be stressful and complicated and makes it feel simple.

At some point, while sitting on a train, we started wondering: why isn’t there something like Flighty, but built specifically for train travel?

We wanted an app that could genuinely feel like a travel companion — something you can trust enough to stop constantly checking departure boards, operator apps, connection times, and delay notifications. An app that lets you relax and enjoy the journey while it takes care of the details.

That idea became Blitz.

**What it does**

Blitz is an intelligent train tracker that brings together information from many different sources to make train travel as simple and enjoyable as possible.

It keeps you informed about delays, connections, missed trains, onboard amenities, train formations, and what your train actually looks like. It also gives you a beautiful travel log where you can look back at your journeys and see how far you’ve traveled over time.

What we wanted most was to make adding a journey feel effortless. Instead of manually searching for trains, you can simply press the share button inside your train operator’s app and add the trip directly to Blitz.

For the journey itself, we added Live Activities and Dynamic Island support so the information you need is always easy to glance at.

And because trains have a habit of passing through tunnels, mountains, and places where mobile service disappears completely, Blitz is designed with offline use in mind. We store country-wide railway data in a surprisingly small footprint, allowing the app to continue following your journey even without an internet connection.

The goal is simple: less time worrying about your trip, and more time enjoying it.

**How we built it**

With such a short timeframe, we decided to move quickly and use tools we already knew well.

The iOS app is built in Swift, while the backend uses Go with Fiber to keep responses as snappy as possible.

For the interface, we prototyped everything in Figma and constantly tested ideas with friends. They were kind enough to become our unofficial test group, telling us what felt intuitive, what was confusing, and what needed to change.

That feedback helped us iterate quickly and build something that felt much more natural to use.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge was the data.

Railway information is incredibly fragmented. We had to gather resources from many different places, build what we call "adapters" for different formats, compile GTFS files, search through obscure government websites, and occasionally create completely custom solutions for data sources that behaved in their own unique way.

It was a lot of detective work, but it was also one of the most interesting parts of building Blitz.

Another surprisingly time-consuming challenge was creating the train formation artwork ourselves. We wanted the trains inside the app to feel recognizable and visually polished, but producing that artwork by hand takes a huge amount of time.

In the future, we’d love to collaborate with 3D artists to create even more detailed and high-quality train models.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

One of our favorite surprises happened while we were posting about Blitz for the Build in Public award.

Our very first post unexpectedly took off. In less than three days, it reached almost 13,000 views and brought us more than 80 followers. Even more exciting were the messages we received from people in the railway and transportation industry offering to help us with APIs, data, and testing.

We also received comments and DMs from people saying they had been looking for exactly this kind of app.

Seeing that response meant a lot to us. Until then, Blitz had mostly been an idea that we personally wanted to exist. Suddenly, we could see that there was a whole community of people who wanted it too.

That was probably the strongest validation we could have asked for.

**What we learned**

We learned very quickly that building a great train-tracking app is about much more than showing a departure time on a screen.

Behind a single journey are dozens of data sources, edge cases, railway systems, operators, formats, and country-specific quirks. Making all of that complexity feel simple for the person using the app became one of the most important lessons of the project.

We also learned how valuable it is to build in public. Sharing Blitz early brought us feedback, encouragement, industry connections, and ideas that we probably never would have discovered on our own.

Most importantly, this hackathon reminded us how much fun it is to build something you genuinely want to use yourself.

**What's next for Blitz**

Because of the hackathon timeframe, we were only able to fully integrate Switzerland.

But Switzerland is just the beginning.

Our next goal is to expand into neighboring European countries and gradually cover the rest of the EU. From there, we’d love to bring Blitz to railway networks in the US, Asia, and eventually anywhere people travel by train.

There are also plenty of features we still want to explore, from richer train information and better formation artwork to even smarter journey assistance and crowd-sourced, organic and direct feedback in the app, while also making the arduous process of collecting and updating transit data more efficient.

Ultimately, we want Blitz to become the app you open whenever you travel by train — no matter where in the world you happen to be.

</details>
