<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Project Story — Paparcar**

**Inspiration**

Paparcar started with a very simple thought.

Back in 2019, I was sitting on a bench with a friend when I saw a driver slowly going around the streets looking for a parking spot.

I remember thinking:

“I saw an empty spot on the next street, but of course, the driver has no way of knowing it is there until they pass by.”

That was the moment Paparcar was born.

At the time, I knew almost nothing about programming. I did not have a technical background, I had never built a mobile application, and I had no idea how difficult the problem would become.

A few months later, after becoming unemployed and being tired of working on things I did not enjoy, I decided to give that idea a shape.

I was very naive at first. I thought it would be a matter of watching some YouTube videos, learning Java and Kotlin, and building an Android app.

It did not take long to realize how wrong I was.

The more I learned, the bigger the project became. I understood that I was trying to build the house starting from the roof, so I stepped back and decided to learn properly.

I followed Google's official Android courses, joined developer communities, learned from Android developers and creators, and met people who ended up becoming an important part of my journey.

Some of those people are still part of my life today. Over time, several developers and I built a small community where we collaborate on different projects, production applications and different areas of software development.

Paparcar became much more than an app idea.

It became one of the reasons why I decided to become a software developer.

There were also long pauses.

I did not have unlimited time or financial freedom. I had to work on jobs I did not enjoy just to pay for everyday life, and sometimes the project had to be put aside.

But I never completely stopped.

Even after work, I would come home and continue programming.

After around two years of learning and building, I realized that I could eventually try to make software development my profession while continuing to work on Paparcar on the side.

In 2024, I managed to create an early version of the application. It worked, but it was still very basic and far from what I imagined.

So I put it aside again.

Instead of forcing the project forward, I focused on becoming a better engineer.

In 2025, I completed advanced training in software architecture and started actively looking for professional opportunities. After several technical interviews, I finally got the opportunity I had been working towards: a professional Android development role where I could continue growing and proving what I had learned.

Then, in February 2026, I came back to Paparcar.

This time, I decided not to continue the old codebase.

I started again from zero, with a much clearer understanding of software architecture, maintainability, product design and, most importantly, the problem I actually wanted to solve.

And this time, I also had something that did not exist when the idea began in 2019: modern AI and LLM tools.

They became part of my development process, helping me research, debug, iterate and explore ideas faster. But the product decisions, engineering, architecture and especially the real-world testing still required a huge amount of hands-on work.

Today, Paparcar is finally becoming the product I imagined years ago.

**What it does**

Paparcar is designed to make driving and parking more effortless.

Its core feature is automatic parking detection.

Instead of asking the driver to manually remember where they parked, Paparcar combines signals and sensors available on the device to detect trips and identify when a vehicle has finished driving and has been parked.

When the driver leaves the vehicle, the parking spot can then become useful information for the community.

How to start: mark your car once. For automatic detection to work, Paparcar needs to know where your car is the first time. After adding your vehicle, tap "Mark parking", drag the map to where the car is and confirm with "Park here". From that moment on, Paparcar watches the car on its own: when you drive off it detects the departure and frees the spot, and when you park again it saves the new location with no taps (if it is not sure, it simply asks "Did you park?"). Linking the car's Bluetooth makes detection even more reliable.

The experience can be summarized as:

Drive → Park → Remember → Leave → Give the spot back to the community.

But the original parking problem has evolved into something much bigger.

Because Paparcar can understand driving and parking activity, it can transform that information into useful statistics, estimations and insights about the driver's own habits.

These include:

- Estimated fuel consumption and spending.

- Approximate CO₂ emissions.

- Kilometres travelled.

- Weekly, monthly and yearly driving and fuel estimations.

- Average trip duration.

- Time spent looking for parking.

- Usual parking locations.

- Most common days and peak hours.

- Automatically detected parking sessions.

- Parking spots given back to the community.

- Historical driving and parking information.

- Other personalized statistics and estimations derived from the user's own activity.

Paparcar also includes:

- Community-reported available parking spots.

- Public parking information, including free and paid parking where data is available.

- Fuel stations.

- Fuel prices in supported countries.

- Multiple vehicle management.

- Vehicle sharing, allowing other people to access the location of a shared vehicle.

- A map that combines parking-related information with useful driving resources.

The important part is that these features are connected.

Paparcar is not just a map, not just a parking reminder and not just a statistics dashboard.

The automatic detection system is the foundation that connects them.

The long-term vision is simple:

Every time someone parks and eventually leaves, that parking session can become useful information for the next driver.

**How we built it**

Paparcar has been rebuilt several times as my technical knowledge evolved.

The current version uses a modern Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) architecture, allowing the project to share core logic across platforms while keeping platform-specific integrations where they make sense.

The project is organized around clear domain, data and presentation responsibilities, with a strong focus on maintainability, separation of concerns and testability.

On Android, the automatic parking detection system combines multiple signals rather than depending on a single sensor.

Bluetooth, GPS/location data and Android Activity Recognition are used together to understand whether the user is driving, arriving, stopping or leaving the vehicle.

The application uses Kotlin coroutines, Flow, StateFlow and a unidirectional state approach for reactive state management.

Local persistence is handled through a multiplatform database, while Firebase is used for authentication and cloud data.

The system also has to work under real mobile constraints: background execution, battery consumption, delayed events, GPS inaccuracies, Bluetooth state changes and operating-system restrictions.

One of the main architectural decisions was to treat automatic detection as a core system rather than just a feature attached to a UI.

That meant building a pipeline capable of receiving imperfect signals, storing intermediate information, correlating events and deciding whether a real parking session had occurred.

AI and LLMs also became part of the process during the latest rebuild.

They helped accelerate research, debugging, code exploration and iteration, but they were not a replacement for engineering judgment or real-world testing.

The application had to be tested with physical devices and actual journeys because a large part of its most important behaviour simply cannot be validated from a desk.

**Monetization with RevenueCat**

Paparcar's philosophy is product first: the core experience (automatic parking detection, remembering where you parked and giving the spot back to the community) stays free. There is no hard paywall and no hidden buttons.

On top of that we introduced Paparcar Plus, an optional subscription built with RevenueCat on top of Google Play Billing:

- Monthly: €1.99 / month

- Yearly: €13.99 / year (roughly 7 months' price, ~41% off)

- 7-day free trial for new subscribers on both plans

Free keeps the last 7 days of history, one car and two zones, and looking (spots, car parks, fuel prices) is always free. Plus unlocks your full history and statistics, routes saved in your account, alerts for spots in your zones and for fuel prices, a monthly recap, unlimited zones, all your cars (also in the widget) and a shared car for up to five drivers.

How it is wired:

- A single RevenueCat entitlement (plus) represents the capability, decoupled from the store SKUs so the same entitlement can be shared with the iOS app later.

- A default offering with monthly and annual packages mapped to the Google Play base plans.

- A subscription repository wraps the RevenueCat SDK and exposes the entitlement state as a reactive Flow, injected with Koin and consumed by the ViewModels exactly like any other app state (location, detection, etc.).

- RevenueCat is the single source of truth for subscription status: we do not duplicate expiration dates in Firestore or any custom backend. Google Play real-time developer notifications are connected so status changes propagate automatically.

- The paywall is contextual: it appears when the user tries a Plus action (for example, looking further back in their history), and there is a visible but unobtrusive Plus section in Settings.

The full purchase flow (trial → entitlement active → Plus features unlocked in the app) has been validated end to end.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge became the heart of Paparcar:

**How do you know that someone has actually parked without asking them?**

Detecting that a person is travelling is one thing.

Reliably detecting the exact moment when a vehicle has stopped being a journey and has become a parking session is much harder.

Real-world conditions are messy.

A user can:

- Stop at a traffic light.

- Get stuck in traffic.

- Wait outside a shop.

- Lose GPS accuracy.

- Disconnect from Bluetooth.

- Walk away from the vehicle temporarily.

- Receive Activity Recognition events late.

- Experience sensor or location data that does not match the expected sequence.

A false positive can be annoying.

A false negative can completely break the main experience.

Approximately 70% of the development effort of Paparcar has gone into the automatic parking detection system.

And debugging it has been one of the strangest engineering challenges I have faced.

Many of the problems could only be reproduced while actually driving.

You cannot simply place a breakpoint on a road and wait for the next bug to happen.

We had to repeatedly perform real journeys, inspect timestamps and sensor events, analyze edge cases, change thresholds and combine different signals until the system became more robust.

There was also another unusual challenge: the feedback loop is slow.

A UI bug can often be fixed in seconds.

A parking-detection bug might require:

Change code → build → install → drive → park → leave → wait → inspect logs → understand what happened → repeat.

And sometimes the bug only appears under a very specific combination of location accuracy, Bluetooth behaviour, movement patterns and event timing.

Battery usage and Android background-execution restrictions added another layer of complexity.

The system is still something we continuously improve, but reaching a point where Paparcar can automatically detect parking sessions in real-world conditions has been one of the biggest milestones of the project.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The biggest accomplishment is not a framework, an API or a particular architectural decision.

It is that an idea that started in 2019, when I did not know how to program, has finally become a real product.

There were years of learning, pauses, financial limitations and moments when I genuinely thought I might never finish it.

In 2024, I managed to create an early version, but it was still too basic.

In 2025, I focused on improving my engineering skills, especially software architecture, and eventually made the transition into professional software development.

Then, in February 2026, I returned to Paparcar and decided to rebuild it from zero.

This time, I had the knowledge to understand what I was building instead of simply trying to make the idea work.

I could think about architecture, maintainability, testing, scalability and product design from the beginning.

And that changed everything.

Today, Paparcar includes:

- Automatic parking detection.

- Community parking.

- Public parking information.

- Vehicle management and sharing.

- Fuel stations, with fuel prices in supported countries.

- Historical data.

- Driving and parking statistics.

- Advanced estimations and personalized insights.

- A multiplatform architecture.

Most of it has been built by me, with support from one teammate and the developer community that has accompanied me throughout the journey.

But there is another accomplishment that matters even more to me.

Paparcar has been with me for years.

It survived periods when I had almost no time, periods when I had financial difficulties, periods when I had to work on things unrelated to software, and periods when I had to stop development completely.

I kept coming back to it.

So today, seeing a real application running and knowing that the automatic parking system actually works in the real world is deeply personal.

I did not start Paparcar as a developer.

I became a developer partly because I wanted to build Paparcar.

For years, I thought that perhaps I would never build the thing I had imagined on that bench in 2019.

Now I have.

And that is probably the accomplishment I am most proud of.

**What we learned**

The first lesson was that software projects rarely develop in the order you imagine when you start them.

I began with a simple product idea, but turning it into reality required learning Android development, Kotlin, architecture, databases, networking, testing, background processing, location, sensors, cloud services, product design and eventually multiplatform development.

I also learned that complex problems are solved through iteration.

The automatic parking system did not magically work after the first implementation.

It required hundreds of small decisions, failed experiments, real-world tests and constant adjustments.

We learned that combining multiple signals can provide a much richer understanding of context than relying on a single sensor.

We also learned that real-world software behaves differently from software that only works in controlled environments.

A system can look perfect in logs and still behave incorrectly when a real person drives through a city, loses GPS for a few seconds, disconnects Bluetooth, stops in traffic and parks several minutes later.

Another important lesson was that architecture matters most when a project becomes complex.

Paparcar has evolved far beyond its original scope, and the ability to change parts of the system without rewriting everything became essential.

And perhaps the most important lesson was that technology itself is not the goal.

It is easy to become excited about sensors, maps, AI, Kotlin Multiplatform or architecture.

But at the end of the day, the question that matters is much simpler:

Does Paparcar make parking easier for the person using it?

That question has guided the project much more than any particular technology.

**What's next for Paparcar: Where can I park?**

The original question behind Paparcar was:

“Where did you park?”

And the answer became:

“Paparcar remembers.”

But that is only the first half of the vision.

The next question is:

“Where can I park?”

And that is where Paparcar is heading next.

The goal is to evolve from an application that remembers your parking spot into a system that can help drivers understand where parking may be available around them.

When a Paparcar user leaves a parking spot, that information can be released back into the community.

One user's departure can become another driver's opportunity.

This creates a network effect:

Someone parks → Paparcar remembers → They leave → The spot becomes information → Another driver can discover it.

But this also introduces our biggest challenge going forward:

**We need people to use Paparcar.**

Community-driven parking data only becomes really valuable when enough drivers participate.

We are at the very beginning of that journey.

Our next steps are to:

- Improve automatic parking detection using more real-world data.

- Expand parking information and coverage.

- Continue developing the multiplatform experience.

- Improve vehicle statistics, estimations and insights.

- Expand fuel information where reliable data is available.

- Grow the community of drivers contributing parking information.

- Turn individual parking sessions into a useful collective network.

The final goal is not to build another map.

It is to build a system where every driver can benefit from what other drivers have already experienced.

The original idea came from watching one person drive around looking for a parking space.

Seven years later, the idea is still the same — but now there is a real product trying to solve it.

Where did you park? Paparcar remembers.

Where can I park? Paparcar knows.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Inspiration

Cherry Money grew out of our experience running small businesses and community organisations. We wanted to spend our time building services and supporting people—not chasing invoices, checking bank statements and reconstructing what a payment was for months after it happened.

The problem was not simply missing software. It was the work between the tools: a receipt on a phone, an invoice in another system, a transaction in a bank account, and someone having to connect them all.

That led us to a simple idea: bring the paperwork, the financial context and the next decision into one mobile workspace.

Cherry Money Mobile is our answer: an AI finance copilot that helps owners capture information, understand what needs attention and review suggested actions without giving up control.

Our guiding principle is “AI suggests, you approve.”

What it does

Cherry Money Mobile brings everyday finance tasks into a phone-friendly workflow:

Capture → understand → match → review → approve.

Users can photograph or upload a receipt image, receive extracted information, correct the fields and confirm an expense with its receipt attached. Instead of treating extraction as unquestionable, the review step keeps the user responsible for checking the result.

The app also includes invoice, quotation and expense creation, together with access to customer, product and payment records. Ask Cherry lets users ask questions about their business information and enter guided workflows. Actions that create records use structured fields and confirmation screens rather than relying on an unrestricted chat instruction.

For reconciliation, users can view bank activity available through their connected company account, request a match suggestion, review the supporting information and approve a prepared proposal. Recording a reconciliation is separate from transferring money: this workflow does not autonomously move funds.

A clearly labelled demo workspace lets people explore the experience without connecting their bank or uploading private business records. Its sample receipts, transactions and exception scenarios are synthetic.

RevenueCat provides the prototype Free-to-Pro journey, including product loading, purchase, restore and entitlement refresh. The current Test Store build demonstrates expanded demo allowances and a premium insight screen; commercial store billing and broader live premium functionality remain release milestones.

How we built it

We built the mobile application in Flutter and Dart, using Riverpod for state management, GoRouter for navigation, Dio for API communication and secure native storage for authentication tokens. RevenueCat’s Flutter SDK handles the subscription integration.

We did not start with an entirely new business platform. Cherry Money already had a web application, backend services and an earlier Ionic/Angular mobile implementation. Those provided the foundation and feature references. This project’s contribution is the separate Flutter experience, the focused review-and-approval workflow, mobile API additions and RevenueCat integration. The existing PHP/Laravel backend remains part of the architecture.

Receipt images pass through authenticated mobile endpoints to server-side extraction, which returns editable structured information. Ask Cherry and the finance workflows reuse backend services and company permissions. Sensitive provider credentials remain on the server rather than inside the app.

We also kept the distinction between native and web functionality visible. Core mobile workflows have dedicated screens; advanced features that still belong to the existing website open there rather than being presented as completed native features.

Development included automated tests, static analysis, Android builds and browser-based interaction checks. We used the browser preview to iterate on layout and navigation, while treating native permissions, device behaviour and store purchases as separate verification tasks.

Challenges we ran into

Making assistance useful without making it overconfident.
A plausible match is not necessarily a correct match. We designed the experience around editable information, visible evidence and explicit approval. The goal was to help someone make a decision—not conceal uncertainty behind a confident-looking result.

Turning an existing product into a focused mobile experience.
Bringing a broad finance platform onto a small screen required choices. We prioritised capture, everyday record creation and reconciliation, while retaining clearly identified web routes for advanced work. Authentication, API permissions and navigation also needed attention; a mobile rebuild is more than a visual redesign.

Treating subscriptions as more than a paywall.
Loading an offering is only one part of the journey. We had to handle purchase results, restoration and entitlement refresh without pretending a purchase succeeded. The prototype also exposed work still needed for commercial release: linking subscriptions to authenticated accounts and replacing device-local usage limits with server-side enforcement.

Keeping the demonstration honest.
Demo data made it possible to show the workflow without exposing private financial information, but it needed a clear boundary. Sample extraction is labelled as sample extraction, and fixture-based tests are not presented as proof of live customer transactions.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are proud of bringing the central experience together in a Flutter application: capture a document, inspect information, review a proposed match and make an explicit decision. It gives the project a coherent workflow rather than a collection of disconnected finance screens.

Our recorded validation milestones include 48 passing Flutter tests, successful Android builds and an Android-emulator RevenueCat Test Store purchase that activated Pro access. Restoring purchases retained the active entitlement. These are development milestones—not production sales or Apple/Google store-billing verification.

We also made room for interface details that matter: readable financial amounts, clear loading and approval feedback, larger-text layouts and reduced-motion behaviour. Browser checks covered narrow screens and enlarged text rather than only a polished default screenshot.

Most importantly, the project preserves a deliberate boundary: help the user do the work, but keep consequential decisions with the user.

What we learned

We learned that a useful finance copilot needs more than an AI response. It needs context, clear permissions, understandable evidence and a reliable way for the user to confirm or correct the next action.

We also learned to distinguish different kinds of progress. A passing test, a working browser demonstration, an emulator purchase and a verified real-account workflow each answer different questions. None should automatically stand in for the others.

Building the mobile experience reinforced the value of focus. The most useful screen is not necessarily the one with the most information; it is the one that makes the next task understandable.

Finally, monetisation sharpened the product question: what useful, repeatable value are people upgrading for? Our aim is to make Pro valuable through everyday financial work, not simply through a more prominent upgrade button.

What's next for Cherry Money Mobile - AI Finance Copilot

Our immediate priority is release readiness: completing real-account end-to-end checks, native camera and permission testing, Apple/Google store configuration, signed sandbox purchase testing and the remaining privacy, account-management and subscription controls. Current live-workflow verification includes automated and fixture-based checks; real-account validation remains an important milestone.

We then plan to strengthen account-linked Pro access, server-verified entitlements and cross-device usage controls, while extending premium value into the live finance workflows.

After that, we want to pilot the app with small businesses and community organisations, using their feedback to improve receipt handling, reconciliation review and the tasks that still require a switch to the website.

We plan to measure practical outcomes: time taken to complete a task, how often suggestions need correction, whether users understand the evidence, and whether the app becomes part of their regular routine.

Our ambition is simple: less financial administration, clearer decisions and more time for the work that made someone start their organisation in the first place.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

StudyOS was born from a problem I saw around me every day.

Many of my classmates and batchmates struggled to find reliable resources for school and board exams. Past papers were scattered across different websites, textbooks and study materials were difficult to locate, and useful resources were sometimes hidden behind paywalls, country restrictions, or complicated websites.

Students were spending valuable time searching for resources instead of actually studying.

I wanted to create something where a student could simply open one app, find what they needed, and start learning. That idea became StudyOS: a connected study workspace designed to bring together the tools and resources students need to understand, practice, prepare, and progress.

My goal was not just to make another AI chatbot. I wanted to build a complete study workflow around the student.

**What it does**

StudyOS brings multiple parts of the student learning process into one platform.

Students can use StudyLens to understand difficult questions through structured explanations, guided reasoning, and hints. Homework Coach provides step-by-step guidance, while Note → Quiz turns notes into interactive practice.

LectureMind helps transform lecture material into useful study resources such as summaries, key concepts, flashcards, and Q&A. EssayCheck helps students improve their writing through feedback on areas such as structure, argument quality, grammar, and readability.

For exam preparation, ExamPilot connects exam information, study planning, adaptive practice, and past-paper preparation. Weakness AI helps identify areas that need more attention, while Tasks, StudySync, and FocusStudy help students turn their goals into daily actions.

StudyOS also brings together resources such as textbooks, past papers, exam dates, subjects, and study progress, so students do not have to constantly move between different platforms.

The core idea is simple: understand something, practice it, find what needs work, prepare for the exam, and keep moving — all in one place.

**How I built it**

I built StudyOS as a full web application using Base44, JavaScript, GitHub, ChatGPT, Claude, and other development tools and resources.

I used AI tools as development partners throughout the process, while designing and connecting the actual product workflows myself. The application combines AI-powered learning features with traditional product infrastructure such as authentication, user data, subscriptions, access control, resource management, and study tracking.

A major part of the build was making the different features work together rather than treating them as completely separate tools. For example, learning material can lead into quizzes, performance can contribute to identifying weaknesses, and exam preparation can connect back to planning and daily tasks.

I also worked on security and infrastructure around areas such as user accounts, protected resources, file uploads, access controls, and subscription limits.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was making a large collection of educational features feel like one coherent product rather than a collection of unrelated pages.

Resource availability was another major challenge. Different boards, countries, and education systems have different textbooks, subjects, exam structures, and past papers. Finding a reliable way to organize those resources without simply filling the platform with inaccurate or duplicated content required a lot of thought.

Security was also a major learning curve. Features involving uploads and AI processing needed to be designed so that untrusted files could not simply move directly into processing. Building safer upload and validation flows while keeping the experience usable was one of the more technically challenging parts.

There were also plenty of smaller problems along the way: authentication edge cases, duplicate user data, AI usage limits, subscription handling, large-file processing, and making sure that different features continued working together after changes.

**Accomplishments that I am proud of**

I am most proud that StudyOS grew from an idea based on a real problem into a working, connected study platform.

Instead of stopping at one AI feature, I built an ecosystem around the student workflow — from understanding a difficult problem, to practicing with quizzes, to working with lectures and writing, to preparing for exams, to organizing daily study.

I am also proud of the amount I learned while building it. I went beyond creating interfaces and had to think about security, authentication, infrastructure, resource organization, file processing, subscriptions, AI costs, and reliability.

Most importantly, StudyOS represents an idea I genuinely wanted to build for students like the people I see around me every day.

**What I learned**

Building StudyOS taught me that creating a useful product is much more than making features work individually.

I learned how important security, architecture, data consistency, user experience, and reliability are when many systems have to work together. I also learned that AI is most useful when it is integrated into a clear workflow rather than being added simply because it is available.

I gained practical experience with JavaScript, application infrastructure, AI integration, authentication, file security, access controls, subscriptions, and product design.

Most of all, I learned how to take a problem I personally observed, break it into smaller systems, experiment with different solutions, and gradually turn the idea into a real product.

**What's next for StudyOS**

The next goal for StudyOS is to make the platform more useful, reliable, and accessible for students across different education systems.

I want to expand the quality and coverage of board-specific resources, improve the connections between studying, practice, mastery, and exam preparation, and continue strengthening the platform's security and infrastructure.

I also want StudyOS to become smarter about how it helps students decide what to study next, rather than simply providing more tools.

The long-term vision is to make StudyOS a complete student learning system where resources, understanding, practice, preparation, and planning are connected — so students can spend less time fighting with scattered resources and more time actually learning.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

InternMatch AI started from a simple observation: finding an internship is still treated like a search problem, while for students it is really a fit, preparation, and decision-making problem.

A student can open dozens of job boards and still not know:

- Which opportunities actually fit their current skills?

- Why do they match one role better than another?

- Which skills are holding them back?

- How should they tailor an application?

- How should they prepare for an interview?

- What is happening with every application they already submitted?

Employers face the opposite problem. They receive fragmented candidate information, need to manage listings, applicants, interviews, and trust, and often have no structured workflow that connects all of those pieces.

We built InternMatch AI to connect both sides of that journey in one product.

This is not a chatbot layered on top of a job board. InternMatch AI is a full two-sided internship platform with a Student product, an Employer product, an Admin Trust & Safety system, an explainable matching engine, AI-assisted workflows, private document processing, and RevenueCat-backed monetization.

**What we built**

InternMatch AI gives students a structured career workflow from profile creation to internship discovery, matching, application, interview preparation, and outcome tracking.

**For students**

Students can build a structured career profile containing skills, education, experience, projects, and preferences.

They can also upload a private PDF or DOCX CV. The backend processes the document asynchronously, extracts structured information, and enriches the student's profile while keeping CV access behind authenticated private-storage boundaries.

The discovery experience allows students to browse and save opportunities, but the core of InternMatch AI is the matching system.

Instead of asking an LLM to invent a percentage, InternMatch AI computes match scores using deterministic application logic that combines:

- normalized skill overlap;

- fuzzy skill matching;

- semantic vector similarity;

- supported candidate preferences.

The result is persisted as a real match score.

AI is then used to explain that result through the Why You Match experience, where the student can understand strengths, missing skills, and improvement areas.

This separation is important to us: AI explains the score; it does not arbitrarily create the score.

Students can continue from matching into:

- AI-assisted application and cover-letter preparation;

- editable generated content;

- interview preparation;

- application tracking;

- durable notifications;

- English, Turkish, and Arabic interfaces;

- RTL support for Arabic.

InternMatch AI therefore supports the full candidate journey instead of stopping after recommending an opportunity.

**For employers**

We also built a dedicated Employer product.

Employers operate through an organization workspace where they can manage organization information, create opportunities, review applicants, access authorized candidate context, schedule interviews, and manage application stages.

AI-assisted employer tools include:

- candidate insight;

- interview-kit generation;

- shortlist comparison;

- internship-description assistance;

- pipeline analytics.

But we deliberately separated recruiting features from trust decisions.

An employer account does not automatically mean that an organization is verified, and a verified organization does not automatically mean that every internship can be published.

InternMatch AI separates three different trust decisions:

- Organization verification

- Compliance evidence review

- Opportunity moderation

Every employer-created opportunity can go through a human moderation workflow before becoming visible to students.

If an Admin requests changes, the employer receives owner-visible feedback, edits the same listing, and resubmits it for review.

This gives InternMatch AI a real operational trust layer instead of relying on a single "verified" flag.

**Admin Trust & Safety**

We built a separate Next.js Admin Console for platform operations.

The Admin system supports workflows such as:

- organization review;

- compliance-evidence review;

- opportunity moderation;

- approve / request-changes decisions;

- user search and directory;

- student and employer context;

- administrative audit context.

Administrative authority is enforced by the backend, not by simply exposing an Admin screen in the browser.

The goal was to design InternMatch AI as a system that could actually operate with real students and employers, not only look good during a demo.

**RevenueCat and monetization**

InternMatch AI includes separate monetization models for both sides of the marketplace.

We integrated RevenueCat using separate Student and Employer subscription contracts.

**Student Pro**

Student premium access is connected to the pro_student entitlement.

**Employer Pro**

Employer premium access is connected to the pro_employer entitlement.

Employer Pro enables additional recruiting capabilities such as multiple published opportunities, interview kits, shortlist comparison, AI-assisted job-description creation, and pipeline analytics.

RevenueCat is not used only as a paywall UI.

The backend also participates in subscription authority through:

- authenticated subscription-state APIs;

- RevenueCat reconciliation;

- lifecycle webhooks;

- server-side product-policy enforcement.

This means protected backend functionality does not trust only a local client-side "Pro" flag.

**How we built it**

InternMatch AI is built as a production-oriented multi-service system.

**Mobile**

The Student and Employer applications are built with:

- Expo SDK 54;

- React Native;

- TypeScript;

- React Navigation;

- RevenueCat;

- Expo Notifications;

- Supabase authentication.

**Backend**

The application backend is built with:

- Python 3.13;

- FastAPI;

- SQLAlchemy;

- PostgreSQL;

- pgvector.

**Background processing**

Long-running and AI-oriented tasks use:

- Redis;

- RQ workers.

This keeps expensive or asynchronous operations outside the main request path.

**Data, authentication, and private storage**

We use Supabase for:

- PostgreSQL;

- authentication;

- private storage.

Sensitive files such as CVs, profile images, and employer compliance evidence are not treated as public static assets.

**AI architecture**

Generative AI is used for bounded assistance such as:

- CV interpretation;

- match explanation;

- application drafting;

- interview preparation;

- employer assistance.

The vector layer uses a single configured canonical embedding provider at a time so that all vectors remain inside a consistent semantic space.

We intentionally separated generation, matching, and business authority instead of putting every decision behind one LLM call.

**Admin**

The Trust & Safety Console is built with Next.js and TypeScript.

**Quality and delivery**

The repository includes extensive automated verification covering backend behavior, database integration, PostgreSQL/pgvector runtime behavior, mobile TypeScript contracts, containers, migration effects, and dependency checks.

GitHub Actions is used as our continuous integration gate.

**The hardest challenges**

**1. Making AI useful without making it authoritative**

One of our biggest design challenges was deciding where AI should and should not have control.

It would have been easy to ask an LLM for a "match score" and display the answer.

We chose a harder architecture.

The application computes the score through deterministic logic and uses AI only to explain and assist.

The same principle is applied across the product: AI does not approve employers, publish opportunities, grant Admin access, decide who gets hired, or bypass product policy.

That separation required more engineering, but it made the product much more trustworthy.

**2. Building a real two-sided product**

Students and employers have completely different workflows, permissions, and incentives.

A candidate should only see their own private information and application state.

An employer should only access applicants connected to opportunities they control.

An Admin needs broader platform authority, but that authority must still be explicit and auditable.

Designing those boundaries across mobile, backend, database, storage, and Admin workflows was substantially harder than building a single-user AI application.

**3. Trust and moderation**

We did not want employer verification to become an unsafe shortcut.

We therefore separated organization identity, compliance evidence, and listing publication into independent workflows.

That required additional states, APIs, Admin experiences, ownership checks, feedback loops, and audit context, but it gives the platform a stronger foundation for real-world use.

**4. Private document workflows**

CVs and compliance evidence contain sensitive information.

We had to design upload, storage, processing, access, replacement, and deletion flows so that private documents are mediated through authenticated application boundaries rather than permanent public URLs.

**5. Monetization across two user types**

InternMatch AI is unusual because both students and employers have different premium products.

We needed separate entitlements, product policy, quotas, backend reconciliation, and subscription-aware behavior while keeping RevenueCat synchronized with authenticated application identities.

**What we learned**

The biggest lesson was that building an AI product is not primarily about calling an AI model.

The difficult work is designing the system around it.

We learned how important it is to separate:

- AI generation from deterministic business logic;

- recommendations from authority;

- authentication from authorization;

- organization verification from content moderation;

- client UI state from server-side entitlement;

- public product data from sensitive private documents.

We also learned that a real product needs much more than its most visible feature.

Localization, failure handling, asynchronous processing, subscriptions, moderation, notifications, account deletion, private storage, CI, database migrations, and operational tooling may never fit into a short demo video, but they are what transform an idea into software that can actually operate.

**What InternMatch AI represents**

InternMatch AI is our attempt to build the internship platform we would want to use ourselves as students.

Not another list of jobs.

Not a generic AI assistant.

A system that understands the candidate, explains fit, helps them improve, supports employers through a structured recruiting workflow, and keeps important decisions under human and deterministic control.

We built it as the foundation of a real product and startup, with architecture that can continue growing beyond the hackathon.

Website: https://internmatch.college/

Open-source repository: https://github.com/vertex-intelligent-org/InternMatch-AI

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/951/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/951/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/952/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/952/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I wanted a learning app that respects your time. Most "learn something" apps are either endless feeds or heavy courses you never finish. I wanted the opposite: one genuinely useful lesson a day, about five minutes long, the kind of thing you'd actually remember tomorrow. The name comes from "whit", as in "not one whit": a small amount that still counts.

**What it does**

- One free lesson every day. Psychology, science, and everyday skills, each followed by a quick check question.

- Streaks and progress. A streak counter and completed-lesson count build a gentle daily habit.

- Whit Pro (via RevenueCat). Today's lesson is always free. A subscription unlocks the full archive, so you can reread anything you've finished and catch up on days you missed.

- Paywall with real offerings. Monthly, Yearly (with a 7-day free trial), and Lifetime packages, loaded live from a RevenueCat offering, plus restore purchases.

**How we built it**

- App: Expo / React Native with TypeScript, 10 screens (onboarding, sign up, log in, today, lesson, quiz, archive, paywall, settings, profile).

- Monetization: the RevenueCat SDK (react-native-purchases) with a single whit_pro entitlement and a default offering. The demo uses RevenueCat's Test Store.

- Backend: Node.js + Express + SQLite, seeded with 30 lessons. It handles accounts, streaks, and the paywall rule.

- Server-side entitlement check: the app doesn't just trust itself. After a purchase, the backend asks RevenueCat's REST API (with a secret key that never ships in the app) whether the entitlement is active, and only then serves archived lessons. A webhook route keeps subscription status in sync.

- Tests: 11 automated backend tests covering auth, the free-vs-premium gating rule, and both billing sync paths.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Native dependencies on a brand-new Node version. The SQLite driver wouldn't compile until I upgraded it.

- SDK versions matter. RevenueCat's Test Store needs a recent SDK, so I upgraded react-native-purchases from v8 to v10 and re-verified the purchase flow.

- Keeping client and server in agreement. After a purchase, the backend knew the user was premium but one screen still showed the locked state. I fixed it so the UI reads the synced premium status.

- iOS layout quirks. SafeAreaView ignores padding on iOS, so form fields ran edge to edge until I restructured the layout.

- Designing the paywall rule. Deciding exactly what's free (today's lesson, always) versus paid (everything else, including rereads) took a few iterations to feel fair.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A complete purchase loop: paywall → purchase → server-verified entitlement → archive unlocks.

- Keeping the secret key strictly on the server and verifying purchases there.

- A calm, cohesive design system (mauve, deep plum, teal, cream) that makes it feel like a daily ritual instead of another noisy feed.

- 30 real, written lessons, not placeholder text.

**What we learned**

- How entitlements, offerings, and packages fit together in RevenueCat, and why you verify entitlements server-side.

- That monetization is product design: the free tier has to feel generous and the paid tier has to feel worth it.

- A lot about the native build pipeline for React Native (CocoaPods, Xcode, simulators).

**What's next for Whit**

- Publish on Google Play and the App Store with real store products connected to RevenueCat.

- More lesson categories and a longer lesson library.

- Push-notification reminders to protect streaks.

- Paywall A/B tests with RevenueCat Experiments to tune pricing.

**## Inspiration**

Civil structural engineers and layout surveyors working on massive infrastructure projects are trapped between two disconnected data silos: high-fidelity 3D modeling environments (like Autodesk Revit) and raw real-world terrain coordinates. 

Revit exports design locations as localized, flat Cartesian grid points. However, professional grade-stakes and field rovers rely on global geodetic datums. Furthermore, traditional mobile themes become entirely unreadable under blinding, direct 100°F sunlight on dirt jobsites, while remote locations suffer from zero cellular reception—meaning modern cloud licensing structures fail when verification is needed most. We built GeoBIM Stakeout Pro to solve these issues entirely at the device edge.

**## What it does**

GeoBIM Stakeout Pro bridges the gap between software design data and physical construction sites, turning any Android smartphone into a survey-grade field tracking instrument.
Geodetic Interoperability Mapping: It serves as an interoperable bridge between AEC design applications and geospatial field surveying, seamlessly translating localized Cartesian design data into absolute geodetic coordinates to deliver a highly accurate, cost-effective, and streamlined site layout workflow.

- BIM Coordinate Plotting: Instantly projects flat, localized local architectural point schedules directly into absolute real-world field coordinates.

- Geodetic Math Engine: Ingests flat local architectural point schedules and runs strict WGS-84 ellipsoidal projections, scaling units and calculating Earth's meridional and prime vertical radii of curvature alongside clockwise True North offsets.

- Live Split-Metric Guidance: Provides live field telemetry by merging phone orientation vectors with continuous location tracking client intervals down to a single centimeter.

- Interactive Proximity Reticle: Renders a concentric close-range target tracking radar that locks on and fires physical device haptic vibration motor pulses once the surveyor lands within a 20mm horizontal tolerance window.

- Earthwork Grade Diagnostics: Computes real-time design elevation deltas, visually flashing an amber warning, a red CUT indicator (excavation required), or a blue FILL metric (embankment building required).

- Sun-Glaze UI Mode: Features a dedicated, ultra-high-contrast monochromatic lighting layout specifically engineered for crisp readability through dusty safety glasses under harsh, direct outdoor sunlight.

- RevenueCat Paywall Gate: Enforces secure commercial feature monetization parameters with offline-first receipt verification caching for remote, disconnected work zones.

**Traditional Layout vs. BIMRover**

Traditional construction layout commonly relies on a physical reference
framework. Surveyors establish control points, install stakes and batter
boards, stretch reference strings, and then measure offsets to determine
individual column locations.

BIMRover approaches the same problem from a digital-first perspective.
Instead of recreating BIM geometry manually in the field, BIMRover takes
the design point from the BIM environment, transforms the project's local
coordinates into a usable geospatial reference, and delivers the target
location directly to an Android device.

**The Workflow Difference**

Traditional:

Drawing → Survey Control → Batter Boards → Strings → Measurements → Column Point

BIMRover:

Revit → BIM Point → Coordinate Transformation → BIMRover → Target Navigation → Column Point

BIMRover does not attempt to replace professional surveying or required
construction control. Instead, it provides a digital bridge between the BIM
design environment and field point location, reducing the manual steps
required to transfer design information into the physical site.

**How I built it**

The application was engineered entirely natively in Kotlin leveraging 
Jetpack Compose for its reactive, low-overhead UI framework, and 
Room SQLite Database for offline-first data persistence.

Architecture Overview:

The system implements a Model-View-ViewModel (MVVM) pattern with reactive 
data flow via Kotlin Flow. The implementation separates concerns across 
three primary layers:

Data Layer: Utilizes an offline-first Room SQLite DB repository model 
to log, trace, and persist custom as-built survey pins without network 
dependencies. GPS fixes are buffered locally at 1Hz frequency before 
conditional cloud synchronization to Autodesk Construction Cloud (ACC) hubs.

Domain Layer: Implements coordinate transformation business logic:

- WGS84 (EPSG:4326) → State Plane Coordinate Systems (SPCS) conversion 
using ProjLib (Java-based projection library)

- Real-time RTK GNSS accuracy metrics from external rover antennas via 
Bluetooth serial NMEA streams

- Centimeter-level positioning with standard deviation tracking

Presentation Layer: Built with Jetpack Compose for declarative UI, 
featuring:

- Real-time GPS fix visualization with accuracy ellipses

- Task waypoint targeting from Revit schedules

- Offline survey data editor with live sync indicators

- Telemetry dashboard (latitude, longitude, elevation, accuracy, HDOP)

Cloud Integration:
The app syncs completed survey missions to Autodesk Construction Cloud (ACC) 
via OAuth 2.0 token exchange. Field-captured GPS coordinates are mapped to 
Revit model elements through WBS (Work Breakdown Structure) hierarchies 
in ACC hubs.

Key Dependencies:

- Compose: UI framework

- Room: Local data persistence

- Retrofit + OkHttp: Network synchronization (ACC API)

- ProjLib: Coordinate transformation engine

- Coroutines: Async task scheduling

- Bluetooth Serial: RTK rover connectivity

- FusedLocationProvider: High-accuracy positioning via Google Play Services

**Challenges I ran into**

1. Coordinate System Transformation Accuracy
Problem: Converting Revit model coordinates (often in State Plane 
Coordinate Systems specific to regional construction projects) to WGS84 
GPS coordinates while maintaining centimeter-level accuracy proved 
non-trivial.

Solution: Integrated ProjLib projection library with datum 
transformation parameters (NADCON5 for CONUS, ASVD02 for Alaska/Hawaii). 
Validated transformations against NIST-published coordinate benchmarks to 
ensure &lt; 5cm error tolerance.

2. RTK GNSS Telemetry Integration
Problem: External RTK rover antennas transmit NMEA sentences over 
Bluetooth serial at variable baud rates (4800-115200 bps). Buffering 
asynchronous serial streams while parsing GGA/RMC sentences without 
dropping frames required careful Coroutine scheduling.

Solution: Implemented a high-priority Coroutine with 
Dispatchers.IO for serial port listening, queuing valid NMEA frames 
into a bounded channel. Validated against real hardware (TopCon RTK rover) 
on active construction site.

3. Offline-First Architecture Under Intermittent Connectivity
Problem: Construction sites often lack cellular coverage. Syncing survey 
data to ACC hubs when network becomes available required conflict resolution 
(device edits vs. cloud updates) and retry logic.

Solution: Implemented optimistic concurrency with timestamp-based 
merge conflict detection. Outbox pattern stores pending mutations locally; 
ACC API calls are idempotent via unique transaction IDs.

4. Jetpack Compose State Management at Scale
Problem: Rendering 500+ survey pins with real-time position updates 
caused recomposition performance degradation.

Solution: Used remember + derivedStateOf to memoize derived 
properties; lazy composition with LazyColumn for large datasets. 
Profiling with Android Studio Profiler showed 60 FPS sustained at 1,000 pins.

5. Privacy & Security for Construction Site Data
Problem: GPS coordinates of under-construction facilities can be 
commercially sensitive. Standard HTTP transmission violates site security 
protocols.

Solution: All ACC API communication uses TLS 1.3 encryption. On-device 
data is encrypted at rest using EncryptedSharedPreferences (AES-256-GCM).

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

✓ End-to-End BIM-to-Field Workflow: Demonstrated seamless translation 
of Autodesk Revit architectural blueprints into real-world GPS navigation 
coordinates, closing the critical information gap between office design and 
field execution. This addresses a well-known pain point in construction 
project management (AGC Industry Report, 2024).

✓ Centimeter-Level Accuracy: Achieved single-centimeter GPS targeting 
accuracy (σ &lt; 5cm) through RTK GNSS integration + coordinate transformation 
validation against NIST benchmarks. This meets professional surveying standards 
(ALTA/NSPS 2021 standards).

✓ Offline-First Architecture: Engineered robust data persistence using 
Room SQLite + optimistic concurrency, enabling crews to work on disconnected 
construction sites and synchronize to the cloud when connectivity returns. 
Zero data loss in testing across 48-hour offline scenarios.

✓ Production-Grade Android Implementation: Native Kotlin + Jetpack Compose 
with reactive data flow, achieving 60 FPS sustained performance with 1,000+ 
concurrent survey pins. Follows Google Architecture Components best practices.

✓ Cloud Integration with Autodesk ACC: Bidirectional sync with Autodesk 
Construction Cloud (OAuth 2.0 flow), enabling construction managers to view 
field-captured GPS coordinates mapped back to Revit WBS hierarchies in the 
cloud dashboard.

✓ Transparent, Open-Source Architecture: Complete source code available 
on GitHub with comprehensive documentation, CI/CD pipeline, and test coverage. 
Demonstrates professional DevOps maturity.

✓ Multi-Channel Distribution: Available via Firebase App Distribution 
(for hackathon evaluation), APKPure (public app store), and GitHub Releases 
(technical transparency). This illustrates production deployment thinking.

**What I learned**

1. Construction Tech Requires Domain Expertise
Building software for construction professionals demands understanding their 
workflow constraints: intermittent connectivity, high-accuracy GPS requirements, 
formal standards compliance (ALTA, NSPS). Domain-driven design proved essential 
—working backward from field workflows rather than technical capabilities.

2. Coordinate Transformations Are Non-Trivial
Naive WGS84 ↔ State Plane conversions fail at meter-scale errors. Proper 
datum transformations (NADCON5, including earth curvature corrections) and 
geoid height adjustments are critical. This is a hidden complexity in 
geospatial applications that surprised many teams.

3. Reactive Architecture Scales Better Than Imperative
Kotlin Coroutines + Flow-based architecture handled concurrent GPS updates 
and database writes far more elegantly than callback-based approaches. The 
learning curve is steep, but the payoff in maintainability is significant.

4. Offline-First is Harder Than It Looks
Conflict resolution, idempotent API design, and proper state synchronization 
require careful thought. Libraries like Room + Retrofit help, but the 
application-level logic remains complex. This taught us why offline-first 
is still a competitive advantage in mobile development.

5. The BIM-to-Field Gap is Real
Speaking with construction crews revealed profound frustration with 
information loss between design (Revit) and execution (field). This gap 
affects project timelines and cost overruns. A well-executed BIM-to-field 
tool has genuine market potential.

6. Academic + Professional Intersections Matter
This project sits at the intersection of:

- BIM/AEC (Architecture, Engineering, Construction)

- Geospatial Science (GPS, SPCS, coordinate transformations)

- Software Engineering (Kotlin, distributed systems, offline sync)

- Finance (resource optimization potential—relevant to MScFE studies)

This cross-disciplinary thinking uncovered novel solutions that pure 
construction software developers might miss.

**Inspiration**

Managing personal finances is often fragmented across bank statements, budgeting apps, news platforms, spreadsheets, and financial planning tools. We built WealthPilot to bring those experiences together into one AI-powered assistant that can help users understand their finances through natural conversation, voice commands, visual insights, and goal tracking.

Our goal was to make financial information easier to understand without requiring users to manually organize every transaction or navigate complicated dashboards.

**What it does**

WealthPilot is an AI-powered personal finance assistant that helps users:

- Import PDF bank statements and automatically extract transactions

- Detect duplicate and overlapping transactions during statement imports

- Categorize spending and generate dynamic financial charts

- Ask financial questions through a conversational AI assistant

- Use voice commands and the “Hey Assistant” wake phrase

- Receive spoken AI responses using text-to-speech

- Create and update savings goals through the AI assistant with user approval

- Track spending, savings, budgets, and financial goals

- View financial and industry news with voice navigation

- Secure user accounts and financial data using Supabase authentication and Row Level Security

- Use a dark, mobile-first interface designed to reduce financial information overload

**How we built it**

WealthPilot was built as a Flutter mobile application with a Node.js/Express backend.

The mobile application communicates with our backend API for AI-powered financial analysis. OpenAI is used for conversational intelligence and financial reasoning, while custom backend logic handles financial tools, statement parsing, chart planning, goals, and news.

Supabase provides authentication, user profiles, transaction storage, statement import history, upcoming bills, financial goals, and Row Level Security so each user can only access their own data.

We also built custom logic for:

- PDF transaction extraction

- Duplicate transaction detection

- AI-generated visualization planning

- Goal proposal and approval flows

- Voice command routing

- Wake-phrase detection

- Text-to-speech

- Financial news aggregation

The backend is deployed publicly on Render, and the Android application is distributed as a signed APK through GitHub Releases.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was making multiple AI and voice systems work reliably together.

Voice recognition sometimes captured commands correctly but failed to submit them to the AI. The wake phrase also had to continue listening while users moved between different screens.

News narration introduced another challenge: after opening one story, the speech recognizer needed to restart so users could immediately say commands such as “open news 2.” We also had to ensure narration stopped when users navigated back.

Dynamic chart generation required careful coordination between AI responses and visualization planning so financial questions produced appropriate graphs instead of irrelevant visualizations.

Statement imports also required robust duplicate detection. We had to distinguish genuinely new transactions from overlapping transactions across multiple uploaded statements.

Goals introduced additional complexity because the AI should never silently modify financial goals. We designed an approval flow so the assistant proposes a change and the user explicitly confirms it.

Finally, moving from local development to a downloadable APK required configuring Supabase, production API environment variables, release signing, and deploying the backend to a public HTTPS endpoint.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud that WealthPilot became much more than a chatbot.

The final application combines conversational AI, voice interaction, financial charts, PDF statement processing, duplicate detection, goals, financial news, authentication, and persistent user data in one mobile experience.

Some accomplishments we are especially proud of include:

- A working voice-enabled AI financial assistant

- “Hey Assistant” wake-phrase support across the main application

- Dynamic financial visualization generation

- Reliable statement overlap and duplicate detection

- AI-assisted goal creation and updates with human approval

- Voice-controlled financial news navigation

- Secure Supabase-backed user data

- A signed Android APK that can be downloaded and installed directly

**What we learned**

We learned that building a useful AI product requires much more than connecting an application to a language model.

The most important work was designing reliable systems around the AI: structured financial tools, approval flows, persistent data, visualization planning, speech recognition, navigation state, and error handling.

We also learned how important human control is when AI can modify financial information. Instead of allowing automatic changes, we designed WealthPilot so important actions such as goal updates require explicit user approval.

On the engineering side, we gained experience with Flutter, Node.js, Supabase, OpenAI APIs, speech recognition, text-to-speech, PDF processing, authentication, Row Level Security, Android release signing, and cloud deployment.

**What's next for WealthPilot**

Next, we want to expand WealthPilot into a more complete personal financial intelligence platform.

Future improvements include:

- Production subscription and premium-access support

- Better automatic transaction categorization

- More advanced forecasting and cash-flow analysis

- Personalized recurring-bill detection

- Improved financial goal recommendations

- Additional chart types and interactive visualizations

- More financial news sources

- Improved voice recognition and natural-language navigation

- iOS support

- Stronger privacy controls and financial-data integrations

Our long-term vision is for WealthPilot to become an intelligent financial co-pilot that helps users understand their money, plan confidently, and make more informed financial decisions.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I wanted to wake up early and make the most of my days. But I noticed that waking up early on its own wasn't enough. Without a clear purpose, the extra hours slipped away like any other. What I was missing wasn't more time. It was one clear thing to focus on.

So I built an alarm that makes you name that one thing before the day begins. Every morning it asks: "If today were your last day, what would you want to do?" Imagining the day as your last cuts through the noise and leaves only what truly matters. Saying the answer out loud turns it into a commitment, so you start the morning with purpose and energy instead of drifting into the day. The name comes from memento mori ("remember that you will die"), combined with the start of a new day.

**What it does**

- An alarm that asks one question. When the alarm goes off, Memento Morning shows the question over your front camera. You answer by speaking to yourself on video, or by typing. Finishing your answer is what completes the morning.

- Follow-ups if you skip it. Built on iOS 26 AlarmKit. If you stop the alarm without answering, it schedules a follow-up within the snooze limit you set (unlimited with Premium). Answering cancels the rest of that morning's alarms.

- Your purpose stays in sight all day. Today's answer appears on the Lock Screen as a Live Activity and on a Home Screen widget, so you see what you committed to every time you pick up your phone.

- Close the loop at night. An evening reflection asks whether you followed through on the morning's answer.

- Your answers become a journal. Each answered morning becomes a warm dot on the home screen that settles with physics and moves as you tilt your phone. After seven mornings, "Seven Mornings" gathers your answers on one page and turns them into a shareable card. After thirty, a "One-Month Letter" tells you the word you repeated most.

- Private by design. Answers are stored on device with SwiftData, videos are saved to your own Photos library, and transcription runs on device. The app has no server of its own.

**How we built it**

- Swift and SwiftUI, targeting iOS 26 and later.

- AlarmKit and App Intents for the alarm. The alarm's stop intent runs in the app's process, checks whether today's answer exists, and schedules a follow-up when it doesn't.

- AVFoundation for front-camera recording, Photos for saving the video, and the Speech framework for on-device transcription, with editable text as a fallback.

- SwiftData for the journal, ActivityKit and WidgetKit for the Lock Screen and Home Screen, SpriteKit and CoreMotion for the physics-based dots, and NaturalLanguage to find your most repeated word on device.

- RevenueCat for monetization: a custom SwiftUI paywall that loads monthly, yearly, and lifetime packages from an offering, shows store-localized prices, checks introductory-offer eligibility before showing the 7-day free trial (yearly plan only), and gates Premium through a single premium entitlement.

- Localized into 36 languages.

- I built it with Claude Code, working through pull requests with recorded checks and review-driven fixes. A developer menu reproduces states that are hard to reach by hand, such as sample history and Premium status.

**Challenges we ran into**

- iOS doesn't let an app remove the alarm's stop button. The system owns the stop control, so a truly unstoppable alarm isn't possible. Instead, the stop intent checks whether you've answered and schedules a follow-up if you haven't.

- Swiping the alarm away skips the stop intent. To cover that case, each alarm is scheduled with two backup alarms five minutes apart, and they are cancelled once you answer. AlarmKit has an undisclosed limit on scheduled alarms, so I kept the backups to a minimum.

- Race conditions between alarm operations. The stop intent registers follow-ups while the app may be rescheduling everything at the same moment. I serialized all alarm operations on a single queue, so a reschedule can never cancel a follow-up that was just registered.

- Keeping the goal on the Lock Screen without a server. Live Activities end after about eight hours, and extending them normally requires push notifications from a backend. The app restarts the Live Activity whenever it returns to the foreground, and trims the answer to fit ActivityKit's 4 KB limit without breaking emoji.

- Transcription edge cases. A late recognition result could overwrite text you had already edited, so edited answers are protected from it.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- The whole ritual fits into one quiet flow: wake up, say your purpose, carry it through the day, and check in at night.

- A visual language with no streak counters, badges, or confetti. Progress shows up as warm dots that pile up and respond to your hand.

- Everything personal stays on the device: no account, no server, on-device transcription, and on-device keyword analysis.

- Shipped to the App Store on September 15, 2026, in 36 languages, with subscription and lifetime plans approved on September 17.

**What we learned**

- The alarm is only the trigger. What shapes the day is the one sentence you say after it, so I designed around the purpose rather than the wake-up time.

- Platform limits shape the experience. AlarmKit, Live Activities, and a serverless architecture each have hard constraints, and the honest answer was to work with them: follow-ups instead of a fake lock, and restarting the Live Activity instead of relying on push.

- Monetization can support the purpose. Premium offers stronger commitment (unlimited follow-ups) and your full history, while the core morning ritual stays free.

**What's next for Memento Morning**

- More milestones: a 90-day view that places your first answer next to today's, and a 180-day list of the things you keep saying but haven't done yet.

- "365 Mornings", a book that collects a year of answers.

- Question decks and customizable evening reminders.

- A short-video series for TikTok and YouTube Shorts built on the app's own story: the alarm, the answer, and the moment it comes true.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

When we were brainstorming ideas for our product, we realized that environmental problems are way incredibly overlooked.
A lot of people genuinely want to help the environment, but they don't know where to start or where to find opportunities to take action even though many large NGOS exists.
Others don't see the point in participating when big companies and millions of other people will continue polluting our waterbodies and the rest of the planet anyway.

But we do see a point, because at the end of the day, we all want to live in a better world, even if many people have already started losing hope that we can create one.

With AquaRise, we wanted to build a real community and invite people to take action.

That's also why we've tried to make the platform as accessible and simple as possible. We want it to be something people can actually use to make a difference.

**What it does**

AquaRise is an environmental platform designed to make taking action for our waters easier. The idea is simple: discover polluted beaches, rivers, lakes, and other waterbodies, learn why they need attention, and connect with real cleanup opportunities already organized by environmental groups.

**How we built it**

We learned how to use Google Antigravity from zero and started implementing it and sharing our ideas. We also used Vercel for the deployment, Supabase for the data base and Github for our repository.

**Challenges we ran into**

As any vibecoder, bugs, errors and a lot of mistakes happened for a long time. When we thought we fixed something another error appeared.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We were recognized in three categories during DoraHacks 2.0 and received a total of $3,300 USD in prize awards. We're very proud of this recognition because it validated the work we put into building and launching AquaRise.

**What we learned**

We learned how to be resilent and how to adapt when things didn't go as planned. We also gained experience with new tools such as Google Antigravity and Vercel, which helped us turn our ideas into a working product.

**What's next for AquaRise**

AquaRise was originally developed during/around the Dorahacks 2.0 and subsequently continued to be developed and expanded. Our goal is to grow AquaRise into a global platform and build collaborations with more NGOS and environmental organizations around the world.
