<details><summary>Description</summary>

Entering: the Next Gen Award. Turn is a student team's entry, submitted with a public repository and a demo video instead of a store listing.

**What it does**

Turn is an augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) app for iPhone. It's for adults who can read and tap but can't rely on their speech, such as people living with ALS or recovering from a stroke.

- Speak. Tap a saved phrase or type, and Turn speaks it in your Personal Voice or a system voice. The bank starts with about 150 editable phrases in categories, and every typed reply joins it.

- Listen. In Listen mode, Turn transcribes the conversation partner on the iPhone. When the partner finishes a line, a row above the grid offers your own saved phrases that answer it: one big button when Turn is confident, up to six otherwise, and no change when nothing fits. For a yes-or-no question, Yes, No, and Not sure come first.

- Nothing speaks until you tap. A reply keeps its slot until a new one wins by a clear margin, and the grid never reorders itself.

- The "aha". A partner asks "How was physio?", and "It was hard" is waiting in the row, though the two share no content word.

**Why it matters**

Aided communication runs at about 8 to 10 words a minute, while speech runs at 125 to 185. By the time a reply is typed, the conversation has moved on. Existing AAC apps sell symbol grids or typing. Newer apps that listen generate replies, and AAC users testing AI suggestions worried about the system "suggesting the wrong thing and making the participants look bad". Turn never writes a word: a hosted decision model chooses which of the person's own phrases answer each line, and whether any do.

**The evaluation**

On September 23, 2026, we evaluated 80 partner lines with the hosted decision model pinned to version 1.13.0. On the 64 lines with an acceptable saved reply besides Yes, No, and Not sure:

Ranker
Top 1
Top 6

chance
5%
26%

keyword
16%
23%

embeddings
22%
45%

hosted decision model
67%
75%

Its top 6 leads embeddings by 29.7 points (95% paired interval, 17.2 to 42.2). Claude subagents wrote the lines, the starter bank, and the labels at our direction, and no clinician has reviewed Turn yet. The repository's eval/results.md has the intervals and caveats.

**How it makes money**

Speaking is always free: the grid, typing, saved phrases, and Personal Voice. Turn Listen, a one-time $24.99 purchase through RevenueCat that grants the listen entitlement, keeps Listen mode on after 20 free partner lines. Listen mode is the part that costs us money on every line, and a one-time price means nobody loses their voice when a payment lapses.

- The RevenueCat Paywall opens on the 21st partner line. Settings holds Unlock Listen mode and Restore Purchases.

- Our relay checks the listen entitlement through RevenueCat's REST API v2 before it calls the model.

- The purchase runs through RevenueCat's Test Store, which the organizers accept for Next Gen: "Test Store is enough for the Next Gen category" (forum). Test Store purchases are sandbox data, so we report no revenue.

**How judges reach the paid part**

- Download Turn.app.zip from the latest release, then install it on an iOS 27 Simulator with xcrun simctl install booted Turn.app.

- Tap Home at the top of the grid, choose Clinic, then tap Listen, Allow, and They agreed.

- Type "How was physio?" as the partner's line, and tap "It was hard" to hear it.

- Open Settings, tap Unlock Listen mode, and complete the Test Store purchase. It's free, so no promo code is needed.

Bundle ID: com.m1ku.turn.

**How we built it**

- App: Expo SDK 57, React Native 0.86, TypeScript, Expo Router, and expo-sqlite, with our own Swift Expo modules for on-device transcription with Apple's SpeechAnalyzer and for Personal Voice.

- Purchases: react-native-purchases and react-native-purchases-ui, with a RevenueCat Paywall configured remotely.

- Relay: a Cloudflare Worker with SQLite-backed Durable Objects. It counts free lines, checks the entitlement, rate-limits, and asks the model to score a 40-phrase shortlist.

- Retrieval before judgment: the phone picks 40 candidates by keyword ranking, the place, and your most-used replies, so the whole phrase bank never leaves the phone.

- Offline: without a network, or when the model is slow or down, the phone ranks phrases itself and says Listen mode is degraded.

**Privacy and consent**

- Before any phrase leaves the phone, you give permission. Then the partner sees a consent card each time listening starts.

- A light shows while Turn listens, and a switch keeps a partner under 18 from being heard.

- There are no accounts and no audio is recorded. Names become tags before a line leaves the phone. The privacy notice is also in the app.

**AI tools we used**

We built Turn with Claude Code and OpenAI Codex as coding agents, and Claude subagents drafted the evaluation lines, starter phrases, and labels. We set the direction, reviewed the work, and tested it on an iPhone and in the Simulator.

**Links**

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

**Wha## Inspiration**

Power users live in their clipboard. Email templates, standup replies, API snippets, that one link you paste five times a week — they end up scattered across Notes, Messages drafts, and random .txt files. I wanted the muscle memory of "copy → paste" without the archaeology of finding things. The constraint I set myself: saving must take under 5 seconds, retrieval under 2 taps. Everything else followed from that.

**What it does**

SnipStack is a single inbox for reusable snippets:

- Save anything reusable — text templates, links, images, files — with a title and loose tags. Four kinds, one place.

- Get it back instantly — live search across titles, content, and tags; pinned items and most-used snippets surface first.

- Two-tap retrieval — open a snippet, hit "Copy to clipboard", get haptic confirmation. A use-counter quietly shows which snippets earn their keep.

- Free vs Pro — the free plan holds 15 snippets (enough to feel the workflow). SnipStack Pro (monthly/yearly, powered by RevenueCat) removes the limit.

**How I built it**

- Expo + React Native (TypeScript)​ for a single iOS/Android codebase.

- Zustand + AsyncStorage for local-first, offline-by-default persistence — no account, no sync latency, nothing between you and your snippets.

- RevenueCat react-native-purchases drives the entire paywall: a pro entitlement, a default Offering with monthly + yearly packages, restore purchases, and real-time entitlement updates via addCustomerInfoUpdateListener. Gating happens exactly once — at the moment a free user tries to save snippet #16 — where the value is most tangible.

- React Navigation (native stack + bottom tabs), expo-haptics for tactile copy confirmation, and a fully custom light/dark theme.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Where to put the paywall. Hard-gating on app open converts worse and feels hostile. Gating at the 15-snippet limit means users hit the wall only after the app has proven its value — a monetization lesson RevenueCat's own content preaches.

- Speed as a feature. Search had to feel instant, so filtering runs in-memory over a denormalized store instead of hitting storage. Every interaction was budgeted: save ≤ 5s, retrieve ≤ 2 taps.

- RevenueCat in Expo. The SDK needs a dev build (no Expo Go), so the repo includes a DEMO_UNLOCK flag to iterate on paywall UI without a store connection.

**Accomplishments I'm proud of**

- The entire save flow really is under 5 seconds — I timed it.

- A clean, honest freemium line: the free tier is genuinely useful, and Pro is a clear upgrade rather than a ransom.

- Shipped as an open-source student project while juggling classes.

**What I learned**

- How RevenueCat abstracts StoreKit / Play Billing into one entitlement model, and how much faster that makes iterating on monetization.

- That "fast" is a design decision you enforce at every layer, not a performance pass at the end.

**What's next for SnipStack**

- iOS Share Sheet + Action Extension (save from any app without opening SnipStack)

- Home Screen / Lock Screen widgets with your top pinned snippets

- Global hotkey companion for iPad keyboard users

- Optional end-to-end-encrypted sync

**BillTrip**

**Inspiration**

The inspiration behind BillTrip came from the need to make travel planning and hotel booking more convenient, organized, and accessible. Many travelers face difficulties when searching for accommodation, managing booking information, and finding a simple platform that brings these activities together. We wanted to create a platform that could simplify the booking experience while giving users a smooth and user-friendly interface.

As a frontend developer, I was also inspired by the opportunity to apply my web development skills to a real-world problem and build a project that could grow into a useful travel solution.

**What it does**

BillTrip is a hotel booking platform designed to help users explore accommodation options and manage their booking activities through a web interface.

The project focuses on providing a simple and responsive experience where users can:

- Create an account and log in securely.

- Browse available accommodation options.

- View relevant hotel information.

- Manage their account details.

- Access booking-related features.

- Reset their password when necessary.

The platform is designed with usability, accessibility, and a clean interface in mind.

**How we built it**

We built BillTrip using a combination of frontend and backend web technologies.

- HTML — Used to structure the web pages.

- CSS — Used to style the interface and create a responsive design.

- JavaScript — Used to add interactivity and improve the user experience.

- Bootstrap — Used for responsive layouts and reusable interface components.

- PHP — Used for server-side processing, authentication, and application logic.

- MySQL — Used to store user and application data.

- XAMPP — Used as the local development environment.

- PDO — Used to establish a more secure connection between PHP and the database.

- SweetAlert2 — Used to provide user-friendly notifications and alerts.

We organized the project into reusable components, including configuration files, headers, footers, authentication processes, and helper functions. This made the code easier to maintain and allowed us to develop and test individual features more efficiently.

**Challenges we ran into**

During development, we encountered several challenges, including:

- Database connection and configuration: Setting up the database correctly and ensuring the application communicated with it properly required careful configuration.

- User authentication: Implementing registration, login, email verification, and password-reset functionality required attention to security and validation.

- Session management: Managing user sessions and displaying success or error messages without triggering alerts at the wrong time was challenging.

- Responsive design: Making the interface look good across different screen sizes required testing and adjusting layouts.

- Debugging: Identifying and fixing errors in PHP, JavaScript, and database queries helped us understand how different parts of the application work together.

We addressed these challenges through research, testing, debugging, and improving the structure of the code.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud of building a functional hotel booking platform that combines frontend design with backend functionality. Some of our key accomplishments include:

- Creating a responsive and user-friendly interface.

- Implementing user registration and login functionality.

- Connecting the application to a MySQL database.

- Adding email verification and password-reset features.

- Organizing the project into reusable and maintainable files.

- Applying security practices such as password hashing and prepared statements.

- Gaining practical experience building a full-stack web application.

Most importantly, the project helped transform our knowledge of web development into a practical application.

**What we learned**

Working on BillTrip taught us that building a web application involves more than creating attractive pages. We learned how frontend and backend technologies communicate, how databases support applications, and how important security and proper error handling are.

We also improved our understanding of:

- PHP and MySQL integration.

- User authentication and session handling.

- Form validation and data processing.

- Responsive web design.

- Debugging and troubleshooting.

- Organizing code for easier maintenance.

- The importance of testing features before deployment.

The project also strengthened our problem-solving skills and taught us to approach development challenges step by step.

**What's next**

Our next goal is to improve BillTrip and make it closer to a complete, production-ready travel platform. Future improvements may include:

- Adding a complete hotel search and filtering system.

- Integrating real-time hotel availability.

- Adding a secure online payment system.

- Implementing booking confirmation emails.

- Creating a user dashboard for managing reservations.

- Adding hotel reviews and ratings.

- Improving security and performance.

- Deploying the platform online for real users.

- Developing an administrator dashboard for managing hotels, users, and bookings.

We hope to continue improving BillTrip by adding features that make travel planning and accommodation booking easier and more reliable.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Last year, our teammate Johnathan came to France for the first time. He loves food, so one of the first things he wanted to do was try as many French restaurants as he could.

At one of the first restaurants he went to, he could not understand the menu. He tried Google Lens, and it translated the words, but a dish name translated word for word still does not tell you what the dish is, how it is cooked, or what is in it. So he called the waiter over, and the waiter started explaining the dishes to him, one by one. Halfway through, the waiter had to leave to look after another table, and Johnathan was left with half a menu explained and the rest still a mystery.

When he told us about it, we realised that what he needed was not a better translation. He needed what the waiter had started to give him: someone who knows the food, explaining each dish, and who does not have to leave for another table. That is what we set out to build with MenuLango.

While building it, we also noticed that many restaurants, especially in France, write part of their menu by hand, on a chalkboard (ardoise) or a sheet of paper, usually for the dish of the day. Those are often the most interesting dishes, and the hardest ones for a visitor to read, so we made sure MenuLango reads handwritten menus as well as printed ones.

**What it does**

MenuLango reads a photo of a restaurant menu and explains every dish on it. It works with printed and handwritten menus, and with menus that have several pages. The dishes appear on the screen one by one while the menu is still being read, so you can start reading long before the whole page is finished.

For each dish, MenuLango tells you what it actually is, in plain words. Ropa vieja, for example, is explained as slow-cooked shredded beef in tomato and peppers, instead of its literal translation, "old clothes." Opening a dish shows how it is made, with the cooking method and roughly how long and how hot, what it most likely contains, including allergens, and a rough estimate of the calories, protein, carbohydrates and fat in one plate. It also shows a photo of how the dish usually looks, from Wikimedia Commons, and a button that opens a Google Images search for more real photos. The "Help me choose" feature allows us to match dishes to your mood: something simple stays with familiar dishes, and something special looks for the ones that require more effort from the kitchen.

Local specialities. When a menu opens, MenuLango picks out the dishes that are hard to find outside that region and shows them at the bottom of the menu, under "Don't leave without trying." For someone who is only in a city for a few days, these are often the dishes they will remember.

Filters and search. You can narrow a menu to vegetarian, vegan, no pork, halal-friendly, kosher-friendly, no offal, nothing raw, not spicy, good for sharing, or local specialities. A filter only appears if it would actually change that menu, so you never see a "Vegan" button on a menu with no vegan dishes. You can also add your own words to avoid, such as "coriander," and they apply to every menu you open. The search works with names, ingredients and prices, so you can type "chicken" or "chicken under 20."

Prices. At the top of each menu, MenuLango shows how many dishes there are and the average price, so you know at a glance whether it is an expensive place. The "Budget" filter shows only the dishes at or below that menu's middle price. And if you turn on price conversion in Settings, every price also shows a rough amount in your own currency, using daily exchange rates for 166 currencies, so a traveller from Nigeria sees "21 € → ≈ ₦34,000" without doing the maths.

Ordering, and showing the waiter. When you are ready to order, you add dishes for each person at the table, with notes such as "no onions, please." MenuLango shows the total, the total in your own currency, and a rough nutrition estimate for each person. Then you tap Show the waiter. The screen switches to the restaurant's side: every dish appears with its name exactly as printed on their menu, and your notes are translated into their language on the phone itself, so the waiter can read the whole order at a glance. A switch at the top lets you flip between "For me," in your language, and "For the restaurant," in theirs.

Every menu is saved on your phone. The app is available in nine languages: English, French, Spanish, Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Russian and Hindi.

MenuLango Plus adds unlimited menus of any length, and three more things:

- Help me choose. When you can't decide, you tell MenuLango your mood, such as something new, something special, something you can only eat here, or something simple, and it suggests dishes as cards you can swipe through, for everyone at the table.

- A record of what you've eaten, so its suggestions keep showing you something new.

- Sharing a menu as a link. Usually only one person at the table has the app, so the link lets friends open the same explained menu on their own phones, look through the dishes themselves, and tell the person with the app what they want. It also gives them a real look at what MenuLango can do, which we hope makes them want to download it too.

**How we built it**

We built MenuLango with Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform, so the screens, the logic, the saved menus and the payments are written once and shared by the iPhone and Android apps. Only a few parts are written separately for each platform, such as the camera, the photo picker and saving backup files.

Our stack:

- App: Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform for iPhone and Android, with a thin Swift layer on iPhone

- Storage on the phone: SQLDelight

- Networking: Ktor

- Dependency injection: Koin

- Reading menus: Google's Gemini API (Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite)

- Translating notes on the phone: Google ML Kit, on both iPhone and Android

- Server: a Cloudflare Worker, written in TypeScript

- Protecting the server: Firebase App Check

- Payments: RevenueCat, with the App Store and Google Play

- Dish photos: Wikipedia and Wikimedia Commons

- Exchange rates: ExchangeRate-API

- Coding partner: Claude

Reading the menu.* A phone camera takes photos of 3 to 10 MB, which can take a long time to send on restaurant Wi-Fi or roaming data. So before a photo is sent, the app shrinks it to 1,536 pixels on its longest side, which brings it down to about 300 KB and gets the first dishes on screen much sooner. That size is still sharp enough for Gemini to read a menu clearly, and it also keeps each scan cheaper, because Gemini charges more to read a bigger image. Gemini then reads it and answers in a fixed format that we define, with the dish's name first. As the answer streams in, the app reads each dish the moment its entry is complete and shows it straight away. Each dish is checked before it is shown, and if the answer is cut off, every dish that arrived complete is kept.

Our server. The app talks to a small Cloudflare Worker that we wrote. Photos are kept in its cache for 30 days and exchange rates for 6 hours, so each is fetched once and shared by everyone. Because the instructions we give Gemini live on the server, we can improve how MenuLango reads a difficult menu without releasing a new version of the app. We have also added Firebase App Check, which confirms that a request comes from the real MenuLango app. It is running in monitoring mode now, and we will switch it on fully once the store versions are live.

Dish photos. We understood early on that the first thing people want to know is what they are about to put in their stomach, and nothing answers that like a picture. But for a student team, getting those pictures was hard. Taking our own photos was not possible: MenuLango reads menus in any language from anywhere in the world, so the dishes it might need to show run into the tens of thousands, across every cuisine, and as students in France, we could never order or cook, and photograph, even a fraction of them. Scraping photos from other websites raises copyright problems. Generating them with AI is slow and expensive, and makes the person wait. And whichever way we got them, we would then have to store all those photos and serve them to everyone, which costs money.

Wikipedia and Wikimedia Commons solved both problems at once. Their photos are free to use as long as the photographer is credited, which MenuLango does under every photo, and Wikimedia hosts them, so we do not have to store them ourselves. Our server only looks each photo up once and keeps a copy in its cache for 30 days, so it is fetched once and shared by everyone. For anything more, a button opens a Google Images search for that dish.

Payments. RevenueCat handles MenuLango Plus. Anyone can read three menus a month for free, with up to three pages per menu, and a free scan is only counted once you have actually seen the dishes. We chose the plans around how people actually use the app. Most travellers are only in a place for a few days, so the 7-day Trip Pass is a weekly subscription made for a single trip. The monthly and yearly plans are for people who have moved to a new country and eat out there regularly. Everything on the paywall, from which plans are shown to which one is highlighted and the headline at the top, comes from the RevenueCat dashboard, and the headline can be written separately for each language. This means we can try a different price or a different highlighted plan with a group of users, or show a different offer in a different country, without releasing a new version of the app.

Design. We designed MenuLango to be practical first, but we did not want it to feel boring. People come back to MenuLango every time they eat out somewhere new, and we want it to feel a little like opening something new each time, with warm colours, paper and fabric textures, and small moments of movement.

How we used AI. Claude wrote MenuLango's code. Our job was to decide what MenuLango should be and how every part of it should work, to explain that clearly, and then to read, question and test what Claude produced until it was right. That meant we still had to understand how Kotlin Multiplatform works: how the shared code reaches each platform, what has to be written separately for iPhone and Android, and why something worked on one phone but not the other. We were lucky that Victoria, on our team, already had experience building with Kotlin Multiplatform, so when something went wrong, we could understand why and steer the fix. Every feature, every wording and every decision in the app, from the privacy choices to how the halal-friendly filter stays safe, came from us. Claude turned those decisions into code.

**Challenges we ran into**

**1. Making a shared app feel like a native one**

This took more time than anything else. When you build an iPhone app in SwiftUI, a lot of motion comes for free: selections slide, lists animate when items are added, buttons react to your touch. With Compose Multiplatform, most of that is not there by default. A filter chip just changes colour, a new item just appears, a selection just jumps. Nothing is broken, but next to a native app it feels flat. So we built the motion ourselves into the tab bar, the paywall as we move from one card selected to another, the filter chips, the search bar, and the "words to avoid" section in the Settings.

**2. Reading real menus, not clean ones**

Real menus are messy, and busy ones caused our first big problem: long pages were being cut off halfway through.

When Gemini reads a menu, it writes its answer back piece by piece, and it charges for every piece, counted in "tokens." AI models also occasionally get stuck repeating themselves. So we set a limit on how much Gemini may write back for one page. That way, a single scan can never cost more than we expect. We already ask Gemini for at most 60 dishes per page, and we estimated that 60 dishes would fit in about 8,000 tokens, so that is where we set the limit.

But each dish is much more than a line of text. It has the name as printed, an explanation, how it is made, its ingredients, allergens, nutrition and price. On busy pages, our logs showed answers needing more than 10,000 tokens, so Gemini stopped in the middle of a dish, and the end of the menu was simply missing.

We raised the limit to 16,000. That fits the busiest page we have seen, with room to spare, while still capping the cost of a scan if something goes wrong. Because the limit lives on our server rather than in the app, the fix reached every phone straight away, without an app update. We also changed the app so that if an answer is ever cut off, it keeps every dish that arrived complete, instead of losing the whole page.

Prices were another problem, because menus write numbers differently from country to country. In France, "8,50 €" means eight euros fifty, with a comma where other countries use a full stop. In other places, "6.000 F" means six thousand, not six, because the full stop separates the thousands. Some dishes also list two prices, for a half and a full portion. We gave Gemini rules for all of this, so it reads each price the way that menu's country writes it. When a dish has more than one price, the app uses the lowest one for filters and totals, and still shows you the full price as it was printed.

**3. Halal, kosher and allergies**

This feature started with feedback. One of our classmates, who is Muslim, tried MenuLango and told us she often avoids restaurants when she travels, because she cannot tell which dishes on a foreign menu are likely to be halal. Knowing that would take away a lot of that worry. We added it for her, but also for everyone who wants to really try the food of a new country but does not feel confident enough to order.

For every dish, the AI model now answers more questions: does it contain pork, alcohol, shellfish, or meat served with dairy? We defined each one carefully. Pork includes lard, gelatine and pork stock. Alcohol includes wine or spirits used in sauces and desserts. Shellfish includes squid and octopus. Meat with dairy includes meat cooked in butter or served with cheese. These answers power the halal-friendly and kosher-friendly filters. How we keep them safe is described in the Safety section below.

**4. Backups on two platforms**

Because MenuLango has no accounts and no server that keeps people's data, there is nowhere for us to save someone's menus and picks for them. But people still need a way to keep them when they change phones. So we built a backup that people make and keep themselves: in Settings, you can choose the "Create backup" option, provide a passphrase, and MenuLango saves everything into one locked file that you can put wherever you like, such as your Google Drive, iCloud Drive or an email to yourself. On your new phone, you open that file in MenuLango, type the same passphrase, and everything comes back.

It took more work than we expected. The goal was to save menus' details and preferences, the dishes they had hidden, their picks and notes, or settings like Calm motion and we discovered whiles trying to do so that:

- Restoring is not just copying. The new phone might already have menus and settings, so we had to decide what wins. For food preferences, we keep the stricter choice from either phone. Your own marks on a menu on the new phone are kept, and tips you have already read do not appear again.

- iPhone needed a bridge. Our shared Kotlin code cannot open Apple's Share menu or file picker by itself, so it passes the backup to a small piece of Swift, which turns it back into a file and opens them.

- Things go wrong. A wrong passphrase, a damaged file, a backup from a newer version of the app, or a file that will not open each get their own clear message, instead of a general error

**5. Pick together only worked between phones of the same kind**

When friends eat together, usually only one of them has MenuLango open, and everyone else leans over to look at that one phone. So we built a feature called Pick together. One person opened a "table" on their phone, the others at the table found it from their own phones and asked to join, and once the host accepted them, each person could pick their own dishes on their own phone while the host's phone gathered everyone's choices into one order, live.

To keep it working without internet, which travellers often do not have, the phones talked to each other directly over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. Android and iPhone each have their own system for this: Google's Nearby Connections on Android, and Apple's Multipeer Connectivity on iPhone. Both worked well, but only with phones of the same kind. The two systems cannot talk to each other, so an iPhone and an Android phone could never find each other at the table.

Most groups of friends have both kinds of phone, and so does our own team. A feature that leaves out half the table did not feel right to release, so we turned it off for now.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Our teacher was most impressed by "Show the waiter." When we presented MenuLango in class, the part that stood out to our teacher was the full ordering flow: choosing dishes for each person at the table, adding notes, and then turning the whole order into the restaurant's own language so it can simply be shown to the waiter. This full flow is what makes MenuLango more than a way to read a menu: it takes you all the way from not understanding a single dish to actually placing your order.

- Our classmates asked for features, and we built them. The halal-friendly filter exists because a classmate told us what would make her more comfortable eating out abroad. Seeing someone want to use what we built, and shaping it around them, was the best part of the project.

- One codebase that feels like a native app on both platforms. The iPhone and Android apps are built from the same code, look the same and behave the same way, down to the animations, in nine languages. Making a shared app feel this close to a native one took most of our time, and we think it shows.

- It reads handwritten menus. Chalkboards and handwritten dishes of the day are often the most interesting part of a menu and the hardest for a visitor to read, and MenuLango reads them as well as printed ones.

- It respects people's privacy. There are no accounts, menu photos are never stored, nothing tracks what people do in the app, and backups can only be opened by the person who made them.

**What we learned**

For all of us, MenuLango was our first time building something that was not just an app, but a small business. We had to decide who it was for, what should be free and what people would pay for, and how to price something for a traveller who is only abroad for a week differently from someone who has moved abroad for years. That is where the 7-day Trip Pass, and the monthly and yearly plans, came from.

Because we are based in France, European privacy rules shaped the app from the very first day. Shipaton pushed us to actually understand them rather than hope for the best. We learned why we needed the paid tier of the Gemini API to serve people in Europe, why adding analytics would mean asking people for their consent first, and why we did not want an account system at all. We are grateful to RevenueCat for giving us a reason to learn this properly.

Kotlin Multiplatform taught us that sharing code between iPhone and Android saves a lot of work, but not all of it. The logic, such as reading menus, filters, saved menus and payments, was easy to share. The feel of the app was not. We had to build the motion by hand, one animation at a time, and check each one on both phones.

Getting an app into the stores was a lesson of its own. For the first time, we set up billing for the Gemini API, including our tax details in France. We paid for an Apple developer account and a Google Play developer account, created our subscriptions in App Store Connect and the Google Play Console, and connected them to RevenueCat. We ran out of time for Apple and Google to finish reviewing the app before the deadline, but we now understand the whole process from start to finish, and we are ready to launch MenuLango across Europe.

**A note on our submission**

We wanted to enter several Shipaton categories, all of which require the app to be live on the App Store and Google Play. We have submitted MenuLango to both stores, but Apple and Google were still reviewing it at the deadline, so it was not live in time. For this reason, we are submitting MenuLango for the Next Gen Award, which is judged on the demo video and our public code repository. We are confident that once the app is published, other people will love MenuLango the way our classmates did.

**What's next for MenuLango**

We have already paid for what we need to launch. We upgraded to the paid tier of the Gemini API, which allows MenuLango to be used by people in Europe, and we paid for our Apple and Google developer accounts. As soon as Apple and Google finish their reviews, MenuLango will be available on both the App Store and Google Play.

Before the official launch, we plan to open public testing, so that people beyond our classmates can try MenuLango and tell us what to improve. After that, our goal is to reach the people who need MenuLango most: travellers like Johnathan, people who have moved to a new country, and people with allergies or dietary requirements.

We also plan to:

- Let people share their picks. Today, only the person with the app can see the order. We want them to be able to send the list of dishes they picked to the rest of the table, so everyone can check their order before the waiter arrives.

- Bring back Pick together, for every phone. Instead of connecting the phones directly over Bluetooth, the person hosting the table will share a short code, and anyone at the table can join with it over the internet, whether they have an iPhone or an Android phone.

- Build our own library of dish photos. Today, a dish only has a photo if Wikipedia has one. With our own photos, many more dishes would have a picture, including local dishes that are not on Wikipedia.

- Start a MenuLango community. We want people to be able to share what they thought of a dish they ordered, so the next person reading that menu can benefit from their experience.

- Bring MenuLango into restaurants. We want to work directly with restaurants, so that when you sit down, you are invited to scan the menu, make your choices in MenuLango, and have your order sent straight to the waiter, in the same way that you can already pay at the table with a card.

- Make the free scans fairer. Today, the three free scans a month are counted on the phone, which means that clearing the app's storage resets the count. We plan to keep this count on our server instead.

- Let Plus move between iPhone and Android. Today, Plus is linked to your Apple or Google account, so if you buy it and later move to a new phone of the same kind, Restore purchases brings it back. What does not work yet is moving from an iPhone to an Android phone, or the other way round, because Apple and Google do not share purchases with each other. For the few people who switch, we will add an optional sign-in so their Plus can come with them. Everyone else will keep using MenuLango without an account, as they do today.

- Filter and search the way you would ask a friend. Today, filters are fixed buttons, and search understands dish names, ingredients and simple prices like "chicken under 20." We want people to be able to just type or say what they want, in their own words, such as "something light without meat, under 15 euros," "what's good for someone who doesn't like spicy food," or "a dessert to share," and have MenuLango narrow the menu to the dishes that fit. It would only use the menu already on the phone, so it can stay fast and private.

**Privacy by design**

We are based in France, and privacy shaped a lot of our decisions from the very first day. Our rule was simple: if we do not need someone's data, we do not collect it, and we do not store it.

- There are no accounts. For our current version of MenuLango, you never sign up, and you never give us an email address or a password. We decided this on day one, because an account would mean storing people's details on a server, and we did not need to. Your purchases are linked to your Apple or Google account instead: on iPhone, Plus follows your Apple ID, and on Android, it follows your Google account, so tapping Restore purchases brings it back on a new phone. We thought this made sense for MenuLango after confirming our hypothesis that very few people move between iPhone and Android. According to CIRP (Consumer Intelligence Research Partners, a US market research firm), about 87% of people who bought an iPhone in the US in early 2026 already had one, and about 86% of Android buyers stayed with Android.

- Your data stays on your phone. Your menus, your picks and notes, the people at your table and the dishes you have eaten are stored only on your phone, not on our server. The only thing our server ever stores is a menu you choose to share with your friends, and it is deleted automatically after 24 hours.

- We do not keep your menu photos. When you scan a menu, the photo goes through our small server to Gemini, only so that the menu can be read, and our server does not save it. This is part of why we pay for the Gemini API. Google's terms only allow the paid service for apps used by people in the EEA, Switzerland and the UK, and on the paid service, Google does not use what we send to improve its products..

- You hold your own backup. Instead of syncing your data to a cloud account, MenuLango saves everything into one locked file, protected by a passphrase you choose. It is locked with strong, standard encryption (AES-GCM, with the key made from your passphrase using 600,000 rounds of PBKDF2, which makes guessing the passphrase very slow). You save the file wherever you want, and we never see it or your passphrase. Because no server stores backups, this also costs us nothing to run.

- Your notes are translated on your phone. Notes such as "no nuts, please" are translated by the phone itself, not by a server.

- MenuLango never uses your location. It never asks for your location. The app works out where a menu comes from, such as its language and its currency, from the menu itself.

- There are no analytics and no tracking. In Europe, tracking what people do in an app requires their consent and careful handling of that data, so we decided not to do it. MenuLango has no analytics, no ads and no tracking. We will measure how the app grows through the number of installs and subscriptions.

- A random ID is only used to prevent abuse. When the app is installed, it creates a random ID. Our server only uses it to limit how many menus one phone can scan in a minute and in an hour, so that nobody can misuse the service. It is not linked to you, to your device or to any advertising.

- Shared menus contain nothing personal. When you share a menu with your friends, the link only includes the dish explanations, never your photo, your picks or anything about you, and it is deleted automatically after 24 hours.

**Safety and trust**

When people choose what to eat based on what an app tells them, the app has to be careful. These are the rules MenuLango follows:

- When MenuLango shows allergens, it tells you what a dish likely contains and what it may contain, and reminds you to ask the restaurant if you have an allergy. It never says that a dish is free of an allergen, because it cannot know for certain how the kitchen prepares it. Allergen information is always free and never behind the paywall.

- When you use the halal-friendly or kosher-friendly filters, MenuLango is judging each dish only from its likely ingredients. It cannot know whether a restaurant is officially certified as halal or kosher, or how the meat was prepared, so whenever one of these filters is on, the app says so and suggests asking the staff. The AI model is also told that whenever it is not sure whether a dish contains pork, alcohol, shellfish, or meat with dairy, it should answer yes. We would rather hide a dish that was fine than show one that was not.

- When the AI model does not recognise a dish, it leaves out the cooking method rather than inventing one, and the explanation is marked as a best guess, so you know to ask the waiter.

- When you see a dish photo, it is labelled as how the dish usually looks, because it comes from Wikipedia, not from the restaurant, and the plate you receive may look different.

- When you see a price in your own currency, it is marked with "≈," because it is based on that day's exchange rates and is not the exact amount your bank will charge.

**Accessibility**

We wanted MenuLango to work just as well for someone who uses a screen reader, or for someone who finds a lot of movement on screen uncomfortable.

- Everything you can swipe, you can also do another way. Every swipe in the app also exists as an action the screen reader can offer: deleting a saved menu, hiding a dish you are not interested in, and keeping or passing on a dish in Help me choose. Help me choose also has visible Keep and Pass buttons, and it tells a screen reader which card you are on.

- Changes on the screen are read out. When you tap a filter and the list changes, a screen reader says how many dishes are left, for example "7 of 20 dishes." The progress while a menu is being read, error messages and payment results are also read out as they happen, without interrupting what the screen reader is already saying.

- Selected filters do not rely on colour alone. When you select a filter, it changes colour and also shows a tick, so people who cannot tell the colours apart can still see which filters are on.

- Movement can be turned down in two ways. MenuLango follows the phone's own "reduce motion" setting, and it also has its own Calm motion switch in Settings, for people who want less movement in MenuLango without changing their whole phone. With either one on, screens change with a simple fade, the paper textures stop moving as you scroll, the small vibrations stop, the example hints in the search field stop changing, and new items simply appear instead of animating in.

- It works right to left, and in your own language. The whole app is translated into nine languages, and when it is set to Arabic, the layout flips to read from right to left. You can also choose MenuLango's language separately from your phone's language, for example to keep your phone in English while using MenuLango in French.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I wanted a puzzle app I would actually keep on my phone. Most of the ones I tried had a timer nagging me, an account I did not want, and, worst of all, puzzles that turned out to need a guess halfway through. A puzzle that needs a guess is not a hard puzzle. It is a broken one.

So the rule for Chalk was set before a single screen existed: every puzzle ships verified by computer to have exactly one solution, and the app never needs the internet, an account or your attention when you did not ask for it.

**What it does**

Nine games, drawn like chalk on a board. Five puzzle games you play alone: Sudoku, Nonograms, Quilt (shikaku), Stitch (a number path game) and Slitherlink, across 2643 puzzles arranged in ladders from small to large. Four board games for two: Tic Tac Toe, Four in a Row, Dots and Boxes and Hex, against a friend, against the computer, or between two phones.

The two phone part is the bit people stop me on. There is no server and no pairing code. The phones either find each other over the local network, or one phone plays a short chirp through its speaker and the other phone hears it and makes the move. It works on a plane.

Around that: a daily puzzle that is the same for everyone, streaks, your fastest times per size, home screen widgets, reminders, a share card, and nine languages. It is free, and one purchase removes the ads.

**How we built it**

Expo SDK 57 and React Native 0.86, in TypeScript, in about two and a half weeks from first commit to both stores.

The puzzles came first and the UI came last. Each game is a pure rules module with no React in it: the board is derived from a list of moves, undo is dropping the last move, and a wrong move comes back as a described problem ("this patch has to be 8 squares, not 12") rather than a boolean. Puzzles are generated by a throwaway script, then re-checked by an independent solver that counts solutions with a cap of two and a node budget. If the search does not finish, the puzzle is thrown away. The suite that checks the shipped data runs on every change.

State is one Legend State observable persisted to SQLite, with the writes coalesced and made async because the stock plugin was doing a synchronous disk write on every move. Animations are Reanimated 4, almost all of them mount and unmount transitions. The native pieces are Nitro Modules: I wrapped ggwave, the data over sound codec, as react-native-ggwave and open sourced it, and wrote a small module over Multipeer Connectivity and Nearby Connections for the wireless link.

Monetisation is RevenueCat with one lifetime entitlement. There is exactly one line in the app that decides whether someone has paid, and buying, restoring and the background listener all go through it. Whether ads show is persisted locally so the answer is right on the first frame and offline. The RevenueCat Test Store meant I could buy the unlock dozens of times during development without a payment sheet, which made the paywall the least stressful part of the app.

**Challenges we ran into**

Difficulty does not live where you think. I assumed sudoku difficulty was about which technique finishes a puzzle. Measured against the shipped ladder, it is clue count: a solver that counts branches finds almost every puzzle solvable by propagation alone. Every game's ladder came out differently, and every one would have been wrong if guessed.

An interaction has to be able to reach every answer. Quilt originally anchored drags on the number clue, which made puzzles with an interior number impossible to draw. The fix was in the generated data, not the UI: every clue now sits on a corner of its patch. A test now simulates the real gesture for every puzzle.

Sound is a modem, and modems have rules. Seven moves sent, six heard, no error anywhere. It turned out one ggwave instance cannot encode while it is decoding, and a send that landed mid-reception destroyed the incoming payload. Two instances fixed it. I also chose the audible band over "ultrasound" on purpose: 15 to 19 kHz is where phone speakers roll off hardest, and most people under 25 can hear it anyway.

No Intl.PluralRules on Hermes. Every i18n library needs a polyfill for the one thing I would ask it to do, so I wrote the plural rules for nine languages by hand and made the English catalogue the type. A missing key or an unfilled placeholder is now a compile error rather than a key drawn on screen.

Reanimated hides a view until its entering animation starts. 125 level tiles mounting inside a sheet that was itself still animating flashed up and vanished forever. That one cost a day and is now written down in the repo with the other traps.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

2643 puzzles, zero ambiguous ones. Every puzzle in the app was re-checked by a solver that is independent of the one that generated it, and the test suite refuses to ship one whose check did not finish. Nobody will ever hit a dead end in Chalk.

Two phones playing over sound, with no server. A move is six bytes and a quarter of a second of chirping. The wrapper that made it possible is open source as react-native-ggwave, so the next person does not have to find the lost move bug themselves.

Nine languages, done properly. Plural rules tested per language, and a suite that refuses Romanian written with the Turkish cedilla, because the two look identical in a diff and different on screen.

Shipped on both stores in under three weeks, with widgets, a daily puzzle, a share card and a paywall that worked the first time.

**What we learned**

Prove the data before drawing a pixel. Measure difficulty instead of guessing it. Check library APIs against the installed types, not the docs. And write down every trap the moment it is solved, because the second time is always in a hurry.

**What's next for Chalk: puzzles you can trust, two phones that talk**

Game Center and Play Games leaderboards are designed and not built. More languages, once the plural rules for them are tested. And real measurements of the sound link in a noisy room, which I have written the test plan for and not yet run.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**About the project**

Nordic Focus is a distraction-free Pomodoro app inspired by Scandinavian minimalism, Nordic soundscapes, and the feeling of watching a small world slowly come to life.

At first glance, it is a simple focus timer.
But behind the timer live two mysterious little creatures.
One feeds on food.
The other purifies water.

As users spend more time focusing, they earn Coins, their companion's affection increases, new dialogue is unlocked, and the world around the creatures gradually comes alive.

I designed Nordic Focus around one idea:
What if time spent focusing could become more than a number?
Instead of treating 25 minutes as just another statistic, Nordic Focus turns those 25 minutes into progress inside a small living world.

**Built for the Next Gen Award**

Nordic Focus is not just another productivity tool; it's a living diorama in your pocket. Submitted for the Next Gen Award, this app is fully developed, perfectly optimized for real iOS devices using StoreKit Sandbox, and ready to demonstrate a flawless RevenueCat ecosystem—even before hitting the App Store.

**Inspiration**

In today's hyper-connected world, maintaining deep focus can be surprisingly difficult.
Many productivity apps add more dashboards, notifications, statistics, social features, or visual stimulation in an attempt to keep users engaged.

I wanted to approach the problem from the opposite direction.
Inspired by Scandinavian minimalism and the calming atmosphere of Nordic landscapes, I designed Nordic Focus to be visually quiet and easy to understand.

The timer itself should not compete for attention.
The app should become almost invisible while the user works.
But I also wanted to answer a second question:

How can we make people want to return without turning productivity into pressure?
My answer was companionship and discovery.
The companions do not interrupt the user while they work. Instead, they quietly react to the user's focus.
A completed session gives Coins.

The selected companion accumulates focus time.
Affection levels increase at 25, 60, 120, and 240 minutes.
New messages then become available in the Fairy Archive, turning accumulated focus time into an unfolding story.

**A World That Grows With Focus**

The two companions are designed around completely different forms of "consumption."

🍓 Appetite Enhancer
This creature's hair is actually living slime.
It can wrap around food and swallow it.
It loves eating so much that when it first meets the user, its first thought is:
"You look... delicious."
It is kind enough not to eat the user, however.

Instead, it happily eats beside them while they work.
As the user's focus time increases, its messages slowly change from playful encouragement into attachment.

What begins as:
"I'll sit here while you work."
eventually becomes:
"I used to enjoy eating by myself. But now... it feels strangely quiet when you're gone."

💧 Appetite Suppressant

This creature's cloak is actually a network of plant roots.
The roots extend into the ground and absorb water.
Polluted water is purified through the creature and eventually returns to the environment as clean vapor, while flowers bloom around it.

It has spent a very long time performing this cycle alone.
At first, it simply accepts the user's presence.
But after many focus sessions, it begins to notice their absence.
"I spent a very long time working alone. Now, I notice when you are gone."

The relationship gradually becomes more personal without ever explicitly explaining what the creature is feeling.
The user discovers the story through the messages they unlock.

**What It Does**

- Distraction-Free Nordic Timer

The core experience is a clean Pomodoro timer with:
25-minute Focus
5-minute Short Break
15-minute Long Break
Custom durations
Quick presets
A 1-minute quick-test mode for demonstrations

I also added quick duration pills directly to the timer so that common durations can be selected without navigating into Settings. The quick-test mode makes it possible to demonstrate the full reward loop immediately during a hackathon presentation.

- Your Work Becomes Part of the Story

I wanted focus tracking to feel personal rather than purely numerical.
Users can select categories such as:

Math & Logic
Study & Reading
Work & Code
Creative & Hobby
Fitness & Health
Other

They can also create their own categories with a custom name and emoji.
Each completed Focus session automatically records time both for the selected category and the currently equipped companion. The data is persisted locally, so it remains after restarting the app.

This means the app can answer two different questions:
What did I spend my time on?
and
Who did I spend that time with?

The Categories tab visualizes total focus time, category breakdown, percentages, and the currently active category.

- Affection and the Fairy Archive

Every companion has an affection level based on accumulated focus time.
The progression is:

Level Focus Time
Acquaintance 0 min
Good Friend 25 min
Trusted Ally 60 min
Best Companion 120 min
Soulbound 240 min

As affection increases, new messages are unlocked.

These messages are collected in the Fairy Archive, where users can see:

Affection level
Total focus time
Progress toward the next level
Unlocked dialogue
Locked dialogue and its unlock condition
Message collection progress

The archive also includes the Categories view, turning the screen into a combination of story collection and personal focus history.
I also designed the message system as a data-driven catalog: adding a new dialogue entry to FairyMessagesCatalog automatically makes it available to the archive at the specified affection level.

- Focus Creates Visible Reactions

The companions do not simply swap between static images.

During a session, the Appetite Enhancer eats different foods, while the Appetite Suppressant absorbs water and grows flowers.

For example, the food sequence cycles through items such as apples, cinnamon rolls, pancakes, cloudberries, and blueberries. The animation was carefully timed so that the food is completely consumed before the companion transitions into its satisfied expression.

This makes the relationship between focus, character, and world visible rather than purely textual.

**Monetization & The RevenueCat In-App Economy**

Rather than gatekeeping essential productivity behind aggressive subscription paywalls, Nordic Focus utilizes RevenueCat (purchases_flutter) to power a balanced, ethical micro-economy:

- Earned Through Focus: Users naturally accumulate coins simply by completing Pomodoro sessions (+10 Coins per session).

- Consumable Coin Store (via RevenueCat): For users eager to instantly unlock premium companions or ambient soundscapes, we offer flexible consumable coin tiers:

- Handful of Coins (+100 Coins): $0.99

- Pouch of Coins (+500 Coins - Unlock Imp!): $3.99 (Most Popular)

- Chest of Coins (+1,200 Coins): $7.99 (Best Value)

- Fair Unlockables: Accumulated coins can be redeemed in the Nordic Shop to unlock additional elemental companions (e.g., Appetite Suppressant Imp for 300 Coins) and exclusive soundscapes (e.g., Glacier Stream BGM for 150 Coins).

**Small Details I Added to Make the World Feel Personal**

One part I especially wanted to avoid was making every visual asset feel like generic game decoration.
To add warmth and variation, I used photographs taken by myself and my family as source material, converted them into pixel art, and incorporated them into the app.

I also used photographs of real flowers as references and converted them into pixel-art patterns using MakeBead.
This gave the app a visual language that is partly designed and partly grounded in real things I have actually seen.

The result is intentionally a little more handmade than a typical productivity app.

**Audio as Part of the Experience**

Nordic Focus also treats sound as part of the environment rather than just background music.

Users can choose how ambient audio behaves around Focus and Break periods:

Always
Focus only
Break only

The selected behavior persists through Settings, and the audio state is coordinated with timer start, pause, resume, and break transitions.

I also integrated additional soundscapes into the same reward system, so users can unlock new ambient tracks through the Shop. Purchased soundscapes immediately become available from the main soundscape interface.

Audio credits and licensing information are also exposed in-app and documented in the repository.

**How I Built It**

- Flutter / Dart

- Riverpod

- just_audio

- RevenueCat / purchases_flutter

- shared_preferences

- Feature-based application architecture

- Flutter app + interactive GitHub Pages demo

The core state is separated into timer, audio, shop, focus statistics, category, companion affection, and message systems.

Focus statistics, category data, unlocked messages, and companion progress are persisted locally with SharedPreferences.

**Challenges We Ran Into**

- Making Character Animations Feel Like Real Characters

One of the more subtle problems was that the companion images did not all have the same proportions.
When a character changed from a normal pose to a larger eating or smiling pose, simply placing every image inside the same centered box caused the character's apparent size and position to shift.

I had to analyze the original image dimensions, establish a consistent scale, and pin every sprite to the same baseline so that only the upper part of the character changed position.

I also had to deal with image flickering during state transitions.
In the web demo, changing an image's src could temporarily display an old image at the new size. In Flutter, asynchronous image decoding could create a one-frame gap where the character disappeared.

I solved this by preloading the sprites and keeping the different poses available simultaneously, switching visibility instantly rather than repeatedly creating and decoding new images.

- The Web Demo and the Real iPhone Were Not Behaving the Same

One of the biggest practical lessons was that a browser demo and a real mobile device can expose completely different problems.

On the real iPhone, I encountered issues such as:

- Horizontal overflow in control bars

- Overflow in the Coin Store

- Overflow in the reward dialog

- Sprite flickering

- Incorrect timer duration synchronization

- Incorrect BGM behavior when pausing and resuming

For example, the reward dialog initially overflowed because long text such as "Appetite Enhancer Friendship" was competing for width with the level indicator. I had to redesign those rows using Expanded, Flexible, wrapping, and ellipsis handling rather than simply shrinking the entire UI.

The same process happened repeatedly:
observe the real-device bug → identify the layout/state cause → change the implementation → test again.

That iterative process became one of the most valuable parts of building the project.

- Synchronizing the App and the Demo

I wanted the GitHub Pages demo to feel like a real extension of the application rather than a static mockup.

That meant synchronizing features such as:

- Fairy Archive

- Categories

- Quick timer presets

- Reward dialogs

- Soundscape unlocking

- BGM behavior

- Character switching

The demo was updated alongside the Flutter implementation, and the project documentation records verification of the JavaScript syntax and deployment process.

- Designing the Animation Around the Artwork

Another challenge was not purely technical.

Because the companion artwork is hand-drawn and each pose has a slightly different canvas size, I had to make implementation decisions around the art itself.

Instead of forcing every image into an identical rectangle, I changed the rendering approach so the original image proportions were preserved with a uniform scale factor and a fixed baseline.

This is a small implementation detail, but it mattered because the artwork is one of the most visible parts of the app.

- Building a Monetization System Without Breaking the Reward Loop

RevenueCat was another area where implementation details mattered.

At one point, failed or cancelled purchases could incorrectly fall through to the success path and add Coins.
I traced that behavior to the purchase error handling and changed the logic so Coins are added only after a confirmed successful purchase.

This also required careful handling of StoreKit testing and fallback product lookup so the purchase flow could be exercised on a real iPhone during development.

**Accomplishments I'm Proud Of**

**A Productivity App With a Memory**

Nordic Focus remembers what the user did and what happened because of it.

A completed session can simultaneously affect:

Coins + Focus Category + Companion Affection + Story Progress

That made the timer feel less like a stopwatch and more like a living system.

**A Character System That Is Actually Extensible**

The companion dialogue was built as a catalog rather than hard-coded into individual screens, so new messages can be added without redesigning the archive system.

The same approach is used across other systems so that categories, audio, unlockables, and companion states remain separate and extensible.

**Real-Device Iteration**

The project was not only tested in a development environment.

I repeatedly tested the behavior on an actual iPhone and fixed issues that only became obvious on the physical device, including layout overflow, sprite transitions, timer synchronization, and audio state handling.

The final project walkthrough records a full-project static analysis result of 0 errors, 0 warnings, and 0 lints.

**What I Learned**

The biggest lesson was that restraint and depth are not opposites.

The UI can stay minimal while the underlying system becomes surprisingly rich.

A user might only see:

a timer, a little creature, and a few buttons.

Underneath that interface, however, the app is tracking categories, companion-specific focus time, affection levels, dialogue unlocks, persistent state, audio modes, purchases, and character animation states.

I also learned how important physical-device testing is.

A layout that looks perfectly reasonable in a simulator or browser can fail immediately on a real phone.

And perhaps most importantly, I learned that story can change the meaning of a productivity metric.

25 minutes focused is a number.

25 minutes that made someone in this little world a little happier is a story.

That is the idea I wanted Nordic Focus to preserve.

**What's Next for Nordic Focus**

I would keep this section shorter than your current one. The current "Apple Watch / cloud sync / seasonal bestiary..." list is fine, but the story-driven direction is stronger.

**A Larger Little World**

Future companions could introduce new environments, mechanics, and stories while keeping the same core loop:

Focus → Affect the world → Build a relationship → Discover the story

Potential future companions could be connected to auroras, forests, frost, sunlight, or other Nordic-inspired phenomena.

The companion archive could also eventually grow into a larger story collection, with hidden narrative fragments that only become visible after enough time has been spent with each creature.

**One thing I'd change about the overall submission**

Your original Project Story has a lot of feature inventory language:

"Flutter & Dart..."
"RevenueCat..."
"just_audio..."
"SharedPreferences..."

Those are useful, but they shouldn't be the thing the judges remember.

I would make the submission's narrative flow:

- Focus problem
↓

- Quiet Nordic design
↓

- Two strange companions
↓

- Focus changes their world
↓

- Affection unlocks story
↓

- Categories and archive make progress personal
↓

- Real-world photos/pixel art make the world yours
↓

- Real-device iteration makes the experience robust

That way, the technical implementation supports the story rather than competing with it.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Vybaa came from a simple frustration: people set goals with good intentions, miss a few days, and then feel like they have failed. Most productivity apps only show the missed days. They dont really help you understand what happened or how to start again.

We wanted to make something that feels more like having someone in your corner.

**What it does**

Vybaa helps people create goals, choose how they want to make progress, check in, and reflect on what is happening over time.

When the day goes badly, users can talk it through with a Rewind partner instead of just dismissing another notification. They can look back at their conversations and progress, notice patterns, and return to a goal without being punished for missing a day.

The idea is not to pretend motivation is always there. It is to help someone understand what is getting in the way and find a realistic next step.

**How we built it**

We built the mobile app with React Native, Expo and TypeScript, with a cloud backend for goals, progress, conversations and user data.

We used Google Gemini for the conversational experience. The conversations are designed to use the person’s own goals, check-ins and reflections instead of giving generic motivational messages.

We also used Remotion and real app screens to create the product video, adding narration, music and sound effects so the experience could be shown properly.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest part was keeping the experience personal without making it complicated. There are a lot of small states to handle: someone changing a goal, missing a day, coming back later, correcting a check-in, or continuing a conversation.

We also had to think carefully about carrying personal context safely between the app and the cloud. AI should help someone think, but it should not make important decisions for them or pretend to know more than it does.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud that Vybaa does not treat a missed day as the end of a goal. Starting again is part of the experience.

We are also proud of the Rewind flow and the way goals, conversations, reflections and progress fit together without turning the app into a complicated dashboard.

**What we learned**

We learned that progress is not always just a number. Sometimes it is understanding why you got stuck, being honest about how your day went, and finding one small next step.

We also learned that AI is much more useful when it has the right context and clear limits. A generic message is easy to generate, but a thoughtful response needs to be grounded in the person’s own story.

**What's next for Vybaa**

We want to make Vybaa better at helping people notice patterns across their goals and reflections, while keeping the experience calm and private.

Next, we are working toward deeper insights, better Rewind conversations, more flexible goal routines, and making it easier to come back after life gets messy.

You dont have to make progress alone.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

“Text me when you get home” is a small promise that carries a lot of care. But what happens when someone forgets to check in, their battery runs low, or the person waiting falls asleep?

We built SafeCircle to give that promise a clear plan. Before walking home, taking a rideshare, or meeting someone new, users can decide who should notice, when to check on them, and what information they are comfortable sharing.

The idea behind SafeCircle is simple: someone should notice—and you should choose who.

**What it does**

SafeCircle organizes personal safety around temporary Safety Sessions. Users choose a session type, destination, and expected-safe time, then check in or mark themselves safe.

Its safety engine evaluates conditions such as missed check-ins, overdue arrival times, and low battery. It explains why a session needs attention instead of claiming to know whether someone is in danger.

The project includes:

- A Guardian Circle with primary and backup contacts.

- Configurable check-in and escalation workflows.

- A Guardian Live web view for authorized session information.

- Safety Capsules containing information approved for sharing.

- Privacy controls for status-only, approximate, or precise-on-escalation sharing.

- SafeCircle+ subscriptions managed through RevenueCat.

Basic Safety Sessions and check-ins remain available without a subscription. SafeCircle is a hackathon prototype, and its remote delivery and background behavior require further real-world validation.

**How we built it**

We built the main app in native Android using Kotlin, Android Views, and Material Components. ViewModels, repositories, and separate domain engines organize session state, safety rules, escalation, and SafePhrase logic.

A FastAPI backend supports session synchronization and the Guardian web experience. WorkManager handles scheduled background tasks, while an offline event queue supports retrying updates after connectivity returns.

The project implements Android Keystore and AES-GCM encryption for local Safety Capsules, alongside expiring Guardian access tokens and privacy-scoped API responses.

We integrated RevenueCat to manage the safecircle_pro entitlement, hosted paywalls, subscription status, purchase restoration, and Customer Center. Monthly and yearly packages share the same entitlement.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest part was coordinating the traveler’s session with the guardian’s view. Starting, extending, escalating, and resolving a session all need consistent behavior across devices and intermittent connections.

Privacy added another challenge: guardians need useful information, but users should control when sensitive details become available.

We also had to separate essential safety functionality from premium customization. Subscription state should not prevent someone from checking in or marking themselves safe.

**Accomplishments that we’re proud of**

We turned a familiar everyday concern into a connected prototype with an Android experience, backend synchronization, a Guardian portal, and RevenueCat integration.

We are especially proud of the explainable session states and consent-based sharing model. Users can understand what changed and how their information is handled.

We also created a repeatable judge demonstration that walks through starting a session, showing concern, reviewing the guardian experience, and resolving the session.

**What we learned**

Personal safety software needs clear communication as much as automation. A missed check-in is a reason to ask for confirmation; it is not proof of an emergency.

We learned to design around delayed updates, offline devices, and session resolution from the beginning. We also learned that privacy must shape the workflow, permissions, and data shared—not just the settings screen.

**What’s next for SafeCircle - Someone Should Notice**

Our next priority is testing with travelers and guardians to understand whether session setup, alerts, and resolution are clear and useful.

We plan to validate background behavior across Android devices, test configured notification delivery, complete accessibility and security reviews, and refine subscription packaging through user feedback.

We also want to develop the iOS reference client further and evaluate family and recurring-commute workflows.

Our goal is to help people coordinate care through temporary, understandable safety plans that respect their choices.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every freelancer knows the feeling. The client call goes great, and then you lose your evening to a proposal: a blank document, a pricing table, a PDF that the client opens on their phone, squints at, and never answers. The work is won or lost in the gap between the call and the signed proposal, and that gap is mostly formatting.

The tools that exist were built for desktops and sales teams. Freelancers, studios and small agencies sell their own work, often from a phone, between jobs. They need something that keeps up with a conversation, not a template library that takes an afternoon to fill in.

So I set out to close that gap. MyProposer turns the notes you took on the call into a priced, branded proposal in about a minute. You send it as one link, the client picks a package and signs on their own phone, and the contract or invoice drafts itself from the deal you just won. The whole loop works from the phone in your pocket, before the client has finished their coffee.

**What it does**

- Paste your notes, AI writes the proposal. Strategy, scope, timeline and three priced packages, all editable.

- Your brand, not a form. Your colours, fonts and logo on every document, on the client's page and in the emails.

- One link, no attachments. The client reads it in a browser, picks a package, and signs on the spot.

- You know the moment it happens. Viewed, approved or declined arrives as a push notification, and revenue updates on the dashboard.

- Approved to contract in one tap. Parties, scope and agreed price are already filled in. Quotes, contracts and invoices work the same way.

- Send from your own Gmail address, export contacts, and manage everything in one pipeline.

**How I built it**

The mobile app is Flutter (Riverpod, go_router), and it talks to a Next.js API and web app backed by Firebase (Auth, Firestore, Cloud Functions, App Hosting). Most of the business logic lives in the API layer, so the phone, the web app and the public client pages all behave the same way.

RevenueCat runs the subscriptions. The app uses the RevenueCat SDK (purchases_flutter) for the Starter and Pro monthly plans: one offering, two packages, two entitlements. The RevenueCat customer ID is the Firebase user ID, so a RevenueCat webhook to my server maps a purchase straight to the right account and plan. Restore purchases and manage subscription are built in, and the app polls until the webhook has landed so the plan on screen is never stale.

Other pieces: FCM and APNs for push, Sign in with Apple, Resend for branded email, and a Remotion project for the store video. Over 700 automated tests run across the mobile and web code.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Deleting an account is harder than it sounds. Firestore doesn't cascade deletes, so removing a user leaves documents, contacts and even an OAuth token behind. Apple also requires deletion to start inside the app. I built in-app deletion that removes every owned document and subcollection, then sends a farewell email.

- One notification, two writers. Trial users got the same notification twice because both a Cloud Function and an API route wrote it. The fix was to make one place the owner.

- A cache that refreshed nothing. After a plan change the UI stayed on Free, because evicting the cache is not the same as making the provider refetch.

- Push that only looks healthy. iOS hands out a device token even if the user tapped Don't Allow, so a registered token proves nothing. I record the actual permission answer and set up the APNs key properly.

- One blue. The brand had drifted into several blues, one with a violet cast. I unified everything to the logo blue and built a contrast ramp so text stays readable at every size.

- The App Store. An early build was rejected for missing terms and privacy links on the paywall. Fixing it taught me to verify what the store shows instead of assuming.

- Sign in with Apple sends your name exactly once, ever. If you miss it on the first sign-in, it is gone, so the capture has to be right the first time.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

A real end-to-end loop: an AI-drafted proposal, opened and signed by a real client on their phone, arrives as a notification, and the approval turns into a contract in one tap. It launched on Google Play on August 29 and is now live on the App Store too, with RevenueCat subscriptions behind it, and I tested it on physical iPhones rather than just the simulator.

**What I learned**

Payments and store rules shape the product as much as the code does. I also learned to treat "it looks healthy" with suspicion: a green status can hide a total failure, and the only proof is watching the real thing work on a real device.

**What's next**

Account linking across Apple, Google and password sign-in, Outlook and iCloud Mail sending, and CRM sync.

</details>
