<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/178/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/178/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/177/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/177/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/176/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/176/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/174/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/174/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/173/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/173/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/175/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/175/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/799/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/799/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

A friend sat three CLEP exams on the strength of a blog post that said they were
"widely accepted". They were heading to a UC. The University of California
awards no CLEP credit whatsoever — not reduced credit, not elective credit,
none. Nobody had lied to them. The blog post was true somewhere else.

That is the whole problem in one sentence: transfer-credit advice is written
nationally and enforced locally, and a student cannot tell which sentence applies
to them until after they have paid.

The number that decided it: the same three exams that are worth $0 at UC
Berkeley clear three of the five general-education requirements at the
University of Florida, dropping what that student still owes from $2,505 to
$1,002. Same exams. Same scores. Same week.

**What it does**

You answer a few quick questions, one per screen — year in school, rough field,
what you can spend, whether you qualify for a fee waiver — pick a state and a
campus, and say which credit you already hold. Degree Route
then prices the requirements you still have to clear, at that campus's own
per-unit rate, and shows three ways to clear them:

- Cheapest — the least money, however many terms it takes

- Fastest — exams instead of semesters

- Lowest risk — only credit backed by statute or a published campus policy

From a first-year at UT Austin with nothing banked:

Do nothing
Cheapest route
Saving

UT Austin (Texas Core, 42 SCH)
$12,600
$875
$11,725

UC Berkeley (Cal-GETC)
$17,825
$969
$16,856

University of Florida (GE Core)
$2,505
$487
$2,018

Then the part that matters more than the saving: every claim on screen carries
its provenance — a source URL, the date it was last read, and a confidence
level. Anything unconfirmed is badged in amber and excluded from the lowest-risk
route by construction, not by convention.

The plan is a map, not a verdict. Tap any requirement to see every other credit
that campus accepts for it, swap it, or say you are handling that one yourself —
the engine re-plans and re-prices on the spot, and the plan persists on the
device.

When you are ready, export an advisor packet: a printable page listing every
row, every source, and — set apart at the top — the specific rows an advisor
needs to confirm. There is a second version framed for a parent or guardian, with
the same evidence and the same unconfirmed rows still marked. Softening those
for a parent would be exactly the dishonesty the document exists to prevent.

**How we built it**

Expo SDK 57 / React Native 0.86 / React 19.2, TypeScript in strict mode, no any.

The core is a pure planning engine with no React in it — it takes a dataset
and a student, and returns routes. That boundary is why it can be tested in Node
with no renderer, and it is where the real correctness work lives: one credit can
only be spent once (AP English Literature clears 1A or 3B, never both), an exam
that clears two requirements is charged once, and a route's unmet requirements
are priced back in so a plan that clears less can never look cheaper than it is.

The dataset is typed TypeScript modules rather than JSON, so a malformed row is a
compile error. It currently holds 79 public campuses across three states, 25 requirement
areas, 113 credit sources across eight credit families — AP, IB, Cambridge A
Level (what Florida calls AICE), CLEP, DSST, DLPT, community-college courses and
third-party providers — and over 5,000 acceptance rules. That is every
family in Florida's credit-by-exam statute still being sat today, plus the two that
are not exams at all.

Coverage is deliberately two-tiered and the app never blurs them. Campus-level
planning — the part that produces a number — is California, Texas and Florida.
On top of that sits a statewide layer: 25 of the 51 US jurisdictions carry
their actual statewide transfer rule (Ohio Transfer 36, the Illinois
Articulation Initiative, the Michigan Transfer Agreement, Missouri's CORE 42,
Arizona's AGEC…). That rule applies to every public campus in the state at once
and is usually the most valuable thing a student can be told. The remaining 26
say honestly that we have not confirmed one.

RevenueCat powers the one-time advisor-packet unlock on both platforms:
react-native-purchases + react-native-purchases-ui (Paywalls and Customer
Center) on device, @revenuecat/purchases-js (Web Billing) on the web. Metro's
platform resolution picks the implementation, so nothing in the app knows which
one it got. With no key configured the app still runs end to end and the paywall
simply reports that purchases are unavailable — it does not crash and it does not
hide anything.

57 tests, and the ones worth naming are invariants rather than examples: no
campus can be handed another state's requirements; every rule points at rows
that exist, in the right framework; every campus in the country plans without
producing a negative saving or spending a credit twice.

**Challenges we ran into**

Every interesting bug was a wrong number that looked right.

An early build showed the lowest-risk route as the biggest saver — "$0, saves
$9,933, clears 0 of 10" — because saving was computed as baseline − cost, which
credits a route for everything it never touched. An empty plan is the cheapest
plan. Savings now count only what a route actually clears.

The engine invented policy. For a campus/exam pair we held no rule for, it
emitted "UC Berkeley counts this toward your degree" — a sentence no source
supported. It now says "We have no record of how UC Berkeley treats this," which
is less satisfying and true.

AP mappings were guessed and the guesses cost money: AP Biology clears 5B and
the 5C laboratory, so students were being sent to sit a lab they had already
satisfied. Fixing it meant satisfies_area: string had to become
satisfies_areas: string[], because "and" and "or" are genuinely different
things and a single field cannot hold both.

Going national surfaced the nastiest one. effectiveCost zeroed community-college
fees for any waiver-eligible student — correct in California, which has the
College Promise Grant, and wrong in Texas and Florida, which have no statewide
equivalent. It would have under-priced every route in those states, in the
student's favour: the direction a wrong number never gets caught, because
nobody complains that they saved too much. The waiver is now a property of the
jurisdiction.

And one that ate an afternoon: Metro inlines process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_* at
transform time and caches the result, so changing the RevenueCat key and
rebuilding silently baked the stale one into the bundle. The key read as an empty
string through several rebuilds. build:web now passes --clear.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The app tells you when it does not know. In Texas and Florida the
lowest-risk route comes back empty, and says so: "We have not yet confirmed any
credit for UT Austin against its own published policy, so there is nothing here
we would stake your money on." We could have made those states look as strong as
California by relaxing one confidence level. The whole product would have been
worth less.

Going from one state to three cost two lines of engine change, because
scoping is a data invariant rather than a filter — a requirement names the
systems that require it, so a Texas campus cannot reach a Californian
requirement even though both live in the same array. A test asserts it rather
than trusting it.

And the thing we would ship even if nothing else survived: a student who has
already spent $285 on the wrong exams is told so, on the first screen, before
they are asked for anything.

**What we learned**

Statewide law is worth more than any campus's policy page, and no campus page
will ever tell you about it — because it is not theirs to give. Texas Education
Code §61.822 says a completed 42-hour core transfers as a block the receiving
university must substitute. Florida §1007.23 has guaranteed AA holders
university admission since 1972. Those two sentences are worth more to a student
than every exam on their plan put together, and they surface above the routes
now, not beneath them.

We also learned to read the limits as carefully as the promises. Florida
guarantees admission to a state university — not the one you want. The app says
that in the same breath as the guarantee.

**What's next for Degree Route**

- Read Florida's Rule 6A-10.024 equivalency table. One binding document that
every public institution in the state must follow. Reading it flips every
Florida AP and CLEP row from "needs confirming" to statute in a single pass,
and turns Florida's empty lowest-risk route into the strongest demo in the app.

- Promote the statewide layer from needs_check to statute. All 25 rules
are one document away each. Ohio Transfer 36, Illinois IAI, Michigan MTA and
Missouri CORE 42 cover the largest student populations.

- Campus pricing for those states, in the same order.

- Third-party credit providers (Sophia, Study.com, Saylor, StraighterLine,
TEEX, Modern States) are listed with price, who recommends them and — the
field that actually decides their worth — whose transcript the credit lands
on. UC publishes a refusal for all of them, so a UC-bound student is told
before they subscribe. See docs/CREDIT-SOURCES.md. There are also some courses with ACE recommendations for transfering to colleges, but not implemented in the app yet.

- Out-of-state coursework. A student who studied in one state and is heading
to another is currently told to retake requirements they may already hold. The
app can now show them both states and still cannot connect them — which got
more pressing with three states in the dataset, not less.

- Community colleges as destinations, which matters most in Florida, where
the statutory guarantee attaches to the Associate in Arts rather than to the
university.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/381/518/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/381/518/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**The Problem**

Studying often becomes a cycle of reading, practicing, forgetting, and not knowing what to study next. Students can spend hours studying without knowing which concepts they actually understand and which ones are holding them back.

**Our Idea**

StudyForge was built around one simple question:

What should a student study next?

Instead of treating every student the same, StudyForge creates an adaptive learning loop:

Learn → Practice → Measure → Detect Weakness → Adapt → Improve

A student starts with a topic. StudyForge breaks it down into understandable concepts, teaches them through Learn Mode, generates practice questions, evaluates their answers, identifies weak concepts, and uses that information to guide what they should study next.

**What We Built**

StudyForge combines:

- Topic Forge — turn a topic into a structured learning path.

- Learn Mode — beginner-friendly explanations, examples, formulas, reasoning, and common mistakes.

- Adaptive Practice — practice based on the student's current learning state.

- Weakness Detection — identify concepts that need more attention.

- Adaptive Learning — recommend what the student should focus on next.

- Progress Tracking — measure mastery and improvement over time.

- Theme Studio — personalized study environments.

- Bug Finder & Bug Shield — reliability features designed to detect and recover from problems.

**The Experience**

A student can enter a topic such as Matrix Inverse, learn the concept, practice it, receive an evaluated result, and see their mastery update. If they struggle, StudyForge can identify that weakness and adapt the next learning step.

The goal isn't simply to give students more questions.

The goal is to help them know what to learn next.

**Why StudyForge**

We wanted to build something that feels less like a static study website and more like a learning system that responds to the student.

StudyForge turns performance into feedback, feedback into adaptation, and adaptation into a personalized path toward mastery.

Learn smarter. Practice better. Turn weak spots into strengths.

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/578/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/578/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/579/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/579/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/584/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/342/584/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**What it does**

Michizure splits trip costs for the trip you are actually on. There are no accounts: a room is a URL plus a passphrase that you send separately. Once a room is open on your phone it keeps working with no signal — every change is saved to the device first and sent to the server afterwards — and it syncs when signal returns. The server stores only ciphertext and thin metadata.

The demo video (75 seconds, on an Android phone) shows the offline path: airplane mode on, an expense added, airplane mode off, and the room returning to "saved". Then the one paid feature — exporting the room's expenses and settlement as CSV, gated behind a one-time purchase powered by RevenueCat. The app's interface is in Japanese.

**Choices we made on purpose**

- No accounts. Nothing to sign up for and nothing to lose but the passphrase. The price is that we cannot recover a lost one.

- Encryption happens in the browser. The key is derived from the passphrase (PBKDF2, 600,000 iterations) and never sent. The passphrase is generated by default: five words from a 1,024-word Japanese list.

- Conflicts are surfaced, not guessed at. Expenses added on each side merge automatically. When two devices change the same expense, the app shows both versions and asks — and until you choose, that device sends nothing to the server.

- Money is divided in whole yen. The remainder is assigned, not rounded away: ¥100 between three people is 34/33/33, and every device agrees on who carries the extra yen.

**How it is built**

TypeScript with no UI framework (an esbuild bundle), a service worker that caches the app shell so it reloads with no network, and Cloudflare Workers with one Durable Object per room on the server. The native shell is Capacitor; we built and launched both the iOS and Android shells to confirm they run — iOS in the Simulator, Android on real hardware, which is also where the demo video was recorded. Apache-2.0.

**How RevenueCat is used**

The hard part of monetization here is not checkout — it is that the app has no accounts, so there is no user to attach an entitlement to. Attaching it to the room would make the server store "this room is paid"; introducing accounts would undo the premise of the product. We attach it to the device, with a Restore button, and keep paid features to things the device can decide by itself. The RevenueCat SDK runs in the native shell only and is lazy-loaded; the web build never touches it.

In this submission the purchase is configured against RevenueCat's Test Store, as the video shows, so no real-money purchase is possible. The app is not released to any store yet, and the RevenueCat keys are not in the repository.

**What we are honest about**

The README lists these in full; the ones that matter most:

- A lost passphrase cannot be recovered, and a device that has opened a room keeps its contents and key in plaintext in local storage.

- You cannot verify the encryption yourself: we serve the JavaScript that does it.

- Metadata is visible to the server, and Cloudflare keeps request data including IP addresses.

- Room creation is unauthenticated and its rate limit is weak: in a production test on 2026-09-18, about 195 consecutive requests never received a 429. We plan to replace it with a Durable Object counter after submission.

- The connection indicator does not probe reachability.

**What we learned**

We audited every factual claim in the README against the code, with a second reader trying to refute each finding. It found things we had written wrongly — including a limitation we had already fixed, and a rate limit we had described as working when it did not.

Built by waiteu. Source code: https://github.com/waiteu-git/michizure

</details>

## 351. MindMaze

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

MindMaze started with a simple question: how can we discover what people really think but rarely say out loud?

There are thoughts we keep to ourselves because they feel too personal, too unusual, or simply difficult to bring up in everyday conversation. Sometimes, just discovering that someone else thinks the same way can make us feel less alone. At other times, we want to know what other people genuinely think or wish for, especially in relationships, but those honest perspectives can be difficult to hear directly.

I wanted to create a place for those hidden perspectives.

At the same time, I did not want MindMaze to become another social media app where people compete for followers, likes, or attention. I wanted the incentive to be different: contribute something meaningful if you want to discover something meaningful from someone else.

That idea became MindMaze.

**What it does**

MindMaze is an anonymous social app built around a simple exchange:

Post one perspective, discover one perspective from someone else, and rate it.

The app has two modes: Thoughts and Wishes.

Thoughts is a place to share honest opinions, feelings, experiences, and ideas that people may not normally say out loud.

Wishes focuses on what people genuinely want from others, particularly in relationships and social interactions.

MindMaze deliberately avoids endless scrolling. Posting gives you the opportunity to discover another person's post, and after receiving it, you must rate it from 0 to 100 before continuing.

The rating system is also part of a larger idea: improving the quality of what people contribute.

MindMaze calculates a user-level score from the ratings their posts receive. Its matching algorithm then uses that score when selecting posts for the user. In other words, how your posts are rated influences the kinds of posts you are more likely to discover next.

This creates an incentive that is very different from likes or follower counts. Ratings are not about publicly displaying popularity. They help create a private feedback loop in which contributing something valuable can lead to discovering something valuable.

**How we built it**

MindMaze is my first app.

I built it using React Native, Expo, TypeScript, Supabase, RevenueCat, ChatGPT, and Cursor.

When I had the idea for MindMaze, I decided I wanted to turn it into a real app. While figuring out how to make that happen, I discovered Shipaton and decided to take on the challenge. From the initial idea to submitting MindMaze for App Store review, the entire journey took about one week.

Because I started with very little app development experience, AI became an important part of my development workflow.

I used ChatGPT extensively to discuss product design, reason through architecture and edge cases, learn unfamiliar concepts, and plan implementation and testing.

I used Cursor to help inspect, write, debug, and verify the actual code and backend changes.

AI accelerated the implementation, but I still had to decide what MindMaze should be. I designed the product concept, interaction rules, monetization model, rating and matching system, and user experience, and repeatedly tested the resulting behavior on a physical iPhone.

When something did not behave as intended, I went back through the design, investigated it with these tools, changed the implementation, and tested it again.

The app uses Supabase for authentication, the database, server-side logic, and access control. The backend manages profiles, posts, ratings, discovery state, matching, blocking, reporting, moderation, daily limits, and Premium access.

As part of Shipaton, I integrated RevenueCat to build MindMaze Premium. Rather than treating the subscription requirement as a separate feature added just for the hackathon, I wanted Premium to fit naturally into the product.

MindMaze Premium unlocks:

- Wishes

- History

- Increased daily posting limits

I implemented monthly and yearly subscriptions, purchase restoration, entitlement handling, and a webhook that synchronizes subscription events with the backend.

One important design decision was not to rely only on the client to decide whether someone is Premium. Features such as access to Wishes and higher posting limits are also enforced on the backend using subscription state synchronized through RevenueCat.

I also separated the development and production environments and tested the complete production flow on a real iPhone before submitting the app to the App Store.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge was time.

This was my first experience developing an app. I had the idea for MindMaze, decided to build it, and discovered Shipaton while figuring out how to turn the idea into a real product.

I decided to take on the challenge and bring the app from an idea to App Store review in about one week.

That meant learning how mobile app development works while simultaneously designing, building, testing, monetizing, and preparing a real application for the App Store.

I decided to fully commit to it.

AI tools made it possible for me to move much faster than I could have on my own, but moving faster also meant I had to be careful not to confuse generated code with a finished product.

I still needed to understand what behavior I wanted, identify edge cases, verify changes, test them on a real device, and make the final decisions when different approaches were possible.

Along the way, I had to deal with many things I had never encountered before:

- Authentication

- Database design

- Row-level security

- RevenueCat subscriptions and webhooks

- Production environments

- TestFlight

- App Store Connect

- Account deletion

- Moderation

- Release testing

Getting a subscription to appear in an app is one thing. Making sure purchase, restore, expiration, client-side entitlement state, and backend authorization all remain consistent is another.

I spent significant time testing those flows on the actual production build rather than stopping once the paywall worked.

The interaction model itself also created difficult edge cases.

MindMaze is not a normal feed. A user can have an unrated post waiting for them, an unused discovery from a previous post, no eligible post currently available, a daily posting limit, or a change in Premium status. Thoughts and Wishes also have independent state.

All of these states need to work without letting users:

- Skip required ratings

- Repeatedly see the same post

- See their own posts

- Lose an earned discovery

- Bypass Premium restrictions

Another major challenge was designing the system around quality rather than simply quantity.

Anonymous apps can easily encourage low-effort content, so I spent a lot of time thinking about how the product itself could give users a reason to make better contributions.

That led to the rating and matching system that became one of the core ideas behind MindMaze.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

What I am most proud of is getting MindMaze all the way from an idea to App Store review.

This is my first app. I had the idea for MindMaze, decided to turn it into a real app, discovered Shipaton, and took on the challenge.

In about one week, I went from an idea to submitting MindMaze for App Store review.

I am proud not because I wrote every line without help, but because I learned how to use the tools available to me to turn an idea into something real.

ChatGPT and Cursor dramatically accelerated the process, but there was still a long chain of decisions between "I have an idea" and "I have submitted an app."

I had to define the product, decide which features mattered for v1, work through unexpected behavior, test repeatedly, configure production services, integrate monetization, and keep pushing until the app was actually ready to submit.

In about one week, MindMaze went from an idea to a functioning production app with authentication, subscriptions, backend authorization, moderation, account deletion, matching logic, and a tested production environment, and finally to App Store review.

I am also proud that I did not simply build an anonymous posting app.

A central design goal was to think about incentives.

If users can consume unlimited content regardless of what they contribute, there is little reason to put effort into a post.

MindMaze instead connects contribution and discovery, and its matching algorithm creates an additional incentive:

The quality of what you contribute can affect the quality of what you discover.

There is still much more I want to do with this idea, but creating that foundation in v1 is one of the parts of MindMaze I am most proud of.

**What we learned**

Building MindMaze changed my understanding of what it means to build software.

One of the biggest things I learned was how powerful AI-assisted development can be for someone entering an unfamiliar field.

ChatGPT and Cursor allowed me to learn and build at the same time.

Instead of spending weeks learning every technology before starting, I could encounter a real problem, understand what I needed, work through it, test the result, and move on to the next one.

At the same time, I learned that AI does not remove the need for judgment.

A feature is not finished just because code was generated or because it works once.

I had to think about what happens:

- After restarting the app

- When a subscription expires

- When there is nobody eligible to match with

- When a user blocks someone

- When an account is deleted

- When the client and backend disagree about state

I also learned the importance of designing incentives.

For MindMaze, the most interesting question became not just:

"How do I let people post anonymously?"

but:

"How do I make people want to contribute something worth reading?"

That question influenced the one-post-for-one-discovery structure, mandatory ratings, user-level scores, and the matching algorithm.

RevenueCat also taught me that monetization is not just about putting a paywall in front of a feature.

I had to think about the complete subscription lifecycle: purchase, restoration, entitlement state, backend authorization, webhooks, expiration, and how all of those pieces remain consistent.

Because RevenueCat was a core requirement of Shipaton, it pushed me to implement monetization in my very first app. What began as a hackathon requirement became an important part of learning how a real production app works.

Most importantly, this project showed me how much can be accomplished in about one week when I combine strong commitment with tools that allow me to learn and execute quickly.

**What's next for MindMaze**

Submitting v1.0 is only the beginning.

The current version already creates an incentive to make better posts through ratings and matching, but I have more ideas for strengthening that loop.

I want to introduce features that make users actively want to improve the quality of their next contribution, rather than treating posting as merely the price of seeing another post.

Some of those ideas are already designed conceptually, but I deliberately kept them out of v1 so I could focus on making the core experience reliable first.

After launch, real usage will help determine which of those ideas should come next.

I also want to continue improving matching, moderation, safety, and the overall discovery experience as the community grows.

The long-term goal is to make MindMaze a place where anonymity does not reduce the quality of conversation, but instead makes it possible to discover perspectives that people would otherwise never share.

The core idea will remain simple:

The more meaningful your contribution, the more meaningful your discovery can become.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**IELTS Speaking Go**

**Why We Built It**

When I first started to look for IELTS Speaking practice materials, I quickly realized that most tutors were far more expensive than I expected.

So I turned to free LLMs like ChatGPT or Qwen, but almost every time they gave me a band 6.0. Why? Because that reflects the average candidate level, and giving a more conservative score is the safest way for an LLM to avoid unreliable results.

So I thought:

Why don't I build the tool I actually need?

Together with one of my best friends, we decided to build IELTS Speaking Go — an AI-powered IELTS Speaking examiner that makes speaking practice more accessible, affordable, and convenient.

**What We Built**

IELTS Speaking Go lets you practice IELTS Speaking anytime, anywhere with an AI examiner.

It supports more than 5 languages, allowing learners to interact with the app in the language they are most comfortable with.

But it doesn't just give you a score.

It analyzes your speaking performance across areas such as:

- Fluency and coherence

- Vocabulary

- Grammar

- Pronunciation

- Pauses and hesitation

It also identifies grammatical mistakes and provides practical feedback to help you improve.

The goal is simple:

Give IELTS candidates a way to practice speaking without having to pay for a tutor every time they want to practice.

**How We Built It**

We built IELTS Speaking Go by combining AI, speech recognition, language models, and IELTS-specific evaluation criteria.

The system processes a learner's speech, generates a transcript, analyzes their speaking performance, and produces structured feedback.

Behind the scoring system is an AI pipeline designed around IELTS examiner scoring criteria and high-band speaking samples.

We also built our own evaluation and retrieval system so that the feedback is grounded in IELTS-specific criteria rather than being just a generic AI conversation.

Our goal wasn't simply to make an AI that sounds intelligent.

We wanted to build an AI that actually helps students practice.

**The Challenges**

One of our biggest challenges was making the AI scoring feel consistent with real IELTS evaluation.

Any AI that supports voice input can easily generate a convincing-looking IELTS score, but that doesn't necessarily mean the score is useful. Most of the LLM models are able to "score" you, but most of them choose to give a band 6.0. This is due to the lack of official scoring materials and reliable data. And since most of the existing online models don't have a word-level timestamp feature, they can not give accurate pronunciation and fluency scores.

So we had to work on how the system interprets:

- Fluency and hesitation

- Grammar mistakes

- Vocabulary usage

- Pronunciation

- Pauses and speaking rhythm

- Differences between IELTS Speaking Parts 1, 2, and 3

Another challenge was making the experience fast enough to feel natural while still providing detailed feedback after each practice session.

We also had to build the entire product experience around speech — from recording and transcription to analysis, scoring, and presenting feedback in a way learners can actually understand.

**What We're Proud Of**

We're proud that we went from an idea we personally needed to a working app that people can actually use.

We:

- Gathered all the reliable materials online

- Built a database of speaking test mock tests

- Worked on data clustering to better assess fluency and hesitation

- Fine-tuned an LLM model to adapt to the real needs of students

- Reviewed the IELTS official criteria carefully

- Made the LLM assessment more reliable

- Added grammar correction features

- Added multi-language display support

We realized that:

Although AI is strong, there's still a lot of work for us to do. But it truly accelerates our speed of learning.

**What We Learned**

Building IELTS Speaking Go taught us that building an AI product is about much more than connecting an LLM to an app.

The difficult part is turning a model's general intelligence into something reliable, measurable, and useful for a specific problem.

We learned how important it is to combine AI models with domain-specific knowledge(in this case, linguistics), evaluation criteria, structured data, and real user feedback.

We also learned that sometimes the best product ideas come from a problem you are personally frustrated by.

Instead of asking:

"What can AI do?"

we started with:

"What if I could build the solution I needed—and make it available to others too?"

**What's Next for IELTS Speaking Go**

IELTS Speaking Go is just the beginning.

In the future, we want to expand beyond IELTS and support more language proficiency and language-learning exams, e.g., TOEFL, DELE, DELF, JLPT, etc., helping learners prepare for different exams with AI-powered practice and personalized feedback.

But our vision goes beyond exam preparation.

We want to build the largest community for language exam learners — a place where learners can practice, share experiences, exchange resources, track their progress, and learn from each other.

Our long-term goal is to build a platform that brings together AI-powered learning and a global community of language learners.

Because everyone deserves access to quality language exam preparation — not just those who can afford it.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/438/017/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/438/017/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/438/160/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/438/160/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

As a computer engineering student, I noticed gamers often lose track of their backlogs and need a dedicated space to share their gaming journey. GameShelf was inspired by the need to create a clean, interactive, and social game tracker that goes beyond simple spreadsheets and takes full advantage of modern mobile development.

**What it does**

GameShelf is a comprehensive gaming companion and social platform. Users can search for any game using the IGDB API and add it to their personal library. The library allows categorizing games with statuses like "Playing", "Plan to Play", "Completed", or "Dropped". Users can rate games out of 5 stars, write reviews, and select the specific platform they played on. The community tab features an activity feed to see updates from followed friends. Users can also write detailed guides using Markdown, attach images, and create interactive polls for the community. The app includes a premium "PRO" tier that unlocks advanced features, managed through a seamless paywall.

**How we built it**

The mobile application is built from scratch using Flutter and Dart. For the backend, I used Supabase to handle user authentication, PostgreSQL database management (for relations like feeds, likes, and polls), and bucket storage for avatars and post images. Monetization is handled by integrating the RevenueCat SDK using the 'purchases_flutter' package to validate the 'Pro' entitlement and manage the paywall. Game data is fetched via HTTP requests to the IGDB API ('api.igdb.com/v4/games'), implementing a custom keyword filter to exclude unofficial mods, bootlegs, and romhacks from search results.

**Challenges we ran into**

Building a fully functional social feed and real-time polling system required complex database structuring and relational queries in Supabase. Additionally, parsing and filtering the IGDB API data to ensure only official games appeared in the search was a significant technical hurdle. Finally, ensuring that the RevenueCat paywall correctly restored purchases and updated the UI state across the app required careful state management.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I am particularly proud of shipping a complete, full-stack application with a robust monetization flow in a short hackathon timeframe. Successfully implementing a social feed with interactive polls and Markdown support for community posts adds a lot of value beyond a basic tracker. 

**What we learned**

Integrating RevenueCat demonstrated how straightforward setting up in-app subscriptions, managing packages, and handling entitlements can be compared to native solutions. I also deepened my knowledge of handling complex relational database schemas and real-time state updates with Supabase and Flutter.

**What's next for GameShelf**

The plan is to expand the PRO features, introduce push notifications for community interactions, and officially launch the application on both the App Store and Google Play.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

It's midnight before an exam. You're stuck on a problem, so you open a chatbot. The question is clear in your head, but you can't put it into words. You type something close, and the chatbot answers what you typed, not what you meant: a long, generic answer that doesn't help.

We realised the real problem isn't the answer, it's the question. People often can't say what they want. The thought exists before the words for it. Every chatbot makes you do the hard part: describe what's in your mind. So we asked: what if the tutor never made you find the words, and instead learned how you think?

**What it does**

Versa is an adaptive AI tutor that learns your thinking style and teaches you your way.

Versa doesn't ask, it offers. After every answer it lays out a few cards for where the idea could go next, and you tap the one that matches what was already in your mind. The cards come from a library of 16 kinds of next step in four families:

- Make it real: a concrete example, where it's used, try it yourself, real numbers

- Go deeper: why it works, a harder version, prove it, a common mistake

- Make it simpler: an everyday analogy, picture it, the story behind it, the one-line version

- Go wider: what comes next, compare it, connect it to another subject, the debate

Every tap is a clue. Across chats, topics and days, Versa looks for what repeats: where you start, what you pick next, how deep you go. Once a pattern holds, that is your thinking style, and Versa adapts:

- It guesses your next pick before you tap, then shows you: "Versa guessed you'd pick this · 7 of your last 10".

- Your follow-up answers start your way, for example "Shaped to how you explore: example → why". The first answer to anything new is always normal. The shaping only kicks in on follow-ups, so it feels like mind reading, not guessing.

- If none of the cards fit and you type your own question, that "miss" is the most valuable signal of all: Versa reads what you asked for instead and varies what it offers next time.

The thinking style powers four modes:

- Learn a topic: search any subject or bring a PDF or link, pick the branches you want, and Versa builds a full course of chapters and lessons with tracked progress.

- Sandbox: ask anything, anytime, even with a photo of your homework. If a question could mean two things, Versa asks first with one-tap options (clarifying is always free). An animated character acts out the idea while the answer streams in. When you're done, one tap turns the whole chat into revision notes you can download as a PDF.

- Exam prep: your syllabus becomes units, 5-question quizzes and timed mock tests, with a study plan up to exam day.

- Study with others: a group room where Versa joins as a tutor, stays quiet while friends talk, and steps in to give each member the right push.

You can also set your own length, depth and breadth with sliders and regenerate any answer, and the Thinking style page shows every pattern Versa found, with the evidence behind it. You can approve, edit or archive what it believes about you.

**How we built it**

- App: Flutter, one codebase for Android, iOS and web, with Firebase sign-in (Google or email) and a WebSocket that streams every answer as it's written.

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, and PostgreSQL 16 with pgvector for memory and retrieval. It runs on Google Cloud Run, Cloud SQL and Secret Manager.

- AI: Google Gemini. A fast model handles the ambiguity check, the options and the cards, a stronger model writes the final answer, and Gemini embeddings power memory and similarity.

- The thinking-style engine:

- Each answer draws a random pool of cards from the library, and you see a hand of three, one per family.

- Because hands are random, every pick is read against the cards that were actually offered, using a Plackett–Luce choice model, so we measure preference rather than what happened to be shown.

- Every observation is split into lenses: style, range, interest, ability, mood, and what you said. A pick made while you were stuck, or rushed taps, count for less.

- A pattern is only confirmed when it holds across at least 3 sessions and 3 topics, beats other learners at least 1.5×, and predicts your later picks out of sample at \( p &lt; 0.05 \), Bonferroni-corrected for every candidate tested.

- Monetization: RevenueCat for Versa Plus (1-month free trial, monthly or yearly), a one-time Exam Pass, and Spark packs. Sparks are learning credits with one rule: pay for learning, never for confusion. Clarifying a question is always free.

- Trust by design: 22 written invariants. Every store is append-only, every model call is logged with its prompt and output, and the test suite enforces it with an AST check. Every claim Versa makes about a learner traces back to stored, readable evidence.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Our first architecture lost to a plain chatbot. We started with a big learner model: hypotheses, a concept graph, a planner scoring six value terms, and a branching prediction tree. When we tested it head-to-head against a single plain LLM call, it lost at 20–40× the cost. We cut it all and kept only what survived measurement.

- Not inventing a style. In early tests, a random learner was told they had a style 10–22% of the time. Out-of-sample prediction and multiple-testing correction brought that down to 0–4%.

- Not fooling ourselves. If Versa shapes an answer and you then pick the matching card, that pick partly reflects Versa. We mark those picks as steered and keep them out of the evidence, and the cards themselves are never personalised. They are the measuring instrument.

- Telling style apart from mood and ability. A tired student or a hard topic changes your picks for a day. Separating those from your lasting way of thinking took a whole layer of its own.

- Telling topics apart. Raw embedding similarity couldn't tell subjects apart, so we switched to centred embeddings.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A tutor that shows its work: Versa guesses your pick before you tap, tells you how often it was right, and lets you open any belief to see the exact picks behind it.

- In a live run with a simulated student on real Gemini, guess accuracy rose from 5 of 9 in the first third to 8 of 9 in the last, and one pattern was confirmed with 16 of 21 later picks predicted correctly across 8 topics.

- Every first answer to something new stayed normal (10 of 10). Adaptation only appears where it should.

- Four full learning modes, a working subscription system and revision notes, all from one codebase on Android, iOS and web.

**What we learned**

- Personalisation has to be earned and visible. People trust an adaptive tutor when it shows why it adapted, and when they can correct it.

- The best signal about how someone thinks isn't a quiz about learning styles. It's the small, natural choices they make when they're not being asked.

- Measuring against a plain baseline early saved us. Cutting the clever thing that doesn't work is a feature.

**tested with real users:**

Got positive reviews for the app features, especially the exam mode, felt interesting and understanding
the concepts became easier

**What's next for Versa**

- Testing with more real students at scale, and proving that learning in your own style actually helps, with a style-on vs style-off comparison.

- Exam prep as the "under pressure" version of your thinking style: how you revise and react to a wrong answer when the exam is close.

- An interest layer that follows what pulls you, in step with how you think.

- New card types discovered from what students ask for when no card fits, reviewed by people before they join the library.

**Aiming category**

Next Gen award

</details>

**Inspiration## Inspiration**

Difficult workplace conversations can be stressful, especially for new managers and professionals learning to give feedback or set boundaries. ClearTalk gives users a place to practise their responses before having the real conversation.

**What it does**

ClearTalk contains three workplace scenarios:

- Addressing a missed deadline.

- Declining extra work when the team is overloaded.

- Setting boundaries around after-hours messages.

Each scenario has three conversation turns with three response choices per turn. Choices produce different prewritten reactions and affect clarity, empathy, and boundary scores.

After practising, users receive feedback explaining the consequences of their choices. They can retry the scenario and explore a different approach. The scores are based on authored scenario rules; they are learning aids, not validated psychological measurements.

**How we built it**

ClearTalk uses Expo SDK 57, React Native, Expo Router, and TypeScript. Scenario content and scoring run locally without an AI API or backend.

The missed-deadline scenario is free. The other two scenarios use RevenueCat’s premium entitlement for access control. The implementation includes offering retrieval, purchase and restore actions, loading states, cancellation handling, and error messages.

**Challenges we faced**

We resolved an Expo SDK mismatch, configured the development environment on an older Intel Mac, and repaired incomplete dependency installations. We also worked on making feedback specific to each choice while keeping the interface readable on a phone.

**Accomplishments**

We built a working mobile prototype with three complete scenarios, nine conversation turns, and 27 response choices. The core experience runs on a physical iPhone through Expo Go.

**What we learned**

A focused interaction can communicate a product’s value more clearly than a large feature list. We also learned how RevenueCat separates products, offerings, and entitlements, and why native purchase testing needs a development build.

**Current status and next steps**

The app has been tested through Expo Go. RevenueCat runs in Preview API Mode in that environment; a real Test Store transaction has not yet been verified. Store publication, revenue, and user traction are not claimed.

Our next steps are to test purchases in a development build, gather user feedback, and expand the scenario library.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Ordering at a café hasn't changed much over the years. To order, you still need to queue, explain your order to a cashier or scroll through menus on a screen.

We wanted to make a new, natural way to order: what if you could just talk to the café?

That's how we were inspired to build BaristaVoice: an AI voice ordering system for cafés. Our aim was to tie together the entire conversation from the customer to the café's ordering workflow.
We also wanted to build something that could be used in a real café business rather than just another consumer-facing AI app.

**What it does**

BaristaVoice lets customers order from a café using natural speech.

A customer can tap the microphone and say something like:

"I'd like a large iced latte and a chocolate croissant." or ask the AI to recommend something.

They can also choose to type if they are uncomfortable speaking or if it's loud.

BaristaVoice will understand and update the order, showing relevant products and images as they are mentioned. A customer can then freely adjust what is being ordered before confirming and paying.

The order is then sent to the café's POS system.

On the café side, businesses can manage their menu, receive and track live orders, view ordering analytics, get tips on how to improve and manage their BaristaVoice subscription via a dedicated dashboard.
Individual cafés can also have their own QR code for customers to scan to reach the café's menu.
BaristaVoice currently integrates with Square (Sandbox), bringing the voice ordering experience into a real POS workflow.

The business model is B2B: cafés subscribe to BaristaVoice rather than customers paying to use it.

Customers:

- No account needed, making the experience simple and hassle-free

- Customers simply scan the café's QR code or enter their link to start ordering

- Cafés they've ordered from before are stored locally in their profile, in case they visit again

**How we built it**

BaristaVoice was built using Flutter and Dart, with Supabase as our backend/database infrastructure.

The major technologies we used were:

- Flutter / Dart — customer kiosk and café dashboard

- Supabase — database, authentication, storage and realtime updates

- Groq — natural-language AI and order processing

- ElevenLabs — text-to-speech responses

- Square — POS integration and payment functionality

- RevenueCat — café subscription management (recurring, fixed, monthly/yearly)

- Stripe — café usage-based billing infrastructure (5p/item ordered, charged monthly)

- Claude Code — AI-assisted development

The customer ordering experience is login-free, while café administrators log in to access their dashboard.

Orders are stored using a canonical order model before being submitted to the POS, and this flow is designed so additional POS providers can be added in the future.
We also built realtime order updates so that an order can appear in the café's dashboard as soon as it's placed. Staff can have the Live Orders page displayed and mark orders as complete.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the main challenges was to make the AI ordering experience feel like a real conversation rather than a chatbot with a microphone attached.
The AI needed to understand natural requests, extract the correct products and quantities, handle order changes and make sure the visual order state was correct.

We also needed to ensure that the AI couldn't make up a product or price; orders had to be validated against the café's actual menu before being submitted.

Another important challenge for us was the integration to a real POS system. Getting our internal order system to connect to Square involved managing products, orders and transactions.

We also had to work around constraints of APIs and tools while building and testing the project, including AI request limits, payment sandbox environments and subscription testing.

Finally, we had to make sure we kept the UX smooth: adding too many buttons or menu interactions would undermine the reason for using voice in the first place, so we kept the interaction simple while still giving customers enough visual feedback to know what the AI understood.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We're especially proud that BaristaVoice goes beyond just a voice demo and ties the entire ordering workflow together.
A customer can speak an order, see it interpreted on screen, confirm and pay, and have the resulting order appear in the café's dashboard.

We're also proud of building both sides of the app:

- A customer-facing voice ordering experience

- A café management dashboard including:

- Live order tracking

- Menu management

- Analytics

- Subscription infrastructure

The project also gave us the opportunity to work with several production-oriented technologies that we haven't previously used together, including Supabase, Square, RevenueCat and ElevenLabs.

Most importantly, we built BaristaVoice around a real business model. The customer experience is free to use, while cafés are the paying customers so that the product is sustainable beyond the initial demo.

Cafés can test BaristaVoice using the free trial without replacing their existing ordering system, allowing them to try it out alongside their current setup.

**What we learned**

We learned that building an AI product is much more than just connecting an LLM to an interface.
The AI itself is only one part of the system: the difficult part is to make the AI interact reliably with databases, pricing rules, payments, POS systems, and a UI that users can trust.

We also learned a lot about design around AI rather than simply adding AI to an existing interface. Voice works best when the rest of the UI supports the conversation rather than competing with it.

On the business side, we learned how important it is to design the monetisation model alongside the product. Thinking about cafés as the customer influenced many of our decisions around the dashboard, POS integrations and analytics.

Finally, building BaristaVoice taught us how much effort is required to turn an idea into a real product. We spent a lot of time fixing bugs, refining features and making the UX smoother.

**What's next for BaristaVoice**

The current version of BaristaVoice shows the complete customer-to-café ordering workflow, but we have much more to build.

Our future goals include:

- Supporting additional POS systems such as Toast, Lightspeed and Epos Now

- Expanding café analytics and reporting

- Improving automatic menu/product extraction

- Making the conversational ordering experience even more flexible

- Supporting multi-location café businesses

- Refining the pricing model as real usage data becomes available

Our long-term vision is for BaristaVoice to be used in real cafés with real customers, allowing faster, simpler and more efficient ordering without businesses being forced to replace the system they already use.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Quiet: Where should we go? Let's go.
Inspiration

"Where should we go?"

Everyone knows what comes next: 20 minutes of scrolling, cross-checking reviews, dropping pins on a map, polling the group chat... and then someone says, "Honestly, you decide."

We realized the problem isn't a lack of options. It's too many. Every app helps you discover more places, and none helps you actually choose one. So we built Quiet to make that decision effortless.

What it does

Quiet turns a vague intention into a confident decision.

Tell it what you're in the mood for, and instead of a wall of results, you get one focused recommendation with a clear explanation of why it fits. Love it? Save it for later.

Intent → Score → Report → Save

Intent: Say what you want in plain language.
Score: Quiet evaluates nearby places against what you actually asked for.
Report: You get a short, readable case for the top pick, with no noise.
Save: Keep the places worth remembering.

The goal isn't to show you more places. It's to help you stop searching and start going.

How we built it

Quiet is a mobile-first app with an AI decision layer running quietly underneath.

React Native for a fast, smooth mobile experience
Supabase for auth, database, and backend services
PostgreSQL + PostGIS for location-aware place data and proximity queries
AI decision logic that interprets user intent and evaluates candidate places
Scoring and reporting layer that ranks options consistently and explains the reasoning in plain language

Rather than trusting a single LLM answer, Quiet combines structured place data with AI reasoning, so recommendations are grounded, consistent, and explainable.

Challenges we ran into
Making it simple is harder than making it powerful. Every extra feature was a temptation to add friction. We had to keep cutting.
Representing intent. Turning messy human requests ("somewhere chill but not boring") into something a system can score reliably took real design work.
Consistent scoring. Two similar searches should give sensible, comparable results, not random ones.
Structuring AI output. We had to control what the model returns so the report is concise, trustworthy, and handles uncertainty gracefully.
Wiring the full stack. Connecting our local Supabase environment, database functions, API routes, and the React Native frontend meant lots of debugging across layers, and it taught us how a real application fits together.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
Shipping the complete loop end to end: intent, scoring, report, and save, working together in a real mobile app.
Building location-aware logic with PostGIS and database functions that power the recommendations.
Designing an AI experience that stays in the background, where the user sees a decision, not a chatbot.
Making recommendations that explain themselves, so users can trust the pick instead of just accepting it.
What we learned
Building an AI product isn't about dropping an LLM into an app. The real work is designing the decision experience around it.
Controlling what the user sees matters as much as what the model can do.
Structured outputs and honest handling of uncertainty make AI feel reliable.
Working with PostGIS, database functions, and full-stack integration gave us a much deeper understanding of how frontend, backend, and data layers communicate.
The best AI often feels invisible.
What's next for Quiet
Group decisions: blend everyone's preferences into one pick, and end the "you decide" loop for good
Personalization: learn from saved places and past choices to sharpen recommendations
Richer context: time of day, weather, budget, and crowd levels in the scoring
Share and go: send the final pick to friends with one tap, with directions built in

Quiet doesn't give you more choices. It gives you your next move.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**The category I'm entering, and why**

Next Gen — I'm a student, there's no paid developer account behind this. The
whole app runs from source, and the repository is the submission.

One category, on purpose. The app could be argued into others and I'd rather not:
the design is good, but it isn't a design product.

**Inspiration**

I spend my days saving links: tips I want to revisit while coding, a tool someone
mentioned, an article I'll need "later." When that "later" finally arrives, I find
it impossible to locate the specific item buried under the pile of saved links and
videos in my bookmarks — because I've forgotten the title, the source site, and the
exact wording used.

Raindrop (which I've tried extensively) and even note-taking apps filled with
copy-pasted URLs solve the storage problem beautifully. They offer folders,
tags, highlighting, full-text search... Yet, each one requires you to remember a
specific detail about the content — its title, the words it contained, or the
category you filed it under. None of them solve the problem of retrievability.

That is the core idea behind Lymarks: a saved link is worthless if you can't find
it again when you only have a vague memory of it.

This isn't a problem I invented just for my own convenience. Anyone who saves more
content than they actually read ends up with the same digital "graveyard": people
who email articles to themselves all week, those who keep four hundred tabs open,
or those for whom a "read-it-later" app has quietly become a place where links go
to die.

The app is built on a simple promise: you don't need to remember the link itself.
You only need to remember what you were looking for.

**What it does**

You share a link from any app. That's the entire interaction — one tap, no form,
no folder to pick. Two seconds later the sheet is gone and you're back where you
were.

Behind that, Lymarks fetches the page, extracts the text, and asks a model for
three bullets and a category. The card fills itself while you've already
moved on. From then on the link is findable by what it said, not by what it was
called — including semantic search, where you describe what you half-remember and
it surfaces anyway.

Some pages refuse a server. When that happens the phone reads the page itself
and hands the text back to the same pipeline, so a site that blocks robots still
ends up in your memory.

And it works without a network: the library lives on the device, search falls back
to full text locally, and a banner says plainly that you're looking at the last
sync instead of pretending everything is fine.

**Monetization: what the free plan does instead of refusing**

This is the part I'd most like judged.

The obvious free-plan design is a limit that refuses: past 30 links, the
capture fails. I shipped that first. Then I tested it on a real phone and saw how
bad it is — you keep sharing links from other apps, none of them arrive, and you
don't find out until you next open the app. The product quietly loses your data
to protect its own pricing.

So the limit changed nature. Past 30, the link is still saved. It just arrives
locked: there in your library, blurred, with the mascot asleep beside a line that
says "We saved every link you sent. Nothing is lost." No model call is spent on
a locked link, so the free tier still costs nothing to run. The moment the
RevenueCat webhook confirms the entitlement, every locked link unlocks and the
pipeline runs on all of them at once — you don't get an empty Pro, you get your
own backlog, summarised.

The upgrade isn't a gate you hit. It's a key to something you already own.

The HAMM award would have been this work's natural home, but that category expects
an app already published on the stores and Lymarks isn't there yet. Next Gen is the
one I can honestly claim — the monetization work is here all the same, and I'd
rather it be read than not entered at all.

RevenueCat carries that whole flow: offerings drive the paywall prices, the
appUserID is the Clerk user id, and the entitlement is confirmed server side
by the webhook. The app never decides on its own that you're Pro — the store
confirms the payment, the server decides the right.

During the Shipaton the purchases run against RevenueCat's Test Store, so the
whole chain — offering, purchase, webhook, entitlement, unlock — is exercised end
to end without a Play listing. And no screen imports the SDK: purchases sit behind
a Billing contract. That is what makes the paywall testable against a fake store,
and what lets the app run with no store at all — which is exactly what you get when
you clone the repository.

**How we built it**

Flutter app ──► Cloudflare Worker API ──► Neon Postgres (pgvector + full-text)
 │
 ├─► Groq → Gemini Flash summary, 3 bullets, category
 ├─► Gemini embeddings for semantic search
 ├─► Clerk identity
 └─► RevenueCat webhook entitlements

Flutter and Riverpod on the client, Hono on Cloudflare Workers for the API, Neon
Postgres with pgvector and a generated tsvector column for hybrid search. Page
fetching is SSRF-guarded, with DNS resolved over DoH before every request and
every redirect.

Everything is optimistic first: each gesture changes the local list immediately
and reconciles with the server afterwards. Deleting is reversible for five
seconds, and the real purge only leaves once the undo window closes.

**See it in one minute, with no keys**

git clone https://github.com/morel1999/lymarks.git && cd lymarks/app
flutter run

With no API keys the app boots in demo mode: 54 lymarks, every screen
reachable, and no network calls at all. It isn't a mock layer bolted on for
reviewers — it's the same code path the test suite and the reference renders run
against.

The demo needs no server, but there is one, and it is live:
GET https://lymarks-api.lymarks.workers.dev/health answers
{"ok":true,"version":"0.1.0","db":"ok"}. Build the app with a Clerk publishable
key and the same binary talks to it.

It starts you on the Free plan on purpose, because that is where the part I'd
most like judged actually lives: 30 lymarks open, the 24 most recent saved but
locked, and a simulated purchase that opens all 24 at once. The README walks
through the whole thing gesture by gesture.

**Challenges we ran into**

A feature can pass every test and still not exist. Offline reading was green
across the suite and completely unreachable on a real phone: the auth SDK awaited
a session-token fetch during startup, retried it eight times with exponential
backoff, and since that was the only await before the app started, Flutter never
drew a single frame. You saw the launch screen forever. It took an evening of
reading logcat line by line to find it. No unit test would have.

Reference renders that failed at random, on and off for days. The cause was in
the demo data: it called DateTime.now() once per item, so two links saved "nine
days ago" sometimes landed in the same millisecond and sometimes didn't — and
List.sort isn't stable in Dart, so their order flipped between runs.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- The locked-instead-of-refused free tier. It changed how the product feels, and
it came from testing on a device rather than from a spec.

- 121 behaviour tests and 32 reference renders on the app, plus the API's security
suites. The renders caught real regressions, not just cosmetic drift.

- A design system with its own mascot, whose poses are colour-matched by a
reproducible pipeline that lives in the repository: the target hue is measured
off the asset the app actually ships, never written as a constant.

- The onboarding's two 3D scenes, held to that same discipline. Both arrived with
the mascot at the wrong hue — 243° and 258°, where the app's own sits at 220° —
and one of them as a 26 MB 256-colour GIF whose dark gradient was a dither
pattern that crawls on an OLED screen. The build script measures the target hue
off the shipped mascot instead of hard-coding it, removes the dither before
upscaling rather than after, and neutralises a third-party logo that was legible
on a card. 255 KB for both, at the exact pixel width of the screen.

- Documentation kept alive rather than written once, including a build journal
that records what actually broke and why.

**What we learned**

That the gap between "it works" and "it works on a phone" is where the real work
is. Three of the best things in this app — the locked free plan, offline reading,
a launch screen that doesn't flash white — exist because something was wrong on a
device and nothing in CI could see it.

**What's next for Lymarks**

Automatic clustering: category paths currently run on a fixed taxonomy, and the
server doesn't compute clusters yet. The Daily Digest has its schema and its
screen but no scheduled job. Push notifications have no token plumbing. iOS is
untouched, for want of a Mac.

These are in the README too. An honest map of what isn't done is worth more than a
demo that pretends.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**NIPSMAP — Never Ride Unaccounted For**

**Inspiration**

Before entering an unfamiliar taxi or bus, a commuter makes a decision with very little information: What do I know about this vehicle, and who will know where I am if something goes wrong?

In Nigeria, that question is personal. While building NIPSMAP, I spoke with people I know who have experienced frightening situations on public transport. Those conversations shaped the project around a practical need: help people check before boarding and stay connected to someone they trust throughout the journey.

NIPSMAP brings vehicle checks, community reports, journey sharing, and emergency alerts into one mobile app.

**What it does**

NIPSMAP supports three moments in a journey:

Before boarding: Enter a vehicle’s plate number to check available vehicle records and community incident reports. Results distinguish available information from missing records. An unknown result is not treated as proof that a vehicle is safe.

During the ride: Start a trip and share a tracking link with someone you trust. They can view the journey in a browser without installing NIPSMAP.

When help is needed: A deliberate hold-to-activate SOS lets the rider initiate an alert to their emergency contacts with location information. Delivery depends on connectivity and notification availability.

Commuters can also report incidents, create Family Circles, and use an AI assistant for plain-language safety guidance.

The goal is practical accountability: more information before a ride and better visibility during it.

**How I built it**

I built the mobile app with Flutter and Dart for Android and iOS. A Laravel backend manages vehicle checks, incident reports, trips, Family Circles, and subscription access, with PostgreSQL and Redis supporting data storage and background work.

Slow vehicle lookups required special attention. Instead of holding the app on a blocking request, I moved lookup processing into background jobs so the app can check for the result while remaining responsive.

RevenueCat manages in-app subscriptions, with webhook updates synchronizing subscription access to the backend. Free allowances let commuters try the app, while paid plans support higher usage and shared family allowances.

OneSignal supports notification delivery around the journey experience. The purpose is useful communication tied to a rider’s activity, rather than unrelated promotional messages.

**Challenges I faced**

Getting through app review. Seven Google Play rejections made release readiness a substantial part of the project. Permission flows, reviewer access, source attribution, and government-data disclaimers needed the same care as the main features.

Working with slow external services. Vehicle lookups could take around 30 seconds. That forced me to design for waiting, retries, and clear progress instead of assuming every request would finish immediately.

Keeping subscription access consistent. The purchase flow had to work across the app, RevenueCat, and the backend. Webhook authentication and entitlement synchronization were important parts of making that reliable.

Communicating uncertainty honestly. Missing records must not become a reassuring verdict. Likewise, an action queued while offline must not look like an alert that has already been delivered.

**What I learned**

A safety product needs clear boundaries as much as useful features. Finding a vehicle record does not guarantee a safe journey, and initiating an alert does not guarantee that help has arrived.

I also learned that affordability and infrastructure costs have to be designed together. Usage allowances and pooled family plans help balance access with the recurring cost of verification and other services.

Most importantly, the commuter experience has to remain understandable when the network is slow or information is incomplete.

**Accomplishments I’m proud of**

I launched NIPSMAP on Google Play and the Apple App Store, bringing vehicle checks, journey sharing, Family Circles, and emergency alerts together in one cross-platform app.

I also completed a successful ₦1,000 production purchase through RevenueCat, with webhook delivery and backend entitlement updates connecting payment to premium access.

The part I’m proudest of is connecting riders with the people who care about them. A shared journey link makes NIPSMAP useful beyond the person who installed it.

**What’s next**

My next priority is onboarding early users and learning from real journeys: where people hesitate, which information helps them decide, and whether their contacts can follow a trip easily.

Future work includes broader family use cases, fleet and transport-union pilots, and exploring SMS or USSD access for people with limited mobile data.

NIPSMAP starts with a simple belief: you should not have to ride unaccounted for.

</details>
