<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Tutti — Cook in Concert**

Timers beep. Tutti sings.

**Inspiration**

Cooking one dish means following a recipe. Cooking three at once is more like conducting an orchestra. The salmon needs flipping, the rice needs to rest, and the broccoli is starting to char—each with its own timing.

Kitchen timers beep, but they don’t tell you which dish needs attention, what to do next, or how everything fits together. That can be especially challenging for new cooks, people with ADHD time blindness, and anyone with flour on their hands.

Shipaton challenged us to combine two categories that depend on each other. We chose Food × Music because preparing a multi-dish dinner already feels like performing a score: different parts enter at different times, the work sets the tempo, and everything needs to finish together.

In music, that moment has a name: tutti, Italian for “all together.”

**What It Does**

Tutti turns dinner into a piece of music—and the music tells you when to act.

**1. Pick Your Dishes**

Choose your dishes from the crate. Each gets its own instrument and a short, four-note musical signature called a leitmotif.

Dish
Instrument

Salmon
Cello

Rice
Harp

Broccoli
Marimba

Caesar salad
Flute

Mug cake
Celesta

**2. Press the Record**

A scheduler works backwards from the serving time and draws your cooking plan as a vinyl record.

Each dish occupies a slice of the disc, with time moving from the outer rim toward the center label. Solid bands represent hands-on work; fine grooves represent passive cooking.

**3. Drop the Needle**

A live, generative arrangement follows each dish as it cooks:

- Hands-on steps play a rhythm you can work to: chopping at Allegro—104 BPM—and whisking at Presto—126 BPM.

- Passive cooking becomes a quiet drone.

- Upcoming tasks are announced by the dish’s musical signature, gradually fading in and building.

- Action cues combine a bell, a phone vibration, and an amber light.

**4. Re-score Live**

Tap Done or +1 minute, and Tutti replans every step that hasn’t started yet. It tells you whether the original serving time still holds or needs to move.

**5. Serve on the Chord**

When the needle reaches the label, the whole orchestra plays together, marking the planned moment to serve. An encore then plays your dinner back as a short song.

**6. Tip the Band**

Tutti is free, with no locked recipes or instruments. After dinner, the Finale screen offers an optional tip through RevenueCat. Each tip receives a final chord from the whole orchestra.

Hearing the harp come in gives you a cue without having to read three separate countdowns.

**How We Built It**

Tutti is a native Android app built with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, in approximately 3,400 lines of code.

It ships with zero audio files. Every sound is synthesized live on the phone.

**Scheduler — Conductor.kt**

The scheduler works backwards from the final chord and treats the cook’s hands as one shared resource.

- Prevents overlapping hands-on tasks.

- Leaves a 30-second breather between tasks whenever possible.

- Places steps with the tightest timing windows first, using earliest-deadline-first scheduling in reverse with one step of lookahead.

- Uses a hill-climbing optimization pass to reduce waiting within each dish’s allowed hold time.

- Replans during cooking while keeping started steps fixed and preventing tasks from being scheduled before the current moment.

**Synthesizer — Synth.kt**

We built a 48-voice polyphonic synthesizer from scratch. It renders floating-point PCM audio one sample at a time and includes 12 sound patches:

- A filtered-saw cello.

- A plucked harp.

- A marimba with an inharmonic partial.

- An FM bell.

- Pads and drums.

A trimmed version of Freeverb adds room ambience. Voices use preallocated primitive arrays, so the audio render loop never allocates memory.

**Orchestra — Orchestra.kt**

A sample-accurate sixteenth-note sequencer runs on an URGENT_AUDIO thread and feeds AudioTrack at 48 kHz.

At a tempo of b beats per minute, the number of samples per sixteenth note is:

Δ = (60 × fₛ) ÷ (4 × b)

Here, fₛ = 48,000 samples per second. At 104 BPM, each sixteenth note lasts approximately 6,923 samples.

Tempo changes happen on bar lines. The UI reports each dish’s cooking state, while the audio thread makes the musical decisions.

**Tip Jar — RevenueCat**

Tips are consumable products in a RevenueCat offering, loaded through the Android SDK and sorted by price.

We wanted the full cooking experience to remain free, so the optional tip appears only after dinner is served. RevenueCat’s Test Store lets us test the purchase flow without a Play Console account. Builds without a configured key simply omit the tip jar.

**User Interface — Compose + Material 3**

The interface takes the form of a turntable:

- An aluminum plinth and black vinyl record.

- Dish colors used on labels and grooves.

- One amber cue light.

- A record and tonearm drawn with Canvas, animated using the audio engine’s beat clock.

The app supports dark theme, large text, the system’s Remove animations setting, and TalkBack, which announces cooking cues and schedule changes.

**Challenges We Ran Into**

**Coordinating Every Menu**

Five dishes create 31 possible nonempty menu combinations: 2⁵ − 1.

Our unit tests cover every combination, checking that hands-on tasks never overlap, required gaps and hold tolerances are respected, and live rescheduling remains valid. These tests caught two real bugs.

**Keeping Audio and Visuals in Sync**

Our emulator environment lacked a working audio device, and its audio output ran slower than real time. This caused demo recordings to drift out of sync with the screen.

We moved the music’s timing onto the wall clock and checked that count-in clicks landed within 0.1 seconds of the corresponding screen change.

**Working Without Xcode**

The development machine had no iOS tooling, so we built Tutti entirely as a native Android app.

**Making the App Feel Like an Instrument**

Our first interface resembled a paper concert programme, but it didn’t capture the experience we wanted.

Partway through development, we redesigned it as a turntable. A design review identified eight issues, and we fixed all eight before recording the demo.

**What We Learned**

- One pair of hands is a meaningful scheduling constraint. Working backwards from the serving time made the problem manageable.

- Real-time audio requires careful engineering. The render loop must avoid memory allocation, and audio output cannot always be assumed to track real time.

- Sound can guide interaction when hands are busy. A musical signature that builds before a cue helps users anticipate the next task without looking at a screen.

- Exhaustive testing is valuable when the input space is small. Testing all 31 menus helped us find and fix scheduling errors.

**What’s Next**

- Voice controls: Say “done” instead of tapping.

- Recipe imports: Bring in recipes from a link.

- Smart oven integration: Let connected ovens report their own cooking cues.

- Duets: Two cooks, two task lanes, one record.

- Wrist cues: Bring the cue light to a smartwatch.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Breadcrumb is an Android screen-capture app that makes you answer one question before anything is saved: "Why are you saving this?"

**Inspiration**

I save a lot of screenshots of people I might reach out to for projects or business; like a founder whose work I liked, a designer I might collaborate with, a profile that seemed relevant. A few weeks later I open my gallery, find a wall of screenshots, and have no idea who was who or why I saved them.
That's the problem - I remembered the 'what' but rarely the 'why'. There was nothing on my phone that solved that problem.

On my android phone, my gallery allowed me to add tags to pictures, but that would've disrupted my flow if I had open the gallery for every screenshot I took. Notes apps, bookmark managers and clipboard tools are all good at storing content, but almost none of them preserve intent. I wanted a tool that treats the reason as the main object and the capture as secondary.

**What it does**

Breadcrumb lets you capture text, links and images from anywhere on your Android phone. Before anything is saved, a lightweight Save Flow asks one thing: why are you saving this?

**Capture from anywhere**

- Text selection: highlight text in any app and save it in one tap through Android's PROCESS_TEXT menu. 

- Screen snip: an adjustable rectangle to capture part of the screen as an image.

- Create: write or paste something directly in the app.

- Import: pick one or many images from the gallery. Multiple images inherit the same note.

**How we built it**

I built Breadcrumb in Google AI Studio's cloud environment because my hardware can't run a local Android emulator. That constraint shaped the workflow. I iterated and tested the core flows in a cloud emulator primarily.

**Challenges we ran into**

Breadcrumb went through two major rewrites. The transition from version 1 to two was the biggest challenge of all. It made me realize a lot of my own limitations, and helped me shape a friendlier pricing model. 

- Version 1: 
The first design had cloud sync as the paid feature: $2.99 a month or $20.99 a year, with Google sign-in, OCR for text capture, and optional context on every save. It looked like a standard consumer app with a standard subscription.

- Version 2:
I removed cloud sync, auth and OCR, and I moved from a monthly subscription to a one-off payment. The lightweight text-selection path (PROCESS_TEXT) turned out to be clunky. It hides the option in an overflow menu, which costs an extra tap and some hunting, and that goes against "fast" and "low friction". So I moved toward Android's accessibility capabilities, which allow a one-tap floating save. But accessibility is a heavy permission, and anyone who grants it to a third party is trusting that app with a lot. If I was going to ask for that trust, I didn't want to make a promise about it. I wanted to make it impossible to break. So I removed the backend entirely. There is nothing for data to leak into. I don't want any of the app's data to leave the user's device, at least until I'm very sure about security.
I'm not claiming the permission is small. The point is that the architecture offsets the ask.
Monthly pricing made sense when the paid feature was cloud sync, because sync has a recurring cost and a recurring benefit. Once sync was gone, neither existed. Charging rent for a local-only app felt wrong, so I moved to a one-off payment.

**Monetization**

- all users get to capture unlimited snippets, add context, manage by data types.

- Pro unlocks tags, search and tag filtering. 
Why are these paid features?
Those only matter to people with a big, growing inbox, which means people who use the app constantly. That's a stronger signal of willingness to pay than cloud sync, which is a convenience almost anyone might want once. The paywall sits exactly where commitment shows up.

Pro billing runs through RevenueCat's Test Store, and I confirmed test purchases show up in the RevenueCat dashboard.

If no key is configured, the app falls back to a demo mode that unlocks Pro, so anyone can try the full experience. This was deliberately kept this way so evaluation is easier for this hackathon submission.

**What I learned**

How to work under major constraints! Time and hardware were both a limiting factor for this hackathon.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Text description**

Ludo Elemental takes the board game almost everyone has played and gives each colour an elemental power: Fire burns a path through enemies, Water freezes tokens into traps, Earth walls off the road, and Air gusts nine extra steps. Every power charges as you play, so each turn asks a question classic Ludo never did — use it now, or wait?

The four elements are a straight nod to Avatar: The Last Airbender. The show also gives each element a second, rarer form — waterbenders who bend blood, firebenders who throw lightning, earthbenders who bend metal. We looked at giving each colour a second power the same way, and cut it: a 4-player board where everyone has two abilities each turn stops being Ludo and starts being a different, much longer game. So one power per colour stayed, and the balancing lever became something else entirely — a charge meter. Every power costs 40 points to fire, and once one of your tokens gets all the way home, that cost drops to 30. Progress makes you stronger; it does not hand you a second ability.

What it does

- Four elemental powers with their own timing rules, animations and counters (Ice is immune to Fire; walls shove sheltered tokens)

- Pass N Play with any mix of friends and computer players, online matchmaking, and private Party Code rooms

- Host-authoritative online play: one device runs the rules, others send moves, so nobody can cheat by editing their client, and a dropped player can rejoin

- A guided tutorial with Stymite, the game's mascot, that teaches every power in play

How it makes money — RevenueCat
The shop sells premium game boards as one-time, non-consumable Google Play products, powered by the RevenueCat SDK (react-native-purchases):

- Ownership comes only from RevenueCat's CustomerInfo, never from local storage, so unlocks cannot be faked

- Prices are fetched from the store and shown in the player's own currency

- Purchases are tied to the player's account with Purchases.logIn, so a board bought on one phone is there on the next; Restore brings everything back after a reinstall

- An item is owned if its product was bought or an entitlement of the same name is active, so a bundle can be launched from the RevenueCat dashboard with no app update

- Everything sold is cosmetic. Nothing is pay-to-win, and there are no ads

How we built it
Expo SDK 57 and React Native 0.86 with Reanimated 4 for animation; Supabase Auth and Realtime for accounts and multiplayer; RevenueCat for purchases. The rules engine is plain JavaScript with no UI imports, so every power, turn rule and online authority check runs in Node test suites before a build ever happens.

Challenges
Shipping an Android-only game without an Android device: every release is checked with custom scripts that catch the crashes that only happen on a phone (worklets calling plain functions, non-boolean native props, styles web accepts and Android does not), plus an in-app crash screen.

What's next
Dice sets, coin bezels and crest symbols in the shop (the tabs are already there), a discounted all-boards bundle, and ranked online seasons.

</details>

**Inspiration**

**What it does**

**How we built it**

**Challenges we ran into**

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

**What we learned**

**What's next for SecureQuest**

About the Project
Inspiration
Cybersecurity is often taught through definitions, technical concepts, and lists of best practices. We wanted to make cybersecurity learning more practical and interactive.
SecureQuest was inspired by a simple question: what if learning cybersecurity felt like making real security decisions instead of only reading about them?
We designed the experience around realistic cybersecurity situations such as phishing, weak passwords, malicious applications, ransomware, and unsafe public Wi-Fi. Instead of simply reading an explanation, users make a decision and then learn why that decision is safe or risky.
Our goal was to create a cybersecurity learning experience that is practical, engaging, and easier to understand for people who are still developing their security awareness.
What We Built
SecureQuest is an Android cybersecurity learning application built with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose.
The application combines interactive cybersecurity missions with an AI-powered cybersecurity tutor. Users can work through security scenarios, make decisions, receive explanations, track their progress, and explore achievements.
Core features include:
• Interactive cybersecurity missions
• Phishing and threat-detection scenarios
• Decision-based cybersecurity learning
• AI-powered cybersecurity guidance
• Gemini-powered threat analysis and explanations
• Learning progress tracking
• Achievement tracking
• Premium features powered by RevenueCat
• Modern dark cyber-defense user interface
The AI Assistant communicates with a Node.js and Express backend, which connects to the Google Gemini API. The Gemini API key is kept on the backend rather than being embedded directly in the Android client.
The architecture is:
Android Application
 |
 | REST API
 v
SecureQuest Backend
 |
 | Gemini API
 v
Google Gemini
For monetization, we integrated the RevenueCat SDK and configured a premium product, entitlement, offering, package, and paywall. We used RevenueCat Test Store during development to validate the purchase flow without using a real store transaction.
How We Built It
The Android application was developed with:
• Kotlin
• Jetpack Compose
• Material 3
• Navigation 3
• Kotlin Serialization
• OkHttp
• RevenueCat SDK
The backend was developed with:
• Node.js
• Express
• Google Gemini API
The project is organized around the mobile application, cybersecurity learning experience, AI integration, backend services, and monetization layer.
The main application flow is:
Home
 |
 +-- Cybersecurity Mission
 |
 +-- Threat Analysis
 |
 +-- AI Assistant
 |
 +-- Progress
 |
 +-- Achievements
 |
 -- Premium
 |
-- RevenueCat Paywall
We tested the application both through Android tooling and on a physical Android device. This was especially important for validating the AI network connection and the RevenueCat Test Store purchase experience.
Challenges We Faced
One of the biggest challenges was connecting the Android application to the local AI backend while testing on a physical Android device.
The application initially had to distinguish between emulator networking and physical-device networking. We had to configure the backend URL correctly, add Android Internet access, allow local HTTP traffic for development, and use USB port forwarding with adb reverse during testing.
Another challenge was diagnosing the AI connection. The generic message displayed by the application did not immediately reveal whether the problem came from the Android application, local networking, the backend server, or the Gemini API. We therefore tested each layer separately until the complete Android-to-backend-to-Gemini path was working.
RevenueCat was another important part of the project. We configured a Test Store product, connected it to the premium entitlement, created the securequest_premium offering, configured the monthly package, and tested the purchase flow through the RevenueCat paywall.
We also had to refine the user interface extensively. We wanted SecureQuest to feel like a modern cybersecurity product rather than a traditional educational application, so we focused on a dark cyber-defense visual language, structured information cards, neon-inspired accents, mission progression, and consistent navigation.
What We Learned
This project taught us that creating a working mobile application requires much more than building screens.
We learned how different components have to work together:
User Interface
 ↓
Navigation
 ↓
Application Logic
 ↓
Network Layer
 ↓
Backend
 ↓
AI Service
 ↓
Monetization
We gained practical experience with Android development, Jetpack Compose, REST APIs, Node.js, Express, Google Gemini integration, RevenueCat subscriptions, Test Store purchases, local networking, Android debugging, Git, GitHub, and real-device testing.
We also learned that testing on a physical device can reveal problems that are not obvious when developing only on an emulator.
Why SecureQuest Matters
SecureQuest is designed around a simple learning principle:
learn by making decisions, understand the consequences, and improve through immediate feedback.
Instead of presenting cybersecurity as a collection of abstract concepts, SecureQuest turns security awareness into an interactive experience.
The project brings together:
Cybersecurity + Interactive Learning + AI + Mobile Technology + Monetization
in a single Android application.
Our goal is to demonstrate how modern AI and mobile technologies can make cybersecurity education more practical, accessible, and engaging.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I am 17 years old and I have liked computers, coding and development for a long time. Since I was a kid, I always wanted to make something of my own. Not just another normal project, but something that I had never seen before and something that could solve a real problem. The idea of Ranchat came from something I noticed in schools and colleges. There are many things people want to say but cannot say openly. It can be an idea, an opinion, something they are going through, or even something they want to say about something that happened in their classroom. For example, imagine something happens in a classroom involving a teacher, or someone has an opinion about something, but they are scared that if they say it openly, everyone will know it was them. There are also many introverted people who have things to say but don't feel comfortable saying them directly. I kept thinking about this and eventually I thought:What if people could just say what they wanted to say without having to reveal who they are?
That was where the idea of Ranchat came from.Ranchat is an anonymous messaging app where people can communicate and share their thoughts without directly revealing their identity.

**What it does**

Ranchat is made for people who want to communicate without putting their real identity in front of everyone. The main idea is very simple. You can join, start conversations and share your thoughts while staying anonymous. I wanted to make something where people don't have to think, "What will happen if they know I said this?" At the same time, I know that anonymity can also create problems, so I want safety and responsible use to be an important part of Ranchat as I continue developing it.

**How we built it**

I built Ranchat by myself. To be honest, when I started this project, I wasn't a very experienced developer. A lot of what I know about coding now, I learned while building Ranchat. It took me 93 days to build it. I worked on the frontend, backend, database, APIs, UI and many other parts of the app while learning at the same time. There were many times when I didn't know what I was doing and had to search, try different things and learn from my mistakes. I also used AI tools when I got stuck, but I used them mainly to understand problems, find possible solutions and learn things that I didn't know.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest part was definitely debugging. There were times when the frontend was working but the backend wasn't working at all. Then I would fix the backend and somehow something else in the frontend would stop working. Some errors took me four or five days to solve. Sometimes I would spend hours trying different solutions and still get the same error. Another problem was internet connectivity. In my hometown, there are times when the internet is not reliable. When I couldn't work online, I started using a notebook to write down ideas, things I wanted to build next and problems that I needed to solve. There were also many nights when I stayed up until 3 or 4 AM working on the app. My family would often ask me what I was doing with my laptop all day and tell me to study instead of always sitting in front of the computer. I understand why they said that. But I had been thinking about building something of my own for a very long time, and I didn't want to stop just because it was difficult.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

For me, the biggest accomplishment is simply finishing the app. I started Ranchat without knowing everything I needed to know. I learned while building it, and after 93 days I had something that actually worked. There were many points where I thought a problem was too difficult, but eventually I found a way around it. I am also proud that I didn't stop working on Ranchat because of the errors I faced. This project started as an idea in my head, and now I can actually open the app and use something that I built myself. That is probably the part I am most proud of.

**What we learned**

I learned a lot while building Ranchat. I learned frontend and backend development, APIs, databases, debugging, UI/UX and many other things that I had never worked with before. But more than anything, I learned how to keep working when I don't know the answer. Before Ranchat, if I saw a difficult error, I would think that I didn't know how to solve it. While building Ranchat, I learned that not knowing something doesn't mean I can't figure it out. I just have to keep trying.

**What's next for RanChat**

I still have a lot of things I want to add to Ranchat. I want to improve the UI, make the app more stable, improve the anonymous communication experience and add better safety features. I also want to eventually make Ranchat available to more people. One of my dreams since childhood has been to create something that people will know me for. After spending 93 days building Ranchat, I found Shipaton 2026. When I read about Shipaton, I thought this could be the first step towards that dream. There was one problem though. I am only 17, so I don't have my own Google Play Developer or Apple Developer account. Then I found out about the Next Gen category. It meant that I could still submit something I built as a young student developer, without needing my own app store developer account. So I decided to submit Ranchat. I don't think Ranchat is perfect. I still have a lot to learn and a lot more things I want to build. But this app represents 93 days of my life where I learned, failed, fixed things and kept going. And hopefully, one day I will be able to show my family Ranchat and say: "I made it. I actually built this."

For now, this is just the first step.

</details>

- **Repo check:** public repo · ⚠️ proprietary license (not open source) · 47 commits · Kotlin · RevenueCat found in code ✅
- **Other links:** https://apps.apple.com/app/dryrun-say-the-hard-thing/id6811369238
- **Built with:** android, cloudflare-workers, compose-multiplatform, gradle, groq, ios, kotlin, kotlin-multiplatform, ktor, llm, revenuecat, storekit, swift, typescript

**Video (1:50):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rESiZ3Gvck0

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/rESiZ3Gvck0/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rESiZ3Gvck0)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/352/361/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/352/361/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/352/362/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/352/362/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/352/363/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/352/363/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/352/364/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/352/364/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/352/365/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/352/365/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Most advice about difficult conversations is about whether to have them. That was never my problem. I knew what I needed to say. I had said it in the shower, in the car, in my head at 2am. Then I got in the room and it came out as "I just wanted to check in, no worries if not."

The gap is not courage. It is that the sentence changes on the way out of your mouth and you do not hear it happen. I wanted something that would let me hear it, in private, before it cost me anything real.

**What it does**

You pick a conversation you are dreading, or describe your own. The other person answers in character. They are defensive, or tearful, or charming, or simply unmoved, and they do not let a vague opener slide.

Three things happen that do not happen in a normal chat app.

Your hedging underlines as you type. "Just", "maybe", "I think", "sorry to bother you", "does that make sense?" are marked the moment you write them, with a running count. Nothing is blocked. You just get to watch yourself flinch in real time.

When you finally make a clear point, they say nothing. The typing indicator starts, then stops. Three real seconds of dead air. Most people fill it and talk themselves back out of the thing they just said. Sitting in the silence is the whole skill, and it is scored honestly, because the app counts on the device whether silence was offered and whether you filled it, rather than asking a model to guess.

Afterwards you are scored on four things, quoted back word for word: whether you named the specific thing, said what it cost, left them room to answer, and held the point under pushback.

Run the same conversation twice and it shows you the line that changed.

The before and after in the demo video is real and unscripted. The hedged run came back "All criteria unmet, conversation lacks clarity and firmness", zero out of eight, seven hedges. The same conversation said straight came back "User identified specific issues, impact, and deadline, and stayed firm", eight out of eight, and "They went quiet once. You waited."

**How we built it**

Kotlin Multiplatform with Compose Multiplatform. 4,633 of 5,198 lines, 89%, are shared between iOS and Android. The platform specific code is 220 lines of Kotlin for iOS, 276 for Android, 41 lines of Android host and 28 lines of Swift. There is no second UI.

The parts that had to be trustworthy are deterministic Kotlin in commonMain, not model calls.

The hedge detector tokenises and matches phrases against token sequences, never substrings, so "just" does not fire inside "justify" and "a bit" does not fire inside "a bitter argument". It is backed by a hand written probe corpus of ordinary sentences, half hedged and half clean, deliberately seeded with the words that break naive matching.

The silence beat is decided by the server, which holds the counterpart's state, but counted on the device. Those counts are sent into the scoring request as ground truth, overriding whatever the model thinks it saw. Silence is earned rather than random: it is only offered after you make a clear, specific point, at most twice per run, never twice in a row.

The counterpart's state is three numbers: defensiveness, how heard they feel, and whether they have conceded. The model proposes an update and the server clamps every change to one step per turn, so a hostile colleague cannot turn grateful because you asked nicely once.

The backend is a Cloudflare Worker in TypeScript in front of Groq, with its own auth, rate limiting, and a safety check on both what goes in and what comes back.

101 tests: 61 in shared Kotlin, 40 in the Worker.

**Challenges we ran into**

The trial the app never mentioned. The App Store sheet was offering a free week that the paywall had never disclosed. The trial length was being read from defaultOption.pricingPhases, which is a Google Play concept and is null on iOS, so it returned zero there no matter what App Store Connect said. It now reads introductoryDiscount first. Undisclosed trial terms are their own rejection under guideline 3.1.2, and we found it by watching a recording frame by frame rather than by running a test.

A run you could walk out of and lose. Leaving a rehearsal deleted it, because the session lived only in memory and nothing was written until a run was scored. Fixing that introduced a second bug: a scored run was still offered back, and finishing it twice filed two runs with the same number. Both are fixed. Both were found by watching real usage rather than by a test suite that was perfectly green throughout.

A keyboard that swallowed the exit. On iOS, Compose defaults to OnFocusBehavior.FocusableAboveKeyboard, which pans the whole surface up to clear the keyboard. The rehearsal screen keeps the keyboard open for its entire life, so the top bar went off the top of the screen, taking "Leave" and "Done" with it. Users were trapped inside a conversation with no way out. One line of configuration, found only by watching someone else use it.

Apple, three times. Rejected for a missing demo video, then for a Terms of Use link that was inside the app but not in the App Store metadata, which turns out to be a separate requirement. The app is live now.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The silence. It would have been easy to score "left them room to answer" against a transcript and let a model decide. Instead the counterpart genuinely returns nothing, the app shows real dead air, and the thing being scored actually happened. It is the only place we deliberately made the product feel worse to use in order to make it teach something.

And the restraint. There is no share button anywhere in DryRun, on purpose. What you type is about a real colleague, sometimes by name. Transcripts and scores never leave the device, "Delete everything" means it, and the app says so on the screen where you type.

**What we learned**

That the feature which makes the product worth using was also the hardest to justify keeping, because it looks like nothing happening.

And that a green test suite tells you nothing about whether the app can be used. Every serious bug we shipped was found by watching a recording, not by running tests, and the tests were passing the entire time.

**What's next for DryRun: Say the Hard Thing**

Android is in closed testing on Google Play, running the same shared core. After that: difficulty escalation that remembers how you did last time rather than just counting runs, and hedging trends across months rather than within a single conversation.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every student has notes, a syllabus, and a long list of things to revise. Almost nobody has a plan that survives contact with reality. Miss one day and the whole schedule collapses into guilt — so people abandon the plan, not the subject.

The tools that claim to help actually make it worse. To-do and planner apps show you what you failed to do, then quietly accept that you fell behind. Nothing reschedules. Nothing protects the deadline that actually matters.

We wanted the opposite: a planner that treats a missed day as ordinary life, and quietly rebuilds the rest of your plan around it.

**What it does**

- Subjects with real constraints — add each subject with its exam date, priority, and topics with estimated study minutes.

- AI-generated day-by-day plan — StudyPilot builds a realistic schedule that respects your daily study capacity and prioritises the subjects whose exams are nearest. Nearest exam first, and never more than you can actually finish in a day.

- Today view — answers one question: "what should I study right now?", with your streak, exam countdowns and per-subject progress.

- Adaptive replanning — skipped or missed tasks get redistributed across the remaining days, assuming skipped topics still need to be studied. Your exam dates stay protected.

- Focus timer — a per-task pomodoro timer that logs focused minutes toward your streak.

- Never a dead end — if the AI is unreachable, a deterministic local scheduler builds the plan instead. The app stays fully usable offline.

**Monetization (RevenueCat)**

Freemium, enforced through RevenueCat entitlements:

Free
Pro (pro entitlement)

Subjects
1
Unlimited

AI plan generations
3
Unlimited

Offline planner, focus timer, progress
Yes
Yes

The integration uses the full RevenueCat SDK surface: Purchases.configure, getOfferings → default offering with monthly + lifetime packages, purchase flows, restorePurchases, entitlement checks, and a live customer-info listener that flips the entire app into Pro. Subscription management is handled by the RevenueCat Customer Center. As a student entry without a paid store account, purchases were verified end-to-end against RevenueCat's Test Store.

**How we built it**

Flutter (Dart) targeting Android, with Riverpod for state management and Hive for offline-first local persistence. AI plan generation runs through OpenRouter. Monetization is handled entirely by purchases_flutter and purchases_ui_flutter.

Architecture: UI → Controllers (ChangeNotifier + Riverpod) → Services (AiService, LocalScheduler, PlanService, RevenueCatService, Repository).

**Challenges we ran into**

Making an LLM reliable enough to build a product on. A model that returns malformed JSON is not a feature. StudyPilot prompts for strict JSON, retries with a repair call when parsing fails, and detects topics the AI silently dropped so they get re-inserted. If it still fails, a deterministic scheduler takes over — the user never sees an error where a plan should be.

Designing a fallback that's genuinely good, not a stub. The local scheduler sorts pending topics by urgency (daysUntilExam × 10 + priority) and packs them greedily into daily capacity. It's deterministic, unit-tested, and produces plans students actually follow.

A real purchase flow without a paid developer account. Rather than mocking payments, we wired the complete RevenueCat integration and verified it against the Test Store, so the entitlement, paywall, restore and Customer Center paths are all real code.

**Accomplishments we're proud of**

- An AI feature with a guaranteed working fallback — the happy path is AI, but the product never depends on it.

- Entitlement-driven limits: freemium logic lives in one place, driven by RevenueCat state.

- Adaptive replanning that protects exam dates — the actual differentiator.

- Clean flutter analyze, a unit-tested scheduler, MIT-licensed and fully open source.

**What we learned**

- LLM output needs an engineering layer around it — schema, repair, gap detection, fallback — before it becomes something users can rely on.

- Modelling access as a single entitlement makes freemium dramatically simpler.

- A good fallback is a feature, not a compromise.

**What's next**

- Local study reminders and an agenda/calendar view.

- Weekly insights computed from logged focus minutes.

- Publishing to Google Play with real store products.

**Links**

- Open source repo (MIT): https://github.com/Ravish-Paul/studypilot

**Video**

&lt;LINK — 2-minute demo on a physical Android device&gt;

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every AI app is the same shape. You type something, it answers, you leave. Prompting is a skill almost nobody practises deliberately, and one that nobody can put a number on.

Charades is already a game about describing your way around a constraint. Point it at a language model and the roles invert: the machine becomes the thing you are trying to beat, and your prompt becomes the move. That gave me something a chat box never can, which is a score.

**What it does**

One word a day, the same word for everyone.

Five obvious words are blocked. For SANDCASTLE that is sand, beach, build, castle, bucket. You write a clue that goes around them, and a language model gets three guesses.

Scoring is brevity. Par is 30 characters, and every character you come in under par is worth 15 points. fort vs tide is twelve characters, lands on the first guess, and scores 1,270. A clue that says too much gets you mansion, hacienda, adobe and zero.

Everyone plays the same word, so clue length is worth comparing. There is a streak, an archive, and a full record of how short your clues really are.

Today's puzzle is always free. Plus sells difficulty rather than access: the constraint modes (no vowels, one word, twenty characters), the full archive, and your complete statistics.

**How we built it**

Compose Multiplatform, and genuinely shared. Not "Kotlin for the logic, native for the UI". Every screen is shared Kotlin.

shared/src/commonMain 2,970 lines game, UI, networking, billing, storage
shared/src/androidMain 297 lines
shared/src/iosMain 165 lines
androidApp + iosApp 57 lines two thin hosts

That is 85% shared, with eight expect/actual pairs for the rest: platform identity, HTTP client, storage, share sheet, sound, daily reminders, and the store API key.

RevenueCat behind one object. Entitlements, offerings and the purchase flow run through purchases-kmp in commonMain, wrapped in a single Plus object. No other file in the app imports a RevenueCat type, which is what made the next part possible.

A Cloudflare Worker serves the puzzles. They are generated offline and uploaded to KV, so a normal session costs nothing and the model key never ships inside the app. Guesses are cached by a hash of the normalised clue, and players converge hard on the same phrasings, so a cache hit returns in about 20ms instead of about 700ms.

**Challenges we ran into**

I was tuning the wrong knob. The banned word lists felt like the difficulty control, so I hardened them adversarially by asking the model which words it leans on. Then I measured it with self play against the real model, and the first-guess win rate did not move at all. What did move it was length: 100% at 60 characters, 100% at 40, 90% at 25, and 67% at 15. Par went from 60 characters to 30 on the strength of that one graph, and the three-guess framing turned out to be decorative rather than a real tension mechanic.

Substring matching cannot tell a compound from a coincidence. Blocking sting for BEEHIVE also rejected "casting", "lasting" and "fasting". Sand rejected "sandwich" and "thousand". Wind rejected "window". A player experiences a false rejection as a bug in the game, not as a rule, so the minimum containment length went to five characters with a three-character remainder, and every puzzle carries an allow list for the leftovers. The false positive rate is now measured by a probe rather than assumed.

Two App Store rejections, and the second one was my own fault. The first was 3.1.2, a missing Terms of Use link on the paywall. The second was 2.1(b), reviewers could not locate the in-app purchases. My review note had told them to tap any padlocked mode, but that row only renders during the writing phase, so they went looking in the wrong place. The fix was to keep a way into Plus on screen after the round is played.

Play billing is still blocked on bank verification. Rather than ship an Android build full of padlocks that open an empty sheet, Plus.unlocked() takes both the entitlement and whether a store key is configured. With no key the app degrades to a complete free game with no dead paywall anywhere, which is also exactly what avoided a Play rejection.

A tester said: "I didn't quite understand what I am typing and what the machine tries to guess." That is the game failing before it starts. The answer was not more words, it was one worked example on first run: here is a word, here is what you may not say, here is a clue, here is the machine getting it.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A design decision that came from a measurement rather than a feeling. The difficulty curve is entirely clue length, and I can show the numbers.

- Billing that fails open. A build with no store key is a complete game, not a wall of locks. The whole app asks one function whether something is unlocked, so the two can never drift apart.

- 85% shared with no UI compromise, and a platform layer small enough to print in a table.

- Nothing lets a player read ahead. The puzzle number is resolved from a date index server side and never taken from the request. The test asserts that five different smuggling shapes all still resolve to today.

- Live on the App Store inside the submission window, after two rejections.

**What we learned**

Measure before you design. I spent real effort hardening ban lists that moved the difficulty by zero. Thirty minutes of self play would have told me that on day one.

Fail open on billing. Treating "no store configured" as "everything unlocked" rather than "everything locked" turned a blocked payment provider from a launch blocker into a footnote.

Write App Review notes against the actual render conditions. I described a control that only exists in one phase of the game and cost myself a review cycle.

Ask for permission after the win, not on launch. The notification prompt fires only once someone has solved a puzzle, because asking a stranger who has not played yet burns the single chance iOS gives you.

**What's next for Machine Charades**

- Play subscriptions, once the bank verification clears. The mapping is already built on the RevenueCat side; only the key is missing.

- More puzzles. The current schedule runs to 12 October 2026 and needs extending well past that.

- Fix a duplicate-guess bug. The model occasionally repeats a guess it has already made, despite being told not to. It needs a stricter prompt or a server-side reject-and-retry.

- A head-to-head mode, where two players clue the same word and compare character counts directly rather than through par.

- Localised puzzle sets, because the banned word lists are the interesting part and they do not translate.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Why Return Window**

A return deadline is easy to forget while deciding whether to keep a purchase. Return Window keeps those dates in one small list, without asking for an email inbox or a pile of receipts.

Enter the deadline from the shop and a note if you need one. Search the list, mark an item resolved, or reopen it if your decision changes. JSON import and export let you keep your own backup. The app does not decide whether a purchase qualifies for a refund.

**How it is built**

JavaScript, HTML and CSS run inside a Capacitor Android app. Dates are treated as calendar days, and stored records and imported backups are validated. RevenueCat supplies the one-time Window Plus entitlement for on-device reminders. Access is checked against customer information rather than a locally writable purchase flag. The demo uses Test Store: no real charges.

**What testing uncovered**

Returning a Capacitor plugin proxy from an async function caused JavaScript to call a nonexistent then method. Returning the module namespace instead fixed this Android-only failure; regression tests cover that boundary. The project has 33 passing automated tests. Native Test Store purchase and same-installation restore passed. A fresh installation without a purchase stayed locked on restore.

The notification plugin also requested exact-alarm access by default. These reminders do not need that precision, so they now use ordinary notification permission. Three reminders appeared in Android's alarm schedule. Advancing the emulator clock produced an actual notification while the app was in the background; tapping it reopened the app. The clock was restored afterward.

**Where it stands**

This is a student prototype, not a store-launched product. Notification delivery has been checked with a simulated clock, not an overnight physical-device test; battery settings can delay delivery. Cross-device purchase restoration is not yet verified.

The source is public under the MIT license. Item names, notes and dates stay on-device. RevenueCat receives the purchase-related information needed to check access. There is no receipt upload or inbox access.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Takt**

Plan smarter. Prioritize better.

Takt is a calendar-aware competition decision-support system that helps people decide whether and how to pursue a hackathon or competition using evidence from the competition source, their real availability, workload assumptions, and explicit planning constraints.

It does not treat a competition URL as automatically reliable truth, and it does not turn a recommendation into a calendar commitment without the user's approval.

Takt separates the decision into distinct stages:

Competition source
→ Evidence-backed canonical brief
→ Readiness
→ User constraints
→ Workload
→ Candidate planning
→ Feasibility
→ Recommendation
→ Human decision
→ Accepted local commitment

The goal is simple: help users understand what they can realistically take on before they commit.

**Inspiration**

Competition decisions look simple until the information has to survive contact with reality.

A hackathon or competition can have:

- a submission deadline in a specific timezone;

- a separate registration deadline;

- eligibility requirements;

- team-size constraints;

- category-specific rules;

- required technologies;

- required artifacts;

- judging criteria;

- multiple official pages that disagree;

- or a PDF whose useful content needs native extraction or OCR.

Even after those facts are understood, a second problem remains:

Can the required work actually fit into the user's real schedule before the deadline?

Participants often answer that question informally. They skim the rules, estimate the workload mentally, compare it loosely against classes, work, organizations, sleep, and existing commitments, and then commit.

That can produce overloaded schedules, unfinished submissions, unrealistic scopes, and avoidable opportunity cost.

We built Takt to turn that vague judgment into a structured decision process.

Instead of asking only:

“Do I want to join this competition?”

Takt helps the user examine:

- what the competition actually says;

- which facts are verified, missing, unresolved, or conflicting;

- whether the user is ready to evaluate it;

- what work the selected scope requires;

- how uncertain that workload is;

- when the user can actually work;

- which schedules satisfy the hard constraints;

- how robust those schedules are under different effort scenarios;

- and why a recommendation was produced.

Takt is decision support, not an autonomous scheduling agent.

The final decision remains with the user.

**What it does**

Takt can ingest supported competition material from a URL or PDF and transform it into a traceable planning workflow.

The core flow:

- captures the source and preserves provenance;

- performs defensive URL, HTML, PDF, and OCR-capable processing;

- extracts supported competition facts;

- reconciles evidence into a versioned canonical competition report;

- keeps conflict, missingness, and uncertainty explicit;

- evaluates deterministic readiness;

- models user availability and existing commitments;

- validates workload estimates and task dependencies;

- generates bounded candidate plans using OR-Tools CP-SAT;

- independently checks candidate invariants;

- evaluates feasibility across explicit workload scenarios;

- assembles an advisory recommendation;

- lets the user inspect the system-primary plan and valid alternatives;

- requires explicit confirmation before a plan becomes an accepted local commitment;

- preserves accepted history and supports re-evaluation when material inputs change.

Takt helps answer questions such as:

- What does this competition actually require?

- Are any critical facts still missing or conflicting?

- Am I ready to evaluate this opportunity?

- How much work does the selected scope require?

- Does that work fit into my real availability?

- Which candidate schedules are valid?

- What happens if the workload takes longer than expected?

- Is the plan feasible, tight, or infeasible under the current constraints?

- What trade-offs does the recommendation depend on?

- Has the previous recommendation become stale?

- Which parts of the result are facts, assumptions, or recommendations?

The output is a structured Decision Report rather than a single unexplained score.

**Core decision flow**

The end-to-end lifecycle is:

URL / PDF
↓
Source snapshot
↓
Native extraction / OCR evidence
↓
Candidate extraction
↓
Reconciliation
↓
Canonical competition report
↓
Readiness
↓
Availability + workload
↓
CP-SAT candidate plans
↓
Feasibility
↓
Recommendation
↓
Decision Report
↓
Explicit user action
↓
Accepted local plan / progress
↓
Re-evaluation when material inputs change

Several distinctions remain intentionally separate throughout the flow:

source evidence != canonical truth
canonical brief != readiness
readiness != feasibility
feasibility != recommendation
recommendation != commitment
stale history != current truth

**Operational flowchart**

The operational flowchart shows how the system handles validation, extraction, reconciliation, readiness, planning, recommendation, persistence, recovery, and human authority.

Important runtime boundaries include:

- invalid or unsupported source input stops before planning;

- missing information remains missing instead of becoming false information;

- conflicting evidence remains conflict unless deterministic authority or freshness rules justify supersession;

- blocked readiness does not become solver infeasibility;

- technical failure does not become a domain conclusion;

- only valid availability can be used for planning;

- task dependencies and daily capacity constrain candidate schedules;

- a solver candidate is independently validated before it can support a recommendation;

- recommendation remains advisory;

- accepted truth exists only after explicit user action and successful local persistence.

Takt can therefore finish with uncertainty, review, tight capacity, infeasibility, or a supported recommendation instead of forcing every case into a positive answer.

**System architecture**

**Judge-facing architecture**

The simplified architecture keeps the main responsibility boundaries visible:

Flutter mobile client
↓
REST / JSON
↓
FastAPI compute layer
↓
Source processing
↓
Canonical reasoning
↓
Planning + feasibility
↓
Recommendation
↓
Human decision
↓
Local-first persistence

For the current MVP:

DEVICE = personal state
SERVER = compute

The backend primarily performs computation and decision-support evaluation.

The mobile application owns personal state and accepted-plan persistence.

**Full technical architecture**

The full architecture expands the same flow into implementation-oriented components:

- Flutter presentation and local state;

- SQLite + Drift persistence;

- RevenueCat entitlement boundary;

- FastAPI product API;

- Pydantic public contracts;

- URL and PDF ingestion;

- native extraction;

- OCR;

- evidence reconciliation;

- readiness;

- availability;

- workload;

- OR-Tools CP-SAT scheduling;

- feasibility;

- recommendation;

- re-evaluation;

- public failure contracts;

- explicit human acceptance.

The architecture deliberately avoids making a cloud database part of backend correctness for the MVP.

Takt also avoids treating monetization state as decision truth. RevenueCat can control access to a presentation feature, but it cannot change competition facts, readiness, solver results, feasibility, or recommendation correctness.

**Data strategy**

Takt uses a contract-first data strategy.

The project deliberately separates source evidence, deterministic fixtures, future behavioral data, and product runtime state because they answer different questions.

**1. Real public source corpus**

Real competition sources are used for:

- URL and PDF extraction evaluation;

- canonical-field validation;

- provenance evaluation;

- source conflict evaluation;

- extraction and reconciliation testing.

These sources are evaluation evidence, not a custom-model training dataset.

The source hierarchy is:

- official legal or rules source;

- official organizer source;

- official event or platform page;

- official FAQ or update;

- secondary source;

- synthetic fixture for evaluation only.

The system preserves source identity, extraction path, evidence locators, and versioned provenance so downstream decisions can be traced back to supporting evidence.

**2. Synthetic deterministic and adversarial fixtures**

Synthetic fixtures are used where deterministic truth is more useful than pretending to have field data.

They cover areas such as:

- calendar constraints;

- recurrence and exceptions;

- overlapping commitments;

- fragmented capacity;

- CP-SAT invariants;

- native-versus-OCR reconciliation;

- missing fields;

- conflicting sources;

- hard feasibility cases;

- fallback and recovery behavior;

- stale-state transitions;

- release screenshots.

Synthetic fixtures are explicitly treated as:

EXPERIMENTAL
NOT SOURCE OF TRUTH
NOT FINAL TRAINING DATASET
NOT PRODUCT EVIDENCE OF REAL-WORLD OUTCOMES

They are engineering evidence.

**3. Future real behavioral and outcome data**

Real behavioral data is intentionally deferred until the product can collect defensible observations.

Examples include:

- actual task effort;

- estimate-versus-actual history;

- recommendation usefulness;

- accepted, edited, or ignored recommendations;

- completion risk;

- long-term calibration.

Synthetic acceptance labels are not treated as evidence of recommendation quality.

**4. Dataset families**

The preproduction data strategy defines several dataset families:

- DS-01 Source Understanding Corpus for authoritative-source extraction and provenance;

- DS-02 Calendar Constraint Fixtures for schedule and recurrence behavior;

- DS-03 Solver Feasibility Fixtures for task, dependency, capacity, and buffer invariants;

- DS-04 Task Effort Dataset for future effort-estimation work;

- DS-05 Recommendation Evaluation Dataset for future real-user evaluation.

The current MVP does not require a custom-trained ML model to make its decision.

**5. Leakage policy**

Takt treats leakage as a methodology failure, not a cosmetic benchmark problem.

Examples of forbidden leakage include:

- using actual effort before task execution;

- using final completion state to predict initial feasibility;

- using future calendar changes in an earlier recommendation;

- using label-derived variables to predict the same label;

- splitting near-duplicate versions of the same competition source across evaluation partitions.

Where grouped evaluation is required, related entities remain together.

For example:

- source extraction groups by source_family_id or competition_id;

- OCR variants group by original document;

- future unseen-user effort evaluation groups by user_id;

- deterministic solver fixtures use fixture families rather than train/test terminology.

**6. Calibration and uncertainty**

Takt explicitly models uncertainty instead of manufacturing precision.

The system distinguishes:

- source uncertainty;

- effort uncertainty;

- constraint uncertainty;

- recommendation uncertainty.

For workload, the MVP uses:

minimum
likely
maximum

rather than a single forced estimate.

Before any future user-facing probability is introduced, the data strategy requires:

- a defined empirical target;

- held-out calibration measurement;

- reliability analysis;

- appropriate probabilistic metrics;

- and distribution-shift review.

The current release therefore avoids unsupported claims such as “87% feasible.”

**7. Custom-model training gate**

A custom-trained model is allowed only after:

- the target definition is stable;

- prediction-time features are documented;

- leakage audit passes;

- split strategy is frozen;

- baselines and metrics are defined;

- sufficient real labels exist;

- uncertainty and calibration plans exist;

- deterministic rules remain authoritative;

- rollback is possible.

The current release candidate does not include a custom-trained ML model.

That is deliberate.

The MVP relies on explicit contracts, deterministic readiness rules, transparent workload ranges, and CP-SAT planning where those methods match the problem better.

**Logical data model**

The logical ERD represents the relationships behind the complete decision-support lifecycle.

At a high level, the data model connects:

- source records;

- extracted evidence;

- canonical competition reports;

- canonical field states;

- readiness results;

- availability;

- commitments;

- tasks;

- workload ranges;

- candidate plans;

- feasibility results;

- recommendations;

- evaluation basis;

- stale transitions;

- accepted plan revisions;

- task progress;

- and traceability metadata.

The model keeps source evidence, user constraints, planning state, recommendation state, and accepted state as separate responsibilities.

That separation matters because Takt is not storing a generic to-do list.

It preserves the chain from:

what the competition says

through:

what the user can realistically do

to:

why a particular recommendation was produced

and finally:

what the user explicitly chose to accept.

**Why the system separates the decision stages**

Each stage answers a different question.

**Source processing**

“What evidence did we receive?”

Takt captures and processes the source without assuming extracted text is already canonical truth.

**Reconciliation**

“What competition facts can we responsibly publish?”

Supported observations are reconciled into canonical fields with explicit states such as:

VERIFIED
SINGLE_SOURCE
CONFLICT
MISSING
UNVERIFIED

A conflict cannot become a usable fact merely because one extraction path has a higher confidence value.

**Readiness**

“Do we know enough, and does the case satisfy the deterministic conditions needed to evaluate it?”

Readiness remains separate from feasibility.

Examples of readiness outcomes include:

READY_TO_EVALUATE
NEEDS_REVIEW
ELIGIBILITY_BLOCKED
DEADLINE_PASSED
INSUFFICIENT_INFORMATION

Unknown eligibility is not the same as failed eligibility.

**Workload**

“What work does the selected scope require?”

Tasks can preserve:

- identity;

- mandatory status;

- dependencies;

- minimum effort;

- likely effort;

- maximum effort;

- assumptions.

The workload layer validates:

- minimum &lt;= likely &lt;= maximum;

- duplicate IDs;

- dependency references;

- dependency cycles;

- deterministic topological order;

- transitive required closure.

**Availability**

“When can the user actually work?”

Availability is modeled as timezone-aware, minute-aligned intervals.

The system can account for:

- work windows;

- fixed commitments;

- flexible commitments;

- recurrence;

- exceptions;

- accepted project commitments;

- daily capacity;

- focus-duration preferences;

- target buffer.

Aggregate free hours alone are not enough. Ten continuous hours and twenty thirty-minute fragments are different planning states.

**Candidate scheduling**

“Which concrete schedules satisfy the hard constraints?”

OR-Tools CP-SAT is used to generate bounded candidate allocations.

Planning respects:

- available-only scheduling;

- task dependencies;

- finish-to-start semantics;

- deadlines;

- daily capacity;

- task splitting rules;

- scheduling buffers;

- candidate diversity constraints.

Candidate output is independently checked against invariants instead of trusting solver output merely because the solver returned a result.

**Feasibility**

“How does the plan behave under different workload assumptions?”

Takt evaluates explicit workload scenarios, including:

MIN
LIKELY
MAX
FULL_SCOPE

Feasibility can distinguish:

FEASIBLE
FEASIBLE_WITH_TRADEOFFS
TIGHT_CAPACITY
NOT_FEASIBLE_UNDER_CURRENT_CONSTRAINTS

A technical execution failure is not represented as infeasibility.

**Recommendation**

“Given the validated evidence above, what decision-support output should be presented?”

The recommendation can expose:

- recommended candidate identity;

- suggested work windows;

- rationale;

- trade-offs;

- assumptions;

- valid alternatives.

The recommendation does not independently override source truth, readiness, or feasibility.

**Re-evaluation**

“Has the evidence or planning basis materially changed?”

Takt preserves distinct states such as:

UNCHANGED
SUPERSEDED
SESSION OUTDATED

Trusted stale evidence is not silently erased.

A previous accepted plan remains historical truth even when the evaluation that produced it later becomes stale.

**Explicit acceptance**

The final authority boundary is:

Recommendation
↓
User confirms
↓
Local transaction commits
↓
Accepted truth exists

A failed persistence operation does not become an accepted plan.

A suggestion is not a commitment.

**Local-first persistence**

The Flutter application uses SQLite + Drift for personal state.

Persistence covers release-critical state such as:

- schedule commitments;

- recurrence and exceptions;

- analysis snapshots;

- accepted plan revisions;

- accepted schedule blocks;

- task progress;

- stale evaluation state.

The backend remains primarily a stateless compute layer.

This architecture avoids introducing server-side persistence before there is a concrete need for:

- accounts;

- cross-device synchronization;

- shared team workspaces;

- cloud backup;

- asynchronous server jobs;

- server-side accepted-plan history.

**RevenueCat / Takt Pro**

RevenueCat is used as an access boundary, not a correctness boundary.

Canonical Shipaton identifiers include:

entitlement: pro
Test Store product: takt_pro_lifetime_v1
offering: default
package: $rc_lifetime
premium feature: alternative_candidates

The free experience keeps:

- competition facts;

- readiness;

- feasibility;

- the system-primary recommendation;

- and other correctness-critical domain information.

An active pro entitlement unlocks the Alternative Candidate Explorer, allowing the user to inspect and select additional valid candidates already returned by the same backend evaluation.

RevenueCat does not change:

- source provenance;

- canonical facts;

- readiness;

- planning inputs;

- candidate validity;

- solver output;

- feasibility;

- recommendation correctness;

- accepted-plan history.

Unknown or initial entitlement failures fail closed for the premium-only surface.

Refresh failures preserve the last trustworthy entitlement state.

Purchase and restore use RevenueCat's official Flutter SDK.

The Shipaton demo path uses RevenueCat Test Store configuration.

**How we built it**

We used an evaluation-first, contract-driven process.

The project moved through:

Discovery and Problem Framing
↓
Product Requirements
↓
Evaluation and Domain Rules
↓
Data Strategy
↓
Synthetic Evaluation Fixtures
↓
Preproduction Contracts
↓
Implementation Handoff
↓
Production Implementation
↓
Integration
↓
Reliability Work
↓
Backend Release Audit
↓
Mobile + End-to-End Release Audit
↓
Release-Candidate Closure

Before implementation, we defined the behavior that needed to remain stable:

- canonical source semantics;

- readiness states;

- workload invariants;

- availability rules;

- task dependencies;

- feasibility semantics;

- recommendation boundaries;

- human acceptance authority;

- stale evaluation behavior;

- recovery classes;

- persistence semantics.

That let us test the system against explicit contracts instead of treating a successful demo as proof of correctness.

The production stack includes:

Backend
- Python 3.12
- FastAPI
- Pydantic v2
- httpx
- python-multipart
- OR-Tools CP-SAT
- PyMuPDF
- Tesseract OCR

Mobile
- Flutter
- Dart
- Provider
- SQLite
- Drift
- http
- file_picker
- timezone
- RevenueCat purchases_flutter

Quality
- pytest
- Ruff
- flutter_test
- GitHub Actions
- uv

**Evidence and evaluation**

Takt's release process treats evidence as part of the product rather than an afterthought.

**Backend release audit**

Hari 7A completed a full backend release audit.

Audited backend runtime freeze:

650d17ff8dabed273ab50ef5d60581697b777367

Recorded backend gate:

Python Ruff PASS
Python regression 1010 passed
0 failed
0 skipped
known P0 0
known HIGH 0

The audit covered:

- URL ingestion;

- PDF ingestion;

- native extraction;

- OCR;

- source provenance;

- candidate normalization;

- reconciliation;

- canonical report integrity;

- readiness;

- availability;

- workload;

- CP-SAT planning;

- independent candidate validation;

- feasibility;

- recommendation;

- re-evaluation;

- public API failure semantics.

**Mobile and end-to-end release audit**

Hari 7B completed the mobile and end-to-end release audit.

Audited mobile runtime/evidence freeze:

ab44fbe1776afe1a04adeb028aaef6c0e2017622

Exact-head CI recorded:

Flutter analyze PASS
Flutter regression 286 passed
320 px / 2x compact QA PASS
9 screenshot evidence states PASS
390 × 844 crop verification PASS
Android debug build PASS
iOS debug build PASS

The mobile audit covered:

- root navigation;

- schedule CRUD and recurrence;

- Analyze Competition;

- source review and provenance;

- Decision Report;

- alternative candidate presentation;

- explicit acceptance;

- Saved Plans;

- task progress;

- stale and re-evaluation behavior;

- recovery;

- local persistence;

- responsive critical-path QA;

- Android and iOS debug builds.

**Release-candidate closure**

Both release audits are merged.

Current release-candidate blocker count:

P0 / critical = 0 known
P1 / HIGH = 0 known

The release candidate is ready for submission packaging within its documented claim boundary.

**Challenges we ran into**

**Source truth is harder than text extraction**

Extracting characters from HTML or PDF is only the first step.

The harder problem is determining whether multiple observations agree, conflict, represent the same instant in different timezone notation, come from independent sources, or should remain unresolved.

Takt therefore separates extraction from reconciliation.

**Ambiguous source facts**

A single source can contain repeated or contradictory values.

During the backend release audit, ambiguity handling was tightened so the parser fails closed rather than silently selecting the first supported value.

Equivalent timezone instants can still reconcile, but contradictory or partially unsupported alternatives are not silently promoted to canonical truth.

**Unknown is not infeasible**

A missing eligibility attribute, incomplete brief, or technical failure should not become a false negative decision.

Takt keeps these meanings separate:

UNKNOWN != INFEASIBLE
FAILURE != MISSING
EMPTY RESULT != FAILURE
CONFLICT remains CONFLICT

**Free time is not planning capacity**

A total-hour calculation can claim that a project fits even when the work cannot actually be scheduled.

Dependencies, fragmentation, recurring commitments, deadlines, daily limits, and focus blocks matter.

That turned planning into a constraint-satisfaction problem rather than simple arithmetic.

**Workload is uncertain**

One exact estimate creates false precision.

Takt therefore uses minimum, likely, and maximum effort ranges and evaluates multiple scenarios.

**Solver output still needs verification**

A solver returning a candidate is not enough.

Candidate plans are independently checked against hard invariants before they can support feasibility or recommendation.

**Recommendation is not commitment**

The product must not silently convert a suggested window into an accepted commitment.

Acceptance requires explicit confirmation and a successful local transaction.

**Stale state is real state**

When inputs materially change, the previous evaluation can become stale.

But stale historical truth must not be erased.

Takt preserves trusted SUPERSEDED evidence and accepted historical revisions instead of rewriting them as if the earlier decision never happened.

**Monetization can contaminate correctness if designed badly**

RevenueCat could easily have been wired into recommendation behavior.

We deliberately prevented that.

Entitlement controls access to the Alternative Candidate Explorer, not the truth of the analysis.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud that Takt turns a vague question:

“Should I join this competition?”

into a traceable workflow:

Evidence → Canonical Brief → Readiness → Workload → Availability → Candidate Plans → Feasibility → Recommendation → Explicit Acceptance

The release candidate combines:

- URL and PDF source intake;

- native extraction;

- OCR;

- source provenance;

- evidence reconciliation;

- explicit canonical field states;

- deterministic readiness;

- minute-based availability;

- recurrence and exceptions;

- dependency-aware workload models;

- minimum / likely / maximum effort;

- OR-Tools CP-SAT candidate generation;

- independent candidate invariant validation;

- multi-scenario feasibility;

- traceable advisory recommendations;

- multiple valid candidate plans;

- RevenueCat-gated alternative candidate exploration;

- local-first SQLite + Drift persistence;

- accepted-plan revisions;

- task progress;

- stale-state preservation;

- re-evaluation;

- explicit recovery semantics;

- Android and iOS mobile builds;

- backend and mobile release audits.

We are especially proud that correctness boundaries remain visible in the product:

CONFLICT != VERIFIED
UNKNOWN != INFEASIBLE
FAILURE != MISSING
recommendation != commitment
entitlement != correctness

**What we learned**

We learned that useful decision support depends less on producing a confident answer and more on preserving the structure behind the answer.

A recommendation becomes more useful when the user can inspect:

- the evidence;

- the unresolved facts;

- the workload assumptions;

- the available capacity;

- the candidate plan;

- the feasibility classification;

- the trade-offs;

- and the reason the recommendation exists.

We also learned that abstention can be a valid product output.

CONFLICT, MISSING, UNKNOWN, NEEDS_REVIEW, TIGHT_CAPACITY, and explicit infeasibility preserve information that a forced answer would destroy.

Another lesson was that optimization should be used only for the part of the problem it actually owns.

CP-SAT is good at finding schedules under constraints.

It does not determine whether the competition source is trustworthy, whether eligibility is known, whether a recommendation should become a commitment, or whether a paid user deserves a different truth.

Keeping those responsibilities separate made the system easier to audit.

**Known limitations**

The current release candidate intentionally does not claim:

- general multilingual competition-rule understanding;

- a general-purpose LLM extraction system;

- perfect extraction from arbitrary websites;

- universal live-source extraction accuracy;

- a custom-trained ML decision model;

- production authentication;

- production rate limiting;

- production load certification;

- Railway network or egress-policy certification;

- signed Play Store distribution;

- signed TestFlight distribution certification;

- live RevenueCat store-transaction certification;

- cross-device synchronization;

- shared team workspace;

- cloud backup;

- server-side accepted-plan persistence;

- automatic calendar execution;

- exhaustive physical-device certification;

- support for every locale, accessibility mode, device ratio, or OEM environment.

Additional boundaries include:

- the production candidate normalizer uses a bounded explicit grammar;

- unsupported ambiguity fails closed rather than guessing;

- OCR is bounded, but not every synchronous PDF operation is forcibly terminated at one exact global wall-clock threshold;

- CI screenshots are Flutter-renderer evidence, not exhaustive real-device validation;

- unsaved in-memory state is not guaranteed to survive arbitrary OS process death;

- the current file_picker Android integration emits a future Flutter/Kotlin compatibility warning while the audited Android debug build still passes.

These are documented limitations, not hidden promises.

**What's next for Takt**

The next phase should improve the quality of evidence rather than simply add more automation.

Priorities include:

- broader source-language and competition-format coverage;

- richer canonical extraction where it can be validated safely;

- stronger multi-source competition reconciliation;

- collection of real estimate-versus-actual workload history;

- real recommendation usefulness evaluation;

- calibration of future workload estimation from real data;

- calendar integrations that preserve explicit user authority;

- cross-device synchronization when a concrete account model exists;

- team-based planning;

- longer-horizon portfolio planning across multiple competitions;

- production RevenueCat store validation;

- production authentication and deployment hardening.

A future learned effort-estimation model should only be introduced after sufficient real labels, leakage controls, baselines, calibration, and rollback criteria exist.

The point is not to turn Takt into a larger pile of automation.

The point is to make the next decision more defensible.

**Try it**

Hosted API:

https://takt-production-951d.up.railway.app

iOS TestFlight:

https://testflight.apple.com/join/PEfUw9CX

Demo video:

https://youtu.be/aa_vFMYPgjU

Source code:

https://github.com/panjiaryasoma/Takt

Takt

Plan smarter. Prioritize better.

Preserve the source. Keep uncertainty explicit. Model the real constraints. Let the human decide what becomes real.
