## 370. Undo — Regret Journal

> One question every night: what would you do differently? Undo quietly maps where your regrets cluster — across twenty years of notes — so you change the thing, not just record it.

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/undo-regret-journal (gallery page 106) · ❤️ 0 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [Huynh Thien An Nguyen](https://devpost.com/annguyen030205)
- **GitHub (Try it out):** https://github.com/Annguyen0410/Undo
- **Repo check:** public repo · license: MIT · 1 commits · Kotlin · RevenueCat found in code ✅
- **Built with:** android, android-studio, github, gradle, jetpack-compose, junit, kotlin, kotlin-coroutines, kotlin-flow, ksp, material-design-3, mit, python, revenuecat, room, sharedpreferences, sqlite, vico, workmanager

**Video (1:49):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2b89ehOxyOQ

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/2b89ehOxyOQ/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2b89ehOxyOQ)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/359/872/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/359/872/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/359/873/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/359/873/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/359/874/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/359/874/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every journal app I have tried asks me to be prolific. Blank page, streak counter, "you haven't written in 3 days." But the thing I actually do every night is smaller and less comfortable: I lie in bed and think, I should have said something in that meeting, or I wasted the whole evening. Those thoughts never make it into a journal because they are not nice, and by morning they are gone.

They are also not random. I noticed the same three or four of them coming back for years — mostly communication, mostly courage. That is the gap Undo exists to close: a journal that asks one uncomfortable question and then, quietly, shows you where your regrets keep clustering. Not to make you feel bad — to make the pattern impossible to ignore, because a pattern you can see is a pattern you can change.

**What it does**

Undo asks a single question before bed: "Is there anything today you wish you'd done differently?" You write freely — no character limit, as many notes in an evening as you need, and no cap on how old the journal can be — tag it with one of eight categories (Work, Money, Health, Relationships, Time, Courage, Communication, Other) and rate how heavily it sits on you.

Three tabs:

- Check-in — the nightly question, the composer, tonight's stack of notes (each one editable, deletable, undoable), and a From the archive card that hands one evening from years ago back to you ("Ten years ago tonight") with a tap-through to that exact night.

- Journal — the archive: pinned search, category filters, pages of 50 as you scroll, and a jump-to-month control that reaches any month that holds notes in one step.

- Insights — your streak, a category donut, one plain-language sentence naming the pattern ("most of what you'd change this week sits in Communication"), and a monthly trend. Free users see the last 7 days; Premium unlocks the full history and the trend across months.

An unsaved draft is written to disk on every keystroke, so a killed app comes back mid-sentence. Everything is on-device: no account, no sync, no analytics, and the notes database is excluded from Android cloud backup. CSV export and import are deliberately free, because that file is the backup.

**How I built it**

Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, Material 3, single activity, three screens. Room holds one table; there is no backend at all.

The hard constraint I set early: the journal must survive decades. That ruled out the normal "load the list, filter in memory" approach. The Journal reads pages of 50 over a (date, createdAt) index with a date ceiling instead of OFFSET-ing past years; Insights takes every number straight from SQL (GROUP BY category, GROUP BY substr(date,1,7)); the streak comes from a list of distinct dates; the archive card picks its evening from those dates and then loads exactly one day. Nothing in the app ever holds the journal in memory. Against 20 years and 7,185 seeded notes, the first page plus the exact count comes back in about 40 ms warm.

WorkManager schedules the nightly reminder through a notification channel and tolerates Doze. Vico draws the donut and the trend. The insight sentence is pure aggregation over category templates — no AI, no network call.

Design was a real part of the build, not a coat of paint: one palette, one spacing scale and one panel component shared by all three tabs, a near-black plum "midnight observatory" background with a slow star field, a serif pull-quote for the nightly question, and a second premium theme (Midnight Reflection) that pushes the same hues deeper and colder.

**How RevenueCat powers the purchase**

The paywall loads the current RevenueCat offering and renders its packages with the real localised prices the SDK returns, then purchases or restores through purchases. Every premium decision in the app is derived from one place — entitlements["premium"].isActive — in purchase/RevenueCatManager.kt, so there is no second source of truth and no way for the UI to disagree with the store.

premium unlocks four things: the full history, the monthly trend, a custom reminder time, and the Midnight Reflection theme. Free users keep unlimited check-ins, the timeline, the 7-day insights, and CSV export/import.

Undo has not been released to a store yet, so the demo build runs against RevenueCat's Test Store — the same SDK, the same default offering, the same CustomerInfo flow, with sandbox transactions visible in the RevenueCat dashboard. No Apple or Google developer account is involved, and no real card is ever charged.

**Challenges I faced**

The empty-demo problem. A journal app installs empty by design — notes are written by hand and there is no per-day limit, so a fresh install has nothing to demo, screenshot or record. I added a debug-only Sample journal card that back-fills about 90 deterministic days, and a Twenty years card that seeds roughly 8,700 notes across 20 years, so the performance claim is checkable instead of asserted. Both are hidden in release builds.

Bugs that only exist on a device. Reviewing on the emulator rather than in the IDE found two things no amount of reading the code would have: the platform theme painted dark status-bar icons on the near-black canvas, so the clock was effectively invisible in every capture; and a Scaffold with a transparent container left LocalContentColor unset, so every Text relying on the default colour rendered almost black — headings were unreadable on the device while looking perfectly fine in code.

A journal that outlives its layout. Building for decades meant every read had to be re-thought, and it also produced the feature I am happiest with: the From the archive card, which only becomes possible once the journal is old enough to have a past.

The store gate I could not pass in time. I originally aimed at Google Play and found that a new personal Play Console account requires 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days before you can even apply for production access — a schedule the submission window does not allow. That is part of why this is a Next Gen entry: the video and the open-source repo carry it, and no store listing is required.

**What I learned**

The API I re-learned the hard way is not holding data. Designing for twenty years forced SQL-level aggregation, paging and date ceilings into the app from the start, and every screen got simpler as a result. On the purchase side, the lesson was to keep entitlement state in exactly one place and let the UI read it — the moment premium logic is duplicated in a screen, the store and the app start disagreeing.

**What's next**

The obvious next step is a real store listing, which turns the Test Store build into a live one without touching the integration: only the API key changes. After that: optional encrypted export, a monthly "what changed" review, and a widget for the nightly question so the check-in is one tap from the home screen.

Undo is MIT-licensed and fully open source.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**A gaming bucket list that lives in your share sheet**

You're three minutes into a review and something looks good. To save it, every other backlog app wants you to leave the video, open the app, search for the game and file it.

Almost nobody does that, which is why almost nobody's backlog is accurate.

Backlogue is a share target. Share the video, the Reddit thread or the Steam page into it, and the game lands in your pile in one tap, without leaving what you were watching.

Who it's for: anyone whose list of games they meant to play lives in their head, a notes app, or twenty open browser tabs.

**Everyone else is fighting the wrong battle**

Every tracker on the store competes on organising games you have already saved: tags, filters, custom lists, sort orders. All of that assumes the list is complete.

It never is. Games get lost in the gap between hearing about one and getting around to filing it, and no amount of organising fixes a gap that happens before the app is even open. So the product is one gesture, and everything else is bookkeeping.

**The hard part is a text parser**

A Steam share is easy, because the game's name is sitting in the URL: /app/1030300/Hollow_Knight_Silksong/.

A YouTube share is a video title, and video titles are written to be clicked, not parsed: SILKSONG IS FINALLY HERE! First Impressions | IGN.

Backlogue strips bracketed tags, 52 noise phrases ("official trailer", "first impressions", "before you buy"), shouted hype words, and a trailing | Channel, but only when that tail matches a known outlet, so Dark Souls | Remastered survives intact.

It deliberately under-cleans, because search copes with an extra word far better than with a butchered title. When the only way to produce a query is to put back words it had marked as noise, it says so, flags the guess as low confidence, and opens a focused search box instead of pretending it understood.

That file is the least glamorous one in the project and the one everything rests on. It has ten tests built from real share-sheet payloads.

**It remembers where you found it**

Every game keeps a line saying where it came from: "From a YouTube video." "From Reddit." "From Steam."

It costs one database column. Six months later it's the difference between a list that reads like a record of your own taste and one that reads like homework.

**Designed against its own genre**

For most players a backlog is low-grade guilt. Every "pile of shame" joke is someone telling you their tracker made them feel bad. So Backlogue refuses the genre's usual mechanics.

No numbers anywhere. No completion percentage, no "47 unplayed games" counter, no progress rings, no red badges, no overdue states. A status with nothing in it doesn't even get a filter chip, so a new player's filter row is never a row of zeroes.

"Bounced", not "Abandoned". A game you tried and didn't click with is Bounced. Other trackers say Dropped or Abandoned, and both read like an accusation about a perfectly reasonable decision. "I bounced off it" is what players actually say, and it puts the mismatch on the game rather than on you.

Dark-first and art-forward. Cover art is the most beautiful thing on the screen and we didn't draw it, so the interface stays out of its way. In dark mode the app is near-black. On a light-mode phone it follows the system with a light palette built from the same design tokens. Either way, the one loud colour is reserved for adding a game.

**Alerts that earn their notification**

Something has to stay awake to notice when a game you wanted finally gets a release date. A Cloudflare Worker sweeps the watched games every hour and pushes through OneSignal, but only on a real change: a game gained a date, its date moved, or it came out.

The Worker keeps a snapshot of every game between runs. Without it, the obvious implementation re-sends "out now" every hour for a week, which is exactly how an app gets muted and then deleted. The first sighting of a game writes a baseline and sends nothing.

Only unfinished games are watched. A game you've already beaten doesn't need a release alert.

**How it makes money**

The core loop is never gated. Saving, organising and rating up to 30 games is free for good. Backlogue Pro, $1.99 a month through RevenueCat, removes the cap and turns on release alerts.

A cap of five would convert better, and it would contradict the only thing this app is for. A paywall in the middle of saving a game would wreck the two seconds the whole product exists to protect, so the paywall appears in exactly two places: the Pro badge in the pile header, and the moment the free pile is full. Never on launch, and never mid-capture.

**One Kotlin codebase**

Built with Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform. Android and desktop render the same composables, rather than a shared core with two hand-written front ends. The only platform-specific UI is the capture surface, because that's where the operating systems genuinely differ.

The shared Kotlin also compiles and links for iOS. A public GitHub Actions workflow on a macOS runner builds ComposeApp.framework with RevenueCat included. What isn't done yet is the Xcode packaging and an App Store release.

**Awards we're entering, and why**

- Next Gen. A student project, with the full source public and MIT licensed.

- RevenueCat Design Award. The design argument is which mechanics were refused. The Design answer points to the details worth noticing.

- HAMM. A paywall placed where it can't damage the core loop, and a free tier sized from real backlogs rather than from conversion.

- Keep Them Coming Back (OneSignal). Release alerts that only fire on a real change, with snapshotting so nothing ever repeats.

- Ship Kotlin Everywhere. One Compose Multiplatform UI on Android and desktop, with the shared code linking for iOS in CI.

- Influencer Award: Gaming. A bucket list for saving, organising, completing, rating and sharing games that is built, first and foremost, not to feel like a chore.

**A note on versions**

The demo video shows version 0.1.1, submitted to Google Play on Sep 30 and in review as we submit. Compared with 0.1.0, it adds the Pro badge in the pile header, a Share button on each game, and fixes that keep the status bar and the keyboard clear of the content. If Play still serves 0.1.0 when you install, those are the only differences.

**Links**

- Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.chinesepowered.backlogue

- Source, MIT licensed: https://github.com/chinesepowered/hack-backlogue

- iOS build in CI: https://github.com/chinesepowered/hack-backlogue/actions/workflows/ios.yml

- Site and privacy policy: https://backlogue-app.vercel.app/

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

A first-aid instructor once told our class, after demoing infant choking response on a manikin: "Everyone in this room will forget this in three weeks." She was right. Choking first aid is a skill you learn once at a workshop, never rehearse again, and then need at the worst possible moment — often with your own child.

CPR has manikins, apps, and recertification courses. Choking response has a poster on the pediatrician's wall. I wanted something you could actually practice — on a manikin or doll, with your phone watching your form and correcting you in real time, the way an instructor would. And because skills decay, the app should also nag you (kindly) before you forget.

That's Second Breath: a camera-coached choking first-aid trainer aligned to the 2025 AHA Guidelines for CPR & ECC and ILCOR 2025 CoSTR, with distinct protocols for infants (0–12 months: back blows + chest thrusts), children (1–12 years), and adults (back blows + abdominal thrusts). Practice is manikin-only — never on a real person.

**How I built it**

- Client: Flutter (clean architecture: BLoC/Cubits, GetIt DI, go_router), with Google ML Kit pose detection running fully on-device — no video ever leaves the phone.

- Backend: Spring Boot 3 (Java 17), stateless. Serves versioned AHA protocol definitions per age group, consumes RevenueCat webhooks to sync subscription entitlements into Firestore, and runs a daily scheduled job that sends FCM "refresher" reminders on a 90-day skill-decay window.

- Voice coaching: flutter_tts at half speech rate, so instructions land while your hands are busy.

The heart of it is a three-layer pose pipeline:

- Feature extractor — smooths raw landmarks with an exponential moving average and normalizes every measurement by shoulder/torso span, making it invariant to camera distance:

$$\hat{x}t = \alpha x_t + (1-\alpha)\,\hat{x}{t-1}, \qquad \alpha = 0.65$$

- Kinematic classifier — a state machine that detects individual strikes from wrist velocity (in torso-spans/second), stroke depth, and recoil. Infant mode tracks each hand independently; child/adult abdominal thrusts require clasped hands — both wrists close together and moving in unison — to count.

- Phase machine — walks you through the full protocol: positioning (body in frame → hands placed → confirmed ready) → 5 back blows → observed repositioning → 5 chest/abdominal thrusts → reassess and repeat, with TTS coaching at every step.

Sessions end with a scorecard: rhythm score (fraction of inter-strike gaps inside the effective 0.8–4.0s window), sequence score (did you complete milestones organically or skip them?), and a composite of the two. A 3-minute minimum keeps sessions honest.

**Challenges I ran into**

ML Kit lies. It returns all 33 body landmarks even when they're off-screen — it hallucinates plausible positions. Early builds happily counted back blows from an arm that wasn't in frame. The fix was gating every landmark on its likelihood score, but tuning that gate was a trap: too strict and landmarks vanish during fast hand motion (exactly when you need them most), too loose and the ghost limbs return.

My worst performance bug was garbage collection, not the model. Inference would randomly collapse from ~10 FPS to 0.2 FPS. I spent days blaming the model before realizing the camera at 720×480 was generating ~15 MB/s of frame garbage, thrashing the GC and starving inference. Dropping to low resolution roughly tripled effective FPS — ML Kit downscales internally anyway, so the extra pixels were pure cost.

Counting reps from noisy poses is much harder than detecting poses. At 6 FPS, a back blow is 2–3 frames of signal. Meanwhile users wave their arms, adjust their grip, and settle after each strike — all of which look like strikes. The rep counter needed a small army of guards: minimum stroke depth and velocity, lateral-drift rejection (waving), a ≥55% recoil requirement, a &gt;9 spans/s glitch reset for hallucination spikes, and a 550ms cooldown that only re-arms once wrist speed calms below $0.65$ spans/s. That last one killed a maddening bug where the natural bounce after a blow registered as a second blow.

Feedback oscillation. One dropped frame would flip the UI from "you're in position ✓" back to "get in position," and the voice coach would loop. The fix was hysteresis everywhere: landmarks coast 400ms through dropouts, confirmed states stay sticky through brief tracking loss, and duplicate feedback events are deduped before reaching the user.

You can't let users skip the boring step. Repositioning between back blows and thrusts matters medically (especially the infant flip), but users just waited out the timer. Now the phase machine requires observed repositioning motion — real arm velocity after a settling window — before advancing. Annoying to build; it's the difference between a game and training.

Frame-rate diversity on Android. Thresholds tuned at 25 FPS failed at 7 FPS. The classifier now adapts: when frame gaps exceed 140ms it switches to single-frame strike confirmation with a relaxed velocity threshold, and the smoothing factor rises toward 0.85 so stale history doesn't drown fresh motion.

**What I learned**

- On-device ML performance is a systems problem. My worst bottleneck had nothing to do with the model.

- Never trust a model's output structure — trust its confidence scores. "Returns 33 landmarks" and "found 33 landmarks" are very different claims.

- For real-time UX, hysteresis beats accuracy. Users forgive slightly delayed feedback; they never forgive flickering feedback.

- Thresholds need empathy. The "too slow" rhythm bound is tolerant because detection latency, tracker cooldown, and TTS pauses inflate measured gaps — punishing users for my pipeline's latency would be unfair.

- Medical guidelines are a spec. Encoding the 2025 AHA protocols as versioned JSON on the backend (rather than hardcoding them in the app) means guideline updates ship without an app release.

**What's next**

Haptic rhythm cues, a shareable family "readiness score," richer badge progression, and — the dream — validating the camera's scoring against instructor-scored sessions to see how close it gets to a human coach.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Inspiration

Every early-stage founder falls in love with their own idea before the market ever gets a say. Ask a friend "is this good?" and they'll say yes — friends are bad investors. By the time reality delivers its verdict, you've already spent weeks or months building the wrong thing. This is especially costly for student and first-time founders across Nigeria and the wider African market, where capital and runway are scarce and a wrong bet is expensive in a very real way. We wanted something that argues back — before the market has to.

What it does

Council puts your idea in front of four opposing AI personas — The Realist, The Money, The Skeptic, and The Visionary — who debate it from feasibility, monetization, competition, and scalability angles, then return a structured verdict: Validate, Rework, Pivot, or Kill.

If the idea needs work, Council doesn't just rewrite the pitch — it rebuilds the idea specifically around the objections that were raised, then re-runs the Skeptic and Money personas against that new version to check whether it actually resolves the original problem, or just sounds better. Only versions that pass this re-verdict gate move forward.

From there, Council hands you a ready-to-use pitch script — the actual opening line, the differentiator, and the price question — so you know exactly what to say when you go talk to real people, and commits you to one concrete, time-boxed action (a 72-hour Proof-of-Life sprint) instead of an open-ended to-do list. You report back what actually happened, and the Council reconvenes with real evidence instead of speculation. Every idea's full journey is kept as an auditable timeline in your Vault.

How we built it

A React Native app (Expo + NativeWind) backed by Supabase for auth and data, with a single Groq call (openai/gpt-oss-120b) per Council session generating the objections, verdict, repackage, and re-verdict gate together. RevenueCat handles subscriptions, synced back to Supabase via a webhook so pro access unlocks in real time after purchase.

Challenges we ran into

Getting a free-tier LLM to reliably return structured JSON under load was harder than expected — we went through three AI providers before landing on one stable enough to ship, and had to build retry logic and backoff around rate limits along the way. We also had to make a real architectural call: whether the "does this repackage actually fix the objection" check should be a second AI call or folded into the same one — we chose the latter to protect against doubling our failure surface so close to the deadline. And more than once, a bug that looked like an AI problem turned out to be a plain type mismatch between screens and the backend — a reminder that even AI-assisted apps live or die on ordinary engineering discipline.

Accomplishments we're proud of

A monetization loop that's actually wired end-to-end and tested with a real purchase — not just a mocked paywall. And a validation gate that isn't just theater: we tested it against ideas with real structural strengths and real structural weaknesses, and it discriminated correctly between them.

What's next

Tagging real Proof-of-Life field results back to the specific objection categories they resolve, so founders see not just "did this validate" but "which specific concern did the evidence actually answer."

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

PotionTown was born from a love for cozy fantasy games and the satisfying, hands-on craft of alchemy. We wanted to create a mobile experience where players don't just tap a menu to craft, but actively participate in brewing bubbling potions, discovering ancient forgotten recipes, and fulfilling eccentric requests from quirky town villagers. Our goal was to blend deep modular crafting with an elegant, non-intrusive mobile monetization loop powered by RevenueCat.

**What it does**

- Hands-On Cauldron Crafting: Mix, boil, stir, and brew dozens of distinct potions across 5 elemental color categories (Red, Blue, Green, Yellow, White).

- Shop & Economy Management: Balance ingredient costs, customer satisfaction, and shop reputation.

- Modular Recipe Discovery: Experiment with rare herbs, mystical mushrooms, and celestial ores to unlock legendary concoctions.

- Fair & Player-First Monetization: Integrated with RevenueCat to offer consumable ancient currency packs ("Kadim Para"), non-consumable Quality of Life upgrades ("Remove Ads"), and a seasonal "Potion Pass Premium" unlocking exclusive aesthetic cauldron skins and decorative town assets.

**How we built it**

- Engine & Graphics: Built in Unity using the Universal Render Pipeline (URP) 2D with custom shader graph effects for bubbling liquid dynamics, ambient magical lighting, and glow effects.

- Clean Architecture: Designed with a strict ScriptableObject-first architecture (RecipeData, ItemData, CustomerOrderData), decoupling UI logic from game systems for modularity.

- Monetization Engine (RevenueCat): Implemented via RevenueCatManager.cs, wrapping the RevenueCat SDK to handle entitlements (potion_pass_premium, remove_ads) and consumable offerings. We built an offline-safe fallback mechanism and an editor setup wizard to streamline testing.

**Challenges we ran into**

Balancing a fluid 2D fluid simulation and visual feedback on mobile constraints was tough. On the business side, designing a mobile game economy that feels rewarding without turning into a predatory "pay-to-win" wall required multiple iterations. RevenueCat's clear separation between Entitlements and Offerings allowed us to decouple the store UI completely from the game's reward distribution logic.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Delivering a rich, cozy aesthetic with vibrant handcrafted visual effects and reactive audio.

- A rock-solid, decoupled ScriptableObject architecture where game designers can balance recipes without touching code.

- Seamlessly integrating RevenueCat to support multiple purchase flows (consumable currency, season pass entitlement, and ad-free unlocks) cleanly within a Unity C# codebase.

**What we learned**

We gained deep insights into mobile game economies, player retention loops, and the power of RevenueCat in abstracting away platform-specific billing nuances in Unity. 

**What's next for PotionTown**

- Introducing co-op multiplayer potion brewing bench sessions.

- Expanding the town map with foraging expeditions and herbal gardening zones.

- Live-ops seasonal events and dynamic RevenueCat paywall experimentation.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

It started on a walk. I was playing chess against Claude on my phone and kept noticing something: the AI would make moves, but never explain why in a way that actually helped me understand what I'd missed. That bothered me more than losing.

I looked at the tools that existed. They all did roughly the same thing, show you the engine's preferred move, tell you it was inaccurate, move on. Useful, but not corrective. I kept making the same kinds of mistakes because knowing the better move and understanding why I chose wrong are completely different problems.

I wanted something that would ask what I was trying to do, then explain where my thinking broke down. That became Zugzwang.

Zugzwang turns your chess games into saved lessons and targeted practice so you stop repeating the same mistakes.

**What it does**

Zugzwang is built around one loop:

- Upload or import a real chess game.

- Get a post-game review with engine-backed move analysis.

- Find the biggest learning opportunity in the game.

- Explain what you were trying to do in that position.

- Get an intent-aware saved lesson.

- Practise the idea directly on the board.

- Return to the reviewed game without losing context.

The key difference is that Zugzwang does not only say "the engine wanted this move." It asks what the player was trying to accomplish, then explains the mistake relative to their intent, not a generic engine verdict.

The app also includes:

- guest access for immediate review;

- Play mode with adjustable AI opponents;

- Guided Play prompts that teach what to notice, not just what to play;

- Learn / sandbox tools for exploring positions and asking questions;

- saved lessons that persist across sessions;

- an Improvement Profile for recurring mistake patterns across many games;

- light and dark themes;

- RevenueCat Web Billing integration for a Pro tier;

- a tested Android Capacitor wrapper.

**How I built it**

This is my first software project. I had no prior coding experience when I started. Zugzwang was built over approximately one month.

It started as a broken repository from an AI challenge, a basic chess board with a "Make AI Move" button and not much else. I fixed it, then kept going because the core idea wouldn't leave me alone.

The frontend is React, TypeScript, and Vite with a custom UI system built from scratch. The backend is FastAPI with python-chess and Stockfish handling all deterministic chess work. AI explanations sit on top of engine evidence: the chess truth comes from the engine, the language layer turns that evidence into coaching. This separation was the most important architectural decision I made, and I made it early, it's what kept the app honest when everything else was still rough.

I ran a closed beta with real playtesters. Their feedback directly changed the product: the difficulty system was rebuilt from a flat 1–20 scale into Elo-bracket-based opponent personas after testers said low-difficulty felt inhuman. The board layout was stabilized after reports of erratic scaling across different devices. The correction flow was tightened after watching people get lost between review and practice.

Security went through multiple passes, peppered password hashing, per-account AES-GCM encryption, CSRF protection, rate limiting, and session hardening. RevenueCat is integrated with server-side entitlement verification so Pro status is never trusted from the client alone. The app fails closed to Free if verification is unavailable.

The Android wrapper was added close to the deadline, Capacitor wrapping the live web product, built and smoke-tested on a physical Galaxy S23.

**Challenges I faced**

The hardest part wasn't any single technical problem. It was making the app feel like a real learning loop rather than another engine analysis screen with a chat box bolted on. Getting there required solving problems across every layer of the stack.

Getting the architecture right from the start

The most important decision I made early was treating Stockfish as the source of chess truth and the LLM as a language layer on top of it, never the other way around. Chess is a domain where an LLM will confidently explain illegal or objectively bad ideas if you let it reason freely about board state. Every coaching explanation in Zugzwang is grounded in deterministic engine evidence first. The LLM explains what Stockfish found; it never decides what's true. That principle held for the entire build and is the reason the coaching doesn't hallucinate.

Frontend/backend state desync

One of the earliest and most damaging bugs was the frontend's local chess.js copy going stale after AI moves. This caused broken castling, blocked check-escape captures, and general piece freezes that were nearly impossible to reproduce consistently. The fix was re-syncing from the backend's authoritative game state before computing legal moves on the frontend, but finding the root cause required tracing the desync through the full request cycle rather than patching symptoms.

AI provider reliability

Gemini latency occasionally reached 24 seconds, dangerously close to polling windows and causing turn desyncs. An earlier version of the fallback chain could produce seven provider calls for a single user action during retry storms. After tracing the exact call paths, I enforced attempt ceilings, added per-provider cooldowns on 429 and 503 responses, introduced request deadlines, and coalesced in-flight duplicate requests on the backend. Daily API usage dropped dramatically with no loss in product quality. The design principle became: AI should enhance the coaching experience, but the product should not collapse if the provider fails.

Making practice preserve review context

Practice mode had to happen on the main board without destroying the original reviewed game's state. The user needed to enter a correction attempt, make moves, and exit back to exactly the position they were reviewing, with the original PGN intact and review navigation unaffected. This required careful state layering: the practice board runs as a mode over the review state rather than replacing it, with the original game preserved separately and restored on exit.

The correction loop state machine

The full correction flow, select a mistake, capture user intent, generate a grounded explanation, produce a practice position with a verified single-best answer, validate the user's attempt server-side, and return to the original review, required keeping multiple interdependent state objects coherent simultaneously: the original PGN, the current review position, the correction target, the practice board, the answer validation result, and the saved lesson. Getting all of these to update correctly without cross-contaminating each other was one of the harder engineering problems in the build.

Board layout stability

useFittedBoardSize shrinks the board whenever the page overflows the viewport. Three things changed height after load, a practice brief in the identity row, a moves pill that only rendered after the first move, and a take-over hint that went from empty to two lines when the board became playable. Each one triggered a new overflow correction, causing the board to visibly shrink mid-session. The fix required reserving constant height for all three from first paint so the fitter computed size once and had nothing left to correct. Verified stable across 1366×768, 820×1180, and 390×844 viewports.

Security hardening

The app went through multiple security passes: PBKDF2 password hashing with a pepper layer, per-account AES-GCM encryption with wrapped keys, CSRF protection, HTTP-only session cookies with server-side validation, rate limiting on auth endpoints, protected route enforcement, and Row-Level Security on the database verified by actual cross-account access testing. RevenueCat billing is handled with the secret key server-side only, the backend verifies entitlement and fails closed to Free if verification is unavailable. Pro status is never trusted from the client.

A near-disaster with version control

One of the lowest points in the build was a git checkout that silently wiped the first weeks of uncommitted work from the working tree, the anti-repetition fix, the eval bar, the difficulty rework, all of it. Recovered with zero data loss by mathematically reversing the patch that caused it against a verified post-patch copy, independently cross-checked against an older zip archive. Every significant change got committed properly after that. Both patch scripts got double-application guards so it could not recur.

RevenueCat integration complexity

RevenueCat brought its own debugging surface: frontend public key, backend secret key, entitlement ID, offering and package IDs, sandbox checkout, customer and app user ID matching, status refresh timing, Pro gate behavior, fail-closed logic, and a production environment key mismatch that was initially misread as an authentication failure. The final behavior is: frontend opens checkout, backend verifies entitlement, if verification succeeds and entitlement exists Pro is active, if verification fails the app stays Free with a clear reason shown, but getting there required tracing the full provider handshake.

**What I learned**

Building with AI is not about adding a chat box. The real challenge is deciding where AI belongs in the loop, and more importantly, where it doesn't.

The separation of concerns between engine and LLM

The single most important technical lesson was that chess coaching requires a deterministic ground truth layer. An LLM reasoning freely about board state will produce confident, plausible, and sometimes wrong explanations. Stockfish doesn't. Keeping these responsibilities completely separate, engine for evidence, LLM for language, is what makes the coaching trustworthy. This principle now applies to how I think about any AI-assisted system: identify what needs to be deterministically correct, remove the LLM from that responsibility entirely, and use it only where language and reasoning are the actual value.

Graceful degradation as a first-class requirement

AI providers are not reliable infrastructure. They rate-limit, they go down, they return 503 under load. Treating them as enhancement layers rather than foundations, building cooldowns, fallback chains, attempt ceilings, and deterministic fallbacks from the start rather than as patches, is the architecture that survives real usage. The honest "coach could not be reached, so this is the engine's reading only" message in the UI is the right behavior: degrade gracefully and tell the user what happened.

State management at product scale

Managing game state, review state, correction state, practice state, and account state simultaneously, each with their own update rules, persistence requirements, and failure modes, taught me that state is the hardest part of a real product. Not the features. The state transitions between features.

Security is a design decision, not a layer you add later

Adding security after the fact is significantly more expensive than building it in. Peppered hashing, per-account encryption, RLS, and server-side billing verification all went in incrementally, but each one required touching multiple layers of the stack. Designing for these from the beginning, even roughly, would have been faster.

Root-cause debugging over symptom patching

Every significant bug in this build, the frontend desync, the board shrink loop, the API spike, the git incident, had a specific, traceable root cause. Patching the visible symptom without finding the cause would have left the underlying problem intact and made the next bug harder to find. The discipline of always asking "why did this actually happen" rather than "what change makes the error go away" is the single most transferable thing I learned.

Building in public creates accountability

A beta with real playtesters is different from testing yourself. Real users find failure modes you'd never construct intentionally, erratic board scaling on a specific viewport, a piece freeze triggered by a specific move sequence, a billing status that did not refresh correctly after checkout. Fixing things that real people actually hit is a different kind of engineering than fixing things you predicted might break.

The difference between a demo and a product

A demo shows the happy path. A product handles what happens when the happy path breaks, the provider is down, the user imports a malformed PGN, the practice position has no verified answer yet, the checkout conflicts with an existing session. Building the product version of Zugzwang meant explicitly deciding what every failure mode should look like from the user's perspective, and then building that behavior deliberately rather than leaving it to chance.

**What's next**

I want Zugzwang to become genuinely longitudinal.

Right now it can identify a recurring mistake pattern after ten games. What it cannot yet prove is whether a player actually stops making that mistake after completing a correction cycle. That is the real claim, not "here are your errors" but "here is evidence your errors are decreasing", and it is the next thing I want to build toward.

The long-term goal is a personal improvement record that gets more accurate the more you play. One game gives you a lesson. Many games reveal your pattern. Enough practice shows whether the pattern is actually changing.

That is what Zugzwang is trying to become.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Let me paint you a picture. It is the start of a new school year, and I have just spent the last few months grinding through applications for ten different society councils at KGS. Ten. I wrote essays, prepared answers, showed up to trials, and got in. Big win, right?
Wrong.
I am a STEM kid and halfway through the year I had a realisation that hit harder than any exam ever could. Why does the Scrabble Club logistics team belong on my university application? It does not. The Drama Society logistics team? Also no. The First Aid Society logistics team? Genuinely, what was I thinking? I was burning hours every week on things I could not care less about, and nobody told me until I was already knee deep in commitments I could not escape.
Here is the thing though. This is not just a me problem. Students everywhere, in Karachi, London, Toronto, New York, are drowning in opportunities with no structured way to figure out what actually matters. The ones who get it right are usually the ones whose families can afford a university counsellor. And these counsellors are not cheap. In Pakistan alone, they charge upwards of 30 lakhs. In other countries the numbers are just as brutal. For the vast majority of middle class students globally, that kind of guidance is completely out of reach.
I built the thing I wish had existed. That thing is Vetly.

**What it does**

Let's be honest. You could use ChatGPT or Claude for this. And if you really know how to prompt them well, they are decent. But decent is not good enough when your university application is on the line.
Here is the problem with generic AI assistants. They are biased. They do not want to hurt your feelings. They will hype up your mediocre opportunity and call it a great fit because that is what feels good to say. They also cannot give you structured onboarding, and while they can hold context within a conversation, they cannot keep a specific timestamped history of every opportunity you have ever evaluated and let you visualise your own trajectory over time.
Vetly does all of that.
Free tier gives you a 2000 character onboarding where you describe your goals and current situation. From there, you get three evaluations per day. Paste any opportunity as text or a screenshot, and Vetly's AI, currently powered by GPT 5.5, will run it through our system prompt against your full onboarding and give you a brutally honest score. Not a hype job. An actual assessment.
For example, if you are a STEM student gunning for Georgia Tech and you are considering becoming the O-Level head of the Conservation Society, Vetly will acknowledge that it shows leadership and initiative and looks good on paper. And then it will rate it a four or five out of ten, because your time is genuinely better spent on competitive programming or engineering competitions. That is the kind of answer a 30 lakh counsellor gives you. Vetly gives it for free.
You can also edit your goal anytime because you are not a static person and your goals evolve.
Premium tier takes everything further. Your onboarding expands dramatically. Name, university targets, current class, dream university, a 5000 character description of your current situation, a 5000 character goal statement, and a resume upload. The AI cross references all of it every single time it evaluates an opportunity for you. You also get unlimited evaluations, and every single one is saved to your history with a timestamp.It also give you feedback in terms of preperation guidance for that specific opertunity. Over time you can visually compare what you have been evaluating, what you have taken, what you have passed on, and whether that pattern actually lines up with the vision you set for yourself at the start.
It is basically a mirror for your ambitions. And unlike a mirror, it talks back.

**How we built it**

I came into this with a solid foundation. I know React Native, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Python, and FastAPI. I have experience with system design, Git, and GitHub. Building a backend from scratch for a hackathon timeline would have been overkill, so I used Supabase for the database and auth layer, which gave me everything I needed without reinventing the wheel.
The actual development workflow was me paired with Cursor, an AI coding tool. But this was not just vibing blindly and hoping for the best. I designed the architecture myself first, wrote detailed instructions for Cursor on how to structure the code so it would not turn into a bloated mess, specified exactly what to put in the gitignore, and handled all the security considerations myself. I treated Cursor like a very fast junior developer who needed clear direction, not a magic box.
For RevenueCat, I created an account, set up the SDK, built the paywall and billing configuration in their dashboard, then gave Cursor the exact integration instructions and told it precisely where in the codebase it needed to live. Same process for the OpenAI API. I created the account, set my usage limits, got the key, and instructed Cursor to integrate it at exactly the right point in the evaluation flow.
The system prompt that powers Vetly's evaluations I wrote entirely myself. That was not Cursor's job. The brutal honesty, the structured output, the way it weighs opportunities against a user's specific goals, that logic is mine.
Tech stack: React Native with Expo, Supabase for database and auth, OpenAI API for evaluations, RevenueCat for subscription management, AsyncStorage for local data, Git and GitHub for version control.

**Challenges we ran into**

The two things that genuinely gave me trouble had nothing to do with writing code.
The first was configuring the RevenueCat SDK. On paper it should be straightforward. In practice it was one of those things where everything looks right and nothing works. I had to lean on AI guidance more than I would have liked on that one, but eventually it clicked and the integration landed clean.
The second was the system prompt. This took longer than I expected and was honestly the most important engineering decision in the entire project. A bad system prompt means biased, unhelpful evaluations and the whole product falls apart. I went back and forth for a long time, consulting both Gemini and Claude, pushing back on their suggestions, testing outputs, iterating. The recipe I ended up with was not something any single AI gave me. It came out of a long argument between me, the tools, and my own instincts about what brutal honesty actually looks like in a structured output.
The code itself was relatively smooth. I barely wrote any manually, and the minor bugs that came up were quick fixes. The hard problems were not in the syntax. They were in the decisions.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The thing I am most proud of is the system prompt. And I do not mean that as a throwaway line. The system prompt is the product. Everything else, the UI, the database, the subscription logic, is just scaffolding around it.
It took a week of building and arguing to get right. I was going back and forth with Claude and Gemini, pushing back on their suggestions, testing outputs against real scenarios, and iterating until the reasoning felt genuinely intelligent rather than just pattern matched.
Here is what I mean. A naive opportunity evaluator would see someone applying for the International Olympiad of Informatics and rate it 10 out of 10. And for most STEM students it probably is. But what if that student is in their second year of A-Levels with no competitive programming background and exams in three months? Vetly rates that a 1 out of 10. Because context is everything, and blind optimism is not advice.
The same logic works in the other direction. A STEM student joining the First Aid Society logistics team might seem off brand on the surface, and a dumb evaluator would tank the score. But Vetly reasons through it. It shows universities you care about people beyond your own lane. It demonstrates leadership and health awareness. It rounds you out. So it rates it a 6 or 7, not a 4, and explains exactly why.
That kind of nuanced, contextual reasoning is what took a week to build. And I think it is genuinely the hardest part of the whole project.

**What we learned**

**What's next for Vetly**

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We noticed our lives were scattered across half a dozen apps like calendars for meetings, Todoist for tasks, Slack for work, and notes for random thoughts. None of these tools actually talk to each other to give a complete picture of the day. We wanted a single place where you could just dump your thoughts and figure out what actually drives your daily habits. That is why we built Aks. Aks means reflection, and we wanted this app to be exactly that. It is a personal mirror that helps you look at your routines and actually understand yourself better.

**What it does**

Aks acts as your daily sounding board. The core feature is Mirror, a chat interface where you can type or talk normally without feeling like you need to write the perfect prompt. Behind the scenes, it pulls in your real life by connecting securely to Google Calendar, Tasks, Gmail, GitHub, Slack, Notion, and Todoist. Because it already knows what meetings you had or what code you pushed, it actually understands your context. You do not have to spend time explaining your day to it.

**How we built it**

We built the mobile app using React Native and Expo to keep the UI smooth and native feeling, while Supabase handles our backend and authentication. Since this is the RevenueCat Shipaton, getting the subscription model right was a top priority. We integrated RevenueCat to manage the entire premium and free trial lifecycle so we did not have to rebuild that infrastructure from scratch. 

For the voice feature, we hated that typical record, wait, and process delay. To fix that, we built a custom live speech recognition system that types out what you are saying in real time. A massive chunk of our time went into making all these different APIs and microservices play nicely together.

**Challenges we ran into**

Getting the live voice input to feel natural on Android was tough. We had to dig deep into native audio APIs to get the latency down so it actually feels like a fluid conversation. Also, keeping data synced between Supabase, a bunch of different OAuth providers, and RevenueCat was a headache. We ended up having to write custom telemetry just to track what was happening when a user went from the UI, through the backend, and back. It was a huge learning curve in building something production ready versus just a weekend hack.

**Accomplishments that we are proud of**

We are really proud that we managed to turn a massive, complicated idea into an app that actually feels simple to use. Getting real time voice, secure auth, multi platform API connections, and RevenueCat subscriptions working together perfectly was a huge win for us. But honestly, the best part is the user experience. You do not need a tutorial to use Aks. You just open it and talk. Hiding all that crazy backend complexity behind a clean chat interface is what we are most proud of.

**What we learned**

We learned that you have to hold back on features to make a good product. We wanted to add a million technical bells and whistles, but cutting them out to protect the core chat experience made the app so much better. We also learned that handling mobile infrastructure like managing permissions, native builds, and subscription states takes just as much engineering effort as building the actual AI features.

**What is next**

Right now, Aks is great for figuring out your day to day. Next, we are building out pattern recognition so it can spot long term habits you might not notice yourself. Soon, it will be able to point out recurring themes, what triggers your procrastination, or how you are allocating your time based on your connected data. The goal is for Aks to grow from a daily tracker into a lifelong tool for actually understanding yourself.

</details>

**Inspiration**

Design work is often trapped in opaque files. Fanta makes a design a folder of readable source so visual changes can be reviewed in Git and edited by an agent or a person.

**What it does**

Fanta is a native macOS design editor. Start a design or open a Figma .fig file, edit shapes, text, layers and layout on the canvas, and save it as a Fanta project with .fnx page source. The Code workspace edits that source inside Fanta: saving validates the change and refreshes the canvas. The file tree, Git panel, Threads rail, and Agent panel put source review and AI assistance beside the canvas. Agents can inspect design state, make structured canvas edits, verify screenshots, edit files, and place generated media. Fanta exports PNG, SVG and PDF. Local editing is free; signed-in users can spend credits on hosted generation.

**How we built it**

The desktop app uses Rust and GPUI, with Fanta's canvas, renderer, Figma import, and FNX source format. A local MCP server exposes structured design operations to agents, while Fanta's backend routes managed AI and generation requests. Production sign-in uses Clerk. The signed Mac App Store build embeds the RevenueCat SDK through a Swift bridge for Apple in-app purchases: a monthly Pro subscription with 3,000 credits and a one-time 500-credit pack. Purchases are linked to the signed-in Fanta account.

**Challenges and what we learned**

Keeping canvas edits, editable source, and Git history in sync required a validated save path that preserves the last good design when source is invalid or changes during a save. App Store sandboxing required user-selected file access and signed distribution assets. RevenueCat purchases must map to the correct Fanta account before server-side credits are granted.

**What's next**

Verify purchase and credit fulfillment end to end, complete App Review, publish the first Mac App Store version, and improve the editor from real user feedback.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I wanted to make meeting people feel more intentional and interactive than endlessly swiping through profiles. Blink puts people into live dating rooms where they can show their personality, make choices, and connect through a shared experience.

**What it does**

Blink lets people create a profile, set dating preferences, and join or host a room. Participants move through rounds with first impressions, questions, and profile reveals before a host makes a final choice. When two people match, they can continue the conversation in chat. The app also includes AI-generated host commentary and premium features.

**How we built it**

I built Blink as a solo project using Expo, React Native, and TypeScript. I organized the code into screens, reusable components, hooks, service modules, and shared app state with claude code .
 Supabase provides authentication, Postgres data, RPC actions, and realtime updates for rooms and messages.
 AsyncStorage persists the signed-in session and local app data. 
The app can also request host commentary from a Supabase Edge Function, with a local fallback if the request fails

**Challenges we ran into**

One challenge was coordinating room state across multiple users. I used Supabase Realtime subscriptions to keep room phases, participant decisions, and events in sync. 
Another challenge was handling matchmaking when no live room was available, so I added a timeout that moves the user into a local simulation instead of leaving them waiting indefinitely. I also added fallback host lines so the experience can continue if the AI service is unavailable.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I’m proud that I built the complete experience end to end as a solo developer, from the profile and preferences flows to the live room UI and match experience. I’m also proud of the separation between the real Supabase room flow and the local simulation, which lets the app demonstrate the interaction even when matchmaking doesn’t produce a live room.

**What we learned**

I learned how to structure a React Native app around reusable components, shared state, and focused service hooks. I also gained practical experience with Supabase Auth, database RPCs, realtime subscriptions, and persistent storage. Building the fallback paths taught me to design around network services failing or being unavailable.

**What's next for Blink**

Next, I’d improve reconnect and room-transition behavior, add more automated checks for the live multiplayer flows, and make it easier to tell when a user is in a live room versus a local simulation. I’d also continue developing compatibility insights and the post-match conversation experience.

Below are some technical achievements i made 

What technologies I used:

I used Expo, React Native, and TypeScript for the mobile app. Supabase handles authentication, Postgres data, RPC calls, and realtime updates. AsyncStorage handles local persistence. The project also includes RevenueCat integration for premium features and an optional Supabase Edge Function integration for AI-generated host commentary.

**How i implemented a realtime room state :**

When a user enters a real room, the app loads the room, participant roster, and event history from Supabase. A custom React hook then subscribes to database changes for the room, participants, and event feed. The hook removes its realtime channel when it’s no longer needed.

**How did I structure the app:**

I separated screens, reusable UI components, hooks, and service code. Room screens handle presentation and interactions, room action functions wrap Supabase operations, and realtime hooks manage subscriptions. Shared app state connects authentication, profile data, matchmaking, and app flows.

**The matchmaking work:**

The app first tries to join a Supabase matchmaking queue. If a room forms immediately, it opens that room; otherwise, the app listens for a room assignment. If matchmaking hasn’t resolved after about 12 seconds, the current flow falls back to a local room simulation.

**How I handle AI features:**

The app requests host commentary from a Supabase Edge Function. If the request fails or returns no usable line, it falls back to a local bank of lines so the room experience can continue.”
How I handled persistence and authentication:
I use Supabase Auth with AsyncStorage configured as the session storage adapter, so sessions can persist across app restarts. I also save app state such as profile details, preferences, and local matches to local storage. Profile edits can sync to Supabase.
How did I handle chat?
The project has a Supabase-backed path that loads and subscribes to messages for a match, and a separate local mock-message flow for simulated matches. That lets the app support real-time chat while also demonstrating the experience in the local flow.

What would I improve next:
I’d strengthen validation of the live flows, especially reconnect behavior and room transitions. I’d also make the distinction between a live room and a local simulation clearer and expand automated checks around the backend and client.Add real time video and audio.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

For modern Americans, personal wealth is frustratingly fractured. The average household juggles 4+ credit cards across multiple banks, tracks auto loans and maintenance in another app, and keeps health, life, and home insurance policies tucked away in forgotten folders.

For most Americans, vehicles represent their second-largest financial asset—yet vehicle equity, municipal citations, DMV compliance, and auto insurance policies remain entirely divorced from daily net worth management.

We envisioned a unified solution: Aegis. An editorial dark-luxury command center engineered specifically for the US market. Aegis combines comprehensive net worth intelligence with an interactive 3D virtual garage powered by live federal US Department of Transportation (NHTSA) APIs, and a comprehensive insurance and telematics tracking vault. It turns administrative financial chores into an engaging, rewarded cornerstone of personal wealth—all without ever needing to hold customer deposits or act as a custodial money transmitter.

**What It Does**

Aegis re-imagines daily wealth management as an interactive, rewarded experience across three pillars:

- Unified Net Worth & Credit Card Due-Date Radar:

- Aggregates revolving card debt (Chase Sapphire Reserve, Amex Gold, Capital One Venture X) with dynamic credit health tracking (( \text{Utilization} &lt; 10\% ) rewarded as "Excellent", ( &gt; 30\% ) flagged as "Danger").

- Interactive 3D Card Flips: Realistic Y-axis 3D flips revealing real-time interest rates, statement balances, and APRs.

- Zero-MTL Non-Custodial Verification: Users pay their cards through their existing banking apps. Aegis detects the statement drop and mints Aegis Coins with celebratory bursts.

- 3D US Garage with Live NHTSA Federal APIs:

- Live US DOT vPIC VIN Decoding Engine: Connects live over HTTP directly to vpic.nhtsa.dot.gov to decode official manufacturer specifications, assembly plant locations (e.g., Fremont, CA; Flat Rock, MI; Normal, IL), electrification classification (BEV), body class, and drivetrain (AWD).

- Live Federal Safety Recalls Database: Hits api.nhtsa.gov/recalls/recallsByVehicle to pull active federal safety defect campaigns with official NHTSA campaign numbers, defective components, legal safety consequences, and manufacturer remedies.

- Touch-Drag 3D Rotation Stage: 360° perspective transforms with authentic embossed US state plates (CALIFORNIA, NEW YORK, TEXAS, WASHINGTON).

- Municipal Citations & Compliance: Tracks and clears municipal traffic camera tickets (SFMTA, NYC DOF) awarding 2X Aegis Coins.

- Live Automotive Insurance & Telematics Tracker (UBI):

- Usage-Based Insurance (UBI) Driving Telematics: Live driver score (e.g., ( 96/100 )) calculating annual discount percentages (saving up to ( -28\% ) or (\$386.40/\text{yr})) with smooth braking, speed compliance, and phone distraction telemetry.

- Active Claims Pipeline: Step-by-step interactive timeline (( \text{Filed} \rightarrow \text{Review} \rightarrow \text{Approved} \rightarrow \text{Paid} )) with direct-pay zero-deductible glass repairs and 1-tap rapid claim filing.

- Insurance Commerce Marketplace: Compare quotes from GEICO, Progressive Premier, and State Farm. Users can Sell Insurance for household/friends to earn a (\$200) commission (+2,000 coins) or Buy for (\$100) instant cashback (+1,000 coins).

- Personal & Family Insurance Vault:

- Family Health & Rx Protection (BCBS Gold PPO): Tracks family deductible progress ((\$1,450 / \$3,000\text{ Met})), out-of-pocket maximums, and individual member deductibles across policyholders and dependents with mobile ID card barcodes.

- Term Life Protection: (\$1,000,000) 20-Year Level Term Life policy tracking with designated beneficiary allocation percentages (Spouse 70%, Family Trust 30%).

- Homeowners & Property (Lemonade HO-3): Dwelling ((\$650,000)), personal property, and liability protection with past property claim settlements.

- Dual-Screen Samsung Galaxy Z Fold & Tablet Adaptation:

- Seamless responsive layout adapting from mobile candy-bar screens to side-by-side foldable dual-pane master-detail workspaces.

**How We Built It**

- Client Architecture: Built using Flutter 3.x (Dart) utilizing hardware-accelerated 60/120fps rendering, custom matrix transformations (Matrix4) for 3D vehicle and card interactions, and clean Provider-based state management.

- Subscription Monetization: Integrated the RevenueCat SDK (purchases_flutter) powering multi-tier paywalls (Gold Pass (\$4.99/\text{mo}) and Black Edition (\$9.99/\text{mo})) with introductory annual discounts, feature gatekeepers, and entitlement verification.

- Automated Push & Retention: Integrated OneSignal Flutter SDK v5 (onesignal_flutter) with custom subscription observers and tags triggering automated due-date nudges, NHTSA safety recall bulletins, and coin minting celebrations.

- Automotive Intelligence: Direct, live integration with the US Department of Transportation's open vPIC and NHTSA Recall APIs without requiring authentication tokens or intermediate proxies.

- Viral Growth Loop: Integrated Layers SDK referral and reward loops for unlocking VIP perks through friend invites.

- Mathematical Modeling:

- Unified Net Worth calculation:
$$ \text{Net Worth} = \sum \text{Cash} + \sum \text{Investments} + \sum (\text{Vehicle Market Value} - \text{Loan Balance}) - \sum \text{Card Liabilities} $$

- Usage-Based Insurance (UBI) telematics discount function:
$$ \text{Discount}{\text{UBI}} = \text{BasePremium} \times \left( \frac{\text{Score}{\text{telematics}}}{100} \times 0.30 \right) $$

**Challenges We Overcame**

- Navigating US Fintech Regulations (Zero-MTL Architecture): Traditional bill-pay platforms in the US face crippling regulatory hurdles and require state-by-state Money Transmitter Licenses (MTLs). We designed a non-custodial balance-verification model: tracking external balance reductions to reward users without ever holding customer funds.

- Real-Time Integration with Federal Government APIs: NHTSA endpoints have subtle routing nuances (e.g., VIN recall lookups require AWS API Gateway authorization, whereas vehicle make/model/year queries are open and public). We architected a two-stage resolution engine that decodes VINs via vPIC and seamlessly links safety recall defect databases in real time.

- Dual-Pane Foldable Ergonomics: Engineering an interface that transitions from single-handed smartphone use to an expansive Samsung Galaxy Z Fold dual-pane command center without layout overflows or rendering hitches.

**What We Learned**

- Public APIs are Goldmines: The US DOT NHTSA vPIC dataset provides over 100 vehicle attributes (plant state, electrification level, vehicle type, drive system) that make fintech apps feel remarkably personal and tangible.

- Gamification Drives Real Financial Discipline: Tying everyday liabilities (credit cards, traffic citations, insurance renewals) to a tangible coin economy and tiered multipliers transforms administrative friction into an enjoyable daily routine.

- Non-Glossy Dark Luxury UI Design: Moving away from generic "AI-generated" glossy glassmorphism into matte titanium and carbon palettes with crisp typographic hierarchy creates an immediate sense of trustworthiness and sophistication.

**What's Next for Aegis**

We are building Aegis into the definitive financial operating system for American households. Our roadmap includes:

- Direct Connected-Car Telematics (Tesla Fleet & Smartcar APIs):

- Transitioning from static odometer entries to live vehicle telemetry (battery state of health, real-time tire pressure alerts, and instant crash detection that pre-populates insurance claims with collision telemetry).

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Tax notices can be intimidating even when the underlying issue is straightforward. We wanted to build something that helps an ordinary taxpayer move from “What does this notice mean?” to “What exactly should I do next?” NoticeLens was created around that simple idea: make complex GST and Income Tax notices easier to understand and act on.

**What it does**

NoticeLens turns a tax notice into a structured action plan. Users can upload a notice, understand why they received it, identify important dates and amounts, see what documents or actions are required, and track their progress.

It also provides source-linked information so users can trace important facts back to the original notice, an Ask My Notice experience for questions about the document, notice history, and a concise brief that can be shared with a tax professional.

**How we built it**

NoticeLens is built as a web application with a product-focused interface designed around a simple flow: Receive → Understand → Verify → Prepare → Respond → Remember.

The application uses document extraction and structured notice intelligence to identify important information from uploaded documents. We designed the analysis around the notice itself and a structured NoticeLens knowledge base rather than relying on a generic chatbot to invent answers.

RevenueCat is integrated for subscription management, allowing premium functionality to be unlocked through a real purchase and entitlement flow.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge was making notice analysis useful without turning the product into a generic AI chatbot. Tax notices contain dates, amounts, references, legal sections and requested documents that need to remain connected to their original source.

We also had to design a subscription experience that felt like a natural part of the product rather than an unrelated payment screen, while keeping the core experience useful for free users.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud of turning a traditionally intimidating document into a clear, navigable workflow rather than simply generating a long summary.

The combination of a structured Notice Room, action plan, source-linked facts, original-document access, Ask My Notice, history and Notice Brief gives users a complete path from receiving a notice to preparing their next step.

**What we learned**

We learned that solving a complex problem does not necessarily require adding more features. The most valuable part of NoticeLens is the way information is organized: separating facts from explanations, connecting important information to its source, and turning understanding into concrete actions.

We also learned that trust is especially important when building products around financial and tax information.

**What's next for NoticeLens**

Next, we want to expand verified coverage across more GST and Income Tax notice types, improve document and OCR handling, make source references even more precise, and expand the Notice Brief and reminder workflow.

Longer term, NoticeLens could become a personal tax-notice workspace that helps users understand, prepare and keep track of their notices while making collaboration with their tax professional easier.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/385/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/385/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/391/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/391/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/427/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/427/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/428/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/428/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/429/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/429/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/431/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/431/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

In Thailand, eating out with friends almost always ends the same way: one person pays the whole bill, then spends the next 20 minutes typing receipt lines into a group chat, adding the service charge and VAT, and chasing everyone for money. It gets worse when you travel and can't even read the receipt.

Sabai (สบาย) means relaxed or at ease in Thai. I wanted splitting the Bill to feel sabai, so the motto became "Split the bill, not the mood."

**What it does**

SabaiB turns a photo of a receipt into a fair, itemized split that everyone can pay in seconds.

- Scan a receipt in any language. Gemini reads the photo, pulls out every line item, and translates each one into English while keeping the original name, so travellers and mixed-language groups know exactly what they're paying for.

- Review and fix. Edit names, quantities, and prices, remove lines, and set the service charge, VAT, and discounts.

- Open a bill room. Friends join from their own phones with a group code or QR.

- Claim what you ate. Each person taps their items. Shared dishes split automatically between everyone who claimed them, or the host can split the bill evenly.

- Payment Status Each participant gets their exact total (and optional a PromptPay QR of the host), and the host can see who has paid.

- Groups and history. Recurring friend groups and past payments stay in one place.

- SabaiB+. Free users get 1 AI scan every 30 days. SabaiB+ unlocks unlimited scans as a monthly subscription through RevenueCat.

**The math behind a fair split**

For an item ( i ) with unit price ( p_i ) and quantity ( q_i ), the service charge rate ( s ) and VAT rate ( v ) are folded into each item (with ( v = 0 ) when VAT is already included):

$$
\tilde{p}_i = p_i \, q_i \,(1 + s)(1 + v)
$$

If ( S_i ) is the set of people who claimed item ( i ), then person ( k )'s share before discounts is

$$
F_k = \sum_{i \,:\, k \in S_i} \frac{\tilde{p}_i}{|S_i|}
$$

A bill-level discount ( D ) is shared in proportion to each person's raw food cost, so the person who ate more also gets more of the discount:

$$
T_k = F_k - D \cdot \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i \,:\, k \in S_i} \frac{p_i q_i}{|S_i|}}{\displaystyle\sum_i p_i q_i}
$$

That way nobody overpays because they shared a dish or ordered something cheap.

**How we built it**

- Kotlin and Jetpack Compose for a fully native Android UI, using MVVM with StateFlow

- Supabase (Postgres, Auth, Edge Functions) for accounts, profiles, groups, and the shared bill rooms that sync between the host's and participants' phones

- Gemini vision API with a strict JSON response schema for receipt parsing and translation, plus ML Kit text recognition and a regex parser as an on-device fallback

- RevenueCat with Google Play Billing for the SabaiB+ subscription, with RevenueCat's app user ID aliased to the Supabase user ID so a purchase follows the account

**Challenges we ran into**

- Real-time sync. Keeping the host's and every participant's view consistent while several people claim items at once took several rounds of fixes to the join, claim, and payment flows.

- Messy receipts. Receipts mix scripts, abbreviations, local number formats (is 1.200 one point two or one thousand two hundred?), and metadata lines. Prompting Gemini with a schema, and letting users correct the result instead of trusting it blindly, made scanning reliable.

- On-device OCR limits. ML Kit can't read Thai script, so the fallback recovers prices, and the AI path handles names and translation.

- Privacy and trust. I added explicit consent before any image is sent to AI, an age gate, and full in-app account deletion through a Supabase Edge Function.

- Monetization without breaking the social loop. Everyone at the table has to be able to join for free, so only the host-side feature that actually costs money (AI scanning) sits behind the paywall.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- Shipping a complete end-to-end flow on my own: scan → translate → claim → pay → subscribe

- A split that is actually fair, including shared dishes, service charge, VAT, and proportional discounts

- Multi-device bill rooms that feel live

- Translating receipts in any language, which makes SabaiB useful for travellers as well as locals

- A working RevenueCat subscription with restore purchases and account-linked entitlements

**What I learned**

- How to design a backend schema and sync model for multi-user, real-time features with Supabase

- How to make an LLM reliable in production: structured JSON schemas, clear extraction rules, and always letting the user edit the output

- How to integrate RevenueCat and Google Play Billing, and how to think about pricing and paywall placement

- That privacy features like consent screens and account deletion should be designed in from the start, not added at the end

**What's next for SabaiB**

- An iOS version so whole friend groups can join, whatever phone they use

- Currency conversion for travellers, showing totals in both the local and home currency

- LINE sharing and payment reminders for friends who haven't paid yet

- Multiple receipts in one trip with a running "who owes whom" balance

- Galaxy Store release and more local payment rails beyond PromptPay

</details>
