<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every year, companies lose $47 million per 1,000 employees due to knowledge loss when team members leave. When a developer, manager, or key employee exits, they take years of institutional knowledge, context, and undocumented processes with them. The remaining team spends months trying to reconstruct what was lost.

We asked ourselves: What if knowledge could be captured automatically, continuously, and intelligently?

That question became VEQ - The Knowledge Continuity Platform.

**What it does**

VEQ is an AI-powered platform that automatically captures, organizes, and transfers institutional knowledge when employees transition out of a company. It integrates seamlessly with the tools teams already use every day:

- GitHub - Captures code context, pull request decisions, and technical debt documentation

- Google Calendar & Drive - Preserves meeting insights, decisions, and important documents

- Slack - Archives critical conversations, channel knowledge, and team activity

- Notion - Maintains documentation continuity and company knowledge bases

- Linear & Jira - Tracks project history, sprint decisions, and bug resolution context

- Zoom - Preserves meeting recordings, transcripts, and AI-generated summaries

- Zendesk - Maintains customer support context and organizational knowledge

VEQ creates a "Continuity Vault" - a living knowledge graph that ensures no critical information is ever lost, regardless of team changes.

**How we built it**

We built VEQ using a modern, scalable tech stack:

- Frontend: Next.js 15 with TypeScript for a fast, type-safe user experience

- Backend: Next.js API Routes with server-side rendering

- Authentication: Clerk for secure, multi-tenant user management

- Database: Supabase (PostgreSQL) with Row Level Security for data isolation

- AI Integration: OpenAI GPT-4 and Gemini for intelligent knowledge extraction and Brain Map generation

- Integrations: OAuth 2.0 flows for 7+ major platforms (GitHub, Google, Slack, Notion, Linear, Jira, Zoom, Zendesk)

- Deployment: Vercel for global edge deployment

- Email: Resend for automated notifications and weekly AI digests

The platform features a beautiful, professional UI with a warm cream and brown color palette, designed to feel approachable yet enterprise-grade.

**Challenges we ran into**

- OAuth Integration Complexity: Integrating 7 different OAuth providers, each with unique scopes, callback URLs, and token refresh mechanisms, was a significant challenge. We had to implement robust error handling and token management for each provider.

- Database Schema Design: Designing a multi-tenant schema that securely isolates company data while enabling efficient knowledge graph queries required multiple iterations. We implemented Row Level Security in Supabase to ensure data isolation.

- Knowledge Graph Architecture: Creating an AI-powered system that can intelligently extract, link, and present knowledge from disparate sources required careful prompt engineering and data modeling.

- Real-time Synchronization: Ensuring that knowledge captured from various integrations stays up-to-date and consistent across the platform required implementing efficient webhook handlers and background sync processes.

- Performance Optimization: With multiple integrations and AI processing, we had to carefully optimize our API routes and database queries to maintain fast load times and responsive interactions.

**What we learned**

- Multi-tenant Architecture: We gained deep experience in building secure, scalable multi-tenant applications with proper data isolation

- OAuth & API Integrations: We learned the intricacies of integrating with multiple third-party APIs and handling various authentication flows

- AI Prompt Engineering: We discovered how to effectively use AI to extract meaningful insights from unstructured data

- Product Design: We learned to balance enterprise-grade functionality with an approachable, beautiful user interface

- Rapid Development: Building a production-ready platform in a hackathon timeframe taught us prioritization and efficient development practices

**What's next for VEQ**

- Microsoft Teams & Dropbox Integration: Expanding our integration ecosystem

- Advanced AI Agents: Implementing autonomous agents that can proactively identify knowledge gaps and suggest documentation

- Team Collaboration Features: Real-time collaboration on knowledge continuity plans

- Analytics Dashboard: Insights into knowledge health and risk assessment for organizations

- Enterprise SSO & Compliance: SOC 2 compliance and enterprise-grade security features

- Mobile App: iOS and Android apps for on-the-go knowledge access

VEQ isn't just a tool - it's a paradigm shift in how organizations think about knowledge management and employee transitions.

</details>

## 386. Cueback — Live Translation & Script-Linked Q&A

> Cueback breaks language barriers in global competitions with real-time translation and script-linked Q&A. It matches live questions to anticipated ones, surfacing the answers you've prepared.

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/cueback-live-translation-script-linked-q-a (gallery page 110) · ❤️ 0 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [안성주 An](https://devpost.com/PastelJ321)
- **GitHub (Try it out):** https://github.com/PastelJ321/cueback
- **Repo check:** public repo · license: MIT · 11 commits · TypeScript · RevenueCat found in code ✅ · ⚠️ last commit 2026-10-02 (after Sep 30 deadline)
- **Built with:** expo.io, ios, react-native, typescript

**Video (1:42):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JIvsPv9X3xQ

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/JIvsPv9X3xQ/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JIvsPv9X3xQ)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/434/302/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/434/302/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/434/843/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/434/843/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Cueback started from a problem I experienced while preparing for the Wharton Global High School Investment Competition.

I was comfortable with portfolio management, company analysis, and explaining why I made certain investment decisions. The part I struggled with was different: listening to a judge's question in English, understanding it immediately, organizing my thoughts, and answering naturally in English within only a few seconds.

Even if I had already thought about the question before, retrieving the right answer under pressure was difficult.

That made me ask a simple question:

What if I could prepare my answers in advance, and have the right one appear the moment a similar question was asked?

I did not want an AI system that generated answers for me during a presentation. I wanted something that would preserve my own thinking and help me retrieve it at the right moment.

That idea became Cueback.

**What it does**

Cueback is a presentation Q&A assistant that helps presenters quickly find their own prepared answers during live questions.

Before a presentation, the user creates a presentation, writes expected questions, and prepares the exact answer scripts they want to use.

During a live Q&A session, Cueback:

- listens to an English question,

- transcribes it using speech recognition,

- compares the recognized question with the user's prepared questions,

- ranks the most semantically similar questions,

- shows the most relevant prepared answer,

- and provides a Korean translation of the recognized question when supported.

Cueback also shows multiple likely matches instead of blindly assuming that the top result is always correct.

If the similarity is not strong enough, Cueback does not automatically display an answer. It keeps a No confident match state and allows the presenter to choose a candidate manually.

Most importantly, Cueback never generates the answer itself.

Every answer displayed during a presentation was written by the user beforehand.

**How we built it**

Cueback is built with Expo, React Native, TypeScript, and React Navigation.

Presentation data, expected questions, and answer scripts are stored locally with AsyncStorage, allowing the core preparation workflow to remain simple and account-free.

For live questions, Cueback uses expo-speech-recognition to capture English speech.

The recognized question is then processed by a multilingual MiniLM embedding model running on-device through react-native-executorch.

Each prepared question is converted into an embedding, and Cueback uses cosine similarity to compare the live question against the prepared question bank.

Instead of matching only one transcript, Cueback can evaluate multiple speech-recognition alternatives and select the transcript that produces the strongest semantic match.

To improve performance, prepared-question embeddings are cached together with a model identifier and a hash of the question text. If a question is edited, Cueback detects that the old embedding is no longer valid and generates a new one.

We also built a native translation bridge so that the recognized English question can be translated into Korean on supported iOS and Android devices.

For monetization, Cueback uses the RevenueCat React Native SDK and RevenueCat Test Store.

The free version provides:

- one presentation,

- up to five expected questions per presentation,

- speech recognition,

- semantic matching,

- and prepared-answer display.

Cueback Pro removes the presentation and question limits.

RevenueCat is not just used as a decorative purchase button. The application checks the active pro entitlement from CustomerInfo, and the actual data-creation logic uses that entitlement to decide whether additional presentations or questions can be created.

Purchases, cancellations, failures, restoration, entitlement refresh, and subscription expiration are all handled through RevenueCat.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was making semantic matching reliable enough for a live presentation.

A judge may ask the same question using completely different vocabulary or sentence structure from the version I prepared beforehand. Simple keyword matching was therefore not enough.

Semantic embeddings solved much of this problem, but another challenge appeared: being wrong confidently is worse than showing no answer at all.

Because of that, Cueback uses a confidence threshold and comparison between the strongest candidates. If the match is too weak or ambiguous, Cueback refuses to automatically select an answer.

Another challenge was asynchronous behavior.

Speech recognition, embedding generation, semantic matching, local storage, and RevenueCat entitlement updates can all finish at different times.

An older matching request could potentially finish after a newer one and overwrite the correct result. Similarly, overlapping AsyncStorage writes could cause recent edits to be replaced by stale application state.

We addressed these problems by introducing request-generation checks for semantic matching and a serialized local-data store that always applies changes against the latest successfully persisted state.

The RevenueCat integration introduced similar edge cases. We had to ensure that pressing the purchase button did not automatically grant Pro. Cueback only unlocks Pro after RevenueCat returns a CustomerInfo object with an active pro entitlement.

We also protected the purchase and restore flows against duplicate operations.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The part of Cueback I am most proud of is that it keeps the presenter in control.

Many AI presentation tools focus on generating more content. Cueback does the opposite.

It assumes that the presenter has already done the thinking.

The app's job is simply to help retrieve that thinking at exactly the right moment.

I am also proud that Cueback can handle meaning rather than exact wording. A judge does not need to ask the question in the same way it was written in the question bank.

The app can recognize a semantically similar question, rank multiple possibilities, and still refuse to choose when the confidence is too low.

The final application also combines several native and on-device systems in one workflow:

- live speech recognition,

- multilingual semantic embeddings,

- local question and answer storage,

- question translation,

- responsive iPad presentation UI,

- and RevenueCat entitlement-based monetization.

**What we learned**

Building Cueback taught me that reliability is often more important than adding another AI feature.

At first, the main problem seemed to be semantic similarity.

But as the application became more complete, I learned that many of the hardest problems were about state, timing, and uncertainty.

What happens if an old model request finishes late?

What happens if a question is edited while its embedding is being generated?

What happens if storage fails?

What happens if a purchase succeeds but the expected entitlement is missing?

What happens when the model is unsure?

Those questions changed how I approached the project.

Instead of trying to make Cueback always produce an answer, I designed it to recognize when it should not.

I also learned that monetization is not only about putting a paywall in front of a feature. RevenueCat became part of the application's state model: the active entitlement directly controls the limits of the local presentation library.

**What's next**

Cueback began as a tool for investment-competition Q&A, but the same problem exists in many other situations.

Students face it during academic presentations.
Founders face it during pitch Q&A.
Job applicants face it during interviews.
People presenting in a second language face it almost everywhere.

The next step is to make Cueback useful for all of these scenarios while keeping the same principle:

The system should help people communicate what they already know, not replace what they think.

For Cueback Pro, I also want to explore more advanced AI-assisted processing to improve the quality of the live Q&A experience.

This could include AI-enhanced speech recognition that is more robust to accents, pronunciation differences, background noise, and presentation-specific terminology, as well as stronger semantic matching models that can better recognize when two differently worded questions are actually asking the same thing.

AI could also be used to rerank recognition candidates and matching results, improving retrieval accuracy without generating the answer itself.

The user's prepared answer would still remain the source of truth. AI would improve how Cueback understands the question and finds the right script, rather than writing a response for the presenter.

Other future directions include better rehearsal tools, question-bank analytics, confidence calibration, faster model startup, and optional synchronization across devices.

The long-term goal is for Cueback to become a lightweight layer between preparation and real-time communication — helping a presenter turn preparation into confidence when the question finally arrives.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/477/243/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/477/243/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/477/863/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/477/863/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/477/244/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/477/244/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/479/724/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/479/724/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/478/611/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/478/611/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/478/862/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/478/862/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/479/570/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/479/570/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/462/731/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/462/731/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I’m a student, and one of the things I’ve always struggled with is studying consistently. I’ve had periods where I managed to study every day for a while, but sooner or later something would happen and I’d lose the routine. I know a lot of other students who have had the same experience.

While thinking about this, I started researching why it’s so common for students to struggle with studying consistently. I found something really interesting: according to several articles I read, one of the main reasons is that studying itself rarely feels rewarding. In many cases, it can actually feel more like a punishment, where you have to put in a lot of effort now for a reward that only comes much later, with an exam result or a grade.

That was the idea I wanted to explore with Yutori: what if the effort itself could feel a little more rewarding?

Since I’m a student myself, making something for other students felt like the most natural place to start. I wanted to create a study tracker where you could keep all your study time and statistics in one place, but also have a visual representation of that effort. Something that would slowly build up as you kept studying, instead of resetting after every session.

A big part of the inspiration behind that idea came from Japan.

I’ve been interested in Japan since I was a kid. Both of my older brothers have always been really into Japanese culture, so I was exposed to it from a very young age. As I got older, that interest became my own. I started researching things by myself, learning about the culture, the food, the design, and just generally trying to understand what I found so interesting about it.

One of the things that fascinates me is the value placed on effort and patience. There’s something that fascinates me about the idea of improving little by little, rather than expecting everything to happen immediately. That felt very connected to what I wanted the app to be about.

I started exploring different ways of representing progress visually, and eventually came across Japanese food bowls. I’m fascinated by Japanese food, and I liked the idea of having something simple that could change and evolve as you put more time into studying.

That became the visual foundation of Yutori.

The name came from the same place. Yutori (ゆとり) is a Japanese word that can refer to having extra space, time, or mental room. I chose it because I liked what the word represented. Studying can often feel rushed and stressful, and I wanted the app to have the opposite feeling, something that makes the process feel a little calmer while still encouraging you to keep moving forward.

At its core, Yutori is a tool designed to make studying feel more fun, visual, and rewarding. An app with a clear purpose: to make the study experience more enjoyable and give students that extra push to stay motivated and keep going.

**What it does**

Yutori combines study tracking with a collection of Japanese bowls. You choose a course and a bowl, then start studying. Every hour adds another stage to your bowl until it reaches level 5 and you can collect it. Progress carries over between sessions, and your total study time unlocks new bowls to work towards.

You can organise courses by name, colour and icon, pause and resume sessions, and follow your timer through Live Activities and Dynamic Island. Your session history, weekly charts, calendar and streaks let you look back at the work you’ve done.

I also wanted users to be able to correct their recorded study time. These edits only affect statistics, though: bowl evolution and unlocks still use the time actually recorded by the timer, so you can’t skip the progression by adding hours manually.

The smaller interactions were a big part of building Yutori. There are evolution animations, sound effects, ingredient descriptions and full English and Spanish support. Even deleting your account has its own interaction: you tap one of your collected bowls to gradually crack and break it, with a sound on each hit and a final sound when it breaks.

The free version includes one course and the core study and collection experience. Yutori Pro unlocks unlimited courses and personalised app icons, combining collected bowls with Japanese-patterned backgrounds. Both plans include the same features: $9.99 per month, or $34.99 per year. The yearly plan is billed once a year and works out to around $2.92 per month, making it the more affordable option for someone who wants to keep using Yutori throughout their studies.

**How I built it**

I built Yutori completely from scratch, by myself, using Swift and Xcode. I used GitHub to manage the project, and I occasionally used Codex when I was stuck on a technical problem or needed help working out a particular piece of logic.

I had never built an app like this before, so a lot of the process was figuring things out as I went.

The artwork was another big part of the project. I used AI to help generate the initial bowl artwork, but I was very careful with the results. I spent a lot of time selecting, iterating and refining them so the whole collection felt consistent and each bowl had its own identity.

In total, that meant creating 126 different bowl evolutions.

The actual development took around a month and a half of working on it seriously.

**Challenges I ran into**

The hardest part was probably getting the Live Activity and Dynamic Island experience working properly.
I had never worked with them before, and there were definitely a few points where I got completely stuck. 

Getting the timer, state and UI to behave correctly outside the main app took a lot more work than I expected.

Another challenge was learning how quickly a project grows once you start caring about the details.

A feature that sounds like “just add an app icon” can suddenly involve different states, unlocked content, backgrounds, settings and a lot of little edge cases.

That happened more times than I can count.

**Accomplishment I’m proud of**

The main thing I’m proud of is that I actually finished it.

This is my first app, and I had been wanting to build one for a long time. There were plenty of moments where it would have been easy to leave things unfinished, but I kept going and ended up with something that I’m genuinely happy with.

I’m also really proud of the amount of care that went into the bowls. Creating them was a very meticulous process, with a lot of hours spent supervising, reviewing, comparing and thinking about how each one could be improved.

I didn’t want the collection to feel like the same bowl repeated 21 times. I wanted every bowl to have its own identity while still feeling like part of the same world.

More than anything, I’m proud of the final result because I know how much work went into getting every part of it to where it is.

**What I learned**

The biggest thing I learned is how different it is to actually build an app compared to just having an idea for one.

Things that look simple from the outside often become much more complicated once you have to make every part of them work together.

I learned a lot about iOS development, UI design, planning and managing my time. I also learned how to deal with getting stuck instead of abandoning an idea when something doesn’t work.

I even learned things outside of development, like how to promote a project and post about my work online, something I had never really done before.

Most importantly, I learned that sometimes the hardest part is simply starting.

**What's next for Yutori**

I had wanted to build my own app for a long time, but I never really found the right moment to start. Shipaton was the excuse I needed to finally take that step.

Finishing Yutori feels like a pretty big milestone for me, especially because it’s my first app and something I had wanted to do for so long.

I’m genuinely really happy with how it turned out, and I don’t really want to stop here.

After Shipaton, I’m seriously considering paying for the Apple Developer Program and publishing Yutori on the App Store.

I’d love to get my first real users, see what they actually think of it, and keep improving the app based on real feedback.

For me, that would be the next step: taking the first app I’ve ever built and actually putting it in the hands of other students.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**The Academy**

A GED-focused academic RPG wrapped in a retro CRT desktop metaphor. Players pick starter perks and traits, then study, take assignments, and progress through a simulated 1980s-style institutional operating system — complete with windows, apps, and a taskbar rendered in phosphor green.

An AI description engine enriches the text adventure's flavor text, and a companion Android/Expo app brings the whole experience to mobile with a fully offline-first game engine.

**Features**

- Retro CRT desktop OS — boot screen, draggable windows, taskbar, and a period-accurate terminal aesthetic (Space Mono, phosphor-green palette)

- GED curriculum gameplay — study and quiz across math, language arts, science, and social studies

- Character progression — starter perks/traits, stats, and study history

- NPC dialogue — tone-aware conversations with faculty and students

- AI description engine — server-side OpenAI endpoint enhances location and object descriptions ("Location" and "Examine" modes), with client-side caching

- Offline-first mobile companion — the Expo app plays fully offline via a deterministic on-device engine, and enriches responses with the live AI when online

**Project structure**

This is a pnpm multi-artifact monorepo:

Path
Description

artifacts/academy/
Web frontend (React + Vite + wouter), served at /

artifacts/academy-mobile/
Android/iOS companion app (Expo + expo-router), offline-first

artifacts/api-server/
Express 5 backend, served at /api

lib/db/
Drizzle ORM schema for PostgreSQL

artifacts/academy/src/shared/
Shared game modules (schema, perks, stats, curriculum, content packs)

**Tech stack**

- Runtime: Node.js 24, TypeScript 5.9, pnpm workspaces

- Web: React, Vite, wouter, Radix UI

- Mobile: Expo, expo-router, React Native

- API: Express 5, Zod validation, Orval OpenAPI codegen

- Database: PostgreSQL + Drizzle ORM

- AI: OpenAI (gpt-5-mini) for description enrichment

**Getting started**

**Prerequisites**

- Node.js 24+

- pnpm 10+

- A PostgreSQL database

**Setup**

pnpm install

Required environment variables:

- DATABASE_URL — Postgres connection string

**Development**

**API server (port 5000)**
pnpm --filter @workspace/api-server run dev

**Web frontend**
pnpm --filter @workspace/academy run dev

**Mobile app (Expo)**
pnpm --filter @workspace/academy-mobile run dev

**Other commands**

pnpm run typecheck # typecheck all packages
pnpm run build # typecheck + build everything
pnpm --filter @workspace/api-spec run codegen # regenerate API hooks/Zod schemas from OpenAPI
pnpm --filter @workspace/db run push # push DB schema changes (dev only)

**Building an Android APK**

The mobile app ships with an EAS build config (artifacts/academy-mobile/eas.json). With an Expo account:

cd artifacts/academy-mobile
pnpm run release:preview

The preview profile produces an installable .apk; the production
profile produces a Play Store app bundle. These release commands verify the
published API health and AI enrichment endpoint before starting EAS.

**License**

MIT

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

My friends and I often take photos of assignments, quizzes, classroom announcements, and instructions so we can remember them later.

The problem is that those photos quickly get buried in our galleries. When a deadline gets close, we either forget the task exists or spend time scrolling through old screenshots trying to find the original photo.

Before building Duely, I surveyed 107 respondents to see if this problem was common. 66.4% said they sometimes, often, or very often forget or nearly miss assignment deadlines, while 60.7% said they rely on memory to keep track of assignments.

Assignments also come from scattered sources. 72.0% receive them through Messenger or group chats, and 61.7% through professor announcements.

The idea itself also received strong interest: 86.9% rated the photo-to-task concept 4 or 5 out of 5, and 80.4% said they would be likely to use Duely if it were available today.

That led me to build Duely, an Android-first student organizer that turns an assignment image into an editable task with a deadline, reminder, and clear next steps.

**What it does**

Duely lets students take a photo of an assignment or choose one from their gallery.

The app reads the text, suggests task details, and lets the student review everything before saving.

It includes:

- On-device text recognition

- Optional AI-assisted extraction

- Editable suggested fields

- Warnings for missing or uncertain information

- Manual task creation and editing

- Search, filters, and deadline-based prioritization

- Today, Upcoming, and calendar views

- Local reminders

- Guest access

- Google sign-in with optional cloud backup

- Duely Plus through RevenueCat's Test Store

Duely never silently saves extracted information as final. The student can correct every suggested field first.

**How I built it**

I built Duely using React Native, Expo, and TypeScript.

Expo Router handles navigation, AsyncStorage stores tasks locally, and Expo Notifications manages reminders.

For scanning, Google ML Kit performs text recognition directly on the Android device. A deterministic parser then suggests details such as the task title, deadline, type, priority, workload, and reminder timing.

Students can also enable AI Assist after signing in and giving consent. In that flow, Duely sends the recognized text, not the original assignment image, to a server-side Gemini integration for better structured suggestions.

If AI Assist is unavailable or declined, the local OCR and parser still work.

Supabase handles authentication, optional cloud backup, consent records, usage allowances, and account-level authorization.

For monetization, Duely Plus uses RevenueCat's Test Store. During beta, Plus provides a configurable allowance of 20 AI-assisted scans per month, while manual tasks and on-device scanning remain free.

RevenueCat manages the Plus entitlement and restore flow, while the backend controls the related AI usage allowance.

**Challenges I faced**

One of the hardest problems was handling imperfect assignment images.

OCR can make mistakes, deadlines may be missing, and one image may contain several assignments. Instead of treating every extracted value as correct, I added conservative parsing, field-level warnings, and an editable review step.

If Duely detects multiple possible assignments, it asks the student to crop the image or choose one instead of automatically creating several unreliable tasks.

I also had to account for offline use, denied permissions, cancelled requests, and failed cloud services. Because of this, the core workflow stays local and does not depend on an account, subscription, or AI connection.

Subscription handling also required server-side checks rather than trusting client state. RevenueCat verifies the Plus entitlement, while the backend controls the AI-scan allowance tied to it.

**Accomplishments**

Duely now has a working Android beta covering the complete flow:

Assignment image → text recognition → review → saved task → schedule → calendar → reminder

The project currently has 316 passing automated tests covering areas such as extraction, reminders, storage, cloud backup, permissions, AI assistance, and Duely Plus entitlement handling.

I also ran a controlled OCR evaluation using 12 synthetic assignment images. Duely achieved 99.5% aggregate OCR token accuracy, and all 12 produced parser-ready text.

This is an early result from a small synthetic dataset, not a claim of accuracy across all real student assignments.

The survey also influenced the review flow. 81.3% of respondents said they would always or usually review AI-extracted information before saving it, which supported my decision to keep the student in control of the final task.

**What I learned**

Building Duely taught me that recognizing text is only part of the problem.

A useful scan-to-task system also needs to handle uncertainty, make corrections easy, and fail gracefully when information is incomplete.

I also learned how local storage, authentication, notifications, cloud backup, AI services, usage limits, and subscription entitlements interact inside one mobile app.

Most importantly, I learned that AI works better here as an assistant rather than the final decision-maker. Duely can suggest what an assignment says, but the student should decide what becomes a task.

**What's next for Duely**

Next, I plan to test Duely with a wider range of synthetic and consented assignment formats and improve extraction quality based on those results.

I also want to improve accessibility, privacy controls, data export and deletion, device compatibility, and account management.

The long-term goal is to release Duely publicly, starting with Android on the Google Play Store and later expanding to iOS.

Duely is currently an Android beta and is not yet published on an app marketplace.

The Shipaton build uses RevenueCat's Test Store, so all purchases shown in the demo are simulated and no real money is charged.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Inspiration:

ChangeAIPay started with a simple question: why should moving your own money have to come with a transaction fee?

I wanted to explore what a payment experience could look like if payments were designed around zero transaction fees, fast settlement, cross-border use, and AI from the beginning rather than adding AI as a separate chatbot after the payment system already exists.

The idea evolved into ChangeAIPay: an AI-native payment platform with dedicated Personal and Merchant experiences. Personal users can send, receive, request, and make QR payments, while merchants have their own payment and dashboard experience. Fina, the Personal AI assistant, is designed to make payment actions conversational while keeping traditional interfaces available for users who prefer them.

What it does:

ChangeAIPay is designed as an AI-native payment platform for consumers and merchants.

Users can explore payment flows such as sending and receiving money, requesting payments, QR payments, merchant payments, wallet management, and cross-border payment experiences. The platform is designed around zero transaction fees for payments, with Nano providing the underlying payment infrastructure.

The project also introduces Fina, an AI financial assistant concept designed to help users interact with their finances through natural language rather than navigating every financial action manually.

How I built it:

I built ChangeAIPay as a web application that can also be packaged for Android.

The project uses:

- React + TypeScript for the application

- Vite for development and builds

- Tailwind CSS for the interface

- Nano as the planned payment infrastructure

- RevenueCat for subscription and entitlement management

- Capacitor/Android for the mobile application layer

The application includes Personal and Merchant experiences, payment flows, QR interactions, Nano wallet concepts, subscription experiences, and the Fina AI assistant concept.

The submitted application demonstrates the product experience through prototype/demo flows rather than processing real-money transactions.

Challenges I ran into:

One of the biggest challenges was building a complex financial product as a solo founder while keeping the experience simple for the end user.

I had to think through both sides of the payment ecosystem—people sending money and businesses accepting it—while also designing around a zero-transaction-fee model.

Another challenge was deciding what to build first. ChangeAIPay has a much larger long-term vision, so I focused on creating a coherent prototype that demonstrates the core product experience instead of trying to make every planned feature production-ready at once.

Accomplishments that I'm proud of:

I’m proud of turning a broad fintech concept into a working, interactive product experience covering both consumer and merchant use cases.

The project brings together payments, QR interactions, Nano-based payment concepts, subscriptions, mobile deployment, and an AI-native financial assistant into one product.

Most importantly, I built the project as a solo founder, taking the idea from concept and product design through implementation and mobile packaging.

What I learned:

Building ChangeAIPay taught me that creating a fintech product is much more than designing a payment screen.

The difficult part is connecting identity, account creation, payment flows, merchant experiences, security concepts, subscriptions, currencies, AI interaction, and mobile deployment into one coherent experience.

I also learned the importance of clearly separating what is demonstrated today from what belongs to the long-term product architecture. That helped me build the prototype honestly while keeping the larger vision clear.

What's next for ChangeAIPayApp:

The next stage is to continue moving ChangeAIPay from an interactive prototype toward a production-ready financial platform.

That includes expanding the real payment infrastructure, strengthening security and identity flows, developing Fina into a functional AI financial assistant, expanding merchant capabilities, and improving the Android experience.

The long-term vision is to make payments feel less like navigating financial infrastructure and more like simply telling your money what to do—while keeping the underlying payment experience fast, accessible, and free of transaction fees.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**FitDesi AI — Offline-First Fitness Intelligence**

**Inspiration**

FitDesi started from a very practical problem I kept running into while training: different people gave different advice about exercises and technique, and even when I found useful fitness apps, many of them became much less useful when connectivity was unreliable.

That made me ask a simple question: what if the core fitness experience stayed useful even when the internet did not?

FitDesi AI is my answer to that. It is a native Android fitness companion designed around offline-first usefulness, structured fitness guidance, and South Asian depth. The goal is not to replace professional medical advice or make an LLM the source of truth. The goal is to give people a practical system they can actually use day to day.

**What FitDesi does**

FitDesi brings the main fitness journey into one Android experience:

- Offline AI Coach — practical training guidance grounded in local FitDesi knowledge and validated profile context.

- Personalized Workout Planner — structured weekly routines based on goals, experience, available days, and equipment.

- Structured workout generation — deterministic programming logic creates workouts without inventing exercise identities.

- Live workout tracking — sets, reps, weight, rest timers, progress, and session summaries.

- Saved routines and history — persistent local workout plans, completed sessions, and progress review.

- Progress insights — training trends, workout history, and practical review tools.

- Nutrition and fitness tools — calorie, macro, BMR/TDEE, one-rep-max, hydration, and food logging workflows.

- South Asian food context — culturally familiar food identities alongside a verified public nutrition layer.

- RevenueCat-powered monetization architecture — a useful Basic core, Plus for deeper planning and progress tools, and Pro reserved for future advanced intelligence.

The public-safe nutrition layer currently includes 39 verified USDA nutrition records plus 20 South Asian discovery identities that are searchable but intentionally do not claim unverified nutrition values.

**Why offline-first matters**

A lot of AI products become nearly useless when a remote model or internet connection is unavailable. I did not want FitDesi to work that way.

The core product keeps deterministic logic and reviewed local data authoritative for things like:

- canonical exercise identities;

- workout programming rules;

- nutrition facts;

- persistence;

- subscription and entitlement truth.

AI is used to explain and personalize inside those boundaries rather than overwrite them.

That means the Basic experience can still provide useful planning, tracking, calculators, local coaching, and progress workflows without requiring a paid model API.

**RevenueCat and the business model**

FitDesi is designed around three permanent product tiers:

- Basic — the useful local/offline core.

- Plus — deeper workout planning, broader routine flexibility, and expanded progress tools.

- Pro — planned advanced remote coaching and adaptive intelligence.

RevenueCat is the commercial authority for subscription state. The current Shipaton QA candidate uses RevenueCat Test Store flows to validate purchase, entitlement, restore, and feature-gating behavior without pretending that test purchases are production revenue.

FitDesi also includes a bounded Rewarded Boost concept for selected premium experiences. Boost is temporary access, not a subscription tier, and it does not override subscription authority.

**How it works**

FitDesi uses a hybrid architecture:

**Android**

- Kotlin

- Jetpack Compose

- Material 3

- Room

- DataStore

- Firebase Authentication

- RevenueCat

**Backend**

- Node.js

- Express

- server-side entitlement and remote-admission boundaries

- Firestore-backed commercial/remote accounting architecture

Provider secrets stay server-side and never ship inside the APK. Production Remote AI remains intentionally default-off until its deployment, authorization, quota, privacy, and cost controls are fully closed.

**The hardest parts**

This project was not just about adding screens. The hardest work was keeping the product truthful while making it more capable.

**1. Keeping AI from becoming the source of truth**

Workout IDs, programming rules, nutrition values, entitlement state, and persistence cannot be guessed by a model. I had to keep deterministic engines and validated data in control while still making the Coach feel useful and conversational.

**2. Preserving workout identity and programming invariants**

FitDesi has canonical exercise IDs that must stay exact across generation, tracking, saving, and history. Small ID or metadata mistakes can break a workout flow in ways that are hard to notice, so these contracts became protected invariants.

**3. Nutrition provenance**

Food data is easy to overclaim. I had to separate verified nutrition from discovery-only food identities, keep provenance visible, and exclude unresolved historical data from the public runtime instead of presenting estimates as facts.

**4. Persistence and real-device behavior**

Passing JVM tests is not the same as surviving a real app update. I repeatedly checked that routines, workout logs, nutrition history, subscription state, and navigation still behaved correctly on a physical phone.

**5. Subscription truth**

RevenueCat integration had to be more than a paywall screen. Entitlements, restore behavior, paid-feature gates, and remote admission all needed clear authority boundaries so the client could not simply claim premium access.

**6. Preparing a safe public repository**

The private development repository contained internal history and assets that were not appropriate for public redistribution. Before submission I created a fresh, sanitized public-source export, re-audited its contents, removed unverified media references, and published it with fresh Git history rather than exposing private repository history.

**What I am proud of**

By the end of Shipaton, FitDesi had moved well beyond a static prototype:

- a working native Android app;

- offline-first coaching and deterministic workout planning;

- persistent workout, routine, nutrition, and progress workflows;

- RevenueCat Test Store purchase and entitlement QA;

- a signed Codemagic QA candidate;

- physical-device testing on the final candidate;

- 899 Android debug JVM tests across 97 suites with zero failures and one existing skip on the validated candidate;

- a public, sanitized source repository;

- and a public 1:44 product demo showing the real app experience.

I am especially proud that the app remains useful without pretending every feature needs a cloud model.

**What I learned**

The biggest lesson was that a working feature is not the same as a trustworthy product.

For FitDesi, shipping responsibly meant thinking about data provenance, deterministic boundaries, persistence compatibility, subscription authority, secret handling, CI validation, physical-device behavior, and what should not be activated yet.

That discipline made the product slower to build in some places, but much stronger overall.

**What's next**

FitDesi is still early. The long-term vision is to make both the offline and online experience significantly more intelligent without giving up the reliability of the current core.

Planned directions include:

- compact on-device ML intelligence designed for low battery and memory use;

- stronger offline personalization and recommendation support;

- a recipe-to-nutrition engine for structured meal analysis;

- a Food Analyzer that can help users interpret meals and ingredients;

- posture and movement-correction assistance using on-device vision where practical;

- a full-time Remote AI Coach for Pro with validated account, quota, privacy, and cost controls;

- richer progress intelligence and long-term adaptation;

- broader regional food coverage beyond South Asia;

- and a tighter bridge between local deterministic intelligence and optional cloud AI.

The goal is not to make FitDesi “AI everywhere.” The goal is to use the right intelligence in the right place: deterministic where truth matters, lightweight ML where it can run locally, and remote AI where deeper reasoning genuinely adds value.

FitDesi AI is targeting the RevenueCat Shipaton 2026 Next Gen Award through the student video + public-source route.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/401/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/401/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/403/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/403/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/404/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/404/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/413/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/413/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/420/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/420/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/421/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/421/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/422/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/422/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/423/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/372/423/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every store owner has the same nightmare: a checkout quietly breaks at 3am, or a critical plugin goes unpatched, and nobody notices until sales flatline or the site gets hacked. After 20 years building for small shops, I wanted an agent that watches the store like a good ops engineer would — and actually acts, not just alerts.

**What it does**

Store Medic runs a team of always-on AI agents on a Watch → Verify → Approve loop:

- Watch — monitors your store 24/7: uptime, response speed, SSL certificate, HTTPS, PHP version, WooCommerce health, failed orders, out-of-stock bestsellers, and outdated/vulnerable plugins.

- Verify — re-checks each signal to kill false alarms and attaches evidence (with cited sources) so you can trust it.

- Approve — you tap once, and for self-hosted stores it performs the real fix (e.g. actually runs the plugin update) and reports the result. Nothing changes without your approval.
It works on any store at the monitoring level (uptime, speed, SSL — just a URL, no integration), and goes deep with real auto-fix on self-hosted stores (WooCommerce today; Magento/PrestaShop next).

**How we built it**

Solo — one founder + an AI coding team — in about two weeks. A TypeScript engine (the shared Watch→Verify→Approve brain) runs as an always-on cloud service; the mobile app is React Native / Expo. Fixes execute via WP-CLI on self-hosted stores. RevenueCat powers the subscription that unlocks Pro (multi-store, faster checks, and one-tap auto-fix). Honestly? Almost none of this was typed by hand — it's an AI agent team shipping a product about AI agents.

**Challenges we ran into**

Making "Approve fix" genuinely safe: it only ever acts after explicit approval, is scoped to whitelisted actions on a configured store, and every mutating call is API-key protected.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The Approve button performs a REAL fix — not a ticket, not another
notification. One tap runs the actual plugin update on the live store
and reports the result back. That single behaviour is the whole product.

Shipped solo to Google Play production in under two weeks, with the
engine genuinely live and monitoring a real store — an 88% health score
you can watch move, not a mock screen.

It also degrades gracefully: any store on earth gets uptime, speed and
SSL monitoring from nothing but a URL, and self-hosted WooCommerce
stores get the deep integration and one-tap fixes on top.

**What we learned**

Alert fatigue IS the product problem. Store owners don't need more
notifications — they need the thing fixed. That realisation is what
turned the design from Watch→Notify into Watch→Verify→Approve.

Verification turned out to matter more than detection. Re-checking every
signal before surfacing it killed almost all the false alarms, and trust
is the only thing that earns you permission to act on someone's store.

Shipping to Google Play in 2026 is its own engineering project —
targeting API 36 and Play Billing 8 forced a full SDK upgrade late in
the build. Budget real time for the store, not just the app.

RevenueCat erased an entire category of work: entitlements and offerings
were configured once, and the paywall logic stayed trivial for the rest
of the build.

**What's next for Store Medic — the AI agent that watches and fixes your store**

Write-scoped connectors for hosted platforms, starting with Shopify ops
and inventory. Staging-test-then-rollback so fixes are verified on a
copy before they touch production. A nightly digest so owners wake up to
one honest summary instead of a feed. And expanding auto-fix beyond
plugins into failed crons, broken checkouts and stuck orders.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/971/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/971/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/980/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/980/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/981/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/981/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/982/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/982/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/985/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/415/985/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every dog at our shelter has a story.
Some were abandoned. Some were rescued from the streets. Some are old, injured, or have medical needs that make them difficult to adopt.
We started our family shelter four years ago, and while the number of dogs we care for has continued to grow, donations have not.
We wanted to build something that could make supporting these dogs more personal and meaningful. Instead of a generic donation page, we wanted people to discover an individual dog, understand their story, and feel connected to the life they're helping.

That idea became Angelic Friends.

**What it does**

Angelic Friends lets people discover the rescue dogs at our shelter and become an Angel to the ones they want to support.

Each dog has a profile with their story, personality, needs, and a live funding meter. Supporters subscribe monthly to earn Angel credits, then pledge those credits directly to a specific dog — or to a shared feeding fund for strays who aren't sponsored yet. From there, they can chat directly with the shelter's own team about the dog they're supporting, and get weekly video updates so they can actually watch that dog's story unfold.

The goal is simple: turn a donation into an ongoing connection.

Because every dog deserves someone in their corner.

**How we built it**

Angelic Friends is a Flutter app, built once and shipped natively to both iOS and Android from a single codebase, with a clean separation between the app's UI, its business logic, and the shelter's backend data.

Supabase runs the backend: Postgres for every dog, sponsorship, and message, with row-level security enforcing who can see and write what, and Edge Functions handling anything that needs to run outside the app itself.

Subscriptions and credits run on RevenueCat — a supporter subscribes to become an Angel, and a webhook grants that tier's credits into our own ledger every renewal, so unspent credits always roll over rather than resetting. Purchases, paywalls, and subscription management all go through RevenueCat's hosted UI rather than anything custom-built, which also keeps us aligned with both app stores' billing rules for free.

Getting in the door is deliberately frictionless: sign in with Google or Apple, or skip straight in as a guest with just a name. Firebase Analytics and Crashlytics tell us what's actually being used and what's breaking.

We also designed the whole experience around transparency, so supporters can see exactly where their support is going and keep following that dog's journey long after they've contributed.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge was finding the balance between building a meaningful product and keeping it realistic for a small shelter to operate.

We did not want to create a system that required the shelter team to spend hours creating content or managing complicated workflows.

We also had to think carefully about how to communicate a dog's needs without reducing them to a donation target. We wanted supporters to understand the real impact of their contribution while still seeing each dog as an individual.

Another challenge was designing a model that could eventually scale beyond our own shelter without losing the personal connection that makes the idea meaningful.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We're proud that Angelic Friends started with a real problem from a real shelter and turned it into something people can actually use.

We built the experience around the dogs themselves rather than around generic fundraising.

Most importantly, we created a way for someone to discover a dog, learn their story, support their care, and keep seeing their progress over time — and Angelic Friends is no longer just an idea. It's live on Google Play today, with an iOS release on the way, already helping dogs at our own shelter find support beyond just us.

**What we learned**

We learned that people can connect much more deeply with impact when they can see who they are helping.

A donation amount is abstract. A dog with a name, a face, a personality, and a story is not.

We also learned that building for a real-world organization means designing around the people doing the work every day. The product has to be simple enough for a shelter team to maintain while still giving supporters a meaningful experience.

**What's next for Angelic Friends: Give a Rescue Dog a Second Chance**

Right now, Angelic Friends is focused on our own shelter and the dogs in our care.

Our next step is to bring more dogs onto the platform, build a larger community of Angels, and make regular care updates a core part of the experience.

Long term, we want Angelic Friends to help more shelters and rescue organizations give their dogs the visibility, support, and ongoing care they deserve.

Because there are countless rescue dogs waiting for someone to see their story.

We want to help them find that someone.

</details>

## 394. Cairn

> Private check-ins with a clear response handoff. Cairn separates alert receipt from human acknowledgement, so your circle knows who is checking without an always-on location feed.

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/cairn-gzc37e (gallery page 111) · ❤️ 0 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [Ahmed Rahimi](https://devpost.com/importante-ahmed)
- **GitHub (Try it out):** https://github.com/Arag0n1421/cairn
- **Repo check:** public repo · license: MIT · 5 commits · TypeScript · RevenueCat found in code ✅
- **Built with:** capacitor, react, revenuecat, typescript

**Video (0:39):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jplWNaZLkco

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/jplWNaZLkco/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jplWNaZLkco)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/405/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/405/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/444/568/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/444/568/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

“I'll text you when I get home” is a small promise with an unclear failure path. If the message never arrives, who notices, who tries calling, and who knows whether someone else is already responding? A live map does not answer those questions.

Cairn explores a different starting point: agree the check-in, ask people to accept the response role, and make the handoff explicit. An alert reaching an inbox and a person taking responsibility must never look like the same event.

**What it does**

Cairn is a mobile engineering prototype for private check-ins and response coordination. Its working local rehearsal uses fictional people and a durable database. A user can register a timed check-in, finish it quietly, cancel it, or let its deadline and grace period expire. The service records the resulting incident and local inbox receipt. A separate responder identity can acknowledge it, and the sender can close it.

The interface distinguishes service acceptance, local receipt, human acknowledgement and closure. Closing an incident does not imply safe arrival or invent an acknowledgement. Responders must consent, can revoke consent, and lose access after closure. Missing location never blocks a deliberate SOS; a stale position or a gap in wearable samples never automatically creates one.

The free core includes the response drill and a downloadable practice receipt without coordinates or bearer tokens. Cairn Plus adds editable coordination templates with first-response and backup steps, which the user can copy and share themselves. RevenueCat's native SDK loads the current offering and checks the Plus entitlement after purchase or restore.

**How we built it**

React and TypeScript power a Capacitor app for Android and iOS. The optional local service uses Node.js and SQLite with server-owned deadlines, a durable outbox, idempotent mutations, separate sender and responder credentials, and a recorded audit trail. The client reconciles uncertain requests instead of silently declaring success, and hides responder evidence when refresh fails.

RevenueCat separates the commercial layer from incident handling. The coordination kit reads the verified purchase result; billing cannot veto, delay or initiate the core SOS drill. The contest configuration uses RevenueCat Test Store rather than charging users.

**Challenges**

The hardest part was giving uncertainty an honest representation. A notification receipt is not a human response. A closed incident is not proof that someone is safe. A disconnected screen must not keep presenting stale location as current. These distinctions shaped both the service and the interface.

Another challenge was making the commercial feature concrete without putting basic response behavior behind a subscription. The coordination kit gives Plus a small, working function while leaving the complete rehearsal available for free.

**Accomplishments**

A working consent-to-closure local response path; deadline escalation that survives service restarts; protected responder access; safe retries; a clear practice interface; retained acknowledgement evidence after closure; and an entitlement-gated coordination kit. Automated checks cover the safety state machine, UI behavior, API authorization, recovery, billing integration logic and build integrity.

**What we learned**

Response coordination is as much about the meaning of a state as the delivery mechanism. “Delivered,” “someone is checking,” and “closed” answer different questions. Keeping those meanings precise makes the product easier to test and easier to trust.

**What's next**

This entry is a fictional-data engineering prototype, not an operational emergency service. A responsible field version still needs production authentication, real notification-provider integration, encrypted storage, physical-device/background testing and a small informed pilot. Customer interviews must test whether the coordination workflow is useful enough to become a recurring habit.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/659/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/659/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/660/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/660/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/661/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/661/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/662/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/662/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/666/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/666/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/146/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/146/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I found that often when I set the time aside to actually write a letter to someone, I felt that I was able to express myself more freely and that I made a much deeper connection as opposed to just sending them a text. I also enjoyed the anticipation that naturally arises when waiting for a letter or package to arrive. I felt these could easily be combined to develop both a deeper messaging experience that created intentionality and created natural anticipation

**What it does**

Penpal allows users to claim a virtual mailbox at any of the USPS post office locations. You don't share a tag or handle, but you share your virtual address to your friends. You can then either type or draw your letter to your friend. Then across the next 3-5 days your letter will make its way across through nationwide sorting facilities and land at your friends virtual address for them to open. 

**How we built it**

The server was created using a basic python FastAPI server hosted on my own hardware and routed through Cloudflare tunnels, though authentication is done through Firebase Auth. The app was created using native Swift + SwiftUI and optimized for both iOS and iPadOS. 

**Challenges we ran into**

When connecting RevenueCat with App Store Connect products, everything displayed properly and showed as if it was working but the actual application would refuse to acknowledge them. However simply recreating everything using reverse DNS coding fixed the issues as opposed to using dashes. 

There was also an issue that, especially on app boot, presenting a map on the initial render for the tracking page would cause a significant hitch for the user. This was fixed by using a prewarming MapKit while it showed a loader which is quickly swapped for the warmed up map. 

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Penpal was designed from the ground up using a strong MVVM+C architecture which enabled later features such as deep linking, paywall implementation, pre-populated views and automated screenshots much easier to develop. Further it also started with the understanding of an extensive API so I implemented a strong API base which could allow a very "Swift" approach to calls using an enum which then resolved to the actual API call internally. 

**What we learned**

I had never implemented an MVVM+C architecture, nor an app which relied upon a server for its source of truth. I learned a lot about the relationship between apps, websites, and deeplinks (it's important to not kick the user out of what they are doing simply because a deeplink was clicked!). It was also my first time developing an onboarding experience and it was a good learning experience optimizing for a frictionless setup.

**What's next for Penpal**

I'm looking to add a more "penpal" style aspect to the app where you can get connected to another random user to send mail between each other. I would also love to explore this idea further with some form of translation (through drawing would be particularly neat!)

</details>

- **Built with:** appkit, macos, revenuecat, swift, swiftui

**Video (1:42):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3buUP9eKQec

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/3buUP9eKQec/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3buUP9eKQec)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/859/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/859/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/860/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/860/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/861/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/861/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/862/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/862/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/865/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/368/865/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Students switch between essays, code, practice and everyday obligations many times a day. The expensive part is not the interruption; it is rebuilding what you had decided, what failed and where to start again. We wanted a calm place to put that context down, without another guilt-inducing task list.

**What it does**

Tether holds each thing you are in the middle of as a thread with one concrete next move, a short "what you'll wish you remembered" note and optional links. Coming back opens a focused return card instead of a dashboard. Parking a thread adds a checkpoint rather than overwriting earlier thinking. One thread is active at a time, a five-minute filter finds small windows, and there is a menu-bar entry, keyboard shortcuts and full Markdown export. Notes stay on the Mac and are never sent to RevenueCat or an AI model.

**How we built it**

SwiftUI and AppKit on macOS 14+, built with Swift Package Manager. A separate, UI-free TetherCore module holds the domain rules (checkpoints, one-active-thread transitions, the free limit, export) and is covered by standalone checks. Persistence is atomic JSON in Application Support; unreadable data is preserved, and failed saves roll back.

**How RevenueCat is used**

The app uses RevenueCat's purchases-ios SDK 5.90.2, not a REST stand-in:

- Purchases.configure with a public SDK key (the RevenueCat Test Store for this entry);

- offerings() loads the current offering; the Plus screen renders its Monthly ($9.99/month), Yearly ($79.99/year) and Lifetime ($99.99) packages from the returned products, with no hardcoded prices;

- purchase(package:) runs the purchase; on the Test Store the SDK shows its own confirmation;

- access comes only from CustomerInfo.entitlements["plus"].isActive, refreshed on app activation and at the known expiry date, and through the CustomerInfo delegate;

- restorePurchases() restores access and the app confirms the result.

Free: three open threads and the latest checkpoint per thread. Plus: unlimited open threads and the full checkpoint trail. If Plus ends, nothing is deleted or locked, and export always includes every checkpoint.

Verified in the running app on September 22, 2026 and shown in the video: offerings load, a Test Store purchase of Monthly activates plus, the fourth thread that the free plan refused is saved, the full trail appears, and Restore purchases confirms Plus. Test Store purchases are sandbox transactions with no real charge.

**Challenges we ran into**

Recording a real purchase honestly. We captured only Tether's own windows with ScreenCaptureKit and drove the app and RevenueCat's Test Store alert through macOS accessibility, so the film is one continuous recording rather than mockups. The purchase run also exposed three rough edges we fixed: a clipped paywall subtitle, a stale free-limit notice after unlocking, and a restore with no visible result.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

A useful free app first, with a paywall that only adds room: your draft survives the free limit, purchase unlocks it in place, and expiry never holds notes hostage.

**What we learned**

Entitlement state needs refreshing at the moments it can change (activation, expiry), not only at launch. And monetization feels fair when the free tier is complete on its own.

**What's next for Tether**

A production App Store build with Apple products, notarized distribution, and user testing of whether return cards actually shorten restarts. No revenue, users or productivity outcomes are claimed today.

**Try it**

macOS 14+: swift run Tether from https://github.com/ToukoUrsin/tether (MIT). Purchases need a RevenueCat public SDK key in Settings or REVENUECAT_PUBLIC_KEY.

**Team and AI disclosure**

Touko Ursin, solo, Aalto University student (Next Gen category). Development was assisted by OpenAI Codex and Claude (design, code generation, debugging, test preparation, and the video edit). Video narration uses an ElevenLabs stock voice. The app contains no AI features.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every month, almost half of Americans take a prescription drugs this month, but hardly anybody is aware of the effects of the drug inside them. Most medicines work by changing a protein, and many of those proteins have been mapped atom by atom in current databases through 3D models. I wanted to streamline this accessibility for everyone, starting from the medicine box in their cabinet.

**What it does**

Search a medicine or scan the UPC barcode on its box. MoleculeLens shows the protein the drug acts on in an interactive 3D model, with the drug glowing in its pocket where a drug-bound structure exists. Three plain-language cards explain what the protein does, what the drug changes, and why that helps and causes side effects in the user. You can also save your medicines to a virtual cabinet. If two medicines within the cabinet act on the same protein, you get a warning and a suggestion to ask your pharmacist about it. Study mode turns your cabinet, or all 81 medicines, into flashcards and quizzes.

**How we built it**

This was built using Expo SDK 57 and TypeScript in Expo Go. A generator script takes each medicine to ChEMBL for its target, UniProt for the protein's facts, and RCSB PDB for a drug-bound structure, falling back to AlphaFold. It writes a bundled hero list and a verification report I reviewed row by row. The 3D view is 3Dmol.js inside a WebView. Barcodes go UPC → NDC → openFDA, with RxNorm as a fallback. The AI never picks the protein. An optional Cloudflare Worker that asks Gemini to rephrase verified facts is built and tested, but not deployed due to errors during project creation in the site.

**RevenueCat**

The free mode includes unlimited lookups, 3D, the cards, a 3-medicine cabinet and every safety warning. Safety is never paywalled (always free). Lens Pro (monthly or yearly, 7-day free trial) unlocks an unlimited cabinet, side-effect and metabolism deep dives, and a shareable "how my medicines work" sheet. Study Pack is a one-time purchase for flashcards and quizzes. Everything runs on RevenueCat's Test Store inside Expo Go, with my own paywall screen. Expo Go never fires the customer-info listener, so the app re-fetches entitlements after every purchase.

**Challenges we ran into**

- 3D in Expo Go: No native modules, so the viewer is 3Dmol.js in a WebView.

- The NDC hidden in a UPC: A US drug barcode contains a 10-digit NDC, but the digits can split three ways. The app tries all three against openFDA, then RxNorm.

- Salt and ester forms: ChEMBL often stores the mechanism on "atorvastatin calcium", not atorvastatin, and on fluticasone propionate rather than fluticasone. The generator follows parent links and seed overrides.

- Honest fallbacks: Mouse structures, debated mechanisms, germ targets, the bacterial ribosome and ingredients with no protein target each needed their own truthful screen instead of a forced answer.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- 81 medicines, each traced to a database record.

- 11 real drug-bound structures.

- Safety warnings that are free for everyone.

- A report that shows every flag instead of hiding it.

**What we learned**

Biology databases disagree about names, species and what counts as a target, so it became very important to check the actual data instead of just the code.

**What's next for MoleculeLens Rx**

- Live ChEMBL lookup for any medicine

- Reading ingredients from a label photo

- Deploying the Worker

- More hand-written explanations

**Safety Statement**

MoleculeLens Rx is educational only. It gives no prescribed doses or medical advice, and every warning includes "Ask your pharmacist". Animal structures are labelled to alert the viewer they are not looking at a human structure. Never change a prescribed medicine based on advice from MoleculeLens Rx without asking a pharmacist or doctor.

</details>
