**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/708/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/708/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/709/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/709/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/710/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/710/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/711/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/711/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/712/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/712/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/713/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/713/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I was born and raised in Pakistan — a country rich in culture, food, and warmth, but one where a girl is still, in many households, a decision people think twice about. I was privileged: good schools, supportive parents, and a circle of genuinely brilliant, ambitious women around me.

One of them became an influencer. She grew fast — Instagram, TikTok, real fame. Then came a minor scandal, and her comment sections turned into something else entirely: slurs, harassment, coordinated pile-ons. We reported hundreds of comments; Instagram removed a handful of the most obvious ones. Her mental health deteriorated to the point that she deleted her accounts and eventually left the country.

That was the moment I understood how much power an unmoderated comment section has over a real person's life — and how far behind the platforms' own tools were. I remember wishing there was something that could just delete the toxicity the instant it appeared, in whatever language it was written in. I couldn't build that for her in time. toxoff is me building it anyway, so the next person doesn't have to leave the country to feel safe online.

**What it does**

toxoff is an iPhone app that removes abusive Instagram comments, usually before the creator ever reads them.

- Connects to an Instagram Business or Creator account and checks every new comment within about a minute (every 30 seconds on a fresh post).

- Understands any language and any spelling: English, Roman Urdu, Hindi, Arabic script, mixed-language comments and disguised words, the abuse that keyword filters miss.

- Deletes flagged comments by default, or hides them, or deletes only what it is at least 80% sure of. The creator chooses.

- Protects your peace: the Log shows why a comment was removed and in which language, never the words, unless you tap "Read it anyway". Deleted comments can be erased forever, unread.

- Filters: sensitivity, categories (hate speech, harassment, slurs, spam, self-harm promotion), a keyword blocklist and blocked users.

**How it uses RevenueCat**

Subscriptions are the business model, so RevenueCat sits at the centre of billing, and the server, not the phone, decides what a user can do.

- Plans: Free (50 checks a month), Solo (1 account), Plus (5 accounts) and Studio (15 accounts), each monthly or yearly, in one App Store subscription group ordered Studio &gt; Plus &gt; Solo, so moving up is an instant upgrade.

- In the app: react-native-purchases is configured with the user's own account id, so a purchase belongs to the account, not the phone. The paywall loads the current Offering, shows Apple's real price in the user's currency and a yearly saving worked out from the store's own prices, and includes Restore and Manage Subscription.

- On the server: after every purchase or restore, and on every RevenueCat webhook (renewal, cancellation, billing issue, refund, transfer), a Supabase Edge Function re-reads the subscriber from RevenueCat's REST API and updates the user's plan. The app can never unlock a plan by itself.

- Enforced in the database: Postgres functions and row-level security apply the plan: how many Instagram accounts can connect, whether a comment may be checked, and how far back the Log reaches.

- Tested end to end on a TestFlight build on a real iPhone: Apple → RevenueCat → server → database → app, in seconds.

- Ads, ready for later: rewarded ads report every impression and its revenue to RevenueCat's ad tracker. They're switched off in version 1 until the AdMob account is approved.

**How I built it**

- App: Expo SDK 52 (React Native, New Architecture) and TypeScript, built with EAS on Xcode 26 and tested through TestFlight.

- Backend: Supabase: Postgres with row-level security, Auth (email, Google, Apple), Realtime, scheduled jobs and one Deno Edge Function.

- Meta's Instagram API (Instagram Login) to read and delete comments on the creator's own posts.

- AI moderation, cheapest answer first: rules settle emoji, obvious spam and a built-in list of known slurs with spelling variants (no API call); plain English goes to OpenAI's free moderation endpoint; only the unsure and non-English comments reach GPT-5.4 Nano. That costs about 0.05 USD per 1,000 comments, rate-limited per user.

- Tested: strict TypeScript, 36 app tests, 57 backend tests, 17 database tests and a security review with regression tests.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Meta only sends instant comment notifications to verified businesses. As a student without a registered company, I built a polling engine instead that checks fresh posts every 30 seconds while staying inside Meta's rate limits.

- Roman Urdu has no fixed spelling. The AI alone scored one common slur at only 45%, so I added a rule layer for known slurs and their variants that answers instantly, consistently and for free.

- My AdMob account was rejected before launch, so version 1 ships without ads behind a single switch, rather than showing a "watch an ad" button that would always fail.

- Polish bugs that only showed in real builds: iOS 26 switches drawn at the wrong size, and a launch image my own asset script had silently corrupted. Both were fixed and checked frame by frame.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- It works on a real Instagram account: abusive comments are deleted in under a minute, and the creator never has to read them.

- A complete subscription flow through RevenueCat, verified end to end.

- A design that respects the person on the other end: it shows that abuse was removed and why, never the abuse itself.

**What I learned**

Most of a "simple" moderation app is plumbing: entitlements belong on the server, platform rules shape the architecture, and the cheapest reliable answer should always come before the expensive one. Above all, I learned that the best feature for someone being harassed is not seeing it at all.

**What's next for toxoff**

- Launch on the App Store (coming soon).

- Meta Business Verification, so every creator can connect their account.

- TikTok support, and ads on the Free plan once AdMob approves.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Most household food waste isn't one big mistake. It's the yoghurt found three days late and the fourth tin of chickpeas bought because you forgot the other three. Every expiry-tracker app treats those as the same problem, and every one of them is a utility you stop opening after a week.

They're two different problems. Food that's about to expire can't go to a food bank: donations take weeks to sort and hand out. It has to be eaten tonight. Long-life surplus is the opposite: it's exactly what food banks need. So we built an app that knows the difference, and gave people a reason to open it every day.

**What it does**

- Rescue: perishables within 3 days of their date surface on the home screen. Pick them and get one recipe that uses all of them (a built-in recipe for everyone; a Claude-written one for Pro).

- Donate: shelf-stable, unopened, long-dated food that you have too much of (more than 2, untouched for a month, or a duplicate) goes into a donation box: "You have 8 items you'll probably never eat. That's about 6 meals for someone." It finds the nearest food bank from OpenStreetMap. The app never suggests donating food that's about to expire.

- Sprout, the pixel pet: it thrives when you rescue food, celebrates when you donate, and wilts (gently) when food is binned. It grows through six stages, earns badges, keeps a waste-free streak, and wears outfits bought with seeds earned by saving food: 48 items, from a chef hat to a full T-rex costume with its own volcano backdrop.

- Stopping waste at the shop: a shopping list that warns "you already have 5 chickpeas, 17 months left", sends straight to the family chat as text, and moves ticked items into the fridge.

- Quick to use: swipe right for "ate it", left for "binned it", both with undo. Add by barcode, receipt photo, pasting a list, or a scroll-wheel date picker.

**How we built it**

- React Native + Expo SDK 57 (TypeScript, Expo Router), Zustand + AsyncStorage. No database: a fridge is ~50 items.

- All the business rules are pure, tested functions (src/lib/rules): urgency, surplus detection, creature mood, XP and seeds, badges, weekly challenges, shopping-list matching. 68 tests on Node's built-in runner.

- Keyless APIs: Open Food Facts (barcodes), Overpass/OpenStreetMap (food banks), Nominatim (typed locations).

- Claude (claude-opus-5, JSON-schema output) for Pro recipes and receipt scanning, behind a sanitiser that drops carrier bags and totals.

- Sprout is drawn as a 16×20 pixel grid in code, with every accessory, outfit and backdrop as a pixel map. There's no image asset or animation rig.

**How we use RevenueCat**

- Subscriptions: one fridge_rescue_pro entitlement, one offering (monthly $9.99 / annual $79.99), running on RevenueCat's Test Store, so the whole purchase flow works without App Store Connect or Play Console.

- Paywall: RevenueCat's own Paywall component, configured remotely in the dashboard. No prices or copy are hard-coded.

- Second revenue stream: opt-in rewarded ads. In the shop, free users can watch an AdMob rewarded ad for +10 seeds, up to 3 a day. Every ad event (loaded, shown, clicked, paid) is reported to RevenueCat's ad tracker, so ad and subscription revenue sit in one dashboard. Pro users collect the same bonus without the ad.

- The social good is never paywalled. Rescuing and donating are free for everyone. Pro pays for convenience (unlimited items and scans, AI recipes, history and CSV export) and vanity (Pro-only outfits). Seeds can't be bought with money. The app moves food, not money, so it avoids the store rules on in-app charitable donations entirely.

**Challenges we ran into**

- The rescue-versus-donate line: getting the surplus rules right so the app never suggests donating yoghurt that expires Thursday.

- Making a game layer that rewards the habit that actually prevents waste (opening the fridge before food goes off) rather than grinding. Expired food isn't counted as waste straight away: the app asks "did you eat it?" first.

- RevenueCat's Test Store only runs in debuggable builds, which shaped how we ship the demo APK.

**Accomplishments we're proud of**

- A clear idea with a real insight behind it: expiring food and surplus food need opposite answers.

- A pet people want to come back to, with rewards tied to saving food rather than tapping.

- A clean, tested rules layer and a README that explains every threshold.

**What we learned**

Retention in a utility app comes from a reason to open it, not more alerts. Monetisation is easier to defend when the paywall only ever charges for convenience.

**What's next**

- Household sharing (a shared fridge and shopping list for flatmates and families), which needs accounts and sync.

- Verified donations via partner check-in codes at food banks (today, "I dropped these off" is trust-based).

- Better food-bank coverage where OpenStreetMap is thin.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

It started with Amy, a calorie-tracking app that is just a text box. I'm an avid reader and use Goodreads, but filling in countless forms just to do simple things like updating a page number felt like paperwork. So I combined the two ideas: talk naturally, and cactus does the rest.

**What it does**

cactus is a reading tracker you talk to. Type what you did in plain words, like "finished dune, 4.5 stars, started circe yesterday", and it updates your shelf, progress, ratings and streak.

Free

- A classic command grammar, plus an on-device parser that understands everyday sentences, forgives typos and matches titles against your shelf.

- Shelves, series, tags, comments and owned editions.

- Search across Google Books, with an Open Library fallback.

- A yearly reading goal and a reading-days heatmap.

- A real offline mode that syncs when you're back online.

- Goodreads import and CSV export.

cactus pro (a RevenueCat subscription)

- An AI that turns a whole rambling message into several actions.

- Deeper stats, memory notes and recommendations.

- Customisation: themes, fonts and 16 app icons.

**How I built it**

Flutter front end, Supabase backend (Postgres with row-level security, anonymous auth, edge functions), and RevenueCat for subscriptions.

- RevenueCat: the live entitlement drives every pro gate, and every gate fails closed. The paywall is always dismissible, opens on the feature you tapped, and shows the store's own localized prices.

- No sign-up wall: every reader gets an anonymous account on first launch. An optional verified email link secures the library across devices.

- Secrets stay server-side: the AI key lives in a Supabase edge function, never on the device, and each call is rate-limited per reader.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Flaky book data. Google Books returned random 503s and ran out of its free quota. I added a server-side retry proxy, a keyless Open Library fallback and caching.

- Offline writes in the right order. Queued changes have to replay in sequence, or an old value overwrites a newer one after reconnecting.

- Language without a model. The free parser needed fuzzy title matching and date phrases like "yesterday" without misreading titles such as Pride and Prejudice.

- Balancing free and pro. The free tier had to be genuinely useful, or nobody would ever see a reason to upgrade, while pro still had to feel worth paying for.

- Designing for readers, not developers. Most readers won't memorise commands, so I built an on-device parser that understands everyday sentences, and tested it with real readers to see what worked and what didn't.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- A free tier that's genuinely useful, with pro as a real upgrade rather than a lock on the basics.

- 800+ automated tests, and a codebase that passes strict static analysis with zero issues.

- A genuine offline mode.

- Fixing things I found frustrating in other trackers: slow forms, no offline support, and an account wall before you can start.

- Turning flaky book data into a polished search system that rarely misses.

- Heavy customisation, so you can use cactus the way you like.

- The countless easter eggs I hid which create for a fun user experience

**What I learned**

- How to integrate RevenueCat properly: entitlements, gating and a paywall that reflects real subscription state.

- How to build a resilient book search across Google Books and Open Library.

- How to wire in crash reporting and analytics without sending any reader-written content.

- How to design a paywall, and what to put in it.

**What's next for cactus**

- Adding books while offline (it currently needs a connection).

- Stronger recommendations and reading-time insights.

- A release on Google Play and the App Store.

- Wider testing with readers to find and fix pain points.

- Improve speed of Pro mode

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

We live in a world where information, ideas, productivity tools, and AI assistants are everywhere. Yet people often struggle with something more fundamental: turning intention into consistent action.
That inspired MOMENTUM 2.0. We wanted to explore what AI could become if it moved beyond simply answering questions and instead helped people understand their goals, recognize their context, identify the right next step, and keep moving forward.
For the city-reimagining challenge, we extended this idea into a future where AI works quietly in the background as a context-aware intelligence layer around everyday life.

MOMENTUM 2.0 helps turn goals into actionable progress.
The experience is built around a simple journey:
Goal → Context → AI Understanding → Next Action → Progress → Momentum
Instead of overwhelming users with more information, the concept focuses on helping them identify what matters now and what they can realistically do next.
We imagine this intelligence supporting students, professionals, creators, and everyday citizens while remaining human-centered. In our reimagined city, technology reduces friction without taking attention away from the people using it.

We started by identifying the gap between having an intention and taking consistent action. From there, we translated the concept into a digital experience centered around goals, context, actionable guidance, and progress.
We designed the product experience to make AI feel like an intelligent layer rather than just another chatbot. Google Gemini plays an important role as the intelligence layer, helping interpret intent and context and generate relevant, actionable guidance.
We also focused on the visual language of the future city. Rather than relying on generic robots, excessive holograms, or a purely cyberpunk aesthetic, we wanted to show a believable future where intelligent technology is naturally integrated into everyday life.

One of our biggest challenges was turning an abstract concept like “momentum” into something people could immediately understand.
We also had to find the right balance between AI capability and simplicity. An AI system can generate countless suggestions, but too many suggestions can create more friction instead of reducing it.
Another challenge was imagining the concept at a city scale while keeping the experience realistic and human-centered. We wanted the future to feel ambitious without making technology the main character.

We are proud of turning a simple observation about human behavior into a broader vision for how AI could interact with everyday life.
We built a concept that goes beyond the traditional “user asks → AI answers” model and instead explores:
Context-aware assistance
Goal-to-action guidance
Personalized next steps
Progress-oriented interactions
Human-centered AI
AI as an intelligence layer within the environment
Most importantly, we are proud of the central idea behind MOMENTUM 2.0: technology should not simply give people more information; it should help them make meaningful progress.

Building MOMENTUM 2.0 taught us that adding AI to a product is not enough. The more important question is what role AI should play in a person's experience.
We learned to think beyond individual features and focus on the outcome created by those features. We also learned that futuristic technology does not have to look futuristic everywhere. Some of the most useful technology may be the technology that works quietly in the background.
Most importantly, we learned to approach AI from a human perspective: understand the person, understand the context, and help with the next meaningful step.

We see MOMENTUM 2.0 evolving toward a more deeply context-aware AI experience that can understand changing goals, priorities, environments, and progress over time.

</details>

**3D Craft: from an idea to something you can use**

3D Craft turns a text idea or reference image into concept art, then a 3D asset you can inspect, export, animate, or bring into a playable creation. The project includes a native iPhone and iPad studio, a companion web studio, and a cloud creation service.

💡 Idea or photo → 🎨 Choose a concept → 🧊 Generate a 3D model → 🔍 Inspect and export → 🎬 Animate or play

These captures show one path through the current iOS source build. Token amounts shown are examples from that session; the app requests a fresh quote for each model and setting.

Area
Current implementation

iOS studio
SwiftUI with an interactive SceneKit/GLTFKit2 model viewer, lighting controls, and material/solid/wire views.

Concepts
Text or image references, generated concepts, and explicit image selection before 3D generation.

Image to 3D
Atlas options including Tripo H3.1, Seed3D, Hunyuan, HI3D, and Meshy; fal options including Rodin, TRELLIS.2, Hunyuan3D, and hybrid. The iOS picker currently suggests Tripo H3.1.

Animation
Atlas MiniMax H3, Seedance 2.0 Mini, Seedance 2.0, Seedance 2.5, and Wan 3.0 Prime; fal MiniMax H3 and Seedance 2.5. The iOS picker currently suggests Atlas MiniMax H3.

Preview 3D model samples before generating
The 3D confirmation view lets creators inspect interactive sample meshes for supported engines before starting their own generation. Animation choices include Dragon sample videos, with the sample's provider identified clearly.

Themes
Lavender and emerald are independent appearance choices. The lavender gallery uses the blue dragon; the emerald gallery uses the lantern explorer.

Games
Built-in browser games, game-building handoff, and community-submitted game links with review, voting, and reporting controls.

Accounts and billing
Firebase accounts and cloud library; weekly/monthly Creator subscriptions and separate one-time Token packs through Apple purchases and RevenueCat.

Selecting a concept does not start a paid 3D job. After inspecting a model, creators can export it, make a character animation, or use a game-building handoff. Open the full-size walkthrough in the README.

**Why the purchase flow matters**

Different 3D and animation models have different costs. Before a generation starts, 3D Craft requests a quote for the selected model and settings so the creator can see the required Tokens. The iOS app offers weekly and monthly Creator subscriptions plus separate one-time Token packs through Apple purchases and RevenueCat. Purchases are associated with the signed-in account, and the cloud service verifies purchase data before applying Tokens. The explicit concept choice and quote make each paid step understandable.

**What powers it**

Google Gemini creates concept-art options from text and image references. Supported Atlas and fal models turn selected images into 3D assets or create animation videos. The app presents model choices and samples; the public image-to-3D comparison and animation comparison show actual sample outputs from specific test runs. Results can vary with the input and model.

**Architecture at a glance**

The studios share a cloud API. The iOS purchase path uses Apple and RevenueCat, with verification in the API.

The native studio uses SceneKit and GLTFKit2 for interactive 3D viewing. Firebase Authentication, Firestore, and Storage support accounts, background jobs, and the asset library. Firebase Hosting serves the web studio and routes /api/** requests to the FastAPI service on Cloud Run. Signed-in creators can also create scoped, expiring personal API keys for compatible HTTP clients; those calls use the account's production Token balance.

**Designed for creative exploration**

Concepts, models, and animations have separate views, so it is clear which asset is being inspected. Lavender and emerald appearances give the studio distinct visual themes. The model viewer adds lighting and material or wire views for checking geometry. A game-building handoff carries a model and prompt into the next creative step.

**Explore 3D Craft**

Install the iOS app to browse examples, open a 3D model, try its viewer controls, and explore playable creations. Visit the web studio for the companion experience. The public repository documents the current source build and architecture, including features that may reach the App Store in a later release.

3D Craft first appeared on the App Store on September 18, 2026.

</details>

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/31-7EvkX-lw/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=31-7EvkX-lw)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/378/975/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/378/975/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/378/976/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/378/976/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

New managers are surrounded by advice but rarely get a safe chance to practise. A script can tell someone what good feedback sounds like; it cannot recreate the moment when an employee says, “That is not fair,” the manager loses their thread, and the conversation becomes real.

Say It First was inspired by that gap between knowing and doing. It turns difficult management conversations into active rehearsals so people can find the words, hear the resistance, and try again before another person is affected.

**What it does**

A manager enters a realistic underperformance-feedback rehearsal and speaks naturally with Alex, an AI-simulated software engineer who stays in character and pushes back credibly.

The app captures a live transcript and produces structured feedback grounded in the manager's own words. Instead of generic advice, it identifies the manager's strongest moment, explains why it worked, and prepares an exact coached sentence to try next.

The free experience includes the core rehearsal, private debrief, and strongest transcript-grounded moment. Say It First Pro reveals the exact coached sentence and unlocks an immediate focused retry through a contextual RevenueCat-powered monthly or annual offer.

**How we built it**

The Android app uses Expo and React Native with a native development client. A Fastify API owns the trusted AI boundary, provider credentials, session configuration, and evidence-grounded evaluation. OpenAI Realtime runs over WebRTC for low-latency voice, while shared TypeScript contracts keep the mobile, API, and domain layers aligned.

RevenueCat's React Native SDK powers dynamic packages, purchase and restore flows, entitlement refresh, and Customer Center. The coded paywall renders store-provided names and prices and derives annual savings only when the live package currencies are comparable. Development, preview, and production keys are isolated through EAS environments.

Every mobile, API, and provider interaction carries correlation identifiers and privacy-safe diagnostics. Logs include lifecycle, latency, audio receiver quality, package identifiers, and safe error codes, while excluding microphone audio, transcript text, payment details, and credentials.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest failure looked healthy in ordinary logs: an assistant reply completed at the protocol level but the user heard it stop or corrupt in the middle. We treated human listening as the source of truth, removed an accidental response ceiling, took explicit ownership of Android audio focus and speaker routing, and added per-turn receiver evidence for packet loss, jitter, and concealed samples. That made network delivery, decoding, provider completion, and device routing separately debuggable.

Billing exposed a similarly dangerous edge case. RevenueCat's dashboard-created entitlement was the immutable, case-sensitive Pro, while the first implementation checked lowercase pro. An actual Android purchase test caught the mismatch before release, and a regression test now locks the exact production contract.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A real-time spoken rehearsal, live transcript, clean teardown, and quote-validated structured evaluation run on Android.

- Controlled short, 30-second, and 50-second assistant replies reached their spoken completion markers with zero receiver packet loss in the measured runs.

- The native RevenueCat Test Store path loads live packages, completes an annual sandbox purchase, activates Pro, restores access, and opens Customer Center in the actual Android UI.

- The official Play-distributed build completed a no-charge Google Play license-test Annual subscription and activated the same Pro entitlement on a Samsung Galaxy S10.

- A controlled Samsung regression played an approximately 53-second response through the prior 26-second failure point and reached its exact completion phrase; the session then produced a grounded debrief and clean audio teardown.

- Full repository lint, strict TypeScript, 30 automated tests, API/shared builds, Android export, and a separately signed Android lab build pass together.

**What we learned**

Protocol success is not user success. Audio has to be heard to the final word, feedback has to be traceable to something the manager actually said, and a purchase only matters when the exact entitlement unlocks the promised value.

We also learned that observability can improve the product rather than merely support it. The same boundaries that make a failure diagnosable—structured session states, grounded evidence, exact billing identifiers, and privacy-safe traces—make the experience more trustworthy for a nervous manager.

**What's next for Say It First**

Say It First is now publicly available on Google Play in Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The next product step is deliberately narrow: learn from real practice completion, repeat use, conversion, and qualitative manager feedback before expanding the surface area.

The roadmap includes additional scenarios and personas, a highlighted-moment retry, private history and deletion controls, server-side entitlement enforcement, and deeper billing lifecycle verification for cancellation, renewal, expiry, and reinstall. License-test evidence will never be presented as customer revenue.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Why I built Cooly**

Last summer a heat wave hit and the weather app on my phone just told me it was 38°C. Useful, but it didn't answer the actual question I had: where do I go right now? The nearest place with air conditioning, a water fountain, some shade — that's what I needed, and no app was telling me.

Cooly is my answer. It shows the "feels like" temperature and air quality for exactly where you're standing, then points you to the closest cool, safe place — a library, a mall, a cafe — sorted by how far you'd actually have to walk. Water, shade and public toilets sit on the same map. And when heat or air quality turns dangerous, it warns you even if the app is closed.

**What it does**

- Real-time feels-like temperature and a US EPA air-quality reading for your location

- The nearest cool refuge, ranked by walking distance

- Water fountains, shade and toilets nearby, on one map

- Danger alerts for extreme heat and bad air, delivered even when the app is shut

- A home-screen widget for a one-glance safety check

- Watch cities you care about (home, family, a trip) with a 7-day heat outlook

**How I built it**

Cooly is a single Kotlin Multiplatform + Compose Multiplatform project. It isn't shared business logic with two native UIs bolted on — the entire interface, the map screen, the alerts, the paywall, is one Compose codebase that runs on both Android and iOS.

Payments are the same story. Cooly Plus is wired through RevenueCat, so one purchase model covers both stores with the same Kotlin code, and I never had to write platform-specific billing.

Data comes from Open-Meteo (weather and air quality) and OpenStreetMap via Overpass (places) — both free and global, so Cooly works anywhere without an API bill.

**The hard parts**

- Shipping iOS without a Mac dev setup. I don't have a machine that can build and sign an iOS app locally, so I built, signed and shipped the whole iOS side on CI (Codemagic) — fighting through certificates, provisioning profiles and bundle IDs until TestFlight finally accepted it. Proving that a Kotlin Multiplatform app can reach the App Store this way was the single most satisfying moment of the project.

- Getting the danger right. An air-quality alert that cries wolf is worse than none. I reworked the risk model to follow the real US EPA categories, so a "danger" alert only fires when the air is genuinely at that level — not one category early.

- Alerts without tracking you. People shouldn't have to hand over background location for a safety app. Alerts run on the last location you already loaded, checked periodically in the background, with no background GPS.

**What I learned**

Kotlin Multiplatform has quietly crossed the line from "share your models" to "share your product." Watching the same Compose screen render on an emulator and an iPhone, from one file, changed how I think about what a solo developer can ship.

**What's next**

Community-sourced cooling shelters, offline maps for low-signal areas, and localized heat thresholds so "dangerous" means the right thing in Seoul, Phoenix and Lagos alike.

Cooly is one small tool for staying safe as summers get hotter — built end to end in Kotlin, on both platforms, by one person.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I came back to volleyball in July 2026 after almost three years away from the sport. I had finally started training again, and then, on my way to a tryout in the city where I study, I got injured. I already knew how easily time away from volleyball can stretch from a few weeks into months and, eventually, years, so this time I wanted to approach being away differently: not as being "out" of the sport, but as being part of a different stage of it.

That's where Still In The Game started.

**What it does**

Still In The Game is a daily companion for athletes who can't participate normally right now. You pick your sport, say where you are in your comeback and what you miss most, and the app gives you one small activity that keeps you connected to your sport or community.

When you complete it, your comeback court comes back to life. There are no streaks to lose and progress never goes backwards. If you have a bad day, take a day off, or simply don't feel like doing the activity, everything you've already built stays there.

The court is a night volleyball court that grows one piece at a time. The first 12 activities rebuild the court itself: the lines, net, ball, bench, street lamp, lights and scoreboard. The next 12 bring the players onto the court, taking turns between your team and the other team until it becomes six against six. After that, the ball starts moving around the court like an actual rally.

Recovery doesn't have a fixed end date, so the journey continues in seasons instead of ending at an arbitrary percentage. Right now the app is volleyball-only; basketball, football and running are planned next.

**How I built it**

I built the app with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, using DataStore to keep progress locally on the device, with no account or backend required for the core experience. The comeback court is made from 31 illustrations generated through a Python script, so every stage is included in the repository and can be regenerated.

I integrated RevenueCat's Android SDK (10.24) for Still In The Game+. The app reads the current offering and displays monthly and yearly plans, with the yearly savings badge calculated from the actual prices. Plus is controlled through the plus entitlement, and the app listens for entitlement changes so the experience updates when a purchase, restore, or granted entitlement becomes active. I also added an optional username flow using RevenueCat App User IDs and a promo code for judges.

The free version includes the complete daily connection loop. Plus allows users to complete more than one activity per day and request new suggestions without the daily limit. I kept the pricing intentionally low at $2.99/month or $19.99/year because the people this app is designed for may already have other costs associated with being away from their sport, including recovery and physiotherapy.

I designed the visual direction before building: dark athletic navy, warm chalk, court orange, electric blue and rally yellow. I used Sora for the more expressive athletic typography, Inter for the interface, and Caveat for handwritten notes. I wanted it to feel like a sports app without becoming another fitness tracker built around numbers, streaks and performance charts.

I also used Claude, Anthropic's AI assistant, as a coding partner during the hackathon. It helped write a large part of the implementation and generate the court illustrations from my direction. I made the product and UX decisions myself: the idea, target user, tone, visual direction, comeback system, court progression, pricing and what made it into the MVP.

**Challenges I ran into**

The biggest challenge was figuring out how to motivate someone without turning recovery into another competition.

I didn't want streaks, rankings or performance metrics where missing a day could make someone feel like they were falling behind. That didn't make sense for the problem I was trying to solve. Being injured already makes you feel like you're behind everyone else sometimes; I didn't want the app to reinforce that.

I also had to keep the app firmly non-medical. Still In The Game doesn't tell athletes how to recover, what exercises to do, or when they should return to their sport. It focuses on something different: helping them stay connected while they're away.

And then there was the obvious challenge: building all of this in two days. I had to be very strict about the MVP. Every feature had to answer the same question: does this help someone feel like they're still part of their sport?

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

I'm most proud of the comeback court. I didn't want progress to be another number like "43% recovered." Instead, progress changes something the user can actually see. The court starts almost empty, gradually gets rebuilt, and eventually your team shows up. It gives the user somewhere to come back to rather than just something to measure.

I'm also proud of the tone of the app. I wanted it to be encouraging without being overly motivational or cheesy. When you're actually going through an injury, sometimes you don't need someone telling you "YOU GOT THIS!" You just need something that makes the time away feel a little less like you're being left behind.

**What I learned**

This project made me think a lot more carefully about design psychology and motivation. A progress system isn't automatically motivating. If it constantly shows you what you haven't done, it can make you feel worse instead.

I also got much more comfortable with Jetpack Compose, DataStore and RevenueCat, especially with making the monetization part feel like it belongs to the product instead of being a paywall randomly added at the end.

Most importantly, I learned how much product thinking matters when you're building under a time limit. I had a lot of ideas for Still In The Game, but I couldn't build all of them. I had to keep coming back to the same question: what is the smallest version of this idea that still makes someone feel like they're part of their sport?

**What's next for Still In The Game**

The first step is expanding beyond volleyball with courts and comeback journeys for basketball, football and running. After that, I'd like to make the app more useful at the team level, so coaches and teammates can help injured players stay connected instead of having their relationship with the team disappear while they're away.

I'd also like to add Spanish and eventually explore the same idea beyond sports. Dance, art and other passions can become a huge part of someone's identity too, and the same feeling of being "away" can happen there.

The bigger idea behind Still In The Game is simple:

You might be away from what you love for a while. But that doesn't mean you stopped being part of it.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every day when visiting local shops, I noticed customers asking shopkeepers to write down their daily purchases in physical paper notebooks (khata) as udhar (credit). Watching this sparked a question: what happens if that notebook gets lost, the pages tear, or liquid spills on it? All those transaction records and hard-earned money would be gone in an instant. I built Udhar Kitab to replace risky paper logs with a simple, reliable digital ledger.

**What it does**

Udhar Kitab (उधार किताब) is a digital credit book for small shopkeepers in India. It replaces the paper udhar khata with an app that works the way shopkeepers already think.

- Tracks credit and payments: add entries, record partial or full settlements, and see a running balance for every customer.

- Flags overdue payments: a home-screen banner and per-customer indicators show who is late, and the due date can be changed in one tap.

- Works offline: all data lives on the phone first, so the app is fully usable with no signal.

- Backs up to the cloud (optional): shopkeepers can turn on Google Sign-In and cloud sync to restore their book on a new phone, so a lost phone no longer means lost records.

- Speaks Hindi and English: the whole app is bilingual, with locale-aware dates and numbers.

- Sends reminders: one-tap WhatsApp messages (no due date, due today, overdue) or a direct phone call. The app never sends anything on the shopkeeper's behalf.

- Shows analytics: outstanding totals, period-over-period comparison, monthly history, and a top-debtors list.

- Offers a 90-day free trial and Udhar Kitab Pro, a custom paywall built on RevenueCat subscriptions.

**How we built it**

- App: React Native 0.81 and React 19 with Expo (SDK 54) and Expo Router for file-based navigation.

- Local storage: expo-sqlite is the single source of truth for every read and write.

- Cloud and auth: Firebase Auth (Google Sign-In) and Firestore, used as a one-way, best-effort mirror of the local data.

- Subscriptions: RevenueCat (react-native-purchases) powers a fully custom paywall. It handles purchase, restore, and the udhar_kitab_premium entitlement check, all wrapped in a central SubscriptionContext.

- Language: a context-driven i18n layer with English and Hindi translation tables and a persisted language choice.

- Motion and UI: react-native-reanimated for smooth, tactile interactions.

- Builds: EAS Build for Android APKs.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Offline-first without breaking the user's data: cloud sync had to be best-effort so that a failed network call never blocks or corrupts a local write.

- Making the free trial reinstall-proof: the 90-day trial is written to both Firestore and local SQLite, so it survives offline periods and reinstalls once the account is re-linked.

- Native modules vs. Expo Go: Google Sign-In and RevenueCat don't run in plain Expo Go, so development needed dev-client builds.

- Designing for a first-time app user: keeping the interface simple and fully Hindi-friendly, so someone who has never used a business app can pick it up quickly.

- Building a custom paywall: wiring purchase, restore, and entitlement state into a screen that fits the app's design, instead of using a hosted template.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A complete, working credit-book app that a shopkeeper can install and use today, with no signal needed.

- True Hindi/English support across the whole app, not just translated labels.

- Cloud backup that is opt-in and never touches the offline experience.

- A polished custom paywall with working purchase and restore flows through RevenueCat.

- An APK anyone can sideload, plus an open-source codebase with a full README and privacy policy.

**What we learned**

- Offline-first design changes how you structure everything. Treating local storage as the source of truth and the cloud as a mirror kept the app simple and reliable.

- Localization goes beyond translation: dates, numbers, and tone all matter for real users.

- Managing subscription state in one place (a single context around RevenueCat) makes entitlement checks much easier to reason about.

- Building for users who are not tech-savvy means fewer screens, clearer wording, and fewer decisions.

**What's next for Udhar Kitab**

- Customer Center integration for in-app subscription management.

- Export ledgers to PDF and CSV.

- Scheduled reminders, beyond manual WhatsApp and call nudges.

- More regional languages, so shopkeepers across India can use it in their own language.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Finding internships and jobs as a student can be really confusing. You have to work on your resume, search for jobs, prepare for interviews, figure out what skills you are missing, and constantly look for career advice.

I wanted to build something that could bring these things together in one place. Instead of using different tools for every part of the job-hunting process, I wanted RoleEase to feel like a personal AI career assistant that can help throughout the journey.

**What it does**

RoleEase is an AI-powered career companion for students and job seekers.

It includes an AI career chat where users can ask questions and get personalized career guidance. Users can also upload their resumes and other documents for analysis, find how well their profile matches a job, prepare for interviews, and follow career roadmaps based on their goals.

The app also supports document attachments with on-device OCR, allowing information to be extracted from uploaded documents and used during the conversation.

The idea is to make the entire process feel connected rather than having separate tools for resumes, interviews, job matching, and career guidance.

**How we built it**

RoleEase is built natively for iOS using Swift and SwiftUI, with SwiftData for storing application data.

For the AI experience, I built a backend that communicates with the AI model and supports streaming responses. This allows users to see the response being generated in real time instead of waiting for the entire response to finish.

I also implemented document and image attachments, on-device OCR, conversation history, authentication, resume analysis, job matching, interview preparation, and career roadmap features.

For subscriptions, I integrated RevenueCat to manage the subscription system and premium features. I connected the products from App Store Connect with RevenueCat and implemented the paywall and entitlement system inside the app.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was bringing many different features into one application while keeping the interface simple and easy to understand.

The AI chat was another challenging part. Streaming responses meant that I had to carefully handle the incoming text, conversation state, and scrolling behavior so that the latest response stays visible to the user.

Getting subscriptions working correctly was also a learning experience. I had to understand how App Store Connect products, subscription groups, RevenueCat offerings, and entitlements all work together.

Another challenge was making the AI useful for actual career-related tasks instead of just creating a basic chatbot. I wanted the different parts of the app, such as resumes, jobs, interviews, and career goals, to work together and provide more relevant guidance.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I'm proud that I was able to build RoleEase as a complete working iOS application rather than just a prototype.

I built the main features from the ground up, including the AI chat experience, resume analysis, job matching, interview preparation, career roadmaps, document processing, and the subscription system.

I'm also particularly proud of integrating RevenueCat and getting the subscription and paywall flow working as part of the actual app. It was my first time putting together this many different parts of an AI-powered product into one application.

**What we learned**

Building RoleEase taught me that creating an AI application is much more than just connecting an API to a chatbot.

I learned a lot about streaming AI responses, backend communication, document processing, OCR, subscription management, and designing an interface around AI.

I also learned how important the user experience is when working with AI. The response itself is only one part of the experience. Things like loading states, streaming, scrolling, attachments, conversation history, and how information is presented can make a big difference.

Working with RevenueCat also helped me understand the complete subscription workflow, from creating products in App Store Connect to configuring offerings and entitlements and connecting them to the app.

**What's next for RoleEase**

I want to continue improving RoleEase and make the career guidance more personalized.

Some of the things I want to work on next are improving the AI's understanding of a user's career goals, making job matching more useful, improving interview preparation, and providing better career roadmaps.

I also want to continue refining the overall UI and making the experience faster and easier to use.

The long-term goal is for RoleEase to become a single place where students can manage their career preparation, understand where they currently stand, and get clear guidance on what they should do next.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/292/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/292/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/293/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/293/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Two screens. Two cities. One pause button.
Press pause, and the person you're watching with pauses too, wherever they are.

Next Gen Award entry · Android-first · open source (AGPL-3.0) · working RevenueCat integration on Test Store (no real charges) · Download the APK

**Inspiration**

The best part of watching a movie together was never the movie. It's the gasp at the twist, the "wait, go back," the laugh you share half a second later.

Long-distance movie nights lose all of that. They start with a countdown over text, "3, 2, 1… play," and restart every time someone grabs a snack. The conversation lives in another app, and twenty minutes in nobody is sure you're on the same scene. We built MeowWatch so the person on the other side feels like they're on the couch with you. It's made for couples first, and works just as well for friends and family.

**What it does**

Start a room in one tap. Send the invite as a link, QR code or short code. Your partner joins free, with no sign-up. If you're already watching a direct video link, the invite carries it, so they land on the same movie.

Press pause, both pause. Either person can play, pause or skip, and the other screen follows. If a connection drops, the room waits, paused, until you're both back.

Talk without leaving the movie. Chat, reactions and "who's here" sit right beside the player.

Pick up where you left off. Continue Watching remembers your spot, and recent rooms make the next movie night one tap away. You can also watch solo in Local Player mode.

Phone or computer. The Android app joins the same rooms as our open-source MeowWatch for Windows, which is what you see syncing in the demo video.

What you need: both people open the same video, either a direct video link or their own copy of the file. MeowWatch syncs the playback and never uploads your files. Streaming-site pages and DRM-protected services aren't supported.

**How RevenueCat powers the business**

Guests always watch free. Hosting is where the cost and the value sit, so the host gets one free movie night per day. It only counts once someone has joined and you've actually pressed play. Reconnecting or switching videos never uses it up.

MeowWatch Plus is for people who host more often: unlimited rooms, player themes (Glass Aurora, Cinema Noir) and a premium "Movie night" reaction your partner sees live.

- The RevenueCat Flutter SDK loads the current Offering, so plan and price come from the dashboard, not the app.

- The meowwatch_plus entitlement unlocks real behavior: the hosting limit lifts, and the themes and premium reaction switch on.

- Purchase, cancel, failure and Restore are all handled. They were tested end to end with RevenueCat Test Store on emulators and on a physical Android phone.

What we haven't proven yet is willingness to pay. The next step is to learn from real hosts whether they value unlimited rooms, a couple plan or a one-off "movie night pass" most. RevenueCat Offerings let us test that without shipping a new app.

**How we built it**

- Flutter + Kotlin for Android phones and tablets. The room protocol, hosting quota and entitlement logic are kept separate from the UI and covered by tests.

- It builds on our open-source MeowWatch desktop app and speaks the same Syncplay protocol over encrypted connections.

- Android-specific work: a native player that reports its real position, auto-pause for calls and audio interruptions, fullscreen landscape, and progress saved across restarts.

- Tested like a product: CI runs full journeys on two independent Android clients (join, play/pause/seek in both directions, chat, reactions, quota, purchase, Restore), plus a Windows desktop ↔ Android room.

- AI coding assistants helped with implementation and test automation.

**Challenges we ran into**

Syncing looks simple until the player, the room and the network disagree. A phone call interrupts audio, a decoder fails, or Wi-Fi drops mid-scene. We learned to trust the player's actual state rather than what we asked it to do, and to recover into a paused room instead of letting two people drift apart.

**What we learned**

- The hard part of "watch together" isn't the Play button. It's getting both people onto the same video in the first place, which is why invites now carry the movie.

- A paywall only works when the free experience is complete. That's why guests never pay.

**What's next**

- Google Play release, then iOS

- Casting to the TV (sender built, still needs testing on a real receiver)

- Pricing experiments with real hosts through RevenueCat Offerings

**Current limits**

- Judging build = Test Store APK. No Google Play production billing yet.

- Sync is verified on a physical Android phone with Windows desktop, on two independent Android emulators, and on Windows ↔ cloud Android. It hasn't been tested on two physical phones.

- Chromecast receiver playback and chat relay through the paired desktop "Nearby" remote are not yet verified.

- Full evidence: acceptance ledger

**Try it**

- Source: https://github.com/PeterShanxin/MeowWatch-Mobile

- MeowWatch for Windows: https://github.com/PeterShanxin/MeowWatch/releases/tag/v0.51.0-alpha

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Getting older often means your social circle quietly shrinks — friends move, retire, or life just gets smaller. Most social apps are built for dating or for a much younger crowd, and don't feel right for someone in their 60s, 70s, or beyond looking for genuine friendship and things to do nearby. We wanted to build something warm and straightforward: no swiping, no games, just a simple way to meet people close by who share your interests and do something together.

**What it does**

60+ Friends lets people 60 and over discover others nearby, express interest, and match when it's mutual — then chat directly, no pressure. Beyond one-on-one connections, users can create or join local activities like walks, coffee mornings, and card games, making it easy to turn a match into an actual get-together.

Privacy is built in from the start: only an approximate area is ever shown, never an exact address, and block/report tools keep the community safe. A Premium subscription (with a 2-week free trial via RevenueCat) unlocks seeing who's already interested in you, unlimited interest, and a wider search radius.

**How we built it**

The app is built with Flutter and Riverpod for state management, with go_router handling a redirect-based auth flow (splash → intro → onboarding → app). Firebase powers the backend: Firebase Auth for sign-in, Firestore for profiles/matches/activities/messages, and Firebase Storage for photos, all behind tightened security rules that restrict writes to field-level ownership. RevenueCat and StoreKit handle the Premium subscription end-to-end, from the paywall to entitlement checks throughout the app.

**Challenges we ran into**

Several bugs only showed up through real device testing rather than in the simulator. One crash traced back — via actual .ips crash logs pulled from the physical device — to a race condition between an anonymous RevenueCat configuration call and a signed-in login call firing at nearly the same moment; we fixed it by serializing the configuration through a single tracked future.

Another bug was purely visual: a privacy-consent sheet was silently covering the new intro screen on every launch, which only became obvious once we started comparing actual screenshots frame-by-frame instead of relying on debug logs — the logs looked completely correct the whole time.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Getting a real, working subscription flow live end-to-end — RevenueCat entitlements, a genuine sandbox purchase with a free trial, and a build submitted to Apple for review — inside the Shipaton's timeframe, on top of shipping a polished onboarding flow, a custom intro screen, and a full bilingual privacy policy/terms hosted at a real public URL.

**What we learned**

That the visual truth (screenshots) and the logical truth (logs) can tell completely different stories — some bugs are invisible until you actually look at the screen. Also, a lot of the real work in a subscription-based app happens outside the code: App Store Connect's privacy questionnaire, subscription group setup, and review requirements took as much careful attention as the Flutter/Firebase implementation itself.

**What's next for 60+ Friends**

Smarter geo-based matching (the current MVP pages through the whole user pool rather than filtering by real distance), push notifications for new matches and messages, and expanding activities with RSVPs and reminders.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/499/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/499/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/500/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/500/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/501/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/501/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/502/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/380/502/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Many alarm apps are easy to dismiss while half asleep. I wanted to build an alarm that helps people physically leave their bed and complete a deliberate action before the sound stops.

**What it does**

QRAlarm is an iOS alarm clock that can require the user to scan a chosen QR code before dismissing an alarm. A user can place the code somewhere away from the bed, such as near a bathroom mirror or desk.

The app supports one-time and weekly alarms, local notifications, snoozing, alarm editing, and a dedicated ringing screen. QR Code Unlock is offered as a Pro feature through RevenueCat. The custom paywall supports Test Store purchases, cancellations, failures, entitlement refresh, and purchase restoration.

**How we built it**

QRAlarm was built with Swift and SwiftUI for iOS 17 and later. UserNotifications handles alarm scheduling and delivery, while AVFoundation powers QR code scanning. RevenueCat Purchases for iOS manages the monthly Pro entitlement through RevenueCat Test Store.

The Test Store public SDK key is enabled only in Debug builds. Release builds do not contain or initialize the test configuration.

**Challenges we ran into**

The original alarm service was only a mock, so the main challenge was replacing it with reliable local notification scheduling for one-time and repeating alarms. We also had to handle foreground notifications, notification taps, snoozing, and alarm cancellation consistently.

Another challenge was keeping the RevenueCat product, current Offering, and entitlement identifiers synchronized with the app while ensuring that QR alarms could not be dismissed through the normal stop button.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Replaced the mock alarm service with working local notifications

- Added one-time and weekly alarm scheduling

- Built a QR-gated alarm dismissal flow

- Integrated RevenueCat Test Store with a custom SwiftUI paywall

- Added purchase, cancellation, failure, refresh, and restore states

- Kept Test Store configuration isolated from Release builds

- Successfully built, analyzed, and launched the app in the iOS Simulator

**What we learned**

We learned how iOS notification lifecycles behave across foreground and background states, how RevenueCat Offerings and entitlements control feature access, and how to design a purchase flow that clearly communicates every result to the user.

**What's next for QRAlarm**

Next, we will complete real-device testing for camera scanning and all Test Store purchase outcomes, improve accessibility and alarm sounds, add more wake-up challenges, and prepare a production App Store configuration.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every fitness app I tried had the same three problems. Rep counters were boring. The "smart" ones wanted to upload video of my body to a server. And the gamified ones sold you progress - pay to skip the grind, pay to save your streak.

I wanted the opposite: a game where the workout is the combat system, where the camera watches you without anything ever leaving your phone, and where money can buy content but never strength.

**What it does**

REPforged is a fitness RPG. Your real repetitions are the controller: a squat swings the Forge Hammer, a push-up launches a Flame Strike, a plank holds a shield. Across seven regions, each boss teaches one movement mechanic - consistent depth builds combos, only fault-free reps break a guard, steady pacing stops an overheat.

- Camera witness - an on-device pose model finds your joints; a transparent state machine counts the reps and coaches your form live.

- Multiplayer without footage - Ghost Duels race a rival's signed rep timings, and community raids store only aggregate totals. No video is ever exchanged.

- Privacy Glass - live counters in every session: frames saved 0, frames uploaded 0. The Privacy Vault shows everything stored and deletes it in one tap.

- Recovery quests - a logged rest day keeps your streak, so nobody trains through pain to protect a number.

- Forge Pass - three regions are free forever; the Pass adds four more, Workshop publishing and cosmetics. It never sells combat strength.

**How I built it**

The app is Expo SDK 57 / React Native 0.86 / TypeScript, running on Android, iOS and the web from one codebase.

Pose detection runs MediaPipe's pose_landmarker_lite entirely on device - a custom native module on mobile, MediaPipe Tasks for Web in the browser. The model only locates 33 joints. Everything after that is deterministic: each exercise is a YAML file defining the joint angle to measure, the thresholds for each state, and the form faults to watch for. The angle at joint \( b \) formed with \( a \) and \( c \) is

$$\theta = \left|\operatorname{atan2}(c_y - b_y,\ c_x - b_x) - \operatorname{atan2}(a_y - b_y,\ a_x - b_x)\right|$$

folded into \( [0^\circ, 180^\circ] \), and a rep only counts when the angle crosses each threshold and holds it long enough to rule out jitter.

Scoring is deliberately anti-grind - it measures you against your own calibrated baseline, and volume can never win:

$$\text{Forge Score} = 60\%\ \text{completion} + 25\%\ \text{rhythm} + 15\%\ \text{range}$$

with completion clamped at 100%, so doing extra reps earns nothing.

Monetisation uses the RevenueCat SDK with a forge_pass entitlement and annual, monthly and lifetime packages. RevenueCat is configured with no app user ID, so it only ever sees an anonymous ID — never a name, workout or body data. A Spring Boot 3.4 / Java 21 backend receives RevenueCat webhooks, deduplicates them, and mirrors entitlement state into an admin console alongside moderation, raid totals and Motion Ghost verification.

The code has 104 TypeScript tests and 36 Java tests. The client and server safety rules for player-built battles are mirrored, and both test suites must agree.

**Challenges I ran into**

My push-up counter was wrong, and I only found out by measuring it. I built a tool that replays real footage through the shipped engine and reports every threshold crossing. A clip with its own burned-in counter showed 9 reps; my engine counted 4. Every descent was detected — the misses were all at the top. I required the elbow to hold past 160° for 200 ms, but a fast athlete's lockout lasts 0–170 ms. Loosening it to 150° for 100 ms gave 9 out of 9. Squats keep the longer hold, because people really do stand still at the top of a squat.

MediaPipe's confidence scores lied to me. I tried ignoring frames where joints had low "visibility". It turned out a side-on squat scores about 0.99 while a push-up scores about 0.23 — with the arms plainly in shot. Any useful threshold stopped counting push-ups entirely, so I reverted it and wrote down why.

Camera angle matters more than the model. A front-on squat counts zero reps, because the knee angle is foreshortened and never appears to bend enough. Every threshold assumes a side-on camera.

A purchase that grants nothing. In early sandbox testing, purchases succeeded but unlocked nothing, because the products weren't attached to the entitlement. Instead of celebrating a fake unlock, the app now says exactly that. It also refuses to start billing if a Test Store key ever reaches a release build.

**What I learned**

Measure, don't guess. My most confident code was my least accurate until I tested it against real footage. I also learned that privacy is most convincing when it's visible - a counter reading zero, live on screen, persuades people more than any policy page.

**What's next**

Recording my own exercise footage for every movement, validating the lunge, plank and jumping-jack thresholds the same way I fixed push-ups, and running the seasonal expeditions the Pass is built for.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

CraveWise was inspired by the idea of helping people make healthier food choices without guilt or rigid dieting. It turns everyday hunger moments into practical, personalized nutrition guidance.

**What it does**

CraveWise lets users tell the app what they are hungry for and provides simple, actionable recommendations to make the meal more balanced and satisfying.

**How we built it**

I built CraveWise using React Native with Expo for the mobile experience and a FastAPI backend for recommendations. The architecture is designed to support personalized nutrition intelligence while keeping the experience simple and fast.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenges were connecting the mobile application reliably to the backend , Gemini , managing the Expo/EAS build process, guardrails and designing recommendations that are useful without being restrictive or judgmental.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I built a working end-to-end mobile experience where users can express their immediate food cravings and receive practical guidance. I am especially proud of making healthy eating feel realistic and compatible with the foods people actually enjoy.

**What we learned**

I learned that nutrition guidance works better when it fits real-life eating habits rather than asking users to completely change them. I also gained valuable experience integrating a React Native/Expo ,Gemin model ,application with a production-oriented backend.

**What's next for CraveWise**

Next, i plan to make recommendations more personalized using user preferences, eating patterns, and nutritional context. I also want to expand restaurant and food-item intelligence so CraveWise can provide useful guidance wherever users decide to eat.

</details>
