<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Journaling usually happens in a notebook, like a diary. The problem is that old entries are hard to look back on, so I kept running into the same worries again and again without noticing the pattern.

I wanted a journal where entries live as notes on a calendar timeline, so that the problems I'm facing right now, and the thought loops I keep falling into, become visible. Once you can see those patterns, you can discover for yourself what you can do to live a better life.

My goal is simple: help anyone treat each day as a fresh start toward living better, and make journaling effortless enough to actually stick.

**What it does**

journal-mate is a conversational journaling app: just talk to the AI, and your journal entry is done.

- AI-guided journaling: Chat with Claude about your day, and it turns the conversation into a structured journal entry.

- Calendar overview: Browse your journals on a calendar and look back: "What was I worried about back then? Have I grown since?"

- PARA-structured folders: Entries are organized with the PARA method (Projects / Areas / Resources / Archives), so the things you care about most rise to the surface.

- Notes app, too: It doubles as a general-purpose Markdown notes app.

- No lock-in: Export everything as an Obsidian-compatible vault at any time.

**How we built it**

**Tech stack**

- UI: SwiftUI (iOS 18)

- The calendar embeds UIKit's UICalendarView for fine-grained, per-day decorations

- Language: Swift 6

- Strict concurrency checking enabled to catch data races at compile time

- Persistence: SQLite, called directly through libsqlite3 with a ~200-line custom wrapper

- Skipped SwiftData because it doesn't support full-text search (FTS5)

- Skipped GRDB and similar libraries to keep zero external dependencies

- Full-text search: SQLite FTS5 with the trigram tokenizer

- The default unicode61 tokenizer can't do substring matching on Japanese text

- Relay server: Cloudflare Workers (TypeScript) + Durable Objects + KV

- Streams Claude's SSE responses straight to the device without buffering

- Durable Objects process each user's usage ledger serially

- Device authentication: App Attest + DeviceCheck

- App Attest verifies requests come from the genuine app

- DeviceCheck ties the free tier to the physical device

**1. Data model: Markdown as a value**

Note bodies are stored as plain Markdown in the database.

- The single source of truth is one SQLite file

- Bodies are kept as raw Markdown strings, not a proprietary format

- The folder structure is virtual and exists only in the database

- Reclassifying a note never moves a file, so links never break

- Generating a journal, creating nodes, and updating the index all happen in one transaction

No lock-in.

- The app can export an Obsidian-compatible vault (.md files with YAML frontmatter in a real folder hierarchy) as a zip at any time

- Exported vaults can be imported back

Making search fast.

- FTS5 full-text search: Unlike opening and reading .md files every time, it searches 10,000 notes in a few milliseconds. Since the design relies on search to feed context to the AI, this speed matters.

- An index that doesn't duplicate content: FTS5 runs with content='notes' (external content), so the index holds no copy of the body. Triggers keep the index in sync on every insert, update, and delete.

- Fallback for short queries: trigram can't match queries under 3 characters, so queries of 2 characters or fewer fall back to LIKE.

- Composite indexes per screen:

- Calendar: notes(day_key, occurred_at)

- Folder tree: notes(node_id, layer, occurred_at)

- Chat history: messages(session_id, created_at)

**2. PARA × Medallion structure with numbered hierarchy**

Deriving codes from hierarchy paths.

- A path like Areas / Life / Travel / Insurance gets a code such as 1152

- The first digit is the PARA category (0 = Projects, 1 = Areas, 2 = Resources, 3 = Archives)

- Each following digit is the node's position within its level

- The code is also prefixed to file names (e.g. 1152_202609191330.md)

Fetching an entire subtree in one query.

- Codes are precomputed and stored in the database

- A single code LIKE '115%' fetches everything under "Travel," so context for the AI can be assembled instantly

Moving folders and non-destructive reclassification.

- When a folder moves, a recursive CTE renumbers the codes and paths of all descendants in one pass

- Inspired by the Medallion architecture, every folder has three layers:

- raw: original sources, never rewritten

- knowledge: lessons derived from raw and journal

- journal: daily records, append-only

- Because originals are never rewritten, no information is lost no matter how many times you reorganize

**3. A gateway that keeps the API key out of the app**

Why a relay server? An API key embedded in the app binary can be extracted, and I'd be billed for whoever uses it. So a relay on Workers runs four checks before anything reaches Claude.

- App Attest (401): Validates Apple's certificate chain to confirm the request comes from the genuine app.

- RevenueCat (402): Checks subscription status via the REST API and webhooks. If RevenueCat is down, it falls back to the last cached state instead of locking everyone out.

- Durable Object ledger (429): One ledger per user. KV is only eventually consistent, so two simultaneous requests could read the same remaining balance, both pass, and exceed the limit.

- Allowlist validation (400): Only approved models, keys, and max_tokens values pass. Otherwise anyone who found the URL could use it as a free Claude proxy.

Enforcing limits even while streaming.

- Before a request starts, max_tokens worth of quota is reserved; after it finishes, the actual usage is settled

- Reservations from dropped connections expire after 5 minutes

- Day boundaries are fixed to UTC, so changing the device's time zone doesn't reset the quota

**4. A free tier that survives reinstalls (DeviceCheck)**

Problem. App Attest key IDs, anonymous IDs, and identifierForVendor are all regenerated when the app is deleted. Reinstalling the app would reset the free tier.

Solution.

- Record "this device has started using this month's free tier" in DeviceCheck's two bits, which Apple keeps even after the app is deleted

- Whether a new month has begun is determined from the bits' last_update_time, so no cron jobs or scheduled tasks are needed

- If DeviceCheck is down, requests are allowed through so free users aren't locked out

Keeping costs down. Free-tier calls are pinned to Haiku on the server side, with a tighter output limit.

**Challenges we ran into**

Time. I built this in roughly one week, right after moving to a new place.

Working solo. This was a one-person project, so whenever I got stuck, there was no one to ask. I had to attack every unknown myself, with Claude Code as my coding partner.

Learning Swift from zero. I didn't know Swift, so my process looked like this:
learn the basics from YouTube and books → focus on the overall structure rather than every detail → decide a calendar-based UI felt right → search for UI references I liked → hand that context to Claude Code → iterate.

Designing the structure. The hardest design question was how to bring the ideas behind the PARA method and the Medallion architecture into journaling. I kept imagining what kind of structure would actually help a user live a better life. Separating sources and information from personal journals made everything much easier to organize.

Making AI search fast. I was particular about the architecture here. Plain SwiftData couldn't do full-text search, so I dropped it for raw SQLite + FTS5. I also assigned numeric codes to the PARA folder hierarchy so that a whole directory's contents can be pulled with a single indexed query, which keeps context retrieval for the AI fast.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A working demo, built in about a week

- A native Swift app built from scratch, without knowing Swift beforehand

- Turning inspiration into a product: In the middle of moving, I took the essence of a YouTube video about "personal AI agents" and turned it into an actual app

- Caring about the user experience: the calendar view, a visible folder structure, and a fair free-usage limit were all designed with ease of use in mind

**What we learned**

- Xcode is a great development experience. Being able to run the app right on my MacBook was a pleasure.

- Mobile is a whole new world. This was my first mobile app. SwiftUI's calendar UI looks and feels wonderful, and apps like Apple's built-in Weather app are genuinely impressive. I realized that mobile development is full of people obsessed with making experiences feel good.

- Short, intense sprints are tough. Pressure builds up fast, and building alone can be stressful and lonely.

- Scope matters. Building with no team, on a whim, with no clear deadline or scope, taught me that app development without a plan is a reckless bet. Next time I'll define the scope first.

**What's next for journal-mate**

- Smarter folder structure: Trim the hierarchy when it grows too large and make it easier to use from the user's point of view

- Capture from anywhere: Share a link from any app → save it as a note → land it in journal-mate. I want it to become an app that gathers information and organizes what the user cares about

- Faster AI search, plus year-over-year comparison with past journals

- Discovery mode: When you have a spare moment, rediscover old entries: "Wow, I was journaling about this back then?"

- Supporting self-actualization: If you want to travel to Paris, journal-mate pulls up your Paris folder and helps you plan the trip

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/416/301/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/416/301/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/416/302/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/416/302/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/416/308/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/416/308/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Wellness apps often ask for more attention at exactly the moment a person has the least to give. Long libraries, streaks, dashboards, and perfect routines can turn care into another task. Next Ten starts with a smaller promise: tell it how you feel, where you are carrying tension, and how much time you actually have. It gives you one useful thing to do next.

**What it does**

Next Ten turns three quick signals - energy, body tension, and available time - into a focused movement, breathing, or recovery plan. Each plan is broken into calm, timed cues with an animated pacing surface. There are no streak penalties and no crowded content feed.

The free experience includes a useful daily reset. Next Ten Pro unlocks adaptive weekly plans, the full movement and recovery library, gentle progress patterns, and new guided resets. A seven-day trial lets judges and new users experience the complete product before paying.

**How we built it**

Next Ten is built with React Native, Expo, and TypeScript for iOS and Android. The interface uses a responsive native layout, custom plan-generation logic, haptic transitions, and an animated session timer.

RevenueCat is part of the product architecture rather than a decorative checkout. The app checks the active next_ten_pro entitlement at launch, reads the current offering so pricing can be changed without an app release, purchases the configured annual package, and supports restore purchases. Premium packaging matches the product's low-pressure philosophy: one clear annual plan with a trial, no confusing tier matrix, and no artificial countdown.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest product problem was information restraint. A wellness app can easily become a content catalog; Next Ten needed to remain useful while showing only the next decision. The plan builder therefore reduces the input to three signals and presents one recommendation, while still creating meaningful variation in pacing and cues.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A complete check-in-to-completion flow that can be used one-handed

- Personalized routines across energy, tension, and time combinations

- A calm animated timer with haptic step transitions

- A real RevenueCat entitlement, offering, purchase, and restore architecture

- An original store-ready visual identity and icon

**What we learned**

Monetization works best when it follows the value boundary users already understand. The free reset proves the core promise immediately; Pro expands continuity and personalization. RevenueCat makes that boundary easy to evolve without coupling product experiments to release cycles.

**What's next for Next Ten**

Next Ten will add on-device routine feedback, accessibility-first audio cues, and adaptive weekly planning based on what genuinely helps. The goal is not more time in the app. It is a better next ten minutes outside it.

**Category fit**

Yoga & Fitness - Simone Sharice: Next Ten personalizes movement and recovery to the user's present energy, tension, and available time. It converts those needs into one achievable plan for today and deliberately avoids content overload.

RevenueCat Design Award: The app uses expressive editorial typography, tactile color, a breathing animation, haptic transitions, and a restrained one-decision-at-a-time interface.

HAMM Award: The model uses a free daily reset to demonstrate value and a single annual subscription with a seven-day trial. RevenueCat offerings allow pricing and packaging to evolve without an app update, while entitlement state keeps premium access consistent across reinstalls.

RevenueCat Peace Prize: Next Ten makes simple recovery support accessible without shame, streak pressure, calorie tracking, or an expensive upfront commitment. Short plans can fit into work breaks, caregiving, study, or periods of low energy.

</details>

src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/444/491/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Our lives are scattered across camera rolls, notes, voice recordings, and cloud folders. These tools preserve files, but they often lose the story surrounding them.

I built Relive because I wanted a private place where small moments could remain connected to their words, time, place, feelings, and meaning—without becoming social posts or disappearing into an endless gallery.

Relive is designed around a simple idea:

Capture now. Let time organize it. Rediscover it later.

**What it does**

Relive is a private, local-first personal memory timeline for Android and iOS.

A Moment can combine writing, photos, video, audio, a place, tags, and a feeling in one entry.

Instead of showing memories as a database-like list, Relive presents them through a warm, editorial timeline designed to feel like a personal life archive.

Every Moment automatically belongs to the main archive and can also appear in multiple custom timelines such as College, Family, or Japan 2026, without duplicating its underlying data.

Relive also helps people rediscover what they have saved through:

- On This Day memories from previous years

- From Your Past collections

- Favourites

- A dedicated media collection

- Local search across writing, tags, and saved places

- Calendar-based navigation

- Mood insights calculated privately on the device

- Printable Keepsake PDF exports

- Portable .relive archive exports

- Optional Google Drive backup and restore

- Custom palettes, wallpapers, and timeline themes

There are no followers, public profiles, advertisements, or engagement algorithms.

Memories stay inside private app storage unless the user explicitly chooses to back them up or export them.

**How I built it**

Relive is built using Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform, allowing the app to share its domain logic, persistence, presentation layer, and much of its interface across Android and iOS.

The architecture follows clear boundaries:

Android + iOS hosts
 ↓
Shared Compose UI and presentation
 ↓
Domain models and policies
 ↑
Repositories and shared data layer
 ↓
SQLDelight + app-owned media storage

The archive uses SQLDelight over SQLite, with verified migrations and relational integrity.

Media is copied into app-owned storage so Moments never depend on temporary or fragile external file references.

Platform-specific capabilities such as:

- Camera capture

- Location

- Media playback

- Secure storage

- File exports

are placed behind shared interfaces.

This keeps the core product independent of Android and iOS APIs while still allowing each platform to use its native capabilities.

For subscriptions, Relive integrates RevenueCat Purchases KMP.

RevenueCat acts as the source of truth for the relive_pro entitlement, including:

- Monthly subscription

- Annual subscription

- Lifetime purchase

The demo build uses the RevenueCat Test Store, allowing the real purchase and restore lifecycle to be demonstrated without introducing a fake local unlock mechanism.

Optional Android backups use the narrow Google Drive appdata scope.

Portable archives contain versioned metadata, media, relationships, byte counts, and SHA-256 integrity hashes.

On Android, the live database is protected using SQLCipher, with a locally generated encryption key wrapped by Android Keystore.

**Challenges I faced**

**Making memories feel worth revisiting**

One of the hardest challenges was making the timeline feel like a personal life archive rather than another notes app.

That required careful work on:

- Typography

- Spacing

- Media presentation

- Motion

- Themes

- Timeline behavior

- The continuous timeline rail

Visual polish was not separate from the product. It was essential to making old memories feel meaningful when encountered again.

**Handling years of data efficiently**

A personal archive may eventually contain years of Moments and media.

Loading everything when the app launches would not scale well.

To solve this, I designed bounded SQL-backed projections and paged feeds so each screen loads only the data it actually needs.

**Cross-platform media**

Photos, videos, audio recording, camera capture, storage, and playback behave differently across Android and iOS.

Keeping these capabilities behind platform-specific interfaces allowed the shared application logic to remain clean while each platform handled its native implementation.

**Safe backup and restore**

Backup restoration required especially defensive engineering because imported archives must be treated as untrusted input.

Before accepting an archive, Relive validates:

- File paths

- File counts

- Relationships

- File sizes

- Metadata

- Checksums

Restore operations are transactional, so an invalid or interrupted restore cannot silently corrupt the existing archive.

**Time-based memories**

Features such as On This Day introduced several subtle edge cases:

- Local calendar boundaries

- Leap days

- Future timestamps

- Anniversary calculations

- Deterministic daily selections

These features needed to work correctly without sending personal memory data to a remote server.

**What I learned**

Building Relive taught me that local-first is much more than storing information in SQLite.

It requires deliberate decisions around:

- Data ownership

- Secure storage

- Database migrations

- Query performance

- Backup behavior

- Export formats

- Privacy boundaries

I also learned how valuable strict architecture boundaries become as a product grows.

Sharing business logic across platforms while isolating native integrations made the codebase much easier to test, maintain, and evolve.

Most importantly, I learned that software designed around personal memories should optimize for trust and emotional longevity rather than attention.

Relive does not try to make people post more.

It tries to make what they already chose to preserve feel meaningful when they encounter it again.

**What’s next**

The next step for Relive is production polish, including:

- Broader device testing

- Accessibility refinement

- iOS validation

- Performance profiling with larger archives

- Final release preparation

The long-term goal remains simple:

Make Relive a beautiful, dependable home for the moments people want to carry forward.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/464/756/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/464/756/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/387/029/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/387/029/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

QR codes are everywhere—flat, static, and easy to ignore. We kept seeing them on posters, flyers, packaging, and especially in advertising, where they blend into the background and get zero attention. But motion naturally grabs the eye. What if a QR code could move? What if it could be a visual asset, not just a link? That’s how AnimQR was born: a tool that turns ordinary links into animated, scannable QR codes built for advertising.

**What it does**

AnimQR is an animated art QR code generator. You paste a link, choose a style, and it creates a QR code that moves, glows, and still scans perfectly. It’s designed for advertising first—digital billboards, social media ads, video pre-rolls, event screens, out-of-home displays, retail screens, and promotional landing pages.

In simpler words, it merges a GIF file with your QR code.

**Key features:**

Built-in animations: rocket, car, flame (procedural, no external files).

Custom GIF upload: drag and drop your mascot, animated logo, or meme—AnimQR fuses it into the QR while keeping it scannable.

Fancy borders: neon, floral, starry, pixel, circuit, Chinese, gold.

Center logo support, batch generation, error correction levels (L/M/Q/H), module shapes (square, liquid, dot).

Fine-grained rendering controls: detail strength, hue coherence, soften, dark/light luminance, vividness, module size.

Export as GIF or PNG, or share directly.

Monetization: Free preview of every style and premium feature. But if you use any Pro element (custom GIF, premium border, batch mode, center logo) and try to export, a soft paywall appears. Pro unlocks watermark-free HD GIF/PNG exports, unlimited history, and all premium features. Plans include 7-day free trial, monthly, yearly, lifetime, and a limited 3-day Pro pass.

**How we built it**

We built AnimQR as a single-page web app using vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with:

QRCode.js for QR generation.

Canvas for all rendering, including subpixel-level animation (6×6 subpixels per QR module).

gif.js for GIF encoding, with web workers for performance.

RevenueCat (via Capacitor) for in-app purchases on native, with a web mock for UI testing.

A custom GIF decoder (with fallback to ImageDecoder) to parse uploaded GIFs into full frames.

Color science utilities: HSL conversion, hue coherence, palette snapping, luminance capping to keep contrast high enough for scanning.

The core pipeline:
Generate QR → decode/load animation frames → map each frame onto QR modules
→ apply borders, logo, and effects → play in preview → export GIF/PNG

**Challenges we ran into**

Keeping it scannable: Adding animation, borders, and logos easily breaks QR scanning. We had to enforce quiet zones, luminance caps/floors, and error correction. We also built a “gray-frame color guard” to prevent frames from losing contrast.

Subpixel rendering performance: Rendering 6×6 subpixels per module for every frame on mobile required careful optimization. We used offscreen canvases and typed arrays.

GIF decoding: Browsers don’t natively expose full GIF frames easily. We wrote an inline LZW decoder and a compositor to handle transparency, disposal methods, and interlacing.

Soft paywall UX: We wanted users to try everything for free, but still convert. The challenge was making the paywall appear only on export when Pro features are used—without feeling like a bait-and-switch.

Cross-platform IAP: RevenueCat integration works on native via Capacitor, but on web we needed a mock. We had to design the code to gracefully fall back.

Mobile layout: The QR preview was initially too large on phones, pushing the controls off-screen. We had to rework the mobile CSS to shrink the preview and make it collapsible.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

A fully functional animated QR generator that produces scannable codes even with complex animations and decorative borders.

The soft paywall model: free users can preview every premium feature, but export triggers an upgrade prompt only if they’ve used Pro elements. It feels fair and converts.
The subpixel rendering engine that lets you dial detail strength, hue coherence, and luminance while maintaining scanability.
A wide range of borders and themes (neon, floral, starry, circuit, Chinese, gold) that are procedurally drawn, not just static images.
Custom GIF upload with full frame decoding, so users can bring their own brand assets.
A clean, responsive UI that works on desktop and mobile, with sticky export controls and history.

**What we learned**

QR error correction and quiet zones are non-negotiable. You can push the art far, but you must respect the underlying encoding.

Animation on Canvas is fast, but mobile Safari and low-end Android devices need careful memory management.

A soft paywall is a powerful model: give value first, gate the export. It builds trust and still drives conversions.

GIF encoding is CPU-heavy; web workers and frame count limits are essential.

RevenueCat + Capacitor works well, but testing IAP requires a real device—web mock is fine for UI but not for store review.

Users love customization, but too many sliders can overwhelm. We kept advanced settings collapsed by default.

**What's next for AnimQR**

More built-in animations (e.g., product demos, seasonal effects, brand-specific loops).
Template marketplace for ad campaigns—pre-made animated QR designs for different industries.
Video export (MP4/WebM) in addition to GIF, for higher quality on large screens.
Direct integrations with ad platforms (e.g., Google Ads, Meta Ads) to generate animated QR codes from campaign links.
A/B testing tools to compare scan rates between static and animated QR codes.
More Pro features: team collaboration, brand kits, custom watermarks, analytics on scans.
Native mobile apps (iOS/Android) with full RevenueCat IAP, offline generation, and camera preview.
Open-source contributions: we’re on GitHub and welcome stars, issues, and pull requests.

**Additional information**

For quick preview, you can just download the index.html in the www folder and open it locally in your browser(certain browser may not support). Npm install the app for full features.

AnimQR – Motion Beyond Pixels.
Stop settling for static squares. Bring your links to life.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**PackBack**

**Inspiration**

University life has a surprisingly simple problem: there is always something to remember.

A laptop for one class. A calculator for another. An assignment due tomorrow. A different classroom this week. An umbrella because it is going to rain. And after class, the charger you plugged into the wall and forgot to take home.

We realized that existing calendars and to-do lists still depend heavily on the student remembering to create, check, and manage reminders themselves.

That led us to PackBack.

PackBack is a student memory copilot designed around one idea: you should not have to remember to remind yourself.

Instead of being another static checklist, PackBack uses your timetable, class requirements, tasks, previous preferences, and contextual information to determine what matters for your day and remind you at the right moment.

**What it does**

PackBack organizes a student's day around three simple questions:

What do I need to bring?

What do I need to do?

What do I need to bring back?

Students can import their timetable from a screenshot or create events manually. PackBack turns their schedule into a dynamic daily checklist containing the items and tasks relevant to each event.

Before an event, PackBack reminds the student where they need to go and what they need to bring.

After an event, PackBack switches context and reminds them to take their belongings with them, helping prevent chargers, calculators, bottles, and other items from being left behind.

Students can also import lecturer instructions. AI extracts useful information such as required items, tasks, deadlines, and event details into structured information that the student can review before saving.

PackBack also uses contextual information such as weather. If rain is expected while the student is travelling between events, an umbrella can become part of that day's checklist automatically.

Over time, PackBack can remember recurring requirements and forgetting patterns. If a calculator is regularly needed for a particular class, for example, the student should not have to add it every single week.

The goal is not to build a chatbot that waits for the student to ask, "What am I forgetting?"

PackBack should tell them before they forget.

**How we built it**

PackBack is built as a native Android application with a C++ core responsible for the application's core domain logic and state transitions.

The Android layer provides the mobile interface, notifications, timetable management, imports, and integrations, while the shared core handles events, Bring/Do/Bring Back states, checklist behaviour, and reminder logic.

A backend provides services that are better suited to the server, including AI-powered extraction, contextual integrations, synchronization, and semantic memory capabilities.

For AI-assisted imports, screenshots and lecturer instructions are processed into structured data rather than allowing generated text to directly modify the user's schedule. The extracted information is shown to the student for confirmation before it becomes part of their timetable or checklist.

This gives us the convenience of AI while keeping important changes understandable and user-controlled.

We also integrated RevenueCat to support PackBack's monetization layer and premium functionality while keeping the core student-day experience useful.

**Challenges we faced**

One of our biggest design challenges was deciding where AI actually adds value.

It would have been easy to place a chatbot inside the app and call it an AI assistant. However, that conflicts with the problem we are trying to solve. A student who forgets to bring their charger may also forget to ask an assistant what they need.

We therefore focused on proactive assistance rather than prompt-first assistance.

Another challenge was separating structured information from semantic memory. Information such as "bring calculator to Math" is more reliable as structured checklist data than something that needs to be retrieved from a vector database every time. Semantic memory is therefore treated as a supporting capability for richer unstructured context rather than replacing deterministic reminder logic.

We also had to combine native Android functionality, C++ domain logic, backend services, AI extraction, external context, notifications, and monetization without making the everyday experience complicated.

That constraint shaped PackBack into something intentionally simple on the surface:

Bring it. Do it. Bring it back.

**What we learned**

Building PackBack taught us that adding intelligence to an application does not necessarily mean adding more interaction.

Sometimes the better intelligent experience is the one that requires the user to do less.

We learned to distinguish between information that should be handled deterministically and information where AI is genuinely useful. We also learned how to connect native mobile development, C++, backend APIs, structured AI outputs, contextual data, semantic retrieval, automated testing, and RevenueCat into a single product.

Most importantly, we learned to design around the moment when assistance is actually useful rather than simply exposing another feature for the user to find.

**What's next**

We want PackBack to become increasingly personalized without becoming increasingly complicated.

Future versions can learn which items an individual student tends to forget, improve reminder timing based on behaviour, understand more forms of university information, surface relevant long-term context automatically, and provide deeper insights into recurring forgetting patterns.

The long-term vision is simple:

PackBack remembers the small things so students can focus on the important ones.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Modern health tracking is often fragmented, expensive, and tied down by proprietary app stores or platform-specific walled gardens. Traditional movement analysis requires specialized biomechanics hardware, while livestock and pet health monitoring relies on delayed, periodic manual checks.We created PulseVibe to democratize health telemetry and biomechanical analysis. Inspired by the need for universal, real-time health intelligence across species—humans, domestic pets, livestock, and poultry—we set out to build a platform that turns standard hardware sensors and cameras into powerful AI biomechanics tools, distributed instantly via a Multi-OS web streamer without mandatory app store barriers.

**What it does**

PulseVibe is a multi-species AI health and biomechanics telemetry platform paired with a low-latency, native binary distribution hub.Real-Time Biomechanics & Motion Analytics: Tracks physical form and movement using camera feeds and edge pose detection models (TensorFlow Lite), rendering live 3D muscle heatmaps and kinetic stress overlays with Three.js.Multi-Species Health Telemetry: Ingests sensor data across four distinct categories:Humans: Movement posture, rep counter, joint angles, and range of motion.Pets (Dogs/Cats): Limb kinetic balance, gait irregularity, and collar accelerometer telemetry.Livestock (Cattle/Swine): Thermal camera stress alerts, mobility tracking, and herd movement anomalies.Poultry: Automated flock movement heatmaps and activity density indices.Universal Multi-OS Installer Hub: Streams signed native binaries (.apk for Android & Google Wear OS, .ipa for iOS, .msix for Windows, .AppImage for Linux, and .crx for ChromeOS) directly from the web application with automated cryptographic SHA-256 integrity verification.Granular Enterprise Access & Monetization: Integrates Google Authentication, Firebase/Firestore dynamic One-Time Passcodes (OTP) for hackathon judges, an Admin Management Dashboard, and RevenueCat + Stripe integration for Pro tier entitlements.

**How we built it**

[ Camera / Web Bluetooth Sensors ] ──► [ TFLite Edge Inference ] ──► [ Three.js 3D Heatmaps ]
 │
[ Google Cloud Run & CDN ] ◄── [ Google Storage / SHA-256 ] ◄── [ Express Streaming Engine ]
PulseVibe is architected with a decoupled, high-performance web and cloud engine:Frontend & 3D Visualization Engine: Built with TypeScript, React, WebGL, and Three.js. Skeletal angle vectors ($\theta$) are calculated in real time using local joint coordinate tensors:$$\theta = \arccos\left( \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\Vert{}\mathbf{u}\Vert{} \Vert{}\mathbf{v}\Vert{}} \right)$$Backend & Streaming Infrastructure: Hosted on Google Cloud Run in the asia-east1 region, integrated with Google Cloud Storage buckets for release artifact management and Google Cloud CDN edge caching for low-latency global package delivery.Security & Anti-Hotlinking: Protected by Google Cloud Armor WAF with rate-limiting rules (30 req/min per IP) and strict referer checking to protect binary downloads.Authentication & Data Management: Configured with Firebase Auth and Firestore for multi-role dynamic access control across Super Admin, Judges, and Standard Users.Monetization Layer: Powered by RevenueCat SDK bindings and Stripe payment APIs for seamlessly unlocking active entitlements (fitpulse_pro).

**Challenges we ran into**

Zero-Lag WebGL & Pose Sync: Rendering complex 3D skeletal muscle heatmaps at 60 FPS alongside real-time pose estimation required heavy optimization to prevent main-thread blockages and memory leaks.Multi-Region CDN Cache Handling: Ensuring immediate distribution of binary hotfixes without invalidating global edge nodes incorrectly required building dedicated cache invalidation triggers and strict cache-control header policies (s-maxage=31536000, immutable).Cross-Platform Installer Packaging: Generating reliable SHA-256 checksums on the fly for high-volume binary stream downloads across six distinct operating systems without maxing out Cloud Run memory buffers.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

End-to-End Infrastructure Deployment: Built and provisioned a fully automated CI/CD pipeline using GitHub Actions, Terraform, Cloud Run, Cloud CDN, and Cloud Armor.Real-Time Edge Inference: Achieved sub-30ms latency for on-device pose estimation and 3D kinetic heatmap updates directly inside standard browser environments.Storeless Multi-OS Delivery Hub: Successfully deployed a streaming hub capable of delivering platform-native packages directly to iOS, Android, Wear OS, Windows, Linux, and ChromeOS users with built-in cryptographic integrity checks.

**What we learned**

Building PulseVibe pushed our boundaries across cloud architecture, security, and WebGL rendering. We mastered infrastructure-as-code (IaC) deployment with Terraform on GCP, gained deep expertise in configuring Cloud Armor WAF rules against hotlinking and DDoS attacks, and learned how to build resilient multi-platform entitlement systems using RevenueCat and Stripe.

**What's next for PulseVibe**

Edge IoT Thermal Camera Sync: Expanding livestock health tracking by integrating direct MQTT streams from thermal imaging hardware on edge IoT gateways.Automated Biomechanical Diagnostics: Fine-tuning specialized pose estimation models to automatically flag early signs of joint strain and pet dysplasia.Expanded Wearable SDK Support: Adding direct Web Bluetooth integration for open-source livestock collars and smart fitness wearables.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Inspiration

Daylite Digital was inspired by a simple gap: travel and accommodation commerce can be digitally connected without excluding smaller providers or the people who help distribute them.

I wanted to create more than a booking interface. Daylite Digital connects travelers and accommodation providers through a digital commerce ecosystem, while the Daylite Digital Ambassador Programme and Daylite Ambassador Hub create a human participation layer around that ecosystem.

Built from Africa and designed for international markets, my goal is to connect digital technology, travel commerce and economic participation in one system.

What it does

Daylite Digital is an AI-assisted digital travel and accommodation commerce platform connecting travelers, accommodation providers and digital distribution opportunities.

Travelers can discover and engage with accommodation and travel offerings, while accommodation providers can participate in digital distribution. The connected Daylite Ambassador Hub provides approved participants with structured resources and guidance to promote Daylite Digital and participate in its commercial ecosystem.

Together, the two websites operate as one connected ecosystem: two websites, one connected ecosystem.

For this Shipaton submission, I use RevenueCat to power the monetization layer, connecting digital product access with a working purchase experience.

How I built it

I built Daylite Digital as a web-based digital commerce ecosystem, with the product experience, accommodation marketplace, provider participation and ambassador distribution layer designed to work together.

The system combines web technologies, e-commerce infrastructure, AI-assisted customer interaction and third-party integrations. Shopify is used within the commerce architecture, while the Daylite Ambassador Hub provides the structured participation and resource layer.

For the Shipaton build, I integrated RevenueCat into the monetization flow so that a digital purchase can be presented, processed and connected to entitlement and access logic.

I built the product primarily myself as the founder and principal developer while studying full-time at university.

Challenges I ran into

The biggest challenge was not starting with an empty idea — it was turning an already-built ecosystem into a focused, demonstrable product for a technical competition with a very short submission window.

I had to connect an existing travel and accommodation commerce model with a new monetization requirement while keeping the product experience clear and authentic.

Other challenges included integrating multiple systems, designing around real-world accommodation and provider requirements, creating an ecosystem that can work across markets, and communicating a relatively broad business model through a short technical demonstration.

Accomplishments I am proud of

I am proud that Daylite Digital is already a functioning digital commerce ecosystem created from Africa for international markets.

The product connects multiple participants rather than treating travel as a single transaction: travelers, accommodation providers and human digital distribution participants can operate within the same ecosystem.

I am also proud to have built the ecosystem while studying full-time at university and serving as its founder and principal developer.

For Shipaton, I extended that existing foundation with RevenueCat-powered monetization, demonstrating how digital access and commerce can be connected within the product.

What I learned

I learned that building the technology is only one part of creating a scalable digital product.

The user journey, monetization model, distribution network, provider experience and technical integrations all need to work together.

I also learned that an existing business ecosystem needs to be communicated differently from a prototype: judges and users need to see the real product, the real interaction and the real value quickly.

Integrating RevenueCat reinforced the importance of designing monetization as part of the product experience rather than treating payments as an afterthought.

What's next for Daylite Digital

The next stage is scaling the technology and commercial infrastructure behind Daylite Digital.

This includes deeper travel and accommodation integrations, expanded payment and monetization capabilities, broader accommodation-provider participation, growth of the Daylite Ambassador Programme and expansion into additional international markets.

My long-term objective is to grow Daylite Digital into a connected international digital travel and accommodation commerce ecosystem built from Africa — linking travelers, providers, technology and human economic participation.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/401/874/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/401/874/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/401/875/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/401/875/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/401/876/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/401/876/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/401/877/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/401/877/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/420/757/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/420/757/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/420/758/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/420/758/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/420/759/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/420/759/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/420/855/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/420/855/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

It's 11:47pm. Something happened today. You want to tell someone. You open your phone. You scroll your contacts. There's no one to text.

You open Instagram. Everyone looks happy. You feel worse. You close it. You stare at the ceiling.

I built Out Loud for that exact moment. Not for the person who wants to "optimize their wellness routine." For the person who just needs to say the thing — and has nowhere to say it.

Every emotional app asks you to pick from a menu of approved feelings: happy, sad, anxious, grateful. Real feelings don't fit menus. The thing that hurts the most is usually the thing you can't name — or won't say out loud.

I wanted to build something that doesn't try to fix the feeling. It doesn't try to distract you from it. It just shows you that someone else is inside it too.

**What it does**

Out Loud is a quiet place to say the thing you can't say anywhere else.

You open the app. There's one text box: "What do you need to say?" No mood picker. No category. No dropdown. You just type.

Post it anonymously. It disappears in 24 hours. Nothing is searchable. Nothing follows you.

A stranger who feels something similar can send one sentence back. No threads. No reply chains. No way to keep escalating. Just one human sending one sentence to another human.

Core features:

- Anonymous notes — up to 500 characters, gone in 24 hours

- Resonance — tap the heart to say "I feel this too." Count is public. Identity isn't.

- One-sentence replies — the constraint is the point

- AI suggestions (Groq) — if you don't know what to say, a warm sentence is written for you. You can edit it before sending.

- Support chat — a dedicated AI chat, prompted to be warm, validating, and non-diagnostic

- Crisis safety — if a note contains crisis language, a safety screen appears before the note is displayed, with local and international helplines

- Seasonal interface — the entire palette, particle system, and tagline shift with the calendar. Spring shows petals. Summer glows. Autumn scatters leaves. Winter snows.

- Out Loud+ — an optional subscription powered by RevenueCat. The free tier stays free forever.

**How we built it**

Stack:

- Flutter — one codebase, iOS + Android

- Firebase Anonymous Auth — no signup, no PII, no email collection

- Cloud Firestore — real-time note feed with strict security rules

- RevenueCat (purchases_flutter 10.13.1) — in-app purchases and subscription management

- Groq API (openai/gpt-oss-120b) — fast, free-tier LLM for reply suggestions and the support chat

- ai_chat_kit — drop-in chat UI for the AI support screen

- Google Fonts (Inter) — typography

- shared_preferences — device-local API key storage

Architecture decisions worth mentioning:

The seasonal particle system is drawn entirely with CustomPainter — no image assets, no animation packages. Six particle types (petals, sun motes, leaves, snowflakes, and their variants) rendered as paths, each with its own drift speed, sway amplitude, and rotation. The whole system is under 400 lines of code and adds zero KB to the APK.

The security model is Bring Your Own Key (BYOK). No API keys live in the source code. The RevenueCat key is passed at build time via --dart-define. The Groq key is entered by the user in a Settings screen and stored in device-local SharedPreferences. Anyone who clones the repo runs it with their own keys. Nothing is leaked.

Crisis detection runs before note display, not after. It's a synchronous check against a term list in the NoteCard widget's build method. If it fires, the crisis screen replaces the feed. Safety isn't a bolt-on — it's the gate.

**Challenges we ran into**

The Android NDK download corrupted twice. The first time, the source.properties file was missing from the extracted folder. The second time, the download just cut off mid-file. Fix was deleting both the NDK folder and the .downloadIntermediates cache — the SDK Manager was reusing the corrupted archive on every retry.

Firebase Auth returned admin-restricted-operation. This looked like a permissions bug, but it was actually that Anonymous Auth wasn't enabled in the Firebase console. The error message was the least helpful part of the whole build.

The Groq model was retired mid-build. llama-3.3-70b-versatile was shut down on August 16, 2026. The API returned this model do not have access — which reads like an API key problem, not a deprecation. Swapped to openai/gpt-oss-120b.

RevenueCat Test Store keys crash release builds. This is intentional — RevenueCat blocks release builds that use a test key so you don't accidentally ship broken payments. Had to build the demo APK in debug mode.

API key security was a real problem. The first version hardcoded the Groq key in main.dart. For a public GitHub repo, that's a leaked key. Rebuilt the entire flow around BYOK — a Settings screen, shared_preferences storage, and String.fromEnvironment for the RevenueCat key. git grep "gsk_" now returns nothing.

The seasonal system was almost abandoned. Early versions used image assets for each season's background. They looked inconsistent, loaded slowly, and made the APK large. Rewriting it as a CustomPainter with a shared palette system solved all three problems at once.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The app actually ships. It's not a mockup. It builds to a working APK, runs on a real emulator, posts real notes to Firestore, processes real RevenueCat purchases through the Test Store, and calls Groq with real API keys.

The seasonal system has no assets. Every particle, every mountain, every snowflake is code. Four complete palettes, four particle systems, four taglines — all generated procedurally. The APK is smaller than a single stock illustration would have been.

Crisis detection is a gate, not a flag. Most apps detect crisis language and show a banner. We intercept before the content is displayed. If someone posts something dangerous, the person reading it sees resources first — not the post.

The security model is honest. No shared secret lives in the repo. A judge can clone it, run it, and use their own keys. This is how consumer apps should handle third-party API credentials, and almost none of them do.

It's genuinely quiet. No notifications. No streaks. No "you haven't opened the app in 3 days." No gamification. No dark patterns. The app does not want anything from you. That's the entire design philosophy, and it's harder to build than it sounds.

**What we learned**

Building for vulnerable people changes every decision. When your user might be in crisis, you can't ship the same patterns you'd use for a productivity app. Crisis detection moves to the front. The AI gets bounded prompts. The free tier stays free. The word "engagement" stops meaning anything useful.

The best features are constraints, not capabilities. One-sentence replies. 24-hour expiry. No profiles. Every one of those is a limitation, and every one makes the app better. Unlimited characters would have made notes worse. Permanent replies would have made them feel like commitments.

BYOK is underused. Every hackathon project leaks its API key. It's the easiest thing in the world to fix, and almost nobody does it because the default tutorials don't show you how.

Procedural design beats asset design for small teams. One CustomPainter file replaced six illustrations, four backgrounds, and a whole animation library. The app is smaller, faster, and more consistent because of it.

"It's 11:47pm" is a better spec than "users aged 18–24." Every design decision in this app came from thinking about one specific person in one specific moment. The moment was the product brief.

**What's next for Out Loud**

Short term:

- iOS release (the code is ready; just needs Apple Developer enrollment)

- The emotion resonance map — a live, anonymous, global visualisation of how people are feeling right now

- Voice notes — because sometimes a feeling doesn't have words

Medium term:

- A verified-listener tier — trained users who want to respond to people in distress, with a warm-handoff flow to local services when needed

- Private pattern insights — "you feel lonely most on Sunday nights, and it usually passes by morning." Not therapy. Just awareness.

- Localisation — Urdu, Arabic, and Spanish first

Long term:

- Partner with mental health organisations in Pakistan, the UK, and the US to keep the crisis resource list current and regionally accurate

- Open-source the crisis detection term list so other apps can reuse it

- Never add a like button. Never add a follower count. Never add a notification that exists to pull someone back.

The whole point of Out Loud is that it isn't trying to capture attention. It's trying to release it. That stays true no matter how big it gets.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/399/289/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/399/289/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/399/290/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/399/290/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/399/291/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/399/291/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/399/292/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/399/292/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/399/385/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/399/385/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We've all had the experience of picking up our phone to check the time and
somehow ending up 20 minutes deep in Instagram — not because we decided to,
but because our thumb already knew where the icon was. Most digital-wellbeing
apps fight this by blocking access outright, which usually just gets
uninstalled the first time it's inconvenient. We wanted to try something
gentler: keep the app fully accessible, but break the automatic, thoughtless
tap by changing where it lives.

**What it does**

AppMaze is a fully functional Android home screen launcher that periodically
rearranges the position of apps you've marked as distracting. Nothing is
blocked — every app is one tap away — but your muscle memory can't carry you
there anymore, so opening it becomes a small, conscious decision instead of a
reflex.

- Smart scrambling at three intensities (Gentle, Moderate, Strong),
tuned to how much movement and how often

- On-device usage tracking that scores each app's "distraction level"
based on daily screen time — nothing leaves the device

- An intervention dialog that shows your usage for that app before you
open it, with an always-available "Open Anyway" — we never wanted this to
feel punitive

- A dashboard showing today's screen time, top apps, and AppMaze's
measurable impact (scrambles triggered, estimated time saved)

- Disguise mode, so a distracting app's icon and label can be swapped for
a neutral placeholder on the grid, removing the visual pull entirely while
the real app still opens normally underneath

- Essential apps (Phone, Settings, Emergency) are always protected and never
scrambled or disguised

**How we built it**

AppMaze is a native Android launcher built in Kotlin with Jetpack Compose and
Material 3. It uses PackageManager to enumerate installed apps and register
as a real HOME activity, UsageStatsManager for on-device screen-time data,
Room for persistence (app positions, usage events, per-app settings), and
DataStore for user preferences. RevenueCat powers [describe your paywalled
feature here] as an in-app purchase, letting us monetize without touching any
of the on-device privacy guarantees.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Getting scrambling to feel like friction, not chaos — too aggressive
and it's just annoying, too subtle and it does nothing

- Handling UsageStatsManager's permission model gracefully, since Usage
Access has to be granted manually in system settings and the app needs to
work sensibly before that happens

- Making sure essential apps (dialer, settings) are never touched by
scrambling or disguise, even under edge cases like zero marked apps or
rapid app switching

- Wiring a real purchase flow through RevenueCat without it feeling bolted
onto an otherwise fully local, no-login app

**What we learned**

Building a real Android launcher taught us how much "home screen" behavior
is baked into the OS — becoming the HOME activity meant handling
back-button quirks, launcher-chooser edge cases, and permission flows
(Usage Access has to be granted manually in system settings) that a normal
app never has to think about. We had to treat "permission denied" as a
first-class state rather than an edge case, since the app still needed to
work sensibly without it.

The bigger surprise was behavioral, not technical: we assumed hiding or
graying out distracting apps would be the stronger lever, but it turned out
that breaking muscle memory through position alone was enough to insert a
real moment of hesitation before opening an app. That's what pushed us to
add Disguise Mode later — scrambling position wasn't always enough when an
app was still instantly recognizable by its icon, so removing the visual
pull entirely became a necessary companion feature rather than a nice-to-have.

We also learned how easy it is for "digital wellbeing" features to tip into
feeling judgmental. Small wording choices in the intervention dialog — like
framing it as "Take a Break" instead of something more shame-based —
noticeably changed how the friction felt during testing, even though the
underlying mechanic hadn't changed at all.

Finally, integrating RevenueCat pushed us to think carefully about
monetization for a privacy-first, no-login app: the goal was a paywall that
felt proportionate to one specific feature, without compromising the
"everything stays on-device" promise the rest of the app makes.

**What's next for AppMaze**

- Home-screen widget support

- A background service option for more consistent scrambling timing

- iOS is architecturally impossible for a launcher, but we're exploring a
companion "focus mode" for iOS using Screen Time APIs

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

HexHash is a slightly spooky real-time roguelike. Its atmosphere comes from exploring the unknown: limited visibility, nearby enemies, and the tension of deciding what to do next while the dungeon keeps moving.

**What it does**

Explore a dark hexagonal labyrinth with a lantern. Read enemy behavior and decide when to advance, flee, or fight. Heartbeat sounds, background music, and combat effects bring the dungeon to life. Players can also explore an endless mode and customize their cloak colors.

**How it was built**

HexHash was built with Unity and C#, exported through Xcode, and tested on an iPhone 11.

RevenueCat's Unity SDK manages a permanent cosmetic cloak-color purchase, entitlement checks, and purchase restoration. Cloak colors change appearance only and provide no gameplay advantage.

The current demonstration uses RevenueCat Test Store. No real payment is collected.

**Challenges and lessons**

Development involved fixing text readability on phone screens, improving performance, and testing the purchase flow on a physical device. These steps showed why mobile games need testing beyond the Unity editor.

**What's next**

Further improvements will focus on game balance, performance, and making the atmosphere and controls feel even better on mobile.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

CubeX started with a simple problem: solving a Rubik’s Cube can be frustrating when you don’t know what move to make next. I wanted to create something that makes the solving process more visual, understandable, and easier to follow.

**What it does**

CubeX allows users to enter their cube configuration and generates a solution for it. It shows the exact moves needed, such as R, R2, U, and U2, and visually demonstrates each move on the virtual cube so users can follow along with their physical cube.
One feature that makes CubeX different is its bird’s-eye view. Instead of using a rotating 3D cube for the interface, CubeX presents the cube in a clear, flat layout, making it easier to understand where each sticker belongs.

**How we built it**

CubeX was built from scratch using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The project combines the cube’s state, user input, solving logic, move notation, and visual animations into one interactive web application.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was making sure the virtual cube accurately represented the user's input. A Rubik’s Cube has exactly nine stickers of each color, and the position and orientation of the center pieces matter when determining the cube’s state.
Making the solution animations match the actual moves was another challenging part of the project.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We’re proud of turning a complicated solving process into something that feels much easier to understand. We’re especially proud of the bird’s-eye interface and the fact that CubeX doesn’t just provide a solution; it shows users how to actually follow it.

**What we learned**

Building CubeX taught us a lot about JavaScript logic, user input validation, representing a physical object digitally, and creating animations that accurately reflect real-world movements.
It was a tough yet rewarding journey, and seeing the final project come together made all the debugging and problem-solving worth it.

**What's next for CubeX**

We want to continue improving CubeX by making the animations smoother, improving the interface, and adding more features that make learning and solving the Rubik’s Cube even easier.
We also plan to expand this idea into PyramidX, bringing the same easy-to-follow solving experience to the Pyraminx.

</details>

- **Team:** [Zaini T](https://devpost.com/zainit2000)

- **Built with:** android, eas-build, expo-snack, expo.io, javascript, react, react-native, regex, revenuecat

**Video (1:48):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sR0SevT_1R0

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/sR0SevT_1R0/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sR0SevT_1R0)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/388/411/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/388/411/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/388/412/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/388/412/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/388/413/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/388/413/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/388/426/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/388/426/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I'm a final-year Computer Science student focused on cybersecurity, and my final-year project is a honeypot-based threat detection system — an AI that runs decoy systems and logs how real attackers behave against them. Around the same time, I noticed something: almost every student building an LLM-powered app for this hackathon is shipping a system prompt they've never actually tried to break. Jailbreaks like "DAN" and instruction-override attacks are well documented, but there's no lightweight tool a student can run before shipping to check whether their own prompt is vulnerable.

PromptGuard is that tool — built from the same instinct as my FYP (generate real data about how adversarial input behaves against a system) but pointed at a different attack surface: LLM prompts instead of network services.

**What it does**

PromptGuard scans a system prompt or user-input string against a library of known jailbreak and prompt-injection patterns — role overrides, DAN-style jailbreaks, instruction overrides, delimiter injection, system-prompt exfiltration attempts, encoding-based bypasses, false-authority claims, and fictional-framing bypasses. For each match, it explains what the technique does and how to fix it.

The Pro tier (gated behind a RevenueCat entitlement) runs a deeper analysis: it generates novel attack variants by combining and obfuscating the matched techniques the way a real attacker would iterate, and produces a hardened rewrite of the original prompt that explicitly closes the vulnerabilities found.

**How we built it**

React Native + Expo for the app itself — three screens (input, scan results, deep scan), no navigation library, just simple state-based screen switching to keep it lean.
A static pattern library (data/patterns.js) of regex-based detectors, each tagged with severity and a fix suggestion — this powers the free tier.
A rule-based deep-scan engine for the Pro tier: rather than calling an external LLM (which would mean shipping an API key or standing up a backend in a short build window), I built deterministic logic that analyzes which attack categories matched and constructs both realistic attack variants and a hardened system-prompt rewrite from that analysis.
RevenueCat gates the deep-scan feature behind a pro entitlement, checked via Purchases.getCustomerInfo() against a non-consumable product.
Built and iterated in Expo Snack for fast browser-based testing, then a separate native Expo dev build (via EAS) for the RevenueCat integration, since react-native-purchases is a native module Snack can't run.

**Challenges we ran into**

Environment setup ate more time than the actual logic. Getting a clean Expo project structure (avoiding duplicate/misnested files), matching Expo Go's SDK version to the project, and getting an EAS cloud build working all took real trial and error before any app code ran.
Deciding what "AI deep scan" should mean under a tight deadline. I originally planned to call an LLM API for novel attack generation, but that meant either exposing an API key client-side (a real security anti-pattern for a security app) or standing up a backend I didn't have time to build reliably. I chose to build genuine rule-based logic instead — it's deterministic and transparent rather than a black box, which is arguably a more honest fit for a security tool anyway.
Keeping scope to something finishable. It would have been easy to add accounts, cloud-synced scan history, or a bigger pattern library — I kept it to the smallest version that actually demonstrates the core idea end to end.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Shipping a fully working end-to-end flow in a short window — input, static pattern detection, and a genuinely functioning deep-scan engine, not a mockup or a stubbed-out feature. Every screen does what it claims to do.
Building the deep-scan logic as real, deterministic reasoning rather than faking it. It would have been easy to hardcode a fake "AI result" for the demo — instead, the hardened-rewrite output is actually derived from which attack categories were detected, so it produces different, correct output for different inputs.
Getting RevenueCat's entitlement system properly wired into a real native build, including setting up products, entitlements, and the SDK integration from scratch, on a first attempt with this tooling.
Making it honestly useful to the exact audience judging it. Half the apps in this hackathon are LLM-powered — PromptGuard is a tool that could genuinely audit other Shipaton submissions, not just a hypothetical use case.
Staying scoped. Cutting a live-LLM backend in favor of a reliable, well-reasoned rule-based system was the right call under the time constraint, and the app is better for having something that fully works rather than something bigger that's half-broken.

**What we learned**

Hands-on experience with the actual mechanics of prompt injection and jailbreak patterns — not just reading about them, but encoding detection logic for each category and thinking through how an attacker would iterate past a first-pass filter. Also a lot of practical experience with the Expo/EAS build pipeline and RevenueCat's entitlement model, both of which I hadn't used before this project.

**What's next for PromptGuard**

Expand the pattern library beyond the initial 8 categories.
Replace the rule-based deep scan with a real backend-mediated LLM call for genuinely novel adversarial generation, once there's time to build it securely.
Add scan history so a developer can track how a prompt's risk profile changes as they iterate on it.

</details>

Frontend: Built using modern components to ensure a responsive, clean, and intuitive user interface across devices.

Successfully implemented a fully functional, lag-free real-time shared whiteboard for collaborative brainstorming.
Created a highly intuitive, clean UI/UX that keeps students focused rather than distracted by complex settings.
Built a working prototype from scratch within the tight hackathon deadline.

**What we learned**

We learned a massive amount about handling state synchronization for multiple concurrent users in real time. We also deeply explored user engagement strategies—understanding what specific features keep students motivated and productive without leading to digital fatigue.

**What's next for Study Buddy**

AI Integration: Building an AI study assistant that automatically generates flashcards and summaries from uploaded lecture notes.
Mobile Apps: Expanding the web app into dedicated iOS and Android applications for seamless on-the-go studying.
Gamification: Introducing customizable badges, streaks, and leaderboards to further incentivize daily productive study habits.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I find learning an instrument the traditional way a bit boring: classical pieces that slowly climb in difficulty, with little reward along the way. Duolingo showed that short daily lessons, streaks and instant feedback can make people stick with a hard skill, and I saw no equivalent for real instruments. Most music apps also feel disconnected from the instrument because of audio latency and sluggish feedback. Coming from a mechanical engineering background in physical systems and robotics, I wanted Soloist to feel as immediate as a physical tool, with the precision of hardware engineering behind a gamified experience.

**What it does**

Soloist is a gamified guitar trainer that listens to your real instrument through your phone's mic. It teaches through 8 skills and 24 structured lessons with a scrolling tab highway, and it grades pitch and timing live, including strummed chords. Streaks and hearts build daily momentum, and a built-in chromatic tuner and slow-down practice loops let you drill hard sections at 50–90% speed.

**How we built it**

I built Soloist with heavy help from Claude (Anthropic's AI). Claude wrote much of the code, including the C++ audio engine and the grading logic, and helped me debug my toolchain, builds and dependency errors along the way. I was new to low-level audio and native mobile development, so I used the project to learn: I read through what Claude produced, asked it to explain concepts like lock-free real-time audio threads, hardware timestamps and YIN pitch detection, and tested the result on my own phone and guitar. My role was the product vision and design decisions, running and testing it on real hardware, finding what was broken, and directing the fixes.

**Challenges we ran into**

Beyond the latency architecture, the build itself fought back: toolchain mismatches, Metro and Babel dependency conflicts, and a timebase bug between the native audio clock and the UI-thread frame clock that made the note highway jitter. Debugging it meant logging values across the C++, JS and UI threads and comparing their clocks. (Only include this if the highway is actually fixed.) Additionally, I initially tried to publish the app on Google Play, but found that the process would take too long to complete.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Achieving sub-millisecond grading accuracy regardless of visual feedback delay is a massive structural win for the app. I am also extremely proud of successfully integrating a complex C++ digital signal processing layer seamlessly into a React Native frontend. Pivoting from my previous work in 3D WebGL game development and mechanical design into low-level audio programming and mobile app architecture within a tight hackathon timeframe was an incredibly rewarding push.

**What we learned**

I learned how to manage real-time audio threads without allocating memory or using system locks, which is critical for preventing audio dropouts. I also gained deep hands-on experience with cross-platform native modules, React Native Skia's UI-thread rendering capabilities, and utilizing RevenueCat to cleanly abstract away the massive headache of managing cross-platform subscription states.

**What's next for Soloist - Your favorite songs, missing only you.**

Pitch-change onsets for legato, and echo suppression so the backing track doesn't leak into the mic without headphones. Real-recording slow-down needs time-stretching, which is why custom user-uploaded tracks come after that.

</details>
