<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Navigation apps end at a pin on a road. In Doha that is the wrong place to stop.

Doha is above 40 °C for five months of the year. The part of a journey that
decides your day is not the drive — it is the walk from wherever you actually
parked to the door you actually need. Every mainstream app treats that walk as a
rounding error, and treats where the sun is as no part of the problem at all.
If you live here, that is not a minor omission. It is the whole problem.

The second reason is quieter. Navigation is the most intimate telemetry a person
emits: everywhere you go, when, and how often. The industry's answer is to send
it to an advertising company. I wanted to find out whether a student with one
phone could build the other answer — where the server is yours and the app has
no idea who you are.

And one more thing kept bothering me. Navigation apps are confidently wrong all
the time. They will happily route you down a footpath that does not connect,
because admitting "I don't know" is not in the product. I wanted to find out
what a navigation app looks like if refusing is a first-class feature.

**What it does**

Vector is a native Android navigation app with a self-hostable backend. No
account, no login, no analytics SDK, no ads. It declares four Android
permissions — internet, network state, fine location, coarse location — and
no background-location permission; the only two others in the manifest are
the Car App Library's navigation-template permissions.

Driving. Turn-by-turn with voice, in Arabic and English street names. Three
ranked alternatives. Surveyed traffic signals (899 catalogued nationally) and
speed cameras (133) on your route. A 3D navigation camera over a national 3D
basemap — 228,872 building instances across 152,029 footprints.

Walking is a real second mode, not a fallback. It has its own pedestrian
graph: 1,108,269 nodes, 2,374,052 edges, 14,465 crossing facts and 8,707
barriers — of which 2,247 are locked or private gates that remove 3,874 edges,
because a locked gate genuinely splits a pedestrian network.

Shade — the part I care about most. Solar position is computed from a full
NOAA closed-form implementation (Julian centuries, equation of centre, nutation
and aberration, the five-term equation of time, NOAA's refraction fit). It is
deterministic, offline, and validated against published figures — Doha's
solar-noon altitude comes out 68.4° ± 0.5. Vector uses it to draw your walking
route amber where the model puts it in the sun and teal where it does not,
and gives you a slider to scrub the day and watch the route recolour. Both
colours are only ever drawn as an estimate: the copy cannot render a shade
percentage without the word "estimated", and a test enforces that.

The last mile. A journey is drive → park → walk, composed as one object.
Parking comes from a real POI corridor query, and candidates are ranked by the
walk, not by distance to your car — a car park 80 m away on the far side of
a compound wall is a 600 m walk. Then Vector offers you the shadiest of those
walks and tells you plainly what it costs in minutes.

And it refuses. If Vector's footpath data cannot connect two points, it says
so and says why: "No continuous walking route" / "The footpaths Vector knows
about don't connect these two points". It will not draw a straight line, and it
will not quietly fall back to car routing.

**How we built it**

Client: Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, MapLibre GL. Backend: Python services
behind one docker compose up — routing, geocoder, tile server, edge. Data:
OpenStreetMap and Overture, baked locally into vector tiles and two separate
routing graphs.

Two decisions shaped everything else.

1. The interesting code has no Android in it. Solar position, shade
estimation, route following, walking progress and camera policy all live in
core-geo, a pure-Kotlin module with zero Android dependencies. That is why its
675 tests need no device, no emulator and no GPU, and why the shade model can be
validated against published ephemerides in a plain JVM test. Together with the
app module's 1,115 tests, the project carries 1,790 JVM tests that pass with
zero failures, none of which needs hardware.

2. Routability is decided once, at ingestion. One classifier owns the OSM
access model — car, foot, barrier — and the router reads the result rather than
re-deriving it. A second classifier is exactly how a map and a router come to
disagree about whether a gate is locked.

RevenueCat powers Vector Pro. The entitlement state machine (ProAccess.kt)
is pure — no Android imports, no SDK imports — so every branch is a unit test
rather than a device session: the 7-day offline grace, the rule that a known
expiry always beats the grace, relock, and the paywall-rationing gate. The
cache is seeded synchronously before the first frame, so a paying user never
sees an upsell flicker on cold start. And an unconfigured build resolves to
UNCONFIGURED, which unlocks everything and can never draw a paywall — so a
self-hosted user who never touches RevenueCat gets the whole app, and the
classic "paywall nobody can unlock" bug is structurally unreachable.

**Challenges we ran into**

The pedestrian graph is broken, and no amount of code fixes it. Qatar has
3,015 mapped pedestrian crossings in the entire country, and arterial roads are
the connective tissue. So the walking graph is 2,811 components, the largest
holding 32% of all nodes. I spent a long time trying to engineer around this
before accepting it is a data problem, not an algorithm problem. What I built
instead was honesty: component-aware snapping, and a typed refusal that names
its reason.

Shipped is not deployed — and I found out the hard way. Four days of
walking-correctness work was committed, tested and green, and not running in
production. I only caught it by probing the live API rather than trusting my
own notes: a 343 m walk request came back HTTP 200 with a 49 m route, having
silently moved the destination 481 m. It answered a question nobody asked. After
deploying, the same request returns HTTP 422: "endpoint 25.31200,51.53300 is
481 m from the nearest road (limit 400 m)" — re-checked against production on
2026-09-24. That is the single change I am most glad about.

A green test suite is not evidence a service will start. Deploying that fix
took production down. The cause: Optional[str] used without importing it. It
passed every local test because this laptop runs Python 3.14, where PEP 649
makes annotations lazy — and died instantly in the 3.11 container, where they
are not. The fix was one import. The real fix was a deploy step that
smoke-imports the built image in the target interpreter before it replaces
anything.

Wanting a feature does not make the data exist. I wanted entrance-level
arrival. Qatar has 212 entrance tags in the whole OSM extract. I wanted
traffic-light countdowns; there is no public signal-phase feed. Both were cut,
and the timing model is now a sealed type that cannot express a phase without
a freshness window — so the app is structurally unable to invent one.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Shade that is real physics, not a gradient. A full NOAA solar position
implementation, validated to fractions of a degree, driving a visual anyone
understands in three seconds.

- A navigation app that says "I don't know." The refusal path is typed,
tested, and deliberately has no geometry in it at all — it cannot draw a
line it does not believe in.

- 1,115 app tests + 675 core-geo tests, none needing a device. Where a test
pins a defect, I verified it fails against the pre-fix code before accepting
it. A test that cannot fail proves nothing.

- A smaller app, verified on hardware. Enabling R8 shrank the release APK
(23.9 MB → 15.8 MB when measured; today's signed arm64 build is 17.6 MB).
R8 failures are runtime, not build-time, so I installed it on the phone and
drove it through search, routing, the journey card and navigation. Zero
crashes, zero ANRs.

- A limitations section I am not embarrassed by. The README states the graph
fragmentation, the 0.84% height coverage, and that the 3D extrusion was
photographed on the handset in a deterministic simulated GPS replay rather
than a real drive — positions synthesised, everything downstream of them the
shipping app. Saying so is cheaper than being caught.

**What we learned**

That the hardest part of a data product is not the algorithm, it is deciding
what you are entitled to say. Every feature I cut — signal timing, entrance
arrival, shade-aware path selection — was cut for the same reason: the data
could not support the claim, and dressing it up would have been the actual
failure.

I also learned to distrust my own status board. "Shipped", "tested" and
"deployed" are three different things, and I had been treating them as one.
Probing the live system instead of reading my own notes found a class of bug I
would otherwise have demoed with pride.

**What's next**

- An automated pixel-level check that a specific footprint's rendered roof
lands where it should — today the anchoring is asserted on the data (16/16
anchor checks) and the layer graph, and the result is shown in a recording,
but nothing asserts the pixel. Extrusion is photographed on real GPU silicon
inside a deterministic simulated GPS replay, not from a moving car.

- Junction-aware camera framing; ramps and bridges as real 3D form.

- Pedestrian graph quality — synthesised crossings and sidewalk-implied
edges. The only lever that moves 32% meaningfully.

- Genuinely shade-aware routing: an exposure penalty inside the pedestrian cost
model, rather than choosing the shadiest of the walks parking already offers.

- A real store listing and a real product, so Vector Pro stops being
demonstrable only through RevenueCat's Test Store.

**Limitations**

Vector is a real navigation app built on real data, and the data has holes in it.
These are the ones that matter, with the numbers behind them. Everything below
is a fact about the shipped build, not a roadmap.

The pedestrian graph is fragmented, and no amount of routing code fixes it.
Qatar has 3,015 mapped pedestrian crossings in the entire country. Arterial roads
are the connective tissue between neighbourhoods, and OSM has no crossing mapped
on most of them. The result, measured on the deployed bake:

the walking graph
value

nodes
1,108,269

edges
2,374,052

crossing facts
14,465

barriers
8,707

connected components
2,811

largest component's share of all nodes
32%

So walking is not "anywhere in Qatar". It is a real router over a genuinely
disconnected graph. Vector's response is component-aware snapping (it never
snaps a point onto a component that cannot reach the other end) and a typed
refusal that says which of three things happened, rather than a straight line
across a gap. A refusal here is not a bug being excused; it is the honest answer
to a question the data cannot answer.

Shade is an estimate, not geometry. Vector computes the sun's position with a
full NOAA closed-form implementation and scores each walk segment against the
street's orientation and an assumed façade height per road class. It has no
building geometry, no tree data and no ray tracing. A façade height is assumed
because only 1,929 of 228,872 building instances (0.84%) carry an explicit
height_m in the source data — the rest have nothing to cast a shadow with. The
UI therefore cannot render a shade percentage without the word "estimated", and
a test enforces that. Read "62% in shade" as "62% of this walk runs along
streets this model expects to be shadowed at this hour", not as a measurement.

Shade does not choose the path. Vector does not do shade-aware routing —
there is no exposure penalty inside the pedestrian cost model. What exists is
narrower and is described narrowly: the walk is drawn amber where the model puts
the walker in sun and teal where it does not; and where two or more indexed car
parks serve the same destination, Vector offers the shadier of those walks,
having ranked the car parks by the walk rather than by distance to the car, and
tells you what the shadier walk costs in minutes. Choosing a genuinely shadier
route is future work.

3D extrusion is confirmed on real hardware — in a simulated drive, not a real
one. The tile bake carries explicit height attributes for the minority of
buildings that have them, the tile bytes production serves for West Bay are
checked into this repo (docs/evidence/tiles/) so the data can be verified
independently, and a screen recording made on a Galaxy S24 Ultra shows extruded
building volumes with roof planes and wall faces at the 60° navigation camera,
drawn from live production tiles
— that recording is the demo video linked on this submission, from 0:42 to 1:12.

What that recording is not is a real-world drive. The GPS positions are a
deterministic trace replayed into the device's fused location provider through
Google's mock-location API; the navigation, camera, renderer and GPU are the
production application, but the movement is synthesised and no one drove the
route. Nobody has photographed extrusion from a moving car. This is a 3D
basemap, not a height survey.

The demonstration drive is simulated, and is described that way everywhere.
When this submission shows Vector navigating, the positions come from that
replay. It is built to exercise the real navigation, camera-follow, maneuver and
3D rendering paths without a physical drive, and the wording used in the video
and in the written submission says so rather than implying a road test. There is
no automated pixel-level proof that a specific building's rendered roof lands on
a specific screen pixel: such a test has to model the extrusion displacement as a
function of height and pitch, and a test that got that subtly wrong would be worse
than no test. What is asserted automatically is the data (every footprint
georeferenced, buildings and roads in one coordinate space), the layer graph
(buildings and roads share one source, so no independent transform exists) and
the camera policy over a whole replay (centre on the vehicle, tilt at the
documented cap, no rotation the route did not ask for). What is shown is the
recording.

There is no live traffic. The traffic engine has consumed zero probes and
reports edge_count: 0. Vector routes on a static cost model. It does not know
how busy a road is right now, and it does not estimate a delay from conditions
it has not measured.

There is no signal timing and no countdown. Qatar publishes no signal-phase
feed. Rather than guess, the timing model is a sealed type that cannot express
a phase without a freshness window, so the app is structurally unable to invent
a "green in 12 seconds". The signals Vector shows are surveyed locations —
899 catalogued nationally — and speed cameras (133), not states.

Android only. Vector is a native Android app (Kotlin, Jetpack Compose,
MapLibre GL). There is no iOS build, no web build, and no watch or CarPlay
equivalent. The Car App Library integration exists in the manifest but has not
been validated on a real head unit — a sideloaded Car App Library app cannot
appear on Android Auto regardless, so it is untested by construction.

No store listing, no users, no revenue. Vector is not on any app store. It
has no users, no downloads and no revenue, and no growth metrics are claimed.
Purchases are demonstrated through RevenueCat's Test Store on a debug build:
those purchases are simulated, no money moves, and nothing bought there is a
real subscription. The shipping release build compiles no RevenueCat key at all,
which means it has no paid tier — every feature is unlocked — and it also
refuses a Test Store key non-waivably, so a simulated purchase can never be
mistaken for a shipping one.

Entrance-level arrival is not built. Qatar's OSM extract carries 212
entrance nodes in the whole country, which is not enough to route to a door.
Vector stops at the walk from the parking space to the point nearest the
destination it can justify.

If a claim elsewhere in this submission is not supported by the numbers above,
believe the numbers.

**Why Next Gen**

Submitted to Next Gen as an active student (104314@oryx.edu.qa), under the
rule that Next Gen projects are "evaluated using the demonstration video and
code repository" rather than an app-store listing.

Against the criteria:

- A clear, useful idea for its users. Last-mile navigation for a city that
is above 40 °C for five months, which estimates how much of the walk from the
car to the door is in direct sun. Nobody else ships it.

- Meaningful progress toward a working app. It runs on real hardware against
a live backend. 1,115 app tests + 675 core-geo tests, 0 failures. The
repository builds and passes them from a clean clone.

- Thoughtful use of RevenueCat. Pro is a genuine product boundary — free
gets you there, Pro gets you from the car to the door — with a pure,
fully-tested entitlement state machine, and a design where a missing key
unlocks everything rather than locking users out.

- Technical choices, product thinking and care. 57 architecture decision
records in vector-governance/adr/, numbered to ADR-0075; a limitations
section that names real numbers; and a refusal path that is a designed feature
rather than an error case.

Honest note for the judges: Vector has no app-store listing, so purchases are
demonstrated through RevenueCat's Test Store on a debug build — which Next
Gen's rules accommodate. Test Store purchases are simulated: no money moves,
and nothing bought there is a real subscription. The release build refuses a
Test Store key non-waivably, so a simulated purchase can never be mistaken for a
shipping one. There are no users, no downloads, no revenue and no growth metrics
to report, and I have not claimed any.

**Notes for the judges**

Next Gen Award entry — no store listing, per the Next Gen rules. Purchases
are demonstrated through RevenueCat's Test Store on a debug build. Test
Store purchases are simulated: no money moves, and nothing bought there is a
real subscription. The shipping release build refuses a Test Store key
non-waivably, so a simulated purchase can never be mistaken for a real one.

There are no users, no downloads and no revenue to report, and I have not
claimed any.

Three things worth checking in the repository, in order:

- vector-android/app/src/main/java/dev/vector/android/pro/ProAccess.kt — the
entitlement state machine, pure Kotlin, no SDK and no Android imports: the
7-day offline grace, and the rule that a known expiry always beats the
grace.

- vector-android/core-geo/ — solar position and the shade estimate. The
shade is a model with an assumed façade height and no building geometry;
the UI cannot print a shade percentage without the word "estimated", and a
test enforces that.

- docs/evidence/tiles/westbay-z14-*.mvt and westbay-z15-*.mvt — the actual
bytes production serves for West Bay, so the 3D basemap can be checked
against the tiles rather than taken on trust.

The Limitations section of the repository README states what Vector cannot do,
with numbers.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Most habit apps show you a list. A screen full of unchecked items makes you ask "which one first?" and that small moment of hesitation is where habits slip. I also noticed that the real enemy isn't that logging is tedious. It's that you simply forget to open the app.

**What it does**

SpeedTask shows your habits one card at a time.

- Swipe right = done, swipe left = skip ("ask me again later"). Skipped cards come back next time.

- A home screen widget shows how many cards are left today, and you can log directly from the widget or from a notification without opening the app.

- On days you're already done, no notification comes.

- Calendar, history, streaks, and completion rates to look back on. Any day you complete at least one habit counts toward your streak, so busy days don't break you.

- Free for up to 5 habits. SpeedTask Plus (a one-time purchase, no subscription) unlocks up to 10.

- Habit names and records stay on the device. No account needed.

- Japanese and English, switchable in Settings.

**How I built it**

- Swift, SwiftUI, SwiftData, WidgetKit, iOS 17+

- The domain logic lives in a separate Swift package (SpeedTaskCore) with no dependency on UI, StoreKit, or RevenueCat, covered by over 100 unit tests.

- Monetization uses RevenueCat: a non-consumable product mapped to the "plus" entitlement and served through the default offering. When I switched the purchase backend from raw StoreKit to RevenueCat, not a single core test had to change.

- The app and the widget share data through an App Group.

- I used AI tools during development: Claude Code as a pair programmer for the implementation, and Codex for design prototypes (the card motion and onboarding).

**Challenges I ran into**

- Keeping the widget, notifications, and the app in sync so that "cards left" is always correct.

- App Store review: the app and the widget extension must share the same version number, or App Store Connect rejects the upload.

- Designing a paywall that still works honestly when products cannot be loaded.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

SpeedTask 1.0 is live on the App Store, and version 1.1.0 with English support is in review.

**What I learned**

Speed is a feature. Cutting the number of decisions matters more than adding features.

**What's next**

Releasing card themes (already in the code as version 1.2.0), and making the widget experience even faster.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I love organisation. I'm also a student, and I felt I wasn't really having a good time organizing my homework and exams. I used Google Calendar for exams and physical notebook for homework, later replacing it by some TODO apps. However, it always felt pretty messy, as i never had all things in one place. I began my search for an app that would do it all, while also having a nice design. At this point, I had pretty high requirements. I couldn't find a perfect app, so I decided I would build my own.

**What it does**

The main requirement for the app were to be able to differentiate between a piece of homework and exam, while having them appear at the same place. Other requirements included having support for 4 priorities, saving subjects and then easy assigning of the subjects to the homework and exams, having timetable support, android homescreen widgets, etc.
Another thing Schoolarc does is connecting with the Czech school system Bakaláři. That integration enables the user to import their subjects, timetable, but also view the homework assigned by the teacher and easily add it or view the changes in their timetable, such as substitutions or canceled lectures.

**How we built it**

I built Schoolarc using Flutter. While it wasn't the first time I opened a file of code, Flutter was the first time I learned a mobile framework. I chose Flutter because of its multiplatform capatibilities and I enjoyed every step of learning it. Schoolarc is the project I learned Flutter on, so I sometimes had to rewrite whole parts of the app as I gained some new knowledge about the framework.

**Challenges we ran into**

Pretty fun (well not fun when I was coding it) challenge was syncing the order of the homework and exams between devices. I have rewritten that whole part 4 times, going from saving all the tasks in a list to having double-indexed ordering. Double-indexed ordering was truly the best solution to this problem and I'm really proud of it.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Another achievement I'm really proud of is the UI and UX of Schoolarc. It tries to follow the Material 3 Expressive guidelines, which allow the designer to have a freedom in customizing not only the colors and shapes, but also motion. Flutter not supporting Material 3 Expressive fully compeled me to create some elements myself or use packages others have built.

**What we learned**

Building Schoolarc gave me so much - from learning Flutter and some basic coding practices from the ground up, to designing store assets to managing http requests.

**What's next for Schoolarc**

Schoolarc is now released on Google Play, but that version doesn't contain any paid features, duw to the legal complexity of providing paid services in the EU. <details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We grew up on couch games, the kind where four people crowd one screen and everyone's yelling. We wanted that again, except the people we play with now are spread across iPhones, Android phones, Macs and Windows laptops, and half of them aren't in the room.

So we gave ourselves one rule early on: BoatBrawl runs on iPhone, iPad, Android, Mac, Windows and the web, and all of them can join the same online match. If you're at home with friends, you should be able to play on one screen with whatever controllers and phones are lying around.

Boats came from wanting the arena to fight back. On water you get whirlpools that drag you in, currents that push you off your line and geysers that throw you in the air, and walls decide which weapons can actually reach you.

**What it does**

BoatBrawl is an arcade boat-combat game for up to 8 players. You can play against bots, online, or on one screen with friends.

You grab ? crates and fight with whatever comes out. There are 10 weapons:

- torpedoes

- a hold-to-fire deck gun

- a snowball blaster that freezes a boat so you can ram it and shatter it

- depth charges you lob over cover

- the Maelstrom, a slow nuke that hits very hard

- sea mines and decoy buoys

Power-ups like the invincible Ironclad ram and the spinning Cutlass mace change how a fight goes.

There are three arenas, and each one plays differently. Beacon Bay is an open bowl with a whirlpool in the middle, Tropical Forest has a waterfall and vines, and Arctic Vale has falling snow and icebergs. Currents, geysers and boost pads change the lines you take through all three.

Ways to play:

- Offline against bots

- Online with Find Match (bots fill empty seats, so a match always starts)

- A private room code for friends, with a leaderboard and a quick ready-up for the next round

- Local split screen for up to four players

Xbox, PlayStation and other gamepads work on every platform, with rumble. If someone doesn't have a controller, they scan a QR code and their phone becomes one in the browser. There's nothing to install, and they can steer by tilting.

There are six boats. Four are free and unlock as you level up, and the optional Premium Boats pack adds Eclipse and Imperial Tide.

**How we built it**

One Kotlin codebase. The whole game is Kotlin Multiplatform, and every menu and screen is Compose Multiplatform. The shared module is around 70,000 lines and holds the game rules, physics, netcode, audio and input. The same fixed-step engine runs on players' devices and on our server.

Our own renderer. We started on a third-party engine and outgrew it, so we wrote our own: OpenGL ES on Android, Metal on iPhone and iPad, OpenGL on Mac and Windows, and WebGL2 in the browser through Kotlin/Wasm. Boats load from .glb files through a glTF loader we wrote, and split screen draws every player's view into one GPU surface.

Online play. A Ktor server on Google Cloud runs the real game engine at 60 Hz and sends out 20 snapshots a second.

- Your own boat moves the instant you press a button.

- When the server's state arrives, your device corrects to it and replays the inputs the server hasn't seen yet.

- Everyone else's boat is smoothly interpolated.

Game state goes over an unordered WebRTC data channel, so one dropped packet on a bad mobile connection doesn't freeze the match. If WebRTC can't connect, a WebSocket takes over. Servers are versioned by URL, so shipping an update doesn't lock out people who haven't installed it yet.

RevenueCat. Four boats are free. Premium Boats is a one-time lifetime purchase behind a single premium_boats entitlement.

- On iOS and Android, we call the purchases-kmp SDK straight from shared Kotlin and use RevenueCat's native Paywall and Customer Center. Debug builds use the Test Store, and release builds use the real Apple and Google keys.

- The Mac App Store build runs on the JVM, and RevenueCat has no SDK for that, so we wrapped their Apple SDK in a small Swift library called through JNA.

- Customers are identified by the same Firebase user ID the game uses, so a purchase follows you to your other devices. Restore Purchases is in Settings.

- The paywall only opens when you pick a locked premium boat. You never see it at launch or on a free boat, and nothing unlocks until the entitlement is confirmed.

- On Android, there's one ad after each online match, through RevenueCat's AdMob integration. Premium Boats owners never see ads.

Accounts and progress. Firebase Auth with Google and Apple sign-in, plus Google Play Games and Game Center. Only the server writes levels and unlocks, so a modified client can't fake progress.

Tests. There are more than 600 automated tests, including deterministic replays of bad network conditions.

**Challenges we ran into**

Muting the game made it faster. On an iPhone 15 Plus, the game ran 6 fps slower with sound on, and 8.8% of frames were late. Native audio calls were running on the game loop. We moved every audio call to a single background worker, and now sound on and sound off both measure about 59 fps.

Android said 60 fps while the game ran at 39. The screen kept re-showing the last frame while the game itself was stuck, with some frames taking 350 ms. We fixed it in five steps:

- Let the GL thread run on its own instead of waiting on Compose.

- Rendered at 0.8 scale.

- Used cheaper shadows.

- Turned on sustained performance mode.

- Asked the phone for its 60 Hz display mode.

After that, 47 of 50 two-second windows held a steady 60.

Making online play feel smooth. One slow phone could freeze the whole match, inputs piled up behind a busy connection, and boats would surge forward and snap back. We tracked each of these down with deterministic replays and fixed them one at a time.

Why the server decides. Our simulation is almost deterministic, but atan2 gives a slightly different last bit on Android, the JVM and iOS. Over a full match, that's enough for two players to see different winners, so the server is the only source of truth.

Four controller systems. Windows, Apple platforms, Android and the browser all name buttons and flip axes differently, and tilt steering drifted or inverted on some devices. We normalised all of it so every player keeps their seat and their controls.

Selling on the Mac. With no RevenueCat SDK for a JVM app, we built the Swift bridge ourselves. Getting signing, entitlements and App Store review right took a lot of back and forth.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- It's live on the App Store and Google Play, with Mac, Windows and web builds from the same code, and everyone can play together.

- Your phone becomes a controller with one scan, with no app and no account.

- The paywall never nags. It only shows up when you want a premium boat, and buying one removes ads.

- Every performance fix was measured on real devices, in release builds.

- We open-sourced the fixes as Joyframe, a Kotlin Multiplatform library on Maven Central, and wrote a detailed how-to for other Kotlin developers.

**What we learned**

Sharing code across platforms was the easy part. The real work was making the game feel right on each one: smooth frames, fast response and controls that make sense for the device.

Average fps hides the frames players actually notice, and a phone can report 60 while the game is stuck. So we measure frame intervals in release builds on real devices.

In a real-time game, letting the server decide is simpler than trying to keep every device in perfect agreement.

Cross-platform purchases turned out to be mostly about identity. RevenueCat saved us from building a separate integration for every store. The work left for us was making sure an entitlement follows the player everywhere.

**What's next for BoatBrawl**

- More arenas and boats, built with our in-house map editor

- New premium boat packs

- Ranked play and seasonal leaderboards

- The Windows version on the Microsoft Store

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/420/528/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/420/528/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/420/610/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/420/610/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**KATSU — Habits that end**

App Store (iOS, free): https://apps.apple.com/app/id6800968856
Source: https://github.com/kisshiii/shipaton-habit

**The problem**

Most habit apps only make money if you never stop needing them. Streaks you
can't afford to break, re-engagement pushes, a little guilt when you try to
leave. The app's success and your success point in opposite directions.

**What KATSU does**

You set up to three routines with a time. Then you write, in your own words,
what you want to hear on the day you skip one. Not a template. Not
encouragement from a stranger. A short letter from the version of you who
meant it.

When the time passes and the box isn't checked, that line arrives as a
notification. It's hard to ignore your own voice.

When you do everything on your list 66 days in a row, KATSU gives you a
certificate, asks whether you still need this, and shows you where to cancel.
Leaving is the goal.

**Why 66 days**

The research median for a behaviour becoming automatic is about 66 days
(Lally et al., 2010), with enormous individual variation. The popular "21
days" figure has no basis. The streak requirement is not from the research —
it's our design decision, to keep the app from becoming an open-ended
subscription. We say so plainly in the store listing rather than dressing a
product choice up as science.

**Design decisions that follow from the thesis**

- Three routines maximum. Fewer is easier to finish every day. The limit is
the message.

- No streak counter, no score, no graphs. Graduation requires consecutive
days, but we never put the number on screen and never call a missed day a
failure. Break it and the count quietly restarts.

- Check off any time that day. The notification only fires after the time
has passed, so every check is structurally "late." Punishing lateness would
contradict our own design.

- The app never verifies you. You can tap everything at midnight and lie to
yourself. Nobody is watching — that's exactly why the words you wrote matter.

- No backend. Routines, checks and your words stay on the device. The only
network traffic is the RevenueCat SDK for subscription status.

- Safety guardrail. Users are invited to write harsh things to themselves,
so before any text is saved the app runs a local check for self-harm and
suicidal expressions. On a match it declines to save, shows a short
non-judgmental message linking to findahelpline.com, and lets the user carry
on. It runs entirely on device and the result is never stored or transmitted.
The line we drew: attacking what you did is in scope. Attacking who you are
is not.

**Built with**

Expo (React Native), TypeScript, expo-notifications (local only),
expo-sqlite / AsyncStorage, react-native-view-shot, expo-localization
(English + Japanese), RevenueCat, EAS Build. No server.

**Status**

1.0 shipped to the App Store on September 13, 2026. 1.0.1 — consecutive-66-day
graduation, the certificate, a redesign and a clearer plan screen — is in
review as of September 23.

**For the judges**

The paid tier unlocks multiple saved messages and per-routine targeting.
Redeem this offer code for free access: SHIPATON2026JUDGE

To see the notification arrive without waiting: set a routine for two minutes
from now and leave it unchecked. Graduation requires 66 consecutive days, so it
cannot be reached during judging — the store screenshots show that screen.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Our phones fill up with apps, even when many of the services we use also work on the web. Meanwhile, switching between personal, college, and work accounts often means signing out, opening another browser, or keeping track of scattered tabs.

Lite brings those everyday websites into one native iPhone home. The idea is simple: keep access to the services you need, with separate spaces for the different parts of your life.

**What it does**

Lite turns websites into lightweight web apps inside a native iOS library. You can discover a service, search the web with DuckDuckGo, or add a website address, then give that website its own profile.

Each Lite App uses a separate persistent WebKit website-data store. That lets you create multiple profiles for the same service with independent website sessions and cookies. Personal, Work, and Study can live side by side rather than repeatedly replacing one another's sign-in.

Working features include:

- A visual library for opening and organizing your everyday web apps.

- An in-app Discover catalog and DuckDuckGo search, with an Add to Lite flow.

- Multiple profiles for a service, profile customization, and account switching.

- Groups that bring related web apps together in a native carousel.

- Ad and tracker blocking and website permissions configured per container.

- Optional Face ID or device-authentication protection for individual app spaces.

- Saved pages, container downloads, website-data controls, widgets, and Shortcuts.

- A five-screen onboarding flow that explains the product before the first visit.

Using a service's website can reduce the need to install its native app. Actual storage savings depend on the service, its cache, and how it is used; Lite does not promise a fixed amount of storage saved.

**How I built it**

Lite is a native iOS app built with Swift and SwiftUI. WebKit powers the website experience, SwiftData stores the library and organization, and LocalAuthentication protects locked app spaces. WidgetKit and App Intents provide quick ways to reopen selected Lite Apps.

A separate WebKit data-store identity is associated with each profile. Browsing controls, account switching, popup handling, permissions, and saved website data need to respect that identity throughout the app.

RevenueCat manages optional Lite Pro purchases. The app loads offerings, purchases packages, restores purchases, and refreshes entitlement state. Lite Pro unlocks unlimited profile and group creation plus additional customization. The free tier retains the core browsing and privacy tools. Expiry does not delete existing profiles or block access to their saved content.

The current offering includes weekly, monthly, and lifetime options. Pricing shown in the app comes from StoreKit's localized product data. RevenueCat receives purchase-related data; Lite does not send browsing history, website cookies, bookmarks, or downloaded files to RevenueCat.

**Challenges I worked through**

The central challenge was making websites feel organized and comfortable inside a native app while preserving separate sessions. A new profile must remain distinct even when it points to the same service as another profile.

Another challenge was explaining the idea quickly. I iterated on the onboarding, app library, profile sheets, groups, privacy controls, and demo pacing so a new user can understand how a website becomes a Lite App.

The purchase experience also needs to remain honest about state: a pending or failed purchase should not unlock Pro, while existing saved content should remain accessible after a subscription expires.

**What I am proud of**

Lite combines useful profile separation with a deliberate native interface: dark-mode surfaces, clear typography, grouped app cards, focused sheets, and short transitions. The demo follows a continuous journey from onboarding through adding a website, managing accounts and groups, and viewing privacy and Pro controls.

**What I learned**

Good onboarding needs to explain the benefit before exposing the settings. I also learned that a polished demo depends on leaving enough time to understand each interaction, not just moving quickly between screens.

I used Codex during implementation and iteration, debugging, test preparation, and the production of the launch and demo materials. Lite itself does not claim to have an AI assistant or an AI inference feature; its core functionality is native browsing and organization.

**What is next**

I want to improve website compatibility, refine account-management workflows, and use feedback from real users to make common tasks faster. Wider compatibility and additional polish are future work, not claims about features already delivered.

**Demo and scope**

Recording note: Lite runs smoothly during normal use. The demo recording may show occasional stutters or skipped frames due to screen-capture frame drops and editing; it may not fully reflect the app’s on-device smoothness.

The video combines a product introduction with a real dark-mode app walkthrough. Website behavior depends on the service; some native-only features and authentication flows may not work in an embedded browser. Blocking targets known ads and trackers and does not guarantee removal of every advertisement. Profile separation is not anonymity from the websites themselves.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**▸ Project name**

DeskAssist

**▸ Elevator pitch**

Your phone is the button. Tap a tile, your Mac responds — end-to-end encrypted, no account, no cloud.

**▸ Built with (tags)**

expo react-native typescript electron node.js next.js revenuecat x25519 aes-256-gcm applescript vercel

**▸ Description — paste everything between the lines**

**Inspiration**

A Stream Deck is a grid of buttons that costs $150 and lives permanently on your desk. It's a genuinely useful thing: one press launches an app, fires a shortcut, or types a canned reply.

The observation that started this: almost everyone who wants one is already holding a better version of it. A phone is a touchscreen that sits next to the keyboard anyway, and unlike the hardware it can relabel its own buttons, hold as many pages as you like, and rearrange itself for whatever you happen to be doing.

The reason nobody just does this is that it's genuinely awkward to build. A browser can't launch an app on your machine, so a web page is out. Anything that routes your keystrokes through someone else's server is a thing most people should refuse to install. Doing it properly means a real process on the computer and a real cryptographic handshake between the two devices — which is what we built.

**What it does**

DeskAssist turns your phone into a Stream Deck — a grid of tiles that control the computer in front of you. Tap a tile and an app launches, a link opens, a keyboard shortcut fires, or saved text types itself into whatever window you're working in.

The deck. Nine tiles to a page, as many pages as you need. Drag to rearrange. Give any tile an emoji, a short label, or your own image. Make a tile span two cells so the one you reach for most is impossible to miss.

Profiles that follow you. Build a deck per context — writing, calls, coding. Switch on Auto mode and the right deck appears by itself as you move between apps on your Mac. The phone watches the host's focused application and switches on the edge, so a manual override sticks until the focused app actually changes.

Snippets. Save the text you retype — an address, a command, a paragraph you send every week — and send it with one tap. Set a delay first so you have a few seconds to click the window that should receive the typing. A snippet you reach for constantly can be promoted onto the deck as a permanent tile.

Running apps. See what's open on your Mac, jump straight to any of it, and pin an app to your deck while you're there. Tiles carry a live dot for running and frontmost state, so the deck reflects the machine rather than guessing.

Demo mode. Tap "Explore the demo instead" on the first screen and the whole app runs against a simulated Mac — no install, no pairing, no network. Built so anyone can evaluate the product without owning the other half of it.

**How we built it**

Three processes, because a browser is sandboxed and cannot control an operating system. That single constraint shaped the whole architecture.

phone (Expo / React Native)
 | X25519 key exchange at pairing, then AES-256-GCM per command
 v
host (Electron + Node)
 | AppleScript System Events / open / exec
 v
macOS

Pairing is a real handshake, not a shared password. The host shows a QR code carrying an ephemeral X25519 public key and a pairing id. The phone generates its own ephemeral key, derives a shared secret, runs it through HKDF, and proves it saw the QR with an HMAC confirmation tag. Every command afterwards is sealed with AES-256-GCM under that device key, with a monotonic counter for replay protection. The wire format is implemented independently on both sides and checked by interop scripts that fail the build if the two ever disagree.

No server sees your data. There is no DeskAssist account and no relay. The phone talks directly to the computer over your own network. The deck layout, the snippets and the device key never leave the two devices — the key lives in the OS secure store, everything else in local storage.

One switch for demo mode. A single module decides between the encrypted transport and the simulated host, and the branch happens before any sealing, so no demo path can reach the crypto. The UI imports that module rather than the transport and genuinely cannot tell which is live.

Dangerous capability is opt-in. The host can run shell commands, which is arbitrary code execution, so it ships disabled. Enabling it is a deliberate tray toggle with an optional exact-match allowlist, enforced in one function. A paired phone — or a leaked token — cannot execute code unless the human at the computer turned it on.

**Monetization (RevenueCat)**

Built on RevenueCat with one entitlement (deskassist_pro) and a default offering carrying monthly, annual and lifetime packages. Entitlement state is always read from RevenueCat's CustomerInfo rather than a local flag, so lapses, refunds and restores on a second device resolve correctly with no logic of our own.

The tier split is deliberate: the wall sits in front of growth, never in front of function.

Free
Pro

Profiles
1
Unlimited

Pages per profile
1 (nine tiles)
Unlimited

Snippets
3
Unlimited

Image tile faces
—
yes

All five action types — launch an app, open a URL, send a shortcut, type text, run a shell command — are free, as is unlimited ad-hoc text sending. A free user gets a fully working Stream Deck, and nothing that works on day one ever stops working.

Two choices worth calling out. Free gets three snippets rather than none, because a feature nobody can try is a feature nobody buys, and three is enough to feel why you want the fourth. And Auto mode is free but self-limiting — it switches decks to match your focused app, which does nothing useful with one profile. The feature demonstrates its own value and creates the want without a lock icon.

The paywall is reason-aware: reaching for a second profile shows "One deck isn't enough"; a fourth snippet shows "Room for every snippet". The ask names the thing you just reached for.

**Challenges we ran into**

A companion app is nearly unreviewable. DeskAssist does nothing without a Mac running the host. A reviewer opens it, finds a QR scanner, has no host, and rejects it under guideline 2.1 — the standard death of companion apps. Demo mode exists because of that, and it turned out to be a better product for everyone: you can evaluate the whole app before installing anything.

A purchase that granted nothing. The first test purchase completed and unlocked nothing. The code looked for an entitlement named pro; the dashboard's was deskassist_pro. That would have shipped as an app that takes money and gives nothing back — the worst failure available. It's now self-diagnosing: a purchase that doesn't unlock prints which of the three possible causes it was.

A test key kills a release build. RevenueCat's SDK detects a Test Store key in a Release configuration and deliberately terminates the app on launch. A build with no key at all runs fine but cannot sell anything. Both failures are silent until you try them on a real build.

Nine tiles, one page, and a dead button. On the free tier the seed deck fills every slot, so "pin this snippet to the deck" had nowhere to go — a permanently disabled control with no explanation. Found by using the app, not by reading the code. It now names the limit it hit and offers the upgrade that removes it.

A screen with no way back. The pairing screen only rendered when camera permission was denied. Grant it once and every launch dropped straight into a live camera with no exit — and a reviewer following our own instructions to "tap Explore the demo on the first screen" would never see that screen. The camera is now an explicit step you can leave.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The cryptography is real and it is checked. Not a shared secret in a QR code — an ephemeral X25519 exchange with HKDF, an HMAC confirmation that proves the phone saw the code, AES-256-GCM per command, and a monotonic counter that rejects replays. Two independent implementations, kept honest by interop scripts wired into the build.

Nothing leaves your network. No account, no relay, no telemetry, no analytics SDK. The two devices talk to each other and to nobody else. That's a product decision as much as a technical one, and it's the reason the app can be trusted with the ability to type into your windows.

The paywall has an argument. Every free limit is one a real user grows into, and every free feature works completely. Auto mode shipping free — while being nearly useless until you own a second profile — is the part we're happiest with.

Demo mode turned a review problem into a product feature. It exists because of guideline 2.1, and it ended up being the best way for anyone to try the app.

**What we learned**

The interesting constraints are never the ones you plan for. The cryptography was the part we designed carefully. The parts that actually cost days were an unreviewable app shape, a one-word entitlement mismatch, a key type that makes a release build commit suicide, and a permission dialog that silently changes which screen your users land on.

Also that "it compiles" and "it works" are very different claims. Every feature described here was verified by driving the built app — demo mode from a cold launch, a snippet round-tripping with its confirmation, a purchase lifting the gates — rather than by reading the diff.

**What's next**

Windows and Linux hosts (launching apps and opening URLs already work cross-platform; keystrokes and focus detection are macOS-only today). A formal test runner around the pure helpers, which are already exported for exactly that. Optional server-backed deck sync for people who want one deck across several phones — opt-in, and never the default, because the current answer to "where is my data" is "on your two devices" and that's worth keeping.

**Status**

iOS version 1.0.0 was submitted to the App Store on 29 September 2026 and is in review. The source is open under MIT, and the demo video shows the app running on a physical iPhone driving a Mac.

**Note - Demo is also available on GitHub**

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

**What it does**

**How we built it**

**Challenges we ran into**

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

**What we learned**

**What's next for Mily**

I have always hated how I looked on camera. But there were always these tiny moments — on video, mostly — where I actually liked how I looked. A single frame where everything lined up: the pose, the expression, all of it.

That's the whole idea behind Mily: the best version of every person in your group photo already exists — inside the burst you just took. You just can't get at it. I built Mily because I wanted to see the best poses of me, the best parts of me, really. And everyone else in the photo deserves the same.

**What it does**

In every burst of group photos, someone is blinking, mid-word, or caught mid-sneeze. Record a short clip (or pick a burst from Photos), and Mily analyzes every frame with on-device Vision — faces, landmarks, person matting — scores each person's expression per frame (smile, open eyes, mid-word detection), then transplants each person's best moment into one frame. All on-device, in seconds.

The result screen tells you exactly what happened per person — swapped from frame N (checks passed) or left unchanged, and why. Hold the photo to compare before/after. Saving is full-quality and always free.

**The safety policy**

Mily is least-invasive-first, and every stage can answer "no": a donor face must be inside a near-same-pose envelope, and every transplant passes artifact and identity checks — otherwise the person is left unchanged. A real photo of the person you took beats a generated one. That's a product promise, not a fallback.

**How I built it**

The app is SwiftUI on iOS 17; MilyCore, a local Swift package, is the engine: Vision face analysis, expression scoring, a group planner that picks base and donor frames, a landmark-fitted direct transplant synthesizer (weighted by measured landmark jitter so rigid points outvote the moving mouth), grain- and sharpness-matching, and artifact + identity verification.

Monetization runs on RevenueCat: purchases-ios + RevenueCatUI power a one-time tip purchase (mily_lifetime → pro entitlement), with entitlement state streamed through customerInfoStream and an offering-driven paywall. StoreKit 2 is enabled and the repo ships a StoreKit configuration, so the whole funnel — demo burst → result → paywall → purchase — runs in the simulator with zero App Store Connect setup, and is covered by a UI test.

**Challenges**

Making a transplant honest was the hard part: naive face swaps look great in demos and terrible in real life. I gated every edit behind measured landmark jitter, feather-matted compositing, grain/sharpness matching, and identity checks — and gave every stage the power to say "leave this person unchanged."

**What I learned**

- The pipeline is fast because it touches few bytes: strided vDSP gathers lose to sequential passes on interleaved data, and one composite must move ~39 MB no matter what — physics sets the floor. An optimization pass took the composite from 290 ms to ~8.8 ms median (~33×) with decisions unchanged.

- Restraint is a feature. Users trust the app more when it explains who it left alone and why.

- RevenueCat let me ship the entire purchase funnel without writing server code.

Mily is entering the Next Gen Award (student track).

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

As a Nigerian, data poverty is a daily toll. The first time I heard about Shipaton, I had no internet data to even learn what it was about — and that felt crazy to me. I had no job and couldn't afford data, but I had plastic. So I started picking up bottles and trading them for money, then using that money to buy data. That data brought me here. That's the story behind why Oxibyte is entering the Next Gen Award at Shipaton.

**What it does**

Oxibyte removes the barrier that affects millions of youth, especially across Africa, who've never heard of Shipaton and remain disconnected from the internet. It creates a bridge between people and the internet, using plastic. Users deposit plastic and earn internet data in return — credited straight into a data wallet. They can use that data however they want, but most importantly, it opens the door for aspiring app builders to join Shipaton and get access to sponsor tools like ElevenLabs, JetBrains, and more.

**How we built it**

Building Oxibyte started with an extreme decision: I left home with just a few clothes, with no plan for where to stay, and slept outside. It was one of the hardest calls I've made, but I went out with one mindset — if I don't start building, I'm not coming back home. Everything started with Replit, using its free-tier model as the foundation to build Oxibyte.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge, fittingly, was internet data itself. I had to gather plastic bottles, sell them for money, and convert that money into data just to get online — the same cycle Oxibyte is built to solve for others. That's literally how I got access to Replit, signal, and the Shipaton sponsor tools in the first place.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Seeing Oxibyte come out live and make it into the Next Gen Award submission is something I'm deeply proud of. This wouldn't have been possible without pushing through, and I'm optimistic Oxibyte will find its place in the heart of Shipaton.

**What we learned**

Data is knowledge. Building Oxibyte gave me a deep appreciation for that — much like Odin, who gave his eye for wisdom. That idea inspired the Oxibyte logo. It also connects to Einstein's $E = mc^2$: I believe the equation is incomplete without consciousness, and consciousness is the missing data — the piece that makes the whole complete.

**What's next for Oxibyte**

I can't wait to see the first real user. I can't wait to see Oxibyte on the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. Most of all, I can't wait to see that first person — stranded somewhere, disconnected, unable to afford data — turn plastic into their way back online.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**A private phrase. A trusted response.**

A phone can be within reach and still be impossible to use.

An older person has fallen and cannot stand up, but can still speak. Someone facing threats or coercion cannot safely make an obvious call. A person walking home wants a trusted friend to know if they miss an agreed check-in.

These situations share a difficult problem: asking for help may require actions that the person cannot comfortably or safely perform.

**What inspired me**

I was drawn to the gap between having a phone and being able to use it when something goes wrong. I wanted to explore how a person could prepare a simple way to notify trusted people before movement, attention or discretion became limited.

That led me to a simple question:

What if a phrase you had prepared in advance could start an alert to people you trust?

SignalWord is an iPhone app that connects a personal spoken trigger with consenting trusted contacts, private alerts and server-managed check-ins. It helps people prepare and practise a communication plan before they need it.

**How it works**

The user invites trusted contacts, who explicitly confirm their participation. Together, they can rehearse with clearly labelled TEST alerts.

For voice activation, the user configures a personal phrase through Apple Vocal Shortcuts. When iOS recognizes the phrase, it invokes SignalWord’s alert action. SignalWord does not receive the phrase or record ambient audio.

Contacts receive an email containing a private, expiring browser link. They can view the alert, see an optional time-stamped location snapshot and explicitly acknowledge it, without installing an app.

The sender can check the alert’s progress and resolve it separately. Acknowledgement means a contact has acknowledged the message; it does not promise that assistance is coming.

Users can also start a server-managed safety check-in. If its deadline is missed, the configured workflow can create an alert. Closing the app does not cancel the timer.

Voice activation requires prior setup, an available iPhone within hearing range and the necessary connectivity. SignalWord is a trusted-contact communication tool, not an emergency-dispatch service, and cannot guarantee delivery or assistance.

**Why preparation matters**

Sending a message is only one part of a useful safety workflow.

Who will receive it? Have they agreed? Will they recognize a rehearsal? What should they do next?

SignalWord makes those questions part of the experience:

- Consent: contacts confirm participation and can withdraw.

- Rehearsal: TEST alerts let people practise without confusing a drill with a real incident.

- Context: recipients can receive a recent location snapshot when available.

- Clarity: delivery, acknowledgement and resolution remain distinct.

- Recovery: the sender can return to an interrupted workflow and understand its current state.

The potential value is especially meaningful when movement, attention or discretion is limited. For an older adult who can speak but cannot comfortably reach a nearby phone, a prepared voice action could reduce the steps needed to notify family. For someone under pressure, it could offer another way to start a previously agreed communication plan.

The goal is to reduce the effort of sending a clear signal, and the confusion for the person receiving it.

**Safety stays free**

I wanted a business model that respects the purpose of the product.

Core safety features are free. RevenueCat and Apple StoreKit power one optional, non-consumable Supporter Appearance purchase, unlocking Ocean and Lavender accents and a supporter card.

Supporters receive personalization. Purchasing does not change alert priority, delivery or access to help. Purchase restoration and status refresh are available in the app.

**How I built it**

I built the native iPhone experience with SwiftUI and App Intents, with Apple Vocal Shortcuts providing the configured voice trigger. Supabase authentication, PostgreSQL and Edge Functions handle accounts, contacts, alerts and check-ins. A React/TypeScript viewer gives recipients a browser-based way to acknowledge an alert, while Resend supplies email delivery and Cloudflare Turnstile protects verification flows.

I integrated RevenueCat and Apple StoreKit for the optional cosmetic purchase and restoration. I used Codex to assist with implementation, debugging, security review and test development, then checked the resulting behavior through automated tests and physical-iPhone testing. SignalWord does not use generative AI or a danger classifier at runtime.

The engineering challenge was keeping the experience trustworthy when requests are retried, connectivity changes or the app is interrupted.

I implemented idempotent commands, a durable delivery outbox, encrypted delivery payloads, scoped recipient links and explicit acknowledgement actions. Opening a link alone cannot acknowledge an alert.

Privacy shaped the architecture: spoken phrases stay under Apple’s system control, location is optional, recipient access expires, and billing identity remains separate from safety data.

**Challenges I faced**

The hardest challenge was preserving a trustworthy workflow when only part of an operation succeeds. A request can reach the server even if the phone never receives its response. Retrying must not create a duplicate alert. A delivery provider accepting an email is also different from a contact receiving or acknowledging it.

I addressed those boundaries with idempotent commands, a durable delivery outbox, explicit status transitions and recovery after interruption. I tested retries, account isolation, consent withdrawal and the separation between acknowledgement and resolution.

Voice activation introduced another constraint: the experience had to work within iOS's system capabilities. I used Apple Vocal Shortcuts and a narrow App Intent so phrase recognition stays under Apple's control, rather than building an app-owned background microphone.

I also had to make privacy and usability work together. Recipients need enough context to understand an alert, but should not gain access to unrelated account data. Expiring, scoped links and deliberate acknowledgement actions keep that boundary clear.

Finally, I needed to keep monetization independent of safety. Billing failures or an unowned supporter purchase must not block a safety action, so appearance entitlements remain separate from the alert workflow.

**What I am proud of**

I built the complete journey: preparation, contact consent, rehearsal, alert delivery, recipient acknowledgement, sender resolution and check-ins.

SignalWord 1.0, Build 8, has been tested on a physical iPhone through TestFlight. A device demonstration covers registration, login, contact consent, TEST acknowledgement and resolution, check-ins, supporter appearance, restoration and account deletion.

The clean, MIT-licensed source repository includes the app, backend, viewer, tests and evaluator instructions. Apple review is currently pending.

**What I learned**

I learned that for safety software, the words on screen are part of correctness. “Alert created,” “message delivered” and “contact acknowledged” describe different events. A reassuring interface must still tell the truth.

I also learned to treat preparation as part of the product. Consent and TEST rehearsals help both sides understand what a signal means before a stressful moment occurs. Privacy and reliability need to be designed into the workflow, not added after the interface is finished.

Testing taught me to distinguish evidence from assumptions: a passing automated test, a successful physical-device flow and a public store release each establish something different.

**What's next**

My next steps are structured usability testing with older adults and consenting trusted-contact pairs, accessibility improvements and carefully evaluated delivery options.

SignalWord starts with a small act of preparation: choose your people, practise your signal, and make the next step easier when reaching your phone is difficult.

</details>

The Problem That Started DevFlow
Building software is only one part of being a developer. The harder part is keeping track of everything around it — GitHub repositories, pull requests, failed builds, code changes, hackathon deadlines, deployment issues, and the constant stream of information that gets scattered across different tools. As a student participating in hackathons and building multiple projects, I found myself repeatedly switching between GitHub, calendars, notifications, and project dashboards just to answer simple questions: What needs my attention today? Did my build fail? Is someone waiting for my PR review? Which hackathon deadline is coming next?
I wanted one place that could turn all of that noise into something actionable. That idea became DevFlow— an AI-powered command center built specifically for developers and hackathon builders.
 How DevFlow Works:
DevFlow connects directly with GitHub to bring repositories, pull requests, commits, and GitHub Actions activity into a single mobile dashboard. Instead of forcing developers to constantly check multiple services, DevFlow surfaces the events that actually matter through Smart Alerts, including build failures, PR activity, deployments, and approaching hackathon deadlines. Its hackathon tracker keeps important events visible, while the AI layer transforms technical activity into useful summaries — from an AI Daily Brief to PR/code-diff explanations and commit message generation.
I also wanted DevFlow to be more than another dashboard. It needed to behave like a developer companion. That is why notifications are powered through OneSignal, while RevenueCat handles the Pro subscription experience. The free tier provides the core workflow, while DevFlow Pro unlocks unlimited repositories and advanced AI-powered features.
Building It:
I built DevFlow as a React Native + Expo application with TypeScript, focusing on a clean, developer-first mobile experience. I designed the architecture around modular services so GitHub, notifications, AI features, hackathon tracking, and subscriptions can evolve independently. I also built a Demo Mode so the complete experience can be explored even without connecting a personal GitHub account.
One of the biggest challenges was bringing several moving pieces together without making the app feel complicated. Authentication, GitHub API failures, rate limits, notification permissions, subscription state, and AI features all needed to work together while still keeping the interface simple. I spent a significant part of the development process handling these edge cases and making sure the app could gracefully fall back when a service was unavailable.
What I Learned:
DevFlow taught me that building a useful product isn't just about adding more features. It is about reducing the number of decisions and actions a user has to take. Every feature in DevFlow is designed around one question: "What does a developer need to know or do next?"
DevFlow is my attempt to turn the scattered workflow of a modern developer into one focused experience — from the first commit to the final hackathon deadline.

</details>
