<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/490/330/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/490/330/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/351/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/351/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/352/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/352/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/353/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/353/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**BotHouse**

**Inspiration**

When I was 14, I moved to another city and suddenly had a lot of free time. I wanted to get into software development, but programming languages such as Python and Node.js looked intimidating to me. I was afraid that programming would be too difficult.

Around that time, I became more active on Discord, and a friend introduced me to Bot Designer For Discord (BDFD). I downloaded it out of curiosity, and I quickly realized that it was much more than a bot-building application. It was a simple and surprisingly effective way to learn programming fundamentals.

BDFD introduced concepts such as commands, conditions, and basic algorithms without forcing beginners to understand the complexity of a traditional programming language first. Because of its community and accessible structure, I found that some beginners could understand algorithmic thinking through BDFD more easily than they could through Python.

I started teaching BDFD to friends who were interested in programming but were intimidated by English-language resources and traditional programming languages. Eventually, I created my own learning system:

BDFD → JavaScript/Aoi.js → Node.js → Software Development

The idea was to use a simple environment to teach programming fundamentals first, then gradually move students toward real programming.

However, I kept receiving questions about BDFD:

"Why does this function exist?"
"Why doesn't it have this feature?"
"Why can't I do this?"

That led me to a bigger idea:

What if I built the language myself, connected it to a proper server infrastructure, and made it capable of powering bots across different platforms?

At the same time, I realized that the same infrastructure could solve a completely different problem: e-commerce businesses spend significant amounts of money and time building and maintaining automation systems.

For the past three years, I have focused on building the skills required to turn this idea into reality. During the first year, I focused heavily on JavaScript. In the second year, I moved into mobile development. During the third year, I focused on interpreter development, backend architecture, and server management.

That journey eventually became BotHouse.

**What it does**

BotHouse allows users to create and run their own bots using a programming language designed to be significantly easier to understand than traditional programming languages.

Instead of dealing with complex infrastructure, users can provide their bot information to the platform and start building their automation with a simple language.

BotHouse is designed for two major groups:

**Beginners**

People who want to learn programming can create real, functional bots while learning programming concepts along the way.

Instead of starting with thousands of lines of code, users can begin with a much simpler syntax and gradually understand how programming works.

**E-commerce businesses**

Businesses can use BotHouse to automate repetitive operations without having to build and maintain an entire backend infrastructure themselves.

This can reduce the technical complexity and infrastructure costs associated with automation.

BotHouse also introduces an ad-supported hosting model. Users who cannot afford hosting can watch advertisements to help cover their server costs.

For premium features, we use RevenueCat to manage subscriptions and in-app purchases across the platform. This allows us to maintain a centralized and scalable system for handling premium access and revenue while keeping the core platform accessible to users who cannot afford paid hosting.

Our goal is simple:

Make automation accessible to people who know how to code, people who are learning to code, and people who have never coded before.

**How we built it**

The client application was built with Flutter.

I developed the core application logic, service integrations, and platform functionality myself. I also used AI tools to accelerate UI development and iteration, allowing me to spend more time on the underlying architecture.

**Backend**

For the backend, I built a server architecture primarily using Go.

One of the biggest architectural decisions was using a Multi-Tenant, Single-Process approach.

Instead of running a completely independent process for every bot, multiple bots can operate within the same server process while remaining logically isolated.

This was challenging because memory management and resource allocation had to be carefully considered.

I experimented with pooling and resource-management strategies and eventually built an architecture where a bot could operate with approximately 1 MB of RAM on average under our tested workload.

On a server with 6 GB of RAM, I was able to run approximately 1,000 bots in testing.

**Interpreter**

The most technically important part of BotHouse is its interpreter.

I developed the language myself using a traditional:

Lexer → Parser → Interpreter

architecture.

I implemented the core language infrastructure and designed the system so that commands can communicate with different platforms through the appropriate modules or APIs.

This means that the same high-level BotHouse language can eventually interact with different services without forcing the user to learn the implementation details of every platform.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was connecting thousands of potential bot environments to a common language while keeping the server architecture efficient.

Building the multi-tenant architecture, managing bot resources, designing the interpreter, and making everything communicate reliably required solving problems that I had never encountered before.

My previous three years of experience helped me solve many of these problems, but I still had to research unfamiliar concepts and understand new architectures.

I also used AI tools as a learning assistant: rather than simply copying generated code, I used them to summarize complex concepts, compare approaches, and help me understand the underlying systems.

The biggest challenge was not writing the code.

It was understanding why the architecture should work the way it does.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Before building BotHouse, we created an educational community called RUDS Development.

Through BDFD-based programming education and educational content on YouTube, we helped more than 150 people take their first steps into programming.

That experience directly influenced BotHouse.

We learned that beginners don't necessarily need a simpler version of a programming language.

They need a different starting point.

BotHouse is our attempt to build that starting point while also creating infrastructure that can eventually support real-world automation and e-commerce use cases.

Our long-term goal is to take the accessibility that made BDFD successful and remove the limitations that come with it.

**What we learned**

AI has fundamentally changed software development.

Today, someone can describe what they want and generate a working implementation within seconds.

But that does not eliminate the need for programming knowledge.

If something goes wrong, security needs to be reviewed, infrastructure needs to be maintained, or generated code needs to be modified, someone still needs to understand what is happening underneath.

While building BotHouse, I learned much more about:

- Interpreter architecture

- Lexers and parsers

- Memory management

- Multi-tenant systems

- Backend architecture

- Server resource management

- API integration

- Mobile application development

But perhaps the most important lesson was that small systems can become powerful when they are designed to work together.

A simple language, an interpreter, a server architecture, an educational system, and a sustainable business model can become something much larger when they are connected correctly.

**What's next for BotHouse**

There is a lot more planned for BotHouse.

**A better UI**

The current UI was developed under significant time constraints for the competition. We plan to redesign and improve the interface to make the entire experience more intuitive and polished.

**More commands**

We currently have a growing command system, and our next major milestone is reaching approximately 300 supported commands, allowing users to build significantly more complex automations without leaving the BotHouse ecosystem.

**Account synchronization**

We plan to introduce Google Sign-In and a shared cloud database so users can securely access and manage their bots across different devices.

**Security**

Bot tokens and other sensitive credentials require serious protection.

As the platform grows, we plan to implement a stronger security architecture across both the client and server sides, including secure credential handling, isolation, access control, and protection against unauthorized access.

**BotHouse:Block**

Not everyone wants to write code.

For users who cannot read or write code comfortably, or simply don't want to type commands manually, we plan to create a companion platform called BotHouse:Block.

Users will be able to build bot automations using visual blocks instead of writing code.

This would create a progression like:

BotHouse:Block → BotHouse Language → Traditional Programming

Users could start visually and eventually transition into actual programming if they want to.

**AI-powered development**

We also plan to develop an AI assistant specifically designed around the BotHouse language.

The system could be built on top of models such as Qwen or other open-source language models and fine-tuned to understand BotHouse's syntax and ecosystem.

Instead of asking an AI to generate Python or JavaScript, users could simply describe what they want and receive BotHouse code.

Because BotHouse is designed to express common automation tasks with much less code, the same task could potentially require significantly fewer tokens than an equivalent implementation in a traditional language.

**On-device bot execution**

One of our longer-term premium features is local bot execution.

The idea is to allow users to run their bot directly on their own device while using the BotHouse server only for license verification and essential platform services.

This could allow bots to operate without continuously sending their execution data to a third-party server.

**Sustainable monetization**

We want BotHouse to remain accessible while also being financially sustainable.

Our model combines:

Free access + Ad-supported hosting + Premium features

For premium subscriptions and in-app purchases, we use RevenueCat to centralize subscription management and entitlement handling.

This allows us to focus on building the platform itself instead of maintaining separate purchase and subscription infrastructure for every platform.

Ultimately, our goal is to build an ecosystem where learning programming, building bots, deploying automation, and running an online business can exist within the same platform.

BotHouse is not just a bot builder.

It is an attempt to make programming and automation accessible to everyone.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Push your phones together. They become one screen.

**Inspiration**

Put a group of friends around a table and, sooner or later, everyone is looking down at their own phone. We wanted to flip that: what if the phones were the reason everyone leaned in over the same table?

The answer was lying right there. Phones set down side by side already look like the tiles of a board; they just don't know about each other. Make each one aware of its neighbours and every pocket holds a piece of a shared game board, one that grows with every friend who joins.

**What it does**

Bubble Games is a party game where the board is everyone's phones put together. Two to eight players lay their phones on the table and the screens join into one big playing surface: anything that leaves one screen crosses the gap and carries on onto the next.

It comes with 10 competitive minigames, and the twist is that every game rearranges the phones into a different board:

- Pitch Cars: the phones form a winding race track that is randomly generated every round. Flick your car from phone to phone.

- Hot Potato: phones in a ring. Swipe the potato to a neighbour before the fuse runs out.

- Flood: two rows facing each other, two teams, one waterline. Tap to push it onto their screens.

- Guac-a-Mole: avocados in your colour pop up on everyone's phone, so you play it leaning across the table.

- …plus Paint War, Arena, Dodgeball, Cops & Robbers, Marbles Madness and Road Runner.

Between rounds, each phone shows where it goes next, with coloured stripes to line up against its neighbours. Any mix of phones works: the game knows every screen's real size in millimetres, so a marble is the same physical size on all of them.

No account and no server. One phone hosts, and the others join over the same Wi-Fi or a hotspot with a QR code.

**Free to play, one upgrade**

Bubble Games is free, with six minigames ready to play out of the box. A one-time $3.99 USD upgrade unlocks the rest:

- Four more minigames, for ten in total. (And more to come)

- Pick your games. Choose exactly which minigames make up the session instead of leaving it to the lineup.

And the best part? 

Only the host has to pay for premium! All the other players tag along! 

We believe in good old fashioned games that aren't subscription based, and so we are proud to say that BubbleGames Premium requires NO SUBSCRIPTION: pay once and it's yours forever!

**How we built it**

We are a team of four software engineering student from Université Laval in Québec City. We used Flutter for its cross-platform mobile support, with Flame, Forge2D for physics and Rive for animation.

Under the games sits a small game engine we wrote:

- One world, in centimetres. The host phone runs the only simulation, at 60 Hz. Every phone is a camera onto its own slice of that world. Physics keeps running in the gap between two screens, because the bezel is real space.

- A layout engine. Each game asks for a shape (row, grid, brick, ring or random path) and the engine computes where every phone goes from its real dimensions.

- A purpose-built game SDK. A game only declares how many players it takes, where the phones go, its rules and its pixels. Adding one is a folder and one line; networking, sync, layout and scoring never learn its name.

- Local-only networking. WebSockets over the LAN, with discovery over UDP broadcast and Bonjour. No server and no HTTP requests, except for payments.

**Monetization with RevenueCat**

One purchase, whole party unlocked. The game is a party game played across several phones, so the paywall had to fit that. The host buys Premium once, and every player who joins gets the premium games. Nobody else has to pay. 

**How RevenueCat is used**

- One entitlement, one product. A single premium entitlement gates the premium-tier games. It's sold as a one-time lifetime purchase with no subscription, and the paywall shows the localized price from the store.

- Offerings drive the paywall. The paywall reads the current Offering and picks the lifetime package, so we can change price or packaging in the RevenueCat dashboard without shipping an app update.

- One source of truth. A small PremiumStatus notifier initializes the SDK with the right key for iOS/macOS or Android. It listens to RevenueCat's customer-info updates, so the UI unlocks the moment an entitlement becomes active, even if the purchase finishes elsewhere.

- Restore purchases. Restore returns a typed outcome (restored, already active, nothing found, offline, failed), so each case gets a clear message instead of a generic error.

- Failures don't block the game. Store calls have a 10-second timeout and a retry path. A cancelled purchase is not treated as an error, and a missing or misconfigured key shows a friendly message instead of crashing. 

**The paywall**

A sticker-style bottom sheet that matches the game's look. It lists the locked games as chips, shows the price, and has an Unlock Premium button plus Maybe later and Restore purchase links. It can be opened from a specific game ("X is a premium game…") or from the lineup picker. 

**What we learned**

 RevenueCat removed the receipt validation and cross-platform entitlement logic we would otherwise have built ourselves. Most of our work went into the edge cases: offline restore, cancelled purchases, and keeping the UI in sync with the entitlement.

**Challenges we ran into**

Making the seam invisible. If each phone draws the latest state it received, an object steps sideways as it crosses the gap. So every phone, the host included, renders the world 80 ms in the past and interpolates between snapshots. 80 ms was the sweet spot: enough to hide network jitter, short enough to still feel responsive. One early version drifted by 0.8 mm between phones running at different frame rates; a test caught it.

Phones don't know how big they are. Flutter only reports an approximate pixel density, and a few percent of error is several millimetres of misalignment. We read the real DPI natively, and you can calibrate by holding a standard physical card against the screen.

The layout algorithm. It has to minimize the gaps between phones while maximizing the playing surface, with phones of different sizes, for any player count from two to eight.

NameDrop. Put the tops of two iPhones together and iOS covers the game with a contact-sharing sheet. This is enforced at the OS level and cannot be disabled automatically by the game. When triggered, this exits the game (quite problematic). To overcome this we use a clever algorithm that calculates the optimal phone configurations and picks the one that keeps the antennas apart.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Bubble Games isn't a hackathon demo we'll forget next week. It's become our go-to party game: the phones come out at the end of the night, and nobody's looking down at their own screen anymore. Our friends ask for it by name, and some of the best moments we've had building this weren't writing code, but losing to them at our own games.

We're also proud of the engine underneath: all ten games are built on the same SDK, so a new game idea goes from sketch to playable on a table of phones without touching any existing code, networking or layout.

**What we learned**

This project taught us what it takes to ship a mobile app from A to Z. We went from a napkin idea to ten playable games, and we made everything ourselves along the way: the code, the art, the animations and every sound effect. Nobody on the team had done that before. We had to make product decisions ourselves too: which games make the cut, what's free and what's premium, and what a first-time player sees in their first thirty seconds.

The technical side stretched us just as much: real-time networking with no server, physics that has to agree across phones to the millimetre, native code to measure screens, and the geometry behind the layout engine. We started out using game engines; we came out knowing how to build one.

**What's next for Bubble Games**

- Ship it to the App Store and Google Play, with the premium upgrade already wired in. We are halfawy through! The app is already submitted to both posts and pending review!

- Open the SDK. We already build every game with it. Next is letting the community create their own games with pre-selected assets and sounds, and publish them to other players in one tap, like Geometry Dash's level editor.

- More games !!

</details>

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/hLw6xVsFxpE/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hLw6xVsFxpE)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/150/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/150/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/151/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/151/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/152/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/152/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/153/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/153/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/154/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/154/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/159/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/159/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/160/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/160/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every friend group has one. The pool table at the flat, the FIFA rivalry, the Friday table tennis at the office. And every one of those groups has the same argument: who's actually better?

Usually the answer lives in one person's head, or a notes app, or a WhatsApp message from three months ago that everyone remembers differently. The person keeping score always seems to be winning.

I wanted an app that just settles it. Log the game in a couple of taps, and let the table say who's best. But a scoreboard only works if everyone trusts it, so the most important feature turned out to be a rule, not a screen: nothing counts until both players agree.

**What it does**

Krovo keeps score for you and your friends, for any game: pool, darts, FIFA, chess, padel, cards, or the argument you have every week.

- Log a match in seconds. Pick the group, the game and who played. A score is optional.

- Both sides confirm. Your result sits as "waiting on Ahmed" until Ahmed agrees. If he says the score was different, it goes back to you. Only agreed results reach the table.

- Standings that settle it. Win rate, form, streaks and a table per game, per group, per season or all time.

- Head to head. Your full record against any one person.

- Groups for the flat, the five a side, the office. Invite with a link or a code.

- Play people who aren't on Krovo. Log them anyway. If they join later, they get a claim link and their whole record comes with them.

- It works on your own, from the very first match, with no account needed.

- No ads and no tracking. No advertising ID, no contacts, no location.

**How it makes money**

Krovo Pro, through RevenueCat: £5.99 a month or £39.99 a year, on one pro entitlement.

Pro gives you seasons with a champion at the end, your own awards, every stat and a recap card at the end of each season. The interesting part is League Mode: you point your Pro at one of your groups, and the season, table and awards switch on for everyone in that group.

That was a deliberate choice. My first plan was a group subscription, but then everyone in the group gets everything and nobody ever sees a reason to buy. With personal Pro, one person pays and the other five play in their league every week and see what it adds.

It also made the RevenueCat setup more interesting than "check an entitlement":

- The app calls logIn with the user's id, so a purchase is tied to a person and not an anonymous device. Without that, the purchase succeeds, the buyer's own app turns Pro on, and the other five people in the group never get League Mode. It's a nasty bug because the person who paid can't see it.

- A RevenueCat webhook (a Supabase Edge Function) writes entitlements into Postgres. The group's league checks "does a current member have Pro pointed here?" on the server, so no phone ever reads anyone else's billing.

- A small redeem code function hands out Pro through RevenueCat, for testers and judges.

**How I built it**

- Expo and React Native with Expo Router and NativeWind, in TypeScript.

- Local first. Every match is written to SQLite on the phone first and synced through an outbox, so logging works with no signal at the side of a pitch.

- Supabase for accounts and sync: Postgres with row level security on every table, 46 migrations, and Edge Functions for the RevenueCat webhook, redeem codes and a sweep job that closes lapsed votes.

- Sign in with Apple, Google, or a guest account, so nobody has to make a password to keep score of a pool game.

I also wrote the whole system design before writing any code, then reviewed it like someone else had written it. That review found sixteen problems, six of which would have broken the very first database migration. Fixing them on paper cost an afternoon. Fixing them after launch would have cost people their match history.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Making "confirmed" mean something. Once results could be edited, a lot of simple assumptions broke. What happens to a confirmed result someone edits? Who has to agree again? I ended up treating a score like a contract: any change goes back through the same agreement.

- Claim links in in-app browsers. WhatsApp and Instagram often open links in their own browser, which never hands the link to the app. So a claim link now lands on a web page that works either way.

- Everything around the store. Android needs 12 testers for 14 straight days before it can go to production. We hit that on September 17, and the build is in review now.

**Accomplishments I'm proud of**

- A real two sided agreement flow that feels quick instead of like paperwork.

- A pricing model where one purchase makes the app better for a whole group, built on RevenueCat and server side entitlements.

- The design: amber always means you, blue always means your opponent, and colour is never the only signal, so it works in greyscale too.

**What I learned**

The hardest part of a social app isn't the screens, it's trust. Every feature in Krovo ended up being about whether people believe the table, and "nothing counts until you both agree" does more for that than any chart.

**What's next for Krovo**

- Finish Google Play review and ship to the App Store

- Launch with real friend groups first and let them tell me what to build next

- Scan to log: take a photo of a scoreboard and let Krovo read the result

**Why open source**

I'm a student at NUST in Pakistan, and I'm submitting Krovo to the Next Gen track as an open source project. The full client, database migrations and Edge Functions are on GitHub under MIT, with setup instructions in the README. It runs on the device with no backend at all, so anyone can clone it and try it in a browser in a couple of minutes.

</details>

**Video (0:40):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S8ug0gp1BQs

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/S8ug0gp1BQs/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S8ug0gp1BQs)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/192/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/192/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/193/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/193/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/194/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/194/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/195/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/195/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/196/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/196/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/197/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/422/197/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

A craving is a pop-up ad from your brain. You don't have to click it.

That line is the whole app. Cravings for nicotine usually pass in three to five minutes. The hard part isn't knowing that, it's getting through those five minutes at 11pm when the vape is right there.

Most quit apps do one of two things. Either they are a streak counter that resets to zero the first time you slipped (which is exactly when you need the app most), or they are soft, pastel meditation apps full of breathing circles and "you've got this!" Neither feels like something a young person trying to stop vaping would actually open.

I wanted something that:

- does the five minutes with you, right when the craving hits

- never punishes you for a slip

- gives you a reason to open it every day that isn't guilt

That last one is where the Tamagotchi came from.

**What it does**

The craving timer, free forever. Hit the big button when a craving hits and ride out a 5:00 timer. There are three small distraction games built in (pop-ups, smash, hold) and quick notes on what actually helps, like gum, a straw or a walk. When it's done, the app counts it: one more craving outlasted. This is never behind a paywall and no ad ever goes near it.

Slips without a lecture. Caved? Log it. The tally never resets. One bad hour shouldn't erase three good weeks, and an app that wipes your progress teaches you to stop logging.

Money you kept. Tell it what your habit costs, and it shows you what you haven't spent, from your own numbers. Every figure carries a ≈, because it's an estimate and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

A companion that can't die. Quitting leaves a hole: freed money, freed time, freed headspace. In ReinUp, something moves into it. You get an egg, it hatches as you keep checking in, and it becomes Pip, Boo or Nib, a little pixel creature with its own room, decor, mini games and a map to build on. It's a Tamagotchi with everything stressful removed. It can't starve, it can't be neglected and it never asks you for anything.

Gems come from logging your day, measured against your own baseline, so a pack a day smoker doesn't earn more than a light vaper for the same effort. You get paid for showing up, not for how bad your habit was.

NIC. The craving itself, as a grumpy, quarantined pixel virus. He's the villain. He loses.

And the rest: stats, a taper plan whose line only ever moves down, awards, a shareable streak card, and an iOS home screen widget.

Everything stays on your phone. There's no account and no server. Settings has a one tap delete, and the app links to the free 1-800-QUIT-NOW quitline. ReinUp is a habit tracker, not a medical device, and it says so.

**How it makes money**

ReinUp Plus through RevenueCat, on one plus entitlement with two packages:

Weekly
$6.99 a week

Lifetime
$89.99 once

I priced it weekly because a week is how people quitting nicotine think about money. They know exactly what a week of pouches costs. So the paywall doesn't say "only $6.99!", it compares Plus to their own habit: "about a fifth of what you're burning." And there's a lifetime option for people who want to pay once and stop thinking about it.

The rule I set for Plus: it sells depth, never speed. The companion grows at exactly the same rate for free and paid users. A recovery app that sells a faster recovery is selling the wrong thing. Plus gets you every habit tracked instead of just your main one, your whole history, patterns by trigger and time of day, monthly receipts, your own lines in the craving flow, all three widgets, choosing which creature is in your egg, and the full map for its room.

All billing lives in one file, src/billing/purchases.ts, with a web twin so the whole app still runs in a browser. The prices on the paywall always come from the store through RevenueCat, so nobody in Tokyo gets quoted dollars.

**How I built it**

- Expo and React Native in TypeScript.

- An append only event log in SQLite. Nothing is ever edited or deleted (except when you wipe everything). Every number on screen, from the tally to the gems to the companion's growth, is calculated from that log. It's why "the tally never resets" is a rule in the code and not a promise in the copy.

- Money is stored in whole cents, never floats.

- A Swift widget built with @bacons/apple-targets.

- 64 tests covering money, awards, the gem economy and the projections.

- The App Store screenshots and the app icon are generated by scripts from the app's own drawing code, so they can't drift away from what the app really looks like.

**Challenges I ran into**

- App Review. My first build was rejected because the binary included Apple's tracking prompt, and the reviewer could never make it appear. It only showed up inside the ad flow, and in TestFlight the ad flow never started. The ad account was also having issues, so I made a call: ReinUp 1.0 ships with no ads at all and no tracking. Plus is the only way it makes money.

- Fairness in the economy. My first version paid gems for dollars saved, which quietly rewarded people for having been heavier smokers. It also counted "no slip logged" as a clean day, so deleting the app looked like a perfect record. I rebuilt it so you earn relative to your own baseline, and only by actually checking in.

- Tone. Making it funny without making fun of anyone. The rule became: dry text, delighted pixels. The companion never speaks, the narrator is deadpan, and all the warmth comes from the sprite hopping when you open the app.

**Accomplishments I'm proud of**

- The craving timer really works as a five minute tool, and it's free for everyone, forever.

- A companion system that gives people a reason to come back without any guilt, streak loss or pressure.

- An honest paywall that prices Plus against the user's own habit.

**What I learned**

Tiny design rules make the product. "The tally never resets", "every dollar carries a ≈", "the companion never speaks": each one took five minutes to write and changed dozens of decisions.

**What's next for ReinUp**

- Get through App Review and launch on iOS, then Android

- More lands to build on for the companion

- Home screen quick actions to start the craving timer in one tap

**Why open source**

I'm a student at NUST in Pakistan, and I'm submitting ReinUp to the Next Gen track as an open source project. The whole app is on GitHub under MIT with setup instructions, and it runs in a browser with npm run web if you want to try the craving timer yourself.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**RiderMate 2.0**

**AI-Powered Smart Mobility, Rider Safety & Assistance Platform**

Motorcycle riders often depend on multiple disconnected applications for navigation, ride tracking, emergency assistance, vehicle maintenance, weather, memories, and rider communities.

We wanted to build something different: a single motorcycle-focused companion that brings these experiences together while remaining useful when connectivity is unreliable.

That idea became RiderMate 2.0.

**The Problem**

A motorcycle journey involves much more than navigation.

Before and during a ride, riders may need to:

- Check their route

- Monitor their ride

- Access emergency assistance

- Keep track of their motorcycle

- Remember insurance and maintenance information

- Check weather conditions

- Record memorable journeys

- Connect with other riders

- Understand their riding and safety patterns

These experiences are normally spread across different applications.

For a rider, that creates unnecessary friction.

RiderMate was designed around one question:

What if a motorcycle rider could have one intelligent companion for the entire journey?

**Our Solution**

RiderMate 2.0 is an Android-first, offline-first motorcycle companion that combines rider safety, mobility, vehicle management and community features into one application.

The platform brings together:

**🛡️ Rider Safety**

A dedicated Safety Center provides access to safety-focused functionality and emergency workflows, including SOS assistance.

**🚨 Emergency SOS**

RiderMate provides an accessible emergency workflow designed to help riders initiate assistance when they need it.

Safety-critical functionality is kept separate from premium functionality so that essential emergency capabilities are not dependent on a subscription.

**🗺️ Ride Tracking & Navigation**

Riders can track journeys using GPS and maintain ride information locally.

The offline-first architecture allows important ride information to remain available even when network connectivity is unreliable.

**🤖 AI Safety Assistance**

RiderMate incorporates AI-assisted safety functionality to provide riders with contextual guidance and safety-oriented insights.

**🏍️ Motorcycle Garage**

The Garage organizes motorcycle information in one place.

It is designed to help riders keep track of their vehicle, documents, maintenance and related information.

**🔧 Vehicle Intelligence**

RiderMate brings vehicle management into the riding experience, including maintenance-related information and reminders for documents such as insurance and PUC.

**🏆 Safety Points**

The application includes a safety-points system intended to encourage traffic-rule awareness and safer riding behavior.

The idea is to make safety more visible instead of treating every ride as only a distance or speed measurement.

**🌦️ Weather**

Weather information is integrated into the rider experience so environmental conditions can be considered alongside a journey.

**📸 Ride Memories**

Riders can create memories from their journeys using photos and ride/location information.

The Memories system follows the same offline-first philosophy, allowing riders to capture experiences without depending entirely on network connectivity.

**👥 Rider Community**

RiderMate also provides social functionality for riders.

The platform is designed around rider-to-rider interaction, posts, friends, communities and group-oriented riding experiences.

**Offline-First by Design**

One of the central architectural decisions behind RiderMate is offline-first development.

Motorcyclists frequently travel through areas where connectivity may be weak or unavailable.

Instead of assuming that every action requires a permanent internet connection, RiderMate stores important information locally and synchronizes with cloud services when connectivity becomes available.

The application uses local SQLite storage alongside cloud APIs and synchronization services.

This approach makes the application more resilient during real-world rides.

**Technology**

RiderMate 2.0 is primarily built with:

**Mobile**

- Flutter

- Dart

- Android

- SQLite

- GPS/location services

- Camera/gallery integration

**Backend & Cloud**

- FastAPI

- Python

- REST APIs

- Microsoft Azure

- Cloud storage

- Application monitoring

**Intelligence**

- AI-assisted safety functionality

- Ride intelligence

- Safety scoring

- Traffic-rule points

**Monetization**

For Shipaton, RiderMate uses RevenueCat to manage the premium subscription experience, including products, entitlements and offerings.

The premium layer is designed around optional advanced functionality while keeping essential rider safety functionality accessible.

**Why RevenueCat?**

RiderMate is designed as a long-term product rather than only a prototype.

RevenueCat gives us a way to experiment with monetization without building and maintaining separate purchase-management logic for the application.

The architecture separates:

Product → Entitlement → Rider access

This allows the application to evolve its pricing and package structure while keeping the feature-access logic independent from individual store product identifiers.

For example, RiderMate can offer a Pro tier containing advanced ride intelligence, AI assistance, advanced analytics and expanded rider features.

The goal is to build a sustainable product while keeping safety-related functionality accessible.

**How We Built It**

The project was developed as a modular Flutter application.

The mobile application contains independent functional areas for authentication, rides, safety, memories, vehicle management, weather, community and cloud synchronization.

SQLite provides local persistence while the backend provides cloud-connected functionality.

The architecture was designed so that important operations can continue locally and synchronize later.

This became particularly important when working on ride tracking and memories because those features should not stop functioning simply because a rider temporarily loses connectivity.

**Challenges**

**1. Offline Synchronization**

Designing an application that behaves correctly both online and offline was one of the biggest technical challenges.

Data has to remain useful locally while eventually synchronizing with cloud services without creating inconsistent states or duplicate operations.

**2. Integrating Many Features**

RiderMate combines many different domains:

- GPS

- Safety

- Emergency workflows

- Vehicle management

- Weather

- AI

- Social functionality

- Cloud synchronization

- Local databases

The challenge was not simply implementing each feature independently, but making them work together as one coherent application.

**3. Safety-Critical UX**

Emergency features require a different design mindset from ordinary application features.

We focused on making important safety actions easy to discover and reducing unnecessary interaction during critical situations.

**4. Android Testing**

We tested the application through Android builds and emulator workflows, paying particular attention to authentication, local database behavior, GPS workflows, UI layout, offline behavior and application stability.

**What We Learned**

Building RiderMate taught us that a large application is ultimately a systems-integration problem.

A feature may work perfectly on its own but still fail when combined with authentication, local storage, synchronization, navigation and other modules.

We learned to think about:

- Offline states

- Error recovery

- Data synchronization

- User isolation

- API reliability

- Mobile UX

- Cloud architecture

- Subscription access

- Real-world testing

We also learned that product design and engineering have to evolve together.

**What Makes RiderMate Different**

RiderMate is not intended to be just another navigation application.

It is designed around the complete motorcycle journey:

Prepare → Ride → Stay Safe → Manage → Remember → Connect

The application combines these stages into a single rider-focused experience.

**What's Next**

The current platform provides the foundation for a larger smart-mobility ecosystem.

Future development includes:

- More advanced offline navigation

- Richer AI ride assistance

- Real-time group riding

- Improved rider-to-rider communication

- Advanced ride analytics

- Deeper vehicle intelligence

- Expanded cloud synchronization

- Smarter safety recommendations

**Our Vision**

We want RiderMate to become a digital companion for motorcycle riders rather than another isolated utility.

A rider should be able to start a journey, understand their environment, manage their motorcycle, respond to emergencies, remember their experiences and connect with other riders from one platform.

RiderMate 2.0 — one companion for the entire ride.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every software engineer, researcher, and creative builder shares an unspoken frustration: the "save later" cemetery.

Throughout our day, creative epiphanies strike unpredictably. We record hurried voice memos while walking, snap screenshots of elegant architecture diagrams, and bookmark technical discussions across Twitter/X, GitHub, and browser tabs. But days later, these insights sit disconnected in camera rolls and notes apps, rotting away. The friction between chaotic creative inspiration and disciplined engineering execution is massive: scattered thoughts almost never turn into shipped products.

Existing note-taking tools are passive silos. They force users into tedious manual filing, tagging, and folder hierarchies. We asked ourselves:

What if your second brain wasn’t just a digital filing cabinet, but an active, privacy-preserving thinking partner that works in the background to weave scattered research fragments into structured, executable build plans?

This question gave birth to MindMesh AI: a local-first, privacy-native cognitive copilot engineered to eliminate capture friction and automatically synthesize disparate research fragments into production-ready PRDs, database schemas, and engineering blueprints.

**What it does**

MindMesh AI transforms chaotic, multi-modal research into actionable, structured engineering plans through four core capabilities:

- Zero-Friction Multi-Modal Capture: Ingests thoughts from any source in seconds—Whisper voice memos, camera viewfinder captures, screenshots, text snippets, and native Android Share Sheet intents from Twitter/X, Instagram, and Chrome.

- Local-First SQLite Vault: Stores every note, memory, and embedding inside an encrypted on-device SQLite database. MindMesh guarantees complete data sovereignty with zero tracking, zero telemetry, and a Bring-Your-Own-Key (BYOK) architecture for Gemini and Groq APIs.

- The Serendipity Engine: Periodically scans your vector memory graph in the background to detect hidden semantic relationships between memories created weeks or months apart. When strong thematic correlations are detected, it proactively drafts an end-to-end Product Requirements Document (PRD) with architecture schemas and implementation task lists.

- Universal Markdown & Obsidian Bridge: Generates deterministic Markdown files (YYYY-MM-DD-[topic-slug].md) with bidirectional [[wikilinks]] that mirror automatically to your desktop for use in Obsidian, Notion, and VS Code.

- Native RevenueCat Monetization: Features a quiet, transparent subscription model offering a 7-day free trial, flexible monthly/annual tiers, single-tap cross-device entitlement restoration, and zero hard-paywall lockout.

**How we built it**

MindMesh AI is engineered with a hybrid edge-first topology: an on-device React Native client coupled with encrypted local storage, client-side vector search, a secure serverless AI proxy, and native RevenueCat monetization.

**1. Client & Ingestion Pipeline**

- Framework: React Native 0.86 with Expo 57 and Expo Router.

- Audio Pipeline: expo-audio records high-fidelity voice notes, processed via local transcription and fast serverless Whisper pipelines.

- Vision & Media Pipeline: Full-screen camera viewfinder (expo-camera) and asset picker (expo-image-picker) feeding an OCR and visual feature extraction engine.

- Android Share Sheet Integration: Native Android intent filters capturing SEND and SEND_MULTIPLE intents across text, images, and URLs (*/*).

- Storage Engine: High-performance local database via expo-sqlite, storing memories, metadata, tags, and embeddings entirely on the user's hardware.

**2. The Serendipity Engine & Mathematical Formulation**

Rather than relying on basic keyword searches, MindMesh implements a vector clustering model to uncover latent connections between chronologically distant memories.

The similarity between memory vectors u and v is evaluated using cosine similarity:

Sim(u, v) = (u · v) / (‖u‖₂ ‖v‖₂)

Equivalently:

Sim(u, v) = Σᵢ₌₁ᵈ uᵢvᵢ / (√(Σᵢ₌₁ᵈ uᵢ²) × √(Σᵢ₌₁ᵈ vᵢ²))

To balance semantic relevance with unexpected discovery (preventing redundant clustering), we define our Serendipity Convergence Score S(u, v, Δt) as a function of semantic proximity and temporal distance:

Δt = |tᵤ − tᵥ|

S(u, v, Δt) = Sim(u, v) × [1 + λ ln(1 + Δt / τ)]

where τ is a temporal scaling baseline (e.g., 7 days) and λ ∈ [0.1, 0.3] rewards serendipitous cross-pollination between older memories and fresh ideas.

When candidate clusters exceed a convergence threshold θ₍conv₎, MindMesh triggers the synthesis pipeline to compile the connected memories into an actionable engineering PRD.

**3. RevenueCat Subscription Monetization**

We integrated RevenueCat (react-native-purchases) to establish a clean indie software business model:

- Two-Tier Architecture:

- Community Tier ($0/forever): Full local SQLite autonomy, offline access, standard Markdown export, BYOK keys, and 3 weekly synthesis scans.

- MindMesh Pro ($4.16/mo billed annually or $9.99/mo): Unlimited continuous background Serendipity convergence, automated multi-device vault synchronization, priority multi-modal synthesis, and restorable cross-device entitlements.

- Entitlement State Verification: Entitlement states are cached locally and verified asynchronously:

AccessState =

- PRO_UNLOCKED, if entitlements["pro"].isActive = true

- COMMUNITY, otherwise

- Aesthetics: Styled with a quiet obsidian canvas (#030308) and signature Burgundy pop accent (#8B1A2B / #B8334F), completely free of emojis and distracting visual noise.

**4. Companion Web Platform**

- Deployed live on Vercel at https://mindsmeshai.vercel.app using Next.js 16 (Turbopack), Tailwind CSS, and GSAP ScrollTrigger for interactive landing showcase and APK distribution.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Local-First Performance vs. Mobile Battery:
Executing semantic comparisons across hundreds of stored memory fragments without introducing UI lag or battery drain required disciplined optimization. We solved this by precomputing dense vector embeddings during initial capture and executing similarity scans in batched background workers during device idle states.

- Handling Dynamic Android Share Sheet Data:
Social media apps pass wildly inconsistent data through Android Share Intents. Some apps send raw bitmaps, others pass nested text bundles with tracking parameters, and others send raw HTML. We engineered an enrichment pipeline with headless scraper fallbacks to reliably extract clean metadata, OpenGraph tags, and media URLs.

- Purging Visual Fluff & Unifying Aesthetics:
Early iterations suffered from fragmented style tokens, which caused blinding white modal flashes in dark environments. We audited and purged all legacy styles, refactoring both the React Native paywall and Next.js web application to a unified dark design system with Burgundy accents and zero circular artifacts.

- Designing a Non-Hostile Monetization UX:
We refused to implement predatory paywalls that hold user data hostage. Designing an ethical monetization UX meant keeping all stored notes, SQLite databases, and standard exports 100% free and offline forever, while reserving continuous background synthesis and multi-device sync for RevenueCat Pro subscribers.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Complete Edge Autonomy: Built an AI-powered cognitive second brain that operates entirely offline on local SQLite storage without forcing users to upload their private notes to third-party databases.

- Production-Grade RevenueCat Integration: Shipped a seamless subscription system with 7-day trials, restorable entitlements, and offline entitlement caching on native Android.

- Deterministic PRD Synthesis: Successfully demonstrated an AI pipeline that doesn't just summarize notes, but transforms disconnected voice memos and UI screenshots into structured engineering blueprints with database schemas and actionable checklists.

- Minimalist Design Discipline: Created an obsidian-dark luxury aesthetic with a signature Burgundy accent, strictly adhering to high-contrast typography, zero emojis, and zero visual clutter.

- Full Stack Ship: Completed the native Android APK (v0.1.5, versionCode: 3), the companion Next.js web application live on Vercel, and the Express AI proxy backend.

**What we learned**

- Local-First is the Future of Personal AI: Users are deeply protective of their raw thoughts, unreleased project ideas, and personal research. By keeping storage on-device in SQLite and enabling BYOK, users feel safe entrusting MindMesh with their most ambitious plans.

- RevenueCat Accelerates Developer Velocity: Integrating in-app purchases natively on Android can take weeks of boilerplate handling billing client states, receipt validation, and edge-case network recovery. RevenueCat abstracted this into concise SDK calls (Purchases.purchasePackage(), Purchases.restorePurchases()), allowing us to focus on building the core Serendipity Engine.

- Serendipity Beats Hoarding: The true value of an AI second brain isn't in saving more content—it's in synthesizing what you've already captured into something you can actually build and ship.

**What's next for Mind Mesh AI**

- Local On-Device SLM Ingestion: Integrate quantized on-device small language models (such as Gemma 2B or Llama 3.2 1B via ExecuTorch / ONNX Runtime) to perform synthesis without needing any cloud API calls.

- Bidirectional Obsidian Vault Sync: Release an official MindMesh Obsidian Community Plugin to allow live two-way sync between your mobile SQLite vault and desktop Obsidian workspaces.

- Voice-First Interactive Brainstorming: Expand voice memo capture into conversational voice threads, allowing builders to interrogate their synthesized PRDs while driving or commuting.

- Cross-Platform iOS & Desktop Release: Bring MindMesh's RevenueCat subscription architecture and local SQLite vault to iOS and macOS with synchronized universal purchases.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Modern consumer software has perfected the science of behavioral extraction. Algorithms intentionally exploit dopamine loops, pulling young minds and adults into silent, corrosive struggles like compulsive pornography consumption, body dysmorphia fueled by altered beauty standards, late-night binge food cravings, and hours wasted in hypnotic doomscrolling. 

Most blocking applications treat users like inmates because they impose rigid, punitive restrictions, flash aggressive shame banners, or lock essential mental wellness tools behind predatory subscriptions during a user's most vulnerable moments.

As a Computer Science student at University of the People (UoPeople) in Pasadena, California, I set out to build an open-source sanctuary that restores human agency. Aurora App inverts the industry paradigm because it treats users with dignity, operates on genuine neurobiology, provides an active physical exit into the real world, and ensures that crisis intervention is 100% free forever through an ethical RevenueCat patron model.

**What it does**

Aurora App is a privacy-first mobile companion engineered to neutralize behavioral compulsions and reconnect users with the physical world:

- Neural Clarity Sphere (Neurobiological Recovery Arc): 
Rather than arbitrary streaks, the native SVG Clarity Sphere visualizes recovery through five clinical neurochemical phases:

- Phase I (Days 1–3): Neurochemical reset and breaking craving loops.

- Phase II (Days 4–14): Dopamine D2 receptor upregulation and restorative REM sleep stabilization.

- Phase III (Days 15–45): Prefrontal cortex activation and executive control consolidation.

- Phase IV (Days 46–90): Deepened neuroplasticity and attentional autonomy.

- Phase V (Day 90+): Total sovereign mastery.

- Multi-Vector Habit Shield:
An on-device defense system targeting three modern behavioral traps:

- Adult & Pornography Filter: Real-time domain interception and safe-search enforcement to protect dopamine receptor baseline.

- Doomscrolling & Infinite Feed Friction: Deliberate 5-second intercept delays that disrupt mindless algorithmic loops on social feeds.

- Late-Night Binge Eating & Food Craving Lock: Active time-window protection against compulsive midnight delivery apps.

- Anti-Impulsive Deliberate Friction:
Neuroscience demonstrates that chemical craving spikes peak between 3 to 5 minutes. To eliminate impulse overrides, disabling any shield requires the user to manually type out their core personal commitment (e.g., "I deserve mental peace and respect in my daily life"). This intentional friction engages the rational prefrontal cortex and halts knee-jerk relapses.

- Mindful Grounding & Urge Interceptor (SOS):
When an acute urge strikes, a single tactile tap launches an immediate intervention. Instead of trapping the user in front of the screen, Aurora App provides a Mindfulness & Grounding Observation Mission where users are guided to step onto a balcony, look out a window, or take a 3-minute walk, transitioning directly into the live map to discover quiet havens or contribute a calm community signal.

- 50-Meter Privacy-Quantized Live Map (Mapbox):
Streets should be spaces for physical presence. Aurora App features a live map of community-reported safe havens, well-lit pedestrian corridors, and caution zones. Coordinates are mathematically quantized to a 50-meter grid on Cloudflare D1 to achieve zero exact GPS tracking, zero follower graphs, and zero surveillance.

- RevenueCat Ethical Patron Commons:
All core sobriety metrics, urge shields, and crisis tools remain completely free forever. Users who wish to subsidize server costs and map nodes can voluntarily become Guardian or Pioneer Patrons via RevenueCat. Judges can unlock the entire patron experience with the bypass code SHIPATON2026. We believe in disruptive business models: providing transformative value first and requesting voluntary patronage after users experience real changes in their lives is the path forward.

**How we built it**

- Multiplatform Architecture: Built on a unified codebase targeting iOS, iPadOS, and Android powered by React Native (0.86) and Expo (SDK 57) in TypeScript strict mode.

- Subscription & Monetization Engine: Powered by the RevenueCat SDK (react-native-purchases), seamlessly bridging Apple StoreKit 2 on iOS and Google Play Billing on Android to orchestrate Guardian memberships and Pioneer passes with instant entitlement verification.

- On-Device Interception: Custom mobile accessibility and native intent interception that operates strictly locally on the device with zero outbound network egress.

- Spatial & Urban Safety Engine: High-performance Mapbox GL rendering with custom dark obsidian vector tiles, bound directly to native gesture engines and Cloudflare D1 spatial tables with 50-meter bounding boxes.

- Design System: Hand-crafted Obsidian Dark Paper Brutalism (#08070C and #130F1E backgrounds, crisp 1px borders, and calming #42C7F5 Zima blue accents), strictly adhering to an anti-AI-slop standard.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Balancing Anti-Impulse Friction with Accessibility: Building an interceptor that stops relapses without frustrating users required designing the "Deliberate Friction" paradigm—requiring typed personal values instead of arbitrary puzzles.

- Zero-Knowledge Urban Safety: Ensuring community signals provided meaningful street context without ever leaking individual user coordinates required strict client-side and server-side spatial quantization down to 50-meter discrete buckets.

- Ethical Monetization: Building a paywall that never coerces or gatekeeps someone experiencing an urge. RevenueCat's flexible Offerings architecture allowed us to separate emergency utilities from voluntary patron support.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Complete Open-Source Multiplatform Client: Released publicly on GitHub under the MIT License with a signed, production-ready Android APK and native iOS parity.

- Zero AI-Slop Design Language: A dignified, premium dark aesthetic engineered to soothe the nervous system rather than stimulate it.

- True On-Device Privacy: 100% of habit logs, streak calculations, and personal commitments remain exclusively on the user's phone.

**What we learned**

Building Aurora App reinforced that recovery cannot happen in isolation from physical reality. Digital self-regulation is intrinsically tied to real-world movement and community presence. By pairing dopamine habit shields with a live neighborhood safety map, we turn digital defense into real-world peace of mind.

**What's next for Aurora App**

- Expanding cross-platform Bluetooth low-energy (BLE) walking beacons for physical companion walks.

- Offline-first neural tracking syncing across local companion browsers (Orion by Aurora App).

- Expanding local safety networks across student campuses globally.

## 512. Inventivus

**Video (1:14):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bvLGwtVjaAM

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/bvLGwtVjaAM/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bvLGwtVjaAM)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/905/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/905/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/923/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/923/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/924/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/924/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

From kindergarten, children are asked what they want to be when they grow up. While answers tend to be simple but broad at first—police officer, firefighter, rescue worker, or pilot—children are eventually told to be realistic and specialize in one thing. Such specialization provides focus, but only at the cost of siloing expertise and preventing cooperation.

Bring this same attitude into the engineering world, and you can kill entire projects. This is the root of the problem we set out to solve: How do we enable individual expertise while maintaining all parts as elements of a single, cohesive system?

But why? Why would we spend so much time building this? Because we aren't approaching this problem from the outside. We are engineers ourselves. We founded our own engineering team and built real machines, and we have personally experienced projects going through iteration after iteration only to fail because one person had a measurement wrong and nobody caught it. We've seen firsthand how difficult it is to keep an entire team together when everyone is working on different parts of the same machine.

Inventivus came from that experience. We built it because we wanted the tools we needed to build better machines ourselves.

**What it does**

Inventivus provides each person or engineer within a system with a real-time, comprehensive picture of the total system.

One could think of this as every soldier, from the basic infantry fighter to the unit leader, having complete access to a full, real-time picture of the battle—or project—as it unfolds.

Built on an AI backend system called Athena, Inventivus maintains an evolving model of an entire project. Yet this is fundamentally different from simply storing project information.

Instead of treating every CAD file, code file, measurement, design decision, and conversation as separate pieces of information, Athena connects them into a model of the machine itself. It understands not only what each piece contains, but how those pieces relate to one another and how changes propagate through the system.

When an engineer changes something, Athena can reason about that change in the context of the entire project. It can identify inconsistent dimensions, conflicting components, missing information, violated requirements, or changes that no longer make sense based on earlier decisions.

If something is wrong, or Athena has a suggestion or idea, Athena can bring it to the team's attention while they are working, help determine what needs to change, and update the project's shared context.

If the team wants to try something new, Athena can help them reason through the idea, prototype it, and develop it alongside the rest of the machine.

The goal isn't to replace engineers. It's to make sure engineers have the full context they need to do their jobs, regardless of their specialization, and to stop the constant checking of scattered files and fragmented context.

An electrical engineer should be able to understand how their changes affect the mechanical system. Inventivus gives the entire team a shared understanding of what they are building, so the project doesn't slowly drift apart as it evolves.

**How we built it**

We built Inventivus entirely from the ground up using an Electron JS, Typescript, CSS, and HTML. 

All of the programming was done completely by hand, by just me. Debugging of the code and de-spagghetifying of the code was partially done by services such as Claude Code, but 99% of the coding was done by hand. 

The backend is an agentic harness called Athena that can be run with local models, or through the Inventivus AI provider system. This allows Athena to reason about relationships between different parts of the project. When one component or decision changes, the system can consider how that change affects the rest of the machine rather than treating it as an isolated modification. 

Workspace file paths are stored in the Inventivus database/context, enabling the Athena system to access them at any given time. All user data as well as project data is stored locally on the machine, in the paths that they normally would be stored at unless otherwise specified, to avoid overcrowding the Inventivus app files. 

The system is designed around the workflow we experienced while building our own machines. Instead of forcing engineers to constantly search through different files, ask other team members for context, or manually check whether a change has caused problems elsewhere, Inventivus aims to maintain that context continuously.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge was that engineering projects are inherently interconnected.

A single measurement can affect a component, which can affect another component, which can affect a requirement, which can ultimately affect the entire machine. Important information also exists in many different forms—from CAD files and code to measurements, design decisions, and conversations.

This meant that simply storing project information wasn't enough. We needed to think about how all of that information relates to everything else and how those relationships change as a project evolves.

Another challenge was making sure Inventivus solved a real engineering problem rather than becoming another productivity application. We wanted the system to be built around problems we had actually experienced ourselves.

We've seen firsthand how a small mistake or missing piece of context can survive through multiple iterations and eventually cause an entire prototype to fail. Designing around that experience became one of the central challenges—and motivations—behind Inventivus.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We're proud that Inventivus came directly from our own experience as engineers.

We didn't start by trying to make another productivity app or chase quick cash. We started by building our own engineering team and real machines, and we experienced the problems of fragmented information ourselves.

We're also proud of the concept behind Athena: an AI system that doesn't simply store or retrieve information about a machine, but builds an evolving understanding of the machine itself and the relationships between its components. Athena was particularly difficult to build, due to things like low model context, and live speak, which is difficult to implement. 

Most importantly, we're proud of the fact that the app has come to fruition at all. We accomplished something incredibly difficult that could have a real positive impact on a community that we love. 

**What we learned**

We learned that engineering problems are rarely isolated.

A decision made by one person can have consequences for dozens of other parts of a system, even when those consequences aren't immediately obvious. Specialization is necessary, but specialization without shared context can cause teams to lose sight of the system as a whole.

We also learned that AI becomes significantly more useful it's not in your way, and not there to Athena isn't intended to simply answer questions about a project. Its purpose is to understand how the project's information connects, how those relationships evolve, and what those changes mean for the rest of the system.

Most importantly, we learned the value of building around problems that have a real impact. Inventivus exists because we encountered this problem ourselves, and using it with our team has shown us how much of a positive impact a couple engineers with a dream can have. 

**What's next for Inventivus**

Our goal is to continue developing Inventivus into a system that can even better support an engineering team throughout the entire process of creating a machine.

We want Athena to become increasingly capable of understanding project context, identifying problems before they become failures, helping engineers explore new ideas, and assisting teams as they prototype and iterate.

Ultimately, we want Inventivus to make it possible for engineers to specialize without becoming isolated. We want to scale Inventivus to a real product that other engineers around the world can use to their benifit as we did. 

We aren't trying to replace engineers. We're building a system that gives them the context they need to work together.

Inventivus is built by engineers, for engineers—to help teams build better, build faster, and turn ideas into real machines that change the world.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I wanted to make a game around one small moment: “oh no—oh no—saved it.” A tiny, very serious worker
pushes a coffee cup much too big for him. Hold to accelerate; release to brake. That was the starting
point. The difficult part was making the coffee something you could learn to control, rather than
something you watched while hoping it would behave.

**What it does**

Don’t Spill is a portrait arcade game for iPhone. Deliver before the customer leaves, collect tips,
and keep going through Old Town, the Market, Uptown and the Docks. Acceleration, braking and pavement
disturb the coffee. One drop ends the run. Routes change between attempts, but the liquid follows
consistent rules.

The street also has a sense of humour. A cat can join the trolley. An outrageously long limousine
passes through Uptown. At the Docks, a seagull can interrupt work with a little pixel-art battle.

**How I built it**

I developed the game iteratively with Claude and Codex, using plain JavaScript, Canvas and Web Audio,
then packaged it for iPhone with Capacitor. The simulation runs in fixed steps, and the rendered
coffee surface and spill check share the same underlying state. Recorded playtests and repeatable
scenarios helped compare input strategies and catch regressions.

RevenueCat handles the Regular’s Card: one non-consumable purchase unlocking all ten cosmetic sets,
the character creator and additional colour choices. Sets can also be earned with tips. The card
changes your appearance, never your speed or coffee physics; badge trophies remain earned through play.

**Challenges**

My first concern was that I was only managing speed, not balancing coffee. We tried changes, rejected
a test scene, restored some difficulty, and returned to the problem. When I finally caught myself
watching the wave, it felt like progress. Further tests also exposed a shortcut: repeated quick taps
could be too effective. That sent us back to testing decisions, rather than just increasing difficulty.

**Accomplishments**

The result is a small playable world with a consistent visual identity, absurd interruptions and
customization visible on the actual trolley. The iPhone build has been tested for purchase cancellation,
successful purchase and ownership after offline reopening, and submitted to Apple for review.

**What I learned**

A simple control scheme still needs careful feedback. Automated comparisons can show that inputs
change an outcome; playing on a phone tells me whether I can understand that change. Neither replaces
the other.

**What’s next**

Release, listen to players, and improve the confusing moments they actually encounter. I want to earn
the next addition through playtesting, rather than bury the central idea under more features.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Research Pro**

Research Pro helps a writer keep a claim connected to the passage that supports it—and explain why the claim changed. Reading a paper is only part of research. The harder step is deciding what its evidence allows you to say, then keeping that reasoning available for someone else to question.

The native iOS prototype brings that work into one project: import a selectable-text PDF, locate an exact quotation on a page, connect it to a claim, review potentially overstated wording, and explicitly accept a revision with a reason. Defense Lab asks the writer to explain the evidence and acknowledge a limitation. A readable brief and local archive carry the source, claim history and explanation forward.

Our current demonstration uses Kross et al. (2013), Facebook Use Predicts Declines in Subjective Well-Being in Young Adults, with author/source and Creative Commons Attribution credit. We deliberately enter a false causal claim as test input. The writer returns to page 5, types a narrower claim and reason, previews the change, accepts it, and saves a source-linked defense. These deterministic checks prompt review; they do not decide scientific truth.

The project also holds seven scope/protocol fields and a separately authored manuscript. Three built-in profiles—PLOS ONE Research Article, ICLR 2027 Initial submission and Generic research—check supported rules and render the same saved manuscript. They are partial formatting previews, not certified venue-ready submissions; Generic makes no venue claim. Custom style import is unavailable. The manuscript shown was typed separately, not generated from the repaired claim.

We built on the earlier Research OS/Challa, Research Flight Recorder/Reverie and Mobile V2 foundation. Pranav Reddy Challa supplied native handoffs, UI/publication direction, the export-review and wording patch, and presentation drafts. Aditya Chandran Arvind coordinated product direction, Mac integration, verification, source/evidence packaging and media with Codex assistance. We do not present the inherited foundation as entirely created during this event. This latest pass preserves application source and adds capture drivers, fresh verification and clearer evidence.

The SwiftUI client uses PDFKit and versioned local project records. Its archive retains extracted pages and the original file’s fingerprint, not the original PDF bytes. Candidate 53e32f408d16c5cc6afa4d0230af76fd927853c9 freshly passed 147 native tests, 51 Python tests, six release guards and five selected UI scenarios. Two earlier scope-driver attempts failed and remain disclosed. A separately configured RevenueCat Test Store build passed a zero-charge annual purchase, actual Restore, relaunch, two-project access, and saving/reopening a seven-answer advanced Defense session. That is development Test Store evidence, not Apple production billing.

The remaining gaps are concrete: the readable brief omits Primary outcome and Change policy despite persisting both; legacy Claims & evidence shows zero links while the newer argument workflow holds the repaired claim; a nonfatal frame-dimension warning remains. All recordings are scripted simulator QA, not physical-device or student-outcome validation. The next work is synchronizing those views and exports, completing publication formats, and testing with people on devices.

OpenAI Codex, including verified gpt-6-astra sessions, assisted engineering, testing, review, documentation and media. Other contributors’ historical model use is not fully confirmed. The demonstrated local checks need no runtime generative-model service. The current film is silent and captioned.

</details>
