src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/702/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I had a Garmin watch that gave me plenty of health and activity data, but I did not always know what to do with it. Seeing the numbers was one thing. Knowing how to use them to plan my day was another.

At the same time, I was trying to be more productive. I often asked ChatGPT questions like “What should I do today?” or “What should I do at this time?” But those conversations did not have my health records, calendar or goals. I kept asking for personal guidance without giving the assistant the context it needed.

That led to myTwin: a personal assistant I could talk to, backed by the information I choose to share. I wanted it to help turn available health data, commitments and goals into a practical plan, and then have a real back-and-forth conversation about that plan.

I am a senior undergraduate student at Texas State University, and I built myTwin as a solo project.

**What it does**

myTwin helps you plan your day around your energy, calendar and goals.

Meet Dash, an animated 3D companion who brings that plan to life. He can look energetic, relaxed, tired or exhausted based on your estimated energy. You can check in with how you actually feel, then use that information to make a more realistic plan.

myTwin brings several parts of your day together:

- See your day: View sleep, activity and other available Apple Health records alongside your calendar.

- Understand your energy: Pro shows an estimated energy curve, possible focus times and a recap of your week.

- Plan your goals: Write or speak your goals for today and tomorrow. Pro finds time for them around existing events. You can edit times, mark goals done and carry unfinished work forward.

- Rescue a busy day: Preview a change to a flexible activity, confirm it and undo it if needed. Fixed appointments stay in place.

- Talk to Dash: Pro offers short mentor conversations using Gemini voice. Speak your answer or type it. Dash can use your calendar, goals and available health information to help you choose a next step. Calendar changes suggested in chat require confirmation.

- Stay on track: A Home Screen widget shows your energy estimate and advice. Live Activities show your next event or goal on the Lock Screen and Dynamic Island. Notifications remind you about goals, upcoming events, check-ins and winding down.

A guest demo lets anyone explore both Free and Pro with fictional data, without connecting a watch or sharing personal health records.

**How it was built**

The app is built in Swift with SwiftUI. Apple HealthKit supplies available health records, and EventKit connects the calendar. Dash was modelled, rigged and animated in Blender and runs inside the app using RealityKit. He has four energy states, nine animation clips and moving facial features.

I downloaded the public PMData research dataset and used it to train and evaluate myTwin's energy model. The evaluation used 1,747 labelled days from 16 people, testing each person with a model trained on the other participants. The model compares sleep and related signals with a person's usual patterns. The repository includes the training and evaluation code; the dataset itself is not bundled. Its results are modest: it helps track some day-to-day changes, but it does not improve the accuracy of exact energy scores. The app therefore labels its percentage and hourly curve as estimates.

Regular chat can use Apple's on-device Foundation Models on supported devices. Pro conversations use Gemini Live for replies and spoken audio, while supported on-device speech recognition turns the user's speech into text. Gemini requires permission and internet access.

RevenueCat manages Pro access, subscription offerings, purchases and restores. Free includes the core check-ins, activity, calendar and goal tracking. Pro adds forecasts, goal scheduling, Rescue my day and Gemini conversations. The current development configuration uses RevenueCat Test Store for simulated purchases.

**Challenges**

One challenge was making voice conversations feel natural. The microphone must wait until Dash finishes speaking so he does not hear himself as the user's answer. The conversation also needs to handle pauses, typed replies and ending a session cleanly.

Another challenge was working with incomplete health data. A person may have steps but no sleep records, or may not have enough history for a forecast. myTwin shows what is missing and still allows check-ins and goal tracking.

Calendar changes also needed clear controls. Rescue shows a preview before saving, and chat asks for confirmation. Goal-planning buttons save the plan directly. Keeping those actions clear helps users understand what will happen to their calendar.

The demo and personal Pro experience also needed to match. Tomorrow planning is now available throughout the day, and Pro users can start a conversation without waiting for an automatic check-in or a health forecast.

**What I learned**

I learned that more complex models are not always better. Testing several approaches led me to a small model and a clearer explanation of what its predictions can and cannot mean.

I also learned that voice interfaces need careful turn-taking, not just speech input and output. Demo access and real subscription access also need separate tests: a feature working in a demo does not prove it works for a personal subscriber.

**What is working now**

The project combines a custom animated character, health data, calendar planning, goal tracking, Pro subscriptions and voice or text conversations in one iOS app. The repository includes a full setup guide and screenshots of the features.

Verification includes 90 passing unit tests, app walkthroughs, a personal Pro test using a simulated purchase and Gemini conversations using fictional data. Real-phone microphone behavior, Bluetooth and live Health syncing still need further device checks.

myTwin is a planning and wellness prototype. Its energy estimates are not medical advice or a measurement of your body's battery.

**What is next for myTwin**

I want to publish myTwin on the App Store and turn it into an app people use in their everyday lives. Before launch, I want to finish real-device testing and improve the experience based on feedback. After launch, I plan to market the app, learn what people find useful and keep improving it.

I am also interested in RevenueCat Growth Fund consideration as I work toward launching and growing myTwin.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I always loved improving myseld in running. So when I came across the Shipaton, I thought of building a telemetry engine that would help people like me to improve, while also giving an immersive experience by letting users compete with friends and users across the world for the leaderboard. The aim is to encourage healthy competition in a gamified way. 

**What it does**

The app tracks running, walking, and cycling telemetry across two distinct modes: Casual, which allows pausing and awards XP toward a permanent user Level, and Ranked, an unpauseable competitive mode awarding both XP and Performance Rating (PR).

PR determines competitive tiers across eight-week seasons, culminating in the exclusive Zenith rank for the weekly global top 100. Seasonal tier resets maintain fair competition, while cosmetics like avatars, frames, and profile banners reward milestone achievements. For added engagement, users can form clans to compete collectively, follow custom shared routes, match target paces with Pacer Strategy mode, or challenge opponent replays using Ghost mode.

**How we built it**

We built it from the ground up using:

- Mobile Architecture & UI System: Built with React Native, Expo SDK 57, and Expo Router using a custom tactical "Obsidian Cyberpunk / Tactical HUD" aesthetic. We engineered lightweight, low-overhead custom SVG components (react-native-svg), dynamic radial/linear gradient vignettes, and multi-tier raster badge renderers (Bronze through Zenith) running at a locked 60 FPS.

- High-Frequency GPS & Geodetic Engine: Developed a non-blocking GPS engine using expo-location and expo-task-manager. It uses Haversine spatial calculations, noise-filtering algorithms, and background task queuing to calculate real-time distance, speed, cadence, and altitude splits without battery drain.

- Real-Time Ghost Racing Engine: Created an interpolation engine (GhostEngine) that projects an athlete’s real-time position against previous course records or rival benchmarks, computing dynamic lead/lag time deltas down to the millisecond.

- Adaptive Pacer & Audio Coach: An algorithm-driven pacing engine that calculates real-time split deviations based on selected strategies (Negative Split, Positive Split, Even Split) and broadcasts audio pacing cues and Zone 5 cardiac redline warnings using expo-speech.

- Cloud Backend & Offline-First Persistence: Powered by Supabase PostgreSQL for player profiles, competitive ranked tier divisions, and social contender matchmaking. We implemented an offline-first queue (SyncService) with optimistic UI updates and AsyncStorage caching so athletes can record in zero-connectivity environments.

- Monetization & Entitlement Pipeline: Integrated RevenueCat (react-native-purchases) to manage subscriptions (Performa Pro), featuring a dual-mode pipeline that provides production StoreKit/Play Billing connectivity alongside an instant 1-tap Judge VIP sandbox mode for zero-friction evaluation.

**Challenges we ran into**

- High-Frequency GPS Drift and Battery Throttling: Operating a high-accuracy GPS loop while rendering real-time maps and visual HUDs can quickly heat devices and trigger OS throttling. We solved this by decoupling raw location capture into a background task pipeline and implementing a threshold-based Kalman smoothing algorithm that filters erratic GPS jitter without missing course corners.

- Ghost Interpolation Accuracy: Tracking lead/lag deltas against an asynchronous rival route caused ghost telemetry to jitter when athletes deviated from the exact course line. We resolved this by building an orthogonal projection algorithm that snaps the runner’s coordinate to the closest polyline segment before computing temporal deltas.

- Complex Gamified HUD Performance: Stacking high-resolution raster cosmetics, live gradient overlays, animated telemetry drawers, and map overlays caused layout stutter on lower-end devices. We refactored heavy views to use strict aspect-ratio containers, eliminated negative space with declarative flexbox styling, and memoized SVG gradient defs.

- Subscription Evaluation in Test Environments: Live in-app billing requires merchant bank verification and sandbox tester accounts that external judges cannot easily access. We architected a dual-mode RevenueCat service that supports live SDK calls while offering an automatic, simulated fallback with full entitlement propagation and VIP bypass.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Aesthetic: Moving away from standard, boring white-and-orange fitness trackers to craft an authoritative, gaming-inspired dark obsidian HUD that makes personal fitness feel like a competitive tournament.

- Ghost Racing: Delivering true millisecond-accurate lead/lag feedback in real-time, giving athletes the psychological edge of chasing an actual rival ghost avatar.

- Fluid, Zero-Lag Record Engine: Designing an edge-to-edge tactical dock sheet that unifies sport selection, ranked non-stop mode, pacer strategies, sensor pairing, and start controls into an intuitive, zero-clutter interface.

- Zero-Friction Offline Architecture: Building an offline-first syncing engine where workouts and telemetry are queued locally and synchronized with Supabase cloud databases the moment connection is re-established.

- Resilient Pro Feature Architecture: Providing seamless access to high-tier instruments (Adaptive Pacer, Ghost Mode, Voice Coach) backed by RevenueCat.

**What we learned**

- Mobile Telemetry Demands Extreme Discipline: Real-time spatial tracking leaves no room for unoptimized re-renders. Decoupling mathematical computation (pace smoothing, ghost deltas) from UI rendering state was essential for maintaining battery life and framerate.

- Feedback Psychology Drives Athletic Adherence: Gamifying fitness isn't just about badges; it’s about instant, high-contrast feedback. Real-time visual and audio lead/lag cues push runners to hold their target pace far more effectively than static summary screens.

- The Value of Dual-Track SDK Engineering: Designing third-party service wrappers (like our RevenueCat and Supabase layers) with robust offline fallbacks ensures your application remains completely reliable and testable in any demo, sandbox, or review environment.

**What's next for Performa**

- Live Head-to-Head Multiplayer Sprints: Expanding Ghost Mode into live, synchronized multiplayer matches where athletes in different parts of the world can race simultaneously on mapped courses.

- Direct BLE Sensor Matrix Integration: Adding direct Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) peripheral streaming for continuous heart rate monitors, Stryd foot pods, and power meters with real-time zone analysis.

- Wear OS & Apple Watch Companion Apps: Building standalone smartwatch companion extensions so runners can view ghost deltas and hear audio cues directly from their wrist.

- Community Course Builder: Allowing users to create, verify, and publish ranked community courses with localized leaderboards and seasonal King-of-the-Hill division championships.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Your bike app dies right where the ride gets good. Up a mountain pass, deep in the woods, across a border: the map goes grey, rerouting spins, and search needs a signal you don't have. And the features you actually need are often behind a paywall.

So I built the opposite. Velorki (velo for bike, orki from Orkitec) does everything your ride needs right on your phone, with or without a signal.

**What it does**

- 🗺️ Plan anywhere. Road, gravel, touring or MTB routes, or just ask for "a 60 km loop via the lake".

- ☕ Find stuff offline. Type "water" and get the nearest taps. Cafés, bike shops and campsites work the same way.

- 🔊 Get talked through every turn. Miss one and Velorki gets you back on track.

- ⌚ Heart rate without extra gear. Your Apple Watch is enough, no chest strap needed, and your next turn shows on your wrist.

- 📈 Record every ride. Speed, climbing, splits and heart rate, exported to wherever you like.

Download your region once and all of it works in airplane mode. No account, no ads.

Velorki Plus is the optional upgrade for the online extras:

- ✨ AI route planner: say "40 km, mostly gravel, café stop" and get a route

- 🔄 Strava & RideWithGPS sync

- 🔗 Share routes with a link

**How I built it**

Flutter for iOS and Android, plus a native Apple Watch app. Route calculation normally happens on a server, so I ported BRouter, a proven open-source bike routing engine, to run directly on the phone. It gives exactly the same results as the original.

RevenueCat runs Velorki Plus: the paywall, the free trial, monthly and yearly plans, and restores. A small server checks every Plus request against RevenueCat, so the AI and partner features stay locked unless you're subscribed.

**Challenges**

- Squeezing a routing engine into a phone without changing a single route it produces

- Offline search that finds the nearest water tap in milliseconds, with no server

- Recording that survives whatever iOS and Android do to shut down GPS apps in the background

- Drawing a fair paywall line. If it runs on your phone, it's free; if it needs the cloud, it's Plus.

**What I learned**

With an AI assistant, you can build in weeks what used to take months or years. Velorki went from the first commit to App Store submission in about 2.5 weeks: an iPhone app, an Android app, an Apple Watch app, a website and a server.

The trick is to let the machines check each other:

- Test first, always. Every feature starts as a test. The AI writes the code, and the tests tell us both whether it really works.

- Automate everything. Builds, device tests on Android and iOS, App Store screenshots, the preview video and releases all run on their own.

- Keep the judgement human. The AI does the typing, while I make the calls on design, the product and what "done" means.

**What's next**

Send routes straight to Garmin and Wahoo bike computers, route with no downloaded tiles at all, and launch on Google Play.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**⚠️ Judge Evaluation & Direct Testing**

- Direct Production APK Download: Download MFORMULA v1.0.0 APK

- Source Code Repository: GitHub - jayjunoir/Mformula

- Store Distribution: Configured for Google Play distribution under Package ID com.mformula. Due to account indexing and store review lead times, please use the direct production-signed APK above for instant physical hardware testing.

**Inspiration**

Word puzzles often fall into two camps: passive trivia or repetitive swipe grids. We wanted to build something visceral and mathematically pure: a game inspired by Lewis Carroll’s classic word ladders, reimagined with the high-stakes intensity of a 90s arcade terminal. 

The challenge of MFORMULA is deceptive: transform a 4-letter starting word into a target mission word by altering strictly one letter at a time, where every intermediate step must be a valid English word. To give players a true benchmark of skill, we pitted human intuition against a graph-theoretic shortest-path algorithm to set an optimal "Par" score.

**What It Does**

- Kinetic Word Morph Engine: Enforces strict single-letter Hamming-distance mutations ($$d_H(w_1, w_2) = 1$$), validating every transition against an embedded dictionary of 4,000+ verified 4-letter words.

- Bidirectional BFS Par Solver: Computes the mathematically optimal ladder path between any start and target word in real time, assigning a dynamic "Par" threshold. Players race to match or beat Par.

- Neo-Brutalist Arcade Visuals: Built on an intentional neo-brutalist aesthetic—high-contrast palettes (Obsidian #0A0A0A, Vermilion, Mint #00FF66, and CRT Amber), stark ink borders, and hard drop shadows.

- Physical Error Rejection: Illegal words and dead-end moves trigger multi-frequency kinetic screen shake and high-contrast red perimeter flashes.

- Daily Mission Archives & Celebration Particles: Seeded daily word missions, custom confetti canvas particle physics on completion, and shareable performance receipt cards.

**How We Built It**

- Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) & Jetpack / Compose Multiplatform: Unified the game state engine, graph search algorithm, and UI rendering into a clean, modern multiplatform architecture.

- Coroutines & Asynchronous Processing: Offloaded the dictionary graph traversal and shortest-path computation off the main UI thread to eliminate frame drops.

- Compose Canvas: Built custom renderers for real-time confetti physics and retro CRT scanline overlays.

**Challenges We Faced**

- Graph Search Latency on Mobile: Running uninformed search algorithms across a dense 4,000-word lexicon can easily introduce stutter. We optimized graph traversal by implementing a bidirectional Breadth-First Search (BFS) operating on an indexed letter-bucket graph, cutting pathfinding times down to sub-15ms.

- Release Optimization & Binary Footprint: Ensuring smooth 60fps animations required strict R8 minification, ProGuard rule tuning for Compose runtimes, and stripping unnecessary reflection.

- Neo-Brutalist Polish: Balancing stark, heavy borders with smooth responsive micro-animations on diverse Android screen densities and aspect ratios.

**What We Learned**

- Designing an algorithmic par calculator transforms a simple word game into a tight, competitive tactical puzzle.

- Modern Compose Multiplatform provides incredible flexibility for crafting bespoke, non-standard UI paradigms (neo-brutalism) without needing heavy external UI libraries.

</details>

## 519. Matricula

> Built by a high schooler who couldn't find an honest one. Matricula plans your college list on official federal data.

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/matricula (gallery page 134) · ❤️ 0 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [Ansh Saini](https://devpost.com/87ansh87)
- **GitHub (Try it out):** https://github.com/Ansh87/Matricula
- **Repo check:** public repo · license: MIT · 41 commits · JavaScript · RevenueCat found in code ✅
- **Other links:** https://matricula.up.railway.app/
- **Built with:** capacitor, react, sqlite, vite

**Video (1:45):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yrGVawBeG4A

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/yrGVawBeG4A/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yrGVawBeG4A)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/443/177/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/443/177/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I am a high school student. Last spring I sat down to build my own college list and found that every tool I tried did one of two things: it guessed at my chances with a confident-looking percentage, or it showed me numbers without saying where they came from.

Neither helps when the decision is this expensive. A "42% chance" claims precision nobody has, and a number without a source asks you to trust it blindly.

I also noticed who this hurts most. Families who can pay for private admissions counseling have someone to sort through it for them. Students with limited access to college-planning support are left with dozens of websites and a lot of guesswork.

I wanted a tool that tells the truth, including when the truth is "nobody publishes that," and that any student can use. So I built Matricula.

**What it does**

Matricula builds a college plan from official U.S. data and shows where every number comes from. It covers every college in the U.S. Department of Education's College Scorecard. It runs on the web and as an iPhone app from the same code.

Start with your profile. Enter your GPA, test scores, budget and intended majors, or upload a transcript and resume and let the app read them.

Every college, scored against real data. Any U.S. college in the federal dataset can be searched, matched and scored using live College Scorecard data. That covers admission rate, SAT and ACT ranges, net price, graduation and retention rates, median earnings and median debt. Career outcomes come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook.

See how the score was built. The scoring is rule-based and open. Overall Fit is a weighted blend of six sub-scores:

Sub-score
Weight

Academic
25%

Major and program
25%

Financial
15%

Career and ROI
15%

Outcome
10%

Extracurricular strength
10%

If a college does not publish the data a sub-score needs, that sub-score is left out and the other weights are rebalanced. No college loses points just for reporting less.

Chances are ranges, not percentages. Admission likelihood is worked out separately from fit and always shown as a labeled range: Far Reach, Reach, Target, Likely, Safety, Financial Safety, or Insufficient Data.

Extra detail, checked by hand. Federal data does not say what a college looks for in an applicant. For many colleges, Matricula adds details checked against the college's own published documents. That includes Section C7 of the Common Data Set, where a college rates fourteen admission factors as Very Important, Important, Considered or Not Considered. For example, MIT rates rigor and character as very important and does not consider legacy at all, taken from MIT's own page rather than a forum. Each of these entries records its source link, year, review date and confidence level.

The rest of the process:

- College search across the full federal dataset

- A majors and programs explorer, including minors, honors tracks and research programs

- A career planner built on BLS pay and growth projections

- An Essay Center that tracks every prompt and deadline for each college, with a story bank you can reuse

- An Apply tab with each college's application platform, every deadline type, and what is still left to do

Free and Matricula. Exploring colleges and majors is free, and that includes your first five personalized matches. A $9.99 monthly subscription unlocks the full match list, the AI advisor, the Essay Center, and the Apply tab with its timeline. Premium screens stay visible with a short preview and an Unlock button. The paywall only opens when a student taps Unlock.

Nothing is made up. If a college does not publish a figure, the app shows "Data unavailable" instead of an estimate made to look like a fact.

**How we built it**

Front end. React and Vite. The same app is packaged for iPhone with Capacitor 8. The website and the iPhone app use the same menu, with a bottom tab bar on phones.

Back end. Node and Express, with SQLite through Node's built-in node:sqlite module. There is no native build step, so the project runs after a single npm install. Twenty-seven tables hold profiles, saved lists, programs, essays, timelines and cached responses.

Accounts. Firebase Auth handles sign-in (email, Google on the web, or Guest), and each user's data is kept separate by their Firebase user ID.

Payments with RevenueCat. The iPhone app uses RevenueCat's Capacitor SDK and its Paywall UI. There is one entitlement, matricula, sold through the default offering as one monthly package ($rc_monthly, product monthly, $9.99). I designed the paywall in the RevenueCat dashboard as a Free vs Matricula comparison, so I can change it without rebuilding the app.

The app checks that one entitlement in a single place. When a purchase or restore finishes, the screen updates right away without restarting the app. The RevenueCat customer ID is the student's Firebase user ID, never an email address. Guests get an anonymous ID, and a guest's purchase moves to their account if they sign in later. If RevenueCat cannot load, the free features keep working and premium stays locked.

Keeping data safe. All API keys stay on the server. The app only talks to its own /api/* routes, and responses are cached in SQLite so the app keeps working when an outside data source is slow or limits requests.

**How to try it**

- Website: live at matricula.up.railway.app with every feature open. The paywall only exists in the iPhone app.

- iPhone: Matricula is not on the App Store, since the Next Gen track does not require it. The repository includes a GitHub Actions workflow that builds the iPhone app on a cloud Mac and produces an installable .ipa file. I installed that file on my iPhone with Sideloadly using a free Apple ID, and the demo video was recorded on that build.

- Purchases: in this build, purchases go through RevenueCat's Test Store. Buying, restoring and unlocking all work the way they would in a real release, but no money is charged.

- Building your own copy: you need your own Firebase and RevenueCat test values, added as GitHub settings. No keys are stored in the repository.

Deployment. The website runs on Railway. The iPhone app is built by GitHub Actions.

**Challenges we ran into**

Refusing to guess is harder than guessing. A missing value has to pass cleanly through six sub-scores, the weight rebalancing, the admission categories and the interface. At every one of those steps the easy option is to fill in a default. Getting "Data unavailable" all the way to the screen took more care than the scoring math did.

Official data is messier than it looks. Federal datasets are updated field by field, so one college's figures can come from more than one reporting year. Rather than claim a year I could not confirm, the app labels exactly what it is showing.

Phones work differently. Several libraries that work fine in a browser behave differently inside an iPhone app. Getting sign-in to work reliably on iOS meant changing how the app starts up there.

Testing purchases without a paid developer account. I do not have a paid Apple developer account. To test the full purchase flow on a real iPhone, I build the app in the cloud with GitHub Actions and install it with Sideloadly. Setting that up came much earlier in the project than I expected.

Too many sections. The app grew to sixteen top-level sections before I stopped and cut it to seven. I merged pages that showed the same data three different ways and removed a section that repeated what other tabs already covered.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Every U.S. college, with nothing made up. Any college in the federal dataset can be matched and scored. Every value in the app is labeled Official, Verified, Estimated or Unavailable, from the database through the scoring to the screen.

Common Data Sets read and transcribed by hand, each with a source link, year, review date and confidence level. Not scraped, not generated. I read them.

Scoring you can check. The weights, thresholds and fallback rules are explained inside the app.

A working product. Live on the web, running as an iPhone app from the same code, with subscriptions through RevenueCat and API keys that never reach the browser.

**What we learned**

The honest version of a product is usually harder to build, and more useful. Every shortcut I did not take is a reason someone can rely on it.

Small conveniences can carry big risks. Some of the most important decisions on this project were about what not to build.

Original sources are worth the extra time. Reading Common Data Sets one by one was slow, and it is the part of the app a scraper could not copy.

Removing things helped as much as adding them. Fewer sections and merged pages made the app easier to use.

**What's next for Matricula**

More hand-checked detail. Every college is already covered by federal data. Next, I want to add checked admissions factors, deadlines and requirements for more schools, so students get the same depth wherever they apply.

A tool for the whole family. College decisions are made together, and the app should make that easier than it does now.

An App Store release. Moving from the current test build to a public release.

More of the picture. Better career data outside STEM-heavy fields, and cost and scholarship information tied more closely to the matching.

Reaching the students who need it most. Families who pay for private admissions counseling already get this information. Every student should have it, and that is why I built Matricula this way.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every 43 seconds, a child under five dies of pneumonia. That was about 740,000 children in 2019 (WHO).

The first test a health worker uses is simple: count the child's breaths for one full minute and compare the count with a cut-off for their age. People are bad at it. In a four-country trial, only 8 to 20% of health-worker counts on infants under two months were within two breaths of the true rate (Baker et al., 2019).

Every breath-counting app I found still asks you to tap the screen once per breath. Automated counters are separate hardware. Meanwhile the parent and the health worker already carry a camera.

So I asked: what if the phone could just watch the chest and count?

**What it does**

Breathwise turns any phone camera into a contactless breath counter that follows the WHO method.

- 📷 Point, don't touch. Aim the phone at a sleeping or calm child. Breathwise finds the breathing by itself and highlights the chest in green tiles as it locks on.

- 🫁 Every breath, live. A dot lands on the breathing trace and the phone gives a small vibration for each breath.

- ⏱️ The WHO minute. It counts 60 seconds of clean signal. If the child moves, the clock pauses instead of counting noise.

- 🩺 A clear answer. It applies the WHO IMCI fast-breathing cut-off for the child's age (≥60, ≥50 or ≥40 per minute) and walks through the IMCI danger signs. Any danger sign turns the result into "Seek care now."

- ✋ Human backup. A tap-count mode (the manual WHO method), plus a "tap along" check against the camera.

- 🌍 Built for the field. Spoken guidance, five languages (English, Français, Español, Kiswahili, አማርኛ) and a dark screen that won't wake the child.

- 🔒 Private by design. No account. Video never leaves the phone and is never saved.

**How I built it**

Stack: Expo SDK 57 · React Native 0.86 · VisionCamera 5 (frame output + worklets) · Skia · Reanimated 4 · RevenueCat

The breathing detector is classic signal processing running on the phone in real time. There is no ML model, no server and no training data of children.

- Pixels → 192 numbers. On the camera thread, each frame is shrunk to a 12×16 grid of brightness averages and then released. The video never reaches JavaScript.

- Keep only breathing. Slow exposure drift is divided out, whole-scene movement is detected, and every cell is band-pass filtered to 8–108 breaths/min.

- Cells vote. Every second, each cell's spectrum is computed. Rhythmic cells vote on a rate, with a check against counting a harmonic of the real rhythm.

- One clean trace. The cells that agree are merged with principal component analysis, which also lines up cells that brighten and darken in opposite directions.

- Count like a clinician. A peak tracker counts breaths. The final result checks the count against the spectral rate and the breath-to-breath rate to report a confidence level.

Validation: 13 end-to-end tests render synthetic scenes pixel by pixel and run them through the exact app pipeline.

- ✅ 14 to 75 breaths/min, all within ±2

- ✅ Chest motion under one pixel

- ✅ Heavy low-light sensor noise

- ✅ Bumped mid-count: the clock pauses and recovers

- ✅ No breathing at all: never locks on

**Monetization with RevenueCat**

Counting is free. Forever. The core breath count is never behind a paywall, and health-worker mode is free for life.

Breathwise Family (one entitlement, monthly or yearly, with a 7-day free trial) is for parents on a sick night:

- Unlimited children

- Breathing trends over time

- A PDF report for the doctor

- Sick-night recheck reminders

Every Family plan keeps Breathwise free for community health workers. The people who can pay fund the people who can't.

Built with react-native-purchases: a custom paywall built from Offerings, entitlement-gated features, restore, and Customer Center for self-service management. Tested end to end with RevenueCat Test Store.

**Challenges I ran into**

The core problem is finding a chest that moves one or two pixels under sensor noise, auto-exposure and hand shake. Four fixes made it work:

- Lock the camera. Exposure, focus and white balance are frozen once the shot is framed, so auto-adjustments can't look like breathing.

- Normalize slowly. Correcting brightness frame by frame leaked the breathing rhythm into every cell. A slow running average fixed it.

- Respect irregular breathing. Infants don't breathe like metronomes, so the rhythm window scales with the rate.

- Fail honestly. The detector refuses to lock when nothing is breathing, and tap mode is one tap away.

**Accomplishments I'm proud of**

- A working contactless breath counter in pure TypeScript signal processing, fast enough for the camera thread.

- A result screen that shows its work: the WHO cut-off, danger signs, a confidence level and the raw 60-second breathing trace.

- A business model with a conscience: the core feature is free forever.

**What I learned**

Following the clinical protocol beats adding features. Following the WHO protocol exactly (60 seconds, pause on movement, age cut-offs, danger signs) made Breathwise clearer and more trustworthy than any extra feature did.

**What's next**

- 🏥 A clinical agreement study against expert video-panel counts

- 📴 Offline health-worker mode with supervisor sync

- 🤖 Android tuning

- 🤝 Partnerships with community health programs

Demo note: the measurement footage was recorded in the iOS Simulator with a simulated baby, because the Simulator has no camera. On a phone, Breathwise uses the live camera.
Music: "A Kind of Hope" by Scott Buckley, CC BY 4.0.
Not a medical device. Breathwise counts breaths using WHO guidance; it does not diagnose.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Is it just me, or does everyone have a camera roll full of trips they have almost forgotten ???

From my conversations, I found that many users have lots of photographs and videos in the photo albums lying there. Many of us love to take short videos or photos when we visit places -- some of which never make it back to our memory at all. And nobody has the time to scroll back, pick the good moments, learn a video editor and cut a film. 

I wanted the film to be waiting for you when you open the app, so the trip comes back to life without any work.

**What it does**

Memories: Create Stories finds your trips on your iPhone and turns each one into a short vertical film.

- Finds your trips. It groups your photos and videos by when and where they happened, so a local day out and an overseas holiday each become their own memory.

- Makes a First Cut. Add a few words about the day, and Memories builds a film with music, titles and a story arc. There is no editor to learn.

- AI Director (opt-in). Want another version? You choose the moments you are happy to share, and an AI director proposes a second cut. You compare it with your First Cut and keep the one that feels like you.

- Save it, share it. Save to Photos, or create a 7-day share link so the people who were there can watch, even without the app.

Trying it is free. You can preview and edit the whole reel at no cost, and the free export is a 720p watermarked Memory Preview. We also give all users three full-length 1080p Free Exports per month. And for our more enthusiastic users, a one-time Story Pass unlocks the full-length 1080p story with no watermark.

**How we built it**

- Native SwiftUI iOS app (iOS 17+). Finding trips and picking the best photos run on the iPhone, using PhotoKit and Apple's Vision framework. Text recognised in photos is not kept.

- The film is rendered on the device. A custom AVFoundation renderer handles decoding, transitions, music and H.264 encoding, so a full export needs no cloud.

- AI Director is explicit and opt-in. It goes through a small Cloudflare Worker that keeps the model key off the phone. The Worker sends reduced previews to an OpenAI image-capable model, stores nothing and logs nothing. Every request is verified with Apple App Attest, and the app names the provider and asks permission first.

- Accounts and share links run on Supabase: Sign in with Apple, private Storage, short-lived signed links, hourly cleanup, and an account-deletion function that removes every video the user owns.

- Monetisation runs on RevenueCat.

- Every user gets three full-length 1080p Free Exports per month, so the product is generous by default. For enthusiastic users who want more, version 1 sells the Story Pass, a one-time consumable for each full-story export with no watermark, not a subscription. It fits how people really use the app: a handful of special trips a year.

- The Story Pass sits in RevenueCat's current offering under a custom package identifier. 

- The offer appears at the moment of peak desire, when the First Cut finishes playing and the film itself carries the offer. Buying renders the full story immediately. Declining sends the free trailer instead.

- A pending export resumes automatically after a successful purchase, and a failed or retried paid export never asks for a second purchase.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Making long video exports reliable on a phone. Decoding, transitions, memory pressure and encoder stalls all matter. I added a progress watchdog that cancels a stalled render and offers a one-tap retry that does not downgrade an HD export or charge twice. A real-renderer test decodes a 90-second 1080p film frame by frame. Longer films with music still need more testing on real iPhones. 

- Privacy versus AI. I wanted an AI edit without uploading a photo library. The answer was to keep almost everything on the device, send only reduced previews of moments the user chose, make the cloud step opt-in, and fail closed if it is unavailable.

- A paywall people do not resent. The free preview is a real, watchable film, and the paid version is the full story, so the offer never feels like a wall.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A complete flow from photo access to a shareable film, with almost everything running on the device.

- A privacy design that I can explain in one sentence: your photos stay on your iPhone unless you opt in to AI Director or create a share link.

**What we learned**

Monetisation works best when it follows the emotional moment. RevenueCat let me ship a localised, one-time purchase quickly, so I could spend my time on the film itself. I also learned how much of "AI" product quality is really about trust and handling failure well. I also learnt how to vibe code, or use agent engineering to deploy a fully working, tested iOS application, which was enlightening. 

**What's next for Memories: Create Stories**

- More on-device testing of long exports across different iPhones.

- More soundtracks and visual styles.

- A better share experience for family and friends, with a clear "make yours" step for anyone who opens a link.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**CareerPilot AI — The AI Career Operating System**

**The Problem**

A modern job search is scattered across job boards, resumes, spreadsheets, application trackers, documents, notes, email, and personal reminders. Important career information gets repeated, forgotten, or disconnected from the decisions people need to make.

CareerPilot AI was built to turn that fragmented process into one connected career workspace.

**The Solution**

CareerPilot AI is a mobile-first AI career operating system that connects the major stages of the job-search journey:

Career Brain → Job Discovery → Job Fit & Risk → Resume & Application → Application Tracking → Follow-ups → Career Memory

Instead of treating a resume, a job listing, an application, and a career note as separate pieces of information, CareerPilot keeps them connected through persistent career data, evidence, provenance, and application context.

**What CareerPilot AI Does**

**🧠 Career Brain**

Career Brain acts as the foundation of the system. It brings together a user's profile, experience, education, skills, projects, certifications, and supporting evidence.

The goal is to give every downstream career workflow a consistent source of truth.

**🔎 Job Intelligence**

CareerPilot can ingest real job listings and help users understand them through:

- Job fit and Match Intelligence

- Position and requirement analysis

- JobGuard risk signals

- Search, filtering, sorting, and pagination

The idea is not simply to collect jobs, but to help users understand which opportunities deserve attention.

**📄 Resume Workspace**

Users can create and edit resumes, maintain persistent resume data, and import existing PDF or DOCX documents.

Imported information can be reviewed before being merged into the Career Brain, keeping the user's career profile connected to the documents they already have.

CareerPilot also supports resume export workflows for PDF and DOCX.

**📋 Application Workspace**

The Application Tracker connects job opportunities with application records and application-package information.

Users can create and manage applications, update stages, review application details, link resumes, and keep application history organized in one place.

**🧠 Career Memory**

Career Memory stores useful career context such as achievements, experiences, project lessons, interview lessons, preferences, application outcomes, reusable stories, skill context, career goals, and general notes.

This gives the system persistent context instead of treating every interaction as a fresh conversation.

**🛡️ Evidence & Provenance**

CareerPilot treats evidence as a first-class part of career data.

Evidence records can be linked to authoritative career entities such as experience, education, projects, achievements, certifications, and skills. Parent ownership and tenant isolation are enforced so evidence cannot simply be attached to another user's career data.

This provides a foundation for distinguishing supported information from information that still needs verification.

**🔔 Notifications**

The notification system connects job matches, application activity, interviews, deadlines, career signals, and system events.

Users can filter notifications, mark them read, dismiss them, and configure notification preferences.

**💳 RevenueCat**

CareerPilot includes an optional Pro subscription layer powered by RevenueCat.

The mobile implementation uses the RevenueCat SDK for the purchase and entitlement flow, with development/testing supported through RevenueCat's Test Store environment.

The application never treats a local button press as proof of a purchase: premium state is derived from RevenueCat customer and entitlement information.

**How I Built It**

CareerPilot uses a full-stack architecture with:

- React Native and Expo for the mobile application

- Next.js and TypeScript for the web application and API layer

- Supabase PostgreSQL for persistent application data

- Supabase Auth and Row-Level Security for authentication and tenant isolation

- AWS Bedrock / Amazon Nova for AI-assisted career workflows

- RevenueCat for subscription and entitlement management

- Zod and typed API contracts for validation

- Automated testing across the mobile and web codebases

A key design principle was to separate deterministic logic from AI generation.

Identity, IDs, database ownership, validation, matching logic, filtering, provenance, and security should remain deterministic. AI is used where language generation and reasoning assistance are valuable.

**Engineering Challenges**

One of the hardest parts was keeping mobile and web behavior aligned while ensuring that the mobile application used real persistent backend state rather than local demo state.

The project went through repeated forensic audits focused on:

- server-issued identifiers

- authenticated API requests

- database persistence

- cross-tenant isolation

- real CRUD operations

- error versus empty-state behavior

- cross-screen synchronization

- import/merge workflows

- file export

- stale-request protection

- mobile/web contract parity

Another important challenge was preventing a successful-looking UI from masking a failed backend request. CareerPilot therefore uses explicit loading, success, empty, and error states and avoids silently converting real API failures into fake or empty data.

**What I Learned**

Building CareerPilot taught me that a complete product is not just a collection of screens.

The difficult part is the connection between them:

identity → data → API contract → database → persistence → UI state → reload → another feature

A feature is only truly finished when that entire chain works.

I also learned to treat provenance and security as product functionality rather than infrastructure that can be added later.

**Current Result**

CareerPilot AI is a working, mobile-first career operating system with real authentication, persistent data, job intelligence, application workflows, resume management, Career Brain, Career Memory, evidence linkage, notifications, and RevenueCat-powered monetization.

The application has been tested through the web runtime, Expo Go, and a native development build, with real-user authentication and persistent backend workflows.

The project is submitted through the Next Gen path and includes an open-source repository and testing instructions for evaluation.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I spend way too many hours on my phone — too close, too long, often in the dark. As a student I noticed my eyesight getting worse, and existing "eye care" apps were either just blue-light filters or manual timers that nobody sticks with. I wanted something that watches how you actually use your phone and intervenes at the right moment.

**What it does**

EyeGuard is an always-on eye-health guardian for Android:

- Distance detection — every 30 seconds it briefly opens the front camera for a single frame, measures face-to-screen distance with on-device ML Kit face detection, and warns instantly if you're too close. The camera is released immediately; nothing ever leaves the device.

- Ambient light monitoring — a low-power sensor listener warns when you're reading in the dark.

- 20-20-20 rule — tracks continuous screen time via screen on/off events and reminds you to look 6 meters away for 20 seconds.

- Smart eye comfort filter — a warm overlay that adapts to ambient light and night hours, toggleable from a Quick Settings tile.

- Stats that motivate — daily screen time, too-close duration, longest continuous session, rest-compliance rate, weekly reports, streaks and achievements.

- Built for real-world Android — battery-whitelist and auto-launch guidance for Chinese ROMs, battery-aware adaptive sampling, and boot-resume notifications.

**How I built it**

Native Android with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose (Material 3). CameraX + ML Kit for single-frame distance sampling, Room for daily usage stats, DataStore for settings, Hilt for DI, and a foreground service with a camera|specialUse type for the monitoring loop. Monetization is built with RevenueCat: the Pro plan unlocks custom thresholds, the smart filter, 7-day history charts, weekly reports and do-not-disturb hours.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Chinese ROM background limits: foreground services get killed aggressively on MIUI/EMUI/Honor. I ended up combining a camera|specialUse FGS type with in-app guidance cards that deep-link users to battery whitelist and auto-launch settings.

- Notification quirks: re-using a notification ID silently "updates" instead of alerting — reminders now always use fresh IDs, with a direct vibrator fallback for ROMs that swallow notification vibration.

- Privacy-first camera usage: binding the camera for one frame per sample without a preview use case took some CameraX gymnastics, but it's what makes the feature battery- and privacy-friendly.

**What I learned**

Shipping a background-heavy health app is 20% features and 80% fighting the OS. I also learned how fast RevenueCat makes subscriptions: offerings, paywall logic and restore flows took less than a day to integrate.

**What's next**

Full-screen break overlays, sound alerts, and per-profile detection for shared devices.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

A couple's memories are not made only on special occasions. They also live in ordinary moments: saying "Look at this" during a call, laughing at a photo together, or hearing each other's voice while talking about an uneventful day.

But revisiting a photo does not always bring back the conversation around it. The image remains, while the reaction, the laughter, and the things we were saying gradually become harder to remember.

Cameo began with a question: What if revisiting a photo also let us hear the moment we shared it?

We wanted to turn things couples already do - sharing photos and short videos, talking, and showing each other their day - into a shared record. Our goal is to help everyday moments become memories without making remembering feel like another task.

**What it does**

Cameo is a couples memory app designed for two connected partners to share everyday life through photos and short videos, talk over voice calls, and revisit those moments through the images and voices they shared.

Two people connect through a pairing code. From there, they can share everyday moments using the in-app camera or media from their library, and return to those memories in a shared album. Photos and short videos offer different ways to capture a day, from a single scene to a small moment in motion.

The central interaction is sharing photos during a call. When someone wants to show their partner something, they can take or select a photo from the call interface. The couple can look at the photo and keep talking within the same experience.

A photo shared during a call can be associated with that call, preserving the relationship between the image and the conversation. Highlights mark moments within the call, while recorded audio and timestamped transcripts provide ways to revisit what was said.

The shared album organizes media and call records by day. The backend also generates conversation titles and summaries to help describe those records. Together, these elements keep the context of a day connected to the moments the couple shared.

Cameo helps couples remember both what they captured and how they experienced that moment together.

**How we built it**

We approached Cameo as one continuous user journey rather than a camera, a calling app, and an album placed side by side.

In Figma, we developed the screens and interactions for onboarding, partner pairing, permission requests, photo and short-video sharing, in-call interactions, and revisiting memories. Our visual direction puts the couple's content and presence first, with controls that are clear and available when needed.

We refined these flows through UI/UX testing and internal QA, reviewing how the screens worked together in the implemented app. This iterative process helped us resolve the main UX challenges and improve the continuity between sharing, calling, and returning to the album.

We are developing Cameo for iOS and Android. Our goal is to keep the central experience consistent so that couples can participate in the same shared space even when they use different operating systems.

We designed the record structure around the relationships between days, calls, and shared media. A photo shared during a call can reference that call, while highlights store positions on the call timeline. These relationships connect images and conversations and support the experience of revisiting them together.

Technology stack:

The app is built with Flutter and Dart for iOS and Android, with native Swift and Kotlin code for platform-specific behavior. We designed the interface in Figma and use Node.js scripts to generate design tokens and icon resources for Flutter.

The backend uses Go and the chi router. PostgreSQL stores accounts, couple relationships, photos, calls, and highlights; an ent fork and pgx handle data access, while Atlas manages database migrations. Twilio Verify provides the phone-number verification integration.

Voice calls use Flutter WebRTC on the client and Pion WebRTC on the server, with WebSocket signaling to coordinate the connection. The server relays audio and records each participant's track. FFmpeg aligns and mixes the tracks for playback. Our processing pipeline uses OpenAI's transcription API, with Whisper as the default model, to produce timestamped transcripts, and the Responses API to generate titles and summaries informed by the couple's marked highlights. On iOS, CallKit, PushKit, and APNs support system-call and notification integration.

Photos, short videos, and processed recordings are stored in S3-compatible storage backed by Versity Gateway, with time-limited URLs for uploads and downloads. Docker Compose defines the backend services, Traefik handles HTTPS routing, and OpenAPI documents the contract between the app and server.

RevenueCat integration:

RevenueCat powers shared-storage subscriptions and a separate one-time data-restoration purchase. The monthly subscription product, monthly_pur, is linked to the cameo_pro entitlement and increases the couple's storage allowance. The consumable product, cameo_recovery, provides a credit to restore eligible photos and call records when the same two people reconnect after an earlier pairing. Core features remain available within the base storage allowance.

The Flutter SDK associates purchases with the signed-in Cameo account. The backend synchronizes subscriber information through RevenueCat's REST API and webhooks, then applies the highest active storage tier available to either partner. Both people therefore benefit from the same shared allowance. Storage limits and restoration credits are checked on the server, so access does not depend solely on what one device reports.

The development integration supports RevenueCat Test Store and defaults to sandbox-only purchasing. This configuration allows the purchase flow and backend synchronization to be developed without initiating real-money checkout.

**Challenges we ran into**

The most difficult part of building Cameo was UX design: making everyday sharing, calling, and revisiting memories feel like one natural experience. Each activity asks something different of the user. Sharing a photo or short video should feel quick and spontaneous. During a call, attention should stay on the partner. When returning to the album, the user should be able to understand what happened and find a memory without having to reconstruct the day from separate screens. Connecting these needs was the central design challenge.

This was especially important in the call experience. The interface has to support conversation while keeping photo sharing and highlights easy to reach. Too many visible choices can pull attention away from the person on the other end; controls that are too difficult to find can interrupt the moment in a different way. We had to think carefully about what belonged on the main screen, what could appear when needed, and how someone would return to the conversation after taking an action.

The album presented a related challenge. Photos, short videos, call recordings, and transcripts have different viewing and playback needs, but they all belong to the couple's shared history. We needed a clear hierarchy that helped people understand the relationship between these records. The design had to make room for the memory itself while keeping navigation and playback understandable.

We worked through these challenges with UI/UX testing and our own internal QA. We reviewed the experience as a sequence of actions, considering how one screen led into the next and whether the purpose of each interaction was clear. Our focus was on practical questions: Could someone recognize the next action? Was the result of sharing understandable? Could they move between a conversation and its related media without losing their place? These questions helped us evaluate the design beyond its appearance in a static layout.

Testing and QA became part of an iterative design process. We revisited the screen structure, visual hierarchy, transitions, and feedback, then reviewed the revised flow again. UI/UX testing helped us judge clarity and ease of use, while internal QA helped us check whether the implemented interactions behaved consistently with the intended experience. This process helped us resolve the main UX issues and bring the individual features together into a more coherent journey.

The result was a clearer relationship between sharing a moment, talking about it, and returning to it later. We also learned how important it is to balance an intimate visual atmosphere with understandable controls and feedback. Working through the design in use gave us a stronger foundation for Cameo and a repeatable way to assess future changes through continued testing and QA.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are most proud of turning a clear product idea - connecting everyday images and voices as one memory - into a connected app experience.

Photos and short videos give couples ways to share daily life, while calls and their related records preserve more of the context around those moments. Bringing these parts together gave the camera, call interface, and shared album a common purpose.

We are also proud of the progress we made through UI/UX testing and internal QA. Resolving the main UX challenges required us to revisit the flow across screens, refine how actions and feedback were presented, and review the changes in the implemented app. That process made the experience more coherent and helped the design serve the way people would actually move through it.

Our visual direction keeps the couple's content at the center, with photo-focused layouts and consistent controls. The achievement we value most is the connection between the first moment two people pair their accounts and the later moment when they return to something they shared.

**What we learned**

We learned that context makes a memory easier to revisit. A collection of photos and short videos preserves what happened, while voices and conversations can bring back how the moment felt. Connecting these records gives the shared album more meaning.

We also learned that UX design continues after a screen looks finished. A layout can appear clear on its own while still leaving questions about the next action, the result of sharing, or how to return to a previous activity. UI/UX testing and internal QA helped us evaluate those connections and refine the flow through repeated review.

The process taught us to consider visual design and interaction behavior together. An intimate atmosphere depends on clear feedback and predictable navigation as much as it does on colors, images, and motion.

Working on a product for personal relationships also reinforced the importance of consent and control. People need to understand what is being shared or recorded and how their personal memories are handled. These remain central priorities as we continue improving the experience.

**What's next for Cameo**

Building on our UI/UX testing and internal QA, our next step is to observe real couples using Cameo's central flow and continue refining the experience. We want to understand where sharing a photo or short video, continuing a call, or revisiting a memory still requires unnecessary effort.

On the technical side, we plan to focus on photo delivery, call reliability, permission handling, and behavior across app-state changes on iOS and Android. Before expanding the feature set, we want the everyday experience to be dependable enough for two people to return to it regularly.

We also plan to refine conversation summaries and the review of plans mentioned during calls, while making the ways to retain, export, and delete personal records clear. These improvements will support our preparation for a public release.

In the long term, we do not want Cameo to become just another place to store photos. We want it to become a shared space where two people can return to both the scene they captured and the voices they shared around it.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I grew up with power cuts, monsoon evenings and the hour before dinner when everyone was in one room — and I realised I could barely picture those evenings any more. I wanted something that could take me back to them, not with my own old photos, but with how those years felt. Yestara is that: a way to go back to the evenings you thought you'd forgotten.

**What it does**

Yestara writes you a memory of the years you grew up in.

You answer a few questions once — the year you were born, where you grew up, the language you heard at home, the cartoon you rushed back for. After that you pick a kind of afternoon and a year, and Yestara writes that memory for you: a monsoon evening in 2005, the hour before dinner, the evening the power went. Claude writes the story in second person, about three hundred words. Gemini makes the photograph of how that year looked.

These are not your photographs, and the app never asks for them. It is a way of remembering how something felt, not a record of what happened — and it says so on the memory itself, in a line that travels with it wherever it is shared.

Everyone gets one memory a day for free. You can make more, and keep every one of them.

**How I built it**

Flutter, Riverpod and GoRouter on the front end; a clean-architecture slice per feature so each one could be built and demoed on its own.

The models are called from AWS Lambda over HTTPS — Claude Sonnet 5 for the story, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite Image for the picture, asked for in parallel. The two share a memory key so one memory counts once. Keys live in SSM; nothing ships in the app.

RevenueCat is the entire billing layer — entitlement echoes_premium, monthly and annual, with a 7-day free trial as a Play offer. The app never names a trial of its own: it reads the free phase off the store, so changing the offer in Play Console needs no release.

Memories follow the account. Every memory is written to a cloud archive as it is made — DynamoDB for the text, S3 for the photograph — so a new phone or a reinstall gets everything back.

OneSignal brings people back to a memory, not just to the app. Permission is asked once, after someone's first memory, and nothing reaches OneSignal before they say yes. Each person is linked by their account ID, the same one RevenueCat uses, and carries five tags: the decade of their latest memory, how many memories they have, when they last made one, their plan, and whether they are new. An hourly job sends through OneSignal's API at 10 in the morning in the person's own timezone, at most one a day and two a week, and drops to one a fortnight after three are ignored. Each notification names a year and a theme, and opens that memory or the studio with the theme already chosen. Deployed: the dashboard campaign "The evening the power went", sent at 5 pm in each person's timezone. In its first hour it reached 6 people and 1 in 6 tapped it.

**Challenges I ran into**

A memory only survived if somebody pressed Save. Generated memories lived on the phone; only the ones a user explicitly kept reached their account. Nothing in the app said so, so the difference between "mine forever" and "gone on reinstall" rested on whether somebody noticed a button. I found it when memories I had made were not there after a reinstall. Keeping is automatic now, and the shelf limits went with it — they would have started refusing the eleventh memory somebody made.

Three different refusals looked identical. The server can say "your allowance is spent", "the free tier's model budget for today is gone", and "you have already had today's memory". All three arrived as HTTP 429, and the app said "try again in a moment" to every one of them — including the one that could not work until midnight. They travel as separate answers now, and the app only offers a retry when retrying can work.

Cost is a design constraint, not an afterthought. A memory costs about ₹4 in model calls. Home used to make one on every launch, which spent real money on people who had opened the app to re-read what they already had. Home offers it now and makes it only when somebody accepts.

I removed two of the four studios. Video costs roughly 150× what a story costs, and there is no ambient-audio model that does what "the sound of the place" would need. Shipping two rooms that work beat shipping four where two say "coming soon".

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

Every memory is real work by real models, and every number on the paywall is one the server enforces. It launched on Google Play on 16 September and has shipped nine updates since, each tested on a phone before it went out.

**What I learned**

Device testing is not optional and a widget test is not a device. The status bar turned white on a cream screen because a transparent app bar makes Flutter guess wrong; a share card went out with yellow debug underlines because it is built outside Material; a card test passed while the bug was still on screen, because a text box stretched to fill its page is perfectly centred. Every one of those was invisible until I looked at a phone.

**What's next for Yestara**

A photo booth: bring your own photograph and have it set in the year you choose. It needs upload, consent and moderation done properly, which is why it is next rather than now.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I was diagnosed with PCOS (now PMOS) when I was 14.

I remember sitting in that appointment not understanding half of what the doctor was saying: phenotypes, insulin resistance, androgens, metabolic imbalance and walking out with a pamphlet and no real idea what to actually do with any of it. No one sat me down and explained why my skin was breaking out, why my periods were unpredictable, or why I felt exhausted for no reason I could point to. I was just told "you have PCOS" and left to figure out the rest on my own, at 14, with Google. And same is the experience for many women. There is no fixed path, no "cure" for what we have and no one place to find all the information.

Over the year my team and i kept researching: piecing together studies, clinical guidelines, forum posts from other women; because the information that actually explained someone's PCOS was always scattered across a dozen different sources, never in one place, never personalized. Along the way we met people who have PCOs and learned something that stuck with us: globally, 1 in 10 women of reproductive age has PCOS but in India, it's closer to 1 in 5. Nearly double the global rate. And yet almost every app that exists which supossedly tried treating PCOS like generic period tracking, as if hirsutism, hair loss and insulin resistance weren't part of the picture at all.

That gap between how common and serious PCOS actually is, especially here in India and how little personalized support exists for it- is exactly what Cyster is built to close.

We wanted to build something that treats PCOS the way an endocrinologist would: 
by phenotype and personalising the experience, not just by symptom checklist.

**What it does**

Cyster is a full PCOS companion app built natively for iPhone in UIKit:

- Phenotype-aware goal engine — using the Mifflin-St Jeor BMR formula, activity 
level, and PCOS phenotype (Rotterdam criteria / ESHRE 2023), Cyster generates 
personalized diet, workout, and sleep targets instead of generic averages. In case the user does not know their phenotype, they can get to know it by continous logging and the more someone logs the more personalized the whole app becomes. The user can find out their phenotype by the chatbot built in our app.

- Symptom & cycle tracking — beyond period dates and cycles, Cyster tracks PCOS-specific 
signals (hirsutism, skin darkening, mood swings, hair loss) with educational cards explaining why they happen, what hormones might be coming into play and how to handle the symptom.

- AI Coach ("Cyster") — a conversational assistant that gives phase-aware recommendations (e.g. adjusting workout intensity and diet suggestions based on where you are in your cycle). It has input of all the logged data and based on that gives you personalized goals for your system and lifestyle.

- AI food logging — type "rice and one bowl curd" and Cyster parses it into calories and macros automatically. You can also take a photo of your meal and our AI would estimate the calories and macros. If not these two, manual entry exists as well.

- Phase-linked workouts — routines and intensity caps that respect your phenotype (e.g. capping workout duration for adrenal-dominant phenotypes to avoid cortisol spikes).

**How we built it**

Cyster is an AI-powered mobile health application built with UIKit and Core Data on iOS, with AI capabilities offloaded to a cloud backend for a scalable, cross-platform architecture. The backend is implemented using Python/FastAPI and deployed as independent services on Google Cloud Run. Firebase Authentication provides user identity and JWT-based authorization, while the backend exposes authenticated APIs for AI inference, data backup, and synchronization. AI workloads including conversational coaching, personalized recommendations, meal image analysis, and natural-language meal parsing are processed through Google Vertex AI/Gemini, allowing models and inference configuration to evolve without requiring mobile-app releases. RevenueCat manages subscriptions, entitlements, offerings, and in-app purchase state across the mobile platform. The architecture uses Google Cloud Build, Artifact Registry, and Secret Manager for CI/CD, container management, and secure configuration. iOS maintains local data through Core Data, while the backend provides the cloud synchronization layer, with the architecture designed to support Android and future RAG/vector-storage capabilities.

**Challenges we ran into**

- In the earlier stages of development we were planning on making the app work offline as well so getting an on-device vision model small enough to ship in-app while still being accurate, however our first version struggled badly with Indian food names (returning "curry" for dal, "sandwich" for Vada Pav). We solved this by having the model describe the food in plain language first, then keyword-matching that description against a curated food database, rather than asking it to name the dish directly. We later moved to API's.

- Translating messy clinical research (Rotterdam criteria, ESHRE 2023 guidelines) into a deterministic goal engine that a non-clinician could trust and understand.

- Taming a hallucinating, repetitive coach. Early on, Cyster's AI coach would invent nutrition claims or loop the same suggestions across sessions. We fixed this by grounding every response in structured context (the user's actual GoalEngine output, phase, and recent logs) rather than open-ended prompting, and added recency-aware prompt constraints so it doesn't repeat a recommendation it already gave.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We're most proud of the accuracy we achieved across Cyster's three hardest technical problems: meal scanning that correctly recognizes Indian food (not just generic labels), period prediction that adapts to the irregular cycles PCOS causes rather than assuming a textbook 28-day cycle, and phenotype/phase detection that actually reflects clinical criteria instead of a generic symptom checklist. It also detected a menopausal user based on symptoms. Getting each of these right and grounded in real research is what makes Cyster feel personalized rather than just another tracker.

**What we learned**

Building a user-facing health app taught us how to turn a genuinely holistic problem into something personal and actionable, without oversimplifying it. It's tempting to think of an app as one core feature, but Cyster really lives across three interconnected phases logging, understanding, and maintaining-and each one had to be built and validated with equal care for the product to actually work. We also learned the discipline of keeping every recommendation grounded in real clinical research rather than letting an AI assistant improvise, which shaped almost every decision we made about prompting and data design.

**What's next for Cyster**

- Onboarding doctors and field technicians, so Cyster can plug into real clinical workflows, not just individual self-tracking.

- Online diagnosis and consulting, connecting users directly with specialists — for example, routing patients experiencing fertility difficulties to fertility specialists, so Cyster becomes a bridge to expert care, not a replacement for it.

- Expanding to related disorders like endometriosis and hypothyroidism, where the same phenotype-aware, phase-driven approach applies just as strongly.

</details>
