<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/429/670/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/429/670/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/429/671/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/429/671/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/429/668/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/429/668/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/429/667/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/429/667/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/429/669/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/429/669/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/429/765/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/429/765/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

About 10 million people in South Africa speak isiXhosa at home, 16.3% of the population (Stats SA, Census 2022). The language has 15 click sounds built on three basic clicks, c, x and q. It is also tonal, and tone is not written, so a learner who only reads words learns them wrong.

Duolingo announced an isiXhosa course in 2021 and never shipped it. The dedicated apps we found are thin, and none of them drills the clicks as a core mechanic. The founder is Norwegian and enrolled at the University of Cape Town. Molo is the course he wanted, for English and Norwegian speakers.

**What it does**

Molo looks like Duolingo: a path of units and short lessons, hearts, streaks, XP, weekly leagues and spaced-repetition review. Inside it runs on one rule, and the rule is enforced in code:

No learner ever sees content that a human isiXhosa editor has not approved.

Unit 1, "Say hello and say who you are", is live on hellomolo.com and in the app. It has five lessons in three skills: greeting someone and saying goodbye, hearing the difference between c, x and q, and saying yes, no and thank you. Its 14 exercises are of four kinds:

- Click identification: hear a bare click and pick its letter. First the three basic clicks, then plain against aspirated (c and ch, x and xh, q and qh).

- Listen and select: hear a word, pick what it means.

- Match pairs: match words to meanings. Tapping an isiXhosa tile plays the word.

- Culture cards: short notes an editor approved, for example that molo greets one person and molweni more than one.

Every word in the unit, and each of the six clicks it drills, is a studio recording by our tutor, Thandeka. Each click letter has its own colour wherever isiXhosa appears, so a learner sees the click before hearing it. The interface is in English and Norwegian. Glosses are stored per source language, because a Norwegian learner needs different notes than an English one.

New on 28 September:

- New words come before practice (web and app). A card shows the word, plays its recording once and gives its meaning, then the exercise starts.

- Hearts in the lesson header (web and app). A lost heart pops, shakes and drops away while the count ticks down. With reduced motion only the number changes. Screen readers hear how many hearts are left.

- Out of hearts is a card in the lesson (app), not a sheet on top of it: practise to earn a heart, get Plus, or continue later.

- A trail joins the path (web and app). It is solid where you have walked and dashed ahead, and the newest stretch draws itself once after a lesson.

- Screens do not wait (web and app). They draw from what the device already has, fetch the next lesson before the tap, warm its first recordings, and show a skeleton shaped like the real screen in the one cold case left.

- Offline units are a Molo Plus perk (app), behind one pill in the unit header.

- Match pairs never gives an answer away (web and app). The old shuffle left at least one meaning in its own word's row in about 3 of 5 exercises; the new order is a derangement, the same for everyone.

- Reminders at the learner's own time (app, with email as a fallback). After the first finished lesson the mascot asks whether it may send a nudge, at a time the learner picks. A yes brings a daily reminder at that local time, an evening streak saver, and win-back messages on days 1, 3 and 7 that then stop. At most two a day, and nothing between 21:30 and 08:00.

**How we built it**

- A TypeScript monorepo on Bun. A Hono API on Cloudflare Workers; a TanStack Start web app that is both the learner app and the editor dashboard; an Expo app for iOS and Android with an encrypted offline cache (op-sqlite with SQLCipher). PlanetScale Postgres through Hyperdrive, R2 for audio, Queues for audio processing, Better Auth with email, Apple and Google sign-in, Sentry in the EU, infrastructure as code with Alchemy.

- Three Rust crates where correctness earns it. xh-morph generates noun-class forms from rules and is tested against golden forms a native speaker signed off; a rule without a golden case is a rejected change. xh-audio trims each recording, normalises it to −16 LUFS, encodes it and writes a manifest. xh-fsrs wraps fsrs-rs, the scheduler Anki ships, compiled to WebAssembly and run inside the Worker that schedules reviews.

- A publish gate in the code, not in a document. Every content row carries a status, and learner endpoints read published only. Anything a language model drafts enters as ai_draft and cannot reach published without a human editor in the dashboard. An integrity suite of 38 test files runs against a real Postgres and asserts this, among other things; weakening it fails CI. 1,121 unit tests, Playwright end-to-end tests, mobile Jest tests and cargo test run on every pull request.

- Tools built around the tutor's hour. Thandeka records in a browser studio; her takes go through xh-audio and into review. She answers golden cards for the rule engine, writes the sentences a unit asks for, and can leave a note on any item in the studio.

- Licensed sources, not scraped ones. The lexicon is adapted from IsiXhosa.click (CC BY-SA 4.0, a student-led dictionary supported by UCT and SADiLaR). The Gothenburg Corpus of Spoken isiXhosa (CC BY 4.0) and the NCHLT text corpora (CC BY 2.5 ZA) rank the vocabulary. Our adapted lexicon goes back out under CC BY-SA at hellomolo.com/lexicon. An Oxford school dictionary is looked up word by word, and its corrections change only drafts no human has touched.

- An ops CLI for a person and an agent alike (molo). Every command that writes or spends is a dry run unless --live, and every command has --json. molo content promote can send content to review but never publish it; publishing happens only in the dashboard.

- One person and AI coding agents. Claude Code and Codex wrote much of the TypeScript and Rust under written project rules, which the test suite enforces. None of them writes isiXhosa.

**How we use RevenueCat**

- One entitlement, plus, two products (molo_plus_monthly, molo_plus_yearly) in one offering, configured in App Store Connect and Google Play, with list prices of NOK 79 / 599 and USD 6.99 / 49.99.

- The server is the source of truth. RevenueCat's webhook posts to POST /webhooks/revenuecat with a shared secret. One pure module maps the events: purchase, renewal, uncancellation, product change and transfer grant; a cancellation keeps access until expiry; expiration and refund revoke; a billing issue changes nothing until the store expires the subscription. It is idempotent on the event id.

- The app trusts the SDK for a moment. An active plus entitlement from the SDK means unlimited hearts at once, while the server catches up through the webhook. The paywall feels instant and the ledger stays on the server. Every price on the paywall comes from the store.

- Web Billing is wired on hellomolo.com/plus through @revenuecat/purchases-js, with the 14-day withdrawal right of Norwegian and EU consumer law and an express-start consent built into the checkout. It is limited to accounts registered in Norway until VAT registration elsewhere is done, and it is not yet switched on in production.

- What Plus buys is honest: unlimited hearts, a streak freeze every week, offline units, and it funds the recordings and the editors who check every word. Hearts cannot be bought one by one.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Tone is not written. Text corpora silently lose a feature of the language, so audio is the only carrier. A word without a native recording cannot be published, and synthetic speech never satisfies the gate.

- Trusting a model exactly as far as it deserves. Language models write fluent, plausible, wrong isiXhosa. So a model drafts English and Norwegian glosses for words the lexicon already has, never the isiXhosa itself, and forms like plurals come from the rule engine or not at all.

- The tutor's time is the scarcest resource. Every editor tool asks one clear question per card and saves as she goes. Locatives are asked on golden cards before any locative rule exists, and agreement will be asked as whole sentences to say rather than as grammar terms.

- Selling a subscription lawfully in Norway, the EU and South Africa. That took a legal review and rewrites of the terms and privacy policy: an age gate (13+, and 18+ in South Africa), withdrawal rights, POPIA, and data processing agreements on file.

- Shipping daily while the app is in store review. Over-the-air updates are gated on a fingerprint of the native build. A copy change once looked native to that fingerprint and held updates back until we found why.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Unit 1 is published, and every word and click in it is a native speaker's recording.

- Thandeka has signed off the first 11 plural forms the rule engine is tested against.

- The editor gate is a test, not a promise, and it has never been weakened to ship a feature.

- A production stack on Cloudflare deployed from CI, both stores configured (privacy questionnaires, age ratings, subscriptions), and the app submitted to both 24 days after the first commit on 3 September.

- The lexicon goes back to the community under the licence it came with.

**What we learned**

Content, not code, is the product. The realistic way a project like this dies is a beautiful app with forty features and two hundred unvalidated words. So the plan puts the content risk first: a native speaker's hour, recordings for each unit, and nothing published until a person says it is right.

**What's next**

isiXhosa is where we started, not the only language the system is built for. Courses, words and sentences each record the language they belong to, so a second course is new content in the same tables, not a new app. The editor gate, the recording studio, the audio pipeline, the review queue and the scheduler carry over as they are. isiZulu would be the natural next course: it is mutually intelligible with isiXhosa, and our rule engine follows ZulMorph, a finite-state approach first built for isiZulu. Sesotho, Setswana and other languages that few apps teach well would each need their own sources, rule engine and native editors, the way isiXhosa did.

- Units 2 to 10 exist as drafts in the curriculum. Each opens when it is recorded and an editor approves it.

- 136 golden cases in the rule engine's test file still wait for Thandeka's answer, and locative cards are on her page before any locative rule exists.

- Sentences for Unit 1, which Thandeka writes from English and Norwegian prompts, and the grammar notes, once a speaker has checked the rule behind each one.

- The code in the open under an open-source licence.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We are the most informed generation in history, and at the same time, it seems, the least thoughtful. How is that possible? We have unlimited access to information: we read, we learn, we grow. But what is our privilege has also become our curse. Our lives are fragmented. Our time is cut into pieces, our focus keeps switching, distractions are everywhere. And in all that noise, there is often simply no room left for thinking.

I felt this myself. I'm a student, originally from Ukraine, and my head is always full of thoughts, ideas and things I can't forget. I think everyone knows this feeling of overload. To clear my head, I wrote my thoughts down wherever was closest: in a notebook, in a notes app, in a Telegram chat, on some random scrap of paper. And in the end, everything got lost.

So one day in April, I decided to build myself a tool that would always be at hand. Something that would appear out of nowhere, as if with a wave of a magic wand, take everything extra off my mind, and disappear as soon as I no longer needed it.

The small project pulled me in, and instead of one evening, I spent six months building Embar.

**What it does**

Embar is a sidebar notebook for Mac that lets you write things down at the speed of thought. The problem with most note-taking apps is friction: you have to open them, find the right place, switch away from your work. Embar works differently. It is a layer on top of the whole system.

The panel sits just beyond the right edge of the screen and appears over any active window when you move the cursor to the edge or press the ⌥E hotkey. The cursor is already in the input field, so you can write a thought down the very second it appears. When the cursor leaves the panel, it hides, and focus returns to where you were working. And when you have time to go through everything you've collected, you can lock the panel open and widen it, while sorting, filters, walls and palettes let you organize your work exactly the way that suits you.

Inside are three surfaces, each for a different scale of thought, on top of one shared data store.

Stickies are for instant capture. One thought takes one sticky. Stickies are sorted into walls (themed collections), and they have colors, deadlines, reminders, pinning and a "done" mark, while counters and filters help you quickly sort through what has piled up. Any sticky can literally be dragged out of the panel, and it becomes a separate note on your desktop, like a widget that is always right in front of you.

Reader is a working notebook for a source: a book, an article, a lecture or a podcast. Each notebook has a cover and a link to the source, and inside is a chronological stream of thoughts and quotes, colored highlights, photos, voice notes, and threads that group entries by chapter. Its purpose is to be there while you study and to appear on screen when you need it, without wasting time switching between apps.

Notes are for longer writing: formatting, photos, quotes, lists, folders. With [[ one note links to another, and every note shows where it is mentioned.

The surfaces are not isolated. A sticky can be turned into a full note, and the link between them is kept on both sides. An entry from Reader can be added to an existing note or start a new one. A thought travels from a quick capture to a developed idea without leaving the app and without losing where it came from.

That is why Embar isn't tied to one specific scenario, but adapts to any:

- a student in a lecture with full-screen slides takes notes without splitting the screen or switching windows;

- a designer in Figma writes down an idea for another project without leaving the canvas;

- a researcher reading a paper saves a quote with a link to the source without opening a separate document;

- anyone in the middle of a workday records a task with a deadline and a reminder in a few seconds.

How it differs from classic notebooks and workspaces. These tools demand decisions before you write: open the app, find the right place, define the structure. Embar moves those decisions to later. Capture happens immediately, in your current context, while organizing, expanding and linking become a separate step for when you have time. And no accounts: all data is stored locally on your Mac.

Embar is my entry for the Next Gen Award.

**The method behind Embar: Zettelkasten**

For decades, the German sociologist Niklas Luhmann kept a card index of around 90,000 cards. He credited it for his productivity: more than 70 books and nearly 400 scholarly articles. Luhmann called his card index his partner in conversation. The method became known as Zettelkasten, "a box of slips".

The method rests on two principles. First: one card holds one thought, written so that it can be understood on its own. Second: connections matter more than structure.

The modern reading of the method, popularized by Sönke Ahrens in How to Take Smart Notes, distinguishes three types of notes. Embar is built on exactly these:

Zettelkasten
Embar
How it works

Fleeting notes: raw thoughts, written down immediately
Stickies
One thought takes one sticky. Capture it in a second, sort it out later.

Literature notes: the key points from what you read, tied to the source
Reader
A notebook for a book, an article or a lecture: quotes, thoughts, highlights, a link to the source.

Permanent notes: mature ideas in your own words, connected to others
Notes
A sticky or a Reader entry develops into a note; notes link through [[ and show backlinks.

But the method assumes that a thought can be written down instantly. Luhmann always had paper and a pen at hand. On a computer, there is a whole sequence of steps between a thought and writing it down, and every step is a chance for the thought to disappear. And a thought that was never written down will never connect to anything.

Embar brings Zettelkasten into the working environment of a laptop. The panel is always one cursor movement away, capture happens before any decisions about structure, and sorting, developing and linking thoughts become a separate step for when you have time.

**How I built it**

I started with no experience in development or app design, just an idea and a wish to learn. The first version of Embar was an HTML prototype that I made for myself while sharpening my HTML skills. I opened it in the browser and used it every day, like a normal tool. But one day in a café, a girl at the next table asked me what app it was, because, as she said, she really needed something like that too. That was when I decided to turn it into a real Mac app. Knowing that I wouldn't be able to write a native app on my own for at least the next couple of years, I remembered a phrase everyone has probably heard dozens of times: AI is our future. So in the end, Claude Code wrote the code, and the product, the design and every decision were mine.

Research

- Surveyed more than 25 students at my university

- Based on their answers, I made a list of features that would actually be useful, removed some of the features that existed at the time, and reworked the onboarding several times

Design

- Sketches of every screen, drawn by hand on paper

- The HTML prototype as the reference for how everything looks and behaves

App

- SwiftUI for the interface

- AppKit NSPanel for the panel at the edge of the screen

- SwiftData for local storage

Monetization

- RevenueCat + StoreKit

Development

- Claude Code + Xcode

- About 43,000 lines of Swift, 407 automated tests

Website

- embar.studio on Cloudflare Workers

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- I turned an idea into a product on my own. Along the way, starting from zero, I learned the basics of programming, design and product decision-making.

- People asked for the app themselves. I used Embar for myself: in lectures, at the summer school, in cafés and on trains. Again and again, people asked me to share it, because they needed the same thing. Every time I was over the moon, and every time it confirmed that the product is really needed by the people I was building it for.

- Dozens of positive reviews from people using Embar through TestFlight.

- Submitted to the App Store, with the code open on GitHub under GPL-3.0.

**Monetization with RevenueCat**

Trial

- 14 days of full access, no card and no account. Asking for a card upfront scares off many people, especially students on a budget.

- The trial is not an App Store subscription. On first launch the app writes the start date to the Keychain, so reinstalling doesn't restart it.

Products

- Lifetime, $19.99. After consulting people from the industry, I chose one-time payment as the main model.

- Monthly, $2.99, for those who need more than two weeks to decide.

RevenueCat integration

- Offerings, a pro entitlement, a custom paywall, Restore Purchases

- A 16-day grace period for failed subscription payments

- Purchases are tied to the Apple Account, so access returns after reinstalling through Restore Purchases

Nothing gets locked

- After the trial, the app becomes read-only: everything you wrote can still be viewed, copied, edited, exported and deleted. Only creating something new requires a purchase.

- If RevenueCat doesn't respond (offline, a firewall), the app stays fully open. Better to give access than to lock someone out of their own notes.

Third-degree price discrimination

- Ukraine: $14.99 Lifetime, $1.99 per month

- Ukraine is one of the main launch markets, and I know it well. Regional pricing will expand to other countries as the audience grows.

**Challenges and what I learned**

- Apple's rejection. Apple rejected Embar because it was missing the standard window controls (traffic lights). I thought a sidebar panel didn't need them, but I realized: Embar isn't a background utility, it's a full app, and users expect it to behave the way macOS apps do. I added all three buttons and submitted the app again.
→ A platform has its rules for a reason: they are what users expect.

- Lost progress. At the start, I didn't know what GitHub and version control were, and I lost a significant part of my work.
→ Now every finished step ends with a commit. AI is a powerful tool, but like any tool, you have to know how to use it and how to lead it.

- Security without loss. Notes are personal thoughts, so Embar works fully locally: no accounts, no cloud, no analytics. That means data must not disappear under any circumstances. Deleted items are archived and can be restored, data stays in the app's container even after the app is deleted, the trial is stored in the Keychain, and purchases are tied to the Apple Account. The flip side: until there is iCloud sync, notes live on one Mac.
→ Every decision has a price, and prioritizing some things always costs you others.

- Flexibility vs. simplicity. It was hard to draw the line between wanting to add every feature and not overloading the app. Many features that took a lot of time were eventually removed.
→ Analyze the user: not everything I like is what they need.

- Perfectionism. It was hard for me to release a first MVP that, in my opinion, wasn't perfect. I kept wanting to add one more feature, and one more. That cost me the time I needed to get through Apple's review before the end of the hackathon.
→ Polishing can go on forever. It matters to know when to put a full stop and ship.

- Everything at once. It was hard to combine full-time studies, work, two moves and Embar. There were nights when I wanted to give up, but in the morning I woke up, opened my laptop and kept going.
→ Time management is everything.

- Marketing. This is the next big step, and I'm honestly still very scared of it.

**What's next for Embar**

- App Store approval and public release

- iCloud sync across multiple Macs

- Voice input for quick thoughts

- An app for iPhone and iPad, because a laptop isn't always at hand

- More customization: dark mode, a glass look for the panel, a choice of fonts, new languages

- Marketing and social media: bringing Embar to students and everyone else who works with information every day

**How I would use the prize money**

- Time. Right now I combine full-time studies with a job to support myself. The prize would let me work fewer hours and give that time to Embar instead.

- An independent security audit. The security of user data is Embar's top priority, so I want it checked not only by me, but by cybersecurity professionals.

- Marketing. A social media campaign aimed at students, to bring Embar to the people it was built for.

- User research. Paid usability testing sessions with real people, so that the next decisions rest on data rather than guesses.

- Professional localization of the app and its App Store page into new languages.

- Basic development costs: the Apple Developer Program membership and tools, so Embar can keep growing.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I’ve always liked playing games, especially reasoning and brain-teaser games. So instead of building another generic app, I decided to build something I would actually want to play.

I wanted a game that was fun to play with friends, easy to understand, and didn’t require a lot of time. I also wanted the competition to come from thinking and solving problems rather than complicated game mechanics.

That’s how Rivals started: a quick daily game where I could solve different challenges, compare my score with friends, and try to beat them the next day.

**What it does**

Rivals gives every player one Daily Arena with three quick challenges:

- Word Duel

- Cipher Break

- Number Rush

Your performance across all three becomes one Arena Score. You can then compare your score with friends, climb daily and all-time leaderboards, maintain a streak, and challenge friends using virtual coins.

The entire Daily Arena is designed to take less than five minutes, so it feels easy to fit into your day instead of becoming another long game. 

**How we built it**

I built Rivals completely on my own.

The mobile app is built with React Native and Expo for iOS and Android. I used FastAPI for the backend and Supabase for authentication, PostgreSQL, Row Level Security, and Realtime. RevenueCat handles subscription management. 

I wanted the important parts of the game to be secure, so the mobile app isn't trusted with things like final scores, coin balances, wagers, or leaderboard results. These are validated and handled on the server side. 

For development, I first defined what I wanted the product and its features to do, then used AI as a coding assistant to help me write and iterate on code faster. I reviewed, tested, debugged, and integrated the code myself.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge was making the game simple for the player while keeping everything reliable behind the scenes.

A player should just be able to open the app, solve the puzzles, and see their score. Behind that simple experience, I had to handle authentication, server-side scoring, database security, wagers, leaderboards, game state, and real-time updates.

Security was another important challenge. I had to make sure players couldn't manipulate scores, access answers too early, or directly change important game data. This led to using server-side validation, JWT authentication, PostgreSQL Row Level Security, and protected database access. 

I also had to make architectural decisions during development. For example, I initially considered using WebSockets and Redis, but after reviewing the actual requirements and implementation, I simplified the architecture to FastAPI REST + PostgreSQL + Supabase Realtime. 

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I’m proud that I took Rivals from an idea to a complete working product by myself.

The biggest accomplishment for me is that it isn't just a collection of puzzle screens. It has a complete gameplay loop: daily challenges, scoring, leaderboards, friends, streaks, virtual coins, and friend challenges. 

I’m also proud of the backend architecture. I put a lot of effort into making the important game logic server-authoritative instead of trusting the mobile client.

Another thing I’m proud of is building the project while learning along the way. I had to work across mobile development, backend development, databases, authentication, security, real-time systems, and monetization to bring the whole idea together.

**What we learned**

Building Rivals taught me that making something feel simple to the player can require a lot of engineering behind the scenes.

I learned a lot about designing game backends, server-side validation, database security, real-time synchronization, and handling different states safely.

I also learned how useful AI can be as a development tool. Instead of relying on it to decide what to build, I used it to help turn my own ideas and requirements into code faster, then reviewed and tested the results myself.

Most importantly, I learned that building something you personally enjoy makes the process much more motivating. I like games and reasoning challenges, so creating Rivals gave me a project I actually wanted to keep improving.

**What's next for Rivals**

The next step is to keep turning Rivals into a game that people want to return to every day.

I want to improve the gameplay based on real player feedback, make the competition between friends even better, and continue improving the overall game experience.

I also want to expand Rivals beyond the initial three puzzle types over time, while keeping the core idea intact:

A quick daily challenge that is easy to pick up, fun to solve, and more exciting when your friends are trying to beat your score.

</details>

**🐈 Initial idea**

I hate workout apps, so I used to just dump all my gym logs to a ginormous file in the notes app. It turned out I'm not the only one, so I built Beau. You can still type (or even dictate) your workout in natural language, and it logs everything on its own, so the only thing left for you is to track your progress.

**How it works**

You pop into the app and jot down the activity you want to log - there are hundreds of strength, cardio, and recreational activities you can log. The app turns your raw input into structured workout logs that allow for overtime progress tracking and (estimated) calorie expenditure counting. Faster and much more frictionless than traditional gym apps due to lack of heavy interfaces.

**How I built it**

The app itself is a native SwiftUI app sprinkled with custom drawings, animations, and funky UI components. The language processing is done through Google AI Labs' Gemini 3.1 Flash API with a large set of instructions and other optimizations that allow for speed and high precision.

**Challenges we faced**

First of all, I am BAD at drawing, so producing the various drawings and animating them was an.. insightful experience.

That said, challenge number one was getting the model to recognize different writing styles and shortcuts (e.g. 8-8-8 reps, 2x3 reps, etc.) based on the context. It consumed the most time.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

On the technical side, I'm proud that, given such a small and relatively cheap model, we reached the point where the app can decompose and process even large multiple-paragraph chunks of text (like when the user copy-pastes the workout from the notes app) in under a few seconds.

On the front end side, I quite like the visual style and the micro interactions that were achieved here (especially the mascot artworks and animations).

**What was learned**

A LOT. It was the first iOS-native consumer app I ever developed, so pretty much the entirety of the late production stages were completely new to me.

**What's next for Beau Workout Journal**

I have been sharing every single day of development of Instagram, and the waitlist signups count just surpassed 50 people. So I expect a smooth launch in a month or so (if Apple ever approves my developer account at all, the process is extremely slow right now).

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**🚀 Warnly — Autonomous Severe Weather & Storm Defense**

**💡 Inspiration**

- The Problem: Standard weather applications are built for sunny days: they provide a 7-day forecast and serve banner ads. However, when violent convective squalls, cloudbursts, or sudden lightning barrages strike, cellular towers routinely lose power, cloud-dependent push notifications fail, and traditional apps go completely dark. Furthermore, victims frequently sleep through imminent danger because consumer smartphones are locked in Do Not Disturb or silent mode.

- The Next Gen Spark: As a student developer entering the Next Gen Track, I believe emergency software should operate like an airplane flight recorder—completely autonomous, mathematically deterministic, and 100% operational with zero bars of cellular signal. I built Warnly to prove that a next-generation software engineer can solve critical life-safety problems using resilient, offline-first native architectures that function independently of external cloud servers.

**💻 What it does**

Warnly turns any smartphone into an autonomous emergency command station that monitors atmospheric trends, intercepts severe threats locally, and triggers life-saving alerts even when electrical and cellular grids fail.

- Deterministic Threat Tracking: Evaluates real-time atmospheric telemetry (such as CAPE &gt; 2,800 J/kg, Blitzortung VLF pulse arrival, and barometric plunge rates) to calculate a localized threat index.

- Hardware Siren Override: Bypasses Android's silent and Do Not Disturb constraints by directly binding to the low-level alarm audio stream (AudioAttributes.USAGE_ALARM), blasting a 960Hz dual-tone emergency siren when severe weather is within 10 km.

- Tactical Radar & METAR Decoding: Blends high-resolution satellite imagery with RainViewer Doppler reflectivity sweeps to trace storm cells while decoding local airport METAR feeds for ground truth verification.

- Aegis Action Compiler: Translates raw sensor telemetry into actionable, life-saving shelter directives, tracking safety thresholds deterministically.

**🛠️ How I built it**

I architected Warnly around an offline-first system capable of executing complex thermodynamic and tactical routing logic directly on-device:

- Frontend Framework: Built using React Native and TypeScript styled with NativeWind for zero-lag 60 FPS mobile performance.

- Monetization & Entitlement (RevenueCat): Deeply integrated the official RevenueCat SDK (react-native-purchases) to manage Pro entitlements (warnly_pro), dynamically loading offerings with local cryptographic caching so user safety tiers remain active during total infrastructure blackouts.

- Hardware HAL Layer: Leveraged native Android SDK hooks to utilize AudioAttributes.USAGE_ALARM for critical volume overrides and Sensor.TYPE_PRESSURE for continuous barometric microburst analysis without internet access.

- Mapping & Telemetry: Combined ESRI satellite baseline layers with RainViewer Doppler radar composites and Blitzortung time-of-arrival (TOA) lightning strokes.

- Next Gen Store-Exempt Delivery: Fully compliant with Next Gen track submission rules—hosted a live interactive web app on Cloudflare Workers, published open-source code under the Apache 2.0 license, and built direct installable Android APKs via an automated GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline.

**🧠 Challenges I ran into**

- Android Audio HAL Bypass: Android aggressively mutes background audio streams when Do Not Disturb is active. I overcame this restriction by routing my alert tones through low-level STREAM_ALARM parameters, ensuring critical life-safety audio punches through system constraints without requiring root permissions.

- 60 FPS Doppler Sweeps: Rendering animated storm cell radar loops seamlessly over satellite textures caused immediate frame drops and thermal spikes on physical hardware. I optimized this by designing an efficient client-side image processing layer to preserve silky-smooth rendering.

- Next Gen Presentation Constraints: Condensing deep atmospheric physics, hardware sensor feeds, 10 mathematical Astra engines, and live RevenueCat billing telemetry into a digestible presentation was tough. I solved this by engineering a fast-paced 16:9 widescreen demonstration that delivers absolute proof in exactly 01:52, safely inside the 2-minute hackathon limit.

**🏅 Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- Built & Tested on Physical Hardware: Successfully compiled, validated, and screen-recorded live workflows directly on real Android hardware (Realme Narzo 5G RMX3381).

- Deep RevenueCat Subscription Stack: Configured sandbox paywalls, product packages, and real-time customer update listeners to demonstrate sustainable, professional app monetization as a solo Next Gen creator.

- Single-Digit Millisecond Offline Engines: Engineered 10 specialized offline calculation engines (such as AEGIS, FLASH, and SURGE) running raw local physics and acoustic triangulation completely isolated from cloud dependencies.

- Next Gen Compliance: 100% compliant with the Next Gen Award track criteria (open source Apache 2.0, direct installable release build, working video demo, and deep RevenueCat integration).

**📖 What I learned**

- Low-Level Native Engineering: Developed deep knowledge of Android hardware background lifecycles, real-time sensor processing pipelines, and raw audio routing rules.

- Ethical Subscription Architecture: Gained hands-on experience structuring tier capabilities with RevenueCat, ensuring that fundamental life-safety alerts remain free and universally accessible, while advanced multi-zone Family Shield tracking funds long-term development.

- Next Gen Agility: Learned how modern developer tooling and clean architecture allow a solo student developer to build software with the stability and polish of industrial defense tools.

**🚀 What's next for Warnly**

- P2P Mesh Expansion: Refine underlying Bluetooth LE and Wi-Fi Direct mesh relays to allow wider, automated text alert hopping across local ad-hoc topologies when cell towers go down.

- Cross-Platform Parity: Port my native hardware sensor hooks into an identical iOS package using Swift Native Audio and CoreMotion sensor loops.

- Expanded Hazard Graph: Incorporate localized seismic P-wave and flash-flood inundation mapping to widen defensive tracking capabilities across a broader spectrum of natural hazards.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

News moves quickly, but verifying what we see online is often slow and difficult. This becomes more challenging when information is shared across different Indian languages and when AI-generated answers can confidently state things without sufficient evidence.

I wanted to build something that makes two tasks simple: discover what is happening and check whether a claim is actually supported by evidence.

That led to NewzWale — "Only Facts News."

**What it does**

NewzWale combines a live Indian news discovery platform with an evidence-grounded fact-checking system.

The news side aggregates current headlines across categories and Indian languages and links users to the original publisher rather than rewriting or republishing the article.

The core feature is the Fact Check Explorer. A user can enter a headline, claim, or article URL. NewzWale retrieves evidence from two independent paths:

- Published fact-checks through the Google Fact Check Tools API.

- Live web evidence through web search and page retrieval.

These sources are processed together before the system produces a verdict.

The fact-checker supports six outcomes:

- True

- False

- Partly true

- Misleading

- Needs context

- Unverified

The important design decision is that the AI model does not get the final say. The model reasons over the retrieved evidence and proposes a verdict, while a deterministic verification gate applies the final rules. Definite True/False verdicts require independent corroboration; otherwise the system can downgrade the result to a more cautious verdict such as Unverified.

Every result exposes the evidence used so users can inspect the basis for the conclusion.

**How I built it**

NewzWale is built with Astro and deployed as a Cloudflare Worker.

The architecture uses:

- Astro SSR for the web application

- Cloudflare Workers for edge deployment

- Cloudflare KV for caching

- Cloudflare Workers AI for evidence-grounded reasoning

- Tailwind CSS for the design system

- NewsData.io and RSS feeds for news ingestion

- Google Fact Check Tools API for published fact-check retrieval

- Tavily for live web evidence retrieval

- Vitest for automated testing

The fact-check pipeline is deliberately separated into retrieval, evidence processing, model reasoning, and deterministic verdict assessment. This makes it possible to test the individual stages instead of treating the entire AI response as a black box.

The application also includes features such as multilingual headline browsing, saved articles, fact-check history, topic customization, dark mode, search, an installable PWA, and accessibility checks.

**Challenges**

The hardest part was not calling an AI model. It was deciding when the system should trust an answer and when it should refuse to make a definitive claim.

A naive implementation could simply ask an LLM whether a statement is true. That creates a serious problem: the model may produce a convincing answer even when it has insufficient evidence.

I therefore designed the pipeline so that evidence is retrieved first and the model reasons only over that retrieved evidence. A separate deterministic gate then controls which verdicts are actually allowed to reach the user.

Another challenge was handling unreliable upstream data. News APIs can fail or become rate-limited, so the news ingestion layer includes RSS fallbacks and caching.

I also built automated tests around the fact-checking logic, security headers, database schema, and accessibility rather than relying only on manual testing.

**What I learned**

The biggest lesson was that building an AI product is often more about controlling what the model is allowed to do than simply choosing a better model.

Grounding, evidence retrieval, deterministic rules, conservative fallbacks, caching, and testing are all important when the product is making claims about the real world.

I also learned that multilingual products require more than translating an English interface. Search, ranking, tokenization, evidence retrieval, and data availability can behave differently across languages.

**What's next**

The next stage for NewzWale is to improve evidence coverage, expand the multilingual experience, provision the remaining production data infrastructure, and add image/screenshot claim verification.

The long-term goal is to make NewzWale a practical verification layer for Indian digital news — helping users move from "I saw this online" to "Here is the evidence behind this claim."

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

The spark for Pack-a-Bunch came during a postgraduate research trip. While struggling to pack the back of a bakkie (pickup truck) under the blazing sun, my supervisor jokingly remarked, "Why can't we just magically poof it packs itself like Tetris?" Finding a way to make everything fit efficiently was incredibly frustrating, and that exact comment ignited the idea. I wanted to take the spatial puzzle of Tetris and apply it directly to real-world loading, moving, and packing headaches.

**What it does**

Pack-a-Bunch takes the stressful guesswork out of arranging objects into tight physical zones. 

- Space Mapping: Scan irregular volumes, such as a car boot with awkward wheel arches or a cupboard with built-in shelving via your device's camera, or manually input physical internal dimensions. 

- Item Library: Log the items you need to pack by adding names, dimensions, quantities, stacking limits, and allowable rotations.

- Deterministic Solver: A custom pure Kotlin heuristic engine calculates a logical layout arrangement. Instead of giving confusing optimization scores, it reports clean, modeled fill volume and states exactly what could not fit and why.

- Visual Packing Guide: Walks users through a physical layer-by-layer arrangement via an elegant, native 3D isometric interface, showing you exactly what piece goes where from the bottom up.

**How I built it**

Pack-a-Bunch is designed with a strict layer separation to maximize speed, portability, and native UI consistency:

- UI & Frontend: Built natively using Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, and Material 3. Custom motion design tokens and high-fidelity animations were modeled in Figma and rendered smoothly using Lottie.

- Core Logic Engine: A highly performant, unit-testable Pure Kotlin module completely isolated from Android framework dependencies. Lengths are processed strictly as integer millimeters.

- Computer Vision Hybrid Stack: A local Python engine running NumPy and OpenCV embedded directly on the mobile device via Chaquopy. It parses ML Kit object bounds and ARCore spatial anchors to map object depth surfaces and identify physical dimensions.

- Data & Infrastructure: Powered by Supabase Auth and a PostgreSQL cloud backend, alongside local Room database synchronization.

- Monetization & Frameworks: Integrated via the RevenueCat SDK to handle tiered free/premium boundaries alongside native Google Pay Billing integrations.

**Challenges I ran into**

The absolute toughest hurdle was overcoming camera-scanning imprecision. Translating raw physical spaces and uneven item depths into clean mathematical bounds proved notoriously difficult. Initial camera-based dimension estimations were inaccurate and fell far short of the pixel-perfect layouts I had structured on my Figma artboards. 

To conquer this, I engineered a robust fallback system: the app enforces a persistent manual dimensions input flow that is never hidden from the user, and the architecture catches Python/Chaquopy scanning anomalies gracefully by shifting dynamically to the Kotlin ScanMath.kt local module.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- High-Fidelity UI Motion: Creating highly responsive, well-received interface animations on my very first attempt. 

- Algorithmic Craft: Building an isolated, high-speed spatial heuristic engine that operates independently of the platform UI and behaves identically regardless of user subscription tiers.

- Asset Modeling: Spending grueling, dedicated hours modeling 3D representations for every conceivable daily object I had th time to model so that the user's packing guide renders realistic, easily recognizable canvas shapes.

**What I learned**

This project pushed me far past the boundaries of a traditional designer. I learned how to move beyond static layouts into fully responsive animation generation in Figma. On the technical side, I significantly expanded my mobile system knowledge by figuring out how to successfully interface a localized Python data-science pipeline (Chaquopy, OpenCV, NumPy) right inside a native Kotlin Android structure. 

**What's next for Pack-a-Bunch**

- Global App Market Launch: Successfully publishing the production build directly onto the Google Play Store to help everyday people solve real-life packing struggles.

- Cross-Platform Portability: Rewriting the frontend architecture into a multiplatform format to deploy a native iOS version.

- Bypassing Spatial Roadblocks: Replacing the ARCore layer with an independent, universally compatible spatial measuring method that functions fluidly on older, lower-spec mobile devices without hardware barriers.

- Scaling Infrastructure: Expanding the backend cloud database architecture to handle high-concurrency automated sync states for extensive user asset libraries.

- Recognizable Space Modeling: Expanding the 3D library to include fully recognizable environment templates and structures, allowing the packing guide to perfectly mirror specific, real-world spaces.

- Advanced Gap Optimization: Refining the algorithmic solver to support hyper-dense, gap-filling calculations that push space utility to its absolute limit.

- Interactive Layer Customization: Implementing manual item manipulation directly within the layered 3D view, giving users the perfect hybrid balance of automated packing logic and precise, custom control.

</details>

**Inspiration**

when someone wanted to try/learn something new, the process is not easy they may encounter questions like where should i start ?, what i get from learning this ?, how much time i need to spend on this ?, how can i manage my time ? etc . in that barrage of questions they may end up without actually starting their project/work or something they want to try. Myself I experienced this a lot, always confused about what i am about to do. that's when i realized i don't need more time, i just need a proper structure and people who support me. I tried to maintain diary with to-do list but its not that easy to carry a diary with you wherever you go if you do you will be seen as a nerd even though its ok it will affect your motivation, social circle and mental peace as many people always try to mock you.
 thats when i started working on this project to help others reach their goals without embarrassment . i inspired from my experience of being seen as nerd and diary. its better to be a wolf in sheep's clothing to reach your goals without any guilt. I am certain , this will help someone who go through some experiences that can never be said.

**What it does**

it addresses the problems mentioned above It lets users:

- Create multi-day plans with tasks, subtasks, schedules, dates, and reminders.

- Check off daily tasks and track completion progress.

- Add journal notes and view plan history.

- Monitor streaks, consistency, completion speed, badges, and analytics charts.

- Browse, save, vote on, discuss, and join community-created plans.

- Follow creators, view creator profiles, and publish personal plans.

- Message other users through conversations and chat.

- Receive notifications for reminders, community activity, and messages.

- Customize profile, appearance, timezone, privacy, accessibility, and notification settings.

- Continue using locally stored plans offline
The main navigation is:

- Home: personal plans and community activity.

- Create: create a new plan and task templates.

- Explore: search community plans and creators.

- Profile: personal analytics, plans, and social profile.

- Settings: account, notifications, backup, export, and appearance options.
**How we built it**
build it using native android frameworks
**Challenges we ran into**
Making an app offline-first is exponentially harder than building an online-only app. We had local Room SQLite databases acting as the immediate source of truth, but users also needed to publish routines, fork public plans, track check-ins across multiple days, and sync to Supabase.
Plans created offline were failing to sync remote tasks because the Sync Outbox Repository wasn’t wired cleanly into Create PlanView Model Factory.
When users imported community plans, the original creator tasks and multi-day check-in timelines would either drop or fail to deserialize due to PostgREST array decoding errors and schema mismatches.
Supabase RLS policies rejected conversation inserts because authenticated user IDs and creator foreign keys were out of sync.
lot of time spent on designing the particular architecture that addresses this problems and developing the backend
**Accomplishments that we're proud of**
the project is successfully working(both offline and online) and helping my classmates , i am very proud of this.

**What's next for Taxent planner**

even though it is running properly it needs some upgrades and improvements like:
1.Interactive Home Screen Widgets (Jetpack Glance):
Expand the home screen widget so users can check off daily subtasks directly from their Android home screen without launching the full app.
2.Hook into Google Health Connect to auto-complete physical habits (e.g., step goals, sleep tracking, or workout duration) without manual entry.
3."Prompt-to-Plan" AI Blueprint Generator. Users type natural language goals (e.g., "Prepare for a half marathon in 8 weeks with 3 running days and 2 strength days").

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/075/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/075/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/076/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/076/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/077/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/077/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/078/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/436/078/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

In a recent cybersecurity class we discussed a simple idea: attacks will happen so the real question is how well you've prepared to limit the damage. That made me think about physical safety in the same way. If a real attack or a severe storm hit, would I know where to go? Today the main option is MSB's official shelter map, which I found slow and hard to use. I wanted to build something fast and easy to explore that shows how many shelters are actually around you and the quickest route to the nearest one. I also hope it sparks some curiosity: what is it like inside a shelter and how many people does it hold?

**What it does**

Shelter Locator public shelters and helps you find the fastest route to one nearby. You can search for an address or drop a pin and choose walking, cycling, driving or public transport. Each shelter shows its address and official capacity. The shelters can also be used for severe weather and other emergencies, not just attacks. There is also a live layer where people can check in and share basic information about how full a shelter is and what resources are available. The live check-in layer is currently offline while the backend is being upgraded.

**How I built it**

The app is a single-page web app with a native Android version built in Kotlin/Compose. I used Sweden’s official shelter data from MSB, MapLibre for the map, OSRM for routing and Trafiklab for public transport. Supabase handles the live check-ins and privacy rules.

**Challenges**

The biggest challenge was dealing with the official shelter data. The dataset was large, incomplete in some places and difficult to download reliably, so I had to clean it and connect shelters to the correct municipalities. Routing was another challenge. With over 63 000 shelters, I couldn't calculate every route individually. Instead, I use travel-time matrices to find the fastest options. Privacy was also important. I wanted useful information about shelter occupancy without exposing personal information. Check-in data is therefore separated and protected using database-level access rules.

**Accomplishments that I am proud of**

Someone with devtools open cannot forge an occupancy number, edit someone else's check-in, inflate several shelters at once, or read another shelter's roster.
I am proud that it is now faster and visually more fun and interactive to play with than the available page for this.

**What I learned**

**Inspiration**

I wanted to build something simple that could make sharing images a little easier. Sometimes sending an image directly or sharing a long URL is not convenient, especially for posters, presentations, or printed content.

That gave me the idea to create a tool that turns an image into a QR code so it can be opened quickly by scanning it.

**What it does**

This project lets users turn an image into a QR code in just a few steps.

You can upload an image or enter an image URL, generate a QR code, and then scan it to access the image. The interface is kept simple so users can understand what to do without going through a complicated process.

**How we built it**

We focused on building a simple web interface where the whole process happens in one place.

The user provides an image or image URL, the application creates a QR code for it, and the result is shown on the screen so it can be shared or saved.

While building it, we focused mostly on keeping the interface clean and making the process quick.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the main challenges was making sure the generated QR code actually worked correctly when scanned.

We also had to handle different types of image input and make the interface clear enough that users would not get confused.

Getting the functionality and the user experience to work smoothly together took some testing and adjustments.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are happy that we turned a simple idea into a working tool that can be useful in everyday situations.

The best part is that the process is very straightforward. You provide an image, generate the QR code, and you are ready to share it.

**What we learned**

This project taught us a lot about connecting different parts of a web application and handling user input properly.

We also learned that even a small idea can become a useful project when the experience is simple and focused.

**What's next for Turn an image into a QR code.**

We would like to add more customization options in the future, such as different QR styles, more download options, and better support for different devices.

We also want to keep improving the overall experience and make the tool even easier to use.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

**What it does**

**How we built it**

**Challenges we ran into**

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

**What we learned**

**What's next for PortalX**

**💡 Inspiration**

In today's digital age, physical ID cards and static KYC documents leave a permanent, vulnerable data trail. Inspired by the concept of "self-destructing messages," we wanted to build a Universal Temporary Identity Layer. The goal was to give users complete control over their identity by ensuring their data exists only for the exact duration of a transaction, completely eliminating the risk of data breaches.

**⚙️ What it does**

PortalX is a NextGen Ephemeral Identity Layer. Instead of sharing a physical ID, users generate a time-bound "Secure Enclave" authenticated via 3-Factor Biometric Convergence (Retina, Voiceprint, and Liveness). Once the verification timer expires, the identity packet self-destructs completely, leaving zero data trail.

**💰 Business Model (RevenueCat Integration)**

To make PortalX a sustainable business, we designed a highly scalable SaaS model using RevenueCat:

- PortalX Pro (B2C): Basic ephemeral IDs are free. Users can upgrade via RevenueCat in-app subscriptions to unlock premium features like extended token lifespans, multi-device identity sync, and advanced privacy audit logs. RevenueCat makes handling these cross-platform subscriptions seamless.

- Enterprise API (B2B): Businesses pay a tier-based subscription to access our verification API, allowing them to verify users without the liability of storing KYC data.

**🛠️ How we built it**

We architected the system to achieve strictly enforced OWASP MSTG-L2 compliance. A massive part of our engineering went into mapping the architecture to comply with 11 major regulatory frameworks, including RBI, NPCI, PCI DSS, FIU-IND, UIDAI, and the DPDP Act. We built automated Python scripts to generate our Master Compliance Architecture dossier.

**🚧 Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge was architecting a system that satisfies 11 different legal and regulatory authorities simultaneously while keeping the user experience frictionless (under 2 seconds for generation). Designing the "zero-knowledge self-destruct" mechanism without violating financial audit trail requirements took intense architectural planning.

**🚀 What's next for PortalX**

We plan to fully deploy the Enterprise API and expand our RevenueCat subscription tiers to include "Family Privacy" plans. We also aim to integrate hardware-level secure enclaves on mobile devices for faster biometric processing.

</details>

🌐 joingrabit.com

Grab It is a local giving marketplace: a mobile app where people list items they no longer need and others claim them for free pickup. Listing, claiming, and pickup messaging stay free forever; optional paid upgrades (Grab It Pro) add extra listing photos, priority reserves, and a supporter badge.

Less waste, more reuse, and a small but real boost to community trust, since listing and claiming cost nothing. The only paid tier is a small convenience upgrade; the core act of giving never sits behind a paywall.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Studying can mean working alone, comparing answers with friends, and needing somewhere to sketch an idea before writing an answer. MindMesh brings those activities into one study app: shared quiz rooms, independent practice, private feedback, and a drawing workspace for rough working.

**What it does**

MindMesh lets students join a study room, mark themselves ready, answer the same timed questions and compare their results. Each participant can review their own answers, marks and explanations. The backend controls quiz progress and scoring, and reconnecting clients recover the shared state.

The source also includes self-paced solo practice, Studio/Wood/Glass/Paper appearance choices with light and dark modes, private drawing scratchwork with geometry tools, and an earned cosmetic pet system. Companions have simple personalities and reactions; coins reward qualifying participation and buy cosmetic choices rather than better quiz scores.

Adaptive preparation creates a subject/topic-based question set and runs validation and verification before play. Multiple-choice and numerical answers are marked deterministically. Room written answers and eligible longer solo responses use a bounded AI rubric-grading path. Short solo written responses use an explicitly labelled self-assessment step. AI feedback can be wrong, and self-assessed marks are not independent grading.

The starter catalogue covers six GCSE subjects and eighteen topics. It is not a complete syllabus or a claim of exam-board accreditation. Drawing is private rough working, not submitted handwriting. Learning illustrations are curated examples rather than images generated for each question.

**How it is built**

MindMesh uses Expo, React Native and strict TypeScript for the client; FastAPI and PostgreSQL for application state; and Supabase Auth for sign-in. Server-side adapters handle adaptive generation and eligible written marking. Provider secrets stay on the backend. The public source targets Expo SDK 57 and includes database migrations through 0012_learning_companions.

The project began under the working name StudyRoom, which remains in technical identifiers for compatibility. The app’s own visible branding is now MindMesh and MindMesh Pro. The published repository excludes the earlier music assets and playback controls.

**RevenueCat integration**

The source integrates the RevenueCat SDK for a development Pro offering and entitlement, with backend checks for Pro room capacity and client-side cosmetic presentation gates. It supports RevenueCat Test Store configuration; the public source contains no configured credentials and does not claim production App Store products, real payments or revenue. Test Store is a development integration, not a live commercial store launch.

**Challenges and what the implementation taught us**

Keeping two clients consistent required server-owned question transitions, answer locking and reconnect recovery. Written grading introduced another failure path: a response could be accepted while marking was unavailable. The implementation exposes that state and supports controlled marking recovery rather than inventing a score.

The solo and rewards paths required separate ownership and idempotency rules. A drawing workspace also needed to preserve geometry, respect the selected theme and avoid competing with quiz navigation and timers. The main engineering lesson was to distinguish a successful interface interaction from authoritative completion, and to keep reward issuance, private review and recovery tied to server state.

The submission package separates project source from external media and documents dependency licences, outstanding evidence gaps and validation limits.

**Accomplishments and validation**

An earlier native development build completed a two-device multiplayer test through questions, matching results, return to the waiting room and background/reconnect recovery. One adaptive five-mark geometry test reached completion with both participants' private reviews after a marking interruption was recovered. These are observations from earlier builds, not a broad assessment of educational accuracy.

The no-music source snapshot passed strict TypeScript, 605 mobile tests and an offline iOS JavaScript export. After the visible-branding update, strict TypeScript and all 606 default mobile tests passed on the public source. Selected backend tests also passed; database-dependent skips are documented and are not passes. The exact upgraded snapshot has not received a full native build or end-to-end device validation. Later solo, drawing, theme and companion features are source implementations; earlier device testing does not establish full runtime coverage of those additions.

**What is next**

Our future ambition is live voice study rooms, screen sharing and a shared whiteboard, with student-led peer teaching. We also plan personalised daily practice that adapts to mistakes and progress, using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to ground questions and explanations in trusted learning materials. These are future roadmap ideas. The immediate priorities are validating the upgraded client and backend together on devices, broadening educational evaluation and curriculum coverage, and completing production deployment and store configuration. This is a development-stage Next Gen Award entry.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration## Inspiration**

Perimenopause is one of the most under-supported health transitions a woman goes through, and it's especially invisible for Gen X women in their mid-40s to mid-50s. Research shows 61% of women feel their doctors dismiss their symptoms, and a JAMA study found emotional and cognitive symptoms like brain fog and rage show up far more often in women's own words online than in their actual medical records — meaning doctors are literally documenting a different, narrower set of symptoms than what women are actually experiencing. We wanted to build something that closes that gap: an app that takes women seriously from day one, and gives them the tools to be taken seriously by their doctors too.

**What it does**

GirlyCycle is a perimenopause companion app that lets women:

- Log symptoms daily, ordered by real-world frequency (fatigue, irritability, and poor sleep first — not just hot flashes)

- See pattern insights, like correlations between poor sleep and brain fog

- Generate a Doctor Dossier — a clean, exportable report built to actually get read and taken seriously in an appointment

- Access an Atelier Membership for deeper insights and reports, with a 21-day free trial powered by RevenueCat

- Preview a community space for shared validation and support (full peer circles coming next)

Daily symptom logging is free forever. We only gate the deeper insights and doctor reports — because the core habit of tracking your body shouldn't cost anything.

**How we built it**

- Kotlin + Jetpack Compose for a native Android app with a warm, editorial, non-clinical design system

- Room database for local, private symptom storage

- MVVM architecture to keep logic clean and testable

- RevenueCat powers our entire subscription and paywall system — offerings, purchase flow, entitlement checks, and restore purchases, all wired through a single EntitlementManager so premium features unlock the moment a purchase (or trial) is active

- Built with the help of AI-assisted coding tools to move fast as a solo/student builder

**Challenges we ran into**

As a student building solo, the biggest challenges weren't the app logic — they were the build pipeline itself. We hit Gradle wrapper issues, network timeouts pulling dependencies, missing debug keystores, and Google Services config errors, all while racing the deadline. Debugging Android build tooling from scratch, without a pre-existing dev environment, ended up being one of the most valuable (and stressful) parts of the whole hackathon.

**What we learned**

Real research changes real product decisions. Reordering our symptom list by actual reported frequency, giving emotional symptoms equal visual weight, and building the Doctor Dossier around what doctors actually document (not what patients experience) all came directly from digging into real complaints on forums like Reddit's r/Menopause — not assumptions.

**What's next**

- Full RevenueCat production setup with live Google Play products

- Complete the peer community feature (currently a preview)

- Localization for Asian markets, where perimenopause support and menopause-specific health apps remain especially underserved

- Expand the correlation engine with more rule-based insights

</details>

**Video (1:51):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m3O65pUAlHA

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/m3O65pUAlHA/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m3O65pUAlHA)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/437/000/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/437/000/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Screen-time dashboards show you a number and a guilty feeling. Hard blockers work until the first time you genuinely need the app — then you switch them off for good. I wanted something in between: a reason to stay away that feels good, and an honest way back in that doesn't break the habit.

**What it does**

QuestLog flips the screen-time tracker around: instead of scolding you for time spent, it rewards the time you didn't spend. Pick your distracting apps (with optional daily allowances), and every minute you stay off them earns XP and gold.

- Build a city — gold buys buildings for your realm: Market, Library, Zen Garden and more.

- Daily quests and streaks — three fresh quests a day, and a streak that multiplies your rewards.

- Mindful Unlocks — need the app anyway? Type why. A small AI judgment model (TypeSafe) checks whether it's a real task. If it is, you get five minutes that don't count against you. Just bored? It tells you honestly and still lets you in. No lectures, no blocking, and what you typed is never stored.

- Progress — all-time time reclaimed, best day, level and a 7-day chart.

- Share your skyline — a card of your city and the hours you've taken back.

**How RevenueCat powers it**

- QuestLog Pro is a RevenueCat subscription: double XP and gold, a weekly Streak Freeze, unlimited Mindful Unlocks (free players get one a day) and two exclusive buildings.

- Offer-driven paywall — price and trial text come live from the current RevenueCat Offering, so pricing and trial experiments are dashboard-only changes.

- The trial appears when it's earned — the first time a free player reaches a 7-day streak, the paywall slides up once with a 1-week free trial. Trial eligibility comes from Google Play, so ineligible users never see false "free trial" copy.

- Safe entitlement handling — "Pro status unknown" is treated differently from "free", so a paying user on a slow cold start never sees a paywall.

**How I built it**

- Kotlin Multiplatform core with all the domain logic, plus a Jetpack Compose Android UI.

- Room (KMP) with versioned, tested migrations; Koin for DI; MVI-style ViewModels.

- Screen time comes from Android's UsageStatsManager, and stays on the device.

- Idempotent reward accounting — a daily high-water mark means rewards are never double-counted, however often the tracker ticks.

- A Cloudflare Worker proxy for the AI call: the API key never ships in the app, with per-install rate limiting and request-size limits.

- 228 automated tests run in CI on every change.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Making rewards fair: an app blocked at any point today keeps counting until midnight, so unblocking can't game the reward, and allowances only charge overage.

- Keeping the AI useful without being preachy — the verdict is typed (purposeful or not, and what kind of task), and it never blocks you.

- Google Play's new-account rule: a closed test with 12 testers for 14 days before production. QuestLog is complete and in closed testing, and I'm recruiting testers to go public.

**Accomplishments I'm proud of**

A calm, single-accent editorial design; a skyline realm that grows as you scroll less; and a paywall that shows up at a moment of pride (your first 7-day streak) instead of as a nag.

**What I learned**

How to design entitlement logic that fails safe, how to run AI as a small decision-maker rather than a chatbot, and everything involved in shipping a real app to Google Play.

**What's next**

- Public launch on Google Play once the closed test completes.

- iOS — the Kotlin Multiplatform core is already shared; the UI is the remaining work.

- RevenueCat Experiments on trial length and price.

- More buildings and seasonal quests.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/440/265/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/440/265/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/440/266/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/440/266/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/440/267/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/440/267/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/440/268/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/440/268/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**About the Project**

**Inspiration**

We were inspired by a simple problem with the way people learn languages: you can spend months memorizing vocabulary and studying grammar, but still struggle when it is time to actually speak.

We wanted to build something focused on the part that matters most: using the language.

That idea led to VOCES, a voice-first language immersion app where learners practice through natural conversations instead of relying mainly on word lists and traditional exercises.

Our goal was to make speaking practice feel less like taking a lesson and more like having an actual conversation.

**How We Built It**

VOCES is built around voice interaction. Users choose a language and a realistic scenario, then speak naturally with an AI conversation partner through their microphone.

The conversation engine maintains context throughout each session, allowing the AI to respond based on what has already been discussed rather than treating every interaction as an isolated question.

One of our main design decisions was corrections after the conversation.

Instead of interrupting learners every time they make a mistake, VOCES lets them stay focused on communicating. After the session, the app provides corrections, useful feedback, and areas they can improve.

We also built a smart vocabulary system that tracks when words are introduced, how strongly they have been reinforced, and which words the learner struggles to use.

Those weaker words can then be naturally brought back into future conversations and review sessions.

VOCES currently supports English, Spanish, Italian, German, and French, with the architecture designed to support additional languages in the future.

**What We Learned**

Building VOCES taught us that adding AI to an application is only part of the challenge. The bigger challenge is designing how the AI should interact with the learner.

We learned how important conversation context is for making AI interactions feel natural. We also learned that personalization becomes much more useful when it is based on actual user behavior rather than simply asking users what they want to practice.

Most importantly, we learned that speaking practice, feedback, and vocabulary reinforcement do not need to exist as separate activities.

They can work together as one continuous learning loop:

$$
\text{Conversation} \rightarrow \text{Feedback} \rightarrow \text{Reinforcement} \rightarrow \text{Better Conversation}
$$

**Challenges**

One of our biggest challenges was making AI conversations feel natural while still keeping them useful for learning.

We did not want VOCES to feel like a chatbot randomly asking questions, but we also did not want conversations to become completely unstructured. The conversation engine needed to understand the current context while still guiding the learner toward meaningful language practice.

Voice interaction created another challenge. Speech recognition, AI response generation, and voice output all need to work together quickly enough that the conversation does not feel broken or delayed.

We also had to figure out how to provide useful corrections without overwhelming the learner. This is why we chose to move detailed corrections to the end of the session.

These challenges shaped VOCES around one core principle:

Speak first. Learn from the conversation. Then speak better next time.

</details>
