<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Oculo**

plan your shot before you shoot

Oculo is a mobile spatial-cinematography workspace. A filmmaker steps into a photorealistic 3D scene, frames real camera and lens choices, saves annotated shots, and shares a shot plan the crew can read, all on an iPhone.

**The problem**

Location scouting and shot planning usually mean photos, sketches and long messages, and a collaborator still can't see the exact framing you meant. Oculo lets you walk a captured scene, compose the shot with real lens controls, and hand over a plan that shows exactly what you framed.

**What it does**

Explore a real place. Import a .spz scene from a real capture, or open one of the bundled photorealistic scenes: Small Garden, La Nuit, Pantheon, The Moon and the International Space Station. The bundled scenes work offline.
Compose with real camera controls. Choose the lens (focal length and aperture), set the frame's aspect ratio, and move through the scene by touch. On iPhone, Magic Window turns the phone's motion into a handheld camera.
Save annotated shots. Name each shot, add notes, and keep a saved reference frame.
Plan camera moves. Build a move from keyframes with a speed curve, then preview it as a short MP4.
Share a shot plan. Export printable PNG shot sheets with each frame, its lens and its notes, readable by someone who doesn't have the app. Each sheet includes the credits for the scene.
Local-first. Projects live on the device and reopen after a restart. Nothing is uploaded unless you choose to share it.

**How RevenueCat powers the app**

Oculo is free for one saved project, with the full workflow: import, shots, notes, moves, PNG sheets and video previews. Oculo Pro is a single one-time, non-consumable purchase that removes the project limit.

The RevenueCat SDK loads the default offering and the Oculo_Pro_Lifetime package , and runs the purchase.
Unlock is decided by the oculo_pro entitlement. The app checks it and gates only the creation of additional projects.
Trying to create a second project opens the paywall. After the purchase, the second project is created straight away.
Restore Purchases works without any account or login.
Existing projects are never locked or lost if the entitlement changes, so users keep access to their own work.

**How we built it**

A shared TypeScript codebase using React and Vite in a Capacitor iOS shell, with Three.js and the Spark renderer for the 3D scenes. Scenes are stored in the on-device database (IndexedDB), and the shot sheets and video previews are rendered on the device. The app has 709 automated tests.

**Challenges**

Keeping large 3D scenes smooth on a phone. We cap each scene's splat count and re-encode scenes for mobile.
Making local-first storage reliable: atomic writes, safe imports and deleting shared scene files correctly.
Keeping the free tier genuinely useful while giving Pro a clear reason to exist.

**What's next**

Android support, optional accounts and cloud backup, and generating scenes directly in the app.

Built with: TypeScript, React, Vite, Capacitor, Three.js, Spark, RevenueCat, IndexedDB, Mediabunny

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Inspiration

Most AI assistants are designed as tools: you open them, ask something, get an answer, and leave.

We wanted to build something different — an AI companion that feels more personal and interactive. The idea behind MAXie came from the simplicity of virtual pets combined with modern AI: instead of just watching an animated character, users can interact with a companion that remembers interactions, develops personality, reacts to them, and grows over time.

Our goal was to make AI feel less like another app and more like a companion that users enjoy coming back to.

What it does

MAXie is an AI-powered interactive companion for mobile, with a companion experience designed around personality, memory, emotions, and interaction.

Users can:

💬 Interact with MAXie through AI conversations
🧠 Build persistent memories and interaction history
❤️ Develop a friendship/XP relationship with MAXie
🎭 Experience different moods, reactions, and expressions
🐾 Interact with MAXie as a virtual companion
🎁 Unlock interactions and rewards
📱 Use MAXie through a dedicated mobile experience
💎 Access premium functionality through our monetization system

The project also includes a desktop version, while the mobile experience is our Shipaton Next Gen submission.

How we built it

MAXie was built as an open-source project with a Flutter-based mobile application and a separate desktop implementation.

The mobile experience uses Flutter for the cross-platform application layer, while MAXie's companion systems handle interaction, personality, memory, moods, and progression.

We also integrated RevenueCat to handle the monetization layer and premium entitlements.

The project is structured as an open-source GitHub repository so developers can explore the implementation, understand how the different systems work, and contribute to the project.

Challenges we ran into

One of the biggest challenges was making MAXie feel like a companion rather than a normal chatbot.

We had to think about how memory, personality, emotions, progression, and interactions could work together without making the experience complicated.

We also faced the usual challenges of mobile development: managing application state, keeping animations and interactions smooth, handling different device configurations, and making sure the companion remained reliable during repeated interactions.

Another challenge was integrating monetization without making the core experience feel unnecessarily restricted. We wanted MAXie to remain useful as a free experience while providing a clear path for premium features.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're proud that MAXie evolved from a simple virtual-pet concept into a much broader AI companion system.

Some things we're particularly proud of:

🧠 Building a memory-driven companion experience
❤️ Creating a friendship and XP progression system
🎭 Implementing moods, reactions, and personality
📱 Turning the concept into a working mobile application
🖥️ Building both mobile and desktop experiences
💰 Integrating RevenueCat for monetization
🌐 Making the project open source
🚀 Shipping MAXie as a real project rather than leaving it as a prototype

Most importantly, MAXie is something we can continue developing after the hackathon.

What we learned

We learned that building an AI product is much more than connecting an AI model to a chat interface.

The experience around the model matters just as much: memory, personality, interaction design, feedback, progression, and user motivation all influence how people perceive an AI companion.

We also learned a lot about designing mobile experiences, managing application state, integrating monetization, debugging across platforms, and turning an evolving project into something that can actually be shipped.

Most importantly, we learned to focus on the user's experience rather than simply adding more technology.

What's next for MAXie — AI Companion

MAXie is only the beginning.

Next, we want to expand MAXie's personality and memory systems, introduce richer interactions and mini-games, improve personalization, and create deeper connections between the mobile and desktop experiences.

We also want to explore better AI models, stronger privacy controls, cloud synchronization, more customization options, and a larger ecosystem of characters and experiences.

Our long-term vision is to make MAXie an AI companion that grows with the user instead of simply responding to the user.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

The hardest talks at work are the ones we never get to practice: pushing back on a deadline, giving tough feedback, or managing a friend who used to be your teammate. You usually get one shot. Pilots practice in flight simulators before they fly. We wanted the same thing for hard conversations: a safe place to practice first.

**What it does**

HardSync lets you practice hard conversations with AI, on iPhone and iPad.

- 29 real workplace scenarios, like managing a former teammate, saying no to extra work, or explaining a change to your boss.

- 10 realistic AI people to practice with, each with their own role and personality.

- A short briefing before each session: your goal and what to expect.

- Live video calls with an AI person who reacts to what you say (Ultra).

- Free text practice for every scenario.

- Feedback after every session: what went well, what didn't, and a better way to say it next time.

**How we built it**

- App: Flutter, one app for iPhone and iPad.

- AI: Google Gemini runs the conversations and the feedback. Tavus powers the video avatars.

- Backend: Python (FastAPI) and Supabase for accounts and data. Sign in with Apple and Google.

- Payments with RevenueCat: Free includes all text practice; Ultra adds live video calls. You buy with Apple In-App Purchase, RevenueCat unlocks Ultra right away, and our server double-checks with RevenueCat before every video call.

**Challenges we ran into**

Building an iPhone app without a Mac

- We developed everything on Windows, so every iOS build had to be made in the cloud. Code signing failed again and again with confusing errors, and App Store Connect rejected uploads that reused a build number. We moved from GitHub Actions to Codemagic, which finally made TestFlight uploads reliable.

Making live AI calls actually work and feel natural

- Real-time Live AI calls were the hardest part. We fixed calls that went silent, a mic that cut off whenever you paused to think, and permission prompts that froze the call. In the end we focused on doing video really well instead of offering both voice and video.

- Live calls crashed on our server before reaching the AI, because the hosting platform pointed to security certificate files that didn't exist. The AI models were also sometimes too busy, so we added automatic retries and a backup model.

- If a call was interrupted, the old session stayed open and blocked the next one. We added an "end previous call and retry" option, plus tests for duplicate and late events from the video service.

Payments and pricing

- A paywall bug could charge for the cheaper plan while showing Ultra. We now match each plan to its exact product in RevenueCat, re-check after purchase while Apple catches up, and verify access on our server before every video call.

- Live AI video costs real money per minute. We tried pay-per-minute credits, credit packs, and even rewarded ads before choosing something simple: Free for text, Ultra for video, with 10-minute calls to keep costs predictable.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Practicing a hard conversation face to face with a realistic AI person.

- Feedback that uses your own words and shows you a better way to say them.

**What we learned**

The hardest bugs were invisible ones: a silent avatar fallback, audio blocked by iOS, a wrong price behind the right label. We learned to test the real thing on a real device, keep payments simple, and cut features that aren't ready so the core experience works well.

**What's next for HardSync**

- Group calls with multiple AI people. Practice the hardest real meetings, like presenting to your boss and their boss, or handling a disagreement between two teammates, with several AI people in the same call who react to you and to each other.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

It started with my grandparents. When I went back to India, I saw how chaotic the streets were, and how hard it was for them to get around with a cane. Then I noticed the same struggle right here on the UIUC campus.

We all carry phones with LiDAR and AI built in. So why is the cane still a 100-year-old stick? We wanted to make it smart for less than $5.

**What it does**

OpenCane is a phone-only smart cane. You clip your iPhone onto the cane you already own, and it becomes the only computer on the cane. There's no extra hardware and no microcontrollers, and it costs less than $5 in plastic.

- 3D-printed mount: holds the iPhone on the cane shaft and passes the Taptic Engine's vibration straight into your palm. Left, right and head-height obstacles each feel different.

- LiDAR obstacle radar: reads depth about 30 times a second across 3 lanes (left, center, right) and 2 heights (waist and head), so it catches the branches, scaffolding and signposts a cane tip never touches.

- Spatial audio beacon: AirPods Pro play a click that floats ahead of you on the route. You just walk toward the sound. Spoken turns and Apple Watch taps back it up.

- Earcons over chatter: short tones (180 ms or less) replace slow spoken status lines, and a self-hear filter stops the app from answering its own voice.

- Indoors to outdoors: someone records a building once ("Main desk on your right"). Step counting walks you out, and OpenCane hands off to GPS once you're outside.

- Hands-free: Siri, the Action button and a short voice menu run everything. Say "Where am I" and it describes what's in front of you, even offline.

- Honest by design: if iOS pauses sensing, the Dynamic Island tells you instead of showing a false "clear". Fall detection can alert your family with your last GPS location via Grok Bot.

- Safety is free, forever: obstacle warnings, navigation and emergency calls never sit behind a paywall. OpenCane Premium, built on RevenueCat, adds AI hazard watch (cones, barriers, scooters), naming people ahead, and family alerts, at $49.99 a year with the first month free. The paywall never shows up while you're walking.

**How we built it**

Hardware

We started with a smart handle: an ESP32, a battery, vibration motors and a distance sensor. We scrapped it on day one. The iPhone already has better sensors, a faster chip and its own battery, so the phone became the whole system.

Then we designed the mount in OpenSCAD and printed it on Creality SPARKX i7 printers in PETG:

- v1 was a split collar with M4 screws and a 72-tooth hinge. It needed bought hardware, and ball joints slip when a cane sweeps.

- v2 is screwless: 4 printed parts and zero screws. A slotted cone grips the cane and a printed ring tightens over it like a drill chuck. The arm and the phone cradle slide on a dovetail.

- The mount is rigid on purpose. The Taptic Engine's vibration has to reach your palm, so there's no foam or rubber in the way.

- Every part prints in under 2 hours (collar 1 h 43 min, cradle 1 h 34 min) and the full set weighs about 88 g.

- Before anything prints, a script runs 32 checks: no parts collide, the thread turns through its full travel, and every part is one solid piece.

Software

Native Swift 6 and SwiftUI, about 66,000 lines, built in 3 weeks.

- Depth to height. ARKit gives us LiDAR depth, and we place every point by its real height above the ground using the camera's angle:

$$h = c + d \cdot g(u, v)$$

where \(c \approx 95\) cm is where the phone sits on the cane and \(d\) is the depth. Points below 25 cm are the floor, 25 to 140 cm is your torso, and above 140 cm is your head.

- Lanes. The view splits into 3 lanes and 2 heights. Each cell reports its closest 10% of readings, so one bad pixel can't fake an obstacle and a thin pole can't hide.

- Haptics. For anything straight ahead, the cane pulses faster as you get closer:

$$f(d) = \min\left(8,\ \max\left(2,\ \frac{4}{d}\right)\right) \text{ Hz}$$

That's 2 pulses a second at 2 m and 8 at half a meter.

- Branch or wall? A wall is just as close at your chest as at your head. A branch isn't. A head-height reading \(H\) only counts when the torso reading \(T\) below it is clear:

$$T - H \ge 0.5 \text{ m}$$

- Speech that never talks over danger. Every line has a priority, safety &gt; navigation &gt; obstacles &gt; scene, so "Head height." always wins.

- Navigation. MapKit routes, our own waypoint engine, and a spatial audio beacon. You only "arrive" when the GPS is good enough to trust:

$$d + \frac{\sigma}{2} \le 20 \text{ m}$$

on two fixes in a row, where \(\sigma\) is the GPS accuracy.

- RevenueCat. One file talks to RevenueCat. Every rule about who gets Premium, and when, is a tested function. Purchases, renewals, expiry and refunds update live, and nothing ever turns off in the middle of a walk.

Testing

GPS replays of real walks (clean, missed turn, noisy GPS, wrong turn), and stress tests on 1,000 simulated walks with bad GPS. Beyond simulated routes and map stress tests, we took it into the field: we had a friend navigate a live walk all the way from Townsend to Siebel relying on the cane, along with hands-on trials with other testers to validate audio cues and obstacle detection in real pedestrian traffic

**Challenges we ran into**

Hardware

- The thread that wasn't there. Our collar looked threaded in CAD, but the thread came out 0.03 mm thick, and the slicer turned it into a smooth cylinder. We rebuilt it at 0.6 to 0.75 mm.

- Parts that jammed or fell off. The first printed thread jammed two turns in. The dovetails had no stops, so the phone cradle slid right off. In one version the arm went straight through the phone. Every one of these became a check we now run before printing.

- Prints that wouldn't stick. One arm touched the print bed with only 0.3 mm², so we redesigned it to 814 mm².

- Real canes are thin. We tested on a 27.65 mm broom handle, but real white canes are 9.5 to 13 mm. The next collar has to fit both.

Software

- Our first cane walk was a mess. With the phone tilted 45° down, the "head" sensor was actually looking at knees. We got 137 head warnings and 8 "Head height." alerts in 12 minutes, and none of them were real. We rebuilt everything around true height above the ground.

- Walls looked like branches. 349 of our first 360 head-height readings were just walls. The branch-or-wall check fixed it.

- The app heard itself. Speech recognition picked up the app saying "Head height." and treated it as the user talking. We couldn't use echo cancellation because it kills the spatial audio, so we built our own filter that ignores anything the app just said.

- Too much talking. Hearing "Head height." 10 times in 2 minutes indoors is noise, not safety. We added priorities, cooldowns, and short tones instead of sentences.

- A false "all clear". LiDAR can't see anything closer than about 10 cm, so a wall right against the phone showed up as six green "clear" tiles. Now a blind spot means stop, and the lock screen never says "clear" unless sensing is actually running.

- A crash judges would have hit. RevenueCat deliberately crashes a release build that uses a test key, which would have broken any TestFlight build we sent. Our reviewers caught it, and that build now runs safely with everything unlocked.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Our LinkedIn post blew up: 100,000+ impressions. That got us the attention of Founders at UIUC, the club that works with YC companies, and the Landuyt Center for Entrepreneurship here at UIUC.

- Going system-wide: we're bringing OpenCane to the whole University of Illinois system: Urbana-Champaign, Chicago and Springfield.

- Outreach from the West Coast: UCSD's medical school, UCLA and UC Santa Cruz have all reached out.

- Rural Punjab: through connections we made, we're planning to test and deploy OpenCane at schools in rural Punjab that teach students with disabilities.

- 50+ testers right now. We also use OpenCane ourselves every day to get from class to class. Every bug we hit, we fix that week, and that's made the app better than any spec could.

We love this idea. The more people use OpenCane, the better it gets.

**What we learned**

- "It compiles" is never the bar. When someone trusts your app to get them across a street, every number needs proof. Anything we haven't tested on a real cane ships turned off.

- Fewer words beat more words. For a blind walker, their ears are their eyes. Every sentence the app says costs attention, so it has to earn its place.

- Test it the way it's actually used. The phone held in your hand and the phone tilted down on a cane see completely different worlds. We only trust numbers from a mounted cane.

- CAD lies, prints don't. A part can look perfect on screen and come out of the printer as a smooth cylinder. Measure the real print.

- Trust is the product. One false "all clear" undoes a hundred correct warnings. That's also why safety will never sit behind a paywall.

- Use it yourself. Taking OpenCane to class every day taught us more than any spec sheet.

**What's next for OpenCane**

- Fit every cane. Print and walk the full screwless mount, and shrink the collar to fit real white canes (9.5 to 13 mm).

- Tune it on real walks. Use data from cane-mounted walks to set the head-height, drop-off and fall-detection thresholds.

- Test with experts. Paid sessions with blind walkers and orientation and mobility instructors, through campus disability services, NFB Illinois and the Chicago Lighthouse.

- Scale the pilots. Roll out across the University of Illinois system, to the schools in rural Punjab, and to elder-care homes in Champaign-Urbana.

- Ship it. Launch on the App Store and add RevenueCat web purchases, so a family member, school or rehab program can pay for someone's Premium.

- Grow from 50 testers to thousands. Every walk makes OpenCane smarter, and we want this in the hands of everyone who needs it.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We are university juniors who love building apps, AI products, and tools, but every project eventually hits the same first mountain: how do we get our first actual users? We realized this is a problem almost every student builder, solopreneur, and indie hacker faces. You can spend weeks building something you're genuinely proud of, only to launch to crickets — and that can be pretty discouraging. We realized that distribution at scale has become the new bottleneck for builders.

Even in Shipaton, thousands of us are building great apps, but the goal is not just to ship them — it is to get real people to find them, use them, and talk about them. Short-form UGC is one of the strongest ways to break through the noise, but constantly creating fresh hooks, ideas, and videos can become a second full-time job. We wanted to build something that agentically took action and saved builders like ourselves hours of work. That became HypeJuice, a growth tool for builders that learns your product inside out and turns its best features into scroll-stopping AI UGC-style content.

**What it does**

HypeJuice puts an AI growth partner at your fingertips. From a simple product link, it analyzes what you built, maps your audience and strongest selling points, and turns real app footage into UGC-style videos across different tones — funny, candid, relatable, trend-driven, and more.

Builders can generate hundreds of fresh hooks and content variations in minutes, teach HypeJuice their creative taste through swipe feedback, create new angles in Studio, then instantly save and download ready-to-post content while tracking performance over time.

Watch our demo to see HypeJuice in action as it creates content for LinguaChirp, a fun AI language-learning app. You’ll see the full flow from understanding the product to generating fresh hooks and ready-to-post UGC-style content. Note: LinguaChirp is a fictional app we made just for this showcase, not a real third-party product or trademark.

**How we built it**

We built HypeJuice with Expo, React Native, Expo Router, and TypeScript so we could support both iOS and Android while moving quickly during Shipaton. For rapid iteration, we primarily tested through Expo Go on iOS, which made it easy to refine the workflow as we built.

We used a Hono/Node.js backend for the API layer and Supabase for auth, Postgres, and private media storage across creator assets and rendered content.

- We built a custom content + video orchestration pipeline that pairs real app demos with reusable AI creator footage, then uses FFmpeg to normalize, sequence, stitch, and render vertical videos with text overlays.

- We added a Studio path that can branch into custom creator generation through Seedance 2.0 via Higgsfield, while reusable creator footage keeps the main workflow fast.

- We use Gemini across the shared-context agentic workflow for product analysis, audience mapping, hooks, creative angles, captions, and performance insights, so each stage builds on what HypeJuice already knows.

- We use Keep/Toss swipe feedback to personalize future generations, helping HypeJuice learn each builder’s taste and surface better-fitting hooks, tones, and creative angles without starting from scratch every time.

- We also designed the creator library to grow beyond the current hook + demo format. Before release, we plan to test more reactions, creator styles, and formats like green-screen commentary, agent-led explainers, and reaction-driven UGC, then use feedback to decide what deserves to ship.

**RevenueCat Integration + Subscriptions**

HypeJuice is currently an open-source Next Gen submission (Github Repo with MIT License) and has not yet been published to the App Store / Google Play. We still integrated the RevenueCat SDK and used RevenueCat Test Store to validate the subscription flow end-to-end, including a successful sandbox Pro trial. 

For release, we plan to split HypeJuice into two subscription tiers based on how our users actually build:

- Plus Plan: for solo developers, student builders, and early-stage solopreneurs who want to get started quickly with fast content generation & core growth workflows.

- Pro Plan:for power users and small hobby/dev teams who want more creative control, higher generation volume, and deeper Studio features like custom creator workflows.

**What's next for HypeJuice**

We want HypeJuice to become a tool that anyone who has built an app can use – from student builders and hobby developers to solopreneurs and small teams. The bigger vision is for HypeJuice to become a true growth partner for builders, with more agentic workflows that take on real growth work instead of just suggesting what to do.

If you’ve shipped an app or consumer tool you’re proud of but are still struggling to find those first real users, we’d love for you to try HypeJuice. Watch this space for updates – we’ll be sharing more here as we get through App review & get closer to release! 

We’ve been shaping HypeJuice around real pain points from other builders, so if there’s anything you think could improve the product or its workflow, feel free to share it with us.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We wanted to build something that goes against the typical betting-app experience. Most football betting platforms require users to spend real money to put their football knowledge to the test. We wanted to create a different kind of experience.

**What it does**

Clash Eleven is a free football prediction game where fans can predict real match scores, earn points based on their accuracy, and compete with friends and other football fans without risking real money.

**How we built it**

We built Clash Eleven using Flutter as our multi-platform mobile framework and Supabase as our backend. We connected the app to real football APIs to manage match data, predictions, and results.

To speed up development, we used Google Antigravity to assist with code generation and Google Stitch to help design the UI.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was making all the different parts of the app work together reliably. We had to learn how to structure our database, synchronize data with external football APIs, and handle runtime and in-app errors without compromising the user experience.

We also had to learn how to integrate RevenueCat and work with in-app purchases, which introduced another part of the application architecture that we had to understand and implement.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We're proud that we were able to turn our idea into a real, working app that actually met the needs we had in mind.

Seeing Clash Eleven go from an idea to something we could actually use — and seeing the final product look and feel like what we originally imagined — was one of the most rewarding parts of the project. It was exciting to see something we had envisioned come to life as a real application.

**What we learned**

Building Clash Eleven taught us a lot about mobile app development and the different systems required to make a real-time, data-driven app work reliably.

We learned how to:

- Design and structure a database to support our app's features.

- Synchronize our data with real football APIs.

- Handle runtime errors and in-app errors while maintaining a good user experience.

- Build a reliable flow for retrieving and displaying live football data.

- Integrate RevenueCat and work with in-app purchases.

One of the biggest lessons was understanding that building an app is not only about creating the features themselves, but also about making sure all the different systems work together reliably and provide a smooth experience for the user.

**What's next for Clash Eleven**

Our next goal is to launch Clash Eleven as soon as possible and continue improving the overall user experience.

We're also planning to expand the prediction system with more detailed match predictions. Users will eventually be able to predict things such as the number of cards, shots on target, and goal scorers, giving them more ways to test their football knowledge.

Beyond predictions, we want to introduce more social features and interactions to make Clash Eleven more engaging and create a stronger sense of competition between friends and football fans.

</details>

**Inspiration**

**Inspiration**

I froze in an interview when asked "Tell me about a time you failed badly?" My mind went blank. I realized mirror practice has zero pressure. Real conversations have pressure. I wanted an app that creates that pressure safely — to practice speaking when your heart is racing.

**What it does**

ToughTalk is a 60-second pressure speaking trainer.

- 3 modes: Interview, Confrontation, Negotiation

- Tough question cards (e.g., "Why should we pay you that much?")

- 60s countdown timer — you MUST speak non-stop

- Start / Pause / Reset

- Next Tough Question to build a streak

No AI judge, no score — just you vs the clock. Do 5 cards a day and you become unshakeable.

**How we built it**

- Expo SDK 57 + React Native + TypeScript

- Built in 2 days in Lagos with Samsung + HP laptop

- Used Expo Go for Android testing

- Timer with useEffect, state management with React hooks

- Deployed to GitHub: github.com/Josephine2016/ToughTalk

**Challenges we ran into**

- Expo CLI network issues on mobile data — fixed by switching to Expo Go tunnel

- CapCut TTS 500 char limit — solved by splitting script into 5 clips

- Recording 3-min demo at midnight with street noise — used CapCut AI voice (Rachel/Warm Storyteller)

- Pushing to GitHub from Termux — learned git push with PAT token

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Shipped working MVP on deadline night!

- From red screen errors to public YouTube demo: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/hA4suyiFs2E

- Built something I personally need — I now practice 5 tough questions daily

**What we learned**

How to ship fast under pressure, use AI voice for demo when mic fails, and that confidence comes from forced repetition, not perfect preparation.

**What's next for ToughTalk**

V2: AI feedback on filler words ("um", "ah"), voice recording + playback, progress streaks, and community tough questions library.

Built for Shipathon 2026 by Josephine Chukwu-Onwuchuruba from Lagos, Nigeria.

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/145/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/145/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/146/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/146/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/147/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/147/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/442/716/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/442/716/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Google quietly shut down its free Interview Warmup tool in April 2026. What's left is either a $39/month subscription or generic advice — "be confident, be yourself." I wanted something that reads like it was written by someone who's actually run these interviews: specific scenarios, real phrasing, scripts you can say out loud.

**What it does**

Interview Playbook is ten categories of real interview-prep content: behavioral interview fundamentals, the STAR method with fully worked example answers, six industry-specific question banks (tech, sales, healthcare, finance, marketing, customer service), word-for-word salary-negotiation scripts, and how to close an interview strong — smart questions to ask plus follow-up message templates. Two categories are free; the other eight unlock with a single one-time $9.99 purchase. Progress is tracked locally per section so you can see what you've practiced.

**How I built it**

Expo / React Native / TypeScript, with expo-router for navigation and AsyncStorage for local progress state. RevenueCat's SDK (react-native-purchases) powers the single "Full Playbook" non-consumable entitlement. The purchase layer runs in a dual mock/real mode — same UI, same code path, swappable backend — so the full purchase-and-unlock flow works and is fully testable without a live RevenueCat project connected yet; dropping in a real API key activates real purchases with zero code changes (details in the repo README).

I'm not a professional engineer — I built this by directing Claude Code (Anthropic's coding agent) end to end: architecture, all ten content sets, the UI, the RevenueCat integration, and testing on a real iOS Simulator build. The demo video's screen recording is a genuine simulator run, not a mockup, and the narration is my own voice.

**Challenges I ran into**

Designing the purchases layer without ever touching a live RevenueCat account mid-build — the mock and real code paths had to be identical from the app's point of view, not a stub that gets thrown away later.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

Every entry across the ten categories is specific and concrete, not generic filler — that's the entire differentiation from every other interview-tips app. And the purchase flow is genuinely verified end to end on a real device build (checked out, unlocked, persisted across a full rebuild), not just described.

**What I learned**

Directing an AI agent through a full build taught me to verify, not trust. An early cut of the demo video was reported as fully synced — it wasn't. Beats two through seven were dead silent because of a subtle timestamp bug in how the audio clips were cut, and I only caught it by actually watching the video myself, not by trusting the summary that said it worked. That became the rule for the rest of the build: check the real thing, not the report about the real thing.

**What's next**

Connect a real RevenueCat project and ship to the App Store and Google Play, expand the industry question banks, and add a few more categories.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/879/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/441/879/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/452/846/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/452/846/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We all take dozens of screenshots, save photos, download PDFs, and bookmark receipts every week, only to completely forget where they are when we actually need them. Traditional search only works if you remember exact file names or tags. I was inspired to build MemoryOS to give everyone an "extended digital memory", an AI assistant that instantly connects the dots across all your saved visual and textual information so you never lose track of important details again.

**What it does**

MemoryOS turns your chaotic collection of screenshots, photos, receipts, tickets, and documents into an instantly searchable, interactive personal memory vault. Instead of digging through endless photo albums or folders, users can simply ask natural questions like "Where was that Tokyo hotel my friend recommended?" or "How much did I pay for my last flight?" MemoryOS analyzes the content, extracts relevant context via OCR and multimodal reasoning, and delivers exact, verified answers instantly.

**How i built it**

- Mobile App: Built for cross-platform performance and a seamless capture-to-search user experience.

- AI & Vision Pipeline: Powered by advanced multimodal models and OCR to process images, parse unstructured text, and build semantic contextual embeddings for accurate document reasoning.

**Challenges we ran into**

Structuring and cross-referencing completely unstructured visual data (like low-res receipts or crowded screenshots) posed a significant challenge. Ensuring high-accuracy semantic retrieval without high latency required fine-tuning our prompt pipeline and optimizing local/cloud hybrid data extraction.

**Accomplishments that i'm proud of**

- Delivering accurate, conversational answers across hundreds of mixed screenshots and files in under two seconds.

- Implementing a complete, end-to-end monetization and retention workflow using RevenueCat.

- Creating an intuitive "Ask My Memory" interface that feels like talking to a personal assistant who has perfect recall.

**What i learned**

I learned how to effectively design AI-native utility applications around real-world user habits, balance complex AI reasoning latency with fast client UI updates, and build scalable subscription architecture for mobile apps.

**What's next for MemoryOS**

- Timeline Intelligence: Automatically generating chronological trip/event recaps from imported media.

- Privacy-Safe Shared Memories: Allowing users to curate and share specific memory collections (e.g., "My Favorite Tokyo Spots") without exposing private data.

- On-Device Search: Bringing core indexing local for offline-first privacy and speed.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/455/136/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/455/136/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/455/198/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/455/198/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/098/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/098/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/102/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/102/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/145/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/145/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

When students face serious problems, the hardest question is not always “What happened?” Sometimes it is “What can I do?”

Students may not know how to protect themselves, what their rights are, or where to find reliable information. I have seen people face problems like bullying, unsafe touching, domestic violence, scams, and online problems, but not know what to do next. This is why I created Justice Hub.

I wanted to make something that feels less scary than searching complicated legal websites alone. Justice Hub is meant to be a first step for students who need help and want to understand their situation.

**What it does**

Justice Hub lets users describe their situation in their own words and choose their location.

The app looks for important words in the user’s question, such as words connected to bullying, harassment, touching, violence, scams, or privacy. It then gives the user a clearer answer with:

What the app understands about the situation

Possible relevant legal information in simple language

Important vocabulary explained clearly

Practical next steps

Evidence-saving guidance when it is appropriate

Emergency and support contact numbers

Links to official or legal sources

The current prototype supports China and Thailand. It includes information for situations such as bullying, unsafe touching, sexual violence, domestic violence, workplace issues, scams, and privacy problems.

For serious situations, Justice Hub focuses on safety first. For example, it reminds users to contact emergency services, go somewhere safe, tell a trusted adult, or seek medical care when needed.

**How we built it**

I built Justice Hub as both a website and a mobile app.

The website lets people try the legal-information experience in a browser. The mobile app was built with Expo and React Native. I wanted the app to feel warm, calm, and easy to read because someone using it may already feel stressed or scared.

I organized the answers into clear sections like “What I Understand,” “What May Be Relevant,” “Important Vocabulary,” “What You Can Do Next,” and “Find Real Help.” I also added country-based contacts, so the phone numbers are different for China and Thailand.

For the competition, I integrated RevenueCat Test Store into the mobile app. It has an optional supporter-demo purchase, but no real money is charged. Justice Hub’s legal information, safety guidance, and emergency contacts stay free for every student.

**Challenges we ran into**

One challenge was making sure the app is helpful without acting like a lawyer or making decisions for people. Laws are different depending on the country, location, and exact situation. I needed to make the wording careful and clear.

I tried to solve this by showing possible relevant laws instead of saying that a law definitely applies. I also added official-source links and reminders that Justice Hub gives general information, not legal advice.

Another challenge was testing RevenueCat in a real mobile app. Expo Go was useful for seeing the design, but it could not fully test a native RevenueCat purchase. I learned how to create an Android development build, connect it to RevenueCat Test Store, and complete a successful test purchase without real money.

It was also difficult to organize legal information in a way that students can understand. Legal words can be confusing, so I focused on explaining important vocabulary and giving simple next steps.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I am proud that Justice Hub became a working project instead of only an idea.

I created:

A working legal-information website

A working Expo / React Native mobile app

China and Thailand legal-information flows

Country-based emergency and support contacts

Safety guidance for serious situations

Important legal vocabulary in simple language

Official-source links

A successful RevenueCat Test Store purchase demo

A public GitHub repository with an MIT license

I am also proud that the app does not put help behind a payment wall. The supporter purchase is only a competition demo. Safety, legal information, and emergency contacts remain free.

**What we learned**

I learned that creating an app is not only about coding. It is also about thinking carefully about the people who may use it.

I learned how to build a mobile app with Expo and React Native, connect RevenueCat Test Store, create an Android development build, organize legal information by country, and publish code with an open-source license on GitHub.

I also learned that legal technology needs to be responsible. It should not guess too much or make users think it can replace a real professional. It should be clear about its limits and encourage users to contact trusted adults, emergency services, hospitals, or lawyers when they need more help.

**What's next for Justice Hub**

Next, I want to add more verified legal sources, more countries, and more local support organizations.

I also want to improve translations so users can choose languages more easily. I would like to make the topic matching more accurate and add more resources for students who need help at school, at home, online, or at work.

Justice Hub is for people who need help and want to be understood. Sometimes knowing that something is wrong is not enough if you do not know what to do next.

I hope Justice Hub can make that first step a little clearer.

</details>

src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/464/948/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every desk already has a spare touch screen with a keyboard you type on faster than any other: the phone in your pocket. Yet controlling a computer from across the room still means a dongle, a clicker, or a "remote mouse" app whose closed-source helper sits on your computer and sees every keystroke, and you just have to take its word for what it does with them.

I kept finding myself reaching for a keyboard, mouse, TV remote, or presentation clicker depending on what I was doing — and wishing my phone could simply be all of them. The last straw was a presentation where the clicker died mid-talk, while the phone that could have done its job sat in my pocket. The existing apps were usually built for just one job, so I decided to build Remotype: one app that turns my phone into the keyboard, trackpad, presenter and remote for my computers, my TV, my slides and my media.

**What it does**

Remotype turns an iPhone or Android phone into a real keyboard, trackpad, presenter remote, second screen and TV remote for Mac, Windows and Linux.

- Keyboard and trackpad — swipe-typing, real modifiers and shortcuts, a precision trackpad with scroll, pinch and drag-select. Free forever.

- Presenter — a spotlight, laser dot and freehand ink drawn on the computer, so they show up in Zoom and screen recordings (a physical laser pointer never does), plus a slide timer and blank-screen key.

- Second screen — the computer's screen and audio on your phone, and casting to a TV.

- A dozen modes — numpad, media keys, macros, dictation, clipboard sync, and saved passwords typed out after Face ID or a fingerprint.

- Every computer you own — switch between them, or let the cursor flow from one screen edge to the next.

- On Android, nothing to install for keyboard & mouse — the phone pairs as a genuine Bluetooth keyboard and mouse, so it works on a locked-down work laptop or a smart TV.

Keyboard and trackpad are free forever. Everything else is free for 14 days — no card, no account — then 30 free premium minutes every month, or $4.99/month, $39.99/year, or $99.99 once.

**How we built it**

- Native apps on both platforms: Swift/SwiftUI on iOS, Kotlin/Jetpack Compose on Android. Android also registers as a Bluetooth HID keyboard and mouse.

- Three computer hosts: a Swift macOS host (Accessibility for input, ScreenCaptureKit for screen and audio) and Go hosts for Windows and Linux. Their full source is public under Apache-2.0.

- Our own protocol: Bonjour discovery, with Connect-by-IP for Tailscale (or any VPN). You pair once with a code shown on the computer, and every message after that is AES-256-GCM encrypted. The host makes no internet connection at all.

- Monetization on RevenueCat: one offering (monthly, annual, lifetime) mapped to App Store and Google Play products, one entitlement both apps check, and RevenueCat's hosted paywall on both platforms.

- One tiny server: a Cloudflare Worker with D1 that activates the 14-day trial once per device, so reinstalling can't restart it.

**Challenges we ran into**

- iPhones can't be Bluetooth keyboards. Apple doesn't allow it, so iOS talks to a host app over Wi-Fi while Android goes direct over Bluetooth. That means one product with two transports.

- macOS forgets permissions. Accessibility grants are tied to the app's code signature, so an unsigned update silently broke typing. We moved to consistent Developer ID signing and a setup check that tests whether permission is really granted, instead of trusting a cached "yes".

- Realtime input backs up. Sending every pointer event as it happened let a burst queue up and lag everything after it. Pointer, scroll and overlay streams now drop and merge stale events instead of queueing them.

- Some things can't be done, and we say so. Linux on Wayland blocks screen capture and global overlays, so the Linux host is input-first. Tracking the text cursor inside Electron apps isn't possible through macOS Accessibility, so it falls back to following the mouse.

- App Review. Our first submission was rejected twice: once for a missing Terms of Use link, and once because the subscriptions weren't attached to the version. We also learned that App Review runs on the same sandbox as TestFlight - so anything meant only for testers has to be hidden from reviewers too.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Shipped on the App Store and Google Play with native apps on both, plus hosts for macOS, Windows and Linux.

- A trust story we can prove rather than claim: pairing codes, end-to-end encryption, a host with no network access to the internet, and open-source hosts anyone can read before running.

- A pricing model that never nags: the core stays free forever, the trial needs no account, and after it you keep a monthly free allowance instead of hitting a wall.

- An interface built on our own design language, MILLED (keys with real travel and haptics), with every piece of text at a 6:1 contrast ratio or higher, and full VoiceOver and TalkBack support.

**What we learned**

The feature list is the easy half; trust is the hard half. Our closed testers asked us to open-source the host, stop it touching the internet, explain why macOS needs Accessibility permission, and simplify the UI. All four shipped, and every one of them made the product better. We also learned to test on real devices early: one pairing bug only ever appeared on a physical iPhone, never in the simulator.

**What's next for Remotype**

- File transfer between your computers.

- Clipboard, vitals and app launching on the Linux host.

- A notice on your phone when your computer's host app has an update.

- Direct low-latency casting to Chromecast, using our own receiver.

</details>

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/LNWAhJpwO8s/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LNWAhJpwO8s)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/479/943/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/479/943/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/307/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/307/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/305/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/305/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/308/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/308/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/311/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/311/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/479/944/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/479/944/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/306/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/306/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

There are so many people in the world I haven't met yet. Some of them would be people I really click with. But when I think about how to actually find them today, the path is full of small walls: endless swiping, first messages that go nowhere, awkward back-and-forth just to pick a day. A lot of people who want something real give up somewhere in the middle.

I think AI can do more than save time. It can help people get closer to each other. That's the idea behind WingWard. Your AI agent, Ward, takes care of the online part, all the way to suggesting where and when to meet, so you can spend your energy on meeting someone in person. For me, a relationship starts when two people are actually in the same room. Ward's job is to get you there faster, and you still make every decision.

**What it does**

WingWard is an iOS app. Here's the flow as it works today:

- You answer a 10-question quiz, then have three short real-time voice conversations with AI voices you pick. The aim: people show more of who they are when they talk than when they fill in a form. If you skip a question, it's treated as unknown, not held against you.

- The app builds a profile from those conversations. You read it and confirm it before it's used for anything.

- Matching scores compatibility across 14 features in three layers. Then your Ward has a text conversation with the other person's Ward. You see the match along with the reasons.

- If you both tap "I'd like to meet," that's free and has to be mutual.

- Before scheduling, both people have to pass an identity-verification gate. Then Ward suggests a place and a time for you, so nobody has to go back and forth about where and when. Both of you approve it, and that's the plan. Arranging the meetup is the paid step.

- After you meet, you talk it through with Ward by voice. The traits you confirm and Ward's understanding of you get updated for next time.

I'm not claiming WingWard can predict who you'll fall for. What it tries to do is shrink the distance between "we might get along" and "let's meet."

**How we built it**

The iOS app is SwiftUI (iOS 17+). The API is Hono 4.9 on Cloudflare Workers, written in TypeScript 5.9, and the Ward-to-Ward conversations run inside Durable Objects. Supabase (PostgreSQL 17) handles auth and data, with row-level security so only the two people in a match can read it.

For voice I use OpenAI gpt-realtime-2.1-mini, with gpt-4o-mini-transcribe for transcripts. The phone only ever gets a short-lived session credential, never a permanent key. Analysis happens after the call with Mistral (mistral-large-2512 and ministral-8b-2512). I kept analysis out of the live conversation on purpose, so the voice side can just listen and ask one thing at a time.

**RevenueCat**

Signing up, matching, and saying you'd like to meet are all free. You pay at the point where you're most sure: when you're actually arranging to see someone, once you're past the free allowance.

The app uses the RevenueCat Purchases iOS SDK (5.88). It shows the current Offering and supports purchase and restore. There are two products: a monthly subscription, wingward_premium_monthly (entitlement premium), and a consumable wingward_meetup_credit. RevenueCat webhooks hit our API, where they're authenticated and checked with HMAC, then written to the database in one transaction that updates entitlements and the credit ledger. The app asks our API for billing status, so a purchase on the device alone never unlocks anything on the server.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest part was keeping everything consistent when things go wrong halfway. A voice call drops, someone cancels, transcripts arrive out of order. I ended up tying completion to the session, checking ownership on every write, and writing tests for exactly those broken cases.

Another one was stopping the AI from deciding who you are. That's why skipped answers stay unknown, profiles need your OK, and every match comes with its reasons.

And payments had to be trusted on the server, not the phone, which is why everything goes through the webhook path above.

**What I learned**

Finding someone you truly click with shouldn't take this much effort. Working on WingWard taught me to keep lowering the barriers for the user, as far as they can go, until the app can step out of the way and let people have a real, human experience offline.

I also spent a lot of time on where to ask for money, and where the paywall should even appear. If it shows up too early, before you've seen a single match, people just leave. If you have to pay to say "I'd like to meet," it feels like paying for a maybe. So I put the paywall at the point where both people have already said yes and are actually arranging the meetup, beyond the free allowance. That's when Ward is picking a place and time for both of you, the moment the app is doing real work for you, and I think it's the moment people understand why it costs something.

**What's next**

- Research. I'm planning to do neuroscience research at university, focused on what it really means for two people to click. The goal is to use voice conversation data to make better matches between people who genuinely get along. This is future research, not something the app does now.

- Cafés. Cafés have quiet hours with empty tables. I want to partner with them and send WingWard meetups into exactly those hours. The café gets customers it wouldn't have had, and WingWard earns a referral fee for each real visit. That would give WingWard a second revenue stream next to in-app purchases, one that only grows when people actually meet. No partnerships exist yet.

- ID review. The verification gate is built. Document upload and review come next.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Organizations regularly change the people responsible for important roles, but the knowledge needed to perform those roles often leaves with them.

Picture a student society's treasurer graduating. The new treasurer doesn't know which approvals the budget needs, which vendor requires a purchase order, or why last year's process was changed. That knowledge lives in old chats, spreadsheets, shared drives, and one person's head.

When it isn't transferred properly, incoming Role Holders waste time reconstructing processes, lose the context behind past decisions, repeat mistakes, and risk missing important work.

I saw this problem firsthand as a student leader in my university society. When my term ended, almost everything I had learned (who to contact, which approvals were needed, what deadlines to watch, what had gone wrong the year before) lived in my head, my chats and scattered files. My successor had to rebuild it from scratch, and I couldn't capture it all in one last meeting.

This isn't unique to student societies. It happens anywhere responsibility changes hands: companies, nonprofits, committees, volunteer groups and project teams. Relay is built so the knowledge doesn't leave when the person does

**What it does**

Relay turns scattered operational knowledge into a living, role-specific memory that survives people changing.

Throughout their time in a role, the Role Holder captures what they learn. Relay organizes it into useful operational knowledge (contacts, deadlines, processes, warnings and lessons), and the Role Holder reviews and approves what becomes part of the trusted handoff. When the role changes hands, the successor receives the published handoff, can ask Relay questions about it, and starts a new living handoff of their own. Over time, Relay shows what changed from one period to the next and, when evidence supports it, why.

Why it's different: notes apps and wikis store information. Relay adds human-approved knowledge, immutable published handoffs, source provenance, and change tracking across service periods.

**How I built it**

## 559. BearFetch - AI for Students

> BearFetch is a gamified AI learning app for K–12 students, built to make AI understandable, practical, and engaging. BearFetch helps students move from just using AI, to understanding and applying it.

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/bearfetch-ai-for-students (gallery page 144) · ❤️ 1 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [Sachin Kandan](https://devpost.com/sk51004)
- **GitHub (Try it out):** https://github.com/skand5/bearfetch-app.git
- **Repo check:** public repo · license: MIT · 35 commits · Dart · RevenueCat found in code ✅
- **Other links:** http://bearfetch.com · https://www.linkedin.com/company/bearfetch-com/
- **Built with:** android-studio, dart, figma, flutter, java, onesignal, recend, revenuecat, supabase

**Video (5:14):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mnj2gOy2i-E

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/Mnj2gOy2i-E/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mnj2gOy2i-E)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/556/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/556/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/819/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/819/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/549/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/549/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/548/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/548/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/550/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/550/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/547/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/450/547/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Students are already growing up around AI. They use it to search, write, create, and solve problems, but being able to use an AI tool is different from understanding what it is doing, how it can be used responsibly, and how to apply it effectively.

That gap is what led me to build BearFetch.

I wanted to approach AI education differently from a traditional course. Instead of asking students to read through long explanations and then answer a quiz, I wanted the learning itself to be interactive. BearFetch was designed as a gamified learning environment where students can learn an AI concept, immediately interact with it, receive feedback, and continue building on that understanding.

I also wanted AI education to feel practical. A student should not finish a lesson knowing only a definition of a chatbot or a prompt. They should understand what those concepts mean and eventually be able to use them to solve problems and build something of their own.

That became the foundation of BearFetch: make AI understandable, interactive, and useful for students.

**What it does**

BearFetch is a gamified AI learning app for K–12 students. The current app is centered around my first course, From Understanding to Building LLMs, which contains 5 units and 36 steps at a beginner level.

The course is intentionally built around different forms of interaction rather than repeating the same quiz format. Students identify examples of AI in everyday life, complete fill-in-the-blank activities, construct sentences using word blocks, interact with a simulated chatbot, compare how different prompts change the style of an AI response, and assemble the components of a chatbot in the correct order.

The course also progresses beyond explaining AI concepts. In the capstone, students choose a chatbot type such as a Math Bot, Fun Bot, or Study Coach, select training examples for it, test it with a prompt, see the resulting response, and decide whether the response was helpful. This gives students a first hands-on experience with the process behind building and testing an AI system rather than only answering questions about one.

When a student completes the course, BearFetch summarizes the topics they mastered, including AI Chatbots, Tokens & Words, Prediction, Prompting, and Bot Building. The student also receives an AI Explorer Badge, an LLM Starter Certificate, XP, and Honey Jars.

Honey Jars connect learning to the rest of the app. Students can spend them in the Shop on cosmetic items such as hats, glasses, backpacks, and other accessories, and those items can be visibly equipped on their bear. This makes the reward system part of the actual experience rather than something disconnected from the learning.

The app also includes a parent side. BearFetch uses a family-account structure so the parent creates the account and learner profile, while the child does not need their own email or phone number. In Parent Settings, the app also makes its data model explicit: family-account information, learner profiles, progress, rewards, and accessories are stored, while the app states that activity answers and chatbot simulations are not stored.

**How I built it**

I built BearFetch as a mobile application using React Native with Expo, while designing the product around a structured progression from individual activities to complete courses, rewards, and parent-facing progress information. The interface, visual system, mascot, course experience, and activity structure were designed specifically around making a technical subject approachable to younger learners.

A major part of the build was creating enough variety in the learning interactions that students are actively doing something at every step. The course moves between questions, construction-based activities, simulations, comparisons, and a hands-on chatbot-building capstone instead of treating AI education as a sequence of static reading screens.

I also built the student and parent experiences as connected parts of the same product. Students have their own learning progression, rewards, and customization, while parents have a separate view into the family account and the student's progress.

For monetization, I integrated the RevenueCat SDK into the parent side of the app. The current implementation uses RevenueCat to power Progress Insight, a one-time $4.99 purchase associated with the product bearfetch_progress_insight_lifetime. In the submitted build, the purchase is demonstrated through RevenueCat's Test Store, which is a development/testing environment rather than a live customer transaction. The test purchase updates the purchase state and activates the corresponding entitlement inside BearFetch. RevenueCat's documentation describes Test Store purchases as sandbox data that behave like real purchases for testing, including triggering entitlements and updating customer information. 

The important part for me was not simply adding a purchase button. I wanted the purchase to have a clear relationship with the product itself: the student generates measurable learning progress, the parent can access a deeper Progress Insight experience, and RevenueCat provides the entitlement layer that determines whether that experience is unlocked.

**Challenges I ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was deciding how to make AI education both technically meaningful and accessible to younger students.

AI concepts can become abstract very quickly. Terms such as tokens, prediction, prompting, training data, and chatbot architecture are not naturally intuitive for a younger learner, so I had to think carefully about how to turn each concept into something a student could actually interact with.

That is why the course uses several different activity formats. A student may first encounter an idea through a simple explanation, then apply it in a word-building activity, see the concept behave inside a simulated chatbot, and eventually use it in the capstone. The goal was to make the progression feel understandable without stripping away the underlying idea.

Another challenge was balancing gamification with the learning itself. I did not want rewards to become the entire reason students continue using the app. Honey Jars, XP, badges, certificates, and cosmetics are meant to reinforce progress that already comes from learning.

I also had to think about the parent/student relationship. BearFetch is designed around a family account rather than requiring a child to independently manage an email or phone number. The parent experience therefore needed to provide meaningful visibility into progress without turning the student side of the app into an adult-facing dashboard.

Finally, I had to think about monetization in a way that actually belongs in an educational product. RevenueCat gave me the infrastructure to implement and test a purchase flow, but the harder product question was what a parent should receive in return and how that purchase could eventually create value beyond a single transaction.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

I am proud that BearFetch is more than a collection of UI screens or a concept prototype. The current build contains a complete first AI course with 5 units and 36 steps, a variety of interactive activities, a chatbot-building capstone, course-completion rewards, a functioning in-app reward economy, student customization, and a separate parent experience.

The learning experience also has a clear progression. A student begins by understanding basic AI concepts and everyday examples, moves into more specific ideas such as tokens, prediction, and prompting, and finishes by applying those concepts to a chatbot they configure and test.

I am also proud of the connection between learning and the rest of the product. Completing lessons produces XP and Honey Jars, those Honey Jars can be used in the Shop, and the resulting customization is visible on the student's bear.

On the parent side, I successfully integrated RevenueCat into a real purchase flow. The current hackathon build demonstrates the $4.99 Progress Insight purchase through RevenueCat Test Store, and BearFetch responds to the resulting entitlement by showing that lifetime access is active. This gives me a working foundation for the monetization system I plan to develop further.

Most importantly, I am proud that the product reflects an idea I have continued refining: AI education should not stop at explaining what AI is. Students should have opportunities to interact with it, understand its behavior, and eventually build with it.

**What I learned**

Building BearFetch taught me that educational software requires a different kind of product thinking from simply building a functional app.

An activity can be technically correct and still fail to teach effectively. A concept can also be simplified too far and lose the substance that made it worth learning in the first place. I learned to think more carefully about the progression between activities and about what the student is actually doing, not just what information appears on screen.

I also learned that gamification works best when it reinforces an existing behavior. XP, Honey Jars, badges, certificates, and customization have value because they are attached to learning progress. They are not the product by themselves.

Another lesson was that the parent and student experiences need to support one another without becoming the same experience. Students need an environment that is engaging and understandable; parents need a clear way to understand whether that learning is actually happening.

The RevenueCat integration reinforced a similar lesson on the business side. A monetization system is much stronger when it is tied to a clear piece of product value. Integrating the SDK was the technical step; deciding what a parent should actually be paying for was the more important product question.

**What's next for BearFetch - AI for Students**

The current Progress Insight purchase is the beginning of the monetization model I want to develop, not the final version.

My longer-term concept is to turn the parent-facing experience into a continuous learning loop:

Learn → Measure → Report → Recommend → Practice → Improve

Instead of treating a progress report as the end of the process, I want student performance to become an input into what happens next.

A future version could use the student's demonstrated strengths and gaps to generate a more useful Progress Insight for the parent, then connect those results directly to the student's next learning actions. A student who is struggling with prompting, for example, could be directed toward a specific follow-up lesson or targeted practice set. A student who is already strong in one topic could move forward rather than repeating material they have already mastered.

This is also where I see the RevenueCat integration evolving.

The current implementation demonstrates a one-time Progress Insight entitlement through RevenueCat. My longer-term concept is to adapt that foundation into an ongoing parent-to-student learning loop, potentially through a recurring plan that unlocks continued progress insights, personalized recommendations, and targeted practice.

The important distinction is that I do not want to monetize access to learning itself in a way that undermines the product's purpose. Instead, the paid experience is intended to provide parents with deeper visibility into the student's development and then turn that information into something useful for the student.

In other words, I want the value of the purchase to extend beyond a report.

The report tells a parent where the student is.

The recommendation tells them what to do next.

The practice experience gives the student a way to act on that information.

And the next progress measurement shows whether that intervention actually helped.

That creates a much more connected product than a standalone paid document, while giving RevenueCat a meaningful role in the product architecture: managing the entitlement that unlocks the parent-facing growth experience.

This is a future direction, not functionality I am claiming is already shipped in the hackathon build.

Beyond monetization, I plan to expand BearFetch's curriculum, add additional AI topics and building experiences, and continue developing the platform around the same principle that shaped the first course: students should leave BearFetch with more than familiarity with AI. They should have a practical understanding of how it works, how to use it responsibly, and how they can use it to create and solve problems themselves.

THANK YOU!!!

</details>
