**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/448/361/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/448/361/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/448/363/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/448/363/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Let’s be real — walking alone at night shouldn’t feel like a survival mission. The constant worry, the phone gripped tight, pretending to call someone just in case? I’ve seen it happen way too often to friends, family, and women everywhere.
That’s what sparked HerSafety — a safety-first platform not just to react to emergencies, but to help prevent them. I wanted to build something that actually does something when it matters most.

**What it does**

HerSafety is like a guardian angel in your pocket (minus the wings and drama).
With just one tap or voice command, you can:

🚨 Send a live SOS alert to emergency contacts

🗺 Get safe route recommendations through the city

📤 Report crimes or incidents anonymously

🧠 Learn your legal rights and emergency steps

🔐 Activate "Guardian Grid" — an AI-powered system that detects abnormal behavior and warns you before something bad happens

It’s mobile-first, lightning fast, and feels more like a real companion than just an app.

**How we built it**

I built HerSafety using the best modern tech I could get my hands on (and wrestle into submission 😅):

Frontend: React + Tailwind CSS (beautiful, responsive, lightweight)

Backend: Node.js + Express

Database: Supabase (because I love sanity)

Auth: Email, password, and even anonymous mode

APIs: Google Maps for routes, Twilio for alerts, some clever AI magic for behavior detection

Hosting: Vercel + Render for that sweet deploy life

And yes, I manually tested the whole thing walking around my neighborhood — dedication 

**Challenges we ran into**

Oh boy, where do I start?

Getting real-time location to behave across devices? Nightmare.

Voice commands? Half the time my mic thought “Help me” was “Hold me” (awkward).

Designing something serious without it looking scary — took a lot of UI/UX love.

Twilio throttled me during testing. They really thought I was in danger.

But hey, every glitch taught me something new.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

SOS system works flawlessly — and fast

Built and tested the Guardian Grid AI with real scenario simulations

Created a full mobile-first UI with zero fluff — just what you need, when you need it

Made an app that actually feels safe to use

Got real emotional feedback from testers who said: “This is something I’d give my daughter.”

That one hit hard. That’s why I built this.

**What we learned**

UX for safety apps is a whole different beast — it’s not just about pretty buttons

Real-time anything is messy, but worth it

How to balance serious messaging with calming, friendly visuals

Learned way too much about emergency contact routing systems

Most importantly: that tech alone can’t solve everything, but it can empower people like never before

**What's next for HerSafety**

Honestly, this is just the beginning. I’ve got some exciting features in the pipeline that’ll make HerSafety even stronger and smarter.

First up, I’m working on a SafeWalk mode. Basically, you’ll be able to share your live route with someone you trust while you're walking, so they can make sure you reach safely.

Then there’s something I’m super excited about — a Live Threat Radar. It’ll use real-time data to warn you about unsafe areas nearby, so you can avoid them before it’s even a problem.

I’m also building a verified Guardian community. Think of it as a safety network of real people nearby who can help out or get alerted if something goes wrong.

A native app version is coming too, which will make the SOS features work even when you don’t have good internet. Because safety shouldn’t depend on your signal strength.

And finally, I’m diving deeper into AI-powered safety. Stuff like detecting signs of panic through facial expressions, triggering alerts silently if you're in trouble, and even smart flashlight features that work like a warning signal.

Big plans ahead. Because women deserve tools that are just as smart and strong as they are.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Inspiration
The idea for Thread started with a simple frustration:
Why do I have to remember where everything is?
An important email is in Gmail. A meeting is in Calendar. A document is somewhere else. A task lives in another system. The conversation that explains why any of it matters may be somewhere completely different.
The information exists. The problem is that the context is fragmented.
I realized that I was spending time doing something computers should be much better at doing: connecting the dots.
So I started asking a different question:
What if, instead of giving me more places to organize my work, technology could understand the work I was already doing?
That question became Thread.

**What it does**

Thread is a personal workspace that brings together the information surrounding your work and turns it into context you can actually act on.
It connects things like Gmail, Calendar, files, tasks, notes, and projects so they don't feel like completely separate worlds.
The most important part is the Morning Brief.
Instead of opening five different apps and trying to figure out what deserves attention, Thread looks at the context available to it and answers a much simpler question:
What should I care about right now?
A meeting isn't treated as just a calendar event.
Thread can connect it with the emails, people, documents, commitments, and tasks surrounding it.
Search isn't just about finding a file.
It's about being able to ask for something in the way you naturally remember it.
Threads bring related information together around the projects and topics you're actually working on.
The goal is not to add another place where information lives.
The goal is to make the information you already have make sense.

**How we built it**

I started with the experience rather than the technology.
I didn't want to build another dashboard covered in charts, notifications, and AI buttons. I wanted to open Thread and immediately understand what mattered.
From there, I built the product piece by piece.
The interface was built around a clean, focused workspace, while the backend handles authentication, data, integrations, retrieval, and the relationships between different pieces of information.
Thread connects to services such as Gmail, Calendar, and Drive, retrieves relevant information, and uses AI to reason over the context rather than simply generating isolated responses.
One of the most important parts of building it was creating a system where AI responses were grounded in the information actually available to Thread.
I wanted the product to be able to say why something was important, not simply make something up that sounded intelligent.
I also kept rebuilding the interface whenever something felt unnecessary.
That became one of the defining principles of Thread:
If a feature adds complexity without adding understanding, it probably shouldn't be there.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest challenge wasn't getting AI to generate text.
It was getting the system to understand relationships.
An email, a calendar event, a document, and a task can all refer to the same underlying piece of work without explicitly saying so.
Making those connections useful—and doing it without overwhelming the user—was much harder than I expected.
Another challenge was deciding what the product should not do.
It is incredibly easy to keep adding features to an AI product.
I had to repeatedly step back and ask:
Does this make Thread more useful, or does it just make Thread bigger?
There were also plenty of technical challenges along the way: authentication, integrations, data models, retrieval, API limitations, debugging, redesigning parts of the application, and rebuilding things when an approach simply wasn't good enough.
And I was doing all of this while still being a student.
There were moments when the project would have been much easier to abandon as a prototype.
Instead, every time something didn't work, I treated it as another reason to make the product better.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I'm proud that Thread became more than the original idea I had in my head.
I started with a frustration about fragmented information.
I ended up building a working system that can bring together multiple sources of context and turn them into an experience designed around what matters now.
I'm especially proud of the Morning Brief because it represents the central idea behind Thread.
It isn't simply:
"Here are the things that happened."
It tries to answer:
"Here's what you should probably pay attention to—and here's the context behind it."
I'm also proud of how much I learned by actually building the product instead of stopping at the idea.
Thread forced me to think about product design, AI, APIs, authentication, data architecture, information retrieval, user experience, and, most importantly, what makes a product genuinely useful.
But perhaps the accomplishment I'm most proud of is much simpler:
I turned an idea that existed in my head into something another person can actually open and use.

**What we learned**

The biggest thing I learned is that AI itself isn't the product. Context is.
Anyone can ask an AI to write something.
The interesting question is:
What does the AI know when it answers?
Give it isolated information, and you get an isolated answer.
Give it the right context—what happened, who was involved, what is coming next, what has already been discussed—and suddenly the interaction becomes much more useful.
I also learned that great product design is often about subtraction.
My first instinct was constantly to add.
More features. More controls. More information.
Over time, I learned that the best version of Thread was usually the version where I removed something and made the remaining experience clearer.
And I learned something personally important:
Being a student doesn't mean you have to build student-sized ideas.
You may have fewer resources, less experience, and a lot more things competing for your time.
But you can still start with a problem that feels enormous and try to solve it.

**What's next for Thread**

**What's next**

What you're seeing today is only the beginning of Thread.

The first version brings together a part of the Google ecosystem—Gmail, Calendar, Drive—and shows what becomes possible when those tools stop behaving like completely separate products.

But that is only one ecosystem.

Imagine adding Slack. Notion. Microsoft 365. WhatsApp. Linear. GitHub. CRM systems. Project management tools. Notes. Files. Travel. Personal planning. And eventually, the services that haven't even been built yet.

The exciting part isn't simply having more integrations.

It's what happens when Thread can understand the information flowing through all of them.

Today, an email might live in Gmail, a decision might be buried in a conversation, the deadline might be in a calendar, and the work itself might be sitting in a project-management tool.

Thread's opportunity is to make those pieces feel like one story.

The more context Thread can responsibly understand, the less the user has to do manually.

And that creates a very different kind of product.

Instead of asking:

"Which app do I need to open?"

You start asking:

"What do I need to know?"

And Thread figures out where the answer lives.

**From workspace to personal context**

The long-term vision goes beyond work.

The same problem exists everywhere.

You shouldn't have to remember which conversation contains the restaurant someone recommended, where the booking confirmation went, which calendar contains the trip dates, or which document has the information you need.

A system that understands those connections could eventually become useful far beyond productivity.

That is where I see Thread going:

from a workspace that understands your work to a layer that understands the context surrounding your life.

**The opportunity grows with every connection**

There is also something I find particularly exciting about the architecture of the idea.

Thread doesn't need to replace every tool.

It can let the tools people already love continue doing what they're good at, while Thread becomes the layer that helps them work together.

Gmail can remain Gmail.

Calendar can remain Calendar.

Notion can remain Notion.

Slack can remain Slack.

Thread can sit above them and answer the question none of them is designed to answer on its own:

"How does all of this connect?"

That means the vision doesn't depend on convincing the world to abandon the tools it already uses.

It depends on making those tools more useful together.

**And this is just version one**

I'm still a student, and I built the first version with the resources I have today.

That makes the future especially exciting to me.

With a larger engineering team, deeper integrations, stronger infrastructure, and more time to develop the underlying intelligence, there is so much further this idea can go.

I can imagine Thread becoming increasingly proactive—not simply waiting for someone to search for information, but recognizing when context could genuinely help and surfacing it at the right moment.

The goal isn't to create an app with hundreds of integrations just so we can say we have hundreds of integrations.

The goal is to reach a point where the boundaries between those tools stop mattering to the person using them.

Because that's what I think the next generation of software should feel like.

You shouldn't have to think about where your information lives.

You should be able to think about what you're trying to accomplish.

Thread is my first step toward that.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**LIFEQUEST — Practice Life Before Life Tests You**

**Inspiration**

LIFEQUEST started from a simple observation: people are frequently evaluated on what they can remember, list on a resume, or prove through certificates, while many important real-world capabilities are revealed only when a person has to make a decision.

A student can complete a course and still feel unprepared for a workplace conversation. A job seeker can know interview theory but struggle with an unfamiliar situation. An employer can see a resume but still have limited visibility into how a candidate prioritizes, communicates, reasons, or responds to consequences.

We wanted to build something that lets people practice life before life tests them.

LIFEQUEST therefore treats capability as something that can be practiced through realistic situations, observed through decisions, reflected on through consequences, and represented with transparent evidence.

The central loop is:

Situation → Decision → Consequence → Feedback → Evidence → Replay

The product is designed as one extensible capability platform connecting career readiness, practical decision-making, assessment, skill evidence, practical problem-solving, safety awareness, and social-impact directions.

**What It Does**

LIFEQUEST is an interactive capability-practice platform built around Missions.

Instead of presenting every experience as a conventional quiz, a Mission can place the user inside a situation, ask them to choose an action, evaluate the decision, show consequences, and provide structured feedback.

The platform includes directions for:

- Career readiness

- Mental ability and reasoning

- Aptitude and quantitative practice

- Puzzle-based practice

- Situational judgment

- Workplace decision making

- Communication practice

- Interview preparation

- Employer assessment

- Skill Passport

- Impact Passport

- Practical problem-solving

- Women's-safety decision practice direction

- Broader social-impact and community-action direction

The important distinction is that LIFEQUEST does not automatically turn simulated performance into professional credentials.

A completed simulation means the user practiced a situation. It does not, by itself, prove real-world experience.

**One platform, multiple real-life capability domains**

LIFEQUEST is intentionally broader than a single career-preparation app. Its common Mission and evidence architecture can support different moments where people need to think, decide, communicate, verify, or act.

The product experience is organized around:

CAREER
 → Aptitude • Reasoning • Puzzles • Workplace • Interview

ASSESS
 → Employer Tests • Skills • Questions • Preview • Organization

PROVE
 → Skill Passport • Evidence • Provenance

IMPACT
 → Impact Passport • Action • Outcome • Timeline

SOLVE
 → Claims • Documents • Scam Awareness • Legal Awareness • Practical Action

SAFETY
 → Situational Awareness • Risk Recognition • Communication • Appropriate Response

The important architectural idea is that these are not intended to be isolated mini-apps. They share the same capability philosophy: practice or perform an action, capture what happened, communicate the limits of the evidence, and use the result for improvement.

**The Core Experience**

A conventional quiz often looks like:

Question → Answer → Score

LIFEQUEST is designed around a richer loop:

Realistic Situation
 ↓
Understand Context
 ↓
Make a Decision
 ↓
Observe Consequence
 ↓
Receive Feedback
 ↓
Generate Transparent Evidence
 ↓
Replay
 ↓
Improve

This allows the user to learn not only whether an answer was accepted, but why a decision produced a particular outcome.

The architecture is intentionally reusable: different scenarios can use the same Mission Engine while representing different skills and domains.

**Career Readiness**

LIFEQUEST's career ecosystem is designed to practice capabilities that are difficult to capture through certificates alone.

**Aptitude & Math**

Practice directions include:

- Percentage

- Ratio

- Profit and Loss

- Number Series

- Quantitative problem solving

**Logical Reasoning**

Practice directions include:

- Coding / Decoding

- Analogy

- Sequence

- Pattern recognition

- Structured reasoning

**Puzzle Lab**

Practice directions include:

- Matrix

- Pattern

- Logic puzzle

- Spatial reasoning

- Adaptive reasoning concepts

**Situational Judgment**

Users practice workplace situations involving:

- Judgment

- Risk awareness

- Prioritization

- Stakeholder handling

- Professional decision making

**Workplace**

Practice directions include:

- Prioritization

- Decision making

- Collaboration

- Managing competing demands

- Professional response

**Communication**

Practice directions include:

- Professional communication

- Workplace responses

- Stakeholder interaction

- Clear communication

- Appropriate professional tone

**Interview Prep**

Practice directions include:

- HR

- Technical

- Situational questions

- STAR-style behavioral responses

The objective is not to make users memorize a "correct" interview script. It is to help them practice thinking and communicating under realistic constraints.

**Employer Assessment**

LIFEQUEST also includes an employer-oriented assessment direction.

The intended workflow is:

Employer
 ↓
Add Test
 ↓
Select Assessment Type
 ↓
Select Skills
 ↓
Add / Reorder Questions
 ↓
Preview
 ↓
Organize Test

This provides a foundation for assessments organized around explicit capabilities instead of only resume keywords.

The assessment architecture includes employer assessment and reporting components.

The long-term direction is to help employers observe structured evidence of capabilities such as:

- Reasoning

- Decision making

- Communication

- Prioritization

- Collaboration

- Technical capability

without claiming that a simulation alone is equivalent to professional experience.

**Skill Passport**

The Skill Passport organizes evidence around capabilities rather than simply collecting generic certificates.

Examples of capability areas include:

- Problem solving

- Decision making

- Communication

- Collaboration

- Reasoning

- Workplace judgment

- Technical capability

- Practical action

The Skill Passport is designed to answer a more useful question than "How many certificates do you have?"

It asks:

What did you practice, what did you demonstrate, and what evidence actually exists?

**Evidence Integrity**

Evidence integrity is a core design principle of LIFEQUEST.

Skill platforms can easily create a misleading impression if every completed simulation is presented as a real credential.

We deliberately avoid that.

LIFEQUEST uses provenance states such as:

- Simulated

- Simulated Model

- Demonstrated

- Projected

- Field Verified

These states communicate what a piece of evidence actually represents.

For example:

A completed workplace simulation can be Simulated.

A modeled expected result can be Projected.

An appropriate practical activity can produce Demonstrated evidence.

Evidence genuinely validated in a real-world context can eventually become Field Verified.

The principle is simple:

Practice is not automatically proof of experience.

This distinction is important for both learners and employers because it prevents the platform from overclaiming what its results mean.

**Impact Passport**

LIFEQUEST extends beyond employability through an Impact Passport direction.

The idea is to make meaningful action visible without pretending that simulated activity is real-world impact.

A potential impact flow is:

Identify a Problem
 ↓
Choose an Action
 ↓
Take Action
 ↓
Record Evidence
 ↓
Describe Outcome
 ↓
Build Impact Timeline

This can support directions such as:

- Community contribution

- Social impact

- Responsible action

- Inclusion

- Peace-oriented contribution

- Women's safety

- Community problem solving

The same provenance principle applies:

A simulated impact scenario is practice. Real-world impact requires real-world action and appropriate evidence.

**Women's Safety Direction**

One important social-impact direction of LIFEQUEST is women's safety.

The same decision-practice engine can be used to create educational scenarios involving:

- Situational awareness

- Risk recognition

- Emergency decision making

- Communication under pressure

- Seeking appropriate assistance

- Supporting others in difficult situations

The goal is not to replace emergency services, trained professionals, law enforcement, medical services, or established safety systems.

The goal is to provide structured practice for recognizing situations and thinking through appropriate responses.

A safety-oriented practice flow can be represented as:

Recognize Situation
 ↓
Assess Risk
 ↓
Consider Options
 ↓
Choose an Appropriate Response
 ↓
Understand Consequence
 ↓
Review / Replay

This makes the same capability framework useful beyond employment.

**Social Impact and Peace-Oriented Direction**

LIFEQUEST also has a broader social-impact direction.

The underlying idea is:

A person's capability should not only improve their employability; it can also increase their ability to contribute positively to their community.

The platform can therefore extend toward:

- Peace

- Community contribution

- Social awareness

- Inclusion

- Responsible decision making

- Women's safety

- Practical problem solving

- Positive community action

These are directions supported by the product architecture rather than claims that every area is already fully implemented.

**Solve**

The Solve area extends LIFEQUEST beyond tests and preparation into practical action.

Its purpose is to move the user from:

Identify → Understand → Decide → Act → Document

The broader product direction includes practical workflows such as:

- ClaimKit-style claim/document support

- Structured document and evidence workflows

- Scam-awareness and investigation-oriented guidance

- Legal-awareness and responsible decision-support

- Practical problem solving

- Safety-oriented decision practice

- Evidence organization

These tools are designed to help users understand a problem and organize useful evidence or next steps. They are not presented as a replacement for qualified legal, emergency, financial, or professional advice.

The same product philosophy applies across Solve:

Understand the situation → make a better decision → document what matters → learn from the outcome.

**How We Built It**

LIFEQUEST is built as a mobile-first React Native application using Expo and TypeScript.

**Core stack**

- React Native

- Expo

- TypeScript

- Expo Router

- React Hooks

- Structured mission datasets

- Branching simulation logic

- Evidence provenance tracking

- Assessment Lab models

- Skill Passport evidence components

- Employer assessment components

- Employer reporting components

- RevenueCat

RevenueCat is integrated for subscription, paywall, and entitlement management.

We deliberately avoided unnecessary dependencies. The final product upgrade added zero new npm packages and preserved the existing native configuration.

**Architecture**

The application is organized around reusable product concepts rather than treating every feature as an isolated screen.

 LIFEQUEST
 |
 +--------------+--------------+
 | |
 UI / Screens Shared Components
 | |
 +--------------+--------------+
 |
 Mission Engine
 |
 +---------------+---------------+
 | | |
 Missions Evaluation Progress
 | | |
 +---------------+---------------+
 |
 Evidence Model
 |
 Skill Passport
 |
 +---------------+---------------+
 | |
 Learner Flow Employer Flow
 | |
 Practice Assessment Builder
 | |
 Feedback Reporting
 |
 Impact / Action

This structure allows multiple product experiences to share the same underlying practice and evidence concepts.

**Mission Engine**

The Mission Engine is the central product mechanism.

A Mission can represent:

- A scenario

- A decision

- Multiple choices

- Feedback

- Consequences

- Progress

- Replay state

- Skill association

- Evidence state

The architecture allows new Missions to be introduced without redesigning the entire application.

This is important because the product can expand across career readiness, workplace judgment, social impact, and other domains while retaining one consistent interaction model.

**Branching Simulation Logic**

Instead of reducing every activity to a binary correct/wrong result, LIFEQUEST can represent decision consequences.

Conceptually:

Situation
 |
 +---- Choice A ----&gt; Consequence A ----&gt; Feedback
 |
 +---- Choice B ----&gt; Consequence B ----&gt; Feedback
 |
 +---- Choice C ----&gt; Consequence C ----&gt; Feedback

This makes the experience closer to decision practice.

It also provides a foundation for replay:

What happens if I choose differently?

**Observable Skills**

LIFEQUEST is designed around observable behavior.

Rather than simply claiming:

"You are a strong leader."

the platform can associate an activity with observable actions such as:

- Prioritized competing tasks

- Considered stakeholder impact

- Identified risk

- Communicated appropriately

- Selected an action

- Responded to feedback

- Replayed a scenario

This creates a more transparent relationship between practice and capability.

**Technical Design Decisions**

We intentionally kept the architecture lightweight.

Instead of introducing a large backend or additional frameworks solely for the hackathon, we extended the existing Expo/React Native architecture.

This allowed us to focus engineering effort on:

- Product coherence

- Simulation logic

- Evidence integrity

- Reusable components

- Assessment workflows

- Demonstrable functionality

rather than infrastructure that was not necessary to demonstrate the core idea.

**RevenueCat**

RevenueCat is used for subscription/paywall and entitlement management.

This keeps monetization concerns separated from the Mission Engine.

The architecture can therefore distinguish between:

- Free experiences

- Pro experiences

- Entitlements

- Paywall presentation

- Judge/demo access where applicable

**Document and Evidence Workflow**

For document-related functionality, the current implementation uses a structured text/photo fallback rather than depending entirely on native camera OCR.

This was a deliberate stability trade-off.

It keeps the workflow usable across web and development environments while avoiding unnecessary native complexity for the core product.

**Challenges We Faced**

**1. Building one coherent product**

The biggest challenge was expanding LIFEQUEST without turning it into a collection of disconnected screens.

The solution was to keep the Mission Engine as the central experience and connect different modes through the same:

Practice → Consequence → Evidence

model.

**2. Separating practice from proof**

A major product-design challenge was preventing simulated performance from being mistaken for real professional experience.

We addressed this through explicit evidence provenance states.

**3. Maintaining stability during rapid development**

The project needed to evolve quickly without introducing unnecessary native configuration changes.

We therefore reused the existing Expo/React Native architecture and avoided unnecessary dependencies.

**4. Supporting different environments**

The product needed to remain practical across mobile development and web environments.

For document-related workflows, a structured text/photo fallback helped avoid making native OCR infrastructure mandatory for the core experience.

**5. Designing for extensibility**

Career preparation, employer assessment, skill evidence, and social impact could easily become separate applications.

The challenge was finding a shared model.

The Mission Engine and evidence model became that shared foundation.

**Accomplishments That We Are Proud Of**

We are proud that LIFEQUEST evolved beyond a conventional quiz or interview-preparation application.

The product now brings together:

- Interactive Missions

- Decision practice

- Consequence-based feedback

- Skill evidence

- Evidence provenance

- Career readiness

- Employer assessment

- Interview preparation

- Workplace simulations

- Impact-oriented experiences

- Women's-safety decision-practice direction

Most importantly, these areas are connected by a common product philosophy rather than being completely independent features.

**What We Learned**

We learned that a useful practice product is not just a collection of questions.

The important part is the complete loop:

Situation → Decision → Consequence → Feedback → Evidence → Replay

That loop makes the experience closer to practicing a decision than simply consuming information.

We also learned that transparency matters when building systems around skills and evidence.

A simulation can demonstrate how someone approached a scenario, but it should not pretend to be proof of something that has not actually happened.

We learned that product architecture matters as much as feature count.

A reusable Mission Engine allowed us to extend the platform into different capability areas without creating a separate architecture for every feature.

We also learned that social impact needs the same evidence discipline as employability. A user should be able to practice a safety or community scenario without the system incorrectly presenting that simulation as real-world impact.

**What's Next**

The next stage of LIFEQUEST can expand the same foundation into:

- More adaptive Missions

- Larger reasoning and aptitude libraries

- More workplace simulations

- Deeper interview practice

- More employer assessment templates

- Richer Skill Passport evidence

- Real-world evidence verification workflows

- More Impact Passport experiences

- Women's-safety scenarios

- Community problem-solving Missions

- More structured communication practice

- More technical interview simulations

- Improved assessment analytics

The goal is not simply to add more screens.

The goal is to increase the quality and usefulness of the:

Practice → Evidence → Improvement → Action

loop.

**Why LIFEQUEST**

LIFEQUEST is built around a simple idea:

Don't just tell people what they should know. Let them practice what they need to do.

A certificate can show that someone completed something.

A score can show how someone performed on a particular test.

But realistic practice can reveal how someone thinks through a situation.

LIFEQUEST combines that practice with transparent evidence so users can understand what they actually demonstrated.

The long-term vision is a capability layer connecting:

Learning → Practice → Decision → Evidence → Employability → Real-world Contribution

**Responsible Product Positioning**

LIFEQUEST does not claim that:

- A simulation equals professional experience.

- A score predicts a person's future with certainty.

- A practice result is a clinical or psychological diagnosis.

- A safety simulation replaces emergency services or professionals.

- A simulated social-impact action equals real-world impact.

Instead, the product focuses on:

- Practice

- Reflection

- Observable behavior

- Feedback

- Evidence provenance

- Repeatability

- Responsible communication of results

**Built With**

- React Native

- Expo

- TypeScript

- Expo Router

- React Hooks

- RevenueCat

- Structured Mission Engine

- Branching Simulation Logic

- Assessment Lab

- Skill Passport

- Evidence Provenance Model

**Final Product Principle**

LIFEQUEST is based on one simple principle:

Practice life before life tests you.

The product brings decision practice, career preparation, structured assessment, transparent evidence, and social-impact directions into one extensible platform.

The central loop remains:

Situation
 ↓
Decision
 ↓
Consequence
 ↓
Feedback
 ↓
Evidence
 ↓
Replay
 ↓
Improvement

That loop is the foundation of LIFEQUEST.

**LIFEQUEST #EdTech #CareerReadiness #SkillDevelopment #SocialImpact #WomenSafety #DigitalSafety #LegalAwareness #AI #ReactNative #Expo #TypeScript**

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I’m heading into aerospace engineering one of the top Universities in Pakistan and kept running into the same problem: single AI tools give confident answers that are sometimes wrong, and doing every structural check by hand takes too much time. I wanted a tool that students like me could actually trust for preliminary calculations. Something fast, mobile, and verified.

**What it does**

Neometrist is a mobile structural calculator that runs two independent methods on every problem:

- Physics Solver — closed-form Euler-Bernoulli solution

- Numerical Auditor — independent numerical integration

A result is only accepted when both methods agree within 1% (Verified Consensus). It includes material presets, screening limits (L/360), calculation history, and a three-tier RevenueCat subscription system.

**How we built it**

Neometrist was built as a mobile-first app using React Native and Expo , with TypeScript for the main application logic. The core calculation engine is deterministic and runs locally — it uses closed-form Euler-Bernoulli beam equations for the Physics Solver and an independent numerical integration method (composite trapezoidal integration of curvature) for the Numerical Auditor.

The dual-lane system is orchestrated in JavaScript/TypeScript: both methods receive the same raw inputs, compute separately, and a reconciler compares the final deflection values. If the variance is ≤ 1%, the app issues a Verified Consensus badge. The AI layer (OpenAI) is only used for plain-language explanations and never modifies the numerical results.

Development was accelerated with help from Replit, which was used for rapid prototyping of agent prompts, and backend-style routing before moving the code into the Expo project. The project structure includes separate modules for:

- Deterministic physics and numerical solvers

- Tier-aware routing (Freemium / Promium / Premium)

- RevenueCat subscription handling

- Calculation history (local storage)

- UI components for the beam visualization, result cards, and paywall

RevenueCat powers the three subscription tiers and gates access to advanced materials and the second verification lane. The entire math pipeline is designed so that even if the advisory AI service is unavailable, the core calculations still work.

**Challenges we ran into**

Getting the two calculation lanes to be truly independent (not just the same formula twice) took several iterations. Making the mobile UI feel clean while still showing technical depth was also difficult. Balancing freemium limits with a real reason to upgrade required careful design.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Real dual-lane verification with measurable variance

- Working RevenueCat paywall and tier gating

- Clean mobile experience with presets for Civil, Architecture, Automotive, and Aerospace engineers and students

- Fully open calculation trace so anyone can audit the math

**What we learned**

Building a tool for engineering students taught me that reliability matters more than flashy AI features. Separating deterministic math from AI explanation made the product much stronger. I also learned how important clear monetization and presentation are in a competition setting.

**What's next for Neometrist AI**

I plan to expand support conditions, add more materials, improve the visualization, and eventually open it to more engineering students who need fast, verifiable preliminary checks on mobile.

</details>

## 579. Yumetan

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/yumetan (gallery page 148) · ❤️ 0 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [DoyleRampo Yamauchi](https://devpost.com/DoyleRampo)

- **Repo check:** public repo · ⚠️ no license detected · 46 commits · HTML · RevenueCat found in code ✅
- **Built with:** actions, api, app, apple, authentication, cloud, css3, express.js, firebase, firestore, github, google, gpt, html5, ios, javascript, line, login, node.js, openai, purchase, render, revenuecat, swift

**Video (2:35):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uAxh0XgluB0

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/uAxh0XgluB0/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uAxh0XgluB0)

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

People around me love telling me about their dreams. Honestly, it was a little tiring. So I asked myself: in an age of AI, why do they tell me and not a chatbot? The answer I landed on was that they believe I understand them — their week, their moods, their recurring nightmares — better than a generic model ever could.

That became the idea for Yumetan: a dream journal where the AI reading is grounded in your own dream history and diary, not in a one-off prompt, and where a character that only you can grow makes the habit of writing dreams down feel rewarding.

**What it does**

- 24-question dream-type quiz sorts you into one of 16 playful dream types across four groups (nightmare, prophetic, lucid, recurring), each with its own character — a human "Dreamwalker" or an animal "Moonlight companion". The type is recomputed from your recent dreams, so it drifts as you do.

- Dream & diary journal with typed, dictated (on-device speech recognition) or photographed (handwritten-note OCR) entries, sleep check-ins, and a dream level that rises as you keep writing.

- AI dream reading: GPT reads the dream together with your recent diary and returns a reflection on your current state of mind plus a light-hearted "fortune of the day" — clearly labelled as entertainment, never a diagnosis.

- Members' dream feed: share one dream a day, anonymised under a nickname and your character, and react to others' dreams of today with 12 stamps. Yesterday's dreams disappear at midnight, so the feed feels like a shared morning.

- Four languages (Japanese, English, Korean, Simplified Chinese), account sync across devices, in-app account deletion, and store subscriptions (Free / Starter / Standard) verified server-side.

**How we built it**

- One codebase, three targets: plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript modules served as a PWA, wrapped with Capacitor for iOS. Rules that decide a dream type or a dream level live in public/core/ and are shared by the app, the server and the tests.

- Node.js + Express API on Render: verifies Firebase ID tokens, meters plan quotas in Firestore transactions, calls the OpenAI API for readings and OCR, and syncs subscriptions from RevenueCat (webhook + REST) so the client never grants itself a plan.

- Firebase Authentication (Google, native Sign in with Apple, native LINE Login, email) and Cloud Firestore with owner-only rules for journals; a small Swift plugin hands off browser-based OAuth to the app with two independent proofs so a stolen link can't log anyone in.

- App Store In-App Purchase through RevenueCat, Terms of Use / Privacy Policy pages served by the API, and a GitHub Actions pipeline that archives and uploads every develop push to TestFlight.

- Quality: ~80 Node unit tests for the domain rules, billing, moderation and account deletion, plus ~80 Playwright browser tests covering onboarding, sync, purchases, the feed and account deletion in all four languages.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Dreams break content filters. Our first feed ran every post through OpenAI moderation — and rejected "I jumped off a collapsing building" as self-harm. Dreams are full of falling, dying and disasters, so we removed automatic filtering and kept operator-side hiding and suspension instead.

- App Review. We were rejected for missing in-app account deletion, for subscription screens without terms/price disclosure, and for mentioning Google Play inside an iOS app. Each round meant server-side deletion of every trace of a user (posts, stamps on other people's posts, usage counters, RevenueCat subscriber), a purchase screen that states name, length and price next to the button, and a text sweep across four languages.

- OAuth inside a WKWebView. Pop-ups don't work in a Capacitor app, so we built a browser hand-off with a challenge/verifier pair, then replaced it with native Apple and LINE SDK sign-in for iOS.

- Store sandboxes. A RevenueCat Test Store key silently crashes a release build; the build script now refuses it unless explicitly allowed.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A dream journal that is fun on day one (quiz → character) and gets more personal the longer you use it.

- Shipping iOS and web from one codebase with full localisation in four languages.

- A server that never trusts the client for anything that costs money: plans, AI quotas and account deletion are all verified with Firebase tokens and Firestore transactions.

- Surviving three App Review rounds and coming out with a cleaner, more honest product (no Google Play copy, real legal pages, complete account deletion).

**What we learned**

- "Understanding someone" is mostly context. The AI reading felt generic until it started reading the previous day's diary alongside the dream.

- Content moderation tuned for social media is wrong for dreams; the operator, not a classifier, has to be the safety net.

- App Store rules (5.1.1 account deletion, 3.1.2 subscription disclosure, 2.3.10 metadata) are easier to design in from the start than to retrofit.

- Writing tests for the rules (type scoring, quotas, deletion) rather than the UI let us change the UI many times without fear.

**What's next for Yumetan**

- Make the AI reading remember: longer-term patterns across weeks of dreams and diary entries, so the reading truly knows you the way a friend would.

- Report and block controls in the feed, and a gentle "dream streak" to reward daily writing.

- Traditional Chinese and more character sets, plus a shareable "dream card" image for each reading.

</details>

**Inspiration : I wanted a lightweight, fast, and native Android way to track my backlog without bloated social features or cluttered interfaces.**

**What it does: GameTracker allows users to add games, categorize them into statuses (Backlog, Playing, Completed), and search their collection instantly. It operates on a freemium model: users can track up to 5 games for free. Adding a 6th game triggers a RevenueCat-powered paywall, offering a lifetime "Pro" unlock for unlimited tracking.**

**How we built it: App is built natively for Android using Kotlin and Jetpack Compose. State management is handled through Compose's reactive data flows (State Hoisting). For local persistence, we utilized SharedPreferences and Gson to serialize the game lists directly to the device. We integrated the RevenueCat SDK (purchases and purchases-ui) to manage user entitlements and subscription logic.**

**Challenges we ran into: Gradle & Memory Issues: Integrating the RevenueCat SDK initially crashed our builds due to JVM heap space limits. We had to manually configure gradle.properties to allocate 2GB of memory to the Gradle daemon.**

**Accomplishments that we're proud of: Successfully navigating complex SDK dependency issues and building a bulletproof workaround for the hackathon. We engineered a custom Jetpack Compose "Mock Paywall" that intercepts the RevenueCat limit, simulates a successful purchase, saves the Pro state persistently, and instantly unlocks the UI—allowing us to demonstrate the architecture without paying store fees.**

**What we learned: A deep dive into Gradle memory management, Jetpack Compose reactive filtering (combining tab states with search queries without excessive recomposition), and the strict platform realities of integrating production billing SDKs outside of live app store environments.**

**What's next for Untitled: Upgrading from local JSON storage to a cloud database, integrating the IGDB API to automatically pull official game box art, and eventually launching officially on the Google Play Store with live RevenueCat transactions.**

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

As a university baseball player, I have struggled to understand pitching mechanics from video alone. It is difficult to quantitatively compare two pitching motions just by watching them, while professional motion-capture systems are expensive and require specialized equipment.

I wanted to make pitching analysis more accessible by using ordinary smartphone video and AI.

**What I Built**

Outpose Baseball is an AI-powered pitching analysis application that analyzes pitching motion from video.

The application uses AI pose estimation to detect the pitcher's body keypoints and converts the motion into visual and quantitative feedback.

Key features include:

- AI-based pitching pose analysis

- Automatic pitch-speed estimation

- Pitching motion and joint-movement analysis

- Frame-by-frame motion analysis

- 2-Pitch Comparison for comparing two pitching videos

- Overlay visualization of two pitching motions

- 3D visualization of pitching motion and ball trajectory

- Pitch movement visualization

- Strike/ball classification

- Pitch history and data visualization

- A simulation feature for estimating potential velocity improvement from changes in pitching mechanics

The goal is to make useful pitching analysis possible with equipment that players already have: a smartphone and a computer.

**How I Built It**

The application was developed primarily in Python using computer vision and AI pose estimation.

The main technologies include:

- Python

- YOLO pose estimation

- OpenCV

- NumPy

- Pandas

- Plotly

- Streamlit

- Android WebView

- RevenueCat

The web application is deployed using Streamlit Community Cloud, and I also created an Android WebView version that connects to the deployed application.

RevenueCat is used to implement the Pro subscription and control access to premium pitching-analysis features.

**Challenges**

One of the biggest challenges was analyzing fast pitching motions from ordinary video.

Pitching involves rapid movements, and the detected body keypoints can be affected by camera angle, lighting, video quality, and temporary body occlusion.

Another challenge was turning raw pose-estimation data into information that is actually useful to baseball players. Rather than simply displaying keypoints, I focused on visualizations and comparisons that allow players to understand differences between pitches.

I also had to design the application so that the analysis results were understandable without specialized motion-capture equipment.

**What I Learned**

This project taught me that building an AI application is not only about choosing a powerful model.

The AI output needs to be transformed into clear visual feedback that users can understand and act on.

Through this project, I learned about computer vision, pose estimation, video processing, data visualization, web application development, Android integration, and subscription implementation with RevenueCat.

**What's Next**

I plan to improve pose-estimation accuracy, develop more detailed pitching metrics, and provide more personalized feedback based on individual pitching mechanics.

In the future, I also want to make the system more accessible to younger players and baseball teams by focusing on smartphone-based analysis that does not require specialized equipment.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

As Chemical Engineering sophomores returning from summer vacation, we were hit with a massive wall of heavy problem sets, assignments and upcoming mid sem date all at once. Going from zero to a hundred overnight gave us severe deadline anxiety. Staring down pages of heat transfer and fluid mechanics homework, traditional productivity apps just felt like cold, corporate spreadsheets that made our stress worse. We realized students don't need another generic task list-we need a sanctuary. So,we built "Aurora Room" to create a cozy, ambient lo-fi study space that understands heavy academic workloads, visualize deadline urgency through a stress reactive sky, and keeps students focused when late night problem sets get intense.

**What it does**

Aurora Room transforms your device into an ambient , stress aware study sanctuary with tools designed for heavy academic workloads:
-Stress Reactive Aurora Sky: The sky's ambient colour , wave animation speed and pitch darkness dynamically adjust based on active assignment deadlines, feelings of anxiety and upcoming exams.
-7-Day deadline horizon:A horizontal calendar strip in the assignment drawer that visualizes upcoming homework, lab report, and pinned campus dates.
-Emergency Cram Scheduler:Tapping cram mode on high priority deadlines due within 48 hours instantly generates a stress calibrated , hour by hour study and rest timetable.
-Strict Panic Mode:An anti doomscroll focus lock that enforces study sessions with a 3 second hold to quit penalty. Abandoning early triggers Critical Storm mode in your room.
-Weekly Report:Features an animated focus ring that calculates actual focus time against your planned target time, tracking true study completion and top distractions.
-Honest Introspection Check:Prompts students after every session to reflect on actual focused vs wastes doomscroll minutes.
-Powered by Revenuecat: Integrates the RevenueCat SDK to manage live offerings , package fetching , and subscription entitlements for Aurora Pro($2.99/mo or $19.99/yr)
-Free Tier: Default Midnight Cyan sky theme, 3 free AI assignment scans, 1 course tracking, and 1 tap emergency cram tools.
-Aurora Pro Subscription($2.99/mo or $19.99/yr):Unlocks all 5 premium glowing aurora sky paletes, individual $0.99/mo theme passes, unlimited AI document scans, and full study vault storage.
-6 Glowing Aurora Sky palettes: Customize your study space with distinct sky theme palettes(Midnight Cyan, Sakura Bloom, Deep Ocean, Cosmic Violet, Ember Sunset, Forest Canopy). Each theme dramatically transforms the sky wave colours across all 4 stress levels.

**How we built it**

Coming from Chemical Engineering background, neither of us knew how to write mobile app code when shipaton 2026 started. But as ChemE sophomores drowning in Heat transfer and Fluid mechanics assignments ,we had a clear product vision for the exact app we needed to survive.
To bring "Aurora Room" to life , we embraced modern AI assisted development. We conceptualized every UX flow, designed the student psychology loops, and used AI models prompting to generated React Native code blocks, which are carefully integrated , tested , and iterated on in VS Code.
Tech Stack and Architecture:
-Frontend Framework: Built with React Native(Expo) to run cross platform on Android and iOS.
-Animations:Powered by React Native Reanimated 3 to render the 60 FPS continuous Aurora sky waves, glowing ambient overlays, and animated report rings.
-Charts and indicators: Custom SVG rendering with react native svg for the 7 day deadline horizon and weekly progress reports.
-State and local storage:Centralized state using React Context(AuroraContext) and 'AsyncStorage" to persist tasks, streaks and study logs locally on device.
-Monetization Infrastructure:Integrated the official RevenueCat SDK to handle the entitlement checks(pro) , live package fetching, paywall display, and subscription restores.

**Challenges we ran into**

As non cs ChemE students with no coding background, building a complete mobile app from scratch was a really hectic and annoying process ,every step was a steep learning curve:
-AI Prompting and architecture limits: Translating our exact vision into working code required endless trial and error. Making AI understand complex React Native state logic , 60 FPS reanimated sky wave math, and custom context took dozens of prompt iterations.
-Debugging red screens: Fixing crash logs , expo go native module limits, and android permission errors without formal CS training was really hard.
API limits and environment issues: Managing AI rate limits and keeping local storage clean forced us to pivot away from fragile network dependencies toward 100% reliable, zero crash local logic.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We actually shipped!: As chemE majors who literally couldn't write a line of code, even entering a massive global hackathon felt crazy. Going from zero knowledge to a fully working app is wild.
Mastering RevenueCat SDK: Successfully integrating the 'react native purchases' SDK, setting up paywalls, and handling Pro memberships without a CS background felt like a huge win.
Building something we need: We built Aurora Room for ourselves, and it' genuinely helping us survive our hectic ChemE courses.
Smooth vibe, Zero Crashes:Making an app that looks dark, cozy, runs at 60 FPS and actually works on our phones without crashing.

**What we learned**

Building Aurora Room taught us how to take a raw idea and turn it into a real , working product. We leaned how to think like product designers, turn student deadline into clean UX loops, and prompt AI effectively to build complex app logic. Wiring up the RevenueCat SDK showed us how real world app monetization and subscriptions work, and debugging endless screens taught us serious problem solving patience. Most importantly , we proved to ourselves that two ChemE sophomores can overcome technical hurdles and ship software we're proud of.

**What's next for Aurora Room**

-3-D Customizable Lo-Fi Room engine: Our original vision was an interactive, fully customizable 3D room with unlockable desk items, lava lamps and pets that double as monetization features. Due to our limited technical background, time constraints, ad resources, we settled for our current 2D frame engine, but building a real 3D room builder is the next goal.
-Deeper canvas and moodie integration:Automatically syncing deadlines and syllabus changes directly from student university portals.
-Refined UI and app polish: Smooth sound effects, custom widget support for phone home screens, and an even sleeker, stress free user experience.
-Expanded RevenueCat Paywalls: Adding custom A/B testing paywalls, students discount tiers, and expanded theme packs through RevenueCat.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

In December 2023, Cyclone Michaung flooded Chennai. Again, the worst-hit streets were the ones built over lakes and marshes. The city had grown over its own water, and the water came back to where it used to be.

The people buying or renting there never saw that history. What they got was this:

 Broker ──► "Found you the perfect plot 👌"
 ──► 📍 location pin
 ──► "Great price. Sign this week?"

 Buyer ──► no idea what the ground was, 10 or 40 years ago

Yet the answer already exists, scattered across open datasets: forty years of satellite water, elevation models, a century of earthquakes, decades of daily rain, global soil maps. Nobody puts them together for one plot, in plain words, before you sign.

So I built Temen: you core a plot the way a geologist pulls a core sample, and read what the ground remembers.

 SATELLITES REMEMBER + PLAIN WORDS + HONEST LIMITS
 "What was this ground before?" "What does it mean?" "What can't it see?"

Every source runs in parallel with its own timeout, so one slow server never blocks the rest. Parsed readings are cached, so saved places reopen offline.

**Reading the satellites pixel by pixel**

There is no water or terrain API here: Temen reads the raw map tiles itself. A point becomes a tile pixel through Web Mercator:

$$ x = \frac{\lambda + 180}{360} \cdot 256 \cdot 2^{z} \qquad y = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 - \frac{\ln(\tan\varphi + \sec\varphi)}{\pi}\right) \cdot 256 \cdot 2^{z} $$

At zoom 13 one JRC pixel covers about 18.6 m on the ground in Chennai:

$$ m = \frac{156543.03 \cdot \cos\varphi}{2^{z}} $$

Ground heights come straight out of the colour of each terrain pixel:

$$ h = 256R + G + \frac{B}{256} - 32768 $$

**The water verdict**

Temen reads the 9 × 9 JRC pixels around the pin (about a 170 m square). For each group of water classes K, the share is:

$$ s(K) = \frac{\left| \lbrace p \in W : c(p) \in K \rbrace \right|}{81} $$

Verdict
Rule

You're on water
water now covers at least 50%

Water was here and is gone
lost water covers at least 20%

This ground floods seasonally
seasonal water covers at least 20%

Water came and went
brief water covers at least 20%

Water nearby
any water at all

Buffer flag
any water pixel within 30 m

**The bowl test**

Temen samples 16 points on a 400 m ring around the pin and compares their median height with the pin's own:

$$ d = \operatorname{median}\big(h(r1), \dots, h(r16)\big) - h(p) $$

$$ \text{bowl} \iff d \ge 1.5\text{ m} \quad\text{and}\quad \frac{N}{16} \ge 0.75 $$

Here N is the number of ring points higher than the pin. Rain runs towards a bowl.

**Rain in the Indian Meteorological Department's terms**

$$ \text{heavy days per year} = \frac{\left|\lbrace t : r(t) \ge 64.5\text{ mm} \rbrace\right|}{\text{years}} $$

Very heavy is 115.6 mm and extreme is 204.5 mm, the Indian Meteorological Department's own thresholds.

**Soil where the city covers it**

SoilGrids masks built-up ground, and a city centre is exactly where people buy. So Temen fetches a 10 km grid of about 250 m cells and uses the pin's own cell, or the nearest modelled cell by great-circle distance:

$$ d(p, c) = 2R \arcsin\sqrt{\sin^{2}\frac{\varphi' - \varphi}{2} + \cos\varphi \cos\varphi' \sin^{2}\frac{\lambda' - \lambda}{2}} $$

SoilGrids' three fractions always add up to 1000 g/kg, so silt is never downloaded. It's computed:

$$ \text{silt} = 1000 - \text{clay} - \text{sand} \quad (\text{g/kg}) $$

**Challenges I ran into**

**1. A colour key nobody published**

JRC's 2024 water tiles encode each water class as a colour, and the 2024 palette isn't published. I inferred it by cross-tabbing the 2024 tiles against the 2021 release, then locked it with the golden-site tests.

**2. Soil held the whole core hostage**

SoilGrids' point API takes 2–14 s, and city centres are masked. I switched to its grid service, but that server answers in bursts, roughly one request at a time.

 BEFORE AFTER
 6 grids, one after another 4 grids (silt = 1000 − clay − sand)
 ──► up to 16 s, core stuck at 94% ──► one shared fetch per spot
 ──► "Soil took longer than 16 s" ──► the core seals without waiting
 ──► soil fills in when it lands

The core now seals as soon as the other sources are in, giving soil a short grace period:

$$ T = \max\Big(T', \min\big(t(\text{soil}), T' + 2.5\text{ s}\big)\Big) $$

Here T' is the time the slowest non-soil source takes. On a phone, the core now seals in about 3.5 s.

**3. The date line**

Near ±180° a 400 m ring made the tile window span the whole world: 32,784 tile fetches for one point. I fixed it by unwrapping longitudes, so the window stays in one piece across the date line.

**4. Honesty over drama**

Satellites mistake skyscraper shadows for water, and no dataset shows legal lake boundaries. So Temen never says safe or unsafe, always shows what it can't see, and its questions send you to the authority for official full-tank-line maps.

**5. Every way people share a location**

WhatsApp location links, Google Maps short links that resolve to a search path, geo: URIs, degrees-minutes-seconds, decimal pairs and plus codes all parse into a pin, mostly offline.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Every investor believes they would have held through 2008. Almost nobody did.

The gap between how people think they behave under a drawdown and how they
actually behave is the most expensive gap in personal finance, and it is
invisible until real money is on the line. By then it is too late to learn
anything cheaply.

HistoX closes that gap with virtual capital. You find out what you do when
the tape is falling and you do not know when it stops, before it costs you
anything.

**What it does**

You start already invested, in a real historical crash that has already
begun. You are not told which crash it is, what you are holding, or what
year it is. The tape rolls forward, and at scripted moments it stops and
asks one question: hold, sell all, or buy the dip. There is no timer.

Afterwards the Debrief scores your discipline out of 100 against what price
actually did next, breaks every call down with its real outcome, and
compares this run against your earlier ones: how often you sold into a fall
before, how often this time, and how deep the fall usually was when you did.

Seventeen playable crashes, across eight US equity events, seven Indian
market events and two crypto cycles. Black Monday 1987, the dot-com
collapse, the 2008 financial crisis, Ketan Parekh 2001, demonetisation,
COVID, the crypto winter, SVB. Every price, date and historically optimal
move is computed from a real price series by an importer in the repository.
Nothing is typed by hand.

Three more pillars sit alongside the simulator:

Daily Pivot, one sealed call a day on whether Bitcoin closes above a strike,
set at 09:00 IST and resolved at 17:00 IST against Binance.

Time Machine, a what-if compounding calculator with a shareable result card
and no login.

Live Markets, a read-only watchlist across US, Indian and crypto markets
where every price displays its source and whether it is delayed.

And a Nerve Profile, a five-axis read of how you trade under stress.

No real money anywhere. Every position is virtual, the app cannot place a
trade, and Daily Pivot points have no cash value.

**How we built it**

Flutter and Dart, one codebase for iOS and Android, around 26,000 lines in
lib/. Riverpod 3 for state. A custom CustomPainter chart engine with
pan/zoom, a crosshair, four chart types, six indicators and three drawing
tools, shared by every screen that draws prices. shared_preferences for
progress, scores and run history.

One simulator engine. Every campaign level, Endless window and Custom
Simulation runs through it, because a level is data rather than code.

RevenueCat powers HistoX Pro, the subscription that unlocks fifteen of the
seventeen crashes and the full Nerve Profile. The app talks to the store
through a single PurchasesService interface, so tests and the web demo swap
it out without touching a screen. Prices come from the current offering's
annual and monthly packages exactly as the store formats them. Pro is the
pro entitlement, and a customer-info listener pushes renewals, expiries and
purchases made on other devices to every locked screen. A build with no key
falls back to an honest "store not connected" state rather than showing a
price it cannot charge.

Market data is queried live and never bundled for the live pillars: Binance
for crypto in real time, Yahoo for US and Indian equity with a delay.

CI runs the analyzer, the full test suite, and an offline validation pass
that recomputes every level and the scoring from the shipped data and fails
if the committed validation report has drifted.

**Challenges we ran into**

Scoring hindsight as though it were nerve. Nine of the 130 pause points are
marked ambiguous in the level data, meaning price neither recovered nor fell
further. Nothing read that flag, so selling at a moment the importer itself
calls unanswerable scored zero and counted as a panic. Those are now
reported in the breakdown and excluded from the score.

A release build that would have given every user Pro for free. With no
RevenueCat key the app falls back to the unconnected store, and the paywall
offered a "continue without Pro" button to everyone, unlocking all fifteen
Pro levels. The only guard was "is a store connected", which in that build
is exactly false. It is now refused in release builds whatever the store is
doing, and proven fixed on a device rather than only in code.

An Android manifest with no INTERNET permission. Flutter only declares it in
the debug and profile manifests, so a release APK could have shipped unable
to reach Live Markets, the Daily Pivot, Time Machine or RevenueCat itself. A
plugin usually contributes it during merge, but relying on that means a
dependency change can silently kill networking in release.

Proving the campaign is not reducible to one button. Always holding averages
72 across the campaign, always buying the dip 66, always selling 21, random
play 53. The shape is right, but five levels are still beatable with a
single repeated action, and that is recorded as open rather than quietly
reweighted.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The audit. AUDIT_REPORT.md was written against our own code before
submitting, and it names a blocker that would have handed the paywall away,
a manifest that would have shipped with no network access, and five levels
where a player can score 100 by tapping Hold repeatedly. That last one is
still open and stated as open.

Reproducibility. tool/validation/ recomputes every level and the entire
Discipline Score from the shipped data with no network, and CI fails if the
committed report no longer matches. Any claim in the README can be rechecked
by anyone with a clone.

Sourced numbers only. Every historical price, date and optimal move traces
to a real series through an importer. Where data was not sourced, the level
is hidden rather than filled in.

**What we learned**

That a build that looks successful can be a failed one. Piping a Gradle
failure through tail made the shell report exit code zero, and a broken
release build read as a working one until it was installed.

That "is the store connected" is not the same question as "is this a release
build", and conflating them is how a paywall gets given away.

That honesty is cheaper than polish. Writing down the five levels that can
be beaten by tapping one button was more useful than tuning the score until
the problem disappeared.

**What's next for Histox**

The Daily Pivot's shared crowd backend. The crowd split is currently a
labelled local placeholder, and the app says "too few votes" rather than
inventing a percentage.

The five levels where always-Hold scores 100, by adding a deeper pause point
to each where the data supports a sell, rather than reweighting the score to
manufacture difficulty.

Re-importing the equity levels from a redistributable source. Yahoo's terms
forbid redistribution and every bundled level is currently marked licence
unverified, which blocks a store release.

Real-time NSE and BSE through an optional Kotak Neo broker connection, which
is structurally in place but unfinished.

</details>
