<details><summary>Description</summary>

Voyage is a free, open-source iPhone study timer that turns a focus session into a flight. You pick a route, and its real flight time becomes your session. You check your tasks as bags, tear the boarding pass to begin, and study while the plane flies. For Shipaton, Voyage gained an airline loyalty program built on the psychology of habit and goals, and Voyage First, a subscription through RevenueCat that sells comfort, never progress. This entry runs on RevenueCat's Test Store, so no money moved.

**Inspiration**

Starting to study is the hard part, and quitting halfway is the easy part. Airlines have spent decades getting people to come back: status tiers, miles that pile up, a seat up front you can almost reach. I wanted that pull aimed at studying, with the rules pointed the other way. Nobody can buy their way to status, and nothing you need to study is ever behind a paywall.

**What it does**

- A session is a flight. Pick a destination on the globe; the route's real flight time is your focus time. Leave the app for more than 30 seconds and the flight diverts.

- An if-then plan. Scheduling a departure writes one line, when and where you'll board ("When it's 7:00 PM at the library, I'll board…"). The pass and the boarding call read it back.

- One bag tag per task. Each thing you plan to do prints as its own tag with a three-letter code. Peel the claim check to check them, tear the pass to board.

- Baggage claim. After landing, you tear the stub on each bag you finished. Unclaimed bags are "mishandled": they come back first on your next flight.

- Customs. "Anything to declare?" asks three quick recall questions, no notes. One tap skips it.

- Voyage Miles. Every flight earns miles toward Silver, Gold and Platinum. You start with a 500-mile welcome bonus (every threshold was raised by the same 500, so nobody's real effort changes). The miles still needed show up as a real trip, such as "SFO–SEA 7 times". A tier-up carries your surplus miles into the next bar. Your status lives in the Logbook, so Home stays just the globe.

- Status unlocks perks, free. Silver opens the First Class cabin, Gold unlocks priority bag tags, Platinum unlocks the airline liveries. Fly enough and you get everything without paying.

- The Flight Manual. An in-app page with the research behind each mechanic, cited and linked, plus how Voyage First is sold.

**The psychology (cited in the app)**

Mechanic
Finding

If-then plan, one tag per task
Implementation intentions had a medium-to-large effect (d = .65) across 94 tests. Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology

500-mile welcome bonus
A loyalty card with two stamps already on it gets finished more often than a shorter blank one. Nunes & Drèze, 2006, Journal of Consumer Research

Miles to Silver as a real route; surplus carried over after a tier
People speed up as the goal gets closer, and slow down right after a reward. Kivetz, Urminsky & Zheng, 2006, Journal of Marketing Research

Customs recall
Recalling without notes beat rereading when students were tested two days and a week later. Roediger & Karpicke, 2006, Psychological Science

Tearing the pass
A ritual before a hard task lowered anxiety and improved performance. Brooks et al., 2016, OBHDP

Picking the route length
Self-set deadlines helped students. Ariely & Wertenbroch, 2002, Psychological Science

What we won't do
Paying people for something they already enjoy can make them enjoy it less, so miles are a record, not a wage. Deci, Koestner & Ryan, 1999, Psychological Bulletin

**How Voyage uses RevenueCat**

Status is earned; comfort is for sale. Voyage First is one entitlement, voyage_first, sold as two products in the default offering: voyage_first_annual ($19.99/year with a 7-day free trial, preselected) and voyage_first_monthly ($2.99/month). The prices sit deliberately below RevenueCat's own Education and Productivity medians, because the buyers are students. It opens early what status earns for free: the First Class cabin (free at Silver), priority tags (free at Gold) and the six fictional carriers' livery tags (free at Platinum). It never buys miles, tiers, routes or anything you need to study, and nothing in the app is only for sale.

- The paywall appears at the moment of want, next to the free path. The front cabin opens at Silver. Tap a First seat before you've earned it and an upgrade sheet offers both ways there: Earn it, with your real miles to go and a real route, or Fly Voyage First. Only the second opens the paywall.

- RevenueCat's own paywall, designed in RevenueCat's paywall editor and shown with RevenueCatUI's PaywallView, so the pitch changes with a dashboard publish, not an App Store release. It says, in its own footer, "Studying stays free. Status can't be bought."

- Never mid-flight. FirstClassPaywallGate allows the paywall at home, at booking and after landing, and never during a flight, a layover or a diversion (unit-tested). Mid-flight is the moment Voyage exists to protect.

- State, not a boolean. Membership is unknown, economy or firstClass, driven by customerInfoStream. A failed refresh never demotes a member, and unknown never locks anything the free app already does.

- Customer Center for managing or cancelling, right in Settings, and a real trial reminder: when a trial starts, Voyage schedules a notification two days before it ends.

- Open-source safe. With no key the SDK stays unconfigured and the membership UI hides, so anyone can clone and run Voyage. Debug carries the public Test Store key; a pre-build script refuses any Release build with a test_ key.

- Proven on CI. A UI test on a CI simulator taps a locked First seat, opens the paywall, completes a Test Store purchase, watches the seat unlock and checks that Settings reads "Voyage First · Active". That run is the footage in the video.

**What building on RevenueCat taught us (feedback)**

- The setup wizard derives the entitlement identifier and never shows it. Typing the display name "Voyage First" silently created the identifier voyage_first. Our code checked first, so a paid customer would have stayed locked out, and nothing would have crashed to tell us. Fix: show the identifier inline in the wizard, editable, labelled "your code checks this string".

- Suggested prices ignore the category you just picked. We chose Education and were offered $79.99/year and $9.99/month. RevenueCat's own report puts Education's yearly price at $44.99. Fix: seed suggestions from the chosen category's medians.

- Test Store prices can't be edited once created. Rico, the dashboard AI, correctly refused to change a price in place. We had to create new products and repoint the offering, which left two orphaned "legacy" products on the entitlement. Fix: allow price edits on Test Store products, which never reach a real store.

- A fresh AI-generated paywall is attached to no offering. It reads "No offering" until you find that dropdown, and the app shows nothing. Fix: attach to the only offering by default, or flag it in the issues badge.

- RevenueCatUI's convenience modifier traps when the SDK was never configured. Open-source and CI builds are exactly the builds with no key. Fix: no-op and log when Purchases.isConfigured is false.

- customerInfoStream can't say "I don't know yet". Offline with no cache, it yields nothing. Fix: publish an explicit "no answer yet" state.

- Keep: Rico's per-write approvals before touching products; the test_ key prefix, which made "never ship a Test Store key" a one-line build check; and a free tier up to $2,500 in monthly tracked revenue, which works as a startup program for students.

**How I built it**

SwiftUI on iOS 17+, with one third-party dependency (RevenueCat and RevenueCatUI 5.91.0, pinned exactly), a MIT licence, and an XcodeGen project. Membership follows RevenueCat's own SwiftUI samples in purchases-ios (SampleCat, MagicWeatherSwiftUI). The loyalty rules, the perk ladder, the paywall gate and the membership states are unit-tested. GitHub Actions builds on a macOS runner, runs the tests and records the demo videos on a simulator against RevenueCat's Test Store.

**Challenges**

- Selling something without selling out the study. The rule that shaped every choice: a paid perk may be comfort, never progress. It's why First seats open free at Silver and the upgrade sheet puts the free path first.

- The identifier mismatch above, caught before it could lock out a paying user.

- A broken Xcode in the last stretch, so every build, test and recording ran on CI.

**What's next**

Shipping Voyage First in the App Store build (the live App Store version stays free, and its listing is unchanged until the subscription ships), a Web Purchase Link for students who study on a laptop, and a co-pilot mode for studying with a friend.

**About the video**

All app footage is the real app on an iOS simulator, recorded on GitHub Actions by UI tests (ShipatonDemoUITests, ShipatonFlightUITests). The flight is a shortened demo leg (-VoyageDemoFlight). The purchase is a real RevenueCat Test Store transaction that makes the voyage_first entitlement active; no money moved. The dashboard shots are the Voyage RevenueCat project. Narration is Kokoro text-to-speech. The video was edited as code with HyperFrames. The music and sound effects are original, synthesized for this video.

**Since the deadline (added Oct 2, 2026)**

Everything in this section was built after Shipaton submissions closed on Sept 30, and it is not part of the judged entry. It ships in Voyage 1.7, which is scheduled to reach the App Store on Oct 13, after judging ends.

- Airplane Mode. Pick the apps that distract you, and Voyage blocks them from takeoff until you land, through Apple's Screen Time (Family Controls). Wi-Fi and the map keep working. The design follows the open-source Foqos app.

- Open skies. A 25-minute flight with no destination. Tap to fly it yourself; let go and the autopilot lands you at a real airport nearby.

- Customs by voice. After landing, three questions are asked out loud from your bags and calendar, on the iPhone.

- Chase camera, widgets and a Live Activity, plus a cleaner seat panel and Settings.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Coordinating bridal-party outfits is fragmented across group chats, reference photos and separate shopping decisions. Brides struggle to communicate a consistent color direction, and "sage" or "emerald" can mean very different shades from one store to the next. Bridesmaids often want the freedom to choose a dress they love, but they cannot easily tell whether it fits the bride's palette, how it will look on them, or how it will sit alongside the rest of the party before committing. The result is guesswork, returns and a lot of back-and-forth.

**What it does**

Vows & Vibe brings that process into one Android app. The bride defines the wedding style and color palette, invites each bridesmaid, and reviews everyone together in a shared lineup.

Bridesmaids are free to explore dresses beyond the bride's exact picks. For any dress, the app identifies its color family, suggests related shades that stay within the palette, and uses the CIEDE2000 color-difference formula, which measures color distance the way the human eye perceives it, to show how close the dress is to the bride's chosen colors. Each participant can virtually try on dresses, confirm a look and exchange private suggestions with the bride.

The result is a bridal party that looks coordinated without everyone wearing the same dress, with fewer uncertain purchases and less back-and-forth.

**Inspiration**

Practicing spontaneous argumentation and public speaking is notoriously difficult to do alone. Most people freeze up when asked to defend an unfamiliar position without warning, yet traditional debate clubs and speaking coaches require extensive scheduling and rarely provide rapid, bite-sized practice. Without structured repetition and immediate pacing feedback, debaters and students struggle to build fluency under pressure.

Argueo was created to turn impromptu public speaking into a fast, gamified daily habit that fits into a busy student schedule.

**What it does**

Argueo is a tactile, gamified mobile application designed to train spontaneous argumentation, impromptu public speaking, and critical reasoning under realistic time constraints:

- Random Topic & Stance Assignment: Assigns curated debate resolutions across four core categories (Technology, Ethics, School & Education, Current Events) with an enforced random FOR or AGAINST stance to build intellectual flexibility.

- Structured Three-Phase Sprints:

- Prep Phase: 30 seconds to formulate primary arguments and counter-points.

- Sprint Phase: 60 seconds of focused impromptu delivery with visual pacing and countdown feedback.

- Review Phase: Summary of time spent, arguments delivered, and XP reward attribution.

- Streak & Habit Tracking: Tracks daily practice streaks, goal progress, and XP milestones to reinforce daily speaking consistency.

- Custom Topic Creation (Pro): Allows users to input and save custom debate resolutions directly to local storage, instantly starting a sprint with an assigned stance.

- In-App Purchase & Pro Entitlements: Powered by RevenueCat to offer unlimited daily sprints, infinite lives, custom topic creation, and unlimited vault storage.

**RevenueCat Integration & Hackathon Judge Access**

Argueo integrates the official purchases_flutter SDK for subscription management and paywall entitlement enforcement:

- SDK Configuration: RevenueCatService initializes the Purchases SDK, registers sandbox offerings, and syncs entitlement status with local app state.

- Paywall Screen: Displays active package offerings, pricing information, feature breakdowns, and handles native purchase and restoration flows.

- Unified Access Control (ProAccess): All gated features (custom topic creation, unlimited lives, vault saves) evaluate Pro status via a single source of truth that checks both RevenueCat customer entitlements and local promo unlock status.

- Judge Access Code ("JUDGE2026"): In accordance with the Shipaton rules, hackathon judges can redeem the access code JUDGE2026 on the Paywall screen. Entering this code unlocks all Pro capabilities immediately without requiring payment, persists across full application restarts via shared_preferences, and updates all gated interfaces in real time.

**How we built it**

- Framework & Language: Built using Flutter and Dart for smooth cross-platform performance.

- Monetization: Integrated purchases_flutter (RevenueCat SDK) for paywalls and entitlement checking.

- Design & UI: Built with a tactile 3D-extruded dark obsidian theme (#121214 surface with #FF8C00 amber accents) using google_fonts (Nunito text theme).

- Persistence: Local state, streak counters, daily goals, custom topics, and promo code redemptions are saved via shared_preferences.

**Challenges we faced**

Integrating RevenueCat entitlement flows while maintaining a seamless offline/online user experience presented unique architecture challenges. Ensuring that gated Pro features (like custom topics and vault storage) instantly unlocked without requiring full app restarts required creating a unified ProAccessService single source-of-truth class. Additionally, engineering a responsive 3-phase countdown timer that smoothly transitions visual states during the prep, sprint, and review phases took careful Dart state management.

**What we learned**

I learned how to integrate production-grade monetization SDKs with Flutter using RevenueCat, structure modular Dart state managers, design high-contrast tactile UI tokens, and leverage AI agent tools during development to maintain high code quality (0 errors, 0 warnings across analysis).

**What's next for Argueo**

- Adding real-time AI audio transcription and speech-to-text analysis during the 60-second sprint.

- Launching peer-to-peer audio debate duels and community leaderboard rankings.

- Expanding curated prompt databanks to include competitive high school and college debate league topics.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**💡 Inspiration: The Trust Crisis in Tech Hiring**

Every hiring season, millions of aspiring software engineers and students face a brutal paradox:

- The Generative AI Slop Dilemma: Candidates copy-paste job descriptions into ChatGPT, synthesizing resumes inundated with generic, unverifiable claims ("Architected distributed, fault-tolerant microservices with high scalability"). Recruiters, having developed automated cynicism, spend less than 6 seconds per resume and discount ungrounded text at scale.

- The Absence-of-Evidence Problem: Early-career builders, student hackers, and open-source contributors do not have an absence of work — they have an absence of verifiable evidence. Hundreds of intricate Git commits, university capstones, architectural trade-offs, and late-night pull requests sit scattered across GitHub branches. When applying, they either generate artificial AI buzzwords or severely undersell what they actually built.

"Your resume should describe what you can prove. Evident remembers what you have done. Apply knows when it matters."

Brand Thesis: Don't Claim It. Prove It.

We created Evident to eradicate AI resume hallucination by establishing an unbroken, verifiable chain of custody between raw Git commits and professional career claims.

**⚡ What It Does**

Evident is a Code-Grounded Career Intelligence Engine that continuously analyzes connected Git repositories, constructs a dynamic Interactive Evidence Graph, and grounds every professional claim in concrete commit history and source code syntax trees.

**🌟 Core Capabilities & The 4-Stage Loop**

- 1. Living Evidence & Interactive Force Graph: Rather than static text lists, candidate capabilities are rendered as an interactive, relational force-directed canvas. Skills, projects, and commits exist as interconnected nodes with live physics, visual telemetry, and instant node inspection.

- 2. Transparent Opportunity Matching: Ingests any real-world job posting and outputs an objective Evidence Coverage Matrix (such as 5 Direct, 2 Supported, 1 Gap) rather than an arbitrary, opaque match percentage. Critical skill gaps are surfaced honestly alongside remediation roadmaps.

- 3. Application Studio & The 1-Tap Provenance Inspector (The Hero): Synthesizes grounded resume bullets linked directly to retrieved evidence. Tapping [Why this claim?] slides up an instant mobile provenance drawer revealing:

- Target repository (RIFT, KALMAN, SYNTRA)

- Relative source file path (src/auth/tokenRotation.ts)

- Matching Git Commit SHA (b81c44a)

- Syntax-highlighted code extract proving first-party authorship

- 4. Architectural Defense Arena: Moving beyond static resumes, Evident prepares candidates for real technical interview grillings by generating questions derived directly from their own code ("Why did you choose database-backed token rotation in tokenRotation.ts instead of stateless JWTs?"), scoring their trade-off defense across technical rigor and failure-mode preparedness.

- 5. Cryptographic ProofPack Export: Packages verified evidence and commit proofs into an immutable, portable dossier with SHA-256 integrity checksums for technical recruiters and hiring committees.

**📐 The 5-Dimensional Evidence Model**

Rather than collapsing candidate competency into a subjective number, Evident models technical evidence across five orthogonal dimensions:

Evidence Vector = { Status, Artifact, Authorship, Confidence, Freshness }

- 1. Evidence Status: Direct Source (first-party algorithmic logic and API routes), Supported (build configs and manifests), Partial (adjacent conceptual paradigms), Evidence Gap (zero signal detected), and User-Declared.

- 2. Source Artifact: Exact pointer to Git commit hash, syntax AST node, and relative file path.

- 3. Authorship Attribution: Filters out cloned boilerplate; weights signals by author contribution diffs (1.0 for primary author, 0.6 for collaborator).

- 4. Confidence Tier: Deterministic heuristic calculated from code line density, test coverage, and implementation depth.

- 5. Temporal Freshness: Exponential decay modeling recency based on time elapsed since the last verified commit.

**Objective Coverage Metric Formula**

Coverage Score = [ (Weighted Signal Strength Sum) / (Total Requirement Weights) ] × Must-Have Penalty Multiplier

Where requirements carry weighted priorities (2.0 for must-have, 1.0 for preferred), evidence strength scales objectively from 1.0 (Direct Source) to 0.0 (Gap), and missing critical requirements automatically apply a 35% gap penalty to prevent artificial inflation.

**🛠️ How We Built It**

Evident is engineered to the highest production standards, adhering strictly to Clean Architecture (Robert C. Martin) and A Philosophy of Software Design (John Ousterhout):

**System Architecture Pipeline**

- Ingestion & Normalization: The GitHub ingestion service indexes Git trees, extracts commit logs, and parses AST signals into normalized evidence fixtures.

- Core Domain Layer (Pure TypeScript): Framework-agnostic domain modules including proofGraph (relational node linking), matchingEngine (deterministic scoring), and claimAuditor (anti-hallucination verification).

- Deep RevenueCat Integration (react-native-purchases): Native commerce engine powered by PurchaseService and our subscription state store:

- Living Career Memory Entitlement (evident_pro): Monetizes continuous background repository sync, unlimited Architectural Defense interview rounds, and cryptographic ProofPack exports.

- Tier Packaging: Annual Career Pass ($49.99/year, Save 48% with trial) for continuous yearly monitoring, and Monthly Career Sprint ($7.99/month) for active recruitment windows.

- Zero-Friction Judge Sandbox Controller: Seamlessly switches between live RevenueCat SDK configuration and a local Test Store state machine, allowing judges to test purchases and restores with 1 tap and zero credential friction.

- Presentation & Experience: Built with React Native and Expo (SDK 54) using TypeScript. Features an autonomous Ambient Aurora shader background, Apple-style frosted glass cards, and Alan Cooper's rich floating undo toasts in place of jarring modal popups.

**🚧 Challenges We Ran Into**

- The Anti-Hallucination Barrier: Generative AI models naturally tend to invent credentials to please the user. We engineered a strict, multi-pass Claim Auditor. Any synthesized bullet asserting skills absent from the proof graph (e.g., claiming Kubernetes or AWS without commit provenance) is rejected and flagged as an unverified gap.

- Mobile Relational Graph Physics: Rendering interconnected multi-repo dependency graphs on mobile devices without frame drops required designing a lightweight, flattened layout engine with spatial memoization and decoupled touch responders.

- Frictionless Commerce Evaluation for Judges: Mobile hackathons often suffer when judges cannot test paywalls due to missing StoreKit sandbox credentials. We resolved this by building a resilient Test Store fallback state machine in PurchaseService that provides instant entitlement toggling across both physical devices and web simulators.

**🏆 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of**

- 29/29 Automated Unit Tests Passing (100% Deterministic Coverage): Comprehensive Jest test harness validating all critical system invariants across 7 suites (proof graph, matching engine, claim auditor, interview defense service, purchase service, proof pack service, and tutorial onboarding).

- The 1-Tap Provenance Inspector: Achieving an effortless, tactile mobile interaction where tapping a resume bullet point instantly slides up the exact Git commit SHA and syntax extract.

- Deep RevenueCat Value Alignment: Designing a monetization model where Pro genuinely provides ongoing utility (continuous repository sync and living career memory) rather than artificially gating basic features.

**📚 What We Learned**

- Provenance is the Antidote to Cynicism: When AI generation is constrained to cite specific Git commit hashes and AST syntax nodes, applicant materials transform from dubious claims into verifiable engineering portfolios.

- Deep Sponsor Architecture: Integrating RevenueCat through clean domain ports and reactive listeners makes mobile subscription engineering resilient, testable, and maintainable across development, testing, and production environments.

**🚀 What's Next for Evident — Code-Grounded Career Intelligence**

- Automated GitHub App & Webhook Ingestion: Deploying an official GitHub App that automatically detects merged pull requests on main and continuously updates candidate evidence profiles in the background.

- Public Recruiter Verification Gateways: Hosted, cryptographically signed web portfolios allowing engineering managers to inspect code provenance directly from a shared link without needing to clone repositories.

- Multi-Platform Desktop Suite: Expanding Evident to native macOS and Linux environments for integrated IDE workflow support.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

ReavenueCat project app6d52ac5626

**Inspiration**

WisdomBound started with a simple idea: what if learning was a real game, rather than an educational app with a few game elements added on top?

Many educational games are built around learning first, with gamification used mainly as a reward system. I wanted to approach it from the opposite direction. WisdomBound is designed as an RPG first, where learning is the actual gameplay mechanic.

The player enters a fantasy world where knowledge is power. Instead of simply fighting enemies with traditional attacks, players answer questions to influence battles, earn rewards, unlock equipment, summon companions, and build their own team.

I also wanted learning to be personal. People are naturally more motivated to learn about subjects they actually care about, so WisdomBound allows players to generate quizzes around topics that interest them using AI. Players can also learn from books available in the game or upload their own materials, translate individual words, save them, and later turn them into quizzes.

The goal is to make learning feel less like completing an assignment and more like progressing in a game.

**How it works**

The core gameplay loop combines learning and RPG progression.

Players enter battles where quizzes determine their actions and outcomes. Correct answers help them progress and earn different in-game currencies and rewards.

Players can create quizzes in multiple ways. They can choose topics they are interested in and use an AI-powered generator to create questions. They can also learn from books and other materials, including their own uploaded content. Individual words can be translated and saved for later practice through quizzes.

Progression is handled through achievements, statistics, equipment, currencies, chests, and companions. Equipment can be equipped directly on the character and is visually reflected on the character. Players can also summon companions using tickets and combine them into teams with different strengths.

The game also includes a shop, reward chests, rewarded advertisements, in-app purchases, and subscriptions.

**How I built it**

WisdomBound is built with Kotlin Multiplatform, with the goal of sharing as much code and game logic as possible between Android and iOS.

The application uses modern Kotlin technologies and a modular architecture. The UI is built with Jetpack Compose, while the project uses technologies such as MVVM, coroutines, dependency injection, local storage, and cloud services.

Firebase is used for authentication and cloud functionality, while other backend and data services are used where appropriate. RevenueCat is integrated for handling in-app purchases and subscriptions.

One of the most interesting technical challenges was designing the game logic so that important gameplay state could be validated rather than simply trusting the client. This became especially important for an RPG with currencies, rewards, battles, and progression.

I also had to balance shared Kotlin Multiplatform code with platform-specific functionality, particularly when building features that behave differently between Android and iOS.

**Challenges**

One of the biggest challenges was that I was not building a simple educational application. WisdomBound combines an RPG, quiz system, learning tools, AI-generated content, progression systems, inventory, companions, monetization, and cross-platform support.

Keeping all of these systems connected while maintaining a consistent player experience required a lot of iteration.

Another challenge was designing the learning mechanics so that they actually felt like gameplay. I didn't want quizzes to feel like separate tests that interrupt the game. They needed to be part of the core progression loop.

Building for both Android and iOS with Kotlin Multiplatform also introduced challenges around shared architecture, platform-specific APIs, testing, and deployment.

Finally, integrating real-world features such as subscriptions, in-app purchases, rewarded ads, authentication, cloud data, and account management added another layer of complexity beyond the game itself.

**What I learned**

Building WisdomBound taught me a lot about developing a complete product rather than just implementing individual features.

I learned how different systems interact in a real application: game state, networking, persistence, authentication, monetization, UI, animations, and platform-specific functionality all have to work together.

I also gained much more practical experience with Kotlin Multiplatform and learned how to decide what should be shared between platforms and what should remain platform-specific.

Most importantly, I learned that designing a game around learning requires thinking about motivation differently. The challenge isn't only to make learning possible — it is to make the player want to keep learning because it helps them progress.

WisdomBound is my attempt to turn that idea into a complete playable experience: a game where the knowledge you gain outside the game can become the power you use inside it.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

As a 13-year-old student, I spend a lot of time learning from notes, diagrams, equations, and explanations, and I kept noticing how much harder some ideas are to understand when everything is static.

A pendulum is easier to understand when you can actually see it swing. A graph makes more sense when you can move a variable and watch it change. And when you make a mistake in a solution, seeing exactly where your reasoning went wrong can be much more useful than just being shown the final answer.

Most AI tools also pull you away from your notes into a chat box, so I wanted to try the opposite idea:

What if the page itself could think, move, and react?

That became InkMind.

**What it does**

InkMind is a local-first handwritten notebook where you can animate your original ink, change simulations with handwritten modifiers, debug your reasoning, turn equations into interactive visuals, explain selected notes, and generate quizzes directly on the page.

**How I built it**

I built InkMind with Flutter and Dart. Handwriting is stored as editable vector strokes with timing data, which powers Animate Ink and InkDebug. Interactive visuals are generated through InkScript, a constrained language that is parsed, validated, and rendered by InkMind's deterministic runtime. RevenueCat manages InkMind Pro subscriptions and entitlements.

**Challenges I ran into**

The hardest parts were making animations preserve the user's exact original strokes, keeping local AI fast enough on limited hardware, and deciding what should be handled by AI versus deterministic code. I also had to make generated visuals safe and reliable instead of simply running arbitrary model-generated code.

**Accomplishments that I’m proud of**

I’m especially proud of Animate Ink, InkMatter, and InkDebug. A hand-drawn pendulum can actually swing, writing "Moon" can change its gravity, and InkDebug can rewind handwritten work to the point where the reasoning went wrong.

**What I learned**

I learned a lot about Flutter rendering, vector graphics, physics, local AI inference, model routing, structured generation, and RevenueCat. The biggest lesson was that a smaller AI model can become much more useful when it is supported by strong deterministic tools.

**What's next for InkMind**

Next, I want to expand InkDebug beyond basic math, add more Animate Ink behaviors and simulations, improve local-model performance, and make InkMind an even more capable tablet-first notebook where handwriting becomes interactive computation.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/440/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/440/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/441/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/441/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/477/207/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/477/207/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/477/206/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/477/206/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**The Problem**

We all think out loud.

A single voice note can contain a bug to fix, a UI idea, a reminder for tomorrow, a decision made with a teammate, and a message that needs to be sent to a team channel.

But after speaking, someone still has to manually turn those thoughts into GitHub issues, tasks, notes, and messages.

VoiceFlow AI removes that friction.

Instead of forcing users to organize their speech before they speak, VoiceFlow AI lets them talk naturally and turns the conversation into structured actions.

**The Inspiration**

The idea came from a simple question:

What if a voice interface could understand not just what I said, but what I actually need to do with each part of it?

For example, a user can say:

"The result page has a bug. I also think the dashboard needs a better dark theme. Remind me tomorrow at 10 AM to check the API key. We decided that the onboarding flow should require email verification."

VoiceFlow AI understands that this is not one task. It is multiple independent thoughts with different destinations.

The bug and UI idea can become GitHub issues, the reminder becomes a Todoist task, and the onboarding decision becomes a Notion note.

**How It Works**

VoiceFlow AI follows:

Speak → Transcribe → Segment → Understand → Route → Execute

- Voice Capture
The user speaks naturally through the mobile application.

- Transcription
AssemblyAI converts the voice input into text.

- Semantic Segmentation
The transcript is separated into individual thoughts instead of treating the entire recording as one instruction.

- Intent Classification
Each thought is classified as a bug, idea, reminder, decision/note, explicit Slack request, or something that should be skipped.

- Smart Routing

- GitHub → bugs and ideas

- Todoist → reminders

- Notion → decisions and notes

- Slack → only when the user explicitly asks to send something

- Skip → secrets, credentials, or irrelevant content

- Execution
VoiceFlow AI performs the appropriate action through the connected APIs.

The system also uses confidence-aware handling so ambiguous instructions are not blindly executed.

**Mobile + Monetization**

For Shipaton, we brought VoiceFlow AI into a mobile experience and integrated "RevenueCat" for subscription management.

The free experience lets users try the core voice-to-action workflow, while VoiceFlow Pro provides the premium experience through RevenueCat's entitlement and purchase system.

This makes the project more than a voice demo: it is designed as a product that can actually be shipped and monetized.

**What We Built**

The project combines a mobile interface with an agentic processing pipeline.

The backend handles transcription, semantic segmentation, classification, routing, and execution, while the mobile application provides the user-facing voice experience and subscription layer.

We also made an important architectural decision: external integrations run after voice capture finishes.

That means a GitHub, Todoist, Notion, or Slack failure does not interrupt the user's recording.

**Challenges**

The hardest challenge was understanding the boundaries between thoughts.

Human speech is messy. People change topics, add supporting sentences, correct themselves, and combine multiple requests into one voice recording.

For example:

"Ali will handle the onboarding flow that should require email verification."

The second part should remain attached to the decision instead of becoming a separate action.

We therefore combined semantic AI processing with deterministic routing rules for explicit actions such as Slack requests.

Another challenge was avoiding unwanted automation. An agent that creates tasks or sends messages incorrectly can be more frustrating than an agent that does nothing.

This led us to design explicit rules and confidence handling around high-impact actions.

**What We Learned**

Building an AI agent is not simply about connecting an LLM to APIs.

The difficult part is creating "reliable boundaries around AI decisions".

We learned how important semantic segmentation, deterministic safeguards, confidence thresholds, API failure handling, and delayed execution are when building an agent that can take real-world actions.

We also learned that a good voice interface should adapt to the way people naturally communicate rather than forcing users to speak in commands.

**What's Next**

Our long-term vision is to make VoiceFlow AI a personal action layer between people and their digital workspace.

Instead of remembering which application to open, users could simply speak naturally and let VoiceFlow AI determine where each thought belongs.

One voice. Multiple thoughts. Real actions.

</details>

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/Ap06GWVHIP4/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ap06GWVHIP4)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/270/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/270/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Quasar started from a problem I kept running into as a student: I could understand something perfectly while studying it, then struggle to recall it a few days later. At the same time, AI made getting explanations almost effortless, so the bottleneck no longer felt like access to information, it felt like retention. I became interested in memory techniques like visual associations, memory palaces, sound connections, spaced repetition, and active recall, and I started wondering what would happen if an app could automatically turn difficult material into something your brain actually wants to remember. That idea became Quasar: not another place to consume more information, but a memory layer that helps what you learn stay with you.

**What it does**

Quasar is an AI-powered learning and memory app that transforms difficult material into memorable experiences. Instead of only giving students explanations, it turns information into visual stories, sound-based connections, personalized mnemonics, and active recall exercises.
Some of the current experiences include:

- Visual vocabulary and mnemonic learning

- Korean language learning that connects sound, script, imagery, and meaning

- Cell City, where cellular respiration becomes an episodic visual story

- Teach-Back, where learners explain concepts in their own words

- Why Ladder and Case Lab for deeper understanding and application

- Error Memory, which creates new memory hooks around repeated mistakes
Quasar also uses spaced repetition so concepts come back before they completely fade

**How I built it**

Quasar is built as a cross-platform app using React Native, Expo, React, and TypeScript, with Supabase handling authentication, Postgres, storage, and Edge Functions.
The main stack includes:

- Claude through Anthropic’s API for mnemonic generation, quizzes, feedback, and memory hooks

- FSRS for spaced repetition scheduling

- React Native Reanimated, Moti, and SVG for visual interactions

- RevenueCat for subscriptions

- Playwright for end-to-end testing
The AI does not run directly from the client. Requests go through Supabase Edge Functions so API keys stay protected and responses can be validated before they are shown to the learner. I also designed the AI outputs to be structured instead of relying on unrestricted chatbot responses.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was realizing that something being memorable does not automatically make it useful. A strange image might stick in your head, but if it does not help you reconstruct the original word, concept, or meaning, then it has failed as a mnemonic.
I also had to make sure Quasar did not slowly become another generic AI study app. While building each feature, I kept coming back to one question: does this actually help the learner retain, retrieve, or apply the information later?
Other challenges included making AI outputs reliable, keeping the experience useful without constant AI access, and designing one memory system that can still work across very different subjects.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I am most proud that Quasar grew from a simple mnemonic generator into a much broader learning system. It now combines memory creation, retrieval, understanding, application, and spaced review instead of focusing on just one part of studying.
A few milestones I am especially proud of are:

- Building a working cross-platform product for web, iOS, and Android

- Creating Cell City and other visual learning experiences

- Building Teach-Back, Error Memory, and deeper reasoning tools

- Creating a secure AI pipeline rather than simply placing a chatbot inside the app
I also like that AI enhances the product rather than being the entire product. The underlying learning experience still matters even without the model.

**What we learned**

The biggest thing I learned is that good learning design is not just about explaining something clearly. The harder question is what happens after the explanation disappears.
A student can understand something but fail to recall it, remember an image but forget the meaning, or repeatedly choose the same wrong answer. Those are different problems, and they need different types of support.
On the technical side, I learned a lot about building AI as a controlled part of a product through structured outputs, validation, authentication, quotas, and fallback behavior.
I also realized that real personalization should go beyond difficulty. The more interesting question is how does this particular person remember best?

**What's next for Quasar**

Next, I want Quasar to make learning much more immersive and personal. For biology, that means interactive 3D models students can explore in their own space with their fingers, instead of only looking at diagrams. I also want users to generate custom memory episodes in different art styles, from cartoon to cinematic, depending on what helps them remember best. A built-in Quasar bot would be available anywhere in the app, even while watching reference videos, to answer questions the moment they come up. At the same time, I want to keep improving the mnemonic engine so the connections between visuals, sounds, meanings, and concepts become much stronger and more personalized.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Most of my projects start from an indie developer mindset focused on building and shipping, but AI Feelings Wheel was different. This one was genuinely close to my heart, and I built it more for the experience than for making money.

I'm really interested in psychology, lifestyle, and productivity, and I've personally wanted a better way to understand and get clarity over my emotions. That's where the idea came from.

I wanted to build something that didn't just ask "How are you feeling?" but actually encouraged me to slow down, explore what I was feeling, and understand it better. I also had a lot of fun adding things like sound effects and Easter eggs because I wanted the app to feel enjoyable, not clinical.

**What it does**

AI Feelings Wheel starts with an interactive feeling wheel where users can explore emotions and progressively select more specific sub-emotions.

After selecting a feeling, users can add more context, such as the intensity of the emotion and what they were experiencing at that moment.

The Awareness feature goes a step further by asking questions designed to make the user have a conversation with themselves. The goal isn't simply to record an emotion, but to help users understand what they're actually feeling and gain more clarity.

The app also uses AI to help users understand their emotions and reflect on them more deeply.

**How we built it**

AI Feelings Wheel is built with Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform, using my open-source KMP Starter Template as the foundation.

The template helped me move extremely fast by already providing things like purchases, onboarding, paywalls, remote configuration, analytics, and other common infrastructure.

The feeling wheel itself is built using Canvas, while the sound effects use platform-specific APIs. I also contributed improvements back to the KMP Starter Template while building this project.

A lot of the infrastructure that would normally take significant time was already available, letting me focus more on the actual product and experience.

**Challenges we ran into**

Honestly, I didn't run into many major development challenges because the KMP Starter Template handled a lot of the usual infrastructure for me.

The biggest unexpected issue was having my AI API key exposed and subsequently stolen. I fixed the issue in the latest build, which is currently under review.

It was a good reminder that even when the product itself is working well, security around AI integrations needs to be considered from the beginning.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I became surprisingly attached to this app while building it. I genuinely love using the final product, which isn't something I can say about every project I've made.

One of my favorite details is an Easter egg in the feeling wheel: if you rotate it extremely fast, the wheel actually breaks and you have to fix it.

I also spent time creating custom sound effects using ElevenLabs. They turned out much better than I expected and completely changed how the app feels.

Those small details weren't necessary for the core functionality, but they made the experience feel much more alive. That's probably what I'm most proud of — I built something that I genuinely enjoy interacting with.

**What we learned**

One of the biggest things I learned is how much sound can change the perception of a UI.

Even a relatively simple interface can feel significantly more polished and premium when the right sound effects and interactions are added.

I also saw firsthand how much a good foundation can accelerate development. Because the KMP Starter Template already had analytics, purchases, and other infrastructure prepared, I didn't have to spend much time reinventing those parts. I could focus on the actual experience instead.

**What's next for AI Feelings Wheel**

For now, I don't have a specific roadmap for the app. I'll continue fixing bugs, improving the existing experience, and listening to how people use it.

If I get an idea that genuinely makes the experience better, I'll build it. For now, I'm happy letting the app evolve naturally rather than adding features just for the sake of having a bigger roadmap.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**LifeAdmin AI**

**Inspiration**

LifeAdmin AI started from a simple problem: life gets scattered very quickly.

Tasks live in one place, reminders somewhere else, important documents get forgotten, expenses are difficult to keep track of, and small responsibilities pile up until they become stressful.

I wanted to build something that acts like a personal control center for everyday life — an app that helps you remember what matters, stay organized, and reduce the mental load of managing everything yourself.

Instead of building another basic to-do list, I wanted LifeAdmin to feel more like a personal assistant that brings organization, reminders, automation, and AI into one experience.

**What it does**

LifeAdmin AI helps users organize and manage everyday responsibilities from one mobile app.

The app brings together features such as:

- Task and responsibility management

- Reminders for important activities

- Phone notifications for upcoming responsibilities

- Expense and personal information organization

- Document management

- AI-assisted features

- Automated assistance for repetitive life-admin tasks

- A central dashboard for seeing what needs attention

- Premium functionality powered by RevenueCat

The goal is simple: instead of remembering everything yourself, LifeAdmin helps keep track of it for you.

**How I built it**

LifeAdmin AI was built as a Flutter mobile application using Dart.

I focused heavily on making the application feel like a real product rather than just a hackathon prototype. The interface was designed around quick access to the information and actions users need most.

The project includes multiple connected screens and workflows for managing different areas of a user's life while keeping the overall experience consistent.

For monetization, I integrated RevenueCat into the application.

RevenueCat manages the premium subscription state and entitlement system, allowing LifeAdmin to distinguish between free and premium users without building an entire subscription backend from scratch.

The application uses a premium entitlement to determine access to premium functionality and includes an in-app paywall experience.

This allowed me to focus more time on the actual product while RevenueCat handled a major part of the subscription infrastructure.

**RevenueCat integration**

RevenueCat is not just included as an SDK dependency — it is part of LifeAdmin's product model.

LifeAdmin follows a freemium approach.

Users can access the core experience for free, while more advanced functionality can be offered through LifeAdmin Premium.

RevenueCat handles the subscription and entitlement layer behind that experience.

Building this taught me how important subscription state management is. A paywall is only one part of monetization — the application also needs to correctly determine whether a user has access, react when their subscription state changes, and provide a smooth experience between free and premium features.

**Challenges I faced**

One of the biggest challenges was turning a large idea into a usable mobile application.

Life administration covers many different areas, so it would have been easy to create an app filled with disconnected features. I had to continuously think about how each feature fits into the same experience.

Another major challenge was implementing and debugging the subscription flow.

Connecting the application, RevenueCat configuration, products, offerings, and entitlements required careful testing. Small configuration differences can affect whether a paywall or premium status works correctly.

I also had to deal with the normal challenges that come with building a real Flutter application: fixing UI issues, managing application state, testing on a physical Android device, handling notifications, improving navigation, and making sure new features did not break existing ones.

The project went through multiple iterations as I improved both the design and functionality.

**What I learned**

Building LifeAdmin taught me much more than simply how to add features to an app.

I learned more about:

- Flutter application architecture

- Dart development

- Mobile UI/UX design

- Subscription-based product design

- RevenueCat entitlements and paywalls

- Premium feature gating

- Android testing and debugging

- Notification-driven user experiences

- Managing application state

- Designing AI features around real user problems

- Building a product under hackathon time constraints

Most importantly, I learned to think about the application as a product instead of only as code.

A feature is only valuable when users understand why they need it and can use it easily.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

I'm proud that LifeAdmin became a working mobile application rather than remaining just an idea or design.

I was able to build and test the application on an actual Android device, integrate RevenueCat, create a premium experience, implement several life-management features, add reminders and notifications, and bring AI-assisted functionality into the product.

Seeing all of those systems work together inside one application was one of the most rewarding parts of the project.

I'm also proud of how much the app evolved during development. Several parts had to be rebuilt, redesigned, debugged, and improved before they felt right.

**What's next for LifeAdmin AI**

LifeAdmin is designed around a much larger vision.

Future versions could provide deeper automation between different areas of a user's life, smarter AI assistance, improved document intelligence, more advanced financial organization, better recurring routines, richer notification controls, and additional premium personalization.

I also want the assistant to become increasingly proactive — not simply waiting for the user to open the app, but helping them recognize what needs attention before they forget about it.

The long-term goal is for LifeAdmin to become a personal operating system for everyday responsibilities.

One place to manage the small things that take up a surprisingly large amount of life.

</details>

**The resume button for your brain**

 Don't save the task. Save your place.

 CueBack is an Android app that detects when you step away from work,

 remembers where you left off, and brings you back with the exact next step.

 Website

**The problem**

It's 9:14 pm, the night before a test. You're on problem 7, you've just worked out that 7b is wrong because you forgot to convert kilometres to metres, and you know exactly what to try next. Then the group chat lights up.

Twenty minutes later you're back in the browser, scrolling up and down the page, trying to remember what you were about to do.

Interruptions rarely make you forget the goal. They make you forget where you were: what you'd already done, what was failing, and what you meant to do next. Research on task resumption calls this resumption lag. To-do apps record what needs doing. CueBack records the working state you need to continue, and gives back only as much of it as the length of the break calls for.

**How it works**

The whole loop below was recorded on a real phone (a Moto g34 on Android 15). The pause and the return were detected by the live app, not staged.

 1. Save your place.
Share the page to CueBack and write the next step in your own words.

 2. You're back.
Open the same app later and CueBack notices, with your next step in the notification.

 3. Welcome back, then Resume.
The card leads with your next step. Resume reopens the exact page you saved.

 4. Back in 21 seconds.
CueBack measures how long it took to get back to real work.

Everything runs on the phone, in a small context engine written in pure Kotlin:

- Pause score. CueBack watches only the apps you pick, and only which one is in front and when the screen locks. Signals add up to a pause score: locking the screen weighs 0.60, switching to an app you didn't pick 0.35, being away for 5 minutes 0.30. At 0.60 the session closes. In practice, a pause counts after 30 seconds locked or 5 minutes in another app.

- Context capsules. A closed session becomes a capsule: the app, what you shared, your notes, and a confidence score. If the confidence is low, CueBack asks one question, "What were you about to do next?", which you can answer from the notification.

- Provenance labels. Every fact on the welcome-back card says where it came from: Detected, Inferred, You said or Unknown. CueBack never presents a guess as a fact.

- Return matching. When you open a watched app again, a matcher scores the open capsules on app, artifacts, keywords and recency, and only interrupts you when it's confident. Returns within 2 minutes reattach silently, so a quick glance at a message doesn't trigger anything.

- Recovery depth. A break under 5 minutes gets a one-line cue. A longer one gets the recovery card. After 2 hours, or when a lot changed, you get a full reconstruction: goal, work done, artifacts and what happened while you were away.

Every threshold lives in one file, EngineConfig.kt. They're engineering defaults, meant to be tuned, not scientific constants. More in docs/CONTEXT_ENGINE.md.

**Not just for studying**

CueBack works in any app you choose to watch, and with anything you can share:

- A lecture video, at the minute you left. Share the video from YouTube and note the minute you stopped at.

- A code review, on the file you were checking. Share the GitHub page and note the line you were about to comment on.

- Research for an essay, on the article you were citing. Save the page and the sentence you were paraphrasing.

- A long application form. Save the page and what's still missing. With Pro, you get one reminder if you leave it waiting.

 Every place you've saved lives in the library, searchable, one tap from Resume.

Also:

- Reopens your exact spot. Links shared to CueBack reopen at the same page or anchor, through a scheme allowlist.

- Respectful notifications. Quiet hours (22:00–07:00 by default), lock-screen privacy (only "Your next action is ready"), and at most one reminder per context.

- Two detection modes. Live detection recognizes returns within seconds using a small foreground service. Without it, WorkManager checks every 15 minutes.

- Cue, the owl. An animated guide that hovers, glances around, leans as you tilt the phone, reacts when tapped and changes pose with what the app is doing. All motion stops when the system's animations are turned off.

- One dark "Ember" look across every screen: smoked-glass panels on a lit, grainy backdrop, set in Inter Tight. See the design system.

**Business model**

CueBack is freemium, with billing through RevenueCat. The full write-up is in docs/BUSINESS_MODEL.md.

Who pays, and why. The cost of an interruption grows with the number of things you're juggling. One problem set in one browser is fully covered by Free, which is enough to feel the product work. People with several open loops across several apps (students with lectures, readings and problem sets; developers with code reviews; researchers with a stack of articles) hit the Free limits, and they're also the ones CueBack saves the most time.

Free and Pro. The limits come from FeatureGate.kt:

- Free watches 1 app and keeps 3 open contexts. When automatic detection needs a fourth, the oldest moves to the library archive instead of blocking anything.

- Pro unlocks unlimited apps and contexts, the full reconstruction, voice capture, the context timeline and smart reminders.

- Export, delete-everything and the welcome-back card are never paywalled.

Plans. The app shows whatever the current RevenueCat offering contains. The Test Store configuration has three:

Plan
Price

Annual (default, with its per-month price shown)
$79.99 / year

Monthly
$9.99 / month

Lifetime
$99.99 once

These are starting prices to test, not market findings.

Value first. The paywall opens once, right after your first successful return, when CueBack has just said "Back in 21 seconds". Its headline is "Keep that continuity across every project." It never blocks the core loop: Continue free is always one tap away, and after that first time the paywall appears only when you reach for a Pro feature or tap See Pro.

 A real RevenueCat Test Store purchase on the phone, ending on "You have CueBack Pro".

How RevenueCat is integrated (billing/):

- Offerings. Plans load live from offerings.current, with store-formatted prices and any free trial. Product IDs are free-form.

- Purchase and restore go through the SDK, with clear messages for cancelled ("Nothing was charged"), pending and failed purchases, and for a restore that finds nothing.

- One source of truth. Pro is unlocked only when the cueback_pro entitlement is active in CustomerInfo. Nothing in the app can set Pro locally. With no key, billing shows an explicit "not configured" state instead of fake plans.

- Privacy. RevenueCat gets a random ID generated on the phone (cb_…), never a name, email or task content.

- Test Store for development, goog_ key for release. Release builds drop a test_ key on purpose, because Test Store keys crash the SDK in non-debuggable builds.

Verified on a real phone: plans load live from the offering, a valid Test Store purchase unlocks cueback_pro and survives restarts, Restore works, failed and cancelled purchases show clear messages, and the purchase controls hide once you have Pro.

What RevenueCat gives us: prices and packages that change from the dashboard without an app release, Experiments for testing prices and a trial, charts and a per-customer entitlement history, and receipt validation without a CueBack backend.

Next: Google Play products and the goog_ key, a price experiment, a free trial on annual, paywall copy variants, and promo access for judges. CueBack isn't on the Play Store yet, so there's no revenue to report; the dashboard holds only Test Store sandbox data from our own testing.

**Keep Them Coming Back Award (OneSignal)**

OneSignal App ID: c9ad4529-e30c-4ff5-a578-73c954a6737b

CueBack exists to get people back to unfinished work, so OneSignal is part of the core product. Full write-up: docs/ONESIGNAL.md.

Integration. OneSignal SDK 5.10 is connected through Firebase Cloud Messaging and logs each install in with a random on-device ID (no account, no email). After every detection pass, CueBack syncs privacy-safe tags: open_contexts, unresolved_with_next, last_pause_at, use_case and pro. These are counts and timestamps only; task titles, notes, links and app names never leave the phone. Tapping a push deep-links into the app: a context_id in Additional Data opens that exact place's welcome-back card, and a launch URL like cueback://library opens the library. Opens and accepted welcome-back cards are reported as OneSignal outcomes (notification_opened, warm_start_accepted).

Deployed campaign. Built in the OneSignal dashboard:

- A segment, "Unfinished work" (unresolved_with_next &gt; 0): people who saved a place and wrote down their next step but haven't finished it.

- A push, "Your place is still saved. You left a next step waiting. Tap to pick up where you stopped.", with launch URL cueback://library.

- A live Journey, "Unfinished work reminder": enter on the segment, wait 1 day, send the push, exit. Users exit early if they open CueBack on their own or finish the work, and can enter only once, so nobody is nagged.

Value to users. The reminder is about the user's own unfinished work, backed by a next step they wrote themselves, not a generic "we miss you". One tap lands them in the library, and one more reopens the exact page they left.

Reliability. If OneSignal fails to start, the app keeps working, and CueBack's local "You're back" notifications don't depend on push.

Results. The app hasn't launched publicly, so results come from our own test phone (Moto g34, Android 15): the campaign message was delivered to 1 device and clicked once (100% click-through), and it opened the library with the saved place and its next step. Next, we'd test the reminder delay (one day vs. the same evening) and add an in-app message for users who return without opening a place.

**Privacy**

CueBack is private by design:

- Only the apps you choose, and only which app is in front and when the screen locks. No screen capture, audio, keystrokes, messages or content from other apps.

- Everything stays on the phone. There is no CueBack server and no CueBack account.

- Cloud AI is off by default. Turn it on and only a short, redacted summary goes to the endpoint you configure. Tokens and keys are stripped first, and your API key is encrypted with the Android Keystore.

- You're in control. Pause collection, export everything as JSON, or delete everything from Settings.

Read the privacy policy and the privacy and security design.

**How to use CueBack from this repo**

CueBack isn't on the Play Store yet. You can build it from the GitHub repository and install it on your own Android phone. No keys are needed.

**1. What you need**

- A computer with JDK 21 and the Android SDK (the easiest way to get both is Android Studio)

- An Android 9 or later phone and a USB cable (an emulator works too, but automatic detection is best tried on a real phone)

- Git

**2. Get the code**

git clone https://github.com/LSUDOKO/CueBack.git
cd CueBack
cp local.properties.example local.properties

Open local.properties and set sdk.dir to your Android SDK path (Android Studio shows it under Settings → Languages & Frameworks → Android SDK). Leave the two keys blank for now. This file is git-ignored and never committed.

**3. Connect your phone**

- On the phone, open Settings → About phone and tap Build number seven times to turn on Developer options.

- Open Developer options and switch on USB debugging.

- Plug the phone in and accept the Allow USB debugging? prompt.

- Check that it's connected:

adb devices # your phone should be listed as "device"

**4. Build and install**

./gradlew installDebug

CueBack appears in your app drawer.

**5. First Run**

 Meet Cue, personalize your experience, and set up CueBack in a few simple steps.

Get started with CueBack in just a few steps:

- Meet Cue — Discover what CueBack can see, what it never records, and how it protects your privacy.

- Choose your primary use case — Select coding, studying, writing, research, design, or general use. This only personalizes the wording of your prompts.

- Enable usage access — Open Android's usage access settings and grant permission to CueBack.

- Select apps to monitor — Choose which apps CueBack should watch, such as Chrome. The free plan supports monitoring one app.

- Enable notifications — Allow notifications so Cue can greet you with a "You're back" message and help you decide what to do next.

- Activate live detection — Enable real-time detection to recognize when you return within seconds. A small persistent notification keeps the detection service visible.

Your setup, your choice. Every step is optional. You can skip the entire onboarding process and still manually save your place whenever you need to.

**6. Try it in two minutes**

The quickest way to see the welcome-back card, in debug builds:

- Open Settings → Developer → Replay demo story.

- CueBack plays a recorded coding session (a JWT refresh bug) through the real engine and opens the welcome-back card. Demo contexts are labelled and can be deleted.

Then try the real loop:

- Open the app you chose to watch (say Chrome) and use it for at least a minute.

- Share the page to CueBack and write your next step, or just carry on.

- Lock the phone for more than 30 seconds, or spend more than 5 minutes in another app.

- Come back to Chrome. You'll get a "You're back in Chrome" notification; tap it for the welcome-back card, then Resume.

**7. Optional: turn on billing and push**

The app runs fully without keys. Billing and push then show a clear "not configured" state. To try them, add to local.properties:

REVENUECAT_API_KEY=test_xxx # RevenueCat Test Store key, debug builds only (goog_xxx for release)
ONESIGNAL_APP_ID=xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx

- RevenueCat: create an entitlement named exactly cueback_pro, attach your products, and mark an offering containing them as Current.

- OneSignal: create an app, then upload a Firebase service-account JSON under Settings → Push & In-App → Google Android (FCM).

Rebuild with ./gradlew installDebug. Step-by-step instructions are in docs/SETUP.md.

**Troubleshooting**

What you see
Why, and what to do

No notifications in the evening
Quiet hours hold them back from 22:00 to 07:00 by default. Turn quiet hours off in CueBack's Settings when testing at night

Nothing happens when you leave
A pause counts only after 30 seconds with the screen locked, or 5 minutes in another app. Without a saved note or link, a session also needs at least a minute in a watched app

Nothing happens when you come back
Returns within 2 minutes reattach silently. Stay away longer, and stay in the app for about 15 seconds so the return counts

Returns are only noticed after a while
Live detection is off, so CueBack checks every 15 minutes. Turn it on in Settings → Detection

Only one of your apps is watched
Free watches one app, the first alphabetically by package name

Settings says "Billing isn't configured in this build"
No REVENUECAT_API_KEY in local.properties. Add one and rebuild

A purchase succeeds but Pro doesn't unlock
The entitlement isn't named cueback_pro. Check the customer page in the RevenueCat dashboard

A release build has no billing
Expected with a test_ key. Release builds need the goog_ key

Handy commands for testing:

adb shell appops set com.cueback.app GET_USAGE_STATS allow # grant usage access
adb shell pm grant com.cueback.app android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS # allow notifications

**Architecture**

A single-module Android app with manual dependency injection (AppContainer). The engine is pure Kotlin with no Android dependencies, so it's fully unit-testable.

app/src/main/java/com/cueback/app/
├── core/engine segmentation, capsule builder, return matcher, recovery depth, config
├── core/model domain models and provenance labels
├── data Room database, DAOs, repositories, DataStore settings
├── detect live detection service, WorkManager fallback, detection coordinator, demo fixture
├── platform usage collector, app catalog, artifact launcher
├── billing RevenueCat wrapper, entitlement state, feature gates
├── notify local notifications, OneSignal, deep links, notification policy
├── ai optional cloud refinement, redactor, Keystore-encrypted key store
└── ui Compose screens and design system

Browse the source: app/src/main/java/com/cueback/app

More detail: context engine · product spec · UX spec · design system

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/459/740/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/459/740/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/459/749/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/459/749/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/462/554/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/462/554/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/462/555/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/462/555/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/462/556/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/462/556/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/462/557/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/462/557/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/462/558/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/462/558/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I published my first mobile app this year, BlueBaħar (https://bluebahar.com/) and it now has about 3,800 active users in Malta. Building it gave me an opportunity to see how a community of passionate people genuinely forms and creates a virtuous cycle of improving the product cause they care about it. 

For my next app I wanted to try that with something lighter, that could still captivate people but could also transcend the borders of a small country like Malta so I built a game. People always argue about what things cost, like a flat in Rome, a luxury watch, or a car: I thought that argument could become a daily game for all ages.

Did you know that I got pictures for the expensive sailboats myself strolling around the Maltese Grand Harbour?

**The Game**

Every day everyone gets the same five items. You don't guess an exact price. You drag a slider to bet on a range, and the narrower the range, the bigger your multiplier. If the price falls outside your range, you get zero points. There's also a quick mode and head-to-head matches against friends.

**How I built it**

CashOrTrash is a React Native app built with Expo, for iOS and Android. The backend is NestJS with Postgres to store user data, a Redis cache and Bull queue to handle background jobs like points expiry and push notifications. 

All game logic runs on the server while the app is just a UI, it shows the round and sends in the user bet and the server decides everything else to avoid cheating.

**Challenges**

Definitely finding good images, resizing them and removing the background was a hellish job. Every item needs a real photo of a real thing with a real price. The photos come from many different sources, in different sizes, formats and shapes. 

I first cropped and polished each image in Figma, then built a pipeline that crops every image to the same 5:4 card, removes the metadata and renames the file to a hash. Before that, the file name itself could give the price away and the user could just inspect the app with a proxy to find out.

**Preventing cheats**

In a price-guessing game, anything that leaks the answer is a cheat.

- The server sets the 10-second timer once, and the app never sends a timestamp. Reloading a round shows you the time you have left, not a fresh 10 seconds

- You can't bet on a round the server hasn't dealt you yet

- The slider itself turned out to leak the answer. In early versions the real price almost always sat about a quarter of the way along, so a narrow bet placed there beat people who actually knew the item. Now the price's position on the slider and the slider's width are both randomised separately.

**What I learned**

**Monetisation**

The app is freemium. Daily games and matches are free and premium unlocks unlimited quick rounds. I learned to implement RevenueCat and implement monetisation in an app. What to monetise is equally important as well as the pricing logic.

**Proper error handling**

Handling app closures mid-game. Phones pause timers when an app goes to the background. If you left during a round and came back, the old countdown would pick up where it stopped. Now the app gets the remaining time from the server whenever it comes back, so if your time ran out while you were away, the round shows as lost.

**Game fairness**

My first scoring system had a big hole. Stretching the range across the whole slider was always a hit and the multiplier stopped dropping after 60% width. A lazy player could beat people making real, narrow guesses.
I fixed it with some math magic. Now the lazy bet can never be the right strategy!

</details>
