<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Everyone has a Downloads folder like mine. Mine is buried under too many PDFs of courses, scanned documents, tickets and bills.

In Morocco it is worse than usual. Bills, bank statements and leases arrive in French, Arabic and English, often mixed inside one page, as scans and WhatsApp forwards named WhatsApp Doc 2023-10-22 at 07.05.19.pdf. Every file manager searches names and nothing files it for you.

I wanted the folder to sort itself, without any of it leaving my phone.

**What it does**

Free, with no ads and no account. A real document scanner with edge detection, perspective correction and OCR, plus fourteen PDF tools: merge, split, extract, rotate, reorder and delete pages, sign, compress, add or remove a password, watermark, page numbers, and PDF to and from images. The page tools open a document as thumbnails you drag, so you never type a page number.

Librarian, the paid tier:

- Sort. Point Dewey at a folder and tap once. It reads every PDF, works out what each one is, creates folders and files them. Anything it is not sure about goes to a review queue instead of being guessed at, and the whole sort can be undone.

- Ask. "When is my Lydec bill due and how much is it?" The answer comes out of the documents themselves, with the files it used shown beside it.

- Bills and notes. Detected bills with vendor, amount and due date, grouped by what is due first, plus notes of your own. Both have home screen widgets.

**How we built it**

- Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, Room, WorkManager. Sorting four hundred files is a WorkManager job, not a screen's, so closing the app does not cancel it.

- On-device embeddings. multilingual-e5-small through ONNX Runtime, with a Kotlin SentencePiece tokenizer checked token for token against HuggingFace on French, Arabic, mixed script and malformed input.

- Sorting is a nearest neighbour lookup, not a cloud call. A category is another point in the same embedding space as the documents, so filing a whole folder sends nothing anywhere.

- Storage Access Framework, not MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE. You grant one folder and Dewey gets that folder, nothing else.

- Gemini through Firebase AI Logic composes answers from retrieved passages only, so no API key lives in the source.

- RevenueCat for the entire purchase path.

**How we used RevenueCat**

Librarian is a single entitlement, dewey_app_pro, sold as monthly and annual packages on the current offering.

- Purchases.configure at app start, with the signed in user's id as appUserID, so a returning subscriber is never briefly anonymous.

- UpdatedCustomerInfoListener plus an initial awaitCustomerInfo, so every screen reacts the moment the entitlement changes.

- A custom paywall driven entirely by the offering. Prices, the per month price, the "Save 44%" badge computed from the two real products, and trial wording all come from awaitOfferings. Nothing is hardcoded.

- awaitPurchase on the main thread, and awaitRestore, which only reports success when the entitlement actually came back.

- An optional account. Firebase email sign in calls awaitLogIn(uid), so a purchase follows the person to a new phone; signing out calls awaitLogOut.

- RevenueCat's Customer Center for restores, cancellations and plan changes inside the app, plus the managementURL link.

- The paywall appears where the value is: on the locked Documents, Notes and assistant screens, which show what they would do before asking for anything.

It runs on RevenueCat's Test Store deliberately. This entry is judged on a repo and a video, so a separate demo build type carries the test key and the release variant carries no purchase key at all.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Arabic that looks right but reads wrong. Text extraction loses content at direction boundaries. Every generated test document is round tripped and gated at 92% token recall, so a corrupted document cannot quietly skew the evaluation.

- A tokenizer that is subtly wrong never crashes. It just produces slightly worse vectors forever, which is why it is tested against the reference implementation rather than eyeballed.

- Confident misfiles cost more than review. The sort threshold sits high on purpose. A looser one pulled an English transcript into "Papers", so it was dropped.

- Android refuses to grant the Download root through SAF since Android 11. We kept SAF anyway and documented the trade rather than asking for the whole disk.

- PDFBox's importPage already appends the page. Wrapping it in addPage put every page in twice. Found on a real device, fixed, and pinned by tests that read the output PDFs back.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- On a live run in the demo, 100 unnamed documents became 11 folders in one tap: 98 filed, 2 held for review rather than guessed at.

- Sorting makes zero network calls.

- 81% recall@1 and 95% recall@3 for search across three languages.

- Over 760 unit tests, including PDFBox round trips on real documents.

- The free half is a complete app on its own: a scanner and fourteen PDF tools, no ads, no account.

**What we learned**

The honest place for a paywall is the part that costs something to build and saves someone an afternoon. The scanner and the PDF tools are a complete free app. What Librarian sells is the reading.

**What's next for Dewey**

App Check on the Firebase config, a Play Store listing with real products on the same RevenueCat offering, and learning categories from the folders people already keep. That last one is already measured: a folder of your own documents describes them about three times more sharply than any description we wrote.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/517/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/517/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/524/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/524/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/530/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/530/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/543/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/543/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/559/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/559/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/560/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/560/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/561/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/463/561/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/464/033/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/464/033/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration :**

I love hardware. I have so many things I want to invent, but components are always my problem. I don't always know exactly what a build needs until I'm halfway through it. Parts are expensive here and can take weeks to arrive, so buying the wrong one really hurts. And I already own a pile of parts I forget about, so I end up planning around things I don't have instead of the things I do.
Tutorials show someone else's build with someone else's parts, and to-do apps treat a build like a flat list. So I built the thing I needed: tell it what you're making and what's on your bench, and it plans the build around those parts and remembers where you left off.

**What it does :**

FORGE is mission control for the things you build: robots, drones, synths, CNC machines, solar rigs, anything with parts and steps.

- You tell it what you're building and the parts you already have. The AI plans the build around those parts: areas (like Frame, Power, Firmware) and real tasks, starting with checking what you don't know yet and ending with a test of the whole build. It never guesses voltages or pin numbers it wasn't told.

- You look over the plan, pick an icon, and every build becomes a folder on your Home shelf with its progress on the front.

- Open a build and the blueprint shows everything at once: what's done, what's stuck, what hasn't started.

- Tick tasks off and watch it climb to 100%. Pin your next step, and NEXT UP on Home tells you exactly where you left off.

- Search across every build, area and task. Dark mode for late nights, light mode for the workbench.

- Free accounts get 3 builds. FORGE Pro (through RevenueCat) unlocks unlimited builds, templates and blueprint sharing. The paywall shows up right when you try to start a 4th build, and buying Pro finishes creating that build, so you don't type it again.

**How we built it :**

FORGE is built with Expo and React Native, with expo-router and Reanimated for the motion. The backend is Supabase: Postgres with Row Level Security on every table, so the database itself only gives you your own builds. Progress is calculated live from your tasks, so it can't drift out of date. The AI planning runs in a Supabase Edge Function that calls Claude, so the API key never lives in the app, with a daily limit per person. Payments and the Pro entitlement run through RevenueCat. I designed every screen myself around a dot-matrix look and one orange accent, and I used Claude as my coding partner the whole way.

**Challenges we ran into :**

The Apple developer account. I forgot my Apple password, recovery locked me out for days, and when I finally paid for the Developer Program it still had to be activated. So there's no App Store listing yet, and I'm entering Next Gen with a public repo instead. My server also gave me problems along the way. And I had built voice input ("say it out loud"), but it needs a proper iPhone build, which needs that same Apple account, so I parked it for this version.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of :**

I found out about the hackathon 11 days ago. In that time I came up with the idea, designed it, and built a working app with AI planning, payments, light and dark mode, and a design I'm really proud of. More than anything, I'm proud of the energy and effort I put into this one. My last project didn't get this from me. I'm really glad this one did.

**What we learned :**

React Native is completely different from React.js. No divs, no CSS files, and some packages only work in a real build and not in Expo Go. I also learned how much of an app's security can live in the database itself, and that a feature isn't done until it works on the actual phone.

**What's next for FORGE :**

A lot.

- Voice input, as soon as my Apple developer account is active.

- The App Store, in about a week.

- FORGE Community: a place to show off your builds, share blueprints and give each other feedback.

- ForgeBot: a guide for first-timers with no hardware experience, teaching the basics as simply as I can make it.

- My own AI model, trained for planning builds.

- And along the way, answering the big question honestly: why use FORGE instead of an Instructables guide or a YouTube video? My answer so far is that those show you someone else's build. FORGE is about yours: your parts, your progress, and your next step.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/468/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/468/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/146/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/146/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/144/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/144/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/147/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/147/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/143/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/143/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/528/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/528/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/145/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/460/145/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

When you help look after someone, the work that slips is never the big stuff.
It is the small moments: did she drink water, did anyone actually check in,
who is visiting on Sunday. One person in a family quietly becomes the
organiser, usually the one who lives closest, and carries all of it in their
head. Collos exists to make that invisible work visible, and shareable.

**What it does**

Collos turns care into a short daily plan. Each person you care for gets a
plan of small moments: a morning check-in, a water break, fresh air, an
evening note. You confirm or skip each one, and the plan remembers it on
device, instantly, across restarts.

The idea the app is built around: skipping is not losing. A skipped moment
offers to move itself to tomorrow, and the next day it comes back wearing a
"Moved here" chip, so nothing you meant to do falls off the plan. Moments can
repeat on their own days (every day, weekdays, weekends), so the plan can be
one person's real week. The free plan keeps one shared note a day per person;
Collos Pro lifts that limit.

**How we built it**

One React Native (0.86) + Expo (SDK 57) + TypeScript codebase running native
on iOS and Android, and exported to web with react-native-web. Care state is
device-local with no account and no server copy; every confirmation survives
a restart. Behaviour is covered by 29 tests (node:test) and CI on every push.

RevenueCat integration. react-native-purchases is initialised per
platform. The paywall renders live packages from the default offering with
real prices and a per-month breakdown, annual preselected. purchasePackage,
getCustomerInfo and restorePurchases are all implemented; the
collos_pro entitlement is checked on launch and after every purchase, and
cancelled and failed purchases are handled separately from success. The
purchase you see in the demo video is real: it completes through RevenueCat's
Test Store, which records the transaction without charging anyone, and the
app labels that store honestly in Settings rather than pretending it is the
App Store. When no store key is configured the app degrades to a clearly
labelled preview mode, so the public demo never dead-ends.

**Challenges we ran into**

Two stand out. First, a blank white page in production: a floating
transitive dependency (@expo/vector-icons pulling expo-font: "*") dragged
in a copy of expo-modules-core without registerWebModule, killing the app
before first render. The fix was pinning exact versions and adding an
overrides entry. Lesson: wildcard peer ranges are load-bearing in a pinned
SDK tree.

Second, the project was upgraded across three SDK majors (51 → 54 → 57) to
match what Expo Go carries. Every breakage landed in the same three places
(file-system APIs moving behind /legacy, absoluteFillObject removed in
RN 0.86, and the expo-font override), and no state-engine code was touched
to make any of it pass.

**What we learned**

That honesty is a feature. Labelling the Test Store as the Test Store, saying
plainly that there is no account and no server copy, and letting the reset
button describe exactly what it deletes all made the product feel more
trustworthy, not less impressive.

**What's next**

A backend so a care circle can genuinely share between phones, scheduled
reminders, and store releases for iOS and Android.

Built by a student for the RevenueCat Shipaton Next Gen Award. The repository
is public and MIT licensed.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Aquí tienes la versión en inglés de la sección "About the project" sin los emojis:

Inspiration
Spending long hours sitting in front of a computer is a reality for millions of desk workers and developers. Over time, this takes a toll on the body, leading to eye strain, muscle stiffness, poor posture, and a noticeable drop in productivity. The inspiration behind ErgoBreak came from a real, personal need: how can we take care of our physical health without disrupting our workflow? We wanted to create a smart, friendly, and automated tool that gently reminds users when it's time to stand up, stretch, rest their eyes, and move.

How we built it
We developed ErgoBreak as a mobile application focused on user experience and daily wellness.

Interface & Core Logic: Built with a clean architecture to ensure smooth notifications, personalized reminders, and tracking of break habits.

Freemium Model & Monetization: Integrated advanced features (ErgoBreak Pro) managed seamlessly through Google Play Billing and RevenueCat, offering a robust free experience with secure and accessible upgrade options.

Compliance & Deployment: Configured the entire infrastructure on the Google Play Console, navigating data security requirements, health and fitness content declarations, and internal testing tracks for a clean, professional release.

Challenges we ran into
The biggest challenge during development wasn't just coding the timers or the UI, but navigating the strict regulations and policies of the Google Play Console for health and wellness apps. From properly structuring privacy policies and app content forms to correctly setting up testing tracks for evaluators, every step required precision to ensure a smooth deployment.

What we learned
This project taught us valuable lessons about the modern mobile development ecosystem:

The importance of digital ergonomics: Designing with user health in mind completely shifts the product perspective.

App store compliance: Deeply understanding Google Play’s compliance requirements (privacy, data safety, and testing management) is crucial for successfully bringing an app to market.

Seamless monetization: We saw firsthand how efficient it is to implement subscription management and billing to scale a health app's business model professionally.

</details>

## 616. Tapline

> The finger-tapping test that decides Parkinson's medication, measured on your iPhone.

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/tapline (gallery page 153) · ❤️ 0 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [Ashraf A](https://devpost.com/ashrafahmed1232)
- **GitHub (Try it out):** https://github.com/AshrafAhmed9/tapline
- **Repo check:** public repo · license: MIT · 13 commits · Swift · RevenueCat found in code ✅
- **Built with:** apple-vision, avfoundation, ios, revenuecat, swift, swift-charts, swiftdata, swiftui, xcodegen

**Video (1:03):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c-vnQ-g9zl8

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/c-vnQ-g9zl8/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c-vnQ-g9zl8)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/461/121/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/461/121/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/461/125/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/461/125/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Parkinson's medication timing is set from the MDS-UPDRS finger-tapping test: tap your thumb and index finger together, as wide and as fast as you can, for ten seconds. It happens once every few months, scored by eye. Five movement disorder specialists scoring the same recorded trials only agree with each other 74% of the time (ICC 0.74 — VisionMD, npj Parkinson's Disease 2025). What matters clinically isn't just how fast someone taps — it's whether the taps get smaller as the trial goes on (amplitude decrement), which a stopwatch or a simple screen-tapping app can't see. A phone camera can.

**What it does**

Tapline runs that exact test on an iPhone, entirely on-device:

- Prop your phone up, tap for ten seconds.

- Apple's Vision framework tracks your thumb and index fingertip, frame by frame.

- Tapline measures tap count, rate, per-tap width, and how much the taps shrink by the end — the same signal a clinician watches for, quantified.

- A quality gate refuses a trial it can't measure reliably (hand out of frame, too much motion) instead of guessing.

- History links results over time, so a patient can show a neurologist what a whole day looks like, not a fifteen-minute visit.

Not a medical device. Tapline doesn't diagnose anything or output a clinical score — it's a log to bring to a neurologist, not a verdict.

**How we built it**

The core is a shared Swift package (TapCore) used by both the iPhone app and a command-line benchmark tool — one analysis path, not a demo path and a separate real path. It uses Apple's new DetectHumanHandPoseRequest Vision API to track joints, a hysteresis-based tap detector with thresholds that adapt to a trailing window (so it keeps tracking taps even as they shrink), and AVAssetWriter/AVAssetReader for real-time recording and frame-accurate offline analysis.

We didn't just build it — we checked it, against HUBU-FIS, a public, CC-BY 4.0 dataset of 234 real, clinician-scored Parkinson's and control finger-tapping videos. On that dataset, evaluated under a protocol declared before the full run:

- In the last third of each trial — where amplitude decrement actually shows up — our adaptive detector caught 8.10 taps on average, versus 2.13 for a detector calibrated once at the start.

- Adding amplitude and decrement to tap rate improved separation of Parkinson's from control from AUC 0.58 to 0.68, and correlation with the clinician's score from Spearman ρ 0.38 to 0.47.

RevenueCat gates the product, not the science: tests are free forever, and Tapline Plus (monthly, annual with a trial, or lifetime) unlocks a one-tap visit report via a contextual paywall — shown when you ask for the report, not as an upfront wall.

**Challenges we ran into**

Running the benchmark against real clinical footage surfaced real bugs a synthetic test never would have: a CSV parser that silently broke on CRLF line endings (Swift treats "\r\n" as a single grapheme cluster), and a case-mismatch bug that flagged every single video as Parkinson's regardless of its actual label. Both are fixed and documented in the commit history, not swept under the rug.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Building a benchmark tool that runs the exact same analysis code as the live app, so a claim proven on 234 real patient videos is a claim about the actual shipping product — not a separate demo path.

**What we learned**

That the hardest bugs to catch are the ones synthetic tests can't see — real-world data surfaces problems (encoding quirks, label mismatches) that clean, constructed test cases never will.

**What's next for Tapline**

Expanding the benchmark to a second public dataset, and exploring a companion Apple Watch app for passive tremor logging between tests.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

As a final year medical student, I understand the need for medical students and resident doctors to receive a high quality education to inform their clinical decision making. Each patient presents a different challenge, both in diagnosis and treatment, and having a solid foundation of knowledge to guide treatment for patients is imperative.

My own experience through medical school has left me searching for a better way to learn physiology. Physiology was taught to me with static diagrams, but it is a set of dynamic systems. Cardiac output is where two curves meet, not a number to memorise. I want medical students to interact with their teaching, and watch how the physiology responds in real time. As a visual learner, this helps me to understand the processes that keep our bodies functioning much better than simply reading from a textbook or website.

Bentara Physiology Lab is a collection of interactive simulators across multiple physiological themes, built for exams including the UKMLA, USMLE Step 1, MRCP Part 1, MRCS Part A and FRCA Primary. Each one runs a real quantitative model: Guyton's venous return and cardiac output curves, Suga-Sagawa ventricular elastance, Hodgkin-Huxley, and acid-base via Henderson-Hasselbalch:

$$\mathrm{pH} = 6.1 + \log_{10}\frac{[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}{0.03\cdot P_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}$$

and Winter's formula for expected respiratory compensation, \(P_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 1.5\,[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}] + 8 \pm 2\).

A product this useful to students also has to be sustainable and financially viable, and that is where RevenueCat came in.

**What it does**

- Predict-then-run practice, and pattern discrimination with the controls hidden.

- A formula reference, a pharmacology hub and an AI tutor.

- Progress in localStorage, or synced to Postgres when signed in.

- Three simulators (cardiovascular, respiratory, glucose regulation) plus the formula reference and medications hub are free; everything else sits behind one entitlement, full_access.

**How I built it**

One subscription, every platform. The web app (Vite, React, TypeScript, Supabase, Vercel) uses @revenuecat/purchases-js for Web Billing. The Expo companion uses react-native-purchases for App Store and Play. Both use the same offering, the same entitlement, and the Supabase user id as the RevenueCat App User ID. A subscriber who buys on the web is unlocked on their phone with no mapping table and no "restore" dance.

A webhook as the single source of truth. A Supabase edge function receives RevenueCat events and is the only writer of profiles.subscription_status; the client has no column grant on it. It:

- authenticates with a shared secret, compared in constant time;

- is idempotent on the event id, via a billing_events table;

- returns 500 on a failed write so RevenueCat retries;

- handles TRANSFER by demoting the old account and promoting the new one.

Status derived from expiry, not event type. A CANCELLATION or BILLING_ISSUE does not end access. Only an expiry in the past, or EXPIRATION, does:

$$\text{status}=\begin{cases}\text{free} & t_{\text{expiry}} \le t_{\text{now}}\ \text{trialing} & t_{\text{expiry}} &gt; t_{\text{now}},\ \text{period}=\text{TRIAL}\ \text{active} & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

This makes the webhook correct even when events arrive out of order.

Live pricing, honest claims. Prices come from the current offering ($rc_monthly, $rc_annual); hard-coded fallbacks only show if RevenueCat is unreachable. The "Save £X a year" line is computed from live prices as \(12m - a\) (monthly £9.99, annual £99, so £20.88), rather than hand-typed. A typed "two months free" claim would have been misleading under UK consumer law.

Testable by design. The webhook logic is plain shared code imported by both the Deno function and a Vitest suite, so the tests exercise the deployed code. The repo has over 3,800 tests.

Institutions. Schools pay by purchase order against a Stripe invoice and get a licence; the entitlement hook resolves access as institution, subscription or none.

**Challenges**

- Webhook ordering and retries. Naively mapping event type to status breaks on cancel-then-renew and out-of-order delivery. Deriving status from the expiry timestamp fixed it.

- Account transfers. Anonymous-to-signed-in and account switches needed TRANSFER handling and changeUser/logIn/logOut care.

- SDK packaging. purchases-js advertises a stylesheet export that does not ship in 1.55, so the build failed until I stopped importing it. I also load the SDK dynamically so it only downloads on the pricing page.

- Native setup races. A double configure from concurrent callers, and an empty platform key that needed to fall through to the Test Store key. One shared in-flight setup promise fixed the first.

- Store and legal compliance. Auto-renew disclosure next to the Subscribe button (App Store 3.1.2, Consumer Contracts Regulations), an always-reachable Restore, in-app account deletion (5.1.1(v)), and a privacy manifest. I also removed sending exam and training stage to RevenueCat as attributes, for data minimisation.

- Expo Go cannot load the native SDK, so testing purchases needs an EAS development build. RevenueCat's Test Store made this practical.

**What I learned**

- Let the server decide entitlement; let the client only ask.

- Use one stable identifier across platforms and most sync problems disappear.

- Derive state from facts (expiry) rather than from event streams.

- Compliance is product work, not an afterthought.

**What's next**

The app will continue to expand, focusing on increasing the scope of the physiology taught, as well as moving into the other core areas of medical education, such as: Microbiology, Radiology, Pathology, Biochemistry, Pharmacology & Anatomy.

Developing the UI further to increase the educational value is a key priority, and seeking collaboration with institutions and medical schools to enhance the capabilities and accuracy of the models is another goal.

Eventually, the goal is to take the app live on the App Store and Play Store, and launching a web app in tandem, so that users can access the software regardless of what type of device they are using.

</details>

src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/462/300/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

This is the second of my two Shipaton apps. The first one, Stick, is about getting off the scroll. This one is about what I want to do with the time I get back.

When I got my first phone I didn't install a single game. I installed Duolingo and started learning English that same day. I'm on a 301-day streak now. The owl taught me something I didn't expect: the lessons weren't what kept me coming back. The path did. A little circle waiting for me every day, small enough to say yes to.

And then I'd want to learn something that wasn't a language, and the path disappeared. Chess openings, how to code a website, a book everyone keeps quoting. What I got instead was forty open tabs, a three-hour YouTube playlist and a plan I'd abandon by Thursday. The content exists. What doesn't exist is the path.

So the question for ilo was simple. What if Duolingo worked for anything?

The first goal I typed into it, before any of it existed, was "salsa for my grandma's wedding". I kept that example the whole way through, because it's the hardest kind of goal to teach. It's physical, it's rhythmic, it has a deadline, and it matters to someone. If an app can turn that into a daily path you can actually follow, it can handle "learn Atomic Habits".

**What it does**

You type a goal. ilo asks you five quick questions: why it matters, when you need it, how much you already know, how you like to learn, and how many minutes you have a day. Then you watch it build your path live.

- Research, then a path. Claude searches the web for your goal, reads the best sources, and designs a Duolingo-style path of units and nodes. Every node gets a brief: what to teach, 2–4 concrete facts, the common mistake to fix, and what you should be able to do afterwards.

- Lessons written when you tap. A lesson doesn't exist until you tap its node. ilo then writes it from the brief, adapted to your level and your last mistakes. The next two lessons are generated in the background while you play, so you never wait.

- 23 kinds of exercises. The AI picks and arranges them per lesson and per topic:

- Learn: story cards, audio lessons with karaoke captions, flashcards.

- Practice: quizzes, swipe true/false, match, reorder, word bricks, fill-the-gap, free answers graded by AI, roleplay chats.

- Real world: photo-proof missions, a live code lab with a preview, a camera coach that counts your reps with Vision, a haptic metronome that taps "1-2-3 · 5-6-7" into your hand for salsa, and live voice calls with ilo.

- Ones I invented: Guess it, Spot the mistake, Sort it, Teach ilo (explain it like ilo is five), Speed round, What would you do?, Find it.

- The game around it. XP and levels, streaks with freezes, daily quests and a friend quest, 15 badges, chests, gems, and eight weekly leagues named after the mascot's shapes, from Pebble to Apex. Real cohorts need the backend. Offline, the league runs on simulated rivals, and the screen says so.

- ilo, the mascot. An animated blob with sixteen expressions that reacts to every answer. It looks at what you type, falls asleep when you haven't played today, and turns into three thinking dots while the AI works. Every player also designs their own blob, which becomes their avatar in the leagues.

Two rules I cared about more than any feature:

- The learning has to leave the screen. A salsa course that only asks multiple-choice questions teaches you to pass a quiz about salsa. So there are missions ("dance the basic step in your kitchen for two minutes, send a photo"), a metronome that counts beats in haptics, and a camera coach that counts your steps.

- You see what you get before you pay. The path is built during onboarding, before the paywall, so the price is for something you've already seen.

**How I built it**

I built ilo in one day, September 30: 29 commits, about 26,000 lines of Swift, from an empty folder at 1:43 am. I don't write Swift by hand. I built it with Claude Code, and my job was the precision of what I asked for and the shape of the system: what the AI is allowed to decide, what the code decides, and what happens when something fails.

Five builders at once. I first wrote the shared foundation myself with Claude: the data models, the design system, the mascot engine, and one contract every lesson module had to follow. Then I ran five agents in parallel, each in its own copy of the repo with its own simulator:

- onboarding and paywall,

- the lesson player and 15 core modules,

- the 8 real-world modules,

- home, path, leagues and profile,

- the AI brain and the backend.

After that I merged everything and spent the rest of the day making it one app.

The model writes, the code checks. Every lesson module is one flat JSON object with a type and the fields that type needs. The model can pick any module it wants, but the app validates every one (options present, answer index in range, every sorting item in a real bucket), drops the ones that can't be played, and shuffles answers so the right one isn't always A. A lesson with a broken quiz loses the quiz. The lesson still plays.

Bring your own Claude. In onboarding you connect your own Anthropic API key (i don't have the money to afford Claude because i'm a student so i decided to go after BYOK method for Shipaton until the app goes live on the App Store):

- The key is stored in the iPhone's Keychain and sent only to api.anthropic.com.

- Planning is two calls: a research call with live web search, then a design call that returns the path as structured output. They're separate because citations and structured outputs can't share a request.

- Lessons, grading and voice conversations run on Claude Opus 5.5, with server-side refusal fallback.

Everything has a plan B. Skip the key, lose the network, or run out of credit, and ilo switches to its offline brain:

- three hand-written flagship courses (salsa, a first website, Atomic Habits) with 18 full lessons,

- a composer that builds a sensible path for any other goal,

- Apple's on-device model when the phone has one.

A 12-second probe and a circuit breaker make sure the on-device model can never hang a lesson.

The mascot is real code. ilo started as an open-source SVG animation. I ported its geometry to Swift: 64-point silhouettes that morph between eight shapes, eyes projected on a virtual sphere with yaw, pitch and roll, and a blink schedule from a seeded random generator.

Feel. Native iOS 26 Liquid Glass on the floating controls; solid, pressable 3D buttons where your thumb lands, like Duolingo. Custom Core Haptics patterns for correct, wrong, streak, level-up, the hold-to-commit charge and every metronome beat. Every sound effect is synthesized in code, so the app ships with zero audio files.

Tests that tap. 22 UI tests drive the real app with real taps:

- the whole onboarding, through the paywall and the purchase;

- a full lesson from the path to the celebration;

- every tab, and one test per core module.

They found ten bugs I would have shipped, including the Create flow landing on a blank screen.

**How it makes money (RevenueCat)**

The product is a learning habit, so the main product is a subscription with a real trial.

- Plans. Annual at $79.99 with a 7-day free trial, shown as about $1.53 a week, computed from the store price in the user's currency. Weekly at $7.99 as the anchor. The paywall shows the trial as a timeline: today, full access; day 5, we remind you; day 7, you're billed, with the actual date.

- Hard paywall at the moment of proof. It comes after you've watched your own path being built and made a promise to yourself, not before. Its headline is your course title: "Your Salsa, wedding-ready path is ready."

- One pro entitlement, one default offering with $rc_annual and $rc_weekly packages, so prices and plans change from the dashboard without an update.

- Live access. customerInfoStream drives access, so renewals, expiries, refunds and restores unlock or lock ilo without a relaunch. Trial eligibility is checked before the paywall promises a free week.

- Anyone can test it. The Test Store in development means anyone who clones the repo can buy in the simulator without an Apple account. When no key is configured, a StoreKit configuration file is the fallback.

- One identity. When the backend is on, the RevenueCat app user ID is the Supabase user ID, so the server can check pro before spending anything.

- Bring-your-own-Claude protects the margin. The expensive part of an AI tutor is tokens, and a heavy learner can cost more than their subscription. With your own key, the subscription pays for the product (the path engine, the 23 modules, the game, the mascot) and the AI is billed at cost by Anthropic. Nobody sits in the middle marking it up.

**Challenges I ran into**

Five agents, one app. Parallel builders are fast until you merge.

- Tapping Continue twice skipped a module.

- Opening a node while it was prefetching generated the same lesson twice, and paid for it twice.

- "Pass a code lab" unlocked when you failed the code lab.

- Two files had the same name and the build refused to start.

None of these were visible in any one agent's work. I fixed them with a QA pass over every flow, then the UI tests.

A machine at load 380. Six simulators booted at once, five compilers and a screen recorder: the Mac's load average hit 387 and the simulators froze mid-screenshot. I shut down every simulator I didn't need and moved all testing to one device.

The mascot I loved wasn't mine. The blob I built ilo around is an MIT-licensed recreation of another company's bot avatar. The license let me use it, but I didn't want my app's face to be a copy. So ilo got its own colour, electric blue, and its own name, and the original author is credited in the repo.

Who pays for the AI. My first backend routed every lesson through my own server and my own API key. That's fine for ten users and a disaster for a thousand. Letting learners bring their own Claude fixed the economics, and the offline brain means nobody is locked out.

Honest offline mode. My first offline brain showed "Reading Wikipedia…" while building a path, and it wasn't reading anything. It now says what it actually does ("Drawing on ilo's expert library, curated, offline"). The live "Claude is researching the web" line appears only when Claude really is.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

My favourite moment in ilo is halfway through the salsa lesson, when the quiz stops and your phone starts tapping "one, two, three… five, six, seven" into your hand. That's where it stops being a quiz app.

- A 15-step onboarding that builds your real path before you pay.

- 23 module types, and lessons that survive a bad AI answer instead of crashing on it.

- An app that works fully offline and gets smarter the moment you connect Claude.

- A mascot engine with 16 expressions that reacts to everything you do.

- 22 UI tests that play the app like a person would.

**What I learned**

- The model picks, the code verifies. The AI can choose any exercise it wants. The app decides whether it's playable.

- Build the contract before the team. Five agents could work at once only because every module had the same small interface. The bugs all lived where two agents' work met.

- The path is the product. Content is everywhere. A small circle that's waiting for you today is not.

- Show before you charge. People can say yes to a price when they're looking at the thing they're paying for.

**What's next for ilo**

- Ship it on the App Store, with the backend on for real leagues and friend quests.

- Shared courses: when a hundred people type "learn chess openings", build the path once and let everyone start instantly.

- Camera coach for more than steps: posture, form, and hand positions for instruments.

- A path you can share with a friend, so you can race each other to the wedding.

</details>

## 619. FashionU

> Stop guessing if it fits. FashionU uses YouCam's Apparel VTO plus AI reasoning to show you outfits on your own photo and explain why they actually work (YouCam,Gemini, Groq, React Native, Expo, App)

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/fashionu-83j5c7 (gallery page 154) · ❤️ 0 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [Jaya Dubey](https://devpost.com/jaya6400)
- **GitHub (Try it out):** https://github.com/jaya6400/fashionU-app
- **Repo check:** public repo · license: MIT · 21 commits · TypeScript · RevenueCat not found in manifests
- **Other links:** https://youtube.com/shorts/MH3qpa8b4Dc?feature=share
- **Built with:** reactnative

**Video (2:56):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH3qpa8b4Dc

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/MH3qpa8b4Dc/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH3qpa8b4Dc)

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Online shopping still runs on a guess. Will this fit, will this actually look right on me, is it worth the risk of a return. Most virtual try on tools stop at showing you a picture. They don't tell you why something works, so the guessing continues even after you've seen the render.

This was also my first mobile app project. My hackathon background was in web based tools using Gemini APIs and Elasticsearch, so building a full React Native and Expo app end to end, integrated with a third party YouCam API, was new ground for me going in.

**What it does**

A shopper self reports their

body shape through a short quiz using proportion based categories, never inferred from a photo and never framed around size or weight.
They

pick an occasion,
upload their own full body image, and
browse a garment catalogue.
Selecting a garment triggers

YouCam's Apparel Virtual Try On (cloth v3), rendering that outfit on their own photo.
Gemini then analyzes the result for concrete fit details, neckline, waist, sleeve, length, cut, and an AI styling model turns those details into specific, positively framed advice for that person's shape, not generic praise.
Every look is saved with its image and its reasoning.

**How we built it**

Frontend: React Native with Expo (SDK 54), Expo Router, TypeScript in strict mode
Try on: YouCam Apparel VTO, the cloth v3 endpoint, called after a garment is selected
AI pipeline: Gemini extracts fit and silhouette details from the try on result, which feed into a styling model (Groq, with a Gemini fallback) that generates the actual advice
Persistence: Supabase, Postgres with pgvector, storing saved looks and their embeddings
No auth: local state and AsyncStorage, kept deliberately simple for the hackathon scope

**Challenges we ran into**

Silent hangs on real devices. Early on, image analysis would intermittently hang with no clear error. It traced back to React Native's fetch().blob() bridge being unreliable for local file:// URIs on device, even though it worked fine in quick tests. The fix was reading local files directly through expo-file-system instead of routing them through fetch.

Generic AI output- The styling advice technically worked, but it read like a template, this flatters your figure, regardless of the actual outfit. The real fix was not a better instruction to the styling model, it was upstream: the vision step was not extracting fit specific detail, neckline, waist, sleeve, cut, in the first place, so the styling model had nothing concrete to reason from. Fixing the vision prompt fixed the advice.

A model got decommissioned mid build. With days left before submission, Groq announced our primary styling model would be decommissioned, with the cutoff landing before our own deadline. I migrated to their recommended replacement model, added retry with backoff for rate limiting while we were in there, and retested before recording the demo.

A security gap before going public. Supabase flagged a table with row level security disabled right as I was preparing to make the repository public. Since the app only ever reads and inserts, I was able to lock it down to anon select and insert only with a migration, closing the gap without changing any app behavior.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

A working end to end pipeline, not a mockup: real photo in, real YouCam try on, real AI reasoning grounded in the actual garment, real persistence. And a product principle we held onto under deadline pressure rather than cutting for time, styling advice that is specific and honest without ever framing a body as something to be judged.

**What we learned**

How much of the AI gives generic answers is actually an upstream data problem rather than a prompt problem, how unreliable some React Native bridges can be for local files on real devices versus a simulator, and more broadly, how to take a hackathon idea through a full mobile app build for the first time, from onboarding flow to a live third party API integration to a public facing repository.

**What's next**

A match_saved_looks similarity search using the pgvector embeddings we're already generating, replacing the placeholder garment catalogue with a larger real one, and exploring how this same pipeline could plug into an actual retail catalogue rather than a hardcoded set of outfits.

</details>

## 620. SkillSwap

> Tired of expensive classes and endless tutorials? SkillSwap connects you with people who teach what you want to learn while learning what you know with AI finding the perfect match.

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/skillswap-gs9moh (gallery page 154) · ❤️ 1 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [Uwayo Pascaline](https://devpost.com/uwayopascaline87)

- **Repo check:** ⚠️ repo not found / private
- **Built with:** cursor, openrouter, revenuecat, swift

**Video (1:51):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5RzWegCoLUo

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/5RzWegCoLUo/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5RzWegCoLUo)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/174/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/174/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

The idea for SkillSwap came from something I personally experienced. I wanted to learn graphic design, so I started looking at online tutorials and using generative AI. It was easy to find information, but I realized that information wasn't the same as having someone who could actually guide me.

AI can explain how to design something, but when you make a mistake, you often need someone to look at your work, correct you, and explain how they would approach a real project. That human experience is difficult to get from a tutorial.

At the same time, I realized that I already had skills that someone else might want to learn. That led to a simple question: "What if people could exchange skills instead of paying for another course?"

That's how SkillSwap started.

**What it does**

SkillSwap connects people who want to learn with people who can teach.

Users create a profile showing what they can teach, what they want to learn, their experience level, availability, and learning preferences. Our AI finds complementary people, explains why they could be a good match, and helps them start a skill exchange.

From there, users can connect, message, schedule sessions, and learn together.

Premium adds AI-powered learning support such as preparation packs, session summaries and transcripts, and quizzes to help users retain what they learn.

**How we built it**

We built the iOS experience using "Swift and SwiftUI", with a web platform for broader access. The backend manages users, skills, matching, sessions, messaging, and learning progress.

We use "OpenRouter" to power our AI features, including complementary skill matching, match explanations, and learning support. "RevenueCat" handles our Premium subscriptions and entitlements.

Our goal was to keep the core skill-exchange experience accessible while using AI to make the learning process more personalized.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was figuring out what makes a good match.

Simply matching two people who want to learn the same thing doesn't solve the problem. We wanted to connect people whose skills complement each other for example, someone who knows Python but wants to learn Figma with someone who knows Figma but wants to learn Python.

We also had to think about how to use AI without making it the center of the experience. SkillSwap is about people learning from people, with AI helping them find each other and learn more effectively.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We're proud that we turned a personal frustration into a product that could help other learners.

We're especially proud of the idea of skill exchange itself. Instead of treating people only as students or teachers, SkillSwap lets everyone be both.

We're also proud of integrating AI and RevenueCat in ways that support the core experience rather than simply adding features for the sake of adding them.

**What we learned**

Building SkillSwap taught us that having access to information isn't always the same as having access to learning.

We learned that technology can help people find knowledge, but human interaction provides something different: feedback, real experience, accountability, and the ability to ask questions in the moment.

We also learned that a good AI feature shouldn't replace the human experience. It should make that experience easier and more useful.

**What's next for SkillSwap**

We want SkillSwap to grow into a larger community where people can exchange skills across technology, design, languages, academics, hobbies, and professional development.

Next, we want to improve our matching system, expand collaborative learning tools, make sessions more interactive, and give users better ways to track their progress over time.

Ultimately, we want SkillSwap to make learning something new feel less like searching for the right course and more like finding the right person.

Learn what you want. Teach what you know. Grow together.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/391/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/391/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/419/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/419/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/420/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/420/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/421/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/421/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/422/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/465/422/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We all have hundreds of videos sitting in our phone galleries that we rarely watch again.

Usually, when we want to watch something, we have to open the gallery, scroll through thumbnails, remember what each video is, and choose one manually. But sometimes you don't actually know what you want to watch — you just want to see something interesting.

That idea inspired me to create Gallery Tok.

I wanted to turn the personal video gallery into something closer to the feeling of scrolling through Reels: open the app, start watching, swipe, and discover something you didn't know you wanted to see.

The most important part of the idea is the unpredictability. When videos are shuffled, you never know what the next video will be. It could be a funny moment, an old memory, or a video you completely forgot about.

**What I Built**

Gallery Tok turns the videos already stored on your phone into a vertical, Reels-style video feed.

Instead of searching for a specific video, you can simply start watching and swipe through your own collection.

The app includes:

- Reels-style vertical video browsing

- Random / Shuffle playback

- Saving videos you want to revisit

- Blocking videos you don't want to see again

- Auto-scroll to the next video

- Folder exclusion

- Browsing videos by date

- Arabic and English support

The goal is not to create another social network.

It's to make your own gallery feel discoverable again.

**How I Built It**

I'm a UI/UX designer, not a traditional software developer.

I designed the product concept, user experience, interface, and interaction patterns first. I then used AI-assisted development to turn those designs and product decisions into a working Android application.

AI was heavily involved in the implementation, debugging, and development process. I continuously tested the application, refined the user experience, and made product and design decisions based on how the app actually felt to use.

The project was built for Android using Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, with libraries such as Media3/ExoPlayer for video playback and Room/DataStore for local application data and preferences.

**What I Learned**

The biggest thing I learned was that building a product is not only about implementing features.

As a designer, I already think a lot about interfaces and user flows, but building Gallery Tok made me think much more deeply about how those decisions behave in a real application.

I learned how to:

- Turn a simple product idea into a working application

- Use AI as a development tool to bridge the gap between design and implementation

- Think about application state, video playback, and user preferences

- Test interactions repeatedly and refine them based on real usage

- Balance simplicity with useful customization

Most importantly, I learned that a strong user experience can start with a very simple idea.

**Challenges**

One of the biggest challenges was making random video playback feel intentional rather than chaotic.

The whole concept depends on surprise, but the experience still needs to feel smooth and predictable from a UX perspective. The transition between videos, playback behavior, saving and blocking content, and the overall navigation all had to work together.

Another challenge was building an Android application without coming from a traditional programming background. AI-assisted development made that possible, but it also meant I had to learn enough about the underlying project and code to understand errors, test different approaches, and make sure the final product behaved the way I intended.

I also had to constantly switch between thinking like a designer and thinking like a product builder.

**Why Gallery Tok?**

Most gallery apps help you find a specific photo or video.

Gallery Tok is designed for the opposite.

You don't know what you want to watch.

You just want to discover something.

Instead of searching through your memories, Gallery Tok lets your memories surprise you.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

For most of high school, I noticed the same pattern. Tests would come back days, sometimes weeks, after we wrote them. I later realized it wasn't because my teachers didn't care. It was because they cared too much to rush it. Many of them wanted to coach the volleyball team, run clubs, or simply go home to their families, but instead they spent their evenings hunched over stacks of paper, marking long after the school day had ended. By the time our feedback finally reached us, the lesson had already moved on. I wanted to build something that gives teachers that time back, so they can be at the game, at the dinner table, and still hand back tests while they still matter.

U mark less. U teach more.

**What it does**

UMarkless is an Android app that marks paper tests from a photo. A teacher snaps a picture of a handwritten test (or uploads a PDF), and within minutes almost every question, including open-ended handwritten responses marked against a rubric, has a score and a short written reason explaining it. If a response is questionable, it gets set aside so the teacher can review its marking comments. That reason matters to me more than the score itself, because it means a teacher can read the AI's thinking and disagree with it instead of just trusting a number.

It also knows when to step back. If a question includes a diagram, it gets an amber "?" rather than a guess. And if a student reaches the right answer through a different method, it gets flagged so the teacher can take a look.

For a whole class, a teacher can include an answer key to make marking fast and cheap. Without one, UMarkless marks the first paper carefully, learns the key from it, and uses that for the rest of the class. Marked tests can be saved automatically to Google Drive as Google Docs if the teacher turns that on. Student names never leave the phone; only anonymized answers are sent for marking.

**How it makes money**

I chose not to have a free tier or ads. Every test costs me real money to mark, so a free tier would lose money on every teacher who never upgrades. Ads wouldn't fix that either. Teachers open the app to mark a stack of tests, not to scroll for hours, and a teacher marking their students' work shouldn't have to sit through ads to do their job. Instead, teachers get a 7-day trial (approximately 30 tests), and every plan after that is priced above what it actually costs me to run.

There are three monthly plans: Starter is $6.99 for approximately 120 tests, Pro is $14.99 for approximately 400 tests, and School is $24.99 for approximately 900 tests. Every plan is also available as a discounted annual plan. All of the plans and the paywall run through RevenueCat.

Marking with an answer key costs me around 1.5¢ per paper. Even the School plan, the cheapest per test at $24.99 for approximately 900 tests (about 2.8¢ each), still covers its costs after 10% of every subscription goes back to charity. During the trial, a small line in the app shows how much free marking is left ("68% of your free marking used") and disappears once a teacher subscribes.

**How we built it**

The app is built in Flutter and tested on a Pixel 7. Supabase handles sign-in (including Google), the database, and the server functions. RevenueCat runs the subscriptions, the Plans screen and Customer Center, and a webhook on the server updates each teacher's plan when they buy.

For the marking itself, Claude handles handwriting and open-ended answers, while simpler questions with an answer key go to a cheaper open model. Every mark is logged with what it actually cost, so my prices are based on real numbers rather than guesses.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest problem was cost. My first version cost about 12¢ to mark a single paper, which made an affordable subscription impossible. Routing keyed questions to a cheaper model, and learning the key from the first paper in a class set, brought that down to around 1.5¢.

The second was getting the AI to admit when it wasn't sure. Its instinct is to answer confidently no matter what, and teaching it to flag diagrams and questionable answers instead of inventing a score took far more work than I expected. Real handwriting was its own challenge too; pen on paper, photographed at an angle, is much less forgiving than a clean PDF.

I also ran into payment problems I didn't know existed. RevenueCat purposely crashes release builds that use a test key, and I realized a webhook that trusted test purchases would let anyone unlock a paid plan for free, so the server now ignores them by default.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I'm proudest of how quickly UMarkless turns a stack of tests into marked, explained results. What used to take a teacher an entire evening now takes minutes, and it works across subjects, from math and science to language classes. What meant the most, though, was handing it to a real teacher to test. Their reaction was, "This is cool, it works just like you told me it would." Hearing that from someone who marks tests every week told me I was building something that matters beyond a hackathon.

**What we learned**

The biggest lesson was that an honest AI is worth more than a confident one; accuracy means very little if a system can't recognize its own limits. I also learned how much thinking goes into a business model, from unit costs to deciding between a trial and a free tier, and I learned mobile payments and Supabase from the ground up.

**What's next for UMarkless: AI Test Marking for Teachers**

A few teachers at Thornlea Secondary School, Thornhill Secondary School, and Dr. Roberta Bondar Public School are already testing it. The Android app is being submitted to Google Play. The same Flutter code can run on iPhone, but the iOS build isn't working yet, and I'm waiting on an Apple developer account to test and fix it, so the App Store version will follow. After that, I plan to expand to more subjects and curricula beyond Ontario.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Student flats don’t break over big drama — they break over tiny things: who cleaned the bathroom, who still owes money for Friday dinner, whose cousin is sleeping on the sofa, and who needs silence for finals. Every fight starts the same way: a WhatsApp message that half the flat ignores.

We wanted an app that removes that friction. Not another generic to-do list — a shared flat board where:

- chores have photo proof and roommates approve or dispute with a reason

- absences, quiet/exam days, and visits live on the flat calendar (not in chat)

- the app reassigns / rotates tasks around who is actually home

- money reminders are automatic — if someone doesn’t pay, they get nudged; if they mark “I paid”, the creditor gets an alert that opens the expense to settle

Less “did you see my message?” — more “it’s already on the calendar.”

**What it does**

- Tasks: assign (or auto-rotate), swap, complete with proof, approve / dispute

- Proof settings: if the flat sets photo required, you cannot skip the photo; if optional, camera / gallery / complete without

- Expenses: splits, “you owe / they owe you”, settle flow with payment confirmation alerts

- Feed: flat health, weekly reputation leaderboard, balances

- Agenda + Flat life: calendar, absences, quiet mode (exams), visits, house rules — add once, everyone sees it

- Alerts inbox: overdue, review, approved, disputed, you-owe, settle-request, quiet, roommate returns, visits

- HOMPANY Plus (RevenueCat): optional Plus — find flats and roommates more easily, and know who you’re really moving in with thanks to the reputation you build in the app; core flat tools stay free

**How we built it**

- React Native + Expo Router + TypeScript

- Supabase (Postgres, Auth, RLS by home_id, Storage)

- RevenueCat for optional Plus later

- NativeWind, Zod, Jest, full ES/EN i18n

npm install
npm run db:start && npm run db:reset
npm start

Demo login: ana@hompany.local / password123 · invite DEMO2026

Repo: github.com/Celsiita/Hompany

**Challenges we ran into**

Multi-tenant RLS so one flat never leaks into another; a real task lifecycle (PENDING → SUBMITTED → COMPLETED / disputed); recurring chores that respect absences; and proving RevenueCat in a Shipaton demo without locking the free roommate experience. On top of that, recurrence had to feel as simple as possible for the user (few taps, clear days) while still being practical, functional, and realistic for a real flat — weekly chores, monthly bills, and one-off plans that still make sense when someone is away or in quiet/exam mode.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Building something by students, for students — the everyday friction of shared living, not a generic productivity tool

- Keeping almost all of the useful features free: tasks, expenses, calendar, alerts, and reputation stay available to the whole flat

- Turning a real problem (“did you see my WhatsApp?”) into a shared board with photo proof, clear debts, and a calendar everyone can trust

- Making recurring chores feel simple on the outside while still working like a real house schedule

**What we learned**

I learned that shipping a first app is less about knowing every tool and more about listening to the daily mess of living with people. Small copy, clear screens, and one idea at a time beat a complicated system nobody opens. I also learned to cut features when they made the flat harder — and to keep asking: would I actually use this with my roommates next week?

**What's next for Hompany**

Next I want to grow reputation into something you can trust when you look for a flat — so students can find homes and roommates more easily, and know a bit about who they’re about to share with before they move in.

</details>

Every time I make account on random service and I need to type one-time password in, it has been soooo annoying.

It's so simple. All you need to do is just download the app, and register email. 

**How we built it**

I used Jev API, which is pretty cheap and fast, to chose which mail include one-time password. I also use RevenueCat for payment, SwiftUI for UI and so many OSS like SwiftMail. And I only used Windows PC for this project, because I don't have Macbook.

I needed apple developer program to make Autofill, so I used the simulator on the GitHub, but it was really hard. 

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I'm really proud of how I found this problem, and how smart I solved this problem. Jev is really fast, cheap, and accurate. If we didn't use any AI to chose the email, the accurate go down. 

**What we learned**

I have learned how to find the actual problem that we are solving manually, and so annoying. If I was over 18 years old, I surely upload this app on the app store, and do it as a buisiness.

**What's next for SkiPass**

This product is actually really good idea of business because cost price is almost 0, and solving massive problem.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Colombian Sign Language (LSC) has almost no accessible practice material online. Courses are expensive and hard to find, interpreters are booked weeks in advance, and most of what is free is a static word list with no video. Anyone who wants to learn ends up giving up halfway.

I wanted something that runs completely offline on an everyday phone with zero connectivity, for the real-life cases where an interpreter is not around.

**What it does**

A gamified course. Five units covering 112 signs you can actually practice, complete with hearts, streaks, XP, and a reward chest at the end of each unit.

A visual dictionary. All 201 signs from the interpreter's course. 158 have verified video recordings today. The app prints that exact coverage ratio on screen instead of hiding the gap.

An offline translator. Type any Spanish sentence and get back an LSC sign sequence with glosses, speed control (0.75× / 1×), and offline text-to-speech. No network, no API, no account required.

A sustainable freemium model (RevenueCat). Signo Pro unlocks infinite hearts, unlimited practice modules, and offline video copies ($49.99/year with a 7-day free trial, or $9.99/month), with dynamic offerings and entitlements powered by RevenueCat.

The core rule connecting everything: Every sign you can practice is a sign you can watch. A sign only enters the course if a real human video clip exists for it, so nothing on the learning path is ever a dead end.

**How we built it**

Built with Flutter, organized feature-first inside signo_app/ — learn, translator, dictionary, profile, and paywall over a lean core, using Riverpod for clean, reactive state management.

Course content ships pre-compiled. A Dart pipeline reads the interpreter's CSV and emits a typed vocab.json plus a grammar-rules asset. Clips are dynamically bound by matching that output against manifest.json, ensuring a course row cannot claim a video the app does not ship.

The translator is a local rule engine. Colombian Sign Language drops copulas, fronts time expressions, and places the verb at the end (SOV). The mapper rewrites Spanish syntactic order into LSC order before looking up signs. 

RevenueCat (purchases_flutter) manages active customer entitlements ('pro'), package offerings, purchases, and state restoration.

flutter analyze is 100% clean. 232 automated tests pass.

**Challenges we ran into**

Word order. Spanish is SVO; LSC is verb-final without copulas. "Quiero café" is not a word-for-word swap. The linguistic rules live in grammar.json, and they remain the component I intend to refine most.

43 signs have no video. Because the course only teaches signs that have verified clips, 43 of the 201 vocabulary items cannot enter the path yet. The dictionary transparently reports how many are missing and which ones, while each sign card indicates that the video is in production.

Billing. RevenueCat's hosted paywall lets the buyer select any plan, which created the risk that tapping "USD 9.99/month" could settle the annual subscription instead. We engineered strict package resolution during checkout that surfaces an explicit error if a package is missing from the active offering.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The coverage metric is calculated directly from shipped assets at runtime rather than hardcoded into a string, guaranteeing that what the app claims can never drift from what it actually ships.

That same manifest is what governs which signs are teachable. One strict rule explains why 43 signs are absent from the course today, and why the app can state that plainly instead of pretending the curriculum is finished.

**What we learned**

Working with a Deaf collaborator fundamentally redefined our definition of "done." A sign could look visually acceptable on screen and still be linguistically wrong — a subtle handshape angle or movement trajectory was off — and only a daily LSC signer catches that. All 198 clips were recorded and verified that way.

Content provenance determines credibility. Keeping MonikLSC/ in the repository preserves the certified interpreter's raw curriculum, serving as the shortest and most authoritative answer to the first question anyone asks: "Is this authentic LSC?"

**What's next**

- Record the remaining 43 clips, bringing dictionary video coverage from 158 to 201 and unlocking those signs for course inclusion.

- Extend the learning path: 46 signs already have video clips but no course node yet, representing the next unit waiting to be designed.

- Publish Signo to Google Play.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Endless runners on mobile are often too simple and strictly horizontal. I wanted to push the boundaries of the genre by bringing the adrenaline of high-speed, vertical parkour to mobile touch screens. Inspired by the disorienting, gravity-bending architecture of movies like Inception and the fluid movement of modern parkour games, I set out to build a dystopian world where the floor isn't your only path—and where split-second vertical wall-running is the only way to survive.

**What it does**

6D Runner is a hyper-fast 3D endless runner built for Android. Players navigate a brutalist, ruined urban landscape at breakneck speeds. Instead of just switching lanes, players can transition seamlessly onto sheer vertical walls to dodge massive concrete obstacles. The game features a dynamic camera system that shifts FOV and tilt based on your gravity plane, alongside a custom MemoryTracker UI that calculates distance survived in real-time, instantly punishing mistakes and rewarding high-risk maneuvers.

**How we built it**

I developed the entire project from scratch in Unity 6, explicitly targeting the Android platform. The core mechanics, including high-speed physics, obstacle generation, and the custom WallRunner scripts, were coded purely in C#. For the environment, I used heavy 3D assets to build the ruined city aesthetic. The project was version-controlled via GitHub Desktop and compiled directly into an Android APK, ensuring the final build was fully standalone and mobile-ready for the Next Gen track.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest roadblock was extreme mobile optimization. Initially, the heavy PC-level PBR materials in the city environments caused massive shader variant compilation bottlenecks (spiking to over 140,000 variants!). This thermal-throttled the phone and blocked Gradle builds. I had to systematically strip the project down to custom, lightweight mobile diffuse shaders that kept the gritty aesthetic without killing the GPU. 

Additionally, version control became a massive hurdle just hours before the deadline. A 100MB+ 1dcity.glb environment model nearly broke the GitHub push due to server limits, forcing a quick pivot to strict .gitignore rules and modular asset management to keep the repo clean and public for the judges. Lastly, fine-tuning the C# collision detection to prevent the player from clipping through geometry at terminal velocity required intense debugging.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Successfully taking a visually heavy 3D concept and optimizing it to hit stable frame rates on mobile hardware.

- Nailing the fluid transition of the wall-running mechanic—getting the camera and physics to snap cleanly to a 90-degree surface feels incredible.

- Overcoming deep technical build pipeline bottlenecks (shaders and Git binary limits) under the extreme pressure of a hackathon deadline.

- Designing, programming, and shipping a complete, compiled Android APK and open-source repository as a solo 17-year-old developer.

**What we learned**

I gained deep, hands-on experience with the Android Gradle build pipeline and Unity 6's shader stripping capabilities. I also learned a hard but valuable lesson about version control and file size limits, mastering how to properly manage large binaries in game development using .gitignore. Most importantly, I learned how to balance ambitious visual fidelity with strict mobile hardware constraints without sacrificing the core game feel.

**What's next for 6D Runner**

Currently, the track is a hand-crafted high-speed gauntlet. The next major technical step is implementing a fully procedural generation algorithm so the ruins truly become an infinite, unpredictable endless runner. I also plan to integrate online leaderboards, unlockable cosmetic runner skins, and advanced mobile haptic feedback to make every jump, wall-run, and near-miss feel physically impactful.

</details>
