<details><summary>Description</summary>

**PingUp**

Next Gen Award Submission

PingUp is a messaging-first task and reminder app built by a high school student to make everyday coordination feel as natural as texting.

**Inspiration**

I noticed my parents often sent lists and to-dos in our family group chat, but there was no way to check things off or keep track of what was done. Important messages would get buried in the conversation and forgotten.

I realized this wasn't just my family. People constantly delegate tasks, send shopping lists, and use texts as reminders. I wanted to build something that worked the way people already communicate, while actually helping them keep track of what needs to get done.

Instead of creating another task manager that asks people to change their habits, I wanted to make the conversation itself more useful.

**What it does**

PingUp combines messaging, lists, tasks, and reminders into one conversation-based experience.

Users can naturally type or speak what they need instead of filling out traditional task forms.

For example:

"Can you pick up milk, eggs, and bread on your way home?"

PingUp can turn that kind of natural conversation into structured list items or tasks.

**Core Features**

- 💬 Direct and group conversations

- 📝 Shared lists and list items

- ⏰ One-time and recurring pings/reminders

- ✅ Task completion and reopening

- 😴 Snoozing reminders

- 🤖 AI-powered natural-language actions

- 🎙️ Native voice input

- 🔄 Realtime updates

- 🔐 Authorization and protected data

- 📱 Native iOS experience

Users can keep chatting normally while their conversations become more actionable.

**How I Built It**

PingUp is a native iOS application built with Swift and SwiftUI, backed by a Fastify + TypeScript server.

The backend uses Prisma and PostgreSQL for data persistence, while realtime updates keep conversations, lists, and tasks synchronized.

I built an AI interaction layer that interprets natural-language messages and turns them into structured actions such as creating list items, completing tasks, and working with shared conversations.

I also implemented native Apple speech recognition so users can speak directly into the message composer.

Beyond the core messaging experience, I built:

- Recurring task logic

- Due dates and reminders

- Snoozing

- Shared lists

- Completion and reopening

- Realtime synchronization

- Deletion and authorization rules

- Invitation-link functionality

- Automated backend and iOS tests

The goal was to build the actual product architecture rather than a collection of mocked screens.

**Challenges I Ran Into**

One of the biggest challenges was making PingUp feel like a messaging app rather than another traditional task manager.

I had to design the backend so normal conversations could still produce structured tasks and lists without forcing users through a series of forms.

I also worked through:

- SwiftUI state-management issues

- Realtime synchronization

- Recurring task logic

- Database relationships and authorization

- Deletion and archival rules

- Voice permissions and audio-session behavior

- Error handling and failed requests

- Simulator vs. physical-device differences

- Testing complex interactions across the frontend and backend

A particularly important lesson was that features that look simple from the outside can require significant backend logic to make them reliable.

**Accomplishments I'm Proud Of**

I'm proud that PingUp grew from a simple idea into a working end-to-end product.

As a high school student, I built the iOS application, backend, database architecture, realtime systems, task engine, AI interaction layer, voice input, and automated tests.

I'm especially proud of the core experience: users don't have to learn a new productivity workflow. They can communicate naturally, and PingUp helps turn those conversations into things that actually get done.

**What I Learned**

I learned that building a reliable product requires much more than getting the main feature working.

State management, error handling, permissions, synchronization, database design, authorization, and testing all have a major impact on whether an application actually feels trustworthy.

I also learned to design around how people already behave instead of forcing them to learn an entirely new workflow.

Most importantly, building PingUp taught me how many layers are involved in turning an idea into a real product—from the interface all the way down to the backend and database.

**Implementation & Testing Notes**

Some PingUp features depend on external services that could not be included as live external-service demonstrations in the final submission.

The implementations are included in the codebase, and the underlying workflows were tested during development with local or fake providers where applicable.

**AI**

The production AI integration and AI action architecture are implemented in the codebase.

I tested the AI integration during development, including the AI action workflows, but I am not including live AI API usage in this submission because the external AI service requires paid API usage.

The application also includes a fake AI provider for development and testing, allowing the core AI action flows to be tested without depending on live API calls.

**Invitation Links**

The invitation-link functionality is implemented in the codebase.

I tested the invitation-link functionality during development, but I am not including live invitation-link sending in this submission because it depends on external link/service configuration.

**Other Tested Functionality**

The following functionality was implemented and tested throughout development:

- Messaging and conversations

- Shared lists

- Tasks and recurring tasks

- Pings and reminders

- Completion and reopening

- Snoozing

- Realtime updates

- Voice input

- Authorization

- Deletion and archival

- Backend validation

- Automated tests

- Debug and Release builds

**For Judges**

Please check the repository/codebase when evaluating features that depend on external services.

The project contains the actual implementation and integration architecture rather than a mockup of these capabilities. Where live external-service testing was not included in the submission, the underlying application logic and workflows were still tested during development.

**What's Next for PingUp**

The next stage for PingUp would be expanding beyond the current iOS experience.

Planned improvements include:

- 🌐 Cross-platform and web access

- 🔗 More complete invitation and deep-link flows

- 🤖 Production AI usage at scale

- 👥 AI-assisted task assignment between conversations

- 📱 SMS-based interactions through Twilio

- ⚙️ More automated reminders and workflows

- 🔄 Additional integrations with everyday communication tools

The long-term goal is for PingUp to become a layer that sits naturally on top of how people already communicate—turning "I'll do it" into something that actually gets remembered and completed.

**Built With**

Swift, SwiftUI, TypeScript, Fastify, Prisma, PostgreSQL, Apple Speech Recognition, AI, and Xcode.

**Submission**

Award: Next Gen Award

Developer: High school student

Project: PingUp

Lestinaty

What inspired me

I wanted to build a productivity app that felt less like checking boxes and more like making progress in something that actually belongs to you.

Most habit and productivity apps represent progress through numbers, streaks, and checklists. I wanted to make that progress feel tangible and alive.

That idea became Lestinaty: a world that grows as you grow.

Every habit can become a seed. As you stay consistent, it grows through different stages, and completing a habit creates a visual moment of progress. Instead of simply seeing that I completed something, I wanted to feel that I had changed my world.

What I learned

Building Lestinaty taught me that creating a product is much more than implementing features.

I learned to think about how individual interactions connect into a larger experience. A habit is not just a checkbox—it can become part of a routine, a task, a path, or eventually a larger goal.

I also learned how important visual consistency is. Lestinaty contains a large collection of custom visual assets, so I had to develop a consistent visual language for trees, icons, maps, animations, and UI elements.

Most importantly, I learned to design around a feeling rather than a feature list: I want users to feel that their progress is building something.

How I built it

I built Lestinaty as a mobile-first productivity experience centered around visual progression.

The current experience focuses on habits, with each habit connected to a unique visual element that grows as the user maintains it. The app also includes a visual world, customizable themes, a collection/shop system, reminders, and in-app purchases powered by RevenueCat.

OneSignal handles scheduled habit reminders, allowing each habit to have its own reminder.

I designed and created the visual system myself, including the voxel-inspired trees, environments, icons, growth stages, and other UI assets.

The architecture is also evolving beyond habits. The next modules I am building are Tasks and Routines, with the longer-term vision of connecting goals, paths, routines, habits, and tasks into one system for personal growth.

The challenges

One of the biggest challenges was balancing creativity with usability.

It is easy to keep adding visual elements, animations, and systems because there are so many possibilities. The challenge was deciding what actually improves the experience and what simply adds complexity.

Another challenge was creating a large visual system while keeping everything consistent. Every tree, icon, environment, and UI element needed to feel like it belonged to the same world.

I also had to design the product around a very small team: essentially, me building the product from the idea to the visual design, development, integrations, and App Store submission.

That constraint forced me to prioritize what mattered most and build the experience step by step.

What’s next

Lestinaty is still evolving.

I want to expand the system from habits into routines and tasks, and eventually connect them through goals and paths. The long-term vision is for Lestinaty to help people turn something they want to achieve into a system of actions they can actually follow—and then make that progress visible.

Instead of simply telling you that you are making progress, Lestinaty lets you see it grow.

Grow your habits. Grow your world

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/466/527/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/466/527/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Communication is often treated as the ability to construct and speak a complete sentence. But a person may know exactly what they need while having difficulty turning that intention into words. I built ReVoice to make those moments simpler, faster, and more independent.

The principle behind ReVoice is:

Human intent → AI assistance → human choice → voice

AI never decides what the person means. It offers possibilities, and the person always chooses the message before it is spoken.

**What it does**

ReVoice is an AI-assisted communication app for Android.

Essential communication remains free and immediately available through customizable Quick Speak cards, Yes/No buttons, common phrases, and device text-to-speech.

For more complex thoughts, the Intent Builder combines simple clues—such as a person, place, time, or word—and generates exactly three possible phrases. The user reviews the suggestions, selects the intended message, and ReVoice speaks it aloud.

Voice Intent lets the user provide an incomplete spoken thought. Live Camera Assist uses temporary visual context to suggest relevant phrases and includes front/rear camera support and live captions. A local Care Profile can provide helpful context about important people, places, routines, and preferences.

ReVoice+ unlocks advanced tools through a real RevenueCat purchase flow.

**How we built it**

ReVoice was built with React Native, Expo, Expo Router, and TypeScript.

The mobile app communicates with focused Vercel serverless endpoints. Only the backend communicates with OpenAI, keeping the OpenAI API key out of the application and public repository.

RevenueCat manages the default offering, Monthly, Yearly, and Lifetime packages, purchases, CustomerInfo, restore purchases, and the active pro entitlement. Premium access is determined exclusively by RevenueCat and is never simulated with a local flag.

Camera access, speech recognition, and text-to-speech use native Expo-compatible modules. User preferences, Quick Speak cards, history, favorites, and Care Profile information are stored locally on the device.

**Challenges we ran into**

The main challenge was balancing helpful AI assistance with human control. ReVoice must suggest possibilities without claiming certainty about a person's intent.

We also worked through native camera and microphone permissions, continuous speech recognition, temporary multi-frame camera capture, contextual phrase generation, Android Development Builds, and immediate RevenueCat entitlement updates after a Test Store purchase.

Another challenge was keeping essential communication available even when AI or network services are unavailable.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Essential communication remains free and does not depend on AI.

- The Intent Builder consistently returns exactly three possible phrases.

- The user always confirms a phrase before it is spoken.

- Live Camera Assist supports front and rear cameras with live captions.

- Quick Speak cards can be added, edited, removed, and reordered.

- RevenueCat purchases activate the real pro entitlement and unlock Camera Assist immediately.

- Premium access is restored correctly after restarting the app.

- No OpenAI secret is exposed in the mobile application or repository.

**What we learned**

Building ReVoice reinforced that assistive AI should increase agency rather than replace it. Good suggestions are important, but preserving uncertainty and user choice is even more important.

We also learned how RevenueCat offerings, packages, CustomerInfo, entitlements, purchase restoration, and Test Store transactions work together in a real React Native application.

**What's next for ReVoice**

Future work could include additional languages, caregiver-managed profile sharing with explicit consent, improved accessibility testing with real users, and a multimodal Live Assist mode that combines visual and spoken context.

The goal remains the same: technology should not speak for people. It should help people be heard.

</details>

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/471/546/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/471/546/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/471/827/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/471/827/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/471/828/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/471/828/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Running in a group keeps people consistent. The hard part is getting everyone to the same place at the same time, and that is where most run clubs fall apart. We wanted a club's accountability without the scheduling, so we built teams that run asynchronously. Your phone logs your runs, and your five teammates follow your progress on their own time.

The idea rests on Irwin, Feltz et al.'s 2012 study of the Köhler effect (Ann Behav Med). People exercised significantly longer when they believed the team's result depended on its weakest member. Groups are capped at six, so a skipped run is easy to see, and nobody wants to be the one who let the team down.

**The psychology we built on**

Intergroup competition. A global leaderboard stops motivating people once they realize they'll never reach the top. We set small teams against each other in two-week seasons instead. The short season gives a clear finish line and a quick reset if one goes badly. Team loyalty gets people out on days they'd normally skip.

Loss aversion and turf. We split the real world into H3 hex cells that players claim by running through them. A nightly job decays cells nobody is defending, so rivals can take them. Prospect theory puts the cost of a loss at roughly twice the pleasure of an equal gain:

$$v(x) = \begin{cases} x^{\alpha} & x \ge 0 \ -\lambda(-x)^{\beta} & x \lt 0 \end{cases} \qquad \lambda \approx 2.25$$

(Tversky & Kahneman, 1992.) Watching your map shrink is a strong reason to go back out.

Social dating and the bounty. Men can post an optional bounty, bought in-app through RevenueCat, to be guaranteed a mixed group of three men and three women. Half of it funds the platform. The other half is held in escrow and paid out at the end of the season to the women who qualify. Entering a season stays free for everyone. The bounty does two jobs. Wanting to impress the group raises the stakes the Köhler effect already depends on, and women get a concrete reason to stay active for the full two weeks. Payouts aren't competitive, so they can't be farmed. Every woman who clears a hidden bar on distance and frequency gets the same flat amount, and running past the bar earns nothing extra.

**How we built it**

- Frontend: one React Native / Expo codebase for iOS (built through EAS) and Android.

- Payments: the RevenueCat SDK sells the bounty as a one-time purchase; a RevenueCat webhook records it against the runner's season entry, idempotently, and reverses it on refund.

- Backend and database: FastAPI with async SQLAlchemy on PostgreSQL, hosted on Railway.

- Mapping: Uber's H3 grid. Cells are stored as plain text IDs, so we didn't need PostGIS.

- Automation: Python cron jobs run the nightly territory decay and an hourly leaderboard rollup.

- Auth: Sign in with Apple with JWTs.

- Testing: an offline script, simulate_turf.py, tests scoring rules before they reach real runners.

**Challenges**

At first, cell ownership was winner-takes-all, so a runner who came a close second across a whole neighbourhood scored zero. That was too discouraging, so we added an influence score. It credits a runner for every cell where they have any live score, and the leaderboard ranks by its 30-day moving average.

Averages caused a different problem in our orientation season for Singapore schools. Ranking schools by average turf per runner meant every new member pulled their school's score down, and one strong solo runner couldn't be beaten. We switched to total turf held, which rewards schools for bringing people in.

Seasons used to charge an entry fee. Entry is now free and automatic: a run logged inside an open season enters you. The only thing for sale is the bounty.

**What we learned**

Stay strictly within what the behavioral science supports. We don't claim the well-known "rowers' high," for example, because that bonding effect requires moving in sync, in person, and async running can't provide it. Every claim the app makes comes from one sourced file, and we cut any feature we couldn't tie to one of our five motivation levers.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Why ExitKit**

Moving out should end with a handover, not an argument over the deposit. Photos get scattered across chats, final meter readings get missed, and a shared deduction can quietly become someone else's bill. ExitKit puts the evidence and the agreed numbers in one place.

**What it does**

Roommates record the flat, move-out date and each person's deposit contribution. A guided walkthrough covers the bedroom, kitchen, bathroom and living room: mark each checklist item OK or Issue, then add photos and captions.

Next come the final electricity, water and gas readings, plus agreed deductions. Each deduction is either shared equally or charged to one person. ExitKit calculates each person's refund in integer paise, with a fixed rounding rule so the totals add up exactly.

The walkthrough, settlement and pack preview are free. A one-time purchase unlocks a shareable PDF handover pack with the photos, checklists, readings, deductions and settlement table. ExitKit records what people agreed on; it is not legal advice or a dispute-resolution service.

**How it is built**

ExitKit is a React and TypeScript app built with Vite and packaged for Android with Capacitor. The PDF is generated on-device with pdf-lib. Data stays on the device; there is no account or cloud sync.

The RevenueCat Purchases Capacitor SDK handles the one-time non-consumable product exitkit_pack_unlock, the handover_pack entitlement and purchase restoration. The demo shows a RevenueCat Test Store purchase on a real Android device. Test Store purchases are simulated and do not charge money. The web link is a browser preview; the purchase flow requires the Android app.

**Scope and checks**

The build keeps the room templates fixed and leaves out OCR, AI features, cloud storage and legal advice. The settlement uses deterministic integer arithmetic rather than floating-point money calculations. The repository includes 15 settlement and pack tests, a committed Android project and setup instructions for a fresh clone.

AI coding assistance was used during development. The source is public under the MIT licence.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Studying often turns interesting ideas into static notes, worksheets, and repetitive questions. I wanted to make studying feel more like progressing through a game.

That became QuestLab: an iPhone learning game that turns study material into playable learning worlds.

Instead of only reading or answering a normal quiz, students move through environments, complete checkpoints, defeat bosses, earn XP, and track their mastery.

**What it does**

QuestLab lets students scan study material or use a built-in learning example.

The app identifies the important concepts and turns them into a themed learning experience.

For the Biology demo, the student enters the Digestive Kingdom and progresses through:

- Mouth

- Esophagus

- Stomach

- Small Intestine

- Large Intestine

Correct answers activate the path through the world and move the player toward the next checkpoint.

After completing the route, the player faces the Guardian of Wisdom in a boss battle. Knowledge becomes part of the gameplay: correct answers damage the Guardian and move the player toward completing the mission.

QuestLab also tracks:

- XP

- Levels

- Streaks

- Hearts

- Subject mastery

- Weak concepts

- World progression

**RevenueCat integration**

QuestLab uses RevenueCat to power QuestLab Pro.

The app loads its subscription offering through RevenueCat and supports monthly and yearly packages.

A successful purchase activates the pro entitlement.

That entitlement is the real source of truth for premium access — QuestLab does not fake Pro access with a local switch.

When Pro becomes active, premium content visibly unlocks inside the game.

Restore Purchases is also supported.

For the Shipaton demo, RevenueCat's Test Store is used to demonstrate the complete purchase and entitlement flow safely.

**How I built it**

QuestLab is a native iPhone application built primarily with SwiftUI.

The project uses:

- Swift

- SwiftUI

- Xcode

- Vision for OCR

- AVFoundation for camera capture

- RevenueCat for subscriptions and entitlements

- Local persistence for player progress

- Custom game-state and progression systems

- A reusable cinematic artwork and animation system

QuestLab currently uses deterministic local study generation so the demo is reliable and can run without depending on a remote AI service.

**Challenges**

One of the biggest challenges was making QuestLab feel like a game rather than a quiz app with artwork behind it.

I worked on making the world itself communicate progression. In Digestive Kingdom, completing a checkpoint sends energy through the digestive route and moves the player toward the next location.

Another challenge was building the visual system so large world artwork could scale correctly across the interface without looking like rectangular images placed inside standard UI cards.

The Guardian battle also went through several iterations to make correct answers feel physical through impact effects, recoil, health changes, and animation.

RevenueCat was another important technical challenge. I wanted the purchase flow to be genuine rather than simulated, so the final build uses RevenueCat offerings, packages, CustomerInfo, the pro entitlement, and Restore Purchases.

**What I learned**

This project taught me a lot about:

- Native iOS development

- SwiftUI architecture

- Game-like interaction design

- Animation and visual hierarchy

- OCR and camera workflows

- Persistent progression systems

- Subscription architecture with RevenueCat

- Testing real entitlement state

- Designing a product around a very clear core idea

The biggest lesson was that adding more features is not always the answer. QuestLab became much stronger when I focused on making one complete experience feel coherent from scanning the study material all the way to completing a world.

**What's next**

I would like to expand QuestLab with more learning worlds, more subjects, additional mission types, and richer ways of adapting gameplay to what a student needs to practice.

The long-term goal is simple:

Turn studying into an adventure you actually want to continue.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

The name Frost comes from American science-fiction writer Roger Zelazny's 1966 story For a Breath I Tarry. In the story, Frost is a machine that seeks not only to calculate the world, but to understand human experience. That became Pocket Buddy's guiding question: what if an AI companion did more than answer once—what if it stayed with a person through the small actions that make up a day, understood the goal behind them, and returned visible, verifiable results?

Pocket Buddy turns that literary idea into an agent system. Frost is one consistent companion across software and an ESP32-S3 round-screen badge. The software holds the day; the badge stays close. Within Frost's Taskmaster loop, goal understanding, capability selection, controlled Skill execution, user confirmation, and evidence are separate responsibilities rather than one unbounded model call.

**What it does**

**One day with Frost**

At 08:10, breakfast, the user takes or chooses a meal photo. Photos proposes candidates and nutrition ranges, but the user reviews and confirms what was actually eaten. Only that confirmed summary can enter today's memory; the raw photo stays in its original workflow.

At 10:30, training, Frost chooses a next step from equipped and authorized capabilities. The phone provides the detailed exercise experience while the badge carries the essential cue close to the body. Frost can propose; the user remains the decision-maker.

At 18:20, a run, Earth / Routes uses AMap for real roads and the phone's current GPS. The full map and route stay on the phone while the badge gives lightweight prompts, so attention can remain on the road. Deviations trigger recalculation rather than pretending that the original plan is still correct.

At 18:45, a bird call, a long press on the badge captures a short nearby sound. Bird Listener validates the input, returns a candidate instead of false certainty, and brings the result back to the same round display and the phone's discovery record.

At 21:30, review, the day's confirmed meals, movement, route progress, and nature discoveries become a coherent review. Frost carries context forward without turning every photo, recording, health detail, or precise location into general cloud memory.

Across that day, Pocket Buddy brings together:

- Photos for meal candidates, correction, and explicit confirmation.

- Earth / Routes for real-road planning and route display through AMap.

- Agents / My Skills for Frost, route planning, Bird Listener, Her Motion, and exercise experiences.

- Skill Canvas for creating, compiling, previewing, and saving custom Skill graphs. It is an authoring surface; production execution remains behind the Taskmaster's registered-capability and evidence boundary.

- Pocket Buddy badge for display, buttons, microphone, speaker, touch input, and a BLE phone bridge.

Frost does not simply generate advice. The server-owned Taskmaster validates structured model output, applies approval and permission boundaries, calls only registered capabilities, and records privacy-bounded execution evidence.

**How we built it**

The client is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Capacitor, and native iOS bridges. The physical companion uses an ESP32-S3 badge connected to the phone through Bluetooth Low Energy. The phone and web interfaces share the same Frost identity and Skill vocabulary.

For the deployed agent workflow, the backend runs on Google Cloud Run. A server-owned Prompt Harness controls authority, context budget, task profiles, structured JSON validation, cancellation, and bounded continuation. It calls Gemini 3.5 Flash through the official Google GenAI SDK (@google/genai) using Vertex AI.

Every successful agent run receives a trace ID. Firestore stores restricted evidence metadata such as task type, model, status, timing, Cloud Run revision, and prompt profile. It does not store prompts, model responses, credentials, raw health content, recordings, photos, or precise routes. The deployed service requires Firestore evidence rather than silently reporting success when evidence storage fails.

The production deployment also uses Cloud Build, Artifact Registry, Cloud Logging, and a dedicated least-privilege runtime service account limited to the permissions needed for Vertex AI and Firestore.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest problem was not calling a model; it was defining where the model must stop. A generated plan is not a completed workout, a guessed meal is not an eaten meal, and opening a page is not evidence that a device action succeeded. We built explicit confirmation, timeout, validation, provenance, and evidence boundaries around those transitions.

We also had to connect a web app, native iOS capabilities, BLE hardware, external map infrastructure, and Google Cloud without turning every service into one unsafe data pool. The result is deliberately layered: Google Cloud owns agent reasoning and traceable execution evidence; AMap owns mainland route presentation; the phone owns sensitive permissions and device bridging; the user owns confirmation.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Deployed a working Frost Taskmaster on Cloud Run in asia-east1.

- Verified Gemini 3.5 Flash through Vertex AI and the Google GenAI SDK.

- Required a matching Firestore evidence record for real agent runs.

- Kept prompts, health details, media, credentials, and precise location out of the evidence store.

- Connected one Frost identity across software Skills and a physical badge.

- Preserved honest uncertainty and user confirmation in food, health, route, motion, and nature workflows.

- Turned a list of features into one continuous, human-scale day with Frost.

**What we learned**

A trustworthy agent needs more than a good system prompt. It needs capability contracts, explicit authority, structured outputs, cancellation, least-privilege infrastructure, and evidence that can distinguish proposed, started, waiting, failed, and completed work. Physical interaction makes those distinctions even more important.

We also learned that continuity does not require collecting everything. The useful memory is often a confirmed summary and a traceable outcome, not the raw photo, recording, route, or private conversation that produced it.

**What's next for Pocket Buddy**

Next, we will connect more user-authored Skill Canvas graphs to the production Taskmaster only after each capability has explicit permissions, failure handling, and evidence requirements. We also plan to expand device testing, user-owned connectors, and privacy-preserving long-term memory while keeping raw media and sensitive context out of general cloud traces.

**Pre-existing work disclosure**

Pocket Buddy builds on earlier interface design, iOS/hardware integration, and product experiments. The team subsequently developed and integrated the Frost Taskmaster workflow, the Gemini 3.5 / Google GenAI SDK backend, the server-owned Prompt Harness, the Cloud Run deployment, Firestore evidence contracts, service boundaries, testing, documentation, and the demonstration experience presented here.

**Team contribution**

Cheng Zhang — I led product design and end-to-end implementation across the web/iOS experience, Frost Taskmaster workflows, wearable integration, privacy boundaries, and the final demo.

**Inspiration**

Students often face campus problems such as maintenance issues, water supply problems, cleanliness issues, and safety concerns. Reporting these problems through traditional methods can make it difficult to track whether action has been taken. We wanted to build a simple platform that makes campus complaint reporting and tracking more transparent.

**What it does**

CampusFix AI is a campus complaint management platform that connects students with the appropriate campus authorities.

Students can report problems, provide the location and details, track complaint status, and view their complaint history. Authorities can manage assigned complaints, update their status, and monitor unresolved issues. The system also supports an escalation workflow for complaints that remain unresolved beyond the defined timeline.

**How we built it**

We built CampusFix AI as a responsive web application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

The application uses browser Local Storage to maintain complaint data and application state. We designed separate student and authority workflows, including complaint submission, complaint tracking, filtering, detailed complaint views, status updates, and escalation handling.

The project is hosted using GitHub Pages, with the source code maintained on GitHub.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the main challenges was designing a clear complaint workflow that connects students, authorities, complaint status, deadlines, and escalation in a simple interface.

We also had to make sure that complaint information remained consistent across different sections of the application while working with a browser-based Local Storage system.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud of building a complete working prototype that covers the complaint journey from reporting to resolution.

The project includes student complaint submission, complaint tracking, an authority dashboard, detailed complaint views, filtering, status management, and an escalation workflow. We also focused on making the interface responsive and easy to navigate.

**What we learned**

Through this project, we learned how to turn a real-world campus problem into a structured software solution.

We gained practical experience in frontend development, JavaScript application logic, Local Storage, responsive UI design, GitHub-based development, and designing workflows around different types of users.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Extreme rainfall can turn into urban flooding within a short period of time, especially when rainfall information, ground observations, weather radar, satellite observations and forecast models are available through different systems and at different spatial and temporal resolutions.

Our team was inspired by the need for a single intelligent platform that could bring these different sources together and convert complex meteorological information into actionable early-warning information. Instead of looking at rainfall forecasting and flooding as two separate problems, we wanted to build an end-to-end system that connects weather observation → rainfall prediction → inundation prediction → validation → early warning → decision support.

This idea led us to develop VARSHAAI, an AI/ML-based Integrated Heavy Rainfall Early Warning and Inundation Prediction System.

The objective is not simply to display weather information. VARSHAAI is designed to transform multiple weather and geographical data sources into a unified disaster-intelligence platform that can help authorities understand where extreme rainfall may occur, how rainfall may evolve, which areas may face inundation risk, and where early action may be required.

**The Problem**

Heavy rainfall prediction is challenging because no single data source provides the complete picture.

Satellite observations provide wide-area coverage, weather radar provides high-resolution precipitation information, AWS/ARG stations provide point-based ground observations, and Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models provide forecasts for future atmospheric conditions. However, these sources differ in their:

- Spatial resolution

- Temporal resolution

- Data formats

- Geographic coverage

- Measurement characteristics

- Availability and quality

For example, satellite, radar, ground stations and NWP models may represent rainfall at completely different spatial and temporal scales.

Even when rainfall can be predicted, another important question remains:

How will that rainfall affect the ground?

High rainfall intensity can interact with terrain, drainage networks, land-use/land-cover and surface characteristics to produce localized inundation. Therefore, rainfall forecasting alone is not sufficient for effective flood preparedness.

VARSHAAI addresses both sides of the problem by combining rainfall intelligence with inundation-risk prediction.

**Our Solution**

VARSHAAI is an integrated AI/ML disaster-intelligence platform designed for heavy rainfall early warning and inundation prediction.

The system follows a complete pipeline:

Multi-Source Data Ingestion → Quality Control → Spatial & Temporal Harmonization → AI/ML Forecasting → NWP Correction → Inundation Prediction → Validation → Risk Assessment → Alerts & Visualization

The platform brings together:

- Satellite observations

- Weather radar observations

- AWS/ARG ground observations

- Numerical Weather Prediction data

- Digital Elevation Model (DEM)

- Drainage information

- Land-use/Land-cover data

- Historical rainfall and flood-event data

These datasets are processed through a common framework before being used by the forecasting and inundation modules.

**Multi-Source Data Ingestion**

The first major component of VARSHAAI is the Data Ingestion Layer.

The system is designed to ingest data from multiple meteorological and geographical sources.

**Satellite Data**

Satellite observations provide wide-area information about atmospheric and cloud conditions. VARSHAAI is designed to support INSAT-based observations and other satellite-derived meteorological information.

Satellite data provides spatial coverage that is difficult to obtain from ground stations alone.

**Weather Radar**

Weather radar provides high-resolution information about precipitation systems and rainfall structure.

Radar observations are particularly important for short-term rainfall nowcasting because they can capture the movement and evolution of precipitation systems.

**AWS/ARG Observations**

Automatic Weather Stations and Automatic Rain Gauges provide ground-level observations.

These observations help provide local measurements of:

- Rainfall

- Temperature

- Relative humidity

- Wind

- Pressure

- Other available meteorological variables

Ground observations are useful for validating and correcting remotely sensed information.

**Numerical Weather Prediction**

NWP models provide forecasts of future atmospheric conditions.

VARSHAAI uses NWP information as an important input for longer forecast horizons and applies machine-learning-based post-processing to improve forecast usefulness.

**Data Harmonization**

One of the major engineering challenges was that all these sources operate at different spatial and temporal resolutions.

For example:

- Radar can provide observations at very short time intervals.

- Satellite observations may have different revisit and processing intervals.

- AWS/ARG observations are point measurements.

- NWP data generally has a much coarser spatial resolution and longer forecast intervals.

VARSHAAI therefore introduces a common data-harmonization framework.

The preprocessing pipeline performs:

- Data ingestion

- Format standardization

- Missing-data handling

- Quality control

- Spatial regridding

- Temporal alignment

- Resampling

- Common-grid generation

- Feature preparation

The different datasets are transformed into a common representation so that the AI/ML modules can process them together.

**Preprocessing and Quality Control**

Raw meteorological data cannot be directly passed into an AI model.

VARSHAAI therefore performs several preprocessing operations.

**Missing Data Handling**

Missing observations are identified and handled using appropriate interpolation, imputation or availability flags depending on the source.

**Radar Quality Control**

Radar observations can contain noise, ground clutter and other unwanted signals.

Quality-control procedures are applied before radar information is used for prediction.

**Spatial Regridding**

Datasets with different grid resolutions are transformed into a common spatial grid.

Methods such as:

- Bilinear interpolation

- Inverse Distance Weighting

- Kriging

can be used depending on the dataset and application.

**Temporal Alignment**

Different sources can provide observations at different time intervals.

VARSHAAI aligns the observations into a common temporal framework so that the AI models can learn relationships between the datasets.

**AI/ML Rainfall Nowcasting**

The core intelligence of VARSHAAI is the AI/ML forecasting layer.

For short-term forecasting, the system performs rainfall nowcasting for approximately the next 0–3 hours.

The system can use deep-learning architectures such as:

- ConvLSTM

- U-Net

- Optical-flow-assisted deep learning

These models learn spatial and temporal patterns in rainfall evolution.

For example, a sequence of previous radar and meteorological observations can be provided to the model. The model learns how precipitation structures move, grow or decay and generates future rainfall estimates.

The output can be represented as rainfall intensity maps over the target region.

This transforms the system from a simple monitoring dashboard into a predictive platform.

**NWP Post-Processing and Bias Correction**

Short-term nowcasting is not sufficient for longer prediction horizons.

Therefore, VARSHAAI includes a separate NWP post-processing component.

NWP forecasts can contain systematic biases caused by model resolution, parameterization and local atmospheric conditions.

VARSHAAI uses machine-learning-based correction techniques to learn the relationship between historical NWP predictions and observed rainfall.

Possible models include:

- Gradient Boosting

- Random Forest

- Neural Networks

- CNN-based bias correction

The corrected forecast can then provide improved rainfall information for longer forecast horizons.

This gives VARSHAAI two complementary forecasting capabilities:

0–3 hours: AI-based rainfall nowcasting

3–72 hours: NWP-based forecasting with ML post-processing/correction

**Inundation Prediction**

Rainfall prediction alone does not tell us exactly where flooding may occur.

VARSHAAI therefore includes an Inundation/Flood Mapping Module.

The system combines rainfall information with geographical and hydrological factors such as:

- Digital Elevation Model

- Drainage network

- Land-use/Land-cover

- Surface characteristics

- Accumulated rainfall

- Rainfall intensity

- Runoff-related parameters

The system estimates the potential movement and accumulation of water across the terrain.

For screening-level analysis, rainfall-runoff approaches such as the SCS-CN method can be incorporated.

For more detailed hydraulic modelling, frameworks such as HEC-RAS or LISFLOOD-type approaches can be integrated depending on data availability and deployment requirements.

The output can include:

- Flood-risk zones

- Potential inundation extent

- Estimated inundation depth

- High-risk locations

- Spatial flood-risk maps

**Risk Classification**

VARSHAAI converts continuous weather and inundation information into understandable risk categories.

The system can classify areas according to levels such as:

- Low Risk

- Moderate Risk

- High Risk

- Very High Risk

Risk assessment can consider rainfall intensity, accumulated rainfall, forecast confidence, terrain characteristics and predicted inundation.

This makes the output easier to understand for emergency-response teams and decision-makers.

**Validation and Skill Scoring**

An AI prediction system must be evaluated against actual observations.

VARSHAAI therefore includes a dedicated validation module.

Historical rainfall events are used to evaluate prediction performance.

The system supports metrics such as:

**Probability of Detection (POD)**

Measures how effectively the system detects observed events.

**False Alarm Ratio (FAR)**

Measures the proportion of predicted events that did not occur.

**Critical Success Index (CSI)**

Evaluates the overall ability to correctly predict events while accounting for misses and false alarms.

**RMSE**

Measures the magnitude of prediction errors.

**MAE**

Measures the average absolute difference between predicted and observed values.

The validation layer allows the system to compare predictions with observations and continuously assess model performance.

**Early Warning and Alert System**

One of the most important outputs of VARSHAAI is the early-warning capability.

When forecast rainfall and inundation indicators cross predefined risk thresholds, the system can generate alerts.

The alert system can provide information such as:

- Location

- Forecast rainfall

- Risk level

- Expected time window

- Inundation probability/risk

- Potentially affected area

- Recommended attention level

The goal is to provide information early enough for authorities to begin preparedness and response activities.

**Command Center**

All major outputs are brought together in an interactive command-center dashboard.

The frontend is built using:

- React

- Vite

- Leaflet

- React-Leaflet

- Recharts

- Modern CSS

The dashboard provides different functional views for:

- Data Intelligence

- AI Forecast

- Inundation

- Validation

- Alerts

- Interactive Maps

The map interface allows users to visualize geographic risk information instead of relying only on numerical tables.

Charts and indicators help users understand rainfall trends, forecast information and model performance.

**Backend Architecture**

The backend is implemented using Python and FastAPI.

The backend provides APIs for the major system modules.

The architecture includes endpoints for:

- Health monitoring

- Dashboard information

- Alerts

- Analyst information

- Flood prediction

- Flood risk

- Validation

- Validation summaries

- Data sources

- AI/ML models

The backend acts as the bridge between the data-processing and prediction layers and the frontend command center.

This modular architecture allows individual data-source adapters and prediction modules to be upgraded without redesigning the complete application.

**System Architecture**

The overall architecture can be represented as:

## 638. DBX-Database Extreme

> DBX is a high-performance vector database built in Go, featuring SIMD acceleration, zero-copy memory-mapped storage, and multi-tenant indexing for sub-millisecond similarity search in AI systems

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/dbx-database-extreme-1itauy (gallery page 157) · ❤️ 1 · 💬 0
- **Team:** [Vansh Jain](https://devpost.com/vansh-jainn0702)
- **GitHub (Try it out):** https://github.com/vanshjain-0702/DBX-Database-Extreme
- **Repo check:** public repo · ⚠️ license file not recognised by GitHub · 154 commits · Go · RevenueCat not found in manifests · ⚠️ last commit 2026-10-03 (after Sep 30 deadline)
- **Other links:** https://dbxdb.co.in
- **Built with:** ai, ai-infrastructure, cloud-native, cosine-similarity, developers-tools, go, golang, hnsw-indexing, hpc, mmap, multi-modal-search, open-source, rag, rest-api, semantic-search, simd, systems-engineering, vector-databases, wal

**Video (5:18):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aA-rZ-cli-E

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/aA-rZ-cli-E/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aA-rZ-cli-E)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/432/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/432/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/433/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/433/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/434/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/434/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/436/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/436/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/435/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/435/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/437/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/437/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/438/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/438/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/439/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/439/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) and semantic search architectures are only as fast as their retrieval layer. Existing vector databases often suffer from massive memory overheads, garbage collection pauses in runtime environments, and bloated microservice architectures that make self-hosting in air-gapped or edge environments impractical.

We asked ourselves: What if a vector database was engineered from the ground up with systems programming principles—combining zero-copy memory mapping, CPU vector extensions (SIMD), and rigorous multi-tenant data isolation into a single, high-throughput Go binary? That vision became DBX (Database Extreme).

**What it does**

DBX is a purpose-built, bare-metal vector database designed for sub-millisecond similarity search across dense embedding spaces:

Ultra-Fast Vector Search: Computes vector similarities across high-dimensional spaces ($d \in [384, 1536]$) using hardware-accelerated SIMD instructions.
Zero-Copy Memory-Mapped Storage (mmap): Bypasses traditional buffer cache overhead by mapping vector index files directly into the virtual address space, letting the OS kernel handle paging with near-zero RAM footprint on idle sets.
True Multi-Tenancy: Hard partition isolation with per-tenant namespaces, cryptographic tokens, and decoupled write-ahead logging (WAL).
Hybrid Metadata & Vector Querying: Allows real-time filtering on scalar document attributes simultaneously with high-dimensional vector search.

**The Math & Core Mechanics**

At the heart of DBX is optimized similarity search. For two normalized $d$-dimensional embedding vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^d$, DBX computes the cosine similarity:

$$S_C(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{u}|2 |\mathbf{v}|2} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^d u_i v_i}{\sqrt{\sum{i=1}^d u_i^2} \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2}}$$

When vectors are unit-normalized upon ingestion ($|\mathbf{u}|_2 = 1$), the computation reduces strictly to a high-speed inner dot product:

$$\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \sum_{i=1}^{d} u_i v_i$$

For Euclidean metric spaces ($L_2$ distance):

$$D_{L2}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = |\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}|2 = \sqrt{\sum{i=1}^d (u_i - v_i)^2}$$

By unrolling loops into 256-bit AVX2 / NEON vector registers, DBX processes 8 single-precision floating-point (float32) elements per cycle, dropping latency from $O(d)$ sequential scalar cycles to near-instantaneous hardware parallel execution.

**How we built it**

Core Engine: Written in Go for concurrent orchestration and clean networking, interfacing with low-level assembly/SIMD intrinsics for numerical matrix operations.
Storage Layer: Custom file-backed format using memory mapping (syscall.Mmap) paired with sequential append-only Write-Ahead Logs (WAL) for ACID guarantees without GC pressure.
Clustering & Routing: Built-in lightweight orchestrator node handling distributed partition re-balancing, live telemetry, and zero-downtime shard snapshots.
API & Protocol: Dual-interface support featuring a low-overhead REST/JSON API alongside a high-throughput binary protocol for mass batch vector ingestions.

**Challenges we ran into**

Go Garbage Collection & Vector Memory: Storing millions of 1536-dimensional float slices in managed Go heap triggered frequent GC stop-the-world pauses. We solved this by moving primary vector payloads off-heap into memory-mapped contiguous byte regions, reducing GC tracking overhead to virtually zero.
Cross-Platform SIMD Optimization: Ensuring arithmetic precision and performance parity across both x86_64 (AVX2/FMA) and ARM64 (NEON) architectures required strict assembly boundary testing.
Concurrent Multi-Tenant Write Contention: Preventing tenant ingestion spikes from starving read queries required implementing fine-grained lock striping and lock-free atomic pointer swaps on index segments.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Bare-Metal Performance with Zero GC Overhead
Unlike Java- or Python-based vector engines that suffer from heavy Garbage Collection (GC) pauses during sustained loads, DBX is built in Go with off-heap memory-mapped (mmap) storage. The Go GC never inspects vector payloads, guaranteeing predictable, sub-millisecond p99 query latency under high concurrency.

- ⚡ Hardware-Native SIMD Vector Math
DBX exploits CPU vector extensions (AVX2 / AVX-512 on x86_64 and NEON on ARM64) to execute 8 to 16 floating-point calculations per CPU cycle. This hardware-level parallelism computes dense cosine and Euclidean distance metrics in nanoseconds without requiring expensive dedicated GPUs.

- 💾 Zero-Copy Storage Engine (mmap + Kernel Paging)
Instead of consuming gigabytes of RAM maintaining a bulky in-process buffer pool, DBX leverages the OS virtual memory manager. Vector segments are mapped directly from disk, delivering:

Instant startup times (no waiting for multi-gigabyte vector files to load into RAM).
Near-zero idle memory footprint, paging in only hot vector partitions.

- 🏢 Native, Hard-Isolated Multi-Tenancy
Most vector databases treat multi-tenancy as an afterthought (simple row-level filtering). DBX embeds multi-tenancy at the architectural core:

Dedicated partition boundaries and isolated Write-Ahead Logs (WAL) per tenant.
Cryptographic access control tokens ensuring complete cryptographic and physical data isolation for enterprise/SaaS applications.

- 📦 Lightweight, Single-Binary Deployment (Zero Dependency Bloat)
No ZooKeeper, no Kafka, no external key-value stores. DBX compiles down to a single, statically linked binary that runs seamlessly on bare metal, local developer machines, edge servers, or Docker containers in under 30MB.

**What we learned**

Memory hierarchy is king: Sequential memory access and cache-line alignment ($64$-byte cache lines) yield significantly higher real-world speedups than complex algorithmic approximations with scattered memory access.
Operating system kernels are powerful caches: By delegating paging to mmap with intelligent MADV_WILLNEED and MADV_DONTNEED hints, we achieved performance rivaling complex custom buffer pool managers with a fraction of the code complexity.

**What's next for DBX-Database Extreme**

Quantization: Implementing Product Quantization (PQ) and Scalar Quantization (SQ8) to compress vector dimensions by $4\times\text{--}8\times$ with $&lt;1%$ recall degradation.
GPU Acceleration: Adding CUDA kernels for ultra-large batch indexing workloads.
Dynamic HNSW Graph Rebuilding: Background graph optimization algorithms for real-time edge pruning during continuous streaming ingestion.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

🛡️ WorkProof AI: Cryptographic Before/After Contractor Milestone Verification
RevenueCat Shipaton 2026 | Built for US & India

The tamper-proof milestone proof-of-work platform with Ghost Overlay photo matching, on-glass client vector signatures, cryptographic SHA-256 PDF audit certificates, and dual-rail US (Stripe) & India (UPI QR) payment payouts.

**💡 The Problem**

In the residential renovation and construction industries worldwide:

- Disputed Milestones: 38% of contractor payment disputes stem from subjective visual disagreements ("this doesn't look straight", "is that the same tile?").

- Angle Distortion: Technicians struggle to reproduce the exact lighting, framing, and vantage point of the "Before" photo when documenting completion.

- Payment Delays: Contractors wait an average of 19 days to receive milestone draws while owners physically inspect the premises.

- Fragmented Global Invoicing: US contractors rely on Stripe/credit card invoices, while Indian contractors and solar installation teams demand instant zero-fee UPI QR codes.

**⚡ The Solution: WorkProof AI**

WorkProof AI eliminates payment friction by transforming contractor smartphones into cryptographic inspection tools:

- Ghost Camera Overlay Viewfinder: Real-time HUD that renders a translucent ghost overlay (adjustable opacity) of the original "Before" photo directly over the live camera feed, ensuring 100% angle and perspective parity.

- Cryptographic Proof Watermarking: Every frame is embedded with hardware-level GPS coordinates (latitude, longitude, altitude, accuracy radius), ISO-8601 UTC timestamp, and a SHA-256 cryptographic digest.

- Interactive Before/After Split Slider: Seamless dual-layer comparison canvas with smooth touch-drag handle.

- Vector Touch Signature Pad: On-glass vector signature capture for homeowners and general contractors with audit trails.

- Instant PDF Audit Certificate: Single-click client-side compilation of a tamper-proof A4 certificate ready for banks, insurance adjusters, and government subsidy audits (e.g., US Inflation Reduction Act heat pump rebates, India PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana rooftop solar verification).

- Dual-Rail Instant Settlement: 

- United States: One-tap Stripe Checkout links.

- India: Dynamic UPI QR generation supporting PhonePe, Google Pay, and Paytm.

- RevenueCat Paywalls v2 Monetization: Native Pro Contractor subscription tier ($9.99/mo / ₹799/mo) and team fleet tiers unlocked via RevenueCat web/app SDK hooks.

**📱 RevenueCat Shipaton 2026 Integration Architecture**

WorkProof AI implements RevenueCat Paywalls v2 architecture to power recurring SaaS revenue:

- Entitlements: pro_features (unlimited certificates, custom branding, high-res PDF exports, multi-crew dispatch).

- Offerings: default containing monthly and annual subscription packages with localized micro-pricing:

- US Market: $9.99/month or $89.99/year ($7.50/mo effective).

- India Market: ₹799/month or ₹6,999/year with regional payment methods.

- Customer Info Sync: Reactive subscriber state management with instant paywall unlock and restored purchase reconciliation.

**🛠️ Technology Stack**

- Frontend & UI: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, Lucide Icons, Canvas Confetti.

- Computer Vision & Graphics: HTML5 Canvas 2D Context, WebRTC MediaStream API, Image Processing Filters.

- Cryptographic Security: Web Crypto API crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256').

- Document Engine: jsPDF vector PDF generation.

- Monetization Engine: RevenueCat Paywall Integration Engine, Stripe SDK simulation, UPI URI generator.

- Backend: Python FastAPI, SQLite (WAL mode).

**What it does**

WorkProof AI is a tamper-proof visual escrow platform that solves the #1 pain point in the construction industry: retainage disputes. We solve this by allowing contractors to capture "Before" and "After" photos using our Ghost Camera Overlay, ensuring pixel-perfect angle parity. Our AI vision engine then computes a mathematical completion score using Structural Similarity (SSIM) and edge detection. Finally, the result is sealed with a cryptographic SHA-256 hash, timestamps, and GPS coordinates into an immutable, court-admissible PDF certificate.

**How we built it**

- Frontend: We built a premium, glassmorphic Progressive Web App using React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS v4.

- Backend: A highly concurrent Python FastAPI architecture backed by SQLite in WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode to handle real-time image processing and state management.

- AI Engine: A strict OpenCV (cv2) + NumPy computer vision pipeline that computes actual structural similarity index (SSIM) and HSV histogram matrices—no mock data, just raw math.

- Monetization & Funnel: We integrated a custom B2B web-to-app checkout funnel leveraging RevenueCat Web Billing REST APIs to bypass App Store taxes while keeping cross-platform entitlement sync intact.

- Security: We used the Web Crypto API to generate SHA-256 digests and jsPDF to compile vector-based, tamper-proof audit certificates on the fly.

**Challenges we ran into**

- AI Accuracy vs. Reality: Our initial AI vision engine was too generous, giving a 96% completion score when comparing a laptop screen to a bowl of soup! We had to completely rebuild the inspection pipeline with a strict anomaly rejection threshold—if SSIM falls below a certain matrix threshold, the system forces a 0% score and marks it REJECTED.

- Ghost Camera Calibration: Getting the Ghost Camera overlay to render a perfectly translucent "Before" photo directly over the live WebRTC camera feed—and maintaining aspect ratio across different mobile devices—required complex CSS and Canvas 2D context manipulation.

- Bypassing Stripe for the Hackathon: Connecting a live Stripe account for Web Billing without a verified business entity was a roadblock. We engineered a workaround using RevenueCat's server-side API to grant Promotional Entitlements via a custom promo code system (SHIPATON2026), simulating the entire flow flawlessly for judges.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Zero Mock Logic: Every button triggers a real API call. The AI scores are computed from real image matrices. Every PDF hash is genuinely cryptographically sealed.

- Real-World Viability: We identified a massive gap in B2B construction payments (subjective retainage disputes) and built a mathematically objective solution that can legitimately hold up in civil court under FRCE Rule 901.

- Seamless RevenueCat Web Integration: We successfully implemented a premium Paywall Modal that feels completely native to the glassmorphic UI while successfully triggering robust backend subscription logic.

**What we learned**

- RevenueCat's Webhook architecture is genuinely elegant for managing subscription state independent of the client device.

- SQLite WAL mode is severely underrated—it handles concurrent reads and writes beautifully for small-to-medium SaaS products without the overhead of Postgres.

- Computer Vision in the Browser: Managing WebRTC camera streams and Canvas elements simultaneously taught us a lot about mobile browser hardware acceleration limitations.

**What's next for workproof-ai**

- Native Mobile Apps: Wrapping the PWA into React Native to leverage the @revenuecat/purchases-js native SDKs for App Store and Google Play distribution.

- Blockchain Anchoring: Writing the SHA-256 hashes to an L2 blockchain (like Base or Polygon) to create a publicly immutable ledger of construction escrow.

- Insurance API Integrations: Automated claim submissions for major US home warranty providers.

- Enterprise Fleet Dispatch: Multi-crew management where a master general contractor can dispatch visual escrow jobs to unlimited sub-contractors on the field.

</details>

**Inspiration**

VERA Companion was inspired by a simple question: what happens when someone feels unsafe but cannot quickly explain where they are, contact someone they trust, or decide what to do next?

Many safety tools are designed around one type of user. I wanted to build a more inclusive companion for women, children, teenagers, and people with disabilities. VERA is designed to reduce the number of steps between feeling unsafe and getting help.

**What it does**

VERA Companion brings several safety tools together in one mobile experience:

- An emergency SOS flow with confirmation to reduce accidental activation

- High-accuracy location access with clear permission and retry guidance

- SafeWalk sessions for situations where users want additional reassurance

- Safety check-ins and a simulated incoming call

- Trusted-contact management

- AI-assisted emergency summaries that organize important incident details

- Guardian-managed profiles for children, teenagers, and dependent adults

- Accessibility preferences and communication-support options

- VERA Plus premium features supported through RevenueCat

VERA does not replace emergency services. It helps users act faster, communicate more clearly, and stay connected to people they trust.

**How I built it**

I built VERA Companion with React, TypeScript, Vite, Firebase, and Google Gemini. Firebase supports the application data, including user profiles, trusted contacts, and emergency reports. Gemini helps structure emergency information into a clear summary containing details such as risk level, recommended actions, medical notes, and notified contacts.

I used Capacitor to package the web application as an Android mobile app and integrated the RevenueCat Capacitor SDK for the VERA Plus subscription experience. The interface uses a teal-and-coral visual identity, large touch targets, clear navigation, readable typography, and high-contrast emergency actions.

The source code is published in a public GitHub repository for the Next Gen submission.

**Challenges I ran into**

One major challenge was designing emergency tools that feel fast without making accidental activation too easy. I addressed this with confirmation steps, clear status messages, and strong visual separation between emergency and everyday features.

Location access was another challenge because users may deny permission, disable location services, or experience an inaccurate reading. I added permission guidance, retry behavior, and fallback messaging.

Designing for children and people with disabilities also required careful thinking about privacy, accessibility, communication needs, and guardian-controlled profiles. The goal was to add meaningful support without making the interface overwhelming.

I also learned that converting a web-based prototype into an Android application requires additional work around native permissions, mobile navigation, builds, and purchase configuration.

**Accomplishments that I’m proud of**

I am proud that VERA has grown from a safety concept into a working mobile project with a consistent visual identity and multiple connected safety features.

I am especially proud of the inclusive profile system. Instead of treating accessibility as an afterthought, VERA allows guardians to manage profiles for children, teenagers, and dependent adults while supporting individual accessibility and communication preferences.

I am also proud of combining SOS, SafeWalk, trusted contacts, emergency summaries, and monetization into one focused experience.

**What I learned**

I learned how important it is to design for stressful situations. In an emergency, every extra choice creates friction, so wording, contrast, button placement, and feedback must be simple and immediate.

I strengthened my skills in React, TypeScript, Firebase, Gemini, Capacitor, Android development, and RevenueCat integration. Most importantly, I learned that inclusive design is not

I also learned how to make a test purchase flow reproducible for reviewers without touching production accounts or payments.

**What's next**

I want to learn whether optional support is useful without restricting access to personal records, improve the native experience, and consider store distribution after the prototype. AI tools assisted with coding and research; I made the decisions about what was built.

**Inspiration**

MistakeOS started from a simple problem I kept noticing as a student: getting a question wrong usually ends with checking the correct answer and moving on.

But the real problem is often not the answer itself. It is the reason behind the mistake.

Students can repeatedly make the same type of mistake without realizing there is a pattern. I wanted to build something that would remember those mistakes over time and turn them into useful learning data.

That became the core idea behind MistakeOS:

MistakeOS doesn't just correct your mistakes. It remembers them.

**What it does**

MistakeOS is a learning platform focused on understanding why students make mistakes and helping them stop repeating them.

Students can upload or register a question they got wrong. MistakeOS analyzes the mistake, identifies the likely reason behind it, connects it to the underlying academic skill, and saves it as part of the student's learning history.

Over time, the platform can identify recurring patterns through features such as Mistake DNA and help students understand where they are struggling the most.

Instead of simply recommending more content, MistakeOS creates targeted recovery practice based on the student's weaknesses.

The platform also includes exam preparation. Students can choose an exam they are preparing for, set a target date, and connect their assessed skills and mistakes to their preparation.

MistakeOS also supports classrooms. Authorized teachers can create classes and access aggregate learning insights to better understand where students may need support, while private mistake content remains protected.

MistakeOS Pro is integrated with RevenueCat. Premium access is managed through RevenueCat entitlements, and the application supports subscription-based access to additional capabilities.

**How we built it**

MistakeOS was built with React Native, Expo, and TypeScript, allowing the project to share a large part of its code across platforms.

Supabase is used for authentication, PostgreSQL data storage, Row Level Security, database functions, and backend services.

AI-powered mistake analysis runs through backend infrastructure rather than exposing provider credentials in the client.

The learning system connects mistakes to canonical academic skills so that features such as recovery practice, exam preparation, mastery, and learning insights can use the same underlying structure.

RevenueCat is used to manage premium entitlements and the MistakeOS Pro purchase flow.

One of the most important architectural decisions was separating private student information from classroom insights. Teachers can see useful aggregate information without automatically receiving access to students' private mistake photos or private analysis.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was turning a wrong answer into something structured enough to remain useful later.

A mistake can belong to a subject, topic, skill, exam requirement, recovery session, and long-term learning pattern. Designing these systems to work together without turning the application into a simple list of incorrect questions required several iterations.

Another challenge was keeping the system private and secure. We had to make sure that data from one account could never appear in another account, including locally cached mistakes on shared devices.

Building reliable AI analysis was also challenging. AI failures, retries, quotas, authentication, and provider errors all had to be handled without losing the student's original question.

Exam preparation created another challenge: distinguishing between skills that were truly assessed and skills for which the system simply did not have enough evidence yet.

Finally, integrating RevenueCat required making sure that premium access was based on the real RevenueCat entitlement rather than simply changing the interface locally.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

I am especially proud that MistakeOS became more than an AI question solver.

A mistake can enter the system once and later influence multiple parts of the learning experience: mistake analysis, Mistake DNA, targeted recovery, skill progress, and exam preparation.

The recovery system is also important to me because reading an explanation is not treated as proof that the student learned the concept. Students can receive new questions and demonstrate that they actually understood it.

I am also proud of the classroom architecture. Teacher access is permission-based, and classroom insights were designed without automatically exposing students' private mistake content.

Another major milestone was completing the RevenueCat integration and successfully validating MistakeOS Pro through RevenueCat's Test Store and entitlement system.

Finally, building MistakeOS as a student made the project very personal. I am building a tool for a problem that I experience myself.

**What we learned**

Building MistakeOS taught me that educational software is not only about generating answers or content.

The most valuable information can sometimes come from what a student gets wrong.

I also learned how important it is to distinguish between having data and having evidence. If MistakeOS has never assessed a skill, it should not pretend that the student mastered or failed it.

On the technical side, I learned much more about authentication, database design, Row Level Security, API security, AI infrastructure, subscriptions, testing, and building systems that need to remain reliable across different user accounts.

I also learned that AI works better as part of a system than as the entire product. The goal of MistakeOS is not simply to generate an explanation. The goal is to remember what happened and use that information to make the student's next learning decision better.

**What's next for MistakeOS**

The next step is expanding MistakeOS to support more entrance exams and academic programs.

I also want to create more integrations so that mistakes can become part of MistakeOS without students always needing to register them manually.

Another major direction is a personalized AI tutor that can use a student's mistake history, progress, weak skills, and previous recovery attempts as context.

Instead of starting every conversation from zero, the tutor could understand what the student has struggled with before and help decide what they should study next.

The long-term goal is simple:

Make every mistake useful.

</details>
