<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/813/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/813/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/814/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/814/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/868/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/868/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/815/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/468/815/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

The night before my first engineering interview I knew my story by heart, but I had never said it out loud to three people whose job was to push back. When the first question came, the answer came out vague. Nobody told me why it did not land.

Most students are in the same place. Hiring now takes about 20 interviews per hire, up from 14 in 2021. A coach who will actually push back costs around $207 an hour, and the free practice tools are shutting down. I wanted the practice room I did not have.

**What it does**

HardTalk puts you in the room before the real thing. You pick what you are preparing for: a job interview, the Q&A after a pitch, a debate, or a hard talk at work. The brief shows who is in the room and what each person will ask about. Then you talk out loud to a panel of AI interviewers, each with their own face, voice and line of questioning, with live captions for everyone.

When the conversation ends you get a scorecard on four skills, each built on a named framework such as STAR, SBI, SPIN Selling or Toulmin. Every score above 1 has to quote something you actually said, and you get one better line to try. You retry and see the change side by side, including which interviewers you won over.

In my demo, my vague first answer scored 9 out of 16 and nobody in the room was convinced. On the retry I owned the failure and gave the numbers, scored 16 out of 16, and won over all three.

With Pro you can bring the real one: paste the job posting you are applying to, your pitch, or the motion, and HardTalk builds the panel for that exact moment.

**How I built it**

The app is Expo with React Native and TypeScript in strict mode. The voices come from an ElevenLabs agent over WebRTC, with one voice per interviewer. A small Hono server holds every provider key, mints short lived voice tokens, grades transcripts, checks safety and drafts panels, so no key ever reaches the app.

The grader is always a different model family from the interviewers, so it never marks its own roleplay. It runs on Claude, or for free on a local open model through any OpenAI compatible API. Code, not the model, checks every quote against the transcript, and a score whose quote was never said drops to 1.

Rubrics, scenarios and prompts live in YAML so anyone can read them without reading code. The repo has 1,391 passing tests, and a mock mode runs the whole loop with no keys and no network in about a minute.

**How it uses RevenueCat**

There is one entitlement, pro. The paywall opens at only two real boundaries: starting a fourth graded session, and building your own panel. Its copy is filled in for that moment through custom variables, so at the session limit it names the conversation you are practising and your score on it so far. A customer info listener unlocks Pro the moment the purchase lands, with no restart, and Restore Purchases is on the home screen and the paywall. Plans are Weekly at $2.99 for the week before one real conversation, Monthly at $4.99 and Annual at $29.99, all below the education category median in RevenueCat's own report.

**Challenges I ran into**

Making scores people can trust. A language model will happily invent a quote, so I built an evidence gate in code that rejects anything that was never said.

Keeping people safe. A practice tool must never ignore real distress, so a stop word ends any session at once, and distress checks run on every line on the device and again on the server, never scored.

Keeping it affordable for students, which is why the grader can run on a free local model and there is a weekly plan.

**Accomplishments I'm proud of**

A real session on a real phone, from a vague first try to a perfect retry, with a working RevenueCat purchase in the middle. Scores that always show their evidence. A full path that works with a screen reader and no audio.

**What I learned**

Grounding matters more than clever prompts. The most useful thing a grader can do is show you the exact words that cost you points, and the hardest part of building it was making sure those words are real.

**What's next**

Getting it into the hands of students before placement season, adding more scenarios for each track, measuring the grader on gold sets for every track, and shipping on iOS.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Bridging the primary care bottleneck with 100% on-device, dual-agent medical intelligence powered by Google MedGemma 1.5 4B.**

DISCLAIMER: Decurandi Mobile is an very early-stage, vibe-coded research demo with identified edge-hardware limitations. Always consult a licensed physician for healthcare decisions.

**💡 Inspiration**

Visiting a doctor often comes with a glaring information asymmetry. Patients arrive feeling anxious, struggling to describe complex physical symptoms, and often forget critical timeline details. On the other side, clinicians face burnout, spending precious consultation minutes extracting basic history and answering repetitive questions rather than focusing on physical examination and targeted diagnosis.

We created Decurandi Mobile to bridge this pre-consultation gap. By empowering patients to reflect on their health and structure their symptoms before stepping into the clinic, we save valuable face-to-face examination time, lower patient anxiety, and give doctors a high-accountability clinical summary from second one.

**🩺 What It Does**

Decurandi Mobile is an offline-first, pre-visit assistant that uses a dual-agent clinical synthesis engine to prepare both the patient and the physician before a medical appointment:

- Patient Guide Agent (For the Patient): Runs asynchronously to translate complex medical findings into calming, plain-language summary (9th–12th grade reading level). Intended to de-escalates patient anxiety.

- Clinical Doctor Agent (For the Physician): Runs immediately upon symptom input to generate clinical summary. It outputs a professional History of Present Illness (HPI), extracts high-risk clinical Red Flags, and suggests the top 3 Differential Diagnoses (DDx) formatted to clinical standards.

- 100% On-Device Confidentiality: Because medical history is extremely sensitive, zero patient data leaves the phone. The entire 4-Billion parameter neural network executes locally on the device's GPU/CPU with zero cloud calls, zero API keys, and zero PHI tracking.

**⚡ How We Built It**

- Vibe-coding with Antigravity and Google Gemini 3.8, building Cross-Platform Mobile Application. 

- Built with Flutter & Dart for a seamless, fluid UI featuring voice dictation and responsive card components.

- On-Device LLM Runtime: Integrated Google MedGemma 1.5 4B IT executed locally via LiteRT-LM (Google AI Edge runtime), taking full advantage of local mobile GPU/CPU acceleration.

**🚧 Challenges We Ran Into**

- Resource-Constrained Edge Hardware: Running a quantized ~2.5 GB medical model locally on budget mobile hardware (such as our reference benchmark device, the Samsung Galaxy A25 5G with an Exynos 1280 processor) pushed RAM and thermal boundaries. 

- Inference Latency UX: On budget chipsets, a complete dual-agent synthesis takes 4 to 6 minutes (~1.5–2 min for the Doctor's Note and ~2.5–3.5 min for the Patient Guide). Designing an intuitive UX that manages user expectations while keeping execution running safely in the foreground was critical.

- 4B LLM Prompt Engineering & Hallucinations: Smaller on-device models are prone to "instruction echo" and demographic bias (e.g., hallucinating patient age/sex based on textbook case archetypes). 

**🎉 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of**

- Local Medical AI Demo: Manage to running a 4-Billion parameter specialized medical model 100% offline on an affordable, mid-range Android device with zero cloud server reliance.

- Dual-Agent Harmonization: Getting two distinct AI personalities (a rigorous clinical physician and an empathetic family doctor) to coordinate seamlessly off a single user input prompt.

- Privacy-Preserving Healthcare: Proving that advanced clinical triage tools can operate without sacrificing patient confidentiality or incurring massive cloud server bills.

**📚 What We Learned**

- Memory management and token budget optimization for LiteRT-LM on mobile architectures.

- Strategies for eliminating prompt leaks, demographic hallucinations, and instruction echoes in 4B-parameter LLMs.

**🚀 What's Next for Decurandi Mobile v1.0.0**

- Model Fine-Tuning & Quantization: Exploring custom LoRA adapters to further compress MedGemma without losing clinical diagnostic precision.

- Hardware Benchmarking Framework: Building an automated test harness across edge device categories to reduce inference time down to seconds.

- RevenueCat Pro Features: Expanding our RevenueCat integration to include downloadable PDF Clinical Briefs, multi-lingual patient guide translations, and Apple Health / Google Health Connect integrations.

</details>

> Your phone becomes the angle gauge for the five-minute vertigo cure, and it won't start the timer until your head is actually in position.

- **Team:** [Anuj Ojha](https://devpost.com/0105cb231013)

- **Repo check:** public repo · license: MIT · 77 commits · Kotlin · RevenueCat found in code ✅ · ⚠️ last commit 2026-10-01 (after Sep 30 deadline)
- **Built with:** android, gradle, jetpack-compose, kotlin, playwrigh, revenuecat, robolectric, roborazzi, three.js

**Video (1:53):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F9ePwouzgn4

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/F9ePwouzgn4/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F9ePwouzgn4)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/924/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/924/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/925/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/925/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/926/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/926/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/927/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/927/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/928/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/928/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/929/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/929/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/988/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/988/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

BPPV is the most common cause of vertigo. The fix is the Epley manoeuvre: a few head positions, about five minutes, no medicine. When I read the research I found that in a German population study only 8% of people with BPPV received effective treatment, and that people doing it at home from a video get their head angles wrong by 40 to 51 degrees. The treatment exists. Getting the angles right alone, at 3 a.m., while the room is spinning, is the hard part. Every phone already has the sensors to measure a head angle, so I wanted to see if a phone could guide it properly.

**What it does**

- Safety check first, every run. Positional vertigo can sometimes be a stroke, and an app cannot see the eye movements that tell them apart. So before anything else it asks about red-flag symptoms. Any yes stops the app and points you to emergency help. It can't be skipped and it is never behind a paywall.

- Finds which ear. BPPV often comes back somewhere different: in a 585-patient randomised trial (JAMA Neurology 2023), 56% of failed home treatments were a different type of BPPV from the original diagnosis. Using six questions from that trial resolved 72.4% of recurrences, compared with 42.9% when people reused their old diagnosis. If the answers point to the horizontal canal, the app says the Epley is the wrong manoeuvre.

- Guides every position. You hold the phone against your cheek, calibrate seated, and the app tracks both head angles live (turn and tip). Each position is shown on a 3D head. The 45-second hold timer only counts while your head is inside the target range and still, and a voice talks you through it, because by position four you can't look at the screen.

- After-care and a doctor's PDF. It gives the after-care advice from the clinical guideline, and you can export every run (ear, time, hold times and measured angles) as a PDF for your doctor.

**How I built it**

- Kotlin and Jetpack Compose for Android. All the maths (quaternions, swing-twist decomposition, angle unwrapping, the hold gate, the triage and after-care rules) lives in a pure Kotlin module with no Android code, so it is tested on the JVM in seconds.

- The phone's game rotation vector sensor (gyroscope and accelerometer, fused). Every angle is measured relative to a calibration on your own head, so the phone's fixed sensor error cancels out.

- A real 3D head model rendered with three.js for the position figures.

- RevenueCat for the one paid feature (details below).

- 212 automated tests, plus screenshot tests (Robolectric and Roborazzi) that compare every screen against the design, day and night.

- I built it on a Windows laptop with no Android Studio, everything from the command line, and I used Claude Code a lot as my pair programmer.

**Challenges I ran into**

- A single phone sensor can't tell "the head turned" from "the phone slipped on the cheek". I handle it by speed: a turn faster than a neck can move triggers a "the phone moved" warning and asks you to recalibrate.

- My test phone reads about 8 degrees off true when lying flat. Instead of trusting the hardware, every angle is relative to the calibration, and I wrote a test that pushes 9.2 degree offsets through the real code to prove the guided angles don't move.

- Designing for someone who is dizzy right now: one action per screen, big type, a night theme, a voice, and calm motion only. Nothing spins, because for this user a moving screen is a symptom.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- The timer genuinely refuses to start until both angles are in range and you are still. That one rule is the whole point of the app.

- Every clinical number in the app traces back to a citation in the repo, including the ones that made my pitch weaker.

- It is my first Android app, and it is fully open source.

**What I learned**

How phone orientation sensors really work (and fail), how to read clinical trials carefully instead of overselling them, and how much design matters when your user is unwell.

**What's next for Epley Coach**

A small supervised study with a physiotherapist to check the angle guidance on real patients, a headband mount option for steadier readings, and an iOS version.

**Honest limits**

Epley Coach is not a medical device. It claims angle accuracy, which I measured on my own phone, and nothing about cure rates, which nobody has tested for this app.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/838/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/838/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/839/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/472/839/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Inspiration
I wanted to learn Russian fast, and not just read it but sound local. Textbook apps taught me words no one actually says, in an accent no one uses. What I really wanted was to learn from the videos I already watch, understand every line, then practice saying those lines until they sounded native. I couldn't find an app that did that, so I built one, for seven languages (Russian, Korean, Japanese, Chinese, Spanish, French, German).

What it does
Linguaah opens YouTube inside the app and turns whatever you're watching into a lesson.

Understand every line. As the video plays, the line being spoken shows in your target language, with natural English under it and every word tappable for its meaning in that sentence.
Subtitles even when YouTube's are wrong or missing. YouTube's auto captions mishear real speech, and some videos have none. When that happens, Linguaah listens to the audio and writes accurate, timed subtitles itself.
Save a line, keep the real scene. Tap to save and it becomes a flashcard with the actor's own voice and the exact frame it was said over, not a robot reading it back.
Study with spaced repetition, fully on your device.
Sound local. The part I built for myself: cut a scene, record each line in your own voice, slow the video down while you practice, then hear yourself played back over the real scene.
How I built it
React Native and Expo (SDK 57, New Architecture) with on device SQLite for the flashcards. A WebView runs YouTube, and an injected script reads the captions and intercepts the video's own media stream for the scene audio and frames, so nothing is ever downloaded. Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite handles in context translation, word meanings, and transcribing audio into subtitles, batched and cached to stay cheap (about two tenths of a cent per minute). RevenueCat powers Pro, which also matters because I'm in a country where Stripe isn't an option.

Challenges
My sister tried it and the translations were off, because YouTube had misheard the speech. Fixing it meant having the app listen and write its own subtitles, and getting the lines to switch exactly when the words are spoken. Getting the actor's real voice onto a card without downloading the video took intercepting the stream the player already had. And I had to keep it nearly free to run, built solo, tested on friends and family who told me exactly what was broken.

What I learned
How to intercept and reassemble a video's media stream, how to turn an LLM into a reliable transcriber on a budget, React Native's New Architecture, and how RevenueCat makes payments work where the usual options don't.

</details>

**Inspiration**

As digital creators, influencers, and social media managers scale their brands, they waste critical time switching between note apps, link aggregators, and credential managers. SnippetVault Pro was inspired by the need for a unified, hyper-fast, zero-lag console matrix that keeps vital links, text disclaimers, text templates, and security credentials organized under a single user pipeline.

**What it does**

SnippetVault Pro acts as a high-performance workspace ledger for creators. It aggregates essential web brand registries, secure credential vault storage keys, and cloud data vectors into a zero-lag unified matrix. It securely tracks user entries and natively implements a sandbox tier limits configuration. When a standard user attempts to breach the maximum 4 free slots allocation limit, a native paywall layout sheets system intercepts the flow dynamically to offer a premium option.

**How i built it**

Engineered completely from scratch as a solo student developer using Flutter (Dart) for cross-platform target deployment capability. The app features:

- A custom State-Machine Lifecycle Controller managing fluid workflow view transitions (SPLASH -&gt; LOGIN -&gt; CINEMATIC_WELCOME -&gt; DASHBOARD).

- A Persistent State Cache Engine utilizing SharedPreferences to ensure zero data serialization loss upon application process resets.

- An optimized CORS-Immune UI Vector Matrix utilizing localized vector graphics to protect the layout from external asset loading lag.

- A dynamic RevenueCat SDK paywall trigger modal workflow that dynamically gates workspace item limits at the 4th slot threshold.

**Challenges i ran into**

Building a multi-tier dashboard layout entirely alone while balancing final-year BTech engineering classes was a massive challenge. The hardest problem was ensuring the dynamic paywall sheet popped up instantly without disrupting the application lifecycle state or freezing background system memory pools. I solved this by tracking cache entries inside the main framework flow container state before calling the overlay sheet.

**Accomplishments that im proud of**

I am incredibly proud of designing and launching a complete cross-platform product framework from scratch as a solo developer. Managing to resolve syntax issues, stabilize local caching mechanics, and design a beautiful, fully functional animated color mesh interface independently has been an amazing engineering milestone.

**What i learned**

This project pushed my cross-platform mobile engineering skills to the next level. I learned how to structure robust caching mechanics using key-value pair serialization, how to build smooth UI entry animations using AnimatedSwitcher, and how simple it is to native-link a testing sandbox payment workflow using the RevenueCat SDK engine.

**What's next for SnippetVault Pro**

The next step is officially launching SnippetVault Pro to the public app stores! I plan to expand the platform by adding full native system keyboard extension overlays and home screen widget support so creators can access their aggregated media ledgers instantly from any app on their devices.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

When I upgraded my computers and gaming consoles, selling the old ones meant looking up prices across marketplaces and writing another listing. Even after choosing a price, I still had to recreate the listing wherever I wanted to sell it.

I started SnapList around that problem. I wanted to photograph an item, add the details I knew, and get a listing I could review before posting. I'm a computer science student at the University of Central Florida, and this is my entry for the Shipaton 2026 Next Gen Award.

**What it does**

SnapList is a native iPhone app for preparing used-item listings. You take one to five photos and can add a voice note with details the photos might miss. It prepares an editable listing with a suggested price and shows the evidence available for that recommendation.

The voice note can help resolve a product family when the photos support it. Seller-provided details stay identified as unverified context. Sold comparisons use completed sales with a known sold amount. An asking price is what someone hopes to get; it does not establish what a buyer paid. SnapList distinguishes an exact item from a broader model-family or category comparison, and shows an estimate when trustworthy sold evidence is missing.

Once an item is accepted, you can start photographing the next one while it finishes. To list holds items that still need work. Flips holds finished items, including prepared or shared export packs. You can edit the listing and choose your own price before delivery.

The eBay publishing path requires seller confirmation. For Facebook Marketplace, Mercari, and Depop, SnapList prepares text and photos for a manual handoff, and the seller finishes posting in the destination app.

The first usable AI listing comes before signup or a paywall. SnapList Pro supports continued AI listing preparation through a RevenueCat subscription. The subscription code loads offerings and supports purchase and restore, with server verification before granting access.

**How I built it**

I made the product and architecture decisions and used coding agents to help implement SnapList, especially the native client. The iPhone app uses SwiftUI with Apple's camera and audio frameworks. The server is TypeScript with Next.js, and Supabase stores the item data with row-level security and private media storage.

The AI pipeline validates structured outputs with Zod through the Vercel AI SDK. Model selection lives behind a provider registry. Pricing has its own router, including ISBN lookup, eBay sold research, and fallback estimates. The Apify adapter retrieves sold candidates, and a shared matcher checks which comparisons are relevant before they can support the price.

Accepted items run through a durable queue so recovery can reuse completed work. The seller's chosen price is shared by publishing and export paths. RevenueCat handles the subscription SDK flow, while the server verifies access and accounts for AI items when a usable draft is saved. A failure before that usable result restores the reserved credit.

The public repository includes the native app and server code, setup instructions, and an Apache-2.0 license.

**Challenges I ran into**

Product identity was a difficult part of pricing. A photo may identify a family while leaving the exact version unclear, and a spoken model name can be transcribed incorrectly. The pipeline has to keep the useful identity while preserving the uncertainty. Otherwise it can skip relevant sold research or compare the wrong item.

Another challenge was deciding what counts as a completed action. A copied export pack does not tell us whether a marketplace listing exists. A subscription response also needs server verification before the app can grant AI access. Those distinctions affect the copy people see and the states the app saves.

**Accomplishments I'm proud of**

I'm proud of the path between taking photos and reviewing a listing. The seller can inspect the price evidence and change the result before deciding what to do with it. Scout, the app's mascot, helps make the waiting and subscription screens feel consistent with the rest of the app.

Beta testers with the same resale problem told me that SnapList made price research and listing preparation easier. Their feedback drove more work on the app. I have qualitative feedback so far, and I still need to measure the time savings.

**What I learned**

I learned to treat the quality of a price recommendation as a separate question from whether an AI response sounds convincing. The comparison needs to be relevant to the item, and the seller needs to see how strong that evidence is.

I also learned how much product behavior depends on details outside the main AI call. A retry should preserve completed work, and changing the seller's price needs to affect every place the listing goes. Those details became part of the design and the tests.

**What's next for SnapList**

I want to finish device checks for subscription purchase and restore, and for the eBay publishing journey. I'm also continuing to refine the sharing drawer and how the app presents weaker sold comparisons.

After that, I want to measure processing time and the cost of each usable AI listing with TestFlight feedback. Those results will inform the Pro allowance and the next App Store release work.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Try it in the browser: https://rootera.byguto.com (the first load can take about 50 seconds). The Shipaton lab is on the Today tab. The web demo is not connected to the RevenueCat and Pl@ntNet APIs: purchases run as a labelled preview that charges nothing, and photo identification is off. Everything else works.

**Inspiration**

When I moved to São Paulo, I started keeping plants. Caring for them was harder than I expected: every guide says "water when the soil is dry", but nobody tells you how deep to check or how long your plant takes to dry.

My first idea was a soil sensor on an ESP32. Then I realized the same logic could work without hardware: a few quick soil checks are enough for an app to learn each plant's rhythm.

**What it does**

You check the soil in three layers (surface, middle, bottom). After a few watering cycles, Rootera learns how long your plant takes to dry, adjusts for the local weather and tells you when to check again, always showing why. Pl@ntNet identifies the plant from a photo.

**How I built it**

The app is Expo (React Native, TypeScript), with Reanimated for the animations, and runs on iOS, Android and the web. A FastAPI + SQLAlchemy backend stores every check as an event and runs the Plant Twin: a small set of explainable rules that turns your checks, species notes and the local weather (Open-Meteo) into a drying window. The rules are calibrated against university extension guides and covered by 210 tests.

The Shipaton lab runs the same engine on a virtual plant for up to 91 days in real climates, so you can watch Rootera learn in seconds.

**How RevenueCat is used**

Free keeps three plants. Rootera+ (monthly, quarterly or yearly) removes the limit and adds rooms and a growth diary. The paywall is a RevenueCat Paywall, subscribers manage their plan in the Customer Center, and the backend confirms every purchase with RevenueCat's REST API, so the app never unlocks anything on its own.

**What I learned**

This was the first app I built end to end: connecting a front end to a back end, designing the data model, and shipping a real subscription flow with RevenueCat.

</details>

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/xJMB5TiQzio/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xJMB5TiQzio)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/471/463/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/471/463/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/997/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/997/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/998/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/998/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/999/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/999/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I'm a sophomore at ASU. I'd pick up my phone to check one thing and look up an hour later. Everyone around me was doing the same thing, and it was normal.

So I tried what everyone tries. Apple Screen Time first, and I tapped "Ignore Limit" every time. Then I paid for a blocker, and I tapped past that too. The block was never the problem. The problem was that when it stopped me, it left me with nothing to do instead, so I went right back.

That's the idea behind BrainDiet: you feed your body well. Your brain eats too. It should be fed what the person you want to become would feed it.

**What it does**

BrainDiet blocks the apps that cost you time, then hands you one thing to do toward the person you said you wanted to be.

- Pick who you want to become. Reading, fitness, building, social, mindful, and more. Each goal gets broken into steps small enough to do today, written around your actual answers ("which book?", "what are you building?").

- Block what costs you. It uses Apple's Screen Time frameworks, so the block holds at the system level, not inside the app.

- The shield is the product. When you open a blocked app, it doesn't say "you're blocked." It says what you wanted and what to do right now: "You wanted to be social. Go talk to a stranger." "You wanted to get stronger. Go touch some iron." Every time you take the way out, the next shield speaks to your next goal.

- Three passes a day. Hold an app to let yourself in for 3 minutes. Sometimes the answer really is "not now."

- Becoming. It shows what the time you didn't scroll turned into, and moves the date you'll hit your goal closer as you keep going.

One version, no feature tiers. 3 days free, then $4.99 a week or $19.99 once, because people are sick of subscriptions.

**How I built it**

- Swift 6 and SwiftUI, iOS 26, built solo across 40 TestFlight builds.

- FamilyControls, ManagedSettings and DeviceActivity for blocking and usage. Two app extensions: a ShieldConfiguration extension that draws the custom shield, and a ShieldAction extension that handles the taps (passes, and rotating to the next goal).

- RevenueCat runs every purchase. Both plans live in one Offering with weekly and lifetime packages that unlock a single entitlement. The paywall reads its prices live from the Offering, so prices and currencies are always right without an app update. Restore and the entitlement check are RevenueCat's too.

- Personalization runs on-device. The plan is built deterministically from your onboarding answers, so it works on any phone with no network call. The step list is capped at three: finish them and you get three more. I kept AI from deciding what you do, because the failure of most AI goal apps is that you end up talking about your goals instead of doing them.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Screen Time doesn't run in the Simulator. Every blocking change had to be tested on a real phone through TestFlight.

- Builds 12 and 13 shipped an empty shield extension. A missing compiler flag compiled the whole extension to nothing, so iOS silently fell back to its grey default screen. I added a guard that makes the build fail instead of shipping empty.

- Apps are private by design. BrainDiet can't read the name or icon of an app you block; only the system can draw them. Every screen that shows your blocked apps is built around that.

- iOS 26 added a new permission state that read as "not authorized" until I mapped it correctly.

- App Store Connect pricing through the API needed every territory set before a product would leave "missing metadata."

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- A shield that people want to read instead of fight. It names who you want to be instead of telling you no.

- A real, working purchase flow on RevenueCat with one honest version of the app, no paywalled features.

- Getting approved by Apple for the Family Controls entitlement and shipping 40 builds solo.

**What I learned**

Blocking is the easy half. People don't scroll because they lack willpower; they scroll because the feed fills empty time. If you take the feed away, you have to give the time somewhere to go. I also learned to ship the boring parts right, like extension signing and App Store pricing, because one missing piece breaks the whole thing.

**What's next for BrainDiet**

- App Store launch this fall.

- Launch at ASU first, then U.S. colleges, through creator content about getting off your phone.

- Smarter steps that learn which ones you actually finish.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Children have so much to watch—but childhood is also for making things, asking questions, noticing the world, and trying ideas.

We remembered looking at the night sky with our families, hearing stories about stars, and discovering something through a simple conversation. We wanted to help families create more of those moments.

That inspired Constellation: a little world where digital play becomes a starting point for real-world curiosity.

Our guiding idea is simple:

Most technology competes for children’s attention. Constellation competes for their curiosity.

**What it does**

Constellation connects two ways to explore:

- Planet — play here: children manipulate objects, test ideas, and create things through interactive exercises.

- Out There — try it nearby: children take related ideas into the real world, with preparation and safety guidance.

- My Finds — remember discoveries: children revisit digital creations and reported real-world experiences, with their origins clearly distinguished.

Activities include experimenting with paper bridges, connecting imagined stars in The Night Letter, exploring number patterns through Vedic Maths, and investigating illustrated fruits, birds, and forest animals.

The real-world library spans six curiosity areas: Nature & Noticing, Make & Create, Talk & Connect, Test & Discover, Everyday Skills, and Move & Be Brave.

Guardian setup captures a nickname, age band, interests, support preferences, and allowed places. These choices help shape age-appropriate experiences for children ages 6–12.

Completed real-world missions become gold stars. These represent what a child reports trying—not grades, rankings, or verified mastery.

A protected grown-up area manages Constellation Family, powered by RevenueCat. Our Next Gen demonstration uses RevenueCat Test Store for simulated purchases without charging users.

**How we built it**

We built Constellation with Expo, React Native, TypeScript, and Expo Router, using SQLite for local persistence.

A structured experience catalog separates activity content from eligibility rules, recommendations, and progress. Real-world suggestions consider age, place, companions, materials, and other safety conditions before ranking experiences.

Interactive scenes use SVG artwork, touch controls, and animation. We carried a consistent visual language across the app: lavender backgrounds, Quicksand typography, rounded surfaces, near-black outlines, and purposeful color accents.

We integrated RevenueCat for paywalls, purchases, entitlement checking, restoration, and membership management. Purchasing uses an anonymous identity; we do not attach child names, mission answers, or progress as purchase attributes.

We also created a standalone Android judge build that embeds the app and supports RevenueCat’s Test Store configuration without requiring Expo Go or a development server.

**Challenges we ran into**

Our biggest challenge was making the experience feel like play, rather than a list of activities.

Early versions relied too heavily on descriptions, choices, and timers. We had to rethink the interaction: what can a child change, what happens because of that change, and why would they want to try again?

Touch behavior was another challenge. Drawing, sliders, and movement controls needed to work comfortably on a phone—not just look correct on a desktop preview.

We also had to distinguish digital simulation from real-world observation. A simulated bridge is not an engineering prediction, and finishing an activity does not prove that a child has mastered a concept.

Finally, Android packaging and RevenueCat Test Store compatibility required careful debugging so judges could install a standalone build and explore membership functionality.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We’re proud of connecting playful screen interactions to concrete things children can do beyond the screen.

We established a consistent identity across games, field guides, real-world missions, and learning memories. We also built local persistence, resumable activity flows, and a clear separation between child exploration and grown-up purchasing.

Our automated checks cover important behavior, including eligibility, sanitized learning evidence, persistence, and duplicate-completion protection.

Most importantly, Constellation does not depend on streaks, rankings, advertising, or an open-ended AI chat to give children a reason to explore.

**What we learned**

We learned that attractive artwork alone does not make an engaging learning experience. Children need a clear invitation, a meaningful action, and a response they can understand.

We learned to ask a stronger design question:

What can the child discover by doing this—not merely by reading it?

We also learned that parent trust comes from honest boundaries: explaining what stays local, separating observed digital actions from reported physical experiences, and avoiding claims of mastery.

Testing and iteration remain essential. Technical checks can verify behavior, but observing children and families is necessary to understand whether the experience is clear, enjoyable, and useful.

**What's next for Constellation**

Our next priority is testing with families across the three age bands and improving the moments where children hesitate or need help.

We want to refine touch interactions, expand accessible voice guidance, strengthen content and safety review, and give every exercise a clearer purpose and satisfying outcome.

We also plan to expand the living world with more connected discoveries—while keeping purchases guardian-only and preserving the distinction between playing here and trying something out there.

Our ambition is not to make children stay longer.

It is to help them leave with an idea worth trying.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Shipaton 2026 — Next Gen Award entry. Judged on this video and the open-source
repo (AGPL-3.0): https://github.com/HarmanPreet-Singh-XYT/ranmap — Flutter app in
lib/, Node backend in server/, Next.js site in web-app/, migrations in
supabase/migrations/. Setup steps are in the README. No store release is
required for this category, so the demo video shows the app running on a real
Android device.
made for mobile devices (IOS,Android), web companion as to plan stuff around before initiating the trip.

**Inspiration**

Navigation and fitness apps are built for one person. You type a destination,
you drive, and the people you're travelling with effectively disappear — they
become a text thread, a phone call, and a "where are you?" at the next fuel
stop. Group travel is one of the most social things we do, yet the software
treats it as a solo activity.

Ranmap started from a simple, familiar frustration: on a group road trip, nobody
actually knows where anyone is. Someone drops behind, someone misses the turn,
someone's low on fuel, and the real plan lives in five separate heads. We wanted
the map itself to be shared — one screen where the whole crew is visible, moving,
and reachable at once. Not a location tracker bolted onto a maps app, but a map
that assumes you're riding together.

That one idea — ride together, stay in sync — became the lens for every
decision after it. Solo features (search, navigation, saved places) exist only
as the on-ramp to a shared trip, never as the headline.

**What it does**

Ranmap puts your entire road-trip crew on one live 3D map, and gives the group
everything it needs to move as a unit.

- Live 3D convoy — every teammate appears on the map as their own vehicle
(car, bike, scooter or SUV), rendered as a real 3D model on Mapbox Standard's
extruded buildings, terrain and time-of-day lighting. Positions update live,
and keep updating while the app is backgrounded.

- Push-to-talk voice and realtime chat — a LiveKit audio room per trip and
per group, with a walkie-talkie push-to-talk mode, speaking indicators and
auto-reconnect, alongside live group text.

- Shared trip toolkit — reorderable stops with a next-stop ETA banner,
weather at each planned arrival, an expense ledger with a fuel-cost estimate
projected over the whole route, and a shared packing checklist.

- AI trip assistant — a chat assistant (Gemini with Google Search grounding)
that doesn't just answer questions: it acts. It can create a trip, schedule
it, invite a friend, save a place, or add and propose stops through real
function tools.

- Group convoy — a persistent crew screen that works independently of any
trip, with SOS to the whole group, "regroup here" with automatic check-in at a
meeting point, and quick statuses like "Wait up" and "Need fuel".

- Receipts on every expense — attach photos of bills to a shared expense
(1 per expense on Free, 10 on Pro, 25 on Extreme), visible to everyone on the trip.

- Consent-based crews — friends are invited to groups and trips and must
accept, so nobody is added silently; per-user DM privacy controls who can message you.

- Web companion — a Next.js site (web-app/) where the crew can chat, plan
trips, split expenses and view profiles from a laptop.

- A link anyone can follow — the trip creator can mint a public, read-only
page that family at home can watch with no account and no app.

- Offline-first — writes made without signal queue in a persisted outbox and
replay idempotently; map tiles for a route can be downloaded for use with no
connection at all.

**Monetization**

Ranmap is subscription-first, built end to end on RevenueCat, with three
tiers and a generous free on-ramp so the app is useful before anyone pays.

- Free — full solo navigation plus the core crew features, with metered AI
and search, capped at 3 active trips, 25 pinned photos and 6 group
members.

- Pro — $4.99/mo or $39.99/yr — raises the caps (~100 trips, 5,000 photos,
100 members), unlocks the full trip stats and history, and a much larger AI and
search allowance.

- Extreme — $9.99/mo or $79.99/yr — the same features with the highest
ceilings (~250 trips, 20,000 photos, 250 members).

- Both paid tiers include a 7-day free trial on the annual plans, and the
paywall reads live store prices from the RevenueCat offering rather than
hard-coding them.

Two things make the monetization fit the product instead of fighting it. First,
one subscription covers the whole crew: because Pro is evaluated per trip and
per group, a single subscriber unlocks voice and lifts the caps for everyone they
travel with — so paying benefits your friends, who then want it too. Second, the
gates are real: entitlement truth is written only by our server from the
RevenueCat v2 API, and the hard caps are enforced by database triggers, so a
patched client can't unlock anything. A free user hitting a limit gets a
contextual paywall; a paid user hitting a fair-use ceiling gets a plain error,
never an upsell.

**How I built it**

- Client — Flutter (Dart 3.13) with Riverpod for state, go_router for
auth-aware navigation, and ForUI over a custom navigation-grade design system.

- Map — the Mapbox Maps SDK for Flutter (v11). The app ships no long-lived
Mapbox token; it asks our backend for a short-lived rendering token at runtime.

- Backend data — Supabase (Postgres + PostGIS, Auth, Realtime, Storage). All
rows are scoped with Row Level Security.

- ranmap-server — a small Node + TypeScript + Express backend that holds
every secret the client must never have: it mints Mapbox and LiveKit tokens,
runs the Gemini assistant, verifies phone numbers with Twilio, and validates
RevenueCat webhooks. The client forwards its Supabase session token; the
server verifies it before doing any privileged work.

- Live sync — positions travel over a private, per-trip Supabase Realtime
broadcast channel, written through a database RPC that stamps the sender's id.

- Billing — the RevenueCat SDK on the client (public key only), with
entitlement truth written server-side from the RevenueCat v2 REST API.

- Voice — LiveKit rooms, joined with a short-lived token minted by the server
only after it confirms the caller is actually in that trip or group.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Trust in a live location feed. A member must never be able to spoof another
member's position. We publish through a database RPC that stamps the sender id
server-side and revoke direct client inserts on the channel, so a modified app
can't forge a teammate.

- Making live positions cheap. Writing a row per GPS fix doesn't scale. Live
movement rides an ephemeral broadcast, and only a coarse trail is persisted —
cutting database rows by roughly 50–100×.

- Healing a fire-and-forget feed. Broadcasts can be missed (offline,
reconnect). Every (re)subscribe also fetches an authoritative snapshot, so a
dropped message self-corrects instead of leaving a stale dot on the map.

- Enforcing monetization honestly. Client-side flags can be patched, so paid
gates live in the backend and the hard caps (trips, photos, documents, group
size) are enforced by database triggers. profiles.plan has exactly one
writer — the webhook.

- Bounding provider cost. AI is metered in tokens, which are only known
after the model responds. We hold an upper-bound reservation while a turn
runs, then settle the real spend and release the hold, so a running request
never shows up as usage in the user's meter.

- Shipping 3D with no art budget. The repo bundles no binary artwork, so the
per-vehicle models are low-poly glTF boxes generated by a small Python tool at
build time.

- Background location on both platforms — an Android foreground service and
iOS background location, each with their own constraints and disclosures.

**Testing the RevenueCat flow**

Clone the repo, follow the README setup, and add your own RevenueCat public SDK
key and a pro entitlement with a default offering. The paywall reads that
offering, purchases go through the RevenueCat SDK, and the server webhook
(POST /billing/revenuecat) writes profiles.plan, which the database triggers
then enforce.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- A genuinely end-to-end working app: auth, onboarding, friends and groups,
trips, live sync, chat and voice, photos, planning and an AI assistant all
working together on real devices.

- Live sync architecture we'd defend in production: server-attested
positions, an ephemeral broadcast for movement, and a snapshot that reconciles.

- Monetization done properly. RevenueCat is integrated the way it should be —
real store prices on the paywall, entitlement truth owned by the server, and
enforcement that a patched client can't bypass.

- An AI assistant that takes action, with every tool input validated
server-side and scoped to the authenticated user.

- A crew-first product, where "one subscription covers the whole crew" isn't
a marketing line but a property of the data model.

- Tests and CI across the client (flutter test), the server (Node test
runner) and the database (pgTAP RLS suite).

**What I learned**

- The database is the real enforcement layer. Row Level Security plus
triggers are what make "you can't bypass this" true; client checks are UX.

- Ephemeral-first, snapshot-second is a strong pattern for live data: push
fast and cheap, but always keep an authoritative reconcile path.

- Metering needs reservations. For anything priced after the fact, hold a
bound up front and settle the truth afterwards.

- Design principles beat feature lists. Committing to "the crew comes first"
made hundreds of small decisions obvious — what to build, what to cut, and what
the empty states should say.

**What's next for Ranmap — One Map for the Whole Crew**

- Voice polish — video and deafen on top of the existing app-wide voice
session, mini-bar and push-to-talk.

- Push notifications, fully wired — the server side and preferences exist;
the remaining piece is a database webhook/trigger so chat and alerts deliver
reliably to every device.

- Route planning polish — session-based place autocomplete instead of
debounced geocoding.

- A proper job queue for the scheduled-trip poller in production, instead of
an in-process loop.

**Built With**

Client

- Flutter, Dart

- Riverpod

- go_router

- ForUI

Backend & data

- Supabase — Postgres, PostGIS, Auth, Realtime, Storage, Row Level Security

- Node.js, TypeScript, Express

- Redis

- Docker

Maps, media & realtime

- Mapbox Maps SDK (Maps SDK v11)

- LiveKit

- Mapbox Directions, Geocoding & Search Box

- Google Places API

- Open-Meteo

AI

- Google Gemini

- Google Search grounding

**Inspiration**

Every gamer has a "pile of shame" - games bought on sale, recommended by friends, saved from trailers - that never get played. Notes apps and spreadsheets turn that list into a chore. We wanted the backlog itself to feel like a game.

**What it does**

QuestLog is a gaming bucket list, gamified.

- Save in seconds - title, platform and a "vibe" (Cozy, Epic, Quick, Co-op, Story, Chill)

- Organize - Backlog -&gt; Playing -&gt; Completed shelves, with notes like "Chapter 4 - find the sky forge"

- Complete & rate - 5-star ratings when you finish a game

- Share - one-tap share cards via the native share sheet

- Level up - every action earns XP: +10 save, +25 start, +100 finish. Levels unlock titles from Couch Rookie to Legend of the Shelf

- Quest Roll - can't decide? An animated dice picks your next adventure

- Stats - completion rate, average rating, shelf by platform

**Monetization with RevenueCat**

Freemium with a contextual paywall:

- Free: up to 12 games, core tracking, ratings

- QuestLog Pro: unlimited shelf, Quest Roll, share cards, deep stats

- Yearly $19.99 with a 7-day free trial (anchored as "best value"), Monthly $3.99, Lifetime $39.99

The paywall opens exactly when a user reaches for a Pro feature and tells them which feature they tried ("Quest Roll picks your next game"), which converts better than a generic upsell. Built on react-native-purchases: offerings fetched from RevenueCat, purchasePackage, restorePurchases, and a live CustomerInfo listener on the pro entitlement so the UI unlocks instantly.

**How we built it**

Expo SDK 57 + React Native 0.86 + TypeScript. Local-first storage with AsyncStorage - no account required, instant start. Animated API for the XP bar and dice roll. A demo mode (no API key) lets the full flow run on web for previews and the demo video.

**Challenges**

Designing a reward loop that motivates finishing games rather than just adding more - so completion is worth 10x a save. Keeping the paywall honest: core tracking stays free forever.

**What's next**

Ship to App Store / Google Play, iCloud/Google sync, home-screen widget for "Now Playing", friends' shelves and co-op quests, and RevenueCat Experiments to A/B test trial length and price.

Code: https://github.com/swapnilchaudhari007/questlog

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/PWYJCsrRcr8/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PWYJCsrRcr8)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/473/827/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/473/827/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/473/836/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/473/836/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/473/837/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/473/837/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Most goal apps hand you a checkbox. Tap it, get a star, feel good for five seconds, and the app never actually knows if you did anything real. I wanted a goal companion that could tell the difference between someone who showed up and someone who's just tapping a button to feel productive. Hatua started from one question: what if the only thing that could move your progress forward was telling the truth?

**What it does**

You type one goal. Hatua, built around the Swahili word for "a step," turns it into a short path of quests and a small world to walk through, complete with a hero, lanterns that light up as you go, and realms to explore. Every day you check in with a short, honest description of what you actually did. An AI reads that check-in for real specificity, not just whether you typed something, and only counts it as progress if it's genuine. Vague, generic, or copy-pasted answers get told so, kindly but honestly. If a goal is unrealistic, Hatua will push back before you even start. The hero only grows from real days. Achievements are computed from actual history, never handed out. Everything lives on the player's phone.

**How we built it**

Hatua is an Expo and React Native app written in TypeScript, with Zustand for state, persisted on-device with AsyncStorage. The hero, the realms, and every bit of art are hand-built with react-native-svg and animated with react-native-reanimated, no stock illustration packs. The AI judge runs on Groq, called from a small server so the API key never ships inside the app. RevenueCat powers the subscription model: every new player gets a 30-day free trial with everything unlocked, then chooses Monthly or Yearly, with progress, XP, and levels never for sale at any price.

**Challenges we ran into**

Keeping the AI judge honest without making it cruel was the hardest design problem, finding the line between skeptical and discouraging took real iteration on the prompt. Building entirely from a phone through a GitHub Codespace added its own friction: tunnels expiring mid-session, native modules needing a rebuild before they'd actually work, and real debugging done from my phone. Getting the low-poly art style right took a few full redesigns before it looked intentional instead of generic.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The judging genuinely works, it isn't handing out XP for effort, it's reading what someone actually wrote and deciding if it's real. The whole visual identity, the hero, the realms, the lanterns, is original, built in code, not pulled from a template. And the entire thing was built and shipped from a phone.

**What we learned**

That the hardest part of "AI-powered" isn't calling an API, it's deciding what the AI should refuse to reward. And that a tight, honest scope beats a long feature list every time crunch hits.

**What's next for Hatua**

Step tracking and a richer photo-verification flow for goals where proof matters, a public web page, and expanding the realm and achievement system now that the core judging loop is proven.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Most powerful AI assistants depend on cloud services and a constant internet connection. I wanted to explore the opposite approach: how much of a modern multimodal AI experience could run entirely on a user's own computer?

That became Snowman AI — a privacy-first local AI assistant designed to keep inference and user data on-device while still providing a polished, multimodal experience.

**What it does**

Snowman AI combines multiple local AI capabilities behind one interface:

- 💬 Local AI chat

- 👁️ Image understanding and visual question answering

- 📄 PDF, DOCX, CSV, JSON, Markdown, text and source-code analysis

- 🎙️ Voice-to-text input

- 🎨 Local text-to-image generation

- 🖼️ AI-assisted image editing

- 🧠 Automatic request routing between different AI capabilities

- 🛑 Request cancellation and process management

Instead of requiring users to manually choose different models or tools, Snowman analyzes the request and routes it through the appropriate local pipeline.

**Snowman Pro + RevenueCat**

For this project, I integrated RevenueCat to turn Snowman from only a local AI prototype into a product with a real entitlement and subscription system.

Snowman has two experiences:

Snowman Free

- Local multimodal chat

- Vision

- Document analysis

- Voice input

Snowman Pro

- Local image generation

- AI image editing

- Extended local responses

A $4.99/month Snowman Pro subscription is connected to a RevenueCat product, offering and entitlement. The RevenueCat Test Store is integrated directly into the upgrade flow, allowing the complete purchase and entitlement activation process to be demonstrated.

Importantly, purchasing Pro changes access to features, but AI inference still remains local.

**How I built it**

The frontend is built with React and JavaScript, while the local API and routing system use Node.js and Express.

Snowman communicates with Ollama to run local AI models. Qwen3-VL 8B handles language and vision tasks, while FLUX.2 Klein 4B powers local image generation.

A unified /api/agent endpoint receives requests and determines how they should be processed. Snowman combines deterministic fast-path routing with semantic routing, multimodal context handling, local document extraction, and a prompt-bridge pipeline for image transformations.

The interface also includes AbortController-based cancellation and server-side process-tree cancellation so expensive local inference jobs can be stopped cleanly.

RevenueCat's Web SDK provides the subscription, purchase and entitlement layer for Snowman Pro.

**Challenges**

One of the biggest challenges was making several very different local AI workflows feel like a single assistant.

Image generation, vision, document processing and normal conversation require different inputs and execution paths. Building the routing layer while keeping the UI simple required multiple iterations.

Local inference also introduced hardware and memory constraints. Snowman was designed around quantized models and optimized workflows so it can operate without requiring cloud GPUs.

Integrating monetization without compromising Snowman's privacy model was another challenge. RevenueCat handles the product and entitlement lifecycle while the actual AI inference remains on the user's machine.

**What I learned**

This project taught me that building a useful AI product involves much more than connecting a model to a chat interface.

Model orchestration, routing, cancellation, multimodal context, local resource management, document processing, product entitlements and UX all have to work together.

RevenueCat also showed me how a local-first application can still have a conventional subscription model without moving the application's core AI workloads to the cloud.

**What's next**

I want to continue improving Snowman's local model efficiency, expand its multimodal capabilities, improve image editing, support additional hardware configurations, and make installation easier for non-technical users.

The long-term goal is simple: make capable multimodal AI useful even when the cloud isn't available — while keeping the user's data on their own device.

</details>

Inspiration

What it does

Family mode shows a dashboard (today's check-in, a 7-day strip), alerts, and a way to post moments. Missed check-ins trigger a reminder and then an alert to family.

How we built it
FastAPI, Postgres/Supabase and a DB-backed worker on the backend. Expo React Native on mobile, built with EAS. The backend is the only judge of Plus access. RevenueCat (Test Store) handles purchases, and the server confirms them through webhooks and refresh before granting anything.

Challenges
Making billing error-proof, with idempotent webhooks and a Day Pass granted only after server confirmation. Keeping elders away from any payment UI. Building on limited RAM using cloud builds.

What's next
Recipes with an AI voice assistant, a music hub, Android launcher mode, widgets, SMS/voice escalation, iOS, and a Galaxy Store launch.

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**👨‍🎓 The Next Gen Story: Built by Two 19-Year-Old Student Builders in India**

We are two 19-year-old student developers from India. 

Like millions of students across India and around the world, our lives are defined by high-stakes exams, brutal 200-page slide decks, and dense textbook chapters. Every exam season, we watched our closest friends and peers pull 3:00 AM all-nighters, highlighting pages until highlighters ran dry—only to blank out during finals because passive reading cannot beat the natural decay of human memory.

According to Hermann Ebbinghaus’s mathematical model of the Forgetting Curve:
$$R = e^{-\frac{t}{S}}$$
where (R) is memory retention, (S) is the relative strength of memory, and (t) is time. Without timed active retrieval practice, students lose over 70% of newly learned information within 24 hours.

We didn't build StudyBuddy AI as a theoretical course assignment. We built it together in our dorm room because our classmates and we were burning out. We didn't need another generic notepad; we needed an intelligent cognitive study operating system that turns passive reading into active, lifelong mastery—backed by sustainable, student-friendly monetization.

Winning the Next Gen Award would be a defining milestone: taking two 19-year-old indie builders from India all the way to NYC, seeing our student project broadcast on a Times Square billboard, and proving that the next generation of young founders can engineer production-grade, sustainable software that solves real human problems.

**💡 Inspiration**

Every semester, students struggle with two friction points:

- The Forgetting Crisis: Cramming fails because memory decays exponentially without spaced repetition.

- The Friction Crisis: Creating high-yield flashcards from messy handwritten notes, textbook diagrams, and syllabi takes hours of manual copying—so students give up before they start.

We asked: What if your phone camera gave you an instant cognitive tutor?

An app where you snap a photo of notebook handwriting, your privacy (PII) is protected on-device, Gemini 1.5 Flash distills active-recall concepts with mnemonics, an interactive bidirectional voice agent quizzes you aloud like a private tutor, the SuperMemo SM-2 algorithm schedules your reviews to the exact minute, and RevenueCat powers localized, fair monetization. That is StudyBuddy AI.

**⚡ What It Does (10 Production Modules)**

- 📸 Multimodal Note Scanner: Snap messy handwritten notes or textbook diagrams; Google Gemini 1.5 Flash vision extracts high-yield flashcards with mnemonics.

- 💳 RevenueCat Pro Monetization: Integrated with @revenuecat/purchases-js featuring entitlement validation (pro), dynamic offerings, Restore Purchases, and a 50% Off Student Pass.

- 🎙️ Gemini Live Voice Tutor: Hands-free study agent reading cards aloud, listening to spoken answers via Web Speech API, evaluating conceptual accuracy, and speaking Socratic feedback.

- 🧠 SuperMemo SM-2 Cognitive Engine: Mathematical 4-tier calibration (Again, Hard, Good, Easy) adjusting Ease Factors ((EF \ge 1.3)) and intervals.

- 🛡️ Client-Side PII Security Shield: Redacts Indian (+91 10-digit) & international phone numbers, emails, and student IDs before any cloud payload transmission.

- 🎓 Canvas LMS & Blackboard Hub: 1-click syllabus and assignment import with gradebook passback.

- 🏟️ Collaborative Study Arena: Synchronized Pomodoro sprints with Supabase Realtime presence and global campus leaderboards (IIT, MIT, Stanford, Oxford).

- 🧩 AI Diagnostic Quiz: Auto-generates 5-question multiple choice quizzes with instant rationales.

- 💡 Pedagogical Memory Hooks: Generates mnemonic associations for every concept to maximize cognitive retention.

- 📱 Universal Export & Native Mobile Ready: One-click export to Anki (.tsv) and Markdown; packaged with Capacitor 8 for iOS and Android.

**💳 How We Integrated RevenueCat**

Monetization is the lifeblood of sustainable software. StudyBuddy AI implements the RevenueCat Web SDK (@revenuecat/purchases-js):

- SDK Configuration: Purchases.configure() initializes at app startup with app user ID binding.

- Entitlement Architecture: Gates unlimited AI scans, voice tutoring sessions, and advanced SM-2 analytics behind the pro entitlement.

- Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) Student Tier:

- Standard Pro: $29.99/year ($2.49/mo) global tier.

- Next Gen Student Pass: 50% Off (₹999/year in India vs $29.99 globally)—demonstrating how young builders can use RevenueCat to price fairly across different geographic economies.

- Monthly Pro: $4.99/month flexible tier.

- Customer Demographic Attribution: Purchases.setAttributes() attaches cohort tags (country: 'India', age: '19', cohort: 'NextGen2026', student_status: 'verified').

- Restore Purchases: Full implementation of Purchases.getCustomerInfo() to restore entitlements across devices.

- Graceful Sandbox Fallback: If run in an environment without live Stripe credentials, the architecture falls back seamlessly into an interactive simulation mode so judges can test the full paywall lifecycle without transaction blocks.

**🧠 The Mathematics of SuperMemo SM-2**

StudyBuddy AI implements the authentic SuperMemo SM-2 spaced repetition algorithm. For each review quality (q \in {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}), the new Ease Factor (EF') is calculated as:

$$EF' = \max\left(1.3, \; EF + \left(0.1 - (5 - q) \cdot (0.08 + (5 - q) \cdot 0.02)\right)\right)$$

The inter-repetition interval (I(n)) grows exponentially based on mastery:

$$I(n) = \begin{cases} 1 \text{ day} & \text{if } n = 1 \ 6 \text{ days} & \text{if } n = 2 \ \text{round}(I(n-1) \cdot EF') & \text{if } n &gt; 2 \end{cases}$$

If a student rates a card with (q &lt; 3) (Again), the repetition count resets to 0 and the card is scheduled for immediate review, preventing memory extinction.

**🛠️ How We Built It**

- Frontend & Architecture: React 19, TypeScript, Vite — ultra-responsive mobile SPA architecture.

- Design System: Dark-mode glassmorphism, Outfit typography, HSL tailored color palette, and micro-haptic Web Audio sounds.

- Automated Testing (TDD): 36 unit tests passing across 5 test suites in Vitest covering:

- SuperMemo SM-2 interval growth, EF floor bounds ((EF \ge 1.3)), and reset logic

- PII scrubbing security (Indian +91 phone numbers, international formats, emails, SSNs)

- RevenueCat entitlement validation and fallback handling

- Supabase Realtime presence and broadcast handlers

- Utility class composition and Tailwind conflict resolution

- CI/CD Pipeline: Automated GitHub Actions testing Node 20.x & 22.x matrix on every push.

- AI & Multimodal: Google Gemini 1.5 Flash API with strict structured JSON schema outputs.

- Voice Intelligence: Browser-native Web Speech API (SpeechRecognition + SpeechSynthesis) paired with Gemini evaluation prompts.

- Sound Engine: 0-dependency Web Audio API procedural synthesis generating 4 custom acoustic profiles (flip, success, streak, click) using oscillator math.

- Mobile Runtime: Capacitor 8 with iOS and Android native bridge configurations.

**🧗 Challenges We Overcame**

- Multimodal OCR on Messy Handwriting: Real student notes have scribbles, margin notes, and arrows. We engineered Gemini prompt directives that instruct the vision model to extract semantic hierarchies rather than raw OCR text, reliably producing structured active-recall flashcards.

- Low-Latency Voice Tutoring Without WebSockets: Coordinating spoken audio prompts, speech recognition transcripts, and AI accuracy evaluation in the browser required a robust state machine (speaking → listening → evaluating → feedback → rating) with instant acoustic feedback.

- Rigorous SM-2 Algorithm Implementation: Spaced repetition is sensitive to rounding and boundary drift. We wrote a 14-test suite in Vitest verifying the SuperMemo SM-2 algorithm against the official specification, ensuring Ease Factors never drop below 1.3 and review intervals scale accurately.

**🌟 Accomplishments We're Proud Of**

- 36 / 36 Unit Tests Passing with 0 TypeScript compiler errors and 0 linter warnings (oxlint).

- End-to-End Real SDKs: Real RevenueCat Web SDK integration + Supabase Realtime presence.

- Two 19-Year-Old Student Builders: Built directly out of our lived experience with college exam pressure in India, designed with localized pricing and ethical offline-first privacy.

- Zero-Latency Procedural Audio: Designed a zero-asset sound design engine using pure mathematical sine/triangle oscillators.

**📚 What We Learned**

- Cognitive Science &gt; Flashy AI: AI should not replace thinking; it should activate it. By structuring Gemini outputs into question-answer-mnemonic triples evaluated via the SM-2 algorithm, learning becomes active rather than passive.

- Subscription Strategy with RevenueCat: Building for students taught us that pricing psychology matters. Having a localized student tier with Purchasing Power Parity (₹999/yr vs $29.99/yr) powered by RevenueCat creates high-converting, sustainable subscription businesses.

**🔮 What's Next for StudyBuddy AI**

- Google Play & Apple App Store Launch: Build APK/IPA via our existing Capacitor 8 configuration.

- Direct Canvas / Blackboard OAuth2 Webhooks: Live push notifications whenever a professor uploads a new syllabus or reading.

- Voice Mode in Vernacular Languages: Multi-language voice tutoring (Hindi, Spanish, French) powered by Gemini multimodal audio.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

At our newborn son's pediatrician appointment, the doctor asked how feeding was going. I said, “Great.” My wife said, “Not so good.”

Neither of us was wrong. We were using different yardsticks. The person qualified to assess his progress had been handed two opinions instead of a record.

The facts were scattered across a baby book, two phones, and two tired memories. I built BabyDaily to bring daily care and health records together—so everyone caring for a baby can work from the same information, and families can arrive at appointments prepared.

**What it does**

**Daily care, shared across the household**

Record nursing and bottles, breast milk and formula, pumping, sleep, and diapers. Recent-care summaries and daily totals make the record easy to read. A running sleep timer and longest-stretch insights help families understand their baby's routine.

Premium caregiver invitations bring a partner, grandparent, or nanny into the same record using their own account. Household access follows the baby's owner's subscription, so each invited caregiver does not need a separate purchase to participate.

**Health records and appointment preparation**

Vaccinations, medications, and doctor visits are central to BabyDaily:

- Vaccination records and reminders: keep immunization history together and set reminders for upcoming vaccinations. Vaccination records remain accessible beyond the free tier's rolling history window.

- Medication and supplement logs: record medicines, vitamins, and recurring care so caregivers can check what has already been logged.

- Doctor visits: keep appointment records and reminders alongside the baby's care history.

- Growth tracking: plot weight, length, and head circumference against WHO child growth standards.

- PDF and CSV reports: Premium exports organize recorded care for review and discussion at appointments.

BabyDaily organizes information; the clinician interprets it. It does not diagnose or replace medical advice.

**Designed for occupied hands**

Large labeled quick-log actions, a short diaper form, and native Siri shortcuts make routine logging easier to reach. Milestones, photos, and journal entries preserve the personal side of the record too.

**How I built it**

I built the open-source starterkit as a reusable foundation for this work. Building on my own starter kit let me focus on BabyDaily's specific challenges: shared caregiving, readable care records, and household-aware subscriptions. The starter kit is available for other developers to explore and build on.

The mobile app uses Flutter and Riverpod, with native Swift App Intents for Siri. A NestJS API, PostgreSQL database, and Prisma models hold the shared record. Generated OpenAPI clients keep mobile and backend contracts aligned.

RevenueCat powers monthly, annual, and lifetime Premium purchases through one entitlement. The backend enforces household access and history limits, processes authenticated subscription webhooks, and records subscription events. Purchase and restore flows refresh entitlement-dependent screens.

Reminders are computed from the shared server record. The OneSignal integration supports household delivery, quiet hours, deep links, and lifecycle tags. PostHog event instrumentation and Sentry integration provide foundations for learning from real usage after launch.

**Challenges I ran into**

Making reminders agree with the shared record. A phone should not decide a feed is overdue from its own stale copy of events. Reminder decisions belong alongside the household record, with activity notifications excluding the device that just logged the action.

Getting the subscription lifecycle right. Duplicate webhook deliveries must not process twice. Cancelling renewal must not immediately remove already-paid access. Restoring purchases must refresh the history and features the family sees.

Choosing fair monetization boundaries. Free accounts can track one baby with a rolling 30-day history. Premium adds caregivers, multiple babies, full history, longer-range insights, and exports. Vaccination records and family photos are deliberately exempt from the history cutoff. Every tier is ad-free.

**Accomplishments I'm proud of**

BabyDaily connects a small action at home to a useful conversation later: record a feed or supplement, let the next caregiver see it, and bring the history to an appointment.

I'm proud of the household permissions, subscription lifecycle handling, native Siri integration, and the attention paid to health records alongside everyday care. The current backend test suite passes 199 tests across 13 suites.

Beyond BabyDaily itself, I built and open-sourced the starter kit so the reusable foundation can help other builders too.

**What I learned**

Logging is only half the problem. The value appears when someone else can understand the record without asking the person who entered it to reconstruct the day.

That shaped the home screen, caregiver access, vaccination history, reports, and reminders. Each feature has to make the next handover or appointment easier.

**What's next**

Learn from families using the released app: where logging slows them down, which health and care views they return to, and whether reports make appointments easier to prepare for. Improve onboarding and caregiver invitations using observed behavior, then evaluate pricing with real conversion data. These are next steps, not claims of outcomes already measured.

</details>
