<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Long-form podcasts are where some of the best conversations happen, and they are almost impossible to skim. You cannot search inside them, you cannot quote them, and you cannot tell whether minute 74 is the part you care about.

**What it does**

Podcasterium processes each episode once and gives it back in three ways:

- Watch or listen with a chapter list next to the player, background audio and speed control.

- Read an article that retells the episode chapter by chapter, with the timestamp of every section one tap away.

- Search the whole archive by keyword or by meaning, and open a person page that shows every episode someone speaks in or is talked about, with the minute of each mention.

The archive today holds 49 channels, 3,246 episodes and 3,112 hours of processed audio: mostly Croatian-language shows, plus English-language ones such as RevenueCat's own Sub Club (181 episodes) and Launched (116). Articles are currently written in Croatian; the interface is English and Croatian.

Podcasterium Plus is an optional subscription sold through RevenueCat: monthly or yearly, with a 7-day free trial. Today it unlocks 30 search results instead of 12 and a supporter badge. We list only what exists; the roadmap is shown separately and is never part of the purchase.

**How we built it**

One Flutter codebase for iPhone, iPad, Android, Android TV and the web. RevenueCat (purchases_flutter) handles the subscription on both stores, with one entitlement and one offering. Supabase handles accounts (Sign in with Apple, Google, email), Cloudflare serves the processed episodes as static files from R2 plus a Worker for server-rendered web pages, and Meilisearch powers keyword search.

The app is a white-label shell: all brand-specific material lives in one configuration object, and the same engine already runs a second, independent brand in production. Podcasterium is the open, brand-neutral edition of it. The shell is MIT-licensed on GitHub.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Brand leaks a white-label app hides until you look at every screen: the app opening in the wrong language, a footer naming the other brand, a paywall offering a plan that did not exist.

- Store consoles: an App Store subscription stays "Missing Metadata" until it has a price in every territory; App Review could not find our paywall and account deletion because both lived only inside the account screen, so both are now one tap from the home screen.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

Reading as a first-class way to consume a podcast: chapters with timestamps, a speaker-labelled transcript, and a person hub that links every mention of a public figure to the exact second of the original recording.

**What we learned**

A paywall that promises two real things converts trust better than one that promises seven future ones. And a green store console is not a working app: verify sign-in and purchase end to end before every submission.

**What's next for Podcasterium**

Articles in the episode's own language for English shows, RSS ingestion beyond YouTube, and white-label instances for newsrooms, universities and podcast networks, each with its own RevenueCat project.

**Awards**

We are entering the RevenueCat Design Award and the RevenueCat Peace Prize (accessibility of spoken public debate for deaf and hard-of-hearing people and for long-tail languages).

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We noticed that taking notes is easy, but actually doing something with those notes is where things get difficult. Information gets scattered across notes, tasks, and different apps. We wanted to build something that could turn that scattered information into a more focused and useful workflow.

**What it does**

NeuroNotes is an AI-powered productivity and note-taking app that helps users capture, organize, understand, and turn their notes into actionable tasks all in one simple workspace.
Instead of treating notes as just stored information, NeuroNotes helps users work with them and turn ideas into action.

**How we built it**

NeuroNotes was built with a modern full-stack architecture.

Frontend: React
Backend: FastAPI
Database & Authentication: Supabase
AI: AI-powered features integrated into the application

We focused on creating a clean, simple interface while connecting the AI capabilities with the user's notes and productivity workflow.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was connecting multiple parts of the application into one smooth experience.
We had to handle authentication, database operations, frontend and backend communication, AI integration, and environment configuration while making sure everything worked together reliably.
Another challenge was designing the experience so that AI features felt useful rather than simply being added for the sake of using AI.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We're proud of turning an idea into a working end-to-end application.
We successfully connected the frontend, backend, database, authentication, and AI functionality into a single product. We're also proud of creating an interface that keeps the experience focused instead of overwhelming users with too many features.
Most importantly, NeuroNotes helped us explore how AI can be integrated into an everyday workflow in a practical way.

**What we learned**

We learned that building an application is about much more than writing code.
We learned how important it is to design the user experience around a real problem, connect different technologies together, manage environment variables and authentication securely, and continuously test the entire system rather than treating each feature separately.
We also learned that a good AI feature should solve a real user problem—not just exist because it uses AI.

**What's next for NeuroNotes**

We want to take NeuroNotes further by making its AI capabilities more personalized and useful over time.
Future improvements could include smarter note organization, better task generation, deeper personalization, improved search and knowledge retrieval, and additional tools that help users move from “I need to remember this” to “I know what to do next.”

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**LagoonLink (Mobile Game)**

LagoonLink is a mobile game. The player earns points by connecting a given element with other identical elements. It is a highly engaging game consisting of 24 levels and featuring 5 difficulty settings.

🔍

**LagoonLink: 10s Dataset Match Puzzle**

An Android-style mobile matching puzzle game built with React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vite PWA, and Firebase (Firestore & Google Auth). Players connect matching target items scattered among 10 decoys over a tropical beach lagoon backdrop within a 10-second countdown per step.

**Key Features**

- 100-Item Dataset & /images/ Folder:

- Includes all 100 dataset items (50 Fruits, 30 Animals, 9 Nature elements, and 11 Objects, from #001 Apple to #100 Bottle, including #061 Dog) stored in /images/ and /public/images/ alongside manifest.json.

- Features photorealistic custom sprites for Kiwi, Pear, Spoon, Cycle, and Pen bundled via Vite asset imports and copied into /public/ for production deployments.

- 10-Second Target Linking Gameplay:

- Each step spawns the target item (3 to 6 copies depending on difficulty) amidst 10 distractor items (or 10 total board items mode).

- Tap or drag across matching target items to draw a glowing cobalt-blue link trail before the 10.0s timer expires.

- Ocean wave transition animation sweeps across the lagoon between levels to reset and buoyantly pop in the new wave of tokens.

- 5 Selectable Progressive Difficulty Levels:

- Level 1 (Easy): 3 targets · 10s window · gentle drift · mixed decoys (+100 pts/target).

- Level 2 (Medium): 4 targets · 10s window · moderate drift · category/color-matched decoys (+140 pts/target).

- Level 3 (Hard): 5 targets · 10s window · faster drift · lookalike decoys (+180 pts/target).

- Level 4 (Expert): 5 targets · 10s window · rapid currents · lookalike decoys (+230 pts/target).

- Level 5 (Master): 6 targets · 10s window · cyclone currents · lookalike decoys (+250+ pts/target).

- 5-Heart Life System, 3-Level Flawless Milestone & Daily Bonus:

- Players start each run with 5 Hearts.

- 3-Level Flawless Milestone: Completing 3 consecutive levels without failure automatically recovers +1 lost Heart (up to the maximum of 5 Hearts, or awards +500 bonus points if already at 5/5 Hearts).

- Daily Heart Bonus: Claimable once per day from the bottom control bar or the Levels tab for +1 Heart (up to 5) and +250 bonus points.

- 360px Mobile Phone UI & Installable PWA:

- Designed for a 360px mobile smartphone viewport with a compact 46px top app bar, thumb-zone game controls (Hint, Clear, +1 Heart, Pause), and a 52px 4-tab bottom navigation bar (Play, Levels, Ranks, Dataset).

- Configured with vite-plugin-pwa, Web App Manifest (standalone portrait display), 192x192 / 512x512 / maskable icons, and offline asset precaching.

- Live Firebase Leaderboards:

- Real-time global Top 10 leaderboard (/leaderboards/global) and personal score history (/scores/{scoreId}) backed by Cloud Firestore and Google Sign-In, with automatic localStorage fallback when playing offline or signed out.

**Project Structure**

├── images/ # 100 generated dataset SVG sprites + manifest.json
├── public/
│ ├── images/ # Publicly served dataset sprites & stage backdrops
│ ├── pwa-192x192.png # Android / Chromium home screen icon (192x192)
│ ├── pwa-512x512.png # Android / Chromium splash & store icon (512x512)
│ ├── pwa-maskable-512x512.png # Android adaptive maskable icon (512x512)
│ └── apple-touch-icon.png # iOS Safari home screen icon (180x180)
├── scripts/
│ └── scrape_dataset_images.mjs # Script to regenerate all 100 dataset item sprites
├── src/
│ ├── assets/images/ # Bundled stage backdrops & custom item sprites
│ ├── data/datasetItems.ts # 100 dataset item definitions & 5 level configs
│ ├── utils/sound.ts # Web Audio API synthesized sound effects
│ ├── firebase.ts # Firebase Auth & Firestore leaderboard client
│ ├── usePWAInstall.ts # PWA install prompt & online/offline status hooks
│ ├── PWAInstallButton.tsx # In-app Install / Download App modal & offline badge
│ ├── App.tsx # 360px mobile game shell, arena, levels, ranks & dataset tabs
│ └── main.tsx # App entry point & PWA service worker registration
├── capacitor.config.json # Capacitor configuration for native Android APK builds
├── firestore.rules # Hardened Cloud Firestore security rules
├── vercel.json # Vercel static asset & SPA rewrite configuration
└── vite.config.ts # Vite + Tailwind CSS + VitePWA configuration

**Getting Started Locally**

**1. Install Dependencies**

npm install

**2. Regenerate Dataset Sprites (Optional)**

node scripts/scrape_dataset_images.mjs

**3. Run Development Server**

npm run dev

The app starts on http://localhost:3000.

**4. Type-Check & Build for Production**

npm run lint
npm run build

**Deploying & Packaging as a Mobile App**

**Deploy to Vercel**

The repository includes vercel.json and Vite ES module asset imports so the tropical beach lagoon backdrop and all 100 dataset sprites bundle cleanly into dist/.

- Push the project to GitHub/GitLab or run npx vercel.

- Framework Preset: Vite (npm run build, output directory: dist).

**Install as a Mobile PWA (Android & iOS)**

- Open the deployed URL on your phone and tap the green Get App / Install on Phone button.

- On Android (Chrome/Edge): Tap Install Directly to Home Screen or open the browser menu (⋮) → Install app.

- On iOS (Safari): Tap Share → Add to Home Screen.

**Build a Native Android .APK / .AAB**

- Via PWABuilder: Paste your deployed URL into PWABuilder.com and select Package for Stores → Android to download a signed .apk and .aab.

- Via Capacitor & Android Studio:
bash
npm run build
npm install @capacitor/core @capacitor/cli @capacitor/android
npx cap add android
npx cap sync
npx cap open android

**Video (1:22):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zP7o59w6gxs

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/zP7o59w6gxs/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zP7o59w6gxs)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/693/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/693/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/737/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/737/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Moving out for the first time is exciting until you realize nobody is telling you to drink water, go to bed, or put your phone down. Most health apps feel like forms and dashboards, and they're easy to ignore. A mom's nagging is hard to ignore because it comes with warmth and a little guilt. We wanted to put that in your pocket: Mothrly, an AI companion for anyone living away from home for the first time.

**What it does**

Mothrly is a warm, slightly nagging presence that:

- Reminds you to hydrate, sleep on time, and stay focused, and says it out loud with persona-specific text-to-speech.

- Changes personality: pick Gentle, Strict, Funny, or Motivational, and all the copy is rewritten in that voice.

- Supervises your scrolling: when you cross a time threshold in a watched app, Mothrly draws a nudge over that app, so the nag lands while you're still in TikTok, not when you next open Mothrly.

- Keeps it fun with daily streaks and GIF mood check-ins instead of boring forms.

- Monetizes through RevenueCat, with premium personas and voices unlocked via entitlement.

**How we built it**

- App: Expo SDK 57, React Native 0.86, React 19, and strict TypeScript, with Expo Router for file-based navigation and Zustand for state.

- Navigation: onboarding and the main app are separated with Stack.Protected guards, so flipping one flag moves the user between them with no imperative navigation.

- Offline-first storage: there is no server. A three-tier synchronous key-value store (MMKV → expo-sqlite → in-memory) sits behind Zustand's persist, and each tier is loaded defensively so a missing native module can't crash startup.

- Supervise mode: a custom local Expo module with a Kotlin foreground service polls Android's UsageStatsManager and draws the overlay nudge. It keeps running and restarts itself without JavaScript, and any nudges raised while JS was dead are folded back in on next launch.

- Personas as pure data: nothing in the code branches on which persona is active, so adding a fifth persona is a single data entry.

- Subscriptions: RevenueCat (react-native-purchases + -ui) handles the premium_personas entitlement and paywall.

- Polish: hand-drawn SVG icons, Reanimated animations, and a hidden 7-step guided demo mode we built for screen recordings.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Counting screen time correctly. Aggregated usage buckets can start before midnight and would count last night as today. We switched to raw resume/pause events and compute today's usage as:

$$T_{\text{today}} = \sum_{i} \left( \min(t^{\text{pause}}i,\, t{\text{now}}) - \max(t^{\text{resume}}i,\, t{\text{midnight}}) \right)$$

Event types are matched numerically because constant names differ across Android versions.

- Awkward permissions. Usage access and "Display over other apps" have no runtime prompt and live deep in system settings, so we built explanation screens that walk people there.

- A service that must outlive JavaScript. Config is passed to the Kotlin service as a JSON string it persists verbatim, so it can restart itself with no JS running.

- Native code vs. Expo Go. The local native module means Expo Go can't run the app, so a dev build is required. Everything reports "unsupported" rather than throwing, so iOS falls back to seeded data.

- Fragile startup. A missing native module throws during module evaluation, which is why every storage tier is loaded inside a try.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- The overlay nudge works: Mothrly nags you inside the app you're overusing.

- The persona system is clean and extensible, and every persona comes with its own voice.

- Reminders run end to end, with rolling-horizon scheduling that tops up on each launch.

- The full RevenueCat flow works, including the paywall UI.

- The codebase is well documented and has zero TODO/FIXME comments.

**What we learned**

- Writing a native Android service and bridging it into Expo through a local module.

- How Android usage stats really work, and why raw events are more trustworthy than aggregates.

- Designing offline-first state that degrades gracefully when native modules are missing.

- Wiring up RevenueCat entitlements so purchases drive real feature unlocks.

- Treating tone as a product feature: the same reminder lands very differently in a Gentle voice versus a Strict one.

**What's next for Mothrly**

- Real data on Home: the hydration, sleep, and focus tiles currently use placeholder values.

- Better iOS support, where supervise mode currently runs on seeded data.

- Production RevenueCat: platform-specific store keys instead of the shared Test Store key, then a Play Store release (with a justification for the foreground service type).

- Fully customizable voices: users will be able to upload or record their own voice samples, so Mothrly can sound just like their own mother's voice, with the reminders and nudges delivered in a voice they actually miss.

- Adaptive personas: instead of picking one personality, Mothrly will switch between Gentle, Strict, Funny, and Motivational based on the user's mood and on how many times she has had to interrupt them to stop scrolling. A stressed user gets gentleness, and a repeat offender gets the strict voice.

- Personal reminders: users will be able to hand Mothrly their own to-dos, like "call the landlord" or "submit the assignment by Friday", and she'll remind them in her own persona's voice so nothing slips through the cracks.

</details>

## 678. MeteoWatch -The AeroGuard AI

> AeroGuard AI is a real-time aviation monitoring and alerting platform that combines live aircraft data, flight route information, and aviation weather hazards to identify potential risks to aircraft.

- **Devpost:** https://devpost.com/software/meteowatch-the-aeroguard-ai (gallery page 162) · ❤️ 13 · 💬 1
- **Team:** [SURYAT1 cse](https://devpost.com/suryat1-cse2025), [BHARADWAJ K S](https://devpost.com/bharadwajks-cse2025)
- **GitHub (Try it out):** https://github.com/bharad07-cyber/AeroGruard-AI--MeteoWatch
- **Repo check:** public repo · ⚠️ no license detected · 2 commits · Python · RevenueCat not found in manifests
- **Built with:** ai, deeplearning, eventhouse, eventstream, fabric, github, kql, machine-learning, notebook, openai, pipeline, powerbi, python

**Video (2:41):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pn07HIoCN70

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/pn07HIoCN70/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pn07HIoCN70)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/127/044/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/127/044/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

We wanted to explore how real-time intelligence could be used to solve a practical problem using open data. While looking for a use case that combined real-time data, geospatial analytics, and AI, we discovered that aviation provides a rich ecosystem of publicly available data.

We were inspired by the possibility of combining live aircraft positions, flight routes, and aviation weather hazards to answer a simple but important question:

“What if we could automatically identify which flights are likely to be affected by a weather hazard and warn them in real time?”

This idea led to AeroGuard AI — a real-time aviation intelligence platform that brings together aircraft tracking, weather hazard detection, geospatial analysis, and generative AI.

**What it does**

AeroGuard AI continuously monitors aircraft and aviation weather conditions to identify potential risks to flights.

The system combines data from OpenSky Network, ADSDB, and AviationWeather to understand:

- Where aircraft are currently located

- The routes they are following

- Where significant weather hazards are present

- Whether a flight could be affected by a particular hazard

Using geospatial analysis, AeroGuard AI checks whether aircraft trajectories intersect with SIGMET hazard areas.

When a potential risk is detected, the system generates an alert and uses Azure OpenAI to convert technical weather information into a clear, natural-language warning that can be tailored to the affected flight.

A real-time dashboard allows users to visualize aircraft, flight routes, weather hazards, and active alerts in one place.

**How we built it**

AeroGuard AI was built using Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence as the core data platform.

The architecture follows a real-time intelligence medallion architecture:

Data Sources → Notebooks → Eventstream → Eventhouse → Silver Layer → Gold Layer → AI Alerts & Dashboard

**Data ingestion**

We retrieve aviation and weather information through web APIs using notebooks. The data is then sent through Eventstream and ingested into a Fabric Eventhouse.

**Data processing**

The raw data is organized into different layers:

- Bronze: Raw aircraft, route, and weather data

- Silver: Cleaned and transformed data using update policies

- Gold: Enriched information used for analytics, visualization, and alert generation

**Geospatial intelligence**

Materialized views are used to perform real-time processing, including:

- Creating geographic geometries

- Processing aircraft trajectories

- Representing weather hazard areas

- Detecting intersections between routes and hazards

- Tracking active alerts

- Aggregating the latest flight information

We worked with geospatial formats such as GeoJSON and WKT to represent aircraft positions, flight paths, and hazard zones.

**Generative AI**

When a potential flight hazard is identified, the relevant information is passed to Azure OpenAI.

The AI converts the technical information into a meaningful warning message that is easier for a pilot or aviation stakeholder to understand.

**Visualization and alerting**

A real-time dashboard displays aircraft positions, routes, weather hazards, and detected risks.

The alert pipeline can also send generated warnings through Reflex to notification channels such as email or Microsoft Teams, depending on the available environment.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was real-time API ingestion. We initially explored calling web APIs directly from Eventhouse using KQL, but the available functionality was not sufficient for all our ingestion requirements. We therefore used notebooks to retrieve and process the external API data.

We also encountered limitations with Azure OpenAI access and rate limits. In a real-time aviation scenario, multiple flights may require alerts simultaneously, but the available rate limits made it difficult to process every alert immediately.

Another limitation was the availability of communication channels in our development environment. Since we were working with personal Azure/onmicrosoft accounts, we could not fully test integrations with Teams and Outlook.

We also wanted to experiment with text-to-speech, which could potentially turn generated warnings into spoken alerts. However, the required model was not available in our hackathon environment.

Additionally, Copilot capabilities were not available in our Fabric trial environment, limiting some of the AI-assisted features we wanted to explore.

Finally, aviation is a highly specialized domain. Since we were not aviation experts, understanding SIGMETs, flight operations, and the appropriate interpretation of weather hazards was itself an important learning challenge.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We are proud of building a complete real-time aviation intelligence pipeline within the limited time and resources available during the hackathon.

Instead of creating a simple dashboard, we developed an end-to-end system that connects:

Live Data → Real-Time Processing → Geospatial Analysis → Risk Detection → Generative AI → Intelligent Alerts → Visualization

We successfully brought together multiple independent aviation data sources and demonstrated how Microsoft Fabric can process and analyze them in a real-time environment.

We are particularly proud of the ability to identify potential interactions between flight trajectories and weather hazard zones and then transform those technical findings into understandable AI-generated warnings.

**What we learned**

This project was our first experience building a complex solution focused specifically on real-time intelligence.

We gained practical experience with:

- Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence

- Eventstream and Eventhouse

- KQL

- Real-time data processing

- Medallion architecture

- Geospatial analytics

- GeoJSON and WKT

- Materialized views

- Generative AI with Azure OpenAI

- Real-time alerting architectures

- Integrating multiple external APIs

We also learned that building a real-time system involves more than simply processing data quickly. Data ingestion, latency, API limitations, rate limits, data quality, geospatial accuracy, and domain knowledge all play an important role.

Most importantly, AeroGuard AI showed us how real-time data and generative AI can work together to transform raw information into actionable intelligence.

**What's next for AeroGuard AI**

We see AeroGuard AI as a foundation that can be expanded into a more intelligent aviation decision-support platform.

Our next steps include:

**🔊 Text-to-Speech Alerts**

Enable AI-generated warnings to be converted into speech, allowing alerts to potentially be delivered as voice messages.

**🤖 RAG-Powered Aviation Assistant**

Build a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture that allows users to ask questions such as:

“Which flights are currently approaching severe weather?”

“What hazards are affecting this flight route?”

“Why was this flight flagged?”

The assistant could use real-time flight and weather information to provide contextual answers.

**🔮 Predictive Risk Analysis**

Move beyond detecting current intersections and explore whether a flight may enter a hazard zone in the future, providing earlier warnings.

**📡 Improved Real-Time Processing**

Optimize ingestion and alert processing to handle larger numbers of aircraft and simultaneous hazards while reducing latency.

**📊 Enhanced Dashboard**

Add more advanced flight analytics, historical hazard information, risk scores, and detailed flight-impact visualization.

**☁️ Production-Ready Architecture**

Replace some of the hackathon-specific workarounds with a more robust production architecture designed for scalability, reliability, and continuous real-time operation.

Ultimately, our vision is for AeroGuard AI to evolve from a monitoring system into an intelligent aviation safety and decision-support platform, helping aviation stakeholders understand risks faster and make better-informed decisions.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

This is the third of my Shipaton apps. Stick is about getting off the scroll. ilo is about what I want to do with the time I get back. Mémoire is about who I want to spend it with, while I still can.

My grandmother isn't here anymore. A while ago I asked my mom a simple question: how did her parents meet? She didn't know. They had never told her. It was one of those things that just wasn't talked about at home, and by the time anyone thought to ask properly, there was no one left to answer. It's a small question, and it's the one I regret most.

Then, going through old family photos, I found out something nobody had ever told me: my grandfather and my great-grandmother adored each other. Not in a polite, Sunday-lunch way. They were close, they laughed together, they had their own jokes. I learned it secondhand, years too late to hear either of them tell it.

That's the thing about family stories. Nobody is against keeping them, and almost nobody does. The kids don't dare, don't have time, and don't know what to ask: "we'll do it next Christmas." The grandparents find writing hard at 85, apps are a wall, and most of them think "my life isn't interesting anyway."

StoryWorth proved the demand: more than a million printed books from one emailed question a week. But a question in an inbox is still a blank page, and nobody asks the follow-up: "wait, what was that soldier's name?"

So the question for Mémoire was simple. What if someone called her every Sunday and actually listened? And what if, twenty years later, her great-grandchildren could still ask her how she met Grandpa, and hear her answer in her own voice?

**What it does**

You gift Mémoire to a parent or grandparent. Every Sunday, Louise, a warm AI biographer, calls them. They install nothing and need no password. They just pick up. That night, the whole family gets the story in the app.

- The gift, in four minutes. The buyer writes a short portrait: where she lived, her work, her close family, the topics never to raise (a recent loss, a war, an illness), the call day and time, and the biographer's voice. Then the app gives them a script to tell her about it themselves. Nobody gets a call from an AI without being told first.

- Louise, the biographer. A real-time voice conversation using the oral-history method:

- concrete before abstract: "describe the kitchen", not "tell me about your childhood";

- a follow-up on every detail, and always the names of people and places;

- a thread between calls: "last week you told me about your first school in Ariège."

- She listens patiently. Elderly people pause in the middle of a sentence, so Louise waits much longer than a normal assistant before she speaks. In my test call, Jeanne told her about her father's bakery in Oran, and Louise came back with: "What was the name of the street where the bakery was located?"

- A chapter in her own words. When the call ends, the app writes a chapter from the transcript. It removes the hesitations and keeps her expressions. It is forbidden to add a fact, a name or a date. People, places and years go into a living dossier that Louise reads before the next call.

- Her real voice, in sync. Every story plays with the transcript highlighted sentence by sentence, like lyrics. Tap any sentence to jump to that moment.

- Ask, and she answers. A grandson types "How did Grandma meet Grandpa?" Mémoire finds the passage where she tells it, plays exactly those seconds and highlights each sentence as she says it. If the answer isn't there yet, one tap sends the question to Louise for next Sunday. That's the feature I built for myself.

- The family takes part. Anyone can add a question for the next call, and the family votes on them. Louise picks the top question and says who asked it. Everyone can react to each story, and the app shows the people she talks about and a timeline of her life.

Two rules I cared about more than any feature:

- We never clone her voice. Every answer in the archive is a real excerpt of a real call. This holds even after she's gone, even if the family asks.

- The storyteller is the real customer. Louise says she's an AI, asks consent before recording, never raises the topics the family flagged, and is not a companion. She sends her back to her real family.

**How I built it**

- The voice, with no SDK. Louise runs on Gemini Live (gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking) over a raw WebSocket:

- the microphone is converted to 16 kHz audio and her voice comes back at 24 kHz;

- echo cancellation stops the AI from hearing itself;

- end-of-speech detection is set to its least sensitive level, with 1.6 seconds of silence before it's her turn.

- Only her side is recorded. The archive records the storyteller only, and pauses while Louise speaks. Each turn gets a timestamp, which is what makes the synced player and the archive search possible.

- The model writes, the code keeps it honest. The chapter is written by gemini-3.8-flash with high thinking and a JSON schema. The rule "no fact added" is written into the prompt.

- Search that stays on the phone. The archive uses Apple's NaturalLanguage sentence embeddings plus keyword matching, entirely on the iPhone. It returns timestamps, never generated text.

- Every failure has a plan B.

- If Gemini Flash is overloaded, it falls back to Flash-Lite, then to 2.5 Flash.

- If all of them fail, the recording is saved anyway and the chapter waits.

- Without a RevenueCat key, the paywall switches to a demo mode.

- Design. I worked from a reference design system: blue gradients, floating white cards, a wide geometric display face. The storyteller's words are set in a serif, so they read like a book.

**How it makes money (RevenueCat)**

The person who pays (an adult child) is not the person who uses it (the grandparent). The whole integration is built around that.

- One entitlement, family. It unlocks weekly calls, chapters and the archive for everyone.

- One default offering with three packages, all loaded from RevenueCat, so prices can be A/B tested without an update:

- The Gift, the annual plan and the main offer: $79.99 a year in the Test Store. In production I want €119, sold as a gift.

- Monthly, for families who want to try first: $9.99.

- Lifetime archive, a one-time purchase that keeps every recording forever: $99.99.

- The paywall comes last in onboarding. By then the buyer has already written their mother's portrait, which is when the gift feels real. A "start with the free welcome call" option lets them hear it work first.

- Listening stays free. Every invited relative has grandparents of their own, so charging them to listen would break the growth loop.

- Customer attributes. storyteller_relation, call_day and biographer_voice are sent to RevenueCat, so revenue can be split by who the gift is for.

- The rest of the integration:

- customerInfoStream drives access live;

- restore purchases;

- RevenueCatUI's Customer Center to manage the subscription;

- a RevenueCat Test Store, so anyone who clones the repo can buy in the simulator without an Apple account.

- The printed book is paid on the web. Apple doesn't allow in-app purchases for physical goods.

**Challenges I ran into**

- My first Shipaton app blocked my third. The simulator I used still had Stick's Screen Time shield running, and it blocked Mémoire at launch with "Not today." I had to create a fresh simulator just for Mémoire.

- The disk hit 100% in the middle of the build. I couldn't even run df. I freed 10 GB of Xcode caches and kept going.

- Gemini was saturated. gemini-3.8-flash kept answering "high demand", which is why the app falls back to lighter models and never loses a recording.

- Ten requests a day. The free tier allows only 10 text-to-speech requests per day per model, and I needed 38 sentences for the sample stories. So I made one request per story and asked the voice to pause between sentences. Then I found the pauses in the waveform and placed each sentence on the nearest real pause to where its length says it should start. That gives sentence-level sync from 6 requests.

- A silent simulator. The simulator's microphone gave Louise nothing to hear. I added a test hook that streams a recorded answer as if it were the mic, and only starts once Louise has finished her question.

- "itis" and "aboutour". Live transcription arrives in word-sized pieces that sometimes lose their space. Small, but it made Louise look sloppy.

- A demo video with no sound. Xcode 27 no longer ships a separate Simulator app, and the simulator's screen recording has no audio. In an app where the voice is the product, that was a problem. I wrote a small ScreenCaptureKit recorder for the system audio, a tool to merge it with the video, and an editor for the cuts and captions.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

My favourite moment is when Jeanne finishes her story about the bakery and Louise, without being told, asks for the name of the street. That's when it stops being a chatbot and starts being a biographer.

- A full loop that works: gift, live call, chapter, synced player, voice search.

- A red line written into the product, not just the pitch: no cloned voice, ever.

- An archive that answers with a real recording instead of generating text.

- An app that never loses a recording, even when the AI is down.

**What I learned**

- Ask now. I didn't build Mémoire because the technology finally allows it. I built it because I waited too long to ask one question.

- The voice is the product. Text is easy to generate. A grandmother's laugh isn't.

- Patience is a setting. The difference between a good and a bad AI call for an 81-year-old is a few hundred milliseconds of silence.

- The buyer isn't the user. The paywall, the onboarding and the pricing all had to be designed for the person who gives the gift, while the experience is designed for the person who receives it.

- Say what's real. The sample stories in the demo are voiced by a TTS voice, and the app says so on each one. A product about trust can't fake its own demo.

**What's next for Mémoire**

- A real phone line (Twilio or Telnyx, with a French number) so Louise calls a landline. Today she talks through the app's test call.

- An EU backend for families, sharing and the living dossier.

- Five real grandparents first. Success means at least 4 out of 5 say yes to a second call.

- The printed book, with a QR code to her voice in every chapter.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**🎙️ EasyEnglish: The Zero-Cloud-Cost, E2EE English Speaking Companion**

**🌟 About the Project**

**💡 What Inspired Us**

Over 1.5 billion people worldwide are learning English. Yet, the vast majority hit an invisible barrier: the conversational freeze. Traditional apps like Duolingo turn language acquisition into gamified vocabulary drills, but fail to build spontaneous speaking fluency. The few apps offering live conversations route every voice packet through centralized media servers (SFUs/MCUs), racking up massive cloud bandwidth bills that force founders to shut down or hide behind exorbitant subscriptions. Worse, users are exposed to eavesdropping, data harvesting, and safety risks.

We set out to answer a single question:

Can we build a world-class, real-time speaking companion that guarantees absolute cryptographic privacy, offers 24/7 AI conversational coaching, and costs the developer exactly \$0.00 in idle and streaming infrastructure?

The answer is EasyEnglish.

**🛠️ How We Built It**

We designed EasyEnglish around three core pillars: Zero-Trust Privacy, Free-Tier Sustainability, and Seamless RevenueCat Monetization.

flowchart LR
 subgraph Client ["Flutter Mobile Client"]
 UI["Riverpod UI Engine"]
 E2EE["E2EE Cryptography Engine\nX25519 + HKDF + AES-GCM"]
 MOD["On-Device Moderation\nRegex & Rolling PCM Buffer"]
 end

 subgraph Monetization ["Monetization & Auth"]
 RC["RevenueCat SDK v10+\nEntitlement: easy_english_pro"]
 end

 subgraph Serverless ["Zero-Cost Edge Infrastructure"]
 Vercel["Vercel Edge Proxy\napi/coach.js"]
 Upstash["Upstash Redis\nDaily Quota Limiter"]
 Gemini["Google Gemini 1.5 Flash\nGrammar & Fluency Coach"]
 end

 Client --&gt;|1. In-App Purchase| RC
 Client --&gt;|2. Direct P2P Video Call| Client
 Client --&gt;|3. Bearer Token Auth| Vercel
 Vercel --&gt;|4. Verify Entitlement| RC
 Vercel --&gt;|5. Check 50 req/day limit| Upstash
 Vercel --&gt;|6. Grammar Analysis| Gemini

**1. Peer-to-Peer WebRTC with Zero-Trust E2EE**

Free 1-on-1 human matchmaking connects two learners directly device-to-device. We implemented an on-device cryptographic handshake using the Diffie-Hellman problem on Curve25519 ($X25519$):

- Both endpoints generate ephemeral key pairs: $(sk_A, pk_A)$ and $(sk_B, pk_B)$.

- The shared secret $K_{shared}$ is derived via:
$$K_{shared} = X25519(sk_A, pk_B) = X25519(sk_B, pk_A)$$

- Symmetric keys are extracted using HKDF-SHA256:
$$K_{session} = \text{HKDF-Extract-Expand}(K_{shared}, \text{info} = \text{"EasyEnglish-E2EE-v1"})$$

- Audio, video, and text data channels are authenticated with AES-256-GCM with monotonic sequence numbers $S_{seq} \in \mathbb{N}$ to eliminate replay attacks.

- To defeat Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks without centralized certificate authorities, we calculate a deterministic 4-digit numeric code and 4-emoji Short Authentication String (SAS):
$$\text{SAS} = \text{SHA-256}\Big(\min(pk_A, pk_B) \mathbin{\Vert} \max(pk_A, pk_B)\Big)$$
Users simply confirm they see the same emojis (e.g., 🚀 🐱 💎 🌟) on their screens.

**2. The Gemini AI Speaking Coach & Zero-Cost Cloud Model**

For learners too shy to speak to a stranger, or who want round-the-clock structured practice, we built the Gemini AI Speaking Coach. 

- Powered by gemini-1.5-flash, the tutor engages in realistic roleplays (ordering coffee, job interviews, airport navigation) and outputs structured grammar corrections.

- The Developer-Cost-Shield: The client passes its RevenueCat app_user_id as a Bearer token to a serverless Vercel Edge proxy (/api/coach). The proxy verifies active entitlement (easy_english_pro) against the RevenueCat REST API and checks an Upstash Redis rolling counter. If the user is unentitled or exceeds 50 requests/day, requests are halted at the edge before incurring upstream API costs.

**3. RevenueCat In-App Purchase Engine**

Integrated using modern purchases_flutter (v10+) and purchases_ui_flutter:

- Configured dynamic paywalls using RevenueCatUI.presentPaywallIfNeeded('easy_english_pro').

- Built custom localized package pickers with a 48% savings badge for the yearly plan vs. monthly.

- Integrated RevenueCatUI.presentCustomerCenter() to provide subscribers self-serve management, cancellation prevention, and purchase restoration.

**4. Client-Side Content Moderation & Safety Shield**

Because P2P media cannot be inspected by a central server, safety is enforced entirely on the client:

- Homoglyph & Leetspeak Normalizer: Strips zero-width unicode characters and normalizes obfuscations (b!tch $\to$ bitch) in $&lt;1\text{ms}$.

- Scunthorpe-Safe Token Regex: Prevents false alarms on innocent everyday words ("classic", "pass", "assistant").

- 15-Second Audio Safety Buffer: A rolling FIFO buffer of raw PCM audio ($16\text{kHz} \times 16\text{-bit} = 32\,\text{KB/s} \times 15\,\text{s} = 480\,\text{KB}$) kept entirely in memory. Only if a user taps Report & Block is the buffer packaged for abuse review.

**📈 The Economics: Marginal Cost Function**

For typical cloud apps, the total server cost $C_{total}$ scales linearly with total minutes spoken $M$ and concurrent streams $N$:

$$C_{\text{traditional}}(N, M) = N \cdot (\text{Signaling}) + M \cdot (\text{Bandwidth}_{\text{SFU}}) + M \cdot (\text{Transcoding})$$

In EasyEnglish, WebRTC media streams directly peer-to-peer ($0\,\text{bytes}$ through our servers), and AI calls are strictly capped:

$$C_{\text{EasyEnglish}}(N, M) = \$0.00 + \sum_{i \in \text{Pro}} \min(\text{Requests}i, 50) \times C{\text{Gemini}}$$

Since Pro users generate monthly subscription revenue $R_{sub} \gg 50 \times 30 \times C_{\text{Gemini}}$, our gross margin satisfies:

$$\text{Gross Margin} = \frac{R_{sub} - C_{compute}}{R_{sub}} &gt; 92\%$$

**🥊 Challenges We Faced & What We Learned**

- Building on Low-Spec Hardware:

- Challenge: Our development machine is an Intel Core i5 dual-core laptop with limited RAM. Heavy Android Studio emulators and standard 8GB Gradle daemons caused thermal throttling and out-of-memory crashes.

- Solution: We tuned android/gradle.properties (-Xmx1536m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m, 2 workers), used headless Dart/Flutter testing (flutter test ran 23 tests in 13 seconds), and automated continuous APK builds via GitHub Actions on cloud runners.

- Mitigating Scunthorpe False-Positives on Mobile:

- Challenge: Naive regex filters flagged words like "classic literature", "pass the salt", or "teaching assistant".

- Solution: We designed tokenized boundary matching combined with character homoglyph decoders that evaluate only complete leetspeak words without degrading UI framerates.

- Eliminating Relay Latency with Direct E2EE:

- Challenge: Implementing Diffie-Hellman key derivation asynchronously without delaying the instant WebRTC media track attachment.

- Solution: Key pairs are computed during ICE candidate gathering so that symmetric session keys are ready the millisecond the RTCDataChannel opens.

**🚀 Key Takeaways & What's Next**

Building EasyEnglish proved that privacy and profitability do not have to be opposing forces. By pushing heavy media compute to the edge (user devices) and using RevenueCat to unlock AI capabilities, single-developer startups can launch resilient consumer platforms capable of supporting millions of users without risking cloud bankruptcies.

Next, we are preparing for app store publication across Google Play and the Samsung Galaxy Store for the RevenueCat Shipaton 2026.

**Inspiration**

Students already have the material — lectures, PDFs, slides, YouTube — but still rewrite it by hand into notes, then again into flashcards, then again into quizzes. Darwinity started from that loop: one upload should become a full study set, not another blank page at midnight.

**What it does**

Darwinity is a native iOS/Android study app. Upload a lecture recording, PDF, or YouTube link once; the app builds:

- AI notes from the source you were actually taught from

- Flashcards for spaced repetition

- Quizzes to test recall

- Podcasts for learning on the go

- Exam prep practice from the same set

Free to start. Pro unlocks higher limits and premium features via in-app subscriptions.

**How I built it**

- Client: Expo / React Native (TypeScript), React Navigation, TanStack Query, Zustand

- Monetization: RevenueCat (react-native-purchases) for Pro monthly/yearly offerings, purchase, restore, and entitlement sync

- Auth: Apple Sign In + Google Sign In

- Backend: Darwinity API (notes, quizzes, flashcards, podcasts, billing status)

- Native extras: local Expo modules for focus shields / study alarm

Public open-source client (MIT): github.com/schandu-eng/darwinity-mobile

**RevenueCat**

Pro is powered end-to-end by RevenueCat:

- Configure SDK with platform API keys

- logIn with the Darwinity user id so entitlements follow the account

- Load Offerings → monthly / yearly packages

- Purchase + Restore Purchases on Account

- Listen for CustomerInfo updates and map the Pro entitlement to the paywall / limits UI

Product IDs: darwinity_pro_monthly, darwinity_pro_yearly.

**Challenges**

- Keeping store IAP + backend plan status consistent (trial/geo rules vs App Store / Play products)

- Shipping a real study loop on mobile (upload → notes → flashcards → quiz → podcast) without collapsing into a thin API wrapper

- Making the paywall honest: free must be useful; Pro is for volume and premium surfaces, not a brick wall on first open

**What I learned**

Thoughtful monetization is product design: offerings, restore, and entitlement listeners matter as much as the paywall screen. Expo + RevenueCat made cross-platform subscriptions tractable so I could spend time on the study UX.

**What's next**

Polish the demo path for judges, tighten onboarding, and keep iterating on recall quality from real coursework uploads.

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/134/517/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/134/517/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

Inspiration

Billions of people live in communities where internet connectivity is unreliable, expensive, or unavailable. For them, digital payments often stop when the network stops, forcing dependence on cash and intermediaries. We were inspired to build OfflinePay so that a person should not be excluded from the digital economy simply because they lack internet access. Our vision is to make digital transactions accessible to underserved communities, especially in low-connectivity regions, while promoting financial literacy, trust, and safer digital participation.

What it does

OfflinePay enables peer-to-peer and merchant digital payments without requiring continuous internet connectivity. Nearby devices can exchange transaction data through technologies such as Bluetooth, NFC, QR codes, or other local communication methods. Transactions are securely recorded on the devices and can be synchronized when connectivity becomes available. OfflinePay also incorporates a trust and financial-literacy layer that can warn users about suspicious payment requests, fraudulent merchants, and financial scams. A simple, multilingual and voice-friendly experience is designed to support users with limited digital literacy.

How we built it

We designed OfflinePay around an offline-first architecture. The payment flow creates a digitally signed transaction containing essential transaction information and securely stores it locally. Nearby devices communicate directly rather than depending on a continuously connected central server. Security mechanisms such as cryptographic signatures, unique transaction identifiers, local transaction records, spending limits, and synchronization checks are considered to reduce risks such as replay attacks and double spending. When connectivity returns, pending transactions can be synchronized and reconciled with the appropriate payment infrastructure. The prototype focuses on demonstrating the offline transaction experience and the underlying trust model.

Challenges we ran into

The biggest challenge was designing a payment experience that remains useful when there is no internet connection. Offline systems introduce difficult security problems, especially double spending, replay attacks, device theft, delayed synchronization, and conflicting transaction records. We also had to balance security with simplicity because the target users may have limited digital literacy. Another challenge was designing an approach that could work across smartphones and lower-cost devices while remaining adaptable to different connectivity environments and regulated payment systems.

Accomplishments that we’re proud of

We are proud to have transformed the idea of “digital payments without internet” into an offline-first concept focused on inclusion rather than convenience alone. We designed a transaction flow that demonstrates how value can be exchanged locally and synchronized later. We also incorporated financial-literacy and trust features rather than treating payment security as purely a technical problem. Most importantly, OfflinePay is designed around people who are often left behind by internet-dependent technology: rural communities, low-income users, small merchants, and people with limited digital access.

What we learned

We learned that digital inclusion is not simply about providing technology—it is about designing technology for the people who have the least access to it. We learned that offline systems require security to be designed into the architecture from the beginning. We also learned that financial inclusion and information literacy are closely connected: giving someone access to digital payments is not enough if they cannot recognize scams or understand risky financial information. Simplicity, local-language accessibility, community participation, privacy, and trust are just as important as technical innovation.

What’s next for OfflinePay

Our next goal is to develop OfflinePay into a robust, secure and scalable offline payment protocol that can complement existing regulated financial systems rather than replace them. We plan to improve offline double-spending protection, secure synchronization, device-to-device communication, low-cost/basic-phone compatibility, multilingual voice support, and accessibility. We also want to pilot the concept with local merchants and underserved communities, train young people as OfflinePay Trust Guardians, and measure real-world impact through transaction costs reduced, users reached, scams prevented, and successful offline transactions. In the long term, our vision is an interoperable offline payment layer that can help low-connectivity communities participate safely in the digital economy.

</details>

**Inspiration**

Most retail investors focus entirely on external market movements. However, long-term returns are often degraded by our own behavioral mistakes—holding losing positions too long (the Disposition Effect), reluctance to realize losses, and anchoring to past price peaks. We built BiasGuard to help investors see both the risk in their portfolio and the hidden patterns in their own decision-making.

**What it does**

BiasGuard combines institutional-grade portfolio risk analytics with quantitative behavioral finance signals:

- Objective Portfolio Risk Tracking: Calculates Volatility, Sharpe Ratio, Beta, and Maximum Drawdown across your holdings.

- Behavioral Radar: Analyzes trading patterns across key signals (Disposition Effect, Loss Realization Reluctance, Overconfidence Calibration, and Reference-Price Sensitivity) plotted on a multi-axis spider chart.

- Transparent Explainability: Never a black-box score; users can inspect the underlying formulas and transactions that contributed to each behavioral alert.

- Monetization with RevenueCat: Free tier provides basic portfolio tracking and core metrics, while BiasGuard Pro seamlessly unlocks comprehensive behavioral diagnostics, interactive assessments, and deep historical benchmarks.

**How we built it**

- Frontend: React Native, Expo Router, TypeScript, and SVG for the dynamic Behavioral Radar.

- Backend & Auth: Firebase Authentication, Cloud Firestore, and Cloud Functions (Node.js).

- In-App Subscriptions: Integrated via the RevenueCat SDK (react-native-purchases) for cross-platform entitlement and paywall management.

**Challenges we ran into**

Translating behavioral finance literature into rigorous, automated quantitative signals while keeping the user experience intuitive was our biggest hurdle. Ensuring deterministic calculations across timezones and handling edge cases in transaction histories required extensive automated testing.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Delivering a fully functional end-to-end prototype featuring real-time Firebase syncing, automated behavioral metrics, and RevenueCat paywall integration.

- Achieving 100% test suite pass rates with strict feature freeze and regression testing.

**What's next for BiasGuard**

- Automated brokerage syncing (Plaid/SnapTrade).

- v1.1 UI/UX polish and personalized nudge notifications before high-bias trading decisions.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/849/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/849/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/856/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/480/856/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

Early-career software engineers and newly minted engineering managers frequently run into a silent career blocker: high-friction workplace communication. Whether it is pushing back on an impossible 4-day delivery sprint, giving upward critical feedback to leadership, or defending tech-debt refactoring against feature creep, junior professionals often react passively or defensively. We built PocketMentor to give tech talent a safe, interactive simulator to build executive presence, manage boundaries, and practice high-stakes professional dialogue before stepping into real meetings.

**What it does**

PocketMentor is an interactive executive communication coach with a built-in subscription model powered by RevenueCat:

- Real-World Engineering Scenarios: Practice situations ranging from scope creep pushback to communicating critical feedback upward.

- Multi-Dimensional Diagnostics: Analyzes user responses across three distinct leadership indices: Assertiveness, Diplomacy, and Clarity, rather than a vague overall score.

- Staff-Level Alternative Scripts: Provides actionable critiques and generates an executive rewrite showing how a Staff Engineer or Director would frame the exact boundary.

- Local Session Tracking: Persists session histories and progress logs locally so users can measure communication improvements over time.

- RevenueCat Monetization Architecture: Gates advanced executive scenarios behind a pro entitlement with dynamic Monthly and Lifetime tier offerings.

**How we built it**

- Mobile & Web Frontend: Developed using React Native with Expo and TypeScript, styled with a modern dark-matte executive aesthetic.

- Monetization Engine (RevenueCat): Integrated react-native-purchases utilizing RevenueCat's Test Store configuration. Dynamic packages are fetched directly from RevenueCat Offerings and gate access via the active pro entitlement.

- Persistence & State: Local-first session logging and progress persistence powered by @react-native-async-storage/async-storage.

- Diagnostic Evaluator: Multi-vector rubric analyzer scoring contextual boundaries, constructive compromise proposals, and objective data-grounded framing.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Cross-Platform Purchase Abstraction: Handling the differences between native mobile sandbox environments and web preview builds required creating a resilient RevenueCat service layer with graceful sandbox fallbacks so the app could be demonstrated without build crashes.

- Designing a Commercial-Grade Paywall: Structuring a paywall that felt native, clear, and value-driven rather than an intrusive roadblock. We focused heavily on clear tier comparisons, prominent feature value propositions, and dynamic pricing strings.

- Balancing Diagnostic Feedback: Creating an evaluation algorithm that rewards constructive boundary setting rather than just long, polite, or overly passive answers.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Wiring a clean, complete RevenueCat purchase lifecycle with dynamic offerings and instant entitlement checking.

- Designing a focused 2-screen mobile experience with zero visual clutter and immediate user utility.

- Implementing multi-metric feedback that delivers practical, staff-level communication advice in seconds.

**What we learned**

- How RevenueCat decouples product catalog management from app releases, making pricing experiments and entitlement gating seamless.

- How critical the first-time paywall experience is: highlighting specific tangible benefits (like Staff-level rewrites) dramatically clarifies user value.

**What's next for PocketMentor – AI Executive Communication Coach**

- Live Audio Voice Roleplay: Integrating low-latency voice-to-voice simulation so users can practice speaking under pressure rather than typing.

- Team & Enterprise Tiers: Expanding RevenueCat subscription tiers to support engineering team licenses and bootcamps.

- Custom Scenario Builder: Enabling users to paste their own real-world Slack threads or email chains for personalized executive rewrites.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

It all started when me, and my friend decided to learn Japanese. Flash cards such as Anki works, but we eventually found out that we could not write any Japanese characters at all. So, it seems obvious that an app specifically made for this is the right answer. Expanding on this idea is the tug of war aspect. We loved tug of war as kids, and fun. Combining these two ideas became much more than a language learning app, but rather a fun past time for all people.

**What it does**

Tsunahiki is a mobile educational game where you learn kana by playing tug of war against an opponent.

kana appears on screen. You draw it with your finger.

- Correct stroke → you pull the rope toward your side.

- Wrong stroke or miss → the opponent pulls, and you lose ground.

Rounds are short. Matches are tense. You win by pulling the rope past the threshold.
The core loop is: see the kana → draw it → feel the result immediately. No menus, no score screens between reps. Just draw, pull, repeat.

Currently playable: hiragana tug of war with real-time stroke recognition, a working opponent AI, and win/lose states.

**How we built it**

The game itself is UI heavy, thus, a game engine such as Godot does not suit our needs. Thus, we came across Kotlin Multiplatform. Thus, the entire client is built with Kotlin, with a compose UI.

The stroke recognition is namely the hard part. We first tried to use a machine learning approach, but we are worried about its performance on non-powerful devices. We first opted for Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), a time series model that matches points to another points, and gets the similarity cost. However, upon testing, it proves to be bad on handwriting tasks. Then, came the paper from Moussa et al.. It is called DTW_seg, and so, after a few testing, we found that it is better than regular DTW.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Stroke recognition is hard. Kana have specific stroke orders and shapes, and fingers are imprecise. We had to balance forgiving-enough-to-be-fun against strict-enough-to-actually-teach.

- Making losing feel fair. If the opponent pulls too hard, the game feels punishing. Too soft, and there are no stakes. Tuning that was more design work than code.

- Scope. We had a fixed deadline and school on top of it. We cut features aggressively and focused on making one loop feel good instead of five loops feel mediocre.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- A working vertical slice: the core loop is playable and actually fun.

- Real-time stroke recognition running on-device with no noticeable lag.

- A modular architecture that makes future expansion a data problem, not a rewrite.

- Shipping something playable under a tight deadline with competing schoolwork.

**What we learned**

- Constraints force clarity. Not having time to build everything made us decide what Tsunahiki actually is.

- Game feel is not a nice-to-have. The difference between "educational tool" and "game" is entirely in the feedback — sound, timing, screen shake, rope tension.

- Designing for extensibility early pays off, even when it feels like overengineering at the start.

**What's next for Tsunahiki**

Tsunahiki was built on a modular core, and that's the whole point. The whole application can be easily extendable to other languages/scripts. However, we are going to focus on the future our native ancient roots. As a Filipino, we want people to learn the Baybayin script, the original script of the Filipino language.

Additionally, we want to develop the multiplayer in Rust. This was our initial plan, however, due to time constraints, and competing schoolworks, we simply opted for offline enemy AI.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

RevenueCat's own name is built around cats. Their awards are named Catvertising. Their trophy is called Shippy. And yet somehow nobody had shipped an actual cat game for Shipaton. That felt like an open goal.

The specific idea came from thinking about what cats actually do - not the internet meme version, but the real behaviour. Cats are efficient, they take the most direct route, they jump things humans wouldn't attempt, and they absolutely do not care about your obstacles. A delivery cat made perfect sense. The job requires speed and precision, the rooftops give you verticality, and the isometric perspective makes every jump feel deliberate in a way a flat side-scroller doesn't.

Monetization was designed into the game from the start rather than bolted on at the end. Ads appear between runs on the results screen - the one moment the player is naturally paused and not in flow. Watching an ad buys a continue or a coin bonus, so the exchange feels fair. The subscription removes ads and doubles earnings, which is a straightforward value proposition the player can evaluate after a few runs once they know they want to keep playing. We tried to make every RevenueCat touchpoint feel like it belonged in the game rather than interrupting it.

We are both computer science students. We have built tools, web apps, and systems before. We had never shipped a game to a live app store. Shipaton was the reason to finally do it.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

When I moved to Italy, official letters were my biggest source of stress: tax notices, fines, residence-permit appointments, school letters. They're written in dense bureaucratic language, and missing a deadline can mean penalties. Millions of immigrants, refugees and international students across Europe face the same thing, often relying on friends or paid services just to understand one page. I wanted a tool that turns that fear into a clear to-do list, in your own language.

**What it does**

Take a photo of any official letter, bill, form or medicine leaflet, and Label Lens explains it in your language:

- Plain-language summary: what it is, who sent it, what it means

- Deadlines with date boxes and one-tap reminders (3 days and 1 day before)

- Step-by-step "what to do": where to go, what to bring, how to pay

- Key details: amounts, payment codes and reference numbers, copied exactly

- Warnings and a glossary of the bureaucratic terms

- Follow-up questions about that specific letter

- 12 languages (English, Persian, Arabic, Ukrainian, Spanish, French, Bengali, Urdu, Chinese, Turkish, Romanian, simple Italian), with full right-to-left support for Persian, Arabic and Urdu

Dates are only taken from the document or worked out from a date printed on it (e.g. "30 days from notification"), and computed dates are clearly marked. Unreadable parts are flagged instead of guessed.

Monetization (RevenueCat): Free = 3 scans per week. Pro (pro entitlement) = unlimited scans, deadline reminders and follow-up questions. Yearly ($24.99, 1-week free trial) or Monthly ($3.99, 3-day free trial), sold through a RevenueCat Paywall, with Restore and Customer Center. Every scan has a real AI cost, so a small free tier plus a subscription keeps it sustainable.

**How we built it**

- App: Expo / React Native (TypeScript), on-device image resizing, local notifications, local-only history

- Payments: react-native-purchases + react-native-purchases-ui (RevenueCat Paywalls)

- Backend: a small Cloudflare Worker proxy to Google Gemini with a strict JSON schema. The API key never ships in the app. Our proxy stores nothing; the photo is sent to Gemini only to read it.

- Design: warm pastel UI, localized digits for Persian and Arabic

**Challenges we ran into**

- Getting the model to copy payment codes and amounts exactly, and never invent dates

- Computing relative deadlines ("within 60 days of notification") correctly from the date printed on the letter

- Right-to-left layouts across the whole UI

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

A crumpled Italian letter photographed outdoors comes back in a few seconds with the right issuer, the right deadlines and the exact payment code, in the user's own language. It's the app I wish I'd had when I arrived in Italy.

**What we learned**

Strict structured output plus careful prompting makes vision models reliable enough for high-stakes documents, and a simple, well-placed paywall shapes the product as much as the features do.

**What's next for Label Lens**

Google Play launch, PDF export, sharing a result with a family member or caseworker, and partnerships with NGOs and university international offices.

Demo letters in the video are fictional. Voiceover generated with ElevenLabs.

</details>

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/426/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/426/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/427/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/427/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/428/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/428/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/432/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/432/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/433/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/433/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/434/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/434/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/435/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/481/435/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

A parent answers the phone. The voice on the other end sounds exactly like their child — panicked, asking for an emergency transfer.

The problem is no longer just identifying a synthetic voice. A scam can use a real voice, a cloned voice, or social pressure alone. PauseSignal was built for the few seconds between hearing and acting: create a pause, explain the risk, and guide the user toward verification before money moves.

**What it does**

PauseSignal is an AI-assisted voice-scam defense system that combines two independent signals in real time:

- Acoustic forensics analyze real 16 kHz PCM audio using spectral flux, spectral rolloff, and zero-crossing-rate indicators.

- Semantic threat analysis detects urgency, financial demands, secrecy pressure, and impersonation cues in English and Egyptian Arabic.

The two signals are fused into an understandable Threat Score (0–100).

When risk becomes high, PauseSignal does more than show a warning. It explains why the call was flagged and provides concrete verification steps.

The product also includes:

- SafeCall for live microphone sessions and a clearly labeled Demo Attack mode.

- Incident Reports with SHA-256 audio provenance, flagged phrases, evidence, and verification guidance.

- Analyze Recording for local acoustic analysis of saved calls and voice notes.

- Family Shield, a privacy-minimal trusted-circle alert flow that never sends raw audio, transcripts, or phone numbers in its alert payload.

- Full localization across English, Arabic with true RTL, Spanish, and French.

**How we built it**

PauseSignal is built with Flutter 3.41 and Dart 3.11 using a feature/domain/data architecture and flutter_bloc.

Live PCM and generated Demo Attack audio both pass through the same IAudioStreamSource analysis pipeline, so the demonstration exercises the real downstream scoring system rather than a separate fake UI path.

The acoustic engine performs real DSP over PCM audio. The semantic engine uses a deterministic bilingual rule system locally, with optional relay-backed cloud integrations.

Provider secrets are kept out of the mobile client through a minimal Cloudflare Worker relay.

The project currently has:

- 427 passing Flutter tests

- 74 passing relay tests

- GitHub Actions CI

- Automated web deployment

- Android build validation

- 581 localized message keys across each supported locale

**RevenueCat integration**

Subscriptions are implemented using the real purchases_flutter SDK with RevenueCat CustomerInfo as the sole entitlement authority.

PauseSignal uses two paid entitlements:

- sentinel

- family_vault

For Shipaton judging, we validated the integration against RevenueCat's hosted Test Store using the real SDK.

The live Offering observed through the SDK contained:

- $rc_monthly → sentinel_monthly

- $rc_annual → sentinel_annual

- $rc_two_month → family_vault_monthly

- custom Annual → family_vault_annual

We completed genuine RevenueCat Test Store sandbox purchases, observed the expected active CustomerInfo entitlements, verified entitlement-driven UI updates, tested Family Vault precedence, verified Restore Purchases, and confirmed that cancelling a purchase grants nothing.

The purchase shown in the demo video is a RevenueCat Test Store sandbox transaction — no real money is charged.

**Challenges**

One of the hardest parts was keeping the product honest when external integrations were unavailable.

PauseSignal treats degraded capability as a first-class state instead of pretending everything is live. Demo, live, partial-analysis, Test Store, and unavailable states are explicitly labeled.

Another challenge was protecting provider credentials in a mobile architecture. Permanent provider keys stay server-side behind the relay, while release builds reject unsafe direct-key paths.

Egyptian Arabic scam semantics were also implemented as a first-class detection lexicon rather than simply translating the English rules.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

We built a complete consumer-facing safety product rather than a single detection demo.

PauseSignal combines real audio processing, bilingual conversation-risk analysis, evidence-backed incident reports, verification guidance, Family Shield, accessibility and localization work, and a real RevenueCat entitlement architecture.

The repository is fully public, MIT licensed, tested, documented, and continuously validated by CI.

**What we learned**

The biggest lesson was that safety software is as much about truth management as detection.

A risk tool that overstates its capabilities can be more dangerous than one that clearly explains its limits.

We also learned that deterministic bilingual semantic analysis can provide surprisingly useful scam-risk evidence before requiring a large language model.

**What's next**

Next steps include physical-device QA, iOS validation, calibrated acoustic models, and live validation of the optional AssemblyAI, Groq, and OneSignal relay-backed paths.

The longer-term goal is a production-ready assistant that helps people recognize manipulation, pause before acting, and verify suspicious requests through a trusted independent channel.

**Disclosures**

- Demo Attack is simulated using generated audio and scripted dialogue, and is visibly labeled as a demo.

- The subscription purchase shown in the video uses RevenueCat Test Store through the real SDK. It is a genuine sandbox transaction, not a real-money charge.

- AssemblyAI, Groq, and OneSignal relay paths are implemented but are not presented as live-verified in the submission video.

- The demo video was captured on an Android emulator.

</details>
