<details><summary>Description</summary>

**🎓 Entry: Next Gen Award (student)**

I'm Pierre, a student at Audencia (France), and I designed and built TapReply on my own. TapReply is live on TestFlight (App Store review in progress), so this is a Next Gen Award entry with a public open-source repository and a demo video.

**Inspiration**

The Apple logo on the back of your iPhone is actually a button: tap it twice and iOS can run any action (Settings &gt; Accessibility &gt; Touch &gt; Back Tap). Meanwhile, we all do the same tedious dance every day: screenshot a chat, open an AI app, paste it, ask for a reply, copy the answer, go back, paste. I wanted that hidden button to do all of it in one gesture.

**What it does**

TapReply writes your replies for you, from any conversation.

- Double-tap the back of your iPhone, in any chat.

- TapReply reads the conversation on your screen and writes the right reply.

- The reply is copied and shown in the Dynamic Island. You paste it and send it.

- Messy draft? Type "cant tmrw.. busy?? fri maybe", tap twice, and it becomes a clear, natural message that keeps your meaning.

- Tones: Classic, Professional (work emails), Charmer (dating apps), Funny (group chats), and Fact Check, which reads a claim on your screen and tells you if it's TRUE or FALSE.

- Create your own tones in the Studio: name, mascot color and instructions.

- Three shortcuts: Double Tap, Triple Tap and the Action Button, each with its own tone.

- Private history saved on the iPhone only, with favorites.

- A built-in Test tab to try the gesture safely. Available in 6 languages.

**Privacy**

- Screenshots never leave the iPhone: text is read on the device with Apple's Vision framework.

- Only the conversation text is sent, and only after explicit consent (you can turn it off anytime).

- Zero-data-retention AI providers only: the text is processed in real time and never stored.

- No account, no ads, no tracking.

**How RevenueCat powers the business**

- Free: 10 replies granted once by the server as RevenueCat Virtual Currency (RPLY), plus 1 custom tone.

- TapReply Pro (monthly or annual, 3-day free trial on annual): unlimited replies for personal use, extra tone shortcuts, unlimited custom tones, exclusive app icons.

- 50-reply pack: a one-time purchase for people who don't want a subscription.

- Credits can't be faked on the device: the server checks the entitlement and the balance with the RevenueCat REST API v2, debits one credit before calling the AI and refunds it automatically if the generation fails.

- When Pro ends, extra tones and Pro shortcuts lock gracefully with a clear explanation instead of disappearing.

**How I built it**

- iOS app: SwiftUI (iOS 18+), App Intents + a shared Shortcut triggered by Back Tap, Vision OCR with a custom parser (who said what, and the draft in the input field), ActivityKit Live Activities for the Dynamic Island, SwiftData, String Catalogs for 6 languages.

- TapTap, the mascot: a real-time vector animation engine I built for the app: 50+ animation clips in a compact custom format, decoded at runtime and recolored with the user's color.

- Backend: a Supabase Edge Function in TypeScript that verifies the anonymous RevenueCat identity, applies rate limits, manages credits through RevenueCat, and calls AI models through OpenRouter (Gemini, with Claude as fallback).

- Monetization: RevenueCat SDK, offerings, entitlements, virtual currency and REST API v2.

**Challenges I ran into**

- Reading a screenshot reliably: telling my messages from the other person's, ignoring timestamps and app chrome, and finding the draft in the input field.

- Making credits impossible to cheat without any user account, using only the anonymous RevenueCat ID and server-side debits.

- Getting privacy right: explicit consent, zero data retention, and App Store review rules for AI apps.

- Explaining a gesture most people have never used: that's why the onboarding is an animated, step-by-step story with TapTap.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

- A complete product built solo as a student: onboarding, tones, custom tones, history, paywall, subscriptions, credits, privacy, 6 languages, now in App Store review.

- Replying to a message takes two taps instead of seven steps.

- Proof that students don't just learn to build apps: we ship them.

**What I learned**

Shipping is a different job from coding: review rules, privacy labels, pricing, trial terms, onboarding, and above all explaining a new habit in a few seconds.

**What's next**

- App Store release (review in progress).

- Retention offers with RevenueCat for people who cancel.

- More tones and smarter context for long conversations.

</details>

**Video (1:16):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pqMMr9Ek-pQ

[![YouTube video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/pqMMr9Ek-pQ/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pqMMr9Ek-pQ)

**Images:**

<a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/130/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/130/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/131/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/131/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a> <a href="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/132/datas/gallery.jpg"><img src="https://d112y698adiu2z.cloudfront.net/photos/production/software_photos/005/483/132/datas/gallery.jpg" width="150"></a>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

India's gig workforce is projected to grow from 7.7 million workers in 2020-21 to 23.5 million by 2029-30 (NITI Aayog, India's Booming Gig and Platform Economy, 2022). They are paid per hour, per delivery, per task, and when the payout comes up short, the platform holds the only record of what was actually worked. The worker has memory and a screenshot. I wanted to flip that: an independent record that lives on the worker's own phone, works with no signal and no account, and can prove what is missing.

**What it does**

ProofPocket is an offline shift and pay log for gig workers. You log work three ways: per hour, per delivery, or per day, across as many jobs as you have. A live timer with breaks and task counters records shifts as they happen. When the money lands, the payout check compares what you logged against what you were paid and shows the gap in plain language: you logged 39 hours, they paid you for 33, ₹1,080 missing. Once a record is settled and paid, it locks. One tap turns any client's history into a dated PDF evidence packet you can send to a manager or a platform. The money math at the heart of it is simple on purpose:

$$\text{Missing pay} = (\text{units logged} - \text{units paid}) \times \text{rate}$$

Logging, payout checks and CSV export are free forever. Plus unlocks the PDF packets and monthly reports.

**How we built it**

One Expo and React Native codebase in TypeScript, running on Android and iOS. Every rupee calculation lives in a single framework-free ledger module, so the money math is unit-tested on its own: 14 tests cover part payments, per-task rates, settled locks and month boundaries. All records live on-device in AsyncStorage; there is no backend and no account, which is the privacy model, not a missing feature. RevenueCat handles subscriptions through one entitlement with Monthly, Yearly and Lifetime plans. The payments module loads lazily, so the app still runs in Expo Go and on the web, where the paywall honestly shows a preview state instead of pretending a purchase happened. The interface is a token-based Material You system with one strict rule: red appears only for missing pay.

**Challenges we ran into**

RevenueCat cannot load in Expo Go, so the purchase flow had to degrade gracefully without ever faking a successful buy; lazy loading and an explicit preview state solved it. The harder problem was trust in the numbers: part payments, advances, and per-delivery rounding all had to land on the exact rupee, which is why the ledger became a pure, tested module instead of logic scattered through screens. Finally, the timer had to respect reality: people forget to end shifts, take breaks, and close the app mid-shift, so the running shift persists on the device and survives restarts.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

The full loop works end to end, offline: start a shift, end it, check the payout, lock the record, export the proof. The pay math is verified by tests, not by hope. Subscriptions are genuinely wired through RevenueCat, with live prices, restore, and a Test Store purchase demonstrated in the video. And the design holds its discipline: in the whole app, red means exactly one thing.

**What we learned**

The emotional core is not the log, it is the translation. "6 unpaid hours" is information; "₹1,080 missing" is something a worker can act on. I also learned that for this user, offline is not a limitation to apologise for. Cheap phones, dead zones, and a real fear of earnings data leaving the device make local-first the feature. Restraint beat features at every step.

**What's next for ProofPocket**

A store release so workers can install it without a developer build, regional language support starting with Hindi, photo receipts attached to records, and one-tap sharing of evidence packets over WhatsApp, which is where these disputes actually happen. The goal stays the same: no worker should have to take a platform's word for what they earned.

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration## Inspiration**

As an Electrical Engineering student, I've seen how engineering assessments usually work: fixed questions with fixed answers. You can memorize them, or use AI to generate the "right" answer. But real engineering isn't about knowing the static answer—it's about what you do when the facts change mid-problem. I wanted to build something that records adaptation, not just completion. 

**What it does**

Defend is a mobile proof session. 

- You solve a realistic troubleshooting task (e.g., a tripping pump motor).

- Your initial answers lock and timestamp.

- The evidence mutates (the supply is fixed, but the current imbalance remains).

- You revise your diagnosis and explain why in your own words.

- You get an honest, compact record: Submitted, Adapted, Explained, time taken, help disclosed, and a cryptographic record fingerprint.

It explicitly states: auto-checked, not verified. It doesn't certify skill; it shows how you respond to changed evidence.

**How we built it**

- Expo (React Native) + TypeScript: 5-screen flow using expo-router.

- Deterministic Engine: A JSON-driven challenge schema (motor-imbalance.json) with seeded variants (Mulberry32 PRNG), constraint validation, and pure-function grading. No backend, no LLMs.

- RevenueCat Integration: Wired react-native-purchases for monetization. Free tier gives one session; Pro unlocks full JSON packet export and fresh randomized variants. Purchases run against RevenueCat's Test Store in Expo Go.

- State & Persistence: AsyncStorage handles session lifecycle, immutable locking before mutation, and integrity signals (like leaving the app).

**Challenges we ran into**

- Dependency Hell: Expo SDK 57 pins React 19.2.3, but a stray react-dom@19.3.0 peer dependency caused endless ERESOLVE crashes. We had to surgically remove web dependencies and use --legacy-peer-deps for RevenueCat.

- The Generator Bug: Early on, 70% of random variants broke the scenario's physics constraints (e.g., voltage unbalance dropping below 2.8%). We increased the constraint-satisfaction loop from 25 to 5,000 attempts to guarantee valid variants.

- Hotspot Networking: Running the dev server over a mobile hotspot blocked local IPs, forcing us to configure @expo/ngrok tunnels so the physical phone could load the bundle.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- End-to-End RevenueCat Flow: Successfully wired the Test Store paywall, displaying live products ($9.99/mo, $79.99/yr) and executing a test purchase that instantly flips the entitlement to unlock Pro features.

- Honest Limitations: Built the "auto-checked, not verified" disclaimer and help-disclosure directly into the core UX. We didn't fake a backend or human review.

- Zero-Backend Architecture: The entire grading logic, variant generation, and state machine run locally on the device.

**What we learned**

I learned that building an assessment tool requires extreme honesty about its limits. Keyword matching can be fooled, and a self-run app can't prove who did the work. By leaning into those limitations—displaying them plainly on the proof card—we built something more trustworthy than a fake "certificate." I also learned how deeply integrated RevenueCat's Test Store is; getting live offerings and test purchases working in Expo Go was a massive win.

**What's next**

- A second challenge domain (buck-converter ripple) to prove the JSON engine is truly generic.

- Reviewer-style PDF/Markdown export of the proof packet.

- Mentor/Employer dashboard tiers.

</details>

**Inspiration**

Picture this: It’s 11:30 PM. You’re lying in bed, exhausted, scrolling through your phone.
During the day, you had a brilliant startup idea, but you scribbled it in a random notes app. You recorded a voice memo while walking to lunch that you never listened to again. You messaged yourself two reminders, snapped three screenshots, and jotted tasks across sticky notes.
Your day happened, but it’s scattered across five different apps. Instead of winding down with clarity, you go to sleep carrying mental noise, wondering what you forgot.

**What it does**

We built Dusk to be your calm mental sanctuary.
Whenever inspiration strikes—a half-baked thought, a quick voice note, or a photo—you dump it into Dusk in two seconds with zero friction.
Then, at your scheduled evening hour, Dusk brings it all together. Through a calming reflection ritual, it pulls out your actionable tasks, prompts you with thoughtful questions, and synthesizes your day into an editorial Insight Card.
*You don’t just capture your life—you actually understand it,

**What's next for Dusk**

Looking ahead, Dusk is evolving beyond daily reflections into a proactive life companion.
Our goal is to build long-term pattern recognition across weeks and months—uncovering subtle burnout trends, recurring creative sparks, and personal growth trajectories.
With cross-device lock-screen quick capture, on-device local AI models for complete zero-knowledge privacy, and collaborative shared spaces, Dusk aims to become every person's ultimate calm second brain

</details>

<details><summary>Description</summary>

**Inspiration**

I call the same person every night. I built Same Moon for the two of us, and we have used it for 62 nights in a row. Streak apps and couples apps already exist, but none of them felt like the thing we actually share: the same sky, at the same time, from two different places. So the whole app is that sky.

**What it does**

- A pixel-art night sky with the real phase of tonight's moon. Two houses sit on the horizon, one for each of you. A window lights up while that person has the app open, and a string of lights hangs between the houses when you are both there.

- Mark a night after you call and the streak grows. A rare "clouded" night can bridge one bad evening, so a single miss does not erase two months.

- Video calls are peer to peer over WebRTC. The server only carries the handshake, so audio and video go straight from one phone to the other.

- A storybook you build together: notes, photos and drawings from a shared canvas. Arrange a page like a scrapbook, then seal it with a kiss. A sealed page can never be changed again, by anyone.

- Games for during the call (tic-tac-toe, four in a row, pairs) are refereed by the server, so nobody can cheat by editing their phone.
**How we built it**

- Next.js 15 and React 19 in TypeScript, with no UI framework. Every sprite is ASCII art drawn on an integer grid.

- SpacetimeDB is the whole backend. A Rust module holds every rule (who can answer a ring, when a round is scored, that a sealed page stays sealed), and both phones keep a live subscription, so a change on one phone shows up on the other in about half a second.

- The iOS app is a Capacitor 8 shell with the native RevenueCat SDK.

- Tests: 64 unit tests, plus a 168-assertion suite that drives every database rule against a real local SpacetimeDB.
**Challenges we ran into**

- Turning an app built for exactly two people into one any couple can use. Inside the database the two people are now "Moon" and "Star", and their real names live in one row, so a rename never touches a night, a message or a page.

- Keeping a call from double-offering when both phones ring each other at the same moment. Whoever rang first is always the offerer.

- SpacetimeDB treats adding a column to a live table as a breaking change, so every new feature lives in its own table to keep our real data safe through every update.

**Accomplishments that we're proud of**

- Got our friend a girlfriend

- Held my first relationship for longer than 30 days

**What we learned**

- SpacetimeDB treats adding a column to a live table as a breaking change, even when the table is empty. So every new feature gets its own table, which kept our real data safe through every update.

- Realtime apps get glitchy when one kind of event re-renders everything. Typing indicators were rebuilding the whole message thread. Splitting the connection, the messages and the games into separate subscriptions fixed it.

- Building for strangers is a different problem from building for yourself. Names had to come out of the code, and secrets had to come out of the app's bundle. The door word is now checked on the server. I also learned to write down plainly what is and is not private.

- Price the thing that actually costs money. Photos are the only feature with a real storage cost, so they are what Plus pays for. A subscription for two also needs shared state, and in production that state should be set by a RevenueCat webhook on the server, not by the phone.

- iOS zooms into any text field with type smaller than 16px, which pushed our lock screen off the side of the phone. I only found it by running the real app in the simulator, not the website.

**What's next for Same Moon**

Real accounts with each couple scoped to their own rows, the RevenueCat webhook for Plus, a home screen widget with tonight's moon and the streak, and Android.

**instructions**

HOW TO TRY SAME MOON

Live demo: https://same-moon-demo.vercel.app
Door word: moonlit-harbor
Works in any browser. It looks best at phone size or on a phone.

GETTING IN

- Type the door word and tap Come in.

- Pick who you are: Sriyan or Daksha. The couple is already named for the demo.

- You will see tonight's real moon phase, the streak, and two houses on the horizon.

SEE BOTH PHONES AT ONCE
Open the same link in a second browser or a private window, type the same door word, and pick the other person. The second person's window lights up on the first screen, and a string of lights appears between the houses while both are open. Games and the storybook update live in both windows.

THINGS TO TRY

- Mark tonight to see the streak celebration (if tonight is not marked yet).

- Book: add a note page, arrange it like a scrapbook, then tap Seal with a kiss and press and hold the lips. A sealed page can never be edited or removed. The server refuses every change.

- Games: play tic-tac-toe, four in a row or pairs between the two windows.

- Call: with both windows open, tap Call. Allow camera and microphone. Video goes directly between the two browsers.

SAME MOON PLUS
Storybook photos are part of Same Moon Plus, which runs through the RevenueCat SDK in the iPhone app. In a browser, the Plus sheet says "Plus is in the iPhone app." The demo build has no RevenueCat key configured, so a purchase cannot be completed in the demo.

RUN THE IPHONE APP
git clone https://github.com/teameuphoriainv-dot/same-moon
cd same-moon && npm install
CAP_SERVER_URL=https://same-moon-demo.vercel.app npx cap sync ios
Open ios/App/App.xcodeproj in Xcode, choose a signing team, and run it on an iPhone or the simulator. The simulator has no camera, so calls need a real phone.

RUN EVERYTHING LOCALLY
The README covers it: a local SpacetimeDB server, the settings in .env.example, and npm run dev.

KNOWN ISSUES

- On narrow phone screens, the Messages panel is shifted left and partly cut off.

- The presence line under the moon shows "Star" or "Moon" instead of the person's name.

**Inspiration**

Studying can easily become repetitive: read, answer questions, check your score, repeat. We wanted to make that loop feel more engaging by adding something students already understand: competition.

Study Battles was inspired by the idea of turning ordinary revision into a challenge you can share with a friend. Instead of studying completely alone, you can create a battle, compete, see your results, review your mistakes, and practice the topics you struggled with.

**What it does**

Study Battles is a mobile study app built around competitive quiz battles.

A user can choose a subject, topic, difficulty, and number of questions to create a battle. The battle generates a unique share code that can be sent to a friend. Players then answer questions, earn points, and see how they performed.

After the battle, Study Battles goes beyond simply showing a score. Players can review their mistakes and jump into focused practice based on the questions they missed.

The core loop is:

Create → Battle → Review → Practice → Improve

**How I built it**

Study Battles was built with React Native, Expo, TypeScript, and Supabase.

The interface was designed to feel more like a game than a traditional study app, with animated transitions, score feedback, timers, battle states, light and dark mode, and focused result screens.

Supabase handles the battle-sharing functionality, including anonymous authentication, battle creation, share codes, and player participation.

We intentionally kept the architecture focused on the core experience instead of trying to build every possible feature for the MVP.

**Challenges I ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was balancing a polished experience with the limited time available for the hackathon.

I joined late and I had school, so I had to decide which features actually improved the core study loop and which could wait. This meant focusing on the battle experience instead of adding unnecessary complexity such as payments, notifications, deep linking, or a large social system.

Another challenge was connecting the mobile app to Supabase while keeping the existing demo flow stable. I had to handle authentication, database functions, battle creation, and share codes without breaking the UI and navigation that were already working.

**Accomplishments that I'm proud of**

I'm proud that I was able to build a fully functional study battle app within the time I had

**What I learned**

I learned a lot and more about building mobile apps with react native, revenuecat, expo and the mobile ecosystem in general

**What's next for Study battles**

There is still a lot I could build, including real-time multiplayer battles, stronger question generation, battle history, notifications, leaderboards, and deeper progress tracking.

For this MVP, the priority was proving the core idea:

Studying can be something you compete in, share with friends, and actually enjoy.

</details>
